title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Thyroid and Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture certified organic herbal extracts. This month we are very pleased to welcome Dr. Ray Peat onto the show. I know our listeners are keen to hear what 40 years of experience has revealed concerning your areas of expertise, Dr. Peat: progesterone, related hormones, and how physiological differences can be made by relatively simple dietary changes—and in some cases, thyroid hormone supplementation. Thank you for being our guest.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hello.

**Andrew Murray:** For those listeners who are perhaps not familiar with you, could you outline your academic and professional career?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, I was studying the humanities—literature and linguistics—and I worked on master's degrees in several departments. It was about 12 years in which I taught humanities and worked at several universities before I went back to graduate school to work in biology. I had been interested in biology all through the 1950s and 60s, but I considered the dogmatism to be more than I wanted to deal with. After going through five or six other graduate departments, I learned that you can get through just about any department if you keep your mouth shut and don't ask questions or challenge people.

**Andrew Murray:** We've mentioned the importance of thyroid on previous shows. Would you explain the physiological importance of a correctly functioning thyroid, and what symptoms would be experienced by a person with a low thyroid state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the higher animals require thyroid to survive and to differentiate. Without any thyroid function, we would basically be like a fungus. The brain is the organ that is most responsive to the thyroid hormone; it uses the most oxygen and burns fuel at the highest rate. All of the oxidative processes required for high-sensitive functioning depend on the thyroid hormone. The difference between us and a bacterium or a fungus is largely the thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's really a master controller.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's the master gland. It is even more basic than the pituitary, which they often call the master hormone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because the thyroid hormone will affect the pituitary function, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pituitary depends on the metabolism of the brain and gets signals from the whole body, but the thyroid is what regulates the brain and governs the signals that the other cells send out.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if a person's brain isn't utilizing oxygen efficiently, that is probably because of their thyroid gland, and then their pituitary won't operate correctly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The thyroid keeps the energy of all cells up and makes them ready to work. A lot of people have thought of the thyroid as an exciting hormone. They have heard that it will make them burn calories faster and lose weight, so they think of it as similar to speed or adrenaline. Actually, it works in the opposite direction. People who are low in thyroid usually have defective sleep, often insomnia. Taking the right amount of thyroid can bring on deep sleep in an insomniac, sometimes in just a few minutes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that because it helps balance the adrenaline levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Over a period of days, it will lower a person's adrenaline, sometimes 40-fold, down to a normal or low level. At the same time, it raises the cell's stores of energy and lets the cell get into its relaxed condition. When you have a cramp in a muscle, often that's because the energy is depleted. Low thyroid people tend to get muscle cramps very easily.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I have several clients who have calf cramps, and they think it's down to them being hypothyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the old, very meaningful tests for hypothyroidism is to have a person kneel on a chair and thump the Achilles tendon. Rather than looking for the extent of the reflex, you look for the speed of the relaxation. To relax, the muscle has to restore its energy and get ready for another twitch. The brain and all other organs are the same way. When the energy is down, it can't relax.

**Andrew Murray:** Could you explain the adrenal fatigue syndrome? If we're talking about people who are over-stimulated by a low thyroid, compensating with adrenaline, how do the adrenal glands become tired out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the ways you can measure a low thyroid is to measure either the urine adrenaline breakdown products or the blood adrenaline. It will often be 20, 30, or 40 times higher than normal in a hypothyroid person. Adrenaline is the emergency compensation for low energy. When the adrenaline is high, it tries to bring the energy back to normal. First, it draws glucose out of the liver. If you are low thyroid, you tend to deplete your glucose stores. When those are gone, your adrenaline goes even higher and starts pulling fats out of storage. The fats poison your ability to burn glucose and create a diabetes-like condition.

When the fatty acids aren't providing adequate energy, then you resort to producing cortisone. The cortisone usually follows just a few minutes after the surge of adrenaline. The cortisone starts breaking down your tissues—muscles are the first to go. The thymus is dissolved, sometimes in just a few hours, with high cortisone. The breaking down of your tissues provides sugar to help you restore energy. The cortisone should be a very quick, instantaneous reaction; otherwise, it starts destroying all of your essential organs.

**Andrew Murray:** This would be the classic wasting of a hyperactive or sympathetically stimulated person.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen several very hypothyroid men who, no matter how much they ate, couldn't put on weight. They weighed 130 or 135 pounds and were very frail looking. When they took thyroid, they didn't have to eat so much, but they could suddenly put on muscle because their cortisone went down.

At the same time that your adrenaline is driving your adrenal glands to produce more cortisone, your adrenals need the thyroid hormone to convert cholesterol into cortisone. The destruction of your muscles to turn them into food liberates tryptophan and cysteine amino acids, which are signals to turn your thyroid down so that you don't totally destroy yourself in the first two days.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's a vicious cycle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The stress turns your thyroid down. When your thyroid is low, you can't convert cholesterol into cortisone, and that's what is called adrenal failure. But it's really thyroid failure.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why people with low thyroid sometimes end up with high blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can find dozens of articles in PubMed showing that high blood pressure goes with hypothyroidism. Very quickly, you can usually lower the blood pressure by correcting the thyroid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This is contrary to popular opinion. People think thyroid is a stimulant that will raise blood pressure and give you heart palpitations. But in reality, if people don't have enough thyroid, their body will start overcompensating with adrenaline, which gives those stimulatory effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The adrenaline and lack of energy increase the tendency of the blood to clot and for the red cells to become rigid so that they don't go through the capillaries very easily. The blood is thicker and harder to pump, which tends to cause high blood pressure and heart problems.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And even increase the possibility of a stroke?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Meanwhile, since you aren't able to produce the anti-stress hormones when your thyroid is low, the cholesterol simply rises in an attempt to compensate.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's why people with low thyroid have high cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It's a mirror image of your metabolic rate. That has been known since the 1930s: if you take out a person's thyroid, the cholesterol zooms up. If you give them a supplement, the cholesterol comes down in just a matter of a few days. Longevity, intelligence, and resistance to cancer are assisted by high cholesterol. Lowering cholesterol without correcting your thyroid is exactly the wrong thing to do.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's what the statin drugs aim to do.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you force your cholesterol down, you're unable to make progesterone, pregnenolone, DHEA, and the whole range of protective steroids.

**Andrew Murray:** There was a recent Harvard study that proved cholesterol less than 200 was likely to cause more cardiovascular accidents than cholesterol of 230. What's your opinion on the reference range being less than 200?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Framingham study showed that people over 50 are much more likely to have dementia if they have less than 200 cholesterol. There are several indicators that 260 or 270 is the best for longevity and resistance to cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What is your view on why so many Americans seem to be low thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It started back in the 30s or earlier. The food industry was starting to convince people to use vegetable oil, synthetic butter, and synthetic cooking oils made out of cottonseed oil. In the 1930s, George Crile and his wife did surveys around the world of people's oxygen consumption and thyroid function. He showed that in almost every other country—except where they have a high incidence of tuberculosis, cancer, and heart disease—people averaged about 25% higher metabolic rates than Americans.

It was pretty well established that 40% of Americans benefited from taking a thyroid supplement. It's probably the grain-centered diet. In the Yucatan and in Alaska among the Eskimos, the people had higher metabolic rates. Those are cultures that are not bread-centered.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the Eskimos who ate lots of saturated fats had a better utilization of oxygen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. But the Americans with their bread and other starchy foods tended to eat only the muscle meat. In the more primitive, less affluent cultures, they economize and eat the whole animal: the brain, the thyroid glands, the blood, feet, and skin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they have a more balanced ratio of proteins, not just the muscle meat like we eat in America?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Muscle meat is very powerful at suppressing the thyroid because that's its function. When we resort to cortisone, we destroy our muscles. The muscle dissolution coming into the bloodstream suppresses the thyroid. So when you eat a simple steak or hamburger, your body can't tell the difference between stress or eating simple meat. It suppresses your thyroid because of the imbalance of amino acids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What can people do to eat a protein that isn't going to suppress their thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you stew a chicken and skim off the fat after it has cooked the meat loose from the bones, you will get gelatin out of the skin, bones, and connective tissues, which will be about half of the protein of the whole chicken. That would be what the primitive cultures were eating every day—a perfectly balanced set of amino acids. You can approximate that by eating shellfish, shrimps, and oysters, where you eat the whole body of the animal. Milk and cheese are also pretty good for the protein balance.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you explain the methodology of testing thyroid function and why so many people fall through the cracks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, a new type of thyroid hormone was synthesized containing only T4. Around that same time, a blood test came on the market which measured iodine bound to protein (Protein Bound Iodine or PBI). They assumed it was the same as the synthetic hormone they were promoting. The synthetic hormone was tested only on young men, who are the least likely to have a hormone problem.

When they measured the iodine carried on a blood protein, they found that only 5% of the population had low protein-bound iodine. They convinced doctors that 95% of the population didn't need thyroid, even though the clinical symptoms established up to 1940 showed that everyone with those symptoms—dry skin, falling hair, constipation, insomnia, lethargy—benefited from taking thyroid.

In the 1960s, it turned out that this protein-bound iodine had almost nothing to do with thyroid function. It was found that the real thyroid hormone was T3, not thyroxine (T4). It's present in a very small amount in the blood. They were able to measure T3 by the late 1960s, but they standardized the new test against the old idea, which had been established with a completely meaningless measurement. So now, it doesn't matter how accurate your test is; if you keep the idea that statistically only 5% are hypothyroid, you're not going to be treating the people who need it.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's talk about the controversy of polyunsaturated fats—the fats that are supposedly good for your heart—versus the saturated fat of our ancestors, like lard and beef fat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** This really started with the paint and plastics industry learning how to make paint, varnish, and plastics out of petroleum. Previously, fish oil and seed oil—linseed oil in particular—had been the basis of paints. The petroleum chemists learned how to make paint very cheaply, so the farmers and the industry producing paint stock had no market.

First, they used some old research which had already been disproved. In the 1940s, the George and Mildred Burr Company claimed that unsaturated fats were essential nutrients. However, people working on B vitamins showed that what the Burrs had created was a B vitamin deficiency by not feeding their animals a balanced diet. Burr himself demonstrated that animals without the unsaturated fats had an extremely high metabolic rate, about 50% higher than average.

The lab in Texas showed that it was specifically Vitamin B6 and Zinc which were deficient in the diet, not actually the polyunsaturated oils. The polyunsaturated oils were simply suppressing metabolism so that rats didn't need so much food. The pig farmers knew about that and applied it by giving polyunsaturated fats to their pigs to fatten them by suppressing their metabolism.

**Andrew Murray:** So polyunsaturated fats actually increase your weight while lowering the number of calories you can burn?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Is it right to assume that polyunsaturated fatty acids have a slowing effect on thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Experiments in France showed that they block the secretion of the hormone from the thyroid gland itself, block the transport on proteins in the blood, and block all of the cells' functions in response to the thyroid hormone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you list the oils in our food chain today that are very high in polyunsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Safflower oil, cottonseed oil, corn oil, flax, and soy. Canola isn't quite so bad, but it's still toxic. Sunflower is pretty bad.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And what about fish oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's worse. But the good thing about fish oil is that it's so unstable that most of it doesn't survive to reach your bloodstream, or it would inhibit your thyroid function. It breaks down into other compounds which are actually toxic. The first thing you see affected is the immune system. The breakdown products of the spontaneously oxidizing fish oil include acrolein, which is a carcinogen, and ethane. Several of these toxic breakdown products are immunosuppressive. They have an anti-inflammatory effect that in the short run makes them seem beneficial.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why people who take fish oils say they notice a benefit, like easier joint movement or resolved skin conditions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. 50 years ago, they used to treat arthritis and psoriasis with X-rays. You could stop just about any inflammation for a while with X-rays. The polyunsaturated fats work by exactly the same mechanism that the X-rays do: creating an immune deficiency and an inability to produce inflammation.

**Andrew Murray:** How about the news that these polyunsaturated fats are so unstable that the adipose tissue stores the fat, and this product can remain in a body for several years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you totally change your diet from saturated to unsaturated, it takes about four years for the complete change to be reflected in your stores. So you can figure that the average fat molecule is four years old. If you've ever left your cooking oil bottle out of the fridge, you've noticed it gets sticky. That hardening, oxidizing process would be much faster at body temperature.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this what plaque in the artery is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For 30 or 40 years, people have been demonstrating that the chemicals in the lining of the artery are identical to age pigment. Age pigment is produced in proportion to the unsaturated fats in your diet versus the saturated fats, and the amount of oxidants such as heavy metals. Every time you draw fats out of your storage, they have to circulate through the bloodstream, exposing the lining of the arteries to free radicals. Recent experiments have shown that polyunsaturated fats poison a mechanism that normally causes cholesterol to be taken out of the arteries.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's time to throw out the corn and safflower oil and start eating butter and coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that's it.

**Andrew Murray:** We keep getting told that fish oils are the "good" fats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even though it's established that seed oils are carcinogenic and cause heart disease, they've shifted to say the real essential fatty acids are the fish oil type, the Omega-3. That basically comes from a study of Greenland people where they claimed there was very little heart disease. But a more recent study of Alaska Eskimos showed that the ones who eat a lot of fish have no less heart disease than the ones who don't. A study in Canada found that if you look at the amount of Omega-3 fats in their tissues, the pollution—such as PCBs and mercury—exactly corresponds to the amount of fish oil.

**Caller:** On a different show, you talked about how cholesterol itself was not the problem, but something else was the culprit. You said if you took at least 500 milligrams of B12, B2, and something else...

**Andrew Murray:** How do you equate the B vitamins to cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver is constantly detoxifying all the chemicals you absorb. Anything in your bloodstream is processed through the liver. If you're deficient in thyroid, the liver can't handle the cholesterol or free fatty acids. The liver treats the polyunsaturated fats as toxins and destroys them. The cholesterol is recycled. But the liver can't process these things without adequate protein and B vitamins. Thiamine (B1) is essential for making the liver work efficiently. Low thyroid function makes it impossible to use these B vitamins and protein.

I usually advocate eating a diet naturally rich in vitamins. Eggs and liver are probably the richest sources of all the essential nutrients for liver function. But if you eat too much liver, it can act like too much muscle meat and suppress your thyroid. Too much carotene or Vitamin A can also suppress your thyroid. So I recommend lots of liver and eggs, but only if you're balancing with the right amount of thyroid function.

**Caller:** How much Vitamin B12, B6, and B2 do you think a person needs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It varies according to your metabolic rate.

**Caller:** Is it better to eat butter than olive oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, butter and coconut oil. Olive oil is not as good as butter.

**Caller:** Why do you say butter is good for you when so many people say it's bad?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Researchers, specifically Nanji's group, are showing that they can cure liver disease caused by polyunsaturated fats by adding butter and other saturated fats to the diet. It is the polyunsaturated fats that cause alcoholics to get cirrhosis and hepatitis, not just the alcohol.

**Caller:** What about the glop in your arteries?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is caused by the vegetable oils, primarily.

**Caller:** Are you saying that Omega-3s are not good for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they're not. Alzheimer's disease is now definitely associated with inflammatory processes and free radical oxidative processes which are supported by the polyunsaturated fats.

**Caller:** It does seem to make the arthritis in my knee better.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's anti-inflammatory, but those are the oxidized breakdown products that suppress your immune system. At the same time they suppress inflammation, they also suppress your ability to stop infections or the spread of a tumor.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How many times a week would you suggest eating eggs or liver or shellfish?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can eat as many eggs as you want if they're well-fed chickens. But they feed most chickens now the same thing they feed pigs—a lot of corn and soy. So currently for Americans, I advocate only one or two eggs a day because of the polyunsaturated fats.

**Caller (Rosa):** I was curious to hear what Ray Peat thinks about the Ayurvedic oil change. I found it very interesting that he says it takes four years to change out the fatty acid composition of your cells. Would doing an oil change where you're actually drinking a lot of oil speed up the changeover?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you have been eating polyunsaturated fats and you stop, and start eating only butter and coconut oil, does eating an excessive amount of oil speed up the change?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You only see a big problem in someone who's very fat. They'll take thyroid or use coconut oil, which can boost your thyroid while it's in your bloodstream. But as soon as your blood sugar falls and you draw fats out of storage, then your thyroid is suppressed again.

One lawyer who weighed over 300 pounds thought he would lose weight in a hurry, so he drank a cup of coconut oil. He said he really believed he might explode or start on fire because he was so hot for about an hour. So you don't want to take more than about a tablespoon at once because you can notice your heart rate goes up, you breathe harder, and get pinker for about 30 minutes to an hour.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there any way to actually increase that change or do you just have to wait four years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just taking a little bit of coconut oil at a time. It depends on your body weight. I added just a tablespoon per day and lost a pound a week and stabilized 12 pounds lower.

**Caller:** I have Hashimoto's disease. I've been on 175 micrograms of thyroid since 1976, although it goes up and down. I would dearly love to find somebody who knows what is going on because MDs are not doing me any good.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat has offered to consult with clients through either Andrew or myself. We can consult with Dr. Peat on your behalf.

**Caller:** He says butter, coconut oil... what did he say about olive oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In moderation. It's got 10% of the polyunsaturated fats on average. So a teaspoon or two per day isn't enough to hurt.

**Caller:** I had high cholesterol, 330, and I thought I'd better bring it down.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cholesterol is very good for a person. If you take an adrenal gland or an ovary and run blood into it, the amount of progesterone coming out the other side is directly proportional to the amount of cholesterol in the blood. That depends on Vitamin A and thyroid to be converted. So when a person takes thyroid and sees their cholesterol quickly coming down, that's because they're making the defensive hormones like pregnenolone and progesterone.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you have any advice for hepatitis patients and how thyroid hormone would be useful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Having a doctor who understands thyroid is convenient. Mary Shomon's website has a list of doctors all over the country. I've seen people with terminal cirrhosis who, after six months of using saturated fat, thyroid, and in some cases progesterone, saw no evidence of cirrhosis left, even though their liver had been very enlarged and rubbery. It was normal after six or eight months.

**Andrew Murray:** Fantastic. It's been a real pleasure to have you on the show, Dr. Peat. Thank you very much for joining us.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. Thank you, Dr. Peat, for giving a lot of clients hope that with proper nutrition and a good diet, they can become much healthier.

**Andrew Murray:** Like I said at the beginning of the show, the reason we invited you on is because we've actually seen the difference ourselves. Thank you very much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Thyroid, Metabolism and Coconut Oil
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have perhaps never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions. We manufacture all our own certified organic herbal extracts.

Tonight, we are continuing our topic on the thyroid, its role in health, and the use of coconut oil as a means of weight loss and improved thyroid function.

To carry on from last month's exposé on the polyunsaturated versus saturated fat controversy, I wanted to mention right from the get-go that some of this material has been copied from Dr. Raymond Peat. This material is not something that we have produced, although in between the excerpts, the commentary is ours.

I want to continue this exposé of a fairly startling turnaround. Many people believe that polyunsaturated fats are good and saturated fats are bad, but it is seemingly very much the other way around. Our ancestors and grandparents had it right the first time: eating lots of saturated fat, animal fats, butter, milk, cream, and dairy products. They were very healthy and had very low incidences of cancer, diabetes, and obesity—things which have shot up since the 1920s.

**Andrew Murray:** At the end of the Second World War, the seed oil industry was in a crisis. The traditional use of seed oils, such as flaxseed oil in paints and plastics, was being displaced by new compounds made from petroleum. The industry needed new markets. They discovered ways to convince the public that seed oils were better than animal fats, calling their seed oils "heart protective," even though human studies soon showed the same results that animal studies had: they were toxic to the heart and increased the incidence of cancer.

This began in the 1920s and 1930s with experiments on animals in feedlots. Farmers wanted to increase the animals' weight in the last six or eight weeks of life to make them more valuable. They started using coconut oil, a cheap, imported tropical saturated fat. They believed it would be a good feed source to increase weight gain. Lo and behold, rather than gaining weight, the animals actually lost weight.

So, they changed their plans. They switched from coconut oil to corn oil and soy oil. When they did that, the animals started gaining weight. However, the long-term effects of these fats were toxic. The animals were unable to continue eating this for more than six or eight weeks before they started getting serious, life-threatening inflammatory disorders.

Ultimately, coconut oil was thrown out, and a huge campaign was started to alert the American public that these cheap, tropical imported oils were not good for you. They claimed the alternatives should be USA-grown corn and soy. With the chemical and pharmaceutical industry behind this, corn and soy became very important crops to be genetically engineered and owned.

Rapidly, the information was disseminated that soy and corn were good for you—that they were polyunsaturated, good for your heart, and good for cholesterol. The propaganda was promoted by a lot of money.

**Andrew Murray:** Despite the widespread acceptance, the lipid hypothesis has never really been proven. Oil researcher Mary Enig, Ph.D., and Sally Fallon, founder of the Weston A. Price Foundation, point out in their article "The Secrets of the Edible Oil Industry" that the lipid theory was first proposed by David Kritchevsky. In 1954, he published a paper describing the effects of feeding cholesterol to rabbits.

By showing that polyunsaturated oils from vegetable sources lowered serum cholesterol temporarily in humans, Kritchevsky appeared to show that the findings from animal trials were relevant to heart disease. Soon, the United States was on an anti-cholesterol campaign.

In 1956, an American Heart Association fundraiser was shown on TV. Panelists presented the lipid hypothesis as the cause of America's heart disease epidemic and recommended a "prudent diet" in which corn oil, margarine, and chicken replaced butter, lard, beef, and eggs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But the panel was not unanimous. Dr. Paul Dudley White disagreed with his AHA colleagues. He noted that heart disease in the form of myocardial infarction (MI) was non-existent in 1900, when egg consumption was three times what it was in 1956 and when corn oil was completely unavailable. When pressed to support the prudent diet, Dr. White replied, "See here, I began my practice as a cardiologist in 1921 and I never saw an MI patient until 1928. Back in the MI-free days before 1920, the fats were butter and lard. And I think we would all benefit from the kind of diet we had at that time when no one had ever heard the words corn oil."

Unfortunately, his observations fell on deaf ears. Ads in the Journal of the American Medical Association described Wesson oil as a "cholesterol depressant." Mazola advertisements claimed that "science finds corn oil important to your health." Dr. Frederick Stare, head of Harvard University's nutrition department, wrote a syndicated column encouraging the consumption of up to a cup of corn oil per day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Meanwhile, experimenters found that feeding a diet that totally lacked the "essential" fatty acids produced animals with remarkable properties. According to Dr. Ray Peat, they consumed oxygen and calories at a very high rate. Their mitochondria were unusually tough and stable. Their tissues could be transplanted into other animals without provoking immunological rejection. They were very hard to kill by trauma and toxins that easily provoked lethal shock in animals on the usual polyunsaturated oil diet. As German researchers had seen in 1927, they had a low susceptibility to cancer.

Dr. Mary Enig points out that other researchers conducted population studies showing that the animal model used by Kritchevsky—especially using vegetarian animals like rabbits—was not a valid approach to heart disease in human omnivores. She cites studies showing that arterial plaque is a natural process unrelated to diet. American soldiers killed during the Korean War had similar amounts of plaque (75%) as Japanese natives (65%) whose diet was lower in animal products.

In 1957, Dr. Norman Jolliffe launched an "Anti-Coronary Club." All were placed on the prudent diet. Results published in 1966 showed that those on the prudent diet of corn oil, margarine, fish, chicken, and cold cereal had an average serum cholesterol 30 points lower than the control group. However, eight prudent diet followers died of heart disease, while *none* of those who ate meat three times a day died. Jolliffe himself died in 1961 from a vascular thrombosis.

In the 1960s, interest in organ transplantation led to the discovery that polyunsaturated fats prolong graft survival by suppressing the immune system. Immunosuppression was considered to have a role in the carcinogenicity of essential fatty acids.

**Andrew Murray:** Just to reiterate: polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) suppress the immune system.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Yes. Around the same time, studies showed that unsaturated fats retarded brain development and produced obesity. In addition, the age-related glycation products usually blamed on sugar are largely the result of peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids.

**Andrew Murray:** That is one of the important things about PUFAs. Because they are polyunsaturated, they are very susceptible to lipid peroxidation—oxidation of the molecule—because they are not stable. Unlike saturated fats, which are completely saturated and very stable.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And they don't go rancid quickly. Coconut oil has a very long shelf life.

By 1980, it looked as though researchers would see the promotion of cancer, heart disease, mitochondrial damage, hypothyroidism, and immune suppression caused by these fats as their most important feature. But then, fat researchers just started changing the subject.

Dr. Ray Peat advises us to get acquainted with pasture-fed butter, lard, tallow, and coconut oil. Throw away the canola, corn, sunflower, safflower, sesame, and soy oils. Stay away from anything containing polyunsaturated fats. Kiss tofu goodbye and forget soy milk, soy yogurt, and soy protein.

**Andrew Murray:** Animals that eat polyunsaturated fats don't produce saturated fat. When you eat their meat, you are eating polyunsaturated fat with all the adverse effects of soy and corn oil.

**Andrew Murray:** Moving on to the thyroid. In 1995, researchers studied over 25,000 participants at a Colorado health fair. They discovered that among patients not taking thyroid medication, 10% had a thyroid problem that had gone unrecognized. These figures suggest that nationally, there may be as many as 13 million Americans with an undiagnosed thyroid problem.

Endocrinologist Kenneth Blanchard notes that the TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) test is often viewed as a yes-or-no answer, which is fundamentally wrong. TSH is controlled not just by circulating T4 and T3, but by T4 getting converted to T3 at the pituitary level. Excess T3 generated at the pituitary can falsely suppress TSH. Hence, many people who test within the "normal" range are actually suffering from thyroid problems.

Dr. Ridha Arem, author of *The Thyroid Solution*, agrees that hypothyroidism may exist despite normal TSH levels. If we included people with low-grade hypothyroidism, the number would likely double.

Diet plays a major role. We know low iodine leads to goiter, but iodized salt hasn't been the answer. There are foods known as goitrogens that block iodine. Two prevalent ones in the American diet are peanuts (and peanut butter) and soybeans (often used as Textured Vegetable Protein or TVP).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Everyone could benefit from eating coconut oil. It helps improve your metabolism. A real low-fat diet can be very detrimental.

Something you can do at home to assess your thyroid function is to take your temperature. A normal body temperature is 98.0 to 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit. You can use a basal body thermometer to take your temperature before and after breakfast, and before and after lunch. You should also check your pulse, which should be around 70 to 85 beats per minute. If these are low, it may indicate hypothyroidism, though it is best to work with a practitioner.

**Andrew Murray:** Here are some questions to ask yourself. If you answer yes to many of these, you may want to investigate your thyroid health:
*   Have you experienced infertility or miscarriage?
*   Do you feel like you catch every infection, or take a long time to recover?
*   Do you regularly eat significant amounts of uncooked goitrogenic foods such as Brussels sprouts, broccoli, rutabaga, turnips, radishes, cauliflower, millet, cabbage, or kale?
*   Are you experiencing menstrual cycle changes (too short/long, or heavy/light flow)?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Regarding the goitrogenic foods—plants in the Brassica family like broccoli and kale are meant to be cooked. If you cook them until they are soft, you take away the potential for them to cause a goiter. We aren't suggesting you don't eat them, just don't eat them raw.

Also, many dietary polyunsaturated oils negatively affect thyroid health. It is possible they are among the worst offenders. Even as little as one teaspoon a day can be suppressive.

**Caller 1:** I make a distinction in my life between food and "food-like production." When I'm out, I try to educate people to steer away from food-like products.

**Andrew Murray:** Yes, education is what it's all about.

**Caller 1:** When restaurants ask if I want ketchup or jam, I ask if they know it has high fructose corn syrup. Just little spots of education here and there.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Well done. Keep up the good work.

**Andrew Murray:** High fructose corn syrup has become the common sweetener. It is no longer sugar or honey because those are too expensive.

**Caller 2:** You have neglected to discuss the issue regarding Omega-6 and Omega-3 fats and the ratios. I wanted to recommend a book called *The Omega Diet* by Artemis Simopoulos. As I understand it, there is evidence that the ratio makes a big difference. The most affordable oil high in Omega-3 is canola, but also flax and walnut oil. I wanted your feedback.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This brings up the question of "Essential Fatty Acids" (EFAs). Aren't some polyunsaturated fatty acids essential?

Dr. Ray Peat has asked prominent oil researchers for evidence that there is such a thing as an essential fatty acid. One professor cited a single publication about a single patient. Others cited the Burr and Burr study from 1929. It is surprising that people consider research from 1929 definitive. What was known about nutrition then? Most B vitamins weren't even suspected to exist. Burr had no way of understanding what deficiencies or toxicities were present in his experimental diet.

Two years before Burr's experiment, German researchers found that a fat-free diet prevented almost all spontaneous cancers in rats. Later work showed that polyunsaturated fats both promote and initiate cancer.

Logically, look at how we got here. Did our ancestors eat bottles of essential fatty acids or canola oil? No. They ate butter, coconut, and olive oil.

**Andrew Murray:** And how much fish were they eating? Probably not that much unless they lived on the coast.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Exactly. Let's get back to basics.

**Caller 3:** I have a basal temperature of 96.8 consistently. I have a number of symptoms of hypothyroidism. I painted iodine on my skin and it disappeared within 12 hours. Do you think I should get a prescription for Armour Thyroid?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The best thing is to talk to a doctor who is open-minded about thyroid issues, such as Dr. Connie Basch or Dr. Beverly Copeland. Alternatively, you can buy glandular thyroid extracts. However, I recommend working with a practitioner because taking too much is not safe. Diet is the first place to start.

**Andrew Murray:** And stop eating thyroid-suppressive foods.

**Caller 3:** I'll avoid the polyunsaturated oils. I'm thinking of eating seaweed for the thyroid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Be careful. A deficiency of iodine can lead to hypothyroidism, but too much iodine can also suppress the thyroid. It is a delicate balance.

**Caller 4:** My sister's cholesterol is 280. She asked what she can do naturally. I told her to eat the right oils. Can you distill some advice for her?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Cholesterol is often raised because of too much sugar and carbohydrates in the diet. When you say "good oils," remember that heart attacks were unknown before 1920 when people ate butter, lard, and coconut oil.

I recommend organic butter, organic coconut oil, and a small amount of olive oil. Decreasing grains and sugars would be a healthy place to start. Sugars get converted into fat and can raise cholesterol levels.

Also, recent research suggests that people over the age of 50 with cholesterol around 230 were less likely to die of heart attacks and cancer than those with cholesterol below 200. Cholesterol has a protective function in the body.

**Caller 4:** What about plaque buildup?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is now being attributed more to an increase of sugars and polyunsaturated oils (trans fatty acids). Corn oil in large quantities has been shown to suppress the immune system.

**Caller 5:** I have two kids. I don't buy high fructose corn syrup, but I give them chocolate soy milk because my son eats so much dairy and I wanted to balance it out.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Soy has a goitrogenic effect. The soy flavonoids are thyroid suppressive. A study showed that 11 ounces of soy milk a day in a healthy individual is enough to suppress thyroid function.

**Caller 5:** Wow.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My advice is to feed your children the least processed foods. Make your own chocolate milk using regular milk and cocoa.

**Caller 5:** I can do that. I found my 2-year-old prefers eating stuff straight from the garden.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is how it is supposed to be.

**Caller 6:** I was diagnosed with hypothyroidism four weeks ago. I'm on a small dose of Levoxyl. I eat a clean diet, but I drink almond milk and eat peanut butter and almond butter.

**Andrew Murray:** Bad. You should cut those out of your diet now.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Since you are on medication, my advice is to ask your doctor to switch you to Armour Thyroid, Nature-Throid, or Westhroid. These are natural porcine glandulars that contain both T3 and T4. Levoxyl is just T4, which relies on your liver to convert it to the active form (T3). The natural glandulars are often a better alternative.

**Caller 7:** What do you think of tempeh? It's a fermented soy product.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I don't think it is as harmful as other soy products because fermentation makes grains and beans more digestible. However, for someone who is hypothyroid, my advice is do not eat anything that could possibly suppress your thyroid.

**Caller 7:** I also want to comment that I started eating coconut oil three or four years ago and lost about 20 pounds.

**Andrew Murray:** Absolutely. It is a thermogenic product. It increases your body's metabolism and oxygen consumption. Your thyroid governs every metabolic process, including heat production. Coconut oil is a saturated fat that supports your thyroid and allows you to lose fat while eating fat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** In the 1940s, when they experimented with animals, they found the animals lost weight on coconut oil. The American Soy Association boycotted imported oils to sell their corn and soy oil. That is why we haven't heard this research until recently.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Today, it is nearly impossible to eat at restaurants or buy packaged foods that don't have soy oil.

Dr. Ray Peat writes that the sudden surge of polyunsaturated oils into the food chain post-World War II has caused many changes in hormones. The best-understood effect is interference with the thyroid gland. Unsaturated oils block thyroid hormone secretion, its movement in the circulatory system, and the response of tissue to the hormone.

There is a growing body of research concerning soy's detrimental effect. In the 1960s, when soy was introduced into infant formulas, babies started developing goiters. A study by Fort *et al.* showed that teenage children with autoimmune thyroid disease were significantly more likely to have received soy formula as infants (31%) compared to healthy siblings (12%) or controls (13%).

Another study by Ishizuki *et al.* showed that when healthy adults were fed 30 grams of pickled soybeans per day for one month, they developed goiters and elevated TSH levels. One month after stopping, levels returned to normal.

Traditionally, soybean oil has been used for livestock feed because it causes animals to gain weight. Dr. Peat notes that the fattening effect is due to the presence of long-chain fatty acids like linoleic and linolenic acid, which have an anti-thyroid effect. The animal's fat becomes chemically similar to the fats in their food, causing it to be equally toxic and fattening to the consumer.

**Andrew Murray:** We are going to wrap it up now. You've been listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Cholesterol is an Important Molecule
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Good evening and welcome to Ask Your Herb Doctor on KMUD 91.1 FM. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists with degrees in herbal medicine. We consult clients with a wide range of conditions and operate a certified organic medicinal herb farm. This month, we are pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat on the show. Dr. Peat, for those who don't know you, could you give our listeners an overview of your professional and research-based work before we open up tonight's topics?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I did my PhD research in aging of the oxidative respiratory systems and how that is affected mostly by reproductive hormones. I looked at how it causes, for example, middle-aged infertility in people and animals. What I found, which was contrary to the textbooks at the time, was that estrogen became the dominant hormone at middle age, causing distortion of the oxidative metabolic processes.

That got me interested in the factors that contribute to that age-related imbalance. Age pigment was one of the things I studied in connection with that change. Age pigment itself is stimulated by an excess of estrogen and is formed mostly from polyunsaturated oils. It oxidizes fuel and consumes oxygen without producing anything useful except free radicals. I later found that the way to prevent or delay that was to protect the thyroid hormone function. In the years since then, I've worked on ways to use diet to decrease the formation of age pigment, retard the increase in estrogen in the tissues, and maintain optimal thyroid function.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you are keen to emphasize the nutritional side of a lifestyle rather than simply prescribing drugs or herbal supplements. In relation to diet, high cholesterol is a touchy subject given that statin drugs have been implicated in causing severe side effects. What is your opinion about the cause of high cholesterol? How high do you consider "high," and how would you approach its treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a study a few years ago of women in rest homes or convalescent hospitals. They followed them from the time they entered until they died, watching how their cholesterol levels corresponded to their longevity and ability to function. The optimal cholesterol level for living a long time and keeping their mentality sound was 270 mg/dL.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Wow. Current laboratories and doctors recommend that it should be under 200.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a Framingham study about 20 years ago which looked at the cholesterol levels of people as they passed the age of 50 in ordinary life situations. They saw that those who did *not* have a cholesterol level above 200 were more likely to become demented.

It has been known for 80 or 90 years that cholesterol is an antitoxin, an anti-inflammatory, and our basic protective substance. It is like a protective hormone in itself. In experiments with animals, learning ability and maze-running ability improve just by increasing the amount of cholesterol. Cell division involves cholesterol. It stabilizes red blood cells. Every level of physiology is protected by adequate cholesterol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is it true that every one of our cells utilizes cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even the genetic apparatus. Cholesterol is an essential component of every living process. It is stuck to the chromosomes and the structural, architectural microtubules and microfilaments all through the cell. It isn't just a membrane-associated thing. The ability of cells to move requires cholesterol.

**Andrew Murray:** Why does modern mainstream medicine consider a figure over 200 to be associated with a higher incidence of cerebrovascular disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's similar to why the optimal level of blood pressure has been revised downward. They can treat more patients and sell more drugs if more of the population is defined as sick. Thirty or 40 years ago, there was a study looking at blood pressure with aging; those whose pressure kept rising with the years lived the longest. A decrease in blood pressure indicated the nearness of death. As long as the blood pressure was on a steady rise, that was a good indicator.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What values do you consider healthy and normal for blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The lower number is partly an indicator of the elasticity of the system—how much pressure is there when the heart isn't beating. If the system is elastic, the lower number usually approaches 80. The upper number should be less than 50 points higher than that. So, 120 over 80—with a 40-point difference—is very good. A good plumbing engineer knows that keeping the pressure steady without great rises and falls makes the water circulate more smoothly. You don't want the lower number to drop too low, otherwise the blood stops moving.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to cholesterol, is the acceptable value of 270 more for elderly people, or would this apply to younger people?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is for old people. Similar to blood pressure, cholesterol rises when there is a problem to be soothed. When tissues are less efficient, they need more blood supply and care. So, blood pressure and cholesterol tend to rise with aging as the tissues need more attention.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you consider it dangerous for doctors to prescribe statins to older people when their bodies need higher cholesterol for protection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Back in the mid-80s in Hungary, there was a large study which saw that using a drug to lower cholesterol increased the death rate from just about every cause. Cancer, suicide, and even getting murdered were more probable when a person had their cholesterol artificially lowered.

**Andrew Murray:** Could you cover what cholesterol is responsible for helping us with?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the main defensive substance, but it is in turn converted into other protective substances. The first of which are pregnenolone and progesterone, and also DHEA. It should be massively converted into those more specific protective substances, but it can only be converted when the thyroid is adequate.

**Andrew Murray:** Please explain that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In experiments where they put the bloodstream flowing into an organ like an ovary or an adrenal gland, if the blood contains Vitamin A and thyroid hormone, the amount of progesterone being produced by the gland varies directly with the amount of cholesterol going into the gland. It is a massive quantitative conversion.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if you have low blood cholesterol, you will have low production of progesterone coming from that ovary?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. That's why it's dangerous to have it artificially lowered; it is the raw material for making all of the very specific protective steroids.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this why dementia is higher in low-cholesterol clients? Because these protective hormones are not being manufactured in sufficient amounts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There are several lines of reasoning showing that progesterone, for example, is extremely protective to the brain. It promotes healing and regeneration after the brain has been injured. It is now being tested in people who have had car accidents with brain damage, and it makes a tremendous difference in survival and recovery rates. If your cholesterol is artificially lowered, your brain is going to be deficient in progesterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Basically, progesterone is very important for anti-aging and keeping normal cellular processes going. If we don't have enough cholesterol coming from our diet or synthesis, we will likely have low levels of these protective hormones.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and thyroid has to be present for that conversion to take place. As early as 1993, it was found that in cholesterol treatment of rabbits—which caused circulatory disease—if they gave the same amount of cholesterol along with thyroid hormone, it didn't hurt their circulatory system.

Furthermore, the experimental cholesterol treatments turned out to be using a toxic form of oxidized cholesterol. If you leave cholesterol sitting in a bottle too long, or use certain cooking practices, it creates this toxic form. For example, people recommend steaming salmon to cook it at a lower temperature, but the slow oxygen exposure to unsaturated fats actually increases the toxic oxidized cholesterol. Steamed salmon has more toxic cholesterol than a grilled beef steak.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when they slice open someone's arteries and see cholesterol blocking them, what is happening?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cholesterol is there primarily to protect the cells against the free radicals produced by the polyunsaturated fats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For our listeners, polyunsaturated fats come from vegetable oils including soy, corn, safflower, sunflower, fish oil, canola, and cottonseed. Are you saying those oils are so toxic to the lining of our arteries that they cause a breakdown, which the body then tries to patch with cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that was worked out in the 1940s. Lab animals were dying of various symptoms, including infertility and softening of the brain. It was found that this was because they were adding unsaturated vegetable oils to their feed. It turned out that the oils were blocking their thyroid function and preventing them from using the protective cholesterol.

Agriculture took advantage of the anti-thyroid effect of these vegetable oils to use them to fatten animals economically.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So instead of pigs being fed compost, they were fed corn and soy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It was common to use waste food like spoiling apples, vegetables, and whey. But when they learned they could fatten pigs on much less food if it contained these unsaturated oils, that became the basic industrial animal food.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It makes sense because these vegetable oils aren't something we've naturally been eating in such concentrated forms for thousands of years.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In Mark Twain's time, he wrote about hearing merchants talking about how cheap cottonseed oil was and that they were going to teach Americans to eat that instead of butter. That was in the 1880s.

**Andrew Murray:** I believe this is linked to thyroid as well, but diabetes seems to have exploded in terms of diagnoses. What can be done to treat that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The diet of Americans and Europeans has changed over the years in which diabetes has increased, specifically with the greatly increased consumption of polyunsaturated vegetable oils. Even eggs and pork now contain more polyunsaturated fats because the animals are fed so much corn and soy.

In 1963, a researcher named P.J. Randle observed that he could block the oxidation of glucose just by feeding an increased amount of fatty acids. This is now called the Randle Cycle. When it became popular to feed hospitalized patients intravenously with a fat emulsion, they discovered it suppressed the immune system and almost immediately caused an elevation of blood glucose—exactly what Randle had noticed.

Diabetes was basically explained biochemically in the 1960s: if you feed more fats, you block the response to insulin and create insulin resistance. This is now called Type 2 diabetes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this with any kind of fat, or just vegetable fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you feed people or animals a very high sugar diet, you can greatly increase our own synthesis of fats, but these are saturated or monounsaturated fats. Even if you feed so much sugar that you increase triglycerides and fat deposition in the liver, it lowers the toxic effects of free radicals and actually helps to lower blood glucose. Feeding a high sugar diet has an anti-diabetic effect.

Contrasting that with starch—the complex carbohydrate dietitians have recommended for 30 years—starches have the opposite effect. They increase insulin resistance very quickly, just as if you were eating fat, because starches don't support our own production of saturated fat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So vegetable oils lead to increased blood glucose, but saturated fats help protect against it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, with the qualification that eggs, pork, and chicken are now fed so much vegetable oil that their fats are toxic too.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it would only be the more saturated fats like coconut oil or butter.

**Andrew Murray:** What about estrogen as a cofactor?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen causes increased deposition of fat in the liver and increased circulating triglycerides. It interacts closely with unsaturated fatty acids. Women typically have more polyunsaturated fatty acids circulating than men do. It is a peculiarity of estrogen that creates a bias making polyunsaturated fats even more toxic.

**Andrew Murray:** What are the best solutions for high estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 70 years ago, animal studies showed that a deficiency of protein causes the liver to be unable to remove estrogen or activate thyroid hormone. Just eating more protein can sometimes activate metabolism, cause the ratio to shift toward progesterone, and eliminate estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But women must be careful to avoid animals fed polyunsaturated fats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You wouldn't want to eat mainly pork, poultry, and fish because those are anti-thyroid. The number of unsaturations in the fatty acid corresponds with its ability to suppress thyroid function. Cutting those oils out as much as possible allows the thyroid to work more efficiently.

I recommend around 80 to 100 grams of protein a day as a minimum. 120 to 150 grams is very good for an active person. Also, reduce starches and replace them with fruit sugar. In animal experiments, they found that adding Coca-Cola to an animal's diet made it lean and able to eat much more food without gaining weight, just because of the sugar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Were they replacing the starches with Coca-Cola?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Orange juice is the ideal way to get your sucrose. Animal experiments suggest you can increase your metabolic rate by 50%. You would go from getting fat on 1,500 calories a day to getting lean on over 2,000 calories a day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about people who say they can't eat that much protein because they get kidney stones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eating enough calcium is the best protection against that. The sugar in fruit juice acts very much like Vitamin D. In Vitamin D deficient diets, animals eating starch became calcium deficient, but those eating sugar acted as if they were able to assimilate and retain calcium.

When you eat enough calcium, you suppress inflammatory agents, including the parathyroid hormone, so the calcium goes into your bones rather than forming stones in your kidneys or poisoning your arteries.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you suggest a high calcium, high protein, and high fruit diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. As a quick therapy diet, I recommend at least two quarts of milk and two quarts of orange juice every day. This will stimulate the thyroid, suppress inflammation, and help the liver regulate things. As it starts working, it will increase caloric needs.

**Caller:** I heard you talking about cholesterol being important for connective tissue. I was born with a rare disease where I don't have any connective tissue over my whole body. I blister and break open all the time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you tried increased amounts of Vitamin E?

**Caller:** I did when I was younger, but it made me very horny and I couldn't control it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Working on your hormones so that you can use enough of the antioxidants sometimes corrects that blister-susceptible disease.

**Caller:** Could I achieve that goal with a hyperbaric chamber?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. Going to a higher altitude, where you get lower oxygen pressure, is actually more likely to help.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, it's known that hyperthyroidism (high thyroid) can cause high blood pressure. But is there research showing low thyroid also causes high blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In general, research shows that increasing thyroid function lowers blood pressure. I think what has happened over the last 30 or 40 years is that doctors have been confused. I've seen dozens of people diagnosed as hyperthyroid who were actually classical hypothyroid cases.

One thing that happens in hypothyroidism is that the sympathetic nervous system activity and adrenaline production increase to compensate for the lack of thyroid energy production. I've seen hypothyroid people with 40 times the daily output of adrenaline.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So because their metabolism is slow, the body compensates by stimulating adrenaline, which raises blood pressure.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I've seen people with a pulse of 180 beats per minute at rest, which was taken as a sign of hyperthyroidism. But when they took thyroid, within a week they had a normal pulse rate of 80 or 90 because it lowered the adrenaline.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you tell us more about the interaction between high blood pressure and thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Toxemia of pregnancy (preeclampsia) got me interested in this. Starting in the 1950s, drug companies told women to take diuretics and restrict salt to prevent high blood pressure. They were actually starving the developing baby of blood supply by reducing blood volume. Adrenaline rises when you restrict salt intake, just as it does when you restrict thyroid function.

Researchers found they could cure toxemia and bring blood pressure down by giving women adequate salt and protein. I suggested to women with PMS—who often get swollen feet—to eat as much sodium as they crave. They found it prevented swelling. I saw old people with similar syndromes; when they went on salt-restricted diets, they developed insomnia, suggesting high adrenaline. When they started eating as much salt as they liked, they slept better and their blood pressure came down.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is completely counter to what you normally hear.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A man named David McCarron noticed 30 years ago that in government figures, people who ate the most salt had the lowest blood pressure. He showed that it wasn't sodium excess causing high blood pressure, but calcium deficiency. When people didn't eat milk and cheese, they would often eat salty snack foods.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they need to increase salt *and* calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Salt and calcium both increase your metabolic rate and ability to oxidize sugar. The anti-diabetic effect is increased with increasing sodium and calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you have any safe methods for increasing diuresis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Calcium helps. By optimizing sugar metabolism, it energizes the kidneys. Baking soda and sodium chloride both have a diuretic effect. The only chemical diuretic I would recommend is Acetazolamide (Diamox). It increases carbon dioxide in your tissues, which helps regulate salt.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller.

**Caller:** I wondered how olive oil is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it's a small quantity, like a tablespoon a day, it's fine. But it does have 10% polyunsaturated fats.

**Caller:** Is it okay when it's cooked?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, those fats are toxic. Even if you eat cold-pressed unsaturated fats, they warm up in your body, and then the blood pumps catalysts and oxygen through the warm fat. It doesn't matter how fresh they are when you eat them; they are going to get rancid once they are in your body.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you explain how salt can be a diuretic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen suppresses your ability to make albumin, makes blood vessels leaky, and causes you to lose sodium. This decreases blood volume. The kidneys then put out hormones that drive the heart to beat harder and tighten blood vessels to increase circulation.

Albumin doesn't work to retain water without an associated cloud of sodium atoms. By eating sodium, the albumin in your bloodstream can osmotically attract water. Eating salt pulls water back into the bloodstream, increases blood volume, perfuses the kidneys, and energizes them so they stop driving the blood vessels to tighten up.

**Caller:** How does your thyroid relate to Lyme disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The whole immune system is the issue there. A very healthy immune system can throw off chronic infections like Lyme disease. It is best to do it quickly with an antibiotic, but you always want to back up the antibiotic with an optimized immune system. Thyroid, calcium, and Vitamin D are basic things to make your immune system eliminate pathogens without causing inflammation.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you very much, Dr. Peat, for joining us.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For listeners who would like to read more, visit www.raypeat.com. He has numerous free articles and newsletters.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I can usually send a few references for issues I don't have on the website if people email me.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for tuning in. We will join you again next year in 2009. We wish you a Merry Christmas and a prosperous New Year.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Thyroid, Polyunsaturated Fats and Oils
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture our own certified organic herbal extracts.

This month we are very pleased to welcome Dr. Raymond Peat back to the show. We will be examining some common misconceptions surrounding thyroid treatment and the apparently normal thyroid test in clients with obvious manifestations of thyroid imbalance. We have seen remarkable progress made with clients whose symptoms improve dramatically with diet and lifestyle changes that promote thyroid health, revealing a prior lowered thyroid function even in the absence of diagnostic tests that show obvious problems. Welcome again, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat has over 40 years of experience in lecturing, teaching, writing, editing, and nutritional counseling. He has a PhD in biology, but his work was all in physiology and biochemistry. We wanted to talk about thyroid disease because it seems to be a chronic epidemic. Dr. Peat, what would you describe low thyroid disease, or hypothyroidism, to be?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is a slowing of the oxidative metabolism, which means your biological efficiency falls drastically. We rely almost entirely on oxidative metabolism. In emergencies, we can use glycolytic, non-oxidative metabolism, but then we have to make up for it by re-oxidizing the lactic acid that was produced during the oxygen deprivation or energy stress. Everything that is human, mammalian, or even a complex organism depends on the thyroid because all cellular activity requires oxidative metabolism to be efficient.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the thyroid is controlling the oxygen to all the cells in our system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. One of the effects is that our carbon dioxide production is kept at a fairly high rate in relation to oxygen consumption, and that keeps our tendency to produce lactic acid very low. If a person is low thyroid, even at rest, they can seem metabolically as if they are doing stressful activity. They can chronically have elevated lactic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why people experience chronic fatigue? Are their muscles fatigued even though they aren't doing exercises that seem to use their muscles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because when you don't use oxygen efficiently, you have to make lactic acid to keep the cells alive. The lactic acid then has to be re-oxidized in your liver to turn it eventually to carbon dioxide. Just sitting passively for a hypothyroid person can be the same as running at high speed for a healthy person.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 60 years ago, it was well known that a hypothyroid person has trouble relaxing their muscles and nerves. There were publications showing that you can invariably diagnose hypothyroidism with a simple thump of the ankle tendon to the gastrocnemius muscle (the calf muscle). When you are kneeling and you thump that, you can see that the relaxation is delayed. That was established as a good diagnostic method in the 1930s and 40s. However, the labs and pharmaceutical companies couldn't sell anything. You can use a table knife or a wooden hammer handle to thump the tendon, and it takes about two minutes. It is a very uneconomical business for doctors in the pharmaceutical industry to diagnose the condition so simply.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why the blood test came about? The TSH, Thyroid Stimulating Hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For the first 20 years or so, doctors were told not to use the Achilles relaxation test, the basal metabolic oxygen consumption test, or any of the proven absolute confirmations of hypothyroidism because they had what they called the "scientific blood test" to prove it. That was called the Protein Bound Iodine (PBI) test. That convinced doctors all over the country that, where previously 40% of the population had shown evidence of being hypothyroid, the new blood test showed that only 5% were. For 20 years this test was used, convincing the medical world that very few people are seriously hypothyroid. Then, in the 1960s, it turned out that protein bound iodine has essentially nothing to do with thyroid hormone functioning.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about the TSH used today? Do you think that is relevant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the PBI test was thrown out, they looked for other tests—which conveniently proved to be even more expensive—and finally settled on the TSH test. They can measure it very precisely, but it isn't clear what it means in many cases because things other than the absence or excess of thyroid hormone can raise or lower it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So someone can have varying levels of TSH, which doctors say is Thyroid Stimulating Hormone, but it doesn't really relate specifically to thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's true. It also has bad side effects; it promotes inflammation in itself. Low thyroid people not only lack metabolic energy, but they tend to have very high TSH levels, and the TSH is causing chronic tissue damage.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you think is causing low thyroid function in so many people in the U.S. today?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 70 years ago, it sometimes included an iodine deficiency, but with the iodination of table salt, other factors became far more important. Many times it is a protein deficiency or an excess of eating certain foods that inhibit the thyroid, such as raw cabbage, or an excess of any of the cabbage family foods.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That would include kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, mustard, and watercress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, even if they are cooked, if you eat a huge amount of them, that can be enough to make you hypothyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this to do with the sulfur groups?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is a combination of a carbon that contains an oxygen or nitrogen and a sulfur group. These are known medical chemicals used specifically to inhibit the thyroid to treat hyperthyroidism.

**Andrew Murray:** In previous interviews, you have brought out polyunsaturated oils as being antagonists to thyroid function and downright thyroid destructive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They antagonize the thyroid function at several levels. For example, they inhibit the proteolytic enzymes in the gland itself which are needed to form and secrete the hormone. They bind to the protein in the bloodstream that transports thyroid, preventing transport to the tissues. Finally, the polyunsaturated fats block several of the active sites in the cell where thyroid should bind to enliven the cell.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they affect thyroid health at the production location, the transportation through the bloodstream, and at the tissue level.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They also act on several other parts of the system, including indirectly on the TSH.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** These polyunsaturated fatty acids are found in vegetable oils like corn, soy, sesame, safflower, canola (rapeseed), and fish, hemp, and flaxseed oils.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is also one which isn't a fatty acid, but is a highly unsaturated molecule: carotene, the precursor to vitamin A. It not only blocks the cellular sites that use vitamin A, but as a polyunsaturated molecule, it blocks the thyroid function everywhere that the vegetable oils do.

**Andrew Murray:** So this would be ingesting lots of cooked carrots, pumpkin, or anything with high levels of carotene?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some studies confused people because they knew vitamin A was protective against cancer, but they saw that some types of cancer increased with supplementation of carotene. Carotene blocks the receptor so your body can't use the vitamin A. Vitamin A and thyroid work so closely together biologically that the protein transporting them is a single protein called transthyretin (retinol-thyroid transport). In the 1930s, one way of confirming a person had died from hypothyroidism was that the steroid-forming tissues turned red because of accumulated carotene. You can't use vitamin A if you don't have thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this the reason behind people having yellow calluses on their soles or palms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that is one of the old ways to diagnose hypothyroidism.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I want to mention some symptoms and signs that accompany the disease.

**Andrew Murray:** The list is exhaustive: less stamina, long recovery periods after activity, inability to fight infection, cold hands and feet, high or rising cholesterol, dry hair, hair loss, and dry cracking skin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Contrary to dry skin, you can also have acne on the face, shoulders, chest, and back. Dr. Peat, why would both dry skin and acne be symptoms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Partly it is the close connection between vitamin A and thyroid. The skin needs vitamin A to differentiate properly. Mucous membranes require vitamin A too; in an extreme deficiency, the surface of the eye becomes scaly like snakeskin. The lack of both thyroid and vitamin A can cause skin problems including plugging the pores—allowing infection to set in because the thyroid doesn't allow immune cells to function properly—and thinning of the skin because it isn't growing fast enough.

Estrogen is contrary to vitamin A's effect. Progesterone and vitamin A are closely connected. When you have enough vitamin A and thyroid, your skin can produce progesterone and other steroids. When they are lacking, estrogen takes effect and tends to prematurely harden, or keratinize, the skin cells. The juicy cell collapses and becomes a bit of leathery scale material. That is accelerated by estrogen and retarded by thyroid, vitamin A, and progesterone.

**Andrew Murray:** Other symptoms include exhaustion, lack of motivation, broken fingernails, tinnitus, joint pain, fluid retention, and blood pressure problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many doctors are confused about blood pressure. Hypothyroidism typically increases the viscosity of the blood and raises blood pressure. A slightly hypothyroid person might have low blood pressure, but a high percentage of people with hypertension are simply hypothyroid. Correcting it with a supplement of thyroid will lower the blood pressure.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is contrary to what we were taught in medical school. We were taught high blood pressure is a sign of high thyroid function.

**Andrew Murray:** You would think thyroid is a stimulating hormone, but actually, it improves sleep, calms you down, and lowers resting pulse.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen two people who chronically had a pulse around 180 beats per minute. One had it for 20 years. Within a couple of weeks of taking thyroid, both had it down to a normal 90 or 100 beats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you consider a healthy, normal thyroid pulse?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies of different ages. High school kids who were healthy and had the best grades had a resting pulse averaging 85 beats per minute. When old people on heart pacemakers were given mental exams with the pacemaker set at the usual 70 beats, they had the usual old person's memory. When they cranked the pacemaker up to 85, every mental function improved.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is interesting because we are taught that a racing pulse diagnoses hyperthyroidism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is an old doctrine from the beginning of the 20th century called the "Rate of Living Theory"—that the faster your heart beat, the sooner you would die. The experiment that "proved" it involved putting cantaloupe seeds in a saucer of water. The ones that sprouted soonest and grew fastest died soonest. But they didn't put any soil in the dish, so they simply used up all their food. It is an embarrassment for science.
