**Caller 1:** If a person was quite low in thyroid for more than 20 years, what kind of damage could that cause? Also, once taking supplementation, when could you expect to be better? I've been getting supplements for 20 years and am still incapacitated. I don't have a thyroid; it was removed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually doctors prescribe thyroxine (T4). That isn't the thyroid hormone; it has to be turned into the active thyroid hormone, triiodothyronine (T3), in the liver. When a doctor prescribes thyroxine, there is no chance you will be overdosed because as you increase it, it can sometimes suppress function. One patient with myxedema coma had been given increasing doses of Synthroid (T4) up to 500 micrograms and went into a coma. In the hospital, they gave her an injection of the active hormone T3, and she came out of the coma in a few hours.

You can have an amazing recovery from many things in a matter of minutes. For example, a doctor with agonizing breast pain took a 10 microgram tablet of Cytomel (T3). In 10 minutes, the pain stopped.

**Caller 1:** I have taken both. Is the damage from 20 years without a thyroid irreparable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some types of damage, such as osteoporosis, take time. When your thyroid is low, your pituitary tends to swell and overproduce prolactin. Prolactin causes breast pain and is a major factor in bone loss. It can take a long time of correcting your diet along with thyroid to restore bones, but I have seen people increase bone density by 20% in less than a year. Even lifelong things can be corrected quickly. I grew an inch and a half in my 40s when I started taking thyroid.

**Caller 2:** I had thyrotoxicosis and went into a thyroid storm. I was treated with Iodine-131 and have been taking Synthroid for 30 years. Can you explain the connection between the adrenal, the pituitary, and the thyroid? How bad is stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When your thyroid is low, you don't have efficiency with oxidative metabolism, so you turn sugar into lactic acid. Your liver spends energy converting lactic acid back to sugar, so low blood sugar is a constant problem.

To compensate, your adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline to force your liver to release stored sugar. When that isn't enough, the adrenal cortex secretes cortisol to break down protein (muscle tissue) to make sugar. Falling blood sugar and rising adrenaline signal the brain to increase stress hormones like ACTH and prolactin. ACTH drives cortisol up, and cortisol causes acute tissue damage, loss of muscle mass, and bone loss.

**Andrew Murray:** And weight gain, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. As your ability to burn fat decreases with falling thyroid, cortisol eats up the skeletal muscles that burn fat. The unburned fat gets laid down in the trunk, neck, and face.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when doctors diagnose "adrenal fatigue," they really need to look at thyroid function, vitamin A, and cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Many people diagnosed with Addison's disease simply had thyroid so low they couldn't produce steroids. You need cholesterol and thyroid to make steroids like progesterone, pregnenolone, and cortisol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How is temperature affected by low thyroid? What should a waking morning temperature be?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oral temperature should be around 98 degrees.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And after eating?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It should quickly pop up to 98.6 or 98.8. As they get muscle activity going during the day, it can rise to 99 degrees in the afternoon.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Most clients I see have much lower temperatures. If they have low thyroid symptoms in conjunction with low temperatures, is that a diagnosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you look at the whole picture—Achilles reflex, symptoms, calorie burning, sleep quality, and the ability to relax instantly after exertion—all of those go with the good temperature curve.

**Caller 3 (Kevin):** I was diagnosed with Hashimoto's disease. Can Dr. Peat speak about that and the use of Low Dose Naltrexone (LDN)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hashimoto's was originally defined as infiltration of white blood cells into the inflamed thyroid gland. Since they don't like to cut out a piece of the gland to confirm that, they look for antibodies in the blood. However, anti-thyroid antibodies overlap with many other problems, including arthritis, so they aren't strictly diagnostic. They do indicate inflammation. Since the thyroid is the basic anti-inflammatory hormone, often the thyroid is the main problem. Studies show that supplementing with thyroxine can decrease antibodies.

Regarding Naltrexone: When you are hypothyroid and produce lactic acid, you accumulate endorphins. Endorphins limit physiological functions in a protective way, like hibernation. Naltrexone clears those out. Sometimes in two or three days, a person can come out of depression or a lethargic state.

**Caller 3:** Is there any problem with long-term use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but I usually see good results in just two or three days. I think the basic treatment is a good diet and thyroid supplement. Naltrexone is good to try to break up a pattern.

**Caller 4 (Mike):** Earlier you listed vegetables and oils that affect the thyroid. Would cod liver oil be placed in with those oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fish oils are long molecules compared to seed oils. They don't inhibit our enzymes for metabolizing fats as seriously as seed oils (like canola or corn) do. However, they are very unstable to oxidative breakdown. By the time they get in the blood, they are often oxidized.

Studies show fish oils have an anti-inflammatory effect, but only their oxidative breakdown products—which include toxins like acrolein—are the active anti-inflammatory substances. They suppress immunity. Temporarily it alleviates symptoms, but in the long run, it poisons the immune system. There are articles showing fish oils contribute to atherosclerosis, increase metastatic cancer risk, and are toxic to the brain.

**Caller 5 (Jenny):** I've been on Armour Thyroid. My doctors want to switch me to a synthetic. Are there disadvantages? Also, do synthetics contain milk products?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The company that makes Armour also makes a synthetic called Thyrolar, based on the original Armour product. The FDA has required formula changes in natural thyroid, so quality varies. Thyrolar is a synthetic chemical that has been steady for 40 or 50 years and is equivalent to traditional Armour. You can check the manufacturer (Forest Pharmaceuticals) regarding milk content. Other similar products available from Mexico are Novothyral and Cynoplus.

**Caller 6:** I have been diagnosed with staph infections—multiple lesions resembling boils all over my body. My husband caught it too. How do I treat this?

**Andrew Murray:** One product is an allicin-rich garlic extract, used successfully for internal staph. However, Dr. Peat might note the sulfur content.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen chronic infections clear up with just thyroid or thyroid and nutrition. It is good to cover the bases. Tetracycline, for example, has a structure parallel to vitamin K and the active ingredient of aloe and cascara. Those molecules have a beneficial effect on the immune system as well as being slightly suppressive to bacteria.

I had a friend whose doctors wanted to amputate his legs because of gangrene and bone infection. I made him take thyroid. Within two weeks, the sores closed. When his doctor made him stop the thyroid, the infection returned. He cycled through this three times—feet rotting without thyroid, clearing up with thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to call it a night there. Thank you, Dr. Peat, for joining us. Dr. Peat's website is very extensive with researched scientific information. You can find it at www.raypeat.com.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat is also available for nutritional counseling via his website. We can be reached during normal business hours at 1-888-926-4372.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for joining us and good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Bowel Endotoxin
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month’s *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture all our own certified organic herbal extracts.

This month we are very pleased to welcome Dr. Ray Peat back to the show. We will be exploring the emerging revelation concerning endotoxemia and how unsaturated fats further burden our bodies in ways we could never imagine. Welcome to tonight’s show, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thanks.

**Andrew Murray:** Perhaps for those tuning in, could you outline what endotoxin is, how it is formed, and how it is harmful to our health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm not sure that people really know what it's doing in the bacterium, but it's been known since 1892. It was called endotoxin to distinguish it from the older known bacterial toxins that the bacteria secrete to poison something in their environment. Supposedly, the endotoxin only comes out when the bacterium is broken apart, but I think actually it leaks a little bit all the time. So I wouldn't say that it's strictly an endotoxin like the textbooks used to say. It is somewhat of a structural protein, but it's a medium-to-smallish molecule that can leak out in the process of growth and cell division.

Its other name is lipopolysaccharide (LPS) because its structure is a chain of sugar molecules with fatty acids attached. That gives it a soap-like behavior that is part of why it is toxic so generally. They are so common in the environment that organisms have their basic defenses against them. One of our basic defenses is the high-density lipoprotein (HDL). They talk about HDL in terms of carrying cholesterol, but I think its historic main function is that it's our first defense against endotoxin once it gets into the bloodstream.

Normally, the intestine is a good barrier against absorbing the endotoxins. If some of it leaks through the wall of the intestine into the blood vessels and gets carried to the liver, the liver enzymes break it down. It shouldn't normally reach the bloodstream in significant amounts, but it's a matter of tens of milligrams that can circulate into the bloodstream every day.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know if there is an acceptable value or level of endotoxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It stimulates defense reactions, so it's kind of a "toughening up" reaction to have a small amount of it. If you're born in a germ-free environment, your first exposure to bacteria is likely to be lethal. Absorbing a little bit of the endotoxin toughens up the system.

**Andrew Murray:** Perhaps this hearkens back to the germ-prevalent society of 100 years ago producing children that had better immune systems and did not have autism or other syndromes associated with the sterile environments of today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think when you try to be too sterile and then are inevitably exposed to germs, the sudden shock is probably a lot more stressful.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned lipopolysaccharide. How is it harmful to our health if we are exposed to varying amounts of it daily?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It triggers a whole series of reactions. It seems to be a physical-chemical process that stirs up a cell to recognize a threat. It is the things that it sets into action that really cause the chronic, accumulating degenerative damage.

One of the first things it does upon exciting a cell is to cause the cell to take up calcium and to activate the synthesis of nitric oxide. The nitric oxide and the cell excitation that goes with absorbing calcium trigger other reactions. A small amount of endotoxin can stimulate the intestine to contract more, but if the cells are getting overloaded with it, that—and possibly other irritants—can cause cells to produce so much nitric oxide that it becomes a major metabolic disruptor. It will cause the intestine to lose the ability to contract, and it will poison the respiratory apparatus so that cells can't make energy to fight back. At that point, with increased nitric oxide and reduced energy, the cells also take up water.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And then they become basically non-functioning to a degree?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they are under stress. If the body can deliver enough energy to them quickly, they can excrete the water and the calcium, turn off the nitric oxide, and return to normal functioning.

When they swell up, the textbooks give a simplified, mistaken idea of what is involved in bowel damage. They talk about the leakage *between* cells, as if the cells lose the glue that holds them in contact so holes open up. That does happen, but it isn't necessarily the worst way that the endotoxin gets into the cells.

As the cytoplasm takes up water, instead of being fat-like and tending to exclude water, the introduction of this sugar connected to a fat acts like a soap. It makes the cell tend to admit not only more water but pretty much anything that is in its environment. The whole substance of the cell becomes spongy and leaky.

When this starts affecting the whole organism, that kind of change occurs all through the body. Once the stuff has passed through the lining of the intestine, crosses capillaries, and gets into the bloodstream, the endotoxin starts doing the same thing to any cell it comes to. It will leak out of capillaries no matter where it is. If it happens to reach the brain, it will cause the brain capillaries to leak whatever is in the bloodstream, which can contribute to Multiple Sclerosis.

Every organ has its particular way of responding, but there is a generality. No matter what the organ, there are basic defense reactions that will occur not only to endotoxin, but to any radical threat to the survival of the cell. X-rays and gamma rays will produce essentially the same kind of change in brain cells or bowel cells that endotoxin does. If you're overexposed to X-rays, for example, you'll get constipated the same way that overexposure to endotoxin will cause constipation.

**Andrew Murray:** So there's a kind of saponification going on then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, an opening up and loosening up of cell structure. If you imagine a lump of gelatin soaked in oil, it will stay stable in the presence of water. But if you mix a little bit of lecithin with it, it will quickly start taking up water, and then the whole thing is on the road to dissolving and breaking up.

**Andrew Murray:** Many of our listeners have heard the term "leaky gut." Can you outline what causes a leaky gut and how it leads to this translocation of bacteria or endotoxin into the bloodstream?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Endotoxin is always present in the intestine and is the first thing to defend against. But many other stresses and toxins—like radiation, heavy metals, estrogenic substances, or too many polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)—all tend to loosen up or saponify the cell structure. This causes the cell to take up water and let junk enter from the environment into the cell substance itself.

Getting into the cell substance, it can just as easily go out the other side of the cell into the underlying extracellular material, and from there across the capillary cells and into the bloodstream. That is essentially what the leaky gut is: leaky cell substance, which involves leaky capillaries. Ultimately, it can cause leakiness of any tissue.

In pre-cancerous states, for example, you see substance leaking out of the characteristic cell. The prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is just a normal prostate protein that leaks out because the cell is under stress. The same protein leaks out of breast cells when they're under stress.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So literally, the cell is falling apart, breaking down, and leaking.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And something as simple as Vitamin E can tremendously strengthen the cell and help to hold it together so it doesn't leak its protein substance out into the environment.

**Andrew Murray:** What would be the mechanism behind that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No one really knows, but partly it is stopping the free radical damage that nitric oxide is producing. It helps to keep calcium from overloading the cell and keeps the water from associating too closely with the proteins. The natural hormones progesterone and testosterone also help to toughen up the cell. Factors similar to Vitamin E that are associated with energy production—Coenzyme Q10 and Vitamin K—are extremely powerful at defending the respiratory apparatus from nitric oxide and endotoxin.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned the influx of water into the cell due to lack of energy. Would thyroid have a part to play in raising the energy of the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The thyroid is essential for making the enzyme that allows oxygen to absorb electrons out of the mitochondrial system. The mitochondria take up electrons from sugars and fats and derive energy from those electrons as they are passed along to oxygen. Thyroid is the essential factor for making that happen.

There are other supporting factors, such as uncoupling proteins, that make the electrons run more quickly to be taken up by oxygen. What that does is produce carbon dioxide more quickly, which turns off the formation of lactic acid. That, in turn, turns off the nitric oxide forming system. If you can run the system fast enough with plenty of thyroid, you'll make the carbon dioxide, inhibit lactic acid formation, and pretty well defend against producing nitric oxide. This gives you relative immunity to the lipopolysaccharide.

**Andrew Murray:** Is that what they call the electron transport chain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The electrons pass down to oxygen, but they can't do it without thyroid. Temperature is also a factor. When you run the electrons through this system, you produce heat as well as carbon dioxide and ATP. Keeping the temperature up helps turn off the production of nitric oxide and other free radical destructive factors.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So all of these harmful X-rays, LPS from bacteria, and excess estrogen are essentially free radicals that are damaging our oxygen usage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Not all free radicals are toxic, but nitric oxide is one that is widely produced in response to stress. It increases greatly with aging, just because aging involves progressive stress reactions.

**Andrew Murray:** I remember "poppers"—drugs that were nitric oxide-based and very damaging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nitroglycerin has been used as a drug to open the circulation of the heart. Nitric oxide didn't really get much interest scientifically until Viagra came along. That is basically doing the same thing as nitroglycerin, but it's extremely toxic. It's like eating toxins, getting irradiated, and getting old ahead of time.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's a powerful free radical that people don't realize creates damage by depleting their bodies of oxygen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some free radicals can actually defend against the toxic free radicals. When the thyroid and oxygen are working properly, the electron transport chain involves lots of free radical activity, but it is all productive and protective. The faster you run oxygen through the mitochondrion under the influence of thyroid, the less free radical damage you have to the structure of the cell.

If you are low thyroid or lack oxygen acutely, the electrons, instead of being safely passed through this chain, wander off and attack the fats that make up the mitochondrion. Those fats become peroxides, which are a randomly destructive kind of free radical.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** These would be the polyunsaturated fats, which includes corn oil, sunflower seed oil, safflower, canola, fish oil, hemp seed, flax seed, cotton seed, and many packaged foods.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. All of those tend to accumulate in the tissues. When they're given acutely as an emulsion—they used to do it in hospitals to fatten people up, and now they do it to suppress immune systems for kidney transplants—they not only suppress immunity but create an instantaneous diabetes or inability to respire and use sugar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if we eat food fried in these oils, we are essentially ingesting a free radical?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very quickly, yes. An experiment I did illustrates how they spontaneously oxidize even at room temperature. I put a rubber hose in a bottle of safflower oil and the other end in a glass of water. Just at room temperature over a few hours, the bottle was in effect "respiring." It was sucking oxygen up and drawing water up into the tube. The oxygen was combining with the unsaturated fats and forming lipid peroxides.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And the situation is even worse in our body when it's at 98 degrees.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Much faster at that temperature. And we have catalytic amounts of iron and heavy metals floating around to accelerate the reaction.

**Andrew Murray:** What foods promote or prevent the formation of free radicals and endotoxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since polyunsaturated fats are the main material that causes an explosion of free radicals once the process starts with endotoxin and nitric oxide, simply minimizing those in the diet is a basic way to defend yourself.

There have been studies for 100 years showing that a fat-free diet, if you give the required nutrients, extends lifespan and reduces cancer. A 1927 study showed no spontaneous cancer in rats on a fat-free diet. Roughly 100 studies show the beneficial effects of a so-called deficiency of polyunsaturated fats. When a rat is made "deficient"—meaning they don't feed them PUFAs but give them purified nutrients—those animals can stand tremendous physical trauma that would kill a normal rat. They can be given cobra venom and survive. Toxins that would produce diabetes in normal rats don't hurt the deficient rats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So why are we so brainwashed that these are called "Essential Fatty Acids"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Burrs (George and Mildred Burr), who were promoting that idea from 1929 through the 1930s, were working for the lard and vegetable shortening businesses. When independent researchers checked their claims in the 1940s, they found the Burrs had simply produced a Vitamin B6 deficiency. The polyunsaturated fats poison thyroid function, raising the metabolic rate by about 50%. If you feed them only a normal amount of vitamins, they become deficient. Researchers in 1946 cured the syndrome by giving extra Vitamin B6.

However, in the 1950s, the industry went through a change. They discovered they could economize on food for pigs and chickens by poisoning their thyroid glands so they wouldn't eat as much but would still get fat. They found that polyunsaturated fats suppress the metabolic rate. That was when feeding pigs a diet of corn and soy took off.

At the same time, the paint industry discovered how to turn petroleum into paints and plastics, so they didn't need linseed or safflower oil anymore. The soy oil industry needed another market besides animal feed, so they convinced people to eat the production they couldn't sell as paint.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And the story continues into 2009.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After 50 years, the original data—that vegetable oils caused softening of the brain, infertility, and cancer—became too public. Everyone was catching on that linoleic acid was carcinogenic. So about 20 or 30 years ago, marketing shifted to fish oil. The fish industry was being pressured by the EPA to stop dumping waste in bays. They made fish protein from skins and heads, and since the oil spoiled so fast, they marketed it for human medical use.

**Andrew Murray:** It's a lesson through history that wherever there's a waste product, there's an industry to turn it into a profitable product.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Shrimp shells are now a medical product. I'm waiting for used tires to come out.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to go back to the liver breaking down endotoxin. How do you view liver health and how would you approach improving it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver has several ways to catch toxins. The brain is our second most active detoxifying organ. But if the liver is spending too much energy detoxifying, it becomes unable to produce albumin. Albumin circulating in the blood is one of the layers of defense.

When we're being poisoned, the high-density lipoprotein (HDL) made in the liver increases. Estrogen and alcohol increase HDL.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And this is what doctors tell us is the "good cholesterol."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, it is good because it's a reaction to being poisoned, so it helps protect when we're having a bowel problem.

**Andrew Murray:** So if you have low HDL, that may indicate you don't have a high toxin load?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The albumin in the blood binds fatty molecules. Between albumin and lipoproteins, our blood can hold a lot of stuff temporarily to give the liver a chance to catch up.

When the liver is poisoned—estrogen and radiation can do the same thing as endotoxin—the ability to form albumin decreases. Looking at albumin in a blood test is one of the first indicators of a person's basic resistance. If it's high, their prognosis is usually good. If it's down around 3 (where normal is 4.5), you're going to have to clean out the bowel. I've seen people go from below 3 up to over 4 in just a couple of weeks just by eating fiber and fruit juice to reduce the absorption of endotoxin.

**Caller:** I have a question for Dr. Peat, but first I'd like to make a statement. I am living proof that what this man is saying is the truth. I have had Crohn's for about 20 years. I've had four major surgeries, had all but 12 inches of my intestines removed, and have a double ostomy. By changing my diet, I no longer have any Crohn's symptoms whatsoever. My question is: Do common doctors understand these things? And if they do, why don't they tell their families?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The average doctor learns his high school courses very well. Then, the medical school courses on the alimentary canal and digestive physiology are really just a repeat of junior high and high school textbooks. So doctors get a very superficial picture of nutrition and digestion. I've been running into more fairly famous gastroenterologists who are barely better than the junior high textbooks.

**Caller:** I believe they are just trained to be drug pushers. Thank you so much for your wisdom.

**Caller:** You had spoken last month about a raised heartbeat being preferable. Since then, I've heard the opposite on another show.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Why do people feel better when they have a pulse above 80, when we are taught that an athletic heart rate of 60 is healthy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The brain needs oxygen and sugar. Unless you have a very big heart, it usually takes around 80 or 90 beats per minute to pump enough oxygen and sugar to the tissues to keep them warm.

Over the last 30 years, the normal temperature doctors look for has decreased considerably. From the beginning of thermometers, normal was around 37°C (98.6°F). In recent years, the average temperature of Americans has decreased. That means the heart rate can go slower, and the person feels they're getting enough, but they don't really feel as good as they should. I've talked to people who had temporary episodes of hyperthyroidism where their heart rate went to 125 for a couple of months, and consistently they say they never felt so good in their life.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** A previous caller wanted to know if kelp and iodine-rich seaweeds are good for thyroid health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have about 80 articles in my file on the toxic effects of getting excess iodine. Thyroid cancer is increasing at a tremendous rate. Welcome, Dr. Raymond Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hello.

**Andrew Murray:** For listeners who may not have heard you before, could you briefly give an outline of your academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was a student of literature and linguistics for years before I decided to get a degree in biology. In 1968, I went to the University of Oregon intending to get a PhD concentrating in neurology or brain biology. Very quickly, I saw that the nerve and brain people were extremely dogmatic and not really interested in studying the way the organism works. I found that reproductive physiology in that university had a really scientific orientation, so I did my dissertation on the endocrine and metabolic changes in aging of the reproductive system.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you have done a lot of work on thyroid hormone and progesterone. I wanted to ask you to expand on a topic many people suspect: the potential harm of X-rays. The medical establishment purports them to be very safe. Is there an upper limit to exposure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They don't keep a record of how much radiation they're giving patients. I've had many people who had obvious brain symptoms or spinal column symptoms of radiation poisoning. They asked the various doctors that had treated them what their exposure had been—for example, radiation for prostate cancer or fluoroscope visualization during heart surgery. None of the doctors had the vaguest idea how much radiation they had received, but it added up and caused classical degenerative symptoms.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Isn't it true that there isn't really an organization that monitors the X-ray machines in hospitals regarding how much radiation each machine is emitting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that has improved. They are generally supposed to calibrate them once a year.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you describe the principle behind X-radiation and how it causes negative effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The harmful effect is essentially from the ionization of molecules in the body. There is a spectrum ranging from radio waves through infrared, ultraviolet, soft and hard X-rays, and gamma rays. They classify things from the hard ultraviolet category through X-rays and gamma rays as "ionizing radiation." However, there are molecules in the body that ionize spontaneously, so anything from the weakest energy can increase the degree of ionization in the body.

It is a very misleading idea that only the so-called ionizing radiation is harmful. It is the amount of ionization produced that causes the damage. The radiation has to interact and resonate with some atom or molecule in the tissues to cause harm. If it passes through without being absorbed, there is no particular harm done. But if it ends up in your tissue and doesn't come out the other side, that does the harm.

For example, red light can pass through your body harmlessly. Blue and ultraviolet light will give you a sunburn. With soft, lower-energy X-rays, you can get a sunburn on one side while barely exposing film on the other side of your body. They tend to use higher energy, hard X-rays so that you don't fry one side of your body to get a picture of something inside. But still, with a chest X-ray, the side facing the emitter is going to get a higher dose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that shows something is getting stuck in the body; it's not going all the way through.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the same principle as getting sunburned on the side facing the sun. If you are facing the X-ray emitter with the detector on your back, your breasts are going to be at greater risk than if you turned the other way. But since your heart and lungs are right in the middle, they get it either way.

**Andrew Murray:** How would you compare the sun's radiation to radiation from MRIs or X-rays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The atmosphere filters out the harder, higher-energy X-rays and ultraviolet C. The kind of ultraviolet that burns us is ultraviolet A and B. To some extent, blue light can cause a sunburn. The burning effect is very superficial; it goes just a few millimeters into your skin and is absorbed. However, a sunburn can poison you systemically. Even though it's absorbed at the surface, you can suffer general systemic sickness.

The things in your skin that absorb the radiation from ultraviolet are the colored vitamins—folic acid, vitamin B2, and carotene or vitamin A—and the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). The PUFA spread the energy absorbed by these colored substances. The excited or oxidized fatty acids in your skin can travel and cause the release of inflammatory mediators all the way from your skin into your bloodstream and throughout your body.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about cosmic rays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cosmic rays are particles moving at extremely high speed. They pass through our bodies constantly. Because these primary particles are traveling at such high speed, our molecules don't resonate with them. The electrons that are knocked loose usually go back to where they were and don't cause much damage.

However, if you put animals under about a half-inch of lead, these primary cosmic rays hit a nucleus in the lead instead of being shielded. They cause a fission reaction in the lead nucleus, creating an intense shower of secondary cosmic rays. If you are in a building with a very thick roof, especially with metal overhead, you get some of that same effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because the secondary rays are traveling slower?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Essentially. They increase their ionization of the tissue as they slow down. It's analogous to skiing at high speed and falling. If you hit fluffy snow, you slow down gradually. If you hit dense snow, you come to a sudden, damaging stop. All the energy is absorbed by your tissue suddenly. That is what happens with these lower-energy particles.

If you eat an isotope which emits particles—such as those used to scan the thyroid or do PET scans—those are largely absorbed right in the local tissue. Those are extremely carcinogenic.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So not only are you exposed to the carcinogenic effect of the actual PET scan, but the substance you take to show up on the scan is also radioactive?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They often do it to find a tumor that concentrates the radioactive substance. But if you look at the whole body, the brightest spots are usually the brain, the kidneys, and the thyroid gland. They don't mention that those are highly metabolic areas that concentrate the radioactive substance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In Japan, blood tests show that people exposed to the atomic bomb 60 years earlier still have a lingering inflammatory reaction in which their blood is still emitting excited photons.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They still basically have radioactive particles inside their body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not exactly radioactive, but it started a process, sort of like rancidity in oil. If you start an inflammatory reaction with radiation and don't stop it, it can continue for the rest of your life.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** When doctors say a dental X-ray is equivalent to spending all day in the sun, how untrue is that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Totally untrue. An ordinary sunburn is actually slightly good for you, probably by making vitamin D. There is no good produced by the type of radiation from an X-ray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about people working in high-rise buildings?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Above the 25th parallel of latitude, the cosmic rays are intense enough that it probably increases your cancer risk.

They used to believe it was only the direct action of radiation on genetic material that caused cancer. But if you irradiate cells in a dish to cause mutations, and then add fresh, unexposed cells to that dish, the fresh cells will begin to mutate. It is called the "bystander effect." The damaged cells send a signal to the new cells in their environment that causes the same kind of damage, exactly as if they had been irradiated.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this trait heritable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It is undoubtedly a mixture of excitation and chemical signaling. Dentists will often put a lead apron over a pregnant woman and say, "We're just going to X-ray your head so the baby isn't affected." But a study in Seattle looked at pregnant women who had dental X-rays. When their babies were born, they were underdeveloped and smaller, showing that something happened systemically to the mother's physiology that affected the fetus.

Animal experiments in the 1950s established that X-rays act like estrogen. It will even cause rodents to go into heat. For years, people thought it excited the pituitary, but experiments showed that if they just X-rayed the animal's foot, the whole physiology would behave as if they had been given estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the lead shield doesn't fully protect the fetus because the mouth sends estrogen-like signals through the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the line.

**Caller:** Hi, I had a question regarding microwave radiation related to telephones and cell phones. Is that damaging?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 35 years ago, there were laboratories working with that frequency of energy, and there were clusters of brain cancers on the staff. Within a year or two, several people would develop brain cancer working around those high-intensity fields. In that context, the studies suggesting cell phones cause brain tumors are very believable.

**Andrew Murray:** How about acoustic neuromas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Whatever is close to a field is going to be affected. Because of industrial commitments to exposing the population to high energy—radar, microwaves, etc.—government and industry have put pressure on researchers not to see any harm. But from the 1950s on, researchers showed that nerves are seriously disturbed even by very low levels of microwave and radio frequency.

**Caller:** I need dental work, and I realize the dentist is going to do a huge X-ray. Is it better to let my teeth rot rather than have a dental X-ray?

Ultrasound imagery has been proven to work beautifully for teeth—you can see fine detail—but dentists are invested in X-ray technology.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So MRI and ultrasound are radiation-free diagnostic techniques?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The kind of radiation they use is less harmful than gamma rays.

**Caller:** Anyone who flies gets exposed to scattering from the X-raying of luggage. What kind of exposure are they getting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I haven't seen the exposure doses for those machines, but the history of X-ray technologists is not encouraging. Dentists always assured patients the stuff was harmless, but there was an epidemic of dentists losing their index fingers to cancer. Now they make the patient hold the X-ray film.

**Caller:** I had a lot of radiation as a child—liquid isotopes and mammograms as a teenager. What can we do to counteract the cumulative effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you know you are going to be exposed, or to repair damage, you can protect yourself by making sure your thyroid function is good.

**Caller:** What about full-body CAT scans?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A CAT scan typically gives you about 200 times the radiation dose that a single picture does. It is big business, but bad business. John Gofman discussed this extensively in his work.

**Caller:** I'm a midwife. I noticed that around a microwave tower in the countryside, I would see three- and four-eared rabbits.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They have known for a long time that telephone or power line workers—men—have mostly female offspring, and birds that live near power lines have nearly all female offspring. It is reproductive disruption.

**Caller:** I wanted to add seaweed to the list. It is a detoxer of heavy metals and radioactivity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Seaweed is even better than potassium iodide tablets, but it only protects you against **radioactive iodine**. This is the first and worst radiation injury from a nuclear leak, like Three Mile Island. However, it wouldn't help with radiation from a CAT scan or X-ray. Also, iodine is risky to use chronically; getting just two or three times the minimum requirement can increase the risk of goiter, thyroiditis, and thyroid cancer over a long period.

**Andrew Murray:** What are the upcoming techniques that are safer for visualizing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For mammograms, there is now good evidence that MRI and ultrasound will give even better information than X-rays. With an X-ray, you can't tell what is a tumor and what isn't. With an MRI, you can detect the type of chemicals and physiology in the soft tissue.

**Andrew Murray:** If someone is in a traffic accident and may have broken bones, is an X-ray justified?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Except for broken bones, or locating a bone splinter in the brain or lung, X-rays are limited. You can't really see much about the soft tissue.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think will be the long-term effects of our current exposure levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is already showing up. I am getting a huge number of emails from young women, from teens into their 40s, who have a problem with fat around their waist. Obesity is epidemic, and degenerative diseases, allergies, and asthma are increasing tremendously.

**Andrew Murray:** Can you explain the link between allergies, obesity, and inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The things that cause obesity also cause inflammation. Asthma is an inflammatory disease. The cytokines that regulate metabolism trigger cortisone production once you start down the inflammatory pathway. Cortisone directs fat to your face, abdomen, and shoulders. Chronic overproduction of cortisone causes degenerative diseases such as osteoporosis, obesity, and heart disease.

**Caller:** Has there been an increase in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) due to cumulative radiation? And is there a way to treat lupus successfully?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is my impression regarding the increase, though I don't have the figures. Regarding treatment, I have seen lupus patients over the last 30 years recover completely, or at least not die of kidney failure, by using **thyroid, progesterone, and avoiding polyunsaturated fat (PUFA)**.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you very much for joining us again, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** I think I should start by asking you to mention your academic background for those people who perhaps have never heard you.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We have a very experienced nutritionist, physiologist, and endocrinologist joining us tonight. We're very happy to have you on our show.

**Andrew Murray:** We wanted to go over the 10 most toxic things in our food. Incidentally, probably 50% of our interaction with clients is based on modifying their diet—getting them to cut out foods that are negatively impacting their health and switch to foods that positively affect it. In England, there are very descriptive ingredients on all the foods you buy. It almost seems ridiculous sometimes because there is so much information about the ingredients that it covers up the advertising. But it lets people know exactly what is in the product; everything has to be disclosed. Tonight, we will cover 10 products known to cause disease or symptoms leading to disease. These are easy to spot on packaging in England, whereas in America, legislation allows for the non-disclosure of certain ingredients.

One of the main things that has come to light is the ever-increasing processing agents used in foods. Food can basically be broken down into a soup, re-homogenized, put into molds, pressed, and formed. This is becoming an art—not for the sake of being creative, but for selling a product and turning non-edible food into apparently edible food.

The transglutaminases are a group of compounds that are basically "meat glue." These are agents that bind meats together. Dr. Peat, would you talk a little about the transglutaminases and their negative impacts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Celiac disease has been pretty much explained as an overlap between part of the gluten protein molecule and a natural enzyme that we have in all of our cells and systems: transglutaminase, which sticks proteins together. This enzyme is induced by lots of things to increase or decrease its quantity.

For example, ACE inhibitors for treating blood pressure have been discovered to block it to the extent that people's skin can fall off—the epidermis separates, forms blisters, and comes loose because of inhibiting the transglutaminase. The cells are flattened and keratinized under the influence of estrogen, which is antagonized by vitamin A.

For example, scleroderma—the hardening and calcification of the skin and other membranes—can apparently overlap considerably with celiac disease involving over-activation of the transglutaminase enzyme.

I'm not sure how big a role transglutaminase plays in those, but that is one enzyme that is very susceptible to forming autoantibodies under the influence of estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** Typically, what kind of foods will contain larger than normal amounts of these transglutaminases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The worst thing about the use of these products is that they are industrially manufactured in genetically modified microorganisms. When the Japanese pioneered the genetic modification of microorganisms to produce amino acids, people thought they were buying a pure chemical substance. **Andrew Murray:** And these can't be removed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As far as I know, it's impossible to absolutely purify them. But they purify them enough to satisfy government regulation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they're taking bacteria, fungi, and yeast, and genetically engineering them to produce various chemicals. The transglutaminases are one of these things produced through genetic modification.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And they're becoming more and more popular with restaurant chefs to prepare things individually.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That was a very interesting article you sent us talking about chefs wrapping chicken with bacon. If they just applied a little bit of this meat glue, the bacon conveniently stuck to the chicken breast without skewers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're getting very skillful. Soybean protein can be shaped, modified, and glued together to resemble the fibrous texture of meat. Scraps salvaged from the slaughterhouse can be glued together to look like meat. They can form it so that it looks like specific lamb chop cuts, pork chops, or rib steaks. They are very convincing copies.

**Andrew Murray:** They don't want to waste anything.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably where most people are exposed to the transglutaminases would be in the chicken or fish chunks that are very neatly formed to a certain shape. Or in delicatessens, they have so-called roast beef or roast turkey that comes in very symmetrical tubes or loaves.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Fortunately, in California, we are blessed with a lot more natural food stores, but these delicatessen meats are still very prevalent.

**Andrew Murray:** So basically, the pressed meats. Any meat in a delicatessen that's been pressed into a certain shape.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think some of the loaves that have been around for 100 years or more, for example, head cheese made with natural gelatin, would be fine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to recap on these transglutaminases: they are something our body manufactures naturally and have a purpose, but when we take them in increased numbers through these processed foods, that is when it starts to cause the problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Everything that we eat or inhale is processed by our immune system, sampling things that hit the intestinal membranes or leak through the membrane into the bloodstream. The immune system has to decide what to do with these extraneous materials. It can either accept them and allow them to circulate, or it can organize a defensive attack against them. It's the defensive inflammatory attack against extraneous materials, such as microorganism proteins, that can trigger sometimes deadly allergic reactions.

It isn't strictly the proteins. The immunologist doctrine used to say that proteins are the allergens, but many carbohydrates or starch-like gum materials are extremely allergenic. That has actually been known for 60 or 70 years, though allergists are just now barely accepting the fact.

**Andrew Murray:** Before we move on, Dr. Peat, could you mention the health benefits of gelatin? We mentioned the pressed meats using transglutaminase where gelatin was traditionally used.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gelatin constitutes about 50% of the protein in an animal. It has the feature of lacking tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine. Muscle meats are extremely rich in tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine, and those happen to inhibit thyroid function, suppress metabolism, and promote inflammation.

Simply eliminating methionine from the diet in animal experiments has increased the maximum lifespan by about 40%. Adults have an extremely low requirement for tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine. They are used for growth processes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's very important for children.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they're essential for kids to grow up. But once you've achieved your growth, you just need a very small amount to make new skin, antibodies, intestinal membranes, hair, and nails. You don't need the vast quantities that we get in the ordinary average proteins. 40 or 50 years ago, nutritionists wondered how "little old ladies" could be so healthy just eating gelatin and toast because they thought of tryptophan and cysteine as essential amino acids. But old people can essentially live on it with just a trace of the others in things like bread and fruit.

**Andrew Murray:** I think there is conditioning that gelatin is a bad product because it's created from animal parts. But actually, gelatin is extremely important.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Traditional diets made very efficient use of things like chicken feet, pigs' ears and tails, beef and pork skin, and so on. It is really very pleasant and nutritious food.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And there have been studies showing the anti-cancer effect of gelatin as well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, anti-aging and anti-inflammatory. It was used medically very widely up until about 50 years ago.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to the next additive: citric acid and ascorbic acid. These are common ingredients found in juices, especially orange juice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started running into people who had mysterious allergies in Eugene, Oregon. They tended to start with the pollen season and continue with the grass seed field burning in the late summer. But I found that some people had year-round allergies and were consistently taking all of the anti-allergy supplements: pantothenic acid, vitamin A, vitamin C, and so on. I suggested they try stopping those for a while to see what happened. I got essentially 100% results in curing the local allergies.

That was when I started doing a lot of nutrition counseling because everyone was so surprised to see that they had been allergic to the supplement, specifically ascorbic acid. That caused me to investigate the history of it.

Several years later, they developed new ways of manufacturing it. One of the processes Linus Pauling described as the "lead room" for making sulfuric acid. Then corn starch is oxidized with this industrial sulfuric acid and ends up as ascorbic acid containing quite a bit of heavy metal. With these new methods, I found that when people were taking 500 or 1,000 milligrams, they would often develop cold symptoms when they took it. **Andrew Murray:** Even though they might call it the same product, the industrial manufacture produces a very different thing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One researcher dissolved a 500-milligram tablet of commercial ascorbic acid in a liter of water and then put it in a machine that measures free radicals. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And here people are taking vitamin C for its antioxidant effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He said it shows what tremendous antioxidant systems we have in our stomachs that we don't all die with the first 500-milligram dose.

**Andrew Murray:** How about the gums? We see things like guar gum, locust bean gum, carob bean gum, xanthan gum, carrageenan, and agar-agar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And now they're in everything. Most ice creams, cottage cheese.

**Andrew Murray:** So these are basically the thickeners. We find them in ice cream, whipping cream, cottage cheese, bread products, cookies, and tortillas.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Even if it doesn't say it on the label, that doesn't mean it's not in there. A lot of processed foods have them.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's mention PUFAs, the polyunsaturated fatty acids. That's a pretty big problem.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In natural foods, I think there are two or three naturally occurring substances that account for some natural disease and possibly all of the major degenerative diseases. Those are polyunsaturated fats, starches, and sometimes an excess of iron.

If you ate liver every day accompanied by orange juice, you would absorb a toxic amount of iron. But just over the period of several years, you can see the accumulation of polyunsaturated fats in the tissue. Old animals have highly polyunsaturated brain tissue. Long-lived animals that are remarkable for living longer than you would expect are unusually saturated in their fats.

**Andrew Murray:** You'll find these polyunsaturates in corn oil, soy oil, and fish oils to some extent. These are used as frying oils for chips or french fries. Dr. Peat, mention some of the conditions that they can lead to.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Arthritis, cancer, dementia, wrinkly skin, and susceptibility to sunburn. An article that just came out two months ago looked at the pigment epithelium in the retina. They found that linoleic acid in particular, but all of the polyunsaturated fatty acids, created an inflammatory process that basically accelerates the degeneration of the retina. A new article showed that stearic acid or saturated fatty acids don't do that.

For many years, researchers on alcoholic liver disease have been showing that it's the polyunsaturated fats which cause cirrhosis and hepatitis when people drink alcohol. In India, alcoholics who are in the butter, ghee, and milk-eating regions don't get cirrhosis.

**Andrew Murray:** So the cirrhosis is not apparent at all in those people? It's purely those people that would consume alcohol in the presence of polyunsaturated oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A group led by a man named Nanji has demonstrated that saturated fats can basically cure alcoholic cirrhosis and hepatitis.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Even in the presence of them continuing to drink.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Someone did allow them to drink a quart of vodka every day, and they still recovered when they had their saturated fats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** To recap, naturally occurring saturated fats are butter, coconut oil, palm oil, beef and lamb fat, and cocoa butter. The polyunsaturated fats include sesame seed oil, nuts and seeds in high quantities, and corn and soy oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And chickens and pigs if they're fed on a high corn and soy diet. Their fats will be representative of what they were eating.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Even our eggs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They used to talk about the high saturated fat and cholesterol content of eggs, but about 30 years ago, someone decided to reanalyze and found that at that time they were already almost purely polyunsaturated.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, you categorized three toxic things in our foods naturally occurring: polyunsaturates, starches, and excess iron. Let's talk about starches.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A man named Gerhard Volkheimer, an immunologist in Berlin, tested on his medical students by having them drink a solution of corn starch or potato starch stirred into water. He would draw a blood sample periodically. Within about 10 or 15 minutes of drinking the starch solution, you would find a lot of the unprocessed starch pellets in the bloodstream—the same size they were when ingested. In some of these starches, the diameter of the starch grain is as much as 100 microns across, 10 times as wide as the cells that line the intestine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So how did it get through?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The process is called persorption. Basically, they are pressed on one side and they pop out the other side. The cells are much more flexible than people imagine. Since the capillaries are just a few microns across, and a red cell at 10 or 11 microns has to bend a little bit to get through, the starch grains can get stuck. The bigger ones will plug the arterioles before they get to the capillaries.

Volkheimer fed a high starch diet to mice and then sliced them up. He found that every organ contained areas where cells had been killed by plugging up an artery with ischemia, and that it accelerated the aging process by killing areas in the heart, brain, and kidneys.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that's causing heart disease then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically. In his medical students, after the first 15 to 30 minutes, he tested the urine and found that the same unprocessed starch grains were showing up in the urine, right through the kidney organelles. Somewhat later, he found it in the bile. About an hour later, he could find it in the cerebrospinal fluid.

**Caller:** I have a 13-year-old daughter who has allergies. We eat pretty well, mostly organic. Her symptoms are a stuffy nose and sometimes bumps on her face or legs. She tested positive for Johnson grass, molds, and sensitivities to wheat, dairy, and corn. The dairy seemed to make her stuffed up, and the corn and wheat generated the bumps. These allergies started to manifest between 6 and 8 years old.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With allergies, it's similar to autoimmunity, except not so serious. Estrogen begins to rise, especially in girls but in boys too, around the age of seven or eight. The estrogen changes the immune function; it tends to shrink the thymus gland and increase antibody production without the guidance of the thymus cells. That seems to be why it predisposes to allergies, asthma, and autoimmunity.

Asthma is now very well recognized to be increased by birth control pills, menopausal estrogens, or even the cyclic premenstrual rise in estrogen. Partly that's the effect of lowering the blood sugar, because if your blood sugar falls, the immune cells become much more reactive.

An experimenter ranked food allergens. If he lowered the animal's blood sugar with insulin to 50% of normal, the mildest allergens could kill the animals. But if he infused glucose while exposing them to even the worst allergens, the worst allergens might give them the sniffles, but nothing worse. So just increasing glucose or decreasing it can make a total difference in your sensitivity. Since thyroid and progesterone are the main things that allow your liver to store adequate glycogen, and estrogen interferes with that, that's why the sensitivities come on around puberty.

**Andrew Murray:** That's probably another misconception—that sugar is bad for you. Just say a little bit more about sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** White sugar was already being blamed for causing diabetes 150 years ago. The treatment for diabetics was to absolutely forbid sugar, which was a completely crazy idea. A French and an English doctor said that if they're losing a pound of sugar per day in their urine, they're surely going to die sooner if they don't eat any sugar. So he fed them up to 12 or 14 ounces of sugar—the best white granulated sugar he could buy—and he cured his patients just by feeding them as much sugar as they were losing. The process of washing it eliminates most of the allergens. So the finest white sugar is really one of the safest foods available.

**Caller:** I have questions about coconut oil. Could you explain the difference between coconut oils and coconut milks regarding health effects? Also, do you have suggestions for recipes for coconut oil? It works in stir fries, but the flavor isn't conducive to eggs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The coconut water is a pretty safe material. When the coconut is relatively fresh, the liquid should be almost clear and very sweet. It's surprisingly low in allergenicity. But the white material sold as milk is an industrially manufactured substance made by emulsifying some of the solids and oil with the liquid. The solids in coconut are very starchy and can be pretty allergenic.

I recommend using the highly filtered, deodorized form of coconut oil, which is extremely cheap. The aromatic, delicately scented ones that haven't been filtered can make some people very sick from an allergic reaction to the starches left in it. If it's very well filtered, high-quality oil, it tastes fine for frying chicken. I've been frying chicken in coconut oil for many years.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** There have been studies in the Philippines showing that people who used milk traditionally were having health problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, even in the traditional forms, it is probably not a very good food to use.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to answer your question, caller, Tropical Traditions Expeller Pressed Coconut Oil seems to be the best one I've found that doesn't have the coconut flavor.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the very pleasant ways to use the deodorized oil is to emulsify it. A little bit of egg yolk is all it takes. If you warm the oil and the milk, just a touch of egg yolk will allow it to emulsify. You can make ice cream or cheesecake—all kinds of buttery, creamy consistency foods—using the emulsified coconut oil instead of cream or cream cheese.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to the GMO microbial enzymes and vegetarian rennet. Talk a little bit about why natural rennet from a calf's stomach is not being used now, but is being genetically modified on yeasts, and how this contributes to allergies.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's the trace allergens, parts of the fungus or the bacteria. Aspergillosis is a very serious disease, and people who work in some of these enzyme factories are exposed to dust from the microorganisms and develop allergies. But the regulators assume that the people who eat the stuff aren't going to have the same sort of reactions.

All of the organisms used in manufacturing amino acids, proteins, or enzymes have their risk of impurities being left in the product. Food producers are being pressured to give up the natural material and buy their stuff in a can, doing it like they were in a chemical lab rather than a kitchen.

For example, Nancy's used to be natural cottage cheese. The way cottage cheese was always made was to drain the curd and salt it. Draining it left the curd free of lactic acid. But a couple of years ago, someone convinced them to start using what they called a "dressing" consisting of lactic acid and dry milk powder to give the cottage cheese a very long shelf life. Lactic acid suppresses the growth of organisms, but it's also just as toxic to the people who eat it. It can very quickly stimulate the whole inflammatory chain reaction, the same as polyunsaturated fat. If that inflammation is continued chronically, it increases fibrosis and eventually increases the risk of cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And we're told lactic acid is good for us. To summarize: natural sources of rennet are animal rennet, fig juice, nettles, thistles, or lemon juice. Artificial sources are "vegetarian rennet" or microbial enzymes derived from mold or genetically engineered. So vegetarian rennet is not a safe rennet.

**Caller:** What do you think of olive oil and canola oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In small quantities, like a teaspoonful or so of olive oil, it's fine and safe because it's only 10% of the toxic polyunsaturated fats.

Canola oil is very high in the polyunsaturates. It got its reputation as being healthful about 30 years ago when they learned to lower the erucic acid content. But Hans Selye demonstrated that it is not the erucic acid which was causing heart damage; it was the linoleic acid itself—the so-called essential fatty acid—which was causing death of heart cells. He showed that just by adding stearic acid from cocoa butter he could neutralize the toxic effect on the heart. So it's a ratio, and canola oil has a very high content of the dangerous polyunsaturates.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat can be reached on his website: www.raypeat.com. Thank you, Dr. Peat, for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** We probably only got halfway through the food ingredients. People should take more time to look at the ingredient panels on the foods they eat because you will find a lot of hidden material that causes problems. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Food Additives
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** We are finishing up last month's discussion on food additives and the detrimental health effects of ingredients that may not be listed on labels. In England, they have fairly strict food laws where everything has to be disclosed, whereas in America, a certain percentage of food ingredients legally don't have to be detailed.

I want to discuss dough conditioners and rennets. Most people probably don't know dough conditioners exist in bread. Could you say a little bit about potassium bromate, which is a fairly common additive to bread, and what likely negative health effects it has?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Besides any changes that it makes to the proteins and starches—which will make them more likely to be allergenic—any that gets into the system is going to be an antithyroid agent at least.

**Andrew Murray:** So it is thyroid suppressive. Regarding cheeses, our family has leaned toward European cheeses because their manufacturing is more traditional. In the States for the last 15 years, genetically modified yeasts used to culture cheese have become widespread. It is difficult to get a cheese that isn't made using a genetically engineered yeast. What do you know about the trouble with these versus using traditional rennet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The worst problem is that they are using things to carry the microbial enzymes. There is always some debris from the *Aspergillus* or whatever microbe they are using as a source of the enzymes. The genetic modification makes them somewhat different, but they are already toxic and allergenic in themselves. Even if they were naturally evolved organisms, any debris from them that goes along with the enzyme is risky.

Even worse than simply having microbial enzymes where there used to be animal enzymes, they are using seaweed materials—either carrageenan or other things—to distribute, emulsify, or mix the enzymes efficiently so they can be canned and dumped into the batch. One of the compounds being used to make microspheres to enclose the microbial enzymes has been used to make dental molds. One person died shortly after having some of that put in his mouth, and a high proportion of dentistry students had serious allergic reactions when practicing with it. These things are routinely being added to foods to carry other products, and as a packaging or carrying material, they don't show up on the labels at all.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Even on the labels for cheese, sometimes it just says "rennet." That could mean animal rennet, or it could mean vegetable rennet, which never really comes from a vegetable source—it is usually genetically modified or grown on a mold. Of course, there are natural rennets available like fig juice and cardoon thistle, but no companies use those anymore. So you are saying not only are these enzymes problematic, but also the carriers used to make it convenient for the cheese maker.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and they are being used as carriers for other foods. It is increasingly common to use seaweed materials, which are potentially deadly. One of the other most deadly allergens was sulfite, which killed a few people eating restaurant salads or seafoods that had been deodorized with it. Even after it was recognized that it could be deadly, it was still used in drugs sold for treating asthma patients.

There was a product called Alupent. A girl who had almost died in the hospital after being treated once was about to be treated with it again. She grabbed the bottle and ran; right on the bottle, it said "contains sodium metabisulfite." I wrote to the FDA, the drug companies, and the *Journal of the American Medical Association*. They all admitted it was a problem that could kill people, but they went on selling it for years without publishing warnings.

**Andrew Murray:** The wine and beer industry say sulfites keep wines stable. Sulfites are prevalent as sodium metabisulfite, both as a cleaning agent and to halt fermentation. Apart from asthma, what are the toxic side effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The allergic reaction is really the only serious toxic effect, but a person never knows when they are going to have a reaction. If they haven't eaten for a long time or if their thyroid happens to have fallen, there can be a sudden increase in allergic sensitivity because blood sugar powerfully controls the release of histamine. In experiments, they found that the mildest allergen would kill animals with shock if their blood sugar was lowered to 50% of normal. If they doubled the blood sugar of the animals, even the deadly allergen would only cause slight reddening of their nose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That supports the motto of eating frequently throughout the day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Eating frequently avoids several stress reactions, including fluctuations in blood sugar.

**Andrew Murray:** Many people are stuck on the doctrine that sugar is bad for you and causes diabetes. How would you defend sugar's role in a healthy organism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of people cite Otto Warburg's work in the 1920s, in which he showed that cancer cells can't use oxygen efficiently, so they use sugar at an extremely high rate. People argue that if cancer cells live on sugar, you shouldn't eat it. But that isn't a valid argument because when you have even a small tumor, the body senses danger and increases its production of cortisol.

One of the very early events in cancer is a chronic elevation of cortisol. Cortisol turns your tissues to sugar. If you don't eat sugar, your body wastes away faster. The wasting away of the immune system and other tissues is what kills most people with cancer.

There have been experiments where high concentrations of glucose were put into the artery feeding a tumor in an extremity. The sugar itself caused the cancer to die. So, sugar not only spares your immune system, brain, and other tissues, but if delivered at a high enough concentration, it allows something to happen that can kill the cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's discuss the science surrounding current cancer theory versus the "cancer field" theory. We have traditionally been taught that cancer cells are outside the body's control, that they ignore apoptosis (programmed cell death), and that they are immortal.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything is wrong with that belief. Going back to the mid-19th century, people saw that cancer arises in a "field" of visibly abnormal cells. After this inflamed area persisted for a long time, mutant cells might appear. This concept has developed over 150 years: anything irritating or destructive that the body can't overcome will cause progressive stressing or inflammation of the tissue. You can develop a cancer before there is any identifiable mutation.

Harry Rubin at Berkeley has shown that there is definitely a pre-mutational, definitive cancer condition. In the cancer, the tissue as a whole is so unhealthy that mutations occur in the DNA, but the DNA event is down the road from what is actually causing the cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you are suggesting that chronic inflammation or injury to a tissue eventually causes the cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you look at the functioning of a tumor, the cells are very sick and do not have a long lifespan. What you see in a biopsy are very mortal cells that will probably die in the next couple of divisions. The doctrine that cancer cells are immortal and body cells are mortal is completely backwards.

The Hayflick limit—that cells can only divide 50 times—was invented to reinforce the DNA-centric view of biology. Stem cell work has shown that all cells seem to be basically stem cells and immortal given the right circumstances. The function of the tumor is a process of healing and regeneration that can't come to completion. Something is missing that would allow the tumor to let the sick cells die while the healthy cells return to normal functioning.

**Andrew Murray:** How does radiation affect this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies of X-ray treated tumors found that the X-ray accelerated the death of the original tumor cells, but it actually accelerated the ability of the tumor to call for help and recruit stem cells from the bloodstream or adjacent tissues. The same signals sent out by inflammation call for assistance and replacement cells. So, when a tumor is irradiated, it increases its ability to recruit stem cells. The reason the tumor keeps growing after radiation is that you have increased the injury.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you see metastasis in light of cancer being a recruitment of stem cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s through the 50s, tests were made implanting pieces of cancer into people. It was found that people who already had cancer would accept a transplant, while healthy people didn't suffer consequences; their bodies rejected it. Metastasis, which is simply a self-induced transplantation, involves a defect in the whole organism that makes it susceptible to receiving a transplant.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that why radiation is used—because it does kill some tumor cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It stops the cells that are irradiated right in their tracks. But it also stops the growth of healthy tissue. Within 30 minutes of irradiation, there is a burst of histamine, serotonin, and tryptase enzymes that cause inflammation. This leads to a chronic overproduction of collagen and fibrosis. If the body can't heal this scarred, atrophied tissue, it recruits cells to try to repair it, creating a risk of future cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Is the current theory valid that cancer cells have different surface markers (MHCs) than normal body cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are degenerating, so they can go off in many directions and are often killed easily because they are recognized as abnormal. The normal function of the immune system is to maintain the proper development and form of the body. Phagocytosis (eating) of sick or injured tissue is at the center of the immune system. Germs don't necessarily trigger the immune system unless they damage something.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding constant irritation—like smoking leading to lung cancer—how does energy play a role?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The higher a cell's energy capacity, the more it takes to irritate it. Keeping cellular energy at a maximum means you are fairly immune to irritation. If something impairs energy production, almost anything becomes irritating.

In cigarette smoke, there are irritants and Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs). These are carcinogens, but they are also estrogens. Behind those irritants is carbon monoxide, which blocks oxygen use, making the cell more susceptible to stimulation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do those hydrocarbons suppress the thyroid as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The work of the Pullmans in the 1940s and 50s showed that the electronic behavior of these aromatic hydrocarbons acts as signals to cells in the same way estrogen does. Drug and government interests diverted that research, financing the molecular biology approach instead, which tries to explain these hormonal actions as nothing but mutations. But their main mechanism for mutating DNA is by acting as hormones that deplete the energy of the cell while over-exciting it.

**Andrew Murray:** How does a human energize themselves to improve ATP production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, you need essential vitamins, minerals, and adequate protein. But sugar is essential for keeping your thyroid functioning without resorting to cortisone overproduction. Unless the thyroid is specifically signaled to turn off by things like polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and estrogens, essential nutrients plus sugar will allow the thyroid to function.

Once the weakening process starts, the intestine becomes permeable ("leaky gut"), and toxins from bacteria leak into the bloodstream.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** To specify, PUFAs are vegetable oils: corn, soy, canola, cottonseed, and sesame seed oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1980s, French experiments showed that every stage of thyroid hormone production and transport was blocked in proportion to the number of double bonds in the unsaturated fat. Monounsaturated fats were slightly inhibiting. Two double bonds (like linoleic acid) were much more inhibiting. The triply or quadruply unsaturated fats, such as fish oils and omega-3 fats, are the most inhibiting to the energy system.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the bottom line is: eat coconut oil and butter, avoid other oils, use olive oil in moderation, and keep blood sugar up with fruit.

**Caller:** I have questions about sugar. You sound like you are saying "sugar is okay." As far as I know, refined white sugar is addicting and causes obesity and diabetes. I assume fruit sugar is okay, but can you clarify the difference between eating fruit versus candy and cookies with white flour?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Starches and proteins are very powerful stimulants to insulin. The combination of starch and polyunsaturated fats causes the greatest disturbance of blood sugar—much more than eating white sugar. The polyunsaturated fats block the ability to use sugar, so cells experience a sugar deficiency and turn on stress reactions. Starches are pure glucose rather than a 50/50 mix of fructose and glucose, so starches are much more powerful stimulants to insulin and stress reactions.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Starches like bread, pasta, and chips have a glycemic index around 140. White sugar is around 99. Fruit is around 75.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The potassium content of fruit is what keeps the insulin much lower. If you eat bread, you get very little potassium. If you eat fruit with the same amount of sugar, the potassium acts somewhat like insulin, so you have very little stimulation of fat production.
