**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I've also found that white sugar, because it is filtered, is less allergenic than raw brown sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you centrifuge brown sugar, the first wash is blackstrap molasses. I've noticed a smoky taste in blackstrap because it is common practice to burn the cane fields to harvest. Also, if you boil sugar at high temperatures, impurities cause polymerization reactions that create allergens. The brown material contains biological materials that, when heated, can make intense allergens.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the hierarchy is:
1.  Fresh, ripe fruit and milk sugar.
2.  Raw honey.
3.  White sugar (if you must).
4.  Brown sugar (less preferable).
5.  Starches (least preferable due to low minerals and high insulin spike).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. That stimulation of insulin leads to a surge of cortisol, which destroys protein in your tissues to keep sugar up. Eating too much protein without fruit will waste protein. I've seen people eating two pounds of meat a day who showed signs of protein deficiency because of super amounts of cortisol.

**Caller:** I was told that folic acid helps depression. Is that true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fruits are very good sources of folic acid. It is needed to make nerve transmitters.

**Caller:** I cut out everything but butter and stopped using vegetable oils, and it gave me a lot more energy.

**Andrew Murray:** What is being done currently in cancer treatment that you are excited about?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** More people are recognizing the importance of aspirin and stopping inflammation. As we age, we accumulate polyunsaturated fats in our tissues. Under stress, these circulate and produce inflammatory prostaglandins. Aspirin is an anti-aging defense against a lifetime of accumulating PUFAs. It is now known that chronic use prevents essentially all kinds of cancer to some degree.

**Andrew Murray:** How much aspirin would you suggest?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin should always be backed up with plenty of vitamin K—natural K1 and K2, not synthetic. Vitamin K is structurally extremely similar to a botanical drug called Lapacho (or lapachol), which has been used for generations to treat cancer. Emodin from aloe and cascara is also structurally analogous to vitamin K. Tetracycline, the antibiotic, has anti-cancer action not by killing cells, but by protecting the mitochondria from being poisoned, similar to cascara.

**Caller:** Do you have any feelings about quercetin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You get similar things in fruits. I think oranges have substances that are even safer and better than quercetin, such as naringin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Nettle leaf is also high in vitamin K and contains quercetin.

**Caller:** If using white willow bark (MediHerb), what would be an average amount for what Dr. Peat is recommending?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For an anti-inflammatory effect, probably one tablet daily. For an anti-cancer dose, it would likely be much higher, perhaps nine tablets. We use a standardized white willow bark powder because you would have to drink gallons of tea to get the therapeutic dose of salicylic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you think of the American Cancer Society and current cancer treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I see a lot of fraud. They sponsored a lecture tour to show they had cured lung cancer and leukemia, but they used phony statistics. The ending of atomic bomb testing accounted for the drop in childhood leukemia, not their treatments.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Why does research on anti-cancer substances like aspirin or cascara never reach the hospitals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The drug companies want a drug that you pay all your money for and keep taking as long as you are alive. They don't want people getting cured with aspirin, fruit juice, or Pau d'Arco.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to wrap up. As Dr. Peat says in his newsletters: "While a lie spreads around the world, truth is just putting her boots on."

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Altitude
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, which run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions. We manufacture all our own certified organic herbal extracts.

You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD Garberville 91.1 FM. You are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's mixed topic of elevation, the protective effects of CO2, and its many health benefits. We are once again very pleased to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, who will be sharing his research and knowledge of this topic.

For those listeners who perhaps have never heard you speak, Dr. Peat, would you please give us an outline of your academic work before we start this month's show?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started out in literature and painting because I was aware that American biology in particular was pretty backward at the time I was in university. It wasn't until I had got a master's degree, taught linguistics, and tried being a professional painter that finally I decided to go back and study physiology because I had been reading that all along. So academically, I started fairly late in science, but that was sort of an advantage because it kept me from having to conform to the dogmas that rule the scientific world.

**Andrew Murray:** You have extensively lectured and taught at universities, and you have many specialties. Would you briefly outline your particular interests?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Progesterone, thyroid, aging, and for the last 10 or 20 years, I've been thinking a lot about carbon dioxide and its physiology.

**Andrew Murray:** That is what we're going to talk about this month. I know that for some time now, I've been made aware that we are slowly evolving and retraining our minds. My mind certainly has been retrained, Dr. Peat, since I left university. Our physiology and pathology training was very much dictated by the texts at the time, and quite a lot of that seems to be erroneous. You've opened our eyes to certain things that are actually very different.

Let's start with elevation. What does high elevation do for a person? We all know about communities that are famous for having populations with great longevity. How does elevation confer longevity to a human?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the essence of the problem: what is the outstanding feature that affects all of the high populations? 100 years ago, insurance companies already knew—the actuaries were looking at the mortality figures for different diseases—that cancer, for example, was much less common in all of the high cities of the world.

As recently as the 1950s, [scientists] were sure that those figures must be wrong because they knew radiation causes cancer, and the radiation in Denver is much higher than in New Orleans, for example. But the figures show that the cancer rate in New Orleans and San Francisco is much higher than in Denver. They said that just must be a mistake, but the insurance companies have had the figures for over 100 years.

Part of the thing is that the radiation that you get at high altitudes is less harmful because of its lower energy transfer; high-energy cosmic rays basically go through you without causing much damage. But the altitude causes the Haldane-Bohr effect. Everyone knows about that in physiology; it explains what happens when you breathe and when the oxygenated hemoglobin reaches your tissues down in the capillaries.

The Haldane-Bohr effect explains the fact that oxygen, when it sticks to hemoglobin, changes the hemoglobin molecule, causing the carbon dioxide to come loose. And when you have a high concentration of carbon dioxide down in your capillaries, the carbon dioxide sticking to the hemoglobin causes the oxygen to come loose and become available to the tissues.

Strangely, there has been almost no research—just maybe a couple of dozen papers—applying that Haldane effect to other proteins. But in the case of hemoglobin, the molecule just happens to be in the right position to transport oxygen and CO2 in the blood. A few people who have tested other proteins find that the Haldane-Bohr effect applies to proteins in general. When there's a lot of carbon dioxide, it basically changes the pH or the isoelectric point of the protein, making it less accessible to oxygen. That in itself is a protection against the attack of oxygen against proteins.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** But more than that, the particular group that carbon dioxide sticks to on a protein, such as hemoglobin, is an amino group. Any amino group in your body—whether it's on your DNA, your enzymes, or the so-called hormone receptors—these all contain amino groups. When there's enough carbon dioxide, it will stick to those groups. In the absence of carbon dioxide, other stuff will stick to those, such as glycation. Various free radical fragments of unsaturated fats will tend to stick to those and derange the hormones. Insulin, for example, is a different hormone in the presence of CO2 versus in the absence of CO2. So everything in your body is different when it's well saturated with CO2. You can't suffer the side effects of diabetes, for example, if your proteins are well protected.

**Andrew Murray:** I find this yet another example of reorganizing my mind to get to grips with the fundamentals. I think we all think about carbon dioxide as being the "bad guy." It's a bit like the common misconception that sugar is the bad guy or saturated fats are the bad guy. How does carbon dioxide confer more benefits than oxygen when we all think that oxygen is the life-giving molecule?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1940, someone did a survey of organisms, including a great variety of bacteria and amoebas that all require oxygen to live. He found that they can't live more than one generation if they aren't exposed to adequate carbon dioxide. Even the obligate respiring, oxygen-dependent organisms need carbon dioxide. So he concluded that really it's more important as a life-supporting element than oxygen is, because all organisms require it and not all organisms require oxygen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also, Dr. Peat, you explained to us just a few minutes ago how if you increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the bloodstream, that tends to knock those oxygen molecules off the hemoglobin so that the tissues can pick up the oxygen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For example, in the heart, when you increase the amount of carbon dioxide in your blood, you increase the actual amount of oxygen in the heart. It delivers the oxygen to the heart. But more important than that is that it delivers it in the optimum way. It makes the oxygen go to the right places in the heart because it's having the same effect on the heart proteins that it has on the hemoglobin. It retracts the electrons so the oxygen doesn't stick where it shouldn't. The electrons go directly to the oxygen down the electron transport chain, and the electrons are prevented from deviating and attacking the polyunsaturated fats, which is what causes the bad oxidation that people take antioxidants for.

**Andrew Murray:** That's the free radical damage that people know about? So free radical damage is where the electrons are free to interact with things that cause harm, whereas the presence of an increased amount of CO2 actually prevents those electrons from becoming wild and reacting with tissues.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The essential electron-moving cofactor, NAD and NADH, which takes electrons from sugar or fat and moves it to the respiratory system—in the presence of carbon dioxide, that is more oxidized, meaning that the oxygen is doing its work better in the presence of CO2.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Basically, just to recap for our listeners: CO2 is referring to carbon dioxide. We breathe in oxygen-rich air and our hemoglobin picks up that oxygen and carries it to our tissues. What is happening at higher elevations is that you have an increased amount of carbon dioxide in relation to the amount of oxygen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is less oxygen pressure pushing the carbon dioxide out of your body, so your body retains a higher concentration as you go higher in altitude. You can see that in the cornea; it becomes more compact at higher altitude. People often notice that their nearsightedness improves by two or three diopters.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow. I read an article that you published explaining how nocturnal cornea edema can result in swollen eyes because the cornea has to absorb oxygen from the air. When we're awake, our eyes are open and that diffusion is happening, but at nighttime, our eyelids are closed and our cornea swells because it's not able to get oxygen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They've done experiments putting goggles over people and infusing extra carbon dioxide into the goggles. That makes the oxygen get used more efficiently in the cornea where it's depending on the outside for its energy supply. The carbon dioxide helps the oxygen get in and tightens up the energy structure of the cornea.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Why are hospitals so concerned, especially in emergency rooms, with testing your oxygen saturation and giving you oxygen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For one thing, I've tested those meters on my finger. Everyone feels really good when they have a 99% saturation, but I've noticed that when I'm feeling really the best, I can get mine down to 89%. I've watched the different conditions that cause it. Hyperventilating will cause the saturation to go up. Having cold fingers will make the oxygen go up. If you're not using the oxygen, it doesn't do you any good to have your hemoglobin saturated. So those finger meters aren't really very informative unless you know what temperature your fingers are at.

I've talked to doctors specializing in giving oxygen to stroke patients. Way back in the 1930s, Yandell Henderson became famous for providing resuscitation equipment to fire departments which provided 7% carbon dioxide with the oxygen. That was based on physiology. It worked the same for altitude sickness. I have friends now who take a bottle of carbon dioxide with them when they go to Vail for high-altitude skiing. When they start getting mountain sickness, they take some carbon dioxide. Traditionally, people have been using acetazolamide for altitude sickness; that causes you to retain your own carbon dioxide at a higher level.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's go over the health benefits of increasing your CO2, either artificially or when you live at high altitude. I understand it's the inflammatory reactions inside the body that are controlled by an increase in carbon dioxide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you've ever hyperventilated just for fun, sometimes it'll make your hands drop into a cramp or make your toes curl up. Losing carbon dioxide when you hyperventilate is the same as living at a very low altitude. There's too much oxygen and too little carbon dioxide. The cramping effect is just the first immediate thing. It also causes a cramping of your blood vessels, shutting down the diameter of your blood vessels, and it can cause fainting by cutting off the blood supply to your brain.

But it also causes the capillaries to leak. Even though they're tending to close down, they also become leaky and let water leak out. Carbon dioxide at the proper concentration causes the platelets to retain their histamine, serotonin, and other inflammatory substances. When you hyperventilate, your platelets leak these and make your blood vessels leak, causing edema.

If you have something else causing lactic acid to increase other than hyperventilation, you get the same effect. The lactic acid displaces the carbon dioxide, makes your platelets and red blood cells leak, and starts the inflammation cycle. One of the ways that carbon dioxide works is that it combines with ammonia, which is produced by stress and protein metabolism. In combining with the ammonia, it stops the stimulation of the formation of lactic acid. Ammonia accelerates the formation of lactic acid, so carbon dioxide is directly turning off the production of lactic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** Lactic acid is the thing that we feel when we exercise and our muscles cramp.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And it triggers the release of a whole series of mediators of inflammation, also of fibrosis. They're now finding that during abdominal surgery, if they blow in a fairly concentrated carbon dioxide gas, they'll suppress the formation of fibrosis and adhesions.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the common belief that when your muscles hurt it means that they're growing bigger and that's better is a myth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, yeah. Anything that injures your muscle... the lactic acid is probably long gone, but the damage persists. The damage involves the loss of CO2, and that causes the uptake of water, swelling, and so on. The swelling and injury does cause the muscle to get bigger, but not healthier.

**Andrew Murray:** This is another misconception regarding athletes. We look at people doing the Olympics and imagine them to be the most supreme, fit human beings, yet actually, they're in a very stressful state doing what they do.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. There have been studies that found that very well-trained athletes typically go around with an elevated lactic acid in their blood. Even days after their last exercise, they've suppressed their carbon dioxide and become habituated to increased lactic acid, which has those long-range harmful effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I wanted to ask you, Dr. Peat, why people who go to oxygen clinics and have intravenous oxygen or oxygen therapy feel positive health effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are different treatments called oxygen therapy. They range from simply injecting a solution of hydrogen peroxide or exposing the blood to ozone or ultraviolet light. Generally, the treatments are exciting the white blood cells. Some of the effects of excited white blood cells are beneficial; they become more aggressive when they're slightly injured. But they also release substances that trigger the stress hormones, ACTH, leading to activation of your adrenals. Activated adrenals will combat other inflammations. So it's a way of turning on your anti-inflammatory, anti-stress hormones. But there are better ways to just generally suppress your inflammatory responses. For example, things that increase progesterone will decrease cortisol, causing much better consequences in the long run.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people might experience an increased immune system or decreased inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Carbon dioxide activates the phagocyte process of various cells in your blood. That's a part of normal repair and regeneration. For example, the baby gestating in the uterus is completely free of germs normally, but it still has very active phagocytes. Their activity is supported in proportion to the carbon dioxide tension, which is usually high in the uterus. That activity of the phagocytes is part of the developmental process. When a tissue is changing from one form to another, the old form has to be digested and removed to make room for the new form.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the phagocytes will eat up the old cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and so the high concentration of carbon dioxide supports the developmental process of cleaning up the junk.

**Andrew Murray:** Would any of this phagocytosis be involved in destroying cancer cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it's essential. Lacking the cells enter the cancer, but they are unable to produce the right results because the cancer is producing lactic acid which knocks out the suppressing [effect] coded by carbon dioxide.

Also scar formation. The developing fetus is practically resistant to forming scars. Only at a later stage, when it's being exposed to environmental fats that the mother eats, will it form a scar. But healing is ordinarily scarless in the early fetus. It's the things causing loss of carbon dioxide mostly that inhibit the phagocytes, which should clean up the collagen excess.

**Andrew Murray:** Is it in part due to the decreased fibrosis that increased CO2 would also bring about, leading to less scars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think that's a big part of it. Excess oxygen causes malfunction of a lot of things. Displacing the carbon dioxide changes everything systematically.

**Andrew Murray:** It reminds me of a spring that we have here in California called Vichy Springs in Ukiah. Those mineral-rich spring waters are highly carbonated. You get this thing called reactive hyperemia after you've been in the water about five minutes where you get this flushing; your skin turns pink and you feel warm, even though the water is only about 96 degrees.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have a giant plastic bag, like a leaf bag, you can fill it with pure carbon dioxide. It'll be at room temperature or even colder if you just blew it out of a tank. When you step into that, you instantly feel warmth and your skin turns pink. When you're in a hot spring, even though the water doesn't dissolve a very high concentration of CO2, still you absorb it against a gradient. There can be many times higher concentration of CO2 in your tissue, but it moves from a lower concentration into your body as if your body were pumping it in. But it's really a matter of being more soluble in your body.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think you're getting more benefits from CO2 by bathing in Vichy or sitting in a trash bag full of CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's more fun to bathe in a hot spring.

**Andrew Murray:** I know. But actually, from a standard point of view, do you think you're probably going to get more CO2 doing a CO2 therapy in a sealed container?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think so. Just don't put it above your neck.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Don't try to breathe it.

**Andrew Murray:** I think we have a caller.

**Caller:** I have a question. How come when people have weakened lungs, high altitude bothers them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's really the only condition that is bad for a high altitude. When they've done studies, for example in New Mexico, mortality from heart disease as well as cancer decreases for every thousand feet of higher altitude. But asthma is the one condition which is a problem at higher altitude.

However, in Mexico City, there have been surveys through Mexico in which actual incidence and suffering from asthma increases as you go *down* in altitude. So if you have asthma to start with, you don't want to go to Leadville right away. But as a matter of developing the problem, living at a high altitude makes you much less likely to develop it than living at sea level.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's go to the next caller. You're on the air.

**Caller:** Good evening. I have a question about mountaineering in the 6,000 to 8,000-foot range, maybe even up to 11,000 feet. Normally we use a technique of a big abdominal exhale when we're feeling the effects of the altitude. But what you're saying is you should breathe into a bag instead and breathe in your own CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** On one of the Everest expeditions, they were treating people by putting them in a big plastic bag with oxygen. That's a fairly standard way to treat them, and it works. But they found that it was the carbon dioxide that they were breathing out that was accumulating in the bag, which was the really therapeutic agent.

**Caller:** So that would be a good technique to test? To have a paper sack or plastic bag and exhale into it and take maybe 30 seconds of deep breaths into it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. I've seen people with high blood pressure bring their blood pressure down 30 points in a day or two just by bag breathing repeatedly.

**Caller:** Okay, well, thank you. We'll try that this winter.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also, Dr. Peat, you've mentioned before that if you tightly seal the bag around your mouth, you can breathe in and out of that bag for a couple of minutes before you start to feel uncomfortable. Just that small amount of bag breathing can increase your carbon dioxide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. How the adaptation works is that each time you increase the CO2 to an uncomfortable level, it's suppressing the lactate a little bit and lowering the adrenaline, free fatty acids, and many things that cause you to hyperventilate. So you're basically curing your tendency to breathe too much by adapting to repeated exposures to extra CO2.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to bring out a little bit about people with low thyroid. I understand that their CO2 state is generally lower anyway because they have an increased adrenaline, and adrenaline depresses carbon dioxide. So having a better thyroid will increase your likelihood of retaining CO2 and decrease your adrenaline.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and there are many side paths to that. For example, the thyroid helps to lower the estrogen level. Estrogen and many of the related factors tend to cause you to hyperventilate, even to the point of having alkalosis. Diabetes, even though supposedly the diabetic isn't using glucose, typically a diabetic has elevated lactic acid. Carbon dioxide makes a big effect on the diabetic lactate.

**Andrew Murray:** This is another reason not to aerobically exercise—running, jogging, cycling—things that would increase your respiration, increase your oxygen, decrease your CO2, and increase your adrenaline. All of those things are pointing out to be more negative than healthful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** So the kind of exercises for people that do exercise a lot... what would be more beneficial?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think mild muscle-building activity, as well as anything that's fun—enjoyable activity that doesn't cause discomfort. There have been studies of old people with their muscle mitochondria apparently having genetic damage and loss of DNA. By several weeks of concentric exercise—just contracting the muscle against resistance—they repaired the mitochondrial DNA to have restored mitochondrial function. But the eccentric exercise, where your muscle is forced to lengthen while resisting—for example, when you're walking down a hill—that damages the mitochondria.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So this is why you suggest pushing the bicycle up the hill and riding the bicycle down the hill. Or throwing weights or loading firewood.

**Andrew Murray:** I didn't know this, but the positive effects of elevation—say if you go up to a high city for a couple of weeks and come down—can actually linger for several months. How does that work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Russians were the ones that really pioneered this. After Yandell Henderson, the Russians took up the study and found that if an animal was kept at high altitude for a few months, when it went back to low altitude, it lived the rest of its life retaining about twice as many mitochondria as it had at lower altitude. Meaning it was basically twice as efficient.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And it could produce twice as much energy. For those listening, the mitochondria are the powerhouses that utilize fuel and produce energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And it's failure of the mitochondrion that causes the degenerative diseases. Otto Warburg, 80 or 90 years ago, was showing that mitochondria fail in cancer. The same Russian groups that were showing that high altitude causes increased mitochondria produced cancers artificially in rats. The ones that were left at low altitude, 100% of them died. The others that were taken to 17,000 feet, 50% of them spontaneously threw off the cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow. The beach and the seaside in Victorian England was the place to go to, but actually, it's one of the worst things you can do. You need to go to a high elevation if you want to get some positive effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you tell us, Dr. Peat, about those people that live at very high altitudes and their lifespans? You were telling me about a typical lifespan of 130 to 150 years old.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I think it was about 1950, the first time I heard about it was a Peruvian who was brought to tour the United States as an oddity. The church record showed him as being 187 years old. After a couple of weeks visiting around the US, he was sent back to Peru and died shortly after that. And Old Parr in London—he was a guy in the country that was famous for being 150-something. The King had him brought to London to study, and he died shortly after living the high life in London.

**Andrew Murray:** At sea level?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My mother and I just went to Michoacán in Mexico. We were staying in Pátzcuaro, which is a town at 7,200 feet. For the short seven days we were there, the health benefits were very noticeable. Dr. Peat, you're suggesting that if someone spends a week to a month at a higher elevation, the health benefits will last. For how long?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After once, probably a year and a half, something like that. A friend of mine who was there at that altitude last winter for almost two months lost 20 pounds while he was there.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That was the other thing. Their food is so delicious—their wonderful corn tamales, uchepos, and corundas. I ate probably two to three times more than I normally eat, and I came back weighing the same. My mother did the same. We were so hungry, it sped up our metabolism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Indian army noticed that their soldiers, when they were sent to Kashmir or other very high-altitude places, lost weight very quickly. So they've done a lot of studies on how to keep the soldiers' weight up at high altitude.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We hiked up this ancient volcano every morning, and that was a two-hour hike. We didn't notice any change in our breathing as far as being at 7,200 feet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The conventional physiologists for years have noticed what they called the "lactate paradox," which is that you can work full force at a high altitude without producing lactic acid. It's not really a paradox; it's that the oxygen is not at a high enough concentration to displace carbon dioxide. So the carbon dioxide is taking care of the lactic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** So in increased carbon dioxide states, oxygen is utilized way more efficiently and way less of it is available to react in free radical formation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It works one of the ways is that carbamino effect, simply protecting any amino group from attack by oxygen. But it also simply activates the enzymes that direct the electrons to move from glucose or fat down to oxygen. It creates a sort of greased pathway for the electron movement. If you block the carbon dioxide or oxygen, the NAD reflects the increased access to electrons, and those electrons tend to diffuse out through the cell, causing attack of polyunsaturated fats and genetic material.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Basically, the carbon dioxide is acting like a very powerful antioxidant.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Instead [of antioxidants], hospitals have noticed that during surgery their patients often had severe lung damage from free radical oxidation from ventilating them too hard. So now they practice what they call "permissive hypercapnia." They under-respirate them, let the carbon dioxide accumulate, and it has an antioxidant protective effect.

In horses, there were studies in which they raised the blood carbon dioxide concentration three times normal. At that level, there were no free radicals detectable in their bloodstream, where normally there is a certain amount. It's as though we're designed to live with much more carbon dioxide than is available at this altitude.

People studying the early embryo before implantation traditionally were culturing them in an atmosphere with 5% carbon dioxide and maybe 15 or 20% oxygen, and they were having poor results. Someone tried increasing the CO2 and found that at 10 or 15% CO2 and 5% oxygen—much more CO2 than oxygen—the blastocysts were more vigorous. More of them survived and implanted better. So even at the crucial stage of early embryo development, carbon dioxide is the crucial factor, much more important than oxygen.

**Andrew Murray:** Are there any good ways of increasing your CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Shifting your diet away from the polyunsaturated fats is, I think, the basic [step].

**Andrew Murray:** How does that help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The polyunsaturated fats interfere with the enzymes that send electrons to oxygen and shift away from glucose metabolism to fat metabolism. You can show that when they give intravenous fat to people in hospitals to increase their calories, within a few minutes their ability to use glucose is suppressed. The fats simply block the enzymes that produce the oxidized glucose.

When you burn glucose, you get much more carbon dioxide per unit of oxygen used. So at high altitude, a person uses their oxygen more efficiently and they're more reluctant to burn their stored fats. Anything you do to increase the carbon dioxide will tend to protect you against mobilizing your fats and creating that diabetes-like state.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to explain for our listeners, polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs) are those fats that are liquid at room temperature—apart from olive oil, which is mainly monounsaturated. They include the long list of vegetable oils: soy, canola, safflower, cottonseed, corn, sunflower, hemp seed, flaxseed, and fish oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. There is a big push now to sell fish oils in place of those seed oils that were promoted for 50 years. Now they're shifting over to fish oils because they don't produce some of the toxic effects of the seed oils. But part of the reason they don't do that is that they are so unstable that they break down even before they reach your bloodstream. A very high proportion has become the free radical fragments that inhibit your immune system. Even though in the long range they increase your infections and suppress immunity, in the short range they seem to be anti-inflammatory just by their suppressive effect.

Some of the people who are promoting those very oils, DHA and EPA, have been saying that your baby will be smarter if you put it in their baby food. But in the baby food, these things are so unstable, they're about 20 times more broken down into toxic free radicals than even when you get them in the normal food form.

Some of these people believed that the women who ate fish oil and the other highly unsaturated fats would have more intelligent fetuses. So they presented sounds to the gestating baby to see how quickly they could habituate and respond. They were predicting that the women with the highly unsaturated babies would have the smartest fetuses. They found just the opposite: the women showing evidence of a deficiency of fatty acids had the babies that behaved most adaptively.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they had a deficiency of these toxic fatty acids.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And when the baby was born, they measured their head circumference, length, and weight, and they were growth retarded as well as behavior retarded.

**Andrew Murray:** Oh, goodness.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 30 or 40 years ago, animal studies showed the same effect. They fed one group of rats cocoa butter and another safflower oil. The ones that got safflower oil were stupid and had small brains; the others were better learners with bigger brains that had the cocoa butter.

**Andrew Murray:** I think our engineer has a question for you, Dr. Peat.

**Engineer:** I have a couple. One is, prior to 1920, I heard that when corn oil got out in the country, there were more heart attacks. I don't know if that's true or not. And the other is butter and coconut oil—are those two ones I should be eating?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If you eat lots of butter or cream, it can make you fat, but it is protective against the oxidative degenerative diseases. But the coconut oil tends to stimulate your use of oxygen so fast that it protects against even obesity. Milk contains other things that stimulate your safe use of oxygen, so if you're going to use the cream, it's better with milk rather than just in the butter form.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And I think your question about the heart attacks was that prior to the 1920s, studies showed that heart attacks were much less prevalent. It was once people started eating these polyunsaturated fats in the corn oil—the big Mazola corn oil push—that's when the heart attack incidence was on the increase.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And the age pigment is formed from the polyunsaturated fats of corn oil and soy oil. This has been identified repeatedly in the atherosclerotic plaques that are involved in heart disease. So there are direct connections between the polyunsaturated fats and heart disease as well as cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** There's lots of this research out there. You can visit Dr. Ray Peat's website. It's www.raypeat.com.

**Andrew Murray:** There are plenty of articles there about subjects that we've talked about this evening and a lot of other articles that we haven't covered, but well worth checking out. Fully referenced scientific articles. Thank you for listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. Until next month, August the 20th.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Sugar I
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, they run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM. We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal supplements and dietary advice.

This month we want to reassess the role of sugar in the diet and why good sugars are essential for good health. It seems that many things we are told are bad for us are actually the good guys, and we need to see the facts and research that is out there. First, it was saturated animal fats; we were told they were hardening our arteries and leading us into an early grave. Not true. The polyunsaturated alternatives are actually damaging us and are the cause of many disorders. Then salt, which we were told was increasing our blood pressure. Again, not true. Salt is essential and regulates many processes, without which we suffer from increased adrenaline and stress hormones.

Now sugar is the "bad guy." Well, not true. So once again, we're excited to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us this month, and we'll be hearing from him on research-based facts behind the statement that sugar is good for you. Dr. Peat, thank you so much for joining us again. Would you first give the listeners a little bit about your background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 50s and 60s, I was studying and teaching in the humanities, but I spent a lot of time reading at the science library of the University of Oregon. I eventually decided to get a PhD in biology and physiology so I could use their laboratory equipment as well as their library. But I never really considered myself part of the academic scientific community. I just got what I could from their culture and have tried to see things that are useful rather than just abstract. That has meant that I concentrate on small molecules rather than genes and the big fancy molecules. So water, carbon dioxide, salt, calcium, sugar, and fats have been the things that I study most.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you first qualify the term "good sugar" for our listeners? Then we'll get into the facts and figures surrounding sugar and why they're so important for us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar is really the ideal energy exchange substance. It's useful for practically all organisms, and it is something that we can store and use for building all of the big molecules. When it's metabolized, it releases carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is really a more universal substance than oxygen for the support of life.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You had told us in one of our previous shows that there are organisms who can live without oxygen, known as anaerobic organisms, but there are no organisms that can live without carbon dioxide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. It turns out that it isn't just mosquitoes, fleas, and bed bugs that are attracted to carbon dioxide. The flatworms and nematodes that they study as simple models of metabolism and aging seek out a fairly high concentration of carbon dioxide as more favorable for their living conditions.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So as our cells use sugar more effectively, are we producing a larger amount of carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When we produce more carbon dioxide, that means we inhibit the production of lactic acid. Lactic acid is not only a wasteful way to use sugar, but it has a signal function that turns on a whole range of inflammatory processes. They have talked for decades about tumors producing lactic acid, but lactic acid also promotes tumors and all the inflammatory processes. So you want your sugar to metabolize into carbon dioxide, which will then prevent the dangerous overproduction of lactic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can somebody overdose themselves on lactic acid from eating fermented cultured products?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I got interested in that a long time ago when I found a nice kefir product that tasted good. I would drink a pint of it for lunch, and I came down with a migraine every time I did that. That caused me to read more about the metabolism of lactic acid. It is normally produced by stress. When you use your muscles faster than your lungs can keep the oxygen supply adequate, the lactic acid is circulated into your bloodstream and reaches the liver. Your liver has to spend extra energy to turn the lactic acid back into glucose, which it then sends back to the muscles. Meanwhile, it's depleting your liver of any stored glycogen just to get rid of the lactic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's wasting the sugar that your liver has stored as glycogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Because I probably was hypothyroid, I happened to be so sensitive that I got a migraine just from drinking a package of the kefir. Since then, I've run into quite a few people who were having various symptoms every time they ate a fermented product with lactic acid in it. The vinegar type fermentation is slightly toxic, but it doesn't participate in that blood sugar disturbing effect that lactic acid does.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's the probiotic bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of the probiotic bacteria make lactic acid. In themselves, they can produce other substances that are protective, but you don't want them producing lactic acid from the sugar you eat. The sugar you eat should be absorbed in the first part of your intestine where there are no bacteria to speak of.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Or there shouldn't be.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. For various reasons, sometimes the bacteria will migrate up there from a sluggish bowel. Or, if you eat poorly digested materials like too many starches or fibrous mixtures of starch and carbohydrates, these things will not be absorbed. They will go down and feed the bacteria, and then the bacteria can make lactic acid and other worse toxins from them.

**Andrew Murray:** I think it's important to expand on the liver as a storage organ for glycogen. How much glycogen is the liver able to store? How long can people go with just eating proteins or not eating before their liver runs out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your thyroid and other hormones are in the right concentration, your liver should be able to store at least eight hours of glycogen. Everyone should be able to get through the night on the amount of glycogen in their liver without resorting to other sources of energy.

However, when your thyroid is a little low, or if your estrogen is too high, your liver sometimes can hardly store any glycogen. Typically, when your glycogen runs out, you send out a surge of adrenaline, which will squeeze the last little bit of glucose out of your liver. When your liver can't respond to the adrenaline anymore—the first sign of depleted glucose is feeling shaky and cold from the high adrenaline—you then resort to increased cortisol.

Cortisol begins breaking down your tissues, turning protein into fat and carbohydrate for energy. Under that extreme condition, when you've been out of glycogen long enough to run on cortisol for about a day, your thymus will be dissolved just in a few hours. When the quickly dissolved tissues such as the thymus are gone, your muscles will atrophy. People who fast for a week or two will usually lose more muscle weight than fat because of the very rapid conversion of protein into fuel under the influence of cortisol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So whenever you eat a big dose of protein without sugar to back it up, you're going to stimulate the secretion of insulin to dispose of the amino acids.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The insulin, which properly disposes of the amino acids, is going to lower any circulating glucose and tend to turn it into fat. As the glucose goes down, that will drive up your cortisol. Typically, a big protein meal will cause a huge surge of cortisol. Some people become supposedly diabetic or very hyperglycemic because they eat too much meat unaccompanied by sugar or carbohydrates.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's important to keep a balance between proteins and sugars.

**Andrew Murray:** We should always eat sugars with protein.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's clarify the bad sugars versus the good sugars and what food sources they are in.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things that started me thinking about whether a person should follow the government's advice to eat a lot of starch—otherwise known as complex carbohydrates—was reading about it in the 70s. The government and the American Dietetics Association have been promoting the idea that complex carbohydrates have some advantage over sugars for almost 50 years.

I ran across Gerhard Volkheimer's research. He fed different mixtures of starch and water—corn starch, potato starch, and grains—to experimental mice. These starch grains are roughly the size of a cell, anywhere from 5 microns up to 100 microns. He found that with a chronic diet of frequent starch feedings, he could demonstrate particles of starch in their bloodstream just minutes after they ate it, and in all of their body fluids about an hour later. He found that the mice were prematurely aged. When he examined their organs, he found little nests of dead cells where one of these fairly large grains of starch was stuck in an arteriole, killing all of the cells downstream from that plugged-up point.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the starch granules were blocking the arterioles and starving the cells of nutrition?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. He tested it on his medical students. He found that about 30 minutes after you drank some of it, you can find starch grains in your veins. 45 minutes to an hour later, you find it in the urine, the bile, and even in the cerebrospinal fluid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this because people's intestines are out of balance, or just the nature of the starch granule size?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He assumed they are being forced between cells. People have a mechanical conception of the intestine wall, arteries, and capillaries, but it's actually more like a viscous fluid. Things can migrate through as if there was no absolute barrier.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat has mentioned starches as being the bad guys because they block arteries, but there are other things starches do.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the typical starch isn't digested, it goes down and feeds the bacteria. That's a really bad effect they've seen with these so-called "prebiotic" or "probiotic" semi-digestible starches. They have found that poorly digested starches cause behavioral changes in animals, making them anxious and aggressive from the fermentation in their intestine. Some of the products of bacterial action can tremendously increase endotoxins and cause inflammation of the intestine, liver, and eventually the whole body.

However, when a typical well-cooked starch *is* digested, it releases pure glucose. In my first physiology lab, the professor had us feed a dose of corn starch to lab rats. Ten minutes later, there was no trace of starch paste left; it had instantly been turned into glucose and absorbed. When you look at the glycemic index, starch tends to be near the top, very similar to pure glucose. That means you get a quick, powerful stimulation of insulin. The insulin does its work quickly of disposing of the glucose by turning it into fat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So whether you eat a meal that has pure protein or a meal with starch, the end game is the same: it drives up insulin, increases fat production, and doesn't store sugar in your liver effectively. What types of sugars are slow-release and stored in the liver as glycogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sucrose, glucose, fructose, and lactose are very good, well-metabolized sugars.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do those sugars feed bacteria in the lower intestine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, they are so quickly absorbed that usually they will be absorbed partly in your stomach and partly in the first foot or so of the intestine. The presence of fructose partly blocks the release of insulin and changes the effect of insulin so that it helps direct some of the glucose into the liver while blocking its storage as fat. So, you get a lower secretion of insulin, a lower stress effect, and a better glycogen storage effect from either sucrose, the mixture of glucose and fructose, or milk sugar (lactose). In the case of milk, the proteins and fat add to the slowing of the sugar effect.

**Andrew Murray:** How many grams of sugar would you say is a good, healthy amount?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on your total caloric requirement. Some hypothyroid women can maintain their body weight on 700 or 800 calories a day. But if you have a healthy metabolism and can burn between 2,000 and 3,500 calories a day, then your carbohydrate requirement is going to be somewhere in the range of 180 grams to 350 grams.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to give our listeners an idea: one teaspoon of sugar contains 4 grams. In comparison, one cup of brown rice contains 41 grams of sugar, but the glycemic index of the rice is going to be a lot higher. You'll store the sugars from the rice as fat more than you would if you were eating the same amount of grams in white sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you get your sugars in the form of more natural foods rather than refined white sucrose, there are benefits. For example, orange juice is extremely rich in minerals compared to rice, pasta, or bread. Potassium, which is very abundant in all fruits, acts like insulin. So you don't have to secrete very much insulin for the same disposition of glucose. Orange juice also has helpful chemicals like naringin that help prevent inflammation.

In milk, besides the protein and fat slowing the absorption of lactose, the calcium powerfully stimulates energy metabolism, causing you to use your sugar more quickly and preventing it from being stored as fat. Milk drinkers generally tend to be much slimmer than non-milk drinkers largely because of this calcium effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So Dr. Peat, you've mentioned milk and orange juice. What about honey?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Honey is generally better than white sugar because it has some minerals, though not as much as fruits. It's probably the best refined sugar—bees refined it rather than a factory. Honey has been used as a food by all the high civilizations. I think there's good reason to think that sugar goes with high cultural development.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the deal with the link between diabetes and sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The principle in physiology that explains it was proposed a few decades ago called the Randle effect or the Randle cycle. It refers to the fact that free fatty acids block the use of glucose by cells. This was demonstrated in hospitals when giving nutritional support to patients in the form of a soy oil emulsion. About 15 minutes after injecting this emulsified soy oil, people would get hyperglycemic.

When the fatty acids involved in blocking the sugar are *polyunsaturated*, they produce long-range damage. A group led by Fu demonstrated that the glycated proteins seen in diabetic people—which are usually blamed on glucose—are actually caused more powerfully by polyunsaturated fatty acids. Spontaneously oxidized polyunsaturated fats stick to the proteins. So, the free fatty acids not only block sugar use instantaneously (Randle effect), but they produce these advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) associated with diabetes and aging. The chronic effect of a high-fat diet, if the fat is predominantly unsaturated, produces diabetes and all the things that result from glycated proteins.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So in diabetes, people have high levels of free fatty acids blocking the sugar from getting into the cell. Doesn't that feedback to the system to tell the body to raise the blood sugar higher?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's a self-stimulating cycle. When you block the cells from using glucose, they call for more, and the liver obliges by making extra glucose. Diabetics often have very high lactic acid concentrations, showing that the glucose *is* getting into the cell, but it can't be used oxidatively because the fatty acids are blocking the respiratory system. So then lactic acid goes to the liver, which turns it into more glucose.

**Caller:** If I eat a big bowl of cereal with a lot of sugar, then two hours later I get sleepy. What does that mean?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually it's the same effect that a person who has been hypothyroid experiences when they correct their thyroid. When your adrenaline is high, you're being stimulated; you are very alert and on edge. When you either correct your thyroid function or eat a lot of sugar, the sugar helps to lower adrenaline. Sugar and salt will both help to lower adrenaline, so they can both make you sleepy while they're present and circulating. People who have insomnia can often take care of the problem temporarily by taking some sugary and salty food at bedtime.

**Caller:** If a person is diabetic or pre-diabetic, is there a simple way to express what the good sugars and bad sugars are?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The definitions of diabetes and pre-diabetes have been created to sell insulin and drugs. They keep multiplying the definitions—Type 1, Type 2, Syndrome X, gestational diabetes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Basically, the good types of sugars that are going to be more slow-release are the fruit sugars and honey. If they're eaten in combination with fat and protein, they won't require the pancreas to pump out a ton of insulin. Fruits and cheese are very safe things for diabetics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, fruits and cheese are very safe. I wrote a newsletter about an English doctor 150 years ago who noticed exactly that same thing, but it didn't catch on with the medical business. Since the government has been making recommendations to eat starches and polyunsaturated fats, the incidence of so-called diabetes has increased tremendously. In the long range, it's very important to avoid polyunsaturated fats to avoid diabetes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Avoiding vegetable oils: soy, canola, corn, safflower, sunflower, hemp seed, and fish oil.

**Caller:** What about beans and whole grains, like whole grain brown rice or quinoa? Also, a lot of nutritional people claim there's a problem when you combine fruits with proteins and want you to separate them. But what you're saying seems to contradict that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's good to precede a big protein meal by maybe 15 or 20 minutes with fruits so that you get your liver stocked with some glycogen. That way, you don't respond so violently when you eat pure protein.

Regarding whole grains and legumes: they have more nutrients, but only a small amount of minerals compared to fruits. The germs do contain some valuable nutrients, but they also contain enough of the polyunsaturated fats that they go rancid. That was why refining was invented by the Chinese several thousand years ago; they found that the rancidity of the whole grains damaged the nutritional value.

**Caller:** So a good diet would be mostly fruit and protein, staying away from polyunsaturated oils and even the omega-3 oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The virtue of omega-3s is that they are a little less toxic in the sense of causing cancer than the omega-6s, but they tend to break down faster. Their main virtue therapeutically is as an anti-inflammatory agent, but the way they are anti-inflammatory is that their breakdown products interfere with the immune system. In the long run, they are suppressing your immune system, similar to cortisone.

**Caller:** I have a question regarding the role of sugar in yeast infections and systemic fungal infections. If a person has a systemic fungal infection, should they be avoiding sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Things like the yeasts that cause infections love sugar. If someone has a very intense infestation in their stomach, eating sugar can actually make them drunk from the fermentation. But getting drunk on sugar is about the worst effect of the sugar metabolism by the yeast.

When you *starve* yeast, they tend to become invasive. If you have yeast living in your intestine—and they are attracted to estrogen—and you starve them of sugar, they put out filaments long enough to penetrate through cells like fingers reaching through your intestine walls looking for sugar. That starvation condition is what can make them invade your tissues rather than just living free in your intestine. It's only when they invade your tissues that they become deadly.

Correcting the thyroid and hormones is the basic thing. Topically, dusting with sulfur powder is a safe way to kill them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you are saying that if someone has an overgrowth, eating more sugar would feed the yeast and make them happier so they're less invasive?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, actually.

**Andrew Murray:** What would you suggest as a treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The carrot salad. The carrot is indigestible and has antifungal, antibacterial chemicals in it. If you grate a carrot and put some olive oil or coconut oil and vinegar on it, it helps. Vinegar is a bacterial chemical; the acetic acid is the bacteria's way of killing fungus. The fatty acids of coconut oil and olive oil bind to the indigestible fiber of the carrot and are slowly released all the way down your intestine. They have a very profound, safe disinfecting action.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, thank you so much. For those who would like to find out more about Dr. Ray Peat, his website is www.raypeat.com. He has a very informative website with scholarly research articles on salt, polyunsaturated fats, hormones, and cancer. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Sugar II
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicine and dietary advice.

This month, we wanted to continue exploring the positive role that sugar has to play in the diet and why good sugars are essential for good health. It seems that many things we're told are bad for us are actually beneficial, and we need to see the facts and the research that's out there. With an ever-increasing worldwide prevalence of diagnosed diabetes, what is it about sugar that we can defend?

We're excited to have Dr. Ray Peat with us again this month, and we'll be hearing from him on scientific research-based facts. Dr. Peat, thank you for joining us again. Would you please introduce yourself and your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been writing a newsletter on health issues for about 30 years. I started that about eight years after finishing my PhD research at the University of Oregon. Part of the reason for starting my own newsletter was seeing that the science journals are very doctrinaire and influenced by industry. Since doing my study at the University of Oregon, I've been reading lots and experimenting some on my own.

**Andrew Murray:** I know that you've published many articles and your specialisms are hormones—pregnenolone, estrogen, protective hormones—things that we normally would confer some protection to people from aging and free radical damage. Your other specialties are thyroid and polyunsaturated fats.

The sugar issue—you joined us last month, and we got some of the way through expanding on why sugars are good for you. As you mentioned, the common indoctrination is that sugars are bad for you, just like salt and saturated fats are supposedly bad for you. For those listening who may be diagnosed as diabetic, hypothyroid, or hyperthyroid, sugar has had bad press in the last 20 years or so. They would have us eat less sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, that actually started about 200 years ago.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So what's the history behind why we started being told that sugar was bad for us 200 years ago?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At that time, they had defined diabetes as the "sugar disease" because they discovered glucose in urine. The mechanically thinking doctors said if you don't put glucose in, it can't come out. But in fact, the glucose was being produced by dissolving the protein in the person's body. It turned out that the worst thing you can do is to starve them for sugar because that accelerates the breakdown of both protein and fat.

Two doctors, at least in the 19th century, went against that conventional opinion and started giving their patients the amount of sugar extra in their diet that they were losing in the urine, figuring that they would die more slowly from diabetes. They found that they actually recovered very quickly. That curative effect of large amounts of sugar has been fairly recently demonstrated in animal experiments and in vitro experiments in which sugar stimulates the regeneration of pancreatic insulin-producing cells.

**Andrew Murray:** So a basic question then: Do humans need sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Monkeys, for example, who normally live on fruit, develop very high cortisol levels when fruit is scarce. That is something that happens in any animal that habitually has a mixed diet containing carbohydrate. Some animals, like reptiles, can get along nicely on a protein diet. We can turn protein into sugar and fat, but it happens that one of the effects of the sugar is to inhibit the cortisol which turns protein into sugar. So, sugar spares protein; we don't have to eat so much of it.

Cortisol has many side effects other than breaking down the tissue proteins. At the same time that it helps to digest protein foods, it changes the whole arrangement of the way metabolism works. So it's better if we can minimize cortisol. Sugars also inhibit the chronic release of free fatty acids from storage. Our body—our brain in particular, and some tissues such as the red blood cells—strongly prefer sugars over fats and function better. When we get enough sugar, we inhibit the release of fats from storage and allow these tissues to have all the sugar they need.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's basically a backup mechanism. When you don't eat sugar, your body will get the sugar from your protein, your muscles, your bones, and your brain. The cortisol dissolves various organs that will then release different free fatty acids or proteins that the body will convert into sugar. That's a less preferable backup mechanism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The famous arctic explorer, Vilhjalmur Stefansson, reported that people he knew eating a mostly fat and meat diet seemed to be many years older by appearance than they really were.

When people try to lose weight by fasting, what happens is for a day or so, their cortisol is still high and their metabolic rate is fairly high. So, they are living on a meat diet as they dissolve their muscles and fat. The thymus gland is one of the first to be dissolved. Since we would eat ourselves up in just two or three weeks if we kept eating at the same rate, our metabolic rate slows down drastically under the influence of these free amino acids liberated from our tissues. Those turn the thyroid hormone off. The falling blood sugar and the rising free amino acids and free fatty acids all turn our metabolic rate down. Then we can get along on a very low-calorie intake, but it slows down reproductive function, brain function, everything.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So basically, fasting is the worst thing you can do if you're trying to lose weight.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, or pretty much anything. Fasting turns off the liver's ability to detoxify things, so you're exposing yourself to increased toxins rather than decreased. The only thing that benefits is the intestine from not putting bad stuff into it.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of sugar as a quantity to consume, I've heard you say 170 to 250 grams of sugar per day. Is that correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think for a person of normal activity and eating mixed foods.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Let's discuss some of these sugars. Which ones are good sugars and which ones are bad sugars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lactose has a lot of special properties, so it's a very good sugar. It's somewhat slowly absorbed, but it stimulates digestion. It helps with calcium metabolism and absorbing the other nutrients in milk.

Sucrose consists of one unit of glucose and one of fructose. That is fairly quickly broken into the components when we eat it. The glucose stimulates insulin. Fructose, besides not itself stimulating insulin, actually slightly inhibits the release of insulin. So if you ate pure glucose, you would get a stronger insulin reaction. In most situations, if you eat slightly faster than you're metabolizing, a surge of excess glucose is going to turn on your fat metabolism. When you take sucrose with the fructose component, it will moderate the secretion of insulin and the production of fat depots.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because if a sugar stimulates insulin production, your liver is not happy and you store that sugar as fat. So we want to be eating the types of sugars that don't strongly stimulate insulin so we can use the sugar in our liver and stimulate metabolism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Surprisingly, fructose—besides moderating the production of fat—does many other things. It raises your temperature by a variety of mechanisms, which all by itself will increase your metabolic rate. It increases your conversion of carbohydrate to energy by about 20%. It'll do that even in a fairly small amount.

With sucrose, you have a 50/50 ratio, and it activates several components of the thyroid system better than glucose. Glucose is essential for keeping the thyroid functioning optimally, but fructose does some extra things that cause it to raise your temperature and metabolic rate more than glucose alone would.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The foods that these sugars are found in are primarily fruits?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mostly fruits.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And honey and white sugar also have a little bit of fructose in them as well. So when you're looking at the glycemic index, how would you describe why diabetics should eat fruits and honey and stay away from starchy carbohydrates?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 30 or 40 years ago, there was quite a bit of publishing activity relating to the anti-diabetes effects of fructose because of that stimulating effect on the metabolism. But currently, in the last three or four years, besides forgetting all of that, they're inventing a lot of new stuff to direct people away from the anti-diabetic effect of fructose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Supposedly, some of the motivation for this is the popularity of what they call high fructose corn syrup. Those are more fattening than sugar, but it isn't because they are actually high in fructose. They have slightly more fructose than glucose.

However, a group in Los Angeles a few weeks ago measured the amounts in some soft drinks. They found that they accurately reported the content of fructose and glucose, but when they hydrolyzed the material, they found that there was much more carbohydrate in the drink than just the fructose and glucose. There was about four to five times as much caloric value in some kind of carbohydrate present in the drink that was not glucose or fructose. So if you have four or five times more food in your soda pop than you were thinking, you're going to be more likely to get fat—not because fructose is fattening, but just because you're getting a huge amount of pretty much the equivalent of eating flour.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So a huge amount of starch that strongly stimulates insulin, and insulin stores that starchy sugar as fat. Whereas if it was actually sucrose from white sugar, then it would be much easier for your body to store as glycogen in the liver. I know corn syrup is a hot topic, but there have also been reports that high fructose corn syrup is quite high in heavy metals.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, a few years ago, some samples were analyzed and the government decided to drop it as soon as they saw that they were full of mercury. Then the industry supposedly corrected itself, but the government isn't keeping up on it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I've noticed that a couple of different soda pops now are being advertised that have sugar rather than the corn syrup.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I heard that the Coke company was suing the Mexican branch to make them stop using sugar because so many Americans were importing it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I spoke to a chemist that tests products in Mexico, and she said that the Mexican Coca-Cola in Mexico will have sugar sometimes and corn syrup other times. So if you're drinking Coca-Cola in Mexico, you're not guaranteed that it is made with sugar.

**Andrew Murray:** I just wanted to cover the amounts. It's probably eight ounces of sugar a day?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Well, yeah, 250 grams is five to six ounces.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people can eat a lot more, but your appetite is a fairly good guide. Once your liver has enough glycogen, it tends to turn off your appetite for everything, not just for sugar.

**Andrew Murray:** I know last month you outlined that it takes about eight hours for the glycogen stores in the liver to be depleted.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Looking at weights and measures: one glass of orange juice contains 25 grams of sugar. One glass of milk contains 12 grams of sugar. One teaspoon of sugar only contains four grams. One tablespoon of honey contains about 17 grams. So it's easier to get a lot more sugar in fruit than it is actually in white sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And when you're eating fruit, the potassium and other minerals in the fruit really bypass the whole issue of glycemic effect. The potassium itself has an insulin-like action that helps you turn sugar into glycogen. If you ate too much, it would also produce fat, except that the presence of the potassium with your sugar means that it's going to keep your blood sugar pretty level compared to eating starches.

**Andrew Murray:** The general argument is that people defend avoiding sugar by saying sugar will make you fat. But probably what's important to bring across is that sugar will increase your metabolic rate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, a 20% increase in your metabolic rate makes a tremendous difference in how much you can eat without getting fat.

**Andrew Murray:** It's important to get the right kind of sugars—fructose, sucrose, and glucose—so that your liver has an adequate store of glycogen, rather than the sugars found in starchy carbohydrates like pastas and pastries which stimulate cortisol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things that fructose does is protect against the fat deposition effect of insulin. It not only restricts the secretion of insulin itself, but it makes insulin less harmful by blocking its tendency to produce obesity.

A publication that has been cited frequently to say that fructose is dangerous because it has an anti-insulin effect was the conclusion of a group of researchers who gave a 55-week diet to rats. They said at the end of five weeks, those who ate a gigantic amount of fructose were insulin resistant. The implication was, "See, in just five weeks we have made these animals diabetic." But the thing that doesn't get often cited is that those animals gained tremendously different amounts of weight. If you had continued that same diet for the rest of the year, the ones eating the starch would have weighed twice as much as the ones eating the sucrose diet.

**Andrew Murray:** Why do diabetic women have smarter, larger babies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I mentioned Zamenhof's experiments in developing chicks in the egg. He noticed that their brains stopped growing two or three days before they were ready to hatch. He saw that the glucose in the egg was depleted before the chick had finished maturing, and the brain stopped just at the time the glucose was depleted.

He knew from studies on mammals that if you give a pregnant animal either estrogen or insulin, which will lower the supply of glucose, their brain stops growing. So he made a little chip in the eggshell and injected some glucose right at the stage where the brain had stopped growing. He found that caused the brain to keep growing, and the chicken hatched with a brain bigger than chickens had ever normally had.

**Andrew Murray:** Smart chickens.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In humans, they see that at about six months gestation, the brain has many more cells than it will have at birth. So from six to nine months, cells are dying rather than being created. Diabetic women are able to deliver more glucose during that time and prevent the death of this huge number of brain cells.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How do you feel when they give women who have supposedly gestational diabetes instructions to restrict their sugars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I met a woman whose doctor had told her to restrict her sugar when she was pregnant again. I asked about the development of her older boy, and she said he had taught himself to read when he was two years old. I had heard many stories like that from old obstetricians who associated that with so-called diabetes.

That caused me to look up where the idea of gestational diabetes came from. In the 60s, they were promoting the glucose tolerance test to diagnose diabetes very early. It was out of those situations, expanding the definition of diabetes, that they started noticing that most healthy pregnant women tend to have about 130 blood glucose—quite a bit above the non-pregnant normal. That simply was redefined as something off the scale of normal, and so they started thinking of pregnancy in terms of diabetes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But that's just the body's natural response when you're pregnant—to raise the sugar so the baby has more sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. One of the things Zamenhof did, besides adding glucose to the eggs, was adding progesterone. He found that also keeps the brain growing. It helps to stabilize and make more efficient use of glucose. Glucose and progesterone work together. Women with low progesterone tend to have unstable low blood sugar and many more problems through the pregnancy.

**Caller 1 (Gardener):** I have a lady friend who is overweight. I suspect she needs to kick up her thyroid to burn that fat. You're saying certain sugars would do that. She eats a lot of fruits and vegetables and stays away from too much carbohydrates. What's the relationship between the sugars and the thyroid being stimulated to kick up the metabolism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your diet isn't providing either glucose or the mixture of glucose and fructose, your liver can't activate the thyroid hormone as fully. If you're living on a high protein and fat diet, your liver will slow your whole body metabolism down. That's just as effective as if your thyroid gland had shut down.

**Andrew Murray:** You're saying this because the liver converts T4, which is the inactive hormone, into T3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The liver makes about 60% or 70% of the active hormone. Once your liver slows down, if you try to boost it just with the thyroxine (T4), that will tend to turn your own thyroid hormone production down. So if you're going to supplement, it has to be a balanced T3 and T4.

But often, just by avoiding the things that inhibit the conversion of thyroxine to the active form—avoiding too much muscle meat, avoiding the polyunsaturated fats, and getting enough of the pro-thyroid nutrients—you can help. Sucrose and lactose are both effective at maintaining your production of thyroid active hormones.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** To summarize, that would be limiting muscle meat—steaks, burger, fish, and chicken—to a small portion. What would you recommend for an overweight person?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person really wants to concentrate on losing weight, use milk and gelatin as the main protein. Milk and gelatin are the most favorable for weight loss, partly because the milk comes with such a generous supply of calcium. Calcium powerfully stimulates the metabolic rate. Having enough salt in your food is another thing; salt and calcium interact to stimulate your metabolic rate.

The fructose in particular activates the whole range of cells, but specifically activates the production of the active thyroid hormone. Even if you're deficient in thyroid hormone, you can keep the activity going to a great extent with sucrose, salt, and calcium.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that's white sugar, salt, calcium, and avoiding the polyunsaturates. Those are powerfully thyroid-toxic oils found practically everywhere: corn oil, soy oil, canola, safflower, sunflower, hemp, flaxseed, fish oil, cottonseed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.
