There was a whole series of studies that showed that polyunsaturated fats inhibit secretion from the gland by blocking the digestive proteolytic enzymes, and they block the transport in the bloodstream and at several different places in the cells. One of the enzymes that reacts to the thyroid hormone happens to be a key enzyme in the response to fructose. It's activated both by thyroid and fructose. The key respiratory enzyme, cytochrome oxidase, is activated both by thyroid and fructose. The polyunsaturated fats block these intracellular places as well as the transportation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So for the caller's friend: avoid polyunsaturated fats, replace those with coconut oil, butter, and a little bit of olive oil. Coconut oil specifically helps with weight loss. Along with lots of fruit, milk, and some cheese for protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Also, keep the intestine happy. Not eating too many raw, indigestible foods. If you have the wrong bacteria, even supposedly good fiber like grain fiber or bran can support the production of toxic chemicals in your intestine.

**Caller 2:** I have a friend who swears by a diabetes cure of sorts. It's 400 international units of vitamin E and 1200 milligrams of lecithin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lecithin generally is made from soybeans. It could be extracted from eggs, and that would affect the composition if the eggs ate good food. But generally, lecithin is essentially the same as the polyunsaturated fats in corn oil or safflower oil. So a gram or so isn't going to make a big difference, but it does have a slightly toxic effect. I don't think it's safe. It's not very dangerous, but it's not the safest way to approach diabetes.

**Caller 3:** Along with your polyunsaturate list, you mentioned butter. Could ghee be included as well?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Actually, ghee and butter are saturated fats, so they are not thyroid toxic and they are very liver supportive. They would not be amongst that list of corn, canola, soy, etc.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In fact, these saturated fats are being researched as cures for liver disease because they're so protective to cells that are under attack from the polyunsaturated fats. Alcoholic liver disease is being treated with the highly saturated fats such as butter and waxes from palm trees.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't you tell me about a study being done regarding alcoholic hepatitis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think Northwestern University is doing it with butter. A man named Nanji is doing the most research. But there have been studies in the US earlier showing that fructose protects various organs against alcohol in pretty much the same way that it protects against diabetes. They've found that you can stimulate the removal of a toxic amount of ethyl alcohol from the body by giving a person some fructose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if someone's going to drink, they want to have a vodka and orange juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The fructose actually detoxifies the alcohol better than ordinary glucose.

**Caller 4 (Mike):** I've heard that fertilized eggs are supposed to be better for you than non-fertilized eggs. I'd like to get your opinion.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think there actually could be a difference. When chickens are kept in tiny boxes where the eggs won't get fertilized, they're under extreme stress, and the stress is undoubtedly reflected in the egg. If they have the freedom of movement that would be necessary for fertilization, I think the eggs are going to be healthier.

**Caller 5:** My daughter, who is about 38, was told by her doctor that he's not happy with her cholesterol level. He says if it isn't lower in six months, he's going to put her on Lipitor. I have trepidations about Lipitor. What do you think about the cholesterol issue in itself and how much it really relates to heart disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been several studies showing that lowering cholesterol by any drug means has pretty serious side effects. That's because cholesterol is, next to glucose, probably our single most important protective all-purpose molecule. The reason it rises during stress in a fairly healthy person is that it's our defensive molecule and it's the precursor to the anti-stress hormones. It's used massively in making steroids such as pregnenolone, DHEA, and progesterone.

If you artificially lower the supply of cholesterol in the blood, you're going to proportionally push down the amount of progesterone you can make. That seems to be why it causes so many disastrous effects, increasing the general mortality in people who are using drugs to push down the cholesterol.

**Caller 5:** Can you tell me what some of these bad effects are of Lipitor?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things that has turned up a lot in recent years is the breakdown of skeletal muscle—first pains, and then sometimes seepage of enzymes and myoglobin into the blood, damaging the kidneys.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Lipitor is a statin drug. Aren't statins really hard on your liver?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and it's through that effect that they affect the muscles. The muscles are destabilized if they aren't getting enough cholesterol. All of your organs, including the brain, suffer when your liver isn't supplying enough cholesterol.

**Caller 5:** Why are they so upset about cholesterol being a little on the high side?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A study of older people in nursing homes looked at their cholesterol as they aged. The longest-lived people were up around 280 milligrams of cholesterol. A Framingham study about 20 years ago saw that after the age of 50, people who have below 200 cholesterol are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease. It's a very protective substance.

Since the 1930s, it's been known that hypothyroid people are susceptible to many diseases, including heart disease, and that hypothyroidism is the basic cause of increased cholesterol. Cholesterol has to be converted to progesterone under the influence of thyroid hormone. So if you're low in thyroid hormone, your body increases cholesterol to keep the progesterone production going.

**Caller 5:** My daughter actually takes thyroid medication.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The metabolic rate is a mirror image of the blood cholesterol level. As you increase your metabolic rate, your cholesterol will come down. But doctors have disregarded the effect on the metabolic rate and they prescribe only the inactive part of the thyroid hormone. Very often people stay hypometabolic despite taking thyroid.

**Caller 5:** One more quick question. Are you saying that sugars—fruit sugars and even white sugar—are okay, but the bad thing is white flour, white rice, pasta, and simple carbohydrates?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. The starches and the polyunsaturated fats are the main culprits in fatness.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Another thing about cholesterol: think of it as a bandage. Dr. Peat, you told me about a Japanese study showing that arteries are blocked up by polyunsaturated fats, and the body bandages it over with a cholesterol plaque.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The unsaturated fats are very reactive with oxygen, and the bloodstream is where there's the most oxygen. The saturated fats that we make in the liver—if we eat too much sugar and are low thyroid—might cause high triglycerides, but these are saturated and they happen to be protective to the heart. The thing is to avoid the things that cause the distorted blood lipids, not to try to lower the lipids themselves, but to remove the cause.

**Andrew Murray:** The engineer has a question. She wants to know what you think of Splenda and artificial sweeteners.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Splenda is the one that has chlorine in the molecule. Exposed to bacteria, the bacteria can break down the molecule and liberate things in the family of organic chlorine compounds, like chloroform-related toxic substances. So I wouldn't want my intestine exposed to Splenda.

**Andrew Murray:** How about Stevia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's pretty safe.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So basically, you'd recommend our listeners avoid all those artificial sweeteners?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Sugar is so much more nourishing and protective.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Peat. For those listening who want to read more about your research, Dr. Ray Peat is an endocrinologist and research scientist. His website is www.raypeat.com. There are lots of articles on his homepage, all referencing scientific articles.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you for listening.

**Andrew Murray:** We'll see you next month.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Endotoxins
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month’s *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

The last two months we've been talking about the role of good sugars and bad sugars. This month we're very pleased to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, who is going to expose the risk of endotoxin and dietary effects that influence endotoxin production. There's a lot of research now to show that endotoxin is associated with many inflammatory diseases that you wouldn't normally associate with food. So the adage "you are what you eat" is very true, and perhaps we should say that you suffer as a result of what you eat. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for joining. Would you please give an outline of your expertise?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm studying hormones and nutrition mostly. I got my PhD in physiology with a biochemical orientation, concentrating on reproductive aging. That was when I got interested in the interactions of estrogen, oxygen, unsaturated fatty acids, and the toxic interactions of some of our natural materials with environmental materials and processes.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you describe endotoxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Its chemical name is lipopolysaccharide. There are several kinds of bacteria that make similar things, but it's a combination of a starch-like molecule with some fatty acids attached to it. It's so widely distributed that all animals have a system for reacting to it and defending themselves against it. It seems to be partly a bacterial defense against the bacteria's environment. There is an evolved back-and-forth relationship between animals and the bacteria, and it's a matter of things getting out of balance that causes the endotoxin to be a problem.

**Andrew Murray:** I hear of many foods that promote this production. Would you be able to list some specific foods that people should be thinking about before they consume them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mostly it seems to be things that are poorly digested that pass along with a lot of food value down into the intestine where bacteria thrive on them. Things like fruit are so quickly digested by most people—the liquid parts, minerals, and sugars can be largely absorbed before you get down to the bacterial area of the intestine.

The more indigestible the food is, the more risky it is for supporting an overgrowth of bacteria. If your digestion happens to be poor, then more foods will pass along and become bacteria food. Indigestible fibrous materials and types of starch that can't be broken down by animal or human enzymes become good food for bacteria. Many of these are being promoted for intestinal health to stimulate peristalsis, but about 30 years ago, some Australian studies saw that people who ate a lot of oat bran were actually increasing the risk for bowel cancer. Certain types of fiber cause such intense growth of bacteria that the bacteria produce many types of toxins, not just the fragment of the bacterial coat known as endotoxin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when people say, "I can't have a normal bowel movement if I don't eat lots of fiber," what do you say?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, there are some very safe fibers that come from plants that have their own defenses against bacteria and fungi. Raw carrots, for example. If you notice, many vegetables will spoil in the refrigerator, while carrots seem to be completely clean and unattacked by bacteria or molds. That's because there are chemicals that are defensive for those plants. When we eat them, they remain like antibiotics all the way through our intestines, so they are very hard for bacteria to grow on.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And in that way, they also provide a good roughage that doesn't get broken down by bacteria.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and it can also bind some of the toxins produced by bacteria. Rather than increasing the amount produced, it can actually bind it and carry it out, subtracting toxins. It's almost like the activated charcoal that's used for detoxifying ingested chemicals. The carrot is a natural way of doing that.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** When people say, "If I eat a good green salad, then I have a wonderful bowel movement," is that because the bacteria are stimulating peristalsis? Because we don't have cellulose-digesting enzymes, so we are relying on the bacteria to ferment and digest the cellulose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some people get terribly constipated when they eat raw vegetables. For other people, it's enough irritation to stimulate the intestine. Doctors for a long time have warned against using stimulant laxatives, but when they recommend eating vegetables, it's really primarily a stimulant action produced by irritating substances either in the vegetable itself or produced by the bacterial growth. If you've ever left a head of lettuce in a closed container at room temperature, you know how quickly lettuce can decompose compared to a carrot. Lettuce is very good bacterial food, so it can become very toxic if you happen to catch the wrong bacteria.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The last couple of months, we've spent time talking about the different types of sugars. You've been describing the health benefits of an easily digested sugar—one that gets digested in the stomach and very high up in the intestinal tract, thereby not providing food for bacteria further down. These are mainly soft, ripe, juicy fruits, honey, and even white sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And the lactose in milk is another good sugar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Those are all things that our human digestive tracts can absorb quickly and efficiently without having to rely on bacterial degradation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They also have a defensive effect against the products of the bacteria, so that once you are poisoned by the endotoxin, the sugars protect by decreasing the inflammation reaction to them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if you ate starches for dinner, then having some good sugars before bed will help protect against some of the endotoxin produced by the bacteria digesting the starches. The "bad sugars" come from foods more resistant to digestion: breads, pastas, cakes, cookies, flours, grains, beans, and rice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another kind of defensive food is saturated fat. If you think of soap and its antibacterial effect, saturated fats are mildly antiseptic. If you eat butter with your potato, the starch is less likely to become toxic material for the bacteria because the butter's saturated fats will suppress bacterial growth.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So mashed potatoes with lots of milk and butter can protect against eating these starches. Also, if you cook your starches really well—like you say, Dr. Peat, if you boil potatoes for 45 minutes to an hour—they'll be digested more easily in your stomach.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you don't actually sign up for the belief of the commensal organisms in the gut, is that right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, experiments with germ-free animals find they're actually healthier than the normal germ-infected animals. However, if they grow up never exposed to bacteria, they seem very healthy but never develop their immune defenses. So when they are exposed, they are extremely susceptible to infection. If we're going to live in a world with germs, we might as well get used to them.

**Andrew Murray:** When I was looking at research on endotoxin, it was always associated with E. Coli, Salmonella, or Typhoid. But our own gut bacteria can be a reasonable threat to us in terms of toxin production, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. All bacteria produce something that can be sickness-inducing. Even *Lactobacillus*, which is probably favorable, has polysaccharide material in its covering that can produce inflammation and a whole range of pathological reactions. It's really a matter of balance.

**Andrew Murray:** What about the research on cancer and endotoxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that's a very plausible approach. If you look at practically any degenerative disease—arthritis, gout, dementia, epilepsy, hepatitis—almost anything is crucially made worse by endotoxin. Once you get stressed, all of these things are exacerbated by the endotoxin.

**Andrew Murray:** Describe what you mean by "stressed."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just a mental stress, for example, will shift the blood away from your digestive system to your legs and arms—the fight or flight reaction. If that persists or is very intense, the intestine loses its barrier function and bacteria can go right through the membrane lining the intestine into the bloodstream. Even a much lower degree of stress will begin letting the endotoxin flow in at an increased rate. So just thinking stressful thoughts will tend to increase your endotoxin absorption.

**Andrew Murray:** What you can do to help yourself can be a really simple way of improving your health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Women who were going to a fertility clinic were put on a moderate dose of penicillin or other antibiotics by a doctor who theorized their ovaries were infected. Many noticed their mood and headaches were relieved. They also became pregnant. The doctors saw that before they took the antibiotic, they had a stress level of cortisol and a very high ratio of estrogen to progesterone. Taking the antibiotic decreased the cortisol and estrogen, and increased the progesterone.

I've done the same measurements in women who had PMS and infertility. Just two or three days of eating a raw carrot salad every day caused exactly that shift of hormones: increased progesterone, decreased estrogen and cortisol. Other research shows that endotoxin alone will account for those changes. If you inject an animal with endotoxin, its estrogen will go up maybe five times higher than normal, and the progesterone and testosterone fall sharply.

**Andrew Murray:** How about endotoxins and PUFA (polyunsaturated fatty acids)? Is there a link?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they favor the growth of many microorganisms, but they also interact at every stage. For example, the permeability of the intestine is increased by polyunsaturated fat. One of the first reactions when a cell senses endotoxin is to produce nitric oxide. Nitric oxide increases the leakiness of the intestine. If your tissues happen to be well supplied with polyunsaturated fats, the nitric oxide increases the release of free fatty acids in circulation. So, for the person who has eaten a lot of polyunsaturated fat, once a stress triggers the absorption of endotoxin, the reaction can be much more intense.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to describe for our listeners: Estrogen is a very inflammatory hormone involved in a lot of cancers. Progesterone is an anti-aging, fertility hormone. The bacteria tend to increase estrogen in relation to progesterone.

Regarding fats: Polyunsaturated fats come mainly from nuts and seeds—almond oil, sunflower, safflower, corn, soy, cottonseed. Olive oil is only about 10% polyunsaturated. The saturated fats are the ones that are antibacterial. Those include butter, coconut oil, palm oil, and animal fats from animals that haven't been eating corn and soy.

**Andrew Murray:** How about the association of cancer with endotoxin production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every level you look at is a promoting effect. There are a few positive effects of endotoxin—our long exposure builds up basic immunity, like HDL cholesterol, which is a defense against endotoxins. But reactions beyond that simple level are all pro-inflammatory and tend to stimulate fibrosis as a sign of deteriorating tissue function. Fibrosis and atrophy make the tumor harder to get at and more autonomous.

The medical establishment has convinced the public that estrogen has some anabolic protective effects, especially for preventing osteoporosis. But the overall effect of the inflammation produced by endotoxin creates a systemic age-like atrophy of all tissues. Osteoporosis is extremely sensitive to endotoxin; it activates factors that stop bone replacement and accelerate decomposition. Those atrophic processes weaken the immune system's ability to remove a cancer once it starts.

**Andrew Murray:** Sarah, do you want to cover offending substances besides starches?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We mentioned breads, grains, beans, and flours. What other foods encourage bacterial growth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The so-called fibrous materials, many of which are promoted as health foods. Lignins—woody materials in many vegetables and grains.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Like in flaxseeds.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Generally, those tend to have an estrogen-promoting effect and support the growth of bacteria.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Flaxseeds also have PUFA, so those won't be inhibiting bacterial growth like a saturated fat would.

**Andrew Murray:** I was reminded that the Dow Chemical Company was trying to incorporate lignins into bread, and they were doing research at a USDA lab to see if lignins could be a viable starch source.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they've used sawdust for many years. Cellulose is probably the safest fiber if it's a clean kind.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My friend at the USDA labs said, "If people are going to eat bread, why can't they just eat whole grain bread? Why do they have to add sawdust into it?"

**Andrew Murray:** The industry is keen to make sure there are no unsold byproducts. If something isn't naturally occurring, don't be surprised if what you're consuming is a byproduct of another industry—like the paint industry with flaxseed oil becoming a food source.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller question about pediatric Crohn's disease and a diet that would be good for that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's good to try raw carrot. It's important how you use the carrot. Just eating a raw carrot is fine, but if you're going to make a salad, it should be grated longitudinally so that you have longer pieces of fibrous material. You don't want to put it in a blender, and definitely don't want to use a juicer. The juice isn't protective, and it removes most of the fiber.

**Andrew Murray:** So that would be a starting point.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And usually having plenty of milk and cheese in the diet is protective. The bacteria that grow on milk are generally the safer type. Also, quite a few people respond well to a thyroid supplement because there's usually that typical stress pattern of high cortisol, high estrogen, and low progesterone. Thyroid helps restore the protective hormones.

**Andrew Murray:** Thyroid function can be measured by temperature and pulse before and after meals. There is a very definite pattern to how they should rise.

**Caller:** I have a question regarding carrots not being juiced. Many cancer diets call for a lot of vegetable juices, and carrot juice is a big one. Also, have you heard of the Budwig diet? Dr. Budwig introduced combining flaxseed oil with cottage cheese to help cells form a stronger electrical charge. Does combining flaxseed oil with cottage cheese change the bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the oldest treatments for cancer was enemas. A few hundred years ago, laxatives became a standard feature of cancer treatment. About 60 or 70 years ago, Max Gerson cured his own migraines with a change of diet. He was a famous advocate of a mostly vegetable diet, but he did use liver juice and thyroid. It was a nutritionally rational program, but he twice in his book said "absolutely no oils." His followers have changed the book, likely influenced by Johanna Budwig.

In 1954, before Budwig started writing about cancer, a Mexican professor advocated a cup of linseed (flax) oil per day as a purge to clean the intestine. When you drink that much highly unsaturated oil, the fatty acids are converted to prostaglandins and cause intense contraction of the intestine. It’s a very quick, thorough laxative. Budwig changed that to think of linseed oil as a nutritional factor. To the extent that it works as a laxative, it's likely helpful. The rest of her program was curds—cottage cheese—which is a soothing, safe diet that promotes less endotoxin than other proteins.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you explain why carrot juice in particular would be lowering your good hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The carrot is so rich in carotene. When you eat it whole and raw, the fiber keeps you from absorbing almost all of the carotene. When you juice, you get sugar and minerals, but you also get a tremendous amount of carotene. Carotene works like unsaturated fats in blocking thyroid function and progesterone function.

In the early years of treating thyroid patients, doctors noticed infertile women often had a red spot in the ovary in place of the yellow corpus luteum. It was red because a tremendous amount of carotene had accumulated in it. That indicates the thyroid is unable to convert cholesterol into progesterone, and that Vitamin A, which should be used in the conversion, is blocked by the carotene.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if you eat a lot of cooked pumpkin and carrots, you could be blocking your Vitamin A receptors.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person has very vigorous thyroid function and plenty of Vitamin B12, they can take care of a lot of carotene. But if you notice the calluses on your hands and feet starting to get an orange tint, that means you've got too much.

**Caller:** I'm 50 and going through menopause. I'm having horrific night sweats. Somebody recommended borage oil. Also, I'm a vegetarian.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Highly unsaturated oils like borage have some short-range beneficial effects by blocking some immune inflammatory reactions, but that ends up being an immunosuppressive process. In the long run, it will actually increase inflammatory and stress processes.

The quickest way to alleviate night sweats and hot flashes is to increase your sugar and protein intake. Sugar lowers cortisol and adrenaline. Your protein intake should be around 80 grams of good protein. Among vegetables, potato protein is the only one that ranks up with animal proteins—it's even better than egg protein. Milk, cheese, eggs, and potatoes are high-quality proteins.

If you don't get enough sugar or starch, you use protein for energy, starving the liver. When the liver isn't functioning well, it can't store enough sugar to get you through the night. First, adrenaline surges to get sugar from the liver. When the liver is depleted, cortisol rises to turn muscle and tissue into sugar. It's the cortisol surges that cause the hot flashes. Sugary and salty foods are a quick relief.

**Caller:** So borage oil isn't good for me?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. It inhibits your ability to digest protein and inhibits thyroid function.

**Caller:** Is agave a good sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, unless it's been overheated.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I think most agave nectars are boiled down, so they are caramelizing the sugar. When you boil sugars down and don't filter out the caramelized portion, those are allergenic and carcinogenic.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I want to mention some herbs. Cascara is an herb that decreases transit time and is a laxative. If aged properly (sun-dried and aged for one year), the anthraquinones are safe and effective. Dr. Peat, tell us about the structure of tetracycline and Cascara.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a series that starts with Vitamin K. It's a quinone structure that has been studied since about 1910 as anti-cancer, antiviral, and energy-promoting. Vitamin K is now used to strengthen bones and prevent calcification of arteries. The emodin in Cascara is a three-ring substance, and tetracycline is a four-ring substance. They are all quinones intensified by adding the extra ring.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Nature has a very similar compound in Cascara as well as in Tabebuia, otherwise known as Pau d'Arco. It's antibacterial, anti-tumor, antifungal, antiviral, and anti-parasitic. Dr. Peat, you mentioned a doctor who used a decoction of that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** W.F. Koch was a Michigan chemistry professor. He proposed that we have free radicals in the form of quinones in our mitochondria handling energy. He created substances to treat cancer and viral infections. The famous Albert Szent-Györgyi based practically his whole career on working out the meaning of Koch's work with quinones. Ubiquinone (CoQ10) was later discovered in the mitochondria, proving Koch right.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Coming up to this time of year with the flu, stock up on your raw carrot salad, Cascara bark powder, and Tabebuia. Other good herbs are Echinacea, Goldenseal, Barberry, and Oregon Grapefruit.

**Andrew Murray:** For people who'd like to hear more from Dr. Ray Peat, please go to his website, www.raypeat.com. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Radiation
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray, and Sarah will join us in the studio shortly. For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicine and dietary advice.

We are very pleased to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, who has recently published an article about the prevalent effects of radiation in the environment, how subjected we are to it on a daily basis, and how it is something to be aware of rather than accepting it as a normal fact of life. Dr. Peat, thank you for joining us. Would you explain your academic background in biology to the listeners?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started graduate school as a specialist in nerve biology, but I felt that they weren't very scientific; they were dogmatic. I wandered around the various labs until I ran across the reproductive physiology people. They actually seemed to be getting information and thinking about how the organism works, whereas the nerve biology people were really just trying to develop a dogma. So, I did my dissertation on the aging of the reproductive system in mammals.

**Andrew Murray:** With particular relevance to your recent publication, I know there is controversy surrounding the full-body scanners that began rolling out around 2007. What is your opinion of these devices in terms of their potential for causing negative effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the situation is similar to the 1950s. The government was assuring the public that fallout from atomic bomb testing was completely harmless because of their way of explaining the biological effects. They are still promoting those theories. Even though this kind of X-ray examining is much less dangerous than the radioactive isotopes falling out of bomb tests, the science by which they assure us of its safety is exactly as faulty as it was in the 1950s.

John Gofman, who was a government defender of the safety of radioactive isotopes during the 50s, suddenly realized that if the effects are going to be disastrous in the future, it's better to learn about the dangers now rather than wait until we're all dead.

The trick they've been using for almost 100 years is based on early 20th-century findings. People knew you could cause mutations with radiation or toxic chemicals. By the 1920s, people saw genetic changes as being entirely in the chromosomes. As chromosomes were seen to be in the DNA, the doctrine focused on the interaction of radiation with DNA.

However, in the 1960s, people demonstrated that if you do microsurgery on a protozoan and change the orientation of its cilia, its offspring will have backward cilia for generations.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's like a biological memory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and totally separate from the DNA. The frog biologist Gurdon showed that surgery on the surface of a frog egg could cause the whole line of frogs to die out generations later. Even though that egg would mature into an adult that could reproduce, eventually, the line would die out just from treating the surface of the egg. He showed that if you heat a spot on the surface, you will get mutations. It showed that some harmful influence other than direct interaction with DNA is able to eventually cause mutations and death.

**Andrew Murray:** Do we know what is actually transferred several generations down the line?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not really, just some good guesses. A researcher in Hungary named György Csaba has been working on what happens with these early life experiences that are passed on from cell to cell and even from an adult to its offspring.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the whole-body scanners in airports, they tell us they are safe. What are the potential risks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For 70 or 80 years, people have noticed that X-rays, even in moderate doses, seem to accelerate the aging process. The idea of imprinting is that you might get acceleration of the aging process from generation to generation if that is passed on the way other cytoplasmic injuries are.

Many people insisted that the aging process was the result of accumulating mutations. However, someone used a chemical mutagen to produce more mutations than X-ray treatment was producing, and the mice lived just as long as normal mice. But the X-rays, producing even fewer mutations, shortened their life. So it's a physiological effect. Mutations are much less deadly than whatever this other cytoplasmic or general physiological process is.

**Andrew Murray:** They tell us there is a difference between ionizing and non-ionizing radiation. What do you say to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All kinds of electromagnetic radiation interact with matter. Light bounces off something, is absorbed in our retina, and we see things. That light causes a certain amount of electronic excitation. If you use a blue light rather than a full spectrum centered on yellow, the excitation of the electrons is enough to damage mitochondrial energy production. They've seen this for 50 or 60 years growing plants under different colored lights. If you put a plant that thrives in sunlight in pure blue light, the mitochondria are damaged almost as if they were irradiated with X-rays. But when you add back the rest of the spectrum, there's something about the red light that neutralizes the toxic effect of the blue light.

If you put a piece of glass in the desert for many years, it turns purple. With a given energy of radiation, you can bleach that purple out. Electrons are excited by energetic radiation and get trapped. When you shine just the right energy, like red light, you can move an electron out of its trap and restore it to its normal position.

This works in biology too. People who have burned their retina with ultraviolet light can prevent the burning if they get red light soon enough. You can demonstrate this in seeds or hair. So, the excitation and moving of electrons isn't strictly an X-ray or gamma ray phenomenon. However, when you get up to ultraviolet and higher, the main effect is that the electrons get completely knocked out of the system. That constitutes ionization. You actually have some degree of ionization even from blue light.

**Andrew Murray:** And the non-ionizing type doesn't have the energy to displace electrons?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You get very similar chemical effects from ultraviolet and X-rays. The difference is that ultraviolet light is absorbed just a few millimeters into your skin, but you get the same kind of damage to the skin cells that you get to your heart and brain cells from X-rays. It's a very similar biological damage, except the very high-energy radiation goes right through you and affects all your cells.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned red light can calm down the excitation of electrons, which is behind free radicals, tissue destruction, and cancer. So red light is extremely healing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The most surprising experiment was a Russian study where they gave a lethal dose of gamma rays to frogs. The dose was so intense the frogs would only live a few days. But if they shined bright red light on them within the first hour after exposure, they didn't get sick at all.

**Andrew Murray:** Are we talking about infrared or just red light?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Red light. In an ordinary incandescent bulb, the red end is a lot more intense than the blue and green end because the temperature of the bulb isn't nearly as hot as sunlight.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If somebody has been exposed to an X-ray, what would you recommend they sit under?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you can do it very quickly, within the first hour, you can almost completely block the chain of events. However, people exposed to Chernobyl or the Nagasaki bombing still have toxic blood serum decades later. It acts like a systemic dose of estrogen to irradiate any part of the body. **Andrew Murray:** So it penetrates deeply enough to potentially quench excitatory damage within the bone marrow?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you were to advise someone to purchase a light bulb, what type would you recommend?

When you run them on a standard 120-volt circuit, they aren't as blue-biased as ordinary incandescent bulbs. They are much weaker in the blue and stronger in the red. They appear as a yellowish-white, warmer than standard bulbs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So a 130-volt clear front incandescent. What wattage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They come in 150 to 250 watts.

**Andrew Murray:** There is a link where the liver's ability to metabolize waste products can be severely influenced by both estrogen and radiation. What are the consequences of that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The most intense, visible first thing is that both estrogen and radiation interfere with mitochondrial energy production. That is associated with inflammation and adaptive lactic acid production. As carbon dioxide production goes down, lactic acid goes up, and lactic acid triggers inflammatory mediators.

In experiments, when you irradiate one cell, it emits inflammatory mediators that affect other cells in the same dish. It's a chemical that goes into the cell's environment and causes mutations, inflammation, and degeneration in other cells. That's what happens when your foot is irradiated; the fluids escaping those damaged cells circulate throughout your body.

**Andrew Murray:** I read about the "bystander effect," where fish exposed to radiation could affect other fish in the same water.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They've been able to block that by using antagonists to serotonin. Serotonin itself contributes to fibrosis and impaired energy production.

**Andrew Murray:** People in this country are encouraged to use serotonin supplements for mood and sleep. That seems erroneous.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The whole system relating to serotonin is problematic. It's made from tryptophan, and tryptophan has some of the bad effects of serotonin. Tryptophan also happens to be probably the most sensitive amino acid to absorbing radiation. When the lens of the eye is injured by ultraviolet light, it's largely the tryptophan absorbing that energy.

**Andrew Murray:** So consuming a lot of meat isn't a good idea because of the tryptophan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Adults have a very low requirement for tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How many ounces of meat product do you think is a safe limit per day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments with animals show they live 30% to 40% longer when they are almost completely lacking methionine. Similar effects are seen with tryptophan. These are the anti-metabolic amino acids. Some rat experiments suggest that maybe just an ounce or two of meat would be safe. Gelatin, which lacks those amino acids, is safe in very large amounts. Poor people who eat the tough bits of the animal—chicken feet and wings—get more gelatin than rich people who eat the tender steaks.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because you're absorbing light all the way through your body from sunlight. It increases your energy in your liver and brain. Everything is being refreshed. The general saturation with the red light in sunlight protects you to a great extent against the systemic "bystander" stuff seeping out of damaged skin.

**Engineer:** Is near-infrared beneficial too, like sitting by a wood stove?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It mostly just warms you. Keeping your core body temperature close to 99 degrees activates your respiration and protective processes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The red fraction is used for making energy, but if you grow most plants under pure red light, they grow extremely fast but are very weak and tend to fall over. They need some irritation to build the cellulose skeleton for strength. The typical grow light has red, blue, and a little ultraviolet to irritate the cells enough to produce cellulose. The irritating frequencies tend to make crops rich in defensive chemicals, which makes them bitter, but those defensive substances are often antioxidants for humans.

**Caller:** I just had a bunch of dental X-rays, and two days later my back got really insecure. I was interested to hear that you can be irradiated in one place and it causes inflammation elsewhere.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A study in Seattle measured responses to standard dental X-rays where they used lead aprons to shield the body. Women who were pregnant when they got mouth X-rays had smaller babies than women who weren't exposed, even though the baby was shielded. It was the systemic stress or estrogen-like illness effect that caused the embryo to grow at a slower rate.

**Caller:** So is taking something for thyroid a better way to go?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That would be my choice. One of the most interesting recent antidepressants actually has the opposite effect—it *increases* the reuptake of serotonin, just the opposite of the currently popular ones, and it is very effective.

**Caller:** Would that replace the Forteo injections? It's Teriparatide.

**Andrew Murray:** Vitamin K, calcium, and Vitamin D are the most important things Dr. Peat mentioned. Also, make sure your thyroid is working optimally.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even with Hepatitis C, calcium and Vitamin K should help blood pressure.

**Andrew Murray:** For Hepatitis, avoid polyunsaturated fats (PUFA). They are implicated in inflammation. Increase gelatin consumption and get good proteins.

**Caller:** I've read that non-ionizing radiation can cause cellular damage. I'm concerned about the new PG&E Smart Meters and WiFi.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some relatively low-energy radiation can still break chromosomes; it's a matter of how they resonate. For example, men working around power lines have very few male offspring, and birds living near those lines have almost purely female offspring because of cellular and chromosome damage from those low-frequency emissions.

**Caller:** Do you know anything about the frequencies of Smart Meters and WiFi?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have a gauge that I check things with. I went to a flat-screen monitor years ago and use only wire connections. Even with new microwave ovens, it's good to stand back three or four feet because they have intense fields.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you recommend people buy an EMF meter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think they cost about $20.

**Andrew Murray:** Wherever possible, hardwire your internet connection to your computers rather than using WiFi.

**Caller:** That's odd, I'm struggling with healing tendons and taking this at the same time.

**Andrew Murray:** For tendons, one of the best things is Dr. Peat's recommendation of a bone broth or gelatin broth. Gelatin is anti-inflammatory and provides components used in the formation of tendons.

**Caller:** I'm looking to lose weight. Is there any meat that is better than others?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoid pork and non-ruminants because those reflect whatever they ate and are usually highly unsaturated and anti-thyroid. Beef and lamb are saturated.

**Caller:** Do you recommend turkey?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Turkey usually eats the same stuff chickens and pigs do—corn and soybeans.

**Andrew Murray:** We are out of time. Dr. Peat, thank you very much for sharing your research. For those who want to find out more about Dr. Raymond Peat, his website is www.raypeat.com. He has many fully referenced articles there. Thank you for listening, and we will see you next year.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Inflammation I
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We’re in 2011. Happy New Year to you all. For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, which run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

It's become increasingly obvious over the last few years that if you really want to get a point across, you cannot just mention it once or twice. Varied topics encompassing the same root subject will result in a coherent view of the matter in question. Association is an excellent tool for improving the memory. We get a lot of very positive feedback concerning Dr. Ray Peat, who has joined us on many of our shows. He is joining us tonight, and we'll discuss the role of inflammation in the disease process and reiterate some root causes and ways to avoid generating inflammation generally. Good evening, Dr. Peat, and thank you so much for joining us again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Hi, Dr. Peat. Sorry to interrupt, Andrew, but we need to give the disclaimer. The views and opinions expressed throughout this broadcast are our views and opinions, and they do not necessarily reflect the station's thoughts and ideas. Time will be made for other viewpoints.

**Andrew Murray:** Very good. So, to get back to Dr. Peat. For folks who have not listened to our show before, would you just go over your academic and professional career?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was a student and teacher in the humanities for about 10 or 15 years before I studied in the graduate school of biology—basically nerve biology and reproductive biology. I've taught a few courses in biochemistry, immunology, and other things.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you've written fully referenced papers on many different topics. The topic for tonight's discussion is the role of inflammation on the human body: what it does, how it is generated, and how to do something about it. Would you briefly discuss what we all understand when we hear the word "inflammation," and then we'll go over the broad view of inflammation in newer thinking?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 50 years ago, when I was in school, they were teaching that inflammation is part of the curative healing process—we needed it to kill germs and heal. But in the last 10 or 20 years, the change has been seeing it occurring in all of the degenerative diseases: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, heart disease, arthritis, and so on. It was pretty abrupt in the 20th century that there was this sudden change to seeing inflammation as at least not all good, maybe all bad.

**Andrew Murray:** I know from reading about Plato and Aristotelian views of medicine that they had a different metaphor for understanding it. With the view of inflammation that Ilya Metchnikov brought around, would you describe the difference and how fundamentally it makes such a big difference to the way we should understand what causes it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Metchnikoff had worked primarily as an embryologist, understanding the organization of developing primitive organisms. When he saw the phagocyte process—when he put a splinter in an organism and saw cells gathering around it—he interpreted that in the context of what he knew best, which was how the organisms create and maintain their body structure.

The Nobel Prize went simultaneously to him, with that very biological view of immunity, and to Ehrlich, who was working with chemical poisons. The idea of immunity as killing "bad organisms" took over throughout the United States and most of the world for most of the 20th century. As Americans started studying the white blood cells and the thymus gland, they were influenced by the drug industry—Ehrlich looking for the "magic bullets" to kill the evil organisms. That passed over to thinking about antibodies and cells as aimed primarily at organisms that are trying to take over.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It reminds me of how you've described the progression of hepatitis C. We're told that it's this nasty bug, but maybe it's just the body trying to rearrange something, and there's an inflammation process going on from damage.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the retroviruses in general—we've got lots of them, and they seem to be as much part of us as anything. They don't do anything that is for sure harmful. If you mess up an organ, like poison the liver, you get a bunch of these retroviruses. They call them "retro" because normally DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein, but there are enzymes which will turn RNA into DNA. That was first observed in 1979.

At that time, Lamarck had been totally weeded out in the late 1940s with the Cold War. All of Lamarck's followers were fired from teaching positions in the U.S. So in 1979, when the idea that information could go from RNA to DNA was demonstrated, my professors unanimously said it's impossible; that's Lamarckian and not permitted.

**Andrew Murray:** Just so people understand: DNA codes for the manufacture of proteins, and RNA is the messenger. If the retroviruses can manufacture DNA, that DNA can then get into our mitochondria or effect a change in its own right.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of the people inclined in the direction of Lamarck, like Barbara McClintock, proposed that you can get genetic change. Eventually, Barbara McClintock got the Nobel Prize for it—about 40 years too late—demonstrating that information can flow from the environment into the DNA. Some of these people were actually saying that there should be enzymes, such as are seen in retroviruses, that can create new DNA in response to environmental experience.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That reminds me about that test in Egypt regarding schistosomiasis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, there was a chronic schistosomiasis epidemic where a very high percentage of Egyptians had it. They were treated with chemicals that injured their liver. Now they say that it was caused by spreading a virus, but other experiments suggest that the chemical treatment aimed at killing this parasite could have been enough to cause the livers to express retroviruses, one of which is now called hepatitis C.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's looking at the disease as a damaged particle rather than an infectious organism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think this is what Peter Duesberg is suggesting when he says that the retrovirus of HIV, for example, isn't known to be a cause of immunodeficiency. He suggests that it's the result of chemical poisoning.

**Andrew Murray:** Back to the inflammatory process. How does the newer view describe inflammation and how does it differ from what we learned in school?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at the injury of the fetus, it heals without inflammation and it doesn't produce a scar. Basically, it's perfect healing. At a very early stage, you can split the embryo and each part will grow into a complete animal. Later in development, you can cut or injure a part of the fetus and it simply zips itself shut, makes new cells, and doesn't leave a scar or inflammation. It's after being born that inflammation as we know it occurs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We all need to crawl back into our mother's womb.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are two things that happen when we're born. One is our carbon dioxide exposure goes way down and the oxygen availability increases greatly. So there is a shift away from carbon dioxide, which is anti-inflammatory. At the same time, we are no longer protected by the uterus and placenta, which act as a filter and let very little polyunsaturated fat in. Practically all newborns are considered deficient in the so-called "essential fatty acids." But these begin building up during childhood from practically any diet. That, combined with the reduced availability of carbon dioxide, accounts for basically all of the features of inflammation and degeneration that are distinct from the prenatal healing process.

We still have some of the features of prenatal healing, and they can be recovered to some extent. For example, if you pack a wound with sugar, it practically heals without a scar. That's partly because it is giving an extremely generous supply of sugar which can be used to make carbon dioxide.

**Andrew Murray:** This is behind the Greeks using honey in deep wounds.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The sugar makes it unnecessary for the cells to metabolize any of the fatty acids. Even if the organism has been eating them and integrating them into the tissues, the presence of sugar makes it possible to energize and repair cells without drawing down more of these unsaturated fats, which produce all of the features we know of as inflammation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to summarize: polyunsaturated fats are liquid vegetable oils present in almost everybody's diet. You can avoid them to some extent by avoiding any liquid vegetable oil apart from olive oil, and eating coconut oil and butter in their place.

**Andrew Murray:** If people started to increase their carbon dioxide content—we've mentioned bag breathing or living at elevation—and cutting out polyunsaturated fatty acids, what else could be done to lessen the chance of inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another basic thing promoting inflammation is the endotoxin from bacteria that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. If your liver is well nourished and energized, it can cut out practically 100% of the endotoxin. But if the intestine is stressed in any way—which can be nervous stress increasing adrenaline—that cuts down the blood supply. The reduced blood supply releases histamine and serotonin, which make the intestine more permeable, letting more of the endotoxin get into the bloodstream. The endotoxin does the same thing throughout the body: it increases permeability, lowers energy, and increases the inefficiency that shows up as inflammation (swelling, redness, heat).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So stress is a big killer. A lot of people who get extremely stressed are often running on adrenaline to keep their metabolism up rather than running on an adequate amount of thyroid. Dr. Peat, do you have anything else to add to how we can help minimize stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping the intestine as clean as possible and moving stuff along. Raw carrots or bamboo shoots happen to be antiseptic vegetable material that doesn't feed the bacteria and tends to suppress bacterial growth so it doesn't come too far up the intestine. They also bind the endotoxin and other chemicals that should be eliminated.

If the intestine is sluggish, what the liver has excreted into the bile will be reabsorbed farther down the intestine and come back to poison the liver. If you keep a stream of good clean material moving through, you can lower the toxins that should be excreted. That would include unwanted hormones, including estrogen, which the liver should be able to eliminate 100%. It will reduce the endotoxin and shift the serotonin and histamine such that it will also lower cortisol production. That total pattern will increase the good hormones, like progesterone and testosterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For a nice recipe: if you add apple cider vinegar or lemon/lime juice to raw grated carrots with some salt and coconut oil or olive oil, it's even more antimicrobial and antifungal.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about using anti-inflammatories as another means to lower inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of them are very helpful. I mentioned that cleaning the intestine will lower cortisol and raise pregnenolone, testosterone, and progesterone. These are our natural, most powerful anti-inflammatory things. The fetus is exposed to extremely high concentrations of progesterone until it's born. Keeping our production of progesterone as high as possible can make a big difference. Aspirin and related things are also helpful. A lot of fruit chemicals are similar to aspirin and have a protective effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What particular fruit chemicals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm specifically thinking of naringenin in oranges.

**Andrew Murray:** Is that in grapefruit as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's another one in grapefruit that happens to poison an enzyme system in the liver, letting estrogen accumulate tremendously.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This is such a well-known medical fact that in the Fortuna maternity ward, they say they no longer serve grapefruit juice to pregnant mothers because it interferes with the hormones. They didn't specify that it blocked the P450 enzyme that helps the liver excrete excess estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** Have they done animal experiments modeling high CO2 and keeping inflammatory products out to see how long they lived?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 70 years ago, people noticed that food restriction could increase lifespan by 30% or 40%. It has gone through phases where they saw this could happen even in adult animals. Then they started trying different specific foods. It happens that the foods which are eliminated are those which produce inflammation, such as polyunsaturated fats and the amino acids that contribute to inflammation, like tryptophan and methionine. Just eliminating one of these increased longevity by about 30% or 40% in animal studies.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So these Indians that live to 120 years of age in the Andes, are they just not eating any polyunsaturated oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of these long-lived cultures in South America, the Caucasus, and Nepal lived at fairly high altitudes and were surrounded by glaciers. They were drinking water that was fairly recently high-altitude snow, which happens to be isotopically different from sea level water. It's been refined by repeated distillation. As it rains out going to higher altitudes, it becomes metabolically stimulating "light water," whereas average water contains some of the metabolically slowing "heavy water."

At the same time, the atmosphere at high altitudes is very low in oxygen, so people retain more carbon dioxide in their tissues—another resemblance to the prenatal condition. Generally, they are sheep farmers, so they tend to eat vegetables, fruits, and lots of cheese and milk-related dishes.

**Andrew Murray:** The thing about the rainwater is interesting. From an alchemical perspective, the first prerequisite is to distill water seven times to raise the energy of the water. I read an article about water and how different it is energetically and how available it is to the cell.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s, when they first made isotopically heavy water with deuterium replacing hydrogen, they found that it slowed biological processes like nerve conduction. In 1950, they showed in mouse experiments that it tremendously accelerated the aging process. It took about 50 years before people started experimenting with the light water from which the heavy water had been removed. They experimented with it in Russian space vehicles and found that the condensed sweat, which had been filtered, was a very light water resembling glacier water.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So what water do you recommend people drink?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You have to go near a glacier. However, some plants will absorb the water at high altitudes and concentrate it even more. Sugar beets, for example, intrinsically eliminate deuterons. So they have light hydrogen incorporated into their tissues. If they grow in Colorado at a high altitude where they're getting already refined water, then the beet sugar contains the equivalent of glacier water.

**Andrew Murray:** The main thing in our bodies is that everything communicates properly. When things don't communicate properly, problems occur. What do you think about cell-to-cell communication?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it works on many different levels, but the important one has been sketched out by people like Albert Szent-Györgyi, who demonstrated that cells, muscle systems, and secretory systems are tuned electronically. The whole cell is tuned to resonate to certain substances. There's a recent lecture by Luca Turin on pharmacology showing the current vitality of that idea. Mae-Wan Ho has a website talking about the coherence of an organism, showing a worm under a polarizing microscope with coherence on the atomic level all the way through. I think that kind of coherence—electronic or chemical and electrical interaction—is at the basis of cell recognition.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the line. Paula, you're on the air.

**Caller (Paula):** I have a question for Dr. Peat. I've been getting off of Prozac that I took for many years, and I'm having discontinuation syndrome—agitation, sweating, and so on. Are there herbs that one can take to help alleviate that discomfort? I was worried about the influence of these serotonin uptake inhibitors on my bone structure.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The good effects of those serotonin uptake inhibitors, I think, are due to other things, not at all serotonin. It's in spite of the serotonin. In the 1950s, serotonin was discovered to be what makes the carcinoid tumor so bad. These tumors turn the bulk of dietary tryptophan into serotonin. The features of this massive overdosing of serotonin give insight into the drug industry: people flushed, became depressed, anxious, and aggressive. They developed arthritic pains, skin thickening, and fibrotic heart valves. These are things now being seen associated with the uptake inhibitors: osteoporosis, heart disease, breast cancer, obesity.

**Caller (Paula):** Here serotonin is the supposed good guy, but getting off of it is really awful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are good ways to get off. I think pregnenolone, thyroid, and coffee are very helpful.

**Caller (Paula):** Coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, you have to adjust to the coffee, but it goes with thyroid, sugar, progesterone, and so on as part of an anti-inflammatory system. When we were talking about anti-inflammatory substances, I should have mentioned caffeine as one of them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also, if you're already running on a lot of adrenaline and have low blood sugar, caffeine can worsen symptoms. But if you restock your liver's glycogen stores through eating sugars that are lower glycemic index—specifically non-starchy sugars—your body will not respond to the adrenaline like it would if you have low blood sugar.

**Andrew Murray:** Someone had a question about arnica: how it works and how to use it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Arnica is a very anti-inflammatory flower. You want to make a macerated oil from *Arnica montana*. You don't want to take it internally, but rubbing the oil on the affected area immediately after an injury can really help alleviate bruises, tendon sprains, and tears.

**Andrew Murray:** It works really well. Dr. Peat, do you understand the physiological effect of arnica?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, I wanted to ask you about the study you mentioned where cells communicate even through a piece of plastic or quartz.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was Gurwitsch in the 1920s and 30s. They demonstrated that if you used quartz, which passes certain frequencies of ultraviolet, cells could stimulate cell division across the thin sheet of quartz. That is being taken up again in the last 10 years. Most of the work is in the ultraviolet frequency of communication.

**Andrew Murray:** The main thing is that everything communicates properly. That communication is benefited by higher energy, which is the function of the thyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, carbon dioxide is sort of a universal hormone of metabolism, keeping everything in the optimal condition. For example, it holds histamine and serotonin in a bound position. It holds calcium in a bound position. If you hyperventilate and lower your CO2, within a minute your platelets—which carry most of the serotonin—will release it and immediately cause capillaries to become permeable, leaking fluid into your lungs. You can create pulmonary edema with a minute of hyperventilation just because you've messed up the carbon dioxide concentration.

**Andrew Murray:** Back to retroviruses. Are you saying that ultimately we coexist with a wide range of retroviruses, none of which normally give us any problem until some other insult?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, Duesberg said we all contain hundreds of them. When there's an injury to the tissue, we do form antibodies. Some people say that's evidence that they're an alien thing. But many years ago, someone did an experiment with rabbit cartilage. If they removed a piece of cartilage and put it back untampered, it didn't produce any reaction. But if they twisted the cartilage just enough to damage the structure, the rabbit produced antibodies to it. What that means is that antibodies are part of a cleanup process. Something is disturbed, and the antibodies prepare the situation for our phagocytes to remove the damaged material.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So we're looking at the immune system not as a killer attack system, but as a house cleaner.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just fairly recently, someone showed that in a traumatic brain injury, the presence of antibodies to the injured tissue corresponds to the healing. The absence of the antibodies lets the tissue deteriorate. In the thyroid, people think about autoimmune antibodies as causing the problem. But just an excess of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) causes overstimulation and inflammation. The body is cleaning up the damaged cells when it produces antibodies. If you keep the TSH low enough, the cleanup will proceed and the antibodies will disappear.

**Andrew Murray:** We have another caller.

**Caller:** I'm interested in your thoughts on eczema in relationship to leaky gut.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Celiac disease is one of the causes of both skin disease and arthritis. Celiac disease will allow endotoxin into your circulation. Low thyroid is probably the most common thing associated with ordinary eczema. When your thyroid is low, the circulation in your intestine is poor, serotonin is high, and the combination of endotoxin and serotonin will cause the skin to have abnormal growth patterns.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would psoriasis be in the same category?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why when people take liver herbs like dandelion and burdock, they notice an improvement. Working on the digestive tract makes a big difference.

**Caller:** In relationship to celiac disease, do you think the tests for gluten allergies are accurate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They can clearly demonstrate the enzymes involved, but I think gluten is toxic in itself to anyone. It's just that some people are more resistant. It has an overlap with the transglutaminase enzyme, which is activated by estrogen. I think that's why women have more of the problem with it.

Gluten is not intended as a food. The seeds create the protein gluten as a storage form, but also to discourage animals from eating it because it contains amino acids that contribute to inflammation. The seed intends it to cause inflammation in your intestine. A very tough person can withstand it for a long time, but it's not a good idea for anyone to eat it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Traditionally, Europeans ate bread, but it was always soured. The souring process changes the gluten into a less allergenic form.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And soaking it for 12 hours or so increases the protein value tremendously while destroying the gluten.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Modern sourdough bread is risen in three or four hours, maybe even 20 minutes. That's not enough time for the cultures to break down the gluten.

**Andrew Murray:** We are coming to the end of the show. Thank you so much again for joining us, Dr. Peat, and sharing all of your knowledge. Dr. Raymond Peat has a very good website with an extensive list of reference material on many different subjects, from thyroid to progesterone to fish oil. His website is www.raypeat.com.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is R-A-Y-P-E-A-T.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you and good night. Happy New Year.
