**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions. Tonight, we are discussing hormone replacement therapy (HRT), estrogen, and its inflammatory effects, as well as other popularly accepted hormones like serotonin, melatonin, and 5-HTP. We will discuss why they might not actually be that good for us. We are very pleased to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, who will be sharing his research and knowledge surrounding these topics.

Science, whilst responsible for many excellent breakthroughs, is unfortunately subject to the same scandals that beset many excellent thoughts. While studying physiology, I was subject to an indoctrination into an erroneous state of pseudo-fact. One of those things was the receptor model used in physiology regarding estrogen. This has been a perpetrator of much deceit on behalf of Big Pharma. Why was HRT so promoted, and how did the truth behind estrogen's effects get covered up?

Dr. Peat, for those who may have never heard of you, would you open up with your scientific background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As a kid, I was interested in science, but I would read old medical books and encyclopedias. I very early got the impression that education was largely indoctrination. I found that literature as an undergraduate was a field where I could see the actual evidence—the material we were studying—without the interpretation of the professors.

It was years later that I finally decided to go to graduate school in science, when I realized I could get through it without having to fight with the professors; I could just be quiet and do what I wanted to do. I enrolled at the University of Oregon in the biology department, specializing in nerve biology. I was interested in how the brain could handle language and images. I saw that the whole direction of brain biology was towards a very reductionist computer analogy. Looking around the department, I saw that reproductive physiology was much more scientific, so I shifted over to that specialization.

**Andrew Murray:** That word "indoctrination" is a very good place to start tonight's exposé regarding the scandal surrounding HRT. When I was studying, the receptor-ligand interaction was dogmatic. However, you have a very good understanding of the enzymatic background before it was taken over by corporate manufacturing. The whole estrogen receptor is a bit of a non-entity, I understand.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was 1970 when I was working on my dissertation. I was studying the metabolism of the uterus in aging animals, trying to understand why infertility came about in middle age. The particular metabolic studies I was doing corresponded to increased estrogenic stimulation with aging.

All the current textbooks in the 1960s were saying that menopause is when the ovaries wear out and stop producing estrogen. So, I read way back to about 1900 and up to the 1940s. I saw there was a sudden change in 1942. All through the 1930s and into the 1940s, researchers like Soderwall and Blandau were studying the effects of excess estrogen on the uterus. They showed that if you gave a graded dose, increasing amounts of estrogen caused miscarriage. The smallest dose would cause miscarriage at a very early stage. If you waited until very late in the pregnancy, it would take a bigger dose, but it was a continuous graded effect in which a slight excess of estrogen was sufficient to kill the developing embryo.

The hormones of the ovary were identified in the mid-1930s. The major substance produced in the ovary was progesterone, and estrogen was a minor substance. However, people doing research on how estrogen worked found that if you put a spoon in a candle flame and extracted the soot in a solvent, you could get hundreds of different estrogenic substances out of just soot. This was wonderful for the drug industries because everyone could find an estrogen to patent. But there was only one natural progesterone, so that was not a viable drug because no one had a patent on it.

By 1942, the 13 major estrogen companies had their synthetic estrogens. The scientific situation was that estrogen caused infertility and was associated with aging. But since they had products, they said, "Here we have the female hormone, and being female means being able to have babies, so estrogen must be what causes women to have babies." They wanted to sell it to millions of women. They came up with the idea that it would prevent miscarriage, even though the science said the opposite. They got a team at Harvard to promote the idea that Diethylstilbestrol (DES) would prevent miscarriages.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Which is just awful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They were prescribing it for years to prevent miscarriage and make a "healthier baby." It turned out that DES causes cancer and doesn't prevent miscarriage—it actually increases the risk. Just as it was getting recognized that DES causes cancer and deformity, they were getting interested in a new product: the birth control pill.

In the 1940s, they didn't want their drug company known as the "abortion producer." But by 1959 or 1960, contraception was becoming acceptable. They invented a story saying that if you take estrogen, it will suppress your body's estrogen and prevent miscarriage by lowering your estrogen. So, they came out with the contraceptive pill just as it was recognized that DES was causing miscarriages and cancer. They lost one product but immediately came out with another falsified story to sell the birth control pills.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the truth behind whether estrogen binds to a specific receptor, and the lies surrounding the science produced to support the estrogen industry?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The people doing the real science were trying to explain why estrogen had these toxic effects. They saw that natural estrogen was imitated by these polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in soot, which were recognized carcinogens. They were studying the properties of soot and estrogen and finding that the substance tended to produce inflammation and cancer. These were activating enzyme systems in particular ways.

This reached a peak in the 1950s. The government moved some investment from chemical warfare into endocrine research. The opinion of many is that the intention was population control. They gave a big grant to a group led by Elwood Jensen. He wanted to create a new idea for how estrogen worked that would not involve all of this interesting chemistry explaining why estrogen was a toxin and carcinogen. He wanted to say that all it does is activate the "female genes"—that estrogen turns a switch that would only activate those female genes and not involve the nasty chemistry of cancer and inflammation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But they knew that soot caused cancer in the late 1800s from the chimney sweeps.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was exactly what Jensen wanted people to forget. He wanted to say it's like a lock and key. The female organs have a very specific lock, and the estrogen is a key that sticks only into that lock.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Estrogen receptors are now known to be found all throughout the body, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And in men. But at that time, Elwood Jensen was arguing that there was just one little switch molecule in the cell. The Atomic Energy Commission gave him permission to use radioactive isotopes. His competition didn't have the grants or the isotopes. He labeled estrogen and claimed that there were no oxidative reactions in which estrogen participated. He published that in 1962.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they couldn't disprove it because the research up until that point had been showing estrogen causes cancer, but the drug companies wanted to sell the oral contraceptive pill, DES, and HRT.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. Jensen used the fancy isotope demonstration to say estrogen is not oxidized and reduced. But 10 or 15 years later, after the receptor dogma had been imposed, other people started using isotopes and showing that the older enzymologists were right. Estrogen does participate as a catalyst in enzyme reactions, especially transhydrogenation reactions that connect energy production to gene turnover and cell growth.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that's how it initiates cancer cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it allows the energy to be short-circuited over into the growth mechanism rather than the function mechanism. It drains the energy right out of function into growth.

**Andrew Murray:** I'm interested in water. Modern science has shown that H2O exists in many different states. How does estrogen involve itself in redox reactions regarding cancer promotion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fastest change you can see in a cell within a minute or two of exposing it to estrogen is that it instantly starts taking up water. As it takes up water, the water gets out of the cell's control. That's part of this short-circuiting of the energy process. The microtubules, which are an organizing force in the cell, are depolymerized and disorganized in the presence of estrogen. That's part of the cancer problem—the cell can't communicate from one part to the other because the microtubules are messed up.

The water is normally under the control of adjoining surfaces, very unlike bulk water. But in the presence of estrogen, it becomes bulk-like. One of my experiments was to put an old uterus, a young uterus, and an estrogen-treated uterus in an MRI machine. We showed that the old uterus and the estrogen-treated uterus had loose, disorganized water that could be distinguished from the young, healthy uterus.

**Andrew Murray:** Give me your opinion on HRT's effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The industry succeeded so greatly in turning science upside down in the case of estrogen that it took a lot of other hormones with it. Progesterone was suppressed because it would cure the things estrogen was claimed to cure, but it couldn't be patented.

Prolactin had many toxic effects that were well recognized, but since estrogen increases prolactin, there was pressure not to think about the fact that prolactin causes bone loss and osteoporosis.

Serotonin is another thing strongly influenced by this inverted interpretation. Estrogen increases exposure to serotonin. Serotonin is one of the means by which estrogen increases prolactin, and serotonin does many of the harmful things estrogen and prolactin do, including being a direct cause of bone loss. People who take fluoxetine-type antidepressants (SSRIs) are seen to have premature bone loss because of the excess exposure to serotonin. Serotonin is a cofactor for estrogen; estrogen increases serotonin, and serotonin increases the production of estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We're all told that serotonin is the "feel good" hormone and they give you SSRIs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the currently bad effects of serotonin excess that is getting some recognition is hypertension of the pulmonary artery. The drugs that increase serotonin increase this pulmonary hypertension and degeneration of the valves in the right side of the heart. This was known in the 1950s as the main deadly complication of having a serotonin-producing tumor. Finally, 60 years later, it's being recognized as a way to treat pulmonary hypertension by using anti-serotonin drugs.

**Caller:** I sometimes have a tendency toward depression. I resisted trying Zoloft or Prozac, but I was told by nature doctors to try 5-HTP. They said it was natural and would help me use my own serotonin better. Is that not good for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Prozac-type drugs keep the platelets and nerve cells from binding and keeping serotonin out of the way, leading to overexposure. Plain tryptophan is bad enough, but 5-hydroxy-tryptophan (5-HTP) is one step closer to being serotonin.

**Caller:** So you think it's not good for me to take it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything I know suggests that. For example, there is an increased risk of breast cancer and obesity.

**Caller:** How can it increase obesity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By slowing metabolism and suppressing the thyroid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's basically providing the precursor, and your body makes more serotonin out of it. The effects of excess serotonin increase estrogen, which slows your liver's metabolism. That can slow your thyroid down, lead to obesity, and promote cancer.

**Caller:** It says it elevates your mood.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You have to weigh it up. It might elevate your mood, but you also risk these other things. They used to give X-rays for acne, and people got cancer.

**Caller:** I certainly don't want to slow my metabolism. I'm done with menopause, so I figure my estrogen has balanced itself out. I'm specifically talking about 5-HTP from the health food store, which seems benign.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's all part of the same system. If the body naturally produces serotonin in the bowel, and a little bit stimulates inflammation and degeneration, you wouldn't want to increase that even through natural means.

**Caller:** So I should probably do without it and see if my food is okay.

**Andrew Murray:** Unfortunately, the short-term gain is not worth the price of the long-term sequelae of disease processes.

**Caller:** I've talked to you before and I've gotten completely off my serotonin reuptake inhibitors. One effect of stopping is that I've been able to stop using steroids in an inhaler. My asthma has gone away completely. I think you said on your website that serotonin relates to asthma?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, estrogen is related to asthma too. The effect of serotonin is to cause localized contraction of the tubes in your lungs as well as causing them to take up water and promote inflammation. The contraction is the thing best studied in connection with asthma.

**Caller:** It went away within four weeks. I coughed up a lot of fluid for a week, but after that, it cleared up. Getting off the serotonin was painful, but I'm very grateful.

**Caller:** I haven't heard mention of the three different types of estrogen in our bodies: estriol, estrone, and estradiol. They have a hugely disparate impact on our bodies.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are probably a dozen important types of estrogen, but the three main types—estriol, estrone, and estradiol—have pretty much the same effects, just at different potencies. If you can turn your most potent estradiol into the others, you're protected against some of the most toxic effects. During pregnancy, the index of a healthy pregnancy is when estriol is high, because that means you're destroying your estradiol very quickly.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So estradiol is the most dangerous form.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And these different forms are exactly the issue that Elwood Jensen denied happened. He said estradiol can't turn into estrone and estriol, but in fact, that's a major way of inactivating estrogen according to the cell's energy system.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the only reason you'd want high estriol is because that tells us the estradiol is being detoxified. Not that high estriol in itself is protective.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's about 10 times weaker than estrogen. Every little bit of estradiol that you turn to estriol is a down-stepping of your estrogen effect.

**Caller:** What is your opinion on modern birth control methods like the pill or the NuvaRing? Are they safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They tremendously decreased the amount of estrogen in the contraceptives, but if it's strong enough to kill the embryo, it's strong enough to do damage to the woman. About 30 years ago, there was agitation for FDA approval of the traditional cervical cap—a metal casting made to fit the cervix exactly. The FDA wouldn't approve that but approved a rubber one that didn't work well. I think it was because they were simply working for the contraceptive pill.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** As far as IUDs, they now have IUDs that secrete a small amount of hormone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The signal from inside the uterus travels through nerves to prevent the ovary from producing the amount of progesterone it should. So any kind of IUD, with or without hormones, will create a hormonal imbalance.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thereby increasing your estrogen and risk of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** So is there anything else other than natural birth control?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the rhythm cycle method is the best.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think of melatonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has its own endocrine problems. It can disturb your progesterone and thyroid production if you take a lot of it. But its function seems to be a way of detoxifying serotonin. The trigger that turns the conversion in the pineal gland of serotonin into melatonin is the adrenergic stress-related nerves. During the night, your stress increases from the lack of light, and this system causes the pineal to convert serotonin to melatonin.

Biologically, it's evidence that you are responding to stress with a detoxifying process. The enzymes in the pineal activated by stress can also be found in inflamed joint tissue and breast cancer. Serotonin is involved in the pathology of those situations, so if our enzymes could turn it more quickly into melatonin, there would be less of a serotonin problem.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But when people actually take melatonin supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's probably protecting against circulating serotonin. But in itself, in an otherwise healthy person, animal studies showed it was capable of lowering both progesterone and thyroid while increasing estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So in a short-term emergency, it could be okay, but long-term it has negative side effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, though it is much safer than serotonin.

**Caller:** I take a suppository called Vagifem for dryness. The package says it's estradiol. Should I worry?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have been studied using vaginal creams, and their blood level of estrogen was even higher than some of the oral pills were causing. It is definitely a systemic hormonal influence.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What would you recommend to this lady to use in place of her suppository?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known several women who had pharmacists make suppositories with a fairly high dose of vitamin A and a little vitamin E in cocoa butter. The vitamin A helps to strengthen the membranes and normalize mucus production.

**Caller:** What do you think of bioidentical hormones in low doses, derived from wild yams?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All hormones, even bioidentical ones, have to fit into the system in a balanced way. When you supplement estrogen or serotonin, you're most likely increasing something that's already excessive. The doctrine of replacement with natural hormones builds on the history of synthetic hormone replacement.

What they neglect is that as a woman ages from 19 to 39, there is a steady average increase in the amount of estrogen in her bloodstream. In the 40s, progesterone production is no longer able to keep up with this steadily increasing estrogen. As soon as progesterone decreases and can no longer force estrogen out of the cells, the blood estrogen level will drop, but the estrogen *inside* the cells will increase.

Publications have shown that the tissues of old organisms retain much more estrogen than the tissues of young animals. The fact that you don't find it in the blood is simply because estrogen sticks inside the cells in proportion to the deficiency of progesterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the reason they recommended it is because of low blood levels, but Dr. Peat's advice would be to not use it.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat. For anyone listening who wants to find out more, his website is www.raypeat.com.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Fukujima I
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture our own certified organic herbal extracts.

You are listening to KMUD Garberville, 91.1 FM. Today we are discussing the unfolding facts in Japan. First and foremost, we want to extend our heartfelt, sincere wishes for the people of Japan—that their country recovers and the people find relief, food, shelter, and protection.

Last Friday, there was an 8.9 or 9.0 earthquake which resulted in a tsunami. This caused a catastrophic breakdown in the cooling system of the Fukushima nuclear power plant. We are joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, an expert physiologist, chemist, and research scientist. We will be hearing from Dr. Peat about helpful things to do to counter any potential radioactive spread to this country.

Earlier in the week, evidence began to show that the steam leaked from the plants—subsequent to the hydrogen explosions on the buildings housing the reactors—was laden with Iodine-131 and cesium isotopes. These were released as engineers tried to lower the pressure to prevent a breakdown of the containment vessel. One of the reactors, number three, is a mixed oxide fuel reactor containing 6% plutonium and 94% uranium, which would lead to much more serious environmental damage if released.

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) in Vienna, which monitors the atmosphere for radioactive particles from nuclear testing, released information that this cloud was moving east. Today, a CTBTO station in Sacramento recorded very small, but present, particles of Iodine-131. It is likely coming down in the rain or upper air jet stream.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I want to introduce Dr. Peat and ask him if he believes it is true that radioactive iodine has reached our land yet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is probably present in detectable amounts, but probably not yet biologically significant. However, it could quickly become concentrated enough to affect pregnant women because the fetus concentrates elements from the environment at least 100 times faster than other tissues. During the first two or three months after an accident like that, radioactive iodine would be concentrating in the embryo and fetus. Other isotopes, such as cesium and strontium, would continue to be dangerous if they got into the food supply, but radioactive iodine is the most crucial for developing babies.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, what foods and nutrients can help protect us from increasing levels of radioactive iodine, cesium, or strontium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first principle is to dilute the radioactive isotopes with good, stable isotopes. Old food is best. The radioactive iodine isotope is practically gone three months after its production. The others will eventually wash down into the ground. Plants growing in the first few months after an accident will contain those isotopes. If you have canned food, dried milk, or aged cheese, these are very safe and will continue to be safe for months because they were produced before the accident.

The other principle, besides diluting the isotopes, is to increase your resistance to stress and radiation. My very first newsletter 30 years ago was on radiation resistance. I reviewed research from the Atomic Energy Commission and Soviet studies. The main conclusions were that increasing the metabolic rate causes cells to retain magnesium. Magnesium is very important in repairing cell damage. The faster the metabolic rate, generally the more damage can be repaired before it becomes established as a stress factor.

A high metabolic rate produces carbon dioxide, which has an antioxidant, anti-stress effect throughout the organism. If you keep your metabolic rate up and eat a balanced diet, your tissues will retain the magnesium they need and produce the carbon dioxide they need—assuming you are getting adequate protein, sugar, fat, vitamins, and a balance of minerals.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you expand on what types of sugars, fats, and proteins we should be ingesting to keep our metabolic rate high?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ideal fat is coconut oil because the short-chain saturated fatty acids compete with the other fats that normally slow metabolism. For a couple of hours after you eat a tablespoon of coconut oil, your metabolic rate is increased, producing more carbon dioxide and accelerating cell repair processes.

Regarding fruit, the farther south the fruit is grown, the longer it will be free of this high-latitude Japanese radiation. Oranges grown in Mexico, Brazil, and Florida are going to be pretty pure for a very long time. The sugar and minerals in oranges are very close to what we need. So: coconut oil, orange juice, and milk as a good source of calcium.

During the atmospheric bomb tests in the 50s and 60s, the government began recommending people not drink milk because it was contaminated with strontium. However, I looked at the analysis and found that a person getting their nutrition from vegetables would have about five times higher exposure to Strontium-90 than people who got their nutrition primarily from milk and cheese. The cows concentrate the calcium and filter out a little more of the strontium than the vegetables do.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You mentioned that to get enough calcium to protect against bone destruction, one would have to drink one to two quarts of milk and eat cheese daily. To get that same amount of calcium from green leafy vegetables, you would need about three pounds of spinach per day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Something like that.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And by eating that much spinach, you would actually be exposing yourself to much higher levels of strontium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you recommend for elimination methods if we are breathing in or ingesting radioactive particles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Once it gets into your digestive system, if it is incorporated in the food, there is no way to sort it out. But if it is in the water, keeping a lot of fiber flowing through your system helps. Eating fruit or carrots that you know are uncontaminated will sweep the material through your intestine, preventing the absorption of some nutrients at the same time. If you are exposed to a very concentrated dose from rain, it is better to go hungry for a little while while sweeping out your intestine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would you consider the radiation we have been exposed to thus far dangerous enough to avoid milk and vegetables from California and Oregon?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not yet. If the reactors start burning fuel rods, someone is likely to leak the information in time for people to take precautions. If it reached the proportions of Chernobyl, it would take extreme measures for a very long time, using only stored, "antique" food.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It sounds like we need to start stocking up on sugar and dried milk powder.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** There is a lot of hype around using potassium iodide (KI) and kelp. How do these help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It simply dilutes the radioactive isotope. When you take in a lot of old, stable iodine, it saturates your thyroid. Your thyroid shuts down and stops taking up any more. If you add radioactive iodine to a saturated person, it just gradually washes out without concentrating in the thyroid.

However, if a person is deficient in iodine, almost all of it will stick in the thyroid gland once it enters the bloodstream, giving an extremely high dose to the gland—and even more so to a developing embryo.

Potassium iodide is very good protection, but *only* from damage to the thyroid gland. It doesn't protect against other isotopes or other tissues. If you take more than enough to saturate your tissues—the CDC advocates 160mg as one dose—every day for a long time, your thyroid gland would shut down. Your metabolism and defensive reactions would slow down, making you more susceptible to injury throughout the rest of your body.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you are not recommending people take kelp powder or potassium iodide at this current level?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The minimum requirement is only 150 or 200 micrograms. Even one milligram per day continued for a long time increases the risk of thyroiditis.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you know how much is in kelp powder?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably a half teaspoon is adequate to saturate most people. One half-teaspoon dose isn't going to hurt anyone, but you don't want to do that every day for a long time.

**Andrew Murray:** The radioactive iodine in Chernobyl was responsible for the increase in thyroid cancers. You are saying pregnant women are more susceptible than young children?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Ernest Sternglass studied this during the atmospheric bomb tests. The government timed tests in Nevada so the wind blew toward Utah rather than California cities. Utah suffered the most autoimmune diseases and cancer. Occasionally, fallout would reach the East Coast. Sternglass found high radiation levels at his university that the government hadn't mentioned. He showed there were likely tens of thousands of miscarriages. A high percentage of surviving babies were hypothyroid or born without thyroid glands. As long as they were breastfed, the mother's thyroid hormones in the milk covered up the symptoms until they were weaned.

**Andrew Murray:** I found the most up-to-date information coming from *Russia Today*. What is the best source for people in America to find real-time figures?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is an anti-nuclear power site that is getting up-to-date information.

**Andrew Murray:** I was looking at Geiger counters on eBay. They are usually inexpensive, but prices have jumped.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For a while, you could get old Soviet Geiger counters for about $15. Someone told me the price went from $35 to $75 as soon as the radiation scare hit.

**Caller 1:** I'm actually holding mine right here. I got the cheapest one for about $250. The really expensive ones are $10,000 to $20,000. It's not beeping much more than normal right now.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Let's discuss caffeine. How does it protect against radiation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coffee is a good source of magnesium and niacin (Vitamin B3). Caffeine is anti-inflammatory and an antioxidant. If you have mobile isotopes in your bloodstream going through your kidneys, caffeine helps flush them out faster. It has a slight chelating effect.

The radiation effect itself imitates estrogen in the body. Everything estrogen does can be imitated by radiation. If you are in a high-estrogen state, you are more susceptible to radiation injury. That is why progesterone, thyroid, and caffeine—by helping to lower estrogen and inflammation—are protective.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** To recap:
*   **Caffeine/Coffee:** Magnesium, B vitamins.
*   **Progesterone:** Blocks estrogenic effects.
*   **Vitamin E:** Blocks estrogen.
*   **Vitamin C:** Orange juice/tropical fruits.
*   **Vitamin A:** Eggs and liver (helps repair).

What about glutathione?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is confusion there. Anything that harms your cells turns on a defensive reaction and increases glutathione. Many harmful things stimulate that defense. Taking large doses of glutathione was shown in animal studies to be carcinogenic to the liver by starting free radical reactions rather than stopping them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about animal liver? It contains B vitamins and fat-soluble vitamins, but people worry about toxicity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver is the main detoxifying organ, but it cleans itself quickly. Studies on beef showed that while muscle and fat tissues retained chemical contaminants, only a tiny proportion of livers had toxins left. After about 24 hours of exposure, the liver has cleaned itself. The fats are the most risky for chemical poisoning; the liver is the cleanest.

**Caller 2:** I saw a map showing the plume hitting Cape Mendocino. I missed the name of the colon cleanser you mentioned.

**Andrew Murray:** Grated raw carrot.

**Caller 2:** Does garlic help bring iodine into the system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has some antioxidant effect, but I don't think it has a big effect on iodine.

**Caller 2:** We are trying to safeguard with a "potassium iodine salad" made of bananas and seaweed. Is there a cautionary amount?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sea organisms like shrimp, oysters, and clams are good sources of iodine. However, the banana issue brings up an important aspect. Bananas are one of the richest food sources of serotonin.

Biologists have found that low-level ionizing radiation causes cells to produce serotonin. Even if you take the injured cells out, the water they were in becomes equivalent to radiation for other cells due to the chemicals released. Serotonin is one of those communicators of radiation damage (the bystander effect). I think it is good to avoid sources of serotonin, especially bananas.

**Caller 2:** Is there any benefit to dried vs. fresh bananas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think shifting toward gelatinous meats and away from muscle meats helps reduce the tendency to produce serotonin. A good balance of vitamins and minerals helps avoid excess serotonin production.

**Caller 2:** What can men take to preempt the estrogenic effect of radionuclides? And is bottled water better than well water right now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For men, keeping thyroid function high is the main thing. Aspirin and thyroid inhibit the estrogen produced by stress. Regarding water, a good filter for well water is adequate.

**Andrew Murray:** Does a carbon filter sequester iodine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, activated charcoal absorbs almost any solid.

**Caller 3:** Brown seaweeds like kombu contain sodium alginate, which is supposed to take heavy metals out of the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they pass through your intestine, yes. Anything indigestible that stimulates your intestine will sweep out. However, alginate is dangerously allergenic for many people. I wouldn't recommend it unless you are sure you aren't sensitive to it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Raw carrots are absorptive and non-digestible. Also, taking too much seaweed will lower your metabolic rate and suppress the thyroid.

**Caller 4:** I recommend Turkey Tail mushrooms (*Trametes versicolor*). They are used in Asia as an anti-cancer drug and for immune support.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you. People can check that out online.

**Caller 5:** The EPA has a website with graphical representations of raw data from monitoring sites. It is `epa.gov/japan2011/rert/radnet-data.html`.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you. People can compare that to the CTBTO information.

**Caller 6:** I was wondering about using D-Ribose to raise the metabolic rate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main risk is that substances produced industrially often have contaminants not mentioned on the labels. You have to be cautious of allergic reactions to semi-purified chemicals.

**Caller 7:** Are you suggesting we only get vitamins from whole foods, or are supplements okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For an emergency period of two or three weeks while the cloud passes, a B-complex supplement could be helpful to support a maximal metabolic rate. But eating extra eggs and milk is better. A B-vitamin supplement is pretty safe.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If cesium has a half-life of 30 years and is heavier than iodine, will it fall out over the ocean?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There would be a little bit of everything produced in the fallout.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Orange juice is rich in potassium, which helps the body pick up less cesium, similar to how kelp helps with iodine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We had a caller earlier mention swing sets for adults as a health tip for stress.

**Andrew Murray:** That's a good illustration of the ability to defend yourself.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think of that as analogous to concentric muscle exercise, where you are shortening the muscles under force. I think the same sort of thing happens in the nervous system when you can do something protective or constructive.

**Caller 2:** I'm an old farmer. The wheat grown now by big agribusiness has almost 90% more gluten, which is a lectin. Lectins are sticky proteins that protect the plant seed from invaders. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are many defensive chemicals. Bananas are extremely allergenic, probably because of intensive production in poor soils. Ordinary sugars—sucrose, for example—have a tremendously protective effect in resisting all of these inflammation-producing factors. Fructose catalyzes the ability to use glucose efficiently. So sucrose is better than even well-cooked starch at protecting the immune system from these irritants.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's pick up on stress. People always talk about stress being bad for you.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The only mistake Hans Selye made in his work on stress was talking about a limited ability to adapt because we are born with a certain amount of "adaptive energy." I don't think there is such a thing. I think it's substances like sucrose and fructose which let us deal with menacing things like serotonin and endotoxin.

What Selye called a lack of adaptive energy, I think is actually us adapting to a bad environment. We get worse as we adapt to bad things like polyunsaturated fats and chronic excess serotonin. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the immediate response of serotonin—like diarrhea—is a short-term help, but constant exposure causes degenerative disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A high calcium diet and plenty of sugar will keep your thyroid working and keep your carbon dioxide up. Carbon dioxide keeps the serotonin bound and out of trouble. When you're stressed and make lactic acid, that displaces the carbon dioxide and activates the release of serotonin.

**Andrew Murray:** We are going to have to leave it there, I'm afraid, as we are out of time. Dr. Peat, thank you very much for joining us.

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** Kevin, sorry for the technical difficulties. You are creating a Lyme support group, is that correct?

**Andrew Murray:** Will that be for Humboldt County or the surrounding area?

**Kevin Peer:** It will be for the surrounding area. It is going to take place at my office at the AEE building in Redway.

**Andrew Murray:** How are you going to advertise it?

My phone number is 986-7469. They can also contact me through my email: kevin@inneralliancecounseling.com.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What can participants expect besides expressing their symptoms?

**Kevin Peer:** It will be a listening platform for people to share experiences, but also a place to gain information. Myself and guest speakers will present information on the latest treatment modalities in both conventional and alternative medicine. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Will you be discussing how hypnotherapy can help?

**Andrew Murray:** Are you going to be charging for this?

**Kevin Peer:** There will be a nominal fee, probably $5, just to help defray the cost of gas. Nobody will be turned away for financial reasons.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you, Kevin, for your time tonight.

**Andrew Murray:** We have Dr. Raymond Peat on the line. Dr. Peat, for those tuning in for the first time, would you please let people know about your academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied biology at the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology, especially reproductive physiology, and quite a bit of biochemistry. I consider myself an old-fashioned biologist—pre-molecular biology in my way of thinking. My dissertation was on the effects of hormones on oxidative metabolism in relation to the aging of the reproductive system.

**Andrew Murray:** We wanted to discuss hair loss and the mechanism behind it. I know male pattern baldness is often attributed to genetics and testosterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The head of the dermatology department where we trained in London was convinced that male pattern baldness was caused by a sensitivity to testosterone, or DHT. Dr. Peat, how do you explain why males develop baldness? Is it due to testosterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the belief in testosterone as the cause is similar to the old belief that males got prostate cancer because of testosterone. Since males get a particular kind of baldness, it's easy to blame it on testosterone. But in fact, there is no evidence showing that excess testosterone is responsible for it, any more than excess testosterone causes prostate cancer. The idea of "increased sensitivity" came in because there was no evidence of too much of the hormone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Right. When they measured blood levels, the testosterone levels were not important, so they assumed cellular sensitivity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That fills in for a lack of evidence. When you look at the actual hormone situation of people with lots of hair versus those with not much, you see an excess of prolactin and cortisol in the people losing their hair—both men and women. Testosterone actually makes the hair shaft grow thicker and faster. Prolactin tends to cause it to fall out. In birds, prolactin is known as the molting hormone. In humans, it is the milk-producing hormone, but it also regulates practically every other cell in the body. It has the analogous function of terminating the growth cycle of the hair shaft.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So, cortisol and prolactin both rise during stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There is clear evidence they are associated. What links those is low energy production—a thyroid deficiency tendency—letting the metabolism of cholesterol go down towards increased cortisol, and less towards progesterone, testosterone, and DHEA, which are things that promote hair growth.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If men suffering from baldness checked their blood levels, would they see higher than normal prolactin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It wouldn't likely be "higher than normal" on the current lab standards, because they have increased the upper limit of the range. This is probably because of the population's exposure to estrogens. Estrogen increases the production of prolactin, and estrogen itself terminates the growth of hair.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't you say that in the past, the ideal range was lower?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Back in the 70s, they found the healthy range for women was around 12 to 15, and for men, it was about 4 to 7. They've now raised the upper limit for men sometimes as high as 20. But all the men I've talked to who had levels close to 20—even though they were told they were normal—had developing breasts, or gynecomastia. Fertility is best when a man has a level of 4 to 7.

**Andrew Murray:** Speaking of gynecomastia, that is not an uncommon sight in heavy drinkers of very hoppy beer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's not only the phytoestrogens from the hops, but the yeast required for alcoholic drinks. Yeast produces estradiol, the powerful human hormone.

**Andrew Murray:** Interestingly enough, hop extract is the latest miticide for the bee industry.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Female hop pickers are notoriously known to stop menstruating because of the high level of hormones they are exposed to through their skin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The hormones in beer, and to a lesser extent in wine, along with the estrogen from the yeast, will stimulate the adrenals to produce both estrogen and cortisol. Cortisol makes the big belly, and the estrogens contribute to breast growth.

**Andrew Murray:** What about the oral contraceptive pill and its presence in the water supply? Is that a credible source of environmental estrogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, sure. You can identify the specific type of estrogen and progestin from the fields going right through the sewer processing plants into the rivers. It causes fish, muskrats, and anything living in the rivers to be feminized.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is there a filter that takes those compounds out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nothing practical that is in use. If you are going to drink the water, you should run it over activated carbon. Ozone is probably the cheapest, best method for municipalities because it breaks down chemicals like that.

**Andrew Murray:** Back to the connection between hair loss and hormones. You mentioned cortisol and prolactin are stress hormones that decrease hair growth.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They go up with stress. Prolactin responds to different kinds of stress; for example, anything that blocks your thyroid function and energy production tends to increase prolactin.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you speak often about the innate energy level within an organism being responsible for health. You mention thyroid as the driver of cellular respiration.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When your thyroid is low, or if your cholesterol is below average, or if you are deficient in vitamin A, you can't efficiently turn cholesterol into progesterone and the other anti-stress hormones. The emergency anti-stress hormone is cortisol. If you lower your cholesterol with a drug, that forces you to increase reliance on cortisol, which will have degenerative effects, including interference with hair growth.

**Andrew Murray:** This is why statin drugs have degenerative side effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you poison the production of cholesterol, you are also poisoning Coenzyme Q10 and many other metabolic systems.

**Andrew Murray:** You are an advocate of having a reasonably good level of cholesterol because it is a building block for steroid hormones.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Framingham study found that people over 50 who don't have at least 200 mg% of cholesterol are much more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease. It is brain-protective to have over 200. Thyroid will lower cholesterol naturally by producing more of the protective hormones: progesterone, pregnenolone, and DHEA.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can we talk about practical applications? What can people buy to help hair grow back?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D is closely involved in hair development. Also, getting enough calcium in your diet.

**Andrew Murray:** How does Vitamin D work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Vitamin D receptor is a regulatory material in practically every cell in the body, including bones and hair. The receptor itself is involved in making stem cells that produce new hairs. A couple of groups have discovered that if you inhibit the parathyroid hormone, you can increase hair growth. The natural inhibitors of the parathyroid hormone are Vitamin D and calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** Parathyroid is inflammatory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It interrupts the use of oxygen. It is essentially an anti-thyroid function. Thyroid enables you to use oxygen; parathyroid hormone can do useful things like shocking your bones into producing more cartilage by interfering with oxygen production for a moment. But if you keep your parathyroid hormone up continuously, you destroy the bone because it doesn't have enough energy to build.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people can make sure to get lots of calcium—up to 2,000 milligrams a day—and Vitamin D from sunshine. What else?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin A intake helps hold down parathyroid hormone. You want to avoid everything that suppresses thyroid function, such as polyunsaturated fats (vegetable oils).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And get plenty of coconut oil. Vitamin A is found in liver and eggs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the last couple of years, some people have found that topical thyroid hormone (T3) applied to the skin stimulates regeneration. Caffeine, which has some overlapping effects with thyroid hormone, is now being added to lotions to renew hair growth.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would coffee or tea work if you applied it topically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm sure the caffeine would work, but it's cleaner to use pure caffeine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You also mentioned making an oil rub with natural progesterone, DHEA, and olive oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, those regenerate many skin functions, including hair growth.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So, a little olive oil, 25mg of DHEA, and 50mg of natural progesterone mixed together?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen several people do it. If you have hair to start with, it is a sticky mess to put on your scalp every day. That is why caffeine is neater.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take our first caller.

**Caller:** I was wondering about estrogenics from plants versus testosteronics. Does the Yohimbe plant or yohimbine act as a hormone? Are there any natural testosterone sources in plants?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know of any plants that have a testosterone-like action. There are some chemicals that test like progesterone in plants, but I've never seen an actual biological effect from them.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a question from a listener regarding a female ex-bulimic who recovered about a year ago and started experiencing hair loss immediately after.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect it led to hypothyroidism. There is usually high prolactin and high serotonin during those appetite disturbances. It probably started because of hypothyroidism, but at a certain point, hair can start falling when the thyroid is really low and the stress hormones are high.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I'd like to talk about unwanted female hair growth, or hirsutism. What is going on with hormones there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The androgens are usually up, but prolactin excess is also involved. Both hirsutism and hair loss are associated with high prolactin. A thyroid supplement is a very reliable way to control prolactin in most women. Vitamin A and calcium also help.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** From an herbal point of view, Vitex (Chase Tree Berry) blocks prolactin.

**Andrew Murray:** How about graying hair?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen DHEA correct it pretty quickly. However, the enzyme that creates the melanin pigment uses copper as a catalyst. Probably the best food for increasing your copper—while decreasing the iron which competes against it—is shellfish. Shrimp, clams, lobster, crab, and squid all have high copper content.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Since I started eating a serving of shellfish once a week three years ago, I haven't noticed any new gray hairs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since iron accumulates with aging, if a person eats foods high in iron, like meat or liver, it is helpful to have coffee at the same time so you don't absorb all the iron. Iron attacks polyunsaturated fats and tends to increase serotonin. This chronic oxidation of polyunsaturated fats interacting with iron and estrogen forms lipofuscin (age spots).

**Andrew Murray:** I want to ask about osteoporosis. We hear about calcium and brittle bones, but what is your interpretation of the cause?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My current interest is that it is a good way to conceive the unified nature of aging processes. Everyone's bones get thinner with aging, which corresponds to the loss of muscle tissue and the calcification of soft tissues. This is associated with the misapplication of calcium—failing to put it in the bones. All of that is under the control of energy metabolism. When thyroid and oxidative metabolism fail, the parathyroid, lactic acid-producing metabolism replaces it, causing stress atrophy.

**Andrew Murray:** So it is an error of calcium metabolism. What kind of calcium intake is reasonable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Maasai people and other cattle-raising people often get 5,000 mg of calcium a day.

**Andrew Murray:** And this is from milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There has been publicity about calcium supplements not being helpful. The most popular medical supplements have been calcium citrate or lactate. Citric acid itself causes you to lose calcium in your urine. Those supplements have anti-calcification effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They advertise calcium citrate as the only absorbable form, but you are saying it inhibits absorption?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It activates the loss of calcium. Calcium carbonate isn't quite as soluble, but eventually, it has a chance to absorb. It is a very effective and safe supplement because the carbon dioxide is the form that stimulates bone formation rather than breaking it down.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** An easy way to get that is eggshell powder. A quarter teaspoon of finely ground eggshell powder is about 2,000 mg of calcium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Chemical analyses comparing eggshells to commercial supplements find that the lowest concentration of toxic heavy metals is in eggshells. Oyster shells are the next cleanest. Old cows used for bone meal often have high lead content.

**Andrew Murray:** So calcium in the form of eggshells is excellent.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And aspirin. People seldom talk about it, but aspirin improves calcium retention in bones. It isn't as profitable as osteoporosis drugs like bisphosphonates, but it is very safe as long as you take Vitamin K with it. Vitamin K protects your arteries from calcification and allows the bone to use carbon dioxide to bind calcium into the bone.

**Andrew Murray:** What are food sources for Vitamin K?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Kale is the richest vegetable, and liver is a very rich source. A serving of well-cooked kale every other day should provide enough.

**Andrew Murray:** Calcification of the arteries is common, and people think they should avoid calcium, but that is counterintuitive. Consuming adequate calcium drives parathyroid hormone down and deposits calcium in the correct location.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Also, recently, researchers noticed that people taking SSRI antidepressants were getting osteoporosis. They see that serotonin—produced mostly in the intestine—interferes with bone metabolism. Now they are developing drugs to suppress serotonin synthesis to cure osteoporosis.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, we have to cut it short there. Thank you so much for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Raymond Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. You can find references for his statements there. Thank you for tuning in.
