**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our show, we run the third Friday of each month. Sarah and I are both licensed medical herbalists. We graduated in England with a degree in herbal medicine and we run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions.

Tonight, Dr. Raymond Peat has been kind enough to join us again. We had a listener from Rio de Janeiro who has been tuning in regularly on the web. She had plenty of questions about milk consumption, specifically regarding arguments against milk raised in a seminar by Pedro Bastos, who advocates the Paleo diet.

Dr. Peat, thank you for joining the show again. Would you introduce yourself and give a rundown of your professional academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied physiology in the Biology Department at the University of Oregon. I've been interested in endocrine biology and many other themes in biology since I was a child, but I didn't study it academically until 1968 to 1972 because I had a bad opinion of American biology from my high school experience. I have read many other national traditions in biology, so I take a critical approach to most of the things that I read.

**Andrew Murray:** The reason for tonight's show is to address some erroneous science suggesting inherent problems with using milk. Pedro Bastos mentioned that Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF) was stimulated strongly by milk. What do you have to say about IGF and its stimulation by milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has some of the features of insulin, but it and insulin are just two of our regulatory factors. When one of them is slightly distorted, we have so many other regulatory systems that nothing really changes much.

**Andrew Murray:** So you're saying there is no significant negative effect from the stimulation of IGF by milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you look at the functions in a given species, animals that are very big for their species have a high level of IGF. However, big mice have high levels, while elephants have very low levels. So, within a species, it has one kind of effect, but across the spectrum of animal species, it has a very different meaning. It is just part of a system.

Our whole system has long-range adaptive processes. Nutrition research has hardly scratched the surface of how nutrition works in developmental biology. Most nutrition research is done for the agricultural food industry—they want to know how to make big animals, not intelligent, long-lived animals. Some studies have found that your grandmother's nutritional level affects the development of your brain. In animal studies, you can see the influence of diet going on for four to five generations. Focusing on the size of the brain, for example, you can't determine anything in just one generation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when Pedro Bastos says milk is bad because it stimulates IGF, is that a theory not backed by evidence?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is not really enough science to know. It might turn out four or five generations from now that it is either good or bad. For example, people who drink milk might have great-grandchildren who are much smarter than they are.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** He claims it is a stimulator of cancer, but isn't it also a stimulator of healthy tissue growth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For example, a study of radiation effects in Japan looked at all factors of life and diet. They saw that people who didn't drink milk had a much higher risk of becoming demented in old age. A later study in the U.S. saw the same thing—that milk has anti-dementia properties.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there an anti-inflammatory component to it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They don't really know; that is just an association of big populations. But it could involve something like IGF. There are so many factors in milk. The high ratio of calcium to phosphorus is one of the extremely beneficial qualities of milk.

**Andrew Murray:** You are very big on calcium. Perhaps we can discuss how easily bioavailable the calcium in milk is compared to other foods.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The next best food, which people don't usually think of as food, is eggshell. I had a relative who cured his early youthful osteoporosis by having a tablespoon of powdered eggshell every day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That would be about 5,000 milligrams of calcium a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Something like that. That is in the neighborhood of what the Maasai people get during their lifetime—5,000 to 7,000 milligrams on average. A whole eggshell is maybe 2,000 milligrams of calcium carbonate.

However, the absorption of calcium in milk is greatly improved by the presence of lactose. When you compare different sugars, fructose is not as good as lactose, but it is still an important factor in helping to absorb calcium. Starch has a very poor effect on calcium absorption. When bone development was compared in rats made deficient in Vitamin D, one group was given starch as its carbohydrate, and the other was given sucrose. Despite being deficient in Vitamin D, the sucrose-fed rats had strong bones.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So sugar doesn't weaken your bones like we're told?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, it actually works parallel to thyroid and Vitamin D for stimulating metabolism. Calcium, the T3 component of the thyroid hormone, and fructose all have overlapping effects in activating respiratory metabolism.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people who drink lactose-free milk will not be absorbing as much calcium as people who drink normal milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right.

**Andrew Murray:** What about people who say they are lactose intolerant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies in Chinatown in San Francisco compared people who hadn't grown up drinking milk to people who had—same family, same genes. It is a matter of what you grow up exposed to. When you take someone who has grown up without it and have them drink a total of a glass and a half of milk a day—about half a glass at a time—in just two or three weeks, they induce the enzymes in their intestine.

When you look at factors responsible for losing those enzymes, a deficiency of progesterone and thyroid, or a bacterial infection of the small intestine, will cause the loss of those enzymes.

**Andrew Murray:** So a bacterial infection can directly cause a lack of enzyme production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and that usually develops in the upper part of the small intestine in people who are thyroid deficient. Starch tends to support that bacterial overgrowth more than fruit sugar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I found that once people get their overall nutrition in a better state, it becomes easier for them to digest milk.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can we talk about the anti-inflammatory effects of calcium? When we think of calcium, we usually just think of bones.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Adelle Davis talked about this in the 1950s. People think of calcifying kidneys and arteries and are afraid of the calcium in milk. But she pointed out research showing that people who have the least calcium in their diet have the most kidney stones and the most calcified arteries. That is because of the anti-inflammatory effect of calcium.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the extra calcium deposited in the arteries is coming from the bones in response to a deficiency?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The calcium in your diet, by having an anti-inflammatory and pro-thyroid effect, tends to direct the deposition of calcium into your bones. It keeps the production of carbon dioxide up by stimulating cell metabolism. The same carbon dioxide that deposits calcium into the bones prevents calcium from depositing in arteries and kidneys by keeping it in a soluble state.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you take enough in your diet, it goes from the milk to the bone. If you don't, it goes from the bone to your arteries.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the factors in osteoporosis is high cortisol or high prolactin. Both of those are caused by high serotonin. Serotonin, prolactin, and cortisol are all anti-bone formation. Calcium in your diet suppresses prolactin, cortisol, and serotonin, allowing the bone-building factors to be dominant.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Let's talk about how the sugar in milk helps your liver function better to manufacture more carbon dioxide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Any sugar helps. If you eat sucrose, it is similar to lactose, though not quite as effective for absorbing calcium. Sucrose in fruit, honey, or plain sugar is 50% fructose and 50% glucose. It takes a little fructose to catalyze the more energetic burning of glucose to produce carbon dioxide. You don't have to eat a pure sugar diet to have optimal carbon dioxide production, but it is okay to avoid starch entirely.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of keeping CO2 up, I know you've mentioned bag breathing to re-inspire expired air.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Something as simple as baking soda stimulates bone formation. The mechanism is carbon dioxide. The body has such an affinity for carbon dioxide that even though there is a high concentration inside your body compared to the atmosphere, if you put your arm or leg into a bag of carbon dioxide, it will flow into your body. The same applies to carbonated hot springs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why for broken bone treatment, they use CO2 treatment where you put your broken limb into a bag filled with carbon dioxide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you move to a high altitude or live in a submarine, your bones incorporate some of the CO2 out of your blood. People living at very high altitudes, once adapted, have blood coming out of their lungs that is more completely oxygenated. The effect of carbon dioxide improves the diffusion of gas from the air into the blood capillaries in the lungs.

**Andrew Murray:** Some argue that as a human race, we've been around for millions of years and only recently started drinking milk. What do you say to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of people have an imaginary history of the human race. Konrad Lorenz and his followers described the evolution of the "killer ape"—that a carnivorous ape made the transition into humankind, so meat was the basis of human evolution. Others say Africans living along coasts ate fish, so the brain is made of fish oil. But all of that is reading backwards into history from whatever people believe in the present.

**Andrew Murray:** Grains would also have been a fairly recent food.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, for the last 10,000 or 20,000 years civilizations have domesticated grains. Grain eating hasn't done anything great for the human brain or general health. So, insofar as the "Caveman diet" takes people away from a grain-based diet, it starts in the right direction. However, one of the bad features of the grains-and-nuts diet is a high phosphate content.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And a high meat diet also has high phosphate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, a high meat diet has that same drawback unless you eat eggshells or chew on the bones.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Does this bring up grass-fed milk versus grain-fed milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Fresh grass has a high ratio of Vitamin E to fatty acids. In grains, especially if stored, Vitamin E is depleted. Cows need Vitamin E in proportion to fatty acids because the bacteria in the cow's rumen destroy the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) in plant material. The bacteria hydrogenate those PUFAs so that 98% of the polyunsaturated fat is destroyed—*if* the cow has enough Vitamin E.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So fresh grass has more Vitamin E than grain and alfalfa.

**Andrew Murray:** What about organic milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. In the 1960s, Israel had one of the highest rates of breast cancer. They noticed their dairies were using Lindane. As soon as they banned the use of that pesticide, their breast cancer rate came down to the European and U.S. level.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the truth regarding the presence of estrogens in milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The amount in milk is maybe up to 1 microgram per quart. Estrogen is really as much a male hormone as a female one. Natural estrogen is processed in both men and women and detoxified fairly quickly. About 85% of the estrogen in milk is attached to either sulfate or glucuronic acid, which prepares it to be excreted by the kidneys. A birth control pill has 30 micrograms. No one drinks 30 liters of milk in a day.

**Andrew Murray:** What about homogenization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pressure breaks the particle of fat up into such a small size that it doesn't separate. Presumably, that makes unstable fats oxidize faster, so it has a small harmful effect. But considering the alternatives in a supermarket, other foods are going to be much more dangerous as oxidants.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I've heard the theory that homogenization breaks the fat molecule so small it blocks arteries. Is that rubbish?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When we secrete bile, the soapy material in the bile breaks up all the fats we eat into particles of about that same size, which do get directly into the bloodstream. That is the chylomicron system.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So would you consider raw milk nutritionally superior?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. It is nutritionally better. But that doesn't mean you should eat soybeans or bread if you can't get raw milk.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It also depends on what the cows are eating.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you get milk from a dairy with only a few cows, what the cow ate the preceding day has a big effect on taste and allergenicity. If you pool milk from a thousand cows, it becomes a standardized product. Also, most milk has at least 20 times as much progesterone as estrogen. If you did get some active estrogen, the progesterone is more than enough to counteract its effect.

**Caller:** I would like to address the nutritional value of goat milk and fresh goat cheese. I feel like it's less mucus-forming.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The composition is definitely different, but again, it depends on what the goat was eating. When I was a child, a neighbor came back from the war with malaria. As soon as he was able to drink his daily goat milk, he didn't have malaria attacks. Once, when he was in the veterans' hospital for a checkup, he had an attack, they wouldn't let him get his goat milk, and he died.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I've heard goat milk protein is smaller and more easily digestible.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've heard that quite a bit. There are so many chemical differences I wouldn't guess what was most important.

**Andrew Murray:** If people refuse to drink milk or take eggshells, what else can they do to get sufficient calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you eat most of your carbohydrate as fruit and avoid grains to avoid excess phosphate, then probably an eggshell a day will give you all the calcium you need.

**Andrew Murray:** But if they refuse eggshells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suppose a leaf-based diet would eventually provide enough calcium. However, in an experiment where rats were given fresh vegetables versus canned vegetables, the ones getting canned vegetables lived perfectly well, while the others wasted away because they couldn't assimilate the nutrients. The vegetables need to be well-cooked.

**Caller:** I have a question regarding evaporated milk and thickening agents like carrageenan.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have an article on my website about carrageenan. A few years ago, I started getting sick on cream from an organic producer and saw they were using carrageenan. The same happened with ice cream. Many cheeses add gums as carriers for flavoring agents. One researcher has demonstrated in animal experiments that carrageenan is carcinogenic. The FDA allows it because they say only "degraded" carrageenan is carcinogenic, but bacteria in your intestine degrade it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And evaporated milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is heavily oxidized, which is why it tastes bad.

**Caller:** My question is about sprouted grain breads and sourdough breads.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just the soaking process activates enzymes in the dough. 8 to 12 hours of being moistened allows enzymes to break down phytic acid into inositol and phosphate. Gluten is also partly broken down. The protein quality actually increases because gluten carries many nitrogen-rich amino acids which make it allergenic. When enzymes release the nitrogen, it can be used to make new, different proteins.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people eating a lot of grains get a lot of phosphorus, similar to people eating a lot of meat. Both are out of balance regarding calcium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Americans often have a 7-to-1 phosphate-to-calcium ratio. Milk is about 1.3-to-1 in favor of calcium. The long-range optimum is probably between 1-to-1 and 2-to-1 in favor of calcium.

**Caller:** I want to bring up the issue of raw milk availability and government interference.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone should have their own cow next door. My father built a barn that looked like a little cottage, so it made the neighborhood look residential, not like a farm.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You mentioned earlier that pro-pasteurization support comes from the NIH and SAIC.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, one of the articles warning about dangerous estrogen in milk was done by a partnership of the NIH and SAIC (Science Applications International Corporation). They are effectively a branch of the defense and surveillance industry.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Why are they pro-pasteurization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is motivated by a kind of class war to make food cheaper. In the 1930s, there was a campaign against breastfeeding and advocating early feeding of beans and bread. They are doing that again in poor communities. They don't want people on food stamps buying "fancy" food like milk, meat, and eggs.

**Caller:** Would the phosphorus and calcium effect be more wholesome if taken as yogurt?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Normal American yogurt retains the lactic acid-rich whey. Strained Greek yogurt (like Fage) removes the whey and the lactic acid. It is not good to replace milk with tart yogurt because of the harmful effect on the liver.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lactic acid burdens your liver, causing a tendency toward hypoglycemia by preventing glycogen storage. Lactic acid also produces fibrosis, inflammation, and contributes to cancer metabolism.

**Caller:** You usually say serotonin is bad, but I've always heard it's a "feel good" hormone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies of aggression in dogs show that when treated with SSRI drugs, their aggression subsided because their serotonin went *down*. Serotonin is a hormone of withdrawal, anxiety, and metabolic suppression. It is an emergency anti-stress hormone. When you are chronically stressed, it causes stomach ulcers, fibrosis, hardening of the arteries, and osteoporosis. Depression is actually associated with high serotonin conditions.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We've been brainwashed to believe it's a feel-good hormone so drug companies could sell SSRIs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those patents are expiring, so they will be coming out with new antidepressants, and we'll stop hearing so much about serotonin.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for joining us, Dr. Peat. For listeners who want more information, his website is www.raypeat.com. There are plenty of scholarly articles referenced there. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Sugar Myths I
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month’s *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture all our own certified organic herbal extracts.

You’re invited to call in with any questions either related or unrelated to this month's topic. It is perhaps a mixed topic, but a topic about sugar: Sugar is good for you.

We are very pleased and excited to have Dr. Raymond Peat join us on the show to share his years of wisdom and research. He helps us understand the erroneous statements that the medical industry and the scientific community make that so easily fool us into believing what they're saying is true. We want to dedicate the show to exposing some of the myths about sugar, and especially the myths about the link between sugar, obesity, diabetes, and heart disease.

There is another doctor, Dr. Uffe Ravnskov, who has produced many books, one of which is *The Cholesterol Myths*. I know we're talking about sugar, but there are definite links between sugar, lipids, and the general obesity and heart disease epidemic. Dr. Peat will bring those out and show how erroneous some of the statements about sugar have been. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for joining us once again. I’d appreciate it if you would let people know your scientific background.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started in graduate school. I had been reading on my own, but I decided to study physiology in the biology department at the University of Oregon in 1968. Since then, I've been pretty much full-time working in physiology-related things. Reproductive endocrinology was what I did my dissertation on—how oxidative metabolism interacts with aging, estrogen, and so on to regulate fertility and sterility.

Part of that thesis work involved the aging of metabolism and how oxygen came to be wasted more and more with aging, or under the influence of stress or high estrogen. The age pigment, lipofuscin, was one of the things that I found was involved in high estrogen and aging or stress or radiation damage. Lipofuscin is a breakdown product of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), largely with other things bound into little brown lumps in the cells. It consumes oxygen and wastes energy and eventually can kill the cell. But its main function seems to be to waste oxygen and energy.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And those are those little brown spots that people call age spots or liver spots?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, spots on your skin. They form in the brain, on the skin, everywhere. They tend to get formed faster and faster the more stress you're under. Pretty soon, if you're under the influence of unopposed estrogen, they can just eat all the oxygen and not leave any for the cell functions. That was what really started me getting interested in unsaturated fat metabolism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I did that dissertation in 1972. That was the year that John Yudkin published his book, *Pure, White and Deadly*. I read that and was so impressed by his arguments that sugar increases blood lipids, saturated fats, and cholesterol, that that was what started me on the idea of recommending increased sugar for people who are under stress.

I had already become convinced that there was no basis at all for the connection between high cholesterol, saturated fats, and atherosclerosis or heart disease. When I would see someone deficient in progesterone, having too much estrogen and age pigment, they would often recover if they could increase their cholesterol production. The simplest way to do that was to have them eat some extra sugar. That started me seeing the therapeutic possibilities of sugar.

From there I worked backwards, understanding where the lipid hypothesis had come from, and especially the doctrine that essential fatty acids are essential nutritionally. Since they are what lipofuscin is made from, it seemed increasingly important to understand how that theory came about.

I saw that George and Mildred Burr were the ones who created that idea in 1929 and 1930. In their experiment, they didn't at that time know about most of the essential nutrients, vitamins, and minerals. They fed what they thought was a complete diet. When they eliminated the linoleic and related so-called essential fatty acids, their animals developed skin symptoms and various things that they called the "Burr disease."

Their diet used a high sugar content, a little starch, and protein casein that had been highly purified. They recrystallized the sugar and precipitated the casein to eliminate all vitamins and minerals from it, and then added what they thought were the essential nutrients. So the animals, when they removed linoleic acid from their diet, developed these scaly tail symptoms.

Three years after that, George Burr put one of his rats under a bell jar and saw that it was burning oxygen at a 50% faster rate than the rats getting the normal essential fatty acid diet. He decided that was because their skin was leaky. He said the essential fatty acids create a barrier in the skin—just making this up out of whole cloth.

The same journals where George and Mildred Burr published these ideas had already published articles by several well-known researchers showing that animals were healthier *without* fats in their diet, lived longer, and didn't get cancer. But the Burrs absolutely ignored the counter-evidence and published their doctrine. Their financiers supported them, but the world didn't pay much attention to it.

Fifteen years later, in the mid-1940s, Roger Williams' famous lab at the University of Texas had been working on discovering new B vitamins and essential minerals. They created the exact diet that Burr had fed the rats, created the so-called Burr disease, and then cured it by supplementing them with Vitamin B6.

What had happened was that on a high sugar diet, the animals were burning calories 50% faster than normal. On a terribly deficient diet, they got scaly skin largely because of a Vitamin B6 deficiency. That pretty much ruined the Burrs' scientific accomplishment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Meanwhile, the pig industry had problems with the chemical they were using to reduce feed intake, shut down thyroid function, and make pigs get fat cheaply. They found that by substituting a high polyunsaturated fat diet—soybeans and corn—they could suppress the thyroid just as well as using that toxic drug and make them get fat on a small food intake. The Burr's "essential fatty acids" turned out to be what was suppressing the thyroid.

At the same time, the seed oil industry was losing its market for extracting these unsaturated fats to use in paint and plastic manufacture. That turned the whole seed oil industry toward food. They found they could increase the sales of these extracted seed oils by promoting the idea that they were healthful for human consumption. They had been hardening them to make margarine, but by promoting their health benefits, they could sell them directly as liquid cooking oils and salad oils.

To do that, they found that a biological effect was that they lowered cholesterol production or lowered the cholesterol that appeared in the blood (causing it to increase in the liver as a defensive reaction). They created the doctrine of cholesterol as the cause of heart disease and told people to eat more of the unsaturated fats. Even though they knew that they would create obesity, as they did in the pig industry, they convinced doctors by a huge campaign that cholesterol was found in the wall of arteries that were developing atherosclerosis. Since you could lower the cholesterol in the blood, they argued that you would lower the cholesterol in the wall of the artery and prevent heart disease.

Ravnskov much later showed that none of those arguments had any evidence to support them. Atherosclerosis didn't have a direct connection to heart disease mortality. Cholesterol in the blood didn't have a connection directly with the formation of atherosclerosis. And saturated fats didn't create the cholesterol in the blood.

There was a slight backsliding in the ability to sell doctors on the idea of eating unsaturated fats to lower cholesterol. There was a study with veterans in which putting them on the liquid oil diet, eliminating saturated fats, caused more of them to die of heart disease and a lot more of them to die of cancer. So there was some problem with that lipid theory already in the 1960s.

John Yudkin came out in 1972 arguing that sugar caused heart disease because it increased cholesterol. Since I knew that cholesterol didn't have anything to do with heart disease—except protecting against it to some extent—that was where I started realizing that he was right on the issue that sugar would increase cholesterol in some people.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't the Japanese come out with a study recently that showed when they actually took off an atherosclerotic plaque, it had a cholesterol bandage over oxidized, rancid vegetable oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Cholesterol protects every cell. It's increased in the location that's being injured especially, but it's necessary for healthy cell division, DNA replication, nerve function, and learning. It's our most basic anti-stress protective substance.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So those oxidized vegetable oils were damaging the arterial wall, and if the cholesterol wasn't there, it couldn't have stopped the rancidity and oxidation, and it could have caused more problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. And what starts the inflammation in the artery wall and everywhere else is the breakdown of the essential fatty acids into the free radical products and lipofuscin. You can extract lipofuscin from every arterial plaque and every degenerative tissue. You find the breakdown products, but you don't find fresh polyunsaturated fats because they're unstable; they break down quickly. What you find is the cholesterol that's there repairing the tissue, the saturated fats that didn't break down, and the lipofuscin, which is the essential fatty acid insult.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just for our listeners to understand, this unsaturated fatty acid is all liquid vegetable oils that are commonly sold and things are fried in. It also includes fish oils, omega-3 oils, omega-6 oils, flaxseed oil, and hemp seed oil. All of these are very unstable products. They can go rancid outside the body, even at room temperature. Once you ingest them, they can go rancid very quickly because we're warm and full of oxygen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In an experiment, I put a little clear plastic tube into the cork of a bottle of safflower or corn oil and put the other end in a cup of water. Sitting at room temperature, you could see the water being sucked up into the tube as the oil sitting there was consuming oxygen and becoming rancid even at room temperature. It is much faster at body temperature.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, sugar is probably the second most maligned substance after cholesterol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That guy was calling it "Pure, White and Deadly." He said that it raised the cholesterol. Well, now that they've proven that cholesterol doesn't cause heart disease and sugar raises cholesterol, that makes sugar a good guy. So what else are they saying about sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Professor Lustig at the University of California, San Francisco, in his famous lecture uses the words "toxic," "poison," and "evil." Someone counted 18 times in an hour-and-a-half lecture.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** He was referring to fructose. The sugar that's found in fruit is toxic, evil, and deadly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since sucrose is 50% fructose, he was applying it to sucrose too, or the high fructose corn syrup which is almost 50% fructose. He was saying that it's just like alcohol in being toxic to the liver. That's one of the weirdest things he said, because for many years people have been showing that fructose detoxifies many things that enter the liver, including alcohol. It can almost double the rate of destruction of alcohol and prevent liver damage in the process. Many other toxins are detoxified in the presence of fructose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about honey? Honey is mainly fructose, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About half. Honey and more purified fructoses have been used to treat diabetes, stomach ulcers, and other things. Sugar has been used to cure wounds. In emergency situations where they didn't have antibiotics, they found they could do open heart surgery and pack the wound with pure white sucrose to prevent scarring and promote healing better than the fancy antibiotics. Honey was used for thousands of years that way to cure wounds.

In the 1970s, there were many articles advocating the use of fructose in the diabetic diet because it had become economically pretty cheap. It could be added practically to anyone's diet to improve the regulation of blood glucose. But that idea goes back to 1874; someone showed that it metabolized better in diabetics than other sugars. Even earlier, in 1856 or 1857, sucrose was used to cure diabetes.

**Andrew Murray:** Why does mainstream medical science want to promote the idea that sugar is so bad for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's this momentum. They're committed to the mistaken cholesterol lipid theory of heart disease. I think Yudkin sort of tilted the scale, and all of the ranting against cholesterol and animal fat has just slid over to concentrate on sugar and fructose.

**Andrew Murray:** For people listening, a very good scientific reference is Dr. Uffe Ravnskov. He has produced about 10 books and over 80 scientific articles completely disputing the cholesterol myths. It’s a glaring example of where cholesterol has been mentioned as the evil you have to use drugs to lower, when actually it's a very protective compound. I was looking at articles citing the many antimicrobial protective effects of cholesterol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the same with toxins. As early as 1915 or 1920, people were showing that cholesterol would protect against toxins as well as infectious things. Ravnskov did some studies on triglycerides showing that they are also anti-infective. Other people have shown that they are anti-inflammatory.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We're told that HDLs are the good guys and you want high HDL.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're all good in the sense that they are there to protect you.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But when they're in elevated levels, it's showing that there is something else wrong. Like if you're low thyroid, you can have a total cholesterol of 300.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If you take alcohol or estrogen, your HDL will go up. But also if you take chlorinated hydrocarbons and other things, they'll go up.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to sugar and the erroneous link between sugar, obesity, diabetes, and heart disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same thing that Burr demonstrated—his diet was mostly plain sucrose, and his animals respired 50% faster than animals on a normal diet. That's been seen over and over. Fructose in particular, even a small amount added to a standard diet, will catalyze the oxidation of other substances, glucose and fat both. But mostly it catalyzes the use of glucose, turning it to carbon dioxide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it helps your cells use oxygen more efficiently and respire better.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. That increase is just about 30% to 50% in all of the publications where they've looked at it.

**Andrew Murray:** And the increased CO2 is also very beneficial. That's another misconception—that CO2 is bad and oxygen is good—but it's actually the other way around.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experimenters who have given a fructose supplement to diabetics see that they respond just as well or better than people without diabetes in the ability to oxidize fructose and produce energy. One group looked at the fructose that's normally present in everyone's bloodstream and compared it to diabetics. title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Sugar Myths II
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Hi and welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And my name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, we're both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi.

**Andrew Murray:** First of all, for the benefit of any new listeners, would you like to describe your academic and research background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My academic career went from linguistics to biology, and there was a continuity of a sort. From studying grammar and the structure of language, I moved to thinking about strictly biological questions. In linguistics, I was concentrating on how culture interacts with the structure of language. I was seeing the evolution of understanding in the culture as being what shapes the way the grammar itself works.

For various reasons, I switched over to biology, thinking to understand the brain better—the brain as the organ that carries culture and language. When I went from brain work to reproductive physiology, I was still interested in those questions of how the context interacts with the structure. Going from the brain to other aspects of physiology, I saw that the environment is a part of the organism. That accounts for my orientation in biology: concentrating on the interaction moment by moment between the animal and the environment.

**Andrew Murray:** Before we get started on a continuation of last month's subject—sugars and the debunking of the cholesterol heart disease myth—I think it would be useful to understand your perspective. You've spent 40 years researching these areas. How often do you find that mainstream science conflicts with the evidence that you find?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was a constant, almost daily experience in my attending lectures. I was really surprised anytime a professor said anything that I thought really related meaningfully to the biological facts. There was a book used as a text called *Classical Papers in Genetics*. Reading through that, I couldn't find any case in which the facts were honestly presented. It was really a little handbook of ideology. My experience with the academic science people was that they are very heavy on ideology and very light on facts. I almost never saw a science professor in the science library, and I spent many years every day reading in the library.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's get into the meat of this month's program on sugars. In your last newsletter, you mentioned that the addition of fructose to glucose during intraportal infusion increased the net glucose uptake, even when insulin secretion was compromised, as in diabetics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They refer to that as a catalytic property of fructose. It doesn't just increase the metabolism and uptake of glucose, but it increases the whole metabolism of the animal. Restrict the glucose to the baby, and the brain is smaller; feed it extra glucose, and the brain is bigger.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just to go over a little bit of sugar science for our listeners: Everybody's familiar with white sugar, which is sucrose. Sucrose is half fructose and half glucose. All fruits contain approximately the same ratio of fructose and glucose as white sugar. However, other sources of carbohydrates like grains, beans, starches, bread, pasta, and potatoes are almost all glucose; they are devoid of fructose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And the only place fructose slows down glucose is in the absorption from the intestine. Fructose itself is slow to be absorbed compared to glucose. If you eat starch like white rice or white bread, you'll get a very sharp increase in blood glucose. That stimulates insulin to handle the rising glucose, and that stimulates cortisol to prevent the reverse reaction from too much insulin. But when you eat sugar, the glucose half is broken off and the fructose lags a little bit in being absorbed.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's why it's a safer sugar for diabetics?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The glucose from the sugar gets absorbed, and then the smaller amount of fructose coming in accelerates the absorption of the glucose by the various tissues—not just the liver, but brain, kidney, heart, everything. It is fulfilling some of insulin's responsibility without having to call on the insulin. Under some circumstances, it can actually inhibit the release of insulin, preventing the spiking of insulin while taking care of insulin's work.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So, a diabetic's problem is that they have high sugar in their blood, and they need their cells to pick that up. When the fructose is combined with the glucose, the fructose is actually helping the cells pick up the glucose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It stimulates the cells to take up glucose very much the way insulin does. You can't distinguish the effects on some of the crucial enzymes. Fructose, and the pyruvic acid that it turns into, stimulate the enzymes that oxidize pyruvic acid just the same way insulin stimulates that same enzyme. One replaces the other perfectly.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If a diabetic eats whole grains or beans, they don't have the same ability to use that sugar because it's mainly glucose. They end up with elevated sugar numbers and elevated insulin. Diabetics are told to avoid orange juice and white sugar and eat whole grains, but that's exactly the opposite of what I've seen work in our clinic. When diabetics avoid the starches and eat honey, white sugar, and fruits, their sugar numbers become much more manageable.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was in 1874 that someone first published a paper on the fact that fructose is metabolized by diabetics where glucose isn't. After the publication of that paper, it was fairly common for people to recommend the use of fructose or sucrose to diabetics rather than plain glucose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You don't often find a food that just has white sugar or honey in it. It's usually combined with a carbohydrate or fat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Worse than that, polyunsaturated fats are very often combined as shortening in bakery products. The enzyme I mentioned before, pyruvic dehydrogenase—which is activated by insulin or fructose to handle the oxidation of glucose—happens to be activated also by saturated fatty acids, but it is *inhibited* by polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA).

They interfere with the ability to oxidize glucose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Don't they also destroy the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Every place you look, the polyunsaturated fats contribute to diabetes and obesity.

**Andrew Murray:** What's your opinion on the possibility of regenerating islet cells in the pancreas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar itself, sucrose, is known to stimulate the regeneration of beta cells. That was in my newsletter about a year ago, describing the early treatment of diabetes with glucose and looking at new in vitro studies where sugar stimulates regeneration and polyunsaturated fats kill the beta cells. Sugar often gets the blame for things the polyunsaturated fats do, such as the glycation of hemoglobin (HbA1c). Most of the so-called glycation is really the oxidative breakdown fragments of the polyunsaturated fats.

**Andrew Murray:** So a person's HbA1c could be lowered if they avoided all polyunsaturated oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** A really bad example of a way to eat sugar is a donut: white flour (glucose) fried in canola, sunflower, or corn oil (PUFA). There you have a saturated fat and the fruit providing fructose.

**Andrew Murray:** You also mentioned fat peroxidation involved in the degenerative disease process. Despite fructose increasing the production of uric acid, you noted that uric acid is an endogenous anti-inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's considered to be our main antioxidant. Most inflammatory signals come from oxidative breakdown products. Uric acid is our basic antioxidant and a major anti-inflammatory factor.

**Andrew Murray:** But the oxidation of these polyunsaturates has a very strong inflammatory effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The fish oil type breaks down much faster than the seed oils. By the time it gets from your food into your bloodstream, there is so much free radical activity that it poisons some of your enzymes involved in immunity. That immune-suppressive effect is what people mistake for an anti-inflammatory effect in fish oils. The seed oils don't even have that temporary toxic apparent benefit; they are flat-out inflammatory.

**Andrew Murray:** There was a study where people were given a 300-calorie drink containing either glucose, fructose, or orange juice. Those receiving the glucose had a large increase in oxidative inflammatory stress, but it was absent in those receiving the fructose or orange juice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That has ramifications for the immune system and bone cells. About 35 years ago, someone fed groups of rats either a high starch diet or a high sugar diet. Some groups were Vitamin D deficient. The Vitamin D deficient group on starch had rickets-type bones—poorly calcified and weak. But those on the high sucrose diet without Vitamin D had strong, well-calcified bones. It apparently was the increased carbon dioxide production from the catalyzed higher metabolic rate. Carbon dioxide is largely responsible for proper calcification of bone.

**Andrew Murray:** Does a higher CO2 content actually allow extracellular calcium to move into bone stores?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The first bone material laid down is calcium carbonate. In vitro experiments showed that you can have an acidic condition as long as it's based on carbon dioxide and have strong bones. The same amount of lactic acid pH will cause dissolution of the bones. Starch tends to produce a shift towards lactic acid rather than carbon dioxide.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this why you say oxidative exercise like aerobics or jogging is bad for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It has taken about 40 years for the science to get to the trainers, but the East Europeans were the first to limit the training their athletes did. They won a lot of Olympic medals by "under training"—cutting the exercise short before the lactic acid rises enough to poison the system. A minute or two is enough. Lactic acid turns on the stress hormones that destroy your muscles, nerves, and bones.

**Andrew Murray:** And aerobic exercise depletes your own CO2 stores.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The typical well-trained long-distance runner has been found to have basically defective lung function. The chronic elevation of lactic acid causes thickening of the air sacs, making the path of oxygen diffusion longer, so it poorly oxygenates their blood. It leads first to water-logging inflammation and eventually to fibrosis.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's talk about the brown sugar movement—the idea that brown sugar, raw sugar, or molasses is a better replacement for white sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In an extreme situation of poverty, crude brown foods—brown bread, brown rice, molasses—are important sources of nutrients. But when people start eating more fat and protein, they can stand to lose the nutrients in those to gain freedom from toxins and inflammation. In molasses, it turns brown partly because the sugars are being caramelized. Minerals catalyze the oxidation, combining sugar molecules and changing them. These become, to various degrees, toxic, allergenic, and even potentially carcinogenic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's a natural tendency for people who have a hormone imbalance, especially hypothyroidism, to crave sugar. I suddenly had no more sugar cravings and could go eight hours without getting shaky.

**Caller 1:** He's had kidney stones. Aren't those influenced by sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think so. Only in the sense that if you let sugar displace sources of calcium, magnesium, and protein, then you tend to form stones. Parathyroid hormone and inflammatory factors tend to create mineralization of soft tissues and stones.

**Caller 1:** What test should he get?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D3 is one relevant thing.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The fact that he's adding white sugar to his coffee is probably protective. Coffee lowers your blood sugar. If he has pure black coffee, he'll end up lowering his blood sugar. If he's craving sugars, he's probably figured out that coffee with sugar makes him feel better. It's easier for his body to use the white sugar than a pile of pancakes. He should get his thyroid and Vitamin D checked.

**Caller 2 (Tesha):** I want to encourage listeners to listen with an open heart. Could you expound on the importance of balance? When you consume sugar, you need fat and protein, and vice versa.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The amino acids in protein are strong stimulants of insulin secretion. If you eat protein without sugar, the insulin will lower your blood sugar. To prevent the blood sugar from dropping, you produce adrenaline or cortisol. If your liver doesn't have glycogen stored, you depend on cortisol, which activates the conversion of protein to sugar and fat. You end up destroying a big part of the protein you've just eaten.

To handle protein efficiently, you need glucose or fructose to steady your blood sugar. The fat does several things: saturated fat works with fructose and insulin to handle glucose oxidation, and fat slows absorption so you don't get a surge of glucose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So everything has to be kept in balance with proteins and good saturated fats like coconut oil and butter.

**Andrew Murray:** Some top fructose sources that also contain glucose are dates (32% fructose, plus B vitamins and minerals) and raisins. What do you think about agave?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you give us examples of good food combining?

**Caller 3:** I wanted to ask about dextrose. I see it in medicine. Also, regarding Steve Jobs and pancreatic cancer—what helps regenerate pancreatic cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Dextrose is just another word for glucose. Starch turns into that. It is great stuff in itself when balanced with fructose, saturated fat, minerals, and vitamins. **Caller 4:** What about kidney?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Same thing. Endotoxin absorbed from poorly digested plant material interferes with glucose oxidation and prevents the activation of thyroid hormone. **Caller 4:** I stopped doing milk. I eat eggs maybe twice a week.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You want to try to get at least 80 grams of good protein every day. If you aren't doing dairy, calcium would be the main thing to concentrate on. You should try powdering eggshells.

**Andrew Murray:** We need to wrap up. Thank you, Dr. Peat, so much for joining us. For those who have heard this evening's show, please check his website, www.raypeat.com. There are scientific reference articles to back up everything you've heard.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Energy Production, Diabetes and Saturated Fats
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Hi and welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, we're both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in Herbal Medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture all our own certified organic herb extracts.

We're very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us. He is an endocrinologist and researcher with many years of experience, here to illuminate some of the misinformation that's so prevalent in the medical literature. The topic this month is the misinformation concerning energy production, diabetes, and saturated fats. Dr. Peat, thank you for joining us again. For new listeners, could you give an overview of your background and education?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've studied a lot of different things, but my biological study was at the University of Oregon. I spent four years there working on a PhD. I started out thinking I was going to do nerve and brain biology, but the people in that section were so dogmatic. I looked around and found that the reproductive physiology and aging people were actually scientifically oriented. So, I shifted over and did my dissertation on the hormones, physiology, and energy metabolism of the aging reproductive system.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you're very interested in maintaining good thyroid function. We have found that to be a key cornerstone to maintaining biological energy production, which is important in fighting the negative effects of environmental materials that lower our metabolic energy. One of the main stumbling blocks seems to be the misinformation regarding saturated fats versus polyunsaturated fats (PUFA). Is that correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think so. The people who created the idea of the "essential fatty acids" actually did an experiment a few years later with one of their lab people that showed why people should *not* eat the so-called essential fatty acids.

In 1929, when the Burrs published their claim that the polyunsaturated fats—linoleic acid and linolenic acid—were essential for life, other biologists had shown that animals were healthier when they had no fat in their diet. They had almost no cancer spontaneously developing. The Burrs simply ignored the evidence that the fats were harmful. Other biologists ignored the Burrs for about 20 years because the evidence was so overwhelmingly against their claims.

However, in their faith that those fats were essential, one of their lab people agreed to go on a fat-free diet for six months. His health remarkably improved. His blood lipids changed somewhat—cholesterol went down a little and triglycerides went up a little—but the total lipid quantity stayed about the same. Crucially, he didn't get tired after a day's work, as he always had, and his lifelong weekly migraine headaches disappeared forever.

**Andrew Murray:** So how did these oils become so popular?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nothing really assured the support of their position until the seed oil industry wanted to market their liquid seed oil—cottonseed oil, linseed oil, soybean oil, and so on. They brought the Burrs out of obscurity. They said, "Since they have proven that linoleic and linolenic acid are essential for life, we'll get the public to eat them in huge quantities and treat them as drugs rather than as trace nutrients."

They claimed these fats would make the skin healthier. But the counter-evidence showed that many animal diseases—degenerative brain disease, atrophy of the gonads, infertility—were connected with eating too much of the unsaturated fats. Vitamin E was found to protect against that damage.

It was a marketing campaign to sell the idea that not only are those fats essential, but they are good for you and will prevent heart disease. But very soon, people started producing evidence showing that linoleic acid not only causes heart disease but promotes cancer and immune problems.

**Andrew Murray:** These PUFAs are the fish oils, hemp seed oil, canola, etc.?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the 1950s, they were feeding a lot of fish to mink in farms, and they were producing what was called "yellow fat disease," which was related to the age pigment lipofuscin—a brown pigment that develops from the breakdown of the polyunsaturated fats. So, the fish oils, right along with the seed oils, were seen to be toxic in the 50s and 60s.

By the 1970s, linoleic acid was being recognized as a major cause of heart disease and cancer. Since they had sold the public on the idea of essential fatty acids, they just changed the story. They said, "Well, fish oils or linseed oil are a *different* kind of fat. They aren't the Omega-6 oils like the deadly linoleic acid; they're the Omega-3." But those had already been incriminated with yellow fat disease and lipofuscin.

**Andrew Murray:** So they just switched tactics to the Omega-3s.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and that's where we are now with the fish oil craze.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What I find interesting is looking at our clients' blood work. A lot of clients have elevated liver enzymes, and when they start eating coconut oil, those enzymes come down.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A researcher on hepatitis and cirrhosis, Nanji, has shown for years that polyunsaturated fats injure the liver. I think it started with an Indian researcher noticing that in the butter regions of India, alcoholics didn't develop hepatitis or cirrhosis. He tested his observation on rats and found that if he fed them unsaturated oils, alcohol caused cirrhosis and hepatitis. If he fed them saturated fats, it didn't. Nanji tried that on his patients and found that their liver condition improved if he gave them a lot of sugar and saturated fat, and got worse if he fed them fish oils or seed oils.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't you say that when people take fish oils and they have high cholesterol, the cholesterol moves out of the blood and into the tissues as a stress response? So the blood test looks better, but it's just stored in the tissues?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Cholesterol is one of our most important protective antitoxins. For the unsaturated fats to lower the total production and the level in the blood is part of why they are something to avoid. The liver knows to retain any cholesterol it can because it is needed for cell division and function. All internal cellular processes rely on both cholesterol and saturated fatty acids.

If you overdose on polyunsaturated fats, all these intracellular mechanisms are deranged. The spindle that helps the cell divide and separates the chromosomes requires cholesterol and saturated fats to function. You get deranged expression of genes and deranged cell division if you have too much polyunsaturated fat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Humans have been eating saturated fats for thousands of years. They didn't make seed oils or corn oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The safe oils are butter, chocolate fat (which is mostly stearic acid), coconut oil, palm kernel oil, beef fat, lamb fat, and olive oil.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** People think of pork fat and chicken fat as bad fats, and they actually *are* bad fats because of what they feed the pigs and chickens. Unlike ruminant animals with multiple stomachs (beef, lamb), the chicken and pork fats are just as bad as the corn oil because the animals are eating corn.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They're now farming fish and feeding them some of the same foods they feed chickens and pigs. Interestingly, fish that live in cold oceans get their fats from plankton. The plankton fat is made by algae, which is where the Omega-3 fats come from. Basically, what we call fish fat is algae fat.

In experiments, they have given warm-blooded animals extra fish oil, or given fish a diet containing less unsaturated fat—like chicken fat or anchovy oil—and tested their endurance. The rats getting the fish oil had less endurance. Even the salmon on a pure fish oil diet had less endurance than when they were getting chicken fat or a less polyunsaturated fat. Fish oil isn't even so great for fish.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about farmed shrimp?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The good thing about anything growing in the ocean is that it has access to selenium, iodine, and other trace minerals. Things grown inland depend on whatever is in the soil, so they are often deficient in selenium and copper.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you explained that the problems with these oils hinge on the fact that we need an excess of metabolic energy to cope with insults from foods, drugs, or toxins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Diabetes is a good model of the energy-deprived state. Several years ago, someone suggested that Alzheimer's disease was "diabetes of the brain." People are seeing the effects of inflammation in all degenerative diseases. Inflammation involves a failure of energy and a shift to the diabetic metabolism, in which all you can do with glucose is mainly make lactic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** Which poisons you again, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Lactic acid is pro-inflammatory and doesn't produce enough energy for normal function. The essence of diabetes was pointed out by Randle in 1963 when he observed that if you increase the free fatty acids in the blood, you very quickly make the cells unable to use glucose.

**Andrew Murray:** It shifts their metabolism away from glucose directly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's now been worked out that there are two clear points where free fatty acids inhibit the use of glucose: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (which you need to burn glucose) and they stimulate glucagon. Glucagon turns on the synthesis of glucose at the expense of protein. Glucagon then stimulates the release of *more* fatty acids.

There are several points where free fatty acids activate adrenaline, ACTH, cortisol, TSH, and glucagon—all of which increase the release of free fatty acids from your fat storage. It seems illogical for the body to create those vicious circles where an energy failure turns on exactly what caused it. But it turns out that it's only the *polyunsaturated* fatty acids that have those terrible anti-energy effects.

If you compare stearic acid (butter/beef fat) and linoleic acid (corn oil), the butter turns off adrenaline and cortisol, while the corn oil turns them on. The excitotoxic system in the brain that kills brain cells is activated by polyunsaturated fats.

**Andrew Murray:** So these promote Alzheimer's and other degenerative diseases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and they are calmed by stearic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So these bad oils can cause diabetes by blocking your use of sugar, keeping blood sugar high, and also cause Alzheimer's.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look up the "saturation index," studies have found that people with cancer had much more polyunsaturated fat in the tumor and in their bodies than healthy people. Putting rodents on a high saturated fat diet delayed their development of breast cancer. Similarly, adding polyunsaturated fats shortened the lives of animals with a tendency toward heart disease, while a high saturated fat diet greatly extended their lives.

In recent years, people are seeing that the level of free fatty acids—which in our population means mostly unsaturated fats—has an extremely close connection to your likelihood of dying from just about anything: shock, aging, cancer, heart disease, and infection.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Isn't this something good for a diabetic to test?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It's been recognized for years that niacin is effective for not only heart disease but diabetes simply because it lowers the free fatty acids. But that isn't catching on because it's so cheap.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What are food sources of niacinamide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All animal foods have a reasonable amount: liver, milk, eggs. Coffee also has a lot of niacin.

**Caller 1:** I have a friend who has difficulty digesting fats because of hereditary gallbladder difficulties. Are there any enzymes, supplements, or herbs that would help in the digestion of fats? He has difficulty eating red meats and pork, but not so much fish or poultry.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's a great tendency for hypothyroid people to have gallbladder disease and trouble digesting fats. The best thing to do for gallbladder disease is to improve thyroid function. Avoiding unsaturated fats in all forms is very important for thyroid function.

The myth tells us that the only difference between unsaturated and saturated fatty acids is their shape. But really, the absolute difference is the way they bind to proteins. Since the basic framework of the cell is protein, saturated fats bind properly, while unsaturated fats bind to proteins they shouldn't. The protein that transports thyroid hormone has sites that associate with the double bonds in the thyroid hormone molecule. Unsaturated fats bind to those same sites on the transport protein, so the protein carries unsaturated fats instead of thyroid hormone.

**Caller 1:** So this might be a cascading difficulty that originates in the thyroid and prevents the gallbladder from properly producing enzymes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Until he can get that sorted out, there are liver herbs that can help improve bile flow. Gentian, Burdock root, and Dandelion root are very bitter herbs that can stimulate the flow of bile. Swedish Bitters is a traditional European tonic that has those types of herbs.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's get back to the energy balance. How do PUFAs impact the organism's ability to be metabolically active enough to pay off the debt of inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I mentioned the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase, which feeds glucose into the oxidative system. But the mitochondrial oxidative system itself is basically destroyed in proportion to the polyunsaturated fat exposure. The mitochondria produces something like 35 times more energy per molecule of sugar than the diabetic pathway (lactic acid) can produce.

**Andrew Murray:** Because diabetics are forced into a fat-burning mode rather than glucose-burning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If it was purely saturated fat, that would be okay. When we are at rest, our cells can burn saturated fat. But with age, our tissues become more and more concentrated with polyunsaturated fats because the fat cells themselves preferentially burn the "good stuff" (saturated fat) for their own maintenance, leaving the PUFA to accumulate.

When we are under stress and don't get enough sugar, we have to burn the bad stuff. That does many things to the mitochondria, including destroying the genetic material inside them. Saturated fat doesn't do that; it is just quietly oxidized.

**Andrew Murray:** So this would give rise to cancers as a result of damaged DNA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The PUFAs break down into isoprostanes and neuroprostanes, which are inflammatory. Fragment molecules like hydroxy-nonenal attach to hemoglobin, genetic material, enzymes, and signaling molecules. Most of the things called "glycation" are really fat breakdown proteins.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How long would it take if someone stopped eating all these bad oils and just started eating butter and coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The complete changeover takes about four years. But if you eat frequently and thoroughly avoid stress-causing foods—don't let yourself get hungry enough to call on stress hormones to liberate fat—you can very quickly shift over to efficient metabolism. Frequent feeding, always with sugar and absolutely no PUFA, allows the slow disposition of the unsaturated toxic fats. The liver treats PUFA like other toxins; if it has the energy, it detoxifies them for excretion.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why when women go on weight loss programs and lose 60 to 70 pounds quickly, their liver enzymes go up. They burn too many of these polyunsaturates at once.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you're under stress, you not only damage blood vessels and nerve cells, but you specifically knock out the enzymes needed to detoxify things.

**Caller 2:** I've heard of the "Eat Right for Your Blood Type" diet. I'm O positive, and it says beef is good for me. I notice when I'm stressed or tired, I get a yearning for a hamburger or meat. What do you think about the relationship between blood types, food, and cravings?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies showing we have specific nerve systems that tell us what we're deficient in. We crave protein when we're deficient in protein. We crave sugar and salt very specifically if we need those. Hypothyroid people generally crave sugar and salty food. Vitamin C causes a craving for sour, tangy foods.

**Caller 2:** I notice stress brings out cravings. If I'm really stressed, I might want a donut, but I also find I crave beef. I try to buy the lowest fat content beef I can, but I'm hearing your cautionary information regarding animal fats. I'm trying to find a balance.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Beef fat is not a dangerous fat. If the animal is grass-fed and organic, the fat should be clean. It's the chicken, pork, turkey, and fish fats that are dangerous because of what they are fed (corn/soy).

**Caller 2:** You mentioned earlier that with swine and chickens, it's the feed causing the issue. Is that the same with fish?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the fish have almost an absolute reflection of their diet in their fat. Fish in the Amazon contain fat that is as saturated as butter because of the water temperature.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The old story about Eskimos not getting heart disease because they eat fish is actually because they eat whale blubber, which is very saturated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One interesting point is that when cows eat bad food (corn/soy), because they have four stomachs, the bacteria can transfer that bad fat into a saturated fat. So beef fat is not dangerous like the fat of the chicken or pig. The cow's bacteria use Vitamin E to saturate the fat, basically detoxifying the unsaturated fats.

**Andrew Murray:** We lost you for a second. You said Vitamin E helps saturate the fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even in humans, Vitamin E will cause some of that in the intestine if bacteria are present. Vitamin E lets the bacteria saturate and detoxify some of the PUFA.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if someone were to eat french fries, they could take Vitamin E to help prevent some damage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, or make the french fries in coconut oil.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the caller who craved donuts under stress—do you understand that stress as a need for blood sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The most intense connection between need and appetite is between sugar and salt.

**Andrew Murray:** We've heard misinformation that sugar and salt are bad, but they are actually important anti-stress compounds. Could you briefly explain the Randall hypothesis again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some call it the Randall Cycle, but it's just a competition. When you raise your free fatty acids, you inhibit the ability to oxidize glucose. Stress increases free fatty acids. Oxidizing glucose is what you need to overcome stress.

The body is designed to respond to saturated fat because saturated fats block the stress reaction. A properly functioning body under stress would provide saturated fats from storage, which would inhibit the stress hormones and allow the cycle to be broken.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So we are just living in a time where we consume poisonous fats (PUFA) that our bodies aren't used to, and they don't respond the same way as saturated fats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If science had simply been looking to understand the situation since 1950, the systematic differences between saturated and unsaturated fats would have been clear. But advertising swamped the cultural situation.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat. For listeners, Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com, where you can find scholarly referenced articles on these topics.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Water Retention and Salt
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a master's degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we offer alternative medicine and nutritional counseling.

This month we want to explore the misconceptions surrounding water retention and the medical advice to avoid salt, as well as the over-prescription of diuretics. We will make special reference to toxemia of late pregnancy and the role of inflammation and poor energy reserves as a cause for concern. We're going to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat.

This month's show is going to be mainly looking at the topics of salt avoidance with respect to water retention and opening up that misconception with facts and science supporting the use of salt—rather than the avoidance of salt—for decreasing water retention. We will also look at Dr. Tom Brewer's pioneering research work on toxemia of late pregnancy. For those women listening, a noteworthy part of the show will be based on that toxemia and the things that Dr. Brewer proved reduce swelling and actually reduce the occurrence of toxemia completely.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray, and I'm joining Andrew Murray. We have Dr. Raymond Peat on the line.

**Andrew Murray:** Hi, Dr. Peat. Thank you for joining us again to illuminate the way through the misconceptions that we so often repeat as truth. Would you please describe your academic and professional background for listeners who perhaps have never heard your name?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied biology and physiology at the University of Oregon and have taught various hormone and nutrition-related courses, as well as in other fields, psychology and philosophy included.

**Andrew Murray:** Your main interests have been looking into hormones, and much of your research has given you new insights into the treatment of many situations with hormones like progesterone, pregnenolone, and others. Perhaps we should start with modern diuretics. We come into contact with people using diuretics to decrease water retention, whether it's ankles, fingers, or cardiac water retention. Are there any safe diuretics that are prescription medications?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are some that are relatively safe, but it's the whole theory behind why they exist that is the problem. Mercury compounds used to be used; basically, they just killed the kidney cells and let stuff leak out. They were the common diuretics for a very long time until the 1950s, when new compounds came on the market that had a variety of effects on the kidneys. It was really the promotion of those that created an ideology that diuretics are key to treating heart disease and several other problems, such as toxemia of pregnancy. But really, I think it's mostly a marketing strategy to orient physiology around making the kidneys leak out more water.

The real problem is what causes the water retention. Almost anything that seriously injures the organism causes water retention. For example, a problem following surgery is that the person stops forming urine. Shock, or any very serious sickness, is going to cause the reduced ability to form urine properly. It's sort of a plumber's approach to physiology to think of just opening up the kidneys and letting the liquid out faster.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** From a herbal perspective, dandelion leaf—and the root is a little bit less effective than the leaf—works as a diuretic. That's what I thought they had created Furosemide from. Although with Furosemide, I know you have to have a prescription of potassium along with it. Dandelion leaf has a lot of potassium, so you don't need to take extra potassium if you use it. Would you consider Furosemide a safe diuretic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's got a long history of use, and it probably does have an actual beneficial effect on survival. But with almost any leaf extract, the potassium and magnesium are going to have a diuretic effect that is probably safer than the actual drug function on the kidneys.

**Andrew Murray:** So the inflammation in the first place is the main cause for the cessation of diuresis and the increase in water retention in the cells through damage.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You're saying it's much more important to look at what's causing that inflammation rather than just prescribe a diuretic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even before the inflammation, there's the energy problem. Something as simple as drinking too much water in relation to the energy your body is producing can cause issues. For example, a low-thyroid person who can't produce much metabolic energy is very susceptible to drinking too much water and getting a very general disruption of their physiology.

A pint or so of water passing suddenly through your stomach to your intestine causes a surge of serotonin release. That is simply a model of stress or shock. Just a surge of water hitting the intestine is enough to increase serotonin, which then stimulates the production of prolactin. Prolactin is associated with water retention. Serotonin increases the production of aldosterone, which produces water retention and inflammation and sets off a chain of reactions that lead to things such as heart failure.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The unfortunate thing is when someone is low thyroid, they're usually very thirsty all the time anyway. They crave that water.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It causes the tissues to retain water. Even though it's passing through the kidneys mostly, and they aren't producing much evaporation through their lungs or skin, it tends to leak out of their bloodstream into the tissues and produce edema. Edema is harmful to all of the tissues. It turns on a whole anabolic system, shifting away from oxidative metabolism, activating lipolysis (the release of fatty acids), and shifting cell metabolism towards burning fat rather than sugar. This imitates diabetes and aging. It's a generalized shock physiology that's involved when cells get waterlogged. It can start with low thyroid, but it feeds back and makes the low thyroid problem worse.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why you said that any kind of leaf extract or tea is going to have minerals in it that help prevent this from happening. And if you made a cup of tea, you'd sip on it slowly; you wouldn't just drink it down like a pint of water.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And regarding the minerals, it isn't essential that it be magnesium and potassium; calcium and sodium have many of the same functions. If you're in shock, you can relieve the symptoms pretty much by taking more of any one of the alkaline minerals: potassium, sodium, magnesium, or calcium. In heart failure and lung inflammation—many of the things that happen with shock or aging—the lungs and the heart tend to get waterlogged and lose function. Just giving a very concentrated salt solution intravenously will relieve the symptoms. Very often they've doubled the survival or cut the mortality rate in half by just giving extra sodium intravenously.

**Andrew Murray:** Why is it so often that doctors tell people to avoid salt? Why is salt so maligned as a problem element, especially when people are swelling?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It really got a big boost around 1950 when the diuretics came on the market. They found the diuretics took sodium out at the same time they took water out. So they said you should get the same effect by restricting the sodium intake. They applied that to pregnant women.
