Tom Brewer and some other people wrote about the horrible effects of sodium restriction in pregnancy, plus using diuretics. If you combine the two, you get doubly bad, serious effects.

After I had been reading Tom Brewer's work for a long time, I was seeing similarities between premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and the toxemia of pregnancy that he had worked on. I finally decided to suggest to young women who were having premenstrual water retention—and not having any good results just by stopping their salt intake—that they follow Brewer's prescription to *increase* their salt intake when they were having edema problems, and to go according to their craving for salt. The first person that tried it had a total avoidance of premenstrual water retention the very first month.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How much salt did she take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Quite a lot. Even if the food was already salted, she would just add lots more onto it. It absolutely stopped right from then on. She never had a water retention problem again.

**Andrew Murray:** Where do you think the mistaken ideology has come from that salt increases the risk of stroke and heart attack?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** David McCarron, 30 or 40 years ago, was studying the issue. He looked at the figures that the government published recommendations were based on. He thought that if you look at the figures carefully, the people who ate the *least* salt had the highest blood pressure, and the people who ate the *most* salt had the lowest blood pressure. He saw that the figures really showed that low calcium intake was associated with hypertension, and the sodium was really there as an innocent bystander associated with the calcium deficiency.

**Andrew Murray:** So you're saying that calcium deficiency is more responsible for hypertension?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. David McCarron has written maybe 150 articles on the subject. I think he was at a California university when he started saying it's not high sodium, it's low calcium that causes hypertension. I think that university invited him to leave.

**Andrew Murray:** Am I thinking right when you've mentioned in the past that low calcium intakes cause calcium to leak out of the bones and into the blood, and that causes the calcification of the arteries eventually, which gives you hypertension?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The essential idea is that low calcium intake, among other things, increases your parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH pulls calcium out of your bones and favors its movement into cells of all kinds. When calcium is taken up by cells, it stimulates them and tends to make them contract.

That's one of the places that thyroid and energy production comes into the question. Carbon dioxide, produced by the action of thyroid, keeps calcium *out* of cells. Even if you breathe in a bag to increase your carbon dioxide, or take baking soda, the carbon dioxide will relax your blood vessels by helping the calcium to move out of the blood vessels and back into the bones.

**Andrew Murray:** So short-term exposure to higher blood levels of calcium, or tissues picking up the calcium, contributes to that lack of elasticity characteristic of high blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Each of these things sets in motion a whole sequence of events. Low carbon dioxide lets calcium get into cells and excite them and tighten up the blood vessels. Low carbon dioxide also lets the platelets release their serotonin. The serotonin, besides adding to the tension of the blood vessels, makes them permeable and leaky, so that the water isn't retained in the bloodstream but leaks through into the cells. The cells that are taking up calcium are also taking up water.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So basically, 2,000 milligrams of calcium is a really important thing for somebody with hypertension to start implementing into their regime.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and supporting it with the other minerals. The facts that David McCarron looked at showed that the high salt eaters actually had lower blood pressure. One of the things involved there is that sodium helps stimulate the cell to expel calcium. Sodium activates the thyroid function, and the thyroid function pushes calcium out of the cell and lets the cell relax.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I know it's a little bit confusing for our listeners, talking about calcium inside and outside of cells. Basically, the salt helps to put the calcium where it should be and not be deposited in your arteries.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to the diet that Tom Brewer brought about for the treatment of toxemia of late pregnancy—a diet which resulted in none of his thousands of patients ever getting toxemia—he was very big on drinking quite a bit of milk.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** There's the calcium. Also salt and lots of protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, he was talking about the protein and adding salt to your food. But the milk has other things besides the protein. The calcium has its direct effect on blood pressure, and the sugar of milk has a diuretic-like action. So the calcium and sugar add to the quality of the protein.

**Andrew Murray:** We talked a little bit about Furosemide. Are there any safer, effective diuretics?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you think of the sequence of stress effects I mentioned—too much water leading to too much serotonin, aldosterone, and prolactin—those are all inflammatory and cause water retention. If you choose your substances with reference to inhibiting any or all of those, that's going to be an anti-edema, anti-inflammatory treatment.

Thyroid and progesterone, for example, lower all of these things. Progesterone is a very powerful antagonist to aldosterone. Drugs are being developed to be very similar to progesterone but patentable, so they can sell them to treat heart failure and water retention.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do they not have the same effect as the progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They cure heart failure and such, but they have their own side effects. Using any of the natural steroids derived from pregnenolone—either progesterone or DHEA—will help with water retention, edema, and heart failure.

**Andrew Murray:** And that's because they're antagonizing the effects of aldosterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Aldosterone increases inflammation and leads to fibrosis. Prolonged heart failure, vascular disease, kidney disease, and lung disease all tend to end up with fibrosis. 60 or 70 years ago, a researcher named Lipschutz called pregnenolone and progesterone the "anti-fibromatogenic steroids." They start out inhibiting fibrous overproduction and end up protecting against tumors.

**Caller (Rico):** About nine months ago, I was at ICU because my calcium went crazy. I was later diagnosed with sarcoidosis, and my doctor wants me to get down on my calcium level. He's got me on 15 milligrams of prednisone to keep my calcium level down.

**Andrew Murray:** The prednisone is an anti-inflammatory steroid. Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory condition.

**Caller (Rico):** I think he's using prednisone to keep the calcium levels down. But the way you talk sounds like calcium levels are a pretty good idea.

**Andrew Murray:** Well, calcium not in the blood, but in the bones, which is where the calcium should be. Consuming adequate dietary calcium—in the form of powdered eggshells or consuming dairy—getting about 2,000 milligrams of calcium a day will actually let you store the calcium in your bones and prevent it from being in your bloodstream. When you said your blood levels were high, that's because your bones were allowing the calcium to leak out into your blood supply.

**Caller (Rico):** Okay, that does help.

**Andrew Murray:** That would also cause what Dr. Peat was talking about with calcium in the endothelial tissue, making it less elastic. Your body, through parathyroid hormone, starts to pull out calcium from the bone when dietary intake is low.

**Caller (Rico):** Yeah, we want to do the reverse.

**Andrew Murray:** Exactly. Making sure you have a high enough dietary intake of calcium will be the key.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What we've seen with our clients is when people have high calcium in their blood, it's because they're not getting enough in their diet. When they start supplementing their diet with a higher calcium level—closer to 2,000 milligrams—you'll see the blood calcium level come down to a normal range.

**Andrew Murray:** The other thing you should do in conjunction with that is supplement with Vitamin D. The calcium and Vitamin D work synergistically.

**Caller (Rico):** I had a reverse opinion. I thought less was best.

**Andrew Murray:** No, you want to bring your blood levels down by making sure you put it back to the bone.

**Caller (Michael):** I got chickenpox, which is going around. I was wondering what your recommendation would be. I learned from you guys that coconut fat is antiviral, so I'm using that as a salve on my sores and drinking coconut milk.

**Andrew Murray:** From a point of view of anti-infectives, being a viral situation, I don't know how much can be done that quickly. Your own body will certainly get on top of it. When the vesicles burst, they will become quite itchy. Calamine lotion is a fairly good, soothing, calming topical application.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin has been found to have a mild antiviral effect against several types of virus. Someone with AIDS sent me an old publication showing they had begun a trial of aspirin for HIV-infected people and were getting good results. It has been proven somewhat effective for several different kinds of virus, including the herpes/chickenpox type.

**Caller:** I have been studying the Buteyko method, which is an exercise which will actually increase the CO2 levels. It helps with things like insomnia. I didn't quite get the full picture of what raising those CO2 levels impacts.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat has talked extensively about the benefits of CO2. Most of us associate CO2 as a poisonous gas we need to exhale, when actually oxygen itself is probably more poisonous than CO2. CO2 is very anti-inflammatory and associated with longevity. Peoples and cultures that live at high altitudes have much less inflammatory disease and cancer incidence because of the beneficial effects of CO2.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Bag breathing is another way that you can help to lower blood pressure because it helps with that CO2 and putting calcium in the right place.

**Caller (Athlete):** I'm curious how this pertains to athletes. I always have to calculate sweat loss to calculate how much I need to intake. I practice running and cycling sports. How do I calculate how much salt intake I should be taking?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** There's been a study done with baking soda showing that athletes performed better when they took up to a tablespoon of baking soda in one day. That's because it increases their CO2. As an athlete, you're blowing off a lot of CO2 when you're exercising.

**Caller (Athlete):** So in reference to CO2, am I actually looking to put my body in a slightly more hypoxic state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In effect, the carbon dioxide is pulling more oxygen through your cell system. It activates the electron transport chain to use oxygen more quickly and effectively. They've done it with endurance races, giving them a tablespoon of baking soda at the start of the race.

You would think that it would make them more alkaline. Alkaline is not necessarily a good state. The carbon dioxide actually enters the cell and becomes an acidic form. Bicarbonate momentarily makes your blood more alkaline, but the absorbed carbon dioxide becomes acidic inside the cell. The intracellular state should be slightly on the acid side when the oxygen is really working. They call it "oxygen" because it means "acid former," and the acid that it makes is carbon dioxide.

In that slightly acidic state, oxygen is having its full action for producing energy. It's that same energy production which takes the calcium out of the cell and lets the cell relax and recuperate properly. If you aren't producing or retaining enough carbon dioxide, the cell will begin making lactic acid. The lactic acid leaves the cell in an alkaline, stressed condition. Even though it's acidifying the blood, it's leaving the cell in a stressed alkaline condition that causes inflammation. So too much aerobic exercise becomes catabolic and inflammatory.

**Caller:** I'd like to know about the ratio of calcium and magnesium that Dr. Peat might recommend.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ratio isn't as big an issue as a lot of books say. If you're getting a little excess sodium and calcium, it spares the magnesium. The sodium and calcium activate cell respiration, and cell respiration is needed for cells to retain magnesium. So if you're living low in sodium and calcium, you depend on a good thyroid function to retain magnesium. Any stress that increases aldosterone is going to make you lose magnesium. Keeping your aldosterone and inflammation down, and your thyroid, calcium, and sodium up, is going to make you retain magnesium much more efficiently.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding the earlier caller with high calcium: If you're having blood tests, it's good to have your Vitamin D3 in the upper part of the normal range. It would also be good to have the parathyroid hormone (PTH) checked. When you're getting enough Vitamin D and calcium, you will inhibit the parathyroid hormone. Although PTH has its place, you don't want it to be chronically elevated because it is a cancer promoter.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for joining us again, Dr. Peat. For more information, visit his website at www.raypeat.com for scholarly articles and fully referenced scientific literature.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Cancer Treatment
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture our own certified organic herbal extracts.

You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's topic: the misunderstandings in the approach to cancer treatment. We are very fortunate to introduce Dr. Raymond Peat, who has done recent work on the misunderstandings in cancer treatment. In light of President Nixon's 1971 address to fight the "War on Cancer," we've made almost no real advances in cancer therapy, unlike other diseases. Cancer is now almost the number one killer, very close to cardiovascular disease.

Dr. Peat, thank you for joining us. For those who haven't heard of you, could you give an outline of your academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied biology about 40 years ago at the University of Oregon. Since then, I've been writing my newsletter and books, and occasionally doing seminars for medical professionals. Over the years, I've been thinking about the medical culture and what makes it so wrong.

When I was in graduate school in 1968 or '69, we had a seminar on cancer biology. My part was to explain carcinogenesis—what things cause cancer and how they work. I listed 50 different types of carcinogenic agents, including inert objects embedded in tissues, distilled water, and psychological stress. The professors were greatly annoyed because their whole point was to work out the ways that mutations are carcinogenic. They wanted me to talk about polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons causing mutations, but that was just one very small section of what I covered.

Those biologists were still fairly in harmony with the medical view of cancer. But since then, with the cloning and stem cell research of the last 10 years, biology has strongly turned away from that understanding. The active research in cancer is now more in tune with the biology of stem cells rather than mutations.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you find that to be a more accurate approach to understanding cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When I did that seminar, I was gathering research that was 30 or 40 years old at the time, but it was outside academic preferences. Since then, because of the changes in the gene industry, they've looked for natural events to parallel their genetic engineering. They've had to be open to people like Barbara McClintock, who showed that stress mutates corn plants. That opened up the whole issue of psychological factors in the development of cancer and how stress affects immunity.

**Andrew Murray:** Given that the last 40 years have yielded very little in promising approaches to cancer treatment or survival rates, and given the opinion that there is a multi-billion dollar industry focused on patentable treatments rather than cures, why was the direction of excising tumors and radiating tissue chosen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For decades, people in the alternative health business have asked how doctors can forbid experimental treatments to themselves or their families. But it is such a deep cultural thing that they really believe it. They are trained in medical school in a boot camp atmosphere where they don't have time to get philosophical. They are drilled with ideas of genetic determinism.

It was less than 200 years ago that it was discovered that people are made of cells. Shortly after, they discovered cancer is made of cells. Then came the germ theory and the atomic theory, and everything fit into this reductionist approach—explaining things by the subunits they are made of. This fit the idea that a cancer is made of "bad" cells.

When genetics came up 100 years ago, it was used to explain what is different about cancer cells. The doctrine became that they are a special kind of cell explained by a mutated gene, making them completely alien to ourselves. It’s like a new being has come into existence.

The old tradition, going back to the Greeks, was to cut a tumor off or burn it off. Medicine fit the idea of the "alien cell" into that tradition of cutting something out. It was perfectly reinforcing: it is something that is not part of us and must be eliminated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** While that was happening, other people were studying metabolism and physiology. They saw that there are fields governing the relationship of cells in a developing embryo—electrical gradients and chemical fields. If you cut a piece of an embryo, or even an adult animal, you could see a wave of cell division spread out from the injury to replace the cells.

The idea of a cancer field was being demonstrated in the 1930s and 40s. They showed that if you found a cancer in the intestine, and examined rings around the cancer, you would find gradients of abnormality grading off to normal. The center was outright cancer, but the surrounding tissue showed inflammation and deterioration.

However, the molecular revolution came about with a great push from the government, and the DNA doctrine was used to explain everything. They said information comes only from the gene to the cell. When virologists demonstrated reverse transcriptases (RNA viruses), my professors wouldn't believe it because they said information only comes from the gene. Since then, biology has changed, but medicine is still stuck on the idea of the alien, mutated clone of cells.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It sounds like the argument between Louis Pasteur and Antoine Béchamp. Pasteur said it was the bug, and Béchamp said it was the *terroir*—the environment of the body—that determines infection.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but medicine didn't agree. By the time the DNA molecule became stylish, medicine had locked itself into that view. Interestingly, around 1950, there was an article about a man injecting cancer into hundreds of prisoners and patients. He found that if he injected cancer into a sick person, it wouldn't be thrown off immediately like in a healthy person. If he injected it into a person who already had cancer, it would sometimes persist. He concluded there is something in the body that either favors cancer or resists and destroys it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Were they wanting cancer to be something our bodies had no control over—just defective genes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The doctrine says once one cell mutates, it produces a clone, and you have to destroy it. But when you actually look at cancers, they are often polyclonal. Within the cancer, there are zones of "bad" and "worse."

Several people have analyzed cancer closely and found that tissue can be perfectly normal and functioning yet contain more than 1,000 mutated genes. A typical cancer has hundreds of mutated genes before it starts going bad.

Forty years ago, researchers stored bits of cancer tissue in a deep freeze. When they thawed them in the presence of structuring solvents like DMSO or butyrates, the tissue would revert to normal. In another experiment, they took tumor cells from hamsters and mixed them with cells from a normal embryo. The developing embryo normalized the tumor cells, producing a perfectly normal hamster.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That disproves the theory that cancers are purely a defective gene. If you can inject a cancer cell into a growing embryo and get a normal animal, the organism is in control.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. Harry Rubin, Ana Soto, and Carlos Sonnenschein have made the point that the organism is in control for most of the life of the cancer. At some point, the organism loses control, and that's when it becomes a functioning cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What can we do to create an environment in our body that prevents cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything you do is either anti-carcinogenic or carcinogenic. For example, if you avoid sunlight or use sunscreens because you are afraid of skin cancer, the avoidance of sun is very carcinogenic.

**Andrew Murray:** There was a report in England recently that rickets is becoming prevalent again because people are using high SPF sunscreen on their children.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It isn't just the Vitamin D; it is the penetrating light. For 50 years, people have studied the effects of red light. The basic effect of penetrating red light is to activate the respiratory enzyme—mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase. This enzyme is restored by red light.

In rabbit experiments, this enzyme is pretty well destroyed by just 12 to 15 hours of darkness. Mortality goes up at the end of winter because nights are longer. Whether using lasers, incandescent lights, or sunlight, red light penetrates the body and restores the energy-producing enzymes.

Otto Warburg in 1929 demonstrated that cancer differs metabolically from healthy cells by turning glucose into lactic acid even in the presence of oxygen. This happens because something has gone wrong with the mitochondrion. All you have to do to create that metabolism is knock out the cytochrome oxidase enzyme.

Everything that is carcinogenic weakens that enzyme: the wrong kind of fat (PUFA), an imbalance of estrogen to progesterone, thyroid deficiency, or ionizing radiation. Ultraviolet light destroys it in the skin, but sunlight is balanced because the red light restores the enzyme that the UV is destroying. If you avoid sunburn, the sun is a pure benefit.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Especially this time of year, are you talking about intermittent exposure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ideally. Animal experiments show the enzyme gets damaged by eight hours of darkness. We shouldn't be in total darkness for longer than it takes to sleep.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do low-energy fluorescent bulbs vary from incandescent bulbs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those little fluorescent things are going to cause an epidemic of cancer. The beneficial red light comes from incandescent bulbs and sunlight.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You’ve recommended that office workers have a 250 to 300-watt incandescent bulb shining over their workstation. How much skin exposure is needed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As much as possible. For people with brain disease or motor neuron disease, shining it on the head, neck, and back is crucial. But getting the whole body exposed is best because you are sending remedial signals through the nervous system that help stabilize enzymes in cells that aren't getting direct light.

**Andrew Murray:** We understand inflammation is not a good thing. Is inflammation a major part of cancer progression?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Everything that is stressful promotes inflammation. Even things like dropping your blood sugar works the same as cutting off the oxygen supply. It keeps that crucial oxidative enzyme from getting energy from glucose. In the absence of sugar, oxygen, or carbon dioxide, that enzyme fails. The cell produces lactic acid defensively, which triggers chain reactions, causes fats to break down, and produces prostaglandins, leading to more inflammation. Basically, you must keep your energy up so you can respire efficiently.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So small, frequent meals will help prevent that chain reaction.

**Michael (Announcer):** A listener asks: What about red LEDs, tanning beds, and far-infrared saunas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Red LEDs have been demonstrated to reverse many changes of cancer and are being used experimentally. Lasers, incandescent light, sunlight, and LEDs all activate that enzyme efficiently, specifically between 600 and 700 nanometers (orange to red).

**Michael:** How about a far-infrared sauna?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is some benefit, and the heat itself is beneficial, but the specific restoration of the enzyme happens in the orange-to-red spectrum.

**Michael:** And a tanning bed would be pure ultraviolet with no benefit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically. You get Vitamin D, but without the protective red and orange light, it will have a slight immune-suppressive effect. It's better to get your suntan in real sunlight.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to cell excitation. We normally look at an excited state as beneficial, but how does this relate to cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** An energized cell is actually relaxed. Imagine muscles ready to work; they are soft and flexible. If you work them to fatigue, they swell and cramp. The presence of adequate energy relaxes nerves and muscles.

If you are deficient in energy production—because the mitochondrial enzyme is impaired or thyroid is low—it doesn't take much stress to de-energize the cell. A cell that has had more stimulation than it can meet with energy production will swell up, just like a tired muscle. In that state, it releases lactic acid, histamine, and prostaglandins.

If you are chronically low energy, you are susceptible. A tissue like the breast, uterus, or liver that experiences stimulation will shift to glycolysis and produce lactic acid if it can't produce enough energy to return to a relaxed state.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that how you would describe a seizure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the cell is over-excited and can't relax. A cramp is the same thing. People are more likely to have seizures or cramps at night because darkness impairs our respiratory enzymes, bringing us closer to the threshold where excitation can't be turned off.

**Andrew Murray:** If someone gets a cancer diagnosis but hasn't had surgical intervention, what is the rationale that cutting into that area is dangerous?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A professor at the University of California about 60 years ago compared people who declined medical treatment with those who got the best available, and those who declined lived longer.

There is a website by a man named Gershom Zajicek (Z-A-J-I-C-E-K) who presents evidence that cutting out a tumor activates metastases that had been sitting harmlessly. Even some professors acknowledge that cutting out a tumor often causes metastatic growth to spring up. Published studies show people get recurrences much sooner if they have surgery than if they don't.

**Michael:** A caller asks: What about cutting out polyps during routine colonoscopies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that's pretty harmless. If you didn't look for them, I think they would fall off by themselves. They aren't deeply entrenched.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about cutting off moles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is one of the things well established to cause others to pop up. Zajicek talks about that on his website.

**Andrew Murray:** So when the body is energy-depleted, it loses the battle against malformed cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. This relates to the "bystander effect." For 50 years, they believed radiation caused cancer by mutating DNA directly. But recently, they noticed that if you irradiate cells in a dish and then put new cells in, the new cells mutate. Or if you mutate one cell, it sends out substances like serotonin, nitric oxide, and carbon monoxide.

In your body, you don't have to mutate a gene by hitting it with radiation directly. You just have to stress a cell so it emits these substances. Your whole body experiences bystander effects. A study in Seattle found that dental X-rays caused pregnant women to have underdeveloped babies even with lead shielding on the abdomen. The bystander effect from the face and brain poisoned the rest of the body.

**Michael:** A listener asks about Taxol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it has some anti-inflammatory effects which probably account for the good it does, but there are less toxic things that do more good.

**Michael:** Could you comment on the Essiac formula?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm sure it has some of those same anti-inflammatory effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It has liver herbs in it, which helps the liver clear excess hormones.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The crucial respiratory enzyme is protected by progesterone and inactivated by estrogen. One of the oldest bystander effects known is that if you radiate any part of an animal, it will go into heat as if given a shot of estrogen. Any inflammation activates the aromatase enzyme, which makes estrogen. In studies of monkeys, they found that the arms were producing at least as much estrogen as the ovaries. So, a person isn't protected against estrogen just because they have had menopause or ovaries removed. Every part of the body that is stressed becomes an estrogen factory.

**Michael:** Assuming you were going through chemo and radiation, what danger is that to people around you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are starting to recommend that people taking radioactive iodine for thyroid treatment not ride on buses because they are radiating people around them. If you get radiation at the hospital, it won't hurt anyone else later, but if you have radioactive substances in your system (like iodine), you are radioactive.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you have comments on metastasis of cancer that hasn't been surgically intervened with?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, metastases are great for business. Now they are saying maybe breast cancer starts *in utero*. The idea of "metastatic little aliens" is tremendous for business because you can never prove they aren't there. If you injure a person enough, you're going to find some.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Wasn't there a study showing that 100% of people over age 50 who died in accidents had some form of abdominal cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, Harry Rubin mentioned that. Similar studies show that if you look at just two or three organs—breast, uterus, prostate—you find cancer in a high percentage. By age 50, everyone can have it diagnosed.

I think that means be careful about getting a diagnosis. Dentists told me twice when I was about 30 that I had precancerous leukoplakia and should have it biopsied. Since I knew I got lumpy developments in my cheeks when deficient in Vitamin A, I took Vitamin A instead. I cured it in a week.

I told women with abnormal Pap smears and "carcinoma in situ" about that. They applied Vitamin A topically. I kept track of three dozen women; all of them went back to their doctors later with no evidence of abnormality. The doctors lost out on a good hysterectomy, and in every case, they didn't want to know what the women had done.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Natural sources of Vitamin A are eggs and liver. Beta carotene relies on a conversion that isn't very efficient, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you are deficient in thyroid hormone or Vitamin B12, you don't convert beta carotene into Vitamin A.

**Andrew Murray:** We are getting close to the end of the show. Dr. Peat's website is **raypeat.com**, where you can find fully referenced articles. You can also email him at **raypeat@gmail.com**.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you for listening.

**Andrew Murray:** Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Acidity X Alkalinity
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD Garberville. From 7:30 until the end of the show at 8:00, you're invited to call in with any questions either related or unrelated to this month's subject of alkalinity versus acidity with reference to disease.

We're very welcome to have Dr. Raymond Peat to share his wisdom and expertise with us for this next hour. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Hi.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks for joining us. Would you give the listeners who perhaps have never heard you before a rundown of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied biology at the University of Oregon and have since about 1970 just continued on my own, figuring things out, talking to a lot of people, and listening to their problems. Almost every time I talk to someone, I learn something about physiology. It's a very complex, continuing thing.

**Andrew Murray:** You did a PhD in physiology based on hormones, didn't you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, reproductive physiology and aging was the subject of my dissertation.

**Andrew Murray:** We really enjoy having you here because you provide the scientific reference for what most people just spout out as truth. It’s refreshing to have the science behind the reasons why.

This month, I want to discuss alkalinity and acidity. Generally, the main reference for cancer is that cancers seem to predominate in acidic environments. The idea is that our diets—through poor proteins or protein-based foods like beans, seeds, and meats—produce acidic byproducts. How do you look at these traditional ideas about the acid-base balance of food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They usually lead to a pretty good diet. For example, the Indian diet—fruit, vegetables, milk, and cheese—is a good example of the alkaline residue diet. I don't have any disagreement with the dietary recommendations to eat lots of milk, cheese, fruit, and vegetables.

But it's the small details that people use to argue for certain refinements of that diet. For example, the fear of milk. They talk about the loss of calcium in the urine as indicating that maybe it's too much acid. But actually, the residue of milk is on the alkaline side because of the very large amount of potassium and calcium in the milk. It is very similar to the vegetables that the cows eat to make the milk; they accumulate a huge amount of alkaline minerals.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's talk about that subject a little bit more. The residue is what's left behind once the food source has been metabolized, and that dictates whether a food is alkaline or acidic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And grains, nuts, beans, and meats do have a very acidic residue or ash after they're metabolized. The biggest part of that in meat, nuts, and grains is phosphate. Proteins have a lot of sulfur which turns into sulfuric acid when it's metabolized. It is possible to do biological harm by eating too much of those and not enough of the potassium, sodium, magnesium, and calcium side.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Which are predominantly found in fruits and vegetables.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, fruits, vegetables, milk, and cheese.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you run through some of the more commonly experienced acidic production processes in the body, whether respiratory or in producing urine, and how the body deals with maintaining the pH balance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it helps to look at the picture in the very biggest context, which is that mostly we're a huge lump of protein, and protein is, on average, acidic. If you just leave acid sitting around in the environment, it will accumulate the base that neutralizes it. So, if we think of ourselves as a big piece of acidic protein, this spontaneously will associate alkaline material with it. Potassium and magnesium, for example, will neutralize the acidity of the protein.

But as we energize our system by burning carbohydrate and fat, the carbohydrate in particular turns into carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide has to constantly be leaving the organism. What comes in is oxygen. The oxygen combines with the fuel carbon and becomes carbon dioxide. So you have a neutral oxygen coming in, and it was historically called "oxygen" meaning the "acid former." The acid that it forms in this case is carbonic acid.

We're constantly metabolically producing this acid, which is streaming out of our cells and leaving through our lungs primarily. As the carbon dioxide is produced, combining with water, it turns into carbonic acid, which ionizes. So you have the acidic carbonic acid leaving the cell as a charged particle. It takes the oppositely charged sodium with it. Primarily sodium and calcium are constantly being drawn out of the cell by the stream of carbonic acid being produced inside the cell.

The alkaline minerals reach the bloodstream in balance with the carbonic acid. Then the carbonic acid leaves the lungs as carbon dioxide, leaving an alkaline trace in the blood. The cell basically was neutral until it produced the acid. Then that neutralized protein gave up some of its mineral alkaline material, which then shows up in the blood. So the pH of the blood is above neutral, about pH 7.4.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because of the carbonic acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In this healthy metabolism, the mineral gets pulled out of the neutral cell. As it's pulled out with the acid being constantly formed, the cell shows its basic protein acidity. So, the respiring cell is normally slightly on the acidic side. A good, healthy cell with plenty of oxygen will be around pH 6.6 to 6.8.

If you stress a cell so it isn't getting enough carbon dioxide—or stress it in any way, like radiation or lack of oxygen—the cell becomes activated and shifts to the alkaline because it can't make carbon dioxide to acidify itself. It begins producing lactic acid very inefficiently.

The thing about lactic acid is that the sugar, instead of being oxidized all the way to carbon dioxide, comes to the point of pyruvic acid. Instead of that being oxidized, the cell reduces the pyruvic acid to lactic acid. In that process, the lactic acid is taking protons out of the cell and is raising the pH of the cell. The conversion of pyruvic acid to lactic acid increases the pH of the cell—just the opposite of what the production of carbon dioxide was doing. So the stressed cell becomes alkaline.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** When the popular theory is stated that cancer cells like an acidic environment, it sounds like if a cell is stressed, it likes an alkaline environment. That sounds almost exactly opposite.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, it shifts internally to become alkaline when it's stressed. But the produced lactic acid accumulates in its environment, and that's where the acid is—in the surroundings. And then it shows up in the blood.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that's like if you've stressed your muscle out too much, you're producing lactic acid and that makes your muscles sore. That's a stressed cell. Does lactic acid play a big part in cancer as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It not only acidifies the environment—which in itself could be actually protective if it was acidified by carbon dioxide—but it happens that the lactic acid acts as a signal to do all of the things associated with cancer. It stimulates the growth of new blood vessels so that the inflammation continues. It signals a lot of inflammatory changes, vasodilation, and the release of carbon monoxide and nitric oxide, producing free radicals and injury.

The lactic acid is functioning as a local poison or inflammatory agent. The acidity that it produces is a sign that something is wrong, but it isn't the acidity in the tumor that's harmful, because the tumor itself is internally alkaline.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you think of foods that are high in lactic acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even when we make it ourselves, it has these pro-inflammatory, swelling-producing, tumor-promoting functions. When it's made by bacteria, it's somewhat more toxic. When the body receives it—either from a stressed muscle, a tumor, or from too much yogurt or fermented food—it goes to the liver to get detoxified.

Every time you eat something with lactic acid, it's the same as if you had been stressed physically. Your liver has to work extra to detoxify it. It has to have a source of energy to detoxify the lactic acid, turning it back into glucose. And the glucose is right back where you started. So you've lost ground every time your liver has to process lactic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would you consider any amount of lactic acid-containing food to be a stress to the liver, or is there some margin of benefit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A healthy liver doesn't notice an occasional dish of yogurt or sauerkraut. But how I got interested in it was a long time ago. I discovered kefir in a store. It tasted good, so I drank a little more than a cup of it each day for lunch. Every time I did that, I would get a migraine-like headache every afternoon. That started me looking up what happens to your blood sugar and inflammatory mediators when you get more lactic acid than your liver likes.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you think about people's lifestyles promoting an acidic situation from stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The nervous system is in control of metabolism to a great extent, so you don't have to run five miles to shift over into that stress metabolism. If your nervous system and emotional systems are very stressed, just the thought of what you're doing can cause it.

I mentioned before that if you hang an animal by its tail or put it in a tube where it can't move, it will very quickly get an ulcer with lactic acid going to all of its systems, releasing histamine and serotonin. But if you give something for the animal to bite, even though it's in the same restrained, stressful situation, as long as it can defend itself by biting back, it doesn't get the ulcer.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think this explains why people say that as long as you let anger out, you generally don't get cancer, but people who hold it in get cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The rat experiment really suggests that.

**Andrew Murray:** So if we coin the term "an acidic lifestyle"—the stressed businessman trying to meet deadlines—is that a potential situation where cancer could arise because of the acidity from stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, it is actually things like lactic acid and serotonin. The stress really is doing its damage by creating an *intracellular alkaline* condition.

For example, when someone is under surgery, they often get ulcers just from being operated on. That stress will very often give them lung inflammation and brain inflammation. They found, 60 or 70 years after people originally discovered it, that if they don't ventilate patients very thoroughly and let them accumulate quite a bit of carbon dioxide, their lungs and brain are protected and don't swell. So the acidity from carbon dioxide is extremely anti-stress and protective. It's the alkalinity that goes with producing lactic acid which does the harm.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people get stomach ulcers if they're stressed because instead of their cells in their stomach holding onto the acid, it's releasing it into the environment and damaging the stomach lining?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's really the serotonin and other inflammatory things in the stomach rather than just the acid. The stomach is very good at holding extreme acidity safely. But when stress gives the wrong kind of signals and you don't have continuing respiration, then you get the damage.

**Andrew Murray:** How realistic is it to consume alkalizing materials and how would that affect the overall acid-base balance when the stomach is so acidic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's very safe to consume a great excess of the alkaline material, which the fruit, vegetable, milk, and cheese people do. The body can change protein into ammonium. If it doesn't have enough minerals, it will waste protein, turning it into the equivalent of the alkaline material and using the ammonia as the cation equivalent of the sodium so it can save the sodium and calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think consuming things that have an excess of potassium, magnesium, and calcium can actively work to raise the pH of someone's environment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think their main function is sparing protein that you would use for the kidneys to help regulate the minerals. For example, when a person is fasting for several days, they will generally lose more protein than fat because the stress hormones rise. They live on a pure meat diet [internally] when they're fasting, as their tissues break down. If you just drink the minerals—salt water, baking soda, potassium, some magnesium and calcium—any of the alkaline minerals will radically spare the amount of protein that you would be consuming and wasting. So a fast is much less stressful and harmful if you are getting the alkaline minerals.

**Caller:** Is the carbon dioxide circulation or exchange that the doctor just spoke of why it's so calming to rebreathe carbon dioxide when you're in stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Stress shifting to the alkaline and making lactic acid means the cells are in danger of getting into a chronically activated state. The panic attack is a typical thing where the body too easily shifts over into making lactic acid instead of carbon dioxide. The person feels that they're suffocating.

In the long run, that same thing can lead to degenerative diseases or cancer in which the cells are stuck in a "panic attack" condition. If you think of the original state of the cell as being the protein acid which attracts the minerals to neutralize the acid, you can restore that condition with carbon dioxide. Just rebreathing it, getting your percentage of the acidic carbon dioxide dissolved in the blood up where it should be, you can stop the production of lactic acid, reverse these stress processes, and restore the cell to its relaxed, un-panicked condition.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's through bag breathing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. For example, you can generally lower your blood pressure just breathing a minute or two in a paper bag a few times a day. I've seen people take their blood pressure down 30 points in just a day or two that way.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it really is a de-stressor not only for the mental state but for all the other cellular states that are panicking.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Every cell or tissue is protected if you restore the proper amount of carbon dioxide. Breathing in a bag is one of the most powerful ways to restore the proper balance. If you need more bicarbonate, the gaseous carbon dioxide will allow you to make more bicarbonate, and that will help you regulate your minerals and help you retain more of your alkaline minerals.

Taking sodium bicarbonate, for example, will actually acidify cells that are in need of more carbon dioxide. When the bicarbonate has been deficient, when a cell is exposed to the bicarbonate, it will convert it into the acidic carbon dioxide and be able to lower its pH, even though you've taken the alkaline baking soda.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that why you recommend baking soda for athletes? To help balance out high lactic acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, there have been experiments in marathon or bicycle races in Death Valley where the altitude is very low. They found that a tablespoon of baking soda at the start of the race made them tolerate the stress much better.

**Caller:** I heard a study that in Japan, despite being the highest smoking population, the mortality rate is lower than in America. Does smoking increase that carbon dioxide to relax the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The carbon monoxide is something that we produce under stress, and it lowers our ability to use oxygen and to produce carbon dioxide.

**Andrew Murray:** And carbon monoxide is what you inhale as part of cigarette smoking.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** So the carbon monoxide from smoking is pretty damaging and it's not something that would improve your CO2 content.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you have any thoughts as to why the Japanese culture has such longevity compared to us, especially since they consume a lot of tobacco?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, much of that is propaganda. When you look at the actual details of the population, it isn't as great as some of the articles have been saying. For example, one of the articles, if you look at the mortality figures, suggests that the average lifespan is 300 years. If you don't look at the whole structure of the population, it's hard to get an idea of what the real age-specific death rate is.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So back to the caller's question, you don't think that smoking raises carbon dioxide in any way?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does, but it raises the carbon monoxide so seriously that that's the main thing that takes over. It's harmful.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned sodium bicarbonate for the athletes in Death Valley. Is potassium bicarbonate something that could be used similarly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the average person is very good at getting rid of sodium, so sodium bicarbonate is something most people can use without experiencing edema or disturbance of blood pressure. The potassium bicarbonate has a relaxing effect on your blood vessels, so it can help to lower your blood pressure even more than the sodium bicarbonate. But you have to be cautious because too much of it can relax your heart too much.

**Andrew Murray:** What would be an ideal lifestyle that you would suggest for people thinking about acid, alkalinity, and cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The only foods I would suggest eliminating would be the grains, beans, most of the nuts, and probably reducing most meats. Gelatin happens to be the part of the meat that doesn't have so many of the disturbing acidic, pro-inflammatory effects. In the news currently is the "pink slime" issue, which is made from connective tissues. But it seems to me that that might be the best part of the meat.

**Caller:** Whenever I do short walks, I get muscle soreness for a couple of days afterwards. I assumed I'm making too much lactic acid. I started taking baking soda baths with about two pounds of baking soda. Is that safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think it's good. Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salts) and baking soda are all good. The baking soda helps you absorb magnesium if you have Epsom salts mixed with it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that's a good combo, like maybe one pound baking soda and one pound Epsom salts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Experimenters in naturally carbonated mineral springs found that people were absorbing carbon dioxide through their skin. Even though their body contains a lot of carbon dioxide, the body has such an affinity for it that it will soak it up from the mineral water against the gradient. It's as if we had pumps in our skin.

**Andrew Murray:** I recall a reference to cancer treatment purporting the use of ascorbate at the rate of up to 130 grams a day. It was supposedly keeping certain types of cancer from growing. Do you know much about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They keep changing the technology. I don't know exactly what they're doing now, but as recently as about 10 years ago, a free radical chemist dissolved a gram of pure powdered ascorbic acid in a liter of distilled water and found that there were enough heavy metals in that purified Vitamin C to produce as many free radicals as a killing dose of X-rays would have produced.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Oh, my goodness. So citrus season is a great source of Vitamin C.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. All of our foods except the grains and beans are very good sources of Vitamin C. The analytic methods have generally ignored it in meat and some solid foods, but it's present in meats at a very high concentration in the oxidized state. All you have to do is metabolize it and you turn the oxidized ascorbic acid into the common ascorbic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that the theory why concentrated orange juice still has absorbable Vitamin C? It's just a slightly changed form when you boil it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Most of the tests don't really look at the molecule, they just look at the reducing power. In some vegetables and meats, the tissue has oxidized it partly into dehydroascorbic acid, but as soon as you eat it, it turns back into ordinary ascorbic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They say in Britain it was the fish and chips that prevented the British people from developing scurvy because potatoes have quite a lot of Vitamin C in them as well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and fish.

**Andrew Murray:** What would be the best way of maintaining enough energy in the body to deal with cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The so-called alkaline ash diet—lots of fruits, vegetables, milk, and cheese—will help to let the stressed cancer cell repair itself as far as it can. Breathing in a paper bag to increase the carbon dioxide is probably helpful.

As long ago as 1910, the insurance companies knew that people who lived at very high altitudes had a very low cancer mortality. That has been tested experimentally. Fifty years ago, they implanted tumors in rats. Leaving them near sea level, all of them quickly died. Taking them up to 17,000 ft altitude, half of them threw off the cancers and had no symptoms left just from the carbon dioxide retention when the oxygen tension was lowered.

The carbon dioxide assures the delivery of oxygen to the tissues. Heavy breathing, or hyperventilating, is a way to lower the oxygen in your tissues because you blow out the carbon dioxide, and you need a lot of carbon dioxide in your tissue to deliver the oxygen.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about Gerson Therapy and what he was putting forward as a diet for anti-cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I happened to get a copy of his book just a few years after he died in the early 1960s. I was very impressed by his detailed studies. He seemed to have read just about everything about cancer in the first half of the 20th century. The minerals are a very important part of it, and restoring the oxidative metabolism. He regularly gave his people Armour Thyroid. I think two grains was a very common dose for these patients.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you were suddenly without the ability to get Armour Thyroid, how much of a mammal's thyroid would you need to eat to get the dose you needed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Armour product was standardized to imitate the fresh glandular weight. They would defat the gland, powder it, and then dilute it with glucose or lactic acid to increase the weight until it was similar to the fresh piece of gland. They called that the normal dilution. The powder itself was called the 3x concentrate, meaning that the gland is three times more concentrated than the old Armour Thyroid pills. That means that 1 gram of the [dried] gland is equal to 15 grains of Armour Thyroid.

**Caller:** What would a double latte espresso pink slime milkshake with baking soda do for an athlete's performance in the Death Valley race?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the caffeine tends to enhance performance in mysterious ways. The gelatin has an anti-stress effect. That mixture seems like it would be pretty good: baking soda, gelatin content. You would need quite a bit of sugar with it, preferably fructose.

**Andrew Murray:** That brings up another question. I've read that cancers feed on sugar and you've got to starve a cancer from sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Actually, they feed on amino acids and turn the amino acids into sugar, and then turn some of the sugar back into fat. Then they metabolize the fat. With all that silly chemistry, they produce a lot of heat with no light or function to speak of. That's why you can identify a cancer because it's so hot—it's burning protein, turning it into amino acids and into sugar, then into fat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So is that why thermography is quite an accurate way at looking for cancers?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And so if you can feed it as much sugar as it wants, then it won't eat your protein, at least not so fast.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Okay, so it could prevent the wasting disease associated with cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And saturated fats aren't probably as good as sugar for quieting stressed tissues, but they do have specific anti-stress functions. I would recommend avoiding all of the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) because those turn on the stress reactions—increase your adrenal corticoids, adrenaline, pituitary hormones, and so on. The saturated fats inhibit those same stress systems.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just for our listeners, the PUFA is the liquid vegetable oils, not including olive oil. Coconut oil, beef and lamb fat, butter, and cream are the saturated fats.

**Andrew Murray:** Going back to the Gerson diet, what was with the injected liver extracts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was a way to get all of the essential nutrients. Around the time I read his book, I met Leonell Strong, who developed the cancer-prone strains of mice. He had been curing cancer just with an extract of liver. That was my first research project, trying to find out what it was in the liver extracts that could cure cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Gerson also wanted to eliminate salt from a diet. That's strange to me because I know you're an advocate of salt.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another person who studied cancer at the very basic level was William Frederick Koch. Working on the parathyroid hormone, he found that the alkaline minerals to a tremendous extent would substitute for each other. You can take out the parathyroid glands, which causes a calcium problem, but you could cure that with sodium or potassium or magnesium.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the salt could replace the calcium or the potassium or the magnesium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, to a great extent. Any of those alkaline minerals can replace the others. So you don't have to worry about the balance so much because having an excess, your body can sort them out.

**Caller:** I'm vegan and looking for different sources of protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Potatoes are the best vegetable protein known. They're better than eggs in terms of quality. They have 106% of the protein quality ranked next to egg yolk.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Right. So 8 ounces of potato has 8 grams of protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you consider you're eating the starch too, a liter of potato is like a liter of milk on average.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you make potato juice and don't drink the starch that settles out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Make the juice, then it's more like eating pure egg yolk.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And you can even make a scrambled egg-like preparation from potato juice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen it for people with mysterious ailments who seem to be dying. One or two meals and they just popped out of it. No one really knew what was wrong with them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You'd recommend cooking it, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My experience is just with cooking, it's like scrambling an egg.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Yeah. Let the starch settle out before you cook it.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for joining us, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you very much.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Genetics X Environment
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of genetics versus environmental predisposition to disease. We're very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat on the show tonight. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining the show again. Several months ago, a listener sent us an email suggesting a few things they would like to hear your opinion on, and they conform with tonight's subject. First, for those who have never heard you, Dr. Peat, would you briefly outline your academic career?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I got a PhD in Biology from the University of Oregon in 1972. But I had been reading in biology since the late 1940s and avoided academic study because I saw that strange things were happening that didn't seem at all scientific to me. Even as a kid, it was very clear that political doctrines were influencing biological theories.

**Andrew Murray:** Onto the question of the fairly dogmatic, entrenched view that our genes control everything. We are told we are at the mercy of our genes, and if we are genetically predisposed to a disease, we are essentially doomed. I want your opinion on the current model versus alternative, scientifically founded ways of looking at biology—specifically the role of genes versus the environment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The federal government is really involved in this issue. I was horrified when I discovered that the National Library of Medicine maintains an online version of a book called *Mendelian Inheritance in Man*. I bought a copy for 50 cents at a used bookstore just for the humor of it because it's totally absurd. Basing genetic determinism of a disease on two cases—a single family, for example—is enough to prove to the author that there was genetic determinism involved. This neglects the possibility that both people in the family were exposed to the same chemical toxin or the same diet.

Just about the time I was starting to read biology, the government was starting to get involved in helping the dogmatists control biological teaching. Carl Lindegren wrote a book called *The Cold War in Biology* that explained how the change took place in the 1940s. People who didn't conform to the dogma weren't allowed to teach, even in high schools. It was a very totalitarian institution, with the government as a funding agency and the science journals being influenced by the pharmaceutical industry.

In the first half of the 20th century, the embryological view of development and inheritance was defining how a single cell becomes an adult. It does this by proceeding through many stages of organization. The guiding principle for the first 50 years of the century was that a "field" was involved—a gradient field of chemicals, electrical forces, or other physical forces. They could demonstrate that there was a field effect; if you removed a part, the surrounding conditions constituted a force that would create a replacement part—regeneration—according to the place in the field rather than what the cells had done up to that moment. The idea of genes reading out mechanically, as if from a blueprint, was clearly disproved by the embryologists. But that whole idea of a morphogenetic developmental field disappeared about 1960. The last advocates retired between 1950 and 1960.

**Andrew Murray:** So you think a lot of the stagnation was brought around by vested interests in medicine guiding the dogma of genetics to produce a controllable scenario where drugs can be introduced?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you can't find a drug that will neutralize a gene's product, then you have something to blame the disease on. It explains why doctors are powerless—it's "incurable" if it's genetic—unless the drug companies can come up with something to alleviate the symptoms.

But the actual evidence of how genes relate to health is really a complete fantasy. By the 1930s to 1960s, the idea of a "gene" was recognized as a metaphysical construct, even less based on evidence than the idea of a field. Even though they didn't know exactly what the elements of the field were, they could demonstrate it. The gene idea was simply an abstraction until they applied it to certain stretches of DNA. But even the definition of a gene has been changing since the recognition of DNA as a component of inheritance.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Did they want to tell us that if they can't help us because there's no drug, then it's just a genetic disease? It takes the power out of the person to help themselves.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was a very conscious ideology. Konrad Lorenz, who won the Nobel Prize, was a hero of practically all the professors I knew even into the 70s. He was a Nazi who designed his idea that genes control behavior specifically for Hitler's Institute of Racial Hygiene. It was an excuse for killing people who didn't have the behavioral traits they thought were appropriate.

The American view of eugenics had been mostly to sterilize—sometimes they would euthanize babies—but mostly it was used to sterilize people they considered defective. That political idea of genetics derived right from the end of the 19th century. Mendel and August Weismann were consciously trying to destroy the Darwinian or Lamarckian ideas that the environment might be able to improve the intelligence of poor people. They wanted an absolute determinism stating that people of lower intelligence were simply permanent; their children would inherit their traits. It was used to justify everything in society, not just particular sicknesses.

For example, it was applied to toxemia of pregnancy. The fetus was said to have a genetic defect which was poisoning the mother. This denied that better diet could control or prevent pregnancy complications because all of it was "genetically determined." The Scopes trial, in which William Jennings Bryan argued against evolution, was basically him arguing against eugenics, which was justified by the theory of a mechanical kind of evolution.

**Andrew Murray:** How much do genetics actually affect the organism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are several conditions that are distinctly controlled by particular genes, such as the type of dwarfism in which the bones don't develop. There is a definite gene mutation involved. But that doesn't say that the environment hasn't created that mutation in a particular, controllable way.

One way of looking at genetic uniqueness is that every organism requires a certain environment. A frog can't live in the same place an eagle can live. Certain genes make you need more things from the environment. But even the genes that limit you can create a stress reaction, and the stress reaction can lead to changes in the genes. Evidence has been accumulating in universities among well-known researchers demonstrating that stress can produce directional changes in microorganisms. This uses mechanisms similar to what Barbara McClintock recognized in corn: mobile genetic elements that move around under stress and accelerate the ability to adapt.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So our environment is constantly having an effect upon our DNA, and our cells are constantly sensing a change in environment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** James Shapiro was one of the people who discovered that bacteria can adapt to resist antibiotics, and they can pass on that acquired resistance to their descendants or to other bacteria they interact with. It can be transmitted both genetically and horizontally as an acquired trait. Shapiro calls this "natural genetic engineering," in which the organism is adjusting its own inheritance to improve its survival.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's discuss some diseases considered genetic by today's thinking which are probably more environmental, like prion diseases and Huntington's chorea.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those are considered degenerative diseases as well as genetic. Huntington's disease typically becomes apparent when the person is maybe 40 years old. They were perfectly healthy—some say healthier than average—up until the disease set in. When you look at the specific gene involved in Huntington's, it's a protein that gets an extra inserted stretch of glutamine residues. This can change generation after generation, so the victim's offspring can develop it years earlier than the parent. It can change quickly, indicating something is actively contributing to the mutation.

However, the folding doesn't become a problem for 40 years. The factors known to activate the folding problem that creates the symptoms are environmental things accumulating over decades. These are now being identified. For example, unsaturated fatty acids cause misfolding of the prions in CJD and Mad Cow Disease. Radiation and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) are known to accelerate the misfolding of the protein, making it act like an infectious thing that spreads from cell to cell. In Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, similar folding of proteins causes the symptoms. The factors causing that misfolding are environmental dietary factors.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Weren't you saying that even in the test tube, when they add omega-6 oils to these proteins, it stimulates the misfolding?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's been done with prions in all the prion-related diseases. In Parkinson's disease, the protein is called alpha-synuclein. DHA—the long-chain, highly unsaturated fatty acid—is known to induce the misfolding, while saturated fatty acids can block the misfolding. The evidence links this to an aging process. With aging, the brain accumulates more and more DHA. Especially under the influence of estrogen, women accumulate more DHA and circulate more of it in the blood. Very typically, women are more susceptible than men to several of the degenerative inflammatory diseases.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** DHA is one of the omega oils they tout as being anti-inflammatory and good for women. But you're saying it actually works in conjunction with estrogen to be destructive?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does several things. It breaks down and forms acrolein, which is a very reactive fragment that attaches to the tau protein involved in the filament formation in Alzheimer's disease. DHA activates the excitotoxic process; it increases the glutamate excitatory system, increasing free glutamic acid in the brain fluid. In all these brain degenerative diseases, you can see increased breakdown products of the fish oil type of polyunsaturated fats in the cerebrospinal fluid and serum. Everything from the short acrolein up to the larger prostaglandin-like breakdown products called isoprostanes or neuroprostanes show up increasingly with age and dementia.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So as a newborn infant, their brains have very little DHA and EPA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because their fats have been synthesized by their own bodies, mostly from glucose absorbed from the mother. The animal body can produce saturated fats, monounsaturated fats like oleic acid, and our own series called the omega-9 series. At birth, these are the dominant fats in the baby's brain.

Animal studies going back 30 or 40 years showed that if you feed pregnant animals a large amount of polyunsaturated fats, their babies are born with smaller brains and don't learn as well. A group in France two or three years ago fed pregnant women a high polyunsaturated fat diet, hoping to demonstrate increased learning in the fetus. They found that learning was retarded in the presence of the omega-3 fatty diet to the mother, just in line with the animal studies.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Did they think these oils were useful because they did autopsies on adults and found the brains had a lot of these oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. They said, "Your brain is full of fish oil, so it must be good for the brain." But looking at a baby's brain, it doesn't have any. The more demented and old brains have more than young brains.

**Caller:** I've seen several doctors and never had one ask me what I eat, yet they give me weird looks when I tell them both my grandfathers died from type 2 diabetes. It seems like I'm destined to get it. I had an argument with a professor who said there was evidence for genetics based on twins separated at birth. How much of that is actually genetic versus the shared intrauterine environment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is an argument I've been making for a long time. There was a genetically oriented argument that working-class people would never rise to the middle class because of genetic influence on intelligence. I pointed out the evidence of the intrauterine environment and nutrition. The evidence from animal studies is clear: twins have a very similar environment and get the same nutrition. If the mother's health changes from pregnancy to pregnancy, the intelligence of the baby is influenced by what she was eating.

Animal studies show this effect can be passed on for four generations. Studies of people starved during pregnancy in Holland and Russia showed that not only were their babies impaired mentally, but even their grandchildren showed impairment. It is inherited, but it is a physiological, environmental thing. If they had a super-supportive environment, that could be corrected and wouldn't be passed on.

**Caller:** Would the mother's nutrition during gestation explain the variance in how people tolerate a poor diet? Some people suffer more than others. Is that because of hormonal reserves from their mother's diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 30 or 40 years ago, doctors talked about the "thrifty gene" that caused some families to get fat on very little food. That is undoubtedly another example of inheritance by gestational influence. If you are starving, the fetus adjusts to a poor diet and becomes thrifty. They've never identified a thrifty gene or a gene for diabetes.

When the country of Israel was formed, immigrants came from Africa and Europe. The Europeans had a high rate of diabetes, but the immigrants from poor countries had almost no diabetes. After a second generation of living on a relatively abundant European style of eating, the immigrants' children were developing diabetes at the same rate as the Europeans. This totally destroys the idea of genetic diabetes.

**Caller:** I've been told I have cystic fibrosis and tested positive on the chloride sweat test. I've been told this is a malfunction in a sodium transport mechanism. Can you shed any light on this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've suspected that hypothyroidism is sometimes misunderstood and a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis is made. When I worked in the woods, we had a cook who believed that if you sweated a lot, you needed salt replacement. He put a tablespoon of salt in everyone's breakfast. Within a few days, I was tending to faint if I didn't take salt pills, and my skin was so salty I got crystals of salt on my forehead. I would have been considered to have cystic fibrosis from the chloride coming out of my skin, but it was simply an adaptation to my thyroid metabolism and high salt intake.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you have any suggestions for someone with cystic fibrosis regarding environmental changes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They should examine their thyroid function very thoroughly, including measurements of carbon dioxide (bicarbonate) in the blood and exhaled carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is what actually regulates the movement of sodium and other minerals. If you look with a suspicion of hypothyroidism and endocrine involvement, I think you'll likely find the answer in that.

**Caller:** You mentioned field theory versus the concept of a gene. Integrating field theory back into our understanding would do a world of change—realizing your genetic code is more like a field frequency you can willfully affect. It's about integrating holistic medicine with diet and proper herbs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's a shame that field theory was the theory for the first 50 years of this century and didn't seem to carry on.

**Caller:** Science got a little confused. What needs to happen is an integration of the two. You can have a willful effect on it, but those things are also debilitated by your chemistry. If you aren't eating enough, your ability to emanate energy will be debilitated.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is totally right on.

**Caller:** You've mentioned that hypothyroidism can lead to a downward spiral of high estrogen, stress hormones, and low progesterone. You mentioned supplemental desiccated thyroid to get out of that cycle. Is that something that works in the short term, or would you have to continue for the rest of your life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen a few people who needed it just for a few days to break a stress cycle. But if your body is loaded with polyunsaturated fats, every time you get hungry, these come into your bloodstream and interfere with thyroid function. The average person who is hypothyroid at age 20 or 30 has a body so saturated with antithyroid agents that it takes a couple of years of strict diet before they can get along without thyroid.

**Caller:** Would the same thing go for low progesterone? Could a few doses get them out of that cycle?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is much more frequent than the quick response to thyroid. I've seen two or three hundred women who just needed one or a few doses of progesterone to get out of the cycle and get going on their own.

One woman, who since puberty had been very white-skinned with purple lips, put some progesterone on her hand. A little later she telephoned and said she felt something happening. When she got home, her cheeks were pink and her lips were red. Weeks later, her parents asked what happened to her color. It had existed for 18 years, and in just minutes, one dose of progesterone apparently permanently changed her physiology.

**Caller:** I saw a report about a hospital in Sonoma where they sterilized kids whose parents were considered misfits. The report said Hitler used that as a model.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I haven't heard of that particular hospital, but there were several doing that in the US in the 1920s. American geneticists were the model for Hitler's eugenics program. The American journal was called *Annals of Eugenics* until 1954, and another was *The Quarterly of Eugenics* until 1969. Public recognition of their role in Hitler's campaigns finally caused them to change their names.
