**Caller:** My other question is about the upcoming eclipse. If someone injures their eyes, is it possible to regenerate vision with beta-carotene or vitamin K?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the exposure has happened in the first hour, red light—like seeing light through your eyelids—can have a detoxifying effect on the heat damage. It stimulates circulation and lowers inflammation. Anti-inflammatory things like aspirin and vitamin E help to stop inflammation from such injury.

**Caller:** Could you explain how salt affects the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It stimulates cells to use oxygen and works with thyroid to rev up the oxidation of sugar, producing carbon dioxide.

**Caller:** So if you had an overactive thyroid, would it be best not to eat salt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not necessarily. Your body should govern your salt appetite. You won't have a salt appetite if you aren't losing salt fast enough.

**Caller:** Are you saying it's not good to eat nuts like almonds and walnuts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. I think they are major problems [due to polyunsaturated fats].

**Caller:** You talked about bacteria inheriting resistance to antibiotics, which suggests inheriting acquired characteristics. Could you comment on how that impacts the work of Lamarck?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Charles Darwin was actually not an antagonist of Lamarck. Darwin's grandfather was a Lamarckian, and Darwin got his basic ideas from him. In the introduction to one of the editions of *The Descent of Man*, he made several points that he was not saying it's just a matter of random mutations. He pointed out several other mechanisms of inheritance.

The anti-Lamarckians were actually anti-evolutionists who didn't like the idea that organisms could have a purpose or respond reasonably to the environment in a way that could be passed on. Anti-Lamarckism was a creation of late 19th-century anti-evolutionists who became the basis for the neo-Darwinist movement, which suppressed the idea of a purposeful developmental field.

**Caller:** I'm thinking about this from reading Arthur Koestler's *The Case of the Midwife Toad*. So the suppression of Lamarck is dogmatic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, even to the point of being irrational and unscientific. It's like a cultish doctrine.

**Andrew Murray:** Briefly, Dr. Peat, I read in your newsletter that Zajicek had done experiments revealing cell streaming in tissues normally thought of as static, specifically in the pancreas with insulin-secreting cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the pancreas, like other tissues, is constantly regenerating. It's just our bad, dangerous fats in the diet that are constantly killing off the insulin-secreting cells.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's possible to regain insulin-secreting cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The organism is in very vigorous replacement everywhere. All the parts are turning over in a very organized, meaningful way, doing its best to renew everything, including the things associated with diseases such as lack of insulin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And just to wrap up, these oils that Zajicek showed were harming the cells include every vegetable oil apart from olive oil, coconut oil, and animal fats such as butter and ruminant fat.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com, where there are many fully referenced articles. Thanks so much, Dr. Peat, for joining us again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Cellular Repair
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome once again to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to the shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture all our own certified organic herb extracts.

You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's loose subject of cellular repair. We're going to look into avoiding scarring, amongst other things. Once again, we have our very popular, ever-present scientist to share his views and opinions with us on this show, and that's Dr. Raymond Peat. Dr. Peat, thank you for joining us again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi again.

**Andrew Murray:** For those people who perhaps have never listened to the show, if you would just give people a résumé of your background, that would be much appreciated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** From 1968 to 1972, I studied mostly physiology and biochemistry at the University of Oregon and did my dissertation on age-related changes in the uterus—specifically oxidative changes. I found that estrogen and polyunsaturated fats tend to accumulate or increase in the tissues with aging and interfere with the use of oxygen. Since then, I've been working out the implications of that. The topic you mentioned derives from that subject.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned oxidative changes in utero. I'd like you to open up with the parallels between the development that happens in utero—which happens without a scar—versus regular life. Once we are exposed to the things you'll bring out, scarring is pretty common. But there is definitely a way to do something about it, isn't there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the uterus, early in the development of the embryo, there's no blood supply. The cells are just absorbing oxygen, sugar, amino acids, and vitamins from their environment. Every time they divide, the environment for each new cell is different. The more cells there are, the more complex the environment is. If you happen to be next to a hungry cell, you won't get the same supply of oxygen and sugar. The changing shape as the embryo grows interacts with and modifies the supply of nutrients. So, the very shape that the embryo develops into is governed partly by the supplies that the mother can deliver to it.

**Andrew Murray:** Now, this relates to things like brain size or skull size?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For example, they knew in the 50s that if you lowered the blood sugar of a well-developed fetus using either estrogen or insulin, the brain cells would simply stop multiplying as long as the blood sugar was inadequate. If you take a chicken embryo in an egg, its brain stops growing exactly when the hen's provided glucose supply is used up. But if you open the egg and inject a little bit of glucose, the brain will start growing again, and the chicken will develop with a bigger brain than normal chickens ever had.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So this is why it's so important for pregnant mothers to have optimal nutrition—it supports the brain development and growth of their baby to an optimal level.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. From month six to delivery, most of the brain cells develop. In fact, about half of the brain cells that are present at month six die off. That's how you can influence the size of the brain: by providing sugar. The more sugar there is, the fewer of those month-six brain cells will die off.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Maybe pregnant mothers need to just be hooked up to an IV of fructose.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you've mentioned in the past that fructose crosses the placenta like glucose, but it doesn't come back to the mother, so it stays trapped.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it's what the baby wants, apparently, because it doesn't give any back.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Supposedly, it's very traditional in the Steiner philosophy that mothers should eat a lot of honey. Honey is very high in fructose.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's look at the differences between scarring in adults when they are compromised by what they eat, and how in utero—with high levels of progesterone and the absence of polyunsaturated fats—scarring is virtually absent.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's no inflammation involved in repair in the fetus. If you remove some tissue in the fetus or embryo, the adjoining cells simply multiply and fill in with more cells. Apparently, you've left the available nutrient supply increased relatively by taking out some cells, so the neighboring cells have more and can simply grow faster and fill in the space.

In a mature animal, there are many things that interfere with that. The blood supply is interrupted if you have an injury, so the supply of sugar and oxygen is reduced. There are mechanisms to try to increase the delivery of sugar and oxygen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And this is a stress metabolism? It's your emergency backup if your body's not performing under ideal conditions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Glucose is largely provided during stress by breaking down proteins. First, you use up what's stored as glycogen, but when that runs out, then you have to break down protein.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why it's important not to go longer than eight hours without eating, because you use up all of your glycogen in your liver.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The lack of oxygen—or the presence of lactic acid, which is produced by a lack of oxygen—turns on the production of a very simple protein that serves as supporting material, but also as a barrier substance. Cells that are injured put out this framework collagen material. But too much of that will increase the distance that oxygen and sugar have to travel to reach the cell. It can make the problem progressively worse the more a cell embeds itself in collagen as a result of the stress. You get more framework material but less functioning cellular material, and that's a scar.

Ideally, every tissue has to renew itself constantly, like your skin and your intestine. Everyone knows those are streaming from the stem cells at the bottom of the layer. Ideally, that's just a continuation of the development of cells in the embryo: they are fed, they multiply, expand, and complexify. But as things interfere with the ability to use energy or oxygen, the mature animal progressively moves into a generalized inflammatory state. It doesn't take a specific wound to turn on these cytokines, histamine, serotonin, and so on.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Which are all the backup stress signals.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, a generalized systemic stress starts turning these on in your fat cells, your liver, and every organ. That starts to shift the whole body in the same direction that scar formation goes. Your whole body loses vital functioning cells and replaces them with collagen—inert connective tissue. Old meat, for example, is tough because it's full of collagen. An old animal hide is thicker and tougher. Kid gloves are delicate, but mature goatskin is a thicker kind of leather. That happens in all of the tissues—progressive turning towards scar tissue type of function.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What types of processes inhibit the ideal use of oxygen and sugar in our bodies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The thyroid is the basic thing. Thyroid activates the respiratory enzyme for which copper is the crucial cofactor. If you load up on iron, an excess of iron tends to displace this crucial copper. Anything that interferes with your thyroid function will also interfere with the functioning of this copper-containing enzyme. Too much darkness—not enough good light—reduces the activity of this enzyme.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people need to get lots of sunshine this summer. It's the red light that's regenerative and healing and helps your body use oxygen and sugar more efficiently.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the absence of sunlight, if you just shine a very bright incandescent light on your tissues, within a few minutes the oxidative enzymes are activated and reduce stress.

**Andrew Murray:** The concept of healing without scarring is pretty new to most people. You're saying that especially in the absence of PUFA—the polyunsaturates people consume from vegetable oils—the body can heal better. These oils have a very negative and inflammatory effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of the worst inflammatory agents are produced directly from the vegetable oil. Polyunsaturated fats, the Omega-6 class, form the prostaglandins.

**Andrew Murray:** Which are very pro-inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fetus is highly protected against those. People talking about the so-called "essential fatty acids" have noticed that human babies and calves are born in an extremely deficient state, they say. That's been used to sell the addition of fish oil to baby formula.

**Andrew Murray:** When actually it's completely the opposite—they don't need it and don't want it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The placenta protects the baby against those fats. The sugar that the baby does absorb makes the Omega-9 series, which are anti-inflammatory.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Humans haven't eaten these oils in such large quantities ever before until the 1920s. That's part of the reason why there are so many degenerative diseases, like the pancreatic damage that happens to the beta cells from excess Omega-6.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, could you illustrate the role of diabetes as an illustration of this stress reaction and the vicious cycle of inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anytime your blood sugar falls, that's a stress reaction. It first calls up adrenaline to move glycogen into the bloodstream, largely out of your liver. When you run out of stored glycogen and your blood sugar falls more, the adrenaline starts mobilizing free fatty acids out of your fat cells and other tissues. If you've incorporated a lot of polyunsaturated fats into your tissues, these free polyunsaturated fats interfere with sugar metabolism and signal more stress hormone production. They tell your brain that the stress is worse than it was.

**Andrew Murray:** So they have an intensifying effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, as opposed to the saturated fats which tend to inhibit the stress reaction. It's a self-limiting thing. If you've been a sugar or saturated fat eater and have a stress, you release the saturated fats which are anti-inflammatory and turn off the stress hormones.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Just a detail for our listeners, Dr. Peat, can you explain which oils are included in these polyunsaturated fatty acids, otherwise known as PUFA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the things you see widely advertised: corn oil, canola, soybean oil, safflower oil, sunflower oil, walnut oil.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Sesame oil, cottonseed oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the American diet over the last 30 or 35 years, when diabetes and obesity have been increasing so much, polyunsaturated fats are the biggest increase in our diet, not sugar.

If you look at the nature of the pancreas, there's a constant renewal of the beta cells that produce insulin. The idea that once you're diabetic you're doomed because you don't have the cells is wrong. Studies show that glucose stimulates renewal of the beta cells in the pancreas.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So sugar helps a diabetic's pancreas regenerate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but since the polyunsaturated fats and the prostaglandins they form are toxic to the beta cells, if you don't have enough glucose, you'll just keep killing any beta cell that appears.

It happens that the stem cell flow moves from the glucagon-producing alpha cells to the beta cells as they mature. The alpha cells raise blood sugar. If you have a lot of alpha cells in proportion to beta cells, that will create apparent diabetes because the glucagon causes the breakdown of protein tissue and increases glucose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's like a stress reaction. The body is trying to save the lack of sugar by increasing glucagon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. If you have a lot of sugar supplied, you don't need the glucagon-producing cells, so they move on. Under the influence of sugar, the flow is increased and you produce the beta cells. The sugar should be holding down the stress and preventing the free fatty acids which would form the prostaglandins that kill the beta cells.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This is why you mentioned that study done in England where they gave diabetics sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They gave them 12 ounces a day of the highest quality white sugar. They stopped producing so much sugar in their urine as they were eating these huge amounts of sugar. As they stopped destroying their own tissues, they began gaining weight instead of losing weight.

**Andrew Murray:** This moves on to the concept of cell streaming. You've mentioned Gershom Zajicek and the idea that there is a flowing of cells from one type to another.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's easiest to see in the liver. Zajicek demonstrated a flowing from the portal vein side of the lobule towards the center. But over 50 years ago, L.V. Polezhaev demonstrated that kind of renewal in muscle cells and even brain cells.

One of the current places where this is important is the idea of adrenal fatigue. It implies that stress causes the adrenals to die. But if the stress is moderate, the adrenal is very good at renewing itself. You can demonstrate the total renewal of the adrenal cortex by scooping out the contents. The cells of the inside of the fibrous capsule will multiply and, within about three months, produce a fully structured and new adrenal gland.

In the adrenal gland, the cells near the capsule produce aldosterone. As they mature and stream towards the center, they turn into a layer that produces cortisol. At the last stage, they produce the androgens and sex steroids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's amazing how one cell knows how to differentiate into all those different types.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Stress producing things, like serotonin or shock, turn on the activity of the layer that produces aldosterone. Aldosterone intensifies defensive stress reactions. If the organism can get past that shock stage with adequate sugar, then the glucocorticoids are produced, and finally the sex steroids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the sex steroids are the least important in emergency mode, but the most important in a healthy mode.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you are in this healthy state producing an abundance of progesterone and testosterone, these turn off the aldosterone production.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to bring out the point that in Africa, honey has been traditionally used to heal wounds effectively. You also mentioned that sugar can be packed into a wound to heal it properly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In Africa, when there were no antibiotics available and they had to do chest surgery, they simply filled up the chest cavity with massive amounts of sugar. They discovered that it not only didn't get infected, but it healed basically without scarring. Packing a wound with sugar inhibits the formation of excess collagen and causes an almost scarless healing.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Honey never goes bad, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Partly it's the osmolarity—it dehydrates things. But honey also has antimicrobial ingredients and fructose, which promotes actual healing instead of scar formation. Keeping the energy supply equal to the demand is what short-circuits the inflammation system. It goes right to repair, like the fetus.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to toxemia and preeclampsia. You've noted similarities between these conditions and aging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just about everything that happens to a woman in preeclampsia is similar to advanced aging symptoms: hypertension, nerve problems, liver malfunction, inflammatory processes. In the 1950s, Dr. Tom Brewer was shocked when he saw drug companies promoting diuretics to pregnant women to prevent edema. Doctors began advocating salt restriction.

Diuretics reduce blood volume. That tells the kidneys that you need more circulation. The kidneys signal with renin to activate the adrenals to produce more aldosterone to retain sodium. So when you cut down sodium, you make the adrenals produce more aldosterone to retain it.

**Andrew Murray:** Self-defeating.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Tom Brewer reviewed the evidence and showed that more salt was the cure to toxemia. He emphasized protein, plenty of salt, and calcium. Milk was the ideal protein because drinking two quarts of milk provides more than 2,000 milligrams of calcium. Calcium and sodium help turn off aldosterone. Aldosterone is the villain producing symptoms like leakiness of blood vessels, which causes edema.

**Andrew Murray:** To get onto calcium: when you have a low calcium diet, your blood calcium actually increases, and that calcium is damaging to soft tissues.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** David McCarron noticed that according to government figures, people who had the highest blood pressure ate the least salt. He saw that calcium was really the main thing affecting blood pressure. Parathyroid hormone comes down when you eat more calcium and have adequate Vitamin D. Parathyroid hormone increases aldosterone. If you restrict calcium, your parathyroid hormone goes up, making your aldosterone go up, which increases blood pressure and retains sodium.

**Andrew Murray:** So a calcium-deficient diet leads to hardened arteries and high blood pressure.

**Caller 1:** I had an overactive thyroid and atrial fibrillation. My cardiologist thought I should cut out salt to help lose weight and lower blood pressure. I'm now on thyroid medication to balance things out. Is there any advantage to cutting back on salt for me?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hypothyroidism causes you to lose sodium and is probably the main cause of people having high aldosterone. Increased blood viscosity is a major thing causing rhythm problems like atrial fibrillation. Thyroid makes you able to regulate your minerals; it thins the blood and makes it easier for your heart to pump by lowering viscosity.

Investigating your thyroid function in more detail, you might not need the blood thinner because thyroid is the basic thing that keeps blood viscosity low. Hypothyroidism is an extremely common cause of hypertension. A calcium deficiency and low thyroid function make you actually sensitive to salt.

**Caller 1:** Now that I'm getting my thyroid balanced, can I have a normal amount of salt without worrying?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your calcium intake is well over 1,000 mg per day and your Vitamin D is good, then there's very little likelihood that you will be one of those salt-sensitive people.

**Caller 2:** Dr. Peat has mentioned that menopausal women often get estrogen concentrated in their tissues. Progesterone can knock it out of tissues into the blood. Would it be advantageous to take progesterone and then get a phlebotomy (blood draw) to decrease systemic estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. If the liver is working, if you're eating enough protein, and if your thyroid is okay, your liver will send the estrogen straight to your kidneys to be excreted as soon as the progesterone gets it out of your cells. Progesterone destroys the estrogen receptor, destroys the enzyme that releases estrogen to deposit it in cells, and activates the enzymes that remove it. Everything progesterone does shifts the estrogen out of the cells so the liver can send it to the kidneys.

**Caller 3:** I was told that in this culture, our diets are so acidic that the body releases calcium from bones to alkalize the blood, causing osteoporosis. I was told that if you eat a balanced alkaline diet (vegetables), you don't need calcium supplements.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the problems with calcium supplements is that some, like calcium phosphate, have so much phosphate that it increases stress hormones and activates bone breakdown. The main things that take calcium out of the bones are cortisol, prolactin, and serotonin.

**Andrew Murray:** Does an acidic diet have a direct effect on calcium mobilization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Phosphate is the main acidifying thing in the diet, and it mostly comes from beans, whole grains, seeds, nuts, and meat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That sounds like a vegetarian diet plus meat. The generalization is that the American diet is acidic because of meat, but dairy products like milk are neutral or slightly alkaline because of the high calcium. It's actually a calcium deficiency that causes calcium to leach out of the bones.

**Andrew Murray:** We are out of time. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for your time again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Raymond Peat's website is . There are lots of scholarly articles there, fully referenced. In a few days, it will be the solstice. The sun is right in the middle of the sky, so people's thyroids should be doing good from all the sunlight. Keep the polyunsaturated fats out of your diet and you'll go a long way to improving your health. Thanks for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Blood Pressure Regulation, Heart Failure, and Muscle Atrophy
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, which run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture all our own certified organic herbal extracts.

You're invited to call in with any questions either related or unrelated to this month's subject of blood pressure regulation, heart failure, and muscle atrophy. The number here, if you live in the area, is 923-3911. If you live outside the area, the toll-free number is 1-800-KMUD-RAD.

We're very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat to share his experience and wisdom. He has been extensively researching many different areas of health and nutrition for probably 30 years or more.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Over 40.

**Andrew Murray:** Over 40. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us on the show again. For those who may not know you, would you let the listeners know your professional academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied biology for a PhD at the University of Oregon from 1968 to 1972. Before that, I had been in linguistics, art, and taught a variety of health-related courses, psychology, and philosophy. My graduate study in biology concentrated on the aging of the reproductive system. I originally intended to study brain biology because of my previous work in linguistics and psychology—I wanted to understand how the brain handled consciousness and language. However, at the university, I discovered that the biologists were really no more scientific than the people in the humanities. It was very heavily ideological. That was why I shifted over to the other end of the organism where I could look at more physical, biochemical processes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It sounds very well rounded because the psyche affects biochemistry and biochemistry affects the psyche.

**Andrew Murray:** This month's show is based around your newsletter regarding blood pressure regulation, muscle atrophy, heart failure, and edema. You have been purporting that saturated fats are better than polyunsaturates for a long time. How long has that been?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I really started thinking intensively about it at the end of the 70s. But I ran into the question directly in aging research in the reproductive system. Way back in the 1930s and 40s, people were showing that estrogen accelerated the breakdown of polyunsaturated fats (PUFA), which intensified the effects of estrogen and accelerated aging, especially in the reproductive tissues. It took several years after finishing my dissertation before I concentrated on the nutritional implications of that and emphasized the benefits of coconut oil around 1978 or 1979.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So back then, there was already literature showing that saturated fats—coming from animal fats and coconut oil—were better than the polyunsaturates, which are the liquid vegetable oils now present in pork, chicken fat, and fish because of what they're feeding these animals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. By the 1940s or 50s, the polyunsaturated fats, both fish oil and seed oil, had been incriminated in intensifying estrogen and age-related diseases. The Shute family, who were the first to popularize the therapeutic use of Vitamin E, started out with preventing blood clots related to high estrogen. That overlaps with estrogen activating the breakdown of polyunsaturated fats, producing free radicals and causing vascular disease. Vitamin E was a fertility drug and an anti-estrogen nutrient, as well as protection against the polyunsaturated fats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Lots of people consider Vitamin E to be an antioxidant to help protect us against free radicals. But you're saying that the free radical producing substance is this vegetable oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, before the antioxidant concept was introduced, Vitamin E was thought of as an anti-estrogen. But in 1942, the estrogen industry basically took over the FDA and public consciousness and suppressed everything that incriminated estrogen in aging and miscarriage. Since Vitamin E was identified as an anti-estrogen, the industry shifted the emphasis to protection against free radical oxidation.

There was quickly an awareness of an inverse relationship between polyunsaturated fats and Vitamin E. If you increased your Vitamin E greatly, you could prevent damage from either estrogen or polyunsaturated fats. However, with aging and the accumulation of fats in the body, you had to increase the amount of Vitamin E to prevent miscarriage. My thesis advisor, Arnold Soderwall, showed that you could prevent middle-aged infertility just by increasing Vitamin E. Extrapolating to human levels, it would be the equivalent of 400 units of Vitamin E per day by age 45 to maintain fertility. But that amount increases if you increase the amount of polyunsaturated fat in the diet. If you carefully avoid the polyunsaturates, your requirement for Vitamin E is very low.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** With increasing polyunsaturates in the American diet, the need for Vitamin E has gone up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and it very quickly reaches the point where you can no longer stop the free radical production just by increasing the Vitamin E.

**Andrew Murray:** There were two peer-reviewed articles, one from 2009 and one from 2011, which published data proving that saturated fat intake improved mortality and morbidity in patients with heart failure compared to PUFA.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The 2011 study was by Galvao and others. A high intake of saturated fat improves survival while a high intake of polyunsaturated fat does not.

**Andrew Murray:** And how do triglycerides affect this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** According to Horwich and others in the 2009 study, a higher level of lipoproteins—total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides—are all associated with improved survival in heart failure patients.

**Andrew Murray:** So a higher cholesterol is directly responsible for an improved outcome. That is staggering because the medical community tells people not to consume saturated animal fats because it raises cholesterol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The seed oil industry created that myth because they found that eating a lot of seed oil would lower your cholesterol. Since you have cholesterol in atherosclerotic arteries, they said it must be causing the atherosclerosis. That was never demonstrated. In fact, cholesterol protects against atherosclerosis.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Wasn't there a study showing oxidized Omega-3 and Omega-6 in the plaques of deteriorated arteries?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the pigment found in plaques is the product of the breakdown of polyunsaturated fats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So we can look at cholesterol as an antioxidant bandage trying to stop that rapid rate of oxidation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was demonstrated and published in a major medical textbook in 1922.

**Caller:** I'm 68 and very active. I eat yogurt, fruit, and vegetables with olive oil. My doctor recently prescribed a blood pressure medicine, Amlodipine, that makes me unenergetic. For the past two weeks, I've been taking a tablespoon of chia seeds, and they give me energy. What is the doctor's opinion of counteracting the blood pressure medicine with chia seeds?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Did you say the drug was to inhibit the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)? That's the one heart drug that I think is probably beneficial because it lowers inflammation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** She mentioned Amlodipine. Her question is, what do you think about the chia seeds helping re-energize her?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know of anything in the chia seeds that would be beneficial.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They are very mucilaginous. Could they be acting as a laxative?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it works as a bulk laxative, it would make you feel better by lowering bacterial endotoxins.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you mentioned that if someone took a bulk laxative, they would feel better by lowering endotoxin. Can you tell us how endotoxin poisons us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Endotoxin triggers nitric oxide, which is a vasodilator. Both nitric oxide and endotoxin increase the production of serotonin. All of these inhibit the production of energy using oxygen and shift it over to lactic acid production. They also increase the leakiness of blood vessels.

Anything that impairs energy production—whether it's toxins like endotoxin, nitric oxide, and serotonin, or environmental interference—makes your blood vessels leaky. This raises free fatty acids, which interfere with the use of oxygen. Free fatty acids lead to a cascade of inflammatory mediators, especially prostaglandins. Once you get loaded up with polyunsaturated fats, all of these things interact. The fats lower your thyroid function and increase estrogen production, both of which intensify inflammation, leakiness, and loss of energy production.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** To mitigate the bacteria feeding on starches, you recommend carrots and bamboo shoots because they are antibacterial fibers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's extremely rare for a person to have microorganisms that can survive a good supply of either carrots or bamboo fiber.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And saturated fats like coconut oil are also antimicrobial.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is one of their direct effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You wrote in your newsletter about the substitution of iron for copper in the respiratory enzyme. Is this a copper deficiency or iron overload?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Diet can affect it, but stress tends to intensify it. Anything that stresses your energy production system—such as high estrogen, nitric oxide, low thyroid, or too much darkness—will tend to make you lose copper from your respiratory system. As copper gets lost, iron tends to fill in for it, binding to some of the same enzymes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** With the current situation in the Pacific Ocean, what would you recommend as a good source of copper?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Beef liver. It has a lot of iron too, but the copper tends to concentrate in the liver.

**Andrew Murray:** Does the respiratory enzyme have a greater affinity for copper than iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you have an adequate supply of copper, it will get picked up. Iron is problematic because it is very reactive; it acts as another oxidant. Taking a supplement of a free metal—iron, zinc, or copper—can interact with nutrients in your digestive system and oxidize them. Iron is the worst one to take as a supplement.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What else interferes with thyroid hormone regarding heart failure and high blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Polyunsaturated fats and stress are the most common things in Western culture. Traditionally, the cabbage family and beans were the main goitrogens (things that interfere with thyroid hormone formation). In the Andes, parts of southern Mexico, and western China, there is still a tremendous amount of thyroid deficiency and cretinism. Beans and the cabbage family—especially if not cooked well, like coleslaw—are major factors.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about poor protein intake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, studies showed that men coming out of concentration camps who started eating well would often grow breasts. Starvation for protein causes the liver to become unable to destroy estrogen. Thyroid is needed to inactivate estrogen. If you have a protein deficiency, your thyroid slows down defensively to stop eating up muscle protein. This slows the liver, leaving more estrogen in circulation. Estrogen then blocks the enzymes which attach iodine to the protein to make thyroid hormone. It creates a vicious circle.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And liver is one of the best sources for B vitamins, which help the liver inactivate estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Animal studies showed that vitamins B1, B2, and protein were the main things that activate the liver to inactivate estrogen.

**Caller:** I've been on a regimen of Simvastatin, 80 milligrams, for the past three years following a heart attack four years ago. What is the downside of that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on how much it interferes with cholesterol synthesis. When you interfere with cholesterol synthesis, you're also interfering with essential things such as the synthesis of Coenzyme Q10. That can cause muscle problems because Coenzyme Q10 is needed for producing energy.

**Caller:** My cholesterol has come down quite a lot. HDL is 49, LDL is 46, and total is 147.

**Andrew Murray:** That is very low.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it was in the normal range before, you might actually not have had enough protective effect from cholesterol. Cholesterol can protect you from heavy metal poisoning and many kinds of toxins.

**Andrew Murray:** There are several articles on Dr. Peat's website specifically on cholesterol and its cardio-protective effects.

**Speaker D (reading for caller):** A caller asks about atrophy related to a pinched nerve in the neck. Any dietary advice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are several things hormonally and nutritionally related to a pinched nerve. One of the most common situations is swelling of the sheath or membrane around the nerve. It swells up—for example, in a thyroid deficiency or estrogen excess—and the water makes the sheath compress the nerve.

If it's in a neck joint where cartilage might be softened because of hypothyroidism, the disc can spread out and push on the spinal cord. All connective tissues tend to swell up with high estrogen or low thyroid.

In dogs and horses, they found that spinal nerve compression and paralysis were caused by a copper deficiency. Keeping horses indoors eating dry hay contributed to this. The absence of light makes your respiratory enzymes lose necessary copper. The combination of darkness and copper deficiency causes an energy failure, leading to swelling of the connective tissues and pinching of the nerves.

**Andrew Murray:** So check the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The medical community relies on TSH measurement, but TSH itself is the cause of many symptoms blamed on low thyroid. When your hormone is low, TSH is high. TSH has pro-inflammatory actions that increase fibrinogen in your blood, making it more viscous and prone to clotting. It's best to have your TSH at the low end of normal. One study found that a population with TSH below 0.4 had the lowest incidence of thyroid cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How does salt play a part in relieving edema and the leak of water from the blood into surrounding tissues?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Salt has direct effects on the mitochondria, increasing energy production and shifting the balance to produce more carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide helps retain as much sodium as you need. Without sodium or thyroid, you tend to produce more lactic acid, displacing carbon dioxide and causing inflammation and water retention.

Many doctors insist that more salt causes water retention and high blood pressure. However, David McCarron was the first medical person to point out that it's a calcium deficiency rather than a sodium excess that accounts for high blood pressure related to nutrition.

**Andrew Murray:** They used to give troops salt tablets in hot places like North Africa and India.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Increasing sodium intake tends to stabilize blood sugar because it works with thyroid to improve energy efficiency. It also lowers adrenaline, making your system work more efficiently, and prevents hyperventilation.

**Caller:** Do you know of an herbal supplement for Isosorbide? It's a time-release nitroglycerin for my heart.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nitroglycerin increases your nitric oxide, which is an age-accelerating free radical. That's the worst thing about it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** As far as herbs for the heart, Hawthorne is helpful, but there is no direct herbal nitroglycerin.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, regarding coronary artery occlusion, what is the main way people can help themselves avoid blocked arteries?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eating enough calcium is protective of the circulatory system and prevents hardening of the arteries. The parathyroid hormone rises when you don't eat enough calcium or eat too much phosphorus (found in meat, beans, and wheat germ). Vitamin K is also very powerful at preventing calcification of the arteries.

**Speaker D (reading for caller):** A newly diagnosed diabetic would like quick nutrient and dietary advice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A couple of my articles on the website explain why you shouldn't be panicked into avoiding sugar. Polyunsaturated fats are the best-documented cause of diabetes.

Cold-blooded animals, like lizards, move into the sun or exercise when they need to increase their temperature. When a person experiences chills, their temperature is rising. They produce goosebumps, making the hairs stand up, and the skin gets pale as circulation is cut off. Keep your whole grains, beans, or meat to not more than 8 ounces a day. Another thing is eggshell powder; if you take a quarter teaspoon three times a day with meals, that's about 2,000 milligrams.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, recommendations have recently been coming out that phosphate be lowered as an additive in food. Do you think industry is listening to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they will find some other way to make meat weigh more. I'm afraid one of those might be the gluey substances such as carrageenan or gums. That's already in practice where they take waste fragments of meat or fish, add a jelly such as carrageenan or alginate, and then glue the whole mess together with an enzyme so it looks like a real lamb chop or squid patty.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take this next caller.

**Caller:** I just started listening about 30 or 40 minutes ago, and you were talking about these sources being inorganic. So would organic whole wheat pasta or organic meats have less phosphate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. It's a matter of whether they have added it to one product and not to the other. But the way the animal is fed depends more on whether it has a lot of grass versus grains. The grains can be organic, but they're still very high in phosphate. So the animal will be slightly poisoned by eating them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So grass-fed meat and milk will have a lower phosphate level than grain-fed. But because grains are very high in phosphate, whole wheat pasta would be higher in phosphate than white pasta.

**Andrew Murray:** I think there might have been some confusion between the inorganic phosphate that occurs in food and the naturally occurring phosphates.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In physiology, when you say that the organic phosphate is a protein with a phosphorus group on it or the ATP molecule, when that releases the phosphate, you call it inorganic just because it's not attached to another molecule. But we're constantly making our own inorganic phosphate molecules.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you've mentioned the misnomer that increased calcium will cause calcification, where it's actually the opposite. It's possible to reverse arterial calcification?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Japanese have done studies using vitamin K—very high doses of it—to effectively rebuild osteoporotic bones while taking calcium out of arteries in animal studies. Vitamin K works on cellular energy and specifically on the handling of carbon dioxide, which lets the proteins handle calcium.

Things that increase your carbon dioxide work right along with vitamin K in helping to keep the calcium and phosphate in your bones rather than in your arteries. Even baking soda helps to build strong bones. It acts the same as vitamin K or niacinamide: helping the kidneys to excrete phosphate that you don't need, helping to deposit calcium and phosphate in the bones while taking it out of arteries.

**Andrew Murray:** You've also mentioned the link between parathyroid hormone and calcium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People who have good thyroid function and get enough calcium in their diet have a pretty low parathyroid hormone activity—towards the low end of the normal range. At the middle of the so-called normal range, people tend to suffer inflammatory diseases, muscle pains, and bone loss. The higher the parathyroid is, the more of these degenerative inflammatory diseases you have. The first way to suppress that excess parathyroid is by eating enough calcium, but also vitamin D.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if somebody doesn't get enough calcium or vitamin D, they will be eating their bones.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In an experiment with animals 35 years ago, they put one group on a starchy diet and the other group with only sugar as the carbohydrate, both with a vitamin D deficiency. The ones on the starchy diet had very weak, atrophied bones. But the sugar diet built strong bones despite the deficiency in vitamin D. Sugar was lowering phosphate, and apparently, that accounted for the sugar making up for a vitamin D deficiency.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think any of this can be an energy-driven process from the sugar being used directly as fuel for cellular respiration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. As they saw in William Brown's study, the high sugar diet with calcium increased his production of carbon dioxide. When he started the experiment, his metabolic rate was 10 or 12% below normal. When he got on that diet, it came up almost to normal.

**Andrew Murray:** That would be measured by his basal body temperature.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also monitoring carbon dioxide on blood tests. And the phosphate in the blood—there are some comprehensive metabolic panels that include phosphate. The range is like 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL. You were suggesting that it's better if it's between 2 and 3.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** William Brown's was 4 when he started and came down to 2.7 or 3.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So in the wintertime, do you suggest that people eat more sugars because of the decreasing daylight hours and decreased vitamin D exposure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it helps to activate the thyroid, too. Your liver needs sugar to convert thyroxine into the active T3 hormone. I think people tend to crave sweets more in the winter, which is an adaptive instinct.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take this next caller.

**Caller:** I have low thyroid function and I have a low body temperature, like down in 97. I'm curious if you have any suggestions for that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes just a deficiency of protein can create a low thyroid state. But usually, polyunsaturated fats, too much of the cabbage family vegetables, and too many beans and grains—all these have some anti-thyroid agents. Changing your diet away from those towards the fruit, milk, and cheese categories helps. The saturated fats don't have these toxic anti-thyroid effects. So butter and coconut oil can actually help to increase your metabolic rate and thyroid while reducing inflammation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Isn't it only one teaspoon of these polyunsaturated fats a day that starts suppressing the immune system and the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They've looked at various animal studies to see where the influence of polyunsaturated fats in increasing cancer mortality starts, and it's with 4 grams a day for the average human body weight.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Which is one teaspoon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even the saturated fat foods like milk, coconut oil, cheese, and butter have about 2% unsaturated fats. So even when you're avoiding the cooking oils and mayonnaise, you're still getting two or three grams a day of PUFA unavoidably.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So polyunsaturated fats include fish oil, hemp seed oil, flaxseed oil, canola, sunflower, soy, corn oil, and cottonseed.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take this next caller.

**Caller:** You said something about vitamin K and also baking soda working similarly for hardening of the arteries. Do you suggest taking that, and how much would you take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin K, you can get a high potency formula of a mixture of K1 and K2. With that, I think from 1 to 10 milligrams per day is in the safe range as well as probably being therapeutic for the arteries.

**Caller:** Where would you get vitamin K? And if you can't get it, can you use baking soda instead?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Liver and kale are the famously rich sources. I take liver once or twice a month at least. But I've known people who regularly take one or two teaspoons of baking soda with meals or after meals. They notice that it increases their endurance and energy.

**Caller:** Interesting. I use it myself for heartburn. It works incredibly well instantaneously.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They've tested it on athletes. As much as a tablespoon at the start of a race can really improve their endurance and performance. I think usually the amount you take for stomach acidity is a good amount.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Vitamin K, you can buy that online. A brand that's pretty pure is Thorne Research Vitamin K liquid; one drop is 1 milligram. So we're talking about one to ten drops.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's quickly go back to vitamin D. We've talked about vitamin D in relation to calcification and how it can correct calcium deposition.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things currently being studied is the so-called activated vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, which is the kind that you make when you're deficient in calcium or vitamin D. It seems to have bad effects. The anti-aging protein *Klotho* suppresses the formation of that activated stuff. So taking vitamin D and calcium has a similar effect as that anti-aging protein *Klotho*.

**Andrew Murray:** *Klotho* has only been discovered since 1998. It's a beta-glucuronidase, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. No one really understands how it works yet. They just know some of the side effects. They're doing experiments with mice; increasing the production of it makes them live extra long, like 30% longer. But you can do some of the same things with fructose, niacinamide, baking soda, and so on.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Let's talk about some good food sources of niacinamide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Liver, milk, cheese, eggs, tortillas.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah, coffee. Dark roast coffee is a very good source. Also magnesium, which works against phosphate.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How many milligrams of niacinamide is in a cup of coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I figured that with dark roast coffee, I could get close to 40 milligrams a day just from drinking several cups.

**Andrew Murray:** We've got about six minutes left. From the perspective of phosphate to calcium intake, people should take note that they need adequate calcium if they're going to consume foods high in phosphate like beans, nuts, and meats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Whenever you eat high phosphate foods like meat or nuts, if you have some sugar along with it—fructose in the intestine increases the resistance of the intestine to taking up phosphate. So it's like a phosphate blocker in the intestine while a phosphate loss promoter in the kidneys.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Good sugar sources are fresh ripe juicy fruit, honey, and sugar. Milk has a good sugar, lactose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's sort of equivalent to protecting against the high iron content of meat by having some coffee at the same meal. But if you put sugar in the coffee, then you're protecting against the phosphate too.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And protecting your adrenal glands from lowered blood sugar.

**Andrew Murray:** I love it. All of those things that they would have told you are bad for you are actually the things that are good for you. Saturated fats, animal fats, calcium, milk, cheese.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I think our ancestors had it figured out thousands of years ago. We can't reinvent the wheel with all of our modern-day processed foods.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** If you go to www.raypeat.com, you'll find a link to the articles. There are probably about 50 or 60 articles, all fully referenced, around the subjects of aging, phosphate, and the anti-aging effects of hormones like thyroid and progesterone. He's a research endocrinologist, so he knows what he's talking about. Our phone number is 1-888-WBM-HERB. We can be reached anytime after the show, Monday through Friday.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Antioxidants
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome. Every third Friday of the month we produce a program called *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat join us on the show to share his wisdom. This month's subject is antioxidants: some of the myths about them, what they really do, how they are helpful, and how the history of antioxidants has been skewed. Our current understanding has been misled by manufacturers and other parties.

We are coming into the fall, and as the daylight hours decrease, most people are under a certain amount of stress. I think we all know antioxidants as anti-stress or at least free radical quenching agents, but we are going to explore them in more depth. Dr. Peat, for those who haven't heard of you, would you please outline your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have taught at several universities, various courses related to biology and biochemistry. For example, in Mexico, I taught immunology and intermediate metabolism. My research was in reproductive aging at the University of Oregon. My dissertation advisor, Arnold Soderwall, happened to be a major figure in Vitamin E research. He found that hamsters remained fertile much longer if he gave them increasingly large doses of Vitamin E. Although I didn't work with Vitamin E myself, that was the background for my research with estrogen, progesterone, and oxidative metabolism.

**Andrew Murray:** I think most people have a medical understanding of what we commonly know as antioxidants. I know you're going to describe some of the ill effects that some antioxidants can have because they can work both ways. Would you outline the effects of antioxidants and the body's system of antioxidants?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People often talk about the body's innate antioxidant system. They usually refer to the glutathione in cells and the enzymes that reduce glutathione when it has been oxidized. Superoxide dismutase and catalase are considered to be at the center of our own antioxidant system, with uric acid as a circulating major protection against free radicals.

**Andrew Murray:** Can I hold you there for a second? Uric acid is something that I was always led to believe was a cause of gout. Is that true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is involved. Being an antioxidant, it's also involved in protecting against inflammation, because inflammation involves things that are thought of as oxidative damage. Molecules get oxidized and changed. Even though uric acid is probably defensive against inflammation, it tends to eventually get crystallized in the process of defending against the inflammation. You often find crystals of uric acid in an inflamed joint, but people can have crystals of uric acid in the tissue with no symptoms at all. Symptoms like gout can occur without the crystals. Crystals of phosphate are probably more common in gout than uric acid crystals, but without analyzing them, people consider them to be uric acid.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's more the inflammation that someone would have anyway, whether in soft tissue or joint, that uric acid would come onto the scene to be an antioxidant for?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Apparently. It is considered quantitatively our main antioxidant defense inside cells. Glutathione is considered the main one because it's the reductant that can block a lot of oxidative molecules.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned superoxide dismutase.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Recently, some studies of roundworms and aging have found that superoxide dismutase actually might shorten their longevity. A lot of things are being reconsidered regarding superoxide. For example, in the ionized air effect, in which negative air ions have anti-inflammatory effects, it turns out that superoxide—which many people think of as one of the worst oxidants—happens to be produced when we breathe negatively ionized air. It's produced in the lung, and the lung is the main place where serotonin is detoxified and destroyed. Serotonin is destroyed in the lungs under the influence of superoxide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why they say if you walk along the seashore and there are breaking waves, the release of negative ions is supposed to help your lungs, especially for asthmatics? Is that because it's lowering the serotonin in their lungs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There is a series of papers done in Poland that call it the "serotonin irritation syndrome." They concluded, after about a 20-year series of studies, that the ions are helping to destroy serotonin in the lungs. The superoxide dismutase that destroys superoxide has been thought of as a defense against this free radical, but we don't necessarily just want to increase that antioxidant because sometimes it's involved with making inflammation worse if we get rid of too much superoxide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when you hear research coming out about a new antioxidant being discovered, we have to look into it a little bit more because it could be counterproductive to have too much of some of these wonderful antioxidants.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Advertisements often say a chemical is 100 times better as an antioxidant than Vitamin E, but that doesn't mean it's going to be safe in the body. Vitamin E fits into this system of superoxide, glutathione, Vitamin C, and uric acid in a very tightly organized system. If you put in something that's 100 times more active against oxidants or free radicals *in vitro*, you really don't have any idea what it's going to do in the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main plant substances that are now being called antioxidants are mostly polyphenolic compounds. There is almost a 100% overlap between the polyphenolics as antioxidants and the polyphenolics as estrogens. I was thinking about that overlap and how 30 or 40 years ago, these same chemicals were classed together as tannins. 50 or 60 years ago, someone discovered that tannins help to seal the skin of a burned person to prevent seepage—called an eschar. After doing that for maybe 20 or 30 years, they started seeing that it was a carcinogen. In the 70s, tannins were identified as very effective carcinogens.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about the topical use of tannins? That was big in herbal medicine school.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's what turned up in the 70s—people who had been treated topically for burns were getting skin cancer in the area treated.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you list some examples of these polyphenols or tannins that are associated with increasing estrogen and carcinogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's almost an endless series, but the famous ones are ellagic acid and gallic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** So the background from which they've come has changed considerably. Now the industry is calling them yet another compound that can be marketed to people to help them in their quest for the antioxidant effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin E is the famous, oldest sold antioxidant supplement. When it was first discovered, it was called the "fertility vitamin" and was sold to increase virility and fertility. The Shute family in the 1930s found that it not only made infertile women more fertile, but they knew that these women with excess estrogen often suffered from blood clot diseases—venous clots, embolisms in the lung, and strokes. They found that Vitamin E not only made them fertile by antagonizing the estrogen, but it prevented the clotting problems. It showed very clearly its anti-clotting effect was part of its anti-estrogen effect.

During that same period, up to 1940, estrogen was known to intensify the effects of unsaturated fats in oxidizing. It catalyzed their conversion into age pigment by interacting with iron and unsaturated fat. So estrogen was an oxidant, clot former, anti-fertility substance, and pro-inflammatory.

As the oil industry began promoting their seed oils, first for animal fattening, they were adding it to lab chow for research animals. It turned out that the animals were suffering from degenerative brain diseases and testicular degeneration. Someone found that Vitamin E protected against the toxic effects of the unsaturated fats. This was a very sudden shift away from Vitamin E as the anti-estrogen, and it started being called the antioxidant protective against the breakdown of unsaturated fats.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And you were saying they added iron to the animal's feed and then they stopped seeing the beneficial effects of the Vitamin E?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For several years they found that the supplemented feed no longer cured the brain degeneration. They found that the Vitamin E was being destroyed right in the product by the presence of iron. But the same thing happens in the organism. Vitamin E and polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) are very interactive and pro-oxidative. The industries—both the estrogen industry and the seed oil industry—found that this was a way to distract the public from thinking of estrogen and unsaturated fats as being dangerous. If Vitamin E was just protecting against oxidation, then all you needed was fresh oil and Vitamin E. They suppressed the idea that Vitamin E was an anti-estrogen, anti-clot, heart-protecting drug for about 40 years.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This made me think about prenatal vitamins. When a woman is exposed to much higher estrogen levels, prenatal vitamins have a large dose of iron and a large dose of Vitamin C. We were talking about how that gets destroyed with iron as well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. That's analogous to something that happens inside the cell during stress. If you're overloaded with iron when your cell can't use oxygen properly, any reductant, including Vitamin C, will react to turn the highly oxidized iron into the partly reduced form—ferrous iron. In that case, that iron becomes a major oxidant, transferring its electron to fats, proteins, DNA, and so on.

About 10 years ago, a free radical researcher put some Vitamin C—he started with a 500 milligram commercial tablet dissolved in a liter of distilled water—and found it produced a terrible intensity of free radicals. He then got the purest reagent grade available, and the same thing happened. He analyzed it and found there were several heavy metals in it. Since he knew about iron's effect, he used just a very small trace of iron, not adding any of the other oxidants, and found that that amount of iron was enough to turn the commercial ascorbic acid into a powerful oxidant.

**Andrew Murray:** This obviously happens in people's bodies. Iron is prevalent in everybody's body and in foods.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** This chemist said, "Isn't it amazing that this amount of free radicals you would think would kill anything?" He said it shows what amazing defenses our stomachs and intestines must have to survive taking ascorbic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** In this country, there seemed to be a cultural trend towards mega-dosing—five grams or more of Vitamin C a day was not uncommon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Linus Pauling pointed out that a goat that weighs as much as a person would be producing about 4,000 milligrams of Vitamin C a day. I had been taking large amounts of Vitamin C and was reacting badly to it, having a cough and chronic symptoms. So I stopped taking it. After a while, I wondered how much Vitamin C I was putting out in my urine every day. On an ordinary diet at that time—including bread and potatoes, things you don't think of as having Vitamin C—I was still putting out 3,000 milligrams a day consistently.

That got me interested in where the Vitamin C was coming from. It turns out that meat, for example, is extremely rich in dehydroascorbic acid. That is not measured; they measure the reduced form, ordinary ascorbic acid, when they analyze foods. So they're simply not looking at the major form in food. Most foods have more ascorbic acid than the analysts show. It functions in the cell as an oxidant, and that's how it has a major part of its protective effect.

When something goes wrong with the oxidative system—if you have a temporary shut off of the blood supply—the electrons coming from fat, sugar, and protein being metabolized will essentially escape and do random damage. But the presence of the oxidative dehydroascorbate in the cell functions as a substitute for oxygen for a short time. It soaks up these random damaging electrons, being turned back into ordinary ascorbic acid, which then becomes water soluble and leaves the cell.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So there's a huge amount of this form of Vitamin C that plays an extremely important role in our physiology, but food analysts aren't even looking at this level.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People who don't eat a significant amount of bread, pasta, and beans will typically consume in their other foods—fruits, meats, milk—3,000 to 4,000 milligrams of Vitamin C equivalent a day.

**Caller:** I have a question about milk. Dr. Peat, I know you are a proponent of milk drinking. I was increasing my milk drinking, and then I came across a paper titled "How Milk Causes Osteoporosis." It paralleled the high bone density of people in countries where they drink a lot of milk with correlated high rates of osteoporosis. Can you address that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is almost an organization of anti-milk people, and that's one of their worst publications. It is unscientific. Much of it is the lack of Vitamin D in those countries. If you compare someone in Vietnam who eats maybe 600 milligrams of calcium from vegetables, and someone in Sweden who might get 2,000 milligrams from milk and cheese, the people in Vietnam are outside a lot getting sunlight and Vitamin D. Their diet is rich in magnesium and other nutrients. Since milk production is high in the high-latitude countries, part of that effect is the lack of Vitamin D.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's a lack of Vitamin D in the northern hemisphere causing the osteoporosis, even amongst milk drinkers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Caller:** Is there any accuracy to their claim that we have a finite number of osteoblasts and we use them up?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The osteoblasts are regenerating and being renewed. There is no finite population.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's not even normal medical science to say that there's a finite population. You're constantly breaking down bone and building bone. Also, bone mineral density scans don't look at the health of the bone or the protein structure; they just look at the minerals through an X-ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you look at a population that's similar in other ways, the difference between milk drinking and not milk drinking corresponds to strong bones versus weak or smaller bones. Animal experiments are the clearest way to understand medical issues. Whenever a medical doctrine chooses to sell a product that conflicts with animal studies, they say we can't go by anything except double-blind human clinical studies. But much of medicine is based on animal studies, and they are a perfectly valid way for most issues.

**Caller:** I am newly diagnosed with diabetes at age 67. Is a restricted calorie diet helpful? Also, I read an article in the *New York Times* titled "High Stress Can Make Insulin Cells Regress." It said beta cells in mice weren't dead but reverted to an earlier developmental state. I'm trying to control it with diet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cells can replace themselves in several different ways. Regressing and redifferentiating is one way, but a well-established way is that the alpha cells in the pancreas are converted steadily into beta cells. You can completely kill off all the beta cells by eating too much unsaturated fat and have supposedly Type 1 diabetes. But if you stop killing the beta cells, the alpha cells are known to be able to replenish them. The stimulus and the defense to keep the replacement going from the alpha cells is sugar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's just what diabetics avoid. For our listeners, unsaturated fats include all those vegetable oils that are liquid.

**Caller:** Yes, I've been omitting that and using coconut oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You've probably seen news about a hundred-year-old study where they used aspirin to cure diabetes. Aspirin helps you handle glucose fairly quickly to lower your blood glucose. Aspirin happens to be a very powerful antioxidant of a safe kind that prevents the excess electrons from things such as polyunsaturated fats destroying cells like the beta cells. So the aspirin is not only intensifying your ability to immediately use glucose, but it's also protecting against any residual polyunsaturated fats stored in your body.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you take more than one baby aspirin a day, you need to take one milligram (1,000 micrograms) of Vitamin K with each standard 325mg aspirin tablet to prevent bleeding issues.

**Caller:** What about restricted calorie diets? I heard about 600 calories a day giving the pancreas a rest.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of the low-calorie diets were analyzed by a researcher named B.P. Yu. He found that if you simply reduced the polyunsaturated fats but kept the calories the same, you got the same protective effects as a very low-calorie intake. When you reduce your calories to the bare minimum, you burn the polyunsaturated fats for energy, and they don't get loose to do the damage.

**Caller:** So if you didn't have a lot of polyunsaturated fats in the first place, it wouldn't matter if you ate normal-sized meals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. People who have a high metabolic rate aren't hurt so much by the polyunsaturated fats because they burn them for energy. The PUFA inhibit your thyroid function and block your oxidative metabolism, allowing free radicals to get loose and damage things.

**Caller:** Thank you very much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In one of my articles, I mentioned studies done in Paris about 1860 where doctors cured diabetic patients by giving them as much sugar in their diet as they were losing in their urine. They described the recovery of patients on 10 to 12 ounces of sugar added to their diet every day. More recently, people have seen that fructose, in particular, maintains the cell in a state of low phosphate and intense oxidative energy and chelates iron. Iron is one of the major things that interacts with unsaturated fats to produce free radicals. Fructose keeps the cell oxidized, including keeping the iron from catching the electrons that make it toxic.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And white sugar is half fructose, half glucose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** So the old-fashioned sugar diet was not only preventing tissue wasting, but it was having an antioxidant effect in the pancreas. The sugar was an essential factor for supporting the regeneration of the beta cells to produce insulin.

**Engineer:** I have a 13-year-old dog who has a wasting syndrome. He's losing weight and is close to death. Should I try adding sugar to his dog food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I have a friend who has been feeding his dogs mostly meat. One of the dogs he put on a mostly milk diet, and it recovered from cataracts. Another dog he thought was about to die, so he put a tablespoon of sugar on each of its servings of meat, and it is recovering.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I've seen great results recovering injured fowl—ducks and geese—with egg, milk, and sugar. It's a convalescent food.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vanilla also happens to be anti-inflammatory and antioxidant.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Before we move on, regarding Vitamin C supplements: Dr. Peat pointed out that companies can call a vitamin "food-based" even when they take cornstarch and oxidize it with lead to produce the Vitamin C. So if you're having allergic reactions, check your vitamins.

**Andrew Murray:** How about other beneficial antioxidants? I know you mentioned selenium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Selenium activates the thyroid. By making the cell use oxygen and consuming all the potentially harmful electrons, the thyroid functions as an antioxidant. Even though its function is to increase oxidation, it prevents the random, harmful type of oxidative damage. Estrogen, by interfering with thyroid-activated functions, produces a lot of reductive stress to the cell, causes water uptake, and shifts the balance towards the reductants. It's like anti-Vitamin E in its effects. Progesterone opposes those effects, working with thyroid to keep the cell in its resting, oxidized state.

**Caller:** I have a brother who is 10 years sober but consumes great quantities of Mountain Dew and ginger ale. By the evening, he's like Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde—very aggressive. I think the sugar is feeding it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Actually, sugar and alcohol have almost exactly opposite effects on the cell. Fructose, in particular, is almost an absolute defense against the cellular damage done by ethyl alcohol.

**Caller:** But he gets reactive. It's almost like he's high.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The idea that sugar causes behavior issues has been around a long time. It got a big boost in the 50s with the publicity for fat-based damage to the circulatory system and the reaction that "no, it was the fructose, not the fat." One subdivision of that thought is that sugar is addictive and shifts brain transmitters. But those theories are often driven by ideology. For example, they say you need to raise serotonin for peace and tranquility and that sugar spoils that. But in dogs, aggressive ones have high serotonin, and if you lower it, they become peaceful.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It sounds like he might have other nutritional deficiencies.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Magnesium deficiency often goes with having a reaction to a certain food simply because those drinks don't have any magnesium to speak of. When magnesium is low, your brain transmitters leak out and get out of balance. A magnesium supplement would be something for him to try.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Before we wrap up, regarding Vitamin E: if people are going to supplement, especially if they are eating PUFA fats (pork, chicken, fish, vegetable oils), it is important to get a mixed tocopherol, not just the d-alpha tocopherol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The d-alpha was the antioxidant they promoted when they suppressed the information about the complete Vitamin E, which related to preventing clots, tumors, and estrogen symptoms.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So a Vitamin E supplement might be safe, but a Vitamin C supplement definitely isn't?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. You can get as much Vitamin C as your body can use just from foods.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you mentioned lipofuscin, or age pigment, is a product of free radical damage and low thyroid. Is that a good gauge of how much stress someone is under cellularly if they have a lot of age spots?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, definitely. If you can see them on the skin, you're getting them in your brain and other organs. It is dietary. If they're fairly new, Vitamin E, progesterone, and even a tiny bit of vodka can help to remove them.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Peat. For listeners, Dr. Raymond Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. There are many fully referenced scientific articles there. Thanks for listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Energetic Interactions of Ionizing and Non-ionizing Radiation
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture all our own certified organic herbal extracts.
