**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So 400 calories from orange juice is not comparative to 400 calories from baked potatoes and rice. The rice would increase stress hormones and suppress metabolism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. Also, starch particles can enter the bloodstream and trigger stress hormones.

**Caller:** I lose about 5 pounds of weight sleeping some nights. Is it better to be cold or warm at night to lose weight?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on how you respond to the cold. Some people steam up the windows, meaning they lose weight by evaporation. But if your body temperature drops because you are slowing down to resist stress, you turn on inflammatory hormones. If your feet reach 90 degrees Fahrenheit (cold), they are producing toxic stress substances.

**Caller:** So it's better to be comfortable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Don't have a cold head or cold feet. Some people sleep better taking a warm foot bath and wearing wool socks and a cap.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** You mentioned eating food that tastes delicious. Is it good to eat whole grains like brown rice and millet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, there's almost nothing of value in those. White rice is relatively free of toxins, but has very little food value.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** What about ice cream?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has a good balance because it has fat, protein, and sugar. It can help a lot of people go to sleep.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** What about fruit juices other than orange juice? Like berry, peach, or carrot juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many juices are good for minerals and antioxidants. Grape juice is very good. Some tropical fruits like guava and mango are good. Carrot juice should be avoided except in small amounts because the high carotene content antagonizes both thyroid and progesterone.

**Andrew Murray:** We have come to the end of the show. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for your input. For those listening, Dr. Raymond Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. It is full of fully referenced scientific articles.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Join us next month on the third Friday.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Palpitations and Cardiac Events
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who have never listened to our shows, they run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 to 8:00 PM. We are both licensed medical herbalists who qualified in England with a degree in herbal medicine and produce our own certified organic herb extracts here in the USA. We have a practice here in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions.

Once again, we're very pleased to introduce Dr. Raymond Peat to the show to share his wisdom with us. Today's topic is palpitations, but it also interweaves many current subjects related to palpitations, such as hormones—especially progesterone—and factors associated with blood clots, myocardial infarcts, and other cardiac events. Let's welcome Dr. Peat to the show.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** We wanted to focus on palpitations this evening. I know there are many factors involved, but we are going to home in on a couple in detail.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Does Dr. Peat want to give our listeners a brief description of his background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied physiology at the University of Oregon for several years, from 1968 to 1972. The circulatory system wasn't my main interest, but I ran across interesting work done in the 1940s by one of my science heroes, Albert Szent-Györgyi, who happened to be studying the effects of estrogen and progesterone on the heart and blood vessels of animals. His work exactly matched what I was doing in animal aging and the effects of those same hormones. So, I was interested in the circulatory system as it relates to the endocrine system especially.

**Andrew Murray:** I know your main interest is anti-aging and hormones surrounding stress and aging. A lot of what we thought we knew from mainstream medical education and the media seems erroneous in the light of published—albeit rarely included—research. I'm referring to the ongoing hormone debate. With the papers published showing the dangerous effects of estrogen and the beneficial effects of progesterone, testosterone, and thyroid hormone, what are we to understand of the misleading advertising surrounding estrogen's supposedly positive effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the standard thing: what gets into the news, science journals, or universities is strongly influenced by giant corporate interests. Estrogen happens to be very profitable—multi-billions of dollars per year—so they can control the public perception of the hormones in their interest.

Part of the idea of selling estrogen as a beneficial thing was that women live longer than men. Since they were selling estrogen as the "female hormone," they said it must be estrogen that accounts for why women live longer and have a lower incidence of heart disease before menopause. At one point, they actually did a trial of giving estrogen to men. When the men started having more heart attacks, they stopped the experiment. But that didn't kill the idea that estrogen is heart-protective. For 50 years, they carried on promoting the idea of giving estrogen to women to protect their hearts until the Women's Health Initiative results came out, showing women having more heart attacks on the estrogen trial.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Why did they start with estrogen? Why didn't they start with progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Because there is only one substance that really has the effects of progesterone. Conversely, just about anything that interferes with the use of oxygen has estrogenic effects. Several extracts of soot were demonstrated to be estrogenic. The polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are very estrogenic. Even cyanide has some estrogenic effects. Putting a plastic bag over an animal's head or irradiating any part of the animal with X-rays or gamma rays is estrogenic. The concept of estrogen is easily brought to market in a product, whereas progesterone is one single molecule that can't be imitated exactly with any alteration.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about the price difference to manufacture estrogen versus progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fact that soot extracts are estrogenic means you can produce it for less than one cent per dose if you want to. Progesterone has to be exactly duplicated. For years they were extracting it from the corpus luteum of sow ovaries, and it took tons of ovaries to produce a few grams of progesterone. Eventually, they found how to manufacture it from plant steroids that were closely similar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Like wild yam and trillium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. With a few chemical alterations, they could become exact copies of the progesterone molecule. But since no one could patent that one substance, they introduced small changes, making it no longer progesterone. They said it was "close enough" to progesterone—and claimed it would be better because they had a patent on it. They devised tests that had something in common with the real progesterone molecule, such as a certain change in cells of the uterus, which let them call it a progestin or progestogen. They implied that it supported gestation, but in fact, these were the chemicals that were the basis for the birth control pill because they *prevented* gestation. Really, they should be called anti-progestins.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they can patent a drug from soot, but progesterone is expensive and unpatentable.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen affects every system, but in pretty much exactly the opposite way that progesterone does. Any tissue that is injured will begin producing its own estrogen. The idea that a woman is estrogen deficient at menopause is a complete fabrication.

Someone measured the estrogen manufactured in a monkey's ovary by measuring the blood going into and coming out of the ovary. As a control, they measured the blood going into and out of the arm of the same monkey. They found that the monkey's arm was producing more estrogen than the ovary. Since women at menopause still have their arms and legs, there's no way they are going to have a decrease in the basic estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the medical myth is that in menopause you suffer from a lack of estrogen, when in fact you're suffering from a lack of progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That has been demonstrated and published, but in books rather than journals. The journals are so controlled by the industry that you get real science in books that never get into the medical indexes. Medical schools teach what the medical journals publish, and that's always at least a generation behind the science journals.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting to the subject of palpitations, quite a few people we see in practice mention palpitations as a feature of their physiology. It's been shown in research that estrogen precipitates arrhythmias, whilst progesterone has an inhibiting effect. Could you explain the physiological interactions at work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the very recent articles on that topic concluded that estrogen causes sudden cardiac death, and progesterone prevents it. They were talking about the arrhythmia caused by prolonging the excited phase of the heart action.

The electrocardiogram has several phases. The last phase is called the repolarization wave or the T-wave. When the cell has repolarized, it is ready for a good, strong next beat. But if it is delayed by staying in the excited state too long, the atrium might send a signal for a new beat. If it superimposes on that excited state, the cell can't recover enough to have a proper full beat. It will have a slight premature convulsive movement, but not an effective pumping stroke.

Estrogen is the basic thing that tends to extend the excited state. It is similar to what happens in epilepsy. During periods of greatly excessive estrogen, the brain cells can't get out of the excited state and there's an epileptic seizure. Progesterone prevents that by quickly accelerating the restoration of the readiness state, or the relaxed state, of the nerve. It is the same in the heart muscle or skeletal muscle. Any kind of cell that is excited is quickly restored by either progesterone or thyroid. Both have the energy-restoring effect in slightly different ways. Thyroid increases the energy production needed to relax the nerve or muscle. Progesterone stabilizes the relaxed state so that it can hang on to the energy produced by thyroid. Estrogen interferes with both of those processes, slowing the action potential.

**Andrew Murray:** So thyroid hormone is also able to allow muscles to relax, showing that energy is necessary to allow that relaxation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the cell is in its excited state, besides the electrical changes, many other properties change. For example, one of the immediate effects of estrogen excess is that cells take up more water or release water more slowly. In this fraction of a second of excitation, the cell momentarily takes up a little water, swells, and then as it relaxes, it squeezes the water out. If you are having a premature contraction and not letting it relax fully, the cell gets a little waterlogged with each of these false beats. Estrogen causes a slight waterlogging and swelling of the cell wherever it acts—pituitary, uterus, breast tissue, heart, or nerve.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why so many women had heart attacks during the HRT trial? Because the estrogen was suppressing their thyroid, causing waterlogging, and blocking progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. One of the differences between heart failure in women and men is that the diastolic, or relaxation phase, is more often defective in women. In that poor diastolic relaxation, the cells become progressively more waterlogged and unable to relax. In that over-hydrated state, they also can't get rid of the calcium that comes in when the water enters. It ultimately can lead to actual calcification of the heart. There was a picture published by the Mexican Heart Institute of a very old woman's calcified heart that looked somewhat like a bone. It is the end stage of that chronic over-hydration, over-excited inability to relax.

**Andrew Murray:** And oral contraceptive use in women over 37 who smoke was related to a much higher incidence of stroke and heart attack.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect that the fact that estrogen increases the carbon monoxide in tissue probably overlaps with the high chronic exposure to carbon monoxide in smokers. Air pollution carbon monoxide is highly associated with increased heart events.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of palpitations, what is the route to restore normal contractions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are things other than the electrical property or hydration. Blood volume is one factor. For example, high-estrogen women are susceptible to varicose veins, or simply swelling and distension of the veins. Sometimes the veins on the back of the hand swell up, and the legs tend to do that in a high-estrogen phase of the menstrual cycle.

When the veins in the legs are distended, much of the body's blood supply is in the legs, so it isn't coming back to the heart at the normal speed. If the woman stands up and her blood tends to fall into her legs, there will suddenly be a smaller return to the heart. The heart doesn't have very much blood to beat, so it has fast little strokes because the blood simply isn't being returned. That situational arrhythmia or tachycardia is not necessarily connected to electrical instability, but simply to the way the blood isn't getting sent back to the heart.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is linked to high estrogen causing the veins to distend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Progesterone increases the smooth muscle tone in the wall of the veins. If your progesterone is deficient, the veins bulge with very slight pressure. If you hold your hand at your waist, if your progesterone is right, you won't see your veins. But if you're low in progesterone or under stress, even at waist level, you're likely to see bulging veins.

**Caller (New Jersey):** I saw something today on Dr. Peat's site I thought he would want to know about. In the article "Calcium and Disease," the words "protein diet" are a link. When I clicked it, I was taken to a commercial for "Sensa" weight loss system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wasn't aware of that. Thanks for the warning.

**Andrew Murray:** Somebody is obviously inserting a malicious hyperlink into one of your articles.

**Caller (New Jersey):** What is your understanding of Sensa?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never heard of it.

**Caller (New Jersey):** They say you sprinkle it on food and it enhances taste so you don't eat as much. Sounds like MSG.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'll take a look at the link. Thank you.

**Michael (Announcer):** A listener asks: What is the herbology of stinging nettles? I've been eating a lot lately.

**Andrew Murray:** They contain a lot of calcium. We recommend eggshells as a richer source, but this is the most nutritious time of year to eat nettles. When they are about 18 inches tall, cut them down to ground level. Steam them in a colander for about 10 minutes until limp. The liquid is mineral-rich. It's also an antihistamine for allergies.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's a perfect time for nettle salad. I like to put olive oil, a squeeze of lemon, and feta cheese on top.

**Michael (Announcer):** A caller notes that once nettles are wilted or cooked, they don't sting.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If the fiber is too much for sensitive digestions, boil them and drink the liquid where most minerals will come out.

**Caller (Eureka):** You mentioned a connection between seizures/epilepsy and estrogen. Did I understand that correctly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I have an article on my website about that. It's been known for around 70 years that there is a premenstrual type of epilepsy. Animal experiments showed that the ratio between estrogen and progesterone governs the stability of nerve cells. When the ratio is too high (high estrogen), slight stimulation can set off an uncontrollable volley of activity leading to seizures. It's correctable by metabolically lowering that ratio—increasing progesterone and excreting estrogen faster.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You can figure this ratio out by asking your doctor for a blood test for estradiol and progesterone.

**Andrew Murray:** I read that prostaglandin synthesis—prostaglandins being inflammatory mediators causing vasoconstriction—is relieved by progesterone. In angina and myocardial infarct, progesterone is important if it can be administered quickly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very much like cortisol as an anti-inflammatory, inhibiting inflammation-promoting things. Prostaglandins are probably the most important ones for people who eat unsaturated fat. However, progesterone doesn't have the harmful side effects of taking cortisol or synthetic glucocorticoids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if you have a heart attack and take aspirin or progesterone, do they both work by blocking prostaglandins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They both stop the inflammatory process which leads to tissue damage. The brain is more sensitive than the heart. Research shows that if you can get a big dose of progesterone to someone who has had a potentially fatal head injury, they will have a high survival and recovery rate because progesterone stops the progression of brain damage. It does the same thing to any tissue that's injured.

**Caller:** Is it estrogen dominance or low estrogen that typically causes palpitations?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's estrogen dominance or a poor ratio of estradiol to progesterone.

**Caller:** Even if the progesterone is "fake" progesterone in the form of birth control? I had a terrible time while on the Mirena IUD. I believe that triggered my palpitations.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some synthetic progestins actually have some protective effects. There is one called drospirenone that is probably the closest to natural progesterone, and it is used to treat heart failure. However, just the presence of an irritant in the uterus [like an IUD] will lower your natural progesterone. Even if it is releasing progestin, the effect is likely by reducing your ovaries' natural production.

**Caller:** Will my body begin to produce natural progesterone again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, as soon as the irritation stops. If your diet is good, it will recover quickly.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Grated raw carrot is a great way to lower estrogen, along with keeping proteins and saturated fats up.

**Andrew Murray:** The grated raw carrot mops up excess bowel estrogen and toxins.

**Michael (Announcer):** A caller asks: When progesterone is rubbed into the skin, does it absorb properly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you stick your finger in it and are familiar with the taste, in about a minute you can taste the progesterone. It goes right through the skin so you get systemic effects quickly.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I've rubbed olive oil and progesterone on a lady with heart failure. Within half an hour, the elevated veins on her hands were completely flattened.

**Andrew Murray:** You've mentioned aldosterone as being a compound that can be problematic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several things start the process toward hypertension, inflammation, and degeneration. Low blood sugar is enough to signal your kidneys to send out renin, starting the process to produce aldosterone. Not eating enough salt also raises aldosterone. If your blood vessels leak—for example, due to hyperventilating—you lose blood volume.

Anything that lowers blood volume, sugar, or sodium will cause your kidneys to increase aldosterone. Aldosterone's function is to keep sodium inside your bloodstream to prevent edema and nourish tissues. However, the side effect is that instead of losing sodium, you lose potassium and magnesium. The loss of potassium and magnesium causes heart rhythm problems. The repolarizing process of the heart muscle requires the cell to retain magnesium and potassium and excrete the excitatory sodium and calcium.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why women tend to swell premenstrually? With dropping progesterone, they have rising aldosterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Protein deficiency is another thing that will start this whole process. Behind the balance of aldosterone, estrogen, and progesterone is the thyroid function.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** I am dealing with lupus and have a grand mal seizure once a month associated with my menstrual cycle. I've also registered as having low sodium, but doctors debated if it was Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) or cerebral salt wasting from a brain injury.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid is the main cause of that inappropriate loss of sodium. Hospitals seem to realize how important sodium loss is, especially in older people, but it happens under the influence of estrogen too.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** I know from my research that catamenial epilepsy goes along with low progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Caller:** I have rope veins in one leg. What would happen if I rubbed progesterone on my skin as a male?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some men use progesterone successfully, often for varicose veins. However, I think the best thing is to start with **Pregnenolone** orally. It can produce testosterone and DHEA as well as progesterone, so it tends to keep your hormones more in balance than applying big doses of progesterone.

**Michael (Announcer):** How much sodium should a 155-pound, 42-year-old male intake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Your taste and craving are the best way to judge. Everything affects your thyroid hormone. If your thyroid is a little low, you need lots more sodium. If your thyroid function is good, you can get along with very low sodium. Women tend to have salt cravings around ovulation or pregnancy because excess estrogen and low thyroid/progesterone cause sodium loss. If your thyroid and hormones are good, you don't have to worry about adding salt to your food.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also, on a comprehensive metabolic panel, albumin works with sodium and thyroid to regulate blood volume.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much, Dr. Peat. Dr. Raymond Peat can be reached online at `www.raypeat.com`. There is a wealth of information there, including fully referenced scientific articles.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We look forward to joining you next month on the third Friday.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Hormone Replacement Therapy
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to our shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture our own certified organic herbal extracts.

Tonight, you are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's topic: hormone replacement therapy (HRT), estrogen, and its inflammatory effects, as well as other popularly accepted hormones like serotonin, melatonin, and 5-HTP. We will discuss why these materials are not actually that good for us. We are very pleased to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, who will be sharing his research and knowledge surrounding these topics.

Science, whilst responsible for many excellent breakthroughs, is unfortunately subject to the same scandals that beset many excellent thoughts. While studying physiology myself, I was subject to what I now understand as an indoctrination into an erroneous state of pseudo-fact. One of those things was the receptor model used in physiology with one particular hormone, namely estrogen. This has been a perpetrator of much deceit on behalf of Big Pharma. Why was HRT so promoted, and how did the truth behind estrogen's effects get so covered up?

Thank you once again, Dr. Peat, for joining us. Would you open up with your scientific background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As a kid, I was interested in science, but I would read old medical books and encyclopedias. I very early got the impression that education was largely indoctrination. I found that literature as an undergraduate was a field where I could see the actual evidence—the material we were studying—without the interpretation of the professors.

It was years later that I finally decided to go to graduate school in science, when I realized I could get through it without having to fight with the professors; I could just be quiet and do what I wanted to do. I enrolled at the University of Oregon in the biology department, starting by specializing in nerve biology. I was interested in how the brain could do things like handling language and images. I saw that the whole direction of brain biology was towards a very reductionist computer analogy.

Looking around the department, I saw that the other end of the organism—reproductive physiology—was much more scientific. So, I shifted over to that specialization. My professor would say, "If it's repeatable, just go ahead." But in the nerve biology section, if the results or the interpretation were a little off, you had to throw away the evidence.

**Andrew Murray:** The word "indoctrination" is a very good place to start regarding the scandal surrounding HRT. When I was studying, the receptor-ligand interaction was dogmatic. However, you have a very good understanding of the enzymatic background before it was taken over by Big Pharma. The whole estrogen receptor concept is a bit of a non-entity, I understand.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was 1970 when I was working on my dissertation. I was studying the metabolism of the uterus in aging animals, trying to understand why infertility came about in middle age. The particular metabolic studies I was doing corresponded to increased estrogenic stimulation with aging.

All the current textbooks in the 1960s were saying that menopause is when the ovaries wear out and stop producing estrogen. So, I read way back to about 1900 and up to the 1940s. I saw there was a sudden change in 1942. All through the 1930s and into the 1940s, people like Soderwall and Blandau were studying the effects of excess estrogen on the uterus. They showed that increasing amounts of estrogen caused miscarriage. The smallest dose would cause miscarriage at a very early stage, and if you waited until very late in the pregnancy, it would take a bigger dose. But it was a continuous, graded effect in which a slight excess of estrogen was sufficient to kill the developing embryo.

The hormones of the ovary were identified in the mid-1930s. The major substance produced in the ovary was progesterone, and estrogen was a minor substance. However, people doing research on how estrogen worked saw that if you put a spoon in a candle flame and then extracted the soot in a solvent, you could get hundreds of different estrogenic substances out of just soot. This was wonderful for the drug industries because everyone could find an estrogen to patent. But there was only one natural progesterone, so that was not a viable drug because no one had a patent on it.

By 1942, the 13 major estrogen companies had their synthetic estrogens. The scientific situation was that estrogen caused infertility and was associated with aging. But since they had products, they said, "Here we have the female hormone. Being female means being able to have babies, so estrogen must be what causes women to have babies." They wanted to sell it for popular use to millions of women. They came up with the idea that it would prevent miscarriage, even though the science said the opposite.

They got a team at Harvard to promote the idea that Diethylstilbestrol (DES) would prevent miscarriages. They were prescribing it for years to prevent miscarriage and make a "healthier baby." It turned out that DES causes cancer and deformity and actually increases the risk of miscarriage.

Just as it was being recognized that DES was causing miscarriages and cancer, they were getting interested in a new product: the birth control pill. By 1959 or 1960, contraception was becoming acceptable. So, they invented a story saying that if you take estrogen, it will suppress your body's estrogen and prevent miscarriage by lowering your estrogen. They came out with the contraceptive pill just as it was recognized that DES was causing cancer. They lost one product but immediately came out with another falsified story to sell the birth control pills.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the truth behind whether or not estrogen binds to a specific receptor, and the lies surrounding the science produced to support the estrogen industry?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The people doing the real science were trying to explain why estrogen had these toxic effects. They saw that natural estrogen was imitated by these polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in soot, which were famous carcinogens. They were studying the properties of soot and estrogens and finding that the substance tended to produce inflammation and cancer—a very close association electronically in the nature of the molecule. These were activating enzyme systems in particular ways.

This reached a peak in the 1950s. The government moved some of their investment from chemical warfare into endocrine research. A project was funded for Elwood Jensen, who had been working in chemical warfare. He wanted to create a new idea for how estrogen worked that would not involve all of this interesting chemistry explaining why estrogen was a toxin and carcinogen. He wanted to say that all it does is activate the "female genes." He argued that it's like a lock and key: the female organs have a very specific lock, and the estrogen is a key that sticks only into that lock.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And estrogen receptors are now known to be found all throughout the body, and in men.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** But at that time, Elwood Jensen was arguing that there was just one little switch molecule in the cell which would neatly turn on only the female genes, so it wouldn't have the possibility of any of these other actions. The Atomic Energy Commission gave him permission to use radioactive isotopes. His competition didn't have the grants or the isotopes.

He labeled estrogen and found that it concentrated in organs like the uterus. The enzymologists were saying that estrogen affects the whole energy system of the organism and the cell, participating in the chemistry of the cell. Jensen labeled two different kinds of estrogen and said there was no interchange between the two and no oxidative reactions in which estrogen participated. He published that in 1962. He had the only means to demonstrate what he claimed, so his opponents couldn't disprove it.

However, 10 or 15 years later, after the receptor dogma had been imposed on the world of biology, other people started using isotopes and showing that, yes, the older enzymologists were exactly right. Estrogen does participate as a catalyst in enzyme reactions, especially transhydrogenation reactions that connect energy production to gene turnover and cell growth.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that's how it initiates cancer cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It allows the energy to be short-circuited over into the growth rather than the function mechanism.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the cell stops doing its normal cellular functioning and just turns on the cell growth processes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it drains the energy right out of function into growth.

**Andrew Murray:** I'm interested in water. Modern science has shown that H2O exists in many different states. How does estrogen involved in redox reactions affect water in a way that promotes cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fastest change you can see in a cell within a minute or two of exposing it to estrogen is that it instantly starts taking up water. As it takes up water, the water gets out of the cell's control. That's part of this short-circuiting of the energy process. The microtubules, which are an organizing force in the cell that lets it do the work it's supposed to, are depolymerized in the presence of estrogen and disorganized.

That's part of the cancer problem—the cell can't communicate from one part to the other because the microtubules are messed up. The division process can reach the point where it can't separate the chromosomes evenly, leading to an imbalance of chromosomes. The water is normally under the control of adjoining surfaces, very unlike bulk water. But in the presence of estrogen, it becomes bulk-like. One of my experiments at the university was to put an old uterus, a young uterus, and an estrogen-treated uterus in an MRI machine. We showed that the old uterus and the estrogen-treated uterus had loose, disorganized water that could be distinguished from the young, healthy uterus.

**Andrew Murray:** Give me your opinion of HRT's effects and why it was eventually taken out—or rather, why there was a backlash against it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The industry succeeded so greatly in turning science completely upside down in the case of estrogen that it took a lot of other hormones with it. Progesterone was suppressed and ignored because it would cure the things that estrogen was claimed to cure but actually caused.

Prolactin had many toxic effects that were well recognized. But since estrogen increases prolactin, there was great pressure not to think about the fact that prolactin causes bone loss and contributes to osteoporosis.

Serotonin is another thing that has been strongly influenced by this inverted interpretation. Estrogen increases exposure to serotonin. Serotonin is one of the means by which estrogen increases prolactin. Serotonin does many of the harmful things that estrogen and prolactin do, including being a direct cause of bone loss. People who take the fluoxetine (Prozac) type of antidepressants are seen to have a lot of premature bone loss because of the excess exposure to serotonin.

Serotonin is, in a way, a co-factor for estrogen. Estrogen increases prolactin or serotonin systemically, and serotonin in turn increases the production of estrogen. So when one gets out of control, they both tend to become dominant.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We're all told that serotonin is the "feel good" hormone and they give you SSRIs to make you feel better. Is this the same brainwashing they did with estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. One of the currently bad effects of serotonin excess that is getting some recognition is hypertension of the pulmonary artery. The drugs that increase serotonin increase this pulmonary hypertension and degeneration of the valves in the right side of the heart. This was known in the 1950s as the main deadly complication of having a serotonin-producing tumor. Finally, 60 years later, it's being recognized as a way to treat pulmonary hypertension by using *anti*-serotonin drugs.

**Caller:** I sometimes have a tendency toward depression and I like to do natural things. I resisted trying Zoloft or Prozac. I was told by some nature doctors to try 5-HTP. They said it was natural and would help you use your own serotonin better. Is that good for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Prozac-type drugs keep the platelets and nerve cells from binding and keeping serotonin out of the way, leading to overexposure. Plain tryptophan is bad enough, but 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) is one step closer to being serotonin.

**Caller:** So you think it's not good for me to take it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything that I know suggests that. For example, there's increased risk of breast cancer and obesity and many bad effects.

**Caller:** How can it increase obesity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By slowing metabolism and suppressing the thyroid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's basically providing the precursor, and your body makes more serotonin out of it. The effects of serotonin in excess are going to be increasing estrogen, which slows your liver's metabolism. That can slow your thyroid down, lead to obesity, and promote cancer.

**Caller:** It says it elevates your mood.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You have to weigh it up. It might elevate your mood, but you also risk these other things. They used to give X-rays to help with psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis, and people got cancer.

**Caller:** I certainly don't want to slow my metabolism or my thyroid down. I'm done with menopause, so I figure my estrogen has balanced itself out. I don't need to increase my serotonin if it's going to be bad for my heart valve.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Exactly. And when Dr. Peat says that, it's not just his opinion; he has adopted that opinion from researching the evidence.

**Caller:** So I should probably do without it and see if my food is okay anyway?

**Andrew Murray:** Sounds like a good idea.

**Caller:** I've talked to you before and I've gotten completely off of my serotonin reuptake inhibitors. I read a bunch of articles on your site. One effect of stopping these Prozac and serotonin things is that I've now been able to stop using steroids in an inhaler. My asthma has gone away completely.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen is related to asthma too. The effect of the serotonin is to cause localized contraction of the tubes in your lungs as well as causing them to take up water and promote inflammation. But the contraction is the thing that's best studied in connection with asthma.

**Caller:** That's really interesting because it went away within four weeks. Getting off the serotonin was painful, but I'm off of it now for almost two months. Thank you for the information.

**Caller:** I haven't heard mention of the three different types of estrogen in our bodies. They have a hugely disparate impact on our bodies. Please inform us of that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are probably a dozen important types of estrogen, but the three main types—estriol, estrone, and estradiol—are the best known. Those all have pretty much the same effects but at different potencies. If you can turn your most potent estradiol into the others, you're protected against some of the most toxic effects. During pregnancy, enzymes are detoxifying estrogen by many different routes. The index of a healthy pregnancy is when the estriol is high because that means you're destroying your estradiol very quickly.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the estradiol is the most dangerous form.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And these different forms are exactly the issue that Elwood Jensen denied happened. He said estradiol can't turn into estrone and estriol, but in fact, that's a major way of activating or inactivating estrogen according to the cell's energy system.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the only reason you'd want high estriol is because that would tell us that the estradiol is being detoxified, not that high estriol in itself is protective.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's about 10 times weaker than estrogen. So every little bit of estradiol that you turn to estriol is a down-stepping of your estrogen effect.

**Caller:** What is your opinion of modern birth control methods like the pill or the NuvaRing? Do you recommend those as safe contraceptives?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They tremendously decreased the amount of estrogen in the contraceptives, but if it's strong enough to kill the embryo, it's strong enough to do some damage to the woman.

About 30 years ago, there was agitation among women's groups for FDA approval of the traditional cervical cap. The ideal thing was made by a metal worker or a dentist; they would cast silver or gold in the shape of the cervix, and it would form a vacuum seal and could be left in place for weeks. Under pressure, the FDA gave its approval to a rubber "cervical cap," which was actually shaped more like a baby bottle's nipple. It was terribly unsuccessful. The FDA approved that but wouldn't approve the one that actually worked.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And as far as the IUD, they now have IUDs that secrete a small amount of hormone inside the uterine cavity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The signal from inside the uterus travels through nerves up the fallopian tube to prevent the ovary from producing the amount of progesterone that it should. So any kind of IUD, with or without hormones, will create a hormonal imbalance, which is the main thing accounting for the prevention of pregnancy.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And then thereby increasing your estrogen and increasing risk of cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** So the only possible safe method would be the silver or gold cap, but they don't make them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the rhythm cycle method is the best.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think of melatonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has its own endocrine problems. It can disturb your progesterone and thyroid production if you take a lot of it. But its function seems to be as a way of detoxifying serotonin. The trigger that turns the conversion in the pineal gland of serotonin into melatonin is the adrenergic stress-related nerves. During the night, your stress increases from the lack of light, and this adrenergic system causes the pineal to convert serotonin to melatonin.

In general, melatonin is functioning as an antidote to serotonin. Biologically, it's evidence that you're responding to stress with a detoxifying process. The enzymes that exist in the pineal that are activated by the stress can also be found in inflamed joint tissue and in breast cancer. Serotonin is involved in the pathology of both of those situations. If our enzymes could turn it more quickly into melatonin, there would be less of a serotonin problem.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But when people actually take melatonin supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's probably protecting against the circulating serotonin. But in itself, in an otherwise healthy person, animal studies showed it was capable of lowering both progesterone and thyroid while increasing estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So in a short-term emergency situation, it could be okay, but long-term it's going to have negative side effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that depends on the person, but it's much safer than serotonin.

**Caller:** I take a suppository called Vagifem for dryness. It says it's estradiol. Should I worry about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have been studied who were using vaginal creams, and their blood level of estrogen was even higher than some of the oral pills were causing. So it's definitely a systemic hormonal influence, wherever you put it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, what would you recommend to this lady to use in place of her suppository?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known several women who had pharmacists make them up suppositories with a fairly high dose of Vitamin A and a little Vitamin E in cocoa butter. The Vitamin A helps to strengthen the membranes and normalize mucus production.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And in the meantime, if you can't find a pharmacist to make it, you can buy Vitamin A palmitate and Vitamin E capsules and try that.

**Caller:** What do you think of bioidentical hormones in low doses? They come from wild yams.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the hormones that are bioidentical have to fit into the system in a balanced way. It's okay to have a physiological amount of any of these, but when you supplement estrogen or serotonin, you're most likely increasing something that's already excessive.

The doctrine of replacement with natural hormones is building on the history of estrogen replacement with synthetic hormones. What they neglect is that as a woman ages from 19 to 39, there's a steady average increase in the amount of estrogen in her bloodstream. In the 40s, progesterone production is no longer able to fully keep up with this steadily increasing estrogen production.

As soon as progesterone decreases and can no longer force estrogen out of the cells, the blood estrogen level will drop, but the estrogen *inside* the cells will increase. Publications have shown that the tissues of old organisms retain much more estrogen than the tissues of young animals. The fact that you don't find it in the blood is simply because estrogen sticks inside the cells in proportion to the deficiency of progesterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that was probably the reason why they recommended it—because of low blood levels. And so Dr. Peat's advice would be to not use it.

**Andrew Murray:** We are out of time. For anyone who wants to find out more about Dr. Raymond Peat, his website is very informative: www.raypeat.com. Thank you so much, Dr. Peat, for joining us this evening.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Until the same time next month, thank you so much for listening. And to those who have ears, let them hear.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Heart I
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Hi and welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. This month is a slightly different format. My wife, who normally joins us on the show, is not with me as we had a beautiful baby girl last month. So, we're going to run the show tonight with Dr. Raymond Peat. He is going to share his wisdom on the subject of heart failure and hormones.

As usual, people are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's show. There is an ever-growing Ray Peat Facebook fan page, and we get emails from all over the states from people following him. It is always very good to hear anecdotal evidence of people improving fairly drastically by making the changes that he's been advocating for the last 20-plus years.

The thrust of the show is heart failure, although there is hopefully some time to look at new research surrounding the understanding of cancer and metastases in relation to solid tumors and the way the body recruits collagen.

Welcome, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi.

**Andrew Murray:** For the benefit of people who have never heard of you, could you give us an outline of your academic and professional career?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** From 1968 to 1972, I was in graduate school at the University of Oregon. I did my dissertation on reproductive aging and how oxidative metabolism changes with age. I found that the changes causing the menopause equivalent in animals happen in every tissue in the body. It just happens that the uterus is where I did my dissertation work, but I was interested in aging changes in the brain and bones as well. It turns out that the same chemical and biological processes change through time in all of these tissues.

In my dissertation, one of the aging theories that I talked about was the collagen theory of aging: that estrogen excess causes wastage of oxygen, basically suffocating tissues the way radiation would, and destroying the ability to use oxygen. As a result of that, excess collagen is produced by the collagen-producing cells (fibroblasts) in the connective tissue. With aging, the collagen becomes progressively denser and more cross-linked, creating an oxygen-deprived environment. My emphasis at that time was on how estrogen, produced by irritation or aging, causes more collagen to be produced and to become more dense, creating further interference with oxygen consumption.

**Andrew Murray:** Roughly 5.7 million people in the US are suffering from congestive heart failure. Would you explain the pathophysiology of congestive heart failure so listeners can understand what the disease entails?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In congestive heart failure, the heart muscle simply gets weaker and less able to pump a full volume of blood with each stroke. The diastolic phase, which should be a relaxation phase, is inadequate. The heart stays partly contracted, so it has a short stroke. To make up for the shortness of the stroke, it tends to pump faster.

Ordinarily, when a healthy heart muscle pumps faster, it has a bigger stroke so that it doesn't have to simply increase the speed; it can increase the volume with each stroke. But with heart failure, that's impossible. So it tends to lead to a fast but weak heartbeat.

**Andrew Murray:** And the actual muscle of the heart itself becomes more flabby and weak?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It becomes waterlogged—a higher concentration of water in the tissue. That's because it isn't relaxing fully. When you work a muscle tremendously, you can actually make a muscle swell up. In just 15 or 20 minutes of very intense contraction, your muscle will gain weight because it doesn't relax fully and retains calcium and excess water. A very fatigued biceps muscle, for example, is temporarily equivalent to what's happening in the failing heart.

If that condition of retaining water and calcium persists for a long time—because the heart isn't getting enough sugar or oxygen to relax, or if it's being stimulated by estrogen—that prevents full relaxation. Chronically, it tends to produce more collagen, and that collagen tends to become hardened. So at first, it's just a swollen condition. Then it gradually becomes a fibrotic condition, and that can actually lead to the development of a bone in the heart—calcification that actually contains crystalline calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** I understood the basic mechanism of treatment to be diuretics, to remove excess water, and plant derivatives like digoxin from the woolly foxglove as a strengthener of heart contraction.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That steroid from the foxglove is similar in structure and function to progesterone. Albert Szent-Györgyi did experiments 50 or 60 years ago in which he showed that progesterone acts on the heart like digitalis to increase the "staircase effect" of heart contraction. This is where a faster stimulation increases the stroke and amount of blood pumped with each contraction. That's because the progesterone or the digitalis is accelerating the ability to both contract and relax.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, because it's the relaxation that is the important phase for the next contraction to be functional.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's why the failing heart has a very weak, small beat—because it isn't relaxed and it's becoming harder just by being filled up with water.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned this staircase effect. I always believed that the increasing contractions of the heart were a mechanism to compensate for the lack of blood volume being ejected.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you're exercising, you will notice the beats per minute increase as you use your muscles and consume more oxygen. But at the same time that your healthy heart is beating faster, it's beating harder. So when it's going maybe 130 beats per minute, it will also be thumping very hard. You can feel your pulse as a big bulging throb with each beat. That's the staircase effect: it's both going faster and having a bigger stroke with each contraction.

**Andrew Murray:** You've explained the waterlogged effect of cardiac muscles in congestive heart failure. This has a relationship to growing pains, doesn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It turns out that exactly the same things are happening in skeletal muscle and heart muscle. Doctors have seen the changes in their patients for 100 years and found that thyroid would correct those problems of both the heart and the skeletal muscles.

Fairly recently, with analysis of genes and proteins, you can see that exactly the same things are involved in growing pains, which come with somewhat low thyroid function. Around puberty—usually a couple of years before—estrogen is increasing, blocking thyroid function. That makes the cell fatigue more easily, so it retains water. The pain is usually in the late afternoon and evening; the muscles have progressively retained more water and calcium, becoming painful and swollen.

If a person in middle age becomes very hypothyroid, they start getting the same thing. Fibromyalgia is one of the variations on that. The muscle disease of hypothyroidism, or hypothyroid myopathy, involves leakage of enzymes from the skeletal muscles. But in fact, the heart is also leaking those proteins. You can identify proteins coming from both the heart muscle and the skeletal muscles in hypothyroidism or in heart failure.

**Andrew Murray:** So you can pick these up in the blood or urine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Creatine kinase is the first thing to look for if you're suspecting a thyroid-related pain problem.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you understand the myopathy, the muscle weakness in hypothyroidism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In hypothyroidism, you can see it in an electrocardiogram or if you kneel and have someone thump your Achilles tendon. If your thyroid function is good, the relaxation will be instantaneous—your foot will relax with a floppy, instantaneous, complete relaxation. If your thyroid is low, it'll come back slowly to exactly where it started.

The heart is doing the same thing with a prolongation of the QT interval. The T wave represents repolarization or relaxation. When that is slow, that means the cell is retaining water and calcium. In that swollen state, it is permeable; it absorbs things that it shouldn't and it leaks some of the enzymes that it shouldn't leak.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this related to someone's reflexes in general? If someone has very quick reflexes, is that a sign of a well-functioning thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the rate of nervous conduction is slowed in hypothyroidism. A hypothyroid person will tend to react 10 or 20 milliseconds slower than a person with good thyroid function.

**Andrew Murray:** For those listening, if you want to test your own reflexes: kneel on a chair facing the back so your legs are hanging off. Have someone gently tap your Achilles tendon. It's how quickly it returns to its resting state that is the important marker. If they swing out and back down quickly, that's the good sign.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another way of looking at that reflex system is insomnia. Many doctors think that thyroid is a stimulant that will make you stay awake. But when you think of the brain as having exactly the same process of excitation and relaxation as your heart or leg muscle, when the brain is fatigued—if it's somewhat hypothyroid—it gets the equivalent of a growing pain or a cramp and it can't relax fully. That amounts to insomnia. If you can energize the brain cells, you can get sleep to come on quickly. Active thyroid hormone, magnesium, and sugar are the things that most quickly will restore energy to your brain or your muscles.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a question about the best foods for the heart.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fruit is extremely important, as is avoiding polyunsaturated fats (PUFA). The heart is much more efficient using oxygen when it's burning sugar rather than fat. Also, having plenty of all the minerals: calcium, magnesium, sodium, and potassium. Those interact very closely.

People think of calcium as the exciting ion, which it is when the cell is excited and can't get rid of it. But calcium happens to inhibit some of the hormones that maintain inflammation and excitation. So if you are well saturated with all of these alkaline minerals, that will help the heart to relax more quickly and then contract more quickly.

**Andrew Murray:** So calcium from milk or eggshells, and potassium and magnesium from fruits?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Orange juice and watermelon, for example, are good for sodium and potassium. One point about sodium is that if you restrict sodium, you increase your aldosterone. One of the current interests in heart drug treatment is to find an aldosterone inhibitor. But eating enough sodium is the simplest way to inhibit aldosterone.

**Andrew Murray:** It's too cheap and they can't patent it.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** My father died of a heart attack, and since I learned from Dr. Peat that estrogen can cause heart attacks, I feel like that's what happened. I have a grand mal seizure about once a month, known as catamenial epilepsy, because of the ratio between estrogen and progesterone. What can I do to balance my hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keep your cholesterol level up. Fruit is one of the best ways to help the liver make enough cholesterol. If your cholesterol production is good, thyroid and vitamin A are the main things for turning cholesterol into progesterone. Progesterone not only has anti-seizure effects, but it has heart-protective effects—steadying the heart rhythm the way digitalis does and blocking aldosterone, preventing fibrosis of the heart.

**Caller:** Is that operative in the gut, like eating the raw grated carrot?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The effect of having a raw carrot every day, or bamboo shoots, is that these are antiseptic fibers which can't be easily broken down by microorganisms. They don't stimulate bacterial growth; in fact, they tend to sterilize the intestine. At the same time, the fiber binds to the estrogen which your liver is producing and excreting in the bile, preventing it from being reabsorbed. You can see a decrease in your estrogen level a day or two after eating a raw carrot. That reduction of absorption of bacterial products and estrogen very quickly reduces your stress and cortisol production, which allows your progesterone to increase.

**Caller:** What about the GAPS diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The simplest thing is to avoid starches and polyunsaturated fat. Olive oil is saturated enough that it helps the carrot with a germicidal action. Coconut oil, butter, and olive oil, especially associated with the fiber of carrot, help to suppress microorganisms.

**Caller (Minnesota):** What can a person do to recover from getting off of SSRIs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I hear that a lot. Basically, it's doing everything you can to restore a good, intense metabolic rate—restore the energy level of cells so that they don't go into the stress state. The high serotonin trains the nervous system to stay in a stress state because serotonin activates the pituitary ACTH and adrenal system. Ultimately, the way to break that pattern is to increase your cellular energy production, lower stress, keep your thyroid function up, and keep the estrogen down.

**Caller:** Is it something that takes quite a long time to recover from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People seem to take about a year to feel fairly normal again, even doing everything right. The serotonin itself creates an inflammatory state in the nerves and body in general. It affects your whole metabolism, tending to increase fat production and stress. You want to concentrate on keeping your whole body in an unstressed condition. Eating frequently is probably one of the helpful things—not forcing yourself to go on adrenaline.

**Andrew Murray:** We also have a note from a listener regarding a website called drugawareness.org and a contact named Ann Blake Tracy who has information about getting off SSRIs.

**Caller (David from Missouri):** I see people put a cell phone in their pocket right over their heart. What do you think the ramifications are of having that competing frequency right next to the heart?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's pretty well established that you damage the tissue and create stress in the brain. The cancer rate increases when your head is exposed to the microwave frequencies.

**Caller:** Regarding bamboo sprouts, I've been steaming them or boiling them. Do you think there's a benefit in not cooking them too much?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, they still have good fiber even if they're soft.

**Caller:** I've been drinking the water I boil them in. Is there antibiotic material in that water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The Japanese and Chinese have drugs made from ferment extracts of the bamboo plant. I think there is the same antiseptic and probably anti-cancer material in the shoots.

**Caller:** Regarding orange juice, I can't always get fresh oranges. I've read that companies use enzymes to break up the pulp. Is there still a benefit from drinking processed orange juices like Tropicana?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There is a worse process where they use enzymes to break up the pulp to have less waste, but even with frozen orange juice concentrate, you can see a very quick relief from mild heart pains just by drinking a pint of orange juice per day.

**Caller (Miranda):** I have chronic sinusitis that I've had for 10 years. I've been feeling like it might be straining my heart. Can a chronic infection affect the heart?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think there is a definite relation between sinus or tooth infections and the heart, but I don't think it goes *from* the sinus or tooth to the heart. I think it's endotoxin from chronic intestinal inflammation. Sometimes bacteria enter the bloodstream along with the endotoxin, but just the endotoxin alone is enough to cause sinusitis and inflamed periodontal tissues. At the same time, it's causing those changes in the heart: calcium retention, water retention, and easy fatigability.

**Caller:** I have a vegan diet and have been strictly off gluten. I can't seem to get ahead of the sinusitis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When simple foods and fibers to disinfect your intestine aren't enough, the drugs that are most helpful in my experience are aspirin and antihistamines—Benadryl, for example, or cyproheptadine, which is an anti-serotonin antihistamine.

**Caller:** What about colloidal silver?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One other thing that helps the general immune system and avoidance of inflammation is vitamin D.

**Caller:** I take 10,000 units of Vitamin D3 a day. Is that reasonable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, if it's vitamin D3, it is.

**Andrew Murray:** We were discussing cholesterol earlier. You were talking about the harmful effects of lowering cholesterol and its relevance to heart failure.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the accepted side effects of both of the main categories of cholesterol-lowering drugs is occasional muscle breakdown—rhabdomyolysis—where the muscle dissolves itself. One known factor is the interference with the production of Coenzyme Q10, but that isn't the sole reason.

The simple lack of cholesterol is a problem. Cholesterol is a cell-stabilizing substance with hormone-like action. In the absence of progesterone and the other protective steroids, cholesterol actually has a cell-protective effect in the skeletal muscles and in the heart. The same process that causes rhabdomyolysis in skeletal muscles can happen in the heart: cholesterol deficiency tending to kill heart cells.

**Andrew Murray:** You recommend having a cholesterol of 200, especially if someone is over 50.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The Framingham study found that people over 50 who had at least 200 cholesterol or higher had a much lower risk of Alzheimer's disease because it's brain-protective as well as heart-protective.

**Caller (Trinidad):** I am dealing with a tooth infection that I've had for a number of years. I've been treating it with tea tree oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know a dentist who cured chronic dental problems like periodontal disease simply by giving his patients a laxative. He found there was no need to do periodontal surgery if he cleared the intestine.

**Caller:** I'm pretty regular, though my digestion is a little sluggish.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes just avoiding starches, and especially raw vegetables and raw fibrous fruits, helps. Apples are easier on the intestine if they're well cooked, and vegetables ought to be cooked about 40 minutes to be protective to the intestine.

**Caller:** So avoid raw vegetables?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. We don't have enzymes for breaking up the cellulose of vegetable material. The bacteria are favored by the warm, moist conditions in the gut and can thrive on raw vegetables. Raw carrots are the exception because, being a root vegetable, they happen to be very germicidal. Bacteria won't touch them.

**Andrew Murray:** I was always taught that acetylcholine was a very important neurotransmitter, mopped up by acetylcholinesterase to prevent overstimulation. So we are talking about an excess situation?

**Andrew Murray:** This sounds like a death situation—going towards death and away from life.

**Caller:** I have a question about toe fungus. Dr. Peat, you mentioned sulfur was good for fungus. Would it work for toe fungus, and should I use DMSO to get it in there? Also, what are your thoughts on food irradiation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, temperature, pulse rate, and symptoms are good indicators. If you don't have symptoms, you are likely handling it properly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some seeds pass through harmlessly, but tomato seeds are so tender that if crushed by chewing, they release fairly toxic, protein-oxidizing materials. Seeds generally contain toxins to prevent mammalian enzymes from digesting them.

**Caller:** What about potato skins?

**Caller:** What is Dr. Peat's position on salt and fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Saturated fats are good. Clean white salt, like sea salt without additives, is good.

**Caller:** I want to mention that Alzheimer's can come with iron deposits in the brain. Turmeric has been recognized as being able to chelate that iron. Curcumin is the active component. Also, for toe fungus, Neem is a traditional medicine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That fits right into what we've been talking about regarding stress hormones leading to Alzheimer's. Iron is the endpoint of all these changes. Nitric oxide and prostaglandins activate enzymes which release and deposit iron in the brain, where it continues amplifying the destructive reactions.

**Andrew Murray:** It is almost 8 o'clock. Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. He has a big resource there for information on thyroid hormones, fats, salt, sugar, and more. Thank you for joining us, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** We will be back the third Friday of next month. Until then, take care.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Learned Helplessness, Nervous System and Thyroid Questionaire
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome once again to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. My wife and I are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions, and we manufacture our own certified organic herb extracts.

You are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of learned helplessness, the nervous system, and a generalized thyroid questionnaire. We are very pleased to welcome Dr. Raymond Peat to share his wisdom with us. Dr. Peat, for those who have never heard you, would you please give an outline of your academic background in biology?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied mostly at the University of Oregon from 1968 to 1972. I did my PhD dissertation on reproductive aging and how the physiology of oxidative metabolism changes with aging and interacts with changes in all of the hormones. Since then, I have been developing some of the central ideas that were involved in both aging and reproduction.

**Andrew Murray:** I think tonight's introduction regarding the nervous system has some fairly new ideas attached to it. Before we get into the subject, could you discuss briefly the two known arms of the nervous system, the sympathetic and the parasympathetic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The general way doctors still think about them is based on a set of ideas established just about 100 years ago, with opposition between the relaxing side and the mobilizing emergency side. That has tended to be called the "fight or flight" reaction for the sympathetic nervous system, which is based largely on adrenaline. The relaxing parasympathetic side is based mostly on acetylcholine.

In the last 30 or 40 years, a lot of complexity has turned up, even though in a general sense those oppositions are still accurate. It turns out there is a lot of overlap. Each part of the nervous system does things that can also be done by the other side, and each one has more repertoire than just adrenaline or acetylcholine. They can interact in various ways with serotonin, histamine, and so on.

The 100-year-old idea is that the relaxing side [parasympathetic] takes care of peristalsis and secretion largely. It slows the heart rate for relaxation and weakens the strength of the heart contraction, but it strengthens the peristalsis movement of the intestine and wall of the bladder and stimulates secretion of a lot of glands. It relaxes the sphincters of the intestine, bladder, and gallbladder so that it goes with secretion, digestion, and excretion—all of the basically vegetative processes.

**Andrew Murray:** So the parasympathetic nervous system is all about what happens after you eat a meal. You relax, you digest your food, your heart rate slows down. You always think of the parasympathetics being fairly peaceful and "wet," if you like.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And it tends to take over at night. It helps a person go to sleep by slowing the heart rate. But with problems such as diabetes, hypoglycemia, or various metabolic disorders, it can get overactive. Instead of just calming things down, slowing the metabolism, and lowering blood sugar because you don't need so much, it can cause too much insulin secretion and other glandular secretions—for example, causing too much mucus formation. The increased insulin can lower your blood sugar too much, and that can lead to intensified activity of the nerves, intensifying both contraction and relaxation where it shouldn't be happening.

**Andrew Murray:** In light of what we understand about the sympathetics and parasympathetics under the effects of stress, you've written about the stress-induced excitotoxic effects of the parasympathetics. Could you describe that a little more?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The place that it started to be understood was in the learned helplessness situation. They saw that when an animal believed it couldn't escape from a stressful situation, its heart slowed down instead of accelerating. The very same signal that would make an animal's heart race if it was wandering around freely and had the possibility of escaping, if it was in a trapped situation, its heart would slow down. Given a little too much stress and threat, its heart would actually stop in a relaxed position. Without that belief in the impossibility of escape, it would go on struggling for days—swimming in a tank, for example—whereas with the expectation that it wouldn't be able to escape, it might drown in five or six minutes.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow. So this is the rationale for hope being something that can keep a person alive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, exactly. In the 1950s, a biologist shocked a lot of other biologists by talking about the rat's hopelessness causing death.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you mentioned how the standard treatment for Alzheimer's is actually pretty bad science in terms of what's understood now about the two arms of the nervous system, and how the drugs they're currently using might be making it worse.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The brain processes that allow learning and intelligent behavior involve the cholinergic nerves of the brain. Several types of evidence made doctors concentrate on the loss of the cholinergic system. If you stimulate the cholinergic nerves, you can improve learning and behavior. But if you aren't increasing energy to keep up with that increased stimulation, you put the cell in a stress between having to work harder but not having the fuel to do it.

If your cortisol is high, interfering with your ability to use sugar, or if your blood sugar is simply low and you're being stimulated, then the cell tends to die. The reasoning that Alzheimer's disease was simply a wasting away of the cholinergic nerves led to treating it for the first 10 or 15 years just with chemicals to increase excitation of the cholinergic nerves. That wasn't working at all. People were dying at a higher rate of liver disease and such.

From the 1950s, people were already suggesting treating dementia and other brain degenerative diseases with atropine and other chemicals that *block* the cholinergic nerves. Amantadine, which is now used for treating Parkinson's disease, was one of the chemicals considered anticholinergic in the 50s, 60s, and 70s. Since people were seeing actual improvement with the anticholinergic chemicals, they reclassified them as acting against another excitatory nervous system—the system that causes glutamate or MSG nerve toxicity. So they now call it an anti-NMDA chemical. Memantine is very similar to amantadine. It is a chemical which used to be called anticholinergic that's being used for both Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. But they still go on with the doctrine that they have to stimulate the cholinergic system too, even though that has never shown improvement.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask you about estrogen. We've talked about how the revelations are that estrogen is extremely damaging. How do you look at estrogen and its destructive features?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of people by now have heard that there's a premenstrual-related epilepsy that results from an excess of estrogen in relation to progesterone, because estrogen is excitatory while progesterone is calming. It happens that estrogen intensifies the parasympathetic part of the autonomic nervous system, while progesterone tends to relax that. You can see that parasympathetic function of estrogen in the uterus. If there's too much estrogen in pregnancy, it will cause strong contractions of the uterus and can cause miscarriage.

For about 50 years, there was a puzzle about how acetylcholine could inhibit the heart and the sphincters while causing contractions of the various ducts and intestine. The main thing that happens is that acetylcholine causes cells to produce nitric oxide—the chemical that became famous with Viagra—which causes vasodilation.

**Andrew Murray:** People also abuse nitrous oxide, don't they?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's a different chemical; that's actually just an anesthetic. Nitric oxide is the free radical that you find in smog, and it's produced by any cell that's excited too strongly. In the situation where the cholinergic stimulation is causing relaxation in blood vessels, it's acting by way of increased nitric oxide. What the nitric oxide is doing is blocking energy production. So the smooth muscle of the blood vessel or sphincter simply doesn't have the energy to contract. It actually steals oxygen from the mitochondrion and blocks the use of any oxygen that's there. Estrogen happens to activate the enzyme that forms nitric oxide. So it works with the cholinergic system, and both of them act partly through increasing the amount of nitric oxide. Progesterone, with its quieting effect, inhibits the enzyme that forms nitric oxide.

**Andrew Murray:** In the presence of adequate metabolic energy in the form of sufficient thyroid, would nitric oxide still be able to do this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. In situations where they were studying learned helplessness, which produces increased acetylcholine and nitric oxide, they found that either progesterone or thyroid (T3) would block the formation of that behavior and keep them from dying prematurely. Thyroid and progesterone both interfere with the production of nitric oxide.

In situations of under-function of the thyroid gland, it's now pretty well established that high blood pressure is produced by hypothyroidism. Because of the belief that nitric oxide has a beneficial effect of increasing circulation, the thought was that hypothyroidism must be lowering nitric oxide. But in fact, it increases it while still causing contraction of the blood vessels and increasing blood pressure. So the effect of thyroid is to stop excess nitric oxide.

Some of the changes with aging—high blood pressure, incontinence, edema, constipation, leakiness of blood vessels—are all able to be produced and relieved by either increasing or decreasing the amount of nitric oxide in the system. An excess of the cholinergic function leading to overproduction of nitric oxide will cause constipation, incontinence, and swelling of the feet—just about all of the typical symptoms of aging, stress, and shock.

**Andrew Murray:** I had a question regarding DHEA. A bottle of DHEA gave a warning about possibly increasing estrogen. Is it true that estrogen would be produced in a person taking DHEA if they were under stress, but not if they had adequate thyroid and progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. DHEA and progesterone both will break the learned helplessness pattern of too much nitric oxide. But what causes DHEA and testosterone to be turned into estrogen excessively is anything causing stress, irritation, or inflammation. The enzyme that makes estrogen—aromatase—is activated by anything that stresses cells. The processes that are reversed by thyroid and progesterone are activated by, for example, prostaglandins, which are derived from polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Prostaglandins synergize with estrogen in many ways. They activate the formation of estrogen. Progesterone, thyroid, and aspirin will turn off aromatase by inhibiting the activity of the enzyme that makes polyunsaturated fats turn into prostaglandins.

**Jackie:** I have a premenstrual seizure problem. I have a grand mal seizure once a month, and I have a real memory problem because of that. I'm wondering, how do you promote the production of more thyroid hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In an emergency situation, you can have a good probability of either stopping or reducing the severity of seizures just with progesterone. But in the long run, you want to stop the intake of the polyunsaturated fats that activate estrogen and inhibit thyroid. The degree of unsaturation of the fat corresponds to the degree of interference with thyroid hormone. So fish oil is more anti-thyroid than the seed oils. Olive oil is very weakly anti-thyroid. Butter, coconut oil, cream, beef, and lamb fat are not anti-thyroid.

Traditional diets before 1940, even in the industrial countries, included quite a bit of thyroid in the food. If you stewed a chicken or a fish, the thyroid would break up and be consumed. With that traditional diet, a person probably averaged the equivalent of maybe 30 milligrams a day of Armour Thyroid. The removal of natural thyroid from the food supply has contributed to hypothyroidism, resulting in high estrogen. At the same time, the diet has been industrialized to include lots of these seed oils which are both pro-estrogen and anti-thyroid.

**Jackie:** I've been using dandelion root to deal with water retention. My source for progesterone is chaste tree berries (Vitex). I am under the impression that over time it can help rebalance my hormonal imbalance.
