Milk is very important for several reasons: as a source of protein, and the high calcium has an anti-stress effect. So emphasize milk, cheese, protein, eggs, and fruits, while avoiding the starchy fruits like bananas.

If you actually have a problem with high blood sugar, supplementing brewer's yeast and aspirin are things that can help to actually lower the blood sugar. And a thyroid supplement sometimes will help.

**Andrew Murray:** We are going to have to hold it there. Dr. Peat can be found online at www.raypeat.com. There are plenty of scholarly articles there, specifically on metabolic disorders, thyroid disorders, hormones, and aging.

Thank you so much again, Dr. Peat. And thank you to our callers from New York, Washington, Kansas, and Missouri. Until next month.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Diabetes II and How to Restore and Protect Nerves
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. My wife and I are both licensed medical herbalists. We trained in England, graduated there with a master's degree in herbal medicine, and we now run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions.

You're invited to call in with any questions either related or unrelated to this month's subject of how to restore and protect nerves. We're very privileged to have Dr. Raymond Peat and his expertise joining us again this evening. Are you there, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hi.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who have never heard of you or your areas of expertise, would you outline your academic and professional background before we get started on tonight's show?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Relative to nerve biology, that was my intended major when I went to the University of Oregon as a graduate student in 1968 because I had been interested in linguistics and psychology. But as soon as I got there, within two or three months, I decided to switch to aging and reproductive physiology because of the great dogmatism in the nerve biology field. So I spent three or four years working on female reproductive aging in particular. I concentrated on the effects of estrogen, progesterone, thyroid, oxygen, and antioxidants on the age-related changes in metabolism.

**Andrew Murray:** And for the last 40 years, you've been doing your own research and consulting. A lot of what you've spoken about in the past has been fairly controversial. In my education in herbal medicine, the same dogmatic and erroneous ideas in science were perpetrated. A lot of what you've been uncovering has certainly got me thinking differently.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to start by saying that the classical description of diabetes was a wasting disease where excess glucose is lost in the urine as a byproduct of protein metabolism, and the patient simply wastes away. Now, obesity is a universal disease, and obese diabetics are common. Medicine now classes diabetes as insulin resistance as well as insulin dependence. Would you explain the processes that you understand diabetes to stem from and outline your approach to its management?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My father happened to be an example of the traditional, original type of diabetes. He wasted away to under 100 pounds. It was just a few years after insulin had come into medical use, and he didn't want to become dependent on it. My mother looked through the old naturopathic medical literature and found that brewer's yeast had sometimes cured people. He went on a brewer's yeast diet for several weeks, recovered his weight, and lived the rest of his life with no sign of diabetes.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know how much brewer's yeast he was using?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was his only food, basically, for several weeks.

**Andrew Murray:** I know the B vitamins are the important part of brewer's yeast, but what specifically helped?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are steroids in it, a lot of potassium, and phosphate. Phosphate is not for general health—you can very easily get phosphate poisoning—but probably it's one of the factors that could be involved in that effect, maybe by interfering with stress hormones.

**Andrew Murray:** So your father recovered from wasting away using brewer's yeast.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I think there are probably many causes of the traditional wasting form of diabetes. A virus is one plausible theory that can cause inflammation and the temporary killing off of insulin-producing cells. But also just very intense stress. There were experiments in which if part of a dog's pancreas was removed, leaving a smaller reserve of insulin-producing cells, a single injection of a large dose of cortisol was enough to make the dog permanently diabetic.

**Andrew Murray:** So that extreme stress caused by cortisol itself is an inflammatory mediator.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Once the tissues are unable to get glucose just from that one episode of stress-induced lack of insulin, the cells are basically dying because they can't get the glucose they need. So they call on fatty acids from stores, and the fatty acids, in turn, kill the remaining or regenerating insulin-producing cells. So it starts a vicious circle.

**Andrew Murray:** Just in case listeners don't understand what a fatty acid or a free fatty acid is, would you explain what they are and how they're used?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A fat, such as butter, lard, or corn oil, mostly consists of about 18 carbon atoms in a chain with oxygens on one end making it acidic. If the hydrogens are removed, that's called an unsaturated fatty acid. Those chains are attached to a glycerin molecule. When the glycerin is combined with three fatty acids, it becomes very water-insoluble. That is the form in which it's stored in the fat cells.

When you need energy, you have to activate enzymes that break the free fatty acids loose. When that happens from stress, hunger, or fasting, these free fatty acids get into the bloodstream, enter cells, and are available for energy production in the absence of glucose. The trouble is that process also tends to keep the stress going. If the free fatty acids are unsaturated—and especially if they are polyunsaturated, like from corn oil or safflower oil—those have a further stress-inducing action that tends to keep the breakdown of fat going and the stress reproducing itself.

**Andrew Murray:** If somebody is consuming a lot of butter, milk, and coconut oil, the fats therein, when stored, don't have the same destructive or oxidative effects when liberated?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. If you store a very saturated fat—like ghee or coconut oil, which is 98% saturated—those things keep for years without breaking down. But if you leave a bottle of safflower, corn, or linseed oil open, within hours or days you can detect spontaneous oxidation in the air. That happens at body temperature with the high oxygen content of your blood.

Interestingly, the biological oxidation is pretty much the opposite. If you have saturated fatty acids and polyunsaturated fatty acids circulating in your bloodstream, your muscles will be able to oxidize the saturated fat preferentially. The polyunsaturated fat tends to go into storage if you ate more than you can oxidize. So, it tends to be fattening if you eat a little extra of the polyunsaturated because it stores more easily. Your fat cells can also oxidize saturated fat, so they live on the saturated fat they have stored. Over the years, stress is more likely to release the polyunsaturated fats, making stress an increasing problem with age.

**Andrew Murray:** So the obesity we see now, which is generically termed diabetes, is probably directly linked to the polyunsaturated, thyroid-suppressive diets people consume.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It's now increasingly seen as a fat inflammation condition—a mild chronic inflammation. A major thing that causes that is the continual spontaneous release of small amounts of arachidonic acid. This is a highly unsaturated fatty acid that, even if you don't eat it, enzymes in the body will create from linoleic acid. It becomes one of the most toxic stored fats. When released, it turns into prostaglandins, which are probably our biggest inflammatory problem.

**Andrew Murray:** And prostaglandins are associated with inflammation, swelling, and edema.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. They're why aspirin is so great.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you approach diabetes management?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you focus on stopping the liberation of fatty acids from your tissues and inhibit their conversion to prostaglandins, you can usually very quickly lower your blood sugar quite a bit and feel better. The two chemicals that are most practical for lowering free fatty acids and stopping the stress reaction are niacinamide and aspirin.

Niacinamide has many effects, but the first one is inhibiting the lipase that liberates fats from your fat stores. Aspirin also does that, along with several other things relating to the liberation of free fatty acids and their conversion to inflammatory mediators.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know the mechanism by which they work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the case of aspirin, it's both indirect and direct actions on at least two different lipase enzymes: phospholipase and the adipose hormone-sensitive lipase that insulin controls. Insulin deficiency liberates more free fatty acids, so both of these act directly on the enzyme which is overactive due to insulin deficiency.

**Andrew Murray:** Most people are frightened of using aspirin because of potential bleeding. I know you recommend using vitamin K with it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Especially if a person has combined antibiotics with aspirin, they might have lost the intestinal bacteria that make vitamin K. Eating lots of cooked greens, such as kale, and liver are the best sources. Some types of cheese are also good sources of vitamin K.

**Andrew Murray:** What would you suggest as a dose for aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your vitamin K is okay, I think it's fine to take 200 or 300 milligrams every day. If it's to correct a problem such as diabetes or some chronic inflammatory problem, then up to... well, I know people who have temporarily taken 6,000 or 7,000 milligrams a day. Like 20 standard aspirin tablets.

**Caller (Kansas City):** I have a couple of questions. One is about a liver enzyme. I have a high ALT. Any suggestions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When any cell is stressed—for example, hypothyroidism lowers the energy production of a cell—it tends to take up water. When it takes up water, it becomes somewhat porous and its natural enzymes leak out into the bloodstream. Just by looking at the type of enzyme, you can't be sure whether it's coming from a leg muscle you strained, a heart muscle, or the liver. The liver is usually the place they look for enzymes like ALT.

**Caller (Kansas City):** The other question is about leafy greens. I cannot digest vegetables, but I do leafy greens broth and raw juicing. How much would you suggest I have per week to meet nutritional needs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you eat cooked greens by the cups and quarts, it's an adequate source of protein. But if you aren't eating it as your main food for protein, then half a cup to a cup a day will provide your vitamin K and a generous amount of magnesium and calcium. Those are the nutrients that quickly cook out into the broth. If you drink only the water that you cooked a cup or so of leaves in, you get a supplement of magnesium and calcium.

**Caller (Kansas City):** What about raw juicing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's pretty irritating to the intestine. Plants put their most intense defensive toxins into their seeds, but their next most intense irritants and toxins are in the leaves because they don't want to be grazed. They put chemicals in that tend to block your digestive enzymes. Cooking destroys or reduces most of those toxins. If you eat them raw, and if you aren't a ruminant that has evolved a stomach to handle raw leaves, you're most likely to have digestive problems.

**Caller (David, Missouri):** I've heard you mention that aspirin is helpful in reducing tumor growth. Also, I use an aspirin powder called BC that has caffeine in it. I've been putting baking soda, magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt), and sometimes magnesium chloride in a bath with this aspirin/caffeine powder for knee pain. Does the baking soda create a gradient that pulls those things into the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has diuretic effects and some anti-inflammatory effects from the carbon dioxide itself. The caffeine acts on some of the same enzymes that aspirin does with an anti-inflammatory effect. They both increase your cell respiration and suppress nitric oxide, which is one of our central risky pro-inflammatory mediators that poisons mitochondrial respiration. So caffeine and aspirin have multi-levels of defense for the mitochondria.

**Caller (David, Missouri):** Will that be pulled in through the skin effectively?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Caffeine goes in through the skin more easily than aspirin, but yes, some aspirin is absorbed.

**Caller (David, Missouri):** Does that apply to tumor growth as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Inflammation and respiratory defects are the motor for cancer growth. It happens that if you restore energy production in the mitochondria, you're also lowering the inflammatory stimulants that activate cell division and spreading.

**Caller (Sacramento):** I have questions about substances that induce mitochondrial uncoupling, which reduces ATP production and generates body heat instead. Is this reduced ATP production harmful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When it's a mild degree of uncoupling, it prevents some of the stray free radical products that happen in the more relaxed, lower-intensity mitochondria. They know that you reduce free radical damage a little by increasing uncoupling.

Another substance which uncouples mitochondria, lowers ATP a little bit, and greatly protects the mitochondrion from free radicals is fructose. Fructose absorbs excess phosphate ions. The absorption of phosphate ions by fructose is a direct defensive system. The pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme is suppressed in cancer—that's why dichloroacetate is gaining interest, as it reactivates that enzyme. But simply lowering the free phosphate in the cell tends to reactivate this crucial enzyme at the top of the energy-producing chain.

When you are supplied with aspirin, caffeine, and fructose, you are not calling on free fatty acids. If you load up the cell with excess free fatty acids from stress, they reverse all of those processes. They block pyruvate dehydrogenase by making more phosphate ions available. Where sugars bind them and lower free phosphates, fatty acids increase them and tend to poison the crucial enzyme.

**Caller (Sacramento):** Does this process of producing heat negatively affect the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It increases heat, among other things. Keeping your body temperature up to an efficient high level makes all of your tissues more stable. The thyroid is very compatible with that. Keeping yourself slightly hyperthyroid doesn't stress anything; in fact, it keeps down those stress signals.

**Caller (Mike, New York):** regarding niacinamide, is there a minimal dose and an upper limit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen really great results from something in the range of 150 to 300 milligrams per day, divided into three smaller doses. But I also know people who have taken over 1,000 or 1,500 milligrams for a very long time without problems. Because manufactured supplements have trace allergenic impurities, it's best to find the smallest amount that works for you.

**Caller (Mike, New York):** Does niacinamide need to be balanced with other B vitamins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thiamine (B1) works with the respiratory enzymes, and of course, you need all of them. B12, B1, and biotin are very closely involved with the respiratory apparatus.

**Caller (Mike, New York):** Regarding Vitamin B6, some people use the active form (P5P). Are there indicators that a person needs the active form?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With either form of vitamin B6, it's possible to overdose. People are finding that the active form is easier to overdose with. It used to take several hundred milligrams over several months to produce toxic effects on the nerves, but some people are seeing it with as little as 50 milligrams over a long time with the active form. I think it's good to start with 10 milligrams, which is far beyond the normal daily requirement. 10 to 20 milligrams is almost always all a person needs therapeutically.

**Caller (Mike, New York):** You've discussed using carrot salads to lower intestinal bacteria. If that doesn't work for SIBO, would the drug metronidazole (Flagyl) be safe to try?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens to be a pretty toxic antibiotic. I think it's good to try a lot of other things first. There are some bacterial products that are more actively germicidal in the intestine, and I think there are some intestinal detoxifying antibiotics that are a lot safer than metronidazole.

**Caller (Mike, New York):** You mentioned anecdotally about people with leukemia treating it with raw eggnog. Could you elaborate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They were using a whole eggnog. Fresh egg lecithin itself has been shown to have antiviral and antibacterial activities. The white of the egg is peculiar for its ability to bind minerals. The combination of the lecithin and raw egg white probably has some special germicidal effect.

**Engineer:** Two callers asked questions off-air. First: dehydration and water requirements. Second: the difference between nutritional yeast and brewer's yeast.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding yeast, there are many strains and they taste different. Brewer's yeast that actually comes from a brewery generally has hops flavor in it, so it's very bitter. Nutritional yeasts have been grown especially for supplements, and some have added chemical substances like selenium. Basically, yeast chemistry itself is always rich in B vitamins.

Regarding hydration, keeping your cell energy up is the basic thing. You want to keep the cell water under control—neither too hydrated nor too dehydrated. The regulating minerals (sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium) are part of keeping a balance between intracellular and extracellular water.

Drinking extra water when you're not thirsty can disturb your mineral and hormone balance. For example, too much water in relation to minerals tends to increase your prolactin, because prolactin is a water and salt regulating hormone. It's probably more important not to push excess water. Thirst is almost always a good indicator of how much you need. If you're drinking milk and fruit juice, that can provide all the water you need.

**Caller (Oklahoma City):** What would you apply on your face to get rid of age spots?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on what they're made of. Sometimes high estrogen or high polyunsaturated fats can cause a fairly sudden appearance of age spots at an area that's irritated or sun-exposed. Changing your diet away from polyunsaturated fats and rubbing some vitamin E into those spots can help remove them. There are enzymes that can break down even fairly old, long-standing lipofuscin pigment, and vitamin E is an activator of that.

If it's largely a sun-induced spot, you might try rubbing some niacinamide. Dissolve a high-potency niacinamide tablet in a tiny amount of water and apply that to the spot every day for a week or two. It fades a lot of the pigments.

**Caller (Oklahoma City):** Is soy-derived vitamin E okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think a pure, high-potency vitamin E is good. 100 or 200 milligrams orally is probably enough that you can put a little on a spot, and sometimes that helps the enzymes to clear it out.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to the topic of tonight. Even in the presence of supplemented insulin, diabetics still get neuropathies—sensation loss, particularly in the feet. How is this process at odds with excess sugar when sugar is a vital energy-producing currency?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've gone through many articles recently. I watched a video by Gershom Zajicek, a medical professor in Israel who has a very good understanding of physiology. He explains how increased blood glucose is called for by the brain to make up for its needs. But after explaining the compensatory effect of high glucose for the brain, he uses the term "glycotoxic" for the harmful effects of glucose. He just resorted to a word to explain how glucose affects other organs without really explaining the mechanism.

The changes in the nerves include everything that is failing because of a lack of energy. When cells are living on fatty acids, the fatty acids intrinsically disturb the metabolism of phosphate, turn off glucose energy production, and activate nitric oxide, the respiratory inhibitor.

In the pancreas, glucose stimulates the regeneration of new insulin-producing cells. It's the bad balance—too much free fatty acid and not enough glucose to defend the cells—that causes them to die.

In nerves, one of the effects of failing energy is the inability to make cholesterol and convert cholesterol into neurosteroids. When a nerve or its supporting glial cells are injured by anything—including lack of glucose or oxygen—they stop producing the defensive steroids from cholesterol and begin producing estrogen. The diabetic brain and nerves have more aromatase (the enzyme which converts androgens to estrogens) than a normal person. The estrogen sends out signals to surrounding cells, which normally causes them to produce protective nerve steroids like pregnenolone and progesterone. But if you don't have the energy, you get stuck producing just the estrogen, which keeps things excited and stressed.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Memory, Cognition and Nutrition
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us. This is *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD Garberville. My name is Andrew Murray. My wife and I are both licensed medical herbalists; we trained in England, graduated with a master's degree in herbal medicine, and run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions.

Tonight, you are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject: memory, cognition, and nutrition. We have Dr. Raymond Peat with us. Dr. Peat, could you give us a synopsis of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the last 40 years, I've been studying independently. Before that, from 1968 to 1972, I was a graduate student in biology at the University of Oregon for a PhD in biology, specializing in physiology. In the late 50s, I worked on a master's degree at the University of Oregon, taking courses in philosophy and psychology. The reason I decided to study biology was that I didn't think people were working on consciousness in the right way. I thought I could come at it biologically.

**Andrew Murray:** Tonight's topic is cognition, memory, and the nutrition that supports successful memory forming and retention. When looking at the pioneers of this subject in the last hundred years, there are many Russians involved. You previously mentioned Fyodor Dostoevsky and gave an anecdote about a change in his perception and cognition as a result of imprisonment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A biography written by Jim Rice, a professor at the University of Oregon, tells the story about how Dostoevsky's nervous problems improved while he was in prison in Siberia. One of the odd things was that he began eating chopped meat because that was available in the prison. In the winter, they didn't have vegetables, so they had to hunt. His consciousness improved, and the professor thought there might have been a nutritional aspect to this change.

**Andrew Murray:** Are you supporting the necessary protein requirement in the diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you are seriously deficient in protein, it absolutely affects your consciousness. A professor friend of mine in Mexico said that when some of his students couldn't memorize things, he encouraged them to eat some protein. When I was teaching language classes in Mexico City, some of my students absolutely couldn't remember anything. I would start my classes by serving cookies I made out of eggs, sugar, and wheat germ alongside a cup of coffee. Everyone was able to learn their lessons just from that little extra boost of protein, carbohydrate, and coffee.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's explore the philosophy behind current thinking. How have you seen the development of our understanding of the conscious versus the unconscious?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Dostoevsky wrote *The Dream of a Ridiculous Man*, in which the hero is suicidal because he sees the world as full of robots—people operating according to cause and effect, doing nothing other than what they are determined to do. At the time he was writing, Europe was being swept by the mechanistic idea. Thomas Huxley, a friend of Charles Darwin, advocated the idea that molecules in the brain are absolutely in control of our thoughts, and our mind is simply a shadow of this determined mechanism.

That idea has persisted. In my generation, the outstanding figure has been Noam Chomsky, with his idea that genes determine "transformational rules" that limit or determine the form language takes. Cognitive science and artificial intelligence are closely related to the Chomsky position, using the digital computer as a model for understanding human intelligence. This has led to a digitalization of consciousness theories.

**Andrew Murray:** You are saying that Chomsky's position was allied to the digital model?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The idea that brain cells communicate according to an "on/off" or "all-or-nothing" signaling was derived from the quantizing philosophy of the digital computer switch. Biology took this up, assuming that when a nerve fires, that is one bit of information.

However, P.K. Anokhin in Russia was critical of that idea. Many people noticed you can't explain hearing—the full range of volume, frequency, and tonal quality—if nerves are only on/off switches. Anokhin showed that it is likely impossible to explain brain function using the analogy of a computer using binary digits.

**Andrew Murray:** There certainly is much more to thinking and cognition than just straight on/off electrical impulses.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In Anokhin's view, it would be more like a picture traveling down each nerve, transmitting complex information. The essential ideas here are resonance and coherence—the interrelatedness of things separated in space and time.

These ideas were part of biology back when Gestalt psychology was current in the 30s and 40s. They argued that the Gestalt was an image having a space-filling function in the brain, reflecting the spatial and temporal arrangement in the real world. For example, in the nose, a molecule vibrating would stimulate an analogous vibration so that the actual aroma would be reproduced along the nerve and in the brain. Or when light is absorbed by a Vitamin A molecule in the retina, it would excite a resonance of a similar luminous quality. In the Gestalt view, you would actually have something like a luminous event in the brain when you saw light in the world.

**Andrew Murray:** Is that resonance similar to the concept of extra-sensory perception being transmitted across space?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are experiments currently going on regarding this. Michael Persinger, a neurologist, has argued for a resonance between everyone's brain and the electromagnetic resonance frequencies of the earth environment.

**Andrew Murray:** I recall the concept of the "noosphere" proposed by Vladimir Vernadsky.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the priest Teilhard de Chardin followed Vernadsky's idea of the world becoming more and more conscious, supporting the growth of more conscious organisms.

**Caller (Jeff from Mendocino):** I have heard of cases where music is used for therapy for people who are comatose or have spinal injuries. It seems magical and medicinal. Since everything is vibrating, including string theory, how do you respond to the idea of music helping people come back?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's something much more subtle but more powerful than endorphins. I think the very structure of nerves is a kind of resonance and carries a function that is analogous to objective music outside the body. When you give the organism a chance to relax and respond to music, you're reinforcing a process that is basic to the life of the brain cells.

If you believed in the mechanistic interpretation of consciousness, you would see the present moment as an infinitesimally thin division between past and future. But the unreality of that is clear when you listen to music. A performer or director has to see where the particular moment is going and where it has been. The pace and qualities developing in each moment depend on what you perceive is coming and what has recently passed. The brain is like a musical composition that doesn't exist only in the present; the moment of consciousness spans time.

**Andrew Murray:** That reminds me of Buddhist teachings on stilling the mind. You once mentioned a test where people performed measurably better when lying down versus standing up. How do you see stilling the mind as a mechanism for better brain function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's a matter of the breadth of time in your consciousness. When you're standing up, you're ready to react quickly to a short-term influence. When you're lying down, your reference of meaning goes out further in all directions. What you're going to do and what you've been doing come into the picture.

When you're under stress, glucose is the immediate source of energy. Glucose is the material that keeps that conscious process possible. If you are under stress and using glucose too fast, or don't have enough available, your nervous processes go into an emergency state where only the immediate present is relevant. Anxiety associated with hypoglycemia or stress will flatten the way your consciousness works.

**Andrew Murray:** Once again, we are touting glucose as positive and energetic, despite the media saying sugar is bad.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person has been under stress and not eating well, besides protein, Vitamin B1 is sometimes the thing that can make the biggest difference. A mild deficiency can make you feel sluggish, depressed, and have poor short-term memory.

**Andrew Murray:** What kind of dose is physiologically sufficient?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've experienced it with as little as 10 milligrams, but for an emergency, 100 milligrams is okay.

**Caller (New Jersey):** I read a quote about how neurogenesis can take place in the hippocampus and the olfactory bulb. Can one go around smelling things to start firing neurons or creating new neurons?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Luca Turin, a perfume specialist, has some very good videos on the internet regarding olfaction. Along with Heraclitus, who talked about the nose as being at the center of consciousness, the olfactory system is very closely connected with our highest conceptual work.

Becoming conscious of odors in your environment is closely connected with the higher parts of the brain. You can use odors to stimulate memory. Any type of experience helps stimulate the hippocampus. For example, taxi drivers in big cities who have learned all the streets have a bigger hippocampus.

The mechanists proposed an idea of memory like a computer, where you punch a hole in a card or put a signal on a tape—a definite thing you could go back and find. They suggested we make a specific protein or RNA molecule for memory. But if you think about the process you would have to go through to *find* the right memory molecule when you needed it, the apparatus used to find that molecule implies you already know where the memory is. So, you already have the memory, in effect. Otherwise, molecules would just be jumping at you randomly.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's get back to nutrition. You mentioned B1 deficiency. Apart from sunflower seeds and bread, what are good sources of B1?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the animal foods: eggs, milk, cheese.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to question you about Vitamin A. You linked this with anxiety.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin A acts as an antenna for interacting with electromagnetic energy, but it also activates the enzymes that make steroids—especially brain steroids. If your Vitamin A is deficient, your ability to make pregnenolone, progesterone, and DHEA is limited. The brain is probably the most powerful steroid-forming organ when it's working right.

**Andrew Murray:** What about fish oils? I know there is a misplaced belief that they are good for you, but halibut liver oil has concentrated Vitamin A and little PUFA (polyunsaturated fatty acids).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Halibut liver oil gives you a lot of Vitamin A, some Vitamin D, and traces of Vitamin E without too much of the PUFA. It's a good source. Liver itself—fish, chicken, or beef—is a great source. Also eggs, milk, and cheese. Vitamin B12 happens to be crucial for turning carotene into Vitamin A.

**Andrew Murray:** What consumes Vitamin A?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ultraviolet exposure destroys it very easily in your skin. Vitamin A reacts with the ultraviolet and spreads damage to any unsaturated fats in your skin. Vitamin E protects against that breakdown.

**Andrew Murray:** Are there other factors that increase the ability to retain information?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Serotonin. When you are under stress or eating irritating foods, your intestine gets inflamed and releases extra serotonin. Some of it gets to the brain and signals the stress system. Endotoxin triggers nitric oxide and serotonin. Various types of stress and depression tend to slow nerve function. If you feed rats beans containing soluble fibers that feed bacteria, creating irritation and increasing serotonin, the rats become anxious, aggressive, and fearful.

**Andrew Murray:** So anxiety is one of the main things to avoid for competent memory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And hyperventilation. When you are anxious, it is common to breathe harder and lose carbon dioxide (CO2). Carbon dioxide seems to be a nerve stabilizer. As CO2 goes down, your platelets release more serotonin. Anything that increases your ability to retain carbon dioxide tends to help you think calmly and clearly.

**Andrew Murray:** And thyroid helps you retain CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Thyroid, progesterone, and pregnenolone. Also, keeping your brain warm. Just running at a higher temperature, your brain produces more CO2 and generally retains magnesium more efficiently. I've known many people with memory problems who had a body temperature of 96 or 97 degrees. Getting their temperature up toward 98 or 99 degrees improved their memory tremendously.

**Andrew Murray:** What about sodium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Stress and aging tend to make it harder to retain sodium. Thyroid is an important factor in retaining sodium so it isn't lost in the urine. When your body senses a loss of sodium, the adrenals produce aldosterone to save the sodium. However, aldosterone tells the kidneys to lose magnesium. So, if you take enough sodium to keep your adrenals from making aldosterone, your kidneys will save magnesium. Eating extra salt is equivalent to having more magnesium in your diet.

**Andrew Murray:** So salt, protein, progesterone, and thyroid are the main things for keeping the brain functioning well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for joining us again and sharing your wisdom. For those listening, you can find out more at www.raypeat.com.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Vaccination I
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who have never listened to the shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

This month's subject has come around fortuitously in terms of the recent press on the whooping cough outbreaks that have been occurring in California and in different states across the US. I wanted to do the show on vaccinations. I know there are many different opinions out there about how useful they are, how harmful they could potentially be, and the debate regarding autism and the MMR vaccination is still raging.

This evening, we are pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us. For those who have never heard Dr. Peat speak, he provides an opinion from a broad scientific background showing that things are not always as they seem. Even though diseases have raged through humanity since the beginning of time, various changes in our world have made it a harder place to live in terms of exposure to toxins. We are exposed to environmental estrogens, radiation, and dietary factors that have degraded the energy with which human beings fight infection.

As an organism, we have an innate store of energy. Slowly but surely, from infancy to adulthood, our exposure to various things interferes with our bodily systems. The immune system is a complex and finely tuned weapon against infection. Infection has always been present; we coexist with a wide range of organisms, some of which are pathogenic.

Some diseases have had wide media attention, like polio. I remember growing up and seeing pictures of polio victims from 15 or 20 years prior—children wearing braces and calipers. Diseases with severe outcomes like polio struck the population, and modern science took full steam ahead with pharmaceuticals. The campaign to eradicate polio, like smallpox, became a major effort of government and industry.

However, it is a strange concept that a government-sanctioned process can be outside of the law. In medicine, the Hippocratic oath states: "First, do no harm." Yet, vaccine products have been indemnified by the government. If people are damaged by vaccines, the manufacturing company cannot be taken to court. The United States legal standard defines vaccines as "unavoidably unsafe products," meaning they are incapable of being made safe for their intended use because they contain chemicals and elements poisonous to the body.

As we talk to Dr. Peat, keep in mind that the media and corporations often present a one-sided story. Dr. Peat may seem controversial, but his statements are the product of investigative work and scientific review.

**Andrew Murray:** Hi, Dr. Peat. Thanks for joining us. I’ve given the outline of the show, but I’d like to give you the opportunity to share your scientific background before we begin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Although I concentrated on physiology, reproductive aging, and biochemistry during my four years at the University of Oregon, I took a seminar on developmental biology in 1969. The professor was sponsoring an international conference on immunology, so I got to hear the latest research explaining the clonal selection theory of adaptive immunity.

The most memorable thing about the conference was a professor describing his *in vitro* experiments with white blood cells. He showed that even after being clonally deleted, when the concentration was proper, they could reconstitute themselves as if each cell had knowledge of the whole organism. This contradicted the mechanistic assumptions of the clonal selection theory. However, it corresponds closely to what is now seen as epigenetic expression, where each cell knows where it belongs in the whole organism.

The clonal selection theory was developed to justify vaccination practice. Vaccination began as an entirely empirical practice—trial and error—before people even knew cells existed. Early in the 20th century, Paul Ehrlich developed the approach that led to the clonal selection theory, which remains dominant. However, in the last few years, there has been a recognition that the innate immune system—which we share with primitive animals and plants—is involved in the adaptive immune system.

In the same year Paul Ehrlich received his Nobel Prize, Élie Metchnikoff also shared it. Metchnikoff presented information about the innate immune system, viewing immunity as a developmental process of maintaining the integrity of the organism. His work was largely ignored until recently.

In 1969, my professors were uninterested in innate immunity. But I had been reading William F. Koch, who developed evidence early in the century that oxidative cell metabolism is responsible for innate resistance. This was the biochemical explanation for Metchnikoff’s developmental view. Koch showed that the energy of cells—oxidative metabolism—made innate immunity work. He was disparaged because his theory involved free radical reactions breaking down viruses and toxins, and biologists didn't acknowledge free radical chemistry until the 1950s. It is only now coming into scientific awareness that the innate immune system and metabolic processes determine why some people get diseases and others don't.

**Andrew Murray:** Even currently, there are populations that don't come down with a disease during a raging epidemic. These are unvaccinated people who have their own innate defense.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People writing about the economics of immunity often refer to vaccination as the "economically viable" method. They acknowledge that sanitation and nutrition prevent disease, but they argue it is cheaper to vaccinate.

Around 1970, the World Health Organization did an experiment in Central America. They gave one village a medical team with vaccinations and regular medicine. In a second village, they did nothing. In a third village, they provided no medical help but supplied clean water and nutritional supplements to pregnant women and young children. After several years, the health was best in the nutrition and clean water village. The health in the medicalized and vaccinated village was actually worse. Scientifically, this suggests that while it might not be "economically viable" to clean up the environment, it is definitely better than vaccination for improving health.

**Andrew Murray:** I find it staggering that the industry producing vaccinations is completely outside of the law regarding litigation for damages.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I find that incredible, and there is very little talk about the actual damage. However, even in medical literature, which is biased against criticizing vaccines, you see evidence that vaccinated people have serious health problems. These range from baldness, sterility, and ovarian failure to psoriasis and autoimmune skin diseases. Long-range studies suggest a significant increase among vaccinated people of serious degenerative diseases with an autoimmune factor, such as dementia, cancer, and heart disease.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you think our immunity has changed from antiquity to now? We know Egyptians had some diseases, but how has the strength of immunity changed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Current experiments show that diet, sanitation, light exposure, and avoidance of pollution make a tremendous difference. In pre-industrial society, there was much less heavy metal exposure. I believe seed oils—polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)—have been a major contributor to bad health, along with heavy metals. These two interact to destroy our innate immune system.

Experiments preventing animals from consuming the usual polyunsaturated fats show they become extremely resistant to all kinds of injury, including infections. Interestingly, organs like kidneys can be transplanted from an animal deprived of polyunsaturated fats into another animal as if they were genetically related. The antigenicity of the tissues is extremely low simply by avoiding polyunsaturated fats.

**Andrew Murray:** So the organs from the animal with no PUFA in its diet had much less antigenic reaction in the recipient?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even though their genes and proteins should be antigenic, because they are free of the associated free radical breakdown products of oxidized fats, those proteins aren't recognized as foreign. You see similar things in liver transplants among humans. Females have higher levels of circulating polyunsaturated fats, which increase with age. The least successful, most antigenic livers come from older female donors, corresponding to the accumulation of polyunsaturated fats.

**Caller:** I have a question about gluten. You mentioned that estrogen sensitizes the intestines to gluten. If someone stays off gluten, how long before they can try it again? Or do they have to stay off it forever?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think hormone balance makes the difference. If you get your defensive anti-inflammatory hormones up—including thyroid—you can improve. As the anti-inflammatory T3 part of the thyroid increases, the TSH (which is pro-inflammatory) decreases. High estrogen goes with low thyroid function and an inflammatory state resembling autoimmunity. I think the gluten reaction is a type of autoimmune reaction. You have to shift the whole organism so it acts properly rather than overreacting to inflammatory signals.

**Caller:** So if you do that, eventually you could eat gluten without a problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The intestine is a source of serotonin, nitric oxide, and histamine, which promote inflammation. These increase with stress and aging. Recent research shows that nitric oxide turns off steroid synthesis (starting with pregnenolone) in white blood cells. Since nitric oxide halts the anti-autoimmune process, you want to minimize exposure to serotonin, histamine, and nitric oxide while increasing anti-inflammatory processes.

**Caller:** Could you also give practical advice for age-related macular degeneration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid is key. Sometimes aspirin helps by keeping down prostaglandins and polyunsaturated reactive oxygen species. Vitamin E, thyroid, aspirin, pregnenolone, and progesterone are all protective. Caffeine is another generally protective substance that blocks the toxic effects of nitric oxide.

**Caller:** So restoring energy production should regenerate the cells in the eye?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Cells tend to regenerate constantly in the brain, retina, and pancreas. Even in sick people, new stem cells are being born. The problem is keeping them from dying due to the stressful situation in the tissue.

**Caller:** I’m calling from Humboldt. What I don't hear you addressing is that many diseases children get vaccinated for have been wiped out, and they were deadly. My father almost died of diphtheria; his cousin died of polio. Smallpox and tetanus were death sentences. Whatever harm vaccinations might cause, aren't they less harmful than the diseases they wiped out?

**Andrew Murray:** That can be contested, and that is the point of this show. People are currently dying from cancers, dementia, and Alzheimer's. Autism is rife. While these diseases had deadly consequences, Dr. Peat has noted that good hygiene, sanitation, and nutrition have done more to reduce disease than vaccination. It is the health of the organism that is the important factor. We aren't saying *carte blanche* that vaccinations shouldn't be used, but we want to highlight that nutrition, drug use, food quality, and environmental factors play a massive role.

**Caller:** A stronger immune system helps ward off diseases. I just wanted to know what you would do without vaccinations for these deadly diseases.

**Andrew Murray:** The goal is to open people's minds to things they may not have thought about. We often get brainwashed with only one side of the story.

**Caller:** I'm a homeopath. There is a wonderful book by Richard Moskowitz called *Plain Doctoring* that offers a medical assessment of each vaccination. For instance, the whooping cough vaccine is terribly ineffective, which is partly why we see outbreaks despite high vaccination rates. Measles works well, but others like pertussis have terrible consequences. It should be a case-by-case basis. I might be interested in a tetanus shot, but not pertussis.

My great-grandfather died of smallpox. All his children had the vaccine and had horrible reactions—their legs got red and pussy. He was repelled by that and refused the vaccine, but then he caught smallpox and died. There should be some sanity, but currently, it seems driven by money.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for the book recommendation. Dr. Peat, let's discuss the adjuvant side of vaccinations and how these are proven to be toxic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the newer adjuvants of interest is phytol, a plant oily material. Heavy metals have been used as adjuvants for a long time and are pathogens themselves. Conventional immunologists realize that simple "foreignness" of a protein isn't enough to make it reactive or function as an antigen. They need to make the body treat it as dangerous to activate the immune system.

Following the trend Eli Metchnikoff sketched out, a few people brought innate immunity back to look at vaccination. It is now recognized as the "Danger or Damage Theory" of immunity. It used to be thought that the immune system recognized "otherness." Now, it is increasingly seen that *injury* triggers the immune system. The originators of this theory, Jamie Cunliffe and Polly Matzinger, showed that if you view the immune system as a developmental process, then pathogenic agents—radiation, heavy metals, toxic fats—are the real agents of damage. That is why they must be used with the bacterium or virus in a vaccine to trigger a response.

**Andrew Murray:** I remember thimerosal, the mercury-based preservative, caused a lot of damage.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people focus on the amount of mercury as a toxin, but it is really the way the tiny amount of toxin or adjuvant is presented that causes the problem. For example, kids whose mothers ate lots of seafood often have high IQs along with a high body load of mercury. In a healthy body, mercury isn't necessarily toxic. But when presented in a way that activates these adaptive defensive reactions, it can lead to autoimmunity. When they substitute phytol for aluminum or mercury, I think the effects are going to be just as bad, if not worse, because it is about potentiating the disturbing properties.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We had a listener who wanted Dr. Peat to comment on the effects of breastfeeding on the immune health of the child and its relationship to vaccines. Specifically, do the antibodies in breast milk offer a viable alternative to vaccines?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Besides being good nutrition, breast milk is extremely low in iron. Iron accumulates in the environment and leads to oxidative injury. Milk provides nutrition with a relative absence of harmful iron. It also provides immune-protective materials like antibodies and lactoferrin, which helps manipulate the body's iron load and prevents it from reacting with polyunsaturated fats.

Breastfeeding provides undamaged proteins that become part of the baby's immune system. Even RNA and DNA have been demonstrated to pass from the mother's milk into the baby. If you are raised on cow's or goat's milk, you get some protective factors, but you are likely incorporating some of that animal's genetic material.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would a longer duration of breastfeeding, say beyond two years, lead to more active immunity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The mother's immunity shows up in the baby if the baby is breastfed for a couple of years. Part of that transfer is by microvesicles—little particles less than a thousandth the size of a cell containing proteins and RNA. These pass through the intestine wall and circulate as immune cells. They are like miniature stem cell repair kits.

Regarding duration, babies are usually born with an iron overload. By the time a baby is two years old, it has grown into that excess and might need iron-containing food like eggs. But the protective immunity is still being passed along up to three or four years.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, we have just a few minutes left. Could you summarize your current understanding of the immune system and the perceived risks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the last 20 years, the image of the organism has become more like a continuing stream of developmental changes. We are essentially a big, slowly developing embryo. What happens during gestation and the first few years of life is critical because there are fewer cells involved, and each of those cells has a long history of descendants. The more you disturb the organism early in life, the greater the distortion in adulthood.

However, we are still in process even after middle age. Stem cells are still being educated. It is never too late to correct damage, but the early environment should be optimized by avoiding stresses.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there a point where an organism is fully protected?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are two types of experiments in mice and rats that say a lot about human conditions. First, germ-free animals: even though they are susceptible to infection because they've never been exposed, they are very tough and resistant to other stresses. In middle age, their mortality rate is much lower, and they are resistant to obesity and diabetes even on high-sugar/fat diets.

The second line of experimentation involves giving animals a diet completely lacking in so-called "essential fatty acids" (PUFAs). These animals are extremely resistant to trauma, chemical poisoning, and biological toxins. They have an extremely strong immune system and are hard to infect. It takes a huge dose of injected cancer cells or bacteria to produce a viable infection.

**Andrew Murray:** I have to hold you there, Dr. Peat. Thank you so much for joining us. For those who want to know more, Dr. Peat’s website is www.raypeat.com. It is full of fully referenced articles. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Vaccination II
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's Part 2 subject of vaccinations. Safety and efficacy are in question. Once again, I'll be introducing Dr. Raymond Peat to the show. He has some new information regarding facts shown from about 2002 through to now—fairly recent revelations about parts of the vaccination process which are probably more questionable than ever.

I want to open the show by reading what I read last month regarding the "first do no harm" tenet of medicine. The United States legal standard applied to vaccines defines them as "unavoidably unsafe products that are quite incapable of being made safe for their intended and ordinary use." The reason why vaccines are unsafe, or harmful, is because they are made up of chemicals and other elements that are essentially poisonous to the body.

Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us again. For those who have never listened to this show, would you outline your academic and scientific background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s and 60s, I was mostly a student and teacher in the humanities—English literature and painting, for example. Then I decided to go to graduate school in biology and biochemistry at the University of Oregon for a PhD because I had been interested in that for many years, but I considered that the academic approach was pretty futile and misleading.

Since graduating in 1972, I've continued studying, trying to find what I consider the "main line" of science in biology, which is very opposed in many ways to mainstream medical thinking and biology influenced by corporate financing. This main line of biological and chemical thinking I've been following is a more holistic, developmental, time-oriented way of looking at organisms than the reductionist, abstract, molecular approach that has become dominant. That particularly relates to how the immune system works. I did teach a short course in immunology to medical students in Mexico in 1979, but since then, things have radically changed.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to start with something that might stun people. My generation, born in the mid-60s, and subsequent generations probably have very little awareness of the fact that all infectious diseases were in free-fall decline *before* the introduction of vaccines. This doesn't enter the consciousness of most people; it is veiled by the fear and mysticism surrounding disease and its apparent cure.

Starting in the 1800s, massive overcrowding, open sewers, poor hygiene, and poor nutrition were largely responsible for the pandemics and epidemics that ravaged Europe. When socio-economic factors improved—general hygiene, nutrition, working hours, and housing—the figures changed.

There is a book by Dr. Suzanne Humphries entitled *Dissolving Illusions: Disease, Vaccines, and The Forgotten History*. Dr. Humphries is a nephrologist who left mainstream medicine after seeing kidney damage initiated by influenza vaccines. She looked at British records from 1750 to the present for about ten infectious diseases, including measles, smallpox, typhoid, whooping cough, diphtheria, polio, syphilis, and malaria. She found a dramatic decrease in the incidence of these diseases mostly around the early 1900s to the end of the Second World War.

Why do you think vaccines have become what they are now in people's minds—that we can't do without them—when in fact diseases were disappearing due to improved health and sanitary conditions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The medical attitude has been developed for more than 100 years. My parents and grandparents were born before the medical indoctrination got underway in the United States and Europe. There were people teaching doctors to vaccinate, but in my parents' generation, they were pretty immune to it. They were forced to be vaccinated in schools, but it was only a later generation—coinciding with the American Medical Association taking over medicine and abolishing natural approaches like naturopathy for about 60 or 70 years—that the drug treatment approach took over.

Several people have recently pointed out that vaccines are really just a cheap way of controlling some infections. It is recognized that good food and a clean environment will prevent infectious diseases, but it is considered too expensive.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you feel about the argument that it is an economic situation? If we had good, clean food—not contaminated with GMOs or laboratory-produced—and people weren't brainwashed into believing butter or sugar are bad for them, there would automatically be an increase in general health. But that isn't in the interest of industries producing products for our ill health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Last month I mentioned the World Health Organization study in Central America. It showed that giving a tiny bit of economic support, such as clean water and a nutritious porridge supplement for pregnant women and children, improved the health of the study village relative to one that had no intervention. The village that had the intervention with doctors, vaccines, and standard medicine saw health go *down* during the study period. That actually said medicine is bad for you.

Even the cleaning up of the environment led by the Rockefeller Foundation—trying to prevent hookworm infection and improving nutrition in schools—was done because it was realized that sick, undernourished, mentally undeveloped people didn't make good workers. So, cleaning up the environment and feeding people is good for the corporate economy too. But it happens that it's even cheaper to use vaccines, and more profitable. Even if the environment got clean enough and people were well fed, it would still be very profitable to sell the chemical and vaccination approach.

**Andrew Murray:** I have a friend who noted that the regular acellular pertussis vaccination has actually increased *Bordetella parapertussis* colonization in children. She suggests that many children with unknown fevers and unwellness, but without the typical cough, actually have *Bordetella parapertussis* colonization resulting from the vaccination itself. Have you heard anything about this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not at all.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's discuss the vaccine theory. We are a stream of consciousness constantly evolving and affected by our environment. In terms of immunity, would you describe the basic immune system—the innate versus the adaptive—and then how vaccines and adjuvants like aluminum affect this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Currently, the medical community emphasizes the difference between the **innate immune system**, which they view as the first barrier to infection, and the **adaptive system**, which learns to be specifically immune to invading organisms.

The 1908 Nobel Prize was divided between two proponents of theories of immunity: Paul Ehrlich and Élie Metchnikoff.
*   **Metchnikoff** was an embryologist who emphasized the role of phagocytes in destroying or isolating invading material and reconstituting a healthy organism.
*   **Ehrlich** was interested in the staining properties of cells. He showed that chemicals which could stain organisms specifically could also react with equal specificity to pathogens. The idea of a "magic bullet" came from his approach—mercury, arsenic, and later sulfa drugs.

Ehrlich's context dominated thinking about adaptive immunity and how specificity could be evoked by vaccines. Meanwhile, the developmental innate resistance Metchnikoff talked about was ignored until Jamie Cunliffe and Polly Matzinger revived the idea in the 90s around the **Danger Theory**. This was analogous to when Metchnikoff stuck a splinter into a jellyfish and showed it was engulfed by phagocytes—wandering cells that could eat invading material and turn it to nutritious use.

This was a complete rethinking of the specific chemical orientation of adaptive immunity. Since the 1990s, the Danger Theory has been incorporated into the mainstream, but they limit it to thinking of the innate system as a barrier and an amplifier of inflammation, which simply shifts over to making the adaptive system run faster. They've accepted innate immunity but in a subordinate way.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you feel about the introduction of fragments of proteins or RNA to the adaptive system? This supposedly underpins vaccine science—that the body prepares memory T-cells to jump in as soon as they contact the organism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By trial and error, it has been known for generations that "junk" added to an antigen makes it produce more active antibodies. Following that accidental learning, it was found that alum—an aluminum compound—is a good kind of junk to make the peptide or protein adhere and be more effective at forming antibodies.

One theory was that the aluminum condensed the protein into a little ball the immune system could deal with. But in the last five or ten years, the tendency is to see aluminum as an activator of the innate inflammatory process. There is a growing awareness that the adjuvant is there for the purpose of creating a generalized inflammation.

This is where the long-range view of "doing no harm" is being neglected. The embryological approach sees that what happens early in development will have permanent, lifelong effects. If you introduce an inflammatory state early in life, you have to wait 20, 30, or 40 years to see the effects. That hasn't been done.

With the new emphasis on the innate immune system as an inflammation amplifier, it is recognized that throughout our skin and mucous membranes, there are **dendritic cells**. These are the major antigen-presenting cells. In normal exposure to germs, the dendritic cells capture the antigen and present them to thymus cells, which instruct the production of antibodies. But this only works if the antigen is broken down and attached to the organism's own surface compatibility factors.

**Andrew Murray:** The MHCs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It is the combination of the invading peptides with the organism's own normal cell surface that immunity is developed toward. In the extreme form of the Danger Theory, this is the essence of the immune system: it is there to restore and maintain the structure of the organism, not primarily to attack invaders.

**Caller:** What are your thoughts on L-glutamine? I've read about people using it to heal stomach ulcers and restore intestinal integrity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it should be limited to what is available in the proteins of the diet. When an amino acid is manufactured in a pure chemical form, it always has risky contaminants not present in the whole natural protein. Secondly, while people talk about the glucose dependency of cancer cells, glutamine is actually a favorite food for promoting cancer cell growth. An excess of any single amino acid can be harmful, including overloading you with ammonia. If you had a clean source, it would be beneficial in some cases, but I think it's risky.

**Caller:** What is the upper limit for glycine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A few grams per day, divided into doses of half to one gram at a time, would be safe.

**Caller:** You've mentioned activated charcoal to clean up the intestine if carrots and bamboo shoots weren't doing the job. How would you use it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, ensure it is clean and hasn't been exposed to environmental contaminants, because it captures things from the air. If you have a clean source, you can add it to a drink or food.

**Caller:** Is a tablespoon at a time the dose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, depending on what you're using it for.

**Caller:** My question is about skin tags. What is the underlying cause, and is there anything topical to get rid of them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know the underlying cause, but they become very common as a person approaches middle age (40 or 45). That suggests a deficiency of the protective, stabilizing hormones. Since the skin is a major hormone-synthesizing organ, making sure you have enough cholesterol and thyroid in your diet to make protective steroids would be helpful. Some people have used topical DHEA or progesterone dissolved in oil, or micro-pulverized pregnenolone on the skin. Sometimes that will clear up a variety of growths, including skin tags.

**Caller:** How do you feel about turmeric or ginger to reduce inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people are allergic to those. Even though the research looks good, especially for turmeric, you want to be careful with herbal things because they have many other components which can trigger strong allergic reactions.

**Caller (Ed):** I'm hoping Dr. Peat can speak to poor memory, focus, low energy, and ADHD.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Having an adequate amount of protein is an essential first step. For an average-sized person, around 100 grams of good protein per day optimizes mental functioning. A Pentagon study of pilots found a high-fat diet was best for attention and avoiding accidents.

Vitamin B1 is used to produce energy from glucose. If you are deficient, a supplement of 10mg or more can be spectacular for mental focus and clarity.

If it isn't a nutritional problem, it is often low temperature of the brain. If your brain is only 94 or 95 degrees Fahrenheit, it won't function well. Studies showed that heating the head raised memory, quickness, and clarity of reasoning.

**Caller (Ed):** How would one know if their brain is at an optimum temperature?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eardrum thermometers are the closest immediate way to judge brain temperature.

**Caller (Ed):** Would wearing a beanie help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it can help. People with low body temperature often have insomnia due to the stress it causes; they sleep better with warm socks and a warm cap. Dietarily, things that keep your brain temperature up include protein, salt, sugar, and the steroids pregnenolone, DHEA, and progesterone.

**Caller (Ed):** Regarding protein, what would 100 grams equate to in food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Three quarts of milk would provide just about the right amount. Or 15 eggs. Or a combination of a quart and a half of milk, a few eggs, and some cheese. You can't depend on the protein in nuts and beans because their digestibility and quality aren't equal to animal proteins.

**Caller:** Is galanga and galangal the same thing? It looks like ginger. I heard it's used for skin cancers. Do you know anything about growing it or its medicinal uses?

**Andrew Murray:** Yes, galangal is a member of the ginger family. It's an Ayurvedic herb. It requires a tropical environment, so you wouldn't have success growing it in Crescent City without a hot house. I've never used it medicinally, though I've used lots of ginger.

**Caller:** I've heard L-arginine is good for you. Can you tell me what it does?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the precursor to two important substances: creatine phosphate (energy reserve) and nitric oxide. Very often, if you supplement arginine, you boost nitric oxide, which turns *off* your ability to produce energy. I think it's fairly predictably a risk.

**Caller:** Is 5,000 units of Vitamin D3 a day a proper dose? The bottle says every other day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is currently believed to be correct for the average person in the north. I've never heard of it being too much. Many people take it daily. The officially recommended few hundred units is definitely inadequate.

**Andrew Murray:** Reference limits have increased recently. Most people are low and don't reach therapeutically recognized levels. 5,000 units would not seem excessive.

**Caller:** You say sugar is good for you, but do you mean fruit? I heard too much sugar overacts insulin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Generally, getting your sugar from fruit is best because of the minerals and nutrients. Occasionally, if the rest of your diet is good, refined sugar can be helpful. Honey provides basically the same as refined sugar with a few extra helpful chemicals. I recommend refined sugar only for specific therapeutic uses.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I want to return to the innate immune system. The medical world sees it as a source of inflammation, a barrier, and a switch for the adaptive system. However, I think the inflammatory function is, to some extent, a *malfunction* of the innate immune system.

When irritation or damage is not repaired quickly enough, you see noticeable inflammation. I think the innate system is really a repair system. The signals it sends out are calling in repair cells. Its ideal function shouldn't reach the stage of inflammation and shouldn't activate the adaptive system strongly.

Thinking of the organism in a long-range, lifelong pattern, you don't want to overburden and misdirect the system by causing repeated inflammation. An example of why I think it is not primarily a system of producing inflammation is that **pregnenolone** has been discovered to turn *off* the immune cells activated by injury or pathogens. The cells should produce their reaction, call in repair processes, and then switch over to producing pregnenolone to stabilize cells and stop the inflammation.

**Caller:** I was curious about the ketosis concept—eating mostly fat and no grains or sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it activates the stress system if you have to produce the ketones yourself. If you have precursors in your diet that are partly formed ketones, those are great and equivalent to sugar. But if you have to turn on the process of making them, it means you aren't getting enough glucose or fruit.

**Caller:** Everywhere I look says the opposite.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You turn on cortisol production when you don't have enough sugar. Cortisol has chronic, harmful developmental effects. You need sugar from fruit, honey, or milk.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, thank you for joining us. His website is www.raypeat.com. He has many fully referenced articles available for free.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Thinking Outside the Box - New Cancer Treatments
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who have never listened to the shows, we are licensed medical herbalists. We trained and graduated in England with a master's degree in herbal medicine, and we run a clinic in Garberville, California, where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions.

This month's subject is thinking outside the box, specifically regarding novel approaches to cancer treatment. We are looking at a viewpoint other than the deterministic view of killing cancer cells. Cancer has traditionally been viewed as something to destroy, and to this end, the mainstream treatment is either cytotoxic cell-killing drugs, which poison the body, or directed radiation. These are "cidal"—they kill cells directly, often with associated collateral damage and inflammation.

However, novel approaches are making themselves known. Nobel Prize winner James Watson recently made observations regarding cancer treatment, and a very "outside the box" theory has emerged. Dr. Raymond Peat joins us to share his viewpoint.

Most people are under the mistaken belief that antioxidants are always good for you and the more, the better. But this is not always true; sometimes these very antioxidants can fuel cancer metabolism. Dr. Peat will outline the physiology and chemistry of the redox system—the reduction-oxidation processes necessary for regular cell functioning. Once we elucidate the redox activity within the body, we can better understand these novel approaches.

Dr. Peat, thanks for joining us again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi, I'm here.

**Andrew Murray:** To give people who haven't listened before an understanding, could you introduce your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1968, I decided to go to graduate school for a PhD and graduated in 1972, specializing in reproductive aging and oxidative changes. It was the oxidative metabolism that I saw changing with aging, which went against the grain. Already at that time, I saw an increase of *reductive* activity with aging.

For example, you can put a dye in young tissue and old tissue. Reductive enzymes, fueled by the energy-producing system and the internal antioxidant system, will reduce the dye. The older tissue reduced the dye much more energetically, looking like it was "more alive." You can test the vitality of any tissue by the intensity of staining of this tetrazolium chemical. I found that an overdose of estrogen, a deficiency of vitamin E, or any serious injury such as X-rays, will increase the ability of the tissue to stain this dye.

So, aging and these various injuries all increased the reductive activity of the tissue, which involves what are called the antioxidative enzyme defense systems. That got me interested in the fact that cancer is very rich in antioxidative defenses. At that time, people were trying to identify specific chemicals cancers used to defend themselves against oxidative poisons like chemotherapy. But over the last 40 years, it has developed that it isn't just a simple chemical they produce defensively; the very basic life processes are shifted in that direction.

**Andrew Murray:** There is a novel way of looking at cells based on new findings in the extracellular matrix—the fluidity within which cells are mobile. It was previously posited that once a cell differentiated, its fate was sealed. But new studies find a "quantum state" where things are fluid; cells communicate in two directions. What implications does the extracellular matrix have for cancer treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The rigid doctrine of the organism that governs current cancer therapy was imposed on a more basic biological view starting around 1830 with Johannes Peter Müller, who described tumors as a problem of organization, not of defective cells. That approach continued through embryology in the 1930s and 40s, where people showed that dissociated cells could reconstruct the organism.

The environment the cells live in is constantly being constructed to meet their needs. If a cell or organ becomes isolated, it loses its sense of direction. If there is no stimulation and no energy flowing through the system, the cell doesn't know what it should be doing. But ordinary cells, if they see a defect in their environment, will reach out and correct it.

The extracellular matrix consists of collagen for stiffness—rigid linear molecules—and carbohydrate chains (polysaccharides) in between that retain water and create an elastic environment. Cells prefer a certain rigidity. When you take an isolated cell and put it on a surface that varies in stiffness, the cells will creep towards the firmer footing. If you inject broken-down collagen fibers into an organism, the cells will rearrange that disorganized collagen, aligning it like bricklayers.

**Andrew Murray:** Because they have an inherent knowledge of the structure they should be in?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and they like it fairly solid. However, they can create more polysaccharides to hold more water, opening the structure to diffuse nutrients. It has to be just right. There are proteins at the surface chemically connected to the structure of the cell all the way through. The sulfur and sulfhydryl system of the cell gives it much of its toughness, and it has to be constantly broken down and reformed because the cell inside is constantly in motion.

**Andrew Murray:** So there is a constant connection of sulfhydryl from the outside to the center of the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. About 40 years ago, experimenters found that if they blocked those surface sulfur groups, the cell couldn't stick to its environment. The degree of reduction and oxidation of the surface sulfur groups is a big part of how it sticks to its environment, moves, and shapes its environment. That degree of oxidation is governed by what has been called the antioxidant defense system.

**Andrew Murray:** Can you describe how this reduction and oxidation (redox) potential works in the matrix and how this determines disease versus health? Specifically regarding the consumption of antioxidants, which might be a bad choice for cancer strategy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many people think of the cell as a reducing or antioxidative environment. But if you look at specific components, such as the molecule that transfers electrons from glucose to the mitochondrion to be oxidized—NAD is the coenzyme, and it becomes reduced to NADH.

In a healthy cell, the ratio of the oxidized form (NAD) is hundreds of times greater than the reduced form (NADH)—about 500 times greater. That governing antioxidant is actually in a highly oxidized state. This is in balance with ascorbic acid, coenzyme Q10, vitamin E, and the glutathione system. These are all energized by the electron from NADH, which comes from glucose.

So, the normal cell is in a highly oxidized state. If the cell is sick—for example, a cancer cell—the ratio approaches one-to-one. It is almost 50% in the reduced, antioxidant state. If you injure a cell, you turn on this signaling system.
