Anything that irritates the cell is likely to turn on more of the reducing system, pushing it in the direction of stress or cancer with a high ratio of NADH to NAD.

**Andrew Murray:** So you want the cell in an oxidized form? You don't want it to have excess antioxidant activity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Correct. The healthy, active cell has 500 times more of the oxidized NAD. When people sell powerful antioxidants, they often test them in a test tube where they destroy oxidizing fragments. But inside the cell, things like ascorbic acid and vitamin E become oxidized. Dehydroascorbic acid is an oxidant, and it is eight times more concentrated in the cell than outside.

When you irritate the cell, you turn on the defensive antioxidant reductive systems. The system which normally should be oxidized all the way through gets stuck in an over-reduced, over-electrified form. Since the 1930s, people have seen that any cell which is dividing goes into this highly reduced state where everything shifts to the sulfhydryl form rather than the disulfide form.

**Andrew Murray:** And this includes cancer cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Normal cells go into this phase, quickly divide, and then return to their oxidized state. The vitamin E and vitamin C go back to becoming oxidants, keeping the system tightened up and helping to squeeze water out.

The membrane potential of a cell is normally around 100 millivolts. The redox difference is in a range of about 15 millivolts—a very small fraction of the energy available. This 15-millivolt difference governs practically all reactions in the cell: energy production, protein synthesis, and the economy of the cell.

**Andrew Murray:** It sounds like a tight range within which normality exists.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you measure products like pyruvic acid versus lactic acid, these are an index of the oxidative or reductive state. When the cell is in trouble, it turns pyruvic acid into lactic acid by reducing it. That reflects the highly reduced antioxidant state. When oxygen is working properly, the cell consumes pyruvic acid and turns it into carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide is an acid and, in a sense, an oxidant. It causes the retraction of electrons.

**Andrew Murray:** So the fundamental here is mopping up electrons?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** I’ve understood free radical damage to be a result of free radical liberation that isn't mopped up by antioxidants. Are free radicals almost more beneficial than the antioxidants?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is James Watson's interpretation, but I think that is not correct. The antioxidant system does good things defending against toxic free radicals. However, the normal oxidative functions involving ascorbic acid, vitamin E, and the sulfhydryl balancing system are able to control the system without resorting to the toxic chemicals Watson is suggesting.

**Andrew Murray:** You advocate for fruit consumption, vitamin C, and vitamin E as safe, gentle antioxidants compared to the "super antioxidants" on the supplement market.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's because they are electrically tuned to a specific role in the cell. If you put in dynamite instead of alcohol, you can have the same overall energy expense, but it isn't under control. Some of the antioxidants they are selling are more like dynamite.

When the good antioxidants are working properly, the system can run as fast as it wants, oxidizing at full speed. As you rev up the oxidizing process—using thyroid hormone, for example—you actually get *fewer* free radical productions. The good antioxidants work with the mitochondria; the faster that system runs, the fewer electrons get away to cause dangerous free radicals.

**Andrew Murray:** This is like aerobic versus anaerobic glycolysis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the cell gets out of control, oxygen is no longer able to suck up the electrons, so the cell expels them as lactic acid. This is a survival mechanism. However, the desperate production of lactic acid raises the pH inside the cell and lowers the pH outside the cell.

The embryologist Holtfreter demonstrated that if you put an embryo in a slightly acidified solution, the cells simply leave the embryo and float off. So, the cancer or stress metabolism acidifying the outside of the cell tends to destroy the cell's connection to its environment. At the same time, raising the pH inside the cell makes it swell up, take up water, shift the sulfhydryl balance into the reduced state, and turn on constant cell division.

**Andrew Murray:** Exercise generates biological oxidants which could be a valid approach to diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and some cancers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exercise will cause cells to take up glucose in the absence of insulin and make them operate effectively. Uncoupling proteins or increased thyroid are the cell's equivalent of exercise. Exercise should keep everything active, but when it doesn't, the organism can defend itself by running things at a higher speed.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding breast cancer, Mina Bissell presented work showing that the context and architecture of the cell govern whether cancers are present. She showed a cancerous duct cell could be turned back to normal not by poisoning it, but by normalizing the extracellular matrix.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The exercise idea is relevant to breast cancer. Women who are constantly having babies and nursing through their fertile years have a very low risk of breast cancer. What is working keeps working; the cells have a load and a job to do, so they keep their extracellular matrix organized to support what they are doing.

**Andrew Murray:** How much credence do you give to the high exposure to progesterone during pregnancy regarding that low incidence of breast cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is the main thing. If you expose a rabbit to estrogen, connective tissue like tendons becomes stiff and hardened. Every time it becomes pregnant and estrogen goes up, you see a momentary shift toward hardening, but after each pregnancy, it is *less* hardened than before. It is the progesterone which reverses those changes in the extracellular matrix. It also erases intracellular estrogen functions.

**Caller (David):** I was born with some interesting genetics—I was born from two eggs, a chimera. I have both genders because of that. How does that happen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Embryologists have made chimeras. That was one of the early demonstrations that mutations aren't the cause of cancer. The somatic mutation theory was debunked 40 years ago when someone took a cell from a tumor (from a black hamster) and put it in the embryo of a white hamster. The developing organism had four parents and was a mixture of white and black inheritance, showing that what had been a cancer cell developed into an ordinary part of the organism.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you have anything to say about chimeras in the human population?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they are probably not as extremely rare as one would suppose because early embryos, if they get too close, can easily mix and form one organism.

**Andrew Murray:** We had another caller ask about low carb diets—the fat-burning ketone diet. He said it helped him, but wanted your thoughts.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You don't produce ketones unless you are raising your cortisol enough to activate the conversion of protein into glucose. At the same time, you turn some fat into ketones.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's a stressful state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The problem occurs over a few years of exposure to that increased breakdown of protein; the cortisol affects your connective tissues. The Arctic explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson, who advocated a meat diet, noticed that the Eskimos were prematurely aged in appearance. Their skin became very wrinkled. I think that is what you would expect from being exposed to very high cortisol constantly.

**Andrew Murray:** I recently saw a *New Scientist* cover with a piece of bacon spelling "FACT," asking if we got 40 years of dietary advice wrong. It’s good to see them admitting that saturated fat is good and polyunsaturates and fish oils are being questioned.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to bring up Dr. Danopoulos's work with urea therapy from the 1980s regarding liver cancer. How familiar are you with urea as a compound for the treatment of carcinomas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the First World War, it was used as an emergency treatment to stimulate healing in wounds and hold down infections. In the 1920s, it was often used for inoperable cancer.

The effect of forming lactic acid causes the pH of the cell to become more alkaline inside, which causes swelling. Swelling promotes replication and proliferation. Urea happens to be a very innocuous substance that acts somewhat like an osmotic dehydrator. It helps to prevent excess swelling and water retention.

**Andrew Murray:** You think that is one of its main effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The dehydrated cell becomes more oxidatively active and catabolic, burning fuel faster, whereas the swollen cell is anabolic and simply growing. Urea would work well with a good thyroid program, which helps you retain the normal amount of sodium chloride. Hypothyroid people produce a matrix that is over-hydrated. Low thyroid function lets your kidneys lose sodium while retaining water. So, osmotic therapies like urea would work nicely with supplementing thyroid to normalize sodium retention.

**Caller (David):** When you describe these processes, you do it so beautifully. Are you actually seeing images? Do you have visual models of how this works?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I see little models. Not that I've seen anything exactly like it, but I have mental models. For example, regarding the extension of the sulfhydryl groups onto the surface of a cell, I have very concrete pictures of how that works. It helps me when I'm looking for information to check against published research facts.

**Caller (David):** Since you're a painter, I thought that must be an important part of your process.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure. I've always been aware of having a map of where I'm going.

**Caller (David):** If you are seeing it like that, you could be part of the healing process by seeing what is wrong and what needs to be fixed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We were talking about the different theories of what a cancer is. The new theory is called TOFT—Tissue Organization Field Theory. I think that needs another adjective: *organismic*. It isn't just the local tissue organization, but how that tissue fits into the whole organism and how the activity of the organism keeps everything working.

**Andrew Murray:** It is very much a holistic way of looking at it. Nothing is fixed; everything is fluid and dynamic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Individual cells, like pigment cells, can sometimes be seen migrating through tissue. They move at the same rate cells crawl on a glass slide—something like a centimeter and a half per day. A very tiny cell really zips along through the solid tissue.

**Andrew Murray:** We are out of time. Dr. Ray Peat is a wealth of experience. His website is . His articles are fully referenced and cover topics from diabetes to saturated fats, cancer, dementia, and hormones. Thanks for joining us.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Field Biology
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who perhaps have never listened to the shows, which run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM, my wife and I are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a master's degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

You're invited to call in with any questions either related or unrelated to this month's subject of field biology. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us again. For people who perhaps have never listened to you or heard you, would you outline your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was a biology teacher before I studied biology professionally, actually about 10 years before. During those years before I went to graduate school in biology, I had taught English and other subjects, but I had done a lot of experimenting in bioelectric subjects, and that relates to the topic of biological fields. That had been a long-time interest of mine.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to pick up a loose end from last month regarding antioxidants. I think it's very important that our listeners clearly understand that what they've been led to believe by nutraceutical companies as beneficial nutrients may in fact not be so, and that they should be treated with caution with reference to their action of blocking certain reactive oxygen species in the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For example, ascorbic acid functions primarily in the cell as an oxidant, maintaining cell structure and regulating synthetic processes largely by its oxidative form, dehydroascorbic acid. So, you don't want an excess of the reduced form.

Vitamin E had a history really starting as an anti-estrogen regulator of the sex hormones. After it was discovered that the unsaturated fatty acids were causing sexual derangement, sterility—especially in males—and brain decomposition, that was when Vitamin E shifted over to be described as an antioxidant rather than as an anti-estrogen. It's gradually being recognized as an anti-inflammatory agent, but it's still stuck in that mold of being called an antioxidant.

**Andrew Murray:** With reference to cancer and the new understanding of field biology—how cells are actually intelligent and drive the organism—what is the rationale behind suppressing reactive oxygen species as an antioxidant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are several interpretations. One group thinks that if you intensify the reactive oxygen species, you'll be able to kill the cancer cells because they are defending themselves by their excess antioxidant capacity. But others recognize that it's the reactive oxygen species that are causing the de-differentiation and aggressive, destructive processes in the cancer cells. So, reducing the formation of them metabolically is the safe, biological, organized way to go about preventing cancer. Preventing it really is part of curing the disease.

Some people have said that you can never tell when cancer is malignant until the patient is dead, because the organism always has the capacity for spontaneous recovery from any kind of tumor. It's most often seen in melanomas because you can clip off a few bits of the tumor and see that it's definitely cancerous. There is spontaneous regression seen so often in melanomas simply because they're near the surface and visible, but I think that spontaneous regression is probably going on all the time with many kinds of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Am I right in thinking that you don't particularly advocate topical treatment of melanomas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely not. Because so many things will disturb your defensive reactions against them and just annoy them, making them try to survive more intensely rather than more intelligently.

**Andrew Murray:** I ask because bloodroot (*Sanguinaria canadensis*) is a very commonly touted treatment for these tumors. I've met people who have showed me patches on their arms or legs where they've used bloodroot. The site looks a little scarred, but there's no presence of what was previously a discolored mole.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What are the active chemicals in that?

**Andrew Murray:** Sanguinarine and probably hydrastine or some other alkaloids, but it also contains tannins. I know tannins have traditionally been used for skin tumors.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the old things that derived partly from herbal knowledge going back to the start of the 20th century was thinking of the molecular structure of these things as catalysts of energy production. William Frederick Koch was one that first proposed this, and it was developed later by Albert Szent-Györgyi. Particular molecules were explored by each of them. What they had in common was the activated ketone structure—activated carbonyl group—opposed by, for example, activated amine groups or hydroxyl groups. Estrogen is in that general irritating category. There are a lot of the tannin category of chemicals that unbalance, or in their most relevant part of the molecule, have this oxidative catalytic function that can restore the oxygen production of energy.

**Andrew Murray:** Sanguinaria does have a very intense red dye. We've talked about intense red dyes or herbs having this free radical quenching activity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That means they're absorbing high-energy particles.

**Andrew Murray:** But as far as you're concerned, you still don't advocate any topical use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I think systemic is better because everything contains impurities, and just a little bit of the wrong impurity can irritate and possibly direct in the wrong direction. I haven't experimented at all with any of those older traditional things, but I did experiment on my own things.

A couple of doctors at different times were convinced that I had things that were melanomas from their shape and behavior. Probably a total of 15 or 20 times altogether, I've had things popping up that were black and blue, growing quickly, and changing shape. Just by increasing my thyroid systemically and putting some DHEA and/or progesterone on the skin adjacent to—maybe an inch away from—the developing spot, within two or three days you would see very intense changes happening. For example, the color would change from blue and white to maybe an even brown color, and then simply the whole thing would melt away.

It's like giving the cells what they need to differentiate properly. Otherwise, they go off exploring what they want to be to deal with the deficiency that they have. I think the particular areas they choose seem to be areas where the body is able to provide something that sustains their growth. If you can let the body provide more of that, increasing its energy, then those cells can go ahead and differentiate. The reducing or antioxidant direction of a cell is interfering with differentiation. There are several chemicals known as differentiating agents that some doctors are treating cancer with. What they have in common is a shift towards the oxidative balance of the cell.

**Andrew Murray:** From a scientific perspective, irritation has always been known to be cancer-causing. Any cell that gets chronically irritated is at risk. I think that's probably where your hesitancy with topically addressing anything comes from.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Although I know there have been very successful things. I've seen people with pink spots on their skin where they previously had a very aggressive tumor. I know an old woman—I saw her when she was 91, 92, and 93. In between my visits, I saw what had been a mole on the side of her forehead evolve into a hole where the bridge of her nose was eaten away by the melanoma. Next visit, there was nothing wrong with her nose. The nose had grown back.

**Andrew Murray:** Physiology is clearly a subject where nothing is isolated. However, knowledge can move along blind pathways. Last month you touched on James Watson as an example of an extreme reductionist now tending to be a little more open-minded. How is science to be moved in the right direction to allow a paradigm shift in our understanding of disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those people who were insisting on a kind of straight-line causality—Gregor Mendel, for example—wanted traits to be eternal rather than occasional, accidental, or changing. He did his experiments to show that even though the pea plants were changing, they had traits which were eternal. That got adopted by the gene people at the beginning of this century. That led to people like Watson identifying this eternal gene, except with the qualification that although it's like Mendel's eternal gene, it can be changed, but only by chance, not by anything intentionally useful to the individual organism.

At the same time, other people were showing evidence that the whole organism is influencing what happens to those traits—that the traits actually can be blended and changed rather than being discrete, absolutely causal units.

With the development of cybernetics, people saw that each level of organization has its own laws and causal processes. However, there were business interests that promoted the idea of genetic-based medicine. Each drug could identify a causal action on one of these causal genes. All through the 20th century, there were profit motives selling drugs for diseases supporting that idea of genetic causality.

But then the cloning and stem cell businesses started to be seen as viable. Those were things that the reductionists said absolutely couldn't exist—you can't have stem cells, you can't clone an animal from a body cell. Now that they saw that those could be good business, they changed the history. Barbara McClintock, who in the 40s and 50s had been treated rudely, was pulled out of obscurity in the 80s and 90s and given the MacArthur Grant and Nobel Prize to create a new history that would justify cloning as genetic engineering—changing the genes as something like a natural process. Science is really being driven not by what's plausible or ultimately helpful, but by what these powerful institutions see as something in their interest.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you've mentioned people in the 20s and 30s who were prominent in their time coming forward with groundbreaking tenets surrounding field theory and cell intelligence, but that was squashed by the evolving gene people.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Classic embryology is where the field thinking really had its practical influence. In their experiments, someone demonstrated that you could take a part of an early embryo out, and the embryo would replace it. The cells weren't fixed; they could fill in for each other. You could move a cell from one place to another and its fate would be changed by where you put it. It could be developing along the line to become a foot, and putting it in another place, it could become a face.

Knowing that kind of field effect, one researcher took a tumor, cut off a tadpole's tail, and grafted the tumor on where the tail had been. The tumor was converted by the developmental field of the tadpole into a new tail. It's potentially a very useful way of looking at the organism: that cells are shaped by the inner environment as well as modifying the environment.

**Andrew Murray:** I was pointed towards work done by Guenter Albrecht-Buehler in a paper called *Cell Intelligence*. He found that cells were displaying intelligence and would gravitate towards infrared light.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's quite a bit of evidence that light produced by the dividing and metabolizing cells is a signal. He's arguing for infrared as a very important signal. The Gurwitsches in the 1930s provided good evidence regarding ultraviolet frequency. They demonstrated that it could transmit mitogenic signals through quartz glass, but not through ordinary glass that would filter out ultraviolet. Albrecht-Buehler is currently one of the leading people. Fritz-Albert Popp in Germany has been another more recent one.

**Andrew Murray:** How can field theory be applied to conditions like Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and diabetes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Albrecht-Buehler sees fields as working both inside and outside the cell. The cell has to have a very organized meaning/interpretation system for knowing which set of genes to turn on and off in certain environments. Cells have to reach out and manipulate the environment around them, conditioning their surroundings to fit their needs.

The organism as a whole, running into stresses, can change that territory around the individual cells as well as the metabolism available to that cell. The metabolism is creating the structure—for example, collagen to restore and renew its environment is produced more under stress when lactic acid is present because there's not enough oxygen. Lactic acid turns on many of these reactive defensive processes that, as a signal to the organism, will tell the organism to deliver more oxygen, sugar, and nutrients to the cells.

But if the cell doesn't get what it needs from the rest of the organism, or if the field disrupting it is too intense—for example, ionizing radiation or intense radio frequency—it can keep the cell from maturing properly. If the organism can get the necessary materials to the cell, the cell can recover.

Lactic acid is one of the basic disrupting signals if it continues too long. It turns out that one of the basic features of diabetes is that they can't oxidize sugar all the way to carbon dioxide; instead, they produce lactic acid. Lactic acidosis is very often what diabetics used to die from. Any organ that's under too much stress and not getting repair materials will shift over to producing lactic acid. The lactic acid is a stress signal and an immune signal for the rest of the organism.

**Andrew Murray:** This reminds me of the lactic acid felt as a cramp during exercise. Is this the same lactic acid that is a destabilizer of the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A very well-developed athlete will not produce lactic acid too easily. A sedentary person who is forced to exercise will be flooded with lactic acid because they haven't developed the system for delivering oxygen and fuel to the tissues.

Carbon dioxide produced by healthy metabolism directly participates in suppressing lactic acid and in maintaining oxidative energy production. A place where you can see this is people who live at high altitudes. The balance between oxygen and carbon dioxide leaves their bodies having a higher residual carbon dioxide level. They can work very intensely without producing lactic acid. That's sometimes called the "Lactate Paradox," because ordinarily oxygen deficiency is what turns on lactic acid. But once you get adapted and are able to produce a lot of carbon dioxide or hold it in your tissues, that in itself prevents this toxic formation of lactic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this adaptation different to the red blood cell adaptation to altitude?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's part of it. The tissues themselves develop more mitochondria and the enzymes that regulate carbon dioxide shift. The red blood cell itself doesn't deliver all of its carbon dioxide. When it gets to the lungs, it picks up as much oxygen as it can, but at a lower oxygen pressure. That means the blood is still retaining a slightly higher amount of CO2.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think of lactate testing to ascertain if someone is under stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably the time that you're feeling the stress would be the best time to measure it. It's increasingly being used to diagnose cancer and monitor the progress. When the cancer is being regressed, the lactic acid in the serum goes down.

**Andrew Murray:** At what state of development of a tumor would lactic acid be increased?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It starts showing up in the blood at a very early stage. At a certain point, it causes an inactivation of the immune system that should be helping to correct the cancer.

Since everyone over the age of 50 has cells that can be diagnosed as cancer, it's a good idea not to be panicked by any measurement that could indicate cancer. If you ate something very disagreeable, your lactic acid would go up just from the general inflammation. You want to take everything in context. Even if it's being produced by a cancer, most cancers don't kill people. It's something that's naturally being cured spontaneously.

**Andrew Murray:** If carbon dioxide is analogous to an anti-lactate, what is the best method to raise this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything that keeps your free fatty acids from being released. Those are released by too much adrenaline. Many of the pituitary hormones help to increase the toxic free fatty acids. Everything you can do to lower the stress hormones helps. Aspirin, for example, is a good anti-inflammatory, anti-stress agent. Vitamin E is another protective. Ascorbic acid in ordinary foods provides abundant amounts, so I don't recommend that as a supplement in general.

**Andrew Murray:** This is why you're so big on orange juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and meat, eggs, milk—everything. Vegetables of all sorts contain ascorbic acid, but meat contains it in the dehydroascorbate form where people measuring the reduced form overlook it.

**Caller:** I'm from Melbourne, Australia. My question is in relation to electromedicine, where George Lakhovsky and Royal Rife produced certain wavelengths to kill off pathogens. Also, Dr. Robert Beck and Hulda Clark have come up with a machine called the Zapper. Do those machines really work? And is there any health benefit to drinking ozonated water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There definitely is something to the principle, but I've never seen evidence that it is as specific as many of the people claim it to be. I know people who use apparatus of that sort, and I think it's acting probably as a stimulus rather than having that specific action that the Rifians claim for it.

Regarding ozonated water, I think ozone is too toxic in itself. The superoxide radical, which is produced by ionized air and some ionized water, can be beneficial as part of a detox system in the lungs, but I would be very careful with either ozone or peroxide-containing water.

**Caller:** I had a question about an herbal protocol for Lyme disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's a lot on the Internet suggesting that it's a lifetime project, but there's also quite a bit of information that says that two or three weeks with the right combination of antibiotics almost always cures it. I think it's good to look widely—get a second, third, and fourth opinion before you commit yourself to a very prolonged protocol.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you feel about the pathogen itself?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That class of bacteria, the spirochetes in general, can be very harsh. Some of them are very toxic and harmful and long-lasting. If you have any symptoms, it's good to check it and, if necessary, have the proper antibiotic treatment. But there are a lot of selling services; some doctors want to make it a many-year project of treatment recovery.

**Andrew Murray:** The World Health Organization advocates four years of breastfeeding for newborn babies. What do you think would be the best possible start for a newborn in terms of nutrition?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Breastfeeding naturally, but with the mother well-fed, happy, and unstressed. When the mother is under stress or not properly nourished, the composition of the milk shows it. Good milk contains a lot of blood sugar converted into the lactose of the milk, hormones—some thyroid and progesterone—and a lot of immune factors. Even if a baby has an endocrine problem, as long as it's getting good milk, something like hypothyroidism often doesn't show up just because the milk is so rich in these protective factors.

**Caller:** I'm local. You said Lyme disease takes a three-month protocol on antibiotics and that cures it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes it disappears in just two or three weeks.

**Caller:** I know a lot of people with Lyme disease and I've never seen that work that quickly. Is there some special protocol you're speaking of?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can find several articles on PubMed that are very good. I think part of the problem that makes it seem so incurable is that it often is misdiagnosed. They recognize evidence of an infection, but they don't recognize any clear signs of improvement because in many cases the person just isn't eating right or has other passing things in their environment.

**Andrew Murray:** Just to interject, caller, more often than not when people test positive on an ELISA test for *Borrelia* antibodies, they have a lot of other metabolic defects. That is what causes people to be so sick. Especially with the protocols that are used—fairly heavy drugs—these can really play into someone's downfall. It's more of a failure of the organism under the barrage of drugs and chemicals to treat it.

**Caller:** Where in PubMed do I find this protocol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just look for *Borrelia* or Lyme disease and antibiotic treatment.

**Andrew Murray:** Every transaction that we make in this world with our bodies costs something. In terms of metabolic energy to fight disease or digest food, it all costs energy. That ATP has to be derived from something, so nutrition is extremely important. Most people can be chronically malnourished—maybe not to skin and bones, but malnourished by foods that are blocking thyroid function. If that's the case, it's very difficult to generate enough metabolic energy.

**Caller:** One of the things about Lyme disease that hasn't been addressed is that it's from a spirochete, which means it's similar to syphilis. Syphilis has a first, second, and third stage. I've heard that if you catch Lyme in the first or second stages, it can be cured with antibiotics, but if it goes into the third stage before it's treated, that's when it's really difficult.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what do you say about primary, secondary, and tertiary syphilis in relation to *Borrelia*?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's probably analogous. The right antibiotic is needed to treat tertiary syphilis. Something that gets into the brain and nervous system will do it.

**Andrew Murray:** We're getting to the top of the hour. I want to mention a few authors you've discussed so people can look them up. We mentioned Michael Polanyi, who has been dominant in field theory. And the Hungarian astrophysicist, Attila Grandpierre.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's a video by Michael Persinger called *No More Secrets* that talks about some of the field interactions that Grandpierre is writing about. They're very interesting.

**Andrew Murray:** You also mentioned P.K. Anokhin as someone studying CO2 and the "acceptor of action."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that was an antecedent for cybernetics. He was a colleague and student of Pavlov, and he devised this cybernetic interpretation of reflexes which sees the model of the world that we have in our consciousness as determining how the reflex works. It makes a very simple way of interpreting other fields, such as Hans Selye's stress process, if you see it in terms of Anokhin's acceptor of action. The meaning of a particular stress and how the body is responding governs the field all the way down to the cell.

**Andrew Murray:** And then there was Noam Chomsky and William Blake.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Blake saw things in a very holistic, cosmic way as well as very biological, soundly based in the organism.

**Andrew Murray:** And Dostoevsky's *Diary of a Writer*?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, about the essential meaningfulness of experience and reality.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for joining us again, Dr. Peat. We really appreciate your time. Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. It is an excellent resource. We can be reached at www.westernbotanicalmedicine.com.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Longevity
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. I'm a licensed medical herbalist. Every third Friday of the month, we have a topic that we choose to open up, and once again, I'm very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat share his wisdom and expertise. At the end of the show, listeners are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of longevity.

Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us again. I know that a lot of your background has been involved with reproductive physiology and aging. As always, I would ask you to introduce yourself and your professional and academic background for people who have perhaps never listened to you.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started getting interested in aging in childhood. Through the 1950s, when I would mention it to people, a few of the very old people—like a biology professor who studied around the turn of the century—had some interesting ideas about the actual cause of aging that suggested possibilities for preventing it. But most people in the 1950s weren't at all interested in the idea of curing aging; it was inconceivable that anything could be done about it.

When I decided to go to graduate school in biology from 1968 to 1972 at the University of Oregon, I intended to study brain biology. It happened that there were some good people working on reproductive aging, so I did my dissertation on female reproductive aging. That helped to answer some questions that I had been accumulating for 20 years, but it really just opened up a lot of basic biological questions regarding the whole nature of what an organism is and how it develops through time.

The whole process used to be explained as reading out from a pre-established blueprint in the genes. That led to the idea that there must be genes causing aging and death. Rethinking that whole developmental scheme is necessary. If you see development as epigenetic, or open to interaction with the environment, then aging obviously is another epigenetic, environmentally dependent process.

**Andrew Murray:** I appreciate you bringing out different perspectives on previously held scientific facts. Regarding longevity, I read a recent study published by the University of Wisconsin in the journal *eLife*. They subjected a strain of *E. coli* bacteria to normally lethal doses of radiation. They took the survivors, reproduced them, and doubled the dose until, 20 generations later, they had a colony able to withstand 1,000 times the lethal radiation dose for a human. They were looking at DNA repair as a primary objective in facilitating longevity. What do you think about the protection of DNA in our body as a method of sustaining longer life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think there is a parallel between what the bacteria are doing and what happens to humans exposed to stresses like radiation. However, single-celled organisms are essentially different in how they respond to stress. Twenty generations of bacteria would be just a few days, so they couldn't possibly be evolving new DNA sequences to make new functional proteins in such a short time.

The radiation degrades proteins, so it tends to knock out functions when it damages the DNA. The bacteria that died had their DNA so damaged they lost function. The ones that survived simply didn't lose the function, but their defense processes were activated. With each generation, they were getting an intensification of the defense reactions.

Bacteria, yeasts, and protozoa under stress can either decide to reproduce faster—live more intensely and divide more quickly if their genes are still working—or they can go in the direction of dehydration. For radiation, forming a spore and eliminating water makes the DNA very resistant because water is part of the hydroxyl radical that destroys the DNA. Without water tied to the DNA, it is very resistant.

**Andrew Murray:** So that's why spores can live for so long in the desert.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If humans tried to do that, the cells under stress would either multiply very rapidly—which would be a cancer—or they would go into something worse than hibernation, simply drying up into a suspended, mummy-like existence. It just doesn't work for humans.

We have ways of handling damaged genes. What animals do is kill the whole cell when the organism senses that the DNA has been damaged beyond the capacity to repair it. To avoid forming a cancer, they have to let the damaged ones die—a sort of triage. The quicker it can die, the more material is available for cancer-stimulating stem cells to replace it.

I think a major factor in aging is that things interfere with that whole process of either repairing or letting the cells die quickly to be replaced. In old age, the process of cell death is retarded. Cells become old, they can't decide what to do, and so they slow down. The whole organism metabolically slows down. In that slowing down process, they produce undesirable products like lactic acid that cause problems for the whole organism instead of just dying and getting it over with.

**Andrew Murray:** So you're saying that the process of apoptosis, or programmed cell death, is actually slowed down in normal human aging?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. People are now looking for the factors that retard that quick replacement, quick apoptosis, and activation of stem cells.

**Andrew Murray:** Moving onto energy. There is a compound called NAD and another form, NADH, which are very important for energy conveyance. The *E. coli* article mentioned NAD as a target therapy. How important do you see NAD supplements being in our biological systems?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Our cells are constantly in a process of oxidizing. Electrons from things like sugar go to the oxidizing NAD and reduce it so that it becomes NADH. NADH can then pass those electrons on eventually to oxygen. In normal metabolism, you should have 300 to 500 times as much NAD as NADH because it's in a rapidly oxidizing state. Stresses that interfere with oxygen or subtract the NAD cause a failure of the balance, shifting it to a very reduced, NADH-dominant state.

**Andrew Murray:** So stress depletes NAD?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depletes both of them. One thing that depletes them is damage to the DNA, such as radiation. In repairing DNA breaks, enzymes build up a chain of repetitive bases to plug the hole in the DNA. To repair the chain, ADP is attached, which comes from the supply of NAD. When you get a nick in the DNA, you draw down this huge amount of NAD to repair the damage. If you draw it down repairing too many broken DNAs, that interferes with the energy production of the cell. If you have ways to block those enzymes and stop the DNA repair, then the cell can make the decision to die, becoming raw materials for the stem cells.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there anything that would preempt that destructive phase rather than wasting energy trying to repair damaged chromosomes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, there are drugs that block that enzyme, which is called PARP. PARP-inhibiting enzymes can save cells from dying unnecessarily or let them go ahead and die. Niacinamide happens to be a very safe way to inhibit that enzyme. At the same time, it is the precursor for making NAD, so you're plugging the drain and filling up the tank at the same time. We can normally make that from proteins—converting tryptophan to niacin—but if we're deficient in protein or have a vitamin deficiency blocking that conversion, we can't keep the NAD supply adequate.

**Andrew Murray:** The article also mentioned compounds called Sirtuins (SIRT1 and SIRT3) as a factor to improve longevity. What is your opinion of calorie restriction as a way of activating the Sirtuins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In calorie restriction, the organism has to do something to survive, so it starts shutting down and turning off genes. The initials stand for Silent Information Regulators. In yeasts, starvation or stress will turn those on and turn off genes. A group at Harvard argued that longevity in yeast corresponded to long life in humans. They argued that resveratrol, which is chemically very closely related to DES (diethylstilbestrol, a synthetic estrogen), stimulated this. Resveratrol is found in grapes and has estrogenic activity. Yeasts are especially sensitive to estrogen.

In humans, that process of turning off genes moves toward a spore-like or hibernating state of not producing proteins. Two very important proteins that get turned off by the Sirtuins include Klotho—a phosphate-regulating protein where turning it off causes rapid aging—and p53, which is a tumor suppressor protein. You definitely don't want to blindly turn off proteins in defense.

**Andrew Murray:** So you don't want to just shut down and turn your anti-tumor proteins off.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. Several years ago, the Harvard group said we shouldn't supplement niacinamide because it suppresses Sirtuins. They claimed if Sirtuins are the "long life proteins," niacinamide would accelerate aging. However, someone put human cells in a dish, gave them a supplement of niacinamide, and they lived 60% longer.

**Caller (New Jersey):** I understand the importance of consuming high-quality proteins, but there is one exception: the kidneys. You've said in your "Gelatin, Stress, and Longevity" article that if the kidneys are working, glycine is non-toxic, but any amino acid will contribute to the production of ammonia. Is there a way to judge if we are getting enough amino acids without stressing the kidneys?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Normal functioning kidneys aren't stressed by a high-protein diet. However, when something is impairing kidney function, such as hypothyroidism or other sickness, then with low kidney function and bacteria in your intestine breaking down amino acids, you can get accumulated ammonia.

Researchers proposed using ketoacids equivalent to the essential amino acids. These will absorb the ammonia even when a person has no functioning kidney ability to secrete ammonia. By feeding ketoacids, you create protein in your body by absorbing the ammonia from your blood. We did chromatography on potato juice and found that potatoes are rich in these ketoacids, which will function as amino acids even though they contain no ammonia.

**Caller (New Jersey):** So for someone with sore kidneys, would you recommend potato juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A few people who had ammonia on their breath every time they ate protein found that just a couple of meals of potato juice allowed them to start assimilating proteins. Ordinarily, there are many other things you need to do when you have kidney disease. You want to correct all the hormones involved in regulating kidney physiology, especially thyroid, progesterone, estrogen, cortisol, and pituitary stress hormones.

**Caller (New Jersey):** And keep eating the raw carrot daily to keep the ammonia down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that helps with the bacterial ammonia production.

**Caller (Chris, Colorado):** In terms of longevity, I understand the importance of avoiding unsaturated fats. However, regarding proper oxidative energy, how important is it to keep fats low and focus more on sugars like sucrose and lactose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A certain small amount of fat helps to stimulate the intestine and activate absorption of the oily vitamins (K, D, A, and E). About 30 or 40 years ago, I looked at the association of various fats with spontaneous cancer incidence. Coconut oil had the lowest of the natural oils. But someone found that hydrogenated coconut oil, containing zero polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), had the lowest incidence of all—essentially like a completely fat-free diet.

Even eating a moderate amount of butter and coconut oil, the 2% or 3% of polyunsaturated fats accumulate because our muscles quickly oxidize the saturated fats. We preferentially store the polyunsaturated fats. With age, our fat tissues become more concentrated with PUFA. Under stress, fat is released, and the PUFA is more accessible to stress activation. Since we can make all the saturated fats (palmitate, stearate) and desaturate stearic acid to make oleic acid, I think it's best to get as much sugar and starch in your diet—preferably sugars from fruit and milk—and minimize exposure to the unstable Omega-6 and Omega-3 fatty acids.

**Caller (Chris, Colorado):** One off-topic question: My girlfriend grinds her teeth at night without noticing. Any ideas on the cause?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several publications show that high serotonin is probably the major factor in tooth grinding and restless leg syndrome.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the most straightforward way of lowering serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Reducing intestinal inflammation is the quickest way. Low thyroid is a factor, but simply avoiding slowly digested foods like resistant starches or undercooked vegetables helps. Salads are very bad for irritating the intestine. Some soluble fibers, even pectin from fruit, can greatly increase the production of serotonin and disturb sleep.

**Caller (Graham, Los Angeles):** My wife has chronic fatigue. Do you have thoughts on how to deal with mitochondrial dysfunction?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is basically the same stress syndrome: low thyroid, excess production of lactic acid, and high stress mediators like serotonin, histamine, and prolactin. Prolactin generally rises when thyroid goes down and serotonin goes up.

**Andrew Murray:** What would be your dietary suggestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Things that are quickly digested. A raw carrot contains anti-inflammatory chemicals and antibiotics that suppress irritating bacteria and bind toxins. Just having a raw carrot every day can adjust hormones in a good direction.

**Caller (Graham, Los Angeles):** She finds the raw carrot hard to digest.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The point of eating the carrot is that it *isn't* digested, so it releases antiseptic chemicals and stimulates the intestine to carry out material. It acts like a bottle brush. If you shred it with a fine food processor so it's almost like hair, that is the most effective kind of fiber because you get a lot of surface area.

**Caller (Graham, Los Angeles):** I have trouble with Metabolic Syndrome—specifically removing belly fat despite exercise.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Polyunsaturated fats are probably what set up that inability to oxidize sugar efficiently. It keeps free fatty acids in circulation, which block metabolism. An active form of thyroid containing T3 is the basic way to get metabolism going so you can oxidize glucose and turn off the free fatty acids.

**Andrew Murray:** How should he monitor this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keep track of your metabolic rate. Low thyroid people find that a lot of the water they drink comes back as urine, whereas you should be able to evaporate a couple of quarts of water a day. Other indicators are heart rate at rest and temperature. Temperature should rise to around 98.6°F right after breakfast and stay there until close to sunset.

**Andrew Murray:** I know B vitamins are involved in energy generation. What is a good strategy to ensure adequate levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A good diet that includes liver once in a while, milk, cheese, eggs, and seafood regularly. Seafood provides trace minerals you might not get in land foods.

**Andrew Murray:** How realistic is it for people to be low in B vitamins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** B vitamins act very quickly. With Vitamin B1 (thiamine), you can often feel an effect in the first hour. With Vitamin B6, you generally feel an effect in the first day; sometimes one dose of 10 milligrams will take care of a problem that has lingered for a long time.

**Andrew Murray:** What doses do you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person has diabetes or cancer and very high lactic acid production, 300mg of B1 in divided doses can help normalize sugar metabolism. Ordinarily, 10 or 20 milligrams is plenty.

For B3 (Niacinamide), taking 50 or 100 milligrams several times a day can control symptoms of diabetes, arthritis, and degenerative problems. Doctors used to like nicotinic acid because it made people turn red, but that flushing releases serotonin, histamine, and toxic prostaglandins. The market is now flooded with "No Flush Niacin," but if you look at the label, it is inositol hexanicotinate. This is slow-release, so it doesn't cause sudden blushing, but it still releases those toxic substances. It has to be niacinamide.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned specifically for cancer, B1 doses of 200-300mg.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it stimulates the oxidation of lactic acid, producing more carbon dioxide. Lactic acid keeps cancer developing by creating inflammation.

**Caller (Laytonville):** I've always had a low body temp, around 97.4. Is that normal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. If you have consistently low body temperatures that do not rise after food, that suggests metabolic deficiency. Protein deficiency is a possible cause. I've seen people who couldn't respond to thyroid, and it turned out they were eating only 20 grams of protein a day when the requirement is closer to 80 grams.

**Caller (Laytonville):** What are your thoughts on chelation or heavy metal cleanses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good foods will safely activate the process of mobilizing heavy metals from the tissues and passing them out through the kidneys. Coffee drinkers are known to have a lower load of heavy metals like cadmium and lead. Orange juice and milk provide materials that help inactivate the toxic effect of heavy metals while mobilizing them.

**Andrew Murray:** Ebola virus is a careful watchword right now. What are your thoughts on how best to protect yourself?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The effects are basically like the flu and many other infections that activate inflammatory processes. The first thing that happens is the inhibition of interferon—an antiviral defense—and the activation of nitric oxide production, which opens up blood vessels, makes them leaky, and lowers energy production.

Whether it's flu, Ebola, or chemical poisoning, the defense is to lower anything irritating, such as hard-to-digest foods, and lower inflammation and nitric oxide production. Aspirin, coffee, and niacinamide are all defenses against nitric oxide.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there anything to raise interferon?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That will take care of itself if you keep your energy up and hold the inflammatory things, such as nitric oxide, as low as you can.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you very much, Dr. Peat, for joining us. For listeners who want more information, Dr. Peat's website has a wealth of fully referenced articles. The website is www.raypeat.com.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Nitric Oxide
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to Ask Your Herb Doctor on KMUD Garberville, 91.1 FM. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who have perhaps never listened to the show, which runs every third Friday of the month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM, I'm a licensed medical herbalist. My wife and I run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice.

Dr. Raymond Peat is happily joining us on the show to share his latest discoveries and research. You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of nitric oxide. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us again. For those who have never heard you, would you give an outline of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, I studied for a master's degree at the University of Oregon in literature and related things, and then studied linguistics for a while. Finally, I came back to study biology from 1968 to 1972, specializing in the physiology of reproduction and aging, and especially the biochemical side of aging physiology.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask you some questions about your most recent newsletter based on nitric oxide. Given that the compound manufactured by Pfizer—Viagra—is well known, and nitric oxide has a major vasodilatory effect, what is it about nitric oxide that makes it so dangerous? It is responsible for things like cardiac arrest, stroke, arrhythmias, and increased ocular pressure. I've had several people who have used Viagra and had a heart attack or stroke. Also, recreational drug users use "poppers," which is exactly the same compound. What is your take on nitric oxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Speaking of poppers, several of the early theorists of AIDS were blaming it on the chemical—nitric oxide or a nitric compound—produced from the poppers. They were arguing that that in itself was enough to account for AIDS among the people who were using that as a pleasure drug.

In the 1980s, everyone knew nitric oxide primarily as a toxic component of smog. When people started discovering that it was being produced in small amounts in the body, they immediately started looking for parallels with smog poisoning: lung injury, circulatory disease, and so on. One of the first things they found was that it kills the beta cells in the pancreas that produce insulin. So, in the early 1940s, there was a flurry of papers demonstrating that our "internal smog" is just as toxic as Los Angeles smog.

But then the Viagra patent and publicity came out in the later 1990s. Suddenly, the medical publications all found that it was a glorious, natural protector of just about every function you can think of—making you smarter, giving you more endurance, and all kinds of good things. After a few years, the investment in publicity started wearing off and people started coming back to the diabetes-producing effects and looking at what it's actually doing biochemically.

**Andrew Murray:** How does it cause harm?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The basic way it causes harm is probably parallel to the effects of carbon monoxide or cyanide: it is a competitor for oxygen. In the mitochondria—the enzymes that produce most of our energy—it knocks out not only the key final respiratory enzyme, cytochrome oxidase, but it poisons the previous electron-transporting parts of the mitochondrion too. Simply turning off the energy supply can account for a lot of its problems.

When you stop the oxidative run through the mitochondrion, the mitochondrion starts leaking electrons that have no place to go. The whole cell shifts over to a reduced chemical state. If you imagine a stream of electrons falling steadily towards oxygen, when you cut that off, they accumulate and float back. This reducing environment shifts the balance of sulfur compounds, and the surface properties of the cell change.

This cloud of excess electrons flows through an enzyme called NADPH oxidase and directly reduces oxygen on the surface. That produces superoxide, a possibly toxic free radical, which then produces hydrogen peroxide. In immune cells under stress, that's considered productive because it helps break down bacteria. However, this hydrogen peroxide can be used to oxidize chloride—which is always present—into hypochlorite. Basically, it becomes like Clorox.

**Andrew Murray:** So in general, nitric oxide forms a pretty energy-wasteful mechanism and is also damaging in its free radical producing effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, this shift of the whole cell away from oxidation starts a process that people are still just starting to put together. It has effects on the nervous system; for example, Parkinson's disease has signs that nitric oxide is one of the central damaging components of the dopamine system.

**Andrew Murray:** There are three species of nitric oxide. The one most commonly referenced is the inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS). That has been implicated in causing increased severity of disease, including herpes simplex encephalitis and chronic viral hepatitis. What are the most reasonable ways of blocking nitric oxide synthesis in the body, or at least managing its production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The body has various natural ways of keeping it under control. For example, progesterone inhibits the enzyme that makes nitric oxide, while estrogen excites and activates that enzyme. When the cell is stabilized by a generous amount of progesterone and related neurosteroids—including pregnenolone—those hold down the production.

Anything that irritates the cell and excites it, like endotoxin from the intestine, is probably the biggest single constant promoter of nitric oxide production. Sometimes serotonin and histamine, which are produced in reaction to endotoxin, can increase the formation of nitric oxide. Caffeine and similar drugs are known to have protective anti-toxic effects by turning down nitric oxide production locally.

In recent years, an old dye called methylene blue—which was used as a treatment for malaria 100 years ago—is being used for a tremendous variety of therapeutic purposes. Simply by turning down nitric oxide, methylene blue is having very positive effects in a variety of things, including herpes and other chronic viral diseases.

**Andrew Murray:** What would be a good short-term approach to block that from what is available presently?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Niacinamide and progesterone are commonly available. But methylene blue, when available, is probably a good emergency thing to turn off the massive amounts of overproduced nitric oxide.

**Andrew Murray:** I read an article referencing methylene blue having favorable suppressive activity in small amounts, but larger amounts could actually cause harm.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of the toxicity experiments have been ridiculous, feeding rats the equivalent of an ounce or two of crystalline methylene blue. That amount of any concentrated chemical is going to be harmful.

However, 25 years ago, a well-controlled study of severely depressed people showed that 15 milligrams per day was all it took to relieve severe depression. The side effects of even many times higher doses are essentially zero. Two studies gave graded doses up to the equivalent of 4 to 6 grams a day for a person—many times higher than the curative anti-depressive dose—for the whole lifespan of rats and mice. They saw no life-shortening effects. In fact, in female mice, they saw an extension of the maximum lifespan with the highest dose.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think the effects of methylene blue are due to electron quenching or electrical stabilizing activity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the known mechanisms is that it can receive electrons from the mediator that receives them from glucose—NADH, for example—and then pass those electrons onto the part of the mitochondrion that is still working, bypassing damaged parts. So it can act like a missing enzyme, restoring mitochondrial function.

Also, the receptor that causes excitotoxic damage from overdoses of glutamic acid involves two sulfur groups. Methylene blue oxidizes those and turns off the receptor, stopping the excitotoxic process. That excitotoxic process is one of the things that turns on nitric oxide production.

**Andrew Murray:** Methylene blue is not a controlled substance; it's just a dye, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, fish farmers use it to cure various fish infections.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned there were other ways it blocks nitric oxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've counted about six different ways. The excitotoxic thing was one. Preventing excess polymerization of the microtubules is another. Probably increasing progesterone production and inhibiting estrogen production are others. But probably the most important thing people should do is be critical about the tremendous amount of propaganda selling the idea that people should eat more arginine to increase their nitric oxide production.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow. It always amazes me how this stuff comes into circulation as "common knowledge."

**Caller:** I'm from Southern Humboldt. I wanted to know if all of the estrogen imitators in the environment are also something that will put us at risk?

**Andrew Murray:** Very much so.

**Caller:** I think I've seen that Bisphenol A (BPA) activates nitric oxide production.

**Andrew Murray:** There you go. And that's an estrogen promoter mimic. Dr. Peat, what do you think are some of the most damaging environmental estrogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The natural estrogen is damaging enough. It's getting into the rivers through the sewage. I think natural estrogen and birth control estrogens—which are many times stronger—are getting into all the downstream waterways that receive sewage.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** As a sewer board person, I can tell you that one of the ways they tell whether water is coming from a sewage system or from nature is they look for caffeine. That's considered a marker for sewage. So yes, a lot of those chemicals do make it through.

**Caller:** Is there a plant or an herb that mimics methylene blue that you can ingest?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've looked around at various molecules. Methylene blue was a precursor for many drugs like tricyclic antidepressants and antihistamines. It's a three-ring molecule, structurally roughly the same size and shape as steroid hormones.

I've looked at plants that make analogous things. The tetracyclines have many of the same anti-inflammatory effects; I suspect they work against nitric oxide. Vitamin K and Vitamin E are analogous in some ways. Lapacho, a chemical from a South American tree (*Tabebuia impetiginosa* or Pau d'Arco), is a dye that has many of the anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer properties of methylene blue.

Recently, people are talking about an Asian herb, black cumin, which contains thymoquinone. The quinones seem to be the essential model of the protective, pro-oxidant stabilizing chemical. Thymoquinone is considered a very powerful anti-inflammatory, and I suspect it will turn out to be acting against excess nitric oxide.

**Caller:** I'm from Arcata. It was mentioned some time ago about a nutrient that could help remediate the earlobe crease. Does that ring a bell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is mainly a thyroid deficiency.

**Caller:** Was there a simple recommendation for correction?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the main thing causing hypothyroidism in so many people is an excess of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), because they are able to block the production of thyroid hormone, its transport, and its action.

**Andrew Murray:** So avoid nuts and seeds that contain liquid oils. Dr. Peat always recommends coconut oil and butter as the two saturated sources of fat. Avoid liquid polyunsaturates, fish oil being the worst.

**Caller:** What about cod liver oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you don't have any better source, cod liver oil is a great source of Vitamin D, but it's better to get sunlight.

**Caller:** One other question. There was something about eating carrots—an antiseptic aspect. It was recommended that carrots be cut diagonally. As a juicer, I thought that was peculiar.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat has always mentioned grated carrots to increase the surface area. It acts as an antiseptic for the gut, removing excess estrogen and other waste products.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The juice contains a lot of good things, but if you throw away the fiber, you're losing the most important thing for stimulating and cleaning the intestine.

**Caller:** I've got a couple of questions. First, did you say that L-arginine was bad? I've heard that was supposed to be good for you.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The internet is swamped with advertisements for ways to supplement arginine. L-arginine is the natural amino acid, but if you get more than you need, it will increase your tendency to overproduce nitric oxide. Too much tryptophan also boosts that. It's very important to keep your amino acids in good balance, especially avoiding too much cysteine, tryptophan, methionine, and arginine.

**Caller:** So you don't recommend taking an L-arginine supplement?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I think it's very dangerous.

**Caller:** Now, did you say that Viagra is bad for you because it's made out of this nitric oxide stuff?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It inhibits an enzyme that is supposed to inactivate a substance made by the production of nitric oxide. Nitric oxide starts a chain reaction, and Viagra keeps that chain reaction going. In the process, it ends up systemically increasing the effect and level of nitric oxide. So it probably is increasing the aging process in the brain, heart, and pancreas.

**Caller:** But they say having sex is good for you. If that improves sexual function in an older man, isn't there a balance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it would be better to work on the actual physiological problem. Improving natural circulation and restoring good thyroid function will often increase libido and potency.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, I remember you mentioning pregnenolone or progesterone as being very positive. You said it does not block the vasodilatory ability, so it actually promotes erection and is a reasonably safe way of doing that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aging men have decreased amounts of testosterone and progesterone and increasing amounts of estrogen. That shift increases the tendency to have erectile problems. One of the odd side effects of increased nitric oxide is that it decreases the ability to make testosterone. I think in both men and women, nitric oxide opposes and lowers those protective steroids while increasing estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** What are your thoughts on the cancer-promoting effects of nitric oxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's one of the central factors in keeping cancer going. It is a definite promoter of cancer growth and metastasis. Many publications are now recognizing that breast cancer, prostate cancer, and probably every cancer will eventually be discovered to respond badly to nitric oxide.

The Warburg hypothesis was that cancer shifts away from oxygen as the energy source to producing lactic acid. Nitric oxide and carbon monoxide are both able to knock out mitochondrial function and imitate cancer metabolism. Several recent publications show that the Warburg cancer metabolism is created by nitric oxide excess and is turned off by methylene blue.

**Andrew Murray:** I have a question about immunity. Why are some individuals immune to HIV or able to mount a successful response against hepatitis? Why do some have an innate immunity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are new ideas about the immune system from Jamie Cunliffe and Polly Matzinger. I see the body as an ecosystem which is simply so strong in some people at maintaining its own organization that when an invader like a bacterium, virus, or cancer cell enters, the situation is so tightly organized in favor of the host that the invader can't find a place. The niches are all occupied doing business with the owner of the property. I don't see it as killing the invader, but simply using up all the electron space productively so keeping the door shut prevents strange things, like turning sugar into lactic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Two simple questions coming through. First one is MSM (Methylsulfonylmethane)—does it have an influence on libido?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I am very cautious about it. Dimethyl sulfide has its uses, but I'm not sure that there's anything really fully safe with MSM.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about DCA (Dichloroacetate) for cancers?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens to be very similar to methylene blue in the way it is essentially non-toxic in moderate amounts. People are getting as much as 10 or 12 grams per day intravenously and feeling great. What it does is restore the productive oxidation of glucose, getting electrons to go all the way to form carbon dioxide. It reverses the cancer metabolism—the Warburg metabolism—the same way methylene blue does. I see it as a very important way of making up for the toxic effects of nitric oxide, endotoxin, and free radical fat oxidation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You've spoken of antioxidants that are too strong. Could you give a spectrum? Is ALA (Alpha Lipoic Acid) too strong?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin E and ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) in the right proportion and situation are very safe and constructive. Alpha lipoic acid is pretty safe. But I would be very cautious with N-acetylcysteine (NAC). I think large amounts of it can push the balance in the wrong direction.

**Andrew Murray:** I had a question from a woman with hypothyroidism symptoms (depression, weight gain, cold hands/feet). Her TSH was 1.6 and T3 was 3.5. She used to take Armour Thyroid, but when she tried to supplement with T3 or a T3/T4 combination recently, she developed anxiety and tachycardia—even at small doses like 1mg of T3. What causes a person to become sensitive to thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes the product has changed; European forms of thyroid supplements seem unpredictable. But if it is the same product, usually a magnesium deficiency can cause exactly those symptoms. Thyroid makes your cells able to use magnesium. A big organ like your skeletal muscles and bones can take up so much from your blood that your brain and heart have trouble getting the magnesium they need to respond to the thyroid. Then you get an exaggerated stress and adrenaline reaction.

Also, low cholesterol is another limiting factor. If you have very low cholesterol, you can't respond to increasing your thyroid because one of the basic functions of thyroid is to turn cholesterol into progesterone, pregnenolone, and DHEA.

**Andrew Murray:** What dose of magnesium would be suitable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 100 milligrams at a time. If you take one or two micrograms of Cytomel (T3), 100 milligrams of magnesium will be plenty for the first two or three hours of responding to that thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** What is a good magnesium source?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fruit juices and coffee. If you want a really intense source, you can boil leaves like kale or beet greens for just two or three minutes. The green water that comes out is very concentrated in magnesium and calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** I'd love to look into the research about the "third circulatory system" and how we are what we eat next month.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, a German group has been looking at DNA from our foods getting incorporated into our own DNA. Some biologists have been theorizing about this for a hundred years. When you ingest pollen blowing in the air, some of that DNA is probably getting incorporated into our chromosomes.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. It has a wealth of fully referenced scientific material. Thanks so much for joining us.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: You Are What You Eat (2014)
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. I’m Andrew Murray. For those of you who have never listened to the show, I'm a licensed medical herbalist who trained in England and graduated with a degree in Herbal Medicine. I run a clinic in Garberville where I consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicine and dietary advice.

This month's subject is "You Are What You Eat." This phrase has come to us via quite a tortuous route. Anthelme Brillat-Savarin wrote in *Physiologie du Goût* in 1826, "Tell me what you eat and I will tell you what you are." In an essay titled *Concerning Spiritualism and Materialism* (1863), Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach wrote, "Man is what he eats." Neither Brillat-Savarin nor Feuerbach meant their quotations to be taken literally; they were stating that the food one eats has a bearing on one's state of mind and health.

The actual phrase didn't emerge in English until sometime later. In the 1920s and 30s, the nutritionist Victor Lindlahr, who was a strong believer in the idea that food controls health, developed the "catabolic diet." Research now suggests that depression and dementia are affected by the quality of our diets across the life course. Indeed, studies from countries as diverse as Norway, Spain, Japan, China, the UK, the US, and Australia show people whose diets are healthier are less likely to experience depression. The most recent evidence points to the importance of the mother's diet for the mental and physical health of their children.

We are joined by Dr. Raymond Peat to hear his perspective on this subject. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us. For those who may not have heard you, I would appreciate it if you would give an outline of your academic and professional background.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After I had studied in the humanities and taught art and English, I decided to go back to graduate school in Biology in 1968 at the University of Oregon. I wrote my dissertation on the age-related changes in oxidative metabolism in the hamster uterus and how it affects fertility with aging. That involved hormones and nutrition, and how the environment affects those factors, especially the efficiency of metabolism using oxygen. Since then, I've been writing, doing consultations, and trying to figure things out, still working on some of those same themes: oxidative metabolism and aging.

The whole idea of metabolic efficiency is one of my current themes. Lindlahr, whom you just mentioned, had the idea of the catabolic diet: to choose foods for their metabolic *inefficiency*. People eating to satisfy their appetite tend to get fat on the available foods. He found that he could get people to lose fat very consistently and quickly by choosing certain foods that increased their metabolic rate so that they could burn calories faster than they were eating them.

That was in the 1920s. Just by chance, a few years later, George Burr, who was studying the effect of fats in the diet, found that if he made his rats deficient in unsaturated fatty acids, they burned calories at a terrific rate—as much as 50% faster than normal. He thought that was bad. However, he became very popular with the agricultural industry because they found that feeding those polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs) to pigs and chickens caused them to gain weight quickly and cheaply without eating very much food. This was just the opposite of what Lindlahr wanted to do, which was to find foods that would decrease the efficiency of the metabolism so that people would produce heat without gaining weight.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know what kind of foods Lindlahr advocated?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of fruits and vegetables, including fruit juices. Standard nutritional education emphasizes the concept of specific dynamic action, or the thermogenic effect of various foods. It's widely recognized that eating protein increases your body temperature and heat production by quite a bit—15% or 20%. Sugar a little less than that.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you've mentioned coconut oil quite a lot in the past as being thermogenic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think there are many reasons for that. Coconut is a very highly saturated fat. It happens that the unsaturated fats interfere with the mitochondrial use of oxygen in several ways: by producing free radicals, inflammation, and by interfering with thyroid hormone function. So, all along the line, the polyunsaturated fats slow down oxidative metabolism. If your body is soaked in these conventional seed oils, then when you eat coconut oil—especially the shorter, very mobile fatty acids that are only a third or half as long as the standard fats—these move into cells very quickly and oxidize without that anti-thyroid effect that the seed oils mostly have.

**Andrew Murray:** So Victor Lindlahr came up with the catabolic diet. Anabolism is to build muscle, and catabolism is to break it down with the production of heat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s and 60s, people were experimenting with what kind of diet is efficient for losing fat while maintaining health. They did experiments in which people would have just pure water for 10 or 14 days. They analyzed what happened to their bodies and found that they lost almost pure protein during that time, and very little fat.
