However, if they ate maybe 600 to 800 calories per day during that same period, they would lose mostly fat and very little protein.

**Andrew Murray:** Interesting. That protein loss is the muscle mass a person loses when they fast.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's why so many women are dieting constantly and getting fatter. If they eat an extremely low-calorie diet, creating stress, the high cortisol and other stress hormones cause them to break down their protein. Their big muscles shrink. A typical dieter will have calf muscles that become atrophied. The big skeletal muscles, even at rest, burn fat to maintain themselves. So, the more dieting they do, the smaller their muscles get, and the easier it is to get fat the next time they eat a normal diet.

**Andrew Murray:** You said with the addition of some food, protein was conserved. How much fat was in that diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They fed them a mixed diet—a little protein, a little carbohydrate—not especially a low-fat intake, but enough to get some calorie needs from the diet rather than from their tissues.

When you are in the first day of a fast, your body uses up the sugar stored as glycogen. As soon as your blood sugar falls because you've used up your stores, your cortisol rises. First adrenaline, then cortisol. The cortisol, having no food available, starts converting your thymus gland and big skeletal muscles into free amino acids. Some of these are converted to glucose to feed your blood cells, brain, and eyes, because those have an absolute requirement for glucose. Even a plain sugar diet to supply that minimal amount that your brain and blood cells require will greatly prevent the rise in cortisol and loss of good tissue.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to jump onto the subject of the microbiome. It is well established that your gut is your "second brain." There are quite a few journal articles linking disease processes to the microbiome. I know you advocate several dietary factors that modulate the microbiome, such as indigestible fibers like bamboo shoots and carrots. You also talk about cascara, not just for bowel motility, but because it has a structure similar to tetracycline.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's interesting that both emodin (from cascara or Chinese rhubarb) and tetracycline (and related minocycline and doxycycline) are anti-inflammatory as well as antiseptic. They have a surprising range of good effects. Minocycline is being found to prevent or possibly improve dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Emodin seems to have new functions found every year, including improving the flora of the intestine.

**Andrew Murray:** Am I right in thinking that emodin is also present in aloe vera?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, lots of plants. Generally, they are laxative plants. But it isn't the typical purging kind of laxative. If the cascara isn't properly aged, it does have an irritating, purging effect. But aging makes it insoluble in water comparatively; it loses the irritating inflammatory property and becomes anti-inflammatory and sedative. It actually increases the production of energy while having a nerve-calming effect.

**Andrew Murray:** This is that red compound you've mentioned that is energetically favorable in terms of electron quenching and anti-inflammatory activity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As a sideline to my research in graduate school on what causes oxidative metabolism to go down with aging, I would look for all kinds of plants and animals that were colored, do extracts, and look for things that stimulated oxidative metabolism. I got the interest partly from Albert Szent-Györgyi. He found that the color of cells is closely connected to the oxidative process—for example, the deep maroon or purple color of the liver. He knew that semiconductors are generally black because of a peculiar electronic arrangement that causes them to absorb all the light that hits them. He figured that the life process involves semiconduction, so pigments are especially relevant to the use of energy in living things.

**Andrew Murray:** Like methylene blue, which we discussed last month as an artificial electron transporter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Like vitamin C. Vitamin C in its normal form isn't a pigment, but it has some of the same electronic behaviors. Both of those can pick up electrons from nutrients such as glucose and pass them into the mitochondrion. Even if the first two units of the mitochondrion are damaged, methylene blue and vitamin C—and probably many other natural pigments—can deliver energy electrons down to the third complex of the mitochondrion and allow it to keep functioning. Part of that function is to stop producing free radicals.

**Andrew Murray:** What are your thoughts about altering the microbiome so that specific bacteria known to be detrimental can be eradicated?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 1990, I read an article from a fertility clinic where women were trying to conceive, but the fertilized ovum wouldn't implant. The doctors thought it might indicate an infection in the uterus, so they gave all their patients a course of antibiotics. Besides improving their fertility, a lot of the patients said their chronic headaches had disappeared. They gave them hormone tests and found that the antibiotics had lowered their cortisol and estrogen production and increased progesterone.

Following that, I suggested that since estrogen is excreted by a healthy liver into the bile, much of it is reabsorbed if you have a sluggish intestine. I suggested that if they eat a carrot every day to stimulate the intestine, the fiber will bind the bile and lower the serum estrogen level. It is now generally accepted that any fiber tends to lower your absorption of estrogen from bile. Within three or four days, these people tested their estrogen, cortisol, and progesterone, and the carrot was doing the same thing the synthetic antibiotics had done.

Knowing that carrots can get tiresome if you eat one every day for years, I looked around for other foods that were antiseptic. Bamboo shoots are something you don't get too tired of; they don't have much flavor, so you can put them in different foods. Cooking a bamboo shoot doesn't destroy the fiber the way a cooked carrot does. You have to eat raw carrots or cooked bamboo shoots.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know of any other fibers that have that effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mushrooms, I think. Because they grow underground in a very decaying environment, they have to have powerful antibiotics. They have high-value protein, and the protein happens to be pretty low in methionine, which is the most toxic of the amino acids. Methionine slows your metabolism. So with mushrooms, you're getting metabolic stimulants, lowering estrogen, and disinfecting your intestine.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take our first caller. You’re on the air.

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** I have a question. Last month I developed very high blood pressure that spikes. I don't have a family history of it. About two months ago, I had my T3 medicine increased, and I got heart palpitations. I titrated down off of that over six weeks, but I still had palpitations until I started magnesium after hearing your show.

However, in October, I went on a "silly little thing" where I was trying to increase my body temperature by eating more sugar and salt. I increased my salt quite a bit—maybe 3,000 or 4,000 milligrams. My blood pressure skyrocketed. Could coming down off the thyroid and that high salt diet have contributed to this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Was your TSH measured as part of the thyroid exam?

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** When I first was on T4, it was like 3, but then it went down to below zero—like 0.3. It's way low.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** TSH causes a lot of the symptoms of hypothyroidism. If T3 causes your T4 to go down too low, your TSH might come up. TSH does a lot of things that go with hypothyroidism, including high blood pressure. It makes your red cells more rigid, your blood and serum more viscous, and it tightens up small blood vessels. Everything it does tends to create higher blood pressure. If your TSH is currently extremely low, then you probably should have your other hormones, such as adrenaline, checked.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you always advocate a TSH as close to zero as possible just because it's a fairly inflammatory chaperone molecule, don't you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** I think I got mixed up. If TSH gets pretty low, does T3 make it lower?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you had lowered your TSH by taking fairly large amounts of T4...

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** It was 25 micrograms. It got really low. Then they incorporated T3 at 25, then increased it to 50. Then I started having heart palpitations. I titrated down, went to the doctor, and they said my thyroid is fine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Were other things like albumin and blood sugar okay? It's good to have albumin well above 4.0, blood glucose anywhere from 70 to 110, and potassium and sodium around the middle of the scale. Is there anything that might be irritating your digestive system? Sometimes that can cause stress and increased pressure.

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** No. I take Great Lakes gelatin, mix it in cold orange juice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you don't dissolve the gelatin thoroughly, sometimes that can cause gas and irritation by feeding bacteria in the intestine. Is your pulse rate about where it was?

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** It's always been around the 70s.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Magnesium and calcium are two nutrients that help to lower blood pressure, but potassium is probably the most powerful. Orange juice is a very good source of potassium. One other nutrient that can powerfully lower blood pressure is vitamin K. I know a doctor whose blood pressure had been 240 over 140, and within two or three weeks of using a lot of vitamin K, his pressure came down to 140 over 70.

**Andrew Murray:** What would be a reasonable daily trial of vitamin K?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That doctor who got such extreme results was taking 40 or 50 milligrams per day.

**Caller (Eastern Oregon):** Okay, thank you. They put me on lisinopril plus a diuretic now.

**Andrew Murray:** It definitely sounds like something more than just your thyroid because of the rapid onset. It sounds like an alarm reaction or adrenaline producing that blood pressure. Thyroid hormone generally antagonizes that and brings blood pressure down.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take the next caller.

**Caller (David):** I've heard for years that coconut oil is an antibiotic and antifungal. I wanted to ask Dr. Peat if that is true and how it works. Also, I've heard you say that when you eat starch, it can get into the bloodstream and create problems in capillaries, and that saturated fat helps prevent that. How does saturated fat help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It slows digestion enough to keep things in an emulsion, giving enzymes time to start breaking down the starch particles. Gerhard Volkheimer, who did the persorption research, showed that starch without fat would immediately—in 15 or 20 minutes—show up in your bloodstream. With fat, it didn't show up, probably because it gives it time to break down.

But I think the most important effect of the fat is that germicidal action, suppressing the bacteria. If your digestion is working right, your whole small intestine should be sterile. In sluggish digestion or low thyroid, people often get bacteria growing all the way up close to their stomach. In that case, when you eat any starch, it feeds the bacteria. The bacteria produce endotoxin, which causes your intestine to produce nitric oxide, serotonin, and histamine. The nitric oxide is a very powerful poison of oxidative metabolism.

So, the combination of bacteria—especially in the small intestine—and any kind of starch that isn't quickly absorbed is going to feed the bacteria, increase nitric oxide, and basically poison your respiratory metabolism. Germ-free animals eat about 20% or 30% *more* calories than ordinary germ-bearing mice, but they are leaner and don't suffer from anxiety. This means the bacteria are producing something that poisons your metabolism.

**Caller (David):** Is coconut oil better for that action because of the short and medium chains compared to butter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Saturated fats are pretty good antifungals and antibacterials. The athlete's foot remedy that kills fungus efficiently is an 11-carbon saturated fat. The shorter they are, the faster they diffuse. Apparently, they are more active as a toxin or antiseptic if they're a little shorter than the stearic acid of butter.

**Caller (David):** I'm going to try a soup with bamboo sprouts and potato juice. I was going to add shiitake mushrooms. Do you think that's a decent soup?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so, but make sure you don't get toxic mushrooms.

**Andrew Murray:** I have to interject here. The only thing I am allergic to is shiitake mushrooms. I came out in a widespread body rash. It took about four weeks to resolve. It happened again years later, and a third time when I was handling shiitake mushroom powder. I find it a very allergenic product.

**Caller (David):** Dr. Peat has talked about Gerald Pollack and structured water. Pollack mentioned that walking barefoot and getting natural sunlight could possibly help structure the water in the body. He also said red wavelengths of light help structure the water.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. The flow of electrons is the basic thing that structures water. When I talk about energy and structure, I'm thinking primarily of the fine layers of water adjoining proteins and fats in the cells. That is created and maintained by the flow of electrons, mostly from glucose to oxygen. When that flow is interrupted, the structure is lost. Just like if you stir a pot of spaghetti, all the strings line up; energy flow generates structure. A German researcher named Andrei Sommer has been doing interesting research showing exactly that—that red light itself organizes the structure of water.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you talk about red light a lot as a free radical quenching substance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And it desorbs nitric oxide from the cytochrome oxidase.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We had a caller who left a question with the engineer. She is 64 years old and wondering about under-eye puffiness.

**Andrew Murray:** A 64-year-old lady sounds like low thyroid. Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, sometimes low thyroid or something missing in the diet can be a factor, but most often it's low thyroid. For example, if your thyroid is chronically low, your cholesterol is likely to be chronically above average as a compensation. Thyroid should turn cholesterol into the steroids: progesterone, pregnenolone, and DHEA. Those should regulate the water and the inside-outside balance of water in the cell.

**Andrew Murray:** We have another caller. You're on the air.

**Caller (North Coast):** What do you know about sulfites in wine regarding digestive problems?

**Andrew Murray:** Sulfite-free wine can be labeled as such, but others must state "contains sulfites." I know Dr. Peat has mentioned that sulfites are very allergenic and can cause symptoms from headache to respiratory disorders.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is potentially very pro-inflammatory and interferes with the handling of electrons. I think that's why it is so dangerously allergenic for so many people. I've had the experience of sulfited wines giving me vertigo and extreme symptoms for several days, which I think were from causing inflammation of the intestine.

**Caller (North Coast):** What about messing up the digestive system and causing pain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, red wines contain their own histamine, which can cause symptoms in a lot of people.

**Andrew Murray:** We will stop right there. Dr. Peat, thank you so much for spending your time with us again. Dr. Raymond Peat's website has a wealth of information and fully referenced scientific articles at .

This is a couple of days until the winter solstice. I hope everyone pays attention to what they eat over Christmas. Hopefully no polyunsaturates. Hopefully, people are cooking with butter and animal fats and making sure what you eat is organic. The food chain is permeated with chemicals now, so always eat organic. Until the third Friday of next month, Merry Christmas.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Digestion and Emotion
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's and this New Year's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. Happy New Year everybody. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who perhaps have never listened to the shows, I'm a licensed naturopathic doctor who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where I consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicine and dietary advice.

You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of digestion and emotion. Some of it is carrying on from last month's topic of "You Are What You Eat." I had quite a few people writing afterwards on that subject, so thank you for that feedback.

Let's introduce Dr. Peat. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hi.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us again. I want to give people the benefit of understanding your professional and academic background for those who have just tuned in.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After working several years in humanities areas, I decided to study biology because I wanted to get a concrete grasp of how the brain works in making language, images, and so on. I intended to work on a PhD at the University of Oregon starting in 1968 in brain biology. I quickly found that that was the most dogmatic area in biology—genetics and nerve biology. So, I looked around for less dogmatic areas and it turned out that the extreme other end of the organism, the reproductive system, happened to be the most scientific and empirical. I did my dissertation on oxidative changes in the female reproductive system with aging, and that involves a lot of nutrition-related topics that were of interest to me.

**Andrew Murray:** At one time you were actively consulting with people for quite a few years, weren't you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In the 70s, I happened to meet some women who were having hormonal problems in graduate school. I had talked to some girls who, immediately when they came to the university and got a cheap basement apartment, started having terrible PMS. In 1967 or '68, I got interested in the role of light in brain and hormone functions and what I called "winter sickness" from a light deficiency.

When I started running into women in slightly older groups—40, 45, and 50—having really serious problems like multiple sclerosis and other nerve-related conditions, I recognized the work I had been doing with hamsters and hormones as being directly applicable to them. So I started doing nutritional consulting and finally started suggesting that they use progesterone and thyroid supplements because, in some cases, the diet just wasn't enough to take care of acute problems.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to carry on partly from last month's topic on "You Are What You Eat" and take a more focused look at diet, digestion, and emotion. You mentioned previously that a gut peptide called cholecystokinin (CCK) was shown to have a crucial role in mediating the effects of fatty acids on brain activity. They were saying that the receptors for CCK are known not only for their role in digestion but also for roles in memory function, learning, and the modulation of panic and anxiety.

So, the gut is not just for digestion; it also triggers emotive events. What do you infer from the suggestion that CCK's role in the stimulation of bile and the absorption of fats supports a link between mental function and digestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's good to consider at least one other digestive peptide: the Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide (GIP). My general picture of the organism is analogous to the sympathetic nervous system and the parasympathetic nervous system—the day and the night sides of the nervous system. Everywhere you look, you can see this polar opposition in two kinds of function. One is mobilizing, the other is demobilizing and relaxing.

**Andrew Murray:** The parasympathetic is the relaxing and the mobilizing is the sympathetic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. When the organism is young and healthy, that opposition works very nicely for night and day action and rest cycling. In the digestive system, when you eat fats and proteins, you secrete cholecystokinin (CCK). When you eat sugar, you secrete GIP, which is also called the insulinotropic hormone because it calms down and stops your acid digestion—you don't need acid to handle sugar—but it activates the insulin so that you handle the sugar.

When you look at the effect in the brain, CCK activates the corticotropin-releasing hormone, which turns on anxiety and stress, and the pituitary ACTH, which turns on the adrenals to handle stress.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide responding to glucose has pretty much the opposite effects. In the hippocampus, for example—which is a part of the brain that's expanded by opportunity and learning and shrunken by stress—the insulinotropic hormone responding to sugar also has receptors that stimulate the birth of new cells. So learning, stimulating experience, and eating sugar go hand in hand.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Surprisingly, the effects on your brain from eating fat and protein turn on anxiety and stress.

**Andrew Murray:** Even protein?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, that tends to lower your blood sugar because it also stimulates insulin. Lowering the blood sugar turns on stress.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Farther down the intestine, if you could be born without bacteria—they've created situations with cesarean birth of rats, dogs, and pigs, keeping them in a germ-free environment—they find that everything develops perfectly. In fact, the animals live longer and are very resistant to obesity, diabetes, and degenerative diseases.

**Andrew Murray:** They have a very high metabolic rate too, don't they?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, they're very much like the calorie-restricted animals. On fat-free diets where they don't have the so-called "essential fatty acids," those animals have an extremely high metabolic rate too. So, calorie restriction and being free of germs both stimulate your ability to oxidize food, produce energy, prevent obesity, and be generally healthy and long-lived.

Something is happening in the intestine that the bacteria are responsible for. It turns out the main thing the bacteria are doing is usually converting starch. Starch is the main bacteria-promoting food. The bacteria living on these foods that we don't digest produce endotoxin. The endotoxin, everywhere it reaches a human cell, stimulates the production of nitric oxide. Nitric oxide is on the demobilizing side of the balance. It turns off metabolism and slows down oxidation. It is the main reason that having too many bacteria in the intestine creates obesity, lethargy, and short life.

**Andrew Murray:** Is it all forms of starch that will promote the endotoxin production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they're very well cooked, easy to digest, and aren't complex with fibrous material, it is different. For example, a corn tortilla that had been processed in alkali to open up the starch granules makes them easy to digest. Versus the bean carbohydrates—the type of polysaccharide that human enzymes can't work on are ideal for feeding bacteria, hence all the gas.

When they've experimented with rats on this type of soluble indigestible fiber, the ones that get the fiber that supports the bacterial growth become anxious and aggressive. They're fearful and so they fight too easily.

**Andrew Murray:** I'm glad you brought up nitric oxide. I think just like sugar was demonized and polyunsaturated fats were promoted, nitric oxide is now being promoted. L-arginine, which nitric oxide is manufactured from, is becoming a popular supplement, especially in the bodybuilding world. Publications are claiming it is important for endothelial health to prevent stroke and angina. Yet there's so much evidence contrary to that. Why is nitric oxide so dangerous? I know it's been implicated in stroke in people that use Viagra, for example.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I just recently heard about a doctor who treats cancer patients with intravenous arginine. Just before I heard about him, I had been reading way back to the 1940s where people discovered that arginine stimulates cancer growth and that starvation or reduction of arginine stops cancer growth. Through the 50s and 60s, methods to stop the conversion of arginine to nitric oxide were investigated as a way to cure cancer.

So there are these two very opposite things going on. One side proposes nitric oxide to cure cancer, while the other demonstrates that suppressing nitric oxide stops the growth of cancer.

I happened to be interested in endogenous carbon monoxide in the early and mid-80s; it can promote cancer by blocking the respiratory enzymes. Then in the late 80s, people started realizing that something was producing nitric oxide in the body. In 1988 or '89, the enzyme was demonstrated. We actually have the enzyme that makes this smog-like free radical in our tissues. Because it was already known as a major toxin in smog, people immediately investigated what it's really doing in the body.

From about 1990 up until the mid-90s, there were many publications showing that nitric oxide produced in the pancreas kills insulin-producing beta cells. That was massively documented up until about 1996. Then the Viagra people got a patent and started promoting the idea that somehow nitric oxide is associated with virility. Suddenly, the research by the late 90s turned 180 degrees, saying everything nitric oxide does must be wonderful.

**Andrew Murray:** Am I right in thinking also that nitric oxide in smog is a causative agent for asthma?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. There are people recommending arginine and breathing nitric oxide to treat asthma, but others demonstrate that people with asthma are producing it themselves—you can measure it in their breath. The worse their asthma is, the more nitric oxide comes out in their breath. It's the same with hepatitis, cancer, or any major systemic disease. You can find increased amounts of nitric oxide-related chemicals in the blood.

**Andrew Murray:** Nitric oxide is produced in the body and supposedly has beneficial functions. What is its real benefit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It helps cells to dedifferentiate by blocking their energy production. If you think of the mitochondrial high-energy oxidative system as being what creates a complex organism, if you want to dedifferentiate and produce a stem cell, you knock out the energy production and it goes back to becoming amoeba-like or fungus-like.

**Andrew Murray:** So this is like stem cell recruitment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. When a tissue is injured, it secretes a great burst of nitric oxide. That calls up stem cells from the environment, but it also creates them—it dedifferentiates existing cells in adjoining tissues so that they can form whatever new tissue is needed. So dedifferentiation is part of forming the organism in the first place. As the embryo develops, nitric oxide has a constructive role. And for wound healing, it's essential.

But that very same burst that calls up repair cells, if it doesn't have the ability to be turned off, keeps differentiating and stimulating tissue renewal so that you get an unhealing wound. The least bad example would be a keloid scar tissue that just keeps growing. In the worst case, it becomes a tumor and a cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you control nitric oxide so that it's a proportionate response to injury but blocked otherwise?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything that we have that is involved in producing oxidative energy helps to turn it off. Vitamin B1, niacinamide, the anti-inflammatory things like progesterone and pregnenolone, thyroid hormone—all of the differentiating, mobilizing, energy-intensifying substances turn it off. Everything that interferes with those turns it on and keeps it going.

Going into hibernation, an animal produces these demobilizing signals with nitric oxide. Anything that makes the organism tend to give up and stop struggling—demobilizing because of stress or isolation—powerfully turns on nitric oxide. In brain function, when your brain is being turned off, it experiences depression and wants to retreat.

**Andrew Murray:** And things like anxiety and aggression?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You aggress if someone doesn't let you retreat.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask you about the mind-body connection. Through focused attention and positive thinking, can the physical body be improved? Would you use supplements (progesterone, thyroid, B vitamins) to turn this negative cascade off, or would you have a positive mental outlook? Do you see the two being important together?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you look at the example of the psychologists who create depression by torturing animals—convincing them that they can't escape—once they form the idea that they can't escape, they don't try to escape anymore. It's an intellectual switch that happens from the bad experience. If you have made an animal helpless by those experiences, just one experience of escape will cure it.

**Andrew Murray:** It'll have the knowledge.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It's resistant because of that knowledge. The culture is telling people too often that they can't escape, that they have to do what they do. So something as simple as taking a vacation or getting a new job can make a tremendous difference. A person can pop right out of a prolonged depression if they get a new kind of work, for example.

**Andrew Murray:** We've got the first caller of the evening. Caller, you're on the air.

**Caller (Kansas City):** My question for Dr. Peat is: do you think using low-dose Arimidex as an aromatase inhibitor would be appropriate for a female who is correcting her metabolic rate by a thyroid diet but still has a fair amount of fat to lose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those chemicals all have some side effects, so there are much better ways to turn off estrogen production. Just the endotoxin from bacteria is a powerful promoter of aromatase and estrogen production. So taking an antibiotic, or eating a kind of fiber that doesn't support bacterial growth, or avoiding starches, and eating saturated fats—which have a germicidal effect—can help. Saturated fatty acids are very much like antiseptics as far as the intestinal bacteria go. Just by making those dietary changes, you can make a tremendous impact on your balance between estrogen and cortisol versus the protective progesterone and androgens.

**Caller (Kansas City):** Okay. One more question. Could you explain briefly the mechanisms of histamine and good ways to correct someone who has histamine responses periodically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since I was mentioning the saturated fats, some of the shorter-chain saturated fats in coconut oil have an antihistamine effect. Coffee is a very effective signal to turn off histamine production. Anything that energizes and restores cell function tends to prevent the production of histamine.

**Andrew Murray:** How about sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, definitely. A person wrote a book about histamine about 40 years ago and demonstrated that histamine is produced in every kind of cell in the organism when it's sufficiently stressed. That was before nitric oxide was known. But histamine turns on nitric oxide. So those are probably the two universal stress injury signals.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take the next caller.

**Caller (David):** On the last show, you mentioned that tetracycline will kill the harmful bacteria and the beneficial survive. Do we know that for sure? How does it selectively spare the "beneficial"? Also, I've heard there is a symbiotic relationship with certain intestinal bacteria that help absorb nutrients.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the interactions of the intestinal bacteria are too complicated to divide them neatly into beneficial and harmful. In the germ-free animals, they've done experiments introducing a single species of Lactobacillus, and even the supposedly beneficial bacteria will make the germ-free animal susceptible to injury that it wasn't susceptible to before. So it's the context and interaction of the different bacteria. Generally, the healthier a person is, the more sterile their small intestine is.

**Caller (David):** So what do you think of the idea that certain nutrients are absorbed through the actions of so-called beneficial bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think there's a little effect there, but I don't think it makes a big nutritional difference. The totally germ-free animals had extremely efficient digestive systems.

**Caller (David):** Is the term "free fatty acids" always referring to polyunsaturated fat, or are there instances where free fatty acids are actually saturated fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They can be either way. Coconut soap is the salt of the saturated free fatty acids. If you actually could eat a bite of free fatty acids, it would taste like acidic soap.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take the next caller.

**Caller (Kim):** I was wondering what the effect of infrared sauna would have on the cells' mitochondria. It produces nitric oxide, doesn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Water absorbs infrared very powerfully. Real infrared feels warm and it helps to keep your body temperature up. Keeping your body temperature up is essential for the mitochondria. The stress of cold is enough to turn on nitric oxide and that can start down the pathway of hibernation. So infrared, as it keeps your body temperature up, helps your mitochondria.

The far-red visible light—dark red, anywhere from orange to dark red—isn't very well absorbed by water, so it goes right through your tissue. You can see a red light shining through your whole body. That's because it penetrates and is only absorbed by blue. Copper is the main thing that absorbs it—enzymes that contain copper in a blue form. Those happen to be the respiratory enzymes. So the far-red activates the respiratory enzymes. Probably a major reason for that is that it bounces the nitric oxide molecule, loosens it, and frees it from the respiratory enzymes where it has been blocking it.

**Andrew Murray:** Next caller, you're on the air.

**Caller (Sacramento):** This is related to treating corn with alkali to make it more digestible. Are sprouted grain tortillas also considered good for digestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yeah. The starch is largely consumed and used. These storage proteins in the seed happen to have lots of ammonia or amino groups which are used to make actual functioning proteins with the energy from the starch. When you sprout a grain, you get rid of the toxic proteins that could release too much arginine and produce nitric oxide and histamine, and you get rid of most of the starches. So sprouts are basically good nutrition, like leaves.

**Andrew Murray:** The gentleman asked if it mattered whether it was wheat or barley.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All seeds, as far as I know, have some toxic effects built in by the plant to protect their offspring. Once the sprouting has begun, the seed detoxifies those intrinsic chemicals. Especially if it's very well cooked, then it becomes nutritious.

**Caller (Sacramento):** One final question. Is progesterone for men beneficial or harmful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Men who are in good health have a fair amount of progesterone. It's rarely measured in men, but it prevents abnormal excess clotting and it's a precursor for other hormones. If you have a good amount of progesterone, it protects you against fluctuations in the adrenal steroids, aldosterone and cortisol. Progesterone is sort of an all-purpose defensive hormone and it's very highly concentrated in the brain, in men as well as women. So it's definitely not just a female hormone.

But if you have too much of it—if you take a supplement—it opposes testosterone. A man doesn't want to take it regularly and stop his whiskers growing, for example. But for an emergency, a big supplement can be helpful for epilepsy or arthritis.

**Andrew Murray:** How quickly would you metabolize a dose of progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know a doctor who insisted that taking progesterone orally wouldn't show up in the blood. So he took a fourth of a teaspoon and then drew his blood every half hour for 12 hours. He showed that it peaked in around the first hour and then gradually decreased over the next day.

**Andrew Murray:** We have another caller.

**Caller (Garberville):** Is it your opinion that yogurt, for its supposed beneficials, is not so beneficial?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it has had some of the lactic acid drained off, or if it has just coagulated without becoming very sour, then it's fine.

**Caller (Garberville):** Is there a difference between a Greek yogurt and a goat milk yogurt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the Greek, which isn't sour, is safe. But the very acidic ones are problematic. I discovered that by drinking a cup of kefir every day, I would get a migraine for several hours afterwards. The type of lactic acid produced by bacteria is racemic. The kind we make is mostly the one confirmation that works differently. The racemic type made by bacteria is more able to produce inflammation and fibrosis if you're chronically overloaded with it.

**Caller (Garberville):** That dovetails into my main question. I was diagnosed with a skin condition called Hidradenitis suppurativa, which causes cysts. I've been trying to support my system with kefir.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have experimented with killing the lactobacillus, and in itself, even when it's dead, it has a very definite anti-inflammatory effect in the intestine. It seems that it isn't the lactic acid or the metabolism of the bacteria that is anti-inflammatory, but just something about the chemistry of the organism, even if it's dead. Since the inflammation in the intestine is quickly reflected in the physiology of the skin, soothing your intestine will take care of a lot of skin conditions, like acne.

**Caller (Garberville):** So yogurt minus the lactic acid is better.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** From a perspective of Hippocratic medicine, they always mentioned that the liver was the seat of anger. Do you have any comment on how this might come about?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver, to the extent that it's injured, will ruin the whole organism. It's the chemist for the whole organism. If you're starving and not getting enough protein or B vitamins, your liver loses the ability to detoxify and you get gross hormone imbalances. That can lead to progressive inflammation and fibrosis.

As these processes get more serious, the liver becomes a larger source of nitric oxide. When they transplant a liver, they've measured the sick person's nitric oxide as very high. When they put in a new liver, suddenly the nitric oxide is low and the lungs begin working more efficiently, demonstrating that the liver is poisoning the lungs.

With the brain, the same thing is happening. Edema is produced in the brain by the endotoxin-nitric oxide combination. The ammonia produced by the injured liver activates the nerves that are excited by glutamic acid (MSG) and excitatory amino acids. Those act largely through nitric oxide. So depression, anxiety, and I assume aggression is part of this mixture of gradual poisoning.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of exercise, I know you advocate gentle weight-bearing exercise rather than aerobic. What would you suggest as the best food sources for building a healthy physique? You mentioned gelatin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gelatin is at least safe. It doesn't stimulate muscle growth the way other proteins such as meat can do. But the person's history really has to be taken into account. I've known people who ate gigantic amounts of meat and were producing so much cortisol in response to the meat that they had extremely high levels of amino acids in their urine and their muscles were being damaged by that same high level of cortisol.

Ideally, like the germ-free animals, they can run on very little protein and lots of carbohydrate. The carbohydrate gets used for energy and you would assimilate essentially all of the protein that you eat because your cortisol wouldn't be destroying it.

**Andrew Murray:** What kind of carbohydrates? Fruit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. As long as you're getting all of the essential nutrients, for example from some seafoods and eggs, then fruits and gelatin would be a very safe diet for adults.

**Andrew Murray:** Very good. I thank you for your time, Dr. Peat. Dr. Raymond Peat's articles are available at www.raypeat.com. Until the third Friday in February, I wish you a happy New Year. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Uses of Urea
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Hi and good evening to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. I'm a licensed medical herbalist who trained in England and graduated there with a master's degree in herbal medicine.

Tonight, we are discussing the use of urea in the treatment of various pathologies. We're also going to get into a recapitulation regarding isoflavones, soy products, and things that are touted as being healthful but lack scientific backing—such as fish oil. Joining us is Dr. Raymond Peat. Dr. Peat, would you discuss your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Academically, I studied various things for an MA in humanities. From 1968 to 1972, I got a PhD in biology specializing in reproductive physiology and the biochemistry related to it. I've been talking to lots of people about biological ideas for about 50 years, so my education comes in a lot of non-academic ways.

**Andrew Murray:** We discussed the treatment of cancer with urea recently, specifically referencing Dr. Evangelos Danopoulos, a Greek medical doctor. He published peer-reviewed papers in journals like *The Lancet* and *Clinical Oncology* in the late 70s and early 80s. What are your interpretations of the mechanism by which urea affects this anti-cancer activity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think one of the essential things is that it inhibits nitric oxide formation. Nitric oxide formation is probably the main means by which stress of any kind can turn off oxidative energy production. Anything that will turn off nitric oxide excess will restore energy production.

Restoring energy production has structural ramifications. The constant consumption of oxygen maintains and renews the microscopic structure of a cell. About 50 years ago, people argued that the membrane is semi-permeable and has pumps run by cell energy. In fact, there are no demonstrated pumps, and the pumps they postulated would take many times more energy than a cell could ever produce.

The cell is doing something very different from maintaining osmotic balance; it is maintaining the structure in an atomically fine sense—right down to the electronic relations of atoms to each other. Urea participates in this directly as well as helping to prevent the loss of the oxidative production of energy.

**Andrew Murray:** How does the concentration of urea play a role?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The normal amount in the blood is just a few milligrams per hundred cc's of blood. But you can increase that to 1,000 milligrams—almost 1% of the blood—without disturbing things physiologically. Danopoulos found that when he got the blood level up to at least 85mg percent—more than 10 times the normal amount—the cancers would start disappearing.

Even before that concentration, it shuts down the production and action of nitric oxide. It fits right into the way water is structured and increases the ability of the cell's natural hormones to structure the water and protein system the way the cell wants to. Urea supports what the cell wants to do.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this similar to the concept of "structured water"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it is exactly what the oxidative system is doing to the electrons. It is preventing an excess of electrons. Toxins, carcinogens, and radiation do the opposite: they put too many loose electrons into the wrong places.

The chemical system of the proteins contains a lot of sulfhydryl compounds, like glutathione. This is a sulfur compound maintained by energy-rich fuel molecules. It maintains a certain degree of oxidation in balance with sulfhydryl groups attached to the proteins. The proteins are like a reservoir of electrons at the right energy level. Oxygen metabolism, besides providing ATP, prevents an overflow of loose electrons getting into the structure of the proteins. Too many electrons will de-differentiate the cell, moving it towards non-oxidative energy production and the formation of lactic acid.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Danopoulos worked with liver cancers, but also ocular cancers—melanomas and basal cell carcinomas.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** His articles on that have photographs that show very vividly the elimination of the cancer and restoration of normal tissue. One of the interesting things about urea is that at these very high concentrations, it is so stabilizing to normal tissue that it prevents the formation of deforming scars.

In a 1935 publication, someone described its use in treating wounds of all kinds. Packing crystals right into the wound or ulcer would clear up the infection and stimulate healing, but it would heal without visible scarring.

**Andrew Murray:** I read that it promoted rapid granulation tissue.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw a story about an African spiny mouse that can regenerate its tissue very quickly. Punching a hole in the skin, it could close the wound by almost two-thirds in the first day. In three or four days, the wound would be healed without a scar.

**Andrew Murray:** Young children heal rapidly compared to older people. That has to be down to an electronic energy state, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The oxidative metabolism slows down from early embryonic development down to old age.

**Andrew Murray:** How can people stave off that electronic degradation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the uterus, the developing embryo heals without scarring. I think two factors are involved: the high carbon dioxide level and the higher urea-related compounds in the amniotic fluid. In the adult, pure carbon dioxide gas can be blown into an ulcer to stimulate healing and reduce pain.

As soon as an organism is born, it starts interacting with the outside environment. In the uterus, it was getting energy filtered through the placenta and making its own fats out of glucose and fructose. The organism using carbohydrate for energy produces saturated fats or omega-9 unsaturated fats. When we come into the world, we are exposed to fats produced by organisms living at a lower temperature. The colder a plant is exposed to, the more unsaturated its fats are. Those interrupt our oxidative metabolism to the extent that we become saturated with them.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding dosage, Danopoulos used 15 grams of urea in a quart of water to be drunk daily. For skin tumors, he used injections of 15% to 50% urea solution. He quoted blood urea levels of 75-85mg percent. What does that equate to in intake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That requires taking quite a bit more than 15 grams per day. Some studies used up to 120 grams per day divided into doses of about 15 grams. In the 1950s, it was the main treatment for reducing brain edema. Urea isn't osmotically active because it goes right into the cells; it soothes the cell's excitation, changes its electronic balance, and lets the cell give up the water it doesn't need—very much the way progesterone and thyroid work.

**Andrew Murray:** Another study mentioned that common white and brown mushrooms inhibit aromatase. They found 10 grams of cooked mushrooms a day reduced breast cancer by 64%. With the addition of green tea, it was an 89% reduction.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You would think there would be more news about that.

**Caller (David):** Indigenous people used urine for medicinal purposes. Did they intuitively know about the urea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known quite a few people who did it regularly and seemed extremely healthy. The Chinese used it, and one interpretation was that it concentrated metabolites of progesterone and pregnenolone. They used these to extend the lives of the wealthy.

**Caller (David):** If we work backward on physiology, it appears humanity evolved in equatorial, high-altitude areas. This implies we should be eating more saturated fats found in warm climates. If someone studied this, would they find that moving away from the equator causes problems?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is my orientation on origins: high altitude, warm climate, lots of fruit. All foods would be more saturated in a more equatorial environment.

**Caller (David):** Are scientists oblivious to this? They aren't warning us about polyunsaturated fats or lack of sunlight.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I ran across publications in food journals 40 or 50 years ago showing that fats vary with the climate and have a definite function. Some function to protect plants against animal predators by poisoning them. It was recognized 40 years ago that seed oils are a biological defense.

**Caller:** I've taken fish oil, but I'm hearing it has negative effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The majority of the oils we store are unsaturated, but our cells prefer to oxidize saturated fats. With aging, our tissues load up on unsaturated fats. In N-3 fats (omega-3), the double bonds are farther from the acidic end, making them more unstable in the presence of oxygen.

When we are stressed, our bloodstream gets a high concentration of N-6 fatty acids, which produce toxic prostaglandins that cause inflammation. If you take fish oil, these oxidize quickly and interfere with the formation of prostaglandins. You get temporary relief from inflammation because you are suppressing the immune system. In the long run, that does damage because it is so highly oxidizable. In some experiments, N-3 fats increased the metastatic spread of cancer cells.

**Caller:** What would you recommend for healthy brain function instead?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Saturated fats are protective, stabilizing cell membranes and being cardiovascularly protective. Coconut oil, palm oil, butter, and animal fat.

**Andrew Murray:** Note that animal fat needs to be organic, or you risk pesticide and hormone residues.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It also depends on what the animals were fed. Chickens are highly polyunsaturated. Pork for the last 50 years has been full of polyunsaturated fats. Even lard is often treated as a saturated fat in studies, but it can have 35% PUFA (polyunsaturated fatty acids), making it risky.

**Caller:** Can you address urea in reference to breast health and fibroids?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know of specific treatments for those with urea. However, the amino acid arginine can either form nitric oxide or urea. Irritants and toxins tend to shift it away from forming urea toward nitric oxide. Avoiding polyunsaturated fats helps you maintain the proper amount of urea formation.

**Andrew Murray:** Estrogen is likely one of the main contributory factors for fibroids.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. Low thyroid causes the ratio of estrogen to progesterone to be very high. Endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and breast fibrocystic disease all go with high estrogen, low progesterone, and low thyroid function.

**Caller:** I have insomnia. I take three blood pressure pills. I heard tart cherry juice helps.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Checking for thyroid function is important. Blood sugar is always a problem at night. Daylight maintains efficient oxidative metabolism; just 15 minutes of darkness is enough to lower the efficiency of mitochondrial respiration.

Having a carbohydrate meal late in the afternoon or before bed—like a glass of orange juice or milk with honey—helps. Sometimes the dose of sugar puts you to sleep for only an hour or two, so it's good to have another glass ready for when you wake up. Salty snacks at bedtime, like milk with salty tortilla chips or pork rinds, help stabilize blood sugar and energy production.

**Caller:** Is that safe with high blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin K is a very important nutrient for regulating blood sugar, blood calcium, and blood pressure. I've known people who lowered their systolic pressure by 100 points in a week or two using Vitamin K. If you are already at normal blood pressure, be cautious. 5 or 10 milligrams is a pretty safe dose.

Vitamin D is also essential. If you aren't getting sunlight, get a blood test. You want the 25-hydroxycholecalciferol test. Both Vitamin K and D prevent excitatory excess.

**Caller:** If urea is so good for cancer, why is it not a more popular treatment?

**Andrew Murray:** It's likely because it's simple and cheap. It doesn't make money like the pharmaceutical industry requires.

**Caller:** What about MSM and Glucosamine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Be very cautious. Glucosamine is suspected of being a factor in creating diabetes if taken too long. MSM can be toxic in itself. Cells definitely don't need it.

**Caller:** Is fish oil good for the heart?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, the studies have ended up negative. Short term, it may lower blood pressure, but it ends up with toxic immune-suppressive effects.

**Andrew Murray:** They are also specifically thyrotoxic (toxic to the thyroid).

**Caller:** What about sesame tahini or nuts?

**Andrew Murray:** It is a liquid oil, so it is polyunsaturated. To consume oil from nuts is consuming a large amount of product you wouldn't normally get exposed to. They oxidize very quickly.

**Caller:** Is CoQ10 good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is good. It works with Vitamin K to stabilize energy production.

**Caller:** You've said it takes four years to change the saturated fat ratio of your cells. If you are overweight, does it take longer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you lose stored fat, it travels through your bloodstream. You want a steady supply of Vitamin E coming in—maybe 50 milligrams a day—to protect your blood vessels as the fat is removed.

Fruit and orange juice have safe antioxidants that protect you. Keeping your temperature steady at 98.6°F during the day keeps you burning energy productively rather than destructively. If you keep your liver energetic with a good diet (80 to 100 grams of protein) and keep your thyroid function up, your liver will be able to dispose of that unsaturated fat as a toxin without having to oxidize it.

**Andrew Murray:** So: gentle exercise, keep warm, ensure thyroid function is good, consume saturated fats (coconut oil), and drink orange juice.

For more information and scholarly articles, you can visit www.raypeat.com. Thank you for joining us.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Breast Cancer
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** A very good evening to you all. This is *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. This month’s subject is going to be about breast cancer. In the last couple of months, I've been approached by a startling number of people that have either known someone who's going through breast cancer treatment or I've met people that have been dying of breast cancer. It has prompted me to bring this subject up again.

This month's show will be about breast cancer awareness and prevention. I don't think we want to necessarily dwell on the treatment, although we will mention alternative medical treatments that are available and showing pretty good promise for inhibiting estrogen, such as aromatase inhibitors. But the prevention of it is the fundamental key to good health. If we put people's diets and lifestyles in the right place to begin with, that preventive strategy is probably a better payoff.

We're very pleased to welcome Dr. Raymond Peat to the show this evening. My name is Andrew Murray. I graduated in England with a master's degree in herbal medicine. I am joined by my wife, Sarah.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Good evening. My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray and I'm delighted to be on the show talking about ways to help prevent breast cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us. As always, I want to make sure people get an introduction from you about your academic and professional background before we get into tonight's subject.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm a biologist, a PhD from the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology and especially related to aging and reproductive hormone issues.

**Andrew Murray:** Most people will recognize breast cancer awareness and the numbers of people that die from breast cancer as being fairly staggering. I saw an article stating it was the leading cause of cancer death among women worldwide. What's your opinion of the causes of breast cancer, and how does this differ from the medical interpretation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The animal studies have been pretty clear for almost 100 years that it is a matter of an estrogen-like irritation. Even if it isn't exactly estrogen in the narrowest sense, the main carcinogenic substances, such as in smoke and tar, are estrogen-like in their structure and effect. The breast is very sensitive to an imbalance of estrogen-like stimulation. It's susceptible to anything that has an estrogen-like effect, including smoke and pollutants of various sorts.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this down to the fact that the estrogen receptors are most concentrated in the breast tissue or some other reason?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every cell has estrogen receptors, but the way they interact with other functions is more important than the number of receptors. Once you're exposed to estrogen, a cell will produce more and more receptors. Progesterone has a very central function of destroying estrogen receptors. So, a breast that's well balanced and exposed to enough progesterone won't have very many estrogen receptors during the progesterone dominance.

**Andrew Murray:** So the actual exposure to estrogen will cause an upregulation in the expression of estrogen receptors?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, pretty much in any cell. Irritation in general will do that. A failure of energy combined with stimulation will make estrogen receptors start to appear. In old people, as the energy production decreases, any irritation tends to induce estrogen production as well as sensitivity by the receptors.

**Andrew Murray:** You are linking estrogen to irritation and stress. You are saying that estrogen can be directly responsible for cancers?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The animal studies in the 30s and 40s were very clear that it isn't just the normally responsive tissues like the uterus and the breast that will cancerize under the influence of estrogen and similar things—those are just the most sensitive. With increased, uninterrupted exposure to estrogen, the sequence tends to go: first cancer of the uterus, then cancer of the breast, then of the lungs, kidneys, intestine, liver, and brain.

**Andrew Murray:** Are you talking about primaries now or metastases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Primary. Any tissue that is de-energized and irritated will develop not only the ability to respond to estrogen, but the actual ability to make estrogen. Your fat, skin, or liver can become a source of estrogen in proportion to how much stress you're under, even if you don't have ovaries.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's not just our monthly cycling that's exposing women to estrogen. Estrogen is prominent in foods and in our environment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fat is particularly sensitive. It isn't very well supplied with defensive and energetic systems, so it seems to be a major age-related source of estrogen, especially if you're overweight.

**Andrew Murray:** Are we talking polyunsaturated fats or fats in general?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was just your normal, ordinary fat cells. But since the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) increase the deposition and storage of fat, and since they break down to form the inflammation-promoting prostaglandins, they make the fat cells more likely to produce excess estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** You have mentioned increasing the dominance of saturated to unsaturated fat by avoiding polyunsaturates. Ultimately, over three or four years, the body fat composition could be turned back to a more saturated type fat if you avoid the polys.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There is a thing called the saturation index, which is just the ratio between a saturated fat like stearic acid and a polyunsaturated such as linoleic acid. People with cancer have a higher polyunsaturation and lower saturation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** But you're saying a saturated fat cell is still capable of producing estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cell which is more saturated is stabler and less likely to produce estrogen. The more highly polyunsaturated fats are very closely connected with estrogen. The amount in the tissue and in circulation of, say, a 5 or 6 unsaturated fat—such as you find in fish oil—is closely associated with the level of estrogen stimulation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So eating nuts and seeds that are high in those polyunsaturated fats, and fried foods that are fried in corn and canola oil, is going to be more promoting than an estrogenic fat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For 80 or 90 years, about every 10 or 15 years, someone has done a study showing that the more polyunsaturated fat in the diet, the higher the cancer incidence. It goes all the way down to extremely rare cancer incidents when there's no polyunsaturated fat in the diet.

**Andrew Murray:** Cancer is obviously one of those effects of decreasing energy. Because of the thyroid-suppressing effects [of PUFA], there is a direct relationship between low energy and the ability for systems to lose their correct structure and organization.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the diet factors that shows up repeatedly in association with a low rate of cancer is a high fruit intake. Fruit eaters, getting the carbohydrate and the sugar, produce saturated fats of their own. So they keep a relatively high saturation index in their tissues.

**Andrew Murray:** It's always mystified me how HRT (Hormone Replacement Therapy) has carried on for such a long time. Now they're finally admitting that saturated fats are actually better for you than polys, but HRT is still a concept. How did it come to a position where estrogen was promoted as beneficial for bones and age-related dementia, when you have evidence to show it's actually the opposite?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a very good essay on the internet, a Harvard Law School paper by Carla Rothenberg on the history of hormone replacement therapy. It gives the political and economic history of how the 12 big estrogen companies in 1942 got together to basically take over the FDA, medical journals, and universities to indoctrinate the idea that estrogen was the female hormone that would promote fertility and all the good female virtues. This went absolutely against the research of the 1930s, which showed that progesterone was the essential female hormone that promoted fertility and good pregnancy success.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They knew back in the 1800s that the chimney sweeps would die of testicular cancer from the estrogenic effects of the soot.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but this was all turned around by these 12 giant companies getting together to promote the idea of estrogen as the beneficial female hormone. A Harvard husband and wife pair of doctors promoted the idea that you should give pregnant women estrogen to prevent miscarriage. That produced two generations of DES babies; their daughters also were susceptible to cancer.

After the news got out by the late 50s that estrogen was not good for preventing miscarriage, they came out with the contraception idea. They knew in the 30s that estrogen causes miscarriages and abortion, so they sold it for the opposite as long as they could get away with it, then came on the market to sell it to prevent or interrupt pregnancies.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So a lot of contraceptive pills allow fertilization to occur, but inhibit implantation?
