title: Ask the Herb Doctor: California SB 277 / Degradation of the Food Supply
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbal medicines and dietary advice. You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD Garberville, 91.1 FM.

From 7:30 until the end of the show at 8:00, you're invited to call in with questions related to this month's subject: California SB277, as well as the degradation of the food supply. Both are intimately linked; causal effects come from many different places and add up to a decreased quality of life for most people. We're very welcome to have Dr. Raymond Peat joining us on the show this evening. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us again. I know we went over vaccination back in June of 2014. We ran through the introduction of vaccines and mentioned that disease was already in a threefold decline before their introduction due to good food, increased sanitation, and clean water, especially in industrialized countries.

Moving on to what has been described as another bill to wipe out yet more choice, California's Bill 277 seeks to impose mandatory vaccination with no religious or ethical exemptions. This bill only came out yesterday, so it's a last-minute topic for us. We are also going to get into the degraded food chain later, but it all amounts to a decreased health perspective for most people. Would you please start by letting people know your scientific and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My PhD is from the University of Oregon in biology in 1972. I've taught in a few different institutions—State University of Mexico, Veracruz University, and two or three schools in the United States—teaching a variety of science courses, including immunology. Even though I didn't specialize in it, I learned what's going on in the immune system, and that teaching got me interested in following the development.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding Senate Bill 277, it abolishes most opt-outs. I think the only exemption permitted is for immunocompromised children—maybe receiving chemotherapy or immunosuppression drugs—but there will be no choice for people who don't believe the science is pointing in the right direction. Last June, we talked about studies done by the World Health Organization. Dr. Peat, why don't you bring that out again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The World Health Organization did this around 1970. They took three villages in Guatemala. They left one as a control population. To the second, they sent the regular public health team with vaccination and chlorinated water—the usual minimal public health things. To the third, they provided a nutritional supplement to all the pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and children.

Relative to the control village that didn't have any doctors or help, the health in the medically treated village got worse by several measurements. The health in the village that simply got the nutritional supplement was generally better, and the kids were bigger, healthier, and more intelligent.

**Andrew Murray:** So the World Health Organization concluded that the far cheaper and easier thing to do was to use vaccination as a standard of care?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but that isn't a popular thing with the world pharmaceutical industry because they want to sell drugs rather than food.

**Andrew Murray:** California is going to be one of only three states that have mandatory forced vaccination with no opt-outs, the others being Mississippi and West Virginia. For anyone who wants to find out more, visit  to see the senators involved and their funding from Merck.

In terms of the schedule, there are going to be 34 to 36 vaccines mandated by age six, and a total of 69 vaccines scheduled for a child through their teenage years. Dr. Peat, what has been shown in the scientific research regarding healthy standards of living versus vaccination?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The history of looking at the relation of vaccination to disease incidence and mortality goes back more than 100 years. Ivan Illich was one of the first people to do a survey of that research. Suzanne Humphries’ website is a good introduction to that perspective. She also has information on the actual effect of the vaccine material on the baby's immune system and the need for a completely new look at what the immune system is.

There is a relatively new approach called the "danger theory," in which the body is really reacting to the disruption of its tissues. The immune system is there to repair and compensate for the injury. From this point of view, it just happens that the infectious agent gets in the way of that repair process, and it's incidental to what the immune system is doing.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they could just be injecting mercury, aluminum, and other immune system irritants and get the same effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, to a great extent. Suzanne Humphries mentions a study in which they used an actual placebo control rather than a different vaccine—injecting just water versus the vaccine. They didn't see any difference in the specific infection rate for the disease the vaccine was aimed at, but they saw six or seven times greater incidence of *other* infections in the vaccinated kids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** There are organizations now saying that vaccinated children are less healthy than unvaccinated children. It's hard to do a study like this because there are so many vaccinated children and not many unvaccinated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And there is not likely to be any funding to do that kind of study.

**Andrew Murray:** The companies that produce vaccines are indemnified by the government against any and all damage arising out of their use. "First, do no harm," yet you can produce a product and not be held liable when it damages someone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, do you think that unvaccinated children are at risk socializing with vaccinated children?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are cases in which a vaccinated child has spread the vaccine organism—where they use a live polio virus—and the vaccinated kid has infected unvaccinated people. But the senators getting that bill passed were claiming that the unvaccinated children are putting everyone at risk. If most of the kids are vaccinated, aren't they protected? The reasoning seems absolutely crazy. You can't put them at risk if they're protected. Apparently, the senator didn't believe that the vaccines are protecting anyone.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's make the link between degraded food and declining health. It is estimated that starch provides about 70 to 80% of the calories consumed by humans worldwide. Why is that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think cheapness is the main factor. Even dietitians are taught to promote a certain amount of starch. Starting in the 1930s, the US government designed and taught dietitians to promote three levels of nutrition:
1. To simply prevent starvation, emphasizing beans and cereals.
2. A middle-class, more health-oriented diet.
3. The rich person's diet with plenty of animal protein.

Originally, it was valuable to hungry people to know how to get by on a few cents a day for beans and grains. But for economic reasons, the breakfast cereal industry subsidized nutrition journals and taught dietitians to say that these things are healthful. The foods that were originally promoted just to survive are now called health foods.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's gone full circle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, so the rich people are now indoctrinated to eat whole grain bread.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned some pioneering work done by Gerhard Volkheimer regarding starches. Would you describe that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He rediscovered work that had been done 70 or 80 years earlier called **persorption** of particles. Ordinary digestion theory says that even proteins are broken down in the intestine and absorbed as small molecules (amino acids). Volkheimer and his predecessors showed that if you feed starch consisting of naturally formed starch grains—which can range from half the diameter of a red blood cell to about 10 times the diameter—they are much too big to pass through the smallest arterioles.

He demonstrated with people and mice that if you feed a slurry of corn starch and draw blood 15 minutes later, you can find the starch particles in the bloodstream. Later, they show up in the urine and cerebrospinal fluid. He found that it caused mice to age prematurely. When he examined the mice, he found that wherever a starch grain lodged in an arteriole or capillary, the surrounding cells would be starved of nutrients and die. It was like a shotgun working internally, killing little pockets of cells.

**Andrew Murray:** And this affects the immune system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Volkheimer was an immunologist. If big particles get into the bloodstream, they come in contact with the immune system. The simple fact that big particles are in the body means our immune system is constantly being exposed to antigens.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the foods to avoid would be grains and any starchy food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the starch is very well cooked—like boiling it for 40 to 60 minutes—and then eaten with fat, the fat slows down the absorption and allows the digestive enzymes to soften it up so it doesn't get through the intestine without being broken down.

**Andrew Murray:** Presumably, most people's intestines are inflamed from poor diets, making them more at risk for this passage of starch granules.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and that inflammation weakens the barrier function. It becomes a vicious circle. Two nutrients important in stopping that circle are magnesium and vitamin A, both of which are dependent on having adequate protein in the diet.

**Andrew Murray:** You advocate plenty of butter with potatoes for this reason?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And having digestive enzymes produced abundantly requires good total nutrition and thyroid function.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you have low thyroid function, you have low hydrochloric acid, making it hard to break down food.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All the little glands in the digestive system slow down.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** In Mexico, for thousands of years, corn has been prepared specifically to help this.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even in my parents' and grandparents' generation, bread making was different. Letting it rise for 8 or 10 hours, the slow leavening process activated enzymes that broke down the starches into sugar and broke down the gluten. This can actually increase the protein by 100 or 200%. Similarly, boiling corn with lime (nixtamalization) decreases toxins and increases nutrients. Since about 1940, the bread industry discovered they could make instant bread by adding chemicals to blow it up.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the air.

**Caller:** I wanted to mention spinal meningitis. My child contracted it when antibiotics didn't work on an ear infection. I believe that is a dangerous disease. However, I've also known parents whose children were paralyzed by the pertussis vaccine. You might want to read the book *The Poisoned Needle*.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you. We are trying not to get into too many specifics due to time.

**Caller (Missouri):** Is there a difference between the starch in white rice and the starch in potatoes? Also, I've heard you say potatoes have high-quality protein. If I eat well-cooked potatoes with butter and a protein like meat, does the body secrete more enzymes effective in breaking down those starch molecules compared to eating just white rice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Norman Pirie wrote a good book on the quality of plant proteins. He rated rice at about 6% value compared to egg yolk at 100%. Leaf protein is about 70%. The protein in potato was about 105%—slightly better than egg yolk. So it is roughly 15 or 20 times better than rice or bean protein.

Regarding the starch grain: the potato grain is one of the biggest, about 100 microns in diameter. Rice starch grains are down around 10 microns.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you think eating protein with the potato increases the enzymatic digestion of the starch?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the potato is very well cooked, it has such high-quality protein that people subsist very well on a pure potato diet. In New Guinea, traditional diets consisted of potatoes for 50 weeks of the year, with pork eaten only during feasts. These people were found to be well-muscled and healthy, as if they had been eating a perfectly balanced diet.

**Caller (Missouri):** Is it possible for a stomach to adapt to secrete specific enzymes if you eat that food for a long time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just in a few months, a person's digestive system will adapt considerably. In animal experiments, if they eat a highly nutritious diet, the intestine is small. If they eat a poor, high-starch, high-fiber diet, the intestine grows in length and mass—almost like producing an organ specifically for the type of food they're eating.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** A good way to get the protein out of the potato is to juice it. You juice a raw potato, let the starch granules sink to the bottom (which looks like corn starch), pour off the clear liquid, and cook that liquid. It cooks up like scrambled eggs. For a vegetarian, that is high-quality protein.

**Caller (North Carolina):** Is there a way to process beans, perhaps with an alkali, to transmute the negative effects of the starch?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can find information on nixtamalizing beans. I've never tried it, but some people say it works.

**Andrew Murray:** Would it negate the phytates?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it does liberate the minerals from the phytic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Soaking beans is a traditional way to prepare them. Soaking for three days activates enzymes that help break down toxins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That increases the protein value greatly. As they approach sprouting, the storage protein turns to growth protein, which is less toxic and more nutritious.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what do you think of xanthan and carrageenan gums?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, the food industry wanted to add various gums. The FDA looked at the evidence and said they weren't appropriate for food. But 40 or 50 years later, the industry had more power over the FDA. Now they use synthetic gums which are cheaper.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I tell people that additives in dairy, like gums, are often what irritate their intestines, not the dairy itself. Even organic brands have these gums.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they are gradually getting away from carrageenan, which is a powerful allergen and inflammation promoter. Degraded carrageenan is widely recognized as a carcinogen. The industry has promoted the idea that "resistant starches" are health foods because they feed bacteria to produce butyric acid, supposedly preventing bowel cancer. But in fact, absorbing these broken-down products causes changes in the brain and nervous system.

**Caller:** Does it matter which kind of potato we eat? I like Yukon Golds.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Each variety varies in the quantity of starch relative to protein, but the whole family has high-quality protein. The digestibility is the main difference. High carotene content (yellow color) can make them hard to digest for some people.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And if the skins turn green, that is a toxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, solanine. It's a nightshade poison.

**Caller (Honeydew):** Doesn't too much starch cause acid in your stomach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main function of acid in the stomach is digesting proteins. The stomach judges how much acid to secrete in proportion to the amount of protein it senses. Starch doesn't necessarily stimulate acid production, but it might be irritating if it is hard to digest. If it passes through the intestine without breaking down, it can support bacterial or fungal growth.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what do you think of lecithin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When it comes from eggs produced by well-fed chickens, it's okay. But now it all comes from soybeans. Soybeans are highly unsaturated fat, so it's a way of getting too much PUFA (polyunsaturated fatty acids) into your system. A trace amount, like in a chocolate bar, is harmless.

**Andrew Murray:** We are almost out of time. To wrap up, there are many ingredients in food people aren't aware of: aluminum phosphate, propyl gallate, potassium bromate. It gets worse and worse.

For those who want to know more about Dr. Peat, his website is . He has plenty of fully referenced articles there. He's been doing this for at least 45 years. Thanks so much for joining us, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks to our callers and KMUD. Good night.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I got my PhD in biology, specializing in physiology and biochemistry, especially reproductive physiology, at the University of Oregon in 1972. Before that, I had been interested in language, philosophy, and psychology and planned to study brain biology. I found that reproductive physiology seemed more scientific and interesting, so I specialized in that but continued to be interested in the rest of the organism.

The first thing I did after graduating was to write a book on the brain, reviewing Russian science from the 19th through the 20th century on brain biology. I've continued my interest in how basic energy physiology relates to things such as reproduction, aging, and brain functions.

**Andrew Murray:** In your most recent newsletter, you continued your discourse on urea and its use in pathology. You discussed how you see the function of urea benefiting people, despite it perhaps being dismissed by mainstream medical science. You mentioned Danopoulos, the Greek physician who has been successfully using urea as a therapy, injecting it into tumors for cancer. But this newsletter explores other physiological effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Doctor, can you tell us what urea is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Its chemical name is carbamide. It's just a combination of ammonia with carbon dioxide. It is the body's way of detoxifying ammonia, and it requires the oxidative production of carbon dioxide to combine with the ammonia to get rid of it. It regulates cell pH, which regulates water metabolism and everything else in cell function.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's something that our bodies produce.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Given that we understand that excess water in the cell is a central feature of major degenerative diseases like heart failure, dementia, and cancer, how do you explain how this happens? What is the best strategy to prevent this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thinking about water and cells comes up against some of the basic dogmas of what life is and how cells work. I think the reason Danopoulos' amazing results in curing cancer with simply injecting or giving intravenous urea have been ignored is that it involves ideas that don't fit with the mechanical dogmas of 20th-century biology.

The main dogma is the membrane theory—the idea that there are pumps in cell surface membranes that regulate the amount of water and minerals by somehow grabbing molecules and pushing them in or out. It's really a silly, impossible concept, but it's what everything officially is based on.

If you look at the facts of what's happening with water, think in terms of what happens when gelatin gets wet. If you put acid or alkali on it, its relation to water changes. Acid makes it shrink; alkali makes it swell up. Simple physical ideas like that are very useful for thinking about what happens in diseases.

**Andrew Murray:** You said acid makes it shrink and alkaline situations make it swell.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Swelling has an anabolic effect and turns on cell division. Uncontrollable cell division can produce everything from cancer to various skin diseases like dandruff, psoriasis, or an overgrowth of fibrous tissue. The control of cell growth is deeply controlled by water and pH.

People blame everything on this magical membrane pump, but if you think about basic metabolic processes—turning sugar, fat, or protein into energy and carbon dioxide—this constant streaming of substance produces carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is an acid. When you're alive, you are making cells acidic inside. As it leaves, it takes minerals out of the cell with it in the form of carbonic acid and the alkaline minerals associated with it.

**Andrew Murray:** This is a better state than the alkaline state, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The acidic state produced by carbon dioxide causes a shift in the whole balance of electrons in the protein, fat, and nucleic acid system. That shift of electrons accounts for the preference of the cell for potassium over sodium. If the cell is disturbed, it shifts, loses potassium, and takes up calcium and sodium. This is what Gilbert Ling has devoted his life to for the last 60-some years.

**Andrew Murray:** I think laypeople often associate an "acid" situation as cancer-promoting and "alkaline" as beneficial.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's true when you apply it to the blood and the fluid *outside* of cells. But the reason the fluid outside of cells is alkaline is that the protons—the electrons—are being retracted into an acidic state *inside* the cell. That shifts the balance and makes it alkaline outside.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when the inside of the cell becomes alkaline, that's when it becomes swollen and boggy, contributing to heart disease, cancer, and psoriasis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, along with a shift towards acidity in the blood and the outside fluid. When people say you don't want to be acidic metabolically, that refers to the fluids outside of cells. It's only since nuclear magnetic resonance apparatuses have been used in the last 40 years that people have started to recognize that inside cells should be slightly acidic.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How do we make the inside of our cells more acidic and keep the outside alkaline?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By keeping the energy flowing and producing carbon dioxide constantly by consuming oxygen. If you suffocate or turn off the oxygen supply, you stop making a steady supply of carbon dioxide. The metabolism shifts over to making lactic acid. The lactic acid takes acid out of the cell as it leaves, acidifying the environment but leaving the cell interior more alkaline.

**Andrew Murray:** And that's the negative acidic situation most people refer to.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's a local inflammatory situation. Anytime a tissue is injured, it tends to produce excess lactic acid and become inflamed and inefficient.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How does urea help our cells use oxygen better or keep the cell more acidic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cell holds its structure by the way proteins are folded, which requires an interaction with the slightly acidic state—making carbon dioxide and keeping the ATP level at a high energy state. This keeps the water participating in the way proteins are folded so that there's a lot of internal surface area exposed.

You know how the surface of a glass of water has a sort of rubbery film, surface tension, where you can float a piece of steel? Inside the cell, when the proteins are energized, the ATP holds them in a state exposing their surface, keeping the cell water in that energized, tough state that holds the cell together.

When it's de-energized, the structure collapses. Spherical proteins that were exposing all their surface polymerize into stalk-like proteins with less surface exposure. The water becomes more like plain bulk water. That kind of water is involved in cell swelling and uncontrolled cell division.

**Andrew Murray:** The pH inside a cell also regulates the protein's folding ability, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the case of any protein jelly, even some synthetic plastics, alkalinity has the effect of making the jelly swell up and become watery and soft.

**Andrew Murray:** So again, an alkaline internal environment is not helpful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Urea happens to be a strange kind of solvent that is pretty much equally at home inside and outside the cells, but it's slightly *more* at home in a healthy, stable cell. Just by solubility, if you immerse cells in a solution with urea, the urea will come to rest at a higher concentration inside the cells. No pumping is involved. Inside the cell, it participates with the energized state, helping proteins expose the surface that keeps cells in a high-energy state.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's how Danopoulos helped with cancer? By injecting urea, it helped cells maintain their shape and function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and to keep it towards the slightly acidic metabolizing state in which it doesn't tend to proliferate—a relatively slightly dehydrated effect. When you have the right amount of urea mixed with proteins, fats, and water, it creates a new state of matter that has its own solubility properties, including the preference for potassium over sodium and magnesium over calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** You stated that urea itself is not an osmolyte and does not affect pH, is that right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's been known for over 100 years. People used semipermeable membranes and found it doesn't behave like sodium or potassium, which pull water across a membrane. Around World War I, it was demonstrated that you could make urea five or six times more concentrated than it should be osmotically, and it would be in balance and not cause cells to lose water. If you had that concentration of sugar or salt, you would dry up.

**Andrew Murray:** And you mentioned that concentration is very low toxicity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sea organisms, like sharks, have a very high level of urea. Experiments have shown that even more than 100 times what we normally have doesn't cause damage to cells. Therapeutically, Danopoulos found that maybe a hundred times our normal serum urea level is therapeutic for things like cancer and brain function.

**Andrew Murray:** The scientific community seems to play down urea or use analogues which are problematic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sickle cell anemia, for example, was being treated successfully with urea. Normal cells under stress tend to harden the way sickle cells become stiff. During heart surgery, stress causes ordinary red blood cells to stiffen and malfunction. With a supplement of urea, that hardening is prevented.

However, because of the myth of urea being an osmolyte, someone used plain urea without the normal sodium and minerals in the solution. It caused red blood cells to break down immediately. They said, "That can't be good," stopped using it, and shifted over to the very toxic, carcinogenic hydroxyurea, which is still in use.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do you know doctors that use real urea currently?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A few people are using it, for example, to prevent killing patients in heart surgery, but it definitely isn't a well-recognized treatment.

**Andrew Murray:** To clarify, urea in the absence of other electrolytes acts like distilled water regarding osmotic property?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It would take about six times as much urea as normal to not break down the red cells.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about taking it orally?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's been done for over 100 years, treating heart failure. One person reported having heart failure patients doing well on oral urea for as long as nine years.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this because it's a diuretic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was the argument—that it relieved swollen legs in congestive heart failure. But since you also see it bringing people back from brain damage in traumatic head injury and strokes, I think it has much deeper therapeutic effects, stabilizing cells in many ways, not just reducing swelling by causing diuresis.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you have any opinion on traditional diuretics versus urea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mercury was a traditional diuretic, and it apparently worked just by killing the tubes of the kidney and letting the water fall out of the body. I think some chemical diuretics are about as well-founded as mercury. Diuretic chemicals that make the kidneys give up more water don't necessarily improve the person's health.

Any stress involves a series of reactions, all of which relate to the way cells handle water. Nitric oxide is universally produced by injury and stress, and it causes de-energizing and swelling of cells. Estrogen is a physiological producer of swelling, imitating a stress reaction. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is another stress-induced producer of water retention.

Old people and hospitalized trauma patients often develop water retention with sodium loss—hyponatremia, or the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion. Estrogen produces the same effect. Nitric oxide, estrogen, and ADH produce a state of getting waterlogged while losing sodium into the urine.

The normal regulator of carbon dioxide—and thus sodium/water balance—is the thyroid hormone. Hypothyroid people always tend towards this syndrome of being waterlogged and losing sodium. Sodium itself, sodium chloride or sodium bicarbonate, can cure a lot of these stress conditions.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think the same waterlogging could happen in a boggy intestine that fails to move food, contributing to endotoxin reabsorption?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The intestine is especially exposed to things such as endotoxin, which release nitric oxide, causing this de-energizing, swelling effect.

**Andrew Murray:** So bicarbonate of soda would be a good way of liberating CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Surprisingly, even sodium chloride has a diuretic effect in most people. When you use baking soda, the kidneys are able to retain as much sodium as they want, but the bicarbonate can be changed back into carbon dioxide and actually help to acidify cells on the inside while maintaining the sodium on the outside.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people can just swallow a quarter or half teaspoon mixed with water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I know people who have taken a teaspoon two or three times a day with water for many years. Athletes sometimes take a tablespoon with water before an endurance race. I think part of the effect on endurance is helping to prevent excess nitric oxide production.

**Andrew Murray:** Are endurance runners who collapse from cardiac arrest often hyponatremic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that's probably the most common reason for endurance runners collapsing and dying.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding aging and skin, young people have plump, healthy skin. As we age, keratin production increases. Is there anything that can be done to improve skin quality related to water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Plumpness is largely the water content. A fertilized ovum is 92% water; an old cell gets down to about 65% water. As that happens, cell division slows. In old skin, there are fewer cells, so it is thinner.

The piling up of collapsed, keratinized cells accumulates in old skin. This maturing process comes on prematurely with aging or stress. For example, a vitamin A deficiency will cause premature keratinizing. Estrogen does this normally in mucous membranes—first causing faster growth due to water uptake, but then increased keratin formation and hardening.

You can offset some effects of aging and estrogen by supplementing vitamin A, vitamin E, and urea directly into the skin. Old skin has much less urea than young skin, which is likely both a cause and effect of lower water content.

**Caller:** My dad is in the hospital with CHF (Congestive Heart Failure) and dementia. He's on a diuretic and Gabapentin. His lactic acid was normal, but creatinine was not. Would oral urea be better for him, and can he take it with the furosemide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can find articles on PubMed about the use of urea in heart failure comparing it to other diuretics.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would that be something he could use orally?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very tasteless, maybe a little salty. It's usually taken with orange juice or grapefruit juice. A small amount, anywhere from a fourth of a teaspoon to a teaspoon per glass.

**Caller:** Would it be okay to take that with the diuretic he is already prescribed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think it interferes with the diuretics; it just makes them unnecessary.

**Caller:** What should one ingest to make the cells more acidic on the inside and the blood more alkaline on the outside?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Getting adequate protein in your diet is probably the thing that makes the biggest difference. You can measure the increased output of urea in the urine in proportion to the amount of protein you're eating. If your digestion and thyroid function are good, eating protein helps.

**Caller:** Is red meat good for that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Meat is very high in phosphate, so it shouldn't be too high. Gelatin is good as a supplement—making soup with collagenous joint tissue like oxtail or shank. It's better to get a big part of your protein from other foods such as eggs, milk, cheese, and high-quality vegetables like potatoes and mushrooms.

**Caller:** You mentioned sodium chloride. Is salt good for your heart?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Salting your food to taste is the best way to tell. In people who are under stress, for example, women with toxemia of pregnancy, salt helps. I saw the same problems existing in women in their 20s and men in their 80s—inflammatory high blood pressure symptoms. I suggested they salt their food to taste instead of a low sodium diet.

**Caller:** I've been taught salt causes high blood pressure and water retention.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They've disproven that. They only started saying you shouldn't eat salt when they wanted to sell diuretics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The blood volume gets oxygen and nutrients to the kidneys and keeps them working.

**Caller:** What about gout? Is that caused by too much meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doctors aren't too sure what it is either. People can have a lot of uric acid crystals without symptoms. It seems to be endotoxin from an inflamed intestine getting deposited on the crystals causing symptoms. Urea is protective against uric acid.

**Caller:** I've had water retention problems since I was pregnant with my first child 45 years ago. I have an underactive thyroid and take levothyroxine, but I still swell up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For quite a while, it's been known that estrogen interferes with the conversion of levothyroxine (T4) into the active hormone (T3). That accounts for why women have about five times as much thyroid problems as men. Illogically, doctors prescribe thyroxine to women without measuring the liver function of producing the active hormone T3.

**Andrew Murray:** It sounds like you're not converting the hormone because of high estrogen. You'd be better off using a T3 supplement. Even if your TSH test is "normal," your symptoms—low temperature, weight gain, insomnia—indicate otherwise.

**Caller:** Is drinking your own urine a good way to get urea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know quite a few people who have done it and seem to be very healthy. It's been practiced for three or four thousand years. However, I think most people would prefer to use the purified chemical rather than their own urine.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's quickly talk about psoriasis, urea, and inflammatory bowel disease. Is there a parallel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One thing to consider when you have both bowel and skin symptoms is that the bowel is actually causing the skin problem. Eliminating gluten, for example, sometimes clears up both because some of the same enzymes activated by inflammation cause the premature hardening of the skin in psoriasis.

The process of psoriasis is an accelerated cell division, probably caused by over-hydration and possibly a lack of the right balance of estrogen, progesterone, and thyroid. Vitamin A and D can restrain the rate of multiplication.

Urea has been demonstrated to delay or prevent that premature hardening process by governing gene expression, keeping the cell in a vital state longer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So urea can be injected, taken orally, or rubbed on topically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There are creams available containing 5% to 40% urea. A 40% solution is very effective for treating psoriasis and ichthyosis. Some pharmacists might scare you saying it removes fingernails, but the 40% solutions are very soothing and therapeutic. It is now widely used for treating skin inflammation in breast cancer patients exposed to X-rays.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to hold it there. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for your time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who want to find out more about Dr. Peat, visit www.raypeat.com. He has a wide reading list of fully referenced published material.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: On The Back of a Tiger
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed herbalists who trained in England. We recommend personalized advice in nutrition, supplements, herbs, diet, and lifestyle. Tonight is a little departure from the last few years. We are hosting two filmmakers, Brad Abrahams and Jeremy Stewart, who are producing a documentary film called *On the Back of a Tiger*. They have interviewed eight maverick scientists, including Dr. Ray Peat, weaving an alternate story of life from the molecular level to consciousness and perception. They challenge mainstream medical dogma with scientific research, illuminating radical new ways of understanding disease and its treatment. Welcome, Brad and Jeremy.

**Brad Abrahams:** Thanks for the great intro. It sums it up nicely.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And welcome, Dr. Peat, to the show.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hello.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, we have been fortunate to interview you for a number of years. You frequently mention eminent scientists and groundbreaking alternative researchers whose view of mainstream medicine runs contrary to the dogma perpetuated by Big Pharma. Brad and Jeremy have been traveling Europe to track down these scientists. I want to cover the timeline of these interviews, but first, I’d like to ask Brad and Jeremy to outline their professional and academic backgrounds.

**Brad Abrahams:** My background and Jeremy's are quite similar. We both went to film school and soon after graduating entered the advertising and commercial production world. We were trapped there for many years, pining away, trying to figure out a way to work on projects that were more meaningful to us. You can't do that with a full-time job; it takes up so much creative and physical energy. We ended up quitting, still working freelance for funds, but spending more of our time on projects like this. We have focused specifically on this project for the last year.

**Andrew Murray:** Did you have any background reasons for pursuing this health topic?

**Jeremy Stewart:** We are both sort of sensitive people regarding what we eat and the environment. Some people are maybe more hypothyroid than others, as Ray might say. That is how we became friends while working together—reading *World's Healthiest Foods* and realizing we had a lot in common. Seeing health problems in friends and family who couldn't find solutions was always in the background.

**Brad Abrahams:** For myself, it was originally things like really bad digestion, allergies, and fatigue. A lot of it came from overworking and the confines of the modern world. More recently, it has been seeing the deteriorating health of family and friends, particularly my father, who was diagnosed with Alzheimer's. I was already skeptical of the medical establishment, but seeing the bad science and suspect motives with this disease really spurred a sense of urgency.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How did you first find out about Dr. Peat?

**Brad Abrahams:** Originally through Danny Roddy. I had been on the roller coaster of diets and found Danny's site, which mentioned Dr. Peat. I found it fascinating that someone was looking at health and nutrition starting at the molecular level and having such a solid grasp of the biochemistry. The work is dense, so it took a couple of years of reading, listening, and self-experimentation to really grasp the unique view.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, for listeners who haven't heard our show before, what is your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was studying art and literature as an undergraduate and did my master's thesis mostly on William Blake. I was interested in life in general and saw biology as a way to get concrete facts that would confirm alternative views. I saw dogma and political opinions influencing what was teachable in the humanities, and I thought real science might have relevance there.

As soon as I enrolled at the University of Oregon to work on a PhD in biology, I realized that biology was exactly as unscientific as linguistics or philosophy. Ideology was right at the center of nerve biology. I wrote to Gilbert Ling in 1968 and told him what my professors were teaching—things he had shown to be profoundly wrong 20 years previously. He answered and said, "You just don't understand what science is. Science is all about prestige and money."

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What year was that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 1968. After a few more months working with the nerve biology people, I found that the reproductive biologist was actually a scientist. When I observed things contrary to the dogma, he asked, "Is it repeatable? Then go ahead." However, the nerve biologist wouldn't even look at the experiments I was doing. All my experiments showed something contrary to the nerve dogma, and my professor would turn away so he didn't have to see what the instruments were showing.

**Andrew Murray:** That is the thrust of tonight's show. Brad and Jeremy have produced a fantastic movie clip showing the different people they've interviewed. These are all PhDs, professors, and research scientists who are directly refuting long-held tenets of science. You can find out more at . Let's go through the different scientists. How did the idea to interview these specific people come about?

**Brad Abrahams:** It was the original phone conversation with Dr. Peat. He asked if we had thought about talking to Harold Hillman or Mae-Wan Ho. We started diving deeper into their work and realized there is a much larger story to tell. Ray has connected the dots and woven together what seem like disparate theories into a cohesive new model for the workings of life.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's start with Harold Hillman.

**Brad Abrahams:** We started filming with Harold Hillman around April 15th of last year. The crux of his work is his criticism of traditional microscopy and the use of the electron microscope. He argues that most of the structures we see are artifacts caused by the processing that once-living material must go through. It would make your head spin hearing him list the dehydration, dyeing, and smashing involved. What you are left with bears almost no resemblance to a living cell.

**Jeremy Stewart:** He made a film you can find on YouTube. He shows a side-by-side of a living cell, which looks like a transparent blob, and then the same cell after being washed in alcohol and other compounds, looking about a third of the size, squashed and squiggly.

**Brad Abrahams:** His work was so difficult to criticize that people would just leave the room when he spoke at scientific conferences.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a famous Swedish electron microscopy expert named Fritiof Sjöstrand who did a lot of very clear explanations using different fixatives, showing how profound the artifacts are in standard preparations. He was a mainstream researcher, but the mainstream simply overlooked his work on the artifacts.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move to Dr. Mae-Wan Ho.

**Jeremy Stewart:** She has covered a lot of topics, including controversies on GMOs, but we talked to her about her study of quantum biology and the crystalline structure of organisms. She used a microscope generally used in geology that utilizes polarized light. She found that small organisms had the same sort of crystalline structure as rocks, but in liquid form. This fits in with structured water and thinking about the organism in a way that is counter to the mechanistic views of science. She wrote the book *The Rainbow and the Worm*.

**Brad Abrahams:** Those findings connected with criticisms against Neo-Darwinism. If the organism is not fundamentally mechanistic but much more fluid and subtle, it supports theories more in line with Sidney Fox and others.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That image of the worm is one of the most important things people should start thinking about regarding quantum biology. I think Albert Szent-Györgyi was the one who motivated people to start going in the direction of electronic biology and a coherent view of the cell. Mae-Wan Ho is, to a great degree, an extension of some of Szent-Györgyi's ideas.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to Dr. Gerald Pollack, often called the "Water Wizard."

**Jeremy Stewart:** He is known for his TED Talk and his focus on structured water. He is unpopular in his department because he studies something that seems like it should have already been figured out. He shows that there are unusual, electrically based forms of water called EZ water—the Exclusion Zone. Water builds up on a surface and purifies itself, excluding everything else. This seems to be how water is structured inside cells.

**Brad Abrahams:** He found that one of the substances that creates EZ water with the most affinity is aspirin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything he has been doing in recent years is extremely interesting. He has developed theories on how light energy, specifically infrared, is used in building structure in water. There is a young German named Andrei Sommer who is working with red light structuring water—a very concrete demonstration of what Gerald is working on.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that why red light is so anti-inflammatory? Because of its effects on the water of the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think that's part of it.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's talk about Dr. Gilbert Ling.

**Brad Abrahams:** Gilbert is 96. When we saw him, he was in shockingly good health, though recently he had a complication. He is most known for disproving the sodium pump hypothesis, which is at the root of all taught physiology regarding the role of the cell membrane. His hypothesis, the Association Induction Hypothesis, details a totally different model of the cell based only on physics and chemistry.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cell membrane theory relates to Neo-Darwinism and the idea that life is like a machine which has to run to keep itself in a given state. Gilbert Ling showed that even if you turn off the energy supply, a cell is stable for many hours. The sodium keeps going in and out, but the cell retains the lifelike imbalance between sodium and potassium.

In an electron microscope course I took, I tried different fixatives based on Sjöstrand's publications. Simply by using a different fixative, my cells were nothing but membranes all the way through. I looked at the origin of the membrane concept and found that 19th-century doctors treated ulcers and burns with osmic acid (osmium tetroxide) to create what they called a "false membrane." The first preparations for electron microscopy showed no membranes, but scientists believed there *had* to be membranes. Someone recalled that old medical concept, applied osmic acid to living cells, and created a membrane.

**Jeremy Stewart:** Anytime there is a new thing that goes in and out of the cell, they have to create a new pump to explain it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you wash all the ions out of hair and dip the hair in serum, it picks up the proper ions and excludes sodium. So apparently, dead hair has all the necessary working pumps.

**Andrew Murray:** Who is Dr. Michael Persinger?

**Jeremy Stewart:** He studies parapsychology and has done a huge amount of work on the effects of fields on life and consciousness. He is known for the "God Helmet" experiment, showing that electromagnetic stimulation of the right hemisphere induced a "sensed presence" in people. He has done decades of work showing how sensitive life is to electromagnetic fields.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what is your take on Dr. Persinger?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My interest in fields goes way back. My brother was a radio ham, so I had access to electronic equipment from age nine. In 1968, I went to Russia to talk to a man working in magneto-biology. One of my first experiments at the university was looking at the effect of a strong magnet on a crab nerve. I could see that the presence of a magnetic field affected the structure of the water and the delay between stimulation and reaction. Very subtle fields have very big effects on organisms.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's discuss Dr. Fred Kummerow, who is 100 years old.

**Brad Abrahams:** He looks even better than you’d imagine—no age spots, full head of hair. He is known for his 60-year crusade against trans fats. What is not reported is that he says very similar things about polyunsaturated fats. When we told him fish oil is sold as supplements, he physically recoiled. He is horrified that a billion-dollar industry is harming people's health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Trans fats normally occur in butter as an intermediate stage. The next step is Conjugated Linoleic Acid (CLA). The beneficial effects of CLA block some of the toxic effects of normal linoleic acid. So, even though butter contains some trans fats, it also contains the beneficial form.

**Brad Abrahams:** Dr. Kummerow's criticism is about the artificially created trans fats, not the natural ones in dairy. He likes butter.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to Danny Roddy.

**Jeremy Stewart:** There are two sides to the film: the scientists and the "health seekers." Danny is a health blogger focused on hair loss. He has no formal academic background but has learned an incredible amount on his own.

**Brad Abrahams:** He has been on the roller coaster many of us relate to. He has the gift of taking complex scientific theories and translating them so anyone can understand them.

**Andrew Murray:** You also interviewed Dr. Peat. It seems he unifies the theories of all these different scientists.

**Jeremy Stewart:** Working scientists usually focus on a tiny area and aren't fully aware of the larger context. Ray’s work puts all these people into a paradigm that makes sense together in a holistic view.

**Brad Abrahams:** What is the worth of scientific inquiry if you can't apply it practically to people's health? That is where Dr. Peat's work resonates with us.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat helps people take their health into their own hands. He encourages them to look at how they feel after they eat certain foods.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, can you comment on the film?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The bits I have seen are very much fun to watch. It is good to see the newer stuff about Gilbert Ling and the others.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you all for being here. Listeners can find more about the film at . My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For more information, visit . Goodnight.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Longevity and Nootropics
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this evening's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us. As always, Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us on the show. Tonight's subject is longevity and brain foods. Dr. Peat's latest newsletter is on cognition, which is a continuing theme of his, and we want to bring out some new thoughts surrounding that. Dr. Peat, are you there with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Just so that people who perhaps have never listened to the show or have never heard you, would you give an outline of your academic and professional background before we get into tonight's subject?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied humanities first, largely at the University of Oregon, a year at Ohio State, and some in Mexico. Then I went to the University of Oregon for four years to study biology, and I've been concentrating on biology now for 40 years or more.

**Andrew Murray:** Looking at longevity first, we did a show a few months back entitled "You Are What You Eat." You've written in your recent newsletter that the intestinal tract of parrots and ravens contained only a few species of bacteria, and this positively correlated with longevity in these species, the intestines being a major source of toxins. I was quite shocked because ravens are carrion birds; you would think that rotting flesh would be a source of a wide range of bacteria. What have you found about the intestinal population of bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Birds have a very high body temperature and so probably have extremely fast digestion and the ability to extract everything good from the food, taking it away from potential bacteria. It's just so fast that bacteria don't have much of a chance at multiplying. Incidentally, besides being very long-lived, those birds are extremely intelligent and can solve extremely complex problems very quickly. I think cognition and longevity go closely together.

When you cause animals to grow up their whole life free of bacteria, they have some advantage in stress resistance and have a somewhat increased average lifespan. A lot of the stuff produced by bacteria ends up simply slowing metabolism. The aging process itself, right from earliest life, is a process of slowing the metabolic rate. So, things that retard that slowing should extend lifespan as well as good cognition.

**Andrew Murray:** That reminds me of the phrase "wear and tear." The relationship between activity and running at a high metabolic rate is often thought of as running out of energy or wearing out. But this is the opposite—a highly increased metabolic rate is actually productively beneficial for the organism in terms of clearing waste material and processing reactions that would denature toxins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was in grade school and high school, it was common opinion that if you were very active and had a high metabolic rate, you would die young. That always annoyed me—that people had the image of a candle: the brighter it burns, the shorter its life expectancy.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why a baby starts out with such a high pulse rate, is so warm, and has a high metabolism, and then aging changes that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, especially at puberty, it gradually slows down. When a calf is born, for example, its fats all through its body, including its brain, are highly saturated because the mother has been saturating the fats from the food, so it's protected from the environment. As its tissues absorb the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA), its metabolism slows down. You can see it in the ruminants because they start life extremely free of polyunsaturates.

According to some fat experts, human babies are born deficient in essential fatty acids, and so they advocate putting more of them in baby formula. But actually, those are major things in slowing metabolic rate. They tend to accumulate in the brain with aging, slowing metabolism, especially the ability to metabolize glucose all the way to carbon dioxide. The old or demented brain has a chronically high level of lactic acid because it has progressively lost the ability to oxidize glucose to carbon dioxide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I find it strange that the placenta filters out the polyunsaturated fats. If the placenta filters it out, maybe the baby is not supposed to have them. So don't start giving your baby fish oil as soon as it's born.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's why babies are born with a so-called fatty acid deficiency, but that's a natural thing. The baby makes its brain fats out of the glucose or fructose that it's getting from the mother. There have been experiments with rats, dogs, and other animals in which the mother is given a high unsaturated fat diet or a PUFA-free diet. The babies have a bigger brain and better problem-solving ability when their mother was free of PUFA during gestation.

**Andrew Murray:** The intestines being clean prevents the accumulation of inflammatory degradative processes and contributes to a longer lifespan. How about the manipulation of hormones? W.D. Denckla did an experiment removing the pituitary gland, which was shown decisively to increase life and reduce the rate of aging. The hormones borne by the pituitary—like LH, FSH, TSH, and oxytocin—are responsible for a lot of inflammatory processes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He found that, in general, the pituitary extract, if you injected it into an animal, slowed the ability to oxidize glucose. So he called the death hormone the "oxygen blocking hormone." He tried to extract a specific protein; it was closely related to prolactin or growth hormone, but he never did identify a single protein, probably because several pituitary hormones do have some oxygen-blocking function.

Growth hormone is really an adequate model of what Denckla was looking for. It is now widely recognized that the more growth hormone you have, the shorter your life expectancy.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And doctors give patients growth hormone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The famous Methuselah mouse lacks the ability to produce growth hormone. When they genetically modify mice so that they produce more than the normal amount, they are very short-lived.

You don't have to do surgery on the pituitary; you can live in a way that reduces the activity of those hormones. For example, any stress tends to sharply decrease your blood sugar until you adapt. Simply an episode of hypoglycemia increases your growth hormone. That activates the process of changing your type of metabolism, blocking oxygen production and the ability to oxidize glucose to carbon dioxide. It also tends to increase phosphate, which is one of the things that happens under the influence of bowel toxins.

**Andrew Murray:** It's the ratio of phosphates to calcium that you've always mentioned as being important. The phosphate from meats, particularly muscle meats and nuts, can be damaging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's now considered one of the most important uremic toxins in kidney disease—simply natural phosphate that everyone has circulating. But when it increases because of hormonal metabolic problems, that is a typical strong sign of the aging process. The anti-aging hormone or protein called Klotho is a very powerful regulator of the balance and handling of phosphate.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask about the anti-aging effect of diluting your blood serum or lymph to remove toxins. When the kidneys fail, they can damage bowel function. Is it possible that we could practically dialyze ourselves?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Animal experiments have been done for 75 years on this. One is a simple dilution experiment where they took out a dog's blood, centrifuged it, threw away the liquid part, put a saline solution back in to replace the red blood cells, and did that repeatedly. Once the whole animal's body fluids had been turned over and exchanged, a decrepit old dog—something close to 20 years old—became frisky. It was effectively rejuvenated.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Bowel toxins are always entering the blood and having to be removed by the kidneys. But they poison not only the kidneys, but the heart, the brain, the liver, and the intestine in the process of being filtered out. The blood contains some of these toxins, including excess lactic acid and phosphate, as well as specific bacterial toxins.

Also, as these toxins affect the various tissues, the body produces defensive reactions. These defensive reactions, including the pituitary hormones, become part of the toxic environment circulating in the fluids. The shift away from circulating renewal signals produced by the animal becomes, with age, circulating stress signals. If you put young blood into an old animal, you're causing a slight shift back towards some of the renewal signals, but you aren't necessarily decreasing the age and stress signals.

**Andrew Murray:** That's very much like a bystander effect as well, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It definitely is the same process. When you injure a cell or a particular region—for example, with a beam of focused ionizing radiation—that tissue emits signals which are the same as the aging and stress signals. So, radiation damage is very similar to the process of aging. The intrinsic regulatory processes, instead of increasing your ability to adapt, start narrowing the way you're adapting. It creates a vicious circle where something interferes with your oxidation, leading to lactic acid production instead of carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is one of the toxins that turns on the production of nitric oxide, which spreads inflammatory signals and blocks the ability to use oxygen.

**Andrew Murray:** If you were to ask people on the streets whether nitric oxide was bad or good for you, I think most would say it was good.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The September issue of *Life Extension* magazine has an article on their cover: "How to Increase Your Nitric Oxide." It describes their product containing flavonoid compounds extracted from oranges. The theory they use to sell them is that they will increase your nitric oxide. I looked up what hesperidin does to nitric oxide and found 30 or 40 articles saying that these are anti-inflammatory because they *block* nitric oxide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they are selling them on the premise of increasing nitric oxide, when in fact it's the opposite?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's explore the subject of nootropics—substances for improving cognitive ability. Can you support or refute the claims made by manufacturers? Let's start with acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter responsible for memory and learning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The popular medical approach to treating Alzheimer's disease for the last 20 years is to try to increase the level of acetylcholine by blocking the enzyme that breaks it down. They've demonstrated basically that it doesn't work.

Acetylcholine is essential and part of our conscious regulating; it's needed for memory. However, it activates the enzyme that produces nitric oxide. Nitric oxide blocks energy production. This is the process of excitotoxicity, which made monosodium glutamate (MSG) notorious. A little too much MSG activates the production of too much acetylcholine, which makes too much nitric oxide. Nitric oxide poisons the ability to oxidize glucose to carbon dioxide, so it increases lactic acid. The cell has less energy and is more excited by the acetylcholine. Basically, it becomes susceptible to dying in proportion to the overstimulation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is it true that MSG can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause that reaction in the brain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, sure. The amino acids all have to get into the brain to provide brain proteins. It's just one of our normal amino acids, but too much of it becomes toxic. Aspartic acid and cysteine are the other potential nerve toxins, again by increasing acetylcholine, which increases nitric oxide and blocks oxygen metabolism.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think most people have enough acetylcholine in their systems?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, actually, I think the tendency with aging is to have too much. For over 100 years, there has been evidence that overactivity of the vagus nerve and the parasympathetic nervous system produces shock. This is the system that acts primarily through acetylcholine producing nitric oxide. In shock, your blood stays red and full of oxygen, but the tissue can't use it. That happens with aging, heart failure, kidney failure, and dementia. All the tissues relatively have a shock-like metabolism that progresses with aging.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think there's any medical benefit in increasing the breakdown of acetylcholine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, there are therapeutic uses of things that block the overactivity of acetylcholine and accelerate its turnover. A rich environment increases the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine.

**Andrew Murray:** So environmental enrichment would encourage the breakdown of acetylcholine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Having a good life protects you against lots of aging problems.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you mean by "good life"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Reading interesting things, talking to interesting people.

**Andrew Murray:** And having interesting work. Liking your job not because it pays well, but because you're fundamentally interested in it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The opposite is learned helplessness or behavioral despair. Most people treat their jobs with some learned helplessness.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That brings up another product line that is being pushed recently: methylating agents. Learned helplessness is a matter of imprinting—turning off the genes that should enliven you and increase your adaptability. Too much methylation shuts things down and makes you hopeless. That process happens progressively with aging. Too much methylation turns off the genes of renewal.

There are lots of products pushing the idea that we need more methylation. One of the main methyl donors is methionine, the amino acid. If you deprive animals of a major part of their normal methionine, they live 30 or 40% longer than they would otherwise.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What's a common food source that's high in methionine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the high-protein foods, like meat.

**Andrew Murray:** So there's another good reason to advocate that muscle meats in isolation are not good for you, and that balanced proteins from the whole animal—including the connective tissue and gelatin—is the best way to consume protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, gelatin is unique in being free of the pro-aging amino acids. Another bad thing about meat is its very high ratio of phosphate to calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** There's a sentence in your newsletter that said heart rate corresponded with academic standing, and elderly patients improved when their pacemaker was turned up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They noticed that people with a faster heart rate had higher academic records. They thought maybe it was just better brain circulation—that people with a very slow heart rate weren't getting enough oxygen to their brain. So they took patients with adjustable pacemakers and gave them mental tests when set at 70 beats per minute. Then they turned the rate up to 85 beats per minute, gave them the same tests, and they scored better in all types of brain function: memory and reasoning.

**Andrew Murray:** It's so popular in culture to believe that if you have a low pulse rate, you're healthy and super athletic. But these people with pulses of 50 beats a minute often die suddenly of heart attacks. It's a complete brainwashing that low heart rate corresponds with longevity.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to bring out a couple of nootropics in the herb world. Sage has fairly recent articles on PubMed stating it has a cholinesterase-inhibiting property. This is the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every plant has thousands of different chemicals. Sage has components that shift the balance to increased acetylcholine action, but two of its major terpene-type chemicals are inhibitors of nitric oxide. These are very effective inhibitors of nitric oxide, so they're anti-inflammatory and pro-respiratory.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this why it has an action reducing menopausal hot flashes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nitric oxide does cause flushing and is connected with hot flashes. So I think probably the dominant effect is to lower nitric oxide, whereas the cholinesterase inhibitors will tend to increase nitric oxide by stimulating the acetylcholine nerves.

**Andrew Murray:** Moving on to Ginkgo, it has been used for a long time to improve cognitive function. They say it improves blood flow to the brain. I also wanted to bring out the link between monoamine oxidase (MAO) and Ginkgo. Apparently, Ginkgo decreases MAO, which increases dopamine. What are your thoughts on dopamine and MAO?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It definitely makes you feel good; it's sort of an "upper." Anything that increases your dopamine tends to increase adrenaline usually. Certain types of MAO inhibitors will increase serotonin too, and those don't necessarily go with well-being. Brain circulation, for example, is decreased by serotonin. It tightens up the blood vessels, especially the veins leaving the brain. So if you have too much serotonin, you can get brain congestion and a migraine.

I think the most important benefit of Ginkgo is that it's a very good nitric oxide inhibitor and also blocks platelet-activating factor (PAF).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And it blocks prostaglandins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, pretty generally, and they are pro-inflammatory.

**Andrew Murray:** When it comes to marketing brain food as supposedly increasing your intelligence, philosophically, intelligence is not just IQ.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The "Wizard of Oz" idea is that maybe you can just go online, buy a diploma, and become intelligent and qualified. It's starting to look like the mechanical idea of qualification. You accumulate your qualifications in terms of what the culture has to sell.

The IQ idea is that there are certain mental skills that an intelligent person has. One of the silliest kinds of IQ tests had questions that were simply stories they asked people at Oxford to interpret. Then they had uneducated people interpret the same story. If you interpret it the way the Oxford graduate did, you have a high IQ.

A lot of products are being sold with the idea that if you take them, you'll become clever in ways that will make you compete in society. But if the society is set up in an irrational way, then it's not intelligent to succeed in terms that the society presents. The nootropic people are really committed to the idea of intelligence as competition to gain status. But I think there's a more general idea of consciousness and intelligence that applies to life in general: it's an appropriateness of the way you live, not the skill you have to fit into whatever you might encounter in society.

**Andrew Murray:** There are definitely some products that promote life. You mentioned thyroid, pregnenolone, and basic anti-stress compounds. I was going to mention B12 and B1.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamins are important. And caffeine, if it's used properly. But a lot of people are thinking of caffeine as a legal version of crack cocaine. It shouldn't be used as speed; it should be used as a food. It should decrease nitric oxide exposure and so it should have anti-aging properties. But if you take it on an empty stomach, it will drop your blood sugar, turn on nitric oxide, and cause aging stress.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So have caffeine after you've had a big meal.

**Andrew Murray:** I just want to bring out one particular herb pertinent to performance enhancing: Ginseng. It falls under the umbrella of adaptogens, a term coined by Russian research when they were looking for alternatives to drugs. They found that adaptogens improved the organism's resistance to stress.

We are coming to the end of the show. Dr. Peat's website, , is full of fully referenced articles. It's a very good starting point to look at his research. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Current Trends on Nitric Oxide
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions. Tonight’s subject is a continuation of a previous topic on nitric oxide and the current trends surrounding it. In the last year or two, both the sports industry—specifically for muscle building and male performance enhancement—and the medical community have promoted it.

However, there is a lot of recent research showing that nitric oxide is actually a very negative product, even though we produce it naturally. It has wide-ranging damaging effects. Dr. Peat’s research details the evidence supporting what we are going to talk about tonight. Nitric oxide has implications for conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis to diabetes, generalized inflammation, and old age. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks for your time. For those who may not have heard of you, would you describe your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I did my master's degree in humanities at the University of Oregon and then went back years later in biology for a PhD. I intended to study brain biology but quickly shifted to reproductive aging physiology. I concentrated on the biochemistry of the steroid hormones in relation to aging.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to open by discussing what people find if they search online. Unfortunately, the internet is rife with misconceptions. Nitric oxide is touted to help the immune system, regulate blood pressure, improve sleep, and is heavily advertised for endurance, bodybuilding, and sexual performance. Dr. Peat, given that we produce it naturally, why does it have so many negative effects?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And why do they claim it is used for all those conditions when it isn't true? Where are they twisting the truth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My dissertation in 1972 focused on estrogen, but I saw that the effects of estrogen were indistinguishable from the effects of X-rays, aging, and oxygen deprivation. It works by changing the oxidative enzyme function, cytochrome oxidase. It was known that smog produces nitric oxide, but it wasn't known that it occurred naturally in the body until the late 80s. The nitric oxide in smog was known to inhibit or damage that same respiratory enzyme.

At the time I was studying estrogen, it was known that carbon monoxide and cyanide also blocked the effect of oxygen in the cell. No one really thought about what nitric oxide was doing to the cell, except regarding smog exposure. As soon as it was discovered that it was produced in the body, a series of publications identified the harm it did in various tissues. For example, several papers clearly showed how inflammation or stress-increasing nitric oxide damages the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. It is a major cause of diabetes. They saw similar damage to every tissue they looked at, which seemed logical since it was a free radical analogous to cyanide and carbon monoxide.

However, someone noticed that nitric oxide causes vasodilation during arousal, and Viagra came on the scene with a tremendous amount of funding for research.

**Andrew Murray:** This was about 15 years ago?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, around 1997. Suddenly all the bad stuff was forgotten, and everyone wanted to find out the curative effects of the drug that could improve virility. Very soon after it came out, I started hearing from people who were suffering things such as diabetes from taking virility pills.

**Andrew Murray:** There is a positive association between cardiac arrest and Viagra use, isn't there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is probably killing more people than are being identified. Nitric oxide is produced in any stressed cell or tissue, and it decreases the function of the tissue by blocking energy production. It creates a vicious circle, the same way too much estrogen or stress can. It starts a cycle of energy loss, increased production of stress mediators (including nitric oxide), exciting the tissue, blocking the energy of the tissue, and leaving the cell to die.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is there any thread of truth to the claims that it helps muscle growth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It actually does make muscles grow, but that is one of the things Szent-Györgyi and Otto Warburg understood 50 years ago: in the absence of oxygen, life can't do anything but grow and divide. Anything that blocks cytochrome c oxidase—blocking oxidative metabolism—tends to stimulate cell division because that's all life can do on the lactic acid-producing cycle.

Experiments with nitric oxide supplements, or creating conditions like cutting off blood supply to cause muscle tissue to produce its own excess nitric oxide, found that it stimulated the multiplication of cells. The satellite cells surrounding the muscle fiber multiply under the influence of nitric oxide or simply hypoxia.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's a very inflammatory process. Even though they describe it as wonderful for muscle growth, it’s actually damage.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They found you could cause muscle enlargement just by putting on a tourniquet. It causes really big muscle growth from injuring it. Cells divide like cancer when they don't have the energy to do what they should do.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's a negative response to stimulation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Anytime you injure a tissue, whether in the brain, heart, or blood vessel, stem cells multiply. The lack of oxygen temporarily stimulates multiplication of stem-like cells which have the potential of regenerating the tissue.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's a natural process to stimulate cell growth, but they're twisting it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is always a local, microscopic process when it's natural. But if you flood the system hoping to grow all your muscles bigger, then your brain, immune system, and gonads are effectively being deprived of oxygen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So drugs that increase nitric oxide would be classified as carcinogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that is starting to be recognized. It is a very basic factor in promoting cancer development, growth, and spreading.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there any truth to the vasodilatory effects helping people with blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does that. Nitroglycerin was used for a long time to open up heart arteries. You do increase the flow of blood by relaxing the arterioles.
