The trouble is, if you increase it beyond temporary dilation, it starts the damaging process of increasing collagen formation and cell multiplication. You can get a momentary effect from nitroglycerin, but as a chronic or systemic thing, it is not good. In fact, it ages you.

For example, in irritable bowel syndrome, you absorb both nitric oxide and endotoxin. The endotoxin increases the production of nitric oxide everywhere. In the blood vessels, the chronic effect of nitric oxide is to promote thickening, atherosclerosis, and hardening of the arteries.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it actually worsens the condition you're taking it for?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The momentary effect can be helpful if you have a constricted area, but systemically, you are adding to chronic inflammation and degeneration. One of the things it does is increase aldosterone, the adrenal salt-regulating steroid, which produces inflammation and fibrosis as a side effect.

**Andrew Murray:** Aldosterone is also implicated in blood pressure regulation, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, too much aldosterone gives you high blood pressure. So the side effect of chronic nitric oxide can be exactly the opposite of what they're promoting.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of inhibiting nitric oxide, I found two compounds. One was aminoguanidine, which is sold as a blocker of the glycation process.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was its first recognized effect, but it turns out it achieves that by blocking nitric oxide, which leads to the oxidation damage of blood vessels.

**Andrew Murray:** Is aminoguanidine a reasonable approach to systemic inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it probably is, but there are safer things that have been studied more. The safest inhibitors happen to be **niacinamide**, **aspirin**, and **progesterone**.

**Andrew Murray:** I’ve seen **methylene blue** mentioned as well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that is another pretty safe inhibitor. But first I would try aspirin, niacinamide, and progesterone as they are the most physiological.

**Andrew Murray:** What dosage would be reasonable for niacinamide or aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For aspirin, if you take Vitamin K, it is safe up to several grams a day. Usually, two doses of 500mg provide good systemic protection. Vitamin K also helps hold down nitric oxide production. For niacinamide, it is probably safe up to 1,000mg a day, but I've seen people take three or four doses of 125mg (totaling 200-500mg a day) do dramatic things for curing nerve degeneration.

**Caller:** I wanted to know if Dr. Peat could briefly discuss cystic fibrosis and practical strategies for overcoming it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never worked with anyone that had it, except some people who suspected they might have it, and it turned out they were just very hypothyroid. The function of the adrenals can cause you to leak chloride, leading to extreme saltiness of the skin, which is often used to diagnose cystic fibrosis. Just correcting the thyroid and adrenal function in the people I've seen resolved it; they turned out not to have cystic fibrosis, just a bad reaction to low thyroid function.

**Amy (New York):** I'm studying a breathing method that's supposed to increase carbon dioxide levels by always breathing through the nose. I was worried whether that would increase my nitric oxide levels.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. Anything that irritates your membranes will cause nitric oxide. You want to avoid inflammatory things in your food or atmosphere, but breathing through your nose itself doesn't contribute to that. The idea of breathing through your nose is that it extends the dead space so that you keep a higher concentration of CO2.

**Amy:** I have another question. You mentioned a study regarding pigs wearing sweaters that ended up with larger stores of saturated fats. Is that a viable strategy for people in cold climates who want to lose stored unsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping your arms and legs warm is very important for your systemic metabolism. The pig study demonstrated that the production of unsaturated fats is a defense against cold because saturated fats harden at low temperatures. When you synthesize unsaturated fats from sugar or starch, they are going to be safe Omega-9 fats (Mead acid), which are much less unstable than the fish oil type.

**Amy:** So it changed the new stored fat, but didn't change the burning preference of existing stores?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping your body temperature up helps you oxidize fat safely.

**Amy:** What about brown fat? People take cold showers to increase brown fat to burn off white fat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think keeping your thyroid function up is better. Cold activates stress hormones that cause side effects. To oxidize your fats while at rest by having a good resting metabolic rate and high body temperature is the safest way, rather than increasing stress to increase fat burning.

**Caller (Madison, WI):** I've been taking T4. It's working well, but I get some eye pain in the process of titrating it. I started on 7 micrograms and went up to 12. Is that normal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I haven't heard of that, but I would back off on the T4. If your liver isn't effectively converting it to T3, it can have an anti-thyroid effect by accumulating and turning off your pituitary. If your liver isn't converting it, you can accumulate so much T4 that it has stress-activating actions.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think it would be better to try the active hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's always better to use the combination [of T3 and T4] in the traditional way. Or, if you have a sluggish liver, small amounts of active T3 can be used safely.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** T4 on its own doesn't have any action; it has to be converted to T3. If you take enough T4, you turn off your brain's stimulation of the thyroid gland.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, drug companies synthesized thyroxine (T4) and tested it on male medical students, claiming it worked just like real thyroid. But women with high estrogen compared to men always have a more sluggish liver. Thyroxine is very often causing problems in women.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** T4 can actually make low-thyroid people feel worse by increasing adrenaline.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the effects of good thyroid function is to lower nitric oxide. Nitric oxide, contrary to advertising, can increase pressure inside your eye. Hypothyroidism can create enough nitric oxide to cause symptoms such as hardening of the eye and increasing pressure.

**Caller:** That's interesting. I was switching over from cortisol to thyroid and wondered if my eye was running low on energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cortisol increases the pressure in the eye, so it's possible you were still producing too much cortisol relative to the protective pregnenolone and progesterone.

**Caller:** What percentage of popular lab tests are fraudulent or useless? My doctor said my TSH was normal, but when I went off thyroid, I had symptoms.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doctors are taught that the TSH normal range is something like 0.4 to 5.0. However, the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists has lowered it to 0.3 to 3.0. In a population of healthy people without thyroid problems, they average 0.4 TSH or less without supplements.

**Andrew Murray:** So if you are over 1.0 or 1.5, you would likely benefit from the hormone.

**Caller:** I think I was at 3.7.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Isn't it correct that while someone might be taking T4 and not converting it to T3, their TSH would still lower?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and stress hormones will lower it too. So you can't really diagnose anything by TSH alone. High cortisol lowers TSH and simultaneously causes the liver to turn thyroxine into reverse T3, which interferes with active T3 function.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw articles demonstrating that nitric oxide was responsible for damaging DNA, implicating it as a carcinogen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Radiation biologists saw that cells hit by X-rays emitted something that caused radiation damage in the neighborhood. Nitric oxide turned out to be a major transmitter of that effect. It spreads to adjoining cells. Nitric oxide not only breaks DNA strands but also changes methylation, altering the control system for expressing DNA.

**Caller (Eureka):** I wanted to know what alternative there is to blood pressure medicines.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at the symptoms of chronic hypothyroidism, hypertension is one of the prominent things. A very large proportion of people who think they have a high blood pressure problem are simply hypothyroid. TSH itself, which rises when you're hypothyroid, increases stress hormones and blood pressure. So TSH is a pro-inflammatory factor causing hypertension.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You could ask your doctor for a TSH test. If it's above 0.4, perhaps think about taking a thyroid supplement.

**Andrew Murray:** We had a caller ask about Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). How do you see the etiology or treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known several people who had it. One friend in his 80s was blue in the face and panting just sitting down. His brain wasn't getting enough oxygen. I gave his daughter some pregnenolone, progesterone, and thyroid to give him. When I came back two weeks later, he was back at work in his upper-floor office, dramatically improved.

**Andrew Murray:** Is that how someone could regain their breath?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. High estrogen and nitric oxide can cause leakage of fluid into the air sacs and a thickening of the pathway between the air and the capillary. Pregnenolone seems to sometimes very quickly improve oxygenation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What would be a recommended starting dose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With thyroid, you want to start very slowly because it increases your need for oxygen. It's good to start with pregnenolone, which helps prevent edema. 15 to 30 milligrams is often a therapeutic dose. With progesterone, 10 to 30 milligrams can make a big difference.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw articles demonstrating that **minocycline** lowered the inducible form of nitric oxide. What do you think about minocycline?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For several years it's been recognized as helpful for Alzheimer's disease and other brain problems. It directly blocks the enzyme [that creates nitric oxide], the way niacinamide does.

**Andrew Murray:** What about **tetracycline**?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's in the same family. The only problem with tetracycline is that it's too cheap, so doctors are not educated to use it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I wonder if **Cascara** would have a similar effect because it has anthraquinones that are very similar to tetracycline.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think that structure is what is happening.

**Caller (Ukiah):** Can you talk about Human Growth Hormone (HGH)? My friends in weightlifting talk about it to build muscle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You have the same problems that you get from nitric oxide or estrogen. Women chronically have high growth hormone during reproductive years. Growth hormone causes a breakdown of fat into free fatty acids. This increases oxidative damage. That is likely why they see increased thickness in blood vessel walls in the kidneys, causing progressive loss of kidney function from chronic exposure to growth hormone. There is a suspicion that it increases the risk of diabetes, which free fatty acids are known to cause.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's very inflammatory.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And people want to avoid supplements touted to increase nitric oxide, like arginine and citrulline.

**Andrew Murray:** We need to wrap up. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for your time and dedication.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Steiner Schools and Education
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. Clients consult with us regarding their health issues, and we recommend personalized advice in nutrition, supplements, herbs, diet, and lifestyle.

For this month's show, Dr. Raymond Peat is going to join us. We're fortunate to have him on the show, and I know people who listen frequently have heard Dr. Peat speak on a very wide range of topics. Tonight is no exception. I want to bring out the topic of Steiner schools, Rudolf Steiner, anthroposophy, and biodynamic gardening. It all ties into itself as a complete system that Rudolf Steiner brought out in the early 1900s. Dr. Peat has his own very pertinent and personal background in education.

Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us. For those who have just tuned in for the first time, would you give an outline of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied humanities as an undergraduate and eventually went to graduate school in biology, although linguistics and painting had been most of my previous study. Since graduating with a PhD in biology, I've done a lot of counseling in nutrition and general health issues.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of your life's work and education, would you want to mention anything about a college that you were part of at one time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it is very directly related to everything I did before and after. I had been a critical consumer of education right from the first grade. I knew how to read when I went to school, so I didn't take it very seriously when they went through their routines. My third, fourth, and fifth-grade experience was exceptional; it was in a one-room country school where there were eight grades in one room. That made it more interesting, and it was completely unregimented. I think that gave me the idea that maybe kids would do better in a freer learning environment.

In my college experience, I found that there were only two or three professors that knew anything that I wanted to learn. My first teaching experience confirmed my belief that the institution tended to be an impediment to learning. The trustees had their idea of what the students should do with their lives, and the students' and teachers' interests were antagonistic to the trustees. As a result, I got the idea of starting a school in Mexico where we could be somewhat beyond the reach of the trustees and government types who wanted to tell us what we couldn't study.

**Andrew Murray:** What year was this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 1961. I had been reading and studying William Blake's work, so I named the school Blake College. The idea was that we would incorporate it, but the students and teachers would be the only trustees. There would be no curriculum. Students could bring up topics they wanted to study, and instructors could offer courses students didn't have to attend—just complete independence.

We had the idea that since the students would use their bachelor's degree to go on for a master's or PhD, the requirement for getting a degree should be passing the Graduate Record Exam (GRE) that students normally take to qualify for graduate school.

**Andrew Murray:** That is an established standard in the US?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was a very standardized system at that time. We said that if a student could pass at the 87th percentile of American college graduates on that test, they could have their degree, because practically any graduate school in the country would be willing to have someone who scored in the upper 12%.

As it turned out, students generally chose to take that exam after being there only six, seven, or eight months, and their average was over the 90th percentile. No one flunked the tests. You could see the process happening. People would come thinking that they needed to be structured somehow, but what they learned was that they were full of knowledge. Their business was to structure reality for themselves—to make sense out of what they already knew and use that orientation to ask questions about what they really wanted to learn. You could see a very quick change in their sense of confidence about knowledge.

**Andrew Murray:** So within a few months, the students could take this exam and score in the 90th percentile? How much of that was due to them being the "right" kind of people who would choose that environment versus what they learned while they were there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of them had been flunk-outs at state universities. A couple of them had even scored poorly on standardized tests and thought they were idiots. When they had the opportunity not to be imposed upon and to be able to talk to other students and teachers, they realized how much they knew. You could see the change from someone who felt helpless coming around to seeing themselves as a responsible citizen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And did they get accepted into graduate schools?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of the state schools said that simply having that high score wasn't enough, so some had to go to private graduate schools. But all of the good schools let them in on the basis of their scores without having had their previous bachelor's or master's.

**Andrew Murray:** This ties in well with the Steiner school environment. Steiner schools have a very different approach to problem-solving. You mentioned there was no curriculum at Blake College?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically. We only paid a couple of professors; there just wasn't enough money. But there were well-known people—painters, philosophy professors, psychology professors, writers, and even a math professor—doing it just for fun. They would usually end up saying they were learning more from the students than they had to teach the students.

When you look at the ideology of public education over the last couple of hundred years, you see that a whole theory of what an organism is is related to the theory of education. What they're doing is based on an authoritarian social system that relies on a mechanical conception of what the person is. The progress of biological knowledge in the last 50 years has illuminated some of the problems with that theory. The brain is the body's energy organizing system. If you have education that conflicts with the body's own processes, you're going to impair the body's energy system, lead to a reduction of ability, and create a tendency toward a lack of adaptability in biological as well as mental health processes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Are you speaking about children being forced to sit for eight hours a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies in New York City where kids were given an IQ test every year. They saw these slum kids coming in with an average IQ, but each year their scores would get lower as they spent the year sitting in school being oppressed. With our students at Blake, just the opposite happened very quickly. They would come out of their oppression and realize that they were creative minds. That same process was discovered 50 years ago in rat studies. The rat that was given an entertaining, free environment became more intelligent and grew a bigger brain with a thicker cortex. Their offspring would have a bigger brain and be more intelligent.

**Andrew Murray:** Steiner used a humor classification of personalities—melancholic, sanguine, phlegmatic, and choleric—to guide education. What do you think about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We called it student-centered education. Following Carl Rogers' client-centered therapy, he used a non-directive approach of empathy. In our non-curriculum, the sense of empathy was the guiding principle. The teachers and students tried to understand each other and together created questions that none of them had thought about before. If you had them categorized according to humors, that would be a way of organizing that process. With our small group, it was a purely individual, adaptive, empathetic approach.

**Andrew Murray:** Steiner students were taught to observe and depict scientific concepts in their own words and drawings rather than encountering ideas through textbooks. These students were shown to have an above-average number of doctors, engineers, and scientists because they investigated the world objectively.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The typical professor has his understanding of how a student's brain works, and they think they have to impose their abstractions—such as the science textbook idea—on the student's brain. But the actuality of a student's brain and personality is analogous to any organism. A simple mammal, for example, understands physics very well. Birds, crows in particular, are very intelligent and can figure out physical processes and make predictions that many graduate students in physics wouldn't understand.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They can predict that if you left the meat out on that rock the day before, it might be there the next day at the same time.

**Andrew Murray:** In Steiner education, from ages three to seven, there is no pressure to learn ABCs. The child is immersed in nature, gardening, and animals before they do anything structured with math and science.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I think they don't read until they're ten on average.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In my experience, I saw people reading and talking about things they saw in the newspapers. I just spontaneously wanted to see what they were doing; it had nothing to do with a curriculum or being taught.

At the Summerhill School, started by A.S. Neill in England in the 1920s, he had no curriculum at all. Students could stay there for 12 years if they wanted and not study. But the ones who did stay and graduate were superior in their achievement to those who had gone through taking classes every day for 12 years. They demonstrated that the curriculum is completely unnecessary. If the student is aware that there is something to learn, they can learn it in a flash compared to what the schools expect of them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't you tell me you learned to read watching people read the newspaper because you wanted to read the comics?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The funnies were the first things—*Alley Oop* and *Smokey Stover* were my favorites. But then my parents had a shoebox full of the "Little Blue Books," classics printed in a very small size. And regarding the newspapers, I wanted to hear what was going on with the war. So I learned the various types of things that were available.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How old were you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Four.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about the concepts of homeschooling? State schools obviously have their own agendas.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the state can set the curriculum to a great extent, even in homeschooling. The federal government approves the agencies that accredit high schools and universities. There are private accrediting agencies which are really responsible to no one; they are an abstract authority that citizens can't affect directly. The state bureaucracies are set up so that no school can grant degrees or transcripts if they don't conform to those accrediting agencies. So the power to grant a degree is pretty much a matter of mind control.

In my experience in grade school and high school, I just didn't pay too much attention to them. In high school, some of our teachers were openly fascists, Hitler worshipers, and racists. It was just a matter of getting through it without having to interact too much with them.

**Andrew Murray:** You often bring to life concepts that aren't found in mainstream medical journals. You mentioned that when you were studying, most of your professors didn't understand what you were trying to get across because it wasn't typical rote repetition.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The system—not only the explicit accrediting process but the official high-status publications and journals—all have ulterior motives. You have to look for people who are motivated by reality. Remember a few years ago someone in the White House said, "Your problem is that you belong to the reality-based community. We're creating a new reality; you're studying the old one." I think there is a possibility still in the reality-based community.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller from Colorado Springs.

**Caller:** Dr. Peat, I was wondering if you had any suggestions for a person that wants to self-educate in biology?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Having access to a really good university library is important. The journals are too expensive; even buying articles over the internet costs $30 or $40 per article. If you have a good science library nearby, you can find journals, recent books, and old books. If you have questions, just start looking them up in the library. Sometimes professors can be helpful if they don't know what your real purpose is.

**Caller:** Do you have any specific textbook suggestions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. There were good textbooks published many years ago, but in the last 10 or 20 years, even the textbooks that were good have been revised under the name of the good author by committees. These committees look for the professors who have the biggest classes. They say something nice in the textbook about the work of that professor, which means they sell an extra 500 books at $100 profit each. Textbooks have become a matter of profit for the publisher rather than information for the student.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't you recommend a physiology textbook from the 50s or 60s?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are some good ones from the 30s, 40s, and 50s. I have a little *Handbook of Physiology* from about 1965 that has the basic information and doesn't have the misleading stuff on membrane pumps and channels.

**Andrew Murray:** What was the name of the index you mentioned at the university in Oregon? You said *Index Medicus* lagged behind?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was *Biological Abstracts*, which had references to international journals in all fields related to biology. When I would compare *Index Medicus*—which was the paper precursor to PubMed—I found that any interesting discovery of recent years found in *Biological Abstracts* took about 10 or 20 years to show up in *Index Medicus*. And then it would often be a put-down. They would scoff for a few years, and then 30 years after it was published in the science literature, the medical literature would finally accept it.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to touch on medicinals and anthroposophy. You mentioned Iscador, which is an anthroposophical preparation of *Viscum album* (European mistletoe).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been following the issue for more than 50 years. I knew people in the biodynamic Steiner approach, and they told me interesting things about the influence of fields created by the moon cycles. Following up on that, I found there were fairly mainline researchers continuing ideas that Steiner had proposed regarding the interaction between moon cycles and botanical processes. From the 20s through the 40s, there were several people doing very good research showing that organisms are biologically coordinated through the earth and moon fields.

**Andrew Murray:** That's the basis for lunar planting.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For people who want background besides Steiner, Harold Saxton Burr wrote a book called *Fields of Life*. He was a Yale professor who did measurements showing these lunar cycles. A professor named Brown at Indiana University did a whole series of biological cycle studies. Solco Tromp was a Dutch biologist and ecologist who wrote a book called *Psychical Physics* about how the nervous system interacts with these fields.

**Andrew Murray:** Steiner students had a statistically significant lower incidence of gastrointestinal distress compared to mainstream students. What do you think about the mind-body connection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The issue of learned helplessness, or inescapable stress, shows up first in the stomach as ulcers and in the intestine as bleeding, but it's really happening in the brain. If it continues, you can see with MRI studies that chronic stress thins the cortex of the brain.

The main parts of the brain that relate the digestive damage to the nerve damage involve the serotonin system and toxic excitatory amino acids. Glutamic excitation processes release nitric oxide. Nitric oxide reduces the energy-producing capacity of the brain and leads to atrophy. The intestine releases both serotonin and nitric oxide. The system goes back and forth between the brain and the intestine, affecting every other organ.

You can see these same processes even in fruit flies. If a fruit fly has a traumatic brain injury, it develops ulcers and a leaky intestine.

**Andrew Murray:** Really?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fruit flies are just like us.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That makes me think of lemon balm because it's calming on the nervous system but also soothing on the intestinal tract.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping the brain steroids up and the inhibitory GABA transmitters up preserves the brain and all of the organs. Keeping the brain energy up keeps the structure up.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller from Windsor, Ontario.

**Caller:** As far as intestinal problems go, I was wondering how Dr. Peat felt about Chia seeds? They seem to help with stomach problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're good for making funny fuzzy animals.

**Caller:** But not for eating?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. I don't really know any virtue they have as a food.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** They are very mucilaginous.

**Caller:** But the Omega-3s in them aren't bad for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There isn't much. I think the risk is an allergic reaction to some of the proteins in them.

**Caller:** The other thing that's helped is Shirataki noodles. They are made from Konjac root.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yes. I read that they were having a problem with people choking.

**Caller:** They don't digest, but they really help with bowel movements.

**Andrew Murray:** Cascara does the same thing for bowel movements, and it's a lot safer.

**Caller:** I found anytime I ate the Chia seeds or the Konjac noodles, the bowel movements are perfect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat always recommends carrots, but he doesn't like seeds.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know psyllium seeds work for many people, but I've known a few people who had a bad reaction to them.

**Caller:** I've tried psyllium and had cramps.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Then you're obviously having that allergic reaction.

**Andrew Murray:** We only have a few moments left, but I want to ask you about the latest findings on a product called lanosterol and its use in the treatment of cataracts without surgery.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was just a little surprised to see a big publication in *Nature*. A group at the University of California, San Diego, was actually reversing the majority of cataracts in rabbits and dogs, using both eyedrops and injections. They actually got established cataracts to clear up.

When I wrote a newsletter about cataracts a couple of years ago, I noticed that research in treating and curing cataracts had been suppressed because of the immense amount of money there is in removing the lens. Cataract surgery is a multi-billion dollar business. That money interest had just wiped out practically all curative research.

**Andrew Murray:** We'll keep our eyes open for lanosterol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mushrooms happen to be a good source of that steroid. It is a precursor to cholesterol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So boil your mushrooms for 45 minutes to an hour and make a yummy winter soup.

**Andrew Murray:** And don't think of cholesterol as a bad thing, because it's not. Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who would like to find out more about Dr. Raymond Peat, his articles are free online at www.raypeat.com. Thanks for listening, and good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Nitric Oxide, Nitrates, Nitrites, and Fluoride
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to the shows, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbs, supplements, and nutritional counseling.

Tonight, you are invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's continuing subject of nitric oxide, nitrates, nitrites, fluoride, and other components in the food chain that are decreasing fertility. Before I get into the topic, starting with fluoride, I'd like to welcome Dr. Raymond Peat for giving his time so freely to join us. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yes, hi.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us. As always, I want to give you the opportunity to outline your academic and professional background.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** From 1968 to 1972, I studied biology, physiology, and biochemistry at the University of Oregon for a PhD. Before that, I was in linguistics, literature, and painting. Since then, I've been writing newsletters and doing consulting.

**Andrew Murray:** Your background is very much focused on the energetic state of the organism. I know that a lot of your research regarding hormones related to fertility, productivity, and mitochondrial energy production has been key in understanding the mechanism by which disease happens.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had been intending to study brain biology when I went to university, but the dogmatism in the nerve biology department made me look elsewhere. I found that reproductive physiology was an open, more scientific area. After I finished my thesis on the aging of the reproductive system, I went back and applied that information to how the brain works and spent a year or two writing my book, *Mind and Tissue*.

**Andrew Murray:** Did you find the subject of reproductive physiology as dogmatic as the other branches of science?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not at all. My thesis advisor, Arnold Soderwall, had been one of the pioneers in exploring the effects of vitamin E as a fertility nutrient. In the 1930s and 40s, vitamin E was recognized as protection against polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) and against estrogen. Both of those interfered with oxidative energy production. Vitamin E was preserving the ability of tissues to oxidize properly. It has come to be known as an antioxidant, but really it should be thought of as a normalizer of good oxidative metabolism.

**Andrew Murray:** That brings me to another point regarding being informed. Most people, including myself until about eight years ago, are dogmatically brainwashed by the industry providing medical education. It wasn't until I looked at a holistic way of approaching disease that I discovered the lies fed through the system. Wherever there is prestige and big amounts of money, there is a huge amount of corruption.

I want to discuss things we think are good for us because the government allows them, but where the science is actually phony. Let's start with fluoride. The fluoride put in our drinking water is not a pharmaceutical-grade additive; it is an industrial waste byproduct. With increasing aluminum production in the early 20th century, manufacturers needed somewhere to put the fluoride waste. They commissioned research to support adding fluoride to the water supply.

The main fluoride chemical added to water today is hydrofluorosilicic acid, a byproduct from the phosphate fertilizer industry. Fluoride given to rats has been proven to cause bone cancer, liver cancer, and a host of other ailments. Dr. Peat, is there any logic to anything they're saying about fluoride and teeth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I read a few studies in the 1970s in which they compared villages that had high fluoride or zero fluoride added to the water. It happens that the teeth were healthier in the village *without* the fluoride. Some of the early studies were done in Montana towns where the water was naturally mineralized. They were getting trace minerals natural in the mountain water—magnesium, molybdenum, and others—that helped the teeth mature properly. They didn't control for that; they blamed the fluoride content for the good dental health.

I went to hear John Yiamouyiannis talk. He was debating a dentist who claimed to be an expert on fluoridation. Yiamouyiannis had worked for the abstracting service *Biological Abstracts* and was familiar with 15,000 studies on fluoride, so he could make any opponent look ridiculous. Yiamouyiannis and Dean Burk did a study in Los Angeles and found that cancer incidence increased after fluoride was added. Dean Burk was one of the best cancer researchers in the world—a colleague of Otto Warburg—but his reputation was damaged by getting involved with fluoride.

**Andrew Murray:** It is unfortunate that people who align themselves with the truth are often attacked. I want to ask you about nitrates and nitrites. These are common preservatives, but there is no real scientific proof that they are safe.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around 1970, there were studies of nitrosamines—compounds mostly involving proline or other amino acids reacting with nitrates in the stomach. It came out that they were very powerful carcinogens and are formed in cigarette smoke.

The farm industry was forcing greater production by using artificial, high-nitrate fertilizers. Spinach produced with those fertilizers will grow very quickly, but it causes it to contain several times as much nitrate as normal vegetables. The cooking process alone forms the nitrosamines.

**Andrew Murray:** So well-cooked spinach, even when boiled, can form these?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even vegetables which have the reputation for being associated with low cancer incidence can produce the same sort of carcinogen as tobacco smoke if they are industrially over-fertilized with nitrate and cooked thoroughly.

**Michael (Producer):** I found a little information. I believe synthetic fertilizers are not organically listed. The highest nitrogen content I found in a quick search was about 12% in feather meal.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In organic farming, the nitrogen could be in the form of ammonia. That would be the safe way for the plants to get their nitrogen. But when they are forced with an excess of nitrogen, they simply absorb the nitrate or nitrite in a crude chemical form that isn't doing the plant any good.

When you eat it, it circulates in your body and is exposed to many layers of enzymic and non-enzymic interactions. Free radicals, as well as reductases, will convert nitrate to nitrite, and then to nitric oxide. Those increase according to your level of stress. So when you're eating food that contains preservatives like processed meats, or industrially produced vegetables, you're creating the conditions for a bad reaction to stress.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And if you're stressed out when you're eating, that makes it even worse.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With old age, the conversion of the ordinary protein arginine to nitric oxide is accelerated by the various things that interfere with your cellular oxidation. If you add environmental nitrates or nitrites to that, you're making your ability to resist stress weaker because these things accumulate and become a more abundant source of nitric oxide, which then feeds back and blocks the ability to use oxygen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about naturally derived nitrates from celery?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they're just as bad.

**Andrew Murray:** Because the bottom line is they are still producing nitrate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The industry argues that brain circulation supposedly goes with intelligence. If you increase the diameter of the blood vessels by increasing your nitric oxide, you're going to reverse the process of brain aging by getting more blood circulating. It does help the brain to circulate more blood, but the problem is that nitric oxide at the same time is blocking the ability to *use* the oxygen. It is imitating a shock state.

In spontaneously age-accelerated rats, which are genetic mutants that age at three or four times the normal rate, they happen to produce tremendous amounts of nitric oxide. The people arguing for nitric oxide products say that's because they're defective and need more. But when you intervene—for example, exposing an organism to overdoses of ultraviolet light or ionizing radiation—you create changes similar to aging. You can extract the liquid from an irradiated organism, and that liquid will produce the same deterioration in others. This "bystander effect" is largely the result of overproduction of nitric oxide.

**Andrew Murray:** I got an email from a listener in Germany who wanted to know your opinion on cannabis. He was frightened by the negative effects he recognized. What are your views on cannabis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was 10 years old, a doctor prescribed it for migraines. I took a glass of the tea every day for about a month—a big bag full of cannabis leaves—and I didn't notice any effect. I was never impressed by the claims for its sedative or painkilling effects.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think of the potential estrogenic effect of it? It is in the same family as hops (*Humulus lupulus*). In England, women picking hops would often skip their menstrual cycle because it was such a disruptor.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does have an anti-testosterone effect. I think the worst effects are when it's smoked because the smoke itself has an estrogen action.

**Andrew Murray:** And you view estrogen as a negative, pro-inflammatory hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In general. It activates the immune system in a short-term, antibody-producing way that is useful in certain situations. But women have a very high incidence of autoimmune disorders because it impairs the energy resources at the same time that it's making these short-term emergency changes in the immune system.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the line.

**Caller (David from Missouri):** I'm glad you're talking about the government. There is a lot of confusion about political systems, but our government appears to be a corporate structure run by corporations. We are baffled by fluoride being put in our water, but it appears to be part of a larger agenda. Dr. Peat has awakened me to the idea of "learned helplessness." The program seems designed to get the population to learn helplessness so we don't realize what is going on.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I talked to old people when I was young to try to find out what it was like 50 years before my time. My impression is that it has been declining rapidly for about 150 years. In the 60 years that I've been studying politics, the problems I saw in the late 1940s and 50s have grown. Basically, it is corporate control using education and the media to make people think things are progressing. The story that lifespan has been lengthened and the cancer war is being won is simply fraudulent statistics. The adult lifespan in ancient Rome was about the same as 20th-century America.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to open up another subject: an Austrian study finding that eating GE (Genetically Engineered) corn may reduce fertility. The study, led by Dr. Jurgen Zentek, found that mice fed GE corn produced fewer offspring than those fed conventional corn. The effects were particularly pronounced in the third and fourth litters. The authors attributed this to the GE corn feed.

It's no surprise that US regulators did not catch this, as no long-term animal feeding trials are required before allowing GE crops on the market. Also, male corn farm workers who regularly work with Atrazine are found to have lower sperm counts.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And if your corn is not organic, you can bet it's GMO.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, I know you talked about potassium nitrate being a sperm count reducer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There was an experiment giving it to full-grown bulls. They analyzed their testicles and found that immediately, with a moderate dose, their testosterone production went down, then the sperm count went down, and it stayed low. The testicles were permanently damaged after they stopped giving them the doses.

**Andrew Murray:** Is potassium nitrate added directly to feed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The nitrite is actually worse because it's chemically closer to nitric oxide.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take our next caller.

**Caller (Pepperwood):** I've always wondered, are multivitamins good? Should we be taking them as we age? And for women, should we take calcium supplements or just eat calcium-rich foods?

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Iodine, Supplement Reactions, Hormones, and More
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat joining us to share his wisdom. He explains things that are almost certainly not what we would hear in the mainstream, but are nonetheless very well researched. Dr. Peat, for people who perhaps have never heard you or listened to the show, would you give us your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After getting a master's degree in humanities at the University of Oregon, I came back in 1968 through 1972 for a biology PhD, concentrating on reproductive physiology. The hormones involved in reproduction are involved in everything relating to life, and brain development was one of my secondary themes of research.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to get into the subject of iodine. I've heard people touting a product called "nascent iodine." They claim it is a stable ionic form that is more readily taken up by the thyroid gland. However, I’ve also read that nascent iodine is very reactive. Given that iodized salt and seafood are available, do we really need supplementation? Is this product necessary?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1980s, I looked into the iodine nutrition question because I saw women with breast disease who recovered quickly when they took supplements of kelp or thyroid hormone. The safest thing is to correct the thyroid problem directly rather than counting on big doses of iodine. Large doses over many years can be problematic. For example, there are about 70 or more publications looking at iodine intake around the world over a period of decades. They see that over half a milligram, or especially over one milligram of iodine per day, is closely connected with increased risk of thyroiditis and thyroid cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Wow.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the theories of why that happens is that iodine spontaneously reacts—or in the presence of white blood cells, their enzymes can cause iodine to react—with fatty acids that are unsaturated. If you've heard about the "iodine number" to describe the degree of unsaturation of a fat, the food oils that are highly unsaturated have a high iodine number. That means the number of molecules of iodine that will be spontaneously absorbed by the oil. The iodine attacks the double bonds in the fat where they lack hydrogen saturation. The iodine fills in to become an analog to the saturated hydrogen content.

There is this tendency of unsaturated fats to react with iodine. When that happens, the body can interpret that as a signal to the thyroid gland, possibly imitating the thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it doesn't cause an increase of thyroid hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Perhaps it can fill the site where TSH should be acting and interfere with that. It probably can go either way, forcing too much activity or, more likely, blocking the effect of TSH. The polyunsaturated fats by themselves interfere with the enzyme which releases thyroid hormone from the gland. So too much of the unsaturated fats, with or without iodine, will have an anti-thyroid effect. But potentially, the iodine reaction could cause overstimulation by mimicking TSH.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned the iodine binding to the double bonds producing this product, and that in its own right could stimulate inflammatory thyroiditis or cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think that's why high iodine intake is statistically associated with greater risk of thyroid cancer. If there really were a product that contained a "more reactive" form of iodine, that would just mean it would attack more molecules. I looked up the source of that nascent iodine product. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So iodine supplementation is very risky. Basically, you should get your trace minerals from seafood sources rather than isolated iodine supplements, and especially not in combination with vegetable polyunsaturated oils.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think that's true.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the chemistry of "nascent" iodine, the media spin was that because it didn't have a stable octet, it was more suitable for the thyroid. But wouldn't that reactivity be counterproductive? Wouldn't it react with the first thing it touched upon ingestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yes. The whole idea of a newly born or "nascent" molecule comes from chemistry. When I was in school, they talked about nascent oxygen, which is highly reactive for a few seconds after it's formed. That's because the electrons are in an excited state. That electronic excitation passes quickly. In short-term situations of a few seconds, that excited state can make a molecule useful for certain reactions, but it isn't something you'd want to put in your body.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's basically a more dangerous form of iodine that can cause a free radical reaction?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's what they're talking about, but I don't think it even exists in the product.

**Andrew Murray:** I was looking at some abstracts regarding isoflavones. Soy and isoflavones were touted as being healthy, but these abstracts mentioned an alcohol-soluble fraction shown to cause female cancers. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it has seriously harmed lots of kids, partly through the estrogenic effect. The oil itself has a pro-estrogen, anti-thyroid effect. The phenyl group or benzene group is located slightly closer to the keto oxygen in the isoflavones, and that group seems to be the estrogenic group. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main problem with soy, besides it being basically inedible, is that it's almost all grown in the genetically modified form that takes large amounts of toxic pesticides, which are estrogenic too.

**Andrew Murray:** It's important to make the male listeners aware that guys have estrogen too. Soy consumption in males has been associated with gynecomastia. Drinking alcohol excessively can also produce that symptom of male breasts.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With aging, a man's estrogen pretty steadily increases. If he has a heart attack or traumatic injury, it goes up sharply during recovery. But generally, there's an upward trend.
