**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I doubt it because the effect of Vitamin E on many cell processes is anti-inflammatory. It inhibits prostaglandin formation, similar to aspirin.

**Caller 2 (Mexico):** Hi. I know someone who took a few milligrams of extra iodine and went into a hyperthyroid-like crisis state—weak muscles, high pulse. Years later, she still gets that reaction from thyroid medication. Is that related to iodine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Back in the years when people in certain regions like southern Mexico or Ohio were very deficient in iodine, they would develop an enlargement of the thyroid gland (goiter). When they ate iodine, even a normal amount, their gland would suddenly start forming thyroid hormone. If the goiter was very big, they could have serious hyperthyroidism that could last for years. If the gland was just slightly swollen, it would pass in about two months.

**Andrew Murray:** So that's a real sequela of using iodine in that individual?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If they took their iodine in the form of thyroid hormone, they could normalize their body functions and replace iodine in a limited, graded fashion. Getting the required amount of hormone would cause their pituitary to settle down and let the gland gradually shrink.

**Caller 2 (Mexico):** Is there any tip on tolerating thyroid hormone now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People who have trouble with thyroid hormone can be deficient in magnesium. Hypothyroidism makes tissues fail to retain magnesium. When you supplement thyroid, you suddenly experience an extreme magnesium deficiency in the heart and brain. Taking magnesium with the thyroid helps. Others, if deficient in adrenal or gonadal steroids, will suffer stress symptoms. Using a supplement like pregnenolone will make them tolerate the thyroid more easily.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about people who take T4 (thyroxine) and get weak muscles and a pounding heart? Is that because they aren't converting it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When people have been low thyroid for a long time, they likely have high adrenaline and cortisol. That causes them to turn T4 into reverse T3, blocking the active T3 hormone. Accumulating more T4 interferes competitively with the little T3 they do have, exaggerating the hypothyroidism.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you say T4 is only 10% as active as T3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It varies. In the 1940s, they tested it on young male medical students, and it was exactly as effective as Armour Natural Thyroid because young men have good livers that convert it perfectly. But women, especially under stress with high estrogen, won't convert it well. I've seen people get more depressed or psychotic when they increased their thyroxine dose.

**Caller 2 (Mexico):** She was using very small specks of T3, under 1 microgram. Should she hold that low dose and increase very slowly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I've known people who stayed with 1 microgram doses of T3 for a week or two. You have to make sure your whole diet is very good—protein, sugar, calcium, and magnesium.

**Caller 3 (New York):** I have a question about Buteyko breathing. Dr. Buteyko noted that as you retain more CO2, the heart rate decreases. I know you recommend a high heart rate typically. What do you think about this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments with animals show that increasing CO2 relaxes the blood vessels, decreasing peripheral resistance. This makes the heart able to pump more blood more easily with less work, usually meaning a bigger stroke volume.

**Caller 3 (New York):** So even though it's a lower heart rate, the metabolism is still good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Most people are running on adrenaline. I've known people with pulse rates of 130 or 180 who, within two weeks of thyroid supplementation, got down to a normal pulse under 100. Thyroid increases CO2, decreases lactic acid and inflammation, and opens capillaries so the heart doesn't have to work so frantically.

**Andrew Murray:** Benign and malignant thyroid nodules are far more common in females than males. What can be done to offset the estrogenic burden?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies of thyroid slices in vitro found that added estrogen caused cells to keep synthesizing hormone and growing, but fail to secrete it. When they added progesterone, it began secreting. Nodules are basically the process of estrogen activating cell division and synthesis of colloid, while desensitizing the cells to the hormone-secreting effect of TSH. Progesterone, by antagonizing estrogen, will reverse those processes.

**Caller 4 (Local):** I was wondering if Vitamin D, thyroid, and magnesium have anything to do with Restless Leg Syndrome (RLS)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There has been research showing that people taking SSRI antidepressants tended to have episodes of restless legs. They saw that nitric oxide and serotonin were involved. Those are produced largely from an irritated intestine. Hypothyroid people typically overproduce both nitric oxide and serotonin and have sluggish digestion. Serotonin seems to be specifically what pushes those motor nerves that cause the leg jumpiness.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would you recommend aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, pregnenolone, aspirin, and avoiding irritating foods, especially legumes and raw green salads.

**Caller 4 (Local):** That's interesting because my partner has this, and we had just switched to eating a lot more of both of those.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned she had low Vitamin D?

**Caller 4 (Local):** Yes, very low.

**Andrew Murray:** She should really load up. If using a 2000 IU drop, take six to eight drops a day for a few days, then maintain 4000 to 6000 IU, and remeasure in two months.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw a website touting nitric oxide as beneficial and suggesting spinach to increase it. I know you say kale can be thyroid suppressive, but what about spinach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it's organically grown without intense nitrate fertilization, and if it's well cooked, I think spinach is good food.

**Andrew Murray:** What about testing salivary nitrite to assess nitric oxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A recent article suggested measuring nitric oxide products to diagnose hypothyroidism because they are so closely connected. I would guess urine might be better than saliva, because thinking of food or being anxious can change the composition of your saliva. Urine gives a better picture of your level of stress.

**Caller 5 (Shelter Cove):** My 16-year-old daughter is transgender and wants to take testosterone to masculinize. Is that safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that's safe, but it should be backed up with pregnenolone and some progesterone to keep things in balance. The tendency is, if you're under stress, for the testosterone to turn into estrogen. Pregnenolone and progesterone will limit that conversion.

**Andrew Murray:** To wrap up, regarding the female issue of estrogen, inflammation, and cancers: would you typically want to lower the estrogenic burden by offsetting it with progesterone, pregnenolone, and thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, thyroid and adequate nutrition. All the vitamins and minerals are involved in keeping estrogen under the safe limit. When you inhibit the formation of thyroid hormone, TSH fails to make thyroxine and T3. It keeps stimulating the thyroid gland, making it grow, but it also has a related effect on every tissue. Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) is associated with low thyroid and high TSH. TSH drives inflammation, so the so-called autoimmune conditions associated with high estrogen are largely because of high TSH exposure driving tumor necrosis factor and various inflammatory cytokines.

**Andrew Murray:** Excellent. Dr. Peat has an extensive library of fully referenced articles on his website, www.raypeat.com. Thank you for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Allergy
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to the show. You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD Garberville. My name is Andrew Murray. My wife is not here this evening, but we are both licensed medical herbalists who graduated in England with a master's degree in herbal medicine. We advise clients with a wide range of conditions using herbal, dietary, and lifestyle advice.

Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us again this month. The topic is broadly encompassing allergy. It is a pertinent time of year; the clocks have gone forward, we are on summertime, and things are starting to flower. Soon the grasses will be flowering, although that is not the only source of allergy-related effects. There are plenty of other allergies, both food and environmental.

Dr. Peat is going to share his insights into the mechanisms of allergy. You probably won't have heard some of what he is going to say because, while some of it is very old material, it hasn't been accepted by the mainstream. Dr. Peat's rationale on the subject is both fascinating and insightful. Thanks for joining us again, Dr. Peat. For those who haven't heard of you, would you outline your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After I had studied humanities and linguistics for a while, I decided to study biology. I spent four years, 1968 to 1972, studying for a PhD at the University of Oregon. In 1969, I attended their International Immunology Conference. Seeing some of the most famous immunologists in the world, I became skeptical of the standard theories of immunity because they were ignoring some of the papers given at that conference in favor of staying with the stereotyped, official dogma.

**Andrew Murray:** You have done a lot of your own research looking at the reality of the science behind cause and effect. Some of your explanations have been borne out in mainstream science recently.

**Andrew Murray:** Starting off with the medical model of allergy, I’ve understood that IgE is the main mediated antibody product that causes the recognition and reactive processes leading to inflammation. Do you see IgE as the main cause, or do you disagree?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think one of the reasons it gets so much attention is that it fits with a hereditary idea of susceptibility to allergy and other diseases. The facts are that it is as much an effect of allergy as it is a cause. For example, it's known that the determination of the B cells—bone-derived white blood cells—to make the IgE type of antibody is determined by signals in the body.

Histamine is probably the most effective signal in telling the B cells to start making the IgE antibody. If you don't have inflammation from the stressed cells producing histamine, you won't be likely to have so much IgE.

One of the things that turns on the production of more mast cells, or the secretion of histamine from the mast cells, is prostaglandins produced from polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), especially prostaglandin E2. Over the last 15 or 20 years, researchers have seen that allergic women have babies born with higher polyunsaturated fatty acid content, and those babies are more likely to develop allergies at an early age.

The polyunsaturated fats tend to decrease the LDL—so-called "bad" cholesterol—and increase the HDL. HDL is associated with allergy, while higher LDL is associated with less likelihood of allergy. PUFA and HDL, the supposedly good things which have been increasingly promoted, are believed by quite a few allergists now to be responsible for the great increase in allergy in Europe and America.

**Andrew Murray:** Because they're signaling for inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They increase the prostaglandins, which increase histamine production.

**Andrew Murray:** These free fatty acids are the same ones you often talk about as being important to keep down because they are both inflammatory and destructive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Besides making the prostaglandins, they cause changes in cells that disrupt their functions. Every function of the cell can be disrupted by too much of the polyunsaturated fats. One of the worst things they do is interrupt oxidative metabolism. The energy deficit is ultimately the thing that leads to really serious allergy problems.

**Andrew Murray:** When you talk about energy production, I think of the mitochondria—the powerhouse of the cell—and thyroid and progesterone being supportive nutrients for it. Is that correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Babies and very young children can oxidize fatty acids very quickly and get good energy from them. But in proportion to how unsaturated the fats are, over the years they slow down the ability to oxidize anything. Sugar, or glucose, doesn't do that. Glucose doesn't cause the great problems with metabolism and energy production.

**Andrew Murray:** So there is a cumulative effect with free fatty acid buildup that leads to a decrease in energy. That energy decrease is responsible for the arrival of inflammatory mediators triggered by things people wouldn't normally be allergic to.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40 or 50 years ago, people associated with Hans Selye in Canada did research on allergy and the shock produced by allergens. In one study, they graded allergens from the potentially deadly walnut oil down to mild allergens like pollen. They gave that range of allergens to animals that had glucose infused into their bloodstream to give them two to three times the normal concentration. Even the most deadly allergen didn't do anything worse than maybe give them the sniffles when they had high blood sugar. But if they gave them a little insulin to lower their blood sugar, the mildest allergen could kill them with anaphylactic shock.

**Andrew Murray:** So sugar is a stress-reducing substance that prevents that cascade from occurring.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Lots of people have been able to give up their EpiPens just by keeping a Coke on hand. If they are stung by a bee they are allergic to, they drink a Coke quickly.

**Andrew Murray:** It is interesting that the industry wants to demonize things shown to be beneficial. Sugar is important not just for energy production, but for vitalizing the cell and directly reducing inflammation. Do you remember the specific amount of sugar mentioned in those studies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 300 milligrams percent was the completely protective level.

**Andrew Murray:** When most people think about sugar, they've been told how bad it is regarding diabetes. But we know the cause for diabetes has nothing to do with sugar; it involves high fructose corn syrup and polyunsaturates.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you give animals extra glucose, it is able to get around the polyunsaturated fatty acid interference with energy production. It can turn off the production of fatty acids and get directly to the mitochondria to produce energy.

**Andrew Murray:** The underlying pathophysiology of allergy involves immunoregulatory dysfunction similar to that noted in highly stressed populations. Allergies have been considered psychosomatic and worsen in patients with high psychosocial stress. How do you see stress modulating the allergy response?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Remember we talked about learned helplessness? Stress that you can't escape from—even if it's not a very deadly stress—becomes deadly because you can't mobilize the anti-stress system. You get stuck in the cholinergic or parasympathetic side of the system, which tends to slow your heartbeat and weaken defenses. It puts you in a condition predisposed to inflammation.

When they looked at people with inflammatory diseases, it turned out that socioeconomic status is additive to any particular learned helplessness situation. A person with a bad condition is less likely to survive if they have low socioeconomic status. But if they have overcome learned helplessness, they can also overcome their socioeconomic status. Learned helplessness plus low income makes you very susceptible to rheumatoid arthritis, heart disease, dementia, and so on.

**Andrew Murray:** How can people best overcome that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** An enriched environment is how they made animals overcome it. In humans, anything that gets you out of the trapped sensation and makes your life interesting helps. Any life-enriching experience—meeting new people, going new places—helps to break out of those patterns.

**Andrew Murray:** For people allergic to pollen, what is the best advice for combating allergies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It turns out that the same things that cure or help escape from learned helplessness also help to stop the inflammatory reaction and reduce histamine production. T3, the active form of thyroid hormone, was one of the early things discovered to cure learned helplessness. It does several things that prevent overproduction of histamine. It's been known to be anti-inflammatory for a long time, but one of its mechanisms is to stabilize mast cells so they don't secrete serotonin, histamine, and other inflammatory substances.

**Andrew Murray:** What is your rationale for the gut-derived link between inhaled allergens and allergy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes the inflammation in a particular area, like the nose, ears, throat, or eyes, is really something irritating your intestine. You can develop IgE antibodies solely in your nasal membranes without having it in your general bloodstream, so you can have a local reaction. But usually, people getting these throat and nose inflammations have it start from something happening in the intestine. This triggers mast cells, which are very numerous in the lining of the intestine, to produce histamine, serotonin, nitric oxide, and prostaglandins systemically. Those circulate to cause inflammation in all membranes.

Avoiding things that feed bacteria so that you don't produce so much endotoxin can help all types of allergy and inflammatory conditions. The standard theory used to say that only a protein is a potential allergen, but there is perfect evidence that many things that don't contain protein are powerful allergens. For example, the alginate dentists use for making molds of the mouth.

**Andrew Murray:** Alginate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, a cousin of carrageenan, which is now in so many foods. One person died of anaphylactic shock while having a mold made with alginate. It's a polysaccharide. Lots of gums like guar, locust bean gum, and xanthan gum are allergens for some people, but they are used indiscriminately in food today.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think this food-based dietary involvement could be additive, where people get worse because their diet doesn't change?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think this is probably the worst cause of learned helplessness in the biological sense. Your body experiences that inflammatory state, which is psychological as much as biological.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you advocate whole food approaches like good quality dairy products.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Calcium and Vitamin D are very strongly anti-allergic. Magnesium is the most famous because a deficiency causes a range of inflammatory diseases. You could cure skin diseases, heart disease, nerve disease, and liver disease just by correcting a magnesium deficiency. Vitamin D and calcium work with magnesium. Some people cure their allergies just by supplementing Vitamin D or Vitamin K.

**Caller (David):** Do you think there is confusion regarding the common cold being in the same category as an allergy? Around the holidays, people have reduced sunlight, eat unhealthy food, are stressed, and everyone gets a cold. Also, why is mucus a major part of both? Is that the body's intelligence trying to throw off the allergens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mucus binds histamine and keeps it away from the cells, and binds other toxins and irritants. It's our first line of defense against allergens and viruses.

I think there is a great similarity between the variety of viruses that like to attack the intestine. Things we think of as respiratory viruses, I think, are primarily intestinal viruses. Polio, in one of its manifestations, was really just a gastrointestinal infection. The famous gastroenterologist Walter Alvarez experimented on dogs about 80 years ago. When he gave them a respiratory virus, he found they would get a runny nose and inflammation in their head without any virus present in their nose. He found the virus was growing in their intestine and producing symptoms in the upper respiratory system. Later, if they didn't throw it off, the virus would show up all through their system.

What seems to be a nose cold is often irritation in the intestine. I've seen people who learned that at the first sign of a cold—sore throat or runny nose—if they ate a carrot, they could break the pattern and not develop the cold.

**Caller (David):** Doctors prescribe antibiotics for colds, saying it's for a secondary infection. Based on what we've learned from you, is that actually a good thing because it attacks the endotoxin issue in the intestine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think so. You usually don't need the standard dose to clear out a bowel infection if it has just come on. Sometimes a third of the standard dose of penicillin, tetracycline, or erythromycin will work.

**Caller (David):** Do antihistamines disrupt the intelligence of the body getting these allergens out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes they can break the pattern. Vitamin E has an antihistamine effect; it prevents the formation of prostaglandins and consequently prevents the degranulation of mast cells. It can prevent the shift to the IgE antibody. Even various antihistamines and drugs can help to break that vicious cycle.

**Caller (David):** You've said before that nitric oxide is also a vicious loop.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Histamine turns on the production of nitric oxide, and nitric oxide signals a bunch of other inflammatory processes. The worst thing is that it interferes with oxygen energy production.

**Caller (David):** So the mucus flowing is probably a good thing, but it may be part of that vicious cycle we want to stop.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mucus itself is fine and helpful, but you wouldn't have to produce it if you didn't have the inflammation.

**Caller (Christina):** I've been experiencing terrible allergies for the past month, and symptoms flare up right when I go to sleep. Why does that happen, and what do you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is when the parasympathetic system kicks in and lowers your blood sugar. That combination turns on histamine release and inflammation. I had that pattern of sleep-onset asthma. I found that Jimson weed or atropine—the belladonna type chemical—breaks the muscarinic part of the parasympathetic reaction. I found that would keep me from going into that very low blood sugar state. However, relying on anticholinergics tends to dry your mouth and cause tooth decay. It is an emergency treatment.

The real solution is to adjust your thyroid and progesterone. Progesterone has a broad variety of antihistamine effects. Estrogen turns on both the multiplication of mast cells and their tendency to release histamine and serotonin. Getting your thyroid to a good level will reduce estrogen and increase progesterone. Aspirin is another antihistamine that works indirectly by reducing prostaglandin and nitric oxide production.

**Andrew Murray:** You could take three 325mg tablets of aspirin a day, in conjunction with Vitamin K. One drop of Vitamin K per tablet is adequate to offset any potential blood thinning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. Sometimes just taking 300-500mg before bedtime has time to get absorbed before you fall asleep.

**Caller (Christina):** My naturopath said I was getting eczema from eating eggs. I know you say eggs are good, but the eczema comes back when I eat them, and I get a headache.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've had that reaction many times to liver, which is another good food. When you tend to have high histamine or parasympathetic dominance, a dose of very high-quality protein powerfully stimulates insulin production and drops your blood sugar. It's the same reaction that happens when you go to sleep. I learned to never eat more than one egg per 10-ounce glass of sweet orange juice to balance the protein.

**Caller (Coleman):** I used to carry Sudafed in my truck for rattlesnakes, understanding it was a possible use on the way to getting help. Is sugar also something that could help in that regard?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Having a Coca-Cola or Pepsi would work. Most people I know have had Coca-Cola work. A 12-ounce glass contains about eight teaspoons of glucose sugar. I think it's mostly the sugar, but the caffeine contributes to keeping your blood sugar up. Ephedra is more powerful than caffeine but works in the same direction.

**Andrew Murray:** Ephedra used to be an herb par excellence for asthma before it was withdrawn. Was it the sympathetic drive or antihistamine quality responsible?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they are all the same thing. Pharmacologists like to talk about specific receptors, but there is an extreme overlap. Benzedrine, amphetamine, ephedra, dopamine, adrenaline, diphenhydramine, cyproheptadine—all of these have a good antihistamine, pro-blood sugar, pro-respiratory effect.

**Andrew Murray:** Are there any sympathetic stimulants that don't have such a stimulant effect on blood pressure but still have an antihistamine effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The currently popular alternative that is legal is produced in the brain, a close relative of dopamine and adrenaline called phenethylamine (PEA). But people are talking about 500 to 1,500 milligram doses, which I think are crazy. A helpful dose would be maybe 5 or 10 milligrams.

**Andrew Murray:** I read an article stating that 95% of people with chronic atopic dermatitis get colonized with *Staphylococcus aureus*. Do you think atopic dermatitis can be treated through the gut?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the gut and the skin have some antigens and enzymes that are so closely connected that when one is inflamed, the other gets inflamed. Thyroid and Vitamin D are the most common solutions to hypersensitivity of the gut and skin.

**Caller (Jana):** I wake up every night with a hypnic headache at 1:00, 3:00, or 4:00 AM. Coffee is about the only thing that relieves it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is exactly the same thing. The parasympathetic system is overactive, pushes the blood sugar down, and then inflammatory things get loose in the intestine and blood vessels. I've used sugar and milk as a compact way to interrupt the night. If you wake up, have half a glass of milk with a heaping tablespoon of sugar. It will usually help you get through the rest of the night.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you see low thyroid as a mechanism here?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid function develops because of accumulating PUFA in the system. When your thyroid is low, prostaglandins are let loose and activate histamine release. Increasing your thyroid can stabilize your tissues so they don't release so much unsaturated fat during the night.

**Caller (Jana):** Is the coffee enema the same effect as drinking coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think drinking coffee with cream is better because you absorb it slowly and steadily, especially if it's with food like a raw carrot. A coffee enema gives you a very sharp increase that can be stressful.

**Andrew Murray:** How many traditional herbs used for allergies might actually have a gut-related anti-inflammatory effect? For example, turmeric.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect they are. The famous soothing teas such as chamomile are working largely on the intestine. Cooked mushrooms are definitely acting on the intestine primarily.

**Andrew Murray:** Have you heard of cromolyn sodium? It comes from *Ammi visnaga*.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never used them, but I know of them.

**Andrew Murray:** What about methylxanthines like theophylline?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Caffeine is my favorite of the category. There is one used medically that has a few carbons added to make it more stable intracellularly—a medically approved version of caffeine.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned Datura as a good anticholinergic. Can that be tolerated long-term?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The dry mouth is the only serious side effect. I've known people who loved it so much they ruined their teeth because of the absence of saliva flow during the night. It's very good for night seizures or asthma, but bad to do chronically. You can do the same thing safely with the oily vitamins—Vitamin E, D, and K. Vitamin B6 and thiamine are important for stabilizing mast cells and blood sugar. Magnesium is essential and works with thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** So we come back to adequate sugars, adequate thyroid hormone, avoidance of polyunsaturates, and a clean diet to prevent constipation and endotoxin reabsorption.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And cascara is another one. The drug companies seem to be getting interested in it as a cancer treatment and for dementia and heart disease. It has a tremendous range of protective effects besides protecting the intestine.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat. For those listening, Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. He has many fully referenced scientific articles there. We will talk to you next month. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Mitochondria, GABA, Herbs, and More
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this evening's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to the shows, they run every third Friday of the month from 7:00 PM to 8:00 PM. We have our very special guest speaker who is full of information about current events as well as historically accurate past events, which brings everything into context.

Tonight, we will be discussing a loose topic on stress, GABA systems, different herbs that can combat stress, and mitochondrial support. Dr. Peat will be bringing his wisdom and expertise regarding mitochondrial activity and how that plays in with hormones like thyroid, progesterone, and pregnenolone. These support the anti-inflammatory cascade that battles the inflammation most people are constantly under attack with.

Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us. Are you there, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hi.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us again. As usual, I think it's good to outline your professional and academic background so new listeners can understand your expertise.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After 10 or 15 years of working in language and literature, I shifted over to biology, specifically aging, metabolism, and reproduction. I studied at the University of Oregon from 1968 to 1972 for a biology PhD.

**Andrew Murray:** We’ve heard a lot from you in the past regarding thyroid hormone physiology, progesterone, pregnenolone, and aging. Tonight we are discussing mitochondria: what they do, how they operate, and what substances deactivate them over time.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, can you explain simply what the mitochondria is? I've been told it's the "powerhouse of the cell." Can you explain that to our listeners?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's a good enough definition, but there is a very stereotyped, textbook definition of it consisting of a certain kind of membrane, special enzymes, and some DNA separate from the nucleus. It handles various functions other than energy production. Steroid synthesis is one of its very important functions. It converts cholesterol into pregnenolone and progesterone, and those turn into all of the steroid hormones.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that why when people age, their cholesterol goes up? Because their mitochondria aren't as efficient in converting the cholesterol into those hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Thyroid is the main hormone that activates the oxidative metabolism of the mitochondrion. If your thyroid is low, the mitochondria don't pull in the cholesterol and turn it into pregnenolone. The other cofactor working with thyroid happens to be Vitamin A. A protein in the blood carries thyroid and Vitamin A on a single protein and delivers it to the mitochondria, where they act like a factory with a conveyor belt bringing in the raw materials and the catalysts.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's how they make the hormones—the cholesterol plus the Vitamin A makes progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Vitamin A is involved in steroid formation not only in the gonads and adrenals but also in the brain and the skin. The skin and the brain are major steroid endocrine glands.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So every cell in our body has mitochondria doing its job in that particular part of the body. But if you don't have adequate thyroid, you won't be getting adequate oxygen into that mitochondria, and basic energy production and cellular function will be decreased.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Red blood cells have mitochondria, but they depend on sugar—glucose—for their energy.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you’ve mentioned in the past that the physiological explanation of membranes is pretty flawed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was studying, the textbook definition of what a mitochondrion is and how it works used a membrane and the "chemiosmotic hypothesis." The membrane has to have certain metaphysical properties. If you look at a real cell oxidizing, it turns out that the outer surface of the cell has mitochondrial-like properties. The same enzyme reactions using oxygen and consuming electrons happen right at the surface of the cell as well as in the mitochondrion.

**Andrew Murray:** So the supposition that the membrane is a cohesive barrier—not fluid or dynamic, but a skin with channels and pumps—is incorrect?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And what about all the organelles? Is that completely bogus as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are suspected to be largely artifacts of fixation. Things are differentiated, but when you kill them, take out the water, harden them, and slice them, things don't look the way they did when they were alive.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is there no way they can look at the cell while it's alive?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can use a fluorescent stain, for example, and see very amazing things—things swirling around. But sometimes the structures seem to be more like a whirlwind than an organelle.

In the 1940s, when radioactive isotopes became available, the whole idea of the barrier membrane was eliminated. Gilbert Ling reviews the history of that. There is no barrier to sodium; it zips in and out of the cell.

**Andrew Murray:** I was always taught about the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, which needed a molecule of ATP to pump in and pump out a molecule of sodium and potassium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** But if you take a hair, which is perfectly dead, wash out the minerals, and then dip it in blood serum or plasma, you get the same unequal distribution of the minerals—potassium inside and sodium outside. It's exactly the same principle as a water softener, where you charge it with sodium and then it removes calcium from the hard water.

A man named M.Y. Seltz wrote a book on the physics of water softeners. He recognized Gilbert Ling's work in biology as the best explanation for how a water softener works. The physics was so good in describing cells that even physicists recognized it worked for something as common as a water softener. But biologists just don't like that way of looking at cells. It tends to leave out a lot of their favorite beliefs about genes and so on.

**Andrew Murray:** Is that where the word "micelle" was coined from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you mentioned a single protein carries Vitamin A and cholesterol. Do you know the name of that protein?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) that delivers cholesterol, and then prealbumin or transthyretin, which transports the thyroid and Vitamin A.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it would be dangerous to have a low LDL, which most doctors call the "bad cholesterol." It's actually a good one.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Because it brings the stuff to make cholesterol out of.

**Andrew Murray:** Once again, cholesterol is not the enemy. LDL cholesterol chaperones these very important molecules to enable steroid synthesis. Without cholesterol, you'd be in bad shape. I heard recently that the brain's white matter is 95% cholesterol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why studies showed older people with low cholesterol were much more prone to dementia.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you advocate cholesterol should be between 180 and 200, and slightly over 200 after age 50.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. According to the Framingham study, people over 50 who weren't above 200 in cholesterol were more likely to have dementia.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to herbs like Valerian root. It is used for insomnia or anxiety as a mild sedative. I was told its main attribute was that the valerenic acid inhibited the breakdown of GABA. What do you know about GABA as a neurotransmitter, and is Valerian's use warranted?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think Valerian also increases the activity of the enzyme that converts the excitatory glutamic acid into the inhibitory GABA. So it does just about everything needed to protect the brain: increasing GABA and the effect of GABA.

The "GABA receptor" system is probably the most complex bunch of proteins that has the name receptor. Many different things affect it in different ways. Valerian—or Valium—binds to it in a way similar to GABA, but in a slightly different way than progesterone, pregnenolone, probably androgens, and even carbon dioxide. These stabilize a whole system of proteins to turn off the excitatory process in the cell.

**Andrew Murray:** "Excitatory" is a very wasteful state to be in, isn't it? Short-term activity is fine, but long-term excitation is detrimental.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's what causes brain fatigue. If you stay awake too long and don't have a good supply of glucose producing carbon dioxide, you more quickly get into the fatigued state. Glucose substantially contributes to the formation of GABA. Carbon dioxide stabilizes it, and when glutamic acid is converted into GABA, it also releases carbon dioxide that helps with the inhibitory process.

Oxidative metabolism in the brain is doing many things: producing GABA, progesterone, pregnenolone, and carbon dioxide, while keeping down the excitatory things like lactic acid, nitric oxide, glutamic acid, and ammonia.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's estimated that 10% of people respond to Valerian in the opposite way—they get excited, almost like cats do. Can you explain why?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not at all.

**Andrew Murray:** St. John's Wort is also posited to be a reuptake inhibitor of GABA, specifically the compound hyperforin. Lemon balm was shown to be a GABA transaminase inhibitor, blocking the enzyme that converts GABA to succinic semialdehyde and glutamate. The body obviously has a fine tune to keep this homeostasis running.

Regarding mitochondrial disease, one of the main downsides is a kind of somnambulence where people get seizures. Is the optimum state a balance between the GABAergic side and keeping things stable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I call that the "high energy resting state," in which the cells, especially in the brain, have so much energy that they're ready to do anything. But when you get very fatigued, they lack the energy needed to replenish that work-ready condition. They enter a hypersensitive, agitated condition. Their resting voltage goes very low, and they stay in a constantly excited but unable-to-work condition.

Magnesium is one of the things that helps restore the relaxed state. Thyroid helps you retain magnesium. Magnesium stabilizes the high-energy ATP molecule. Without thyroid, you can't make ATP very quickly. If you have adequate thyroid producing oxidative energy and ATP, the cell retains magnesium. That complex holds the cell in a ready-to-work state with lots of reserve energy. A magnesium deficiency will cause seizures, insomnia, and inflammation—everything that a lack of energy leads to.

**Andrew Murray:** So it is important to have small amounts of sugars and foods regularly so the body's energy supply is constantly stocked, rather than going four or six hours without food.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And the B vitamins are essential for using oxygen efficiently in the mitochondria—Vitamin B1, biotin, B2.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to melatonin. Advertising is very pro-sleeping and relaxing. It is naturally produced and found in foods. What is your impression of melatonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The good side is that in the fatigued state of the brain—the excitatory, de-energized condition—nitric oxide rises and starts a vicious circle where it activates acetylcholine, which activates nitric oxide synthesis. This can keep you awake. Melatonin is effective at turning off that cycle. So when your brain is in a bad fatigue state, melatonin can protect it by lowering nitric oxide and excitation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would that be in a small dose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. One publication refers to the physiological dose as equivalent to 5 micrograms per body in an average-sized adult. Others have measured it as up to 2 or 3 milligrams in the whole body. When a person takes 10 milligrams, it will put them to sleep, but it is probably doing lots of other things.

In antioxidant or radiation protection experiments, they've used a thousand or maybe a million times the physiological concentration. It can do amazing things like protect against gamma rays, but the outcome might have unexpected consequences.

In the late 1990s, when the material became cheap, studies claimed it was anti-cancer, anti-stress, and anti-inflammatory. But when I was in graduate school, it was known that pineal extract had specific effects that imitated nighttime and winter. In the winter, the reproductive systems of animals—fish, turtles, lizards, rats, sheep—shrink. The thymus gland also regresses, which affects the immune system. This involution of reproductive glands and the thymus has behavioral consequences, like Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), depression, and weight gain. Melatonin is the main thing that causes this involution.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So in different parts of the world, like Hawaii near the equator, seasonal changes don't exist.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right, you don't have the winter sickness or winter immune disturbance.

**Andrew Murray:** I read conflicting information on PubMed. Some said melatonin suppresses tumor aerobic metabolism (the Warburg effect), and others said it was pro-cancerous.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of that varies with the variety of mouse used. Sometimes it decreases tumors, sometimes it increases them. The effect on the immune system partly depends on the dose. At least two groups, one in China and one in Denver, are seeing very clear pro-inflammatory effects from physiological amounts of melatonin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It doesn't seem like you'd want to take something that triggers the wintertime response.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's what I've always thought. In our hamster lab, even though the lab was temperature-controlled with a 12-hour light cycle, the hamsters had essentially no thymus gland during the winter. That started me thinking about the potential risk of changing your whole endocrine system by supplementing something like that.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the air. Where are you from?

**Caller:** San Francisco, California. Hi, Dr. Peat. I wanted to know what causes tooth decay and how do you reverse it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's stress-related. There is one type of cavity that starts with a white area rather than the usual dark area. It comes on very fast with the mobilization of calcium from the dentin under the influence of stress. Another kind is related to stress starting from the outside with the mobilization of calcium because of imbalances and pro-inflammatory factors in the saliva.

The basic thing is to keep your energy up and stress low so that you don't have either harmful saliva or an internal anti-calcium system. Vitamin D and Vitamin K are very important for keeping calcium in the hard tissue. Serotonin has been found to be a major calcium disruptor in the bones and teeth as well. It's really a matter of your total systemic health more than just what happens in your mouth.

**Caller:** Thank you very much.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what do you think about the use of melatonin in radiotherapy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you're bound to have the radiation, very large doses of melatonin are probably protective against the damaging effect. The trouble with using it for treating tumors is that you can kill off the bulk cells of the tumor, but if you haven't cured the organism's problem, you irritate the region and stimulate the recruitment of new repair cells, which recreate the tumor.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to Rhodiola rosea. It has been used for thousands of years—by the Greeks, Vikings, and Chinese. It is considered an adaptogen. How do you see Rhodiola supporting mitochondria or acting as an anti-stress agent?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was studying the progesterone family of steroids around the same time I ran into Ginseng and Rhodiola research. Hans Selye had the concept of "catatoxic steroids." They protect the organism by blocking the effect of a toxin. I think that's one of the effects of the adaptogens. They have steroids analogous to progesterone and testosterone in that catatoxic or stress-blocking effect.

A Russian heart researcher, Felix Meyerson, applied Selye's concept of stress to the mitochondrial level. Meyerson's idea was that we have many layers of stress-limiting signals. Steroids are one major stress-limiting system. Cortisol, serotonin, nitric oxide, and estrogen activate short-term stress reactions. If those continue, they destroy the organism. You need a stress-ending process—that's where progesterone, testosterone, and pregnenolone come in.

It happens that these plants not only have the steroid level of stress-limiting factors but also polyphenols and flavonoids that specifically turn off nitric oxide production and limit the excitatory serotonin pathway which turns on cortisol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I wanted to ask about hypericin, the red oil from St. John's Wort. I remember you saying red compounds are very antioxidant and protective.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is a big polycyclic molecule. The reason it's red is that the electrons resonate and absorb a lot of light. That makes it analogous to molecules such as cascara emodin, aloe, tetracycline antibiotics, and the tricyclic antidepressants.

**Andrew Murray:** How about Pau d'Arco and Catuaba bark?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly that same type of polycyclic molecule. I think it's analogous to the stabilizing multi-ring steroid molecules. They have a geometric stabilizing action on the microstructure of the cell as well as the electronic withdrawing effect. When a cell is stressed and its voltage goes down, the local electrons become very active and attack molecules they shouldn't. When you don't have enough oxygen, you get loose electrons that cause mischief all through the cell.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's what we term free radical reaction.

**Andrew Murray:** Ubiquinone is another one of those structural molecules. What about BioPQQ? It seems to be the latest kid on the block for mitochondrial stimulation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm not sure how important it is to have the most popular, potent antioxidant in marketing. Vitamin K happens to stabilize ubiquinone, and all of these things work in a system. When you're using Vitamin C, it is in an oxidized form that keeps Vitamin E in the right condition. Progesterone keeps ubiquinone and Vitamin K in the right system. It's a much more organized system on the small molecule level than people usually recognize.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Doesn't CoQ10 stabilize Vitamin K?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, they work together with the mitochondria.

**Andrew Murray:** So B vitamins are also very important in terms of electronic stability.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, keeping the cell free of lactate, because lactate represents the shift towards loose electrons that get in trouble.

**Andrew Murray:** Well, Dr. Peat, thank you so much for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who found the show this evening, Dr. Raymond Peat has a wealth of information on his website: www.raypeat.com. There are plenty of scholarly, fully referenced articles.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And our website is www.westernbotanicalmedicine.com. Thank you for listening.

**Andrew Murray:** Have a good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Exploring Alternatives
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to the show, we are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbs, supplements, and nutritional counseling. You're invited to call in with any questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of "Exploring Alternatives."

I want to introduce our main guest speaker, Dr. Raymond Peat. Are you there, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks for joining us again. For those who have never heard your voice or read your work, would you outline your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I got a master's degree in General Studies with work in literature and philosophy from the University of Oregon. About eight years later, I went back to specialize in biology, especially the physiology of aging and reproduction, for a PhD in 1972.

**Andrew Murray:** In your recent newsletter, "Comments on Cancer Therapy," you discussed a phrase—I think you coined it—"trustanoia." You defined paranoia as the belief that powerful forces are trying to harm you, whereas "trustanoia" is the irrational belief that those in power are working for your benefit.

You outlined a chronology culminating in the Carnegie and Rockefeller foundations at the beginning of the 20th century. This was pivotal in establishing the false religion of mechanistic biology, as opposed to holistic research. This holistic research is only just emerging in publications from scientists like Gilbert Ling, Gerald Pollack, and Mae-Wan Ho. Can you discuss the shift in perception occurring away from the dogma that has been upheld for so long?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, I want to mention that the word "trustanoia" was claimed by Laura Nader, the anthropologist.

Regarding the shift of perception, I think it's only partial. In biology, there is a lot of good science picking up from ideas that were suppressed around the Second World War. At that time, the medical establishment fused itself with state power and foundations. Science developed by the government for warfare was shifted to take advantage of these mechanistic ideas that medicine had developed.

The government and the medical establishment began working together powerfully right after WWII, with money flowing from the government to medical research that was sometimes indistinguishable from biological warfare research. Some of the same people went right from one field to the other. For example, Carleton Gajdusek, who got the Nobel Prize for slow virus research, was working in biological warfare. I suspect the "slow virus" idea was a cover-up for the effects of radiation on the brain and other organisms, rather than this hypothetical virus Gajdusek invented.

The dogma essentially denied all traditional ideas of biology and the nature of life to impose the idea that things are predefined. From Gregor Mendel in the 19th century, the idea of the gene was used to deny that plant and animal breeders were really changing the plants. If they produced big animals from little animals, the textbooks said, "Well, these were genes that existed previously; we have simply revealed them."

It was a metaphysics—making up the story to explain things that could more easily be explained by the idea that the organism is highly adaptive. The gene idea allowed people to claim that now that we are in control of the genes, we can make organisms the way we want them, with no danger of things being unpredictable. However, people like Barbara McClintock in the 1940s and 50s demonstrated that organisms can change their own genes to adapt to situations.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So what do you think is going to happen with genetically modified organisms? Do you think they're going to start changing the genes that have been put in them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you realize how ignorant the molecular biologists and geneticists have been, you have to worry that things could be much worse than anyone has suspected. James Watson, of Watson and Crick who discovered the double helix of DNA, is now 88 years old. A couple of weeks ago, he was quoted in the *New York Times* saying that if he were starting over to understand cancer, he would not study molecular biology; he would study biochemistry. He said he never thought he would have to learn the Krebs cycle, but decided recently it would be necessary. The arrogance of these geneticists meant that they simply didn't have to know anything at all about biology.

**Andrew Murray:** You made an interesting point in your newsletter that science was becoming a private matter, specifically regarding the procuring of radioactive isotopes for research. Governments would be entirely responsible for distributing these substances, allowing them to predict outcomes and control the material.

You also referenced the early stages of the medical industry, where doctors wanted government protection from other practitioners. You mentioned "heroic medicine," which included mercury, bleeding, vomiting, and purgative mechanisms that killed a large proportion of patients. People turned to alternatives because the doctors were overtly killing people.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Recently, anthropologists were able to identify the places where the Lewis and Clark expedition had camped by finding so much mercury in the soil.

**Andrew Murray:** Oh, my goodness. It seems like a protectionist racket. A lot of research is hard to replicate because the products are issued under controlled circumstances. We often find PhD research showing the opposite of what the "authority" tells us—for example, that sugar, salt, and saturated fat are essential, not bad for you.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is one group whose papers I've read over a period of about 50 years. Back in the 50s and 60s, Otto Warburg had completely ignored the gene mutation theory of cancer and was showing that it was understandable in terms of a simple metabolic imbalance. Starting in the 1960s, the Pentagon started financing people to debunk and defame Otto Warburg. One of these groups is still publishing as recently as last year, saying Warburg was wrong. They are misinterpreting what Warburg said, but it's important to note that the Pentagon has consistently financed people to push a doctrine that invalidates the metabolic theory of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** It's as if our tax dollars should be supporting the Pentagon to do such work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When they have hundreds of billions of dollars to spend on their conspiracy, it becomes so pervasive you can hardly say it's a conspiracy; it's an alternate reality that they're constructing.

**Caller:** I'd like to ask the doctor if he could talk about any alternatives for emphysema, other than the pills and respirators they give.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've had a couple of very interesting experiences with people who had a diagnosis of emphysema and extremely inefficient lungs. One person was purple in the face and his memory was affected because he was getting so little oxygen to his brain. The other was a woman in her 30s who had been that way for about 15 years.

In the woman's case, it started when she had multiple estrogen injections when she was about 20. That got me reading about the history of experimental emphysema. They found they could reduce the ability of the lungs to absorb oxygen by 90% in just an hour after an injection of an excess amount of estrogen.

In the case of the man, I suspected it was a combination of too much unsaturated fat in his diet—increasing his estrogen actions—and decreased thyroid function. I gave him some progesterone and pregnenolone and a little thyroid. Two weeks later, I saw him in Toluca, at an altitude well over 8,000 feet. He took me up to his office in a building without an elevator, zooming up the ramps. He was 82 or 83 years old and had fully functional lungs as quickly as two weeks.

The young woman noticed she felt better when a doctor prescribed Armour Thyroid. She kept talking him into giving her bigger doses until she got up to five grains. She then went to another doctor and got another five grains, and then a third doctor. With 15 grains of thyroid a day, she recovered completely over a period of two or three months.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Wow.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you don't activate the thyroxine in Armour Thyroid, which is three-quarters of the active material, you're only getting a fourth of it. So in effect, she was only getting about four grains of activity.

**Andrew Murray:** So emphysema in these cases is really an energy depletion and factors contributing to inflammation, which are pushed back by thyroid hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There were animal studies 30 or 40 years ago in which progesterone resolved their emphysema. Pregnenolone and progesterone both allow cells to handle water properly so that they don't swell up, retaining normal elasticity.

**Caller:** What do you think of using the anti-adrenaline drug Clonidine to reduce adrenaline at night? I've read of people using a 100-microgram dose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A low-thyroid person sometimes compensates by producing gigantic amounts of adrenaline just to keep running. It helps maintain their body temperature and keeps their heart rate up. They can even seem hyperthyroid when they have very little T3 production. When these people have their daily adrenaline measured, some are making 30 or 40 times the normal amount just to compensate for hypothyroidism.

Those people often feel a great reduction of anxiety and tension with Clonidine. However, since the adrenaline is compensating—keeping their blood sugar up, for example—it is important to be very cautious when you oppose the adrenaline, because it can sometimes give you asthma or low blood sugar.

**Caller:** Do you think it could be used safely at 100 micrograms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never experimented with it myself, so I don't know the right dose.

**Caller:** I've also read that it lowers cortisol. Do you think that is direct, or an indirect result of lowering adrenaline?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cortisol generally follows a period of excess adrenaline. If you take your adrenaline down, it might let you lower your cortisol, unless you lower your glucose too much. That can increase your cortisol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Salt and sugar are great ways to lower adrenaline. I recommend to people who get anxious before performing to stir a little salt into a glass of orange juice. It works great.

**Caller:** I read an article recently about the duality of taste buds. It claimed that bitter taste buds are the body's first line of defense, acting as a filter for bacteria in the nose and releasing nitric oxide. Do you think smoking or forest fires could coat these cilia or taste buds and give you symptoms like rhinosinusitis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, smoking and pollution affect the membranes locally, but when you breathe them, you also swallow them because they dissolve in saliva. In the last few years, people have observed taste buds existing in the intestine. Your intestine can detect the chemistry of what's present.

Otologists have noticed for 100 years that inflammation of the nose and throat very often starts in the intestine. If you have a chemical irritant, stretching from gas, constipation, or an infection in the gut, the nose will get inflamed and start running even with no germ present in the nose. There is a very close integration between the respiratory system and the intestine.

People often neglect this. They take vitamin pills thinking it will help their immunity or allergies, but I've seen dozens of people recover from chronic runny nose when they stopped taking their vitamin and mineral supplements.

**Caller:** Is there any food you would recommend avoiding?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoid irritating foods. Green salads, uncooked vegetables, and many seeds and nuts are always irritating. Some people can have a runny nose from having a salad just once a week; it sets up a chronic irritation in their intestine.

**Caller:** I was on a low-carb diet for two years and ate a lot of artificial sweeteners. What negative effects have they had, and is it possible to undo them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Artificial sweeteners sometimes activate insulin and cause weight gain just by acting on your hormones, even without increasing food intake. Some of them are excitotoxins if you eat large quantities. Usually, if you stop using them and eat a proper, non-irritating diet, things will correct themselves nutritionally.

**Caller:** Do you know of any alternatives for seizure medication?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since we were just talking about the intestine, that should always be taken into account. Make sure you aren't disturbing your system by eating green smoothies, too many nuts, or raw foods. Irritation in the digestive system will increase the things that promote seizures or lower the threshold for them.

The brain is one of our biggest steroid-forming organs; it produces considerable amounts of DHEA, progesterone, and pregnenolone. These have a quieting effect. When the brain is under stress, those increase to compensate.

There are foods that specifically excite and damage the nerves and predispose you to seizures. Amino acids including glutamic acid, aspartic acid, cysteine, and tryptophan are the worst for lowering the seizure threshold. Supplements of progesterone have been used to reduce sensitivity. The threshold to excitation increases in proportion to the amount of pregnenolone and progesterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I had a client with grand mal epilepsy who was able to wean herself off all medication and resume driving. She sticks to a strict diet that doesn't feed intestinal bacteria, takes pregnenolone and progesterone, has a thyroid prescription, and takes anti-adrenaline herbs like valerian, skullcap, and passionflower.

**Caller:** My daughter is 35 and has had seizures since she was 5. We tried Progest-E; she was taking about one to two bottles every three days. She reduced her medication by 75%, but she couldn't keep up that volume.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Has she had her thyroid hormones, including Reverse T3, measured? When someone is resistant to progesterone and needs extremely large amounts, it's usually because their liver is letting estrogen and excitatory substances accumulate. It takes a super-normal amount of progesterone to steady things.

If you eat things your liver needs—avoiding proteins with excitatory cysteine and favoring gelatin or glycine—and shift the balance toward more sugar (orange juice) and efficient thyroid function, the liver can store sugar and eliminate the excitatory estrogen.

**Caller:** Within the last six months, my hands have started to shake with a very fine tremor. I notice it when holding a book or writing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Physiologically, vitamins and minerals are the first things I think of. I've known people who thought they had Parkinson's, and all they needed was Vitamin B12. For others, magnesium supplements have a sudden steadying effect. Sometimes more calcium and Vitamin D will do it. All of these antagonize excitotoxicity and inflammation. Pregnenolone is also always protective; when you are under stress, you use up your steadying steroids faster.

**Caller:** My daughter wanted me to ask about Alpha Lipoic Acid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's one of the safer things experimentally. In small amounts, it's safe to experiment with. It is supposed to keep glucose metabolism efficient. Biotin, lipoic acid, Coenzyme Q10, and various B vitamins work together.

**Caller:** You said that higher T3 can lower T4?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you are under stress, your Reverse T3 goes up under the influence of cortisol. If you lower cortisol, your Reverse T3 naturally goes down. Everything that helps lower cortisol—sugar, aspirin, B vitamins, minerals—will help free up normal T3 production.

**Caller:** Can cannabis assist with epilepsy?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I would be skeptical about cannabis for epilepsy due to its estrogenic compounds.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, for some people it soothes the symptoms, but it is good to be cautious, especially if used in a crude form that might have other plant components that could be irritating.

**Caller:** I use Stevia because I have Candida. Is it safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never heard of serious allergic reactions to it; it seems fairly harmless.

Regarding Candida: It thrives when you lack membrane surface antibodies (IgA), which depend on thyroid and progesterone. If you are low thyroid, you will have trouble regulating blood glucose and your immune system will favor Candida overgrowth.

If you starve Candida by cutting off its sugar supply, it can put out filaments and become invasive. If you feed it sugar, it won't invade and become deadly; the worst it does is make too much ethyl alcohol. It can be eradicated easily with a small amount of flowers of sulfur (also called sublimed sulfur). Just 200 milligrams—a large pinch—for two or three days in a row will typically clean up the intestine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That is available at pharmacies over the counter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Also, a carrot salad—shredded raw carrots with olive oil, vinegar, and salt—helps. The oil suppresses Candida multiplication, and the carrot has natural antifungal substances.

**Caller:** So you're saying don't do a strict Candida diet?

**Andrew Murray:** The rationale is that starving yourself of glucose puts you at a disadvantage and causes Candida to invade tissues to seek glucose. Keep a normal diet, don't restrict sugar, and use flowers of sulfur.

**Caller:** What is a safe hormone for a person transitioning to a trans female?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Progesterone is feminizing if used in large amounts; it antagonizes the effects of testosterone. In France, there were studies 40 years ago where women with facial hair applied progesterone topically, and in two or three months, it feminized their facial hair. When a man takes a moderate amount of progesterone orally, it slows whisker growth greatly.

It is safe for men or women, unlike the estrogen they often use to produce breasts. The low-thyroid person increases the risk of cancer if they use anything estrogenic.

**Caller:** What would be the dose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's an individual matter. The quality of your thyroid function, diet, and liver affect the response. If you want to reverse hair growth, you can use it topically. Systemically, it is safe at several milligrams per day. I've experimented with it and saw that I didn't have to shave for a day if I took around 10 milligrams.

**Andrew Murray:** It is coming up to the top of the hour. Thank you to the callers. If you want to listen to the show again, go to kmud.org and check the audio archives for Friday Night Live.

For those who want to find out more about Dr. Peat, his website is raypeat.com. There are many fully referenced articles available there. He is not selling anything or seeking political control. Thank you for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good night.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Good night. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Authoritarianism
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD 91.1 FM. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbs, dietary supplements, and nutritional counseling.

Dr. Raymond Peat will be joining us to share his wisdom. This month, the subject is going to be a little political. I can't say it's not, because the subject we'll be covering involves fundamental tenets of freedom of speech and freedom of assembly that this great nation was founded on. We will invite callers to call in for questions related or unrelated to the political and physiological sides of the topic. The broad topic is authoritarianism. Just to couch those terms, authoritarianism would cover freedom of right, expression, religion, and assembly. We're going to bring out both a physiological perspective as well as mental and political perspectives.

Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us. For those who have just tuned in, would you give an outline of your scientific background and your research?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The relevant part of my science background is that I dissented against some of the fundamental ideas in all of the sciences, especially in biology. I had a master's degree in humanities from the University of Oregon for several years before I went to study biology from 1968 to 1972 for my PhD.

I found that when I followed the college instructor's directions to give the students different perspectives on scientific issues in a course called "Physics for Biology Majors," the trustees really didn't want their students to hear the other side of issues from the 1950s, such as the dangers of fallout from radiation or medical radiation. My whole activity over the years has been looking at dissenting ideas in all of the sciences.

**Andrew Murray:** You've mentioned run-ins with various authoritarian figures within the academic community. There are people who come up with dissenting ideas that are vehemently opposed because they threaten the structures in place. How do you think that manifests itself in academia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1965, I saw a really interesting study by a professor at Oregon State University. She looked at the academic success of graduate students. She ranked the scores on the Miller Analogies Test, which measures mental flexibility as well as vocabulary. It's heavy on flexibility; they change the rules partway through.

She found that from the lowest academic achievers in graduate school, the lowest scores on that test corresponded nicely with academic success up to the straight-A students. But then, as the students' mental scores on the analogies test increased further, their grades decreased. The very highest on the mental abilities were very unsuccessful graduate students.
