title: Ask the Herb Doctor: The Metabolism of Cancer
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month’s Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend dietary supplements, nutritional counseling, and an alternative approach to health management.

We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us once more. This month's topic is based on his May newsletter regarding cancer metabolism. It touches on the concept of "paranoia versus trust-noia"—how most people trust mainstream medicine to do them right, whereas it is often better to choose wisely and find information from alternative sources.

Dr. Raymond Peat is a wealth of information, definitely outside the box, thinking like so many of the great scientists he quotes, from Szent-Györgyi to Gilbert Ling to Mae-Wan Ho. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to outline what has happened in science that has derailed good research—specifically research that didn't align with the corporate, collectivistic controllers from the Carnegie and Rockefeller foundations. Institutionalized medicine often ignores or demonizes good science.

Could you outline the history of oxidative metabolism, elucidated by William Frederick Koch, Otto Warburg, and Albert Szent-Györgyi? This really should have been the direction medicine took if it wanted to help people with cancer. Instead, we have a "cidal" approach—killing cancer cells with chemotherapy and radiotherapy—which destroys the organism. How is metabolism seen through the eyes of these great scientists?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Starting in 1900, the idea of electrons in molecules was just being explored. It was about 1930 or 1935 when mainstream chemists started accepting that there was such a thing as a free radical. But in 1900, Moses Gomberg at the University of Michigan had produced a stable free radical—a free but fairly unreactive electron that produced a deep purple color. This started other chemists thinking about what produces color in molecules.

Over the next few years, chemists theorized about mobile electrons in molecules like benzoquinone. It was only in 1916 that Gilbert Lewis gave his theory of electron bonding, and later Niels Bohr described how electrons orbit around molecules. Linus Pauling then gave a more detailed description of how electrons work in chemical bonds.

So, the very best biochemists were just getting started around 1935 thinking about electrons. Biologists and medical doctors couldn't imagine how electrons could have anything to do with the life process.

The process involved in oxidation is the movement of electrons from a fuel, such as sugar or fat, to oxygen. In that process, there is extractable energy. When biologists finally admitted that electrons had to be explained, they wanted to compartmentalize how the energy is used. They invented little "machines" that would take a quantum of energy out of that moving electron and attach it to pumps or motors to explain muscle contraction. They created a primitive concept of biological energy.

However, the actual process is a flow—a streaming process. There is no standing still for the electron. The cell dies if it isn't constantly moving the electrons from fuel to oxygen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So this process is going on with every breath we take, and every single cell in our body is moving these electrons from sugar or fat to oxygen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you try to measure the electrical energy of a cell—by sticking a needle in to measure voltage, for example—people have a static picture of the cell as a bag of randomized molecules. But what they are actually doing is disrupting this intricate, constant flow from fuel to oxygen. They are measuring an injured cell. Every time they try to stop it to fit their model, they destroy some cell process.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, Szent-Györgyi published work on oxidative processes in muscle. He discovered that ATP literally makes muscle contract. He showed that simply adding ATP made the muscle move. However, he found that the contracted muscle in the presence of ATP didn't break down the ATP molecule. The ATP causes muscle to contract without changing its bond structure.

**Andrew Murray:** That is very interesting. Muscle contraction can occur in the absence of the breakdown of ATP? The classic description is that ATP is reduced to ADP and AMP, and the release of that phosphate group drives the muscle. You are saying that is not the way it is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. When I was in graduate school, muscle biologists said ATP has a high-energy bond of 11 or 14 kilocalories per mole, and that energy explained the "motors" in the muscles. Meanwhile, Gilbert Ling, likely aware of Szent-Györgyi’s work, pointed out that the energy of the whole molecule of ATP sticking to the protein of the muscle has an adsorption energy of 21 kilocalories per mole—twice as much as the hypothetical bond energy. That explains why it makes the protein change without having to break down. Simply the relationship between the molecules shifts the whole structure.

**Andrew Murray:** This is a holistic approach to biology. The whole thing is confluent and constant. Electrons don't stop; they are constantly in action. That is life.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We're not talking about high-adrenaline energy. We're talking about energy from a cell functioning properly and having enough thyroid, which basically means the cell has enough oxygen. It is a very calm state, but the cells have a lot of energy in that calm state.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to this energetic state, how should we understand cancer arising from a depletion of this state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1920s, David Keilin in England was working on cytochromes. He found that when an insect or bird flight muscle was contracting and highly stimulated, the pigment he was studying disappeared, showing there was no oxygen present. The extreme activity had consumed all the oxygen momentarily and shifted the cell into a reduced state of excess electrons.

Szent-Györgyi and Keilin were simultaneously working on ideas that William Frederick Koch had developed independently: it is the flow of electrons through the system to oxygen which has to be continuous.

When something overstimulates or irritates an area—and the irritating effect of things like estrogen was already known—that excitation exhausts the tissue oxygen. This was at the center of the idea of what cancer is. Warburg described it as a defect in respiration where the cancer lacks the Pasteur effect. The Pasteur effect, seen in yeast, is where oxygen normally causes the yeast to stop fermenting (stop producing lactic acid or ethanol).

Szent-Györgyi said there is something wrong with the system that prevents cancer from turning off that excitatory process, even in the presence of oxygen. Something keeps the cell in the excited state.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's a backup mechanism? When the body isn't using oxygen properly, it converts to using sugar inefficiently, creating waste and over-exciting the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When it is either deficient in oxygen or overstimulated so that it uses up all the oxygen, it is the same thing as suffocating. There is no oxygen to turn off the production of lactic acid. The lactic acid itself is an irritant and stimulant. It shifts the cell away from the use of oxygen towards the production of more lactic acid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It’s a vicious cycle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lactic acid produces an imbalance in the electrons. It takes up some electrons to be formed, but in the process, it increases the alkalinity inside the cell. It creates a circle of more electrons than it can take up.

One way the cancer cell tries to return to normal is to use those excess electrons—that can't be consumed by converting pyruvic acid to lactic acid—to synthesize fat. Interestingly, the cancer cell turns on the enzymes that synthesize fat as a way to drain away more electrons. Then, as oxygen becomes available, the respiratory process will burn fat.

So, the cancer cell is eating all the sugar it can get, tearing down the body's tissue to use amino acids, and converting the energy from glycolysis to fat. It then oxidizes the fat with whatever oxygen it has. Oxidizing fat is less efficient regarding oxygen use, so it adds to the problem of oxygen deficiency.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this where the myth comes in that sugar feeds cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Actually, cancer eats sugar, but sugar deprivation turns on the Warburg effect. It turns on the stress reaction.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it makes the lactic acid and makes the cancer cells worse?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you go into ketosis, the stress metabolism turns on the partial oxidation of fatty acids. One of the "ketone bodies" is not actually a ketone; it is a reduced state which increases reductive imbalance. It is almost as bad as lactate.

The stress creates this cycle of excess electron imbalance. This activates things that amplify the stress reaction. For example, the formation of prostaglandins is turned on when there is a shift towards too many electrons (an imbalance towards NADH or reduced sulfhydryl). This turns on aromatase, which makes estrogen, which activates more of the tendency to produce excess electrons.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned the inability to relax, the over-excitation, and how the cancer itself is in a very excited state. You also noted that the presence of oxygen calms that excitation down. I know you are an advocate of CO2 having a health benefit. How is oxygen helpful here if we sometimes view it as toxic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** CO2 does at least three central things related to cancer:
1.  It acts like a calming agent, the way ATP relaxes muscles that aren't stimulated.
2.  It is an analog of the pigment molecules Moses Gomberg visualized. It is a Lewis acid. The double-bonded oxygens on the carbon are the essential feature of the free radical oxidative catalysts that Koch and Szent-Györgyi worked with. This acidic effect modifies the proteins so they are stabilized and calmed down, not forced to shift to lactic acid metabolism.
3.  CO2 fills in and corrects what is missing in the Krebs cycle (tricarboxylic acid cycle). It replenishes the catalytic effect of the fuel that keeps the oxygen process going.

Just by increasing CO2—breathing in a bag for a minute or so several times a day—you will lower your serum lactic acid. It is only in the last few years that people are recognizing you can diagnose cancer just by an increased chronic lactic acid excess in the blood.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why you recommend people with cancer go to high elevation, to increase the amount of CO2 in their bloodstream?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There were studies in Russia in the 1960s where they gave carcinogens to rats. They treated some with chemotherapy and took them to 17,000 feet altitude. The ones at high altitude recovered at a very high rate, with or without chemotherapy. About 100 years ago, the insurance industry was already aware that cancer mortality was about 10% lower in cities at high altitudes.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask about pigments. We mentioned the purple pigment Moses Gomberg discovered. In herbal medicine, we use flavonoids, bilberry, blackberries, and anthraquinones found in plants like Cascara, Chinese Rhubarb, and Pau d'Arco. I read on PubMed that anthraquinones have an anti-cancer effect. How do you see those pigments affecting that electronic change?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been several lines of research on emodin, a pigment in aloe, cascara, and Chinese rhubarb. It has a tremendous, unexpected range of functions, including a sedative or quieting effect. It activates oxidative metabolism in cells, suppresses bacteria, and reduces inflammation. These are all properties that W.F. Koch saw in the simple quinone type of oxidative catalyst.

When Koch went to Brazil, he began studying Lapacho (Pau d'Arco), which has a similar multiple-ring structure and a deep color. What these are doing is the same as carbon dioxide: they are modifying or "tuning up" the electrical system of proteins in cells.

The basic idea from Warburg through Szent-Györgyi is that it is pointless to try to kill the cancer as if it were a parasite. When cells are normally fatigued and replaced, the dying cell stimulates the growth of stem cells. This happens in cancer. The natural cancer cell is weak and defective, but every time it dies, it stimulates the replacement of a similar defective cell. The injury caused by killing it stimulates faster replacement.

The alternative idea is to tune up both the tumor metabolism and the metabolism of the surrounding organism.

**Caller (San Jose):** My question is about the altitudes Dr. Peat mentioned. Is there any other factor, like weather, that influences it? For example, Denver versus Albuquerque—fairly similar altitude, but different weather.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Excess humidity is harmful because our osmotic balance is part of the process of tuning up. There is an interaction between oxidation-reduction, pH, and osmolarity. High humidity is a slight stress to the system. Middle-range humidity is good, and as much daylight as possible. 15 hours of daylight seems to be optimal for recovery from cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So being in the Andes would be a good idea—not humid, close to the equator, and high elevation.

**Andrew Murray:** What about Hawaii? It's sea level, but maybe a volcano?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The top of Mauna Kea.

**Caller (Jordan, Redway):** Dr. Peat, you said cancer cells survive on glucose, and when that is used up, they go to amino acids. Are those the foods of choice for cancer cells? Also, I've heard you say amino acids create a medium that allows cancer to grow, but amino acids are essential. Could you explain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on the type of amino acids. Cysteine, tryptophan, and methionine are the ones that most easily promote cancer growth. However, glutamine and several easily metabolized amino acids fuel the production of lactate even when glucose is not available.

The stress that lactic acid reinforces turns on cortisol production. This shifts the balance away from protein synthesis to protein breakdown, providing amino acids. Fatty acids also come into the bloodstream under stress. If those are polyunsaturated, that adds to prostaglandin inflammation.

There have been experiments where cancer growth can be slowed by giving intravenous glucose. A Russian researcher found that with intravenous glucose and higher oxygen, the Ehrlich ascites carcinoma—a classic example of a cell in the Warburg effect—could be reverted to normal metabolism.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Aside from CO2, high elevation, and antioxidants like cascara and Pau d'Arco, what else is anti-cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at things known to reduce excitation, anesthetics—like lidocaine—will turn off the excitation enough to slow down cancer growth. Lidocaine has been proven effective against several different cancers, including leukemia and solid tumors in the liver, pancreas, breast, and prostate.

**Caller:** If you have a lump that is contained and hasn't metastasized, would you advocate surgically removing it so it won't be a time bomb?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on the context. I've had lumps that doctors advised me to biopsy, and I just changed what I was doing, and the problem went away. If it is hard and stuck to surrounding tissues, then a lumpectomy is probably okay, provided you take precautions against activating the cancer by the surgery itself.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What kind of precautions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For example, surgery done when a woman is in the low progesterone part of the month (before ovulation) is several times more likely to metastasize than in the presence of high progesterone. If you do all the things known to reduce excitation and lactic acid production, then a lumpectomy is relatively safe.

**Caller (Albion):** I recently went through five years of hard stress and have fatigue. My thyroid levels—TSH and free T4—came back normal but on the low end. Is there another test I could ask for?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** T3 is the essential active thyroid hormone. Under stress, T4 is converted to reverse T3, which interferes with function. You cannot interpret thyroid function with just T4 and TSH. You have to consider how much stress is causing it to be converted to the inactive, blocking form.

You want a good ratio of active T3 to reverse T3. If you measure your cortisol, you can usually see what is causing it to be inactive. Glucose is needed to convert T4 to the active T3 form and to hold down cortisol. Any area deficient in oxygen or having excess lactic acid can locally destroy active T3.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to hold it there. Thank you so much, Dr. Peat, for your time.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat. Before we wrap up, the Broadway Cinema is showing the film *Vaxxed*, an investigation into the CDC and vaccines.

**Andrew Murray:** We will be back in September to carry this topic on. Thank you for listening.

The free radical theory of aging was conceived by Denham Harman in the 1950s, when prevailing scientific opinion held that free radicals were too unstable to exist in biological systems. Two sources inspired Harman: the "rate of living" theory, which holds that lifespan is an inverse function of metabolic rate, and Rebecca Gerschman's observation that hyperbaric oxygen toxicity and radiation toxicity could be explained by the same underlying phenomena: oxygen free radicals.

Now, Harman's hypothesis has been seriously challenged by recent studies showing that reactive oxygen species actually evoke metabolic health and longevity. Dr. Peat, you've uncovered research which shows a different perspective on our understanding of antioxidants and how they should actually be referred to as pro-oxidants. Thank you for joining us again. Would you outline your academic background for our listeners?

At that time, I was bringing together information on oxidative metabolism developed over the preceding 50 years. I thought the situation was ripe for a conclusion. I couldn't have imagined that 45 years later, it would have gone backward to the 1890s situation of the government pushing a purely genetic causation of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Harman's hypothesis would have been relevant at that time, in the 1950s?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the 1950s, there were lots of new discoveries. Daniel Mazia and his collaborator Katsuma Dan discovered how the mitotic apparatus works—the controlled cell division. They found that the reduction of sulfur groups (sulfhydryls) increased at the time of cell division. If you look at those as the interface between metabolic energy production and cell growth, it suggests a direct course to curing tumor-producing and inflammatory diseases by working on metabolism. The genes are only in the background; they don't have a role in therapy.

**Andrew Murray:** I think many recognize the terms "oxidant" and "antioxidant" erroneously. We've always looked at antioxidants as being the things we were looking for, yet in autopsies of the brain, they find things like glutathione—a main antioxidant—are not that depleted. How is your current understanding different? Essentially, you are saying antioxidants should be termed pro-oxidants?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ones that are therapeutically useful, such as Vitamin E and Vitamin C, actually shift the balance inside the cell. Vitamin C is known to be in a very highly oxidized condition—it is dehydroascorbate when inside a healthy cell. These maintain a constant flow of electrons, but the balance is pushed in the direction closer to oxygen and farther from the reducing electrons.

If you are deficient in Vitamin E and C, the electrons predominate and shift over to reducing the sulfur groups all through the cell into the sulfhydryl form, promoting inflammation. When any injury happens, you disrupt the ability of the tissue to deliver oxygen and sugar. The cell is starved, can't oxidize, and has an immediate shift over to the antioxidant side. The cell has enzymes that function as antioxidants, but they are only activated during injury. In that condition, the sulfhydryls are reduced, the mitotic apparatus is activated, and cells de-differentiate to grow and repair. If the organism can deliver oxygen and sugar, they differentiate and finish healing.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So this whole theory that we don't want to oxidize things is wrong? We want the cell to be oxidizing, and an injured cell is actually in an anti-oxygen state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you get stuck in the antioxidant state, that keeps the healing process from being completed. That's where cancer is: stuck in the inflamed, antioxidant state, only able to divide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How do CoQ10, naringenin, and apigenin work inside the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coenzyme Q10 fits specifically into the mitochondria to deliver electrons to the electron transport system, delivering them ultimately to oxygen to complete the production of ATP and carbon dioxide. It plugs right into the oxidative system. It is oxidizing everything upstream. It is a necessary link between oxygen and the reducing factors. If you don't have that link, the electrons go into the growth and cell division system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Where the actual "antioxidant" function comes in is when you have an oversupply of polyunsaturated fats (PUFA). When you don't have enough oxygen and go into that inflamed state, the electrons that can't be taken up by oxygen are free to locate on iron atoms. title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Rheumatoid Arthritis
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Good evening and welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England and graduated there with a degree in herbal medicine. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with clients about a wide range of conditions and recommend herbs, supplements, and nutritional counseling.

This month, we are very welcome to have Dr. Raymond Peat’s expertise on the show. He offers a counterculture scientific viewpoint—not mainstream and not even naturopathic. His information is rooted in firm science, some of which has been largely ignored and shelved in favor of new drug treatments because we all know that new drug treatments are hugely profitable and not always beneficial.

For those listening, Dr. Peat has an extensive list of fully referenced scientific articles on his website, raypeat.com. They cover many different conditions and can illuminate the research done back in the 50s and 60s, brought into a 21st-century appreciation.

This month's discussion is on alternative approaches to the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. It is an extremely crippling and debilitating condition that affects approximately 30 million people in the US. To use the term "arthritis," we first need to differentiate rheumatoid arthritis (RA) from osteoarthritis (OA).

Osteoarthritis implies a type of joint disease that results from the breakdown of joint cartilage and underlying bone. Typical visual clues in the skeleton of the hand include masses on the knuckle joints called Bouchard's nodes, and swellings on the fingertips referred to as Heberden's nodes. The inflammation is typically not red or hot, and the underlying cartilage is lost with the bone underneath affected by wear and tear.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-lasting autoimmune disorder that primarily affects the joints, resulting in warm, swollen, painful joints, and stiffness often worse following rest. Commonly the wrists and hands are involved, with the same joints typically involved on both sides of the body. There can be systemic involvement, affecting red blood cell count, causing pleurisy in the lungs, or pericarditis around the heart.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you can look at osteoarthritis as just a wear-and-tear breakdown of the joint with years of use, and rheumatoid as an autoimmune condition where the body is attacking itself.

**Andrew Murray:** RA is three times more common in smokers than non-smokers, and Vitamin D deficiency is more common in people with RA than in the general population. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, we’ve mentioned the failed war on cancer, and the war on rheumatism seems similarly lost. Modern treatments like methotrexate are toxic and not very holistic. How do you see rheumatoid arthritis being produced, and what are your viewpoints on it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First of all, I don't make a clear distinction between any kind of arthritis, or even between heart failure, atherosclerosis, and various degenerative diseases. The interesting thing is to explain how a few basic metabolic problems have these very different-looking expressions. The really interesting research over the last 30 years has been in showing how inflammation relates to metabolism.

In the case of rheumatoid arthritis, many years ago I knew two women who were completely disabled with huge swollen knee joints and hands they couldn't use. The condition developed when they started taking estrogen. One was only in her 30s. Her doctor told her she needed to increase the dose of estrogen because of the deep belief that estrogen is protective against almost everything. She was getting worse and finally decided to stop it. She experienced total relief and clearing of the swellings. The other woman had a similar experience—recovery within a week or two of stopping estrogen.

Later, I saw a man about 48 years old. Every afternoon his knee would swell up hugely, and during the night it would get better. Remembering the women who recovered when they stopped estrogen, I thought he might have the same imbalance. I got him a bottle of 500 milligrams of injectable progesterone, which he applied topically to his leg. About two hours later, the inflammation was down. It didn't return the next day. I saw him 40 years later, and he was just starting to get knee inflammation again.

I was convinced that estrogen had a central role and that progesterone could be more curative than cortisol. Glucocorticoids are the main popular treatment, but people end up using them for years, and a main side effect is loss of bone density.

**Andrew Murray:** That's not what you want.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Rheumatoid arthritis, which tends to involve overgrowth of the bone around the joint, eventually shades over into breaking of the bones from osteoporosis. I started reading about osteoarthritis and saw studies published in books—not medical journals—making a clear association between estrogen and osteoarthritis. Even though journals consistently say osteoarthritis is caused by estrogen deficiency, looking at the research on what activates the osteoclasts that cause bone breakdown, endotoxin is a major activator.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that would have a role to play in both osteoarthritis as well as osteoporosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and in all of the degenerative diseases. Once you start having endotoxin absorbed in your system, you begin overproducing nitric oxide and prostaglandins.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, can you recap where endotoxin mostly comes from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is produced by bacteria. It is a combination of fatty acids and carbohydrate called lipopolysaccharide (LPS).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And the main source is from the intestinal tract?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the intestinal bacteria are always producing it. We absorb a little bit all the time, and it acts as a stimulant to the immune system. In everyday life, a small amount doesn't have a harmful effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This is why you're a proponent of raw carrots, because they help to protect against some of that absorption of endotoxin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The bactericidal effect of the carrot suppresses the growth of the bacteria, and the fiber absorbs and stimulates excretion.

**Andrew Murray:** So even in a healthy person, this lipopolysaccharide is still going to be produced?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, there is always a little getting into the liver and seeping into the general bloodstream. But when liver function slows down, it massively gets past the liver barriers and starts poisoning your systems, increasing nitric oxide and drastically lowering oxygen metabolism.

This is where endotoxin and estrogen come together. They both interfere with the metabolic use of oxygen and turn on glycolysis—turning sugar into lactic acid. The more irritated a tissue is, the more reduced it is, meaning it has an electron excess. This shifts everything through that tissue and eventually the whole organism.

**Andrew Murray:** This is the excitotoxic stage where these electrons need to be quenched?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The concept of "reductive stress" is now pretty well established. Fifty years ago, everyone was thinking about oxidative stress, but the degenerative processes are exactly the opposite: not enough oxygen, too much reduction. Estrogen and endotoxin shift us over to the glycolytic, lactic acid-producing condition. Since we can't oxidize glucose, we are forced to oxidize fats. That is very inefficient and leads to lipid peroxidation and the increased production of prostaglandins.

**Andrew Murray:** Which are mediators of pain and inflammation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If our bodies are loaded with polyunsaturated fats (PUFA)—which we don't want—that tends to increase steadily with aging. As a person increases their stores of polyunsaturated fats, every little stress becomes more reductive and more inflammatory. The prostaglandins act to amplify any little stress.

**Andrew Murray:** How else do you see the energetic aspect of rheumatoid arthritis manifesting in systemic conditions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The thyroid and pituitary systems are affected by the processes of the intestine and the failing organ. An inflamed knee, for example, leaks substances. A weak cell leaks proteins. When a cell is under stress, "stress proteins"—including heat shock proteins and glucose-regulated proteins—are activated. These leak out because of the cell structure being loosened by inflammation. They become immunogenic.

**Andrew Murray:** Right, they act as a stress signal to the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is where, even before there are signs of swollen joints, people can detect the rheumatoid factor antibody.

**Andrew Murray:** I think 70% of rheumatoid sufferers have it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I see it as a sign of stress that isn't being handled. The thyroid responds to the same stress signals that the local connective tissue responds to. Nitric oxide goes up in the organism, shifting the brain and pituitary to increase Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) while blocking the thyroid gland's ability to produce the hormone.

Even within the "normal" range of TSH, the upper part of the range is associated with an increased risk of death from cancer and heart disease. You want to keep your TSH low because it is a factor that promotes inflammation—specifically tumor necrosis factor, interleukins 1 and 6, and the rheumatoid swelling.

**Andrew Murray:** And the antibodies defined as thyroid-specific antibodies turn out to be joint-specific as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The thyroglobulin-specific enzyme is also specific for joint tissue. The known atherosclerosis associated with rheumatoid arthritis doesn't seem to involve an attack on blood vessels by antibodies, but rather something going wrong in the whole organism causing simultaneous degeneration.

This supports the Jamie Cunliffe and Polly Matzinger approach to the immune system. Cunliffe's idea is that the primary function of the immune system is the maintenance of order. When something goes wrong, the immune response is a cleanup process. I don't think you need a specific virus or bacteria to explain RA; when you have an energetically precarious tissue condition, any little cause can tip it over the edge into uncontrolled degeneration.

**Caller:** I listened to a 2013 recording where you mentioned it's beneficial for women to have their monthly menstrual cycles throughout their entire lives. Why is lifelong fertility beneficial, and what do women need to do to achieve that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Rheumatoid arthritis frequently completely resolves during pregnancy and returns afterward. I think it's the huge production of progesterone that the placenta takes over during pregnancy. In both animals and humans, the number of pregnancies correlates with longevity.

From puberty on, there is a steady increase in the risk of dying. I think that is the estrogen risk factor. When the organism detects a threatening environment, it turns on the reproductive apparatus. When that apparatus works efficiently, it produces huge amounts of progesterone that have a life-protecting, anti-inflammatory effect. If estrogen isn't adequately compensated—due to low thyroid or toxins—then estrogen cyclically produces damage and accelerates aging.

What shuts the cycle off is the failure to produce enough progesterone. At menopause, even though estrogen decreases, the inflammatory factors lead to degeneration because they persist in the absence of progesterone.

**Andrew Murray:** Older texts mention arthritis associated with mumps, leprosy, or tuberculosis. Do you have experience with berberine or berberis-containing herbs (like Oregon Grape or Goldenseal) regarding their antimicrobial activity and effect on RA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't have experience with berberine specifically, though I've eaten Oregon grapes as jelly. However, my first thought is that berberine likely blocks nitric oxide. Infections increase nitric oxide and impair oxidative energy production.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And if berberine-containing herbs are antibacterial, they would stop the bacteria in the intestines from making the endotoxin that poisons the system.

**Caller:** Why do stores sell Vitamin D3 and not D2? My doctor prescribed D2, but I noticed when I took D3, my hunger patterns changed and I lost weight.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around 1970, publications argued that D2 contributed to atherosclerosis and calcification of blood vessels. Milk producers shifted from D2 to D3 based on that.

Regarding weight loss, both calcium and Vitamin D suppress parathyroid hormone (PTH). Lowering PTH reduces inflammation. Reduced inflammation goes with a more efficient, higher rate of metabolism, keeping weight gain down and stopping the production of fat from protein and sugar.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You want to monitor your levels. A reference range of 50 to 75 is good. It takes about eight weeks to reach a plateau level before you should test.

**Caller:** I am diabetic, likely Type 1. I read that the pancreatic beta cells die. Is it possible to wake them up or regenerate them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Beta cells are always tending to regenerate, but they die quickly when you have diabetes. The factor that seems to kill them as they are being reborn is lipid peroxidation. Getting your polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) down is key.

Glucose happens to be the thing that maintains the constant regeneration of the beta cells. Keeping metabolism under control so you aren't degenerating PUFAs into lipid peroxides is the thing to keep in mind.

**Caller:** Is aspirin helpful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, aspirin improves insulin sensitivity. However, if you take aspirin chronically, ensure your Vitamin K is adequate, as aspirin can lead to a bleeding syndrome if K is deficient.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For one 325mg aspirin, you'd want to take one milligram of Vitamin K2.

**Caller:** Does T3 affect TSH?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Normally T4 suppresses TSH because the pituitary converts T4 to T3 locally. But if you get enough T3 into your brain and pituitary, it is at least as effective as T4.

**Caller:** What about Reverse T3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Reverse T3 partly occupies the same response site that active T3 would, simply competing against it. Local enzymes can eliminate Reverse T3, but if those are blocked by stress substances, Reverse T3 can accumulate.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why taking temperatures and pulses will tell you if you're getting enough T3 or converting T4 properly.

**Caller:** I have two questions. Is endotoxin related to probiotics—are they good or bad? And how much exercise is too much?

**Andrew Murray:** Any exercise that makes you out of breath is not good. Gentle, moderate, weight-bearing exercise is ideal. You don't want to go into anaerobic respiration and produce lactic acid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding probiotics, usually they are helpful, but not always. It depends on the particular species and the individual. Some people get worse when they take certain prebiotics or probiotics. You should judge by how you feel.

**Caller:** I heard you say having more babies prolongs life. But historically, women died in childbirth often. The Taj Mahal builder's wife died having her 14th child.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a study in Hungary around the late 1960s that looked at the whole population over a lifetime. They graphed the number of babies and the age of death of the mothers. It showed a smooth, straight increase in longevity with the number of babies, up to eight.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to hold it there. Dr. Peat, thank you so much for your time and knowledge.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat's website is raypeat.com. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Thanks for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Vitamin D
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. Sarah won't be with us this month, but she will be back in December. We are both licensed medical herbalists who trained in England. We run a clinic in Garberville where we consult with patients about a wide range of conditions, recommending herbs, supplements, and nutritional counseling.

This month's talk is on Vitamin D. Most people will recognize Vitamin D from rickets in the early 1900s. In England and many countries north of 37 degrees latitude, there is insufficient sunlight, especially in the winter months, to generate Vitamin D. Rickets was a fairly common condition and still is in some parts of the world. We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us. He is a wealth of information, and his insights are, as always, outside the box. Thanks so much for joining us, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Could you outline your professional and academic background for those who haven't listened before?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically, I have a PhD in biology, including reproductive physiology and biochemistry, from the University of Oregon.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you have a research background leading in many directions, including steroids, their production, and anti-aging effects. Now, Vitamin D is actually a pro-hormone; it is not, strictly speaking, a vitamin, is it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the discovery of Vitamin D and its association with rickets, do you think there is adequate Vitamin D in the general population?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For preventing rickets, yes. There is very little rickets left around the world. But since the idea of Vitamin D as a rickets-preventing substance was established, that really cut off thinking and research about what Vitamin D really is and what it is doing.

In the 1950s, there was a period when people started thinking about nutrition for themselves—Adele Davis's books came out, for example—and the medical establishment reacted to discourage the public from using their own therapy. There were stories about how horribly toxic Vitamin A was, claiming it would destroy your brain and make your skin fall off, with very little evidence backing it up. You have to give rats and mice a million or so units of Vitamin A to poison them.

There were similar animal experiments with gigantic doses of Vitamin D. Supposedly, there was a case of a baby whose mother took a million or so units of Vitamin D while pregnant, and it supposedly caused the bones to thicken so much that there was no room for the brain to develop. The newspaper stories in the 50s were saying that Vitamin D causes brain damage. Despite reading Adele Davis, I was directed away from Vitamin D because there was such a taboo about taking anything more than 200 or 300 units per day.

**Andrew Murray:** It is interesting you say rickets is relatively unknown. In England, specifically northern England, reports suggest rickets is starting to appear again. The advent of fear-mongering regarding skin cancer, melanoma, the use of sunscreens, and the inherent phobia about being in the sun has been implicated in the British Medical Journal as causative for the rise in rickets.

Regarding blood tests, the beneficial levels have been raised. The lower limit used to be 20 nanograms per milliliter, and now they have raised that to 30. Many are advocating levels of 50 to 70 nanograms. For athletes, studies show positive associations with 100 nanograms per milliliter. What do you think about the tendency in the population to have low levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several conditions associated with Vitamin D deficiency have doubled and tripled in the last 20 to 30 years. It looks like it is because of that fear of sunlight and using sunscreen. I've talked to people who had levels of 10 nanograms per milliliter or below. One woman in her 60s said she was so weak she could hardly walk; her muscles were simply very weak and shrunken. She had levels of 7 or 8. Within a week of taking a moderate dose—I think it was 5,000 units a day—she could walk around.

When you look at the symptoms of people with levels of 15, 20, or 25, you can see gradations of that weakness, depression, shrinking muscles, insensitivity to insulin, and a tendency to have high blood sugar. These are the most common diseases of stress.

**Andrew Murray:** High blood pressure is also positively associated with lower levels of Vitamin D, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Everything related to aging, degeneration, and stress: atrial fibrillation, enlargement of the ventricle, calcification of the valves, hardening of the arteries, calcification of the coronary arteries, and even calcification to the extent of what they call a "heart stone"—a huge mass of calcium.

**Andrew Murray:** I think most people associate Vitamin D with calcium and phosphorus metabolism, weak bones, and osteomalacia. But there is a clear link to energy production and inflammation. You have spoken before about how inflammatory processes are extremely destructive to energy production.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D helps to balance the relation between calcium and phosphate, preventing the over-accumulation of phosphate and keeping up the right level of calcium. When you look at the relation of that balance to inflammation, it turns out that the amount of phosphate relative to calcium is a serious problem in the population.

**Andrew Murray:** Is that because people aren't eating enough dairy or green leaves?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Green leaves, cheese, and milk are the major good sources of calcium. Meat, nuts, grains, and beans have terrifically high phosphate content. The excess phosphate—and the reaction of the parathyroid hormone (PTH) to that high phosphate intake—is exactly the same as a deficiency of Vitamin D.

Too much phosphate and too little Vitamin D results in what amounts to an early stage of chronic kidney degeneration. Parathyroid hormone and phosphate are called uremic toxins in late-stage kidney disease, but people are starting that process very early when they don't eat enough calcium and Vitamin D.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to talk about the natural conversion in the skin. I read that washing directly after sunbathing was counterproductive because you can wash the precursor metabolite off the skin. I also read that only 20 minutes was necessary to produce peak amounts of the pro-hormone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is only when you are in the middle of the day at a moderate latitude. The UVB is so low most of the year in high latitudes that it takes a long time to get enough. But from 10:00 AM to 2:00 PM in the summer at high latitudes, it only takes 15 or 20 minutes to get enough.

**Andrew Murray:** So if you are in San Francisco, from September through April, you probably aren't getting enough sunlight.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Also, the natural color of your skin makes a tremendous difference, as does age. There is apparently less cholesterol metabolism in an old person. The degree of pigmentation influences the reaction to ultraviolet light. In Mexico, for example, women with dark skin who are outside all day—but only exposing their face and hands—tend to be deficient in Vitamin D, even at high altitude and in brilliant sunlight.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think people get enough Vitamin D from the food they eat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that's almost impossible. Even if you drink two to four quarts of Vitamin D supplemented milk. If it isn't whole milk, legally it has to be supplemented, but that is only around 300 units per quart.

**Andrew Murray:** And modern levels advocated are up to 2,000 to 4,000 IU per day. Are there other Vitamin D rich foods?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mushrooms exposed to light have a lot. Interestingly, during the 40s and 50s, the main form of supplemental Vitamin D was synthetic, created by ultraviolet irradiation of fungus. Research around 1970 claimed that this synthetic form might be responsible for the hardening of arteries in young people. Milk additives switched over to Vitamin D3 right after those articles came out.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned mushrooms exposed to light.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you gather them outside, just being exposed to daylight for a few hours is enough. There have been studies using mushroom powder as a Vitamin D supplement. It only took less than an ounce of powdered mushroom to make a distinct rise in serum levels. It actually depressed Vitamin D3 and increased Vitamin D2.

**Andrew Murray:** You have also been an advocate of mushroom soup for other reasons.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, mainly for the anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer functions.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's look at specific diseases. I don't know how many people are aware of the cancer association with Vitamin D, or TB, Multiple Sclerosis, and Rheumatoid Arthritis. Regarding fibromyalgia, I saw a theoretical mechanism linking it to Vitamin D. I know you associate that condition with hypothyroidism. How do you see fibromyalgia in terms of Vitamin D deficiency?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is parallel, almost identical, to the hypothyroid condition. All the inflammations you get with low thyroid function are structurally and functionally similar to those you get from a Vitamin D deficiency.

The Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) is an agent of those inflammatory processes. TSH itself directly activates and causes tissue to release inflammatory cytokines and interleukins. Parathyroid hormone does that as well. By taking Vitamin D, increasing calcium intake, or decreasing phosphate relative to calcium, you will lower both TSH and parathyroid hormone. Both of these hormones are directly involved in mast cell activation—releasing histamine and serotonin—and increasing cytokines, tumor necrosis factor, and nitric oxide, which promote degenerative inflammatory processes. Functionally, Vitamin D and thyroid are parallel. You can't quite separate them.

**Andrew Murray:** There are also papers on lung pathologies like tuberculosis improving with higher Vitamin D levels.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just looking at people when they are brought into the hospital, the higher the Vitamin D when they come in, the more likely they are to go out alive. HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis are very widespread conditions known to increase morbidity and mortality in proportion to how low the Vitamin D is.

**Andrew Murray:** I read about a compound called cathelicidin, an antiviral defense heightened by Vitamin D.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the viral process is basically an energy process. When the cells are well-energized, they are resistant to infection and the replication of viruses. You can see the energy process in brain conditions associated with Vitamin D deficiency. Brain-injured patients have very low Vitamin D.

**Andrew Murray:** I read that Parkinson's was also implicated with low levels.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And the prion diseases are probably influenced because Vitamin D prevents the polymerization of the prion protein, which is involved in scrapie, Mad Cow Disease, Alzheimer's, and probably several other degenerative brain diseases. Anxiety and depression are also associated with very low Vitamin D.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the conversion of Vitamin D first in the liver and then in the kidneys to become active: Are you aware of anything that would bypass the necessity for healthy livers and kidneys to have adequate Vitamin D?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the low level of Vitamin D and calcium is probably the *cause* of the sick liver and kidneys, rather than being a product. Supplementing with calcium and Vitamin D will often correct the liver and kidney problem. It isn't a matter of curing the disease so they can activate Vitamin D; it's a matter of getting the Vitamin D and calcium into the system.

**Andrew Murray:** What about Vitamin D receptors? Is it reasonable to increase the amount of Vitamin D receptors your genotype expresses to overcome a shortfall?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The receptor is the problem. Some stress conditions make the receptor disappear. Getting enough calcium, Vitamin D, and good nutrition generally is necessary to make sure you aren't suppressing the receptors. Some receptor repression is done by over-methylation. If your mother was deficient in Vitamin D or calcium, that sets up a methylation pattern in offspring that can affect their sensitivity to Vitamin D.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know how long these receptors last?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know specifically, but other receptors typically turn over very fast so the cells can remain adaptable—usually just two or three days.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the air. Where are you from?

**Caller:** Phillipsville. A while back, I had a Vitamin D test and I was low. Later, I was on the low end of normal, and they suggested I take 5,000 units a day. I also take a multivitamin that has 3,000 units in it. If I take both, I'd be getting 8,000 a day. Is that too much?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you figure that being in a bathing suit in the sun for 20 or 30 minutes—enough to just start turning pink—can make 10,000 or 15,000 units, then 5,000 or 10,000 units is never going to be harmful. I've never heard of 10,000 a day being harmful.

**Caller:** Did you say that you need added calcium for the Vitamin D to work better?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You need a good ratio of calcium to phosphate. I think it's really protective to take in well over 1,000 milligrams. I try to get about 2,500 milligrams of calcium per day.

**Caller:** What foods are good for that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Milk, cheese, and leafy greens that are well cooked.

**Caller:** They have to be cooked? I eat a lot of salad.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We can't digest raw leaves, so most of the calcium is not being assimilated from salad greens. One or two big servings of kale or chard would give you a good part of your day's requirement. But I think the best way is to have more than a quart a day of low-fat milk.

**Caller:** I can't possibly drink a quart a day. I eat a little cheese and sour cream.

**Andrew Murray:** Can I ask how much you weigh?

**Caller:** I'm not going to tell you that.

**Andrew Murray:** It is important.

**Caller:** I'm a bit on the heavy side, let's say that.

**Andrew Murray:** There are very positive associations with an inability to absorb Vitamin D in obese people. Body fat has a suppressing effect on Vitamin D absorption.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D and calcium both have a direct suppressive effect on fat formation. The fatty liver, for example, is corrected by both Vitamin D and calcium in animal studies. A high calcium intake by itself, with a normal amount of Vitamin D, is very effective at preventing overweight.

**Caller:** What did you say would happen to the kidneys?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not enough calcium and Vitamin D, or too much phosphate—any of those will cause your parathyroid hormone to increase. Elevated phosphate and elevated parathyroid hormone are very toxic to the kidneys.

**Caller:** I had an overactive thyroid and had radioactive iodine to shrink it. Now I take 88 micrograms of thyroid a day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid works in many ways similarly to Vitamin D and regulates calcium and magnesium in particular.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take the next caller.

**Caller:** I am calling from Finland. I was wondering if you could enlighten me about sediment in the urine. Is this a good thing?

**Andrew Murray:** Is it a solid sediment or a cloudiness?

**Caller:** Like a dust, cloudy. If you let it sit, it would make a cloud. I heard claims from people eating mostly fruit that this might be a sign of good assimilation or kidney function.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have a fairly high protein intake and your urine is on the acid side—down around pH 5—and you have a very high calcium intake, say from the equivalent of 2 liters of milk per day, you will have a lot of calcium appearing in the urine. If the urine is acidic, it isn't likely to form stones. But when it stands, the pH can rise as the carbon dioxide evaporates, and that can precipitate crystals. Other things being equal, it isn't necessarily harmful to have precipitation in the urine.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think people with clear urine are healthier compared to those with opaque urine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think clarity is largely from the amount of fluid you are drinking. If the urine is acidic, I don't think some cloudiness is going to hurt. However, there can be bad causes of cloudiness, like infection. The yellow color of urine is considered to indicate cell turnover. Sometimes the morning urine will be yellow and the afternoon urine clear because, during the night with high stress hormones, a lot of cells are breaking down.

**Andrew Murray:** We are almost out of time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wanted to mention that the Klotho protein we talked about a few months ago is the anti-aging protein. It is very similar to Vitamin D in some of its functions. A Vitamin D deficiency produces the degenerative changes that a mutation or deficiency of the Klotho protein can produce.

**Andrew Murray:** Interesting. I really wanted to talk more about the Vitamin D receptor and how that could be enhanced. Maybe next month we can pick up the last part of Vitamin D and bring the receptor into more light. Thanks so much for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Calcium metabolism and sugar oxidation is another subject.

**Andrew Murray:** Excellent. Thanks for listening, and until next month, good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Food
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to tonight's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And my name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists who graduated in England with a master's degree in herbal medicine. We consult with clients all over the states on wide-ranging subjects. Once again, we are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us to share his wisdom. I just got his latest newsletter. He produces prodigious amounts of written work. Dr. Peat, are you on the line with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Great. For tonight's show, we're going to open up parts of previous shows based on inflammation and Dr. Peat's current work looking at autoimmunity, linking that to estrogen and inflammation, and how the concept of cell energy is something he is constantly advocating. Thyroid hormone is one of the pillars, along with progesterone, pregnenolone, and vitamin D. Dr. Peat, for those hearing you for the first time, would you outline your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I did my PhD study at the University of Oregon from 1968 to 1972. Before that, I had been a graduate student and teacher in linguistics, philosophy, psychology, and English literature, among other things. I see that one of your questions from last month was about the trophoblast theory of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Right.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just when I was starting my biology study in 1968, I had known a famous old cancer genetics researcher, Leonell Strong. He was studying the curability of mammary cancer in the strains of mice that he developed using different types of liver extract. In thinking about that, I realized there might be an overlap with the work he was doing and the old John Beard trophoblast theory of cancer, which was behind the Laetrile treatment.

**Andrew Murray:** That was from apricot seeds, okay.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Laetrile activates a process that its proponents saw just as a poison for the cancer cells. But since it involved activation by the enzyme beta-glucuronidase—which happens to be an enzyme that activates estrogen—I saw a link with Leonell Strong's work. In his work, the cancer-prone animals inherited a tendency to have high estrogen from their mothers' prenatal gestational conditions. When he used a liver extract, the animals he treated not only didn't get cancer themselves, but their offspring for several generations didn't get cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Was that because of the vitamin B6 in the liver helping them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He believed it was one of the nucleotide fractions that has analogs in mainline cancer chemotherapy; he believed it was stabilizing the DNA. My impression was that there were anti-estrogenic substances in the liver, and some of them were also the nucleotides that Strong was talking about.

Even though I think the trophoblast theory is wrong in its details, it's extremely rich in its overlap with the actual facts of how cancer develops. The estrogen factor that Strong was working on, and the role of enzymes such as beta-glucuronidase, link these ideas. The Laetrile theory was based on overlap with the trophoblast theory, and the main treatment people used going by the Beard trophoblast theory involved pancreatic enzymes or extracts of the pancreas.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned the product Laetrile, which some people might recognize as the seed kernel extract from apricots. Wasn't the rationale that it would break down the sugar linkage and release cyanide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was the Krebs idea, that it was poisoning the cell. His theory was very nice, except there was a theory for Laetrile that he defined as the glucuronide. The molecule that he published had glucuronic acid on it, which would be specifically released by cancer cells—or by any inflamed cell—but would be poisonous only to cancer cells because they lack the ability to detoxify cyanide.

**Andrew Murray:** Isn't beta-glucuronidase an enzyme that breaks down the sugar linkages?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and glucuronic acid happens to be how toxic substances are detoxified for excretion by the liver through the kidneys. Estrogen glucuronide is one of the main excreted forms.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I have a great liver mushroom pate recipe for people who want to make that for the holidays. The mushrooms have anti-estrogen compounds in them too, if you boil them down really well before you cook the liver with it.

**Andrew Murray:** We've mentioned the button mushroom extract in the past, which has been used as an aromatase inhibitor. That is interesting in the concept of treating cancers.

**Andrew Murray:** I had a couple of questions based on sugars. One was: Does dextrinization and protein coagulation change complex carbs into simple sugars? Do you know much about this dextrinization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is a process that has been used for about 200 years. The first form of it was basically what they used to make Karo syrup or corn syrup—boiling cornstarch with sulfuric acid. It makes a pale, almost clear syrup. But the longer you cook it, and the harsher the acidic or basic conditions are, the browner it gets. They know that the brown stuff in molasses is mutagenic and carcinogenic, just like any charred carbohydrate, starch, or sugar.

When you sort out the corn starch from the germ, you're still getting enzymes and amino groups spread throughout the starch. Those amino groups participate in the classical browning reaction that makes these mutagenic carcinogens. So, the dextrinization produces some dextrose and simple sugars, but the gumminess depends on how far you carry the breakdown reaction. On average, dextrins are considered to have groups of glucose molecules that are around 5 to 15 molecules long.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So cane juice is very thin because there is basically zero starch in that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the sugar is very thin. It contains sucrose itself, so you don't need to process that.

**Andrew Murray:** Just to recap, anything really to do with temperature and starches involving caramelization can be termed as carcinogenic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At least as far as the combination with amino groups, amino acids, and proteins. Those are the best-known mutagens. Acrylamide turns up every time you heat a natural carbohydrate that contains traces of amino acids or proteins. In the absence of amino acids, instead of acrylamide, you probably get small amounts of acrolein, which is another very toxic carcinogenic material.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about protein like meat and eggs? When they brown, is that also carcinogenic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are traces of sugar in those, so you do get some of the same compounds.

**Andrew Murray:** Another question was: Do amylase or amylopsin help change complex carbs into sugars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Amylopsin is just a pancreatic amylase.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of general nutrition, what would you rate as acceptable calories for a female doing relatively sedentary work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I hope 2,000 is a ballpark. You can be very sedentary and still burn close to 3,000. Some people can be moderately active and get along on 1,700. Lots of people now are hypothyroid enough that they can move around with ordinary daily activity and still gain weight on 700 or 800 calories. You really have to look at your metabolic rate.

**Andrew Murray:** How about protein intake for a female?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The military did a big study on people of military age, both men and women, and found that to do just ordinary work, both needed at least 100 grams of good protein every day. You see lots of people getting by on 25 or 30 grams, but I've known people always with pretty serious symptoms getting only 20 grams or less per day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It's hard if you don't want to eat meat three times a day. You can't eat more than two eggs a day because they contain some PUFA. So then you're left with dairy. I think dairy is the primary source of protein that's healthy for people.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you advocate gelatin a lot, but that's not going to make up to 100 grams of protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you recommend for sugars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It really depends on your digestion and intestinal health. When I was in Mexico, I saw nutritionists trying to justify a bean and rice-based diet. It turns out that potatoes are infinitely better than beans as a source of protein, but that requires your intestine to be in fairly good health. The complex carbohydrates of either can support bacterial growth if you have a sluggish digestion.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If people were going to eat potatoes as a source of protein, they better have a pretty strong intestinal wall, otherwise all that starch will irritate them. I know you advocate potato juice used to make a kind of scramble. That's actually starch-free, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that's for people who have digestive problems but still need a very high-quality protein.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of grams of sugar for somebody in a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies in the late 1800s found that diabetics were putting out about 12 ounces of sugar in their urine every day in extreme terminal diabetes. They reasoned that patients would die less quickly if they replaced that amount of sugar. They gave them a regular diet plus 10 or 12 ounces of plain white sugar and found that instead of dying more slowly, they got well.

It depends on what stress your system is under. Huge amounts of sugar like that can be curative if you're under stress. But if your digestive system is very healthy, you can get along with starch instead of sugar. You still need a few hundred grams of carbohydrate either as starch or sugar every day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We had a client who had extensive surgery and needed up to a pound of sugar a day in various forms—marshmallows, sugar in milk—to lower the stress so he could sleep. He went from not sleeping at all to sleeping all through the night just from increasing his sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen similar things in people with cancer or extreme old age insomnia. When they drank a syrup-like concentrate of sugar in milk or ate a bowl of ice cream during the night, they could get back to sleep.

**Andrew Murray:** What kind of foods do you typically gravitate towards?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Two or three quarts of milk, up to a gallon per day, usually 1%. Usually one big egg fried in butter. Orange juice, as much as is available—if it's good, at least a pint, preferably more. Typically about once a week, some oysters or liver. Almost every day, some kind of gelatinous soup, like kale soup or chicken soup with all the fat skimmed off.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We eat milk powder pancakes every morning. How often do you eat those?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every day when we have the powder supply.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Milk is a very good source of high-quality sugar, lactose. One glass has 12 grams of sugar. One glass of orange juice has 25. You can add extra sugar to your milk to make up your quota.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The lactose in milk is famous for helping to absorb calcium. Some studies indicate that fructose or sucrose can serve the same purpose and spare the calcium in your diet. So you can be slightly deficient in calcium and make it up by having enough sugar to keep the stress down so you don't waste your calcium.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Regarding lactose intolerance: if you're not drinking milk, your body will stop producing the enzyme to break it down. If you just take a tablespoon a day and increase it, within a month you'll have a full spectrum of enzymes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Especially if your thyroid is good, you can change your enzymes more quickly—maybe in two weeks.

**Andrew Murray:** A listener asked if red LEDs would be sufficient for red light therapy, as opposed to the 250-watt heat lamps.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably at least some of the wavelengths are enough to reactivate the respiratory enzyme. That's one of the crucial effects of sunlight, incandescent light, and some LEDs. The respiratory enzyme contains a copper atom. In the darkness, it tends to be displaced from the enzyme, causing failure of the respiratory system. The red light has just the right amount of energy to move the copper back into its proper oxidizing position.

**Caller:** I want to know what you think about being a vegan. Is there any way you can eat that way and be healthy and get enough protein and vitamin B?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The closest you can come to it would be eating potatoes and mushrooms. Mushrooms are very similar to meat protein, and your intestine can make vitamin B12, which is sometimes deficient in a vegan diet. With the trace minerals of mushrooms and the high-quality proteins and vitamins of potatoes, you can do pretty well. But most vegans don't do very well.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think they're really deficient in?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Calcium. They break bones too easily once they get to be 60 or 70.

**Caller:** I heard there were no natural indigenous cultures that were vegan. Is that true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people have studied the Fulani people of Africa and found that they were pretty close to vegan, but very sick. Lots of heart disease.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Probably because of the calcium deficiency. Calcium is very important for your heart. You need about 2,000 mg a day, which is basically two quarts of milk.

**Caller (Spiroc):** I was wondering about the correlation of a high dairy allergy. I'm also a vegan, so what will I do for calcium and protein besides the potato every day?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about eggshells?

**Caller (Spiroc):** That's from an animal. You can't get it from vegetables?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Leafy greens, if you cook them thoroughly and save the water, are a good source of calcium and magnesium.

**Andrew Murray:** How much do you think you would have to eat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About a pound, I think.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You'd have to boil a pound down a day and drink all that water. Also, putting baking soda in it helps neutralize oxalic acid, which blocks calcium absorption.

**Caller (Spiroc):** What about protein intake?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How many pounds of potatoes would you have to eat a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Five pounds.

**Caller (Spiroc):** Are a lot of nuts bad for you?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Nuts have a lot of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) that are very estrogenic.

**Caller (Spiroc):** So better to have more seeds?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Seeds and nuts are both very high in polyunsaturated fatty acids. They're not a great source of protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The only nuts I know of that are fairly safe for the fats would be macadamias. They are pretty saturated fat.

**Caller (Bob):** We're getting involved with fermented vegetables—cabbage and all kinds. It really straightens up the flora in your gut. What do you think about fermented vegetables?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of them taste very nice, like sauerkraut, but I don't think there is much nutritional value in them, and there's a risk of getting bad fungus contamination. In Asia, where fermented vegetables are very popular, they've seen a lot of stomach and throat cancer that they think comes from the fungal contamination.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about the lactic acid content?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lactic acid puts a burden on your liver to turn it back into glucose. It takes more energy than you get out of the glucose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you think it's more nutritious to boil the vegetables rather than ferment them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about the probiotics?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The small intestine is best when it's cleanest. Very vigorous people with good digestion and high thyroid function have almost a sterile small intestine from their mouth to their appendix. You get a chance to absorb all the nutrients without competing with bacteria. In a healthy person, the bacteria grow just in the colon. You don't want to support bacterial growth higher up in your intestine.

**Caller (Colorado):** How would I find out if my methylation is interfering with my vitamin D absorption? I tried a therapeutic dose of 12,000 IU for a couple of months. I brought the level up to 73, but my symptoms persisted.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would guess that any symptoms you have related to vitamin D might be from not having enough calcium and magnesium, or maybe having too much phosphate in your diet. It's important to have more calcium than phosphate on a molar basis. Americans often have five or six times too much phosphate relative to calcium.

**Caller (Colorado):** I drink about two or three quarts of milk a day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What are the symptoms you associate with the vitamin D?

**Caller (Colorado):** I get a headache in the middle of the night.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Do you eat any antiseptic fibrous food like raw carrots?

**Caller (Colorado):** Yes, every day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about your thyroid function?

**Caller (Colorado):** I can only keep my temperature up to about 98. I can't get higher than that.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you're below 98, your immune system is at like half power.

**Caller (Colorado):** I'm up to 1.75 grains of thyroid.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Some people need 2 micrograms, some need 200. If you can't get your temperature up above 98, then you don't have enough thyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes a mysterious headache can be traced to a single supplement or a single food causing an allergic irritation.

**Caller (Colorado):** I think I found that the microbial enzymes in cheeses might be the issue.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The two cheeses we know are made with animal rennet are Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Romano. People with sensitivity to cheese often don't find problems with those two.

**Caller (Ontario):** When raising calcium, I get heartburn. What would be the cause? And secondly, what to do for oily skin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of people get stomach irritation from calcium supplements and magnesium supplements—anything manufactured or in an excessively pure form. Eggshell is almost pure calcium carbonate. Your stomach and intestine have trouble with pure chemistry. Milk is extremely complex and soothing to the digestive membranes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How much eggshell are you taking?

**Caller (Ontario):** About half a teaspoon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would skip it for a week and see what happens. If you're getting two quarts of milk plus cottage cheese, you're probably good.

**Caller (Ontario):** I'm just trying to really push that calcium-phosphate ratio. I'm not eating meat right now.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding oily skin: in general, oily skin is very good. It ages very slowly. If you have oily skin when you're 25 or 30, you'll probably have young-looking skin when you're 60 because it's metabolically so active.

**Andrew Murray:** So it signifies good thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually, yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Are you taking vitamin D?

**Caller (Ontario):** Yes, and vitamins A, E, and K.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes vitamin A can be irritating to the intestine. I had to stop using it orally several years ago and use it only on my skin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That might be too much vitamin A for your thyroid function.

**Andrew Murray:** We are right at the top of the hour. Dr. Peat, thank you very much for joining us again for the last show of 2016. It has been eight years since you first joined us in 2008.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: The Precautionary Principle (Part 1)
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed medical herbalists practicing here in Northern California. We see a wide range of people and are increasingly consulting with people by telephone across the country. We are joined by Dr. Raymond Peat, Ph.D., who has spent the last 50 years in research and providing a wealth of newsletters. He is very altruistic and gives his time freely to answer questions.

Tonight's subject is the "Precautionary Principle." This term is not a new concept; it has its roots in antiquity and is the maxim supporting the heritage of herbal medicine: *First, do no harm*. The Hippocratic oath, by which all practitioners of medicine still swear allegiance, is the same. However, modern practices have swerved off the road and are far from the straight and narrow path leading to safe and effective medicines.

We know the Greek legend of Pandora and her box; once opened, it could never be put back, and the price to humanity was great. Why does nature not come up with the best way forward, and why do we seek to usurp it rather than learn from it? GMOs, for example, are very contentious. It defies logic to have Chernobyls and Fukushimas with waste lasting millennia.

The precautionary principle, as applied to medicines and foods, can be seen in Europe where it is codified into law, but purposely not here in the US. The United States has opposed the use of the term "principle" because this term has special connotations in legal language; a principle of law is a source of law. In the European Union, this has informed policy regarding product safety, additives, waste incineration, and GMOs.

Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us again. Getting into the precautionary principle—given that it is law in Europe and not here—where are you most intimately concerned with this for the good of change?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just after I got out of graduate school and was doing consulting, people were talking about whether natural remedies were any better than pharmaceutical chemical remedies. That started me thinking about what the difference really is.

A substance such as progesterone is a good illustration. Just yesterday someone told me the story of his wife being prescribed a new synthetic progestin. I looked up some articles on it, and they described it as being designed to resemble as closely as possible the natural molecule progesterone. A couple of other molecules in the last 10 years have claimed that they are closer than any of the other synthetic progestins to natural progesterone.

It is very interesting that progesterone has existed in animals since animals began. These other substances—in the case of this recent one—have existed in the universe for only 10 years. We pretty well know that natural progesterone is safe because it has been doing its thing in organisms forever. This new one has a cyanide group attached to it that never was attached to a natural steroid molecule. So, it is undoubtedly doing many things that natural progesterone doesn't do. How soon will we know what the ultimate side effects of this historically unique intervention will be? What will they be 100 years from now in the descendants of the people who are being treated with it now?
