**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Why did they put the cyanide on there? Is that to make it a patentable medicine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's part of it. They are making things as close to progesterone as they can, but they can't patent progesterone. The actual natural substance is cheap, and the drug companies aren't interested in promoting something with very little profit because everyone can compete.

When you use herbal remedies, even if there is one specific active agent you're looking for—like in foxglove—you're not only going to have supporting surrounding metabolites that are acting somewhat like drugs, but you know that the natural form of the molecule has existed in plant cells since the plant became what it is. The structure and biochemistry of plant and animal cells are very similar. We have the same basic types of enzymes and energy-producing reactions. We know that those molecules are compatible with at least many kinds of life. If you invent a molecule, it might seem very similar, but you really can't know until you have tried it for the whole lifetime of a particular organism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the case of diethylstilbestrol (DES), it was introduced to treat menopause and to improve pregnancy. It was called the "female hormone." The argument was that if you were having trouble carrying a pregnancy, it was because something was defective in your femaleness, so they gave you more of the female hormone. There were already many things known about the harm of the molecule at that time, but it was given to millions of women.

Twenty or thirty years later, they were seeing that the children—both male and female—and even the grandchildren apparently have been injured by their mother's use of this synthetic estrogen. That shows that the development of sickness, such as cancer, might not show up until 40 years after the exposure. With a six-month animal study, you aren't going to have a clue as to whether it might cause cancer in the old age of the person who uses it, or even in their children.

In the last 15 or 20 years, the idea of epigenetic change has been accepted. What you do to one individual is now recognized to have effects several generations into the future. One of those common effects, which is now recognized as a type of epigenetic change or damage, is called genomic instability. The DNA might not be mutated in the first day or year of exposure, but the genome itself becomes destabilized even in subsequent generations, so that mutations are created later.

Estrogen and ionizing radiation have many overlapping similarities. You can get a synergy between a certain dose of radiation and a certain dose of estrogen which is more than additive. It's like adding extra radiation to an X-ray if you have an exposure to estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's like a potentiating effect.

**Andrew Murray:** The precautionary principle in the EU seeks to bring legal action against malfeasant activities by companies who bring a product to market and subsequently harm people because they didn't do enough testing or covered it up. The whole tenet of "first do no harm" goes hand in hand with being totally honest and scientific so that you're open to scrutiny.

We mentioned Chris Busby in England earlier. He is bringing up the "Euratom suicide clause." He notes that many more deaths have been attributed to radioactive waste—whether from Sellafield, Chernobyl, or Fukushima. He states that the relative risk was downplayed by the American government to maintain research, and the actual death toll is much higher, amounting to corporate manslaughter.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, if some of these drugs are causing genetic problems and cancers 40 years later, how can drug companies test these products safely? Would they have seen some problems within a reasonable amount of time in animal studies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. By the 1930s, years before the estrogens came on the pharmaceutical market, they were already identified as very potent carcinogens and promoters of brain defects, movement disorders, personality changes, inflammation, and cancer in every organ of the body. They were also identified as abortifacients. Estrogen was clearly identified before 1940 as a powerful birth control or early abortifacient agent. Despite that, it was sold for almost 20 years to prevent miscarriage—exactly the opposite of what it was known to do. Fraud was the driving force behind the whole estrogen replacement therapy.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What do you think about new drugs? Do you think there are ways to safely test them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Often they currently have the knowledge and hide it or don't want to look for it. If someone suspects it might have a certain kind of effect, they will carefully avoid discussion of the mechanisms that could cause it to be harmful in their applications for approval.

The whole DNA revolution happened at the same time that biology was being shifted over to a study of the DNA molecule rather than the actual facts of inheritance. I see it as a coordinated effort, sponsored by the government, to support industry in its ability to evade responsibility. If you look at ordinary liability principles in law, it would make it impossible for many of these industries to function. The insurance needed for a nuclear plant or for vaccines would be prohibitive.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So because the insurance would be so great, they get off without having to get any insurance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even without putting this explicitly into the law as indemnification beforehand, the cleanup projects of the great chemical contaminants around the country are being done at public taxpayer expense rather than holding the profiting corporations responsible.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's a win-win for the offending corporations and a lose-lose for the taxpayers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The government is not only working for the corporations in their immediate liabilities, but if you go back to the late 1930s, the government has intervened in the very nature of how science is done. If you look at ancient science from Aristotle down to the 19th century, cause and effect were central ideas. Around the middle of the last century, with quantum physics ideas, people started questioning whether cause and effect is a real thing. That is very nice for the polluting corporation. There are people now—foundations and lawyers hired by corporations—going around the country denying the common sense idea of cause and effect, saying that if you claim a product is dangerous, you have to prove *absolutely* that you are being harmed by it.

**Andrew Murray:** So this is the "get out" clause that America has, putting the responsibility on the consumer.

**Jeremy (Caller from Atlanta):** My wife and I have been PUFA-free for about two years. We've been trying to overcome her estrogen dominance. She is 32. Her waking temp was 94.9, and removing PUFAs got it up to 97.1. We started Dr. Lee's progesterone therapy, doing about 100mg a day. It started her cycles, but she still had PMS. I found some women were doing 700mg or more, so we increased her dose to 900mg per day topically, broken into three doses. She has been doing that since October.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that topical? And are you cycling it two weeks on, two weeks off?

**Jeremy:** No, because she is still continuing a two-week cycle. The flow never begins; she spots for three or four days and then it stops. I was concerned because that seems like an incredibly high dose. We are also doing desiccated beef thyroid, 40mg tablets, one an hour for 12 hours a day.

**Andrew Murray:** 480mg of desiccated thyroid is quite a bit. Dr. Peat, what do you think about this two-week cycle and that amount of thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With topical progesterone, depending on the vehicle, sometimes only a very tiny fraction—5% or less—is actually getting into the body. It's important to have a blood test occasionally.

The liver is always regulating the hormones. When you use progesterone all month, the liver develops the ability to excrete it quickly over the first two weeks. So in the following weeks, you're excreting it almost as fast as you can put it in. The natural cycle has a rest of two weeks where the liver resets itself so that a small amount will have a full effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's why we recommend taking an internal progesterone, like Progest-E, and cycling it from full moon to new moon, then stopping from new moon to full moon. Hopefully, you'll get into a cycle where you're ovulating at the full moon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding the thyroid, products are extremely variable. It's important to watch for changes in temperature, pulse rate, color of lips, warmth of fingers, quality of sleep, and digestion. Usually, low thyroid/high estrogen people have digestive problems. Estrogen tends to recycle when your thyroid is low; it is reabsorbed after being excreted into the intestine. Fiber in the diet—a raw carrot every day—is sometimes enough to get the estrogen down so that cycles are normalized.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you want a temperature and pulse chart, email us. After eating, the temperature should go up to at least 98.2 or 98.6.

**Jeremy:** She has been hitting 98 after eating, and her waking temp hit 97.5 this morning. We are doing the raw carrot every day. I was just worried about the high dosing.

**Andrew Murray:** There is a wide range of doses people use. Dr. Peat, what do you think about the 40mg of desiccated thyroid every hour?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known people who needed that much of even Armour Thyroid. That would make a five-grain tablet of Armour. Even veterinarians would routinely prescribe that much for a cocker spaniel. It isn't unheard of to need that much, but it's important to watch for the signs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also, 40mg of a beef glandular could be very different than 40mg of Armour Thyroid.

**Jeremy:** We ramped it up until she began to get nauseous, then backed it down. Her pulse has been in the mid-80s.

**Andrew Murray:** Symptoms of overdosing would be sweating with minimal exercise, breathlessness, excessive appetite, or a pulse over 100.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If she starts taking Progest-E internally, she'd probably want to start with an eighth of a teaspoon once or twice a day. An eighth of a teaspoon has 50mg of progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And the cycling is very important—two weeks off every month.

**Caller (San Francisco Bay Area):** Two questions: What can a man do to reverse male pattern baldness? And how can someone heal a lower back herniated disc?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Baldness is often associated with low thyroid function. You should look at the whole picture of your cholesterol, body temperature, and energy needs. Specifically for the scalp, caffeine is a good stimulant of hair follicles. You can dissolve purified caffeine in rubbing alcohol, for example. DHEA is another natural hormone that sometimes activates hair follicle function.

For connective tissue and discs, DHEA and thyroid are crucial. If thyroid function is low, all connective tissues tend to be waterlogged, soft, and lacking elasticity. Normalizing your serum level of DHEA—which might only take 5mg a day—can have very quick, dramatic effects on connective tissues, ligaments, tendons, and discs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You must be careful with DHEA because it can raise your estradiol levels. You might want blood checks to make sure your hormone ratios are good.

**Andrew Murray:** The important thing with DHEA is to make sure your thyroid function is adequate, otherwise that conversion to estradiol is more likely to occur.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the precautionary principle: In this country, the onus is on the consumer to suffer consequences and then sue. However, there is a spirit of entrepreneurship and innovation in America. The argument is often that strict regulations, like in Europe, stifle innovation. How do we avoid mindlessly bureaucratic legislation while ensuring safety?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the government would just stop stifling the exchange of information, that would reduce the need for legislative power and enforcement. For example, when a drug comes on the market with FDA approval, the FDA should make public all the information the drug company had. Instead, they let the drug company keep secrets as "business secrets" that very often relate to the safety of the product. The FDA tends to conspire to keep information away from the public.

**Caller (Pepperwood):** I have reached the age of 60 and everyone tells me I need a colonoscopy, even though I'm not having digestive problems. Is this important, or can I hold off?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My position is pretty extreme. If there is no radiation involved, it's just a matter of the mechanics and the toxic effects of any sedative or anesthetic. I would consider it a potentially justified medical procedure, whereas I would exclude almost always CAT scans and radiation exams.

However, no one really knows the natural history of a polyp because you would have to have a colonoscopy every month for years to watch the development. I suspect that many polyps, the same way that many skin melanomas do, simply fall off and go away without being noticed. In the few areas of the world where almost no one dies of intestinal cancer, colonoscopy is not done. There is a close correlation between doing colonoscopies and having colon cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Also, anybody over the age of 50 will pretty much be found to have some carcinoma somewhere in the body on autopsy, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It has been known since the 1940s. A study published in JAMA showed that all the features used to diagnose cancer in a pathological study can be found in an ordinary healing wound. All of those features—abnormal cell arrangement and structure—can be found in a healing wound.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if they mixed up the slides, they might misdiagnose a healing wound as cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It implies that if you cut it out and study it, you don't know whether it was in the process of healing or not. I think the rational approach is to do what you can that promotes healing rather than doing a biopsy. The areas where they don't get colon cancer are areas of Africa where they eat a high-fiber diet. Milk and fiber are very protective to the colon.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to wrap up, but I wanted you to reiterate the rationale behind pigments and skin melanosis—how that cell change can be mitigated with progesterone, given that estrogenic stimulation can be a trigger.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The tanning process is probably related to the formation of moles and melanomas. It is a reaction to injury. When cells are being injured—for example, by a progesterone deficiency or stressed by substances like estrogen—the stress reaction creates a pigment as a defense because the pigment is a free radical scavenger.

A famous Israeli researcher, Gershom Zajicek, has reviewed the evidence on melanoma surgery. He says it's very common that when you remove one confirmed melanoma, often new ones will pop up almost immediately. He suggests that the presence of one is sending out signals that suppress the formation of new ones.

**Andrew Murray:** Because there is definitely a bystander effect with cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The bystander effect is a vastly under-investigated subject. It relates to radiation, estrogen, or any kind of injury spreading signals everywhere in the body.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat. For those who want to find out more, the website is www.raypeat.com.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: The Precautionary Principle (Part 2)
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this evening's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We are both licensed naturopathic doctors. We practice herbal medicine and nutritional counseling. This month I wanted to continue from last month's topic because we barely had time to get into the meat of it. Last month's topic was the precautionary principle. This is something that Dr. Peat was enlightening me to in terms of a directive in law in Europe, whereas that directive is not in place in the States.

To reiterate, the precautionary principle as applied to medicines and foods can be seen in Europe where it is codified into law, but purposely not here in the US. The World Charter for Nature, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1982, was the first international endorsement of the precautionary principle. The United States has opposed the use of the term "principle" because this term has special connotations in legal language; a principle of law is a source of law.

Later in the show, I want to explore the nature of Chris Busby's article and a recent article from Dr. Ernest J. Sternglass regarding whistleblowing on the dangers of the nuclear industry and the government control of data. Chris Busby's invocation of the Euratom suicide clause looks to pose a credible threat to the nuclear industry, and Dr. Sternglass's publications clearly show the reality that no radiation exposure is safe. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for giving your time. Could you briefly go through the process of the precautionary principle again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The principle is really nothing but saying that common sense should be incorporated into public policy—that it's better to be safe than sorry. It is hard to appreciate why that is so controversial, that you should know something about the probable effects of any action you take.

I was just reading about the first big hydrogen bomb test the US made in the Pacific. Some of the physicists working on it said they had calculated there was a certain probability that the bomb might start a chain reaction in the atmosphere and destroy the world. They went ahead with it because they said that was a small probability.

When they were designing the first hydrogen bomb to make a portable device, instead of having refrigerated hydrogen gas, they used lithium hydride or lithium deuteride as the source of the fusible deuterium. They calculated that they would get a 5-megaton explosion. It didn't occur to them that the lithium itself might undergo fission and provide more fusible material. In fact, that is what happened. The lithium itself entered into the nuclear reaction and produced a 15-megaton explosion—three times bigger than they calculated. It killed a fisherman, irradiated and sickened people on a Japanese fishing boat, and burned a lot of the sailors and military people watching it. They were so confident they were good engineers and physicists that they didn't even think about the simple physical chemistry involved.

That simple ignorance is something you have to take into account when working with anything dangerous. But far beyond that is the ulterior motive. If they have some big goal they are after, it isn't simply a matter of not investigating the dangers, but of actually falsifying the known probable effects. That is where the precautionary principle opens up something much bigger. The government has controlled scientific information so drastically over the last 60 or 70 years that even if you do try to apply the precautionary principle, without the information you need, it's impossible to take precautions that will save lives.

**Andrew Murray:** Because the precautionary principle does not apply in the States, does that give a wider doorway for these procedures rather than being held accountable financially for reparation through the courts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is one possible solution. If the information ever comes out that they really knew they were killing people, then they could be held responsible.

**Andrew Murray:** I think about vaccine-damaged children as a pretty recent revelation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Documents have come out that the insiders in the Center for Disease Control (CDC) knew the dangers and didn't want it made public.

**Andrew Murray:** So that is willful culpable damage.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The insiders knew the research showing the risks of vaccinations, just as they knew the risks of radiation. Not just risks—the actual cause of cancer, premature births, and brain damage. When they are finally forced to admit that there is some damage, they traditionally have falsified the quantities of toxins or the intensity of the damage to be expected. In the story that Chris Busby is telling, the government falsified the Hiroshima and Nagasaki damage—over a hundred-fold shrinkage of the actual damage produced over the years.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is this because the corporations are lobbying the government?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Or owning the government. The people working for the government are assured that if they do favors for the industry, they can quit their job in a few years and go to work for the corporations for ten times as much money. It's slightly delayed bribery.

**Andrew Murray:** How can we develop safe innovations without stifling progress or over-regulation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Information has to be available to the public, and that involves alternative scientific opinion being publishable. But the journals are controlled by the industry. For example, the interference by Monsanto with articles that have been critical—either stopping their publication or pressuring for the retraction of already published articles. In the case of health physics and radiation, the main journal, *Health Physics*, is really a house organ of the nuclear industry. The articles that are published are outrageously favorable to radiation, claiming that it's actually good for people to be irradiated.

**Andrew Murray:** So there is collusion between industry, government, and science. We have mentioned before that clinical trials are skewed and data is hidden.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You try to find something on YouTube and you can hardly find it because there are advertising sites that try to tell you what they want to tell you.

**Andrew Murray:** It is like what you have said about reading abstracts in the library. They started removing original research from the libraries, and now you have a hard time finding it on a web search because algorithms direct you elsewhere.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone seems to trust PubMed, but years ago, a librarian posted a notice for students to be aware that PubMed is not a science database. It is controlled by the government and military. I compared some articles that were listed in *Biological Abstracts* or *Chemical Abstracts* and then looked them up in *Index Medicus* or PubMed. The good articles were simply deleted. I would find a conventional, mainstream idea article right next to a very good article; the bad article would be listed in PubMed, and the good article wouldn't be.

**Andrew Murray:** Are *Biological Abstracts* and *Chemical Abstracts* searchable databases that anyone can look at?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are very expensive to use. If you get your library to subscribe and are a member of the library as staff or a student, that's the only practical way to get in.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to mention Chris Busby's Euratom clause report. It outlines the cover-up and misinformation tactics used by the government to hide the fact that the deaths of survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki are still ongoing, killing tens of thousands every year through cancers and genetic defects.

Regarding Dr. Ernest Sternglass, his work on "no exposure is the only safe approach" can be seen by searching "Nuclear Witness Dr. Ernest J. Sternglass." The UPI has stated there are skyrocketing cancer cases in Fukushima. The Times published that child cancers are up 5,000% in Fukushima. We also see a spike in animal deformities on the West Coast.

How can we continue to defend nuclear energy in the presence of technologies like clean coal, which were being shut down in light of it being a global warming issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Do you remember when the Three Mile Island reactor melted down? The public really started turning against nuclear energy because of the fear of a huge meltdown. Sternglass got in great trouble. The industry defamed him beginning even before that, around 1970. They started saying he was totally uninformed because he had the actual inside information showing that the government was under-declaring the amount of radiation being released by hundreds of millions of times.

The nuclear industry taught everyone who worked in it that people like Sternglass, Gofman, and Alice Stewart were simply incompetent fanatics. Even Linus Pauling was in trouble and ostracized by other chemists and physicists because of his opposition to testing bombs in the atmosphere.

**Andrew Murray:** Part of the Sternglass article mentioned the US Army's readiness to commit hundreds of underground explosions to create caverns to store natural gas.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That whole idea of "Atoms for Peace," such as digging canals and producing natural gas release, was knowingly fraudulent. They had the information right from the 1940s that small amounts of radiation caused infant deformities, stopped brain growth in utero, and caused birth defects. But for their own purposes—to be able to wage nuclear war—they promoted this idea that the bombs had a peaceful use.

Because of the public turning against nuclear power in 1978 as a result of Three Mile Island, a process started in the Pentagon where they had to come up with something more scary than nuclear power. Just at the beginning of 1980, shortly after Three Mile Island, they reversed a trend of predicting a new ice age. From the late 1940s until 1979, they were predicting planetary cooling. But the Pentagon and the CIA came up with this idea of planetary warming.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Or the nuclear power industry told them to do that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, the military too, because they need the nuclear power as a source of fuel for the bombs. So they invented planetary warming, totally reversing the preceding 30 years of climate study, as a way to say there is something worse than nuclear power. If we don't use this clean, cheap nuclear energy, we will overheat the planet.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And polar bears will die, and we won't take into consideration how many women, children, and men die from radiation poisoning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When Chernobyl exploded in 1986, the nuclear industry in this country insisted that only a few dozen people were killed. The Russians, who were best informed on the cleanup, calculated about 10 years ago that 985,000 premature deaths from cancer had already occurred from Chernobyl alone.

**Andrew Murray:** It seems analogous to the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) issue. You have been saying for decades that PUFAs are bad, oxidizable, and cause thyroid suppression. Only recently has that revelation become mainstream.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Actually, my interest in that grew out of my interest in the radiation industry issue in the 1950s. Those are the fats that break down and become toxic under the influence of radiation. An excess of polyunsaturated fats produces the same kind of damage that radiation injury does. Estrogen and ionizing radiation synergize; each one produces the same sort of damage to the organism, and both of those converge on the polyunsaturated fats in the tissues.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller. Where are you from and what's your question?

**Caller (Bay Area):** I found that as my hypothyroidism and estrogen dominance improves, things are less overwhelming. For example, I used to get anxious with simple tasks like grocery shopping. Recently someone told me that I was using my health issues as an excuse for laziness. What are your thoughts on the concept of laziness? Interestingly, I'm the most productive when I feel very healthy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think I've ever run into anyone that had exactly that excuse.

**Andrew Murray:** I think what the caller was saying is that when you are metabolically deficient, it has a psychological effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** When you're metabolically healthy, then you're definitely the most productive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Chronic Fatigue Syndrome for quite a few years was said to be a personality issue. But that's something that can actually be measured metabolically and hormonally.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take the next caller.

**Caller (Finland):** It is 3:00 AM here. I'm interested in two topics. First, is there an ideal body fat percentage to aim for? Second, what does science tell us about how much sleep we really need? Is it smart to sleep just once at night?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think body fat varies according to gender and age. For example, young women in their 20s and 30s who are overweight have a lower incidence of breast cancer than those who are underweight. One of the greatest increases in cancer is occurring among women between the ages of 25 and early 30s. Because of that relationship, it's better for a young woman to be on the plump side.

In older people, being somewhat leaner for women reduces the risk of breast cancer. However, in old people in general, mortality is lower with heavier body weight; they just have greater resistance to stresses. Same with increased cholesterol and a slight increase of blood pressure in old age—it is good.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think that body fat percentage would be? 20%? 24%?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think a little higher.

**Andrew Murray:** How about 30%?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think 30% average.

**Andrew Murray:** And regarding sleep recommendations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The timing and the quality of the sleep is the thing. Your blood sugar has to stay fairly steady and not drop too much during the night. Otherwise, the deep sleep is diminished. In a low thyroid person, they might spend eight or ten hours in bed semi-sleeping, but wake up feeling fatigued.

The level of blood sugar and metabolic rate are the main things that allow deep and restful sleep. The turnover of the brain tissue is very great during the night. That's one of the places where polyunsaturated fats in your thighs and abdomen are released into the bloodstream during the night, and whatever is in the bloodstream gets built into the brain structure. You want to keep your free fatty acids fairly low during the night by keeping your blood sugar up. Having carbohydrates close to bedtime protects the quality of sleep.

They've studied people with cirrhosis of the liver who did much better on all their tests if they had a fairly big dose of carbohydrate at bedtime. The breakdown that happens with aging primarily happens during the night. The calcium loss from the bones is essentially all in the morning urine because that's when the stress hormones rise.

**Andrew Murray:** So 10 hours is not too much sleep?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but you probably don't need that much if it's efficient sleep. But I think it should be more than six hours for almost everyone.

**Andrew Murray:** I think the caller was thinking about the "Neanderthal sleep" pattern where humans used to go through two or three sleep cycles in a night.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the long winter, the night darkness would be stressful. If they wake up and have a lunch in the middle of the night, that replenishes their glycogen stores and makes the night much less stressful. Doctors used to be very negative about night eaters, but studies in the last five years show that it's very protective.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Haven't you said too, Dr. Peat, that no one should get up before 8:00 o'clock?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I haven't ever met a night worker who is healthy.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about people doing night shifts and the imbalance of circadian rhythm?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very bad for the health; it increases the cancer incidence. I think it's very important to avoid it when possible.

**Caller (Bay Area):** Sarah just mentioned that Dr. Peat said you shouldn't wake up before 8. Can you elaborate on that?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that because of cortisol levels that are very high at the early hours of the morning?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For example, people who would go for a jog first thing in the morning without eating—they looked at their blood cells, and the chromosomes in their white blood cells were broken. If they ate and then did their run, there was no chromosome damage. That same morning susceptibility to stress shows up in mortality; there's a morning peak in death from strokes and heart attacks. The blood is thicker in the morning and the cortisol is at its daytime peak. So people are relatively fragile in the morning.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there any easy way for people to find glaring mistakes in clinical trials, or is it completely sewn up by the companies doing the trials?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you think of propaganda analysis, when you're reading a science paper, you have to think about everything that they can do wrong. Sometimes I see a paper with fairly good conclusions in which they did everything wrong.

When you dissociate brain cells and put them in culture, or if you separate mitochondria and do techniques such as a patch clamp recording, there are things that have absolutely no physiological real meaning that are very customary in research papers. So you have to look for connections to what's happening in the real organism.

If you look at studies on animals, they can do things to the intact animal that you can't do to a person. But if you use, for example, a rodent with its night cycle and forget what time of day you're doing the experiment, they're stressed if you do experiments during the daytime when they normally would be sleeping. Typically someone with an ulterior motive will use exactly those tricks. Much of the estrogen industry is based on claims about estrogen and bone health based on rodents. They had been doing studies in dogs and found that estrogen damaged their bones. They gave up the dog studies and went to rodents because they could get opposite results.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, that's why we need you to help us sort out all this information.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** If you want to know more, visit www.raypeat.com. Also, look up Chris Busby and the Euratom clause, and Dr. Ernest Sternglass. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Thanks for listening and have a good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Endocrinology (Part 1): Parkinson's
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** From the Middle East to Ireland, it's this evening's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** We have been very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat joining us for a long time now with various topics. This month is no exception. I wanted to provide an outline or a basis for the listeners. I know people listening to these podcasts from all over the world have found them interesting and informative. It has led them to read research from people Dr. Peat has mentioned, or they’ve had conditions and recovered listening to Dr. Peat's advice. I am very much aware that this is a real resource.

We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat join us. I wanted to start an outline this month with endocrinology as the subject, specifically the nervous system as a whole. We are going to get into Parkinson's disease and Parkinsonism as an introduction to the endocrine system. Later, perhaps next month, we will get into the pituitary, thymus, adrenals, pancreas, ovaries, and testes—how they affect health and how everything we do can consciously interact for good or bad with our health. We're not at the mercy of anything in particular; we make choices. Are you there, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us. I wanted to explore the endocrine system. It is a large topic, but one I feel will be a useful exercise in understanding physiology from your perspective. You make regular mention of pioneering scientists whose works give a better appreciation of the physiological processes occurring in the body. These often provide a new direction away from the hijacked modern scientific theories we're cultured to accept—a lot of which are a Pandora's box of ever-increasing drug dependencies.

Communication systems and appropriate responses are key to good health and functioning. This is the role of the endocrine system. I found records of the Chinese isolating sex and pituitary hormones from human urine in 200 BC. Then obviously the ancient Greeks and Romans—Aristotle, Hippocrates, and Galen—until the emergence of the germ theory in the 19th century. I think that is where it veered off the rails of normality and common sense. Dr. Peat, would you mind giving an overview of the understanding of disease past to present, and how your rationale differs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I see it as a deviation from the Chinese and the Greeks, who had a pretty unified picture of what an organism is. Aristotle was pretty much an organicist in his understanding of the organism. It was really around the time of Descartes, in the early part of the 17th century, when things got formalized on the wrong track.

Descartes described the organism as a machine completely separate from consciousness. Consciousness was guiding the machine, possibly from some contact point in the brain, but mostly people who were persecuted by the monarchies continued to think along the organic, unified understanding of what an animal or a person is. Following Descartes, the organism was seen as made up of parts, just like a steam engine or a clock. Each part could be defined, understood, and mechanically interlocked with the other parts. The consciousness or the soul was seen as something completely separate from this machine.

When the idea of infection—something from the environment causing a disease—came in, it happened that the use of the microscope had developed to the point that people had seen the compartments in plants. They called the compartments "cells." When the plant dried up, it left the cellulose framework—empty little chambers. A more underground approach looked at particles like red blood cells and called the units "corpuscles," or little bodies, rather than empty compartments. This idea of breaking the organism down into cells and seeing those as parts of a machine made up of material, without consciousness or spirit, became the background for seeing a disease as a particular mechanical interference with the operation of the machine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And this is where the term reductionism came from, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. One line of thinking was that it was a particular little particle of evil material—a germ cell analogous to the cells that make up the machine—interfering with our material particles. That became identified as a disease. It was a very concrete, specific interference with the machine.

As people looked more closely at tumors, they saw it was really a matter of organization rather than some particular concrete change or substance. But this idea of organization took about 150 years to finally catch on. Right up until the beginning of this century, people were still stuck on Descartes' picture of a mechanical organism being interrupted by something right down on the cellular or molecular level. Cancer was defined as an evil cell, a mutant cell containing bad genetic material or defective DNA. So, in the case of a germ-caused disease, all you had to do was kill the germ. In the case of cancer interpreted as a mutant cell, all you had to do was eliminate every single individual mutant cell and the disease would be cured.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That's still how they treat cancer now, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** To some degree. Almost everyone is still stuck in this 17th-century idea of what an organism is and what a disease is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even regarding Parkinson's disease... in the 19th century, people recognized that all the symptoms of the disease—stiffness, wobbly tremor, and slowness of movement—are simply extreme old age symptoms coming on stronger and earlier. By the latter part of the 19th century, people had noticed that if sufferers took a long train ride to get to the doctor, their symptoms might disappear. Or if they rode in a carriage or on a horse, their symptoms were greatly alleviated by just moving around through space. Some people proposed a vibration therapy. About 40 years ago, someone noticed that swimming alleviated the symptoms. Simply a different kind of stimulation could reverse the symptoms.

It turns out that in animals, you can create the disease by poisoning them. But by giving them an enriched environment, you can reverse the actual anatomical and chemical changes of their nervous system.

**Andrew Murray:** So in the poisoned animals, if you place them in an enriched environment, they no longer display the symptoms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, similar to what they noticed in people who took a long train ride.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to explore Parkinson's disease and Parkinsonism, as there are several similar situations. The terms describe a long-term degenerative disorder of the central nervous system affecting mainly the motor system, but also the sensory system, with cognitive, sleep, and mood disturbances.

There is a compound called alpha-synuclein present in Lewy bodies found within the substantia nigra in the brain, which are diagnostic for Parkinson's. There is also a protein called Dardarin. The primary symptoms result from the loss of dopamine-secreting cells within the substantia nigra. There are five major pathways in the brain connecting other areas with the basal ganglia: the motor, ocular-motor, associative, limbic, and orbitofrontal circuits. All of them are disrupted, which explains the varied presentations of the disease.

How do you see this motor circuit working in the body? How would you rationalize an alternative approach to the treatment of Parkinson's disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My orientation is very similar to Pavlov's, who saw the motor system as subordinate to the sensory system. He saw the cortex of the brain as primarily an extension of the sense organs, and that this formed the environment for the motor reflexes.

The idea of a "reflex" is another thing that originated with Descartes and is simply wrong. The cells aren't mechanically connected in reflex patterns. One of the first people in the West to analyze this carefully was the French philosopher Maurice Merleau-Ponty. He analyzed the meaning of reflexes and clearly showed that there are no reflexes in the Cartesian sense. If you attend a neurology course, you will probably find people still arguing that there are simple, innate mechanical reflexes. For example, the linguistics system of Noam Chomsky is based entirely on this primitive, false idea of brain function based on mechanical reflexes. It simply doesn't work.

In the Pavlovian picture, especially as developed by his student P.K. Anokhin, the sensory system is fluid and continuously being revised as the organism explores its environment. The sense of exploring and being stimulated by newness—traveling through time and space—is in charge, overriding defects in the motor system.

**Andrew Murray:** Interesting.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is a relevant picture for seeing disease, especially Parkinson's, in a non-mechanical way. You mentioned the protein Dardarin; the interesting thing about it is that it shows up as a defect in Crohn's disease in the intestine as well as in Parkinson's. Parkinson's typically starts with constipation. In 19th-century medicine, people remembered the intestine as well as the brain in treating disease. It was very common to diagnose death as a result of inflammation of the bowel, which pathologists typically overlook as a side issue. But the intestine was recognized as very important, and the brain as the other end of the organism.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And now doctors are taught that if you have a bowel movement once every three days, it's all normal.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you trace out the chemical links between what's going wrong in the intestine and in the rest of the motor system, you can see links, but they're always contextually working. There is no simple pathogenic chemical in the intestine, but the bacteria living there, the food you eat, and the way your intestine responds to it all matter.

**Andrew Murray:** And the stress you're exposed to.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. These act in the activating part of the brain. Around 1950, the reticular activating system was identified. This includes the region where the substantia nigra and the basal ganglia are. This is where sensory input is dished out to activate the upper parts of the brain. When that is happening, it tends to go with an inhibitory effect on the body. So, the stronger your mentality is dreaming, for example, the more relaxed your body tends to be. In Parkinson's, the system tends to be over-activated, unable to relax properly. A characteristic thing is that during sleep and dreams, the person developing Parkinson's doesn't relax properly. If they have a dream, they might scream, thrash around, and hit people. There is a failure of consciousness to override and relax the body.

**Andrew Murray:** This reminds me of inescapable stress and the rat experiments, countered by the environmental enrichment you said could restore a Parkinson's-induced effect. We're saying there's a link between environmental enrichment and the progressive replacement of something good that offsets the negative effects of inflammation, bowel degradation, and endotoxin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** P.K. Anokhin and those in the Pavlovian tradition see a global event or process in the brain that they called the "acceptor of action." It's our intention and expectation in the world. This integrates the motor system and dominates the so-called reflexes. This process—which is like a model of everything we know and intend to do—is supported in the organism not just in the brain, but by sensory nerves from the whole body.

This process of being conscious is involved in the activation of the endocrine glands and the nerves themselves. As they metabolize to be conscious, they make changes internally. For example, they turn energy substances like sugar into cholesterol, and cholesterol into pregnenolone. Right in the nerves of the substantia nigra, this process is going on: energy, sugar, cholesterol, pregnenolone, progesterone. The endocrine process stabilizes the structure and the consciousness. The "flavor" of your consciousness, when successful, is modified by the balance between your progesterone, DHEA, other steroids, and the energy processes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you explain the personality of people that develop Parkinson's?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are experiencing learned helplessness. The way they live, they have incorporated duties and obligations that they can manage very well, but they aren't overcoming the stress adequately.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because they're not exploring new things or they don't have new input to their brain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're stuck in a way so that they aren't getting enough sensory input or stimulation.

**Andrew Murray:** That's interesting because medical texts describe Parkinson's patients as having emotionless expressions, being difficult to engage, and lacking *joie de vivre*. That's very much part of a learned helplessness construct. Stimulation, you're saying, is part of switching on a holistic approach to Parkinson's, outside of the mechanistic view.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So, are you saying new sensory input will increase the dopamine output from the substantia nigra?

**Andrew Murray:** Or the protective progesterone and pregnenolone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The dopamine theory is part of the mechanistic view. At the beginning of the 20th century, they saw the brain as a mechanical thing having defects causing the tremor. They actually started cutting out parts of the brain to remove the tremor.

**Andrew Murray:** Sounds like a good idea, doesn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Norbert Wiener, who invented the word "cybernetics," proposed the best surgery up to that time. He designed radar-searching self-control systems to aim guns. He saw the tremor as a feedback searching process. If his radar gun aiming system was poorly aligned, it would have a tremor—a searching movement back and forth. So he suggested surgery to cut out part of the searching feedback apparatus. It actually worked better than the grosser surgeries. But sometimes it didn't work. Michael J. Fox said he wasn't going to have any more surgical treatments because instead of stopping the tremor on his left side, it started to tremor on the right side.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's get into the medications. The substantia nigra is the site of dopamine production. I think the nervous system wants to fire fairly constantly, and dopamine controls that from happening ad hoc, allowing ordered movement through inhibition.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's integrated with the inhibiting systems. In itself, it is an activator, but it runs into nerves that feedback with an inhibition.

**Andrew Murray:** L-DOPA is considered the gold standard of treatment. Dopamine doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier, but L-DOPA does, and it is converted into dopamine. However, within five years, most patients using L-DOPA have a condition called dyskinesia or bradykinesia, where there are involuntary movements. Most patients using L-DOPA are in worse shape five years down the road than if they weren't treated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the problem is that the whole theory of what L-DOPA and dopamine are doing is mechanistic and mistaken.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So they're just putting a Band-Aid on it? They're not treating the sensory input deficiency?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another drug approved for Parkinson's is amantadine, or memantine more recently. In the 19th century, they were already using belladonna and hyoscyamine—anticholinergics—to treat the tremors. They were pretty effective and didn't have the bad side effects of increasing rigidity that L-DOPA does.

It turns out that amantadine and memantine have anticholinergic, anti-excitatory effects, but they are also anti-excitatory in the glutamatergic system. The glutamate and cholinergic systems are both very powerful and excitatory. The glutamate system ends up producing nitric oxide. Amantadine and anticholinergics are not only stopping the excitation that is part of the tremor, but they end up lowering the exposure to nitric oxide. Nitric oxide is a chronic stress-induced factor in suppressing mitochondrial respiration and energy production, accelerating aging of the brain.

Using these drugs actually gives insight into a much more global, organismic process. Rather than just restoring the lost "dopamine regulatory system," it's restoring energy processes and reducing the effects of stress in a systematic way.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take our first caller.

**Caller:** Hi, I'm from the San Francisco Bay Area. Are there simple stepping stones to get out of learned helplessness? For people overcoming hypothyroidism who still find it overwhelming to do big tasks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Painting. Behavioral things like going to new places, meeting new people, doing very different things that you've never done before but thought you might enjoy. Do this at the same time as you try to correct your energy processes that are suppressed—having more enjoyable, varied meals, for example, and making sure your thyroid function is good.

**Caller:** I remember when I asked you what was a good education for our daughter, you said "introduce her to new people." She loves to meet new people and gets so fired up.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, regarding creative outlets like painting or poetry—do you see those as easier constructs to attain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doing something unexpected, out of the routine. Some people actually quit their job and learn a new profession or trade.

**Andrew Murray:** I'm interested in the approach to supporting mitochondria, whether it's Coenzyme Q10 or nootropics. How do you feel about mitochondrial support in the approach to a Parkinson's patient?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Getting good rest is part of the support. Stopping unnecessary excitatory stimulation. Good stimulation should be fun rather than stressful. Everything that is anti-inflammatory can be relaxing as well as stimulating.

Caffeine is extremely protective against all of the defects in Parkinson's disease. It activates while protecting the mitochondria. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), which is in some plants like the passion flower, helps eliminate stressful over-excitation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You mean the passion fruit, or lilikoi?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, passion fruit. It’s something we make along with GABA which helps to eliminate stressful over-excitation. Synuclein, which is damaged in Parkinson's, happens to have the same effect as rotenone—a toxic thing seen to cause Parkinson's by blocking Complex I of the mitochondrion.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So all the herbs that act on GABA would be useful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and even cannabis, because of its sedative effects, can be protective against toxic types of over-stimulation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And what about alcohol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is an antioxidant and can be anti-inflammatory. In the right circumstance, it can be anti-Parkinson's.

**Andrew Murray:** How about nicotine? I've seen research showing nicotine is significantly protective against Parkinson's.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the population effect, where they see smokers have some protection, is partly because it relieves constipation. It activates the intestine, and that in itself has an anti-inflammatory, anti-toxic effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What is the best method for delivery of nicotine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Absorbing it through the skin in the form of an ointment, or ingesting very small amounts of the tobacco leaf very quickly.

**Andrew Murray:** Nicotine is a neurotoxin, but it's not the poisonous component in tobacco smoke—that's mainly the carcinogens and tar. But nicotine can have therapeutic effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And keeping the intestine healthy is crucial because when endotoxin reaches the nervous system, it activates processes that lead to the same blockage of mitochondrial respiration that rotenone or ionizing radiation does. Having CAT scans of the head is probably part of the reason Parkinson's prevalence has increased so greatly over the last 20 or 30 years.

**Andrew Murray:** They are pretty keen to give you CAT scans for anything.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin is another thing. One of the prostaglandins produced in the substantia nigra is very toxic to the brain. Simply having a regular use of aspirin will protect against that prostaglandin made from polyunsaturated fats (PUFA). The breakdown of polyunsaturated fats produces acrolein, a very toxic material. That is one of the things that turns synuclein into a toxic fibrous material, sort of like the prions in mad cow disease.

**Andrew Murray:** I read that they haven't proved beyond a doubt that these Lewy bodies are pathogenic; they might have a protective role.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the body might be "parking" these synuclein fibrils to get them out of the way, packing them up in little compartments that are relatively safe. But some of the toxic fibrils of synuclein are known to be passed from one cell to another, causing damage to the cell that receives it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** When you were talking about rapid movement and the dream state in people developing Parkinson's—is that not also a symptom of low thyroid because their muscles just can't relax?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the same thing. Nothing in the body can relax fully when your thyroid function is low. That's one of the funny things that came out of the idea of the cell as a compartment. If you think of it as a corpuscle that has to be in a state ready to work, the "rested" state is actually a high-energy state. It is full of energy, ready to go.

If you don't have enough thyroid, glucose, and oxygen to produce the energy, you stay in a semi-contracted, excited state. In Parkinson's, this reaches a chronically deadly, cell-killing condition. In chronic hypothyroidism, it's simply a nuisance that your sleep isn't as restful as it should be. You can't get into the deep, relaxing, restorative sleep because you don't have enough energy. The cells keep churning through the energy-producing process without relaxing and storing up the energy as glycogen, ATP, and creatine phosphate.

**Andrew Murray:** We will carry on this subject next month to break down things like testosterone, reducing estrogen, and other factors. Thanks so much for your time, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat can be reached at www.raypeat.com. He has plenty of fully referenced articles there. He's not selling anything; he's just giving you information. Our phone number is 1-888-WBM-HERB. Thanks for joining us.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thanks for listening. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Endocrinology (Part 2)
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have never listened to the show, we run from 7:00 to 8:00 PM the third Friday of every month. From 7:30 to 8:00 PM, we invite callers to join with any questions related or unrelated to the subject.

This evening's show will be a continuation of endocrinology. Last month, Dr. Raymond Peat was discussing Parkinsonisms, symptoms, and causality. A lot of what we read is subject to bad science, no science at all, or just downright lies. I wanted to give an overview of endocrinology—the organs that secrete the hormones and the target organs that are either stimulated or inhibited by them—to bring out Dr. Peat's understanding of hormone physiology. That is his specialty, for which he has been working and studying for the last 45 years.

In a search for truth, there seems to be an endless variety of rabbit holes. Science's greatest ally is verifiable observation; hard facts speak volumes. How we perceive the world influences our very being in the world. Two ends of the spectrum are learned helplessness and its counterpart, environmental enrichment, both of which have been discussed on previous shows.

How we understand physiology shapes our approach to aberrations within it. The outcome is modulated by a faithful scientific approach through verifiable observation on the one hand, and the holistic realization that the web of life is fluid. Nowhere else does this multiverse exist within our very being more than in the nervous system, and particularly the endocrine system.

Dr. Peat, I had this conversation with you this afternoon. What is a hormone? I know you have a very different outlook on it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was a question I brought up with my endocrinology students at the Naturopathic College in the 1970s. Against the background of classical endocrinology, it has a different meaning than when you look at it against the contemporary theory taught to medical students.

If you look at the standard definition—that a hormone is something secreted by cells somewhere in the body into the body fluids, moves in those fluids, and acts on cells somewhere else—then can't you say that lactic acid and carbon dioxide are just as much hormones as anything else? They are created by various cells, move in the body fluids, and definitely act on cells in other parts of the body.

However, what has developed over the last 50 years incorporates the idea of genes as the controlling agent of any cell. If a substance is going to act on a cell in a different part of the body, the theory assumes it must be activating its genes. The idea of a receptor as something that picks up a substance to activate the genes has come to the center of textbook medical endocrinology.

The way I see the subject is really an extension of the very beginnings. Around the middle of the 19th century, Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard became famous when he claimed that squashing testicles in a watery solution and injecting the solution would rejuvenate a man's virility. He described the changes he saw in himself. But in the 20th century, almost every textbook of endocrinology starts out by ridiculing that as a complete mistake—a placebo—because they say testosterone isn't water-soluble.

But he wasn't saying that he was injecting testosterone. He was making a squash solution of testicles. The testicle is full of hormones, many of which are fairly insoluble in water, but it's also full of lipids which solubilize and emulsify them.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Hasn't that been a part of ancient medicine, the ingestion of ovaries and testicles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, you can eat them and get the same hormones. But if you squash them and make a watery extract, you are getting an emulsified whole range of not just testosterone, but many other steroids closely related to it. It is a very ideological thing that these textbooks and professors have to put down Brown-Séquard before they can get on with their business. He was saying that the gland itself is producing substances that are vitally important and that can simply bypass many medical problems and reverse degenerative processes.

For example, in Parkinson's disease, simply giving testosterone has a very powerful therapeutic effect, but it is outside of the mainline thinking regarding dopamine deficiency.

The whole field changed around the time of August Weismann. He is famous for supposedly disproving Lamarckism by cutting off the tails of mice and observing that the offspring still had tails. He was pretty much an idiot, but his idea was that an animal differentiating tissues from a fertilized ovum involved the progressive loss of genetic information. He believed the brain, skin, and eyes each had their own genetic composition. For the whole organism to function as a unit, these genetically discrete parts had to have some way to communicate.

That ideology was designed for religious and political purposes to explain that an organism is basically mortal—that you can't cure incurable diseases because they are predetermined. That genetic idea took over and displaced the potential-filled biology of people like Brown-Séquard.

**Andrew Murray:** The way you look at it is that the structural organization of neurons leads to a better genetic pattern or blueprint. It is like an environmental enrichment scenario.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Each cell is adapting and adjusting itself to the other parts. When you look at the fact that a skin cell contains all the genes needed to make a brain cell, the idea of cloning an organism from a single cell means that every cell is full of potential.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it is just the environment that it is exposed to that determines its function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The way the organism comes into being is by each cell confronting its environment. When it divides, the new cell becomes part of its environment. The whole development of the organism is a process of perceiving its environment and adapting to what it perceives.

Hormones, as we currently talk about them, are just one of thousands of components produced by cells acting on other cells. One of the meanings of this is that we are all in slightly imperfect environments. Our history is continuously a matter of overcoming environmental limitations.

**Andrew Murray:** That brings me to the point of *in utero* nutrition and how pivotal that is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ratio of the person's brain to body, their longevity, life expectancy, and the amount of energy they have at any stage of life is pretty much set by the intrauterine condition.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller on the line. Where are you from?

**Caller (Australia):** I'm from Australia. I have a question for Dr. Peat. I am hypothyroid and have Hashimoto's. My pulse in the morning is around 56 and at night it's around 75. I have low temperatures in the morning as well. I live in the subtropics, so it is very hot.

My main question is: I haven't had PUFA [polyunsaturated fatty acids] for about five years. I've been trying to increase sugar, having milk and orange juice, and reducing cruciferous vegetables. Despite this, I've ended up being 30 kilos (66 lbs) overweight. I'm desperate to find a way to lose that weight without a starvation routine. I take primarily only T3.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, regarding the weight gain and the sluggish thyroid—she is using T3, not a T4 supplement.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The important thing is to keep your body temperature up. It should be in the range of 98°F to 99.5°F (approx. 37°C) during the daytime. A little higher is fine because it promotes the healthy oxidation of fat.

Keeping your liver well-nourished with protein and B vitamins is essential. The liver is able to throw off the polyunsaturated fats, recognizing them as toxic material. Your liver can get rid of quite a bit of stored fat, largely during the night. Keeping your body temperature up during the night with a good amount of protein, calcium, and trace nutrients is important.

If necessary, supplement T3, progesterone, and either pregnenolone or DHEA. DHEA is anabolic for the muscles, but it activates heat production. It causes you to "waste" heat, but it isn't really wasted because it keeps your nerve function up and inflammation down.

**Caller (Australia):** I do a lot of those things. In Brisbane, it is over 30°C every day and I am sweating all the time. How do you make your body increase its temperature?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How many grams of protein are you getting a day?

**Caller (Australia):** I have about 2 liters of milk and a liter of orange juice. Occasionally some lamb or steak.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is not always 100 grams of protein. If you are at all active, you need 100 grams of protein to keep your metabolic rate up. The calcium in 2 liters of milk is likely enough; calcium promotes heat production. Sodium works with calcium to produce heat. Progesterone helps to set your temperature so it stays up during the day and doesn't drop extremely during the night.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I want to discuss the calories. Two liters of milk is anywhere from 800 to 1200 calories, plus 400+ calories in the juice. If your morning pulse is in the 50s and never gets above 75, your metabolic rate probably isn't burning that amount of calories. For a 50-year-old woman, this might be the issue.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is where the DHEA comes in. Adjusting your T3 and progesterone is important. Estrogen tends to lower your temperature, so you want to keep the ratio of progesterone to estrogen pretty high—100 to 1 is good.

**Andrew Murray:** You said you have been PUFA-free for five years. Have you gained these 30 kilos over those five years?

**Caller (Australia):** Pretty much.

**Andrew Murray:** What are your morning temperatures?

**Caller (Australia):** Around 35.8°C or 36°C (96.4°F - 96.8°F). It does rise, and I feel heat after I eat certain things. I take a squeeze of Progest-E every night.

**Andrew Murray:** And how much T3?

**Caller (Australia):** Between 20 and 40 micrograms a day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One thing that can cause you to produce nitric oxide—which lowers your temperature and works with estrogen to reverse the effects of thyroid—is intestinal inflammation produced by bacteria eating food that isn't fully digested. Avoiding hard-to-digest foods can reduce nitric oxide and estrogen. Sometimes just having a raw carrot every day or a good portion of cooked mushrooms can reduce the endotoxin and nitric oxide production enough to switch your progesterone/estrogen ratio and raise your temperature.

**Andrew Murray:** Did you have a history of estrogen dominance?

**Caller (Australia):** Yes, absolutely. I went through menopause at 43. Prior to that, my estrogen level was about a thousand times what it was supposed to be.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you ever noticed an antibiotic having a good effect?

**Caller (Australia):** Yes, but I'm afraid to take antibiotics due to yeast overgrowth.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For yeast overgrowth, mushrooms and carrots are sometimes enough. But flowers of sulfur—just a pinch of it—will clear up a yeast infection pretty quickly, usually in two or three days.

In a fertility clinic about 30 years ago, they gave antibiotics to improve fertility. A lot of the women noticed drastic improvements in general health, stopping migraines and other estrogen-related symptoms. It turned out the antibiotics were lowering stress hormones and estrogen while raising progesterone. It eliminates the endotoxin to the extent that it stops producing nitric oxide and lets your cells begin oxidizing intensely.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Regarding weight loss, as you get older, your metabolism slows. I found it helpful for some clients to use eggshell powder for calcium so they don't have to drink the same quantity of milk. You can live for several months on milk and orange juice, but if you aren't menstruating and have a slow metabolism, you might not lose weight fast on that volume of liquid.

**Andrew Murray:** The pulse in the mid-50s is definitely suboptimal. Dr. Peat usually recommends a pulse between 75 and 85 as a good indicator of metabolic rate. People who are overweight have an uphill struggle using thyroid to generate metabolic rate because the weight itself creates resistance to the hormone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping your serum Vitamin D around the middle of the range (50 to 60 ng/mL) is helpful for keeping your temperature and metabolic rate up. Also, a little bit of coconut oil can increase heat production.

**Caller (Australia):** I use coconut oil. It sounds like it points to endotoxins in the gut.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The raw carrot slows digestion but helps lose weight because it binds some of the fat and carries it out of the body. It also carries out estrogen excreted in the bile.

**Andrew Murray:** Liver support would be a good direction. Liver stimulants or bitters, or milk thistle, would support hepatic function to remove waste.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Two drugs that help the liver maintain high activity are Cascara sagrada, which is anti-inflammatory and a liver tonic, and aspirin. Also, doing a little muscle-building exercise, such as dumbbell lifting for just two or three minutes at a time, helps to shift the hormone ratio.

**Caller (Garberville):** I have a question about poison oak. I got my first case ever. What botanical aid can I get?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We produce a product called Allergy Ease, sold at Chautauqua. It contains antihistamine herbs. If you start that as soon as you start itching, it helps. Otherwise, a clean diphenhydramine product (Benadryl) if the herbs aren't effective enough. Keeping your good sugars up—fruit sugars and honey—will really help keep histamine from being released.

**Caller (Garberville):** I have one other question. I have a plantar wart on the bottom of my foot. Besides salicylic acid, what do you recommend?

**Andrew Murray:** There is a plant excellent for warts called *Chelidonium majus*, the Greater Celandine. It is in the poppy family and has yellow flowers. If you break the stem, it exudes a bright orange-yellow sap. If you dab that on the plantar wart for about a week, the wart will turn black and the skin will peel off.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It isn't native here, though we have it in our garden. Another option is dandelion sap. It's not as effective as Greater Celandine, but if you pick the stem or flower of a dandelion, a white exudate comes out. You can dab that on the wart. Dr. Peat, what do you recommend for warts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That sounds as good as anything I know. I think salicylic acid is best.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting back to the endocrine system, I wanted to look at the hypothalamus. TRH (Thyrotropin-releasing hormone) stimulates TSH (Thyroid-stimulating hormone) release. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the liver slows down because the thyroid is low, then that little bit being produced by any stressed tissue is going to pile up in the blood because it should be eliminated constantly through the liver and kidney.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: California Proposition 65
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. We have a very special guest speaker with us, Dr. Raymond Peat. I know a lot of people listen purely to glimpse his insights because he always has a different answer for things.

I want to start by discussing California's Proposition 65. I briefly mentioned in July's show that I wanted to highlight some inconsistencies with Prop 65 in the California legislature. I want to outline specific testing we've done personally for products as part of our GMP protocol using ICP-MS testing for metals—specifically the California Proposition 65 metals: arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury.

In 1986, California voters approved an initiative to address concerns about toxic chemicals, which became the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986, better known as Prop 65. It requires the state to publish a list of chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects, or reproductive harm. This list has grown to include approximately 800 chemicals.

While Prop 65 has prompted manufacturers to remove some harmful chemicals—like trichloroethylene in correction fluids or lead in ceramic tableware—it drastically needs reframing within realistic criteria. For example, businesses with fewer than ten employees and government agencies are exempt from these warning requirements and discharge prohibitions.

Furthermore, commonly available foodstuffs are far over the maximum allowable daily limit currently legislated by Prop 65. There isn't a single medical study that demonstrates any public health benefits of Proposition 65, nor evidence that it has lowered cancer incidence among Californians. However, it has been a bonanza for bounty hunter law firms.

Let's look at real-world examples. We periodically test our products for the "Big Four": arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury. We use Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS), which detects levels down to parts per billion (ppb).

We tested raw turmeric root. The quantities in the raw root were:
*   Arsenic: 395 ppb
*   Cadmium: 41.9 ppb
*   Lead: 646 ppb
*   Mercury: Undetected

After extraction, the liquid extract was retested:
*   Arsenic: 68.1 ppb
*   Cadmium: Undetected
*   Lead: 6.6 ppb
*   Mercury: Undetected

We saw similar results with Lobelia and Echinacea root. Extraction typically produces a five- to ten-fold removal of these components, resulting in levels well within Prop 65 limits.

However, we also tested foodstuffs. We tested local crab from Shelter Cove:
*   Arsenic: 12,400 ppb
*   Cadmium: 10.4 ppb
*   Lead: 10.3 ppb
*   Mercury: 109 ppb

The mercury level vastly exceeds the maximum allowable daily limit set by Prop 65, given a typical 8 to 10-ounce serving.

We tested Cod:
*   Arsenic: 115 ppb
*   Lead: 30.3 ppb
*   Mercury: 473 ppb

We tested Halibut:
*   Arsenic: 602 ppb
*   Mercury: 794 ppb

Finally, a small nine-pound Salmon:
*   Arsenic: 428 ppb
*   Mercury: 72 ppb

**Andrew Murray:** It seems there is collusion between companies to protect vested interests. Dr. Carla Rothenberg’s PhD dissertation exposed the bad science used to deem progesterone fit for the list. It is like trying to turn an oil tanker; it takes a long time to change direction.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's well established that endometriosis comes from prolonged, excessive exposure to estrogen without interruption from progesterone. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** When experimenters remove steroid-forming tissue, it causes the pituitary to drive the remaining gland twice as hard to keep up systemic steroid production. title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Economics
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. This month’s subject is a mixed topic involving economics, corporate greed, and idealism. We will be weaving in a couple of characters from the mid-1850s who had visionary thoughts about concepts such as the biosphere and noosphere.

We are at a point in time where, as a species, we are definitely becoming more aware of our surroundings. The Internet has made it extremely easy to find information.
