Unlike in times past, when academia and education were reserved for those with power, influence, and hereditary money, anybody with a desire to know more can get on the Internet and fairly quickly come to an accurate opinion about many things.

However, information can be misleading. In talking with Dr. Peat and looking at research articles—including controlled double-blind studies—we find that even seemingly scientific studies can be misleading. You have to look at the data objectively. If there is money involved, follow the money; that will often reveal the truth.

This month is a medley of things, but with economics and greed at the heart of it. As a species, we are perhaps more relaxed now; there is less physical stress to survive because things are available in convenience stores. We don't have to hunt or grow food. We are becoming less physical and more cerebral. Amazon will deliver to your door.

I want listeners to really think about what I am going to say. It highlights how little most people understand about our economic reality. The largest excuse is, "I'm too busy to get involved." That is true enough; most folks work two or three jobs just to make ends meet. The cost of everything has skyrocketed. Our attention is captivated by working to survive, leaving us less time to organize and steer the government. We are blindsided by the economics of the day and debt.

Dr. Raymond Peat is on the line. He is an open-minded free thinker who has spent most of his life in academia researching subjects that show us a very different way to live.

From an economic perspective, let's look at greed coupled with runaway inflation and the resulting decline in spending power. This fuels the chemically altered world we live in. The struggle to support sustainable and organic foods creates a sense of loss to our environment, both psychologically and physically.

Let's look at the cost of living in real terms from 1950 to the present using three metrics: average family income, average car cost, and median house price.
*   **1950:** Average family income was $3,300. Average car cost was $1,500. Median house price was $7,300.
    *   A car cost roughly half your income.
    *   A house cost just over two times your income.
*   **2014:** Average family income was $51,000. Average car cost was $31,000. Median home price was $188,000.
    *   The home price-to-income ratio jumped to 3.7.

It is no wonder people cannot get on the housing ladder.

**Caller (San Francisco):** I heard you talking about the standard of living from 1973. That corresponds to when Richard Nixon took us off the gold standard. Have you ever interviewed Frances Moore Lappé? She wrote *Food First: Beyond the Myth of Scarcity*. She describes that when Nixon took us off the gold standard, the rich of the world figured they better invest in tangible things as hedges against inflation. They started buying high-quality land.

For example, starvation in Bangladesh occurred because the super-rich bought agricultural land at the foothills of the Himalayas, driving millions of people off the land. This was specifically tied to removing the US dollar from the gold standard.

Also, regarding Amazon: in the past, kids made money as delivery boys for local stores. Amazon does this on a global scale, meaning kids can't make that side income. Worse, the payment is electronic, sucking money out of the local town immediately to corporate headquarters. It decimates the local economy.

**Andrew Murray:** I was going to get into the point of wages in real terms and the importance of supporting local economies. Local economies are not controlled by central government, and we have much more say in them.

Regarding education: In 1950, annual tuition at the University of Pennsylvania was $600. Current tuition is $40,000 a year. Student loans are fueling this, amounting to about a trillion dollars in debt. According to the Economic Policy Institute, entry-level wages for high school graduates have dropped from $16 an hour in 1973 (adjusted) to $12 an hour now.

Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hello.

**Andrew Murray:** Can you outline your academic background for those who haven't heard you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I did my undergraduate study from 1953 to 1956. I had a summer job where I made $500, and with a tuition scholarship, that paid for my nine months of schooling every year. I looked at prices recently, and it is at least 20 times more expensive now. I couldn't afford to go to school currently.

**Andrew Murray:** You have seen the economics change over the last 80 years. What do you think about the decline in real wages and the increase in costs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of popular culture has to do with keeping people from realizing things are getting worse. For example, you mentioned "average" income. Those figures are usually the *median* income. The actual per capita average income in the US is higher because the vast incomes of the upper 1% or 2% skew the average. Since the gold standard was thrown out, the government has had to keep the illusion going. They are increasingly hiding information; they stopped giving out figures for the money supply a few years ago. The stock market seems to be going up because the government is pumping money into it—basically corruption by printing money.

**Andrew Murray:** This is central banks printing money without penalty.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was the same with Saddam Hussein and Gaddafi; they were trying to get off the petrodollar. Venezuela is doing the same.

**Andrew Murray:** I read in your newsletter about Vernadsky and Teilhard de Chardin regarding the concepts of the noosphere and the biosphere. We are living in this biosphere and are subject to stresses made known to us through media and debt.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vernadsky looked at the planet as a metabolic system. He saw the soil, atmosphere, and solar energy being converted to food and living substance. His concept saw carbon dioxide as a promoter of life, increasing the quality of living.

I see the current fear of carbon dioxide as partly a distraction from actual pollution. Deforestation is a major cause of the CO2 increase, but the deforestation itself is doing the damage, not the CO2. Real pollution is degrading the rivers and oceans—petroleum spills and chemical runoff from mass agriculture.

The propaganda machine—for example, *Politico*—recently published an article claiming rising CO2 would degrade the food supply by stimulating plant growth. The reasoning was completely unbiological and backward. Vernadsky was right: carbon dioxide is part of the soil-forming process. Plants secrete acids to dissolve minerals, but CO2 carried into the soil is part of making minerals available to plants. The mass media promotes myths to confuse the argument and make people worry about a false process.

**Andrew Murray:** It steers people away from looking at real pollution.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even health statistics, like longevity and disease incidence, are being falsified. In the 90s, the government declared it had won the war on cancer. I pointed out then that they were using phony statistics. Around the year 2000, the US Bureau of Statistics changed the rules and stopped giving out raw figures, providing only age-standardized figures to keep up the illusion.

**Caller (Blocksburg):** I called years ago about a lump on my neck. Dr. Peat suggested eating carrots and avoiding CAT scans. It went on for years and ended up being a cancer tumor. I had it removed and went through chemo and radiation.

My question is: a year later, I was cutting a small amount of poison oak. Suddenly, a huge rash went over my shoulder and down around the area where the tumor was. My girlfriend thinks it might be shingles. Could that be related to the radiation and chemo?

**Andrew Murray:** Chemo and radiation lower your resistance, for sure. Shingles can be reactivated chickenpox, especially under stress. Was the cancer metastasizing?

**Caller:** It was a skin-type cancer. It took 12 to 15 years to develop into a massive lump. It wasn't spreading, but it was breaking out of the skin.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what is your take on the rash?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just in case it is actually poison oak: I had an experience in my teens where I was extremely sensitive to poison oak. The word went around camp that Vitamin C protected against it. I took a few tablets, and the poison oak disappeared and I never had it again.

**Caller:** I'm not usually sensitive to poison oak. This turned into huge, blackening bubbles all down one side of my body. It is getting better now.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it is a virus like shingles, it is a good idea to have your Vitamin D level checked. Vitamin D is a very powerful antiviral and regulates your immune system. Your serum level should be around 50 nanograms per milliliter.

**Caller (New York):** Does Dr. Peat have advice on finding dentists who use the filling materials he recommends, like calcium oxide for root canals and cements for fillings?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For the root canal, calcium oxide is antiseptic and anesthetic. It is safer than gutta-percha or metal fillings. I think the composite fillings are now high enough in strength that they are good even for chewing teeth.

**Caller:** Do you have advice on finding dentists who use those?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For about 50 years, I have had all my dentistry done in Mexico because they emphasize skill and care rather than speed and profit.

**Caller (Phillipsville):** I have a comment regarding the previous caller. You referred to his cancer as "benign" because it hadn't metastasized. That is an oxymoron. There is no such thing as benign cancer. If it is cancer, it is malignant. If it is not cancer, it is a benign tumor.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of the language used medically in relation to cancer has been to promote the business of oncologists. Fifty or sixty years ago, cancers were things that were definitely identified as benign. The language was escalated so that something which formerly was not cancer was called "pre-cancer" and then "cancer."

An article in JAMA about 40 years ago looked at pathology methods. It demonstrated that a healing wound, if biopsied, will show all the properties used by pathologists to identify cancer—rapid growth, invasive appearance, etc. The article pointed out that you often can't tell the difference; the only way to know if something is malignant is to wait and see.

**Caller:** Why did you tell the previous caller not to go to a doctor?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't remember saying that. I never tell people not to go to doctors, but I tell them to think and question what the doctor tells them to do.

**Caller (Whitethorn):** First, for the caller looking for a dentist, Dr. James Mattson in Fort Bragg is the best I've ever seen. My question is about sclerosing mesenteritis. Are there herbs that might help dissolve internal scar tissue?

**Andrew Murray:** Dissolving organized scar tissue is difficult. Maybe progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've had experience with fibrotic lumps where Vitamin E helped. I had a vaccination scar that was bulgy; I put Vitamin E on it, and it disappeared in a week. However, a hard lump inside might take six months of anti-inflammatory treatment—Vitamin E, progesterone, and total nutrition improvement.

A lot of sclerosing problems involve abnormal calcification. Hans Selye pioneered the study of how to cause and regress calcified tissue. Vitamin D and high calcium intake help lower your parathyroid hormone, which is part of reversing calcification. Vitamin K is another factor that prevents soft tissue calcification.

**Caller (Kansas City):** I was diagnosed with Graves' disease, which is supposed to be hyperthyroid, but I've never been hyperthyroid. I had the bulging eyes and swelling in the feet. I am on thyroid hormone, but I still have issues. My antibodies are elevated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think a more thorough metabolic study would show something other than just antibodies. You want to check steroid hormones—progesterone, cortisol, Vitamin D—and the actual level of thyroid hormones: T3, T4, and Reverse T3.

**Caller:** I have a new doctor, and we checked all those. Everything is normal, though testosterone was slightly low. My Vitamin D is between 60 and 80.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you tracked your temperature and pulse rate?

**Caller:** My temperature is usually 96.6 to 97 in the morning and goes up to 99 by the end of the day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is not consistent with Graves' disease. I have only seen one person who I think really had hyperthyroid Graves' disease. Many people are diagnosed with it but are actually hypothyroid.

**Caller:** They tell me I have Hashimoto's *and* Graves now. I take T4 in the morning, four hours apart from food.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Did they explain why you should do that? Since it takes a couple of days for things to pass through the intestine, there is plenty of time for T4 to absorb. Your body doesn't want it to absorb all in an hour or two. If the liver perceives a huge, unphysiological surge of T4, it induces enzymes to destroy it. You will actually be hypothyroid 12 hours later.

**Andrew Murray:** I am afraid I have to stop you both there as we are at the end of the show. Thank you, Dr. Peat, for your time.

For those wanting to know more about Dr. Peat, his website is **www.raypeat.com**. He has fully referenced scholarly articles on many subjects. As he mentioned, the government often wants to keep information quiet to keep people manageable.

Thanks for joining us. Until next month, happy fall to you all.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Diagnosis
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Good evening and welcome to this evening's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who have just tuned in for the first time, we hold a monthly discussion on various topics with Dr. Raymond Peat, using his wealth of expertise to add to what may or may not be known.

This month's topic is about diagnosis as a double-edged sword, looking at shamanism and other spiritual healing modalities. We will also look at cultural ideas—how they develop and how language is used sometimes as a tool against us, and other times as a tool to further our understanding. A lot of scientific research doesn't make it to the public sphere for quite some time. We go through suffering, being told that liquid oils, for example, are heart-healthy and lower our cholesterol, when actually the exact opposite happens. Forty or fifty years later we get an admission, but it's too late for a lot of people by that point.

We will cover diagnosis, environmental enrichment, and nootropics. I wanted to start the show with Dr. Peat's latest newsletter. He included a sentence: "First deny that harm is done." We know the Hippocratic oath is "first do no harm," but medicine since the 1930s or 40s has been doing a lot of harm. Unfortunately, due to advertising and corporate planning, we aren't told the full story.

My thoughts went to Native American, South American, and Aboriginal cultures where ritualistic dream quests—typically involving some mind-body disengagement—counteract the "kiss of death" given by Western medicine's diagnosis. This is achieved through the environmental enrichment of the quest and the interpretation of healing as a journey.

Dr. Peat wrote: "Where the organism is working meaningfully, useless structures tend to atrophy as new structures develop." The "meaningful" aspect is the environmental enrichment of the pursuit of creativity, altruism, and selflessness. I believe this can bring about what Dr. Peat quotes as an "unveiling of new possibilities for reorganization and repair," which is akin to a cure.

I don't doubt the substances Dr. Peat supports affect physiology for the good of the organism. I also understand that antibiotics would have halted the Black Death. However, I am sure the older arts worked on a more subtle energy underpinning physiology, psychology, and spirituality as a unified system. Let me introduce Dr. Peat. Are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for sharing on the show. For those hearing you for the first time, would you outline your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As a new graduate student in the 1950s, I tried several different departments but mostly concentrated on linguistics and the psychology of language. I dropped out of several departments before going back to get a PhD. After I got my master's degree with a thesis on William Blake, I went back to study biology, intending to investigate how the brain can function in ways that could explain intelligence and language use.

I was partly reacting against Noam Chomsky's doctrine. When I began thinking about linguistics in the late 1950s, he was just taking over the culture of language theory. I considered him one of the great evils of our culture. The way he was treating language left the brain and intelligence out of the whole thing. It became a motor program, actually, for following rules laid down in the genes.

**Andrew Murray:** What was he a proponent of in terms of that discussion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He explicitly said that the behavior that allows us to make language and follow grammatical rules must be in the genes. This is very much the way Konrad Lorenz said that all of our behavior is in the genes, and so to improve the species, we have to kill inferior people. Chomsky doesn't say that, but he has a very arrogant attitude towards people who question his very arbitrary genetic explanation of things.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's a bit like Neo-Darwinism and Mendelian situations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it is a kind of cultural arrogance based in MIT with all the power of the Pentagon behind it. Over the years, I found that he had penetrated every department of universities. A friend and I did a course in the honors college at the University of Oregon on interdepartmental views of human nature. We invited ten different professors—the ones students thought were outstanding in their area—to speak. Each one of them said that his department's contribution to understanding human nature was Noam Chomsky's generative grammar. Sociology, folklore, literature—all the different departments at that time, 1968, thought Noam Chomsky had defined the world for them.

**Andrew Murray:** Oh my goodness. So within education at that point, there was this lie being spread and seeded rapidly through different domains that all agreed on the same thing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You can trace it back to the beginning of the 20th century, financed by various corporate and military interests. All the powers interested in expanding their power were promoting research and teaching in areas that presented a very arbitrary and degraded picture of human nature.

**Andrew Murray:** Looking at your newsletter, you mentioned heroic medicine 200 years ago. The "healing crisis" was a defective understanding, seeking to treat with the use of mercury and arsenic. Then we moved to the concept of hormesis 50 years ago. Would you speak about this planting of concepts in our mind to create a false narrative?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The idea of genes determining the nature of a species had its theological advocates in the 19th century. That genetic definition created a fixed, unchanging organism where accidents were the only things that could change the genes.

On top of that understanding, by the 1940s, industries started producing a reaction to their polluting processes. Atomic bombs were being exploded in Nevada, poisoning everyone downwind all the way to New York. People were getting concerned about the quality of air and water; city smog was killing people. The industries started fighting back, saying, "Look at history; if something didn't kill you, it made you stronger."

**Andrew Murray:** We do hear that, don't we?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you survived the mercury treatment, you were supposedly cured and a strong, healthy organism, even though mercury stayed with you.

**Andrew Murray:** This was the original heroic medicine, and then it morphed into the atomic bomb testing era.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Industries started funneling huge amounts of money. One current professor in Boston has received more than $40 million in research to promote this phony idea of hormesis. About 15 years ago, they started defining it as a biphasic response, meaning a small amount moves biology in one direction, and a larger amount moves it in the other. Basically, the idea was that a little bit of poison is good for you.

They argued that the leak from the nuclear industry and atomic fallout were "low-level radiation." They used upside-down evidence to argue that this pollution was actually causing biological benefit. That developed into the argument by big think tanks that the government should stop regulating industrial pollution because the regulation is causing damage to public health by denying us the "beneficial" pollution.

**Andrew Murray:** It takes a long time for the wool to be pulled from our eyes. We hear that polyunsaturated oils are great, or fluoride is good for us. All the time they tell us it's for our own good and use this hormesis mechanism to justify it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even though John Gofman was a major government nuclear researcher, he eventually started looking at the facts. He gathered evidence showing that most cancer and a large part of heart disease in the United States can be traced to medical X-rays. My brother, who worked in the nuclear industry for most of his life, said that every week they had a seminar teaching them about the benefits of low-level radiation.

**Andrew Murray:** X-rays are so ubiquitous. You go to a dentist or the ER, and they want to X-ray or CT scan. GE is heavily invested in their old technology and needs to recoup costs.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting away from the concept of brainwashing, I've long held the belief that diagnosis can be one of the most dangerous things. For someone to hear they've been diagnosed with a life-threatening disease can be the "kiss of death" because of the strong mind-body connection. In shamanistic medicine, the healer is a mediator to a spirit realm where a different interpretation exists. What are your views on the mind-body-spirit approach to healing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think what you're calling the shamanistic view is the simple, basic reality. The world that the scientists and government people are advocating is a world of manipulation, control, and enforced agreement. If you back away from the academic orthodoxy, you see some of the reality that the shamans are working with. It is a basic participation in the world around you. All organisms do it. The shaman's therapeutic reality is to get the person back in touch with the complex realities they are living in, rather than being attached to the story they are being brought up with.

**Andrew Murray:** It is important to pull people out of this dream state. That view of non-ordinary reality is important for practitioners trying to get into the psyche of a sick person.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of people ask me about a cancer diagnosis they've had. When I ask them exactly how the diagnosis was made and what the actual observations were, they are sometimes annoyed that I question the simple fact that they have terminal cancer. But almost nine times out of ten, it turns out the diagnosis was very exaggerated. They are given the impression that invasion is underway, but if you look at the actual pictures, they basically have slightly abnormal tissue. If you press the pathologist, they'll say, "Well, it's abnormal, it will undoubtedly turn into cancer, so it's good to get rid of it."

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the idea that a little bit of something harmful is good for you: most people agree carbon monoxide is toxic. But then I hear people using nitric oxide, or Laetrile (apricot seeds containing hydrogen cyanide) being useful for cancer. What do you think about those?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The composition of city smog is rich in carbon monoxide and nitric oxide. It is interesting that these have now become medically and biologically "desirable." It makes the fear of smog go away if you think they are a defense. They are calling carbon monoxide a very powerful anti-inflammatory agent.

**Andrew Murray:** Carbon monoxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It happens to make city smog look beneficial. But when you look at how it is produced in the body, it breaks down the heme group, which is involved in all our essential oxidative metabolic processes inside the cell. As it breaks down heme, it releases a molecule of carbon monoxide and an atom of iron. The iron acts randomly as an oxidant.

The first step of degrading heme produces biliverdin, which is quickly turned into bilirubin. Bilirubin is being touted as a powerful anti-inflammatory antioxidant. Something I've been pointing out for many years is that cancer is extremely endowed with antioxidant processes. That is why it can resist chemotherapy and radiation so well.

What makes a cell healthy is the whole system of oxidative processes. If you plug up the oxidative machinery, you go into a reduced state. That is the antioxidant power of a cancer cell. You get the process of inhibiting respiratory enzymes by both carbon monoxide and bilirubin. At the same time, bilirubin excites the nerve cells. This is exactly the formula for excitotoxic death of brain cells. Yet, it is called a powerful protective antioxidant.

**Andrew Murray:** So cancer evades treatment because it has enzymes that turn off the oxidative process?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It turns off the oxidative process, producing things like lactic acid, which is a reductant.

**Andrew Murray:** It took me a while to get this concept because dietary supplements and foods are advertised for their ability to be antioxidants. I always understood "antioxidant" to be beneficial. But you're saying oxidants, like Vitamin E and C, are actually the beneficial substances?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In a healthy cell, Vitamin C exists in the oxidizing form. It stabilizes the structure of the cell by keeping things from being excessively reduced. Vitamin E fits into that mixture too.

**Andrew Murray:** How does the doctrine of hormesis work into our consciousness? Medical abstracts no longer reside in libraries, and real data is hard to find. What is actually proposed in many papers does not reflect the true science.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The theory of consciousness and the brain that is repeatedly taught fits the picture beneficial to industry. They want to present the brain as having programs that are genetically determined or trained by "adaptive learning"—repetition rather than insight. This programmed behavior tends to be digital or have concrete symbolic units.

However, the actual organism deals with holistic, rich patterns. A book called *Eye and Brain* by Gregory in the 60s showed that if you look at different images with each eye, the brain integrates millions of points of information to create a three-dimensional image. That kind of sensory assimilation is denied by the culture that wants controllable, educable people who deal only in symbolic forms.

**Andrew Murray:** It is another example of the reductionist worldview.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Logic and math are distractions from the way the organism is integrating its information.

**Andrew Murray:** What will it take for medicine to change and do no harm?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It will take the public recognizing the extent of the harm. I've seen it happen locally where it only took four or five patients standing up to the doctors to change them 180 degrees. Doctors feel trapped by the system just as much as the patients.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned that substances like pregnenolone, carbon dioxide, glucose, and warmth can affect brain growth during development. Do you think supplementation later in life can make up for a lack of these earlier, or is there a finite window for reorganization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every night we produce masses of stem cells that attempt to renew worn-out tissues. With age, things like polyunsaturated fats, iron, and bilirubin accumulate, making it hard for stem cells to do full repair. Instead of repair, we get fibrosis. But with the right support—both in how the person uses their brain and access to environmental needs—I think at any stage those repair cells can be integrated.

**Andrew Murray:** This supports the idea that sleep is important for repair. You advocate for nine hours or more?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the winter when days are short, more sleep is protective. I've seen examples where very damaged brains show radical restructuring quickly. It is like the brain knows how to rebuild itself when given the opportunity.

**Andrew Murray:** You stated that epigenetic changes produced by stress are reversible, but reversal becomes less likely with age if the environment remains the same. Polyunsaturated fats amplify this by generating carbon monoxide and prostaglandins. Do you see environmental enrichment as paramount to drive change?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I see adaptation as constantly choosing between two directions: one is to become more, to know more, and move into the future; the other is defensive adaptation, simply surviving. Stressed parents tend to have babies with less functional brains. At any point, the brain is eager to repair itself, but if the background has been restricted, the repair situation must be more intense. The conscious attitude has to be deliberate to avoid learned helplessness. You must seek things that stop the production of prostaglandins and reduce the storage of polyunsaturated fats—substances like aspirin and progesterone.

**Caller:** I've been hearing you mention polyunsaturated fats quite a lot. What about monounsaturated fats, like olive oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Monounsaturated fats are fine; they are very much a part of our nature. If we eat nothing but sugar, we will make monounsaturated fats of our own. Those are the n-9 (omega-9) fats, like in olive oil and butter. From that n-9 series, we produce our own polyunsaturated fats called the n-9 series.

It is the lack of those which is the damage done when we eat things like soy oil and safflower oil. They inhibit our ability to produce our own polyunsaturated fats, which are stable and beneficial.

**Caller:** You're saying it's better to consume the sugars that will help us produce that in our bodies as opposed to putting it in our food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some research has found organisms that will make the equivalent n-9 series polyunsaturated fats, and they are very protective anti-inflammatory agents. They are the things we would be producing if we weren't poisoned by PUFA.

**Caller:** What is the major difference between monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mono are almost always the n-9 fats, like oleic acid. Crops that grow in cold climates, like soybeans or seaweed, cannot use saturated fats. They produce their own polyunsaturated fats (n-3, n-6) to remain fluid in cold weather. Those fats are unstable when you make them as warm as we are (98.6°F). They cause very quick oxidative breakdown.

**Caller:** I saw a study on PubMed about hypothyroidism, heat intolerance, and anxiety. I have that. I wake up with a low temperature, but I am very sensitive to heat and become overheated quickly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you checked your temperature during the times when you're feeling overheated?

**Caller:** It usually doesn't seem that high, never usually more than 99.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you are really hypothyroid and have, say, a 97-degree temperature when you wake up, it's important to keep taking your temperature and pulse rate during the day. Lots of people who have discomfort in the heat have very high nitric oxide production. That causes vasodilation and reddening of the skin, but that will lower the core temperature. To understand what's happening metabolically, check your temperature before and after those experiences of heat intolerance.

**Andrew Murray:** I have to stop us there. Thanks so much for your time, Dr. Peat. His website is well-researched, and you will find things there you won't find anywhere else: www.raypeat.com. Thanks for listening, and we will see you next year. Good night.

I have worked with Dr. Peat for the last nine or ten years, and a lot of what we found out from him has been revelational. When I was studying herbal medicine in England, we were trained by doctors, endocrinologists, and pathologists. A lot of things we learned, I later found out from Dr. Peat and further research, contained quite a lot of untruths.

Dr. Peat’s website, raypeat.com, is fully referenced with articles. I will introduce him now. Dr. Peat, thanks for joining us again. Please give us your academic background and your research history.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My PhD study was at the University of Oregon, 1968 to 1972. My dissertation was on reproductive aging. My intention when I went back to graduate school in biology was to study the brain, but I found that brain research was the most doctrinaire, next to genetics. I looked around and found that reproductive physiology was actually oriented towards science.

My background before that had been studying literature, linguistics, and painting. It is probably the background in literature that made me think in an adversarial manner in evaluating science, rather than an authoritarian one—accepting things just because the professor said it's true. I think the legal attitude of looking for truth by an adversarial approach should apply to medicine and science in general.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to start by looking at the evidence regarding traumatic brain injury. The numbers are staggering—whether it's professional sports, auto wrecks, or falls. It has been one of the most difficult conditions to treat.

There were some very good Phase 1 and 2 trials using progesterone that were very promising. These spurred the Phase 3 trials, which had huge numbers—10,000 in one and 1,500 in the other. Both of these studies—the PROTECT III and the SYNAPSE trial—seemingly found no beneficial effect. This contradicts your description of the anti-inflammatory and anti-edema effects of progesterone. Given that the earlier trials were so promising, how do you interpret this negative effect shown in the Phase 3 trials?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been about 15 big studies on brain injury. Interestingly, after overwhelmingly promising results from using intravenous magnesium to reduce swelling and restore metabolism, all of these, by the time they reached the Phase 3 level, suddenly showed the opposite results. Nothing turned out to be beneficial for treating human brain trauma in these big studies, even though previous smaller studies and animal studies were showing increased survival and full recovery.

The fact that something happens at the Phase 3 level is very suspicious. When the government and big corporations get involved, I suspect they are protecting drugs that are not generic the way progesterone is.

For example, urea. I don't think there has ever been a major study of treating brain trauma with simply intravenous urea, but it has had amazingly good results. I think a serious study could be done using all the known beneficial things: urea, magnesium, progesterone, hypertonic saline solution, and so on. If you do everything known to be beneficial to the brain, you'd get even better results than with a single drug-like treatment.

The worst thing about this big PROTECT study was that they not only didn't give a big enough dose, but they gave it emulsified with Intralipid, a soybean oil. The amount of soybean emulsion they were giving intravenously is, in itself, harmful.

**Andrew Murray:** That was a 6% solution.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around 1970, someone injected an emulsified soy oil into rats and showed that on the first pass through the brain, 17% of the oil was taken up into the brain. There is no blood-brain barrier that functions against oil. They dissected the brain and showed that one dose of oil was enough to alter the morphology of brain cells. So, intravenous treatment with something supposedly beneficial, mixed with a known toxin to the brain, is hard to imagine—unless corporate and government interests were involved.

**Andrew Murray:** I noticed from that trial they were only using 2 milligrams of progesterone per milliliter. The drug infusion started with a loading dose of 0.71 mg/kg for one hour, followed by 0.5 mg/kg for the rest of the 119 hours. Can you put 2 milligrams or half a milligram per kilo in perspective regarding the progesterone exposure most females enjoy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people have reported that in the last week or two of a healthy pregnancy, a woman's placenta is producing 800 or 900 milligrams of progesterone per day. That doesn't do anything harmful; it is very protective. Women generally feel great when their progesterone is at a maximum. So, they could easily have given 2,000 milligrams of progesterone per day instead of a few hundred.

**Andrew Murray:** A doctor named Donald Stein, who has been studying brain trauma for 30 years at Emory University, published a paper in the *Journal of Neurotrauma* in 2017 titled "Suboptimal Dosing Parameters as Possible Factors in Negative Phase 3 Clinical Trials." He refuted the dose given and the use of the emulsifying agent—the polyunsaturated fat (PUFA) soybean oil.

You have always talked about PUFAs being pro-estrogenic, and estrogen is a known water-logger of neurons. This works against any tiny dose of progesterone in the trial.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You mentioned the estrogenic effect of the polyunsaturated fats. When there is a trauma, the toxicity of the PUFAs is tremendously amplified by their conversion to pro-inflammatory prostaglandins. In any trauma—sunburn, parasites, broken bones, X-rays—estrogen is produced in the injured tissue and the whole organism. Any harm to the organism increases estrogen production and the conversion of PUFAs to pro-inflammatory mediators.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this what the literature terms the excitotoxic situation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is a specific part that happens under the influence of estrogen and PUFAs. They activate the glutamatergic transmitters in the brain—these excitatory signals—to the point that they become toxic. Progesterone opposes all of these. It blocks the formation of prostaglandins, blocks the release of stored PUFAs, blocks the formation of inflammatory mediators, and antagonizes the glutamatergic excitotoxins. Every function of the organism harmed by trauma is intensified by estrogen and PUFAs, and those are blocked by progesterone.

**Caller (Jeff from NY):** I was listening to the comment about progesterone being a miracle product. Does it only apply to women? I think you've mentioned that pregnenolone is universal, but men have to be careful with progesterone—specifically a 55 to 70-year-old where the risk of endotoxins is increasing.

My second question is about salt and insomnia. I switched from sea salt to canning salt (kosher salt), which is pure salt without other minerals. I think it really helped; I don't wake up at 3:00 AM anymore. Do you agree with that?

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding salt, the Himalayan salts and deep earth crystal salts do contain other trace elements and potentially negative materials like heavy metals. I think a straightforward white sea salt or canning salt is preferable. Dr. Peat, what do you think about progesterone in men?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, on the salt: my interest in salt supplementation was related to the estrogen issue. I saw premenstrual women restricting their salt and making their symptoms worse. I suggested to a friend that she salt her food to taste, and suddenly she didn't retain water; salt was acting as a diuretic.

Years later, I knew old people who were restricting salt and developing serious insomnia. I suggested the same thing, and they got good sleep, and their blood pressure actually came down. Tom Brewer, with his diet for pregnant women in the 1950s and 60s, saw that supplementing pregnant women who had toxemia symptoms with huge amounts of salt essentially cured the toxemia.

Regarding progesterone: I used it myself. After working with aging animals, I tried it on my own migraines. Twice, during an intense migraine, I had a complete reversal of symptoms in one to two minutes after ingesting about 100 milligrams. When I took too much for too long, I noticed it had the effect of a "cold shower" for a day or two—an anti-testosterone effect. But that passes quickly when you stop taking it.

I found as I got older that I could tolerate 5mg or 10mg a day without that anti-testosterone effect. Several people have told me it actually seems to reinforce their testosterone. I think that works because testosterone is converted to estrogen under stress. If you stop that conversion with progesterone—which, like aspirin, inhibits the conversion of testosterone to estrogen—you can actually raise your testosterone.

**Caller (Jeff from NY):** On iodine, I know you've mentioned that even small amounts can be toxic. But outside the laboratory, does more iodine make sense in an environment where we are exposed to fluoridated water? Does it counteract the fluoride?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never seen a test of that idea. When I spent time in San Francisco, I was using a daily supplement of T3 (Cytomel). Within a few days of drinking the fluoridated water, I developed a migraine, which made me assume it was a sudden crash of my thyroid function. If you take T3 with fluoridated water, the fluoride in the stomach will totally knock out the dose. As long as it is circulating as ionic fluoride, I think it will knock out any T3 it runs into.

**Caller (Jeff from NY):** Regarding amino acids, you recommend gelatin for proline and glycine. But are isolated amino acids like taurine or carnosine beneficial?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't discourage people from taking those if they want to try them, but I don't use them myself.

**Caller (Jeff from NY):** Lastly, I am holding my breath to increase CO2. Is there a good target time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Holding your breath has value, but the time depends on your metabolic rate. If you have a high thyroid function, you might be unconscious after a minute because you are consuming oxygen very fast. A hypothyroid person consumes oxygen much slower. A very high proportion of the population is hyperventilating, so breathing slower is beneficial, but you can't set a specific time without an oxygen consumption test.

**Caller (Finland):** I read a recent book by a doctor claiming it is almost impossible to get rid of white fat, and that you just accumulate it. He suggests using cold, but I know you've said the stress of cold makes it worse. Also, does fasting turn good brown fat into bad white fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a lot of interesting research on that. My orientation is that the activation of T3, the active thyroid hormone, is the crucial thing. Prolonged fasting has harmful effects, one of which is knocking out T3 in the tissues.

Even though T3 circulates in the bloodstream, various tissues (muscles, skin, brain) can produce T3 from T4 locally. The crucial factor for producing it locally is partly glucose, but fructose seems to have a special ability to activate that local production of T3. I would say eating enough sugar—having orange juice and fruit regularly—is much better than either chilling yourself or starving yourself.

**Caller (Finland):** If you were to choose a place to live to keep metabolism high, would you choose a high altitude, warm place?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, somewhere like Peru at 12,000 to 14,000 feet near the equator. Or Toluca, Mexico. I feel exhilarated at that altitude.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to talk about the GABA-A receptor. Progesterone and its metabolite, allopregnanolone, bind to this receptor, producing an anxiolytic, calm response. Do you think the metabolite is more active than progesterone per se?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since pregnenolone, the precursor, is pro-GABA, I suspect progesterone itself is too. It is converted to allopregnanolone, which seems to be the most powerful activator of the GABA system. But I think all of them act in the same direction. Besides activating GABA to reduce stress, progesterone also inhibits excitatory processes, including the glutamatergic and NMDA receptor systems.

**Caller (Buffalo John):** If someone has a disc herniation, is it possible to regenerate that gel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know people get well from it, though I've never seen X-ray evidence of the spacing increasing. I think it is possible for the disc to rebuild itself and for the bones to conform to the regenerating cartilage.

**Caller (Buffalo John):** I've had six knee operations and three herniated discs. Being on your diet and mitigating PUFA has almost eliminated my pain. I also use red light. You mentioned putting progesterone on a mole and it moving?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, pigment cells are extremely mobile. If you apply progesterone or DHEA near a mole, the cells may migrate to satisfy their need for the substance. I applied it to a mole on my temple. The pigment cells formed rings behind the mole, and the mole itself constricted and eventually fell off without leaving a scar.

**Caller (Buffalo John):** Can you take GABA as a supplement?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In animal studies, when given to a healthy animal, none of it seemed to get into the brain. But if the animal was sleep-deprived and the brain really needed GABA, then it was able to get in and relax it.

**Caller (Chris from Garberville):** I've been using Monk fruit sugar. It's a melon from southern China. I stopped eating table sugar and switched to this, and my inflammation disappeared. It is zero glycemic. Have you heard of it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I haven't heard of it.

**Andrew Murray:** I suspect it might be mixed with erythritol or stevia. I think those sugar substitutes have more negative effects than positive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The effect I described of ordinary sucrose, for example in orange juice, is able to stimulate weight loss by activating the T3 in your fat cells. Fructose is available in pure form and doesn't increase blood glucose the way starch does.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat. We are out of time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, very good.

**Andrew Murray:** For those listening, check out the SYNAPSE and PROTECT III studies on progesterone and TBI, and then read Dr. Donald Stein's 2017 paper in the *Journal of Neurotrauma* which refutes them. Dr. Peat's website is raypeat.com. We will see you next month.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Progesterone vs Estrogen, Listener Questions (Part 1)
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat with us. For those in the area, the number is 707-923-3911. For those outside the area, the 800 number is 1-800-568-3723.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The 800 number might not work from outside of California, and almost certainly not internationally.

**Andrew Murray:** Notably, you did a lot of research into aging. At that time, progesterone as an anti-aging product was a touchy subject because the estrogen industry was dominant, wasn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Interestingly, Donald Stein [from the progesterone brain injury studies] was studying psychology there right around the same time I was.

**Andrew Murray:** You have mentioned that estrogen is associated with waterlogging of cells and an excitotoxic state where energy is wasted. Do you think progesterone would be useful in a heart attack if given soon enough? I know hawthorn extract reduces ischemia if given within the first few hours.

It is very parallel to the effects of T3, the active thyroid hormone. T3 helps to increase the ratio of progesterone to estrogen. T3 is equally acutely protective to the heart. **Andrew Murray:** I assume thyroid works by stabilizing cells and energizing them, as opposed to the depolarized state promoted by estrogen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the oligodendrocytes where progesterone is produced, T3 is the active thing that promotes its production.

**Andrew Murray:** We have covered the hoax of global warming and the demonization of CO2 in the past. Early fossil records show the Earth had lush vegetation when CO2 levels were significantly higher. You have mentioned the similarities between carbon dioxide and progesterone. Could you equate the beneficial effects of CO2 to progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One more comment on the relation between T3 and progesterone is that both of them increase the production and retention of carbon dioxide.

Regarding giving progesterone for a recent heart attack: the effect of estrogen on energy production delays the restoration of the energy needed to make the heart beat. This shows up as a prolonged QT interval. Progesterone shortens that interval and makes the heart less likely to have a rhythm problem because it accelerates the ability to return to the resting, energized state.

Carbon dioxide has that same muscle-stabilizing effect. At high altitude, they have talked about the "Lactate Paradox" for many years. A person can work full force at high altitude without producing the excess lactic acid they normally would at sea level. That is because the body, at lower oxygen pressure, is able to retain a higher balance of CO2 in the tissues. That stabilizing effect in the working muscle is very similar to what progesterone is doing in the heart and brain.

**Andrew Murray:** Does this lend credence to data showing people living at high altitudes have longer lifespans?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you look at how sleep is affected under stress, when someone has altitude sickness, they develop insomnia. It is primarily low-thyroid people who develop altitude sickness because they were hyperventilating chemically even at sea level. When they go to high altitude, that low retention of CO2 shows up as an acute problem.

However, if your thyroid function is good and you are well saturated with carbon dioxide, your restful, slow-wave sleep is longer in proportion to the amount of CO2 in your tissues. They have experimented with having people sleep in atmospheres with 0.5% to 1.5% CO2. At those moderate but increased levels, there is a dramatic improvement in deep sleep.

**Andrew Murray:** Does that imply that athletes taking oxygen on the sidelines should have carbon dioxide mixed in?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it should be 5% or 6% CO2 in pure oxygen. In some Mount Everest experiments, it was traditional to zip a person inside a bag with oxygen to help them recover from mountain sickness. Someone found that inside that plastic bag, they concentrated their breath CO2. They found that giving the high-altitude sickness patient pure CO2—like a 5% additive—would cure them as well as the oxygen supplement.

**Caller (SoCal):** I have a sibling with a history of infertility and very high prolactin levels. She cannot bring it down with thyroid (two grains a day) or progesterone. She follows your diet carefully. What else can she do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Has she taken her temperature and pulse rate to see how she is responding to the thyroid?

**Caller (SoCal):** Yes, she does that. Do you think the medication isn't working?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is important to look at various indicators. For example, the Achilles relaxation reflex. If you kneel and have someone thump your Achilles tendon, your toe should jump out and relax like a piece of floppy rubber. In about two-thirds of the population, it comes back like it has a door closer on it. It shows up as a delayed repolarization or relaxation of the muscle when thyroid is low.

**Andrew Murray:** I've found that some people need to increase the dose quite a bit more than expected to get an effect. Is there anything else responsible for high prolactin, like a tumor?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If there is a tumor secreting it, bromocriptine is almost always successful at shrinking it. But if the tumor isn't very large, you can do it just as reliably by keeping thyroid function a little above normal for two or three weeks. Watch the prolactin; you should first see the TSH go down close to zero, because the same serotonin which rises in hypothyroidism activates the production of prolactin. The TSH descent will be followed by a slower lowering of the prolactin.

**Caller (SoCal):** She also wanted to know how to safely cook mushrooms and make marmalade.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is safe to eat about a cup of well-cooked white button mushrooms every day. Just boil them. They should stay at the boiling temperature for at least an hour.

**Andrew Murray:** My wife cooks them for at least 40 minutes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are probably safe after 15 or 20 minutes, but just to be sure. Regarding marmalade, it is important to get good organic oranges. You don't want insecticide or fungicide in your marmalade.

**Caller (Finland):** I was wondering about the potential positive or negative effects of donating blood. Does it help get rid of metals? Also, could the longer lifespan of females be linked to the fact that they get rid of blood every month?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As far as heart disease goes, the incidence of heart damage increases at menopause so that women become similar to men. That is probably because they had been throwing away excess iron while they were menstruating.

Besides the red cell iron that you lose, I think you can get a great benefit if you keep your red cells but donate the plasma. It might not be good for the recipient, but it is very good to get rid of some of your stress-induced microspheres.

**Caller (Joe):** Regarding CO2, you mentioned putting CO2 gas in a bag and putting your body in it. If you use that bag on a regular basis, would your body acclimate and get better at retaining CO2? Are you teaching your cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I think that is exactly what happens. You are training your cells to take advantage of the Lactate Paradox effect. The longer you stay under the influence of higher CO2, your bones charge up on it. If you are in a submarine for two months, you are still assimilating CO2 into your bone structure. It lasts a long time.

**Caller (Joe):** So you are training parts of your brain not to be hypersensitive to CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Estrogen makes your nerves overreactive to CO2. Under the influence of too much estrogen, everyone hyperventilates and blows out too much CO2. The CO2 temporarily anesthetizes that process and gradually trains you to stop hyperventilating. In Russian studies where they took animals up [to altitude] for six months, they were still showing greater mitochondrial efficiency at the end of their lives two years later.

**Caller (Joe):** My second question is about hair tests for toxic metals. It seems copper, iron, and manganese balance is complex. Do you believe in hair tests?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hair is extremely able to bind metals, even out of the air. So many people have copper plumbing nowadays. If your water is at all acidic, it will absorb enough copper to totally invalidate any hair test if you wash your hair. Your hair will catch all the copper from the wash water.

**Caller (Joe):** So hair tests are generally not valid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Toenail clippings are considered better, but even your toenails can soak up minerals from the water if you wash your feet too often.

**Caller (Joe):** How do you balance copper and iron over time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Generally speaking, I advocate eating shellfish because they use copper for blood instead of iron. A constant once-a-week shellfish meal will keep your copper up where it should be. With age, as you overload on iron, that tends to displace copper from the enzymes where it is used. Elastase in blood vessels tends to deteriorate as it loses copper with aging.

**Caller (Blue Lake):** I have always had high estrogen. I stopped menstruating at 55. I have Lyme and Candida issues. I've heard Reishi mushrooms can help with inflammation. Also, I have a better sex drive now than in the last 25 years, which is strange.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you have said estrogen is responsible for sex drive, whereas testosterone is usually cited.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It takes the conversion of androgen to estrogen in certain parts of the brain to increase the libido. So it doesn't have to be in your serum.

**Caller (Blue Lake):** What about Reishi mushrooms for inflammation?

If you get your resistance up—using DHEA, pregnenolone, and progesterone—that will favor the right conversion of just the right amount of estrogen. You can boost that regulatory effect with things like mushrooms and aspirin.

**Caller (Blue Lake):** I've been told my whole life I am iron deficient. I've tried to correct it with molasses.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doctors for at least 100 years have been diagnosing iron deficiency in women. 100 years ago, they prescribed arsenic to treat it. High estrogen always tends to cause a slight anemia appearance just by slowing the production of red cells.

**Caller (Blue Lake):** I also have high lead content.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Drinking milk, orange juice, and coffee will correct that over a period of weeks.

**Caller (Sugar Cove):** Why boil mushrooms for an hour?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The hydrazines are heat sensitive. It is believed that the hydrazine compounds are the carcinogens. They evaporate and break down. **Caller (Virginia):** What about taking ornithine at night to mop up excess ammonia for sleep?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It might help with the ammonia, but I would worry about the promotion of cell division if you used it chronically. It is one of the things that activates cell division.

**Caller (Virginia):** What about L-Threonine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think it is very safe to use individual amino acids. Glycine is the only one I know of that is safe by itself because it can be used as energy.

**Caller (Virginia):** Is Monolaurin safe for endotoxin?

She said it made her too stupid to teach. She stopped it and had a seizure. She kept having seizures until she was in her early 50s.

**Andrew Murray:** We will have to hold it there. Dr. Peat's website is raypeat.com. It is full of fully referenced articles on thyroid, aspirin, progesterone, Alzheimer's, and more. Next month, we will finish the progesterone versus estrogen discussion. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Progesterone vs Estrogen, Listener Questions (Part 2)
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. This month’s topic is a roundup of where we left off in March discussing progesterone and estrogen. I want to dissect that a little more with facts and arguments refuting the "facts" about how positive estrogen is and how negative progesterone is.

I want to discuss a paper written by Inger Sundström Poromaa at the University of Uppsala in Sweden, apparently a leading expert on brain metabolism and sex hormones. I mentioned in March that the PROTECT and SYNAPSE trials—regarding progesterone's anti-inflammatory effects in traumatic brain injury—were published and apparently relatively unsuccessful. However, Dr. Donald Stein, a PhD brain injury expert at Emory University, was part of the team publishing in the *Journal of Neurotrauma*. He outlined obvious mistakes in the studies, stating the criteria used did not produce valid results. He strongly opposed findings showing no benefit for progesterone, citing evidence to the contrary.

To discuss the ongoing lies about how positive estrogen is and how dangerous progesterone is, we have Dr. Raymond Peat joining us. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I'm here.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat has been a big advocate of things like thyroid, sugar, and progesterone. Mainstream medicine would argue sugar or pregnenolone are not good for you, despite evidence to the contrary. This is clear in the trials regarding Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT). Women with estrogen dominance are advised to take estrogen for bone health or hot flashes, which is likely the last thing they need.

Dr. Peat, given your PhD was in reproductive hormones, could you outline your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Before I studied biology, I was a literature, linguistics, and art major. I decided to study biology to understand how language, intelligence, and consciousness work. I found that brain biology—so-called cognitive science—was pure dogmatism with very little science.

I shifted to reproductive physiology to study how the organism works from the germ cell to the brain. Brain science is not distinct from reproductive physiology; the brain is the motor for the whole life process. I did my dissertation in 1972 on the oxidative changes in the uterus as it changes with aging.

**Andrew Murray:** Let’s jump into questions left over from March. Regarding catamenial epilepsy and estrogens like estrone, estriol, and estradiol—how do you understand the triggering of epilepsy in susceptible females? It is estrogen-related, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In my research, I looked through physiology regarding the brain and uterus up until 1970. I couldn't find evidence distinguishing the physiology of estrogen stimulation from X-ray stimulation, oxygen deprivation, or vitamin E deficiency. All of those things deplete the energy production of the cell, which is based on oxidation.

When the brain is oversupplied with estrogen or lacks its antagonist, progesterone, the whole system wastes oxygen. It is unable to keep the energy level up to the point where cells are stable. A high-energy state is when a cell is ready to work, but not acting. When forced to work more than it is ready for, the energy level falls, and it enters a constantly active state trying to restore energy.

Hypoglycemia works the same as a lack of oxygen. Estrogen interferes with the supply of glucose to cells. It activates insulin but also activates the release of fatty acids, which block the ability to oxidize glucose. Estrogen activates cells by increasing the function of glutamic acid (glutamate), a brain excitant. By increasing glutamate, it decreases GABA, the inhibiting signal. So, estrogen excites brain cells while interfering with their use of oxygen and glucose.

**Andrew Murray:** So the estrogens really mimic a stress response.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I consider estrogen's function to be "controlled stress." The organism requires a constant supply of energy for development. If that energy supply becomes fatally impaired, the function of estrogen is to erase the developmental program and revert to the single, multiplying cell. Without interference, estrogen tends to produce the cancer cell, but it also activates the production of the egg. Its proper function should be once a month, for a few hours, to activate potential new life.

Catamenial epilepsy tends to begin around age nine, when estrogen is rising but progesterone hasn't risen yet. Brain metabolism slows down at puberty, the body takes it as a threat to survival, and turns on the reproductive process.

**Andrew Murray:** Is it correct that the only real benefit for estrogen is the inflammation it promotes to stimulate implantation of an egg?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Throughout the organism, whenever tissue is stressed, it tends to turn on the local production of estrogen. That is how it leads to cancer; every cell essentially has the apparatus for making estrogen.

After menopause, when progesterone production becomes limited, the body's tissues—breast, uterus, brain, liver, skin, fat, muscle—begin producing estrogen.
