**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s and early 1960s, I was studying literature and painting mostly. Then, from 1968 to 1972, I did a graduate program for a PhD in biology. My approach to research is probably influenced by my literature background—thinking of propaganda analysis and sensitivity to how people use language to manipulate preconceptions. I think everyone looking at the internet has to spend more time thinking about propaganda analysis and how advertising has invaded and practically taken over many of the medical journals.

**Andrew Murray:** Just very quickly, tell people what your specialty was when you graduated and what you looked at in your research.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My dissertation was on the biochemical changes involved in reproductive aging, working on the hamster uterus mostly. I saw how many factors parallel aging in the biochemical pattern that they create. Estrogen excess, progesterone deficiency, vitamin E deficiency, and exposure to radiation all create the same typical age pattern of metabolism. It is at its most extreme in cancer metabolism.

That was why I was so interested in Otto Warburg's work at the time I was starting graduate school. American biochemists were turning against Otto Warburg, despite his Nobel Prize, because he was saying that cancer is a metabolic condition, not a gene mutation. Now, 50 years later, the US and European cultures are finally coming around to looking at what Warburg did almost 100 years ago.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to continue last month's subject of skin cancer. I want to talk about an Italian MD named Tullio Simoncini. He has been controversial and was eventually struck off the medical register, but he was getting successful results treating people with topical cancers—basal cell carcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas, and melanomas—using a 7% iodine solution. He also treats internal cancers with a different protocol.

Simoncini stated categorically that cancer is based on a yeast, and *Candida albicans* is essentially the organism responsible for it. Dr. Peat, what do you think about Tullio Simoncini's approach and his rationale?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40 years ago, there was a big mania in the US blaming everything on Candida. That led me to study how it actually interacts. If you are under stress, hypothyroid, inclined towards diabetes (not being able to oxidize glucose thoroughly), and tending to have high estrogen, it happens that all of those favor and attract Candida growth. The presence of Candida coincides with hypothyroidism, estrogen excess, and poor ability to oxidize glucose.

Inflammation and improper oxidation of glucose are typical of cancer metabolism more intensely than of simple stress metabolism. So, Simoncini is seeing something very central to the metabolism of cancer, which is intensified by the inflammation-promoting effects of the Candida.

Candida itself is attracted to estrogen; estrogen is a sex hormone for the Candida fungus. It contains an enzyme which can aromatize male steroid hormones, so it can become an amplifier of estrogen. Once it gets in a tissue and the immune system is failing, the fungus can convert from a yeast form to a filament form and invade the tissues looking for sugar and estrogen. It is very commonly associated with cancers. The sicker a person is, the weaker their immune system is, and the less they are using their own glucose. They produce histamine and lactic acid in the tumor, and both of these are attractive to the fungus.

If you simply increase the pH—and do it with bicarbonate, which converts to carbon dioxide—that helps to suppress the cancer-promoting lactic acid formation by the tumor itself. So he's really onto something.

**Andrew Murray:** Last month we talked about vitamin D deficiency. You mentioned that the skin's immune system and a deficiency of vitamin D in the skin, especially as people get older, plays a part in the formation of skin cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and that follows from a cholesterol deficiency. With aging, the ability to make cholesterol and steroids goes down. When sunlight hits old skin, it makes much less vitamin D.

Just a few months ago in Poland, there was an interesting article on the so-called "activated" form of vitamin D, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D). They showed that the active form suppresses immunity and creates the ideal environment for causing mammary gland cancer metastasis.

**Andrew Murray:** You're saying the 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not actually the beneficial form?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that is produced under stress. It is sort of the way the steroid hormones under extreme stress can emphasize the estrogen version. Calcitriol is the extreme stress form of vitamin D. It has its use under stress, but like estrogen, it easily becomes counterproductive and, in the case of cancer, can promote the cancer spread.

**Andrew Murray:** Calcitriol is the end of the metabolic pathway for the production of vitamin D.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you are well supplied with calcium and the vitamin D precursors—or sunlight and cholesterol—you have a very low level of calcitriol.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, so that won't be reached if you have adequate levels of thyroid and calcium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. Like pregnenolone is the precursor of the pathway that leads to estrogen and aldosterone, but if you take enough pregnenolone, you will reduce those end products.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding Simoncini's idea that *Candida albicans* is the culprit: he observed that tumors invariably had white centers, which was Candida. You've mentioned that Candida is opportunistic. In the past, you've said that you do *not* want to starve the body of sugar—which is typically what they advise for Candida—because the filamentous form is initiated when the fungal organism is deprived of sugar and wants to go further into the tissues.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If it's happy in the intestine, it grows in the yeast form getting enough sugar. But when there's no sugar in the intestine and it starves, then it will attach itself to the surface of the intestine and send out filaments to find sugar from the bloodstream or the cells.

**Andrew Murray:** Simoncini also uses intravenous injectable sodium bicarbonate. I know you are a big fan of sodium bicarbonate and CO2.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When bicarbonate gets into the bloodstream, the sodium leaves in the urine and the bicarbonate is converted to carbon dioxide as it enters the cell. So, it acidifies the intracellular environment despite temporarily increasing the alkalinity of the bloodstream. The typical cancer metabolism has an alkaline intracellular pH. You are getting right at the heart of the problem when you increase the CO2 inside the cell.

Since the 18th century, carbon dioxide gas has been used to treat visible cancers, such as ulcerated breast cancer. The Japanese are currently using it to treat cancers using that same principle: it acidifies the cell and turns off the growth mechanism of lactic acid production. Several drug companies are working on enzyme inhibitors similar to acetazolamide to increase the internal acidity of cancers.

**Andrew Murray:** Acetazolamide is something you've said is useful for raising your own production of CO2.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it causes the body to retain it and acidifies the whole body when you get a certain amount. But intracellularly, that acidification turns off lactic acid production. Lactic acid is effectively the main carcinogen.

**Caller (Petrolia):** I have a crusty carcinoma type of thing on the back of my hands and the side of my neck. I was wondering what I could do to get rid of the scab or crust. Are you saying a 7% solution of iodine might be the solution?

**Andrew Murray:** Yes. If you go to Amazon and look at 7% iodine, read the customer reviews. Many talk about how basal or squamous cell carcinomas have gone after weeks of treatment. You can also look up Tullio Simoncini.

**Caller (Peter, San Francisco):** I've noticed a benefit from adding sugar to milk and orange juice. I'm wondering what the mechanism is for that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hypotonic liquids hitting the stomach and intestine cause a stress reaction and release serotonin into the bloodstream. Hypertonic things—if within reason, as you can injure your stomach with a big dose of salt or dry sugar—have an anti-inflammatory effect. Moderate hypertonicity helps to regulate energy production and pH. Various hypertonic solutions are being used in resuscitation now; a small volume, like a cupful of hypertonic solution, has a very intense resuscitating effect in shock.

**Caller (Dirk, Redway):** My 96-year-old grandmother had a squamous cell on her nose. The doctor recommended excising it, which would have removed her entire nose. We opted against that and applied cannabis oil in an olive oil suspension. In two weeks, it went away. Do you have comments on the efficacy of the cannabis, or was it the olive oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm inclined to think it's the olive oil that is therapeutic because it has so many anti-inflammatory effects. I think the cannabis oil has some potentially pro-growth, pro-inflammatory components.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think that's the oleanolic component of the olive oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The things related to cannabis—the endogenous cannabinoids like anandamide—are metabolites of very unsaturated fatty acids. The effects that I've seen really are along the line of the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) themselves, which as a group are amplifiers of the estrogen effect. However, there are several things in olive oil that I think can have a protective anti-cancer effect.

**Caller (New York):** First, regarding PUFA: What about sardines? It's a whole fish, so you get minerals and potentially vitamin D. Is the PUFA in sardines problematic? Second, regarding Candida: If you have a fungal toe, do you have to be really healthy to attack it? Could chasing it out of your toe cause it to spread to another area?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding sardines, they have very good general nutritional value, including selenium, iodine, and other trace minerals found in ocean organisms. But it does have a lot of the polyunsaturated fats. I think maybe one meal a week is fine. Everything exposed to sunlight tends to have some vitamin D.

Regarding the fungus, I don't think it would spread if you are using something like 7% iodine on the infected nail. It takes a long time to diffuse through a toenail, but it is a good fungus killer.

**Caller (San Francisco Bay Area):** I was in a very toxic relationship this year involving substance abuse and lying. How do bad relationships affect individuals, and can they affect one's physiology?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's a very powerful stressor. Eating well can help to offset the stress, but the attitude—the way you interpret the experience—is also essential. It should be seen as just one of the challenges of living, not interpreted in any way that impairs your understanding of yourself. It should just be seen as one of the environmental challenges.

**Caller (Finland):** I found out they are selling bags for growers that contain a fungus which generates CO2. Would it be a good idea to have those bags around the house to increase CO2 levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had a bag of Masa Harina from Mexico, and the humidity in Oregon started a fungus growth. For about a year, it was hot and producing carbon dioxide. So it is a very productive, passive way to increase the carbon dioxide in your bedroom. I don't think it emits anything seriously harmful other than the carbon dioxide, which is beneficial. If it has a cloth enclosure, I don't think it's going to put out any spores.

**Caller (Michael, Redway):** We often hear about the Candida diet which involves starving it with no sugar. Does that imply you could get cancer from it latching on? How do you get rid of the overgrowth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just a pinch of flowers of sulfur. If it's internal, a pinch of it every day for three or four days is very reliable for cleaning it out of your intestine. If it's on your skin, you can rub it into the white spot. If it is in the sweaty areas, dust the area with flowers of sulfur. I had a whole-body coverage of some kind of fungus when I was in a tropical area of Mexico, and someone told me about 10% sulfur soap. One bath eradicated it. It's amazingly effective against skin Candida infections.

**Caller:** Is flowers of sulfur the same powder winemakers put on their grapes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they use a cruder, cheaper form, but yes, it's a good fungus killer on plants.

**Caller (Pepperwood):** I was recently diagnosed with Hashimoto's. My TSH was 5. My symptom is erratic blood pressure—sometimes 140s, sometimes lower. What would you suggest to support thyroid function and stabilize blood pressure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Broda Barnes advocated the use of temperature as an important basis for diagnosing functional hypothyroidism. In the 1940s, the drug industry introduced chemical diagnoses that were biologically meaningless but convinced everyone that 95% of the population is not hypothyroid. They eventually switched to TSH as the "gold standard," but they neglect the fact that stress lowers your TSH. You can be under such intense stress with high cortisol that your TSH can be near zero while your thyroid gland is producing nothing.

Also, TSH is an inflammation promoter. It creates hypertension by causing inflammation directly in the blood vessels. One of the effects of the thyroid hormone on your blood pressure is simply that it suppresses TSH. Many people now say the upper limit of TSH should not be higher than 2.0.

Regarding blood pressure, it is good to check your temperature and pulse rate when you first wake up and then later in the day. Broda Barnes believes the waking temperature should be close to 98°F and the mid-afternoon temperature closer to 98.6°F. In my own experience, when I stopped taking thyroid for a while, my blood pressure went up to something like 170/110, and other times as low as 55/28. I felt fine, but I got back to taking more sugar and thyroid quickly.

**Caller (New Jersey):** If you cook vegetables, do you get rid of the PUFA? Also, regarding mushrooms, do they have the same effect as the carrot salad and charcoal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cooked mushrooms have a fair balance of minerals. They are somewhat low in calcium, but not as bad as grains, beans, and meats. They have the fibrous effect that the carrot has of helping to sweep out the intestine just by the bulk effect.

Regarding greens, cooking them makes them more digestible so you get more protein, but greens do have too much PUFA to use them as your main food. If you cook them for hours, much of the PUFA would float to the surface and you could get some of it off, but they are still high in PUFA. The cow's digestive system uses bacteria and vitamin E to eliminate 98% of the PUFA, so it's better to process greens through cows and drink the milk. The best thing about greens is the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio; they are extremely high in calcium relative to phosphate.

**Caller:** Are root vegetables the same?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Turnips, for example, have fructose when they are young and fresh and are relatively nutritious. They have much less of a PUFA problem than the greens.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Skin Cancer Part 3
transcriptText:
**Host:** Andrew Murray
**Guest:** Dr. Raymond Peat

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this January 18th, 2019 edition of Ask Your Herb Doctor. This month’s topic is wrapping up the last two discourses on skin cancer, but we are tying in the topic of oncogenes with viruses and epigenetics, and the viricidal activity of selected medicinal plants. There is a wealth of new articles being published on PubMed and other scientific peer-reviewed sites.

For those people who perhaps haven't heard of you and don't know too much about you, Dr. Peat, we'll just give a rundown of your academic and professional background before we get started.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I did graduate study in biology for a Ph.D. between 1968 and 1972 at the University of Oregon. Since then, I have been following up on some of the ideas that I worked on for my dissertation, which was basically aging and cell energy production. Among other things, that includes how hormones and foods promote viral immunity.

**Andrew Murray:** You're a big advocate of food-based help in terms of helping the organism recover homeostasis to fight infection, whether it's producing natural steroids or fighting bacteria and viruses. You spend a lot of time discussing the nutrition aspects of healing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The immune system ideas go way back. Before I went to graduate school in biology, I had read some of William F. Koch's research. Some of his colleagues found that the treatments he used for curing cancer also worked for curing animal diseases, such as mastitis in cows. He showed that the healthy cow could actually have more bacteria in its udder than the sick cow with mastitis, and that a healthy cow tolerated microorganisms without suffering damage from them.

That led me to get interested in the newer research. Jamie Cunliffe in England has what he calls the "damage theory" of immunity, in which the immune system really is a system for repairing tissue damage. If microorganisms cause damage, then the immune system will clear out the microorganisms, but that is a side effect of repairing the damage. Polly Matzinger, about the same time, came out with the "danger hypothesis." That is very similar, except it isn't quite as realistic as Jamie Cunliffe's, because it still leaves it open for seeing the microorganism as intrinsically dangerous. I think the facts indicate that we can tolerate microorganisms as long as they don't poison us.

**Andrew Murray:** Or if indeed we're not poisoned by the environment in which we live. It’s a grand idea to have that common root—that the body is intrinsically able to heal itself if you give it the right material.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you look at a viral disease epidemic, there are always people who don't succumb to it. You often find that they have contracted the infection and have antibodies to it, but it didn't make them at all sick, or only slightly sick.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to clear up a few questions from last month about melanoma. Apparently, the incidence of melanoma has been on the rise exponentially since the 1980s.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think from before that. I've seen figures that it has increased 500% since about 1940. I'm pretty sure it's not sun exposure because it has an inverse relation with altitude. The change that I think is relevant is the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA), which have increased just about at the same rate melanoma has.

**Andrew Murray:** Are you thinking this is because the polyunsaturates are energy depleting or producing lipid peroxidation in the skin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many of those things. The energy goes down and inflammation goes up. In the Veterans Administration study in the 1960s, supposedly to prevent heart disease, they gave a corn oil-based diet to one group and regular fats—including margarine, butter, and ordinary moderately unsaturated fats—to another. The group that got corn oil in their diet regularly, at the end of eight years, had three times the mortality from cancer. That was one of the industry's own studies. It relates to what you see in the animal studies: if you look at just linoleic acid, which was the original so-called "essential fatty acid," as the proportion of linoleic acid in the diet goes up, the cancer incidence and mortality goes up in proportion. They also interfere with the production and use of cholesterol.

**Andrew Murray:** I was looking at an article with the headline: "Lung cancer incidence decreases with elevation: evidence for oxygen as an inhaled carcinogen." You've always mentioned CO2 being protective, with longevity definitely increasing with elevation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The insurance companies have known for more than 100 years that cancer mortality in general decreases with altitude. It is very low in the high-altitude cities. As the oxygen pressure in the air increases, the carbon dioxide tends to decrease. They are competitive; the pressure of oxygen displaces the carbon dioxide bound to proteins in the blood.

**Andrew Murray:** So people at sea level are much more likely statistically to get cancer because they don't have the protective effect of CO2 that you'd get at altitude?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, CO2 is an anti-inflammatory protective factor.

**Andrew Murray:** I know you're completely against statins. You've always said that the elderly, or even people over 50, want a cholesterol level of 220 to 230. I saw from the pharmacology of statins that they block mevalonate, which is an upstream chemical. This can cause aneuploidy, which is a serious outcome.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you experimentally starve cells for cholesterol—the same thing that a statin does to the person—the cells in vitro are stuck in the tetraploid state. They can't do the reductive separation of chromosomes. Old people's skin is relatively loaded with cells stuck in that state because, with aging, the cells lose their ability to maintain the production of cholesterol. When they get stuck in that condition, if something forces them to divide, they get the number of chromosomes randomized as they divide, and that can produce cancer cells.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you see any protocol for rejuvenating skin cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the cosmetic industry, they're starting to put cholesterol in cosmetics. In effect, it does rejuvenate the cells. It restores their ability to divide healthfully.

**Andrew Murray:** So you can physically, topically apply cholesterol in the form of an ointment or a cream?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's what the experiments show, and the cosmetics companies are taking advantage of it. There is half as much cholesterol in old skin as in young skin.

**Andrew Murray:** From an anti-aging perspective, do you think there's much that can be done to restore the collagen or the scaffold in which the skin is normally elastic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the cells normally are able to turn it over. Energized cells can eat up the hardened, cross-linked, aged collagen and let the cells produce fresh collagen. The cholesterol lets the cells divide normally, so they are more energetic and produce a thicker layer of healthy cells rather than a scaly, hardened layer of aged, flaky cells. The practical way to keep your cholesterol synthesis ability is to avoid polyunsaturated fatty acids because they turn off the synthesis of cholesterol and interfere with its use in the cells.

**Andrew Murray:** You've always said that four years is a rough approximation for the turnover of lipids in the cell. How is this the same with the brain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every night there's a tremendous turnover of the lipids in the brain. But when you're asleep, your blood sugar falls and the free fatty acids tend to be liberated from your fat stores. So if you have bad fat in your fat tissue, during the night it's going to be in the blood vessels when your brain is remaking itself. If you can keep your blood sugar up or get your fat so that it's pretty saturated, then your brain remakes itself considerably every night.

**Andrew Murray:** What about hydroxymethylbutyrate (HMB) as a precursor to cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's a precursor that supposedly helps to increase it. It's very important to get cholesterol up to 160 at least. Bodybuilders are the ones experimenting with this precursor, but I haven't heard much from them about its effectiveness.

**Caller (New York):** You said total cholesterol should be 225 to 230 for older people. Is that the only one that matters? What about triglycerides, LDL, and HDL?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When your low-density cholesterol (LDL) is low, that increases the cancer risk and dementia risk. But the things that poison your liver or stress you increase the HDL. It happens that the protein that forms the HDL is anti-inflammatory, so it's a defensive reaction to stress. Estrogen and alcohol, for example, will increase the HDL defensively.

But the LDL is a protective source of the cholesterol. And if the triglycerides are fairly saturated, they aren't very harmful. They found that heart failure is actually less of a problem if your triglycerides are high. But if the triglycerides are polyunsaturated, that goes with interference with the function of the cholesterol. Free fatty acids are the dangerous form of fats in the blood; they have multiple interferences, for example with oxidative metabolism and the use of sugar. The triglycerides are pretty innocuous; they're just evidence that you're under stress and not using your sugar properly.

**Caller (New York):** If a 22-year-old sprains his ankle—torn ligaments, swelling—what are the three or four things you would do to make sure it heals properly? We're told scar tissue has to form, but we worry that leads to arthritis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Do things to keep the free fatty acids low so that you use your glucose as efficiently as possible to produce anti-inflammatory things like carbon dioxide. Aspirin and niacinamide, for example, are anti-inflammatory things that reduce the disorganizing kind of scar tissue and promote maximum quality healing with a minimum of excess random collagen deposition.

Vitamin D and Vitamin K are very important. Getting enough calcium in your diet with Vitamin D so that you keep your parathyroid hormone suppressed helps keep the tissue energy high. Include salt in your diet to keep the aldosterone to a minimum, because aldosterone promotes disorganized collagen healing and fibrosis. So, some unexpected things: sodium and calcium in the diet are protective to the healing of connective tissue.

**Caller (New York):** If a doctor says the only way it heals is when scar tissue develops?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, good scar tissue is fine, but the worse your metabolism is, the more disorganized the scar tissue is. A keloid, for example, is terrible scar tissue—very disorganized because of polyunsaturated fats in your circulation. A baby in utero with no essential fatty acids in circulation and plenty of carbon dioxide will heal without any disorganized structures.

**Caller (New York):** For a fungal toe, someone suggested mixing equal parts apple cider vinegar and hydrogen peroxide and soaking it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Iodine is a good fungus killer. Vinegar is a pretty fair antagonist to the fungus. In combination with hydrogen peroxide, I imagine they work all right too. It sounds very safe. You can damage the tissue with too much hydrogen peroxide. Once I spilled some 30% peroxide on my finger and it turned strangely paper white. I stuck it in a bottle of ascorbic acid and in a flash it looked normal.

**Caller (Calgary):** I followed your suggestion to take coconut oil, but every time I take it, it causes really bad digestive distress. I've tried the ultra-purified and the unrefined.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I found that the nice-tasting unrefined ones were harder on the intestine. The ultra-refined and even hydrogenated coconut oil, I find, is easiest on the intestine. If you put it on a hot frying pan and it smells, then it's more likely to hurt your intestine. It should be odorless when it hits a hot pan.

**Caller (Toronto):** What can an individual do who has an opportunity to intercept a psychopath? Is there anything that can be done to normalize a psychopath?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping the brain well energized, and that means keeping the blood sugar steady. Sometimes just a very digestible diet can make a person feel so much better that they don't have to exploit and manipulate other people.

**Caller (Toronto):** It might have something to do with the narcissistic quality, not wanting to eat or having low calorie intake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think the addictive personality that needs alcohol or drugs is somewhat in the same boat—needing something that they can't get themselves. They try to control others to make their life better. But if their life suddenly becomes better by changing metabolism... I've seen lifetime addicts to alcohol, heroin, or cocaine just overnight literally drop their addiction.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to ask about the role of viruses. Part of our genome is viral. I've always imagined viruses just to be the bad guys. Is there anything useful about viruses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A very large part of our genome resembles the retroviruses. Since viruses can only exist in the cells of higher animals, they obviously derive in some way from the higher animal's genetic material.

It's only in the last several years that western biochemists are starting to recognize that there are particles circulating in our blood and lymph system carrying genetic information. A Korean scientist 60 years ago claimed he discovered a third circulatory system which carries particles of genetic material. About 10 years ago, this was actually documented—not as a third circulatory system, but the fact that there are very small particles of nucleic acids circulating in the blood and lymph carrying genetic information to repair cells or change their functions.

They call these microvesicles or exosomes. They bud from the surface of cells and carry DNA, RNA, proteins, and other parts of cells that act as signals. For example, between a working organ like the lungs and the bone marrow producing stem cells. All of our organs are communicating with each other through these little particles that are about the size of viruses.

When bacteria are exposed to a dangerous environment, such as antibiotics or starvation, they are able to re-engineer their own genes to produce adaptive changes. When one bacterium achieves immunity, they can conveniently pack it up into a little exosome—a plasmid—which they pass onto their neighbors. So it spreads like a viral infection. It is a self-constructed virus that the bacteria pass on for the defense of the community.

Within our body, we are passing these little plasmids or microvesicles to different parts of the body. When we eat another organism, we incorporate some of their DNA into our own cellular DNA. You eat beef and you get some cow DNA; you eat carrots and you get some carrot DNA. In that sense, we're communicating across species all the time. I imagine that viruses have some of that function. I think we have the ability to look into our genetic reservoir to see what's useful. If our energy is very low, then they can cause trouble and interfere with our adaptation. But if our energy is high, I think getting these particles of genetic information can actually increase our repertoire.

**Caller (West Haven):** My gallbladder is not functioning very well. I have fat intolerance. A friend recommended a grape fast.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Years ago, I read a book called *The Grape Cure* by a South African doctor. That was one of the things that got me interested in the purple pigment in grapes and other fruits as a stimulant to proper oxygen use. Combined with sugar and the minerals in grape juice, it does have great therapeutic effects.

**Andrew Murray:** Caller, do you have obstruction or just deficient bile production?

**Caller (West Haven):** Fat intolerance. Nothing showing on ultrasound, but I have a mix of hypothyroid, mold sensitivity, and SIBO.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The gallbladder is very sensitive to low thyroid function or high estrogen in relation to progesterone. Progesterone relaxes it; estrogen tends to cause spasms. The sick reaction to fats is because the thresholds are lowered by the high estrogen-to-progesterone ratio. The key to it is almost always low thyroid function. Correct your metabolism by getting your body temperature up to daytime levels, typically around 98.6°F (37°C).

**Caller (Eureka):** Do you know of any cause that would lead a person to develop digestive issues—frequent loose bowel movements—as well as high blood pressure? They came out of the blue at the same time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Stress physiology is generally involved in both inflammation and the tendency to diarrhea and high blood pressure. Low thyroid function with a TSH measurement up to 3 is often called normal, but anything above 1.0 is likely to promote inflammation, including in the intestine.

High serotonin is the main thing that contributes to an overactive bowel. It is also named for its ability to constrict blood vessels and raise blood pressure. There are drugs that will lower it, such as cyproheptadine. But usually, you can change your diet to reduce the inflammatory foods, such as starches or raw/undercooked vegetables that support bacteria that cause the intestinal inflammation.

**Caller (Eureka):** So less starch and less raw vegetable matter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Salads, bread, beans, nuts, and even potatoes can sometimes feed the bacteria that cause the inflammation and release serotonin. The simplest approach is to eat a bland fiber. Some people are okay with cooked oat bran as a mush, but some bacteria can feed on that. Cooked mushrooms and cooked bamboo shoots are bland fibers that will often lower the serotonin and diarrhea effect.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, thanks so much for your time. For those who have listened, Dr. Peat can be contacted through his website, www.raypeat.com. He has many well-written articles that are fully referenced. Until the third Friday of next month, good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Viruses
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** It is the third Friday of the month. I'm very pleased to introduce Dr. Raymond Peat onto the live show. We are inviting callers to ask questions related to this month's topic, which is the antiviral activity of medicinal plants and their constituents, and how Dr. Peat interprets antiviral activity. It's not always a straightforward antiviral activity, but rather a host response that is often the remedy or the provoking factor which stimulates the immune system into defense. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us. As always, I'd like to start the show off by asking you to introduce yourself and give a rundown of your professional and academic background.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After undergraduate study in humanities and a master's degree also in general humanities—with a thesis on William Blake—I went to graduate school about 10 years later in biology. I was interested in brain physiology, but ended up working on reproductive physiology because the brain biology people seemed too indoctrinated with membrane theory and other stylish things at the time. So, I worked on reproductive physiology, and that got me interested in how hormones affect consciousness, among other things, and how nutrition and hormones interact with other environmental factors to affect our immunity, development, consciousness, and so on.

**Andrew Murray:** To open up this month's topic, we've been intimately associated with viruses ever since we walked the face of the earth. I've heard various stories of viral DNA being part of our DNA. I think up to 8% is the often-quoted proportion.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Retroviral DNA seems to be around that.

**Andrew Murray:** Given how you understand viruses and any potential benefit that they may confer—although most people consider viral illness a detriment to their health—how are we to interpret the viral inclusion in our DNA and our evolution with them? How should we understand their role and our approach to dealing with the damaging effects of coexisting with viruses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** While bacteria have their own independent existence and can generally live without us, viruses depend on a higher organism to exist. When I was in graduate school, I asked a few people what they thought the origin of viruses was, and no one wanted to suggest anything at all.

At that time, around 1970, people were still very puzzled about how we could have such an immense potential immunity to every sort of conceivable antigen. They were still thinking in terms of being born or created with every gene specifying an antibody. Someone worked out the numbers and saw that it would take something the size of a tennis ball for a nucleus of every cell if it was to contain genes for every antibody that we produce. So, people had to start thinking about innovation—the inventive process happening for the immune system. The origin of viruses seems to be related to that process of cell invention, innovation, and interaction.

People have said that viral diseases became a human problem at the same time that we shifted to an agricultural economy, suggesting that diet could be part of it. Historically, wars, famines, deforestation, and all sorts of natural disasters have led to epidemics. One theory is that stress causes mutations in the virus, causing a benign virus to mutate and become dangerous. But whatever the mechanism is, it's known that viruses appear and circulate during social stresses.

When you look at an individual under stress, each type of tissue or organ sends out messages. Little micro-vesicles, microsomes, or various names for them, are emitted as very fine, sub-microscopic particles which contain nucleic acids (RNA, DNA), proteins, hormones, and a great variety of substances. These travel to other cells in the body and can be assimilated, transmitting differentiated nucleic acid patterns to other cells that are under stress, helping them adapt.

When the individual is under stress, everyone does this constantly. The sicker you are, the more of these micro-vesicles you have circulating around. That seems to be why old serum transmits aging, while young serum transfusions communicate a youthful physiology. Part of the stress of aging is that we're sending more and more of these distress messages around. Since viruses never could develop on their own, it's probable that they are an emission from a stressed population escaping from this therapeutic, corrective, adaptive process that happens constantly within our body. Some of that escapes, and getting into an organism which is in a different state of stress, that can become a virus—or a micro-vesicle—that the recipient organism hasn't learned how to deal with.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to go back to something you touched on regarding the epidemiology of viruses. Viral diseases became a lot more prevalent during urbanization, when people started getting together and growing crops in one location rather than being nomadic. Populations started to increase locally in a concentration that allowed viruses an effective means of spread.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was the grains that made that kind of civilization easy to develop.

**Andrew Murray:** And the grains are bad for you, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Two things in particular: they're very high in phosphate and low in calcium. That in itself, I think, is enough to damage your immunity.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think the practice of growing wheat in large quantities to feed the masses affected the nutritional status of the people enough to allow that negative effect of decreasing calcium and increasing phosphate to become an issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and a high iron content in the diet is another thing that damages immunity because most microorganisms depend on iron as one of their host factors.

**Andrew Murray:** You've always mentioned iron as being a very damaging element in terms of its ability to oxidize things and cause damage, and that high iron is always associated with disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And that has been one of my interests in looking at the role of milk in public health, because it's very low in iron and high in calcium. Babies are immune to many diseases, such as malaria and viral diseases, while they're being breastfed. They're getting a high calcium intake and low iron intake.

**Andrew Murray:** Is it a fact that babies being breastfed have a statistically lower proportion of disease than children that have been weaned?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Some of these, like respiratory infections, are said to be only about 20% as frequent in breastfed babies. In zones where malaria is endemic, babies don't get it until right after they stop being breastfed.

**Andrew Murray:** You've mentioned that viruses, or the genetic information they contain, can be passed down through the DNA and act as a messenger system. How could that possibly benefit the organism? I would imagine anybody with cold sores, measles, or warts wouldn't imagine this could be a beneficial thing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the big historical epidemics, there have always been some people who never caught the disease and were simply naturally immune. I think that's the way everyone is when they aren't subjugated and fed a grain diet. I think the social invention of disease, especially viral disease, is a definite historical thing.

There hasn't been much written about the concept of reductive stress, but it simply means that when your cells are being burdened or overstimulated more than their oxidative metabolism can deal with, they lose their oxidative/pro-oxidative balance and go into reductive stress. That's where iron, for example, becomes toxic. Iron that is harmlessly stored in the oxidizing cell suddenly becomes a source of free radical destruction when the cell goes over into the overstimulated reductive state.

I think that's the central fact of the failure of the immune system: something interfering with the oxidative balance. Calcium deficiency or phosphate excess is another thing that contributes to that reductive stress. The parathyroid hormone shifts the cells in that direction. So, when you're eating too much grain phosphate, you increase your parathyroid hormone, which shifts your balance over in the direction of too much reduction, activating cellular weakness and oxidative destruction.

**Andrew Murray:** You have mentioned fairly regularly about cell stability and how the cell's inherent stability is essential for maintaining good health. Everything in this universe is about energy and order, while entropy is the disease, decay, and chaos state.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For the cell energy system, cancer, bacterial and viral infections, and various types of inflammation are all the same process. It shifts from the production of carbon dioxide, which is an anti-entropic factor. The carbon dioxide spontaneously binds to all of the amino groups in proteins and shifts the acidic balance, maintaining the mineral retaining balance of the cell—stabilizing it in the potassium-retaining, calcium- and sodium-resisting condition. When something interferes with your ability to produce that stabilizing carbon dioxide, we produce lactic acid instead. This adds exactly the opposite effect; it shifts us over into the unstable state, increased pH ionization that attracts calcium and sodium and can't take up enough magnesium and potassium.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to bring up a point about technology. The creation of human embryos that can resist HIV is a fairly controversial subject in China, where they disclosed they'd been using CRISPR technology to edit genes. Do you think this technology is going to become helpful, or is it still going to be plagued by problems?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's exactly the same ideology that was imposed early in the 20th century as Neo-Darwinism. It basically removed some of Darwin's most important ideas. Darwin wouldn't have subscribed to Neo-Darwinism. It's a purely mechanical theory of existence in which random variations in the genetic material are the essential idea—randomness from the bottom up.

Ever since Lamarck and Darwin, practical people working with organisms have known that doesn't work. It's only the academic ideologues who have pushed that abstract view of genetics. James A. Shapiro has worked as a bacterial geneticist and written books describing bacteria as perfect genetic engineers. His view of nature is that life is cognitive all the way down, top to bottom. Instead of randomness, it's cognition on the cellular level.

**Andrew Murray:** What about bacteriophages?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For the intestine or wounds that are infected with bacteria, Eastern Europe and Asia have, over the last 70 or 80 years, developed a great collection of these viruses that specialize in living on bacteria. They're harmless to people, but they will eliminate bacteria that have got out of control in our intestines or in infected wounds.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to ask about Human Papilloma Virus (HPV). In males, it causes genital warts, and in females, dysplasia that can eventually lead to cervical cancer. This is one example of a virus directly interfering with a host's DNA and energy to bring about cellular degradation. What do you think about HPV and the oncogenic effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cervical dysplasia can, if it persists, become *carcinoma in situ* of the cervix. But all of the women that I've known who had cervical dysplasia or *carcinoma in situ* cleared it up in just a few weeks by improving their diet and applying Vitamin A, Vitamin E, and progesterone, and taking supplements of folic acid and thyroid. 100% of them.

**Andrew Murray:** Vitamin A and progesterone—would that be best used topically? How do you see those substances acting as antiviral?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Any irritation increases the reductive balance of the cell and the activation of estrogen production. Estrogen tends to lock it into that reductive and dysplastic condition. Vitamin A opposes the structural changes on epithelial cells as an anti-estrogen differentiating effect. Progesterone knocks out the estrogen and its products. All of the metabolic changes shift the cell away from estrogen and inflammation towards the oxidative, energy-producing condition.

**Andrew Murray:** Mainstream medicine uses colposcopy, where they bore a cone of tissue out of the cervix. That goes against the idea that the alarm signal of the "bystander effect" when cells are in trouble is the trigger for disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you're extremely healthy, you can stand to have a bit of tissue cut away and heal it up with a healthy, almost invisible scar. But to the extent that you're not fully in the oxidative condition, any wound is going to leave its trace as a more or less defective healed area of bad scar tissue. This has lower oxygen tension, puts the cells under stress, and tends to attract repair cells but damage them because the tissue is defective. So, it becomes a center for cancer regrowth. If you can recover your good oxidative health, then you can probably stand having a bit of tissue cut out.

**Caller (Arizona):** Dr. Peat, your article on immunodeficiency mentions autoantibodies. Glutamate is an excitatory amino acid, and glutamate decarboxylase is the enzyme that turns glutamate into GABA, which is associated with relaxation. Some people have autoantibodies to this enzyme, associated with Type 1 diabetes and Stiff-Person Syndrome. How does the system work, and how do things like passion fruit juice influence the autoantibodies in GABA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the energy system should be able to use the antibodies to clean out the defective enzymes and not continue to be produced. Supporting the GABA system with magnesium, glucose, carbon dioxide, anti-inflammatory things, the pro-GABA steroids derived from progesterone, and the anti-immune steroid DHEA helps to redirect the antibody production. Estrogen tends to make us overproduce antibodies but not be able to guide the correction process. Things that shift the whole physiology towards oxidation and the relaxed, highly energized state of the cell are the route out of all of those autoimmune diseases.

**Caller (Arizona):** Do you have any comments on people who have adverse childhood experiences and physical injuries? I had a head injury 20 years ago.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those same things. The things that increase stability, energy production, and carbon dioxide production are constantly causing cells to be born and differentiate in the right direction.

**Caller (Arizona):** Is there any use to GABA supplementation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Normally it doesn't get into the brain because of the so-called blood-brain barrier. But when the brain is very injured, it is taken up because basically the brain needs it. But ordinarily, I think it's enough just to eat a pro-oxidative diet and avoid the excess of phosphate, lactic acid, iron, and so on.

**Caller (New York):** I have a question about dry CO2. I've tried putting bags around my legs and arms and filling them with CO2. If I do it for four or five hours, I wake up and there is a lot of moisture in the bags. Is that a good approach? Does that make you dehydrated?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mechanism is that the carbon dioxide relaxes your skin blood vessels, so your skin gets pink and warm, and then the plastic bag prevents the water from leaving. So it's just natural sweat vaporization. It's an inconvenience, but it doesn't hurt anything.

**Caller (New York):** Is it literally removing poorly structured water from the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People who have had terrible edema keeping their legs or lower body in a bag very efficiently get rid of the edema. Much of the water is going to leave through your kidneys and your lungs, but also some of it is leaving through your warm skin.

**Caller (New York):** Are there downsides?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No problem, except you might get skin fungus if you stay too humid too long. It might favor the growth of microorganisms on your skin in a matter of hours.

**Caller (New York):** My second question relates to the thyroid. You discussed how the adrenal gland can rejuvenate itself. Why wouldn't the same apply to the thyroid gland? Why do older people need to take thyroid medicine forever?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The reason people benefit from taking a thyroid supplement isn't that their gland is weak; it's that their whole body is working to interfere with the function. There can be enough thyroxine circulating in the body of a hypothyroid person for a dozen people, but if your body is not activating it properly—not able to mobilize the mitochondrial respiration—then that thyroxine is counterproductive. In some cases, it interferes with the formation of effective T3.

**Caller (New York):** If someone didn't want to take medicine, what are the most important things to do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you have eliminated most of the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) in your tissues, then your tissues are extremely sensitive to thyroid hormone. So your gland doesn't have to work very hard to keep you in a high metabolic condition.

**Caller (New York):** So the point is the consumption of PUFA interferes with the transport and absorption in the cell, not the gland production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. By the time a person is 45, the body is really soaked in polyunsaturated fats. They talk about the Omega-3 fatty acids as being predominant in the brain, but that's only an old brain. A healthy young 5-year-old brain is highly saturated in comparison to a middle-aged brain.

**Caller (New York):** Mary Enig wrote that you need some Omega-3s in a one-to-one ratio with sixes. Is the goal to get to zero?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at a newborn brain, people are now saying that all newborns are deficient in PUFA. But the reason little kids can learn so spectacularly quickly is that their brains aren't overloaded with PUFA. The metabolic rate is extremely high in the absence of PUFA. That was one of the things that Burr discovered in 1932: his animals that were made deficient in the so-called "essential fatty acids" were consuming oxygen almost twice as fast as the normal rats. People are the same. We have a terrifically high metabolic rate when we're two or three years old, and it is gradually suppressed as we accumulate fish oil and vegetable oil.

**Caller (New York):** Dr. Peat, you've recommended fully hydrogenated oils to improve metabolic rate. Do you think the catalysts they use to hydrogenate the oils, like nickel, are a serious problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's definitely worrisome, and I think we should look for a much better way to get saturated fats. But the experiments, like the Russians who used fully hydrogenated peanut oil and found that old mitochondria were restored to youthful functions just with that highly saturated peanut oil... the results are so good that despite the possible danger of traces of the catalyst, it seems beneficial.

**Caller (New York):** Do you think the more saturated the fat is, the more antiviral and antibacterial it could be?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think it is the saturated fatty acids that are most antibacterial and probably help with viral resistance.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to look at some specific components in plants. The flavonoids from green tea—epicatechin and epicatechin gallate—are said to reduce glutamate excitotoxicity. You've always talked about excitotoxicity as being a negative, wasteful state of a cell.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it puts you in the reductive stress condition.

**Andrew Murray:** So if these flavonoid compounds reduce this excitotoxicity, that's good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Although they're called antioxidants—like Vitamin C is called an antioxidant—when they are in the cell, they function as pro-oxidants. They shift the cell into the healthy oxidized condition.

**Andrew Murray:** What about naringenin, found in grapefruit peel and orange juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Marmalade is a great drug.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you see naringenin having an antiviral mechanism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's exactly the same mechanism that aspirin has for its antiviral function: a pro-oxidative, cell-restorative function.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask about pomegranate extract from the rind. Experiments showed that when mixed with zinc, there was a marked increase in antiviral activity against acyclovir-resistant herpes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect that zinc is a cofactor for Vitamin A. Both of them are very important for healthy protein synthesis. When I was about 50, I had aging eyebrows starting to get stiff. I found that a zinc supplement or a Vitamin A supplement—either one—would reverse the age properties of those eyebrows. I think that's because they accelerate normal differentiated protein synthesis and oppose the degraded estrogen excitation reductive process.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for your time. Next month we'll carry on with other antiviral medicinal plants.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat's website can be found at www.raypeat.com. He has a fully referenced library of articles. Our business is Western Botanical Medicine, found at www.westernbotanicalmedicine.com. Thanks for joining us. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Particles
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. We are going to discuss antiviral herbs, nanoparticles and their negative health effects, and articles surrounding polyunsaturated fats and cancer incidence. The tide is slowly turning, and as Dr. Peat has been famously quoted in the past, "A lie gets around the world quicker than truth can tie up her shoelaces." We are very welcome to have Dr. Peat join us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hello.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to start with a brief introduction to the things we're going to cover, following up on the last couple of months regarding the antiviral activity of selected medicinal plants. If you look at PubMed, you can find clinical trials on plants for specific viruses. While we know information sources may not always be fully accurate, PubMed and ResearchGate are some of the few avenues we have to look for results. I know I've interviewed you, Dr. Peat, and you have pointed out blatant errors in research before. Could you introduce yourself and outline your academic background for those who haven't heard of you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Between 1968 and 1972, I studied biology, emphasizing physiology—especially reproductive physiology—at the University of Oregon. I didn't start the academic study of biology until I had about 20 years of investigating controversies in biology. I had decided that academic biology, especially in the US, was too dogmatic and commercial to really be scientific. I finally decided to go through the academic process to find out some of its weaknesses. After getting the PhD, I continued my independent studying, doing nutrition and hormone counseling, and studying how the brain, reproductive, and immune systems interact with the environment, especially nutrition.

**Andrew Murray:** You've been a big proponent of getting people to stop using polyunsaturated fats (PUFA), quoting Burr and others from the 1930s and 40s. You've mentioned that the paint industry was a big user of these vegetable oils. When the petroleum industry began manufacturing synthetic additives and paints, it put seed oil producers at risk, so they decided to put these oils into the food chain. Growing up in the 70s, margarine and sunflower oil were advertised as heart-healthy, while natural products like saturated animal fats were demonized.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A large study in veterans on the "heart-healthy" diet with margarine found that it not only caused more cancer but also increased deaths from heart disease. That was a turning point against the original "essential fatty acids" and set the background for fish oil to come on the market.

**Andrew Murray:** I came across an article titled "Are Diets high in Omega 6 Polyunsaturated fatty acids unhealthy?" from the Hadassah Medical School in Jerusalem. It stated that Israel has one of the highest dietary PUFA-to-saturated fat ratios in the world, consuming 8% more Omega-6 than the USA. Despite this, there is a high prevalence of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, obesity, and increased cancer incidence. The study suggests high linoleic acid consumption might aggravate hyperinsulinemia and act as a substrate for lipid peroxidation. What do you think of that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good.

**Andrew Murray:** It is difficult to find evidence for the opposite view because the industry pushes the pro-polyunsaturated side so strongly.

**Andrew Murray:** You've talked about naringenin before as an antioxidant. Do you have an explanation for naringenin's potential antiviral effects, specifically regarding herpes simplex?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it works the same way aspirin, progesterone, and all the cell stabilizers work. It increases the oxidative balance of the cell, simply reinforcing the effect of the oxidative respiratory metabolism. That makes the cell able to resist improper excitation and stabilizes it against random irritation. Just about anything that is unphysiological will destabilize the cell in the same direction. These things protect against viruses, radiation, vibration, oxygen deprivation, sugar deprivation, too much polyunsaturated fat, too much phosphate, or too little calcium. Anything that shifts the balance towards meaningless excitation or reducing proper energy production.

**Andrew Murray:** So this is a cell-stabilizing component that has an antiviral effect because it saves energy rather than allowing the cell to become excitedly toxic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When the virus wants to replicate, it excites the cell and gets the cell churning its mechanism. That damages the organism and produces more viruses.

**Andrew Murray:** I also wanted to mention pomegranate. I found an article mentioning the effect of zinc in conjunction with pomegranate rind extract being eight times greater in its viricidal activity than pomegranate extract alone. Do you have anything to say on zinc?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the protein-synthesizing function of zinc is like vitamin A for accelerating healing.

**Andrew Murray:** I read an article from a university in Romania regarding birch bark extract. Betulin and betulinic acid showed good results in treating melanomas, colon, and cervical cancer. The study suggested the extract interfered with angiogenesis (the creation of new blood vessels).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Structurally, betulinic acid is analogous to progesterone. Sarsaparilla has a similar steroid.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding skin cancers, I’ve used a product from Australia called Curiderm, based on the plant *Solanum sodomaeum* (related to eggplant), which contains solasodine glycosides. It targets cancer cells while leaving normal cells intact. I also used 7% iodine on some sun-damaged lesions on my arm, and they disappeared after about 60 days. Dr. Peat, regarding melanoma, do you view it outside of the regular "sunburn causing genetic changes" approach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For melanoma, sun really isn't the main factor. Most melanomas occur in areas that aren't much exposed to the sun, like the back, inside of the thighs, or even the bottom of the feet. It's a very hormone-sensitive thing. Estrogen has been suspected for a long time of being involved. I've seen dozens of apparent melanomas that disappeared. A couple of people who were diagnosed with terminal, metastatic melanoma saw it regress when they changed their diet and used coffee, aspirin, various nutritional things, vitamin D, and a lot of orange juice and milk.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this an anti-estrogenic approach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. So far, all of the melanoma people I've talked to have had a really quick response from changing their diet.

**Andrew Murray:** Have you seen people treated effectively without medical intervention for basal or squamous cell carcinomas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The first one I saw was a man about 80 years old, 45 years ago. He put progesterone on his diagnosed lip cancer, and in a week or so, it was gone.

**Andrew Murray:** Nanotechnology is a rapidly progressing science found in many products, from skin creams to foods. What is your opinion on nanotechnology and where it is heading?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have recognized that particles like soot spontaneously make these highly structured, ultra-microscopic particles. About 35 years ago, the chemical industry sent me samples of their products. One was fumed silica, which floated out like smoke when I opened it. It is now added to toothpaste and foods to make things like salad dressing seem creamy. It worried me that the stuff floats right into the air and is dangerous to be around.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned soot, which reminds me of the chimney sweeps in the late 1800s getting testicular cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and soot contains estrogenic as well as carcinogenic chemicals. But the particles themselves, because of their shape and size, cause issues. The reason asbestos is carcinogenic is its fine, pointed crystalline structure. If a particle is as small as the point of an asbestos crystal, the body interprets it similarly to a virus. It starts an inflammatory process when the particle has a certain fineness or length-to-diameter ratio. A sharp or very small particle activates the inflammatory process, exciting the cell. If you have biological energy, you can tamp down that excitation. But when it becomes too frequent or intense, or your energy level decreases, the balance shifts towards inflammation, degeneration, and the production of fibrous tissues rather than functional tissues.

**Andrew Murray:** I found an article from the National University of Singapore describing "nanomaterial induced endothelial leakiness" (NanoEL). It said nanoparticles created gaps in the endothelium large enough for cancer cells to escape the circulatory system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Most places talk about gaps between cells, but that leakiness is really a basic thing that excess excitation or energy deficiency causes in all cells. The substance of the cell leaks out. In a hypothyroid person, if you exercise a muscle too much, it leaks enzymes right through the surface of the cell. Just giving the cell glucose to get its energy up can stop that leakiness. Interestingly, someone looked at the fluid outside the cells in a tumor and found there was a thousand times more ATP in the fluid of a tumor than in normal tissues. The cells are leaky and losing their necessary materials so fast that they are constantly in this over-stimulated condition.

**Caller:** I'm from Redway. Would you please go over the information about the Australian herbal topical cream for keratosis once again?

**Andrew Murray:** The product is called Curiderm—C-U-R-A-D-E-R-M. It is trademarked and patented. You can find it online; there are several outlets.

**Caller:** Thank you very much.

**Caller:** I'm in Eureka. I have questions about Parkinson's and a good direction to take with that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping testosterone and related steroids up is important. The neurosteroids are very protective. Testosterone has been identified as one thing that goes down in relation to Parkinson's. Pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone are all nerve-protective and restorative. Vitamin D is another steroid that is extremely protective to nerve cells.

**Caller:** How much Vitamin D should I take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You should also reduce phosphate in the diet along with pro-inflammatory fatty acids. Eat more carbohydrate and sugar, and any good source of calcium and magnesium like milk, cheese, and well-cooked green vegetables. Eat less beans, nuts, and meat because of their very high phosphate content.

**Andrew Murray:** To summarize: Testosterone is first and foremost. For males, lightweight bearing exercise is the best way to improve general testosterone. Avoid estrogenic substances like polyunsaturates (nuts, beans, seeds) and plastics. Use thyroid hormone if you are low thyroid, and aspirin is a good anti-inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And fibrous foods, because they help to reduce the reabsorption of estrogen in the intestine. Parkinson's almost always involves sluggish intestinal movement or constipation.

**Caller:** I'm dealing with peripheral neuropathy in my feet caused by chemotherapy. It is incredibly painful. Could you suggest anything to mitigate the inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For nerve regeneration, peripheral as well as central, many animal studies show that vitamin D and progesterone work together to restore nerves. It is a good idea to have a blood test for both. Keep vitamin D in the middle of the normal range (50 or 60 nanograms per milliliter). Progesterone should be in the luteal range; even for a postmenopausal woman, it is good to supplement if it isn't naturally detectable.

**Andrew Murray:** This is because it directly opposes estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. After menopause, estrogen begins forming inside cells all through the body—fat cells, skin cells, breast, and uterine cells. It can be formed from adrenal precursors. Anti-inflammatory things like aspirin, progesterone, thyroid, vitamin D, and calcium all help minimize that inflammatory process of spontaneously forming estrogen in the tissues.

**Caller:** I've been taking Synthroid since 9th grade. My thyroid organ doesn't function.

**Andrew Murray:** I've talked to many people who get no benefit from Synthroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The active thyroid hormone, T3, is itself directly anti-inflammatory. Synthroid does have the good function of suppressing TSH, so if you take enough to keep TSH close to zero, that has an anti-inflammatory effect. But the main anti-inflammatory action of thyroid is through T3.

**Caller:** I think my body has a problem with uptake.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoiding polyunsaturated fat is very important because it blocks the activation of thyroid into T3.

**Caller:** I always thought butter was probably better. I'm also interested in the iodine you mentioned.

**Andrew Murray:** I used 7% liquid iodine topically on lesions. One cleared up in about 35 days, the other took about 65 days.

**Caller:** Thank you very much. This has been so informative.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, you've mentioned an anti-inflammatory lifestyle involving aspirin, progesterone, thyroid, vitamin D, and calcium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Other things people often neglect are getting sunlight as much as possible and doing things that are fun. You've heard of the "enriched environment" rat experiments; it made their brains not only more intelligent but also bigger. That kind of entertaining environment causes rats to produce more progesterone and have lower estrogen. Just doing things that are fun and interesting keeps your hormones in the right direction.

**Andrew Murray:** That backs up animal studies showing that rats given no escape fail quickly, while those in enriched environments thrive. People who feel entrapped need to get outside of themselves, even if it just means stepping outside and looking at the sky.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Speaking of breathing, I should mention that one of the main effects of taking thyroid or having good thyroid function is producing carbon dioxide. So you don't want to over-breathe.

**Andrew Murray:** Good point. Thank you for your questions. Dr. Peat's website is RayPeat.com, where he has many fully referenced articles. We can be reached at 1-888-WBM-HERB or westernbotanicalmedicine.com.

**Andrew Murray:** I ran tests on five different types of fish caught locally on the West Coast. I was staggered at what came back. Tuna, salmon, cod, and bottom fish were loaded with mercury, cadmium, and arsenic—way higher than any wild game like elk or deer. It put me off eating fish.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That information is part of why I'm an advocate of milk. **Andrew Murray:** We had a caller asking about the ingredient in Roundup, glyphosate. I saw that there had been massive punitive damages awarded recently for that product regarding cancer.

Just because a substance binds to the receptor doesn't mean it activates estrogen-like processes. It can inactivate the system depending on what it does to that protein. **Caller:** We have not vaccinated our 6-year-old. Being in California, it looks like we might have to. Is there anything herbal or immune-boosting we can do if we decide to vaccinate?

**Andrew Murray:** To the caller, nutrition is very important. Avoid polyunsaturates and gluten. Support your thyroid. The vitality of our civilization has decreased due to environmental toxins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Flax is much better in some ways, but it is only slightly more stable than fish oil. Fish oil is very quickly degraded. Flax is a little more persistent and can be more toxic in the long run.

**Andrew Murray:** The other question was whether you recommend bentonite clay for flushing toxins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The clay is slightly soluble in stomach acid and releases at least a little aluminum and other toxins. The particles are susceptible to "persorption." If your intestine is irritated, the contraction can force these particles right into the bloodstream. The particle size can be as much as 10 times the diameter of a red blood cell. **Caller:** There is new research about highly sensitive personalities and excess cortisol. What do you think about people who live with gushers of cortisol day-to-day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are lots of things you can do, starting with oxidative metabolism and preserving thyroid function. Cortisol stops inflammation, but it activates degenerative breakdown processes when it isn't backed up by large amounts of these three anti-inflammatory, stabilizing steroids. **Andrew Murray:** What about a strategy to improve the liver's function to metabolize waste? Is that relevant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. All tissues apparently have taste receptors, especially for bitter. Bitters act on these receptors to have a calming, stabilizing effect all through the body. The whole energy and protein synthesizing system is involved in detoxifying. The liver uses glucose or fructose, turning it into glucuronic acid, which is attached to toxins for excretion. If you are well-nourished—adequate B vitamins, carbohydrate, and protein—your liver can catch toxic substances, especially hydrophobic materials, and hold them while enzymes degrade them or attach glucuronic acid or sulfate to make them water-soluble for excretion.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned bitters reduce inflammation. How do you link those two?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a protein—the same we have in our tongues—in stomach, liver, and lung tissue that can detect the bitter substance. In doing so, it activates an anti-inflammatory process.

**Caller:** What is your view on supplemental digestive enzymes like lipase and protease to help break down food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The traditional thing was dehydrated animal pancreas tissue. Those are so similar to our own enzymes that they really do work, though you have to be cautious of infection because they are simply dehydrated. I'm skeptical about enzymes derived from fungus. You can't absolutely purify them, so they drag along fungal antigens. If you are sensitive to the fungus, you might have an allergic reaction.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the political will to make the world a cleaner place—what do you think?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I can mention a book that is very important on that issue called *The Politics of Cancer* by Samuel Epstein (1978). The agencies you think should be protecting the public—the American Cancer Society, National Cancer Institute, and universities—are funded so generously by the polluting industries that they are working against the public.

**Andrew Murray:** That is depressing, but *The Politics of Cancer* is worth looking at. Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat.
