title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Postpartum Depression
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to Ask Your Herb Doctor. This month’s topic covers postpartum depression, steroid hormones, and new drugs with dangerous consequences. As always, Dr. Raymond Peat is here to bring his science-based wisdom to these subjects. Dr. Peat, thanks for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Your latest newsletter on postpartum depression, brain aging, and reductionism continues to discuss the shortsightedness of science and its link to aging and diseases like obesity, Alzheimer's, and diabetes. For those who haven't heard the show before, could you outline your academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After teaching a variety of subjects, including linguistics and literature, I decided to go to graduate school in biology. I got my PhD in 1972 and have been continuing to study mostly physiology, stress, and aging since then.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to talk about a product that was just given FDA approval called Zulresso, also known as brexanolone or allopregnanolone. As we’ve mentioned in the past, this is a naturally occurring metabolite of naturally produced progesterone. However, it has been approved as an injection given over a 60-hour infusion in a hospital to treat postpartum depression, costing $34,000. Why not simply use a $30 bottle of progesterone or pregnenolone, both of which quickly convert in the body to allopregnanolone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it was a natural therapy, it would be cheap and not patented, and no one would make several billion dollars a year from selling it. For the last 10 or 15 years, the FDA has acted as though it is in the business of creating monopolies. They did it with the sedative drug Oxybate several years ago; it went from costing a few dollars for a bottle to thousands of dollars for a course of treatment.

**Andrew Murray:** Because it’s been patented and the company has been allowed to use this as their standard.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. After that, they declared that quinine was a "new drug" and assigned a new drug approval to one company. Since the FDA depends on fees to approve drugs, a large part of their existence sees the money coming in from the drug companies as sustaining their existence. If a doctor wants to use quinine bark or a natural nutritional substance for therapy, and it happens to compete with one of these new drug assignments, the doctor is effectively attempting to break a monopoly. In some situations, doctors are actually losing their licenses for using traditional medical reasoning and avoiding so-called "evidence-based medicine."

**Andrew Murray:** "Evidence-based medicine" has become a very popular phrase recently.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What they mean by "evidence" is a study that costs maybe $150 million. Not just any researcher has that money to test a nutrient or hormone. So, what constitutes good evidence in this monopoly paradigm is a study that no one but the giant corporations can afford. Consequently, the only drugs that have legal approval by the FDA are monopoly drugs. State licensing boards are putting pressure on doctors to conform and follow guidelines. It is getting ridiculous; they are telling doctors not to consider any of the traditional signs of hypothyroidism, but to go only by the TSH—ignoring 200 years of recognized metabolic and functional signs.

**Andrew Murray:** It’s a kind of communism, where there is only one way.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, it's strictly monopoly capitalism.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Maybe totalitarianism.

**Andrew Murray:** Right, very dictatorial. You’ve mentioned that doctors can no longer use reasoning. This evidence-based medicine paradigm seems to prohibit and punish reasoning, which is very dangerous.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the newsletter, I mentioned the movement to abolish the so-called basic science part of medical education—the first two years where they actually study science. One proponent has written articles pointing out that there have been over 350 reversals of traditional medicine by these big corporate studies. He seems like a progressive person wanting truth in science, but he says these big studies are the evidence we must take into account. He argues we only need guidelines on how to use these approved treatments. If we have guidelines for all diseases, everyone will treat the disease in the same way, becoming blind to individual variations and unique histories. It's trying to reduce and abstract medicine to the point that no brain is necessary, only following guidelines.

**Andrew Murray:** If A plus B equals C, go to D.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If that's the case, they don't need the first two years of medical school. But even the sciences themselves—physiology, neurology, endocrinology—have been powerfully invaded by the drug companies over the last hundred years. Their understanding has been shaped by the reductionist ideal that one sickness can be defined for everyone and treated with a specific drug.

**Andrew Murray:** Returning to allopregnanolone, the new patented drug. Why couldn't you just use pregnenolone or progesterone as a precursor?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Someone tested that and found that just a tiny dose of oral progesterone—20 milligrams—tripled the amount of allopregnanolone in the body.

**Andrew Murray:** So there is no reason not to use oral progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another point is that allopregnanolone is essentially the end of a line of metabolites starting with cholesterol. Those are regulated at many steps before they come into existence. When you give the end product without looking at the condition of all the preceding steps, that is a great opportunity for throwing the whole system out of balance. For example, estrogen and aldosterone are other end products of steroid metabolism, and excess of those is very dangerous. I don't know if that will turn out to be true for using simple allopregnanolone without its precursors, but it is something they haven't examined.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw a 2006 study from Sweden noting that allopregnanolone was biphasic—at certain doses it was excitatory, and at others, it was calming. This reminds me of valerian, which acts on GABA receptors; usually, it calms people, but a small subset gets stimulated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the sort of thing you risk when using an end-of-line metabolite. Normally, it can never get above a certain level because it has to go through stages where each precursor produces a smaller amount of product. If you artificially give an amount that the body could never experience on its own, you might anesthetize some of the regulatory inhibitory nerves and release things that are less sensitive to inhibition. You are risking something the organism has never experienced before.

**Andrew Murray:** What is your understanding of the cause of postpartum depression, and how can it be avoided?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It happens in women with a history of stress, difficult pregnancy, or difficult birth. Even if the birth was routine, there may have been a history of stress earlier in life. The burden of pregnancy and birth, building the baby's body and brain, requires resources. If you don't have enough calcium in your diet, you increase parathyroid hormone and take calcium from your bones to build the baby's bones. The baby gets priority over some nutrients. Even in an apparently healthy woman, pregnancy increases the risk of nutritional deficiency. Women who suffer postpartum depression typically have a history of preceding stress.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there a relation to menstrual disorders?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. I think PMS is closely related to postpartum issues.

**Andrew Murray:** If we posit that exposure to high levels of estrogen is responsible for the shrinkage in gray matter—"baby brain"—why isn't progesterone supplementation recommended to speed up recovery? What would be a reasonable amount?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In healthy women, progesterone levels in the cerebrospinal fluid and plasma increase considerably during the time the brain is being repaired after birth. However, cholesterol is the precursor for making progesterone. Women with postpartum depression typically have reduced levels of cholesterol, so they cannot make enough progesterone. Vitamin A and thyroid are other limiting factors. A normal cycling woman produces about 30 milligrams of progesterone daily in the luteal phase. I think that would be a reasonable therapeutic amount postpartum. However, if she is still under stress and not eliminating estrogen well, it might take larger amounts.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you suggest increasing cholesterol levels to enable hormone manufacture?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Having enough carbohydrate and sugar in the diet is very important.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think there is a subset of women who, despite the massive rise of progesterone during pregnancy, are still estrogen dominant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure, especially if they had a history of PMS or biological stress. Most often it's associated with slightly low thyroid function. About 50 years ago, I saw a chart based on a large number of pregnancies showing a steady increase of progesterone to a level 50 times higher than estrogen. If your background estrogen stays high because of low thyroid, low B vitamins, or low protein, it is impossible to produce enough progesterone to offset that falsely high amount of estrogen. No amount of progesterone increase will make that pregnancy healthy; it requires getting the estrogen under control with nutrition and thyroid function.

**Caller (New York):** I’ve read that as long as you aren't running a marathon—say, doing sprints for 20 minutes—it actually increases CO2. Do you agree?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends entirely on your physiology, especially your thyroid function. A person with borderline hypothyroidism will start producing lactic acid with the slightest exertion, which displaces carbon dioxide. If you are in great condition, you can keep your carbon dioxide level up and not produce lactic acid with a moderate amount of exercise.

**Caller (New York):** So for a healthy person, it could be positive, but for an unhealthy person, it adds to their problems?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When lactic acid goes up because you aren't using oxygen properly, you release histamine, which produces soreness and potentially asthma. Histamine causes blood pressure to drop. With greater exercise, you release serotonin from mast cells, which could cause a blood pressure spike—that is much worse than the histamine effect.

**Caller (New York):** If people over 50 are predominantly hypothyroid, what should they do? I’ve heard taking Vitamin E or baking soda before exercise is protective.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, a lot of athletes are starting to use baking soda before stressful exertion to provide extra sodium, bicarbonate, and CO2.

**Caller (New York):** What about Cat's Claw (*Uncaria tomentosa*)? It supposedly repairs DNA.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never studied that.

**Caller (New York):** Regarding Vitamin K—is it necessary to take MK-4 specifically, or are other forms okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you eat animal liver, you get the whole variety. The liver can convert K1 or K2 to the higher chains. I think K1 or K2 is adequate because our liver can make the others.

**Caller (New York):** If someone has low thyroid and active adrenals (high cortisol), is it conceivable they might create crises in their life to maintain that cortisol cycle?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the early 60s, that was a common idea among psychologists. I've known people who seem to typify that condition—they know how to create excitement and turmoil. When they get their thyroid function up, people who had been creating turmoil just sit around, enjoy life, and smile.

**Andrew Murray:** Apart from progesterone, what can be done for gestational diabetes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It isn't just a matter of thyroid and adrenals; all hormones are involved in the energy process. Sodium and calcium are important in pregnancy not just for blood volume and bones, but for avoiding adrenal stress hormone excess. People with a history of stress have an increased requirement for sodium, calcium, and Vitamin D.

**Andrew Murray:** A listener asked about a website claiming chronic Vitamin A toxicity is the cause of autoimmune diseases. What is your view?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin A is used to make all steroid hormones from cholesterol. Thyroid and Vitamin A travel together on a protein in the blood and are taken up by cells together. You don't produce steroid hormones without Vitamin A. It is used in protein synthesis; hair and skin will fail if you are deficient. Mucous membranes stop producing mucus without it. I looked through the book claiming toxicity and couldn't find any facts.

**Andrew Murray:** What about the famous polar bear liver toxicity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That has been cited in textbooks for 80 years as proof Vitamin A is toxic. But polar bears sometimes eat fish poisoned by algae, and their livers store that toxin. The explorers likely got algae toxin via the bear liver. When drug companies were releasing Retin-A, there were sudden news releases about Vitamin A causing blindness. I tried to verify one report at the University of Oregon and couldn't get any confirmation. I think they were made up to create a desire for synthetic Vitamin A.

**Caller (Texas):** Athletes are using pickle juice for cramps and hangovers. Do you know what’s in it that helps?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I imagine it would contain lactic acid (if traditionally made) and salt. Anything salty in the morning can be very settling. It helps regulate blood sugar and lower stress hormones.

**Andrew Murray:** I had an email question about Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). What is your approach to this autoimmune disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Like other autoimmune diseases, it is much more common in women. Animal models can be created with estrogen excess. Estrogen activates inflammatory processes. Women who believed they needed kidney transplants found they had no more symptoms when they took progesterone and thyroid. It can definitely be seen as an estrogen excess symptom.

**Caller (Jersey):** A professor from MIT suggests glyphosate might displace glycine in the body because the molecules are similar. What do you think?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is very toxic at such extremely small amounts that interfering with glycine wouldn't do much at that level. The mechanism is more likely related to DNA regulation interference.

**Caller (Jersey):** Regarding green vegetables—I know you say to boil them to reduce PUFA (polyunsaturated fatty acids). Is steaming the same?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you boil them, you can skim off any fat that rises to the surface. It is an advantage to be able to pour off the fat.

**Caller (Jersey):** But you lose minerals in the water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, a lot of the important magnesium and calcium goes into the water.

**Caller (Jersey):** So, because the PUFA remains in the leaf or you lose minerals in the water, that’s one of the reasons you don't recommend eating green vegetables?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. A lot of the PUFA remains tied to the proteins of the leaf. When you eat it, your bile salts will cause you to absorb most of that PUFA.

**Andrew Murray:** A new drug called Vyleesi, based on melanocortin, was approved for female libido. Do you know anything about it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Melanocortin is the precursor protein for making beta-lipoprotein, endorphins, and ACTH—things that come up during the stress reaction. If you take one of these end products out of context, you have unpredictable effects. Suppression of appetite is associated with those receptors. If a woman lacks desire, there are likely serious metabolic problems. DHEA is a great activator of libido, but it goes down under stress when cortisol rises. You should concentrate on lowering stress and using pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, or thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** And DHEA should be used with adequate thyroid to prevent conversion to estrogen, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for your time, Dr. Peat. For listeners, Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Herbalist Sophie Lamb
transcriptText:
**Host:** Andrew Murray
**Co-Host:** Sarah Johanneson Murray
**Guests:** Dr. Raymond Peat and Sophie Lamb

---

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome once again to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. We broadcast every third Friday of the month on KMUD Garberville. We discuss a wide range of alternative medicines and health topics. I'm very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat join us once more. Dr. Peat, would you please give our listeners a rundown of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After studying and teaching the humanities and linguistics—various things except biology—before 1968, I went to graduate school in biology to get a Ph.D. in 1972. I specialized in the aging physiology of reproduction, but in general studied physiology and biochemistry. Since then, I have been doing short courses and counseling.

**Andrew Murray:** This month, I'm very pleased to welcome Sophie Lamb, daughter of distinguished medical herbalist Brian Lamb. Welcome to the show, Sophie.

**Sophie Lamb:** Thank you so much. I'm delighted to be here.

**Andrew Murray:** I've always called you a second-generation herbalist, but actually, your father's background goes back further.

**Sophie Lamb:** My father's background involves about four generations of doctors and surgeons going back about 200 years. Although they were surgeons and doctors, a big part of the medicines they used at the time was herbal medicine, so they had their apothecaries alongside their surgeries.

**Andrew Murray:** I know Brian is 82 now. He qualified in 1978 from the School of Herbal Medicine and has been in full-time practice since. He also manufactures a wide range of fluid extracts and syrups.

**Sophie Lamb:** He is amazing. He works full-time, gets up with the birds, and works all day long. I think it's driven by the passion he has for his job and the love for the herbs. He is still discovering and exploring because it's something you could study for a lifetime and still not extinguish all there is to know.

**Andrew Murray:** Like Dr. Peat, your father is very scientifically grounded in what he discusses. He is very much into the science in herbal medicine, isn't he?

**Sophie Lamb:** He spends his life researching. When he's not physically preparing herbs or seeing patients, he's researching.

**Andrew Murray:** He also spent time in America working for a Utah company, correct?

**Sophie Lamb:** Yes, he used to tour America giving lectures on herbal applications for cosmetics. He worked for a few network marketing companies designing herbal products. That stretched over about 10 years.

**Andrew Murray:** Sophie, winter coughs and colds are common issues. Let's get an idea of what it was like growing up in a household on the northernmost tip of Scotland with an herbalist father.

**Sophie Lamb:** I have three sisters. When you have four young children, they typically develop coughs and chest infections. We lived at the very top of the map of the UK, looking over the Orkney Islands. We had an Aga stove in the kitchen, and my childhood memories are full of herbs drying on top and syrups being made at the side.

We all had whooping cough as children. What dad did for us was slice up garlic, smear the soles of our feet with Vaseline, apply thin slices of garlic, wrap it in cling film, and apply a sock. Within a few minutes, the volatile oils go through the bloodstream and you're breathing out garlic. That shortened the duration and severity of our whooping cough.

We also used to pick *Tussilago* (Coltsfoot). It makes the most incredible syrup because the flowers smell of honey. We would do a layer of flowers, a layer of sugar, and let them macerate by the side of the hot Aga.

One of the things my dad is most well known for is his thyme syrup. Thyme fits the need of the lungs like a glove. It's an antitussive (reduces the cough reflex), anti-edema on the lungs (reduces swelling), expectorant (helps spit out mucus), and antiseptic. He makes a syrup using Deeside water and molasses.

**Andrew Murray:** That's interesting. Your father uses a specific water.

**Sophie Lamb:** All of his extracts are made using Deeside water. It comes from the Pannanich Wells around Aberdeenshire. My dad worked as a consultant for this water company because he is also an engineer. The Royal Family used to travel to this area of Scotland to drink the healing water.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to give a little background on the law and herbal medicine. In 1154, Henry II institutionalized Common Law, based on the premise that everything is legal unless deemed illegal. Herbal medicine has always been protected under Common Law. In 1542, Henry VIII implemented the Herbalist Charter, protecting the right to practice. Later, Nicholas Culpeper translated medical texts from Latin to English so the general public could use them.

However, European law is based on Napoleonic law—the premise that everything is illegal unless deemed legal. The National Institute of Medical Herbalists is working tirelessly to keep the practice safe from restrictive legislation coming from the European Union.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, regarding autism: what do you see as a safe approach to helping the autistic child, and what do you see as a cause?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think almost any environmental harm to the parents, especially the mother during pregnancy, increases the rate of autism. Environmental estrogens, things that cause hypothyroidism, and obesity are known causes.

A major source of adversity during pregnancy is medical radiation or medicalization in general. This includes too many X-ray exams, bad thyroid or endocrine therapy, and the use of toxic drugs. In Texas, a study showed Latino kids had a much lower rate of autism than the medicalized white residents. Touching has also been identified as essential for the nervous system to develop properly. Enriching the environment, removing toxins, and improving the thyroid and progesterone levels can remedy the autistic condition to some extent.

**Andrew Murray:** Sophie, do you have any anecdotal evidence regarding this?

**Sophie Lamb:** I have friends whose children have been severely autistic. They focused on diet and gut health. One friend's son would go into "stimming"—repetitive physical movements. A pediatrician prescribed a strong antifungal because it was suspected he had a fungal overgrowth producing alcohol in his system. The antifungals hugely modified his behavior.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what do you think about gut organisms metabolizing carbohydrates to produce ethanol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Intestinal flora produce lots of toxins. Yeast, in particular, produces both alcohol and estrogen. The estrogen is, I think, more toxic than the alcohol.

**Andrew Murray:** Sophie, sleep disturbance is a common presentation. How do you treat this?

**Sophie Lamb:** I was a severe insomniac for eight years. I learned from Dr. Peat that if you can get your stress hormones down, you will sleep. I was a chronic under-eater. A healthy individual should be able to get an eight-hour sleep because our glycogen stores feed the active brain through the night.

Sleep is an active process; the brain does a huge amount of repair. If we haven't laid down enough glycogen during the day, we get a rise in stress hormones (cortisol and adrenaline) to catabolize fat and muscle for energy. A side effect of stress hormones is mental alertness, which you don't want at night. Insomnia is actually a daytime disorder presenting itself at night.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, can you speak to the liver's ability to store glycogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid is essential for storing glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. When you run out of glycogen, you mobilize free fatty acids. The free fatty acid condition creates a state of diabetes in the brain, turning off brain metabolism by essentially poisoning the mitochondria and blocking the ability to use glucose.

**Sophie Lamb:** In the UK and the US, we are told to avoid sugar and salt. Some mothers even avoid fructose for children. This creates a perfect storm for insomnia. If I have a patient with insomnia, the first place I look is diet, and the second is herbs.

**Andrew Murray:** Sophie, tell us about your TED Talk.

**Sophie Lamb:** I gave a TED Talk with my sister Naomi titled *Why We Are Dependent on Plants for Medicine*. I felt it was important to reconnect the dots for people who think herbs are archaic. The Essential Medicines List of the World Health Organization has a significant proportion of drugs based on herbs.

Examples include morphine, lidocaine from coca leaves, aspirin, metformin from *Galega* (Goat's Rue), and Taxol from the Yew tree. 90% of our chemotherapeutic drugs have foundations in plants. It's important to realize that when you look out to the fields, you're walking past essential medicines.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, what do you say about the undoing of the instinctual craving for sugar and salt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those doctrines were created by the pharmaceutical industry. Around 1950, they convinced doctors that pregnant women had to use diuretics and restrict salt to prevent weight gain, which destroyed many pregnancies. The sugar ban appeared around the same time to sell polyunsaturated vegetable oils (PUFA). The food industry created the cholesterol myth to sell their oils and explain away heart disease, which is really the result of hypothyroidism.

**Andrew Murray:** Sophie, are fish oils still advertised as healthful in Europe?

**Sophie Lamb:** Definitely still very buoyant. But interestingly, last year a newspaper published a study linking fish oils with liver disease and scarring.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, any thoughts on liver scarring and fish oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of stresses contribute, but definitely not good foods like saturated fats and sugar.

**Caller (Jeff):** I have questions about fulvic and humic acids. Are the enzymes and natural minerals associated with those beneficial?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they're mildly harmful because they can release toxic things. Any minerals would be beneficial, but the substances themselves are not safe.

**Caller (Jeff):** I found them helpful for a skin rash. My other question is about thyroid. If someone improves their diet and lowers PUFA, why isn't it possible to eliminate thyroid supplements eventually?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen people stop or reduce their supplement. For some, it happens in a week. Others take three or four years. A person saturated with unsaturated fats has to get rid of that stored thyroid-inhibiting fat before they can get away from a supplement.

**Andrew Murray:** What about electromagnetic radiation disrupting thyroid activity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That, and environmental estrogens in tooth fillings or food packaging, block the thyroid.

**Caller (Jeff):** What does red light do physiologically compared to CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Red light restores the electronic balance of cytochrome oxidase, the crucial enzyme of oxidative metabolism. Stress lowers that activity. Red light also helps with inflammation. Radiation poisoning can be neutralized by exposure to red light within the first hour.

**Caller:** What are the benefits of drinking 16 ounces of celery juice a day?

**Sophie Lamb:** It's a craze in the UK right now. It has minerals like potassium, and people seem to lose water retention.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main problem is that quite a few people are allergic to it.

**Caller:** Dr. Peat, how much sugar do you consume a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I try to get it all from fruit, but when I don't have good fruit, I fill in with white refined sugar. I try to get more than half of my calories from sugar. Maybe 1,500 to 1,600 calories.

**Caller:** My circulating iron is fine, but my ferritin is quite low (6 micrograms per liter). My doctor suggests iron injections. Should I have them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid is required for absorbing copper, which is needed for integrating iron with the blood. You need to get your waking temperature close to 98°F. Thyroid is the main factor. You can get a high intake of iron safely if you eat liver and eggs every day with orange juice.

**Caller:** I eat liver and eggs, but my stores are still low.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your iron saturation is very low, injections might be justified, but I've seen terrible effects from them. Oysters are another good source.

**Sophie Lamb:** Traditionally, nettle tea and blackstrap molasses help strengthen the blood.

**Caller:** What can be done for someone with a high temperature and pulse but still has chronic fatigue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Check vitamin D and calcium intake. High waking temperature might be adrenaline-based. Check your pulse and temperature again at 10 or 11 a.m. If it's steady after food, it might be something other than adrenaline.

**Caller:** Have you heard of chlorine dioxide for autistic symptoms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are safer antiseptic agents. Long-term use could promote cancer. Fibrous food helps disinfect the intestine.

**Sophie Lamb:** Cat's claw is very anti-inflammatory for the gut and has some research for brain inflammation.

**Caller:** I'm seven months pregnant. There is a potential outbreak of whooping cough here. Are the garlic and thyme syrup treatments safe for infants?

**Sophie Lamb:** Thyme syrup is usually made from dried thyme. I used it on my son from six months onward. For infants, use much reduced doses.

**Caller:** Is the garlic safe?

**Sophie Lamb:** It is innocuous, but don't leave it on so long that it burns. Maybe a couple of minutes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I heard a trick to keep it from burning is to peel it without damaging the skin and put it in a sock against the infant's foot. If you break the skin of the bulb, the oil is more irritating.

**Sophie Lamb:** Yes, a whole peeled clove, not sliced.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for calling. Dr. Peat's website is . Sophie Lamb's sleep-specific site is  and her main site is . I can be reached at . I will be away next month, so we will be back the third Friday of September. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Education and Reeducation
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. For those of you who perhaps have never listened to the show, we talk about a wide range of topics related to health, alternative health, and uncovering some of the lies. That is part of this evening's program.

This month I wanted to go over subjects, some of which we have covered, but I can't emphasize enough the indoctrination that I have been through in medical education. It is very difficult to unlearn. It is far better if you are going to get educated in real medicine and science that you get your facts right the first time around. I know Dr. Peat, when he was studying, had to overcome quite a lot of that bias while he was doing his Ph.D.

I wanted to start off the show with a paragraph that I've written to introduce the subject. There is such a complex web of ignorance, bias, and deceit woven into medicine, its practice, and evaluation. From peer-pressured, competitive education through to the brutal and exhausting residencies, it is the perfect breeding ground for the lack of questioning scientific inquiry and acceptance of the status quo. It is no wonder progress has been slow and that the previously rational, objective principles which it once stood on have now given way to marketing and designer drugs for ever-increasing diagnoses. Couple this with a biological understanding that is no longer holistic, and it's a perfect storm.

Over the last 10 years of doing these interviews with Dr. Peat, time and time again, what I thought was grounded in science has been far from it. It is the reality of "buyer beware." Do your own research, question, and search. Don't just take your doctor's word for it. They are under pressure to perform within standard medical protocols, not thinking outside the box, as this is a surefire way to lose your license for malpractice.

So, how did we get to this point where it was initially "first do no harm," and now iatrogenic death or disease is commonplace? Before we take a look at some examples in which stunning misconceptions are rapidly repeated as truth, let me introduce Dr. Raymond Peat. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us again. Would you give an outline of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was a school teacher in several different subjects. I first taught college introductory physics for biology majors, along with several other courses including art theory and introduction to computers. Then I was mostly teaching English and humanities-related subjects before I went back to get a degree in biology at the University of Oregon in 1968.

I did my dissertation on reproductive physiology—specifically, age-related processes in the uterus and how aging changes the respiratory mechanism of the reproductive system. Since then, I've just been continuing to work on everything between the brain and the reproductive system related to biology.

**Andrew Murray:** Whilst you were going through your education, you probably came across research papers suggesting quite the opposite of what was being pushed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For example, my thesis professor, Soderwall, asked me how my work was going. I said it was looking like the older animals had more intense respiration in their uterus, which would be the same as increased estrogen. He said, "Oh, that's interesting, carry on." Other professors would have said, "Wait, that's contrary to the textbook. Stop and do something else." In fact, I watched professors in other departments say, "Oh, you have to find something that is going to be consistent with our project here."

**Andrew Murray:** How often was that the case where you'd come up with evidence to the contrary?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In this department, Soderwall was on the female reproductive physiology side. He accepted anything we came up with. But even on the male reproductive side, there were old fogey professors that insisted on not departing from the textbook.

**Andrew Murray:** In terms of maintaining their egos and all the hard work they did to get where they were?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the reason for that was that female reproductive physiology was low rank on the totem pole of sciences.

**Andrew Murray:** You've repeated the quote that "a lie spreads around the world faster than truth can get its shoelaces tied." When this lie is promulgated by Big Pharma, advertising, the FDA, and the government, there is little opposition.

Since Sarah and I have been working with you, I've seen definite positive changes in applying the science you talk about—using progesterone, pregnenolone, thyroid, and aspirin as energy-saving, anti-estrogenic substances. These things have flown in the face of everything I was taught.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to visit the question of serotonin and Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) again. We are told serotonin is the "happy hormone." Could you explain what we are told versus what you understand about its activity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have looked at that recently on some of the best-known medical websites, and they are still basically saying the same thing. No one has looked at the critical information in a very public spot.

When serotonin was identified chemically in the body, it was seen to constrict smooth muscles—first the intestine, then blood vessels and the uterus. Then it was discovered to exist in the brain. Up into the mid-to-late 60s, people were still looking at the actual research. They saw that things like the ergot family—LSD and related substances—were able to block it and prevent the actions of constricting muscles in all of the known tissues.

**Andrew Murray:** By blocking serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The main nerves that produce serotonin are just turned off by LSD and psilocybin. But as that was becoming known in the 1960s, the government was also starting to criminalize psychedelic chemicals, which were in the news repeatedly as anti-serotonin agents.

When the government criminalized these, the drug companies saw that they could form the basis of drug products. It was in their interest to say that those evil, illegal drugs are anti-serotonin and naturally make you insane, because the "good stuff" which makes you sane is serotonin. That created a foundation of public opinion to build the whole myth on. The government has been creating political myths, and the chemical companies use the government to support their economic sales myths.

**Andrew Murray:** To protect the companies, no doubt.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The companies are supposedly defending the healthy, sane parts of the organism, and the psychedelic people are threatening the sanity of the population. That implies that if you go crazy when you take an anti-serotonin agent, then what you need is products to *increase* your serotonin.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you know about the harmful effects of serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Animal research has the advantage that they can take fluids from anywhere in the animal or grind up its brain to see what is actually there. If you stress an animal—injure it, suffocate it—you will increase the stress hormones: cortisol, estrogen, and serotonin. Chronic stress increases serotonin in the brain as well as several other tissues.

If you compare an average lab animal to one that has been tortured, or one which has been put in a big vacation space with entertaining things to do, the one that is suffering will have high cortisol and lower adrenaline. Cortisol is driven up by the corticotropin-releasing hormone, which is activated primarily by serotonin. So, in these miserable animals, their serotonin is higher.

The happiest animals have the lowest serotonin, as well as lower acetylcholine and generally a little higher adrenaline. They are very alert, learn very well, and have very low serotonin. If you give these exactly the same chemicals that you are giving to increasingly young kids—if you give SSRIs to adolescent hamsters, for example—they become vicious and aggressive.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you understand the mechanism by which increased serotonin causes aggression?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think anyone does fully. But in general, you can suppress the aggression by giving them hopeless kind of stress. The "hopeless, helpless" stress seems to be put into effect by serotonin. Anti-serotonin drugs are starting to be used as antidepressants, but they have been used to cure learned helplessness.

**Andrew Murray:** That is it in a nutshell. Anti-serotonin drugs are being used.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 35 or 40 years ago, a psychiatrist named Cloninger was defining personality types and relating people to animal studies. He proposed that higher serotonin promoted a personality type of "harm avoidance." Rather than creative activity, the animals figured out different ways to avoid being hurt. They were fearful and anxious.

**Andrew Murray:** Isn't suicide increased as part of the disclaimer literature in SSRIs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Looking at the brains of people who commit suicide, they have found several different kinds of support for the idea that they were suffering from excess serotonin production. 50 years after he and his partner defined the famous experiments for learned helplessness, the researchers revised their theory and decided that in humans, too, it is caused by increased serotonin. Originally, they had suggested it might be the loss of serotonin, but they have changed their minds now.

**Andrew Murray:** Yet we are still brainwashed into thinking serotonin and melatonin are just happy chemicals.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Especially when the people who really defined the context for current discussion have changed their minds.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to talk about Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs). Monoamine oxidase breaks down serotonin, and MAOIs prevent that breakdown to increase serotonin. They are also marketed for improving other monoamines like dopamine and norepinephrine. What do you think about low levels of these other monoamines in depression?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When they all come up together, things tend to stay more in balance. When you have adrenaline, dopamine, and acetylcholine all coming up at the same time.

**Andrew Murray:** Wouldn't you suggest that anti-serotonin drugs would be useful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Interestingly, they are being used for all of the things now known to be promoted by serotonin. There are anti-serotonin products starting to be studied and recommended against cancer, arthritis, autoimmune diseases, depression, psychosis, and lung disease especially.

**Andrew Murray:** I wonder how we go three or four decades under this complete farce while people suffer or die. It seems there is a historical rule that every stupid medical idea lasts about 50 years.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** A local caller got it in five words: How does psilocybin fit in?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think psilocybin works very similarly to LSD in suppressing the serotonin nerves. Some of the others, like amphetamine derivatives, have a little overlap. I don't know that much about mescaline, but it doesn't work exactly on those same nerves.

**Andrew Murray:** All the initial research into LSD and psilocybin was probably going in a pretty good direction until it was scuppered by the serotonin industry.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They were seeing good results in treating alcoholism, depression, and a lot of psychiatric things.

**Andrew Murray:** Is there any instance where you think serotonin is useful? We produce it ourselves, so it must have some activity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the place it operates is so at the heart of things that it's best to let it develop under its own rules. For example, tryptophan, which is turned into serotonin, has a resonant aromatic electron system which is very responsive to light, electromagnetic energy, and oxidation-reduction. This is in practically all proteins. It is sort of like the nerve center of each protein molecule.

The structure of most cells is built on a framework of filaments and tubes—microtubules—that give the cell stiffness and movement. These are increasingly thought to be electronically or reductively interactive, acting like the nerve system of the cell. Serotonin acts on these responsive proteins and microtubules with a special interaction. Serotonin can stop the polymerization of the microstructure of a cell, interrupting it so that it can start de-differentiating and getting ready to divide.

When something is so basic to the existence of a cell, I think it's the worst thing you can do to try to intervene by giving a pill to someone. It's like if you have an electric motor, trying to pour coal into it for fuel.

**Caller:** I'm from New York. I was physically active, then got swelling on my ankle. The doctor diagnosed Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). It looks like hundreds of conditions are called RA, and they treat everybody with steroids. My case seems less severe compared to others. Does Dr. Peat have any ideas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen several people—seems like every couple of years I run across one—where their doctors have told them they are incurable. But I think if you find out what's causing it, sometimes you discover that maybe you didn't have that diagnosis in the first place. Foods you are eating, supplements you are taking, or especially if you are taking a serotonin or estrogen drug—those are enough to bring it on.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you believe in the inflammatory process mediating swollen joints and the presence of rheumatoid factor as a differential diagnosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. It will go away if you don't have it anymore. Same with lupus. Another person with lupus recently stopped thinking she had lupus, corrected her diet, took vitamin D and thyroid, and recovered.

**Andrew Murray:** From an herbal perspective, supporting excretion and the liver is key. Basic things like celery seed and devil's claw act as anti-inflammatories, and waste clearing products like burdock or yellow dock aid bile production.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just avoiding some of the foods that have been causing intestinal inflammation is the first thing to look for. Using a regular fibrous food in the diet sometimes is enough to tremendously reduce inflammation.

**Caller:** I'm from the Bay Area. My dad was at high altitude, experienced shortness of breath, coughing blood, and fatigue. The hospital diagnosed a heart attack based on blood work. A day later, after a CT scan, they said it was just pneumonia. How can you diagnose cardiovascular disease safely without resorting to a CT scan or angiogram?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first thing a person notices is trouble doing their usual energetic activities.

**Andrew Murray:** How reliable do you think enzymes are as a marker for heart attacks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Somewhat, but I wouldn't trust them in myself. Stress and exertion can damage a muscle—like running too far—and release enzymes. If your energy supply is low, if you're hypoglycemic and running on fat, overexertion can damage any muscle, including the heart.

**Andrew Murray:** What about angiograms and the dyes used?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you're not sure your heart has been injured, getting a chemical injected into your heart—especially if you exercise with that chemical in there—is going to irritate things and cause some damage. It isn't an entirely free and safe thing to do.

For about 30 or 40 years now, there has been a treatment called "GIK" or "Polarizing Solution"—standing for Glucose, Insulin, and Potassium (often with Magnesium). They give this to someone at the very beginning of a heart attack. It accelerates the healing of the heart. The glucose and insulin lower the free fatty acids, which are a major damaging factor in a heart attack. The insulin helps the cells take up the potassium and magnesium they need to restore energy.

**Andrew Murray:** In Germany, they have published papers supporting hawthorn extract. If administered within 12 hours of a myocardial infarct, it significantly decreases ischemic damage.

**Caller:** My father battled mental health issues and took Haldol and Thorazine. Was the action of those antipsychotics similar to the antidepressant action you were speaking of?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have the impression that Haldol was a danger to that system. I'm not sure about Thorazine. I think the main problem with that was it was given in such large amounts that people lost functioning. It mostly just quieted people down.

**Caller:** I'm from Utah. Dr. Peat, why do you choose to live in Oregon as opposed to someplace like New Mexico with sun and high elevation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely not for health. It was the location of the University of Oregon Library. I lived close enough that I could walk to the library regularly. In Los Angeles, for example, there was no way to get to a big library simply.

**Caller:** I'm from Arcata. I'd like a pep talk on skillful eating for diabetics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoiding serotonin-promoting drugs is one thing, because that's a factor in creating diabetes.

My experience started with my father having a diagnosis of extreme diabetes. He cured himself primarily with brewer's yeast. That got me interested. I read that in 19th-century England and France, doctors cured mortally sick diabetics by letting them eat as much sugar as they wanted—almost a pound a day. Instead of dying, the conversion of protein to sugar decreased and finally stopped, and they recovered.

They had broken the pattern of stress by letting them follow their appetites. Sugar promotes the regeneration of the beta cells that make insulin. It is the free fatty acids which are killing the beta cells constantly.

**Andrew Murray:** Because if you don't have enough sugar, you break your muscle tissue down and generate free fatty acids in an attempt to raise glucose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There is animal research that explains it, but doctors don't want to listen to that.

**Caller:** Besides altitude, are there other characteristics of a location that affect thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoiding very long winters is important because of the stress of the long nights. But I think altitude is very important because the high oxygen pressure at sea level is constantly creating stress—a random tendency to oxidize fats spontaneously—which disappears at a higher altitude. When you find the right altitude for your adaptation, you're able to retain the right amount of carbon dioxide so that oxidative processes run more smoothly without stress.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Does acetaminophen impact steroid production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nothing that occurs to me right now, but through damage to your liver, it undoubtedly will.

**Andrew Murray:** Undoubtedly. Thank you very much again, Dr. Peat, for giving your time. For those listening, Dr. Peat's website is www.raypeat.com. He has lots of fully referenced scientific articles there. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Tryptophan
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray. Dr. Raymond Peat joins us, as he has for several years now. Tonight, we are discussing the continuing topics of serotonin, inflammation, oxidants, and antioxidants. The number to reach us is 707-923-3911.

Dr. Peat, for those who have perhaps never heard you speak, would you outline your professional and academic background before we get into tonight's topic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I got a Master's degree with a thesis on William Blake from the University of Oregon in 1960. I taught at various schools and colleges, and in 1968 went back for a PhD in biology at the University of Oregon, graduating in 1972. I have been following up on pretty much the same interests since the 50s, studying how the brain and body work.

**Andrew Murray:** Carrying on from where we left off last month, I had some questions about tryptophan and serotonin. Given that serotonin is formed from the amino acid tryptophan, and the premise is that serotonin is an inflammatory molecule responsible for many negative effects, how best can we avoid tryptophan ingestion to limit the serotonin formed from it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Tryptophan and its metabolites, including serotonin, are essential for life. Every kind of organism is built with proteins containing tryptophan. Albert Szent-Györgyi demonstrated the electronic nature of life—fluorescence, luminescence, and electronic conductivity of living systems. Tryptophan is the amino acid that gives proteins that basic property which, according to Szent-Györgyi, is the essential mechanism of life that lets it sense and move.

This electronic property is at the heart of sensation, movement, secretion, and consciousness. When something goes wrong with tryptophan or its metabolites, it disturbs life at its deepest level. Cell division and all other functions depend on this excitability of tryptophan.

In the muscle protein myosin, there is one particular tryptophan which is most sensitive electronically. This tryptophan interacts with cysteine, an oxidizable sulfur protein. These are the "electric motor" of life processes, and they are essential during the growth process. However, if you keep the same ratio coming in via your diet after you stop growing, they are no longer being consumed for growth. They become free actors which can spread excitability and oxidizability randomly in the organism.

During the growth period, you need the full balanced range of amino acids. But when growth stops, all you need is to maintain the renewal of skin, intestine lining, lungs, and brain proteins. That is a very small amount of growth compared to infancy. Those amino acids are now at risk of becoming random, excitatory, inflammation-promoting processes.

Gelatin is a major protein used for building connective tissues, and it has a complete lack of these excitable proteins: cysteine, methionine, and tryptophan. If gelatin becomes a major dietary protein when growth is completed, you reduce the risk of inflammatory and degenerative diseases.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think this could be mitigated through exercise? I know you don't promote stress-inducing aerobic exercise, but I come from a bodybuilding perspective where lightweight bearing exercise is supportive for muscle mass and thyroid stimulation. If someone is doing work, does that warrant a diet containing those amino acids?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By the age of 30 or 40, when growth is completed, the bulk of our energy is spent just maintaining the body. But it has to function to be maintained. If you have a cast on your arm, muscles will atrophy because they aren't being used. So, just to maintain what we have, we have to be active. That includes mental or spiritual activity and keeping a freshness of perspective.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think there is a place for people to actively engage in environmental enrichment to produce a mind-body state that is supportive rather than degenerative?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It always has to involve newness and invention. Even conversations can be relatively athletic.

**Andrew Murray:** You have always mentioned that tryptophan should be balanced, which is why you recommend gelatin-rich products. Muscle meats are where we get the greatest proportion of tryptophan. I watched a documentary about plant-based athletes, specifically regarding an MMA fighter, McGregor. They claimed that meat consumption slowed the organism down and prevented muscles from repolarizing and repairing quickly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The high phosphate content relative to calcium in meat is a big part of that. It wastes energy. It acts like a constant subliminal stimulus that tends to load the cells up with calcium as if they were fatigued already.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you be supportive of a plant-based protein diet over meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The problem is that a lot of plant-based proteins are either overloaded with phosphate, the same as meat, or they have potential allergens and defensive molecules that plants have but animals do not.

**Andrew Murray:** So you still advocate very simple amino acid types—gelatin protein sources, dairy, cheese, milk, and eggs—as good quality, clean proteins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but it is a tremendously important field for research to find what plants have the proper nutrients and don't have the toxins.

**Andrew Murray:** Most proteins contain tryptophan. Do you think it's possible to obtain enough non-tryptophan containing proteins for continued muscle growth and repair?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the proteins other than gelatin that I know of will support proper growth and repair.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to ask about the pH of the blood. It is kept very tightly between 7.35 and 7.45. Is it possible for this to change?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yes. I've seen very sick people with extremely high blood pH—7.5 or 7.6, for example. A person has to get really sick for the blood to change outside that range. You can do it momentarily just by hyperventilating—breathing so fast that your carbon dioxide is lost. That can push your blood pH very high to the point that you might faint or die. When you lose too much CO2, the increased pH tends to cause spasms, including blood vessel spasms, cutting off the circulation to your brain.

**Andrew Murray:** Can you do the opposite of that? I know you are an advocate of increasing CO2.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, rebreathing in a paper bag can correct that and lower the pH of your blood to the point that it can start weakening your muscles and causing too much vasodilation. Muscle weakness is the worst thing that happens in that direction.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to talk about statins. The brain creates its own cholesterol, and generally, cholesterol is too big a molecule to get across the blood-brain barrier. However, statins do pass into the blood-brain barrier.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I imagine what they do to the brain is what they do to the muscles. If you are soaked in statins and do vigorous exercise, the interference with cholesterol can cause your muscle to break down and simply dissolve. I'm afraid that same thing can happen in the brain, accounting for depression and suicidality.

**Andrew Murray:** Since the brain is an energy-hungry organ and the white matter is principally cholesterol, lowering brain cholesterol is a cause for concern.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The old brain is sort of like a clump of atherosclerosis. It has lots of cholesterol, but it is bound to fatty acids. Avoiding vegetable oils helps prevent that.

**Caller (Santa Barbara):** I just had a hair tissue mineral analysis test. My sodium to potassium ratio is very high—sodium is 34 and potassium is 1. What could be causing that?
