**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That puts sodium into the water, so it will skew the hair test.

**Caller (Santa Barbara):** My calcium to potassium ratio is also skewed. Calcium is 46 and potassium is 1.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That could be from hard water. I wouldn't worry about a hair mineral test; a serum test is much more useful.

**Caller (Santa Barbara):** I'm 46 years old. A couple of years ago, I started having symptoms of hypoglycemia, which I still have. I've gained about 40 pounds, have anxiety, high inflammation markers, and high cortisol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D, calcium, and thyroid are likely involved. The amount of calcium in your diet works with both thyroid and vitamin D to keep your metabolic rate up and your blood sugar steady. Two grams a day of calcium is a good level.

**Caller (Santa Barbara):** I drink about 16 ounces of 2% milk.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think twice that much of 1% would be better. Two quarts of skim or 1% helps to lose weight because of the high calcium content. That tends to increase your temperature. If your temperature doesn't rise to 98.6°F by half an hour after breakfast, then you likely need a thyroid supplement too.

**Caller (Santa Barbara):** I tried Nature-Throid, but I started having increased anxiety and aggressive behavior, so I quit.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the effects of thyroid is to make your cells able to retain the magnesium that they need. If your diet doesn't have enough magnesium—and two quarts of milk would give you a generous supply—the thyroid cannot work properly. The normal function of thyroid is to increase your ability to relax both muscles and nerves.

**Caller (Mendocino):** I'm 62 and was recently diagnosed with osteoporosis. I went through menopause early at 45. What is an alternative way to treat that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping the parathyroid hormone under control is essential. Eating a lot of calcium—like two quarts of milk—and keeping your vitamin D serum level up to the middle of the range, around 50 ng/mL, is a good basis.

If your thyroid hormone is low, your prolactin will likely be high. Prolactin has a bone-weakening effect. It normally takes calcium out of the bone to put into milk, but under stress, it causes calcium loss. Prolactin tends to rise along with TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone). The simplest way to normalize prolactin is to normalize your thyroid function.

**Caller (Mendocino):** I do not like milk. Is there something else I could do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cooked greens are the food richest in calcium relative to phosphate, other than milk. If you grind up eggshells, that is a good pure form of calcium carbonate. A couple of grams a day would be good.

**Andrew Murray:** If you use organic eggs, wash out the membrane, bake them at 150°F to sterilize them, and grind them into a fine powder. About an eighth of a teaspoon is roughly 650 milligrams.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Unopposed cortisol is another bone-dissolving hormone. If cortisol is high and not balanced with adrenal DHEA and progesterone, that contributes to osteoporosis. Supplementing progesterone, DHEA, and/or pregnenolone can oppose that effect.

**Andrew Murray:** I'm seeing reports now that the LDL/HDL distinction is a myth, and that oxidized LDL particles are responsible for the initial insult on the endothelium, which causes cholesterol to be laid down as a repair mechanism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** And regarding the brain, low cholesterol is rarely discussed, but you have said people should be around 200 mg/dL.

**Caller (John):** I am 78. Over the last year, my PSA has gone up precipitously from 4 to 20. Are there supplements to drive that down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything anti-inflammatory is the right approach. A diet low in phosphate is basic. Cooked greens, cheese, milk, and eggs are anti-inflammatory foods. Keeping your thyroid function up so that your liver helps balance your hormones and keeps estrogen down is important. Adequate protein, a good calcium-phosphate ratio, and a fairly high-normal body temperature are important to lower inflammation and keep estrogen low.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think herbal aromatase inhibitors like nettle root or saw palmetto work by being anti-estrogenic? Is prostatic hypertrophy due to estrogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, estrogen is a growth and carcinogenic factor in the prostate. The men who live the longest with prostate cancer have the highest testosterone.

**Andrew Murray:** So testosterone is protective?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the early 90s, when they started using the PSA test as a diagnosis, mortality from prostate cancer took a huge surge upward. Some doctors decided maybe it wasn't a good idea to diagnose it so aggressively. A couple of studies found that 100% of people who died at the age of 50 or more had diagnosable cancer somehow, even if they died of other causes.

**Andrew Murray:** Aspirin is also well-tolerated and anti-inflammatory.

**Caller (Redway):** How can I get off Celexa? I've been using it for many years.

**Andrew Murray:** We discussed this last month. Dr. Peat mentioned supporting the physiology with thyroid and lifestyle changes to allow a person to taper off.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the effects of SSRIs is that they tend to increase stress hormones. So, an anti-stress program is key. I've known people to withdraw from several different addictive things, including SSRIs, using progesterone, coffee, thyroid, and a good high-calcium diet.

**Andrew Murray:** Also, consider light exposure. With winter coming, seasonal affective disorder is common as thyroid gets low. Exposure to bright light and opposing estrogen with progesterone can have a beneficial effect.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much, Dr. Peat, for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** If you want to find out more about Dr. Peat, visit www.raypeat.com. He has plenty of well-written articles backed by studies. Sarah will be back in January. Thanks for joining us.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Vibrations/Frequencies
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray. It is 2020, and we are looking forward to a good year. You are invited to call in with any questions related to this month's subject: vibrations, frequencies, and cell repair and regeneration through sound and vibration.

Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us again. He is a wealth of knowledge, and whilst he doesn't express himself as an expert on sound specifically, he knows enough to weigh in on some of the most interesting recent publications regarding the use of sound and electromagnetic frequency in the treatment of cancer.

I run a business called Western Botanical Medicine. I've been a naturopathic doctor for 23 years. For the last ten years, I have been working with Dr. Peat to get his insight on the defects in the understanding and dogma which has unfortunately guided medical decisions. Dr. Peat, thanks for joining us in this next decade.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm planning on it.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who have never listened to the show before, would you outline your professional and academic background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had a master's degree in humanities and after about 10 years went back for a PhD in biology at the University of Oregon in 1972. My dissertation topic was reproductive aging.

**Andrew Murray:** So you've been intimately associated with factors around reproduction and organized cell growth. I know you don't generally advocate a lot of supplements, but progesterone is one of your favorites in terms of its use in organized cell growth and anti-inflammatory processes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Incidentally, some of my experiments had to do with the electrical behavior of tissue under the influence of progesterone, estrogen, prostaglandins, and so on.

**Andrew Murray:** You've always mentioned estrogen as being an excitotoxic molecule. The hormone replacement therapy industry pushed it as a pro-life hormone, claiming it helps bone thinning, but it is actually implicated in inflammation and excitotoxicity.

I was looking for material for this evening's talk regarding sound, vibration, and cell signaling. I found a 2013 article titled *Low Intensity and Frequency Pulsed Electromagnetic Fields Selectively Impair Breast Cancer Cell Viability*. They stated that this pulsed electromagnetic field therapy was a good treatment for breast cancer, didn't affect normal tissues, was non-invasive, and could be combined with existing treatments. Do you have anything to add regarding low-intensity, low-frequency vibrational output affecting cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In that experiment, they weren't paying attention to the effects of specific frequencies, so it was just giving some kind of excitation to the cells. Other people, like the Rife tradition, have been trying to identify particular frequencies that are more effective at either exciting or calming the cells.

In the 1960s, people were trying to use direct current to control cancer growth. A professor at Johns Hopkins published an article saying that he had regressed mouse mammary tumors just using a direct current polarization.

**Andrew Murray:** So just applying current, not pulsing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's known that cancer is electrically excited. It's like a wound that is stuck in an electrically excited, negatively charged condition.

**Andrew Murray:** Cancer cells are not exactly strong; they are fragile in a lot of ways. Some of the work done with vibration or electricity has validity in disrupting that cell stability because they don't have very stable membranes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And being electrically charged and excited, I think makes them more susceptible to vibrating energy fields such as in that experiment.

**Andrew Murray:** In the past, they measured frequency in cycles per second before terming it Hertz. Getting back to how a specific frequency can affect a cell—given that we are over 90% water, our membranes are fluid and respond to vibration.

There are currently protests regarding 5G technology. We are organismic and sensitive to light and vibration. The earth resonates at just under 8 Hertz. The study I mentioned used frequencies between 11 and 80 Hertz.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1960s, the doctrine was that neither sound nor electromagnetic energy below a certain frequency and energy could have any effect on the units of the cell, such as chromosomes or mitochondria. That argument started back in the late 40s when radar was accidentally killing people who stood in front of the radar antenna. The authority opinion was that electromagnetic energy could only harm you by overheating your brain or organs.

However, a researcher working with muscle cells in culture measured the activity of ATPase, which controls the disposition of energy in the cell. They found that the pitch of 440 Hz was very powerful at activating that muscle enzyme. They showed that the conventional theory of the cell was impossible for that low frequency, moderately low energy.

The dogma says that the energy concentration is too low to cause chemical changes. But the person demonstrating the effect showed that the cell structure was acting as an antenna, gathering energy from several microns of space and concentrating it so that it could act on the enzyme.

At that time, conventional opinion stated it would be impossible to make a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) device because of the idea that the cell is organized randomly. It took the interaction between Gilbert Ling and his organized water explanation of cell function, and Raymond Damadian, who realized that if Gilbert Ling was right about how water behaves, you could make pictures of the water in cells electromagnetically. His invention of the MRI device really changed the possibility of explaining cell function.

**Andrew Murray:** That reminds me of the bomb testing where they tried to tell us sonic bombs were harmless. They said the same thing about low frequency, low energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's part of the reason that they deny that Gilbert Ling had an accurate description of the cell. If his picture of the cell is right, then radiation and electromagnetic energy are very relevant to cell function.

**Caller:** Do you think meditation is safe if you're trying to lower breathing rate and increase CO2, or can it have bad effects like increasing serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think most people tend to hyperventilate too much. If you can just relax and stop hyperventilating, you retain more CO2, and that has an anti-inflammatory effect everywhere in the body.

**Caller:** Do you know what could help to reduce the need for sleep aside from increasing CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you're not getting into the deepest phase of sleep, called slow-wave sleep or deep sleep, your tissue isn't being repaired adequately. You need more hours of it. If you do things that will deepen your sleep, then you can reduce it to the normal six to eight hours. Thyroid hormone and vitamin D are two of the most important things for maintaining deep sleep.

**Caller:** Can vitamin D increase serotonin and worsen sleep, or is it just a matter of getting enough calcium to counter that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Serotonin and histamine are both brain excitatory signals. That's why antihistamines are used for improving sleep. Both anti-serotonin and antihistamine drugs improve sleep, but you can do the same thing with good nutrition: lots of calcium, vitamin D, and thyroid.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think there's any difference in the mechanism by which non-drowsy antihistamines work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Histamine is basically an inflammation signal. In insomnia, you have, in effect, an inflamed brain. You can quiet it by getting the energy production up with thyroid, sugar, and nutrients. Adrenaline is antihistamine, but it is also excitatory. Insomnia usually involves both adrenaline and histamine. The adrenaline is attempting to turn off the histamine, but if you get your energy up, you turn off both of them and let the brain relax.

**Andrew Murray:** So relaxation is not negative. Thyroid hormone allows your brain to relax through the correct utilization of sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And most aging changes occur during the hours of sleep and darkness.

**Caller:** I have a question about infrasound. We were just embattled with a factory proposing wind power turbines. The proponent denied that there was any effect from infrasound—sound produced below the audible range. Do you have any thoughts on the biological effects of infrasound?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think cell culture gives an insight into what might be happening. The infrasound frequencies are around 10 to 50 per second. When growing cells in culture, they lose some of the properties they had in the organism. One of the tricks to make cell culture more lifelike is to give it some kind of pulsation, because cell physiology depends on the fact that the blood is rhythmically pulsing through the system. The pulse rate is in the infrasonic frequency.

**Caller:** I take from that you would expect there to be physiological effects from a constant infrasound?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I don't know that anyone has clearly demonstrated it, but you can use equivalent pulsations to show that you are changing the cell physiology *in vitro*.

**Andrew Murray:** I found a 2019 article on bone regeneration titled *Translational Insights into Extremely Low Frequency Pulsed Electromagnetic Fields for Bone Regeneration*. It showed that sound improved osteoblastic activity—bone mineralization and formation.

Another 2019 document discussed ultrasound. What frequencies does ultrasound work at?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For treating things, they use anything from 50,000 to 100,000 Hz, but the imaging is around a million cycles per second.

Around 1970, someone discovered that putting ultrasound on infected tonsils caused them to recover and become uninflamed. Gradually, they found that bone healing and soft tissue wound healing were accelerated. Part of that is thought to be the activation of cell regenerating signals such as nitric oxide and estrogen that accelerate stem cell growth and multiplication in the early stages of healing.

The imaging of bone density or osteoporosis can be done with ultrasound. You can tell the strength of a bone as well as its density. Since ultrasound stimulates bone repair, it would be reasonable if doctors would evaluate aging women's bones using ultrasound. Instead, they X-ray them, and X-rays actually weaken the bone and accelerate osteoporosis.

A friend of mine who had liver enzyme elevation and signs of hepatitis or developing cirrhosis had a very prolonged ultrasound examination of her liver. A couple of weeks later, she went back for another exam and her liver had completely recovered. I suspect it was from that half an hour of looking around with an ultrasound imaging device.

**Andrew Murray:** The mechanism would be an anti-inflammatory effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the only place it shouldn't be used is around the head because it tends to emulsify tissue if it's too energetic. You don't want emulsified brain tissue.

**Caller:** I have an appointment next week to start interferon for my hepatitis C, but I had a very thorough ultrasound on my liver to find that out. Should I ask them if I don't need the treatment?

**Andrew Murray:** I didn't think they used interferon anymore because it was so brutal.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the test to identify Hepatitis C has done more harm than the virus itself because of the desperate attitude they take with treatments like interferon. I think people who probably wouldn't have had any problem if it hadn't been diagnosed have been injured by some of the treatments they get.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, I recall you saying that Ribavirin might not have been a bad compound to try compared to interferon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's less harmful.

**Andrew Murray:** Caller, if your blood work doesn't look bad and you feel fine, it's a personal call. I know people who failed interferon treatment and wound up with cirrhosis, and others who have had Hep C for 50 years and are fine.

**Caller:** I feel really good. One more question: What about hydrogen peroxide treatment? You start with one drop a day and go up to 30.

**Andrew Murray:** That sounds like MMS (Miracle Mineral Supplement), which is actually bleach.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a study in Italy that identified it as a probable carcinogen.

**Andrew Murray:** I would not go down that route.

**Caller:** I was diagnosed with osteoporosis 10 years ago. I have an osteopenic spine and an osteoporotic hip, however, I feel fine. I just walked 4 miles to get a tooth extracted. I also have hypothyroidism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin K is very important, along with vitamin D and calcium intake. Vitamin K prevents the removal of calcium from the bone and keeps it out of the soft tissues. The combination is much more effective than either one alone.

**Andrew Murray:** One abstract I looked at showed that exposure to a cytokine production by lipopolysaccharide (LPS)—which is responsible for inflammation—was modulated by sound waves. The sound blocked pro-inflammatory pathways like protein kinase C.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think normal activity has some of those anti-inflammatory effects. If you're forced into inactivity, you develop generalized inflammation. Normal activity of muscles lowers stress hormones and increases constructive hormones such as progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone. Normal activity in itself is an anti-inflammatory process. I suspect that these certain frequencies are imitating the normal rhythm of proper activity.

**Caller:** I have fibromyalgia. I find that when I get into a big city and I'm around a lot of power lines, I start feeling unwell. Is there a relationship?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think a lot of doctors are coming around to recognize the importance of hormone balance. Good thyroid function, vitamin D, and keeping up the constructive hormones like progesterone, testosterone, and DHEA.

**Andrew Murray:** Since you are female and post-menopausal, you are exposed to estrogen in an unopposed way. It is important to get adequate progesterone because it is the antagonist of inflammatory estrogen. In fibromyalgia, estrogen dominance certainly has a role to play in tired, waterlogged muscles.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cortisol is a bone destroyer and progesterone is the main antagonist of cortisol.

**Caller:** It was Hulda Clark who wrote *The Cure for All Cancers*. I wonder if the doctor approves of the device she created to tone out certain bacterial frequencies.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think she used just a simple low-voltage direct current stimulator. That device can be used productively, but I don't think she understood enough to use it productively.

**Andrew Murray:** We are out of time. Dr. Peat's website is . He has a huge list of fully referenced scientific articles. I encourage everyone to do their own research. My name is Andrew Murray from Western Botanical Medicine. Thanks for your time, and until next month, Happy New Year.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Vibrations/Frequencies Part 2
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray and I'm delighted to be back on the show joining the incredibly knowledgeable Dr. Peat and my wonderful husband.

**Andrew Murray:** We are still able to entreat Dr. Peat to join us on the show to share his wisdom. Last month, very briefly, we were discussing resonant frequencies and the effects of frequencies on cells. I came across a lot of interesting abstracts from 2019 and 2020 related to extremely low frequency (ELF) electromagnetic frequencies.

One of the main studies that caught my eye was regarding the treatment of breast cancer. They showed it was effective as an adjunctive therapy to traditional cancer management and had very significant cell-killing effects. We also touched a little bit on Rife therapy and vaccines in the past. Dr. Peat has a newsletter on vaccines in context which we will get to later.

Dr. Peat, let's introduce you to the show. For people who haven't heard your name or know anything about you, would you give an outline of your academic profession and background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After graduating from college and getting a master's degree in humanities and studying linguistics for several years, I decided to study brain biology for a PhD. When I got to the University of Oregon, I quickly decided that brain biology was a dogmatic topic at the time. I looked around and found reproductive physiology was actually doing empirical science. So, I did my dissertation on reproductive physiology and the changes aging makes in the energy metabolism of the reproductive organs.

**Andrew Murray:** You mentioned that reproductive biology hadn't been swallowed up by the machine at that point.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main professor in female reproduction, Arnold Soderwall, had been working in the field way back in the 40s. He was one of the early people to test the effects of Vitamin E on reproduction. In the 1930s and 40s, it was considered a sex-promoting vitamin, or almost a hormone. He was one of the people that showed that its effect on increasing fertility took place by being an anti-estrogen.

The older an animal got, the earlier it became infertile. He found that by increasing the dose of Vitamin E steadily with aging, he kept the animals from miscarrying well into old middle age. I continued that research and found that it was partly acting by way of improving the production of progesterone as well as lowering the effect of estrogen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I also remember you telling me about those flamingos in the African Rift Valley that don't age reproductively because they have so much CO2 from the elevation and the non-PUFA algae they're eating.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No one is really sure, but I think the high carbon dioxide environment is very likely a big part of it. Their usual mortality curve is a semi-plateau up until middle age, and then it crashes. The mortality rate per year for most organisms increases rapidly after a certain age. With flamingos, it seems that all through their whole lifespan, the annual mortality continues at just about the same rate, mainly by accidents.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And they can breed up until they die from an accident?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Apparently, yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** When you were doing your PhD, what forms of Vitamin E did they know of then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I found a bottle of the very old stuff in the freezer in the lab in 1968 or so. It had been there for decades. It was a very viscous material and a light amber color. I tested it against some of the quinones. Comparing benzoquinone, for example, reacting it with Vitamin E and doing a combination staining experiment, I got chemical reactions that showed that the sensitivity of the quinone reaction was very vivid in that old sample. In the newer samples of so-called pure Vitamin E, I haven't been able to see that same reaction that I got around 1970 using the very old stuff.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Where did they get that Vitamin E from? How did they process it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was bought from Sigma Chemical Co., but it was fairly typical at the time. It was the highest grade available. At that time, all Vitamin E was fairly brown colored and very thick. Some of the studies suggested that it was a waxy, highly saturated, long-chain fatty acid that was part of the endurance-promoting antioxidant effect, not the simple tocopherol itself.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it makes a big difference what form of Vitamin E they're using to test. Does that mean we need to be careful when supplementing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even 10 or 20 years ago, the majority of it was highly diluted with soybean oil—highly unsaturated. That is exactly what my professor found was the antagonistic effect; Vitamin E protected against the pro-aging effect of the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So if your Vitamin E is thin and liquid, it's probably not good. If it's thick and viscous, can we assume that's better quality?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so.

**Andrew Murray:** What makes a good quality Vitamin E supplement?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the mixture of the non-racemic natural forms—alpha and gamma are probably the most important. But I think the mixture as it occurs in nature is much better than any of the synthetic D,L-alpha that has been sold for a long time because it's cheap to make.

**Andrew Murray:** What about wheat germ oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is very full of polyunsaturated fat. I tried some of it in the 1970s and that caused a choking sensation when you took just a little bit of it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you're recommending a mixed tocopherol supplement, not just isolated D-alpha tocopherol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In the 1940s, the anti-estrogen, anti-clotting, and pro-fertility qualities were clearly identified. But with the rise of the estrogen industry starting in 1940, the idea that Vitamin E could be the main fertility vitamin and simultaneously purely anti-estrogenic really put a crimp in the estrogen advertising idea. They were a major factor in creating the doctrine that Vitamin E's action is merely as an antioxidant.

The vegetable oil industry at the same time was trying to sell the idea that seed oils are edible. In feeding them to animals, they were finding that animals became sterile on a high intake of the various seed oils.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Didn't they put on weight too?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, but when they had a really high proportion, they became sterile and the brain deteriorated. My professor identified that as an estrogen-promoting effect. It has continued to be confirmed that estrogen increases the accumulation of polyunsaturated fats in the body and increases their activity. Those fats simultaneously increase the effect of estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** It's a vicious cycle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** So the anti-estrogen effect was identical to the anti-PUFA effect. But both the seed oil industry and the estrogen industry found it convenient to sell the idea that Vitamin E is merely an antioxidant. From the 1940s on, D-alpha tocopherol was identified as the standard because it was the most antioxidant. But it turns out that the gamma and others have very distinct, more important biological activities, including opposition to estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** Moving on to the electromagnetic fields (EMF) discussion. I saw a study on rats regarding high altitude stress and ulcer healing. They said low-frequency pulsed electromagnetic fields could penetrate stomach tissue and promote regeneration.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In that particular experiment, they were using restraint stress to produce the ulcers and happened to combine it with high altitude. So I don't think anything can be inferred from that study for humans. If you're being suspended by your tail at high altitude, you're going to be stressed out.

**Andrew Murray:** Another study was titled "The Neuroprotective Effects of Low Frequency Pulsed Electromagnetic Fields in Ischemic Stroke." This seems related to reducing inflammatory sequelae after an ischemic event.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They mentioned some of the inflammatory cytokines that are reduced by the treatment. Behind those protective changes, I think there's likely to be an increase of some of the basic defensive factors such as heat shock protein. Any kind of stress will bring on these stabilizing proteins. I suspect those are behind the reductions of the inflammatory mediators. Another acute stress-induced protective factor is Hypoxia-Inducible Factor (HIF), which tends to come up at the same time as the heat shock proteins. These help nerve cells get through intense stress, such as glucose or oxygen deprivation.

**Andrew Murray:** How do these electromagnetic fields generate this healing event? How does that actually work physically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Robert Becker's research in biological electrical activity found that organisms are responsive to extremely weak electromagnetic signals, such as pulsations in the earth's electromagnetic field. Older research in the 40s and 50s found that all sorts of organisms govern their metabolic rate by changes picked up from the electromagnetic field.

Currently, the doctrine is that it's simply the light and dark changes that are cueing in the expression of genes. But in this older research, they would put the organism in sealed chambers out of sight of night and day. Some of the changes persisted even in mine shafts 60 feet below the surface. So there are some very penetrating electromagnetic fields that are crucially important for the cycles of plants. The current dogma is really trying to cover up that extreme sensitivity to weak fields and how important it is that we're being bombarded with polluting electrical rhythms.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw another article regarding Alzheimer's using 5 Hertz cycles, showing improvement in cognitive ability and tissue regeneration via heat shock proteins. Another on bacterial infections showed that pulsed EMF blocked tumor necrosis factor and transcription factor kappa beta, slowing down previously untreatable infections.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, would you recommend a practical approach to using these ELF and pulsed EMF treatments?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think there has been enough research. It's clear that these acute treatments can stimulate increased blood circulation and defensive heat shock proteins, but regarding the long-range developmental course, I don't think there's enough information yet.

There is very little interest in following up research that was done 40 or 50 years ago on sound. For example, the dogma says that ordinary speaking frequency sound waves couldn't possibly be interacting with cell chemistry. But several experiments have demonstrated that moderate volume music or speech vibrations affect the activity of muscle enzymes. ATPase, for example, was found to distinctly activate at the pitch A440. Each enzyme probably has its own responsive frequency.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So we're supposed to speak to each other, hear voices, and listen to music?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the pitch affects enzyme activity.

**Caller:** I've been dealing with a chronic problem for a while that pushes me to my limits of mental ability because of a traumatic brain injury. I wonder what Dr. Peat has to say about organic damage to one's brain as far as any of this new research goes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think when the brain has any inefficiency from whatever cause, it's more susceptible to interference from being around a broadcast station, for example. The healthier the brain is, the higher its threshold is to that kind of pollution.

The healing influence of the natural hormones proceeds at any age. In traumatic brain injury, they found that progesterone and Vitamin D are both extremely helpful for facilitating repair and keeping down the inflammatory processes that would amount to scar formation rather than the creation of new functioning nerve circuits.

**Caller:** Where do you get progesterone? Is that something that would be prescribed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There might be three or four doctors in the country who are willing to prescribe those things, but it isn't necessary to have a prescription for them. It's the same molecule that your brain manufactures. The brain has the highest concentration of progesterone of any tissue in the body. It's an essential brain-stabilizing molecule.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** It is usually synthesized from wild yam as a starting material.

**Caller:** What do you know, if anything, about Dr. Hulda Clark's machine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think Hulda Clark's apparatus was a simple direct current device. Robert Becker's research found that he could promote nerve regeneration and establish normal function when nerves had been cut using direct current. However, regarding the use that Hulda Clark made of her device, I don't think there was any research supporting the things she claimed for it.

**Caller:** I'm calling on behalf of my husband who works in the medical field. He was recently denied an influenza vaccination exemption request. Since these healthcare workers have compulsory annual flu vaccination with toxic adjuvants, are there any changes you would recommend to diet or supplementation around the time of vaccination to mitigate the effects of adjuvants on systemic inflammation? For example, is it safe to increase aspirin intake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same things that will protect you against injury from radiation, trauma, or bacterial toxins can be used to protect against the aluminum particulate matter and other random proteins contaminating vaccines. title: Ask the Herb Doctor: Coronavirus
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to the March 20, 2020 edition of *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. You are invited to call in with questions related to this month's very specific topic: the worldwide frenzy surrounding the coronavirus. Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us, and he is bringing a very interesting mental shift to how we are looking at this.

I want to state at the very outset that this is a very emotional subject. No one is taking death lightly; when you have loved ones dying, it is absolutely no joke. While some comments may seem light regarding statistical numbers—referencing presentations from Dr. Wolfgang Wodarg in Germany—I will provide information for people to search this on the internet and see for themselves how some of these statistics have been skewed. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks for joining us. As usual, please introduce yourself so listeners can find out a little more about your background.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I got a Master of Arts degree in 1960 from the University of Oregon, then a PhD in 1972 specializing in physiology and biochemistry. I have been concentrating on reproductive and aging biology, with special attention to the nervous system and how nutrition interacts with those changes. It turns out I never was interested in virology, but this particular virus impinges exactly on the things I've been working on for a long time: inflammation, aging, and cellular respiration.

**Andrew Murray:** I would like to outline influenza for people because the terms can be confusing. There are four types: A, B, C, and D. Only type A really produces the major flus—the Spanish flu, Asian flu, Hong Kong flu, Bird flu, SARS, and MERS.

When most people get a common cold, it is often a coronavirus. The main issue with influenza is the massive amount of inflammation that comes as the body's immune response to the virus. A severe complication is viral pneumonia, which can be secondarily infected by bacteria. This can overwhelm a system that is already crashing because of inflammation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When a person gets a verified influenza virus, a typical analysis will find various other viruses, like common cold viruses and other respiratory pathogens, as well as the true influenza virus. So, even when there is a confirmed flu virus, you can't be sure that is really the culprit.

At present, most of the people getting seriously sick or dying are old—definitely beyond their mid-50s, with the highest mortality over 70. One report stated that 99% of the people dying with the coronavirus were suffering from other very serious conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or stroke symptoms. These things made it much more likely that they would die from stress. Other pathogens take advantage of that weak condition. Just because you have a test for one particular pathogen, you can't be sure that it is the contributing factor when there are so many other pathogens present.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's get into the origin of this. Most people are accepting the standard doctrine that this is of Chinese origin, coming from a wet market via a zoonotic infection. However, you mentioned some interesting facts regarding the gene sequencing indicating a different origin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Virologists in Europe, the United States, South Korea, Taiwan, and China have referred to DNA sequence analysis showing that the "trunk" of the family tree is in the United States. There are five different branches or varieties occurring early in the United States before the strain appeared in China. The strain in China identifies as the fourth or fifth branch off this trunk.

This is based on analyzing substitutions of bases in the DNA chain. If you have a virus with two changes, and then a third one with three changes, the ones with fewer changes necessarily came before the last one. The family tree of this virus shows that the one occurring in November in Wuhan was the fourth or fifth descendant.

**Andrew Murray:** So, people have been pointing out a 2015 article in *Nature* regarding this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It was a news item mentioning that people connected to the CDC, working at Fort Detrick, Maryland, were creating pathogens to develop a vaccine in advance. Normally, it takes 12 to 18 months to prepare a vaccine for a new strain, and by that time the flu season has passed. They wanted to have a vaccine ready before a natural epidemic broke out.

The CDC patented a coronavirus in 2003 specifically to work on that project. However, last summer—around July or August—it was in the news that the CDC ordered the closure of the virus lab at Fort Detrick because they had carelessly let their escape protection system deteriorate. They closed the lab because of the danger of an escaped virus just two months before the outbreak.

Additionally, American soldiers participated in international military athletic contests in Wuhan. Normally, these army athletes are outstanding, Olympic quality. But last year, for unknown reasons, the US team came in 35th rank among all countries. The Chinese were commenting on how poorly they performed, which was unusual.

**Andrew Murray:** That is interesting. However, I know there has been a very recent article published by top-ranked virologists regarding the engineering of this virus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they say that this particular virus was impossible to anticipate. Even though the intent of the CDC for years was to make a pathogen to study, these recent virologists say that the nature of this particular one is such that they can't foresee anyone having engineered it.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's talk about the numbers. This event has paralyzed the world economically. We have Dr. Wolfgang Wodarg, who flat-out refuses to believe this is anything exceptional compared to standard flu seasons.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** John Ioannidis, another well-known professor who analyzes statistical disease situations, is suggesting that this might be history's greatest "evidence fiasco."

Dr. Wodarg and Ioannidis point out that we can't see the evidence clearly because we weren't doing this type of testing in previous years to compare. In China, it first looked like 2.7% of those infected were dying. But as they produced huge amounts of test kits and tested large numbers of people, the mortality rate per infection decreased to 0.6%. Ioannidis suggests the actual mortality figure could range from 0.025% up to 5%, depending on the population.

If you only look at people reporting to hospitals, a 10% mortality rate isn't unreasonable because you are measuring the sickest people. But as the testing population expands, the mortality rate drops, approaching the normal flu mortality of one in a thousand.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, give us an idea about how statistics can be skewed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I compare it to what happened historically with cancer incidence. Years ago, General Electric advertised that if everyone bought their X-ray machines, we could increase the cancer cure rate to 97%. If you diagnose cancer in 100% of the population, but only a small percentage were ever going to die from it, you can claim a high cure rate by treating people who never would have developed symptoms.

However, when you treat cancer aggressively, the mortality rate can increase with the diagnostic rate due to the treatment itself. Similarly, when you use a diagnostic test to herd people into hospitals, you subject them to a high rate of medical accidents. Historically in the US, between 200,000 and 440,000 people are killed by medical mistakes in hospitals annually.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a caller asking about the origins of the Spanish Flu and theories surrounding that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The data is based on very few actual tissue samples compared to the millions of deaths. At that time, the flu was thought to be a bacterial infection. A popular treatment was injecting camphor dissolved in oil.

It turns out that a distillate of petroleum smelled like camphor. About 50 years ago, they purified it and added an amino group to make it water-soluble, creating the drug Amantadine, and its relatives Rimantadine and Memantine. These are broad-spectrum antivirals. They happen to be safe genetically.

In contrast, many antivirals being recommended recently—such as Acyclovir, Ribavirin, and Chloroquine—interfere with human DNA and are recognized as genotoxic. If you have millions of people taking those preventively, you are going to have millions of people with genetic damage. You don't want that in a young population.

**Andrew Murray:** So you consider Memantine safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they are safe genetically and moderately effective against a wide variety of viruses. But aspirin, if it were under patent, would be considered a "super antiviral" because it is active against a wide variety, including influenza, herpes, rhinovirus, and hepatitis.

**Caller:** Since transmission is by droplets from the oral or nasal cavity, wouldn't mandatory wearing of masks stop the spread?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That does seem reasonable since the aerosol will likely be trapped on a fairly fine, porous mask.

**Andrew Murray:** And regular hand washing is the number one preventative.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Soap is a surefire parasiticide for this type of virus. It is very virucidal on the skin.

**Caller:** The Governor of California said around half the population is going to get infected. Do you think that is an accurate projection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is within the historical range, but almost none of them will have a serious sickness. The reason there is a flu season from winter until late spring is that in temperate zones, sun exposure goes down. Most people become Vitamin D deficient and extremely susceptible to infection. By summer, Vitamin D rises, and viral immunity rises strongly, ending the flu season.

**Andrew Murray:** I have a friend using 20,000 IU of Vitamin D per day, and their blood levels are just in the middle of the reference range.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** The best way to know if you are taking enough is with a blood test. Dr. Peat, you recommend not being below 50 ng/mL?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, 50 to 60 ng/mL is a safe range. Probably 95% of people I've seen are below that. Low Vitamin D is connected to fatigue, muscle weakness, and high blood pressure.

Vitamin D and adequate calcium work on the same part of the immune system as the drugs the Chinese have been having success with: Cinanserin (a serotonin blocker) and Losartan (an angiotensin receptor blocker).

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Would you recommend people ask for a prescription of Losartan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A man in Italy emailed me about his friend with confirmed coronavirus. I mentioned the Chinese recommendations. He got a Losartan prescription, and the next day his friend was out of bed. Today he emailed saying his friend feels like he has "new lungs."

**Andrew Murray:** Can you outline the mechanism regarding ACE1 and ACE2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is confusion because some say that since the virus attacks the ACE2 enzyme, anything that increases ACE2 must increase susceptibility. But it is exactly the opposite.

ACE2 is a defensive, anti-inflammatory enzyme that destroys angiotensin. It trims two amino acids off the angiotensin molecule, turning it into Angiotensin 1-7, which prevents fibrotic and inflammatory processes in the lungs and heart. Things that block the AT1 receptor (like Losartan) also increase the ACE2 enzyme, which is protective.

**Andrew Murray:** From an herbal perspective, for the primary pneumonia or "cytokine storm," you want anti-inflammatories. Echinacea root is definitely an anti-inflammatory. Elderberry has also been highlighted. For secondary bacterial infections, volatile oil herbs like Thyme and the mint family are positively antibacterial. But the main goal is to control the inflammation.

**Caller:** What will it take for our economy to bounce back?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The government is talking about giving money to corporations. Milton Friedman, the conservative economist, proposed a minimum basic income decades ago. I think he was on the right track; it is necessary to get money to the consumers, not just to the corporations that are losing money.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, you mentioned an average of 44,000 flu deaths annually in the US. If 10% of those were caused by coronavirus strains in previous years, we would expect a certain baseline.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, Dr. Wodarg made the point that based on the historical curve, the current deaths are actually behind the expected mortality curve in places like Germany.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** In 2017, there were 85,000 pneumonia deaths in the US, and 58,000 of those were people over 70.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Old age causes sepsis and pneumonia as common causes of death. Old age changes the inflammatory system the same way this virus does—increasing the angiotensin receptor and decreasing the protective ACE2 system. Anything you do to protect against viral effects is really protecting against aging.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So, Vitamin D, Vitamin B1, and aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, those move the system in the corrective direction.

**Andrew Murray:** We have to hold it there. Thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Peat. You can be found at www.raypeat.com.

What is your perception of ventilation being the problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw one doctor recently on the internet stating that 92% saturation was the level at which they would intubate patients. That happens to be the percentage I like to keep myself at as much as possible; I think it's a sign of relaxation and using oxygen efficiently.

Regarding ECMO, it can be a solution if done vein-to-vein. But when they involve an artery, the amount of invasion required to connect a machine to arterial blood is so damaging that they have a very high mortality rate.

A doctor in Germany, Dr. Gattinoni, advocates using only a nasal cannula to give oxygen. He compared two hospitals in Germany. One was doing what everyone is recommending in the U.S. and Europe—intubation and forced respiration—and that hospital had a 60% mortality rate in intensive care. One survey found that in 88% of the hospitals they checked, 88% of the patients were dying in the intensive care unit. Some hospitals had 100% mortality in intensive care when they ventilated. Until the 1940s, a mixture of carbon dioxide and oxygen was available for resuscitation, but unsupported theories of respiration knocked that out. **Andrew Murray:** The article I read stated that the membranes of the alveoli are some of the most fragile in the body, so forcing oxygen under pressure is irrational. It seems it takes death for thinking people to question standard medical care. Dr. Kyle-Sidell mentioned that using a nasal cannula and "proning"—getting patients to lie on their stomachs—brought oxygen levels from 40% up to 80-90%, which is acceptable.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even putting them in a prone posture rather than supine makes a big difference. A few doctors have mentioned the oddity of this so-called pneumonia. There is a "ground glass" appearance and water in the lungs, but it is distributed in a widespread way, not in pockets like an infection would cause.

In sepsis and serious trauma, absorption of endotoxin will cause "shock lung" or wet lungs. The lung fills up with water just from stress and trauma. **Andrew Murray:** A Chinese study published in *The Lancet* on March 11th stated that 59% of 191 COVID-19 patients developed sepsis, and sepsis was present in 100% of those who died. It was the most commonly observed complication.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The heart, lungs, and intestine are the main places the virus infects. But sepsis alone can cause both heart and lung symptoms. **Andrew Murray:** I also wanted to mention work looking at Vitamin D as a viable antiviral. They discussed how African Americans are particularly susceptible, potentially due to lower Vitamin D levels.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It revs up the immune system to resist viral and bacterial infections, but a major part of its effect is as an anti-inflammatory. Aspirin is also not only anti-inflammatory but has well-established broad-spectrum antiviral activity.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Our surgeon friend confirmed that simple remedies like aspirin are really helping people because it is so anti-inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw the Kaiser Family Foundation discussing the funding from the CARES Act. If a patient is admitted with a coronavirus diagnosis, the hospital gets about $16,000. **Andrew Murray:** Without being cynical, this might explain why you don't hear about heart disease or pulmonary problems right now—everyone is getting admitted under the COVID diagnosis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, suddenly very few people are dying of the usual things.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Also, if the virus can be present in the intestine and not the nose, nasal swabs might be giving false negatives.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I noticed the CDC's chart of influenza cases and deaths fell off like a cliff around April 1st, with a sudden lurch upward in corona diagnoses. It looked exactly as if you had just redefined influenza as corona.

**Caller (Kirsten):** In the March show, Dr. Peat talked about a lab working on vaccines that had to close last year. I was wondering if he could repeat where that was?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That particular one was Fort Detrick, but there was one at the University of North Carolina working with them. That was a *Nature* article, I believe from November 2015.

**Caller (Kirsten):** Was it shut down for sanitation issues?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but that same lab had been previously closed for a moratorium on a particular kind of virus research. One group of virologists argued this research was intrinsically useless and dangerous. In 2014, the government put a three-year moratorium on that kind of research. Within a few weeks, Tony Fauci took $3.7 million to fund the Wuhan lab to continue the research that was considered questionable or dangerous. **Caller (Kirsten):** This is Dr. Tony Fauci from the White House?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. He apparently ignored the moratorium. I think that would be criminal to continue banned research outside the U.S. where they could get away with it.

**Andrew Murray:** Is this "gain of function"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Generally, it is necessary to create a chimera—a combination of two totally different viruses—to get a really good gain of function. This process was developed for military uses. I think it was Nixon who ordered the end of bio-warfare virology, but it continued under the guise of vaccine research. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** The angiotensin system is responsive to stress and emotions.

**Andrew Murray:** So it's the very thing that would be ramped up in the presence of stress.

**Caller (Corly):** Regarding Losartan, I was under the impression that medication affects the ACE1 inhibitors, but the virus attacks the receptor sites of ACE2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** ACE2 is the enzyme that destroys angiotensin. Angiotensin acts on Angiotensin Receptor Number 1 (AT1). That is the thing that activates constriction of blood vessels, inflammation, and fibrosis of the heart. All the bad stuff is activated at AT1 by angiotensin.

The "receptor" for the virus is ACE2. Its function in the body is to destroy the toxic angiotensin and convert it into a beneficial form called Angiotensin 1-7, which is anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory. The virus sticking to that protein limits its ability to detoxify.

Losartan is an Angiotensin Receptor Inhibitor Number 1. Losartan blocks the bad effects of angiotensin and, at the same time, allows the body to increase the production of the ACE2 enzyme—the protective destroyer of angiotensin.

**Caller (Portland):** Can UV light or ozone be used to disinfect the air? Could you cycle air through a filter?

Standard medical thinking is that viral replication causes the problems, but actually, it's the inflammation that leads to the replication of the virus. If you stop the inflammation, you don't have to worry about the virus.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's not critical to think about sterilizing the air?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is fine to sterilize the air, but you can't sterilize the inside of the body. Some people are advocating treating the blood with ozone, but that could intensify the inflammation.

**Caller (Connecticut):** What are your thoughts on lactoferrin as an antimicrobial? And is there anything you can do to protect against adjuvants in vaccines?
