**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's March 19, 2021 edition of *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** Once again we're joined by Dr. Raymond Peat to bring his expertise to bear on the topic. This month is a continuing topic regarding the current coronavirus pandemic, the science behind some of the facts, and some of the alternatives. Specifically, the rollout of the coronavirus vaccines and the potential implications discussed by professionals and scientists around the world. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hi.

**Andrew Murray:** We’ve spent a while discussing the pandemic's effects, the death figures versus infection numbers, and the CDC admitting numbers have been conflated. Recently, I saw an article by a Belgian virologist, Geert Vanden Bossche. He has a long professional background with the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and companies producing vaccines. 

He argues, similar to Dr. Simone Gold, that for a 99.6% survivable infection, this experimental drug should be the last thing considered. Vanden Bossche suggests that because of the mechanism of the drug, there is a potential for new variants to emerge under selective pressure because of the specific antibodies targeting the virus. He argues that natural killer cells are a far better way to deal with this. Is this a "leaky vaccine" situation? What do you make of his discussion on viral immune escape?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** His point about the mutating virus escaping from a vaccine the way it's being used is good standard opinion. What people can justly disagree on is the risk. He gets very excited thinking the risk is very high. If you aren't convinced that the present virus is so very deadly, then an increase of virulence might not be so dangerous as he is suggesting. It's a possibility, but I personally don't think it compares to other ongoing threats, like the risk of world war breaking out. I think the idea of the vaccine causing a worsening epidemic is a moderate to small risk.

However, another very important point he makes is regarding the vaccine creating a very powerful antibody reaction to knock out one particular pathogen. It is effective for blocking the development of that pathogen, but you've devoted your immune system to reacting to that one very specialized problem. Meanwhile, there is an infinite number of potential immunological dangers in the world. Anytime you suffer an infection or a vaccination that causes a very powerful production of one single type of antibody, you're diverting resources from the ability to respond to that infinite number of immune challenges.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He emphasizes natural killer cells. These exist in any healthy organism. Within about three days of a viral infection, they will go to work to kill the cells damaged by the virus. They don't give their attention to killing a virus, but to getting rid of the cells that are being used to multiply the virus. That's why 99.6% of people not only survive, but most don't even know they're sick. At the very earliest stage, the natural killer cells are knocking out the cells that would be multiplying the virus.

He proposes a different kind of vaccine to improve natural killer cell functions. However, it turns out that all the treatments active against COVID-19—the drugs helpful in reducing mortality—have had very significant anti-inflammatory effects. From the very first, the Chinese noticed that an anti-serotonin drug, cinanserin, prevented the development of the infection. Since then, several antihistamines, natural flavonoids from fruits and vegetables, progesterone, and angiotensin receptor blockers have been found effective.

If you look at the natural killer cell, it knocks out the host cell which gets inflamed. Being inflamed makes it a factory for making more viruses. It's the inflammation which is knocked out at the very beginning. Vitamin D, for example, is a great anti-inflammatory agent that stops the COVID infection, largely through improving the action of natural killer cells.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Are you saying that when you have one of these vaccines, it causes your immune system to be highly specialized in dealing with the spike protein, and it fails to promote natural killer cell formation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not only the natural killer cells, but every other level. We normally have a bunch of antibodies which have an overlapping activity against anything you want to put into the bloodstream. These natural antibodies are just part of our basic defense system. The power of your body to manufacture proteins naturally is limited. When the immune system is swamped by a single antigen and the antibodies for it, it sends waves through the antibody-producing system and directs the attention towards that one antigen.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you could become more susceptible to other infections?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There were several studies in recent years looking at the after-effects of the flu vaccine. They found that vaccinated people had a much greater rate of coronavirus infections the following year—not necessarily this particular one, but coronaviruses in general. It's well established that immunity to one thing makes you more susceptible to infection with other things. 

I talked about immunology at the University of Veracruz 40 years ago, and at that time, it was already a current topic that antibodies are a very touchy thing to mess with. The theory of immunity and resistance has been going through a paradigm shift for the last 10 or 15 years, but the official science establishment is acting as if this isn't happening.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Simone Gold mentioned antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) and predicted a rise in autoimmunity in the coming years.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's an established thing that specialized antibodies increase your risk not only for every other kind of infection but for general inflammatory disease and autoimmunity. There is now an autoimmune disease epidemic going on that corresponds very closely to the huge expansion of the use of vaccines around 1980.

The nature of the immune system has been described to suit the doctrine of antibodies and germ-specific treatment. It goes back about 100 years, following Paul Ehrlich's "magic bullet" concept—the idea that every disease has a very specific poison or antibody to attack it. There never was a real magic bullet of a chemical nature, but this idea dominated the concept of natural immunity.

**Andrew Murray:** You’ve mentioned before that estrogen is extremely inflammatory and confers cancerous risk. You also mentioned that estrogen itself is connected to autoimmunity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. One of the first pro-inflammatory effects understood for estrogen was miscarriage. Estrogen creates an inflammatory state in the uterus leading to the death of the embryo. Progesterone's anti-inflammatory effect protects against miscarriage. 

The effect of estrogen is to increase the B cells—the cells that manufacture antibodies—and to increase inflammatory signals. The more estrogen dominance there is, the more B cells tend to overproduce their antibodies. This leads to autoimmune diseases, which are also just variants of the natural aging process. Many people are now referring to "inflammaging." The paradigm shift is realizing that inflammation is not part of the normal healthy immune process; it's part of a deranged or weakened immune system.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So children have such a healthy immune system with so many natural killer cells that they kill the cells breeding the virus without symptoms, whereas the elderly have fewer natural killer cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A Vitamin D deficiency or an estrogen excess lowers the function of the natural killer cells.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding variants, there is the South American P1 variant and the South African variant. They are saying these variants reduce the effectiveness of neutralizing monoclonal antibodies. Do you think there is a reasonable expectation that a dangerous variant could emerge because of the pressure from the experimental drugs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's always a valid possibility; other viruses have escaped vaccines and become a little more virulent. But regarding COVID-19 itself, its danger has been publicized without revealing the evidence for it. People are suing state and federal health departments asking them to reveal the evidence justifying disruptive policies like lockdowns and vaccination. They are refusing to deliver that evidence.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I saw an article today that said COVID is spiking in over a dozen states, most with high vaccination rates.

**Andrew Murray:** I also saw reports stating, "Don't be surprised when vaccinated people get infected." They say this is entirely expected.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The drug companies are saying it's all coincidence. Hundreds of people are dying right after getting vaccinated, or becoming paralyzed or fainting, and they say that's within the realm of chance. But when you compare the number of deaths between two different vaccines—I think it was Pfizer compared to AstraZeneca—there was a significantly greater mortality among the Pfizer product.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And 20 countries in Europe have banned AstraZeneca because of blood clots.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's an obvious thing to do. I think anticipation of danger is why Merck decided not to come out with a vaccine, even though Pfizer says their vaccine is now the second most profitable drug in history. Merck felt the need for caution in going into something that could kill millions of people.

**Andrew Murray:** What treatments would you suggest? We've mentioned Baical skullcap, pleurisy root, and elderberry.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** From an herbal perspective, licorice is like the herbal equivalent of steroids to quell inflammation. Thyme is also very anti-inflammatory and helps expectorate mucus. Dr. Peat, are there other agents?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Zinc-rich foods are a basic defense mechanism. Adequate Vitamin A is also important; studies show supplementing Vitamin A reduced a wide range of diseases. Generally, broad-spectrum, well-balanced nutrition will increase your general health and resistance.

**Caller (Whitethorn):** I’m curious if the doctor has recommendations for "long haulers," specifically regarding the loss of smell (anosmia) that hasn't come back.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Zinc is one of the essential factors for the olfactory and taste nerves, possibly because it's involved in the carbonic anhydrase enzyme. That enzyme regulates the production of carbon dioxide versus bicarbonate, which is a major anti-inflammatory factor. The anti-inflammatory effects of zinc are largely working through the metabolism of carbon dioxide.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Oysters, mussels, and clams are quite a rich source of zinc.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw a study showing a correlation between low zinc levels and hepatitis infection. Do you think the mechanism for reversing anosmia with zinc is based on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very possibly.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about natural killer cell-based vaccines?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vanden Bossche was working on a vaccine for chickens. It seems like a possibility. But I think the general approach should be things that increase your ability to retain carbon dioxide. Zinc is part of that enzyme reaction, but calcium channel blockers, which showed real benefits in treating COVID patients, also happen to increase carbon dioxide retention ability.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you know someone who has had the shot, is there a risk for the unvaccinated person to be around them? Does it differ between the mRNA and the attenuated virus vaccines?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think continuing to be conscious of washing your hands is good, but I don't think that's a real serious risk to catch something from the vaccinated person. However, other vaccines have turned out to create a vaccine-related epidemic. Currently in Africa, polio entirely dependent on the vaccine is now the main epidemic concern. So there is precedent for the vaccine itself to cause and spread disease.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I guess it's good advice for people that have had the vaccine to continue wearing their masks to minimize the chance of spreading anything.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Since they have participated in a completely unknown experiment, and they are the experimental guinea pigs, they should volunteer to wear the mask.

**Caller (David from SF):** I think mismanaging this epidemic has to do with a land grab. But I wanted to ask: Since this is a new disease, do you think it has its origins in pollution? Wuhan is one of the most polluted cities. Also, is there any natural critter or food that will consume a virus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are good publications showing that the inflammation caused by air pollution does make you much more susceptible to viral infections. As for destroying the virus, sunlight—specifically ultraviolet light—destroys it fairly quickly.

**Caller (David from SF):** I’ve used cheap pot smoke to induce coughing and clear my lungs during bronchitis. I wonder if there is a symptomatic way of getting rid of it, like dust or ash in the lungs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Speaking of herbs, emodin, which is the active ingredient in Chinese rhubarb and cascara sagrada, specifically blocks the coronavirus spike protein and the angiotensin-converting enzyme. Besides being anti-inflammatory and restorative of mitochondrial respiration, it has specific antiviral activity.

**Andrew Murray:** Would the therapeutic dose cause purging effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The sensitivity varies. But if you're going to treat something deadly, like advanced kidney failure—where kidneys are improved by emodin—I don't think anyone worries about a little laxative action.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For people having adverse effects to the first shot of the mRNA vaccine, what would you recommend to help mitigate those effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first thing is to make sure their blood sugar doesn't fall. Falling blood sugar is the most powerful pro-inflammatory thing possible. Any little allergen can become deadly when your blood sugar is very low. Raising the blood sugar quiets the immune inflammatory reactions. Baking soda, providing both bicarbonate (carbon dioxide) and sodium, is another quick-acting anti-inflammatory.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you. We do have cascara available on our website now, westernbotanicalmedicine.com.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat, for your time. For those wanting to look into Dr. Peat's research, you can visit raypeat.com. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: April 2021 KMUD
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray. We run these shows every third Friday of the month. We have been joined for the longest time by Dr. Raymond Peat, PhD, who has been weighing in with his academic take on a lot of different subjects that are sometimes controversial, but always informative. So once again, we're very pleased to have Dr. Peat with us on the show.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I'm here.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who perhaps have never heard you before or would like to find out more about you, would you please give a roundup of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was studying and teaching in the humanities for about 10 years before I decided to go to graduate school in biology. That was 1968 to 1972 at the University of Oregon, where I got a PhD in reproductive physiology and aging. My intention had been to study nerve biology, following up on ideas of how language and the brain work. However, because of dogmatism in the nerve biology section, I ended up with reproductive physiology as a way to concentrate on the interactions of hormones, metabolism, and development. Over the next almost 50 years, I've been continuing to study those areas.

**Andrew Murray:** Much of what I've understood from you in the last 10 years has been related to creative energy production and stemming the dissolution of energy. Tonight's subject is epigenetics. I think I could sum it up by saying it is a heritable phenotype, the change of which does not involve alterations in the DNA sequence.

To clarify for listeners: the *genotype* gives the instruction, and the *phenotype* is the organism's appearance. I read that epigenetics may account for a significant fraction of "missing heritability," as DNA mutations only explain a minority of the expected heritable fraction.

Could you describe the basic outlines of epigenetics? Whether it is DNA changes in methylation, the histones that genes wrap around, or non-coding RNA, how do these changes bring about profound shifts in genetic information?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The established powers in biology have been very resistant to the idea that there could be any transgenerational influence of experience. That has involved reducing and emptying the idea of what happens during adaptation. Why does exercise build stronger muscles? What happens during learning?

The very idea of change was resisted powerfully by people who saw the organism as a compilation of specific traits. The idea was that our traits and parts were like a clock mechanism—the parts allowed the machine to work, but nothing very deep was changing during the adult lifetime. This has an extensive ideological background where the organism was seen as a compilation of eternal, unchangeable parts.

However, when you look at the experience of yourself or other organisms, you see that every day there is learning and change. You can't really do anything twice, because the second time you do it, you're a different person. Every moment of your experience, you are in development. The immune system is constantly operating and recording your interactions. The structure of your brain is constantly changing, and that interacts with your constantly changing immune system.

**Andrew Murray:** So it isn't just a technical mechanism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The ideas constantly changing in your mind are actually changing the properties of brain cells, immune cells, and likely all cells. Pretty much every functional cell in the body is likely to have a fine nervous fiber. The body isn't just chemically communicating like a swarm of insects; there is a deep penetration of fine nerve fibers integrating the whole body with the conscious purpose of the organism.

Technically, people use "epigenetics" to mean certain chemical changes that persist from the state of one cell after that cell divides. But the persistence of a physiological state from moment to moment is the simplest and most basic idea of epigenetics. Every moment, we inherit the whole past of our organism.

An extreme biological analogy would be the transformation of a tadpole to a frog. That involves epigenetic changes of a very drastic sort. It is good to keep that in mind as hidden out of sight; our immune system and nervous system are having these constant little transformations. It's not as drastic as a tadpole turning into a frog, but our immune system and brain are recognizably different over very short time spans.

**Andrew Murray:** This reminds me of the concept that you are what you believe yourself to be. Positive affirmations seem to be a roadmap to a better future because they are a way of changing your perception, mental state, and physical state via epigenetic changes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Positive or negative, the environment imposes changes on us. For example, if you put an animal in isolation—social distancing—the animal becomes more inflamed. The whole immune system is deranged in the direction of inflammation just by the depressing experience of being isolated. If you reverse that and give them social contacts and an enriched environment, that ends the inflammatory processes and starts the organism back on a constructive developmental process.

These ideas have been known to common people for hundreds of years. Lamarck, for example, said that if an organism needs longer legs or stronger arms, it will develop them by striving. Exercise improves physiology and structure. But the Darwinists didn't like the idea of the intelligence of the common organism. They invented the assumption of randomness—a metaphysical idea created out of thin air. They claimed biological changes can only be random and unpredictable.

They view adaptation as simply a summing up of many meaningless, random diffusions of molecules. The avoidance of purposefulness in life processes has been going on for about 200 years.

**Andrew Murray:** We have discussed how isolation and authoritarianism—deficiencies in freedom and social engagement—can be construed as very negative for us epigenetically. While our DNA might not physically change, genes can be switched off by these stresses.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The things activated by authoritarianism and isolation include an excess of serotonin production. That causes a rigid tendency toward conformism. At the same time, it cools the body, slows metabolism, and makes it more passive, leaning towards learned helplessness.

Excess serotonin activates other stress-related hormones, but its worst function is to slow the metabolism and increase inflammation, tending towards degeneration. Estrogen is the other killing, stress-related chemical that lowers body temperature, predisposes the body to inflammation, makes it more receptive to authoritarianism, and creates a failure of adaptiveness.

**Andrew Murray:** So this is a compounding factor—one negative thing after another. But you mentioned this is reversible?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The whole idea of epigenetics is flexibility and reversibility. It is very antagonistic to doctrines that say cancer, advanced heart disease, or kidney disease are incurable. The epigenetic idea explains how they develop from bad environmental opportunities and potentially shows routes by which they can be reversed.

Where the genetic view says you can only develop so far if your genes are bad, the epigenetic approach says genes are only a very sketchy determinant. Many other things determine our vitality. For example, prenatal exposure to too much estrogen lowers body temperature, reduces brain growth, and predisposes the organism to obesity and lifelong weakness. Conversely, exposure to extra glucose or progesterone during gestation increases brain growth, the thickness of the cortex, metabolic rate, and longevity.

**Caller:** I have two questions. First, back in 1899, medical textbooks listed about 45 illnesses allegedly cured or improved by ingesting turpentine. Today the mindset is that it is poison. Do you believe they were right back in 1899?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is still research going on showing that the turpentine family—each type of conifer has its own variant—has beneficial effects. Some stimulate wound healing and are anti-inflammatory; others are antibiotic. I don't know where the culture of fearing turpentine came from, but it coincided with the disappearance of cheap turpentine as paint thinner. It used to cost a couple of dollars a gallon; now it is very expensive and hard to get.

**Caller:** My second question relates to the thyroid. Broda Barnes and others mention taking iodine. In the current environment with halogens that block iodine, is it reasonable to take a pure, bioavailable form of iodine in a very small amount to help the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the last 20 years, several dozen studies have shown that thyroid disease corresponds to the introduction of iodized salt.

**Caller:** I agree, iodized salt is a bad product with other toxins. But if you get a pure form, say 500 to 600 micrograms—literally one drop—is that reasonable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I agree with you. I think over one milligram a day is risky, but 500 micrograms of pure iodine is not crazy. And regarding turpentine, I think that is something that needs fresh research in terms of what we know about cytokines and inflammation.

**Caller:** I heard the guest speak in general terms, but I'm wondering if we could get more specific about how epigenetics works biochemically. My understanding involves DNA methylation and histone modification. Could the guest talk about the limitations? The idea that we can "do anything" with epigenetics seems like a misuse of the science. It doesn't change the DNA; it just modifies whether DNA is turned on or off.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The attachment of methyl groups to DNA has garnered the most interest among standard genetics workers. In principle, with stress and aging, we lose the ability to activate genes. The general idea is that our DNA becomes too methylated, turning off massive amounts of genes so that we are slow to renew cell proteins.

However, certain islands of DNA become *under-methylated* due to hormone imbalances and stress. If a tumor suppressor becomes methylated, you stop repressing tumors. If you have under-methylation of an oncogene, you can activate it.

The second most popular mechanism is changes in histones. There is methylation of histones and also attachment of acetyl groups. When an acetyl group is attached, it lets the DNA become active; deacetylators are gene-suppressive.

Now, the micro-RNA regulatory systems have complicated the area. The unexpressed 97% or 98% of our DNA, which doesn't make genes, is clearly involved in regulatory processes that are not genetic in the ordinary sense but contribute to epigenetic momentum.

I think the emphasis on DNA methylation has been taken out of proportion. Estrogen and progesterone are both major regulators of gene methylation and histone acetylation. The hormones and the system's energy are largely regulated by thyroid hormone and the balance between carbon dioxide and lactate. Carbon dioxide is the quieting, efficiency-promoting, anti-inflammatory substance. Lactate is the excitatory, inflammation-promoting, de-energizing substance associated with low metabolic efficiency.

**Andrew Murray:** To sum up, when the organism is fully energized—plenty of CO2, active thyroid, and metabolism working correctly—there is much less chance of epigenetic changes taking place that would destabilize the system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Energy is the thing that protects and guides the proper expansion of our structures. The energy increase under the influence of thyroid, oxidative metabolism, and carbon dioxide is a constant flow tending to complexify and build structure. If your energy fails, it goes the other way; structure deteriorates.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for giving your time again, Dr. Peat. For those listening, Dr. Raymond Peat's website is . He has a fully referenced library of newsletters and articles.

Next month, we may discuss Dr. Nicholas Gonzalez, a medical doctor who had a successful practice treating pancreatic cancer but faced significant opposition. Until the third Friday of May, thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: May 2021 KMUD
transcriptText:
**Hosts:** Andrew Murray & Sarah Johanneson Murray
**Guest:** Dr. Raymond Peat

---

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Welcome.

**Andrew Murray:** You're invited to call in with any questions related to this month's topic of mitochondria, immunity, and natural resistance. Once again, we're very pleased to be joined by Dr. Raymond Peat to weigh in with his expertise on this subject. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** I'll outline what we're going to talk about. The main thrust of tonight's show is going to be natural resistance and immunity, and we're going to discuss the role of mitochondria. There is some very interesting plant-based material responsible for a cell-stabilizing effect that we're going to describe in terms of stabilizing the cell and producing energy in the mitochondria. Dr. Peat, we should probably start by asking you to describe your academic and professional background.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I didn't study biology professionally until about 12 years after graduating from college. I decided to go back and get a PhD at the University of Oregon from 1968 to 1972. Previously, I had been working in literature, education, and various humanities areas. After finishing my PhD in physiology, I continued using the ideas I had researched to apply to different fields, studying the brain in particular, reproductive hormones, and how nutrition interacts with development and health in general.

**Andrew Murray:** I looked at a wide range of natural products which have been shown to be sources of mast cell stabilizers. In terms of degranulation—the histamine-type reaction upon which inflammation is predicated—there are several different classes of compounds ranging from flavonoids to coumarins, cinnamic acid, resveratrol, and quercetin.

I want to get a discussion going regarding the energy potential of cells. We've mentioned medicinal plants like Lapacho (*Tabebuia impetiginosa*, or Pau d'Arco) and Cat's Claw (*Uncaria tomentosa*). Lapacho produces the compound lapachol, and Cat's Claw is used in the treatment of borreliosis. Both of these, as well as the flavonoids we will look at, have very dark pigments. I know you have a fairly clear answer for their benefits regarding mitochondrial function and ATP production. Do you have anything to say on the nature of the pigment and how that pigment acts electronically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was in graduate school, I was working on how mitochondrial oxidation relates not only to aging and fertility but also to resistance against disease and development. Aging is a bad outcome of development, but development of the organism is something that's always happening. When it is under the influence of oxidation, the outcome is constructive. When it's under the influence of something that blocks mitochondrial oxidation, the outcome is always bad.

It was already known in the 1960s that, in general, purple pigments tended to promote better, more efficient oxidation. I was always running around testing various plant materials, especially the purple and red ones. Several people observed that red pigments tended to be sedating and blue pigments stimulating. My main interest was in how the color related to the structure and why it improved mitochondrial oxidation.

In the early years of the 20th century, Frederick Koch, a biochemistry and physiology professor at the University of Michigan, found that a certain way of preparing a catalyst—he used a hot platinum electrode to oxidize alcohol—produced a very intense deep blue or purple pigment. He found that it catalyzed mitochondrial physiology and function. This was many years before the ubiquinone system (Coenzyme Q10) was known. Koch was working on that chemical structure, which he knew to be a quinone, but he hadn't even attempted to extract that material from cells; he just reasoned that it had to be there to catalyze oxygen.

It turned out that this quinone he was producing involved multiple double-bonded carbon-oxygen bonds resonating in relation to each other. The more you have in a sequence interacting with each other, the more powerful it is as an oxidant. After he was effectively chased out of the U.S. by the FDA and FBI, he went to Brazil and studied natural plant substances there. Lapacho was one that he was interested in because of its color. This turns out to be an analog of our own quinone system, or Coenzyme Q10 system, which is also very closely related to the vitamin K structure and the natural anti-inflammatory antibiotics. Tetracyclines have a very intense system of conjugated double bonds analogous to these other natural activators of respiration.

They happen to activate the production of energy as well as increasing the consumption of oxygen. Going back about 70 or 80 years, it was known that anything that uncoupled—reduced the efficiency of energy production in the form of ATP—would make the oxygen system of the mitochondrion run faster and create a more oxidized state of the cell. This principle was used in diet pills because it would make you burn up fat quickly, but it was also found to intensify immunity in the sense of being able to detect and throw off cancer cells that were disseminated but not yet forming tumors. When you made the cells oxidize probably 50% to 100% more intensely than normal by using this uncoupling chemical, the cancer cells would be attacked by the rest of the body, flare up, and be thrown off.

**Andrew Murray:** This is in the presence of these quinones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** This particular chemical, dinitrophenol, uses the nitro group, which is actually more toxic than the system the body uses—much riskier. A lot of people killed themselves trying to use that chemical for weight loss. But it illustrates the principle that when you run the system so it oxidizes more thoroughly, it does something to the immune system that resists both infectious organisms and cancer.

One of the changes that happens when you uncouple the cell and increase mitochondrial oxidation is that iron becomes safely put into a storage form, the ferric oxidized form. The opposite of that process happens when the cell has some obstruction to oxygen use. Many toxins and microorganisms can interfere with the use of oxygen. In that case, the iron is reduced electronically and goes into the toxic ferrous form, which creates very powerful free radical forms of oxygen—hydroxyl radicals—which then damage everything in the cell. Protectively, the cell has this basic mechanism of increasing fever, for example, to increase the body temperature and oxidation by a natural form of uncoupling.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So going back to what you said about iron and these quinone compounds found in things like Tabebuia and Pau d'Arco—do those also cause the body to put iron in a safer form rather than the very toxic form you mentioned?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, everything that maintains even the normal rate of cellular oxidation maintains a basic stable cell immune condition. It's only when something has caused a dangerous disruption that the body has to resort to fever to increase that state and go back to its resting normal rate of good, high oxidation.

**Andrew Murray:** Just in case people aren't familiar with the mitochondria, they are the machinery that generates the energy—organelles within the cell. They use food converted into a chemical called ATP. Essentially, nutrients increase the energy electrons in the form of a substance called NADH. This is used by protein complexes to pump protons, creating a gradient that catalyzes the production of ATP. It is this currency of energy which is used like thyroid very much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid hormone does increase the uncoupled oxidation of glucose, raising the temperature. When you're feeling maximally energized and efficient with good thyroid function, you aren't really being "efficient" in the sense of making a maximum number of ATP per oxygen. Running the oxygen through the system maintains a favorable balance of NAD (the oxidized form) to NADH.

When you block thyroid function or any aspect of the system in the mitochondrion that consumes oxygen, you pile up too much NADH. That is the reducing stress state of the cell.

Some of these plant substances—flavonoids, for example—look like antioxidants or reductants in the test tube because of their hydroxy group. However, once they get inside the cell, they change their structure, lose the hydrogen, create the quinone keto group (the double-bonded oxygen-carbon), and become a catalyst to maintain the oxidized state of the cell and lower the ratio of NADH to NAD.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding the cell stabilizing effect, Quercetin is one of these flavonoids that has been mentioned in medical journals along with hydroxychloroquine and ivermectin for alternative approaches to treating or preventing viral issues. Quercetin is found richly in citrus fruits and dark berries.

We find a lot of the flavonoids are useful in terms of stabilizing mast cells and preventing degranulation—the inflammation from histamine release that produces vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and respiratory trouble. These flavonoids range from herbs like Dyer's Weld (*Reseda luteola*) containing luteolin, diosmetin from olives, and apigenin from parsley, artichokes, chamomile, and celery. There is also gingetin from Ginkgo, EGCG from green tea (also in berries and apples), silymarin from milk thistle, and scopoletin.

Other compounds include cinnamic acid from cinnamon, ellagic acid from berries and walnuts, and resveratrol from *Polygonum cuspidatum*. All of these are plant-based compounds, either pigment products or other natural products.

**Caller (David):** I tuned in late. Are you saying that list of herbs would make your tissue "pucker up" and make it harder for the virus to grab on? Also, if COVID makes your lungs "pucker up" so much that they turn into "dead coral" (fibrosis), is there something we could eat that would revive the lungs? Like pruning a tree to get a starter growing from live tissue?

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: August 2021 KMUD
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* on KMUD Garberville, 91.1 FM. From 7:30 until the end of the show at 8:00, you are invited to call in with questions related to this month's topic of iron and its dangers. Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us again. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I'm here.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you for joining again. When the subject of iron was suggested as a topic, I started looking at articles from PubMed and the National Institutes of Health. I wanted to preface the show with something I've written to let people know clearly where the show content is going and where the evidence is coming from.

I know you've written several newsletters and articles related to the dangers of iron. It seems pertinent to the information and science surrounding the inflammatory nature of COVID, especially surrounding the thousands of fatalities in people receiving the experimental drug from thromboembolic processes. This is added to the acute and chronic inflammatory processes stimulated by receiving this drug, and the potential massive autoimmune disease going forward.

Tonight, we will be discussing the link between iron, estrogen, and the suppression of peptides like cathelicidin and hepcidin. We will discuss the experimental drug for COVID-19 and the rising numbers of deaths and adverse events reported to VAERS. With this in mind, we are pleased to welcome Dr. Peat to discuss the physiology of inflammation and its relationship to COVID-19.

Dr. Peat, regarding the serious outcomes of COVID—people on ventilators or those who have died—and the relationship between iron and inflammation, would you like to discuss the physiology of this process? Let's put some science to the mechanism of inflammation and look for a strategic solution.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are lots of ways that iron triggers inflammation, but the best way to start thinking about it is that inflammation triggers the excessive uptake and retention of iron. Inflammation often affects hepcidin, which is a germicidal peptide that also regulates iron. Its function is to suppress the absorption of iron. When you have enough iron, you increase your hepcidin, which is virucidal and bactericidal, and it blocks the absorption of iron.

However, one of the effects of inflammation is to increase the absorption and retention of iron. When it is extreme, it ends up damaging cells, such as the red blood cells. When you are stressed by anything, you tend to release free fatty acids into your bloodstream. Too many free fatty acids activate destabilizing things that tend to dissolve your red cells and activate lipid peroxidation. Under stress, the lifespan of your red blood cells is shorter, meaning they are increasing your iron burden—the free, dangerous, uncontrolled iron.

Another effect of inflammation is that it increases the enzyme heme oxygenase. This enzyme breaks down the heme group. When your red blood cells have leaked hemoglobin, the heme itself is a dangerous, wild catalyst leading to lipid peroxidation. It has to be disposed of. But in breaking down heme, this heme oxygenase enzyme liberates bilirubin (the chemical involved in jaundice), creates a molecule of carbon monoxide, and liberates a free atom of iron.

Chronic stress makes you dispose of these heme groups constantly. Especially in the brain, they are very dangerous. This stress-induced heme oxygenase is constantly dropping these random iron atoms along with carbon monoxide and bilirubin. This is probably one of the major factors in iron overload. It is an internal process involving the breaking down of red cells.

At the same time, lowered hepcidin under stress leads you to retain more iron from your food. Inflammation—specifically pro-inflammatory cytokines, interleukins, prostaglandins like PGE2, and tumor necrosis factor—activates aromatase, producing estrogen. So, estrogen goes up in inflammation. Under the influence of high estrogen, a woman will retain several times as much of the iron in her food as a man does who isn't under stress. There are several vicious circles: inflammation leads to heme oxygenase, which leads to estrogen, which leads to more inflammation and iron retention.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This is something that can be easily tested on a blood test, right? You can look at the iron saturation on a blood test.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The transferrin saturation percentage is probably the most useful thing.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is that better than the iron saturation percentage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is what they mean when they say iron saturation—it is how loaded the transferrin molecule is.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** All right, because then you can test the quantity of transferrin as well.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw an article on the NIH website related to COVID outcomes. They found a statistical correlation between high ferritin levels and poor outcomes. They were suggesting iron chelation to lower ferritin levels to mitigate serious outcomes. What do you say about ferritin levels and chelation as a method of helping people with known high ferritin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several people have been talking about protecting against disease, and now the coronavirus, by chelating iron. Going back decades, people realized that free iron is associated with infections—parasites, fungus, bacteria, viruses—and cancer. Cancer acts like an invading pathogen in its hunger for iron. Things that want to grow fast need a supply of available iron.

Ferritin should basically be an intracellular storage form that is invisible to anything in the blood. But as you get stressed and overloaded, it starts leaking out of the cells. Just looking at your blood level, you can't really tell what your stored iron is because inflammation makes the iron leak out. Both transferrin and ferritin in your blood increase during inflammation. So, as you experience inflammation, your blood iron rises apart from the real level inside your cells.

Fifty years ago, doctors were diagnosing iron deficiency based on low hemoglobin and hematocrit and prescribing iron to a high proportion of female patients. It was an Anglo-American custom going back to the 19th century regarding "chlorosis" or "green sickness."

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Was that from too much iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The diagnosis was that because their blood was low in hemoglobin, it was a "weakness typical of young women" that made them look green. The green was likely a combination of poorly oxygenated blood giving a blue tint, combined with yellow bilirubin from the breakdown of red blood cells. It was likely a sluggish liver and low thyroid being unable to get rid of bilirubin.

Arsenic was commonly used to treat it because irritation stimulates the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. In the 1920s, when arsenic was discarded, they kept the same process of stimulating bone marrow using high doses of iron—sometimes horribly high doses of intravenous or intramuscular iron.

**Andrew Murray:** Probably causing massive damage and driving up cancers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I knew women who had black marks all over their legs from injected iron.

**Andrew Murray:** Regarding ferritin, if someone has a level of 800—twice the upper limit—what would you think about iron chelators like deferoxamine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Years ago, I was interested in deferoxamine. Just as I started thinking about using it, I read that it could move the iron into worse places and lead to cancer. I'm a little skeptical about what kind of chelator is used.

**Andrew Murray:** So it wouldn't bind it up for excretion; it would shunt it somewhere else?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens with a lot of chelation. When they think they're chelating mercury, lead, or cadmium out of the bone where it was sitting passively, they often move it into the kidneys and brain.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you know of any safe chelators?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coffee is the only one I feel safe with. It has been shown to reduce the bound heavy metals in kidneys and other crucial organs, especially the liver. Many studies show that coffee drinkers have low ALT, an indicator of liver stress. Heavy coffee drinkers have an extremely low incidence of all kinds of liver diseases, including liver cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Haven't you said also that calcium and eggshell is a good chelator of heavy metals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In a very indirect way. When you analyze the minerals in arteries, kidneys, and brains where you shouldn't have calcium crystals, they find iron and other heavy metals associated with them. This association occurred in calcium-deficient areas. When you are deficient in calcium, you load up on whatever "junk metal" happens to be around.

The reason is that a stressed tissue shifts from oxidative metabolism (producing carbon dioxide) to glycolytic production of lactic acid. When a cell produces lactic acid, it leaves a slightly alkaline shift inside the cell, ionizing the cells and making them retain both calcium and any positively charged metals like iron and aluminum.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What foods are high in iron that we should limit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It matters how much calcium they have, too. If you aren't getting enough calcium to turn off your parathyroid hormone and keep your metabolism towards carbon dioxide, you're going to retain more iron. Meat, and liver in particular, has very low calcium and very high iron. It's extremely important to have coffee when you're eating those to block the iron absorption. Vitamin D also helps avoid iron retention by lowering parathyroid hormone.

**Andrew Murray:** We have a question from a caller asking if fulvates or fulvic minerals would be good for binding iron.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they would probably hold it in your intestine to some extent, the way they bind minerals in the soil.

**Andrew Murray:** So if you ate contaminated food, it might hold it, but it wouldn't necessarily pull it out of the rest of your body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I haven't seen research on that, but it's a possibility. However, if you have a lot of stomach acid, the acid might release minerals associated with what you took in.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I know it's not a good idea to eat clay regularly because it has a lot of iron in it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, when it hits your stomach, there is a slight dissolution of the clay substance.

**Andrew Murray:** Just to wrap up chelation: you don't recommend standard chelators because they pull metals from safe stores into circulation, but coffee has an excretory ability?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Also, when we make acids like citric acid or succinic acid inside our cells, if we make enough that some moves into the bloodstream, that is known to carry aluminum and iron out of the cell into the bloodstream. But if you *eat* those acids, they will pick up heavy metals in your intestine and carry them *into* your body. Our body creates a stream of chelators which are constantly tending to pull cadmium and aluminum out.

**Andrew Murray:** Would it be okay to take capsules of ground coffee or instant coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure, capsules of instant coffee, for example.

**Caller (Eureka):** I'm calling on behalf of my husband. We are regular blood donors. In the last year, he has failed the hematocrit test consistently at the blood center where they take it out of the fingertip. However, when he does a regular lab test from his elbow, he is fine. We've tried iron supplements and Vitamin C, but he still fails the finger prick test.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Capillary hematocrit is not the same as arterial or general system hematocrit. You have to figure out what's going on with the difference between the two.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So his hematocrit is low at the fingertip, but normal in the venous blood.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is important to look at things other than hematocrit. If you are under stress and have an elevated estrogen-to-progesterone ratio, estrogen lowers hepcidin. If estrogen is up, you are retaining iron at the same time that you are lowering your hematocrit. This is the same thing that was happening 100 years ago; women looked anemic but were being poisoned with too much iron. That can happen to men too.

**Caller (New Mexico):** Can niacinamide, aspirin, or lithium detox iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin is known to be very protective against iron. That was established 30 or 40 years ago. It acts as an antioxidant and maybe as an iron binder. It is probably one of the most protective things next to coffee and Vitamin E for preventing the toxicity of iron.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about niacinamide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does all kinds of defensive things to maintain your cell's oxidative capacity. It is the failure of oxidative energy production that makes iron become so toxic. So, niacinamide and aspirin are extremely good bets.

**Andrew Murray:** What about lithium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it can have some adverse effects on your iron system.

**Caller:** I have extreme inflammation. My doctor has me on medicines and vitamins that are "chelated." Is chelation bad or good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think "chelated vitamins" is just a marketing ploy. The way vitamins and minerals exist in food is the safest. If you associate them with other chemicals, there hasn't been enough study to know if they are safe compared to getting them naturally from foods.

**Caller:** I'm allergic to everything. Is there anything I could take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Over the years, I've seen lots of chronic, mysterious ailments clear up as soon as the person stopped all of their supplements for a week or so.

**Caller:** I got the COVID shot 10 days ago. On the eighth day, my arm blew up like a balloon with a rash. Now, the blood seems to be pooling at the ends of my fingers and toes—they are blue and red, and my palms are blotchy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The vaccine creates inflammation. The most dangerous part is that this type of inflammation produces a tendency toward hypercoagulation. When you have areas that aren't circulating fully, there is a tendency to form fibrin layers or clotting material inside the blood vessel. This relates to the "blood sludging" phenomenon.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What would you recommend she use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin, cyproheptadine, milk, and Vitamin D. Serotonin is one of the things that goes crazy under the inflammation of both COVID and the vaccine.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, could you sum up the "rouleaux" formation—where red cells stack up on each other—that has been seen in the blood of people after receiving the vaccine? How does that relate to the coagulopathies, strokes, and myocarditis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Melvin Knisely was a person who studied the "blood sludging" phenomenon in people who were under stress and deteriorating quickly. He saw it as a lack of metabolic energy. People following up on his work emphasized that what was happening was catalyzed fibrin polymerization, creating a layer or blockade film of fibrin inside the blood vessels. This thickens the capillary wall, making it hard for oxygen to get through, and coats red blood cells with a layer of fibrin.

People working with very good microscopes studied these coin-like rolls of red blood cells (rouleaux). When they pulled them apart with microprobes, they would snap back together. They published images showing filaments—assumed to be fibrin polymers—stretched between the red blood cells like rubber bands. That was brought on basically by a reduction in oxidative metabolism and a shift to lactic acid metabolism. That is where you start having iron problems and inflammation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So people's blood could be clumping like that just under a stressful situation, not necessarily just from COVID or the shots.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's an apparently universal thing that happens when you're in very bad condition.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I wanted to mention regarding aspirin: it is only safe to use more than a baby aspirin a day if you are taking Vitamin K. Thorne Research makes a Vitamin K2. For every aspirin (325mg) you take, you need 1 milligram (1000 micrograms) of Vitamin K2 to keep yourself from bleeding excessively.

**Station DJ:** Could you mention natural food sources of K2?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Kale is king, but it may not be in high enough doses if you want to use aspirin to block inflammation in doses of 1 to 3 grams a day. If you take a baby aspirin (90mg), you don't need the supplement. But for high doses, it's not safe unless you have Vitamin K2.

**Andrew Murray:** That's all we have time for. Dr. Peat's information is raypeat.com. We can be reached at westernbotanicalmedicine.com.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you for listening. Good night.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: September 2021 KMUD
transcriptText:
**Michael McCaskill:** The regular hosts, Andrew and Sarah, aren't here yet. I have Dr. Peat online. We thought we were just going to do a random show, but we will open the lines. Dr. Peat, why don't you give a little bit of background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been doing nutrition consulting largely for the last 40 or 50 years, but I'm recently getting more interested in immunology. It's been 40 years since I taught a course in immunology, but because of the pandemic, I started reading more about it. I have been looking at the history and development of corporate and government science, and the way those influences have distorted the understanding of immunology, even in these 40 years since I was studying and teaching it.

**Michael McCaskill:** There has been a lot of conflict around COVID-19 and vaccination. Could you give some herbological or dietary recommendations beneficial for everybody, regardless of whether they are vaccinated or not, to make sure their immune system works its best?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D is probably the single most important thing for Americans. Considering the average American diet, the majority of people are far below the optimal level of vitamin D. Even though the establishment still believes that the lower end of the normal range is adequate, when you look at degenerative diseases—heart disease and even fairly rare things like scleroderma—the whole range of degenerative system failure is associated with a fairly low vitamin D level.

Something that has kept more doctors from prescribing vitamin D is that there have periodically been scares about the dangers of taking too much. It's true that if you take a million units or so, after a while you'll start getting hypercalcemia—calcification of soft tissues. But the most common cause of calcification of the soft tissues is actually from a *deficiency* of vitamin D.

With aging and kidney failure, calcification of the kidney tissue and blood vessels becomes the lethal problem. The mechanism for why kidney failure is associated with calcification is that it is also associated with extreme vitamin D deficiency and an excess of parathyroid hormone. They've seen that removing the parathyroid glands can alleviate some of the symptoms of calcification from kidney failure. Just supplementing a moderate amount of vitamin D, like 5,000 units a day for an adult, can be enough. If you have calcium in your diet, it can be enough to lower the parathyroid hormone. Lowering the parathyroid hormone makes you put your calcium into the bones where it should go, keeping it out of the soft tissues.

**Michael McCaskill:** People can get vitamin D from sunlight, though it depends on skin tone and time spent outside. Are there other things you get from sunlight that might make it a better source than just taking a pill?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because the light that penetrates the ultraviolet spectrum is very superficial; it acts on the skin cells themselves. But the visible light, especially the orange and red light, penetrates very deeply. If you hold your hand up and look at the sunlight shining through it, it's very red on the shaded side, showing that the red light easily penetrates the thickness of your skin.

The red light acts as anti-free radical protection. It effectively quenches excited electrons and reverses the effect of the free radical damage done by ultraviolet light. A tanning bed, which is only UV and some visible light, will produce more aging effects than sunlight of the same tanning effect. The UV by itself causes free radical damage and aging of the skin. But with sunlight, the quenching effect of the red and orange light detoxifies much of the free radical damage done by the ultraviolet.

**Caller (James from Arizona):** I've subscribed to your newsletter for years. In one of the first newsletters about this coronavirus, you said cellular excitation is required for a coronavirus infection. If a person is not "cellularly excited," would they just not be exposed or develop antibodies because they don't need to?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your cells are already in a weakened, excitable state, they are the most susceptible to viral infection. If the cell is stable, even if it's infected by a virus, it will turn off the process rather than letting the virus propagate.

The things that are known to be protective against the infection, or alleviate its worst symptoms, include almost all of the known safe anti-inflammatory substances. Aspirin, naproxen, progesterone, and vitamin D have that calming, quieting effect on cells. The antihistamines, anti-serotonin drugs, and anti-angiotensin blood pressure treatments—such as Losartan and Candesartan—are also protective.

**Caller:** You’ve talked about how some proteins are acidifying; for example, phosphorus gets metabolized into phosphoric acid. You discussed the importance of having adequate alkaline minerals in your cells so the body wouldn't have to sacrifice protein.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens in the kidneys; the kidneys will break down protein to balance the pH. But the phosphate itself has an excitatory action. When ATP is breaking down to do cell work, it liberates inorganic phosphate. Inorganic phosphate has an excitatory effect. When it can get attached back to form ATP again, the cell relaxes. So ATP's effect is relaxing, making the cell stable against infection. An excess of free phosphate antagonizes the stabilizing effect of vitamin D and calcium, putting cells into the excited state susceptible to infections.

**Caller:** How do sulfur and sulfuric acid play into that balance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those are pretty safe. If you add too much sulfur to your diet, you'll disturb the absorption of minerals. For example, you can block the formation of pigment by cutting down your assimilation of copper if you have too much sulfur. But otherwise, sulfur-rich foods are reasonably safe; you can dispose of it as the acid.

**Caller:** My friend's husband, who is in his 70s, had the virus. He survived but has gone back to the hospital recently with kidney issues, and they have him on diuretics. What is good for a "long COVID" autoimmune condition hitting the kidneys?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mentioning the diuretics brings up a perspective on what's actually happening in the infection. In the first weeks of the pandemic, two doctors in New York realized that the symptoms of COVID were essentially the same as the symptoms of high-altitude sickness. People who don't adapt to very high altitudes develop edema of the lungs and general inflammatory systems—a failure of the tissues to use oxygen properly.

One of the established treatments for mountain sickness is a diuretic called acetazolamide. It restores the level of carbon dioxide in your body and the acidity. That acidity has a quieting, sedating effect that also causes the tissue cells to give up excess water. Carbon dioxide itself has many calming, sedative effects. Calcium channel blockers were their other suggestion for both mountain sickness and the COVID infection.

One of these doctors, Cameron Kyle-Sidell, observed that the inflamed lung creates a thickness between the capillary and the air chamber. This is increased by inflammation and by a deficiency of carbon dioxide. It makes it harder for gases to diffuse through this thickened pathway. It happens that carbon dioxide diffuses much faster through liquid than oxygen does. Kyle-Sidell observed the breathing problem is because you are losing carbon dioxide very fast. When your carbon dioxide level goes down, oxygen sticks too firmly to the hemoglobin. It increases the blood's affinity for oxygen to the point that your tissue cells are starving for oxygen despite some oxygen being there. It helps to some extent to get more oxygen in, but it's really the deficiency of carbon dioxide in the blood that keeps the oxygen from being delivered as needed.

**Michael McCaskill:** I've heard complaints about masks increasing the carbon dioxide level people are breathing in. Might that actually be a bonus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that's what the acetazolamide and calcium channel blockers are doing. It's making you retain the carbon dioxide more efficiently.

**Michael McCaskill:** Would drinking carbonated drinks or baking soda help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Marathon runners and cyclists have found that if they put a tablespoon of baking soda in a glass of water, their endurance is greatly increased, apparently by the provision of that bonus of carbon dioxide.

Regarding the hospitals that used forced ventilating machines—putting a tube into the throat and pumping oxygen—they were having terribly high mortality. Some approaching 100% of the intubated people died. Adjoining hospitals simply passively giving them a little extra oxygen had close to zero mortality. The excess of pumped-in oxygen was entering the lungs and driving out too much carbon dioxide, making the problem worse.

This brings up the subject of Carbogen. I haven't heard of any hospital consistently using that as treatment, but it was a treatment from the 1930s up until the mid-1950s. Hospitals recognized that using a mixture of 5% carbon dioxide and 95% oxygen, rather than pure oxygen, prevented the damage to the lungs. Its use dropped off around 1955 because a government medical committee in England declared that asphyxia is synonymous with having too much carbon dioxide. They had no evidence to support it, but since that official statement, its use dropped off. Studies show that it does prevent ventilator lung damage and has an anti-inflammatory effect.

**Caller:** I found a translation of a German paper from 1904 that said sometimes a person doesn't need oxygen, just a little whiff of carbon dioxide, and it improves their oxygen uptake.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is the mechanism. It is recognized that hemoglobin is acidified by the binding of oxygen, but the more acidic carbon dioxide molecule shifts the pH and oxygen affinity of the hemoglobin. It out-competes the oxygen for combining with the hemoglobin.

The mechanism by which carbon dioxide binds to hemoglobin forms a chemical bond called the carbamino group. The textbooks mention that the amino group of certain amino acids chemically combines with carbon dioxide, forming a modified protein. All of our body proteins display some of these same amino groups. Carbon dioxide is going to similarly bind every place in the body where there is protein. So, the toxicity of losing your proper level of carbon dioxide—by going to high altitude, hyperventilating, or being ventilated with pure oxygen—is not only inflaming your lungs but, in effect, inflaming every protein in your body.

**Caller (Ross from Whitethorn):** What do you think of L-Carnitine? I read about it in a book by Dr. Nick Lane.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is active in helping you oxidize fats, so in ordinary metabolism, it is essential. However, when you're under stress, the products of oxidizing pure fat will produce less carbon dioxide in proportion to the oxygen used. In stressful situations, such as a failing heart, carnitine—by increasing your ability to oxidize fats—can actually increase the problem of oxygen availability.

In the 1990s, researchers found that if you could keep the cells oxidizing glucose, they produce more carbon dioxide per oxygen consumed. The effect is to make metabolism more efficient, reduce inflammation via increased carbon dioxide, and leave more oxygen available by changing the affinity of hemoglobin. The chemical that increased the ability to use glucose rather than fat was called Mildronate (or Meldonium). Athletes are using it, and it has disqualified some famous athletes because it improves endurance noticeably. It works by bypassing carnitine. Even though carnitine is normal and essential, under stress, Mildronate can bypass it and get glucose to the cells.

**Caller:** I seem to crave cottage cheese, and I think it might be the whey that I crave. Could you discuss whey?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The physiology of consuming any milk products—both the whey and the casein fractions—has multiple beneficial effects that are approaching hormonal and immune-promoting. One of their virtues is that they are deficient in iron but have almost all other nutrients. Iron happens to be one of the main risks of any stress; stress tends to make iron toxic and increase susceptibility to infections. Milk provides helpful nutrients but is very deficient in iron.

**Caller:** Is there an association with histamine? I also have very itchy skin.

**Michael McCaskill:** Is there a dietary recommendation to help be anti-histamine while supporting the heart?

**Michael McCaskill:** Regarding the caller's comment about craving shellfish—how do cravings work? Does the body know what is good for it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies, mostly in animals, but some people have tested it on their kids. They noticed kids will sometimes seem to have a deranged appetite, wanting only one food for several meals. But when they looked at the food choices over a week or two, it turned out their choices ended up providing a proper balance of nutrients.

They've tested this on animals by creating a deficiency in a particular vitamin or amino acid. They find that the animal knows how to ignore a food that might seem generally good but is deficient in what they need, and instead concentrate on the food richest in what they need. It turns out there are only two or three essential amino acids that act as signals. If they make a food deficient in one of the amino acids that *doesn't* act as a guide, the animal no longer makes the right choice. But in nature, those rare patterns of deficiency don't occur. So, animals given a choice of natural foods will invariably pick out the ones that are nutritionally balanced.

**Caller:** I had a pile of wood chips delivered that turned out to be full of Aspergillus fungus. I inhaled the spores and was wheezing. What kind of antifungal or advice do you have for getting fungus out of my lungs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably your lungs are going to take care of it, but it never hurts to make sure your vitamin D is adequate. Vitamin D is the most important immune-supporting nutrient for Americans. In the world in general, vitamin A and zinc are rivals for protection of the membranes and direct immunity to germs, mechanical, or chemical irritants. A good diet with anti-inflammatory foods helps. Besides milk products, citrus fruits are very rich in flavonoids which are anti-inflammatory and pro-immunity. Coffee is another good source of anti-inflammatory substances such as quercetin.

**Caller:** What is the difference between vitamin D and D3? Which one should we take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** D3 is the normal one that we make when we are in the sunlight. It works the same chemically as the one we make. Some products on the market are vitamin D2; that is metabolized slightly differently and doesn't have all the good protective effects of vitamin D3.

In a medical context, you might hear people talk about calcitriol. You don't want the triol—some people confuse that with vitamin D3. You want cholecalciferol (D3).

**Caller:** I have a brain fog issue. I had COVID about a year ago. Do you have recommendations for mental acuity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Brain fog goes with low energy production and low carbon dioxide. Vitamin B1 is a natural equivalent to acetazolamide and the calcium channel blockers in being an inhibitor of carbonic anhydrase, helping to raise your carbon dioxide. It is often the quickest way to clear up brain fog and get your mental energy back. But all of the anti-inflammatory things help: thyroid hormone, vitamin D, calcium, progesterone, and fruit juice.

**Caller:** I've had diabetes for many years. I have investigated intermittent fasting. So far it seems to be bringing my blood sugar down. What are your thoughts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It will make your blood sugar go down, but anything that you can call fasting is going to be putting you under stress. The long-range thing that corrects chronic diabetes is to get your polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) lower—to completely eliminate them from your diet as far as possible. Use butter for cooking rather than any liquid vegetable oils.

The polyunsaturated fats are specifically toxic to your insulin-producing tissues, create resistance in your tissues, and damage the ability to oxidize sugar. They have no essential need; there is no benefit lost by eating a completely saturated fat component. Regarding carbohydrates, if they are taken in a consistent way, it happens that glucose is constantly activating stem cells in your pancreas to restore the ability to produce insulin. It is the polyunsaturated fats stored in your tissues or coming directly from your food that will keep destroying or damaging your insulin-producing cells.

**Michael McCaskill:** Thank you so much, Dr. Peat, for being flexible and sharing your knowledge. Where can people find more information about you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My website is raypeat.com and the newsletter subscribing information is raypeatsnewsletter.com.

**Michael McCaskill:** Thank you so much for joining us.
