transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome back to Ask Your Herb Doctor. Every month we have a guest speaker, and that guest speaker is the faithful, ever-reliable, factual, and informative Dr. Raymond Peat. This month is no exception. Dr. Peat is joining us to discuss the continuing subject of cancer with reference to autoimmunity and estrogen. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for joining us. For those who perhaps haven't read anything you've written or heard you speak, would you explain your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I graduated from college, it was in the humanities. I was an English major for a while, then art, psychology, and philosophy. I specialized in linguistics and wanted to understand how language works in the brain. I decided to study biology to better understand the brain so I could understand language as a basis for understanding culture and humanities.

When I got to graduate school at the University of Oregon in 1968, I learned that the brain scientists were the most dogmatic. The geneticists were more dogmatic, but the brain science people were high status and very dogmatic. I looked around for people oriented towards science rather than dogmatism and found that reproductive physiology people were actually doing research and not throwing away evidence that contradicted their basic ideas.

I specialized in the physiology of oxidative metabolism as it changes in the reproductive system with aging. That happened to provide a good perspective on how to understand the brain and its energy. I wrote *Mind and Tissue*, a little book about the history of understanding brain metabolism in relation to psychology. Then, for 10 or 20 years, I specialized in the interactions of hormones and nutrition, counseling people on the effects of living and eating on the hormonal system and aging.

**Andrew Murray:** You said the reproductive physiology people were far less likely to throw away good information. Is this because the estrogen industry hadn't really gotten so much traction at this point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My brain nerve biology professor described doing some research in class and said, "And then you throw away the bad data." I would point out an instrument reading to him that was impossible by his ideas, and it just turned off his brain in a flash. I'm sure his memory was that he never saw that happen. I've often wondered how my thesis advisor, Arnold Soderwall, came to be so open to the facts and resistant to the industry position. I think it was partly that he was born and educated before the power of the industry took over. He was aware of the research done in the 1930s that absolutely contradicted everything the estrogen industry has foisted onto the public since 1944.

**Andrew Murray:** Getting to the subject of tonight: estrogen, autoimmunity, and cancer. I want to read a paragraph from a 2021 paper regarding why women are more susceptible to autoimmune diseases. It states:

> "New data suggests that the hormone estrogen may play an important role. A new study now shows that estrogen activates the expression of AID (activation-induced deaminase), which is a protein that drives antibody diversification by deaminating cytosine in DNA to uracil. If estrogen increases the level of AID, increased mutations could transform benign antibodies into self-anti-self pariahs. AID might also contribute to cancer, particularly in breast tissue which is highly responsive to estrogen, by introducing mutations and strand breaks into the genome."

It seems researchers are finally disclosing how estrogen unfavorably influences the immune system to become a self-destructive mechanism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That article is an extremely important landmark. One of the very earliest estrogen-cancer researchers, Leonell Strong, showed that estrogen destabilizes the whole genome and promotes a tendency to develop an uneven number of chromosomes. It is a genetic destabilizer. That article focuses on one single enzyme which, when it functions, helps to produce the essentially infinite variety of antibodies by creating an extreme rate of mutation locally. But that same destabilizing process works on many levels, all the way to the shape and function of the basic cell.

In between the big landmarks, like that article on the AID mutagenic enzyme, you have an almost continuous, seamless bunch of other changes that estrogen is acting on. Increasing the water content of the cell, for example, helps to destabilize the whole system, hardening collagen, lowering oxygen tension, increasing nitric oxide production, and histamine production. It would take an hour just to identify the main pro-inflammatory mechanisms that have been identified. It is a holistic, almost seamlessly interacting process where one factor supports another.

**Andrew Murray:** How do you see estrogen driving autoimmunity specifically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pro-inflammatory part of inflammation and immunity that is activated by estrogen—such as histamine, nitric oxide, and serotonin—is an essential part of getting things started. But the next step is to turn off the excitatory process and focus on maturing the cells. Estrogen, by releasing histamine, activates many other pro-inflammatory things. It activates cell division and increases the production of antibodies. The B cells are activated by estrogen.

Meanwhile, the thymus gland shrinks very quickly in the presence of either estrogen or glucocorticoids. If you knock out the thymus T cells that restrain antibody production, things like this enzyme you just cited (AID) become more and more dominant. The B cells, being activated by estrogen and lacking restraint from the T cells, create a varied, random, irrational activity of antibodies. In that relatively random activity, some of the antibodies cause damage rather than contributing to cleaning up the infection process.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If estrogen is an important stimulator of inflammation for healing purposes, at what point does it go wrong?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is exactly the same thing that happens in pregnancy. Estrogen and histamine create a little focus of activity and inflammation in the uterus that the conceptus takes advantage of to implant. But if that process of local inflammation kept dominating, it would interfere with the oxygen and glucose supply to the fetus. You have to stop the excitation and inflammation to really start delivering glucose and oxygen.

One of the natural functions of estrogen is to evoke the progesterone receptor, making the cells open to being turned off by progesterone. Estrogen should excite and inflame the tissue, but immediately turn the tissue towards looking for relief from progesterone. Progesterone knocks out the estrogen in roughly 10 different ways—turning off the production of estrogen, knocking out the estrogen receptor, and changing the metabolism. That is what happens every time you have a little injury that evokes the estrogen-activated start of the healing process; it should increase the cell's ability to receive and be matured by progesterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** For women that have autoimmune conditions, would you recommend progesterone to help combat the inflammatory effects of estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. People are now recognizing the role of progesterone along with DHEA and thyroid. Over the last 50 years, I've seen several women with seriously debilitating effects of Lupus (SLE) simply take thyroid and progesterone, and all of their symptoms faded away over several weeks.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because the thyroid is combating the estrogen, helping improve the liver's ability to excrete it, and increasing oxygen to the cell.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And making more progesterone.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What role do plastics in our environment play in stimulating estrogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Birth control pills getting into the sewage end up in the rivers and recycle. Just the tremendous flow of estrogen down the sewers is a tremendous polluting source. **Andrew Murray:** I want to ask about the link between viruses and cancer. I saw recent research relating Epstein-Barr virus to autoimmune diseases like Hashimoto's, Graves', and Lupus. Do you go along with the theory of viral interference promoting destabilization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same inflammation that leads to the direct actions of estrogen on the T and B cells—and on their ability to make the safe type of antibodies—affects all of the cells of your body, shifting them a little bit to the unstable tendency to lack enough oxygen and take up more water than is desirable.

**Caller (Joe):** Is there a correlation between the plastics makers and the pharmaceutical industry? It is a known fact that the Roundup company also holds patents to the medicine that treats the symptoms caused by their products.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those are the most powerful industries next to the military arms industry. They have had control of the government regulatory agencies for well over 100 years. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Haven't you told us that estrogen is manufactured from petrochemical products?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The original ones were Diethylstilbestrol (DES). It was so cheap; it was a perfect drug. It cost nothing to manufacture but had very powerful estrogen-like effects. They continued using it to treat prostate cancer right into the very end of the 20th century.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that's what you believe causes prostate cancer, right? The estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That treatment was based on zero evidence. It was a total matter of opinion, contrary to all of the research in animals. But it affected many millions of men for about 55 years.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about Diindolylmethane (DIM) for anti-estrogenic purposes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There were studies in fish in which it had a pro-estrogenic effect, so I've been a little skeptical of it. But to the extent that you can show in humans that it is protective, then it's a pretty safe material. Just eat your cabbage and broccoli.

**Andrew Murray:** I also saw a study on *Momordica charantia* (Bitter Melon), a climbing cucurbit. They are saying it has strong estrogen modulating properties and significant antagonism of estradiol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** [Acknowledged].

**Andrew Murray:** Are there other substances that affect estrogen and decrease its ability to wreak havoc on the chromosomes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are two factors that powerfully go with the inflammation and destabilizing effect of estrogen, adding to the tendency to develop autoimmunity. One is **endotoxin**. If you're overloaded with estrogen, your blood vessels tend to be leaky. That increases the risk of exposure to endotoxin, which intensifies that leakiness and affects all of your cells.

The other main factor is **polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)** and the prostaglandins they are converted to. Free polyunsaturated fatty acids have a direct effect, activating estrogen—for example, knocking out the estrogen-binding protein so that the estrogen is freed to be more active. Under the influence of estrogen, the excitatory prostaglandins are activated. In a healthy situation, prostaglandins are blocked by progesterone. Once you shift over to the estrogen influence, you're at increased risk from the polyunsaturated fats and the endotoxin coming from your intestine.

**Andrew Murray:** I'm glad you mentioned endotoxin and leaky gut. I saw an article associating leaky gut with being the initial insult that allowed fragments like gliadin from gluten to pass into the bloodstream. They said the gliadin molecule was very similar to T3 and T4 structure, causing autoimmune thyroiditis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For a long time, celiac disease has been increasing right along with the exposure to estrogen. It has gone from mostly a childhood disease to mostly in adult women. There are several things that overlap antigenically with the tissues under the influence of estrogen and gluten.

**Caller:** What are three categories of foods one can avoid that are highly carcinogenic? How does that compare to smoking cigarettes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:**
1.  **Polyunsaturated fats (PUFA):** Any vegetable seed oil.
2.  **Pro-inflammatory amino acids:** Tryptophan, Methionine, and Cysteine. These are found in high-quality proteins in excess. You don't want to eat a pound and a half of meat per day.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Olive oil is 90% monounsaturated, so that is okay, but other seed oils are polyunsaturated.

**Andrew Murray:** How does a diet rich in PUFAs compare in cancer risk to smoking a pack a day of cigarettes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** PUFA is probably the biggest carcinogenic part of the American diet.

**Caller:** Does whole wheat flour fall under carcinogenic foods? And is chicken healthy to eat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The reason flour and grains were polished—like white rice and white flour—is that the whole grains get rancid and toxic fairly quickly in storage. If you're going to eat whole wheat flour soon after it's ground, it's probably not so bad. But once it gets in your blood, those excess polyunsaturated fats start to react with iron to produce lipid peroxides and free radical toxins. Polished rice has very little nutritional value, but has fewer storage toxins.

Regarding chicken: On a typical industrial diet, chicken is full of very unstable polyunsaturated fats. In excess, I think it is pretty carcinogenic.

**Andrew Murray:** But if you had access to good, fresh, locally raised chicken from a free diet, is 4 ounces a day okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think so. It's the same with pork. Industrial pork has over 30% PUFA in the fat. If people are careful what they feed their pigs—like the traditional diet of whey and old vegetables—the fat goes down almost like beef, to around 4% PUFA.

**Andrew Murray:** Before we lose the thread on gluten and estrogen...

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The enzyme **transglutaminase** is in common between gluten and the lining of the intestine acted upon by estrogen. If we have antibodies to the foreign protein gluten, they will act against our own tissues as far as they're under the influence of estrogen, which induces transglutaminase. The transglutaminase aspect of estrogen is the cross-linking enzyme that hardens collagen. Under the influence of estrogen producing transglutaminase, collagen itself becomes hardened and carcinogenic rather than flexible.

**Caller:** What is your opinion on eating hemp seed and pumpkin seed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are not necessarily the worst for the PUFA content, but I wouldn't say it's something you should do regularly because of the breakdown products. They're probably fairly rancid by the time you ingest them anyway.

**Caller (Corey):** I'm a construction worker and work with laminated glues, ABS glue, and PVC. I assume these exude bio-estrogens. I would love to know about the risks of these materials.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even the safety law system is really part of a superstructure that enforces the use of dangerous materials. The basic system is designed to direct production towards these cheapest and most dangerous chemicals. In the long run, I think the problem would be solved very economically by using materials like mud and cement. They pollute very little and are chemically inert once in place.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What are some dietary strategies if you've been working all day with these chemicals? How do you get that stuff out of your body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:**
1.  **Fiber:** Any good fiber that isn't too poisonous. Raw carrot (moderately shredded) allows us to absorb very little of the irritating chemicals while absorbing estrogen from the bowel. Other fibers include well-cooked mushrooms, bamboo shoots, or even well-cooked oat bran. This keeps the intestine from recycling poisons to the liver.
2.  **Metabolic Rate:** Watch that your thyroid isn't suppressed. Keeping your metabolic rate up and temperature around 98.6°F during the peak of the day will promote quick peristalsis.
3.  **Calcium & Vitamin D:** Calcium, especially from low-fat milk, supported by Vitamin D. Both are good for weight loss and keeping the metabolic rate higher.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And lastly, progesterone is a direct combat molecule to estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat. For those listening, you can find more information at RayPeat.com and our website westernbotanicalmedicine.com.

I want to finish with a thought on authoritarianism. We are evolving as a species, but nature is not accepting; it selects the fittest. Rules exist—like time, gravity, and death. With increasing authoritarianism and legislation aimed at making us accept everything without boundaries, I leave you with this: resist and live. Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thanks for tuning in tonight. Good night.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us again. For those who may never have heard you, could you let them know a little bit about your expertise?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had been a student of the humanities, teaching painting and English literature. I got interested in language and how the brain can do such a thing as use language. I decided that the only way to make progress was to go to graduate school in biology and study the brain.

**Andrew Murray:** I really appreciate your interweaving of your artistic nature with a fluid understanding of biology. Before we move on, I wanted to cover a couple of things from an herbal perspective surrounding estrogen and aromatase.

This may limit the anti-cancer effects of Tamoxifen and explain why it is inferior compared to other anti-estrogens for preventing disease recurrence.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's kick off with the topic of MSG. The FDA considers monosodium glutamate safe to add to food. It is one of the most abundantly found amino acids in nature, present in foods as a flavor enhancer (E621), hydrolyzed protein, or purified monosodium salt.

Early on, they were claiming benefits of MSG, such as increasing temperature, decreasing body mass, and decreasing fat tissue production. However, the negative effect of this glutamate was that it suppressed the oxidation of glucose. Dr. Peat, there are claims of obesity caused by MSG, whereas before they talked about it increasing metabolism. Can you explain the excitotoxic effects and why the FDA hasn't banned it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the weight loss claim was just a sales ploy to sell the flavoring substance. In the 1970s, J.W. Olney found that when rats were fed just a little more than the amount a person could normally eat, the brain was damaged in a way that led to lifelong obesity. It caused the destruction of enough of the brain that appetite remained out of control, and the metabolic rate wasn't sufficient to keep weight steady.

Over a period of several years, he did many experiments showing that the same sort of molecule—aspartic acid, aspartame, or variations acting through the glutamate or aspartate receptor—had this range of excitatory effects. One of the "positive" things was that it made you seem more alert, but that alertness came at the expense of not having enough energy produced to meet the high energy consumption caused by the excitatory action.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Isn't aspartame the fake sugar, Splenda or NutraSweet?

**Michael:** NutraSweet is aspartic acid with methanol. It degrades into methanol and leaves methanol in your neurons.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspartame is a super-sweet material, sweeter than saccharin, but the amount that is toxic is very small. They've demonstrated that it can cause brain cancer. Olney showed in the late 70s that the sudden appearance of a rising incidence of gliomas—malignant glial cell tumors—followed the introduction of foods loaded with aspartame and MSG by a few years. He demonstrated you could cause those tumors by overfeeding glutamate or MSG to animals.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This goes to show we can't trust the ethics of the FDA if they're allowing that product on the market.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cell phones have shown a similar correspondence. If a person habitually holds their cell phone to the right ear, the incidence of brain tumors on the right side has increased sharply. It happens that they are both causes of excitotoxicity. The electromagnetic field excites the cells, and you need to provide energy to keep up with that, or the cell dies.

Ongoing experiments show that when cells are endangered by things like MSG or aspartame, giving them a super amount of sugar (glucose) will save the neurons simply by feeding whatever is needed to keep up with the high level of excitation.

This excitotoxic conflict—between unavoidable stimulation and something interfering with the oxidation of glucose—applies to aging, gliomas, and epilepsy. If the cells aren't able to keep up their energy production with the excitation, the seizure gets out of control and damages the tissue. Any cell that can be exaggeratedly stimulated can be rescued if you keep the sugar supply up. If it isn't kept up, that cell can become cancerous or die, leading to dementia or brain function loss.

**Andrew Murray:** This is like a kind of wasteful entropy. There's a lack of input of the energy needed to keep the cell going.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and it's made worse by overlapping influences. It isn't just cell phone radiation, aspartame, and MSG; many different things have that same function.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So eating Chinese food with MSG, drinking a diet soda, and talking on your cell phone is a bad combination.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at what any stress does—vibration, laser, telephone overstimulation, glucose deprivation, or oxygen deprivation—they all turn out to be excitatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It happens that feeding energy in the form of sugar has a sedative action that leads to turning down the degree of excitation.

If the cell perceives that it is not getting enough energy to meet its needs, one alternative is to go into hibernation. To do that, it has the equipment for producing serotonin. Serotonin helps prevent heat loss through the skin, but it also turns down the production of heat, leading to a colder state—suspended animation to a degree.

Another universal reaction is the formation of histamine. When a cell is in a desperate, dying condition, it secretes histamine to open up closed blood vessels and get more blood delivered.

Estrogen is another of these short-term emergency things. Estrogen can activate the serotonin system to cool off the energy-consuming apparatus, and it can activate the histamine system. It also activates nitric oxide formation and heme oxygenase. Heme oxygenase breaks down heme (used to make cell energy) to produce bilirubin and carbon monoxide. Under these circumstances, carbon monoxide serves as an antioxidant, blocking the ability to consume oxygen and moving the system into a torpor.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's lots of inflammation and wasteful mechanisms to deplete the organism of energy.

**Michael:** My understanding is that glutamate stimulates the umami flavor, and a lot of high-protein nutritious foods stimulate that too. How is it that the body is benefited by eating a high-protein diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the natural state, protein is a rare delicacy for most animals. The urge to eat protein is a survival urge to build muscle and make new tissue. But when society provides lots of cheap protein, people get in the habit of eating it because it's there, rather than being guided by their appetite.

People tend to overeat protein after the age of 20. As long as you're growing, you respond to the signal action of glutamate and go into an anabolic state to make muscle and brain tissue. But once your size is established, if you keep eating that same amount, you have an excess beyond your needs. You get excess histidine, tryptophan, methionine, cysteine, aspartate, and glutamate—all of which are potentially excitotoxic amino acids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** When you recommend people consume 75 to 100 grams of protein a day, you're not recommending they consume that all in the form of muscle meat or eggs. You typically don't recommend more than two eggs a day, and believe most protein should come from dairy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. After you're grown, you should try to learn to go by your actual biological urges rather than what advertising tells you to eat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How many ounces of muscle protein would you recommend as a safe level for adults?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As your metabolic rate slows down steadily from puberty, the older you are, the more careful you have to be about having an excess of the excitotoxic amino acids. Adelle Davis pointed out that gelatin is considered an incomplete protein, but she said she had seen lots of old women going for years living on a diet of toast, Jell-O, and tea—practically their only protein being gelatin. That was an illustration of what a very tiny amount a very old person needs.

**Andrew Murray:** I pulled out an article describing the exposure of rats to MSG at the neonatal stage. It severely damaged their hypothalamic nuclei, resulting in increased body weight, fat deposition, and decreased growth hormone. MSG appears to be a suitable candidate for inducing obesity which leads to diabetes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I wonder if it's allowed to be in products without being listed as an additive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think legally it has to be listed, but they have alternatives like calling it "vegetable broth" when it's really an MSG extracted from soybean.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about Tamari? That is fermented soy protein. Doesn't that form a natural MSG?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that should be limited in someone's diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw an article stating that curcumin from turmeric protects against MSG neurotoxicity by decreasing the NMDA receptor 2B expression in the rat hippocampus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are lots of flavonoids like quercetin and myricetin in coffee. Coffee has lots of tissue-protective, anti-cancer, and anti-dementia effects that I think are largely an effect of the flavonoid components.

**Andrew Murray:** Another article mentioned that glutamate was involved in increasing levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, like tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), contributing to brain damage.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There has been a lot of study on how excitotoxic things like glutamate make the cell become more active. They found that the addition of extra glucose allowed the cell to extrude more calcium. Normally, responding to an excitotoxin means the cell takes up and retains calcium, leading to inflammation and cell death. Glucose promotes the increase of carbon dioxide formation. The carbon dioxide leaves the cell as carbonic acid, taking the calcium with it. This flow of glucose and carbonic acid out of the cell takes care of the calcium accumulation, which is the basic cause of the inflammation.

**Andrew Murray:** Typical foods that are glutamate-rich include hydrolyzed vegetable protein, autolyzed yeast, yeast extracts, soy extracts, and protein isolates. These form a large part of vegetarian or vegan diets as alternative protein sources.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Even organic bouillons often have yeast extract. I notice if I eat that, I feel like I've had an MSG burn on my tongue.

**Caller:** I live on the Avenue of the Giants. Can you explain inflammation? Is it inflammation of the cells or around the muscle tissue, particularly regarding arthritis and the aches and pains of getting older?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People recently have been talking about "inflammaging," as if that explains something. The process of aging obviously involves increased inflammation. The problem is to see what the basic events are. Cell structure, pain, excitation, inflammation, and aging all have these aspects of cytotoxic cell damage and the inability to remedy the problem by making enough energy.

Regarding heme oxygenase, probably 95% of publications describe carbon monoxide as an antioxidant. But if you look at the deteriorated brain in old age, there is more carbon monoxide in it than at any previous life stage. Carbon monoxide presence is a degenerative aspect of inflammation. If you block the formation of carbon monoxide after a traumatic wound, you prevent most of the damage. The chemistry of aging and inflammation expresses the same idea as excitotoxicity and wasteful energy processes.

**Caller:** I'm from South Central Los Angeles. How long does the body take to heal from damage? If you reduce estrogen, PUFA, and inflammatory things, is there a difference in age regarding recovery time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A young person with a higher metabolic rate can change everything more quickly. If an average person moves from a country that eats a lot of polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) to a country that eats very little, it can take four years to equilibrate to the new balance.

However, if you make an extreme effort—like one researcher who ate a laboratory purified diet absolutely lacking PUFA—his chronic health problems, like migraine, disappeared in about three or four months.

**Caller:** Would that apply to reducing estrogen for my wife, who suffers from fibroids and has had miscarriages?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A friend of mine who was 40 and wanted to get pregnant had a tennis-ball-sized fibroid blocking her uterus. She took a large dose of thyroid. Every month the doctor monitored it, and by the fifth month, it had become about a fourth of its original size, and she was pregnant.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So five months made a big difference just by using natural thyroid hormone to lower estrogen and improve liver function.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are so many other out-of-balance components of diet—too much iron, methionine, aspartate, glutamate, cysteine. By fixing any one component, you can see drastic effects.

**Caller:** I'm from Arcata. My nine-year-old grandson has had two episodes of big intestinal bleeding. Scopes haven't found anything. Could you recommend any foods that would be soothing to the GI tract?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People vary in their sensitivities, but the first thing to do would be to absolutely avoid foods that have added gums, especially carrageenan. A very high percentage of foods now contain vegetable gums or microbial gums, all of which are very pro-inflammatory. Knocking out those foods can stop things like chronic bowel bleeding.

**Caller:** Would aloe vera or slippery elm be helpful?

**Andrew Murray:** In Europe, chamomile is the number one GI anti-inflammatory—"mother of the gut." Gentle tannins would also be indicated to gently astringe the capillaries.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** That can be as simple as black tea or green tea.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very important to check his thyroid and vitamin D levels because a deficiency of either can make the intestine hypersensitive to inflammation.

**Andrew Murray:** Also, check his hemoglobin. If he has had chronic bleeding, he might be anemic. Support that with foods containing naturally present iron, like liver, rather than iron supplements. As Dr. Peat mentioned, iron is very reactive and inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And avoid synthetic vitamin C. Synthetic vitamin C reacts with traces of iron in the body to produce inflammation.

**Caller:** I'm from Queens, New York. What are the consequences of not filling a cavity? Is there damage to the nervous system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Consider if the damage is only into the enamel; that can be remineralized. But once it enters into the dentine, then it really needs to be filled.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We see a holistic dentist in Oregon who recommends Lugol's iodine for cavities that are just invading the enamel. Because it is close on the periodic table to fluoride, but not neurotoxic, it is a safe alternative for remineralizing superficial cavities.

**Michael:** I'll throw a plug out there for flossing. As one wise person said, "Floss only those teeth you wish to keep."

**Andrew Murray:** I want to mention a researcher named Blalock. In the *International Journal of Vaccine Theory, Practice and Research* (Jan 2021), there was an article titled "Excitotoxicity and Immuno-excitotoxicity as a Critical Component of the Cytokine Storm Reaction." It stated that the hyper-immune state during pulmonary viral infections was causative for cytokine storms. They found that co-injection of lipopolysaccharide plus an NMDA agonist (ibotenate from *Amanita muscaria*) caused significant neuronal damage.

I'll leave you with this thought: Nature is not accepting; through evolutionary pressure, it selects the fittest. Rules exist, like time, gravity, and death. Life demands that fitness be preserved and aims at physical and spiritual health. Resist authoritarianism and live.

Until the third Friday of next month, my name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Murray. Thank you for listening.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor: February 2022 KMUD
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's edition of Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who perhaps have never listened to the shows before, we run them every third Friday of the month from 7:00 PM to 8:00 PM. We are both licensed practitioners of herbal medicine. We qualified in England in 2000 and 1999 and have been practicing herbal medicine ever since. We were very pleased to discover Dr. Raymond Peat back in 2008 serendipitously through a breast cancer survivor who was praising him and his protocols. That piqued my wife's interest, she made contact, and the rest is history. Dr. Peat has been sharing his time every third Friday of the month for about 11 years now.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, could you introduce yourself before we get into the subject of this evening? We will be discussing the science and principles behind a mechanistic determinant of cancer described as MTOR (MTOR1 and MTOR2). We will get into the biology of it, how it was discovered in the early 90s, and how it has been targeted in the suppression of cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After studying and teaching for about 10 years in the humanities, I decided to go back to graduate school at the University of Oregon for a PhD in biology, reproductive physiology, and biochemistry. Since 1972, I've been doing a lot of personal consulting. For 40 years, since 1981, I've been writing a newsletter—at first every month, and now quarterly—developing themes that relate to health, aging, fertility, and the nature of life.

**Andrew Murray:** The background of your life was the scientific investigation into aging and reproduction. You've always looked deeper into the cause and effect of what we are taught.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The reason I waited until 1968 to do any academic study in biology was that already in the late 1940s and 50s, I had decided that genetics was based on fraudulent, make-believe science. If you really read the classical papers that molecular biology is based on, there's just no real science there. It's a belief attaching experiments to the belief.

**Andrew Murray:** Before we get into the topic of this evening and the discovery of rapamycin, I want to touch on your views regarding estrogen. You have spoken about the unscrupulous estrogen industry and how estrogen is the prime causative factor behind many different cancers, not just reproductive cancers. The inflammatory effects of estrogen trigger excitotoxic states within cells, disorganizing their energy and allowing spontaneous tumors to arise. You have been a big advocate of the antithesis of estrogen, which is progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Having a child fairly early in life is a huge protection against getting cancer. Animal studies show that if a rabbit is bred starting early and as often as it can for the rest of its life, its tissues at any old age are much younger than if it had been a virgin all those years. That was backed up by looking at the relation between the number of children per woman in Hungary. There was a straight increase in longevity with the number of babies, up to eight.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to remind listeners that estrogen is not just a female hormone; males are also subject to the effects of estrogen, especially with aging. In England, with the pub culture, you see gynecomastia—male breast enlargement—and belly fat in older males. This is an outward expression of estrogen dominance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Old men typically have more estrogen than women. It’s not just the ratio; their testosterone is being massively converted to estrogen by the time they're 65 or 70.

**Andrew Murray:** The enzyme aromatase is expressed in many different cells in the body—liver, placenta, bones, and breast tissue. This converts testosterone to estrone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the early 1940s, one experimenter implanted a very small dose of estrogen in animals that had their ovaries removed. The tiniest amount of uninterrupted estrogen produced cancer in every tissue. But if you interrupted it periodically, even a large amount of estrogen didn't lead to cancer. Similar to the aging rabbits or Hungarian women, the quantity and regularity of the progesterone interruption of estrogen just about completely protects against the development of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's move on to the activity of the enzyme MTOR. This is described as the Mammalian Target of Rapamycin or the Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin. There are two subclades: MTOR1 and MTOR2. Could you describe MTOR, its discovery, and what has happened since 1993?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** This particular antibiotic, rapamycin, was used as a fungus killer. It is broad-spectrum but especially effective against fungus. It happens to be in the same family of antibiotics as azithromycin and erythromycin. It is a ring structure, and those are known to have an amazing spectrum of activity. This class of antibiotics happens to kill viruses as well as fungus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After it was discovered to be a treatment for fungus infections, it was found to have many other effects, such as anti-inflammatory effects. In exploring how the anti-inflammatory effect works, they found that it was acting on a particular kinase—an enzyme that attaches phosphate groups to functional proteins. This phosphorylation directs it towards growth and inflammation. They found that the antibiotic inhibiting this particular phosphorylating enzyme extended lifespan drastically and reduced cancer and inflammatory diseases.

**Andrew Murray:** So, the wastage of energy is common in inflammatory diseases, aging, diabetes, and cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The target of this antibiotic, rapamycin (also called sirolimus), controls energy flow. An abundance of energy intake—especially fats and proteins—are the normal activators of MTOR complex number one. Growth hormone is a major activator of MTOR complex two, which is insensitive to the antibiotics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For matters of diet and treatment, the attention is mostly on MTOR complex one because there are so many foods that activate it. Methionine is probably the main activator of MTOR. Meat, besides being a major source of methionine, is also a major source of iron. It happens that both iron and phosphate are activators of MTOR complex one.

**Andrew Murray:** What about milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Although milk contains a lot of methionine, it happens that parathyroid hormone is an activator of MTOR. Milk's high calcium content, working with vitamin D, lowers parathyroid hormone. So, milk contains its own antidote working against the toxic effects of methionine via the great concentration of calcium and a very low concentration of phosphate and iron.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So, Dr. Peat and Andrew, are you suggesting that MTOR is a trigger for cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Cancer, inflammation, aging degeneration like arthritis, diabetes, osteoporosis, and autoimmune diseases.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Basically, rapamycin is an antifungal antibiotic that blocks MTOR?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And therefore they're finding anti-cancer benefit of the rapamycin because it's blocking the MTOR?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it's now used, or derivatives are used, in treating various cancers—breast cancer, pancreas cancer, prostate cancer, and so on.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Is it true that they found it on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in a soil sample?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep.

**Andrew Murray:** The main thrust of this discussion is about the potential use of substances—drugs or phytochemicals—that block MTOR and how that can be used in a dietary perspective to suppress cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coffee is a source of flavonoids like quercetin and caffeine; both of those are anti-MTOR agents. Orange juice and other fruits are very effective flavonoid sources for reducing MTOR.

**Michael (Station Host):** I have a question. You started giving a list of foods that support bad MTOR and reduce it. I learned about the metabolism of estrogen where different foods switch your metabolism so the byproduct is less bad. Are there foods that would help men if they are converting their testosterone to estrogen? And are there any foods that could get men to convert their testosterone back to progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think back-conversion can happen. Progesterone is a precursor to the glucocorticoids like cortisol, but it doesn't go down the pathway towards either testosterone or estrogen. The precursor to those is DHEA.

**Andrew Murray:** How about aromatase inhibitors to block estrogen production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just about everything that's good for you tends to inhibit aromatase because it's activated by stress, cortisol, and prostaglandins, and inhibited by progesterone. All of the things associated with inflammation and degeneration—for example, angiotensin—work through MTOR. If you block angiotensin, you help lower MTOR. All estrogens promote MTOR; progesterone inhibits it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Do even the weaker estrogens like estrone stimulate MTOR?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, they all add up to the same estrogen effect. But estradiol is at least 10 times stronger than the next one. Progesterone activates the detoxifying enzyme system that adds either glucuronic acid or sulfuric acid to the estrogen so that it can be excreted. It also blocks the enzyme that would turn estrone into estradiol.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's working on three different pathways to help block the estradiol. Do you recommend men who are converting testosterone into estradiol use progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coffee, progesterone, flavonoids, and aspirin. Aspirin is a major MTOR inhibitor and aromatase inhibitor.

**Andrew Murray:** So essentially, most anti-inflammatories will have that blocking activity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not everything. For example, doctors prescribe Tylenol instead of aspirin. But in fact, Tylenol activates MTOR and increases inflammatory degenerative processes. Its antidote is aspirin.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** With anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen and Tylenol, they actually increase your risk of stroke. They do not decrease it like aspirin does.

**Michael (Station Host):** Would glutathione be as bad as methionine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, too much glutathione activates MTOR.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to list some specific flavonoids and herbs that block MTOR.
*   **Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG):** From green tea.
*   **Caffeine:** Another flavonoid useful for blocking MTOR.
*   **Curcumin:** From turmeric.
*   **Berberine:** Found in Goldenseal and Oregon Grape root.
*   **Quercetin:** Found in onions (onion syrup), nettles, and pomegranate.
*   **Resveratrol:** From Japanese Knotweed and grape skins.
*   **Pterostilbene:** Found in blueberries and red grapes.
*   **Fisetin:** Found in apples, strawberries, and persimmons. Used in treating melanoma.

Dr. Peat, regarding calorie restriction and fasting—how do we achieve a low MTOR diet without turning into a skeleton?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think calorie restriction is necessary. What slows down the metabolic rate after age 20 is the accumulation of polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) primarily. That shifts our metabolism to prefer the oxidation of fat rather than glucose. If you are oxidizing glucose at a high rate, the resulting carbon dioxide is our basic anti-inflammatory substance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The aim is to prevent the shift towards oxidizing fatty acids. In diabetes and cancer, you fail to oxidize glucose and instead oxidize fatty acids, leading to inflammation. Instead of inhibiting MTOR with carbon dioxide, you activate it with lactic acid. If you can keep away from the stress that causes you to oxidize fatty acids preferentially, you avoid turning on the MTOR complex one.

**Michael (Station Host):** How much glutathione would be too much in a day? And could you list some protein sources similar to milk so that you get protein without pushing MTOR up?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think calcium is what makes the big difference between milk and other proteins.

**Michael (Station Host):** So a bone broth sort of thing would be better?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, gelatin. Naturally extracted gelatin, like chicken skin and bone broth with the fat skimmed off. That contains a very low level of methionine.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And it contains the amino acid glycine, which has lots of other health benefits.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding glutathione: it is a reductant. If you increase the reductive balance of cells, you're putting them in the worst kind of stress—the aging degenerative condition. Glutathione is the cell's major anti-free radical detoxifying agent, but to add it as a food is very risky and I think almost 100% likely to be harmful rather than helpful.

**Caller (Queens, NY):** I have an off-topic question. Dr. Peat, what is your opinion on wisdom tooth extractions and root canals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the pulp is infected, it's probably good to put in a safe filling material like calcium hydroxide and let the immune system take over once you've cleaned out the infection. But I don't think it's good to pull any tooth that isn't an ongoing issue.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you pull a molar of a rat, they lose cognitive ability just from the extraction of one molar. The brain is participating everywhere in the body. You can't separate body metabolism from brain metabolism.

**Caller (Queens, NY):** I currently have a wisdom tooth with a big cavity. Dentists just want to extract it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you can control the pain by scraping out the decayed material and sticking in a temporary filling—for example, zinc and eugenol makes a plastic that hardens—it reduces pain and stops infection. If your wisdom tooth isn't doing any biting work, a temporary filling would probably take care of it.

**Andrew Murray:** Just as an aside, we found a very good holistic dentist in Medford, Oregon, named Dr. Tanner. He doesn't use injections to numb anything before doing a cavity, and he is very skilled. I encourage you to find a naturopathic dentist.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat. For people listening, Dr. Peat can be reached at `raypeat.com`. He has a website full of fully referenced scientific articles. We can be reached at `westernbotanicalmedicine.com`.

**Andrew Murray:** To all those who've listened, I hope you are able to do your own research and follow up on what we talked about with MTOR. Until the third Friday of next month, good night.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good night. Thank you for listening.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** If you were going to be exposed to X-rays, what foods or supplements would you use to protect yourself?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Basically, cancer involves a lot of inflammation, and these compounds act as anti-inflammatories and increase normal cellular respiration.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take the next caller.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, so it has specific therapeutic effects besides its nutritional effects. It reduces the processes that would amplify inflammation, such as blocking prostaglandin formation.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat, we appreciate you joining us again. Thank you so much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's August 19, 2022 edition of Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

Basically physiological chemistry, specifically the metabolic and physiological changes that happen in the reproductive system during aging. There is a chapter of that dissertation where I concentrated on what was still sometimes called lipofuscan as a basic cause of aging.

**Andrew Murray:** I want to expand on your work regarding lipofuscin. We’ve mentioned it in relation to polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). The evidence against it is clear. For example, you can grow human cells in culture. If you are growing huge masses of cells, you know exactly what they are being fed. Mead acid is an omega-9 series polyunsaturated fat with a long saturated tail—just the opposite of fish oil. The n-3 (omega-3) series has unsaturated groups within three carbons of the tip. **Andrew Murray:** That is important. The erroneous doctrine of them being essential and the fact that we can manufacture them brings into question the fish oil industry and the anti-inflammatory dogma. You have said in the past that the placenta doesn't allow these fats to cross. Is that correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it is a very good filter. Even when the mother is eating fish, grains, and unsaturated fats, babies demonstrate at birth that they are making some of the anti-inflammatory, natural Mead acid. This shows they were assimilating very little of the PUFA from the environment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those studies were done over the last 70 or 80 years in rats, dogs, and other animals. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** An interesting side note: I'm not someone who suffers from heartburn, but when I was pregnant, if I ate any PUFA-rich animal fat—like duck, chicken, or pork fat—I immediately got heartburn. **Andrew Murray:** The essential fatty acid myth has been destroyed. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they should be avoided as far as possible.

**Andrew Murray:** Why are they found in nature then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The nuts and seeds produce oils, and snakes, frogs, and fish use them habitually without problem. Those oils are appropriate for them because they live at a fairly low temperature. Animal fats at room temperature tend to solidify; a snake with solidified fat doesn't work very well. However, if you put these fats—which are designed to be sensitive to heat so they stay flexible—into a very hot animal (98°F), they become extremely unstable. That means you shouldn't eat them if you are going to live at 98 degrees Fahrenheit.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's okay for frogs and snakes because they are cold-blooded and won't oxidize those fats. But because we are warm, we rapidly oxidize them into free radicals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. In some studies, they tested the efficiency of fish oil as an energy source for salmon. They added some animal fat (more saturated) to a salmon diet and put them through an endurance test. The salmon eating the saturated fat had better endurance.

**Andrew Murray:** Can you outline the process by which metal ions and stressors exert their effect on these n-3 and n-6 oils to create lipofuscin?

**Andrew Murray:** Did you say lipofuscin can be soluble?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure, some of it shows up in the urine.

**Andrew Murray:** In that case, would things like bitters or liver stimulants that improve digestion and excretion help remove soluble lipofuscin before it becomes permanent?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. Accelerating your digestive processes in general will help.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the difference between the lipofuscin found in endothelial plaque versus the Lewy bodies or amyloid plaque in neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson's or Alzheimer's?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on the type of injury, the type of fat, and the quantity you are exposed to. If it's an extremely fat-loving material, it will stick in your nerve cells.
