**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hi.

**Andrew Murray:** Well, thank you as always for giving your time. I'm constantly reminded that some people just don't know that there are alternatives to the standard model, whether it's treatment, chemicals, or whatever it is. For those people who are listening now and who will pick this up on the audio archives, would you just give an outline of your academic and professional background?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Before I studied biology in graduate school, I was studying linguistics, literature, and psychology and teaching in those areas. I decided I needed a more technical science background to understand how the brain works in the humanities and language. So in 1968, I went to graduate school at the University of Oregon in biology and finished my dissertation in 1972 in the area of reproductive physiological aging—the changes of oxidative metabolism during aging and its effect on reproduction. I've been applying insights and related things to all sorts of problems in the 50 years since then.

**Andrew Murray:** All right, thank you for that. For those of you who are listening, we take callers from now until the end of the show at 8:00. The number is 707-923-3911.

Dr. Peat, I wanted to carry on last month's topic of the findings around mTOR, the mechanistic target of rapamycin, and its use in cancer. The bulk of the evening's show will remain based on alternative approaches to cancer. We like to give the scientific background for the relevance of certain substances, whether natural or synthetic, as a better approach to the treatment of disease.

Would you give an outline of how alternatives have been usurped by the modern approach to disease, and how the machinery which drives that research is corrupted by financial interests? We really haven't made hardly any significant increases in our knowledge of the treatment of cancer in particular. Could you describe how the thinking of classical biologists, like Szent-Györgyi and numerous others, has changed and what we are currently faced with in medicine, which doesn't seek to treat people holistically, let alone scientifically in some cases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mechanistic materialist view reduces everything to a cause-and-effect relation between two simple bits of matter. That makes everything seem absolutely clear to the people who have defined science that way. But when you focus on the interaction of just a few particles, you can understand those very clearly, but you miss the whole context. People like Warburg and Szent-Györgyi looked at the whole picture of biology. Warburg saw things that happened in yeast and saw them happening in cancer: the production of lactic acid, even in the presence of oxygen. He had the insight that this is something very important about the nature of life.

Szent-Györgyi was following up on insights by other people, such as W.F. Koch, and worked out the classical view of how oxidation and mitochondrial metabolism work. But he kept in mind the whole organism and what's going on at every level of water and energy supply interactions. He didn't focus on a few reductionistic material interactions that ordinary science does. As a result, Warburg's work was ridiculed and ignored for more than 50 years. It was only around the beginning of this century that things he did in the 1920s started to be appreciated, but they were generally misunderstood.

Szent-Györgyi's work on cancer involved things that biologists and doctors had never heard of, or even could think of—the idea of what electrons in water are doing and how motion is the essential feature of life, powered by the organized flow of electrons. He applied that to cancer as well as muscle function and circulation. Every aspect of biology can be re-understood in terms of very simple things that act everywhere. The really scientific work, attempting to understand the organism in terms of everything that can be known about it, is something the mainline science people are blind to because it doesn't at all fit into reductionistic or mechanistic materialism.

**Andrew Murray:** The concept of looking for a cause and an effect, driving that mechanistic approach, largely ignores the concept of a living organism interacting with and being affected directly by its environment. In your newsletter, you mentioned the presence and the absolute knowledge of the cancer field, not as a theory but as a reality.

For people listening, the concept of the bystander effect exists. If a cell is irradiated outside of the body and is introduced into the body, it can have a similarly damaging effect, not because it's releasing high-energy electrons, but because the stress signals that the cell gives out as a result of being irradiated have a direct effect on other cells it comes into contact with, either directly or at a distance. That is a reality. It's almost like a quantum physical event that we can only begin to imagine with the last 10 or 15 years of science opening up to quantum theory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People were demonstrating the phenomenon 60 years ago. They knew that if you X-ray an animal, you didn't have to X-ray the brain and pituitary to cause generalized hormonal changes. For example, if you irradiated a female's foot, it would cause the animal to go into heat. The whole organism would shift its hormonal balance towards reproductive heat. That is an example of the whole body as a cancer field. The signal from the radiation is a holistic stress on the whole organism that spreads something that promotes cancer.

The mainstream biologists and medical people are still insisting that radiation causes spot damage to the DNA, causing a mutation in one gene, and that that mechanistic one-to-one damage somehow works its way out, ending up as a cancer. But that simply isn't a realistic picture. The radiation doesn't have to hit the DNA; it does something excitatory and pro-inflammatory to the organism, separate from anything it might do to the DNA. That general stress reaction to radiation turns on signals that transmit estrogen-like signals all through the body. People have found out that you can treat radiation poisoning and estrogen poisoning in the same way. And if you add radiation to estrogen, you get an additive effect of the damage.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat, this is why you strongly recommend against any form of radiation, but specifically dental X-rays. Because X-rays damage fast-dividing cells, and when you have a dental X-ray, it's affecting your brain, which is very rapidly dividing, your eyes, your thyroid, and your tongue.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cancer of the tonsils, eyes, and brain have all increased along with the incidence or intensity of dental X-rays. A study in Seattle several years ago put a lead shield over the abdomen of pregnant women and found that a full set of dental X-rays, with the thyroid and pelvis shielded by lead, caused the babies to be born underweight and underdeveloped if the mother was pregnant at the time—the same way any stress or excess estrogen would do.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So the stress of that dental X-ray spread all the way down to the uterus and the developing baby.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything in the body.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to briefly get into the term "cancer field" before we get into the subject of mTOR. You wrote in your January newsletter that the cancer field is set up such that the actual tumor itself has differing degrees of damage to the cells in a radiating pattern out from the tumor. Essentially, there's a radiating pattern of damage from the central tumor out to distant, pre-cancerous tissues beyond the tumor, and that is propagated by a direct pathway that is similar to the bystander effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Any of the intense stresses, like oxygen or glucose deficiency, will reduce efficient oxygen metabolism and cause stress signals. When one particular area is responding more intensely to stress, you get a small local version of the organismic bystander effect. The bystander effect refers to things that are well-distributed through the body. But with intense signals, a cell that is approaching or has already turned into cancer will chronically produce an excess of lactic acid, even when it gets oxygen. So there will be a gradient of lactic acid surrounding that cell that irritates and disturbs the nearby cells, which then begin producing lactic acid, and that spreads maybe through a few centimeters of solid tissue.

Just the local diffusion causes a visible gradient, ending up in a gradient of DNA damage and mutations. It's hard to list all of the factors other than lactic acid that are diffusing out of an injured cell. They include carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, and a variety of inflammatory cytokines. Everything that the body uses to respond protectively to damage can help local tissues multiply faster to fill in a wound. It accelerates the movement and replication of cells, so it's an essential part of healing. But when it's being originated from a mutated or seriously damaged group of cells, then it's tending to simply spread the damage rather than accelerate healing.

All of these are normal healing factors, like activating the local production of estrogen. That's a normal part of repairing tissue damage. But when it is prolonged and something causes the body to be unable to turn it off, each of these things adds to the spreading effect. As far as it diffuses locally, you'll see this gradient of deterioration, including mutations. Meanwhile, it's adding a burden to the whole organism with the more likely radiation bystander effect.

**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to Ask Your Herb Doctor on KMUD. Dr. Raymond Peat is joining us.

Before we get into the continued dialogue about mTOR and its importance as a target for the treatment of cancer, I wanted to outline this differentiation I started the show with in terms of mechanistic versus holistic approaches. I read an article that discussed the phospho-inositide 3-kinase (PI3K), AKT, and mTOR pathway as a three-branched signaling pathway. It said that approximately 70% of ovarian and breast cancers are activated by a derangement in this pathway, about 90% of lung adenocarcinomas show an aberrant activation of this pathway, and 40% or so of squamous cell carcinomas are activated by this pathway.

Last month, we talked about mTOR for the first time. You had mentioned mTORC1 and mTORC2 as being subsets of mTOR. We discussed the etiology of mTOR, its discovery, and its reference to rapamycin and how that was discovered to be a good novel treatment to block this inflammatory pathway that cancer uses. Would you briefly outline mTORC1 and mTORC2 again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mTORC1 form is an activating, phosphorylating enzyme. When you're normally fed and growing up, it's what mediates between eating more and growing more. If you overeat at any time, you tend to overproduce this growth factor that necessarily leads to degenerative diseases. Excess calorie intake is very important. The activation of a cell will turn on mTOR, synthesis, and growth. Intracellular calcium, which should mostly be outside the cells, is an activating factor inside the cell that increases mTOR.

The mTORC2 form of the enzyme does similar things, but it's fairly insensitive to the usual signals such as overeating. It depends mostly on growth hormone, and many kinds of stress will turn on an excess of growth hormone. Women have spectacularly high levels of growth hormone compared to men as a result of estrogen's stress-inducing effect. That growth hormone has some particular ways of affecting our handling of fat, but that's basically the way mTORC2 is turned on—through high growth hormone.

**Andrew Murray:** And these growth hormones in their own right are proliferative agents that would promote cancer growth.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** When I read about this mTOR/PI3K/AKT pathway, it looked like it wasn't just about mTOR, but that these other two arms of the same signaling messenger system were also very good targets for shutting down the energy pathway. I found that a little hard to reconcile, given that thyroid hormone and progesterone are anti-inflammatory and energy-conservative mechanisms. It seemed like turning off energy production was something to be done to have a beneficial effect on slowing cancers down. Perhaps this is the same mechanism by which calorie restriction produces greater longevity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Overeating and mTOR tend to favor the oxidation of fats over glucose. When that happens, you're basically slowing down the constructive part of energy metabolism and shifting over towards some of these risky, simple growth pathways.

**Andrew Murray:** What do you think about shutting down not just mTOR but these other two linked pathways as a three-branched target? It's not mechanistic in the sense of looking for a cell-killing effect. A lot of the things that were listed were flavonoids, biologically active molecules found in fruits and vegetables, which is what the "five servings of fruit and vegetables a day" recommendation is based on—not just from a vitamin C perspective, but for the antioxidant flavonoids.

I was looking for mTOR inhibitors and saw things like resveratrol from Japanese knotweed and grape skins. Then there are berries like blueberries, bilberries, and cranberries, and citrus fruits contain these flavonoids. I also saw two other herbs that caught my attention. One was a Chinese herb, *Platycodon grandiflorus*, which contains a compound called Platycodin D. Another Chinese herb, *Magnolia grandiflora*, contains a product called honokiol. They were using those as both AKT-blocking and mTOR-inactivating substances.

When people use flavonoids for a systemic inflammatory disorder, these antioxidants can quench the free-radical-generating effect of inflammation. How can this be part of a holistic anti-cancer approach, rather than mechanistically poisoning the cancer cell, which a lot of chemotherapy and radiotherapy does? I know you promote generating higher-than-physiological levels of CO2 as being protective, along with other protective molecules like progesterone and aspirin. What do you think about the flavonoids and other substances I've mentioned?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Energetically, they do directly quench free radicals and are protective that way. But I think a more basic effect is that they intensify the cell's normal cytochrome oxidase-based oxidation by speeding up the energy-producing oxidation through the electron transport chain. That process prevents or reduces the random oxidation that creates free radical damage. So it's a lot more general and fundamental to intensify respiratory energy than to try to use the antioxidant function.

If you think in terms of antioxidants, it can go wrong because cancer is better than anything at creating antioxidant effects. Part of their wildness is their ability to defend themselves against free radical damage. Chemotherapy and radiation are intended to kill cancer cells by way of free radical damage, but they have an antioxidant system that uses high production of electrons. Basically, the excess of lactic acid causes an excess of electrons that will quench the free radicals, but meanwhile, they're failing to activate normal energy-producing oxidation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** You were talking earlier that if you got dental X-rays or other X-rays, it affected things near it. If you were going to be exposed to X-rays, what sorts of foods or other things would you want to do to help protect yourself?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Things such as thyroid, magnesium, and progesterone, which promote the production of carbon dioxide rather than lactic acid. And then all of these other protective things: the flavonoids, caffeine, aspirin, and so on.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I think what it sounds like you and Andrew are describing is that cancer involves a lot of inflammation, and a lot of these compounds are acting as anti-inflammatories and increasing normal cellular respiration.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that's really a secret of thyroid function. It's anti-inflammatory by directing oxygen towards consuming these electrons that would otherwise cause inflammation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Because when the body's inflamed, it results in lactic acid respiration, which is very damaging and inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And the loose electrons that are susceptible to random oxidation.

**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to Ask Your Herb Doctor. The number to call is 707-923-3911.

In terms of using agents that would block mTOR or the PI3K or AKT pathways, I saw that they've come up with second-generation mTOR inhibitors. I think you mentioned the first-generation ones last month: sirolimus, temsirolimus, and everolimus. But they also talked about second-generation inhibitors, calling them ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors, such as Torin 1 and Torin 2. Do you think these molecules that compete with ATP, the energy currency of the cell, have some value? I have trouble conceptualizing interfering with energy production.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That doesn't sound like it will end well.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Yeah.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The essential thing you need is to stabilize the cells.

**Andrew Murray:** Because you're always mentioning sugar being very important and not to starve someone of sugar, not just for diabetes but for cancer. And it's not at all scientifically rationalized that that is a good way to go.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Because the starving cancer emits signals that tell the body to convert its own tissues—muscles, skin, nerves—to amino acids which can be turned into glucose. So when you starve a cancer cell, it tells the body to start breaking itself down to provide the food it wants.

**Andrew Murray:** They also went on to discuss cancer metabolism and angiogenesis—the creation of novel vessels to bring blood and nutrients to the cancer. We've mentioned before that the activation of the hypoxia-inducible factor was very responsible for driving and promoting cancer, and how things like vascular endothelial growth factor are other substances which drive cancer's production. So blocking the hypoxia-inducible factor is something that I know you've talked about in the past.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That tends to go with activating carbonic anhydrase, which is the cell's way of disposing of acidic carbon dioxide. But when that is too active, it causes the cell to become alkaline, leading to the production of lactic acid. That's very central to cancer metabolism: to create alkalinity inside the cell by activating the enzyme that converts carbon dioxide from its acidic form to the carbonic acid form.

**Andrew Murray:** For those who are listening, I wanted to run through some other natural mTOR inhibitors. I think I mentioned turmeric last month. Turmeric is getting a lot of press for its anti-rheumatic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer effects, and it probably gets its anti-cancer kudos from being a natural mTOR inhibitor. Then resveratrol from *Polygonum cuspidatum*, and a compound whose abbreviation is EGCG, epigallocatechin gallate, from green tea, as well as caffeine. I was pleased to see caffeine, which may inhibit mTOR signaling directly and indirectly.

I saw two other substances that caught my attention. One was a substance called shogaol from ginger root. An article said it inhibited the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway by directly targeting AKT and AKT2, but not the PI3K or mTOR pathway. So ginger was used there specifically for colon cancer. And I know you're not into the pre-diabetes treating drugs, but metformin was actually listed as one of those things to inhibit mTOR. Do you have any good things to say about metformin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The only drawback is that it acts to inhibit part of the electron transport chain, so it's impairing the mitochondria while also doing the beneficial thing of turning off mTOR. So it's good to be cautious about metformin because there's not enough known about it, but still, its effects are generally protective through inhibiting mTOR.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think there's much value in using some of these substances as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's? I saw other references for neurodegenerative disorders, and I think there may have been a Parkinson's indication because of the amyloid-beta that was decreased and the neurofibrillary tangles that could be mitigated by using some of these substances because of their effect on mTOR and mTOR's downstream effects on amyloid production.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, inflammation is involved in all of the degenerative processes. And so the anti-inflammatory, anti-mTOR things are turning out to be protective against obesity, Alzheimer's, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus—anything you can think of turns out to involve inflammation at its root.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, we do have a caller. The number is 707-923-3911. Caller, you're on the air. Where are you from and what's your question?

**Caller:** Hello, Andrew, Sarah, and Dr. Peat. This is Margaret from Garberville. I'm grateful for your show. Your mention of turmeric caught me because I use turmeric daily. I know that there's a tendency in our society to find something like turmeric and say, "Oh, this is so great. I'm going to put it in capsules and take a lot of it every day." I was wondering if you would address whether that's really beneficial, or if it's beneficial enough to take it in your ordinary diet, just as it comes. Do we have to really sock it to our bodies with all of these extracts and pills?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think you can overeat on the so-called protective things. Same with vitamin C; instead of being an antioxidant, it becomes pro-oxidant when it begins producing excess electrons itself.

**Caller:** Turmeric comes to mind because I do use that. I know people that take it in little capsules every day, and it seems excessive to me, but I'm not sure. Is it beneficial at that level?

**Andrew Murray:** I think some of this comes from studying populations in countries that use it in their cuisine, like the Indian subcontinent, where they use a lot of turmeric and ginger. I think they have fairly low incidences of colorectal cancer, and they've kind of put two and two together when they've looked at turmeric and its anti-inflammatory activity, positing that as a potential mechanism.

**Caller:** Well, the thing is, they use it as a matter of course in their daily lives. We tend to say, "This is great, I'm going to load myself up with it." I'm just thinking that maybe that's not as beneficial as we think it might be. Maybe we should just follow that pattern and use it in a more integrated way.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** More in a culinary fashion.

**Caller:** Yes, thanks, Sarah.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So that we're eating our medicine instead of taking capsules. Remember too, a lot of traditional cultures make teas out of these things. They're not just swallowing tablespoons of turmeric root. They're putting some in their cooking, and if they're going to make it into a medicine, they make it into a tea, which helps to extract the medicinal constituents, like a tincture does, without having to have all the extra fiber and potential extra heavy metals that are in herbs that don't get extracted in the tea and the tincture like they would in the root.

**Andrew Murray:** That's a very good point. Having looked at these botanicals and put them through ICP-MS to see what levels of heavy metals—arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury—are within these herbs as part of a GMP process, I know from raw data that the plant root itself contains very high levels in some cases, and the extracts contain virtually none. The extract process is very clean compared to the root of the actual herb if you were going to consume it. We've done shows on this with fish in the ocean and how much arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury is in them. The same goes for any plant material that you would ingest in the powder or capsule form. Which is why we're not at all in agreement with capsules and powders over extracts, because extracts do not bring out the heavy metal content of the raw material.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And also, tinctures concentrate the medicinal constituents.

**Caller:** Well, thank you very much. I appreciate your help.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you, Margaret, for your call.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, I think we have another call on the line. Caller, where are you from and what's your question?

**Caller:** Hi, my name is Margie from Pepperwood. I would like a clarification on when Dr. Peat says "sugar," does that mean just fructose or honey, natural sugars? I can take my answer off the air.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay. So, what about sugar? Do we just want to get that from carbohydrates, or do you want to get it from sugar or honey? I think Dr. Peat would say to get it from honey and sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It can come from healthy starches and other more complex carbohydrates. But the problem is some of those, like sweet potatoes, are such mixtures. They have woody material and fats, indigestible things mixed in with the otherwise useful carbohydrates. So you can't just say that any old starch is going to be equivalent to glucose or sucrose or honey. It depends on whether it's digestible.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can I go back to the sugar and cancer issue that you touched on earlier? Every cell in the body needs glucose to operate. So if you don't eat any kind of sugar, your body's going to turn on a harmful metabolism to make sugar, and that involves lactic acid. Correct, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And high cortisol. Cortisol is necessary to mobilize and break down protein to make amino acids and glucose, which also promotes cancer.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Cortisol also promotes cancer. It's a stress promoter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It weakens your immunity against it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Yeah, it lowers your immune system. Like everybody knows, steroids suppress the immune system, and cortisol is a natural steroid your body will make when you starve your body of glucose. I know, Doctor, you said that honey and white cane sugar are identical in their structure. They both are sucrose, which is half fructose and half glucose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And the pure fructose on the market, for many people, has allergenic effects because of its manufacturing in a more complex way than with sucrose. You simply concentrate the juice and remove the impurities from the cane juice to make white sucrose. But to make fructose, chemical and enzyme processes are used that introduce some trace allergens. So you have to be cautious about using what they call powdered fructose.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So you would recommend honey or cane sugar over fructose because of the process that the fructose goes through, even though fructose is a more nutritious sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And the other thing too is, I know, Doctor, you don't recommend people just eat white sugar by the tablespoon without balancing it with a healthy saturated fat like coconut oil or butter and a protein, or at least with just a protein, so that it's not just an instant sugar spike.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It can be used in a pure form, for example, as a mild analgesic for babies. They give them a bit of pure sucrose as sort of a painkiller. And in areas that lack penicillin, a big wound that otherwise would be fatal has been packed with pure, store-bought white sugar. It has a germicidal effect as well as a protective effect.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Well, honey does too. They pack wounds with honey as well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. So it has specific therapeutic effects besides its protective nutritional effects.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Right. I hope that answered that caller's question.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, good. It's almost three minutes to the hour.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One thing I wanted to mention before we're finished is that vitamin D is a very important inhibitor of mTOR. It works on many other levels. It inhibits things that would promote mTOR and reduces the processes that would amplify a little inflammation into a big inflammation, such as blocking prostaglandin formation.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, excellent. Dr. Peat, I do appreciate you joining us again on the show. Thank you so much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor January 2022
transcriptText:
**Host:** Andrew Murray
**Co-Host:** Sarah Johanneson Murray
**Guest:** Dr. Raymond Peat

---

**Andrew Murray:** I want to remind everybody out there listening far and wide that if you do not support your source of information, then you are the product and your brain space is being sold to whoever does support the source of your news and information. So please support whatever local independent news sources that you consume. You have to keep a broader range of viewpoints alive out there, because sooner or later you'll be caught in a cul-de-sac with nowhere to go, and you'll rue the day you didn't support Redwood Community Radio. Without further ado, let's get into *Ask Your Herb Doctor*.

Good evening and welcome to the January 21, 2022 edition of *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Welcome to our show.

**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to KMUD Garberville 91.1 FM here from the Redwood Coast of California, broadcasting nationwide and internationally to a wide range of open-minded, perceptive individuals who want to know what's really going on.

Don't forget to listen to the audio archives. Unfortunately, the station only keeps them for a month or two at the most, but our website has at least 10 years of archives. I've got another two years to put up—excuse me for that, it's been a bit busy.

**Speaker A:** I'd like to comment on the archive situation. I thought they used to be held for a lot longer. One of my past hosts called me up saying, "Hey, our organization sent you people," so I was able to tell Simon about that and he was able to give them a special link. They're up there for three months as it is right now. It used to be longer, but there is a way that you can find a quick link to yours and put that on your website. We as programmers should talk to KMUD to try to get it back.

**Andrew Murray:** We record all of them, so they are intended to be put on the website. But the same thing happens—I just get so busy that it slips.

You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor* from 7:30 until 8:00. You're invited to call in with questions related or unrelated to this month's subject of MSG and cancer, and a continuation of estrogen and its progressively destructive effects and induction of autoimmunity and cancer. We have a bit of a wrap-up from last month to finish, and then we will get started with MSG, glutamate, and the links to cancer and excitotoxicity. There's also a link to COVID and MSG through its negative effects on the immune system.

The number is 707-923-3911. Please go ahead and call up with any questions you have related to this month's subject, or if you have other questions you want to pose to Dr. Peat. Dr. Peat, are you with us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us again. Let's make sure you are fully introduced to the audience, perhaps for those who may never have heard you. Let them know a little bit about your expertise.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had been a student of the humanities, teaching painting and English literature. I got interested in language and how the brain can do such a thing as use language. I decided that the only way to make progress was to go to graduate school in biology and study the brain.

In 1968, I went back to the University of Oregon. I quickly found that the nerve biology section of the department was very dogmatic and cared more about their theories than the actual experimental evidence. In fact, they didn't like to look too much at experimental results if they didn't absolutely fall in line with the theory.

After looking around for several weeks, I checked into many different labs at the university and found that the aging research—specifically reproductive physiology and how it's affected by aging—was the most concerned with finding out what's really happening. I decided to do my dissertation on that, which I finished in 1972: *Age-related oxidative changes in the hamster uterus*.

Surprisingly, that had a huge amount of information relative to brain function. To thoroughly understand what's going on in aging changes and how the organism redesigns cells so that they can start a new life from a single fertilized ovum involves the same principles that you need to look at to see what the brain is doing in relation to behavior and understanding language. One thing led into another, and I've been working on those subjects ever since.

**Andrew Murray:** From a social perspective, I really appreciate you interweaving your artistic nature with a fluid understanding. Mainstream understanding tends to be fairly dogmatic, but you have a very fluid, plastic way of looking at things. It has brought a very wide spotlight on a lot of subjects we've covered.

As I said many times, the archives we've recorded with you for the last 14 years are going to be a living testimony to what's already been confirmed—somewhat reluctantly by some industries because they'd like to keep control of their dominance. But a lot of these things you've been saying have been confirmed, and slowly but surely people are getting a much better understanding of the way things really are.

**Andrew Murray:** Before we retrace too much, there were several questions I wanted to ask Dr. Peat last month about estrogen, its relationship to autoimmunity, and cancer. Very quickly, I just wanted to cover a couple of things from an herbal perspective surrounding estrogen and aromatase.

Last month I mentioned a cucurbitaceous vine-bearing plant called *Momordica charantia*, which is bitter melon. It has been used to block estrogen and has estrogen-modulating properties. This is an anti-diabetic plant that essentially works with regulating blood glucose.

I also wanted to mention artemisinin, a component of wormwood (*Artemisia annua*). It actually contains not just anti-parasitic, antimicrobial, and antiviral effects, but it's also been shown to reduce the estrogen receptive function in breast cancer cell lines. That's worth people taking a look at on PubMed. Artemisinin does have anti-estrogenic activity.

I wanted to say quickly that tamoxifen may be useful in the treatment of immune-mediated disorders, particularly those arising from aberrant helper T1 cell activity, including allograft rejection. It's also been used with some success in Crohn's. But I wanted to bring out that the induced shift away from cellular immunity represents a significant step in fostering a carcinogenic environment. This may limit the anti-cancer effects of tamoxifen and explain why tamoxifen is inferior compared to other anti-estrogens for preventing disease recurrence in early-stage breast tumors.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's kick off tonight with the topic of MSG. The Food and Drug Administration has considered it safe to add to food. It's one of the most abundantly found amino acids in nature and is present in a heterogeneous group of foods as a flavor enhancer, known as E621 in the form of hydrolyzed protein or as a purified monosodium salt.

Very early on, they were seemingly demonstrating the benefits of monosodium glutamate as responsible for increasing temperature, decreasing body mass, and decreasing production of fat tissues. They claimed it would be readily taken up, not just because of the umami flavor, but that it conferred metabolic benefits.

I was surprised to find that there was a wide variety of foods—including walnuts, garlic, onion, potatoes—that contain natural glutamate. And then chicken, beef, eggs, human milk, and cow milk have it in fairly large amounts.

However, the negative effect of this glutamate was that it suppressed the oxidation of glucose. I'm wondering about the claims of obesity, whereas before they were talking about how it was going to increase your metabolism and burn fat. Dr. Peat, you've been looking at monosodium glutamate and its excitotoxic effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the weight loss thing was just a sales ploy to sell the flavoring substance. In the 1970s, mostly J.W. Olney found that when rats were fed just a little more than the amount that a person could normally eat in various artificial foods or added as flavoring, the brain was damaged in a certain way that led to lifelong obesity. It caused destruction of enough of the brain that appetite remained out of control and the metabolic rate wasn't sufficient to keep weight steady.

Over a period of several years, he did many experiments, including showing that the same sort of molecule—aspartic acid or aspartame or variations—had this range of excitatory effects as long as it was acting through the glutamate receptor or the aspartate receptor. One of the "positive" things was that it made you seem more alert. But that alertness came at the expense of not having enough energy produced to meet the high energy consumption caused by the excitatory action of the aspartate or glutamate.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Isn't aspartate aspartame? Isn't that also like that fake sugar Splenda or something like that?

**Speaker A:** Coke uses NutraSweet. It's aspartic acid with methanol, and then it degrades into methanol and leaves methanol in your neurons.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Oh yeah, that's a nasty chemical.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspartame is a super sweet material, sweeter than saccharin, but the amount that is toxic is very small. They've demonstrated that it can cause brain cancer. Olney, among others in the late 70s, showed that the sudden appearance of a rising incidence of gliomas—malignant glial cell tumors, brain cancer—could be caused by overfeeding glutamates or MSG to animals. The rise in the population incidence and mortality from these tumors followed by a few years the introduction of foods that were loaded with everything from aspartame to MSG.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** This goes to show we can't trust the ethics of the FDA if they're allowing that product on the market.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cell phones have corresponded as well. For example, if a person habitually holds their cell phone to the right ear, the incidence of brain tumors on the right side has increased sharply since the use of cell phones. It happens that they are both causes of excitotoxicity. The electromagnetic field excites the cells, and you need to provide energy to keep up with that, or the cell dies.

Ongoing experiments show that when cells are endangered by such things as MSG or aspartame, if you intervene by giving them a super amount of sugar—glucose or other sugar—it will save the neurons simply by feeding whatever is needed to keep up with the high level of excitation.

This is the image of the excitotoxic conflict: unavoidable stimulation of excitation combined with something interfering with the oxidation of glucose. That isn't applicable only to aging and gliomas; it applies to epilepsy, for example. If the cells aren't able to keep up their energy production with the excitation, the seizure gets out of control and damages the tissue.

It isn't just nerve cells, though they are the most obvious. Any cell that can be exaggeratedly stimulated can be rescued if you keep the sugar supply up. But if it isn't kept up, then that cell can become cancerous, form tumors, or just die, leading to dementia or various types of brain function loss.

**Andrew Murray:** This is like a kind of wasteful entropy. There's a lack of input of the energy needed to keep the cell going.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and it's made worse by overlapping influences. It isn't just cell phone radiation and aspartame and MSG, but many different things all have that same function.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So eating Chinese food with MSG, drinking a diet soda, plus talking on your cell phone holding it up to your head...

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And if you look at what any stress does—no matter what you're doing to yourself, vibration, laser overstimulation, telephone overstimulation, or even simply glucose deprivation or oxygen deprivation—they all turn out to be excitatory.

**Andrew Murray:** I think to coin the term "wasteful" was probably a good way for people listening to understand the term "excitatory." It's a very wasteful blowing off of your energy with inefficient processes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It happens that the feeding of energy in the form of sugar has a sedative action that leads to turning down the degree of excitation.

Any harmful influence—oxygen or glucose deprivation, temperature too cold or too hot—turns out to activate a whole range of short-term solutions if the cell perceives that it is not getting enough energy to meet the needs.

One alternative is to try to go into hibernation to turn off its own needs for energy. To do that, it has the equipment for producing serotonin, which will help to prevent loss of heat through the skin, but it also turns down the production of heat. It leads to a colder and colder state—suspended animation to a degree.

Another universal basic reaction is the formation of histamine. When a cell is in desperate, dying conditions, it forms and secretes histamine into its environment because the histamine will open up any closed blood vessels and get more blood delivered.

Estrogen is another of these short-term emergency things. The estrogen in turn can activate the serotonin system and cool off the whole energy-consuming apparatus. It can activate the histamine system. It activates nitric oxide formation that opens up the blood vessels the same way histamine does. And it can activate heme oxygenase, which breaks down heme. Breaking down the heme will provide some antioxidant function—bilirubin and carbon monoxide are produced. Under these circumstances, the carbon monoxide can serve as an antioxidant, blocking the ability to consume oxygen and so moving the system into a torpor or hibernation.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's all lots of inflammation.

**Andrew Murray:** Lots of wasteful mechanisms to deplete the organism of energy and further send the cell into a desperate state.

**Speaker A:** My understanding is that the glutamate, or the Accent flavor, is stimulating the umami flavor, and a lot of high protein and other nutritious foods stimulate that too. How is it that the body is able to be benefited by eating a nice high-protein diet?

**Andrew Murray:** Yes, hydrolyzed protein, whey, soy protein, and a lot of those products are big sources of MSG. Dr. Peat, how about the flavoring side of MSG versus its natural presence in the diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the natural state, protein is a rare delicacy for most animals. The urge to eat some protein is a definite survival urge—you want to build muscle, make new tissue, and so on. But the trouble is when society provides lots of cheap protein, people get in the habit of not being guided by their appetite and cravings, but just eating it because it's there. Even because it's considered the most valuable food, people tend to overeat on protein after they're around the age of 20 or so.

As their growth slows down, they tend to keep eating for the 15-year-old they were. As long as you're growing, you respond to the signal action of the glutamate. You go into an anabolic state and pick up all of those individual amino acids and make muscle and brain tissue. But once your size is established, if you keep eating that same amount, you're going to have a lot of excess beyond your needs. Excess histidine, tryptophan, methionine, cysteine, aspartate, glutamate—all of these are potentially excitotoxic amino acids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when you recommend people consume 75 to 100 grams of protein a day, you're not recommending they consume that all in the form of muscle meat or eggs. You typically don't recommend more than two eggs a day, and most of your protein requirements you believe should be coming from dairy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. After you're grown up, you should try to learn to go by your actual biological urges rather than what advertising tells you to eat.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So how many ounces of a muscle protein—whether it's fish, shellfish, meat, chicken—would you recommend is a safe level for adults?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As your metabolic rate slows down—and that happens steadily from puberty—the older you are, the more careful you have to be about having an excess of the excitotoxic amino acids.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So I guess it's just based upon your activity level and your age.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was Adelle Davis who pointed out that gelatin is considered an incomplete protein because animals and people can't grow if they aren't getting the amino acids lacking in gelatin. But she said she had seen lots of old women going for years living on a diet of toast, Jell-O, and tea—practically their only protein being the gelatin. That was just an illustration of what a very tiny amount a very old person needs.

**Andrew Murray:** I pulled out an article describing the exposure of rats to monosodium glutamate at the neonatal stage. It severely damaged their hypothalamic nuclei, which resulted in increased body weight, fat deposition, decreased motor activity, and decreased secretion of growth hormone. MSG appears to be a suitable candidate for inducing obesity which leads to diabetes.

Funnily enough, the FDA is still behind it. They haven't thrown it out. I was very surprised that even things like human milk and cow milk had some of the monosodium glutamate component in it.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** I wonder if it's allowed to be in products without being listed as an additive. Dr. Peat, do you know anything about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think legally it has to be listed. They have some alternatives, like calling it a "vegetable broth" or something when it's really an MSG extracted from soybean.

**Speaker A:** Can it be "natural flavor" if it's less than a certain percentage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I suppose so.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What about Tamari? Tamari is a wheat-free soy sauce made of fermented soy protein. Doesn't that form a natural MSG as well? Is that something that should be limited in someone's diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so.

**Andrew Murray:** I saw an article stating that curcumin from turmeric protects against monosodium glutamate neurotoxicity by decreasing NMDA2B expression in the rat hippocampus. That's another good plus point for turmeric and its anti-inflammatory activity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are lots of flavonoids like quercetin and myricetin in coffee. Coffee has lots of tissue-protective, anti-cancer, anti-dementia effects that I think are largely an effect of the flavonoid components.

**Andrew Murray:** Another article mentioned the vital role of the hippocampus in memory formation and regulation of behavior, showing that glutamate was involved in increasing the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines—like tumor necrosis factor alpha—which contributes to brain damage and the death of neurons.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There has been a lot of study of how the excitotoxic things like glutamate actually make the cell become more active. They assumed for many of the studies that glucose was somehow able to reduce the uptake or retention by the cell of the excitotoxic agent. But a more detailed study found that the cells were being protected by high glucose addition without changing the concentration of aspartate or glutamate inside the cell.

What was happening was that normally, the process of responding to the excitotoxin means that the cell is taking up and retaining the excitatory molecule calcium, which should be an extracellular molecule. When the cell retains too much, it goes into the excited, inflamed, energy-wasting state.

They found that the addition of extra glucose allowed the cell to extrude more calcium as it continued to metabolize. Apparently, the mechanism is that glucose promotes the increase of carbon dioxide formation as it's metabolized. The carbon dioxide forming carbonic acid leaves the cell and takes with it the counter ion—the doubly positively charged calcium and some sodium. So the flow of glucose/carbonic acid out of the cell is taking care of the calcium accumulation, which is the basic cause of the inflammation, pain, and cell death.

**Andrew Murray:** Let me just quickly outline the typical foods that are glutamate-rich. It's not a bash at vegetarians, but it just so happens that hydrolyzed vegetable protein is very high in glutamate. Autolyzed yeast, hydrolyzed yeast, yeast extracts, soy extracts, and protein isolate are all very high in glutamate. These form a fairly large part of a vegetarian or vegan diet as an alternative protein source.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Yeah, a lot of bouillons, even if they're organic, have a yeast extract. I notice if I use that, I feel like I've had an MSG burn on my tongue.

**Caller 1 (Kevin):** I live on the Avenue of the Giants where I pick up trash. Can you explain inflammation? Is it inflammation of the cells or inflammation around the muscle tissue, particularly regarding arthritis and the aches and pains of getting older?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People in recent years have been talking about "inflammaging," as if that explains something. The process of aging obviously involves increased inflammation in every sense we know. But the problem is to see what the basic events are in cell structure, pain, excitation, inflammation, and aging. All have these aspects of cytotoxic cell damage and the inability to remedy the problem by making enough energy or delivering enough energy.

Regarding heme oxygenation—one of the emergency enzymes that produces carbon monoxide—probably 95% of the publications describe carbon monoxide as an antioxidant, very protective, and so on. But if you look at the deteriorated brain in old age, there is more carbon monoxide in it than at any previous life stage. Carbon monoxide presence is a degenerative aspect of inflammation and cell deterioration.

If you block the formation of nitric oxide—for example, in a traumatic wound to the head or spinal cord—or if you block the formation of carbon monoxide, you prevent most of the damage development, edema, and cell death. So the chemistry of aging, inflammation, and deterioration is a complex of things that express the same idea as excitotoxicity.

**Andrew Murray:** Wasteful energy processes.

**Caller 2:** I'm from South Central Los Angeles. How long does the body take to heal from all the damage? Let's say you reduce all the estrogen, the polyunsaturated fat (PUFA), and all the inflammatory things. Is there a difference in age or is it the same for everyone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The young person with the higher metabolic rate can change everything more quickly. For the average person, if you move from a country that eats a lot of polyunsaturated fats to a country that eats very little of them, it can take four years to equilibrate to the new balance in the diet.

But if you make an extreme effort... one of the early researchers in the supposed essentiality of polyunsaturated fat demonstrated that he would get sick if he ate a laboratory purified diet absolutely lacking polyunsaturated fats. But about three or four months into the diet, all of his chronic health problems disappeared—chronic migraine and other symptoms—and stayed away. In his case, with an extreme avoidance of just one harmful nutrient, his lifelong problems disappeared in just a few months.

**Caller 2:** Would that also apply if you reduce things to get rid of estrogen? My wife suffers from fibroids and has had a couple of miscarriages because of the fibroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. A friend of mine who was 40 and wanted to get pregnant had a tennis ball-sized fibroid blocking the end of her uterus so the tubes couldn't open to deliver the ovum. She took an overdose of thyroid. Every month the doctor—besides telling her she was going to die from taking too much thyroid—made an image showing that the fibroid was shrunken. Every month it got smaller. I think it was about the fifth month it had become about a fourth of its original size and she was pregnant.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So five months made a big difference just by using natural thyroid hormone, lowering her estrogen, and improving her liver function.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And there are so many other out-of-balance components of diet. Too much iron in most people's food, too much methionine, aspartate, glutamate, cysteine. By fixing any one component, you can see drastic effects. So if you fixed half a dozen of these things that are out of balance, it should produce very huge effects quickly.

**Caller 3:** I'm from Arcata. I have a young grandson, age nine, who has had two episodes of big intestinal bleeding. He's had every scope of his upper and lower GI done, not finding anything. They figure it's something called Meckel's diverticulum, some lesion in the small intestine. Could you recommend any foods that would be soothing to the GI tract?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People vary in their sensitivities. But the first thing to do would be to absolutely avoid foods that have added gums, especially carrageenan. A very high percentage of foods now contain vegetable gums, microbial gums, or carrageenan, all of which are very pro-inflammatory. Just knocking out those foods can stop things like chronic bowel bleeding.

**Caller 3:** Would aloe vera or slippery elm be some kind of panacea to help be soothing?

**Andrew Murray:** Just straight off the top—it might sound a little mild—but in Germany and England where I studied herbal medicine, chamomile was the number one GI anti-inflammatory. It's got a fairly pronounced effect in blocking inflammation and soothing the GI tract. Chamomile is the "mother of the gut." That would be one of the first things I would give somebody.

Depending on what kind of bleeding we're talking about, gentle tannins would also be indicated to gently astringe the capillaries or tissues leaking blood.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And that can be as simple as black tea or green tea.

**Andrew Murray:** Yeah, black tea would be totally indicated, as would many other astringent-containing herbs like potentilla.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very important to check his thyroid and vitamin D levels because a deficiency of either of those can make the intestine hypersensitive to inflammation.

**Andrew Murray:** If you haven't already done it, obviously his hemoglobin should be looked at. If he's had long-term chronic bleeding, he'd be anemic, and that's going to be a negative factor for his energy. To support that, use plenty of foods that contain naturally present iron rather than any iron supplement. As Dr. Peat mentioned, iron is very reactive and inflammatory. Go with foods that would be iron-rich, like liver.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And avoid synthetic vitamin C. The synthetic vitamin C reacts with the traces of iron in your body to produce inflammation.

**Caller 4:** I'm from Queens, New York. What are the basic consequences of not filling a cavity? Is there any damage to the nervous system that takes place if you leave a cavity unfilled?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Consider if the damage is only into the enamel—that can be remineralized. But once it enters into the dentine, then it really needs to be filled.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We see a holistic dentist in Medford, Oregon, and he recommends Lugol's iodine for those cavities that are just invading the enamel rather than going all the way into the dentine. He said because it's so close on the periodic table of elements to fluoride, but is not neurotoxic like fluoride is, it's a safe alternative. Besides being antimicrobial, a low percentage solution of Lugol's iodine is very helpful for remineralizing superficial cavities.

**Speaker A:** And I'll throw a plug out there for flossing. As one wise person said, "Floss only those teeth you wish to keep."

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to get this information out for people to take a look at. I looked up a researcher named Blalock. In the *International Journal of Vaccine Theory, Practice, and Research* dated January 2021, I saw an interesting article titled "Excitotoxicity and Immuno-excitotoxicity as a Critical Component of the Cytokine Storm Reaction in Pulmonary Viral Infection, including SARS-CoV-2."

It basically stated that this hyper-immune state secondary to dysregulation of the immune system was ultimately causative for the cytokine storm. A researcher named Morimoto found that co-injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)—which is a very negative substance in the body—plus the NMDA agonist ibotenic acid (from *Amanita muscaria*) caused significant neuronal damage through the excitotoxic arm of the reaction.

I just want to read out one last thing before we close the show. Europe and Britain have lifted the mandate for everything related to COVID.

Authoritarianism and the age of acceptance: have it all and have nothing. We're evolving as a species and with our evolution comes a concept of deranged acceptance. Nature is not accepting, but rather through evolutionary pressure it selects the fittest and is quite barbaric. It takes no prisoners and is quite merciless. Rules exist and nature obeys them. They are set from the foundation of the world, which we recently have also learned to meddle with and derange—like viruses and gain-of-function research.

The opposite, perhaps, of the all-encompassing embrace of "everything is allowable" are the immutable laws set in place which we're constrained to, like time, gravity, and death. Authoritarianism is at odds with our founding fathers' constitution of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, which is a God-ordained decree, immutable and self-evident.

Like gain-of-function research and authoritarianism, these are set at odds with their counterpart and are to be resisted with your life. Life demands that fitness be preserved and aims at physical and spiritual health. I put it to you that with increasing authoritarianism and draconian legislation aimed at making us happier to coexist with everything, accept everything, have no boundaries, and have no morals... I leave you with this: Have at it, or resist and live.

Until the third Friday of next month, my name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Thank you for listening.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Ask the Herb Doctor June 2022
transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Well, good evening and welcome to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. This is June 17th, 2022. My name's Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to the show. At 7:30, we'll open the lines up to invite callers in with questions related to this month's topic, which is going to be around food, the corporation's control of food, and some ongoing numbers and statistics from the COVID fallout. Then we're going to get into some parts of the political discourse and involvement of big companies in the Ukraine and fertilizer production. Hopefully, we're going to get to the topic of the baby milk shortage, follow that up with some artificial meat topics, and as always, have the great pleasure of having Dr. Peat's superb overview of a lot of things.

I guess it's part of his age that enables him to encompass at least 40 or 50 years of time spent studying the subjects, and another three decades on top of that of living to see the events unfolding that have done so. He's got a pretty good, rounded view of many different subjects, and alternative medicine is one of them. He's been spending a large part of his life and his career looking at the research, which is always the most interesting part of any of this factual information. It's not just opinion. So once again, very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat join us on the show. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay. Well, if you don't mind, for the next five minutes or so, I just wanted to run an introduction to some of the questions that I'll be asking you. But just to wrap up last month's discourse, we talked about genetic modification and corporations with patent rights on intellectual property. Especially Monsanto with their genetically engineered seeds, and the quote-unquote moratorium that was on natural products certainly seems to have been put to one side now, where naturally occurring products like corn, wheat, and potatoes have now been granted patent rights on their genetically modified versions. I think this also runs into vaccine technology and the emerging infections that we've gone through since the mid-1990s up until now, with COVID obviously being the major part of our prior two-year discourse.

I also wanted to remind people that the lawyer Reiner Fuellmich has a huge amount of data on his website, which I would encourage everyone to look at as a superb, chronologically documented series of allegations. He's charging crimes against humanity for many organizations, institutions, and governments.

Also mentioned last month that the United Nations has changed the terminology from "technocracy" to "green economy" and "sustainable development," and how that impacts us all very negatively because it sounds so innocuous and harmless. Sustainable development—who doesn't want sustainability? We all do. I want local markets, I want people growing food locally. I don't want huge corporations shipping food from one side of the world to the other and displacing rural farmers. We want sustainable development. But the words "sustainable development" have been couched in such a way as to embrace this technocracy, which we exposed last month as really beginning from about the 1920s. Dr. Peat certainly weighed in on what he understands of technocracy, having lived through it, and obviously the Rockefeller Foundation and all the other power players that are forming the heads of government institutions and global organizations, from the Codex Alimentarius to the Great Reset.

**Andrew Murray:** Anyway, that was just an overview of last month. I wanted to open up this month with something that caught my eye. The fifth-largest life insurance company in the US has just paid out 163% more for deaths of working people—folks from 18 to 64, not old people. The company cites "non-pandemic-related morbidity" and "unusual claims adjustments" as the explanation of losses from group life insurance businesses. The stock is falling and the CEO has been replaced.

The head of an Indianapolis-based insurance company, OneAmerica, said the death rate is up a stunning 40% from pre-pandemic levels among working-age people. Five months after the CEO of OneAmerica broke this story, a new report is out that a much larger life insurance company, Lincoln National, reported a 163% increase in death benefits paid out under its group life insurance policies in 2021.

To quote the OneAmerica CEO, Scott Davison, he stated, "We are seeing right now the highest death rates we've seen in the history of this business, not just at OneAmerica... it's consistent across every player in the business." OneAmerica is a $100 billion insurance company. Davison said the increase in death represents huge numbers, and that it's not elderly people who are dying, but primarily working-age people, 18 through 64. He said, "What we saw just in third quarter, we're seeing it continue into fourth quarter, and that is that death rates are up 40% over what they were pre-pandemic. Just to give you an idea of how bad that is, a three-sigma or a one-in-200-year catastrophe would be a 10% increase over pre-pandemic. So 40% is just unheard of."

Now, what is driving this unprecedented surge in all-cause mortality? It was not only deaths of working-age people that shot up to unheard-of levels in 2021, but also short- and long-term disability claims. If this holds true, then the genetic vaccines so aggressively promoted have failed, and the clear federal campaign to prevent early treatment with life-saving drugs has contributed to a massive, avoidable loss of life. At worst, this report implies that the federal workplace vaccine mandates have driven what appears to be a true crime against humanity: a massive loss of life in workers that have been forced to accept a toxic vaccine at a higher frequency relative to the general population.

Furthermore, we've also been living through the most massive, globally coordinated propaganda and censorship campaign in the history of the human race. All major mass media and social media technology companies have coordinated to stifle and suppress any discussion of the risks of the genetic vaccines and/or alternative early treatments.

So, Dr. Peat, with that introduction—I'm sure it's not news to you, I know you've been tirelessly talking about this since the very beginning of 2020—what are your interpretations of this insurance company's disclosure of these facts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several other companies since then have reported very similar increased mortality, around 40%, in the working-age group. Insurance companies generally have extremely accurate statistics, better than governments as a rule, because their income depends on exactness. So it's really the scientific basis for saying that it wasn't the virus that's responsible, but the vaccination. That's when the 40% rise began. And it fits what the skeptical virologists have been claiming: that the mortality is going to be far, far worse from the vaccine than from whatever occurred from the virus.

**Andrew Murray:** I think that was the point that was made: it was all-cause mortality in young people, and a lot of it was to do with damage and disability. So whether the death may have been caused by the vaccine or not, the amount of money paid out due to the disabilities that were claimed is a pretty stunning part of the numbers. I think we've mentioned in the past that when we're describing things like mortality and altitude, it was the very insurance companies that let that information out, which supported the claim that lower premiums were imposed on people at higher altitude because they were not as likely as people at sea level to die.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay, so that's the first thing, just seeing some glaring headlines about the deaths and insurance companies making payouts and how this is now just part of the fallout of COVID. Supposedly now what we're seeing is the actuality of it all with Omicron. I don't know if you feel that Omicron is a naturally produced variant or indeed any other type of it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has the most bizarre gene sequences of all of the other variants. Starting with the Wuhan virus, the other variants show a series of mutations building on each other. So the most recent, until Omicron, showed exactly the same series of mutations incorporated. It was definitely that virus improving its survivability by mutating. But the Omicron is unique. It didn't show any mutations after Wuhan. While the Wuhan virus was going through all of these changes, nothing was happening at all to the Omicron. Suddenly when it pops up, it is essentially the pristine Wuhan virus with a new series built right on the original virus, none of the history of natural mutation—as if it was being held aside and going through a different series of mutations, as if it wasn't in the world at all for these intervening years.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So are you saying that basically the original COVID went through mutations and you can track that, and then all of a sudden Omicron was like the original with just some alterations to it, so it looked like it had been lab-produced?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and those mutations made it much less harmful. So if someone was preparing a product to end the pandemic by turning it off with a fairly harmless virus...

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So do you think that if people have Omicron and they've developed antibodies to that and caught that naturally, even though it's not a naturally mutated virus, then will they be better able to fight the original Delta or those other variants?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, it won't especially affect them. If it's the dominant virus and it's very harmless, then the other one just isn't going to be around to cause trouble.

**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to *Ask Your Herb Doctor*. From 7:30 to the end of the show, callers are invited to call in with any questions either related to this month's discussion or any other questions they'd like to pose to Dr. Peat about health-related or alternative medicine. The number is 707-923-3911.

Okay, so moving on to the major content of this next 45 minutes. I read a 2014 article from the Oakland Institute. Eight years later, what we're seeing now in Ukraine and Russia is really a question that's embroiled in health, government control, and takeovers. People have certainly heard a lot about Roundup and Monsanto and GMOs.

So the Oakland Institute published a 2014 paper outlining what was being described then as a global corporate takeover of agricultural land in the Ukraine. Ukraine has been hailed as the breadbasket of Europe with a staggering 32 million-plus hectares of incredibly fertile black arable soil. For those of you who are gardeners or farmers, you're well aware of what this means to crops: lush, rich, fertile growth with excellent crop yields and quality harvests. If you too are Monsanto, one of the biggest agribusinesses on the planet, or one of a handful of other players buying into this hugely profitable location, rights to ownership are extremely lucrative. And corruption, as always, exists at the highest level for the highest returns.

Naturally, Ukraine's agricultural land was under a moratorium that banned its sale through January 1, 2016. When Ukraine separated from the Soviet Union in 1990, collectivized communal farms were disbanded and land was distributed in parcels of approximately four hectares each to people living on the farms. In 2001, Ukraine passed its Land Code legislation that gave people functional titles to land. Since then, there's been a moratorium on the sale of land.

The moratorium on land sales applies only to agricultural land, making it both legal and affordable for investors to build and operate a 100% foreign-owned processing facility on its own industrial land while leasing fields from agricultural landowners. A second way that investors could circumvent the land moratorium was by buying shares of large existing Ukrainian agribusinesses. The system of land distribution in the 1990s often led to the concentration of land in the hands of a few elites. Alongside land opportunities, the development, production, and use of agricultural inputs like seeds, agrochemicals, and fertilizers have attracted investment by agribusiness giants Monsanto, Cargill, Dupont, and others. So I was going to ask you, Dr. Peat, you had lots of other information to tie this in.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone has heard about the International Monetary Fund offering the Ukraine a $40 billion loan if they would stop the moratorium, specifically so Monsanto and the other giant corporations could concentrate ownership on a big corporate scale. There was a coup to make that happen because the elected presidency had rejected the IMF fund. The IMF, working with the World Bank and all of the other so-called Western authorities, wanted to reverse that and stop the moratorium, so they supported the coup. And the coup was very clear that they were going to adapt laws that would let Monsanto take over. When the coup happened, in fact, that did take place. They had to get rid of the legally elected president and establish the Zelensky government supporting the Monsanto privatization system.

**Andrew Murray:** So how do you see Russia's involvement? Because this seems to be a two-sided story.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, part of the Monsanto thing is that they want to use chemicals like Roundup to make the profitability of certain giant land corporations favorable to them. The European Union had opposed the United States' policy of supporting Monsanto and genetic modification. So there was a conflict. Several Western European countries went along with wanting to outlaw GMOs.

It turned out that historically, Russia had been passing laws to promote organic farming and to outlaw GMOs. They were aiming for 100% freedom from GMOs and, naturally, from Monsanto. That really was the polarization for the coup and for the International Monetary Fund loan. When the elected president made a deal with Russia for a loan that would bypass the International Monetary Fund, that was the actual moment when the coup took place and got him out of power in Ukraine.

**Andrew Murray:** I read a couple of years ago, and you can back me up on this, that Vladimir Putin was boasting that he was going to make Russia one of, if not the biggest, organic food producers in the world.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Yeah, that's what one of his goals was. But I thought GMOs are still banned in Europe.

**Andrew Murray:** Well, I think they are in England. I'm pretty sure England had banned GMOs.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** No, I thought in England they're not banned because they're not part of the EU. So the EU has banned GMOs, is that your understanding, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are wobbling on the issue. There is still opposition to it, but now the war for Monsanto has affected the West. They aren't pushing so hard to oppose the GMOs.

**Andrew Murray:** I wonder how the whole fertilizer shortage plays into it. Apparently, Ukraine is a big exporter or manufacturer of fertilizer. I wonder how that plays into it, along with the agriculturally rich diversity that is possible there in Ukraine, and how this quote-unquote food shortage they're talking about now... Before we get into the subject of baby milk, the food shortage issue, I wonder how politically motivated this is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, you can see many specific things in which it's been just openly promoted. For example, Union Pacific Railroad announced that they just weren't going to ship all of the fertilizer that the farmers needed. **Andrew Murray:** Okay, so we've talked about things like soy protein in the past being used as a meat alternative. **Andrew Murray:** Let's take this next call. Caller, where are you from and what's your question?
