title: Ask the Herb Doctor Lipofuscin
transcriptText:
**Host:** Andrew Murray
**Co-host:** Sarah Johanneson Murray
**Guest:** Dr. Raymond Peat

---

**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's August 19th, 2022 edition of Ask Your Herb Doctor. My name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray.

**Andrew Murray:** For those of you who have just tuned in, it's a once-a-month radio show, the third Friday of each month from 7:00 till 8:00 PM. We are joined by the expert scientific viewpoint—not opinion, but scientific viewpoint—of Dr. Raymond Peat. I appreciate all those people that do tune into the show either live or who listen to the archives.

I am very pleased to welcome Dr. Peat to the show. I think he has somewhat recovered from some voice hoarseness due to the wildfires up in Oregon. How are you doing, Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I have a tummy cold. I probably should clarify what I mean by "scientific viewpoint." I'm not like Fauci; I don't have *the* scientific viewpoint. I think of the scientific viewpoint as a critical one—always thinking about the evidence and what you're really implying. So it's a matter of criticism and thinking.

**Andrew Murray:** You're always able to back up what you say with articles, reference journals, or other bona fide published information. Just in case anybody listening doesn't know you, could you give an outline of your academic and professional background before we start the show?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied the humanities first through a master's degree, and then went back in 1968 to the University of Oregon for a PhD in biology. Basically physiological chemistry, specifically the metabolic and physiological changes that happen in the reproductive system in aging. There is a chapter of that dissertation where I concentrated on what at that time was still sometimes called metaplasm, or lipofuscin, as a basic cause of aging.

**Andrew Murray:** I wanted to expand on your work and discourse on lipofuscin. We've mentioned it in the past in relation to polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). Public awareness has exploded in the last 18 months with publications coming out saying that they are not safe, that they are dangerous, and that the thinking of the last three decades was erroneous and has resulted in pathology—not just obesity and diabetes, but other degenerative conditions.

Can I start by going over some basics regarding these so-called "essential fatty acids"? If you look online, it seems to imply that they are only available from the diet. Is that correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, some very simple experiments make that really clear. But that amount of clarity in 80 years has hardly penetrated the beliefs about the facts because industry has found a motive in claiming that they are essential. The evidence for them being essential is of an extremely vague, inferential type.

The evidence against it is clear. For example, you can grow human cells in culture. If you're growing huge masses of cells, you know exactly what they're being fed. You can feed them on a diet absolutely excluding fatty acids, especially the unsaturated fatty acids. They multiply enormously on a diet of no environmental unsaturated fats. Obviously, any unsaturated fat that they contain is something that they have made themselves.

The basic recognized evidence that we aren't getting environmental linoleic or arachidonic acid—and are becoming deficient in these so-called essential fats—is two findings: that we are making something called Mead acid (an omega-9 series of polyunsaturated fats) and having a long saturated tail. This is just the opposite of fish oil. The n-3 (omega-3) has unsaturated groups within three carbons of the tip. The type we make ourselves, the Mead acids, are saturated fats extending down to within only nine carbons at the end. That makes them relatively resistant to external contact with oxygen.

**Andrew Murray:** That is important—the erroneous doctrine of them being essential and the fact that they are able to be manufactured. Haven't you said in the past that the placenta doesn't allow these fats to cross?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's a very good filter. Even when the mother is eating fish, grains, and unsaturated fats, the general recognition is that at birth, babies almost always demonstrate making some of the anti-inflammatory natural Mead acid. This shows that they were assimilating very little of the PUFA from the environment.

Defining the newborn baby as almost always "essential fatty acid deficient," the formula companies argued that they need to add fish oil extract to baby formula to make up for the fact that the newborn brain shows evidence of deficiency of exactly those fats. So they do add it to baby formula. Within a few days of reaching the grocery store, these fats are degrading, oxidizing, and becoming toxic. After about a month in the store, they degrade even more. The evidence is that what you're doing is feeding your baby rancid fish oil products which are toxic in many ways.

**Andrew Murray:** Haven't they done experiments to support the fact that babies fed on these formulas—because of the EPA and other fatty acids—show decreased cognition and awareness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Those studies were done over the last 70 or 80 years in rats, dogs, and other animals. They showed that in proportion to the amount of PUFA in the diet, their brains are reduced in size and in learning ability after they're born. The deficient animals—without the PUFA in their brains—have bigger brains, are higher metabolizers all over, and learn much faster. In the 70s, some studies said the average rodent deficient in PUFA had something like a 140 IQ compared to his EPA-drugged siblings.

If you look at the aging brain right from birth, in all the animals that have been studied, the amount of PUFA in the brain steadily increases from the so-called deficient state at birth up until a heavy overload state in old age and dementia. There is a steady increase in PUFA concentration interfering with cholesterol synthesis. As the PUFA content of tissue increases, the heat production and metabolic energy of the whole animal decreases in proportion. The baby has extremely high overall oxygen consumption and metabolic rate, supporting that fantastic rate of learning that is normal for a newborn.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** An interesting side note: I'm not someone who suffered from heartburn, but when I was pregnant all three times, if I ate any PUFA-rich animal fat—like duck fat, chicken fat, or pork fat—I would get heartburn. Even just the tiniest bit. I was avoiding vegetable oils, but that was the only time I would get heartburn. It was very easy for me to see why I shouldn't be eating any kind of PUFA fats when I was pregnant.

**Andrew Murray:** The essential fatty acid myth has been destroyed. The fish oil industry is a multi-billion dollar conglomerate pushing this stuff, and academia pumps out supporting evidence showing anti-inflammatory effects. But the baby in the mother's womb selectively blocks the transport of these products.

Dr. Peat, the fact that these n-3 and n-6 fats are not essential, but are found in many different foods... I know you've always supported a saturated fat diet. But regarding the liquid oils we've been subjected to for 30 or 40 years—canola, corn, fish oil—do you think they should be consumed at all?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think they should be avoided as far as possible.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you outline your understanding of the process by which things like metal ions and stressors exert their effect on these n-3 and n-6 oils in the presence of our body temperature?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The nuts and seeds that produce the oils—and the snakes, frogs, and fish that use them habitually—do so without any special problem. Those oils are appropriate for manufacturing their own energy stores because they live at a fairly low temperature. Animal fats at room temperature tend to solidify; a snake with solidified fat just doesn't work very well. If you're going to have flexible, active tissues, you need to have fats that are liquid at body temperature.

These fats are appropriate for cold animals. If you put these fats into a very hot animal, that's when they're extremely unstable. High temperature, plus the fact that they are designed to be very sensitive to heat so that they're flexible at room temperature, means that you shouldn't eat them if you're going to live at 98 degrees Fahrenheit.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So it's okay for the frogs and snakes to eat these omega-6 and omega-3 oils because they're cold-blooded and won't heat those fats up to oxidize them. Whereas because we should be around 98 or 99 degrees Fahrenheit, we're going to rapidly oxidize those and turn them into free radicals. Is that what you're saying?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. In some studies, they decided to see how efficient fish oil was as an energy source for fish. Naturally, it has to be liquid enough to function at a cool temperature. But they added some animal fat—more saturated fat—to a salmon diet and then put them through an endurance test. The salmon that were eating salmon fat had the endurance that they would have if you gave them a little more saturated fat.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's focus on lipofuscin—its danger, its buildup, and how it's virtually impossible to detox from. It gets bound up in neurons and is an aging causative factor implicated in neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Starting in the 1930s, to explain why food got rancid, the process of breakdown of fats inside tissues was studied. People learned to manufacture something that looked and functioned like lipofuscin by reacting, for example, copper and vitamin C, iron, and just about any kind of fat and various biological components.

You can see that the free radical process is triggered by the copper or iron and a reductant, such as vitamin C, that attracts the oily materials—especially if they're unsaturated—and causes a spreading catalytic oxidative process that creates more free radicals.

You can identify various things that pour out of tissues depending on which tissue you start the process in. If it's the liver and you're under the influence of estrogen or alcohol, the liver is going to produce lots of porphyrin, a chemical used for making heme. That porphyrin will spontaneously amplify the formation of the lipofuscin.

Tissue injury of any sort releases fragments of the damaged cell material, and all of that contributes to the formation of lipofuscin. At first, it can be only in a soluble form. It can travel outside of cells, between cells, through the connective tissue, through the bloodstream, and back into cells in different parts of the organism. Some of it forms only as particles in lysosomes or mitochondria. It varies with every organ and the momentary conditions of the organ.

It is a very powerful way of explaining disease, degeneration, and aging.

**Andrew Murray:** Did you say that lipofuscin can be soluble?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. The smaller particles form soluble, medium-sized molecules.

**Andrew Murray:** I always related lipofuscin with the age pigment you see on the hands of older people. I thought it was always an insoluble complex of iron, protein, and sugar residues that got laid down into the nervous tissue and was resistant to being removed. But you're saying there is some lipofuscin that is soluble and freely moving about. Is it able to be excreted at that point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure. Some of it shows up in the urine.

**Andrew Murray:** If that's the case, is there any mileage in supposing that bitters or aperitifs—things that stimulate bile and improve digestion—could have a positive effect in removing soluble lipofuscin before it gets converted into something less soluble?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. Accelerating your digestive processes in general will help.

**Andrew Murray:** What is the difference between the lipofuscin found in endothelial plaque and the lipofuscin found as Lewy bodies or amyloid plaque in neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson's or Alzheimer's?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on the type of injury and exposure, the type of fat and the quantity you're exposed to, as well as natural factors such as hormones. There is such variation. If it's going to be extremely fat-loving material, that means it's going to stick in your nerve cells primarily. Huntington's disease is very closely connected to certain types of PUFA-derived lipofuscin. Each variation of lipofuscin molecule is going to affect which kind of nerve is affected in exactly what way.

If you know that it's a matter of balance between how fast you're putting it in and how fast you can remove it, the process of removal is very slow. But if you essentially stop the formation by stopping your excess intake of aluminum, iron, copper, unsaturated fats, and other irritants, then you can reduce the formation almost to zero. At which point the slight attrition by way of vitamin E can gradually reduce the amount in the brain.

**Andrew Murray:** Do you think fish oil would be far more implicated in the production of these lipofuscins over flaxseed oil or corn oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The type of molecule is extremely variable. In some early studies feeding a lot of fish to pigs, horses, dogs, and mink, they identified something called "yellow fat disease" in which the animal's fat became a source of dangerous inflammation. It accumulated in a form that created an intense degenerative inflammation throughout the fat system.

**Andrew Murray:** Let's take a caller. You're on the air.

**Caller:** I'm from Garberville. My question is, as a general rule, I love organic coconut milk and I'm wondering what its benefits are. I'm also wondering what other nut milks you recommend.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm not especially wild about coconut milk. Studies in the Philippines have found that people who cook with it frequently have a high incidence of breast cancer. So I'm not sure about what its natural contents are.

**Caller:** Basically, I'm asking about drinking the coconut milk without heating it, just using it as a general rule on a cool basis.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it's just the actual water—if you puncture an unripe coconut and get the water out—that's fine. But what they call coconut milk or cream is a manufactured process where they grind up some of the solid material and suspend it in the water. I don't think it's safe.

**Caller:** What nut milks do you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think there's such a thing. They can make any emulsion that's white and liquid and call it a milk—grain milk, bean milk, or nut milk—but that doesn't have any nutritional value in a positive sense.

**Caller:** You were mentioning linoleic acid. What other related acids would you highly recommend that we do consume?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coconut oil in itself has some real adaptogenic properties by interfering with the PUFA.

**Andrew Murray:** It's thermogenic, obviously it's saturated, so it doesn't have the side effects of being converted into a lipofuscin product.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can I just clarify for that caller? Dr. Peat really only recommends coconut oil. He does not recommend the omega-3 or omega-6 seed oils, or nut milk, or bean milk.

**Andrew Murray:** I caught you saying a little while ago that other reductants like vitamin C could drive lipofuscin production in the presence of those n-3 and n-6 fats. Did I hear that correctly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Too much vitamin C easily activates any stray atoms you have of aluminum, iron, zinc, mercury, and so on.

**Andrew Murray:** How does that relate to orange juice? If people are drinking lots of orange juice but still eating products containing these oils, wouldn't that vitamin C be a danger?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure, but there are so many chemicals other than vitamin C. Citrus fruit in general, grape juice, fruits and vegetables very widely contain bioflavonoids. **Andrew Murray:** I frequently drink half a gallon of orange juice a day during the summer. I'm obviously not consuming any PUFA at the same time. But you say "in moderation."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You're getting equally large amounts of the other pro-oxidant bioflavonoids [in the juice], and so they are helping to keep the cell oxidizing. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So basically, if you're getting a half a gallon of orange juice, you might have quite a lot of vitamin C there, but it's also balanced by the bioflavonoids—the naringin and the quercetin—so it doesn't cause a problem.

**Andrew Murray:** Would you condone the use of citrus bioflavonoid supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the purified form, some of those can be reductants the same way an excess of vitamin C can. I think one bioflavonoid probably intensifies and works with the system in the same fruit.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** We had a caller with bad reception who wanted to ask: Why do you think cow milk is okay for humans since we're the only species that drinks another species' milk after being weaned?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it has to do with the size of our brain and our culture. We have evolved on a high fruit, high carbohydrate diet. In that diet, a very high calcium intake happens to synergize with the other factors to optimize brain function.

**Andrew Murray:** Can I ask about vitamin E's protective antioxidant role? I've read articles talking about vitamin E mitigating some of the effects of these n-3 and n-6 fats and the formation of lipofuscin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The definition of vitamin E has changed radically since the first studies in the 1920s and 30s. It was originally thought of as a fertility-extending, anti-estrogen chemical. But that has now changed back, and it's coming to be recognized again that it's an anti-inflammatory, estrogen-regulating substance.

**Andrew Murray:** What kind of daily dose would you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Something like 20 or 30 milligrams.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** How does that compare to International Units (IU)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The language has simply changed. You can talk about the different forms in terms of milligrams. Sometimes they're still talking in terms of the antioxidant value or the D-alpha tocopherol concentration. For about 20 years you could only refer to D-alpha tocopherol as vitamin E potency; the gamma and delta mixed tocopherols had to be overlooked. But now that effect is disappearing.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So when you state 20 to 30 milligrams, you're stating 20 to 30 milligrams of a mixed tocopherol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Andrew Murray:** Very lastly, Dr. Peat, regarding estrogen. You've always talked about estrogen being inflammatory and progesterone being the anti-inflammatory molecule. Estrogen's inflammatory nature in terms of its effect on the n-3 and n-6 fats and lipofuscin formation is equivocal, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You can treat all of these things as synergizing either beneficial factors or harmful factors. The amount of PUFA, ionizing radiation, exposure to heavy metals—each of the components is at least additive to the others. If you do something to oppose any one of those—reducing inflammation—you're going to reduce estrogen exposure, rate of aging, tissue fibrosis, and cancer. All of these can be alleviated by simple natural anti-inflammatory things including carbon dioxide, progesterone, and thyroid function.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you very much, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Andrew Murray:** Dr. Peat can be found online at www.raypeat.com.

Until the third Friday of next month, my name is Andrew Murray.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** My name is Sarah Johanneson Murray. Thank you very much for listening.

**Andrew Murray:** Okay. Dr. Peat, thanks so much for giving your time again this month. Would you just let people know more about you from an academic research perspective, and then we can carry on the show?

Just a huge difference from supplementing fish oil versus not having fat. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Dr. Peat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Can you hear me okay?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** So this lipid peroxidation, or rancid fat—when we eat fat, it can go rancid if it's not saturated, and that's known as lipid peroxidation. That applies to not only the fish oils but also all the vegetable seed oils, right? Like canola and soy and all the vegetable oils.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The more highly unsaturated they are, the quicker they break down. And some of the oxidative breakdown is almost immediate. Just as soon as it gets absorbed from your intestine and shows up in your bloodstream, you can find the highly oxidized breakdown fragments of the polyunsaturated fats like fish oil.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Did I hear you correctly stating that metastasis is 1,000 times worse on a fatty diet versus a non-fat diet?

**Andrew Murray:** And this would again lead to... people that have talked about ketogenic diets, this is absolutely the last thing you want to be doing, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In the process of getting the ketogenic effect, it's basically starvation and stress that turns on the so-called ketone production. One of the major ketone bodies is actually not a ketone but an alcohol hydroxyl group. In the hydroxyl state, which is formed during the ketogenic diet, this becomes a reductant having effects similar to lactic acid, which is a trigger to shift oxidation towards the fermentation or the lactic acid metabolism typical of cancer.

**Andrew Murray:** You're listening to Ask Your Herb Doctor on KMUD. Callers are welcome to call in with questions related to this month's continuing topic, cancer and cancer alternatives. The number is 707-923-3911.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And you also said anti-inflammatory things, so maybe like aspirin? Would they have infused aspirin into the bladder?

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Stay home cancer, stay home.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** What's that statistic you quote, Dr. Peat? That 99.9% of people over the age of 50 have some form of abdominal cancer that 99.9% of people will not die of?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In an autopsy, you can find cancer in essentially 100% of the people over 50 if you look for it. It's part of a natural healing process, and most people just coexist with many of these little cancers that aren't really hurting anything.

**Andrew Murray:** On a very quick side note, I had a keratosis on the side of my nose. I spoke to you about this, Dr. Peat, three or four years ago. I had it for two years. It obviously wasn't healthy cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Before we end, I want to mention a book that I think might be the most important book published in the last two or three years. **Andrew Murray:** Yeah, well, he's been there for 40 years or something. Dr. Fauci is pretty entrenched.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, but this book I think is going to change that.

**Andrew Murray:** Yeah, they said that possibly he's perjured himself. Anyway, thanks so much for your time, Dr. Peat. It's five to the hour and we need to give people your information. So thanks so much for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you, Dr. Peat. Good night.

**Andrew Murray:** For those people who've listened to the show before or who just tuned in, Dr. Raymond Peat has a wealth of experience. He's been doing this for over 40 years. He's written several books and published hundreds of articles. His website is raypeat.com, R-A-Y-P-E-A-T.com. His journal articles there are well-referenced. He's a very scientific person.

We can be contacted Monday through Friday at westernbotanicalmedicine.com or 707-986-9506. Until the December version, we will look forward to hearing from you. Thanks so much for your time.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** Thank you. Happy Thanksgiving and thanks for tuning in. My name is Sarah Murray.

transcriptText:
**Andrew Murray:** Welcome to this month's May 2022 edition of Ask Your Herb Doctor. Sarah is not joining us this evening, but next month she'll be back. It is a beautiful spring evening, warm and clear. We are very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat join us with his expertise.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Andrew Murray:** Thanks so much for joining us as always. For those who perhaps have never heard of you before, would you please outline your professional and scientific background so people know where you're coming from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 50s and 60s, I was working in humanities—literature, painting, and philosophy. My interest in how consciousness works led me to decide that understanding language and art would help to understand what the brain is and how the brain is conscious. I went back to graduate school in 1968 at the University of Oregon, intending to concentrate on brain studies. However, I found that the department working on the brain was extremely dogmatic.

I looked around and found that at the other end of the organism—the reproductive system—the professors were actually scientific and didn't throw out data just because it didn't agree with the dogma. I did my dissertation on the oxidative aging process as it relates to the reproductive system. It turned out that gives a very interesting background to things such as how the brain works. This was a theme existing in biology 100 years ago—how electrons and biological energy power perceptions and consciousness—but it had been squeezed out. Right from the early years of science, corporations were squeezing out the freely exploring researchers and subsidizing people who would work for their corporate interests.

**Andrew Murray:** Since the very beginning of 2020, we have been skeptical, to say the least, of the organization and rollout of the COVID pandemic. At this point, it seems to have fizzled into a non-event compared to what was forecast. However, the rhetoric has continued that this is alarming and must be controlled via lockdowns and mandates. This aligns with what the World Economic Forum and Klaus Schwab have been working at since the 1930s.

Regarding transhumanism, Klaus Schwab has said, "You will own nothing and be happy." There is a premise that biological evolution will be overtaken by genetic, wearable, implantable, or injectable technologies that artificially expedite the evolutionary process—called the Great Reset.

In the 1940s and 50s, you knew people involved in Technocracy Incorporated. What are your thoughts on this movement toward transhumanism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s and 50s, I knew people who had become convinced members of Technocracy Incorporated. The stock market has been one of the techniques to take over the assets of the world. Every time the value of the stock collapses, small investors get killed by it, and the giant corporations get bigger. It is like a ratchet to shake loose the bulk of investors and constantly refine ownership to a smaller group.

People injured by the economic breakdown in 1930 had good intentions and said, "The corporate engineers know what needs to be done. If we turn the operation of the economy over to scientists and engineers, they will make sure we don't have these collapses." Except the scientists and engineers are working for the big corporations that engineer the collapse. These people were well-meaning but gullible.

By 1950, it was a turning point when the government came out and said that "Big Science" is the only science, and government has to direct, finance, and control it. There hasn't been any pretense of science being a free enterprise since then. The journals and universities were absolutely taken over by the funding of giant corporations and government agencies.

**Andrew Murray:** When I looked at Technocracy earlier, they couch this in terms of the "green economy" and "sustainable development." While I agree with moving away from polluting fossil fuels, the interpretation of the green economy by the technocrats is a different picture.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The way they manipulate science involves selling an ideology to the general population which justifies a reductionist view of biology and evolution. The intelligence of the organism and development has been ruled out of science in favor of randomness being the key to everything.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cold-blooded organisms—like insects, fish, and frogs—have to survive the winter. A seed also has to survive cold storage. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** When we eat carbohydrates in excess, we make our own saturated fats. If we are free of the polyunsaturated fats, we can modify a certain percentage of our saturated fats. **Interviewer:** That's a really important point. Eating in a caloric surplus can amplify some of these negative consequences because these fats go into storage and build up over time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Someone recently sent me a draft of an extremely good, very readable book on polyunsaturated fats. It has about a thousand references. It's going to be published imminently.

**Interviewer:** Moving on to a slightly controversial topic in the keto and carnivore community: Can you make the case for sugar? What role does sugar play in someone's diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have a highly digestible starch, it quickly breaks down into glucose, and then it can provide very safe energy. But many starches are hard to digest. For someone with sluggish digestion, starches tend to support bacterial overgrowth in the intestine.

Vegetables are fine when your digestive system is working well. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** It doesn't require digestion, so it can start absorbing right in your stomach. **Caller:** What do you think of a substance called L-Carnitine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's active in helping you oxidize fats. In ordinary metabolism, it's essential. But when you're under stress, the products of oxidizing pure fat will produce less carbon dioxide in proportion to the oxygen used. In stressful situations, such as a failing heart, carnitine—by increasing your ability to oxidize fats—can actually increase the problem of oxygen availability.

In the 1990s, people found that if you could keep the cells oxidizing glucose, they produce more carbon dioxide per oxygen consumed. The effect is to make metabolism more efficient, reduce inflammation via increased carbon dioxide, and leave more oxygen available. The chemical that increased the ability to use glucose rather than fat was called Mildronate at first, and more recently they are calling it Meldonium. Athletes are using it, and I think it has disqualified some famous athletes because it improves their endurance noticeably. It works by bypassing carnitine.

**Caller:** I seem to crave cottage cheese and I think it might be the whey that I crave. Could you discuss whey and what it does?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Both the whey and the casein fractions have multiple beneficial effects that are approaching hormonal and immune-promoting. One of their virtues is that they are deficient in iron but have almost all of the other nutrients associated with them. Iron happens to be one of the main risks of any stress; stress tends to make iron toxic and increase your susceptibility to infections. Milk provides all the helpful nutrients but is very deficient in iron.

Also, the high calcium content of milk products works along with vitamin D to suppress parathyroid hormone. Parathyroid hormone is one of our basic pro-inflammatory problems. It lowers our cellular energy production but also increases many of our basic inflammation-producing processes.

**Caller:** Is there any nutritional advice for people with arrhythmia, specifically PVCs (premature ventricle contractions)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the basic medical recommendations is to avoid hyperthyroidism. But in reality, a *chronic lack* of thyroid hormone can create preconditions for having arrhythmia. This includes nutritional imbalances and increases of stress hormones, and an imbalance between the stress steroids (including cortisol and estrogen) and the anti-stress, quieting steroids (pregnenolone, progesterone, and to some extent the androgens).

**Caller:** Is there any association with histamine and arrhythmia? I also have very itchy skin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, serotonin and histamine are closely connected with changing the heart rhythm. Milk products have an antihistamine, anti-inflammatory effect. A good balance of all the essential nutrients is needed for balancing your thyroid function. Seafood at least once a week is helpful for the trace minerals.

**Michael McCaskill:** How do cravings work? How might the body know what is good for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies, mostly in animals, but some people have tested it on their kids. They notice kids will sometimes seem to have a completely crazy, deranged appetite, wanting only one food for several meals in a row. But when they added them up over a period of a week or two, it turned out that their choices resulted in a proper balance of nutrients.

They've tested that on animals by creating a deficiency in a particular vitamin or amino acid. They find that the animal knows how to ignore a food that might seem generally good but is deficient in the nutrient they need, and concentrate on one food that's richest in what they need. It turns out there are only two or three essential amino acids that are taken as signals. But in nature, rare patterns of deficiency don't occur, so the signal of adequacy is always detectable. Animals, given a choice of natural foods, will essentially invariably pick out the ones that are nutritionally balanced.

**Caller:** I had a pile of wood chips delivered that was full of Aspergillus fungus. I inhaled the spores and was wheezing. Do you have advice about getting fungus out of my lungs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably your lungs are going to take care of it, but it never hurts to make sure your vitamin D is adequate. Vitamin D for Americans is the most important immune-supporting nutrient. But in the world in general, vitamin A and zinc are rivals for protection of the membranes and direct immunity to germs, mechanical, or chemical irritants. A good diet with anti-inflammatory foods besides milk products is helpful. Citrus fruits are very rich in flavonoids which are anti-inflammatory and pro-immunity. Coffee is another good source of anti-inflammatory substances such as quercetin.

**Caller:** What is the difference between vitamin D and D3? Which one should we be taking?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D3 is the normal one that we make when we're in the sunlight. It works the same chemically as the one we make in the sunlight. Some of the products on the market are vitamin D2; that is metabolized slightly differently and doesn't have all of the good protective effects of vitamin D3.

In a medical context, you might hear people talk about calcitriol. You don't want the "triol"—some people confuse that with vitamin D3. It's cholecalciferol (D3) that is the usual supplement.

**Caller:** I feel like I have a brain fog issue. I suspect I had Covid a year ago. Do you have recommendations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Brain fog goes with low energy production and low carbon dioxide. Vitamin B1 is a natural equivalent to acetazolamide and the calcium channel blockers in being an inhibitor of carbonic anhydrase, helping to raise your carbon dioxide. It's often the quickest way to clear up brain fog and get your mental energy back. But all of the anti-inflammatory things help: thyroid hormone, vitamin D, calcium, progesterone, and fruit juice.

**Caller:** I've had diabetes for many years. I have investigated intermittent fasting and it seems to be bringing my blood sugar down. What are your thoughts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It will make your blood sugar go down, but anything that you can call fasting is going to be putting you under stress. The long-range thing that corrects chronic diabetes is to get your polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) lower—to completely eliminate them from your diet as far as possible. Use butter for cooking rather than any of the liquid vegetable oils.

The polyunsaturated fats are specifically toxic to your insulin-producing tissues. They create resistance in your tissues and damage the ability to oxidize sugar. There is no essential need for them; there's no benefit that will be lost by eating a completely saturated fat component in your diet.

It happens that glucose is constantly activating stem cells in your pancreas to restore the ability to produce insulin. It's the polyunsaturated fats stored in your tissues, or coming directly from your food, that will keep destroying or damaging your insulin-producing cells.

**Andrew Murray:** You said that the reproductive physiology people were far less likely to throw away good information related to research and were a little bit more careful in sticking to scientific principles. Is this because the estrogen industry hadn't really gotten so much traction at this point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My brain nerve biology professor described doing some research in class, and he said, "And then you throw away the bad data." **Andrew Murray:** Getting back to the subject of tonight: estrogen, autoimmunity, and cancer. I want to read a paragraph from a 2021 university paper. It says:

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That article you cited is an extremely important landmark. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've often wondered how my thesis advisor, Arnold Soderwall, came to be so open to the facts and resistant to the industry position. **Andrew Murray:** How do you see estrogen driving autoimmunity in terms of what you're currently seeing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pro-inflammatory part of inflammation and immunity that is activated by estrogen—such as histamine, nitric oxide, and serotonin—is an essential part of getting things started. In that relatively random activity, that's where some of the antibodies cause damage rather than contributing to cleaning up the infection process.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's exactly the same thing that happens in pregnancy. Estrogen and histamine create a little focus of activity and inflammation in the uterus that the conceptus takes advantage of to get into the uterus. But then, if that process of local inflammation kept dominating, it would interfere with the oxygen and glucose supply to the fetus. Keeping the intestine as clean as possible means keeping a rapid transit time and avoiding irritating foods that could cause inflammation and constipation.

Part of the effect is to watch that your thyroid isn't suppressed, because that will slow the elimination of estrogen. **Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And calcium is definitely one of them that helps to keep estrogen levels low, along with Vitamin D.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Because they keep your metabolic rate higher, the way thyroid does. Calcium, especially from low-fat milk supported by vitamin D, is very good for weight loss.

**Sarah Johanneson Murray:** And lastly, progesterone is a direct combat molecule to estrogen.

**Andrew Murray:** Thank you so much for your time, Dr. Peat. For those who have listened, you can find more at RayPeat.com.

So talking about oxidants, antioxidants might be a good place to finish up questioning you this month. But to start that for next month and then get into the whole issue around tryptophan and how we can cut this out of our diet as best we can. But how obviously it's needed. And oxidation is a bad thing. You know, if we think about a cut apple, the surface of a cut apple turning brown, that's an oxidation reaction, though. And so it. Oxidation is not a good thing. Right. And then maybe we might not feel quite so confused about the antioxidant myth that is surrounding taking antioxidants per se for health benefits.

And what you want to do to restore health is to overcome that antioxidant system. And the Down's syndrome involves probably the crucial genetic problem is a huge overdose of the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase.

**Speaker C** (55:48): The amyloid protein accumulates in many conditions where you're simply hypothyroid, for example, or under stress. But it's possible that there are many other defects, but the spectacular one is the failure of the platelet to oxidize serotonin.

title: Butter Living Podcast: A Casual Conversation with Ray Peat
transcriptText:
**David Butterworth:** Welcome to Butter Living. I'm David Butterworth, and this is a podcast about health and about getting back to our playful roots. On today's show, we will be speaking with a PhD, endocrinologist, artist, and a person who I think is an incredible synthesizer of knowledge. A man who seems to have painted an elaborate and coherent picture of biology in a way that I haven't seen before. His name is Raymond Peat.

Ray once wrote that once we begin to believe in the future, we understand the possibility of learning more and of being more. We appreciate the unexpected and we even anticipate the opportunity to confront it. It is in the spirit of these words that I hope today's conversation inspires thought regarding some ideal future, and how the period from conception to the first two years of life can be instrumental in paving the way for this ideal.

I'd like to reiterate that we are not advising you to do anything. We simply hope that you go out and experiment, explore, and wonder about life.

**David Butterworth:** Hi, Ray. How are you doing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi. Very good.

**David Butterworth:** Thanks for being with us today. As a casual way to start, I thought it would be cool for listeners to hear what you've been up to today and what you have for breakfast.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I usually start with a big glass of *café con leche* with some very strong coffee in it. A couple of glasses like that, maybe some orange juice, and then later scrambled eggs, usually with cheese. So my breakfast takes about three hours.

**David Butterworth:** That's awesome. So you put value on how you start the day.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it gives me an hour or so for thinking about what I'm going to do during the day.

**David Butterworth:** I think it's undoubted that a lot of people who listen to this are going to be familiar with you and your work, but there are going to be some listeners who know nothing about you. Would you mind diving deeply into your background and telling us why you're such a great person to listen to regarding health and life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's relevant that I was born in the middle of the Great Depression. I grew up hearing about the Spanish Civil War and Italy's invasion of Africa. I saw the Dust Bowl immigrants coming into California and wandering homeless men. It was like a precursor to Reagan's time, seeing people on the highway with their bedrolls. Between 1940 and 1980, that was rare, but in the Depression, it was a daily thing.

When the war started, our family moved from Southern California to Southern Oregon. From third to fifth grade, I was in a one-room schoolhouse outside of Grants Pass. We had eight grades in one room, so I could hear all of the lessons. When I was in the third grade, I would hear the seventh and eighth graders' lessons. That gave me an interest in the process of education and why they segregate grades so you only have the opportunity to hear what they deliver to your specific grade.

We always had encyclopedias in the house, and I started reading about education. I learned about Bertrand Russell, who was one of my early heroes, and his wife Dora. They started a school called Beacon Hill in the 1920s. From reading about that, I heard about the Experimental College at the University of Wisconsin started by Alexander Meiklejohn, and then Black Mountain College, an experimental college in the 30s.

By junior high, I discovered that those experimental ideas in education had disappeared from the culture. What was coming in 1947, '48, and '49 was the establishment of totalitarian education in the United States. The word was intended to apply to the Soviet Union, but I saw that things I had become interested in—like Lamarckism in biology, which had been a big thing at the University of Wisconsin with a guy named Guyer—had been banned from education.

When I got to my sophomore high school biology class, I realized it was being taught by a conformist. I became extremely critical and skeptical of biological and political ideas, seeing that education had been cleaned up to eliminate any non-conformist ideas.

In the 1950s, I was very aware of the dangers of atom bomb testing in the atmosphere. I realized that Linus Pauling was the only well-known person talking about the dangers of radiation. I learned that an associate of his at Oregon State University, Ralph Spitzer, had been a very successful researcher and teacher but was fired by the president of the university for writing about Lamarckism. Because of that, Linus Pauling wouldn't step foot on the Oregon State campus for 17 years.

People generally don't appreciate what a crazy culture we had in the 1950s. While I was writing letters to the editor and Linus Pauling was giving talks, they took away his passport so he couldn't leave the country because he opposed atmospheric bomb testing. The government was supporting people like John Gofman to go around lecturing, but the mood was to convince people that radioactive fallout might actually be good for you. One of the projects to study the biological effects of radiation was called Project Sunshine. Occasionally, a professor or government employee would say, "Hey, that stuff is really dangerous," and they would not only get fired, but there would be a campaign of character assassination.

In 1959, I was teaching biology at Urbana College in Ohio. I was teaching about the biological effects of radiation. By chance, I learned that a lecturer had been invited to try out for my job because they wanted someone who *wouldn't* teach about those dangers. He chose to lecture on the biological dangers of radiation, and the weekend after he was there, he got fired from his job at the University of Illinois.

He and I got together to campaign to create a college that would be able to talk about such things, that wouldn't have trustees tied to military research, and could freely investigate any subject. Leo Koch and I started working on creating a new college. Just as I was getting things organized, he got a job as a biologist at a mushroom soup company, so I was left to take over the new college, which we called Blake College.

The idea was to get faculty and students living together in a community, able to teach and study exactly what they wanted. We had it set up so that both teachers and students, after being there for six months, would become automatic trustees. There were no outsiders involved. But that didn't please the US State Department because the Vietnam War was escalating, and they cooked up ways to intervene and shut it down.

After that, I taught linguistics for a year and decided I would be more productive studying biology and trying to recover some of the insights that had been shut out of biology 40 years earlier. I decided to go back to graduate school in biology at the University of Oregon, where I got my PhD in 1972.

**David Butterworth:** That gives us such a good picture of where you've come from. I want to jump right into what we plan to talk about now. What would you envision as the ideal society or living environment 30 years from now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What I did in designing Blake College was writing the fiction about what it would be like to have a place where you could do what you should be doing. That's what I think living should be: a matter of learning and exploring what we should be doing so that it's constantly in control of itself.

In 1981, I started writing a series of monthly newsletters. In one of the first issues, I wrote about the effects of the environment on the gestating brain. I got interested in the effects of education, nutrition, and environment on the brain at an early age. That was integrated into my attitude towards free education—that you shouldn't set the curriculum from outside the people who are actually doing the studying.

Education, learning, and brain development are a continuous process. It isn't a genetic apparatus of the brain which is then stuffed with information. Learning and the development of the brain is one single process. Unfortunately, our language ties into a culture which ties into people who want to manipulate others. As soon as we start learning language in that situation, the way language is controlled by institutions starts making us stupid. A psychologist once compared his daughter's development with a monkey's development. He saw that as soon as his daughter began learning language, she was unable to solve some problems that the monkey at the same age could solve. This shows that language imposes stereotyped ways of evaluating situations.

The brain is constantly being renewed and revised. Its course gets set pretty much during gestation, but you can always revise its course on a finer level at any point if you have energetic support.

Imagining the situation 30 years in the future... as it's going right now, it looks like life might not last more than a couple of weeks if the trend keeps going the way it has been. But if that can be overcome, then everything else becomes possible. We'll assume that the institutions that are indoctrinating people—like the people who control Facebook and Wikipedia—if they can be eliminated, then we can consider the actual physical limits to brain development.

We already have levels of automation so that people really don't have to work more than three or four hours a week to have all of their food and practical needs met. That leaves the question of what to do with essentially all of your free time. I think that would spontaneously tend in the direction of communication, interaction, invention, and moving on to new problems constantly.

**David Butterworth:** What do you think you'll be doing in 30 years, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That sort of thing, I'm hoping. Getting things going that are more interesting than the way they've been going in recent years. There are new generations coming on which are starting to be more critical of the existing institutions. Each generation is freeing itself from the stupefying conditions of the older generations.

One of my longtime definitions of culture is that it is the concept of the limits of what is possible. The culture teaches us that certain things are possible, and by definition, everything else must be impossible. If you simply change your mind, the limits of what is possible become undefined and very open. Changing your mind is the essence of living matter. Biology is changed by every experience. The brain is constantly in development, and that involves what you're learning. So what you learn changes your structure, and therefore your mind has changed. You're changing your past every time you learn something because you become a different organism.

**David Butterworth:** I love that. It reminds me of William Blake, who said something to the effect of, "The man who never alters his opinion is like standing water, and breeds reptiles of the mind."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that sort of thing was why I was attracted to Blake. One of his phrases was "the intellectual fountain."

**David Butterworth:** Let's go back to some of those behaviors and conditions from conception to the first two years of life. Can you be more specific about the things that are valuable in that period, and how being thoughtful about this beginning can pave the way for a biologically energetic future?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A biochemist named Stephen Zamenhof experimented with brain development in chicken embryos. He found that the brain stopped developing at the same time the glucose reserve in the egg was depleted. He added glucose, or amino acids that could be turned into glucose, to the egg. He waited until the day he knew the glucose would disappear, then punched a hole in the egg and injected glucose. He showed that the injection allowed the brain cells to keep multiplying right up until hatching. Those chickens had bigger brains than chickens had ever had and were more intelligent.

About the same time, Marian Diamond at the University of California was studying the effects of environment on the brain. It was very Lamarckian. Just by giving rats an interesting environment—playground toys and other rats to visit with—their brains got bigger and their enzyme activity changed. The thing that was discussed least was that their offspring had bigger, more intelligent brains. I read that over four generations, they saw a progressive increase in both intelligence and brain size.

During the 1960s, other observations were made. Rats and dogs both had their brain development limited by excess estrogen, which lowered their blood sugar and made glucose less available. Glucose is essential for brain development. Too much insulin or too much estrogen—which activates insulin—would lower blood sugar and simply turn off brain cell multiplication.

Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) were the other main thing that would stop brain development by interfering with the use of glucose. It was a well-recognized principle that fats block glucose oxidation.

So, three things were known to limit brain growth and intelligence:
1.  Lack of glucose.
2.  Excess estrogen/insulin.
3.  Polyunsaturated fatty acids.

Progesterone was the main thing that protected against estrogen and the excess insulin effect. Progesterone affecting the hormone balance was found to produce this trans-generational advance of the brain.

After I got my PhD, I found that the Catholic University in Valparaiso, Chile, was about to institute a new branch specifically to study the influence of nutrition on brain development. I was contracted to direct that program, but the 1973 Nixon-Kissinger coup stopped that whole project.

**David Butterworth:** You mentioned the impact of progesterone. If someone were to supplement with progesterone, what kind of dosages do you think would be appropriate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Katharina Dalton in the 40s and 50s was treating premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and menopause patients. She had many patients suffering from poor nutrition who also had PMS. She gave them progesterone injections. After several years, someone noted that her patients' babies were superior intellectually. Dalton doubted this because women with PMS are likely to have pregnancy problems and premature deliveries, and their babies usually average a few points below normal IQ.

She studied it and found that all of the progesterone babies were academically superior. Just like the chickens, they had better brains from being exposed to the protective metabolic regulator. She said they were typically around 130 IQ instead of the 96 IQ average of their older siblings who were untreated. It was about a 34-point improvement in IQ just from that one addition.

Knowing that, I started telling people about her work. At the same time, I realized doctors had been indoctrinated with the idea that oral progesterone is ineffective. By the 1970s, everyone thought you had to give it by injection. The solvents used to inject progesterone—benzyl alcohol and benzyl benzoate—were neurotoxic, yet the progesterone was so nerve-protective that it still had beneficial effects.

I looked for a way to convince doctors to use progesterone orally. I found that it dissolved very well in Vitamin E, which allowed it to be taken up with fat droplets (chylomicrons). This allowed it to bypass the liver's metabolic changes and be delivered directly to the bloodstream and cells. Locally, in the mitochondrion, Vitamin E and progesterone supported each other.

I was giving this mixture to friends who were pregnant. Another friend was raising Afghan dogs. She said Afghan dogs are typically untrainable, but when she treated a dog with pregnancy problems using oral progesterone, the pups not only survived but had bigger brains and were trainable—uncharacteristic of that breed.

My friends with the progesterone babies told stories about the precocious things they would do. One story was about a four-year-old girl. She had started a notebook with her 8-year-old brother's name and her grandfather's name. She drew three lines under her brother's name and five lines under her grandfather's name. She said, "I want each of you to teach me three new things every day." When asked why the grandfather had five lines, she said, "Because you know more than he does."

**David Butterworth:** I'm holding a bottle of Progest-E replenishing oil. What are your thoughts on how much a pregnant woman would want to take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Katharina Dalton divided her patients into those who received around 1,000 milligrams total per pregnancy and those who received at least 1,500 milligrams. There was a clear division in their academic record; the ones that got more were the brightest.

**David Butterworth:** Is there an upper limit? Is it safe to consume?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's a statistical thing. When you look at women with preeclampsia symptoms—caused by low thyroid, high estrogen, and low progesterone—about a third of them only needed one injection to resolve their symptoms for the whole pregnancy. Sometimes a single dose will normalize the whole pregnancy.

But to be sure, it's best to check frequently to see if your progesterone/estrogen ratio and thyroid function are where they should be. Progesterone should rise steadily in a healthy pregnancy from conception straight up to the day of delivery. If it rises steadily, it keeps a great excess over estrogen, so estrogen can't interfere and stop brain development.

**David Butterworth:** You mentioned glucose being one of these protective factors. Are you saying sugar is okay for pregnant women? And where might they get this glucose in their diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Tom Brewer wrote about this. He and others, like Shanklin and Hodin in their book *Maternal Nutrition*, campaigned against pharmaceutical companies that had indoctrinated doctors to control weight gain during pregnancy using diuretics. Along with diuretics, they restricted sodium.

Brewer, Shanklin, and Hodin showed that restricting salt or using diuretics stopped brain development very prematurely. Brewer emphasized salt and protein. He showed that protein deficiency was the main historical cause of eclampsia or toxemia. Pregnant women should get at least 100 grams of good protein a day—130 grams would be better. He also wanted to assure they weren't restricting salt; they should eat salt according to taste.

Shanklin and Hodin reported experiments in Australia where women with signs of developing toxemia were given supplementary salt. One group got 6 grams of extra sodium per day, the other 20 grams. In both cases, they were immediately relieved of the toxemic symptoms.

Salt allows the albumin in your blood to bind water and keep it in your bloodstream. Low thyroid, poorly nourished women lose sodium easily in the urine. Thyroid causes sodium retention, and that sodium binds water, keeping blood volume up. This perfuses the kidney with a good volume of blood, so the kidney stops sending signals to raise blood pressure. Salt alone prevented the hypertension of pregnancy in those cases.

I suggested this to friends with PMS who retained water. They found that salting their food to taste stopped the cycle of salt craving and water retention.

**David Butterworth:** If an expecting mom asked for six or seven foods to eat regularly for a healthy, resilient baby, what would you suggest?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:**
1.  **Milk:** At least two quarts, maybe a gallon, preferably low fat or 1% for protein and calcium.
2.  **Eggs:** Two or three a day.
3.  **Orange Juice:** Lots and lots of orange juice to provide carbohydrate.

The sugar in orange juice helps lower stress hormones. The calcium and sodium in milk both act to lower stress. Sugar supports the anti-stress effect of calcium and sodium, keeping down inflammation. Stress and inflammatory hormones are what progesterone is there to prevent. So when you do these nutritional things, you are supporting the effects of the progesterone.

**David Butterworth:** Would you be partial to fresh-squeezed orange juice over store-bought?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it's important to get the sweetest orange juice you can. You don't want to overload on the citric acid that some juice has in excess. Good, sweet, fresh oranges are ideal.

**David Butterworth:** Can you give some examples of polyunsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the liquid fats: safflower oil, soy oil, canola. Anything that is liquid at room temperature is questionable. If it's still liquid at refrigerator temperature, then it's really seriously toxic.

At birth, a calf has a brain which is almost purely saturated fats. A human baby, even if the mother has been eating a junk diet with a lot of polyunsaturated fat, is usually born with what medical definitions call an "essential fatty acid deficiency." That is actually a normal condition; the baby's brain *should* be very highly saturated.

Glucose is the main energy source for the developing brain, and it provides the substance to make the saturated fats and the Omega-9 unsaturated fats (Mead acid) which are intrinsic to our own production. The presence of Omega-9 fatty acids is natural in healthy, glucose-and-progesterone-supported brain development. However, doctors have been taught to define this as a deficiency of soy/safflower oil fatty acids. When they recognize an ideal situation, they call it a serious nutritional deficiency and start advocating formulas with added algae oil or fish oil—the highly unstable polyunsaturated fatty acids like DHA.

**David Butterworth:** Why are unsaturated fats so unstable and toxic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One argument used to sell fish oil is that it has an anti-inflammatory effect. It interferes slightly with the production of prostaglandins made from the Omega-6 series. That is good, but it comes at the cost of immune suppression. The free radical breakdown products are toxic to white blood cells.

People who follow the course of ingested fish oil find that as soon as it reaches the bloodstream, it is already in a mainly oxidized, breakdown condition. These oxidized products are immune-suppressive.

A little bit of this material is incorporated into the brain. As the baby grows, it dilutes these, so by age 20, the brain hasn't accumulated a great amount. But after age 20, there is a steady accumulation of fish-oil-type fatty acids. When they break down spontaneously—without enzyme action—they produce pro-inflammatory derivatives like isoprostanes and neuroprostanes. These create inflammation and degenerative symptoms.

A baby at birth has an extremely high metabolic rate and an extremely low PUFA content in its tissues. Its learning ability is spectacular. That corresponds to a metabolic rate about 2.5 times faster than an adult. As their tissues accumulate PUFA, by age 20, their metabolism has slowed quite a bit. As they keep accumulating PUFA, the metabolic rate keeps slowing down as degenerative conditions set in.

**David Butterworth:** Is it possible for a young organism to keep tissue content of polyunsaturated fat low through what we consume?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Puberty is one of the things brought on by stress. If you look at plants, when the water supply is deficient, they go to seed earlier. When I worked in the woods, the foreman pointed out that you can make a pine tree produce cones by whacking it with an axe. It senses danger and decides it has to reproduce.

Puberty is similar. When the body senses its metabolism is being slowed down, it turns on the reproductive system. In extreme stress conditions, kids can start becoming pubescent well before age 10. In tropical areas where the traditional diet incorporated lots of coconut fat (a saturated fat), it was normal for girls not to menstruate until around age 18. That is almost twice the years of PUFA-free development compared to 9-year-olds in the US.

That slowdown of metabolism corresponds to the increase of estrogen without proper opposition by progesterone and thyroid. It sets up premature degenerative diseases: menopause, cancer, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, and so on.

**David Butterworth:** So a nice approach would be to keep stress low, cook eggs in coconut oil and butter, and get a lot of sunshine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Sunshine is an extremely important factor. In tropical areas, culture often teaches people to cover up. I've had friends in the tropics who avoided the sun so thoroughly they were Vitamin D deficient.

Calcium intake can make up for a partial Vitamin D deficiency. Sugar helps make up for calcium and Vitamin D deficiencies because part of their effect is to keep the metabolic rate high. Combining good calcium intake, lots of carbohydrate, and lots of sunshine—along with low PUFA intake—is good protective insurance against degenerative diseases.

**David Butterworth:** What are your thoughts on trends like ketogenic diets and intermittent fasting regarding a developing fetus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some of those fad diets are based on experiments in rodents. People usually get it wrong because mice and rats are nocturnal. If you study them in the daytime, you are stressing them because they should be sleeping.

Darkness itself turns on stress hormones. The red component of light has an electron-quenching effect; it calms excited electrons. In sleep experiments, researchers found that in everyone, every 15 minutes of darkness caused cortisol levels to increase, rising to a peak around dawn. Sunlight would then lower it.

Darkness is stressful, increasing all stress hormones. Deep sleep is our defense. But if stress and malnutrition have lowered your hormones (like in hypothyroidism), you don't get into the deepest phase of sleep, so sleep isn't restorative.

Among the stress hormones are those that regulate sodium and calcium. Sodium inhibits the rise of aldosterone, and calcium inhibits the rise of parathyroid hormone (PTH). These rise during the night. Aldosterone and PTH interfere with mitochondrial energy production the same way polyunsaturated fats do.

Having some salty soup or a glass of milk at bedtime helps. Milk (protein and sugar) inhibits the rise of PTH and cortisol. Salty soup (especially with gelatin) helps prevent the rise of aldosterone. This prevents the deterioration of mitochondria during the night. Night and winter are where most aging and degeneration take place.

**David Butterworth:** What are your thoughts about a pregnant woman staying up late with a laptop or cell phone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cell phone environment, especially having one near your head or torso, is a very important factor. The industry claims radiation is harmless if it doesn't increase tissue temperature, but that is based on crude, science-free doctrine. Biologists have demonstrated great sensitivity of cells to even weak electrical fields.

A Russian researcher, Yuri Holodov, demonstrated that the gonads and the brain are the most sensitive tissues. The "bystander effect" refers to the fact that radiation can seem to bypass DNA and cause no immediate mutation, but the poisoned cells will be in a destabilized state. Even years later, the rate of spontaneous mutation becomes higher.

An irradiated cell emits small, irritating particles. Surrounding cells receive these and become destabilized. So, laying in bed with a cell phone right above the womb is an energy drain. Even if it isn't ionizing radiation, the energy drain creates stress, and stressed cells send out those bystander effects.

**David Butterworth:** I want to close with a quote from Bertrand Russell: "When you want to teach children to think, you begin by treating them seriously... you talk to them candidly... and you make them readers and thinkers of significant thoughts from the beginning." How can parents raise a child to inhabit a future that is full of wonder?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly what Bertrand Russell said. When I lived in Mexico, I noticed kids were different from kids in the US. In the US, the idea was to give kids "age-appropriate" information. In Mexico, adults treated children as little adults. They were fully responsible and could be communicated with.

James W. Prescott studied different cultures and found that those free of violence had, from a very early age, touched, held, and moved their babies continuously. In the US, touching has been institutionalized away. Continuous physical stimulation and talking to kids with an adult vocabulary right from infancy is crucial.

I once demonstrated this with a kitten. A girlfriend was talking baby talk to her weaned kitten. I told her she had to enunciate clearly. I told the kitten, "Go look at yourself in the mirror." The kitten ran to the mirror and looked. Later, I told the kitten to pick up a piece of Christmas tree trimming and look in the mirror. It did. I'm sure kids are at least as intelligent as kittens. I think people should start talking to them seriously from the day of birth.

**David Butterworth:** How might play fit into all of this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think everything should be play. Studying needs to be thought of as play. It's a property of life, and it's a type of thinking. If you want to solve a problem in physics, you have to play mentally—play with objects, investigate things playfully. It's an attitude without which you don't have science; you have dogma.

**David Butterworth:** Ray, thank you so much. Where can a listener read more of your work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My website, raypeat.com.

**David Butterworth:** It's been a pleasure. Thank you so much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye.

title: Butter Living Podcast: Fertility, Pregnancy, and Development
transcriptText:
**Host:** Hi, Ray, how's it going?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi. Very good.

**Host:** Thank you for doing this today. I had some help from my wife, and we compiled a list of questions from a Northern California birth community and listeners of the podcast. Before we get into the questions, could you go into your background a little bit, especially as it pertains to women's issues, pregnancy, and human development?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1968, after studying many other things for about 12 years after college, I went to graduate school at the University of Oregon specializing in reproductive physiology. I did my dissertation in 1972 on oxidative changes in the uterus with aging. One of my lifelong interests was the physiology of aging, and it seemed especially relevant to the process of reproduction.

I had seen publications from the 40s and 50s showing that when you make a graph of the baby's birth weight and head circumference, both of these increase with each subsequent pregnancy. The older the mother is, the bigger her baby's brain is. That held true up until about the age of 38. At that time, women were having many more babies, so it tended to be the third, fourth, or fifth baby by the time she reached her late 30s. At that point, instead of increasing, the last birth before she became infertile tended to be lighter with a smaller head. But the general drift of both aging and parity was for the birth weight and brain weight to increase steadily.

I had started out intending to study brain physiology in graduate school, but I found that subject was completely dogmatic, whereas reproductive physiology actually tolerated a scientific approach.

**Host:** One of the questions from a listener was directly related to what you spoke to: maintaining fertility as a woman ages. What can a woman do to maintain fertility as she gets older?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The failure of progesterone statistically starts happening in the mid-30s. Estrogen production and concentration in the body tends to increase steadily from about the age of 20 up until the late 30s. That's about the time when aging and stress symptoms start becoming noticeable. Sometimes a woman is gaining excess weight around that age, and any kind of nutritional or environmental problem limits the ability to produce progesterone.

As the ratio of estrogen continually increases and progesterone reaches a limit determined by stress and nutrition, you start getting the signs of menopause and infertility. There are two processes that tend to extend fertility as well as lifespan in general.

One is the liver. When it is healthy, it excretes 100% of the estrogen arriving in the circulation. It makes it soluble for excretion in the urine or puts it into the bile. The estrogen that goes into the bile tends to be reabsorbed if there's not enough fiber in the diet. So, keeping a steady supply of fiber running through the intestine allows the liver to get rid of the bile-excreted estrogen.

The other is the sulfated or glucuronidated water-soluble form of estrogen that goes out in the urine. To make that happen, B vitamins and protein are the most essential nutrients. Keeping up the B vitamins and good nutrition—adequate protein and calcium—keeps the liver able to minimize estrogen. It should be 100% excreted so it doesn't build up steadily with aging. That makes the problem of producing adequate progesterone manageable because it isn't working against this rising tide of estrogen.

Vitamin A, protein, adequate minerals, a balance of calcium and phosphate, and vitamin D are the main limiting factors for making progesterone. Vitamin A is used in almost a one-to-one relationship with the amount of progesterone you produce. Thyroid hormone travels on the same protein in the blood as vitamin A. That protein, with the vitamin A and thyroid, is taken up by cells along with cholesterol and used in the conversion of cholesterol to progesterone. So, it's essential to maintain a good level of cholesterol in your blood to keep producing adequate progesterone.

**Host:** When you talk about vitamin A and the B vitamins, would it be preferable to get these from food sources rather than supplemental sources?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, supplements always contain manufacturing contaminants and breakdown products. Vitamin A, for example, is extremely oxidizable. Many people get serious side effects when they take vitamin supplements that they don't get at all when they eat foods rich in those nutrients. Eggs, milk, cheese, and liver are very safe sources of vitamin A. To some extent vitamin D as well, but if you don't get sunlight, then you will need a supplement of vitamin D.

**Host:** As a woman ages and progesterone levels decrease, does it make sense to supplement progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s, Katharina Dalton in England was treating women with premenstrual syndrome (PMS) using the main progesterone product available at the time, which was injectable in oil solution. She treated them with monthly or twice-monthly injections and found that the women who suffered from PMS tended to have had babies with a high likelihood of being premature, underweight, and mentally not up to par before treatment.

She found that the patients she treated adequately for PMS were having healthier pregnancies. If they continued having a PMS symptom in the pregnancy, she would continue treating them. Many of these women had previously had monthly bleeding episodes right up into the fifth or sixth months of pregnancy and then delivered prematurely. She found that by preventing the symptoms of depression, anxiety, and headaches, she prevented the monthly bleeding episodes, and the babies were carried to full term.

After doing that for about 15 or 20 years, someone mentioned to her that her patients' babies were remarkably intelligent. She said that wasn't very likely because women who deliver prematurely are known to have children with an average IQ of about 95. She did a study and found that her babies were averaging about 130 IQ. The younger siblings were all many IQ points better. The difference was simply that the mother was a little older and was getting progesterone support.

**Host:** There was a poll where women answered whether progesterone supplementation was effective. Many said yes, but some said they weren't seeing positive effects. Why would some women not see results?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some women have a much higher need, and many products simply aren't able to deliver enough progesterone to be effective.

In 1951, there was a study using commercial progesterone for treating uterine cancer. The doctors saw remarkable improvements in the cancer, but they were giving what they considered a maximum dose—many injections of a couple hundred milligrams per injection per day. They never mentioned the patient being anesthetized or even a sedative effect. It is now recognized that the amount of progesterone the placenta produces in the latter half of pregnancy strongly affects the nervous system, preventing childbirth pain with an actual anesthetic effect and improving sleep quality.

That 1951 study demonstrated that even injecting hundreds of milligrams, it wasn't becoming available to the bloodstream. It was dissolved in oil and simply staying in the muscle or fat tissue where they injected it.

When you take it orally in a powdered form, even micronized progesterone, as it touches the lining of the intestine, a small amount passes into the cell structure. Both the intestine and the liver have enzymes to solubilize it the way the liver handles estrogen. So, any powdered progesterone that touches the intestine tends to go into the soluble form and leave the body quickly. If it gets into the circulation as sulfated progesterone, that will have its own sedative effects, but it definitely doesn't follow the metabolic pathway that natural progesterone produced by the ovaries would.

The closest you can get to natural progesterone is when it's dissolved in oil and taken orally. The digestive system breaks it up into micron-sized particles for absorption directly through the intestine into the lymphatic system. Those particles are transmitted directly to the bloodstream, circulating as fat-dissolved particles (chylomicrons) and bypassing the liver repeatedly. This allows it to be absorbed by the uterus, brain, and all tissues.

**Host:** If you are taking progesterone dissolved in vitamin E and aren't noticing effects, would a good gauge be to try taking more?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A fourth of a teaspoon of the solution containing 100 milligrams will likely bring on sleep very quickly for a man. For a woman, it will have a definite relaxing, sedative effect.

During pregnancy, the ovary (or the placenta) will be stimulated by a given dose of progesterone so that there's a positive feedback loop. It can have a catalytic effect. There were studies where women showing signs of miscarriage at the third or fourth month were given an injection of progesterone. About two-thirds of the group went from the third month all the way to full term with just that one injection. One-third needed another injection around month six. So, there is a positive feedback effect where one good strong dose will often solve the deficiency problem.
