**Host:** Can you talk about the relationship between thyroid and miscarriage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone who is hypothyroid becomes subject to an excess of estrogen relative to the protective hormones: progesterone, pregnenolone, DHEA, and to some extent testosterone.

When the thyroid is low, tissues accumulate water and shift their metabolism toward lactic acid formation rather than carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide that should be produced under the influence of thyroid has a relaxing, sedative effect on the uterus and tends to deliver more oxygen to the fetus. When your thyroid is low and you don't produce that carbon dioxide, you make a lot of lactic acid. This has an excitatory effect on the tissues, tending to over-activate contractions in the uterus, causing stress to the fetus, and triggering cortisol production which tends to induce delivery.

Thyroid acting on the liver lowers estrogen. Estrogen itself activates cortisol production and excites contractions. The direct effect of thyroid and cholesterol on the ovary or placenta is to increase the conversion of cholesterol to progesterone. At every level of metabolism, thyroid works toward maturing the pregnancy, keeping the delivery of sugar for the embryo's brain development, keeping progesterone high, and the uterus relaxed.

**Host:** Would thyroid be appropriate as a supplement for pregnant women?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even before getting pregnant. Many studies show that thyroid hormone is the most important single fertility hormone for both men and women. I've known dozens of people who were unable to get pregnant, and usually the very first month they supplement thyroid, they get pregnant.

Another study looked at women who used a progesterone supplement for just one month preceding conception. The normal percentage of birth defects in that study was 4%, but for women who used progesterone before conceiving, there was only a 1% incidence. Progesterone has a powerful stabilizing effect on the chromosomes, and thyroid works right along with progesterone to stabilize the genetic system.

**Host:** You mentioned lactic acid metabolism being maladaptive for a fetus. Can intense exercise be detrimental to a healthy pregnancy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you look at non-pregnant athletes, one definition of overtraining is the lung's ability to diffuse oxygen. One study found that athletes who thought they were in great condition but were overtraining had a deficient ability to admit oxygen to the blood. The overtraining gave them a chronic oxygen deficit and lingering lactic acid levels.

Those with elevated lactic acid even 12 hours after exercise had lungs that had taken up so much excess water that the diffusion pathway was about twice normal. No matter how fast they breathed, they couldn't get efficient oxygenation. The same thing happens under the influence of too much estrogen. A study in mice gave one injection of estrogen and monitored oxygen movement through the lungs; they found that 95% of the diffusion capacity was knocked out in an hour following a single overdose of estrogen.

**Host:** What is the most important piece of advice you would give an expecting mother?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** To eat well. That means keeping protein up, having a good ratio of calcium to phosphate, getting around 100 grams of good protein every day, and a one-to-one ratio of calcium to phosphate if possible.

**Host:** What are your thoughts on the suggestion that a pregnant mother should consume high volumes of water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Water can be very dangerous. Your requirement for protein and calcium means that once pregnancy gets going, two quarts of milk a day is the minimum, along with maybe a quart of orange juice. With two or three quarts of those going in as food, you have very little need for other liquid.

If you don't balance your water intake with sodium, calcium, magnesium, and potassium, it can have a bad outcome. Sodium is often the most important mineral lacking in pregnancy. In the 1950s, drug companies devised new chemical diuretics and decided pregnant women would be a good market. They invented the idea that you shouldn't gain so much weight during pregnancy. Almost every doctor fell for the advertising, teaching women to control weight gain largely with water pills. This had a disastrous effect on millions of pregnancies.

Progesterone is the basis for the body's ability to regulate water and salt accurately, but you have to take in a generous amount for it to work. In two studies of preeclampsia where women were developing high blood pressure, researchers tried giving large supplements of table salt. The standard prescription was to avoid salt and take diuretics. These studies supplemented several grams of salt per day and cured the preeclampsia.

When progesterone is deficient relative to estrogen, you seem to be retaining water, but you are actually losing sodium too fast. Balancing your minerals will help you get rid of the water. Albumin in the blood binds sodium via negative charges, and that combination attracts water. If you don't have enough sodium, the albumin can't retain water in the blood; it falls out of solution into tissues or out the kidneys. Preeclampsia patients lose a lot of albumin in their urine. Sodium allows albumin to stay in the bloodstream, pulling water out of the tissues and increasing blood volume to perfuse the placenta. Excess water combined with diuretics and salt restriction is a deadly mixture.

**Host:** One woman noted an increase in preeclampsia. Could it be as simple as not having enough salt and consuming too much liquid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, salt and protein. Milk especially, because it comes with the calcium.

**Host:** Are there any good prenatal vitamins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't really know of any. Traditionally, they emphasize iron. The idea that women need more iron than men isn't true because estrogen gives women a powerful advantage for efficient absorption of iron from a meager diet. Estrogen makes you attract about 10 times as much iron into the intestine as a man would.

The reason so many women seem deficient in iron isn't that they are losing it with menstruation. The average diet contains enough iron if they are absorbing it efficiently. The real cause for apparent anemia is low thyroid function. Thyroid governs the formation of red blood cells. I would guess more than half of diagnosed iron deficiencies in women are really thyroid deficiencies. The temperature of your arms and legs governs your ability to make red blood cells. If your thyroid is low, your extremities tend to be cool, slowing down red blood cell production.

**Host:** Regarding iron, a listener asked about her teenage son having high iron. Is there a way to lower it without donating blood?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person goes on a milk and cheese-heavy diet, a couple of eggs per day will provide the required iron without an excess. Milk and cheese are very low in iron. Within a couple of weeks on a meat-free diet, you will probably normalize iron stores.

**Host:** Can you talk about iron excess and polyunsaturated fat (PUFA)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those interacting tend to start causing problems around age 45 or 50. Polyunsaturated fats tend to go into storage while saturated fats are preferentially oxidized. On a typical diet, after several decades, your tissues become very high in PUFA. We are also getting more iron than we need, overloading the liver and marrow.

This stress makes us short of oxygen—the same thing that leads to lactic acid production. It turns iron atoms into sources of reactive electrons, producing hydroxyl ions that cause tissue deterioration. When tissues are overloaded with phospholipids constructed out of PUFA, our tissue structure starts being attacked by free radicals, producing chain reactions of inflammation and toxic breakdown products that destroy mitochondria.

**Host:** So a pregnant woman should avoid polyunsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Studies in cows show that even when eating grass rich in PUFA, the newborn calf's brain is completely free of them. In humans, full-term newborns are typically "deficient" in essential fatty acids, so doctors want to supplement them. However, the brain metabolism of a healthy full-term newborn is very high, and free radical breakdown products are extremely low.

In the first couple of years, the brains of healthy kids tend to be borderline deficient in so-called essential fatty acids, yet their learning ability and brain metabolism are very high. As the brain gets more saturated with PUFA over time, learning ability and metabolism slow down. In an Alzheimer's brain, PUFA levels are extremely high and bound with cholesterol, while available cholesterol is low.

You don't want to supplement a baby with these unstable, highly oxidizable fats. Many hospitals give premature babies intravenous soybean emulsion because of this absurd doctrine. Yet, studies have shown that a single injection of soybean emulsion damages animal brains. Almost all doctors will push pregnant women to eat fish oil or supplement PUFA. It is basically an advertising campaign for industry that is counterfactual and seems fraudulent.

**Host:** What are some non-dietary ways to reduce stress during pregnancy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoiding things that are fatiguing. Resting as much as feels right. Fifty years ago, it was recognized that bed rest was sometimes all that was needed for a healthier delivery.

**Host:** Can you talk about cholestasis of pregnancy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** High estrogen is known to be the villain. Keeping your thyroid up is the essential thing. Thyroid and progesterone are the treatment as well as the prevention.

**Host:** The occurrence of cesarean births has tripled in the past 30 years. How might this impact the generation being born?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's being done for the convenience of doctors and hospitals. They have a mechanical calendar model of when delivery should happen. If a woman is slightly hypothyroid or has a less than optimal progesterone-to-estrogen ratio, they can mature the brain properly if they just stay pregnant for another month. There is nothing wrong with prolongation of pregnancy if the woman is healthy.

By arbitrarily defining when pregnancy should terminate, hospitals are creating underweight babies with underdeveloped brains. In the last month of pregnancy, brain growth is fastest. If allowed to continue, the baby will be healthier in every way—immunity, circulation, and general vitality.

**Host:** It seems doctors are on a schedule rather than following the natural course.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many things are tending in the same direction, such as multiple vaccinations and environmental pollution. In the 1980s, in Japan, Germany, and the US, brains stopped growing statistically. In Germany, the body kept getting heavier, but without a bigger brain in proportion. In Japan and the US, there has been a downward trend in head circumference at birth.

**Host:** Several women asked about the connection between vaccinations and autism. Why is autism increasing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several studies show that a woman's estrogen balance during pregnancy strongly corresponds to the risk of autism. Estrogen creates inflammation and lactic acid. Excess inflammation during gestation in animal experiments creates behavior that resembles autism.

Things that contribute to inflammation include the aluminum adjuvants in vaccinations, as well as contaminants from the culture medium (milk protein, egg protein, synthetic chemicals). The purpose of the adjuvant is deliberately to produce an inflammatory state to activate the immune system, but inflammation during pregnancy damages the nervous system of the fetus.

**Host:** What about the idea of hormesis—that a little bit of stress is good for us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is another advertising ploy. The radiation industry led the development of the idea of hormesis to explain away why commercially valuable poisoning shouldn't be grounds for lawsuits. In the 1950s, the Atomic Energy Commission found that bomb tests were causing cancer, but to explain away radioactive elements in babies' teeth (Project Sunshine), they invented the idea that small doses are good for you.

**Host:** If kids are already on the autism spectrum, how can we mitigate the effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything good for the developing baby's brain is good at any age. Pregnenolone, progesterone, and DHEA are essential brain hormones. Some drugs developed for blood pressure, like ACE inhibitors and calcium blockers, stabilize the cell against high estrogen, lactic acid, and inflammation.

**Host:** What is the best course of action for migraines during pregnancy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My own migraines got me interested in brain physiology. I noticed girls were more likely to have them, which pointed to estrogen.

Eating a carrot every day often prevents headaches because it suppresses inflammatory bacteria in the intestine and carries estrogen out of the body. Antibiotics can have a similar effect by suppressing bacteria, lowering estrogen and cortisol.

Thyroid helps lower estrogen and cortisol. I found that supplementing thyroid and progesterone works. Once, I became hypothyroid due to fluoridated water and developed a migraine. I took about 100 milligrams of progesterone in vitamin E on my tongue. Within seconds, the visual flashing quieted down, and in about two minutes, the headache disappeared.

**Host:** How can one correct PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D is helpful. Animal experiments show that removing the thyroid and giving gonadotropin to increase estrogen produces polycystic ovaries. This implies you want to normalize the thyroid and check the estrogen-to-progesterone balance. When hypothyroidism limits the ovary's ability to make progesterone, the adrenals become hyperactive and make testosterone. You can break this vicious circle with thyroid, progesterone, and vitamin D.

**Host:** What are the most helpful labs during pregnancy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid function is key—waking temperature and pulse rate. The ratio of progesterone to estrogen is very important. Fertility clinics found that women whose progesterone was 50 to 100 times higher than estrogen were the ones who got pregnant. Animal studies show the best pregnancies occur when progesterone continues to rise steadily right up to the last days of pregnancy.

**Host:** Is metabolism linked to the length of gestation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. High thyroid metabolism keeps blood sugar steady and progesterone increasing. Estrogen dominance triggers cortisol, which triggers premature delivery. You want to keep sugar intake high enough that cortisol doesn't rise.

**Host:** Is that because sugar helps brain growth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar is the primary limiting factor for brain growth. In chickens, the brain stops developing when the glucose in the egg is used up. Experimenters injected glucose into eggs and found the brain kept developing, producing chickens with bigger brains. If glucose is limited after six months of pregnancy, the human brain stops developing.

**Host:** What about "gestational diabetes"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They created Type 2 diabetes to sell insulin, and then gestational diabetes. Old obstetricians told me that "diabetic" women often had babies with very large heads. I spoke to a woman whose doctor wanted her to diet because of blood sugar around 130. She told me her previous baby, born under similar conditions, was reading adult literature at age two. I don't think the convention of gestational diabetes is very constructive.

**Host:** For extended breastfeeding (beyond two years), are there additional dietary considerations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Drinking lots of milk. Adding a quart of orange juice helps if milk supply is limited. You need lots of calcium and protein yourself.

**Host:** Does the high prolactin from breastfeeding have a negative impact?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you keep your thyroid function up, you won't experience bad effects. Thyroid supports lactation and keeps the pituitary from overproducing stress-induced prolactin.

**Host:** What causes childhood allergies and eczema?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies found women urged to supplement with omega-3 fats (fish oil) had the most allergic children. It's prenatal inflammation. Check the child's vitamin D and thyroid levels.

**Host:** What about reversing autoimmunity in a toddler?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen is the main villain. Women have five times the incidence of autoimmune disease. Stopping medical estrogen supplements often clears rheumatoid arthritis or scleroderma. Progesterone, thyroid, and vitamin D stabilize the system.

**Host:** What is considered early puberty?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In coconut-based economies, the average age of puberty was 18. Coconut protected against the estrogenic effects of PUFA. Now, puberty is coming earlier—eight years old is becoming common.

**Host:** What about endometriosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen activates cell division and motility. Progesterone changes the tissue into glandular tissue. The basic problem is low thyroid. When I've seen women correct hypothyroidism, endometriosis symptoms turn off immediately.

**Host:** What is the ideal learning environment for a child?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** An interesting environment. This includes adults talking about interesting things and being engaged in meaningful activity. Experiencing adults being interested in life is the most important thing for kids—to see that the world is a matter for exploration, not indoctrination.

**Host:** Do you have a parting message for parents?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Be watchful for imposed doctrines, ideologies, and procedures. Being critical of medical doctrines is just a starting point. The culture has dangerous things it wants to impose, and you have to be watchful.

**Host:** Ray, thank you so much for your time, knowledge, and thoughtfulness.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay. Fun talking to you.

**Host:** Bye.

title: EastWest Healing: The Science Behind The Dangers of Polyunsaturated Fats
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Hey everyone, this is Josh Rubin and Jeannie from Holistic Living. Today we are talking to Dr. Raymond Peat. He is a researcher, an educator, and an artist. A lot of what he teaches and preaches definitely goes against the grain.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Thanks for joining us today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Josh Rubin:** Today we're going to be talking about polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). You have obviously done way more research on this subject than most people. It's quite a controversial topic because a lot of people are promoting taking these oils or eating these foods. We have studied you for years, and it is definitely brain-twisting for a lot of people. Can you give a brief introduction to who you are and why you do what you do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started studying brain physiology in 1968 when I went to the University of Oregon. I found that the best scientists were working in reproductive physiology. Even though the brain was my center of interest, I did my PhD work on reproductive physiology, particularly female aging, studying the effects of estrogen and the changes with aging.

I thought that the old animals actually had more estrogen stimulation in their tissues than younger animals, and it was working basically like contraceptive pills to prevent fertility after middle age. I noticed that the uteruses under the influence of aging and estrogen typically were darkened and contained a brown pigment. That got me interested in how that pigment develops through aging.

Estrogen excess, radiation, or deprivation of oxygen can cause it. I started studying this pigment, which is called lipofuscin, or age pigment. It had been studied quite a lot in the 1930s and 40s. They found that they were killing their animals by feeding them too much of the seeds that were rich in polyunsaturated fats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Animals like mink, which are carnivorous, were being killed by an excess of fish in the diet. Even horse meat was killing animals like mink; if the horses had eaten flax or linseed, their fat was toxic to the carnivorous animals.

Animals that ate too much of the unsaturated fats developed "yellow fat disease." In mink, it developed paralysis of the hindquarters fairly quickly and then killed them. Their fat tissue was inflamed, waterlogged, and eventually turned yellow or brown. That is the same pigment that appears in the uterus that has been overexposed to estrogen, or in the skin of an old person that has been exposed to sunlight.

All the organs develop this pigment with aging, but it develops in proportion to the amount of unsaturated fats in the diet. The essential toxic effect is that it consumes oxygen even faster than the unsaturated fatty acids. It acts as an enzyme equivalent, directly wasting energy and oxygen, producing hydrogen peroxide and a variety of toxic effects.

It also poisons the respiratory enzymes and the cellular cleanup systems—the proteolytic enzymes that should remove defective proteins. This is seen in the brains of Alzheimer's patients. They accumulate a lot of these highly unsaturated oils, such as EPA and DHA. In the process, these fats inactivate the enzymes which should remove toxic proteins.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's rewind a little so people understand. Our diets consist of proteins, carbs, and fats. Can you explain the role of these in the body before we go deeper into PUFAs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The basic structure of the body is built of proteins. The function of the protein is partly to produce energy and to replicate itself. We have to eat protein constantly.

Regarding fats, we can synthesize our own saturated and unsaturated fats. When we synthesize the highly unsaturated fats ourselves from eating either sugar or protein, the longer unsaturated fats are called Mead acid. Sugars are able to produce energy, making it unnecessary to convert protein to energy. But in the absence of sugar or fat, we can easily convert protein into fat and sugar to produce energy.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do you think there is such a misconception about healthy versus non-healthy fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The misconception started very quickly in the 1940s when agricultural chemists found that they could fatten their animals faster if they poisoned their metabolic systems with an antithyroid drug. They would get fat on very little food. However, that turned out to leave a carcinogenic residue in the meat.

They then found that corn and soybeans contained these polyunsaturated fats that would suppress the respiration of the animals and make them get fat on very little food. But in the process, they found that they were getting yellow fat disease, brain degeneration, degeneration of the gonads, infertility, and so on.

The function of Vitamin E in the 1930s had been identified as an anti-estrogen. Researchers saw a connection between excess estrogen and excess polyunsaturated fats. However, as the agricultural industry turned to the very fattening diet of high polyunsaturated oil foods (corn and soybeans), they needed to protect against the toxic effects killing their animals. They used Vitamin E. So, Vitamin E became known as an antioxidant rather than an anti-estrogen.

Medical people noticed that cholesterol was lowered in the process of eating a lot of these polyunsaturated fats. That led to the marketing of unsaturated fats to the human food supply. Since people didn't want to gain weight on the least amount of food, they needed a new reason for selling their fats to humans. Lowering cholesterol became the excuse.

**Josh Rubin:** Nowadays, what are the fats in the current diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People are still talking about "essential fatty acids" as if they were almost a vitamin. When I was a kid in school, nutritionists would say "possibly essential" or mention a controversy.

In 1929, the Burrs (researchers working for the agricultural industry) claimed that linoleic acid and linolenic acid were essential nutrients. Previously, researchers had demonstrated that animals could live perfectly without those if they were given vitamin-rich, protein-rich food. In fact, some German researchers found that animals didn't develop cancer—something like 99% of cancers didn't develop—when animals were deprived of linoleic and linolenic acids.

The Burrs ignored the evidence that these fats are not essential. They produced skin disease and gonadal defects when they deprived the animals of these two fatty acids. However, at that time, only two of the B vitamins were known. About three years later, researchers found that Vitamin B6 deficiency causes exactly the symptoms that were blamed on the linoleic acid deficiency.

They fed their animals the diet that the Burrs had used and created the symptoms. Then they gave the animals only extra Vitamin B6 and cured the condition. What the Burrs had demonstrated was that the essential fatty acids slow metabolism, making the animals need less food, thus preventing a deficiency on a deficient diet. But the oil industry simply ignored the fact that the Burrs' work had been invalidated.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Besides Omega 3 (linolenic) and Omega 6 (linoleic), where else in our food supply do we consume these polyunsaturated fatty acids?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All natural foods contain small amounts. Coconut oil contains about 1%. Beef, lamb, milk, and cheese contain a couple of percent, depending on what the animal ate.

The really risky sources appear when you get above the equivalent of about a teaspoonful of polyunsaturated fats per day (4 grams). That is where the breakdown of these starts showing an increased incidence of cancer and other degenerative diseases.

The foods richest in these unstable and potentially toxic oils are grains, seeds, nuts, vegetables in general, and all of the animals which are not ruminants that have eaten vegetable polyunsaturated fats. Horses, rabbits, chickens, and pigs will reflect in their diet pretty exactly what they've been eating. Fish eat algae and smaller organisms that have eaten algae, so they get a very high concentration of these polyunsaturated fats.

**Josh Rubin:** People are overdoing seeds and nuts. Can you explain why the seeds of plants produce these polyunsaturated fatty acids? And when you say vegetables, are you talking above ground or below ground?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you think of where corn or soybeans normally grow, the seed sits on the ground through the winter. It is basically kept in refrigeration. When it warms up, it sprouts. The seed contains enough Vitamin E that under this refrigerated situation, the polyunsaturated fats are stable.

If the oils were completely saturated, they would be like butter in the refrigerator—hard and immobile. The unsaturated fats are still liquid and mobile at refrigerator temperatures. The unsaturation is a defense to maintain mobility on the molecular level at low temperatures.

However, if you kept the seed warm all winter at the temperature of a human body, these oils would react with oxygen and the seed would be dead by springtime. In your body at 98 degrees, that oxidation happens even faster than at room temperature.

**Josh Rubin:** Would you say you are more in favor of vegetables like squashes or root vegetables that have very little polyunsaturated fatty acids, rather than greens, spinach, and kale?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The leaves are important sources of magnesium and Vitamin K, but you have to take into consideration the high proportion of polyunsaturated fats. For calories, squashes and root vegetables are safer. Fruits are even better because the tissue contains a higher concentration of minerals than starchy vegetables. Potatoes are more like a fruit or an animal protein in their total nutritional value.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Many people think Omega 3s produce non-inflammatory prostaglandins. Do we need essential fatty acids to fight inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some recent work on the anti-inflammatory effect of fish oil (Omega-3) shows that they accumulate with aging. Alzheimer's or dementia patients have a much higher level of these in the brain. They spontaneously oxidize into toxic, anti-metabolic substances—neuroprostanes—and in the process of oxidizing, they suppress the immune system.

When you suppress the cells that produce inflammation, you get an interruption of an existing inflammatory process. However, researchers have found that it is only the oxidized, broken-down form of the fish oil that has this effect. When you prolong the feeding, you start seeing that immunodepression is the long-range result.

The present advocacy of fish oil for its anti-inflammatory effect is very similar to what the X-ray industry was doing 80 years ago. They treated arthritis, acne, and psoriasis with X-rays because the immediate effect is to create lipid peroxides, which are anti-inflammatory immediately, but immunosuppressive and toxic in the long run.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you give us five key points on why PUFAs are dangerous and some alternative fats that are beneficial?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:**
1.  **Olive Oil:** Pretty safe because it has a variety of antioxidants, even though it is 10% PUFA. I recommend not eating more than a couple of teaspoonfuls per day.
2.  **Coconut Oil:** Has only around 1% or 2% polyunsaturated fats. Coconut oil and butter can actually have an antioxidant effect, blocking the effects of the breakdown products of PUFAs.
3.  **Sugar/Fruit:** Sugar is naturally turned into saturated fats. We immediately create an Omega-9 type of fat (Mead acid) when we synthesize fat from sugar.
4.  **Mead Acid:** These are produced from saturated fats and have an anti-inflammatory effect. By avoiding the toxic anti-inflammatory effects of PUFAs, we allow our body to produce the natural anti-inflammatory Mead acid series.
5.  **Saturated Fats:** We can produce protective fats from saturated fats such as cocoa butter (stearic acid).

**Josh Rubin:** You mention that PUFAs store in the tissues and, during stress or low glucose, can create hormonal or hypothyroid symptoms. Can you elaborate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen favors the storage of polyunsaturated fats, and these fats favor the influence of estrogen.

When a mammal is born, the tissues are "deficient" in essential fatty acids by present standards because of the presence of Mead acid. The growth of the fetus is inhibited when you try to "correct" that deficiency by feeding the mother seed oils or fish oils.

35 years ago, experimenters fed pregnant animals diets with corn oil versus coconut oil. They found that the unsaturated fats caused the pregnant animals to have small-brained babies which didn't learn very well. Recently, French researchers tried to demonstrate that pregnant women eating unsaturated fats had smarter babies. In fact, they found the opposite: the babies were less able to learn in proportion to the amount of polyunsaturated fat in the diet, and they were born smaller with smaller brains.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Do you feel that eliminating PUFAs and increasing saturated fats could reverse hormonal imbalances and hypothyroidism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 20 years ago, I decided to experiment by adding half an ounce to an ounce of coconut oil to my food. The immediate thing I noticed was that for about an hour and a half after eating it, my heart was running at a higher rate, I was breathing harder, and my skin was pinker. After a couple of weeks, I saw I was losing weight quickly, even though I was eating more calories.

Constantly, when we draw on stored unsaturated fats, all functions of our thyroid system are inhibited. We produce less hormone, transport it less effectively, and it enters the mitochondria less effectively. If you interrupt that supply of stored unsaturated fats, you immediately feel a surge of respiratory activity.

Conversely, the immediate effect of the presence of unsaturated fats is to block the oxidation of glucose. This is called the **Randle Cycle**. It immediately impairs the ability to oxidize glucose, leading to diabetes-like issues and oxidative damage to the mitochondria.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you summarize why you dislike PUFAs in vegetables and cod liver oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:**
*   It promotes estrogen's effect.
*   It interferes with the synthesis of progesterone and other protective steroids.
*   It inhibits the thyroid.
*   It promotes the accumulation of age pigment (lipofuscin).
*   It makes you more sensitive to radiation exposure.
*   While fish oil is marketed for health, in Japan, the amount of fish in the diet corresponds to several types of cancer, including metastatic cancers.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's take a call.

**Caller 1:** I follow metabolic typing and I am a "protein type," so I can't get many fats other than from meat. If nuts aren't good for us, how do I get the recommended amount of fat? I take coconut oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Tropical foods in general are pretty safe. The nuts that grow at a very high temperature are, like coconuts, very saturated in their fats. Tropical fruits are also good because the small amount of fats in those are highly saturated. Anything that lives or grows at a high temperature is going to be safe when it gets in our body at that same high temperature.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's take one more caller.

**Caller 2:** I was curious about polyunsaturated fats and temperature. How do bears do it? They get a ton of PUFAs and they are at 98 degrees.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Bears eat berries to fatten up in the fall. During hibernation, their body temperature drops quite a bit. With squirrels and other hibernators, they have seen that if they don't let them eat the PUFA nuts—if they give them a saturated diet—they don't hibernate. The serotonin that triggers hibernation comes up when you reach a certain point of unsaturation in your fats.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, we have to wrap it up. Thank you for taking the time to come on our show. We really value your work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: EastWest Healing: Inflammation
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Welcome back to a brand new season of Holistic Living with Josh and Jeannie Rubin. We are really excited this year to launch a series of shows with our one and only Dr. Raymond Peat from RayPeat.com. Today, we are going to be talking about inflammation: his view on where it comes from, what is involved, and what in our environment and bodies creates it. Our goal this year is to give everyone an education, whether you are a practitioner or a layperson. We feel Ray can offer a lot of insight into your physiology. We want to start from the basework and move up to solutions. Jeannie has Ray on the line. Hi, Ray. How are you doing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good. Have you talked anything about the history of what people believe about inflammation?

**Josh Rubin:** Based on your science and research, you have a very different view on a lot of things. Why don't you explain the traditional definition and then give your definition of what inflammation is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Elie Metchnikoff, more than 100 years ago, discovered phagocytes and explored the immune process. He observed that when you put a splinter into an organism, white blood cell-type cells engulfed it. They would eat it if it was edible, or just concentrate and form a sheath or a pus deposit around it.

For Metchnikoff, immunity was this process in which certain cells protect the organism basically by eating the problem. That was considered the essence of inflammation, and it was a good thing. He was looking at primitive organisms and viewed this eating process as part of the developmental process—maintaining and generating the proper structure of the organism.

There is an English doctor, Jamie Cunliffe, who is following up on Metchnikoff's idea of what the immune system is. As she expresses it, it is the process of cleaning up messes. The general idea is that our immune system is primarily to maintain our organism. The idea of it being directed at foreign invaders is really secondary to the process of fixing anything that goes wrong in the organism.

However, Paul Ehrlich, who shared the Nobel Prize with Metchnikoff, was working on toxins to kill invading organisms. The idea of killing invaders came to be identified with immunity and inflammation throughout the 20th century. Inflammation was seen as a good defensive reaction against invaders. But if you try to continue the Metchnikoff-Cunliffe idea, inflammation really is a problem rather than a solution. When things are working smoothly, we can either tolerate the presence of foreign organisms or eliminate them without a big mess being produced.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 20 years ago, people started shifting their thinking and seeing that degenerative diseases are all inflammatory processes. Hardening of the arteries, brain degenerative diseases of all sorts including Alzheimer's, and aging in all its aspects involve inflammation rather than simply cleaning up the mess quietly.

This suggests looking at the earliest stages of development—not just evolutionary, but during gestation. When the fetus or embryo is injured, the tissue is simply repaired without producing a scar or inflammation. The prenatal functioning of the immune system is basically what Metchnikoff was talking about: keeping the integrity of the organism and not worrying about killing invaders.

What happens after the fetus is born? There is no longer the mother's body and the placenta filtering the environment. All mammals have a very low concentration of the so-called "essential fatty acids"—the polyunsaturated fats—at birth. As these are taken in from the environment without the filtering process of the placenta, the action of the immune system starts to produce inflammation, scarring, and defective healing.

It is the progressive accumulation of polyunsaturated fats that starts what we know as inflammation. When cells are inflamed, they shift from an oxygen-based metabolism to a simple sugar-consuming metabolism and are in an excited state that promotes cell division. In this oxygen-wasting environment, the cells produce collagen to repair, but the ability to remove the collagen is impaired by the presence of polyunsaturated fats.

The breakdown of polyunsaturated fats involves the production of prostaglandins. These aren't part of the essential development of the embryo, but they become very important as we begin eating polyunsaturated fats. The presence of these excitatory mediators—prostaglandins and free fatty acids—blocks the cleanup process, keeps the inflammation going, and leads to the production of a scar. That is part of why vitamin E, by opposing those processes, can practically eliminate scarring if you get a very high concentration in the presence of the healing process.

**Jeannie Rubin:** You mentioned the placenta working as a filter to protect the immune system against polyunsaturated fatty acids. If a mother has a diet high in polyunsaturated fatty acids, would the placenta still act as a filtering agent?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Normally, yes. Even people who have been on a high n-3 and n-6 diet have babies that come out "essential fatty acid deficient" according to current definitions. That is the argument for putting fish oil in baby formula. However, if you look at calves, they are extremely deficient at birth. Even the small amount of polyunsaturated fat in milk—maybe 2%—will cause them to gradually load up as they grow.

When people have tried to supplement pregnant women to correct that universal "deficiency" of the newborn, they find that the babies are born smaller and are more susceptible to allergies and inflammatory diseases. The worst part is that their brains are smaller. People trying to show that the brain requires n-3 fats fed these to pregnant women expecting the fetus to learn more easily, but in fact, they found they didn't learn as well.

One of the events caused by the excess of n-3 in particular is that the metabolism of tryptophan, which should go largely to form niacin and melatonin, is diverted. This type of unsaturated fat causes tryptophan to be metabolized in a toxic direction, producing less niacin and more of the excitotoxic quinolinic acid and carcinogenic indole derivatives.

**Josh Rubin:** What do you think causes inflammation? Is it just from polyunsaturated fatty acids in the food, or is it happening in utero? Where is it coming from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The challenge is what starts it. Instead of being a quick corrective process, the presence of unsaturated fats causes inflammation, calcium uptake, accelerated growth, collagen production, and eventually calcification of the fibrotic scar material.

The worst challenge that we are constantly exposed to is bacterial toxin production in the intestine. Everyone has it unless they are germ-free lab rats. The balance of colonic bacteria depends on what we eat, but there are always some producing endotoxins. These are lipopolysaccharide molecules that create stress, poisoning, and physical disruption of cells lining the intestine.

Part of the reaction to this is to produce serotonin. The intestine is where about 95% of our body's serotonin is produced. It stimulates peristalsis and activates defensive processes. But when there is an overbalance of endotoxins, the serotonin starts to be the main problem. Serotonin activates the formation of prostaglandins from fatty acids and the release of nitric oxide.

When there isn't enough energy supplied to the organism and there is too much endotoxin, the nitric oxide and serotonin create inflammation in the wall of the intestine and blood vessels, letting endotoxin get into the bloodstream. This causes systemic effects, releasing more nitric oxide and serotonin. Serotonin then becomes the main factor in aging and accumulated stress effects.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on what endotoxin is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is normally just part of the bacterial cell structure. The covering of the bacteria contains a starch-like molecule with some fatty acids attached to it. Organisms have been dealing with them for so long that they are our basic signal of the need to defend ourselves against the environment. They are very good triggers for the production of serotonin and nitric oxide. All bacteria "leak" these little molecules as they are forming new bacteria or being stressed.

**Josh Rubin:** How do we get exposed to these? From meats or other foods?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are constantly being produced in the lower small intestine and colon. The upper part of the intestine is normally free of bacteria. But when we eat undigestible food—starches, complex fibrous materials, lignins—these feed different combinations of bacteria.

For example, if you feed rats a type of starch that humans can't digest but bacteria can, the rats become anxious and aggressive because of the disturbance of serotonin and nitric oxide. The amount and type of bacterial toxin are determined mostly by the presence of things in our foods that we can't digest. Uncooked vegetables will very quickly start producing bacterial overgrowth. If that material gets mixed with proteinaceous things, like undercooked beans, you get a different category of toxins called indoles, which resemble serotonin and histamine.

**Josh Rubin:** How does endotoxin affect the liver and perpetuate the cycle of inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver should absolutely destroy any toxins that reach it. But when the intestine is in bad shape, or if the liver isn't well-nourished and well-supplied with thyroid hormone, it loses the energy to produce antitoxic processes. A poorly nourished or low-thyroid liver lets the junk absorbed through the permeable intestine into the system. Then you get leakiness of blood vessels, which in the brain can cause symptoms like multiple sclerosis, edema in other organs, and inflammatory processes.

When the liver gets weakened by bacterial toxins, it also begins to fail to regulate the body's own hormones. For example, estrogen accumulates. In a fertility clinic, doctors gave infertile women an antibiotic. Shortly after, the women reported less fatigue and fewer premenstrual symptoms. Their blood tests showed that right after taking the antibiotic, estrogen levels went down sharply, progesterone went up, and cortisol went down. They created a fertile endocrine pattern just by taking an antibiotic.

I've seen the same thing just with a carrot salad. The carrot is an unusual vegetable in being antifungal, antibacterial, and very resistant to the production of endotoxin. It works like an antibiotic on the intestine, reducing endotoxins.

**Josh Rubin:** What happens when these hormones are dysregulated?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the liver is failing and cortisol and estrogen are high, that goes with a systemic excess of serotonin and deficiency of thyroid hormones. Serotonin lowers cellular oxidative metabolism and energy production.

One of the biological effects of high serotonin is to allow rodents to hibernate. When they are under stress, serotonin goes up, allowing them to drop their body temperature and go into a torpor. When people—who can't hibernate—are exposed to the endotoxin, serotonin, free fatty acid, and estrogen pattern, it lowers their ability to produce energy and tends to cause body temperature to fall.

As a defensive system, serotonin increases pituitary hormones to compensate. It drives the thyroid gland harder (stimulating TSH), but it also stimulates ACTH, prolactin, gonadotropins, and growth hormone. It turns on the pituitary to try to drive everything up to compensate for the fact that mitochondrial energy systems are being blocked.

**Josh Rubin:** Just to clarify, you are naming specific hormones that create inflammation, pull calcium from the bone, drop body temperature, and inhibit the immune system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Doctors like to see these pituitary hormones in a "normal" range. They will tell you that if you take thyroid to suppress your TSH, you are going to cause problems. But in fact, the TSH itself causes most of the problems identified with hypothyroidism. High serotonin is associated with low thyroid function and high TSH, but the TSH itself contributes to atherosclerosis, increased blood lipids, high blood pressure, and a range of inflammatory processes.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about foods that are anti-inflammatory versus inflammatory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Calcium is a central thing. It stimulates cell energy production. When the cell has what it needs—sugar, vitamins, and minerals—calcium will increase oxidative metabolism. A calcium deficiency turns on inflammation-related processes to attempt to correct the deficiency. This eventually leads to the calcification of soft tissues.

This is the main reason I recommend using milk rather than meat: the high calcium content. Meat has a very high phosphate ratio to calcium. Eggs would have the right ratio if people would eat the shell as well as the egg. With milk, you get a very good ratio of calcium to phosphorus.

The parathyroid hormone (PTH) is suppressed when we eat enough calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin K. PTH has inflammation-promoting effects. So, keeping our hormones low is really one of the goals of eating right. The pituitary should be quiet, PTH should be low, and estrogen and cortisol should be low. The protective steroids—pregnenolone, progesterone, and DHEA—are produced by getting enough vitamin A, vitamin E, and the oil-soluble vitamins K and D. Keeping polyunsaturated fats down is essential for all of these.

**Jeannie Rubin:** When people think of inflammation, they relate it to redness, swelling, and pain. How would someone know if they are suffering from underlying inflammation aside from arthritic conditions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Defects in the energy process will show up very early as poor sleep quality, a tendency towards insomnia, fatigue, excitability, and nervous problems like an inability to concentrate or being twitchy and tense. The energy of the nervous system is probably the most sensitive indicator of a process tending in the direction of too much inflammation.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Regarding polyunsaturated fatty acids, should people eliminate them 100% or is moderation okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A healthy 8-year-old with an intense metabolic rate can burn a large amount of polyunsaturated fats so they accumulate more slowly. Once your metabolism has slowed down after puberty, a high likelihood of it getting incorporated into your tissues is the rule.

Once your body has incorporated these pro-inflammatory materials, every time you are under stress or haven't eaten for a certain length of time, your body will resort to burning the liberated fats. These come partly from your fat tissue and partly from the breakdown of other cells. If you can dispose of these toxic stored materials through a healthy liver, you can excrete them. But if your liver is losing energy, your tissues will have to oxidize them for energy. That is where they poison the energy-producing apparatus and turn into inflammatory mediators.

You can limit that breakdown by keeping saturated fats in your diet. Coconut oil has enough short-chain, water-soluble fatty acids that they will be taken up by preference and protect the mitochondria from the stress-released polyunsaturated fats. Fruit also helps; the sugar restrains tissue breakdown, and the minerals (potassium, magnesium, calcium) act somewhat like insulin to inhibit tissue breakdown.

**Caller (GP):** What is your advice to reduce cortisol secretion during a workout?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several years ago, a study took blood samples from people before and after a jog. Some ate breakfast before, and some didn't. They found that people who exercised on an empty stomach had broken chromosomes in their white blood cells. It is sort of like radiation injury to exercise on an empty stomach. It seems that the sugars and minerals in breakfast—probably just a glass of orange juice and milk—would be enough to prevent that stress-induced chromosome damage.

**Caller (GP):** How about bitter chocolate to prevent cortisol secretion before a workout?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Chocolate has a very high protein content, specifically leucine. Leucine acts like insulin and helps to prevent tissue breakdown. So chocolate is an anabolic protein.

**Caller (GP):** Is it okay to eat chocolate alone or with other food before training?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's good to have some sugar with it.

**Josh Rubin:** That's a great question. It highlights using nutrition to match the physiology of the body rather than just supplements.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are some supplements that are worse than others. Probably the two most dangerous are the carotenes—because they are polyunsaturated—and tryptophan. Tryptophan and 5-HTP (hydroxy-tryptophan) activate the inflammation process very directly.

**Josh Rubin:** Is there anything else regarding inflammation you want to mention?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Another dangerous thing many people are using now is Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs). To the extent that they raise serotonin, they are being found responsible for increased osteoporosis and breast cancer. I think they will probably be found to contribute to obesity as well.

**Josh Rubin:** What do you recommend for people whose doctors tell them they need these?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Things that promote your real energy production while lowering inflammation. Thyroid hormone itself is anti-inflammatory, partly by suppressing the pituitary thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Things that support the thyroid—such as saturated fats, sugars, salts, and electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, sodium, and potassium—help to protect tissues and work with the thyroid to produce the right kind of steroids, like pregnenolone and progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is one little anti-inflammatory tidbit that is very easy to do. Once inflammation starts to lower your energy, it becomes a vicious circle. Just having cold feet and cold hands creates an inflammatory condition. When the blood drops a few degrees to circulate through your cold feet, it releases inflammatory mediators. Just sleeping with a wool cap and warm socks can help greatly with inflammation as well as insomnia problems.

**Josh Rubin:** We can guarantee we'll be at home tonight sleeping with wool caps.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Also, calcification and osteoporosis are two very important aspects of inflammation. The inflammatory substances—prostaglandins, serotonin, TSH, cytokines, interleukins—break down healthy bone structure and at the same time put calcium into your arteries, brain, and pineal gland. Taking aspirin, for example, to lower inflammation will help to prevent calcification of your arteries and help to strengthen the bones.

**Josh Rubin:** Great stuff. If you want to learn more, check out his website, RayPeat.com. He has tons of articles. Ray, thanks for a great show.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: EastWest Healing: The Thyroid
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Hey everyone, this is Josh Rubin from East West Healing and Performance. Welcome to our Blog Talk Radio show. Today we are going to have Dr. Raymond Peat on again. He has a PhD in Biology from the University of Oregon and specializes in physiology. He started most of his work studying progesterone and hormones back in 1968. Since then, he has been working on practical and theoretical aspects of hormones and the thyroid. The bottom line is the guy is a genius; his work is cutting edge, probably 80 years ahead of its time. We’re going to be talking about the thyroid today. Let's get him on the show. Ray, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm here.

**Josh Rubin:** How's it going, Ray? We really appreciate you taking time out to come on our show and educate people on your science. In a lot of your articles, you focus on the thyroid. Could you enlighten us on why you study the thyroid so much and why you feel the thyroid hormone is the most important hormone in the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Looking at life in general, plants, funguses, and amoebas are the organisms that apparently don't need or want thyroid. But as soon as you get what we think of as real animal life—that includes corals, coelenterates, echinoderms, mollusks, crustaceans, insects, just about everything that has an organization to it—they use thyroid.

The basic function of thyroid is to energize cells and to give them enough energy and efficiency to allow them to differentiate so that they don't just concentrate on eating and growing the way plants, amoebas, and fungi do.

If you look at some of the old experiments in an aquarium with developing frog eggs, as soon as the eggs would hatch into tadpoles, they would either add an anti-thyroid chemical or a little bit of thyroid hormone to the water. If you added the anti-thyroid chemical, the tadpole would never turn into a frog; it would just grow to be a huge tadpole. But if you added thyroid to the aquarium, the tiny hatchling tadpole would turn into a tiny, spider-like frog just about the size of a fly. This shows that the thyroid energizes the cells so that they use oxygen and produce a huge amount of energy. This energy allows the cells to realize their function. Without thyroid, all you have is growth. That's fine for amoebas and trees, but in humans, it can lead to tumors and malformations.

Energy production is really the basis of all organized life. That makes the thyroid, in a sense, the main gland. If you take out the pituitary gland—which people have talked about as the master gland—and give the animal thyroid hormone, in some cases the animals live ten times as long as normal, usually about twice as long as normal for the lack of the pituitary gland, as long as they had adequate thyroid.

**Josh Rubin:** So you're saying the thyroid is the master regulator of metabolism? It keeps your body in an efficient, anti-inflammatory state where you're producing energy more efficiently than you're expending it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. The inflammatory state means that something has gone wrong. It's interesting that doctors very often go entirely on the basis of the pituitary Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) in diagnosing your thyroid status. However, TSH creates all sorts of inflammatory processes. When you have enough actual thyroid hormone to completely shut down your pituitary, you turn off practically all of these toxic inflammatory processes.

**Josh Rubin:** We see so many people in our clinic being diagnosed with hypothyroidism. What's your take on the validity of current labs, and what do you recommend when it comes to measuring thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s, it was standard medical practice to have a little apparatus to allow the person to lie down, usually with an empty stomach, and breathe oxygen for two minutes. They would measure how much oxygen was used. People who had the standard symptoms of low thyroid function would often consume only half the normal amount of oxygen. That usually went with their hands and feet being cold, their core body temperature being below normal, and their heart rate being somewhat slower than normal.

As they looked at biochemical indicators, they saw that cholesterol was almost invariably high in proportion to the reduced consumption of oxygen. The increasing cholesterol was like a mirror image of the decreasing metabolic rate. If you gave a thyroid supplement to someone with excess cholesterol, it would immediately come down exactly in relation to the increasing oxygen use.

Carotene excess was another identifying feature. A doctor would look at a person's palm. A hypothyroid person typically would have cold, pale hands, but usually with orange areas where the skin was thickened in the calluses. That's because vitamin A is used directly in proportion to your metabolic rate and thyroid function. If your thyroid is low, you barely use your carotene and hardly convert it to vitamin A.

Another good indicator developed in the 1930s was the Achilles reflex relaxation speed. A person kneels on a chair so their toes hang over loosely, and you thump the Achilles tendon. In a hypothyroid person, the muscle relaxes so slowly that their foot returns like a door with a pneumatic closer on it—a little jerky relaxation. The electrocardiogram shows the same thing; the T-wave is delayed and flattened out. When your brain is tired, the nerves are slow to relax, so your sleep will not be as restorative as it would be in a high thyroid state.

**Josh Rubin:** Just to clarify regarding the slow relaxation of the calf muscle: Is that because of low blood sugar, increased serotonin, or calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of those things contribute. The thyroid allows you to take up oxygen efficiently and oxidize it completely. In proportion to the lack of thyroid, when you stimulate a muscle or nerve cell, it will use its oxygen inefficiently. It will allow calcium to enter the cell and keep it in an excited state, and it will tend to produce lactic acid rather than carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide produced under the influence of the thyroid is needed to carry the exciting calcium out of the cells and allow the cell to relax.

**Josh Rubin:** You mentioned high cholesterol is a huge indicator of low thyroid, as is the Achilles reflex. What about pulse and temperature? Why do you look at those while everyone else focuses on TSH and Free T4?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The idea of free and bound hormones is purely a laboratory construction. It’s a little bit analogous to reading tea leaves. Actually, when thyroid hormone is stuck to albumin protein in the blood, it has no trouble getting into cells.

Regarding TSH, I don't recommend it as a way to diagnose hypothyroidism, but if you are looking at a blood test, I recommend having as close to zero TSH as you can get. All the known effects of TSH are harmful. Doctors often argue that suppressing TSH causes osteoporosis, but the evidence is the opposite. Thyrotropin (TSH), like estrogen, increases osteoprotegerin, which increases the movement of calcium into your arteries and heart and out of the bones.

Regarding temperature, Dr. Broda Barnes practiced in Colorado and found temperature was an adequate way of diagnosing. He thought waking temperature should be around 97.8°F, rising to around 98.6°F after breakfast.

I observed that in hot, humid summer weather, hypothyroid people could maintain a normal core temperature, but often their pulse rate would still be low—45 to 65 beats per minute. I also saw people with extreme hypothyroidism oscillate between depression and mania. When depressed, their temperature was low. In the manic phase, they would wake up with a pulse of 80 and a normal temperature.

Furthermore, if you see a person's temperature and pulse rate fall after a good meal, that reveals a low metabolic rate that was being held up by emergency stimulation from adrenaline and cortisol. Food reduces stress, so when the stress hormones drop, the true low metabolism is revealed.

**Josh Rubin:** So, if someone has a low resting heart rate, society often thinks that means they are healthy, like Lance Armstrong. But you're saying a low resting heart rate can mean they are down-regulating their metabolism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and it tends to go with fertility problems, hormonal problems, low testosterone, increased estrogen, and degenerative problems.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's talk about T3 and T4. Where does most of the conversion happen in the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Broda Barnes was one of the first to notice the importance of the liver in thyroid function. The Biskinds in the 1940s showed how the liver regulates hormones. If the liver was lacking thyroid, protein, or vitamins, estrogen would skyrocket. There is an antagonism focused on the liver between estrogen and thyroid.

The thyroid works partly by energizing the liver so it can detoxify everything, including removing 100% of the estrogen that reaches it. If your thyroid is low, the liver loses the ability to detoxify estrogen.

The liver is also the source of the most active thyroid hormone. About two-thirds of the thyroid used by the body is produced in the liver. If your liver isn't getting enough glucose or selenium, it is unable to convert thyroxine (T4) into T3. If you starve for 24 hours or exert too much energy, your liver isn't getting enough glucose to convert the T4 into active T3.

If a doctor prescribes only T4, it works fine in healthy young men. But women, because of higher estrogen levels, have more liver issues. A little problem with thyroid or estrogen means the liver allows estrogen to increase, which decreases the production of active thyroid hormone, creating a vicious circle.

**Josh Rubin:** So we need selenium and glucose to make the conversion. And estrogen itself will block the T4 to T3 conversion and back up the liver?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Once that happens, the estrogen can reach the point where it inhibits the thyroid gland itself. It inhibits the proteolytic enzyme that releases the hormone from the gland. This is where women tend to get goiters or thyroid enlargement, often diagnosed as Hashimoto's. Estrogen causes the pituitary to drive the thyroid harder via TSH, but simultaneously blocks the thyroid's ability to secrete, causing enlargement.

**Josh Rubin:** A lot of people have high T4 lab values. What does that mean?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It very often goes with hypothyroidism. If your liver can't activate the hormone, the gland will go on producing it, and T4 will accumulate because your liver isn't using it up. A very high T4 level tends to slow down the production of T3.

I saw a patient who was slightly hypothyroid and prescribed T4. Her symptoms got worse. The doctor increased the dose until she reached 400 or 500 micrograms of T4, at which point she went into a myxedema coma. They injected pure T3, and she came right out of the coma. Her symptoms got worse directly in proportion to the increased dose of T4. It isn't rare for a woman to get worse symptoms—noises in the head, electrical sensations, swollen muscles—as a result of taking too much T4.

**Josh Rubin:** How does hypothyroidism affect systems like blood sugar, adrenaline, and digestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you aren't able to oxidize your sugar all the way to carbon dioxide, you produce lactic acid very easily. Even at rest, a person will produce lactic acid as if they were under strenuous exercise. Lactic acid turns on inflammatory mediators and acts as a toxin. Over time, it leads to fibrosis, arthritis, connective tissue diseases, and calcification of soft tissues.

**Josh Rubin:** It seems like regulating the thyroid affects so many systems—joint pain, digestion, menstrual problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because energy production shapes everything. The body is constantly renewing itself. If you aren't renewing yourself at a high rate, errors accumulate.

One reason thyroid problems get worse over time is that our diets contain thyroid-inhibiting substances, especially polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). The French did studies showing that the first effect of too much PUFA is to block the thyroid gland from secreting hormone. Then, it inhibits transport in the blood. Fish oil (5 and 6 unsaturated bonds) is an almost total inhibitor of thyroid transport. Linoleic acid inhibits it about 30%. Finally, it inhibits the cell's responsiveness to thyroid.

**Josh Rubin:** How do thyroid hormones raise CO2, and what are the advantages of higher CO2 levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Higher CO2 means you are oxidizing things completely. If you oxidize fats completely, you stop producing lactic acid. Carbon dioxide binds to our proteins, protecting them. It binds to hemoglobin and proteins with exposed amine groups. Carbon dioxide binds protectively to proteins, keeping them in the native, youthful state.

All of our peptide hormones—insulin, growth hormone, etc.—bind carbon dioxide, becoming a different substance. If we hyperventilate and blow out too much CO2, or if we are hypothyroid and produce lactic acid instead of CO2, our hormone system is deranged. CO2 is in itself anti-inflammatory.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your recommendations for people who don't have a thyroid, or for general thyroid nutrition?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In a non-industrial culture, people would get dietary thyroid by eating the whole animal—fish heads, sausage with beef thyroid thrown in. A natural diet provides the equivalent of half a grain of thyroid.

Regarding foods, avoid toxic foods like polyunsaturated fats and hard-to-digest starches (like beans) that irritate the intestine and create endotoxin. Emphasize sweet fruits, milk, cheese, eggs, shellfish, and gelatin-rich meats (oxtail, shank). Gelatin is pro-thyroid because it doesn't contain the precursors to serotonin.

**Josh Rubin:** You’ve mentioned the "carrot salad" before. How does that help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The raw carrot contains fiber that cannot be digested, and it has mild antibiotic properties. It absorbs toxins and prevents their absorption. I had women measure their hormones, then eat a raw carrot daily. After just a few days, their hormones were back in a favorable state—reduced estrogen and cortisol, increased progesterone and thyroid—because of the cleansing effect on the intestine and liver.

**Josh Rubin:** What about foods to help the T4 to T3 conversion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very sweet, low-fiber foods. Well-strained orange juice from sweet oranges is the safest. It provides glucose for the liver. Also, if you have a centrifugal juicer, you can juice a raw potato and then cook the juice (like scrambling an egg) to get a safe, high-quality protein without the starch.

**Josh Rubin:** Why strained orange juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Commercial juices often use enzymatic processes to create "pulp" that is actually a type of fiber we can't digest, which feeds bacteria. If you make it yourself, straining it removes the indigestible fibers that would otherwise feed bacteria and create endotoxin.

**Josh Rubin:** And coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coconut oil is pro-thyroid. It helps the liver store glycogen and helps the body detox from unsaturated fats. It is anti-inflammatory. Refined coconut oil is often safer to avoid allergic reactions to the proteins in crude oil.

**Josh Rubin:** Any final nutritional recommendations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If people eat vegetables, I encourage them to cook them to death. Boiling them for 40 minutes makes them much safer. Experiments in the 1940s showed that rats thrived on canned (cooked) vegetables but couldn't live on raw ones.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, we really appreciate you coming on and educating us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks.

**Josh Rubin:** Have a good one. For the listeners, please understand the "why" behind these recommendations before you just start eating carrots or gelatin. Read Ray's articles and books. There are many pieces to the healing puzzle. Thanks for tuning in.

title: EastWest Healing: Estrogen vs Progesterone
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Welcome to Holistic Living. We have Ray Peat on every month, and we want to say thank you to him. Before we introduce Ray, I want to mention that Ray's approach is not just an approach; it's a philosophy and a science. It is a science of how the body works—its biochemistry, biology, and physiology. It's not an "outside-in" type of diet like Paleolithic dieting or vegetarianism. It's based on the science of how the body works.

His articles are technical. It's like finding Waldo and piecing things together. Don't think that just because you eat gelatin, carrots, and broth, you're going to become healthy and lose weight immediately. It is a process.

Today we are talking about estrogen versus progesterone. You can go to Ray Peat's site, RayPeat.com. He has a PhD in Biology from the University of Oregon and specializes in physiology. He started his work with progesterone and related hormones back in 1968. Ray, welcome back.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good, thank you.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's get to it. We're going to be talking about estrogen and progesterone today. What sparked your interest in the hormonal field back in the 1960s?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It started when I was a kid noticing things. One of the old-timers in the woods pointed out that when they wanted a pine tree to bear seeds, they would chop it with an axe, and that made it bear fruit. I heard stories about how stress would bring on puberty prematurely.

Those ideas started blending with what I was seeing in the 50s. A woman took a shot of estrogen and immediately came down with rheumatoid arthritis, which got worse with each injection and cleared up when she stopped using it. A classmate's mother had a shot of estrogen for menopause and within 30 minutes was psychotic. The daughter began using contraceptives shortly after that and died of a stroke. Other young women using those first very high-estrogen contraceptives were being disabled by hemorrhaging.

By the time I decided to go to graduate school in biology, my intention was to study brain biology. However, the real science was being done in the endocrinology department. I had moved from Mexico to Oregon, and I started noticing my own health changing with the dark, rainy winters. I heard stories from girls who would get a cheap basement apartment and spend all winter with PMS. I was seeing the interactions of the environment with hormones.

I ran across Hans Selye's early work. In the 40s, he had characterized the functions of steroid hormones. He demonstrated that a large dose of estrogen created a shock condition. Progesterone imitated all the features of the stress-protecting hormones, so animals didn't need their adrenal glands if they had a steady supply of progesterone.

My thesis advisor had demonstrated that estrogen causes miscarriage—basically infertility—but if you give the right dose at any stage of pregnancy, it will cause abortion. He demonstrated that Vitamin E would delay age-related infertility. My project was studying the oxidative changes in the uterus during aging. I found that the changes in the uterus with aging were the same as those produced by estrogen treatment, a deficiency of Vitamin E, and radiation treatment.

I started seeing how relevant Hans Selye's work was, showing the stress-shock imitating effect of estrogen. In fact, any kind of shock or stress has estrogenic effects. You can make an animal go into estrus by irradiating any part of the body; something is produced that has an estrogenic effect. If you put a plastic bag over a rat's head, it goes into estrus. Suffocation activates the so-called estrogen receptors and will actually increase the production of estrogen.

**Josh Rubin:** Because of synthetic estrogens and our environment, people have the misconception that estrogen is essentially bad. But men and women both have it, correct? We actually need it to survive; it's only a problem when it becomes excessive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is really the essential masculinizing hormone. Females can have it at the crucial developmental stage, but they have a lot of a protein called alpha-fetoprotein that inactivates estrogen. At that stage, estrogen will create a male functioning organism, while it won't affect the healthy female fetus because she is protected by that special protein. Its basic early function is as a masculine hormone.

The estrogen industry is really where the idea came from that it's a female hormone. It was identified in the ovary, but the main ovarian hormone, which is the feminizing hormone, is progesterone. Men have quite a bit of progesterone, but women live longer than men probably because they are able to produce much more progesterone.

**Josh Rubin:** That is super important. There is no such thing as a strictly male or female hormone because we both have them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen is an excitatory transmitter. Its main effects in females are to cause the pituitary to produce prolactin, to cause the breasts to develop, and to cause the uterus to expand in preparation for pregnancy. There is a great surge of estrogen right around the time of ovulation that lasts for about 12 hours; that releases histamine in many tissues and activates a great surge of cell division.

Pregnancy requires that only in the sense that the uterus is activated and made sensitive to the contact of the fertilized ovum. However, you can substitute many other irritants. You can cause implantation to happen just with histamine in the absence of estrogen. So, estrogen isn't really essential for reproduction by the female in that sense.

**Josh Rubin:** There are so many ways to get tested now. People say blood is inaccurate because estrogen and progesterone are bound to proteins like albumin, but in saliva, they aren't. What is your philosophy on which is more accurate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the problems with lab tests is that each lab tends to have its own standard, and they usually use people who are sick to establish the "normal" for a given blood test.

Regarding protein-bound versus free hormones: if you try to dissolve progesterone in water, it is very hard to dissolve. It binds nicely to albumin. The assumption is that what you measure in saliva is "free," but since they aren't soluble in water, what is it bound to when you're measuring it?

The tests done in the lab for "free" hormones are done by dialysis. "Freedom" is purely a metaphysical idea. Everything is moving along on the microscopic level in a solid phase. Several people have attached the hormone covalently to albumin so that it can't get loose, and they find that it works—it goes right into the cell. Albumin has no trouble getting into the cytoplasm or nucleus, taking its hormone with it. The idea that a hormone has to be free from a protein to get into the cell derives from the idea that there is a barrier at the surface of the cell.

There is a very good base of information for blood tests. People vary tremendously in the amount of saliva they produce and its chemical composition. When you look at the functional outcomes of manipulating steroids in fertility clinics, they see that the results in humans are almost exactly the same as established in animals: fertility requires 50 to 100 times as much progesterone as estrogen.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Speaking about infertility and miscarriages, how do we become estrogen dominant or progesterone deficient? What are the environmental components contributing to this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anything stressful in the environment tends to increase estrogen. This research goes back to about 1940. The Biskinds [Morton and Gerson Biskind] showed that malnutrition and other stresses would increase estrogen. Malnutrition caused the liver to be unable to destroy estrogen. Normally, 100% of the estrogen that gets to the liver is prepared for excretion. If the liver is underactive because of a protein, B-vitamin, or thyroid deficiency, 100% of the estrogen reaching the liver can pass right through it back into the bloodstream.

That recirculating estrogen then turns on the adrenal stress hormones directly and blocks the thyroid gland. Thyroid was recognized in the 1940s as the basic fertility drug. Thyroid is needed to turn cholesterol into progesterone to maintain a healthy pregnancy.

Increasingly, one of the environmental factors that impairs liver function, increases estrogen activity, and inhibits thyroid function is the polyunsaturated oils—the so-called "essential fatty acids" (PUFA). These are all anti-thyroid, pro-estrogen, and anti-progesterone.

Some French researchers tried to demonstrate that fetuses are smarter when the mother gets a fish oil supplement. They found that the women getting the fish oil supplement had fetuses with retarded learning reactions. When the babies were born, they were smaller, and their brains were smaller. Animal research had predicted this: polyunsaturated fatty acids retard the development of the fetus's brain by increasing estrogen and lowering thyroid.

**Josh Rubin:** So foods high in unsaturated fats or fish oils can mimic the stress reaction.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The intestine is also a very important factor. The liver excretes part of the estrogen into the bile. If the bowel is sluggish—which happens in hypothyroidism—that estrogen tends to be reabsorbed. Sometimes just an antibiotic will drastically lower your estrogen and stress hormones by limiting that reabsorption. That is what got me interested in the raw carrot effect. You see lower estrogen and cortisol, and higher progesterone, within about three days of eating a raw carrot every day.

**Josh Rubin:** You use the raw carrot almost like charcoal to help prevent toxicity in the liver.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. As well as absorbing the estrogen, it reduces the absorption of endotoxin and serotonin.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's talk about prolactin and its correlation with osteoporosis, cortisol, and histamine.
