**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many people have been taught that mast cells are the only cells that produce histamine, but any cell seems to be able to produce it. There is a network in the brain that specializes in histamine signaling, and it seems to be a stress-organizing influence. Serotonin is the other general stress signaling system. When anything goes wrong, your brain activates the histamine and serotonin systems.

Prolactin is one of the stress-reacting hormones. It tends to increase steadily with aging. The normal range for prolactin was lowered about 30 years ago because they saw that the top number was increased by women using birth control pills. There was an epidemic of prolactin-secreting pituitary tumors resulting from contraceptive estrogen exposure. Just a few years ago, the top number was raised again in some labs because the average person is now in a stressed, hyperprolactinemic condition. Don't feel reassured if your prolactin is "normal" by today's standards; everything is under stress when it's that high.

It has been known for many years that prolactin is a major factor in bone loss. Estrogen increases prolactin, yet people are told that estrogen prevents osteoporosis. Men also develop osteoporosis progressively with age as estrogen creeps up, pushing prolactin up. When progesterone falls at menopause, that is when bone loss really picks up.

**Josh Rubin:** A lot of people don't know that estrogen and progesterone play a part in osteoclast and osteoblast production.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1970, Constance Martin pointed out in her textbook that there was no evidence estrogen increased bone calcium retention. The animal research was the basis for selling estrogen to prevent bone loss, but they used rats. It turns out that cortisol also increases bone density in rats, but their endocrine systems are very different from humans. Estrogen reduces osteoclast activity, so they argued it stops bone turnover. However, in the Beagle dog model, estrogen caused bone loss.

**Josh Rubin:** What are some of the symptoms people might see if they are estrogen dominant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since it is excitatory, it can temporarily increase alertness. It acts on the same enzymes that cocaine acts on to increase adrenaline action in the brain. It increases verbal activity. However, carried on for a long time, it is excitotoxic to the nerves.

Acute effects in the brain can include chorea—uncontrolled movements—and epilepsy. Water retention is the first action of estrogen on the cell. The excitation moves the cell's requirements to a level that can't be sustained, so oxygen becomes deficient, and the cell takes up water. This makes the blood vessels leaky.

The adrenal cortex tries to compensate for that leakiness by increasing sodium retention. You can shift from low blood pressure and swollen feet to high blood pressure. At an extreme, you can get gangrene and calcification of soft tissues. Hans Selye called this "calciphylaxis," where excited blood vessels constrict and load up on calcium. I've seen people recover from scleroderma in just a couple of weeks when they stopped using an estrogen supplement.

**Jeannie Rubin:** In a stress reaction, the body bypasses progesterone production to produce cortisol. How do they work together?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Stress activates the estrogen receptor. Once estrogen is acting, that turns on the cell's production of the progesterone receptor. When progesterone binds to that receptor, it destroys the estrogen receptor. Progesterone is an anti-estrogen in a very absolute sense. It knocks out the protein that keeps estrogen in the cell and activates enzymes that eliminate estrogen.

If your body has thyroid, Vitamin A, and cholesterol, it will make a massive amount of progesterone in response to estrogen stimulation to neutralize it. Progesterone also prevents the toxic effects of excess aldosterone and cortisol.

**Josh Rubin:** What is progesterone's role with magnesium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Jerry Aikawa, a magnesium specialist, showed that the cell needs magnesium to stabilize ATP. If magnesium is deficient, you are energy deficient, and that contributes to cell swelling. Thyroid (T3) is needed by the cell to retain magnesium. The production of ATP and carbon dioxide is the mechanism by which thyroid regulates the retention of magnesium. This antagonizes the improper actions of calcium. When the cell is inflamed or de-energized, it takes up calcium.

**Josh Rubin:** How can one produce progesterone without medications using nutrition?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main thing interfering with thyroid function is polyunsaturated fats. You can block that very quickly with coconut oil because of the short and medium-chain saturated fats. They compete against the polyunsaturated fats for producing oxygen in the mitochondria.

Sugar does the same thing. When you have enough sugar and saturated fatty acids to interrupt the anti-metabolic effect of the polyunsaturated fats, your blood sugar is stable. The liver senses the availability of fuel (glucose) to govern your thyroid function. The liver will allow thyroxine (T4) to be turned into the active T3. As soon as your liver runs out of glucose, your T3 production falls immediately by about 60 or 70%.

**Josh Rubin:** I want to clarify regarding "high carbohydrate." You are talking about tropical fruits, root vegetables, milk, and sugar—not Pop-Tarts and grains.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Correct. I am strongly against the grainy starches. If you have to eat starch, it should be cooked for a minimum of 40 minutes and eaten with fat (cream, butter, coconut oil). Starch grains can enter the bloodstream and cause systemic injury. Sugar helps to regulate adrenaline and thyroid hormones.

I think a person should have at least 80 to 100 grams of good protein every day, but it is important not to eat too much protein by itself. Egg protein, for example, stimulates insulin secretion, which lowers blood sugar and calls for a cortisol reaction. You want protein to be used as protein, not burned for energy, so have it with sugar and fat.

**Jeannie Rubin:** What about women put on HRT for menopause or young women on the pill?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Consumption of menopausal hormones decreased after the 2002 Women's Health Initiative showed that estrogen causes strokes, heart attacks, dementia, and cancer. The short-term benefit is that it peps you up, like cocaine.

Hot flashes are a complex set of reactions involving stress, adrenaline, and cortisol. I noticed young women working very hard in high altitudes suffering hot flashes in their 20s. The simplest way to respond is to keep blood sugar steady. Having carbohydrate at bedtime will normally stop night sweats. A snack of orange juice and milk or salty food during the day will usually stop them.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend taking progesterone supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't believe in hormone replacement therapy generally. I advocate diet and thyroid first. If your cholesterol is okay, you're eating right, and your thyroid is working, you don't need progesterone.

However, for an emergency, I do recommend it for epilepsy, MS, dementia, arthritis, and acute migraines. For brain trauma patients, if you get progesterone to them in the first day, they practically all recover.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You sent a question about Warburg's theory of cancer. People are misinterpreting him, thinking you should go on a sugar-free diet. Warburg said the respiratory apparatus (mitochondria) is impaired. The cancer goes on burning the body's protein and fat stores. If you give it sugar, you can slow down the destruction of the body.

Warburg emphasized that sugar is being converted to lactic acid. Lactic acid turns on stress reactions. The "sugar-free diet" people blame on Warburg doesn't fit what he said.

**Josh Rubin:** So it's the body's incorrect use of sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The instantaneous effect of either estrogen or unsaturated fatty acids is to imitate the Warburg effect—lacking the Pasteur effect, which is for oxygen to turn off lactic acid production. In the presence of high estrogen and PUFA, we make lactic acid and cannot use the energy oxidatively.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, we really appreciate you coming on and sharing your knowledge.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: EastWest Healing: Glycemia, Starch and Sugar in context
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Welcome again for a great show. We're going to have Ray Peat on once again. For those who don't know who we are, we own a wellness company in the San Diego area, East West Healing and Performance. We work with people that have GI problems, hormone problems, and physical problems from all over the world.

Today's show is about sugar. Ray Peat is going to be talking about sugar, dispelling some of the myths, and explaining why we need it and the different types. For those of you that don't know Ray, you can visit his website at raypeat.com. Ray has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon and specializes in physiology. He started his work regarding hormones, such as progesterone, back in the 1960s.

One thing I wanted to bring up: Ray is a very humble guy. He keeps answering your emails, which is why he is so busy. All we ask is that if you keep emailing him and he keeps sending you emails back, please send him some money. It doesn't matter if it's a dollar or $500. This great information can't get out unless he can do the research.

Let me get Ray and Jeannie on. Ray, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Jeannie Rubin:** We just want to make sure that people are respectful of your time and energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm sending fewer, very long answers now that more people are writing. I'm trying to condense my answers.

**Josh Rubin:** We definitely appreciate it. Let's talk about sugar, starches, and glycemia. This is probably the one topic people are most interested in because there is so much conflicting information out there. You have so many people saying, "Don't eat sugar. It causes diabetes, insulin resistance, cancer, and AGEs." Then we look at your research, and it's completely different. What got you started focusing on starch, sugar, and glycemia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things was reading John Yudkin's book. He was the English researcher who wrote a book saying that sugar causes heart disease. He showed that sugar increases cholesterol. That was back when everyone was saying cholesterol causes heart disease. I was very impressed by his research, but since I saw cholesterol as a protective factor from studying progesterone, I interpreted it differently. I saw that if you were deficient in progesterone or under stress, your body would increase the production of cholesterol to make more progesterone to protect your systems.

I believed Yudkin was on the right track, but since I saw cholesterol as protective rather than harmful, I took his evidence to mean that sugar would help resist stress.

That started me along that line. I had been a migraineur all my life. I gradually came to see that a change in my rhythm of eating in relation to activity was usually what brought on a migraine attack. Often, I would have very odd food cravings just before the migraine appeared. I started trusting those cravings. I found that if I ate enough sweet stuff—like a quart of ice cream—when I felt a migraine coming on, it wouldn't happen.

I was also a problem sleeper. If I stayed up an hour or two after my normal bedtime, my sleep would be disturbed. One night I was talking on the radio and wanted to keep going. I had a friend buy me huge milkshakes, about one an hour. I was able to keep talking until 1:00 AM and didn't have any problem going to sleep. I recognized that I had a peculiar need for sugar when I was doing anything unusually stressful. That started me thinking more about the physiology of it.

**Josh Rubin:** Most people out there, like the Paleo community, advocate high protein and low carb. Physiologically, what is the importance of getting sugars into our body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At one time, I was experimenting with chocolate as a source of magnesium. I found that bitter chocolate was extremely high in magnesium. However, chocolate happens to be very high in leucine, and it would give me low blood sugar. I would crave something to eat shortly after eating a lump of black chocolate. That started me thinking about amino acids in relation to blood sugar.

Several amino acids in proteins are powerful insulin stimulants. When you eat protein by itself, you stimulate insulin secretion, which is needed to metabolize the amino acids. But in reaction to the insulin, your liver has to put out glucose to keep your blood sugar going so your brain and tissues can keep working.

If your liver is low on glycogen, every time you eat protein and have an insulin secretion, your body secretes a compensating amount of cortisol to bring your blood sugar back up. The cortisol brings your blood sugar up at the expense of protein. The first tissues that cortisol breaks down are your thymus gland, immune cells, and muscles.

If you eat lots of protein in spite of the high cortisol, you can maintain your muscle mass, but you are running on a constantly high cortisol secretion. In my previous interest in diabetes, I saw that doctors neglected to measure hormones related to blood sugar when prescribing insulin. When we tested cortisol in some of these "diabetics," we saw that many just had very high cortisol. Sugar happens to be the best thing for lowering cortisol to normal. Since high cortisol gives the impression of diabetes by causing high blood sugar, you get the unexpected effect that eating sugar lowers the cortisol, and some of these people had a very quick recovery from their so-called diabetes.

**Josh Rubin:** There is so much out there on adrenal fatigue. My perception is that people took Hans Selye's work and misperceived his General Adaptation Syndrome. You talk about using sugar to lower cortisol. What about people that have low cortisol? Is that possible?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In Selye's studies, he never talked about adrenal fatigue; "exhaustion" was his word. When you stress an animal terribly, it enters the shock phase, then the adaptation phase, and finally the exhaustion phase where the animal would die from stress.

He found that pregnant animals didn't need their adrenal glands. As soon as they would have a litter, the next stress would kill them because their progesterone was no longer being produced to compensate for the adrenal absence. He gave some animals a daily dose of progesterone after taking out their adrenal glands and found that they would live a full, normal, healthy life.

The adrenals are there to regulate your sugar and salt. It happens that progesterone regulates sugar and salt metabolism just as nicely. To produce these hormones, you need various nutrients, but especially thyroid hormone and Vitamin A to convert cholesterol into pregnenolone. If a person is deficient in Vitamin A or thyroid, their cholesterol tends to rise, trying to compensate.

So, with a thyroid or nutritional deficiency, you can be deficient in steroid hormones, but it isn't the fault of the adrenal glands. The adrenal glands are extremely adaptive. You can basically destroy the adrenals, and if you have a few cells left—and good nutrition and thyroid function—the adrenal cortex will regenerate very well.

**Josh Rubin:** Because cortisol is a glucocorticoid, it regulates blood sugar. Are we eating foods that block sugar from getting into the cell?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's where fructose and sucrose come in. Fructose is the most powerful sugar at regulating blood sugar, both up and down. It has been used in diabetics for decades as a small supplement to help bring down their blood sugar. It is also effective in hypoglycemia because it helps to regulate insulin production and slowly turns into glucose.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you give some examples of where listeners would get fructose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Health food stores used to sell pure fructose, though I don't recommend it in prepared foods because it's almost always combined with starches. Starches turn into glucose very quickly, whereas fructose is a very slow, controlled converter into glucose, so it regulates insulin.

**Josh Rubin:** In your articles, you mention that insulin itself accounts for only about 8% of the insulin-like activity in the blood, with potassium being a large factor. Can you elaborate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several things imitate the function of insulin. For example, exercise increases the cell's ability to take up glucose. Leucine acts like insulin. But potassium itself has that effect. Since fruits are one of the best sources of potassium, that makes fruit a good food.

Fruits usually have about a 50/50 balance of fructose and glucose (sucrose is half fructose, half glucose). Besides that balance, fruits contain potassium and magnesium, which help regulate glucose. When you drink orange juice, the high potassium content reduces the amount of insulin you have to secrete to handle the sugar. That accounts for why they are much more smoothly handled than a similar number of calories in the form of starch.

**Josh Rubin:** What types of fruits do you recommend, and which ones could hurt us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Almost all sweet fruits are better than the alternative of bread, pasta, and cereals. However, among sweet fruits, there are factors to watch.

For example, bananas are almost all starch unless they are ripened to the point of being a translucent amber mush. High starch content stimulates insulin. Furthermore, if you don't eat starch with fat, starch grains can get into your bloodstream. Gerhard Volkheimer showed that large starch grains can clog small arterioles and cause chronic tissue injury.

Besides starch, you have the allergy problem. This is partly due to the industrialization of banana farming. The latex allergy corresponds to the banana allergy; both plants produce defensive stress substances (chitinases) to kill insects, which happen to be highly allergenic to humans. Even some apples have a high allergen content. Cooking many allergenic fruits makes them safer.

A third factor is serotonin content. Bananas excel in high serotonin content. Before people were aware of this, doctors were diagnosing intestinal tumors when they found high serotonin in the urine. Prunes, plums, and kiwis are also high in serotonin.

That leaves things like watermelons, grapes, and citrus fruits—oranges in particular—as safer options.

**Josh Rubin:** Would you put mangoes and pineapples in the allergy or serotonin category?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pineapples are known to have a fairly high amount of tryptophan that can contribute to serotonin. Mangoes are in the same family as poison oak. In the tropics, "mango sickness" is well known. It is partly because they are a fibrous fruit; if the fiber isn't handled by the right bacteria, it can cause toxin production in the intestine. Any carbohydrate that isn't sugar can potentially feed bacteria that produce toxins.

**Josh Rubin:** You talk about glucose playing a factor in serotonin levels.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Serotonin is a major trigger of the stress adaptation system. It turns on the hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenals. The internet is full of people saying sugar raises serotonin because you "feel good" after eating it. Actually, it is free fatty acids that cause your brain to take up more tryptophan and make more serotonin. You produce more free fatty acids when your blood sugar is low and when you are under stress. So, stress, starvation, or hypoglycemia will make you produce free fatty acids, which send serotonin into your brain and trigger the cortisol stress reaction.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asked: If they want to lose weight, isn't it important to metabolize fatty acids? You say the opposite—that liberating free fatty acids is harmful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At rest, muscles metabolize fatty acids. At maximal activity, you burn almost pure sugar. If your liver is well-energized with thyroid hormone and sugar, it can treat excess free fatty acids produced by stress as a toxin and excrete them.

However, on our 20th-century diet, our tissues are filled with polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). When these are liberated during stress or fasting, they suppress mitochondrial metabolism by interfering with thyroid hormone. Within two or three days of fasting or low-carb dieting, a person's metabolic rate drops tremendously. They lose mostly muscle tissue because of the stress produced by low blood sugar. It is the degree of free fatty acids being mobilized that suppresses your ability to burn calories.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do you recommend orange juice with no pulp?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Any pulp is potential food for bacteria. Experiments with rats showed that fermentable fiber increased toxin formation in the intestines. Animals became anxious and aggressive with fiber; without it, they were friendly.

Regarding commercial orange juice: about 15 years ago, the EPA told the industry their waste was attracting pests. One technology they used to dispose of it was dissolving the waste with enzymes and leaving it in the juice. Much of the commercial "high pulp" juice contains fiber that has been chemically altered so it never settles out. It acts like gums or fibers that can be intestinal toxins.

**Josh Rubin:** Everyone says the thymus shrinks as we age. You suggest this is due to PUFAs and stress.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cortisol maintains blood sugar by blocking the use of sugar for most purposes. Immune cells, which the thymus consists of, cannot use sugar in the presence of cortisol. Cortisol forces them to metabolize fats, and unsaturated fats will quickly kill the thymus. It only takes about three hours for the thymus gland to disappear during profound stress.

If a person is killed instantly at a young age, they still have a thymus. If it takes them a few hours to die, the thymus disappears. This is why they thought the thymus disappears in adulthood. Given the right nutrition and hormones, the thymus can regenerate.

**Josh Rubin:** What vegetables do you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low fiber, low starch items. Small summer squash, well-cooked with butter, is very similar to fruit. Generally, roots are safer. Leaves are the energy factory of the plant and contain defensive toxins. Roots are protected underground and have antifungal chemicals but are pretty free of the plant defensive toxins found in leaves.

Young turnips and potatoes that haven't maximized starch production, eaten with butter after being thoroughly cooked, are pretty safe.

Potatoes are almost unique. The liquid part of the potato contains ketoacids, which are the equivalent of amino acids. These can be used as fuel by the brain and heart as a substitute for sugar. They are an ideal anti-stress fuel.

I have seen cases where juicing potatoes—using a centrifugal juicer to throw out the starch—and then cooking the juice (it coagulates like scrambled eggs) provided recovery for people who were dying. It provides energy and essential amino acids without stimulating insulin or cortisol.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Would you suggest using that with a carbohydrate and fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** R.L. Veech is a ketone researcher whose ideas are being applied to Alzheimer's. The ketones provide energy the brain can't get from fat or sugar. Potato juice is an economical way to get these ketones. I knew a girl who couldn't digest anything and had wasted away to 65 pounds. She burped ammonia when she ate protein. I made her potato juice; she digested it perfectly, stopped burping ammonia, and recovered to 130 pounds.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your thoughts on honey and maple syrup?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Honey is almost pure sugar with some minerals. It is a good food. Maple syrup has high potassium and magnesium, but it is boiled down. Very hot, oxygen-exposed glucose can create allergens. You have to be cautious with dark, concentrated sugars like molasses or agave.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's talk about sucrose (white table sugar). People like Dr. Lustig talk about its toxicity. Why do you recommend it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For about 45 years, the mechanism of diabetes has been understood. Argentine researchers showed sugar was protective against diabetes. The "Randle Cycle" (named after Philip Randle) describes how fatty acids block the use of glucose. If you increase free fatty acids, your ability to metabolize glucose disappears.

The Randle Cycle is the instantaneous diabetogenic effect of fatty acids. Chronically, this poisons the beta cells in the pancreas. Recent studies have found that sugar stimulates the regeneration of beta cells in the pancreas.

**Josh Rubin:** Why is there so much misconception?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can produce toxic effects in animals if you give them 60% of their diet as sucrose or fructose. However, many studies exaggerate these findings or misinterpret adaptive signs as harmful.

There are studies where animals were given Coca-Cola or sucrose water in addition to their chow. These animals were able to eat 50% more food than the control group without getting fat. This shows a tremendous increase in metabolic rate. Fructose catalyzes the ability to oxidize glucose at a higher rate. It works like thyroid hormone to increase ATP production.

**Josh Rubin:** So it's not the sugars themselves, but our diet high in unsaturated fats that makes sugar look bad?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you look at the national diet over the last 50 years, calorie consumption has increased, but mostly through starch and polyunsaturated fats. There has actually been a slight decrease in the proportion of sugars.

**Josh Rubin:** What causes insulin resistance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the polyunsaturated fats. Sucrose, because of its fructose component, increases the ability to dispose of glucose. You can instantly demonstrate the effect of polyunsaturated fats blocking the ability to use glucose.

**Josh Rubin:** What would cause someone to be unable to store enough glycogen in the liver?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid deficiency is the most common reason. Selenium is needed to activate the thyroid, but to use selenium, you need glucose. Fructose happens to be the best stimulant for the liver to store glycogen. The current phobia is that fructose increases triglycerides. But before it does that, it powerfully helps the liver replenish glycogen stores.

**Josh Rubin:** Can people have an intolerance to fruit? Some people crash after drinking juice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people who have been low thyroid for a long time have bacteria living high up in their intestine, near the stomach. If they drink juice, the bacteria get the sugar first. Some people even get drunk because their stomach is brewing alcohol.

To work around this, you want to experiment with things that suppress bacterial growth, like the raw carrot salad. Raw carrots contain defensive antibiotics. If you eat a grated raw carrot, you suppress the bacteria and fungi that cause food reactions. Bamboo shoots are another option; they are a good source of antibiotics.

**Josh Rubin:** What is your take on Candida? Many say to cut out sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** René Dubos, a bacteriologist, showed that if you starve yeast, they start sending out invasive filaments (pseudohyphae) into the intestine looking for sugar. That is when they can become systemic. Having sugar in your diet is actually a defensive means while you are trying to get rid of the yeast, which carrots will usually do fairly quickly.

**Josh Rubin:** Thoughts on Stevia and Xylitol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In themselves, they are harmless. But the sweet taste activates your sugar metabolizing systems (insulin). This tends to increase appetite and can contribute to chronic stress by confusing your system—telling it sugar is coming when it isn't, which triggers cortisol.

**Josh Rubin:** We notice some people get acne when introducing sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar activates the thyroid, which makes the skin function better (more moisture and oil). However, if you are deficient in Vitamin A, the skin becomes susceptible to infection. You need to balance the increased metabolic rate with adequate Vitamin A from eggs, liver, or milk.

**Caller:** I have problems with cow's milk creating mucus, but goat's milk is fine. If I stop starch, can I tolerate cow's milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If goat's milk is fine, stick with that or cheese. Starches like corn can feed bacteria that cause the reaction. Having a raw carrot regularly helps reduce the allergy effects that cause mucus. Also, try switching brands of cow's milk; sometimes the additives or what the cows ate cause the irritation.

**Caller:** I have stage four melanoma. I was instructed to eat potatoes, sugar, saturated fats, and avoid gluten. I'm very weak.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Are you getting enough calcium? Parathyroid hormone tends to promote tumor growth. Eating plenty of calcium (around 1500mg/day) along with Vitamin D and K helps keep parathyroid hormone down.

**Caller:** I was told not to take calcium. I'm taking Vitamin D. What about fish oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Seeds, nuts, and fish oils are a problem because of the unsaturated fats. I've heard of people using aspirin (up to 4 grams a day) to lower immune factors that promote inflammation and tumor growth. Increasing thyroid to the point of being hyper-metabolic can make visible tumors dry up. I use Cytomel (T3) for this.

**Caller:** I have delayed sleep phase syndrome. I can't fall asleep until 6:00 AM.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes a very small dose of thyroid helps. One doctor who had been awake for days took 10 micrograms of Cytomel and slept. Sugar is the next best thing. A glass of warm milk with 2 or 3 tablespoons of sugar dissolved in it will usually have an effect similar to thyroid.

**Caller:** How do you dose T3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The body produces about 4 micrograms per hour. It's good to supplement in small amounts, like 2 micrograms per hour, or take 10 micrograms with lunch so it spreads out as you digest.

**Josh Rubin:** We covered a lot today. This philosophy isn't cookie-cutter. It's about fine-tuning based on your metabolic demands. Don't just jump on the internet and buy T3; if your nutrition isn't in order, you can cause more harm.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thanks for having the show.

**Josh Rubin:** Thanks, Ray. Have a great day.

title: EastWest Healing: Milk, Calcium and Hormones
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Welcome everyone. This is Josh Rubin from East West Healing and Performance. Jeannie and Ray will be joining us in a couple of minutes. It’s been a little bit of trouble getting Ray back on, but I think the break was good and we have a good show ahead of us on milk, calcium, and hormones. It is a big topic. We have Ray for anywhere from 60 to 120 minutes.

If you want to learn more about Ray Peat, you can visit his website at raypeat.com. Ray has a PhD in Biology from the University of Oregon. He specializes in physiology and has taught at many schools around the U.S. and in Mexico, as well as doing private nutritional counseling. He started his work with progesterone-related hormones back in 1968.

Today’s show is on milk, calcium, and hormones. We will be talking about dairy, the degradation of it, where it comes from, and why Ray recommends so much of it based on his work. We will talk about calcium, blood labs, parathyroid hormone, and how we keep those levels regulated to downregulate inflammation.

*(Ray Peat and Jeannie Rubin join the call)*

**Josh Rubin:** How's it going, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, good.

**Josh Rubin:** Did you want to add anything before we start the show in regards to yourself or the topic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been interested in milk for a long time, probably 55 years or so. I've been studying the cultural antagonisms to it. In the 1950s, the government had been collecting samples of organisms from around the world to monitor the effects of the atom bomb tests. They wanted to know how it was accumulating in young people, so they started collecting baby teeth. The isotope that concentrated most in teeth happened to be Strontium 90.

After they had been doing that for years, it came out that Strontium 90 was causing leukemia in children, among other cancers. When that got into the news, people said, "Baby teeth show the radioactive isotope, which is similar to calcium. Milk is rich in calcium, so milk is probably the main place babies are getting their Strontium 90." A whole wave went through the culture for a few years advising people not to drink milk because of the Strontium 90.

However, already in 1956 or 1957, people had analyzed the composition of diets. They found that the fallout into the soil produced quite a high ratio of Strontium 90 to available calcium. Plants extracted the calcium, since that was what their cells needed, but left behind a good proportion of the strontium. When cows ate the vegetation, they again extracted a high proportion of calcium and filtered out a lot of strontium.

When you add up the essential nutrients, if you get them from vegetable matter rather than milk, you are getting extremely high concentrations of the fallout isotopes. Milk is a good filtering process to eliminate all kinds of contaminants. Especially in a period of high radiation, it filters out the radioactive isotopes.

**Josh Rubin:** There are so many people out there that say, "Stay away from it because we're not cows," or others who say, "You should only drink raw milk; pasteurized milk is bad." Why do you think there is so much degradation of milk itself, and why are we seeing so many allergies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Actually, the United States cleaned up the commercial dairy industry 40 or 50 years ago. They cut out the use of the most dangerous insecticides that had been getting into the milk and were known to cause breast cancer. In the 60s, the EPA and FDA banned the use of these insecticides around cows and dairies. Israel was slower than the US to ban one of these insecticides, but when they did in the 60s, their breast cancer rate plunged tremendously. The US led the world in cleaning up the milk supply, far ahead of cleaning up the meat supply. When you look at the agricultural industry in general, dairy is still probably the cleanest food available.

**Josh Rubin:** In your milk article, you talked about plants producing enzymes when stressed. How do you pronounce it? Chitinase?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Chitinase. That is something you find in foods grown in stressed plants. It is a plant enzyme that is protective against insects, but it is strongly allergenic to animals. In small amounts, it is produced in a stressed animal under the influence of estrogen. It's possible that is a factor in meat, eggs, and milk, but probably not in a practical sense.

The main allergens that get into the milk come from cows grazing on pastures that have lots of allergenic weeds. Enough of the allergens go right into the milk that people can react. You can usually taste the funny food in the milk. If you go around the cow's pasture, see what it's eating, and squeeze some of the leaves, you'll often identify what gives the milk a funny flavor. Some small dairies aren't very alert to what their cows are eating, and that can cause an individual dairy's milk to be more allergenic than average.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding intolerances, everyone says, "I'm intolerant to dairy." I know you talk about how having a damaged metabolism or blood sugar handling issues can create the mechanism in the GI system to create the intolerance. Can you talk about the validity of the food intolerance lab tests?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The tests for allergens are really just a very vague indicator of the fact that your immune system reacts to everything you are exposed to. Usually, finding antibodies to a particular substance means that you have become tolerant to that substance. I just don't pay any attention to the lab tests for allergies.

The intestine adjusts its enzymes within just a few weeks. Usually, it only takes two weeks to have a complete adaptation of the digestive enzymes. Until your intestine has adjusted its enzymes to a new kind of diet, much of that food is going to be undigested and will feed bacteria rather than feeding the person. The strange new growth of bacteria will produce chemicals that can be toxic and allergenic. If a person isn't used to eating vegetables and they eat them, they'll often get a sore throat, runny nose, sore joints, or headaches. Much of the food sensitivity issue is just failing to adapt because they change their diet too suddenly.

**Jeannie Rubin:** So you're saying when somebody introduces milk back into the diet, they should take it very slowly to allow the body to adapt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even if a person does have lactose intolerance from a lactase deficiency, tests have found that if they drink a cup per meal or less, they don't have the diarrhea that could be produced by drinking a pint of milk on an empty stomach. Even if biopsies show a deficiency of the lactase enzyme, that can be induced in about two weeks just by introducing an occasional small amount of milk. The cells sense the presence of a nutrient and the enzymes are gradually induced until the intestine can handle normal amounts.

Bacterial infections and inflammation can cause the loss of lactase enzymes and probably many other important digestive enzymes. Experiments with supplementing thyroid or progesterone have found that you can induce or restore the lactase that has been deficient just by increasing those anti-stress hormones.

**Josh Rubin:** Does that have to do with their effect on increasing metabolism, regulating blood sugar, and downregulating estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Inflammation is probably the basic problem there. Thyroid and progesterone, by restoring energy and normal function, bypass the inflammatory processes. Inflammation shifts the cell function to an emergency state, and you tend to lose a lot of functional enzymes in an inflamed state.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do you feel dairy is so important?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Part of it is the alternatives. In 1960, the main focus against milk was its Strontium 90 content. But when you look at the alternatives, it turned out milk was the best food for avoiding Strontium 90. It's the same with industrial additives and accidental pollutants. Just about every place you look in the food industry, things are far worse than milk. Some fruits, if you can find fruits that aren't grown in large-scale industrial orchards, are okay. Bananas are an example of one of the worst products for chemical use, but if you can find unstressed fruits, those are very free of toxins relative to most other food products.

**Josh Rubin:** It would be safe to say dairy is like a complete macronutrient—carbs, protein, fat—and very balanced regarding blood sugar and inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it even contains some testosterone. Thyroid, progesterone, and testosterone are important for the young animal. In human milk, they found there was enough thyroid hormone that babies whose thyroids were destroyed by living near Three Mile Island during the accident didn't suffer symptoms of hypothyroidism as long as they were being breastfed.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Can you elaborate on how calcium and the parathyroid work together in assisting the body with chronic stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's a subject for a week of seminars. It involves everything at every level of the organism. Calcium is potentially the thing that causes all of the problems—allergies, cancer, heart attacks—but when calcium is regulated properly, it protects against all of those things.

One of the central things in regulating calcium is the parathyroid hormone (PTH). When you are deficient in calcium in your foods, your PTH increases. It can temporarily keep your blood calcium up to the proper level, but it does that by taking it out of the bones. When you eat an excess of calcium, that tends to suppress the PTH.

Since they've been doing dialysis for kidney disease, we've gained better insight into how PTH works. They found that if they remove the parathyroid gland entirely, they can solve many of the deadly effects of chronic kidney dialysis. Hypertension and insomnia, for example, are immediately corrected by removing the parathyroid gland.

When you look at the effects of PTH excess in dialysis patients, you get an idea of the range of things that eating extra calcium can correct by suppressing the hormone. Insomnia is just one of them. Probably everywhere calcium is involved in an excitatory, inflammation-promoting way, you can reverse it just by increasing the calcium in your diet.

Two vitamins are important for making the tissue handle calcium properly and lowering PTH: Vitamin K and Vitamin D. Other nutrients, like Vitamin A and niacinamide, work in the same direction, helping to balance the ratio of calcium to phosphorus.

When they put animals on a Vitamin D deficient diet, giving the animal sugar instead of starch will keep its bones from developing rickets. It isn't that sugar has a Vitamin D action; it lowers the stress and makes the animal adapt better to the deficiency. If there's a calcium deficiency, letting the animal drink salty water will make up for it by helping the kidneys retain calcium, apparently by substituting loss of sodium for loss of calcium.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do so many people think that because their blood calcium levels are low, they need to pump calcium? You're saying we need to downregulate PTH first. Can you take too much calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I often see people with a blood calcium of 11, 12, or 13 (when it should be 9 or 10). By getting them to eat *more* calcium, and maybe take Vitamin D and K, they can very quickly get their calcium down to normal. The reason it is high is generally because they are eating too much phosphate and overdriving their parathyroid hormone.

**Josh Rubin:** Could eating a lot of muscle meats and tryptophan create the facilitation of PTH?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, many things increase the parathyroid. Serotonin has a direct action. Estrogen, cortisol, and prolactin all have promoting effects on PTH. Progesterone and thyroid are the main things that help to inhibit it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Part of the inhibition is that carbon dioxide (CO2) produced in the cell forces calcium to leave the cell. That relaxes the cell because calcium should be outside the cell. When it's inside, it tends to excite the cell and cause inflammation and lactic acid production. Once you get the streaming flow of CO2 out of the cell, you're getting calcium into the safe situation.

PTH activates glycolysis and the formation of lactic acid. That is a big part of how it dissolves the bone to provide calcium for the bloodstream. Everything that shifts the balance away from lactic acid production and towards CO2 production helps get the calcium back into the bloodstream, out of cells, and ready to go back into the bones.

When they do tissue culture of a mouse skull, PTH tends to dissolve it, causing it to produce lactic acid. But if you increase the CO2, it directly starts forming crystals of calcium carbonate and restoring the mineral structure of the bone.

**Josh Rubin:** Can we use things like baking soda or carbonated water to facilitate that process?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The exchange between bicarbonate and CO2 is so quick that when you give a person a dose of sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), the exchange to CO2 is quick at the cell surface of a stressed cell. You can actually acidify and restore a stressed cell to normal with baking soda. The sodium will quickly get lost out the urine, leaving the body acidified with the intracellular CO2, which puts the cell back into its anti-inflammatory resting state.

**Josh Rubin:** You mean actually ingesting the baking soda?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, or salty water. Sometimes that does the same thing because it lets you rearrange the balance of your alkaline minerals.

**Josh Rubin:** You talk about how some people can't handle raw milk and you actually recommend pasteurized for them. Can you elaborate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every cow has its particular balance of bacteria. A healthy cow will have a very high bacteria count in its milk, and the individual cow will change its bacterial balance according to what it's eating and the season. It's extremely variable. If a person has a bad reaction to some of the bacteria they're getting from the cow, they can try a different dairy.

Even pasteurized milk still has enough of these individual herd bacteria that trying a different brand is sometimes all it takes. I know a few people who get gas or diarrhea from most supermarket milks, but if they drink only the ultra-pasteurized milk—which has been heated to about 135 degrees Fahrenheit—they tolerate that nicely. Ultra-pasteurized milk has somewhat lower vitamin content and doesn't taste as good, but some people do tolerate it better.

**Josh Rubin:** What about yogurts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first concern is to make sure it doesn't contain carrageenan and gums. Those are showing up in more and more foods, especially yogurt, kefir, and cheeses. I've seen products intended to add Vitamin A and D to milk that contained a gum, such as alginate or carrageenan.

If it says it's just fermented milk or yogurt, that's the safest kind. Still, it's better not to eat more than a few spoonfuls per day because any lactic acid—especially the kind formed by bacteria—is extra work for your liver. Lactic acid activates the fibrosis-producing system, stimulating collagen production. Chronic exposure increases a general tendency toward inflammation and aging. The immediate effect on the liver is that it consumes glucose to turn lactic acid back into glucose. It is basically a drain on your blood sugar reserves.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on carrageenan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They can inject a solution of carrageenan into roast beef. You can increase the weight of your product and decrease the meat content by 30% by plumping it up with this jelly made from seaweed. This stuff is analogous to our connective tissue and the breakdown material in the bloodstream, heparin. It's a sulfated polysaccharide. It can be interpreted as a sign of damage to our own connective tissue, causing acute immune reactions. It is used experimentally to cause inflammation in research.

The use of it in food is justified by experiments showing that native carrageenan doesn't induce cancer. But if you allow bacteria to break down the carrageenan into smaller fragments, that *will* cause cancer. Our intestine contains bacteria able to do that breakdown.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about dairy regarding saturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A liver disease research group led by A.A. Nanji has demonstrated a curative effect on hepatitis and cirrhosis from adding saturated fats—from coconut oil through butter fats up to the waxy long-chain saturated fats. Similarly, they have shown that fish oils and seed oils (polyunsaturated fats or PUFAs) exacerbate liver diseases. Just by substituting saturated fats, you have an anti-inflammatory effect.

**Josh Rubin:** Dairy is low in iron, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. During pregnancy, estrogen causes the mother to absorb more iron. A woman will typically absorb nine or 10 times as much iron as a man. The fetus accumulates iron partly from estrogen exposure and partly from the oxygen deficit in the womb. The baby is born overcharged with iron and doesn't need to eat any iron for about six months to a year. Milk is designed to let the baby grow into its potentially toxic overcharge with iron.

Men, by the time they're 50, are generally overloaded with iron, which contributes to free radical oxidation, heart disease, and liver disease. Women are protected as long as they are menstruating. Milk and cheese are deficient in iron, so adding them to the diet helps prevent that chronic tendency to overcharge on iron.

**Josh Rubin:** What about cheeses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Recently I saw an advertisement stating that 60-some percent of cheeses now made use commercial cultures. These are cheap bacterial and fungal substitutes for the naturally grown cultures. Traditionally, cheese is made with bovine digestive enzymes (rennet) to clot the cheese. Now they are using fungal and bacterial substitutes. Almost all commercial cheeses are risky because of those microorganisms, besides any additives for texture.

**Josh Rubin:** What about whey protein powders?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40 or 50 years ago, cheese factories would give their fresh liquid whey to hog farmers. It produced healthy pigs. But when it is sold as a powder, the process of dehydrating it oxidizes the protein. Milk products are high in fragile amino acids like tryptophan and cysteine. Dehydrating increases the oxidation, toxicity, and allergenicity. I don't recommend any dehydrated food except in emergencies.

The casein in cheese turns out to be anti-inflammatory and anti-stress. You get the opposite effect from the whey fraction. Also, most of the calcium stays with the cheese. So with whey, you have a protein which is easily degraded, lacks anti-stress factors, and is deficient in calcium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the arguments against milk is that it makes people fat. But research shows milk is probably the best reducing food there is. The calcium alone is a very important metabolic regulator; it inhibits the fat-forming enzyme, fatty acid synthase. At the same time, it activates the uncoupling proteins in the mitochondria, which burn calories faster and protect against free radical oxidation. Milk is the only food that does both of those things simultaneously.

**Josh Rubin:** What about the synthetic vitamins in pasteurized milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is a very small amount. Even though I'm allergic to synthetic Vitamin A—just a trace gives me a headache—I can drink a gallon of milk containing their added Vitamin A. Apparently, other things in the milk protect me from that reaction.

**Josh Rubin:** You drink a gallon of milk a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's been my average for 35 years or so. I probably average two to three quarts now when I can get lots of orange juice.

**Josh Rubin:** Ideally, where do you get your calories?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ideally, I would get half my calories from fruit. The proportion of protein, carbohydrate, and fat should probably be something like a third of each. If you avoid starch, polyunsaturated fats, and high-tryptophan proteins, you could go very high on any one of the major nutrients without problem.

**Josh Rubin:** Can a high protein diet create the overstimulation of parathyroid hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because most protein comes with lots of phosphate. Grains, beans, and meats are high in phosphate. The ratio between phosphate and calcium is the main thing that activates the PTH. Minimizing phosphate or increasing calcium is extremely important.

**Josh Rubin:** Does estrogen and cortisol play a part in demineralization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When estrogen is dominant, PTH is highest. Prolactin and cortisol also increase PTH. All of these are known to dissolve bones. It's interesting that they promote estrogen as a bone strengthener, yet in the 50 or 60 years women have been using estrogen, the rate of breaking hips has increased.

**Josh Rubin:** Progesterone would play a factor in rebuilding bone, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and testosterone. The same factors that interrupt progesterone metabolism also interrupt testosterone. High tryptophan, serotonin, or polyunsaturated fats will lower your testosterone. Testosterone protects against the parathyroid hormone and strengthens the bones.

**Josh Rubin:** What are some other nutritional sources of calcium besides dairy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eggshells. If you boil your eggs to get additives off them, eggshells are the purest form of calcium carbonate. They are even cleaner than oyster shells.

**Josh Rubin:** How would you recommend ingesting them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pulverize them into a powder. Take a fourth to a half teaspoon if a person is not getting their milk calcium.

**Josh Rubin:** What about aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin blocks the prostaglandins that cause inflammation related to PTH. It also inhibits pituitary stress hormones, lowering cortisol and estrogen. This works to strengthen bones and keep calcium out of blood vessels.

**Caller 1:** I haven't seen anything about fluoride on your site. Where is fluoride on your radar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I avoid fluoridated water carefully. During a stay in San Francisco, I wasn't aware the water was fluoridated and I started getting extreme hypothyroid symptoms. The fluoride destroyed the thyroid supplement I was taking. It just takes one fluoride atom to ruin the T3 molecule. It acts as a thyroid toxin. Also, studies by Yiamouyiannis and Burk showed that fluoridated populations have a higher cancer rate.

**Caller 2:** I've noticed an increase in acne when I consume dairy. I'm 24 years old.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect the connection is that dairy is increasing your metabolic rate and increasing your requirement for nutrients. Usually, Vitamin A is the limiting nutrient. Calcium is a powerful stimulant to metabolism. The increased metabolic rate makes you consume Vitamin A.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend rubbing Vitamin A on the skin or ingesting it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I used commercial Vitamin A for years, but they change the products and additives can cause sensitivity. I found that every time I worked outside in the summer or slept with a bright light, I got acne. Light activates the hormonal system and consumes Vitamin A. If I increased Vitamin A in proportion to light exposure, I could prevent acne.

However, giant doses (several hundred thousand units) can suppress your thyroid. Carotenes (plant source) are even more anti-thyroid. You have to be cautious, starting with 5,000 units and watching for allergic symptoms. Very often people have to get up to 20,000 or 30,000 units a day before acne improves.

**Josh Rubin:** The plant source is more toxic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because it depends on Vitamin B12 to be converted, and thyroid function is inhibited if it isn't converted. One serving of liver a week and an egg or two every day is usually plenty of Vitamin A.

**Caller 3:** Anti-milk articles argue that milk drains calcium because it has a higher phosphorus-to-calcium ratio than the human body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, the ratio in milk is very high towards calcium. Even if you eat meat (high phosphate), drinking a good amount of milk will put those phosphates into proportion. It should be 1.5 calcium per phosphate anyway. Milk is, next to eggshells, our best source of calcium.

**Caller 1 (Returning):** There is word that dairy is a source of natural trans fats. Is there a difference between natural and synthetic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you heard about Conjugated Linoleic Acid (CLA)? It is sold therapeutically because it is anti-inflammatory and anti-obesity. That is a natural component of milk fat. The trans fats in dairy are just in the process of forming CLA.

The benefit is that they block polyunsaturated fats (linoleic acid). Linoleic acid is the anti-thyroid, pro-cancer, pro-inflammatory fatty acid. The dairy trans fats are precursors to CLA. Bacteria in the cow's rumen hydrogenate the fats to detoxify the polyunsaturated fats from the vegetation. If the cow eats a natural diet rich in Vitamin E, the bacteria turn unsaturated fats to saturated. The small amount of intermediate material turns out to be trans fats and CLA, which have a protective effect.

**Caller 1:** So is that different than partially hydrogenated oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Partially hydrogenated vegetable oil still has a lot of PUFA left in it, which has toxic effects.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, do you have anything you want to elaborate on before we shut it down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, no.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, we really appreciate you taking the time. Thanks for tuning in, everyone. Have a great weekend.

title: EastWest Healing: Questions and Answers I

Ray, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Josh Rubin:** The first question everyone keeps emailing me is: do you have a timeline for when you are going to start taking new subscribers to the newsletter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think we changed that notice and they are available now.

**Josh Rubin:** A lot of people are gung-ho about probiotics. If people have gas or anything wrong, they take probiotics. You don't talk too much about them. Can you elaborate on your thoughts regarding the pros and cons of taking them? Specifically, are you thinking about lactic acid bacteria, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria, or a combination?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are probably okay to try. One thing that has made me skeptical about them was an article published in *Nature* probably 35 or 40 years ago. It showed that there are antigenic regions on these lactobacilli that exactly match proteins associated with female reproductive action. From puberty to menopause, roughly, there is the risk of having an autoimmune or immunological interaction between intestinal bacteria and body tissues. There hasn't been much follow-up on that, but that is the period when autoimmune-type problems show up in women. Estrogen is probably the main factor involved in that, but it just happens that there is this antigen parallel between the bacteria and the person.

The bacteria do have a direct anti-inflammatory effect on the membranes of the intestine, but one problem is that they produce lactic acid. If you provide them with enough fuel, they can produce lactic acid, which is a potential toxin. It stimulates inflammation and the formation of fibrosis or collagen.

**Josh Rubin:** I think the biggest thing for everyone to understand is that Lactobacillus is lactate-producing. If you take it and don't need it, you might be causing more of a problem.

**Josh Rubin:** From a health perspective, is there any time you would recommend fasting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies in which rheumatoid arthritis and similar conditions are completely relieved during a week-long fast, but they come back as soon as the person eats again. That is partly because cortisol increases tremendously when you aren't eating. The cortisol converts muscle tissue into fuel to live on, and at the same time, it has an anti-inflammatory effect.

However, the bowel is really the basic cause of most degenerative inflammatory diseases. So, there is a good reason for thinking fasting is therapeutic. I've seen animals with huge tumors that refused to eat, and if their owners let them sit around not eating, they would recover and live for years. The lack of appetite during sickness is a natural opportunity to fast.

Since the bowel is connected to inflammatory diseases—via bacteria producing lactic acid and endotoxin—the intestine itself produces a tremendous amount of serotonin. If serotonin isn't detoxified right away, it promotes fibrosis, inflammation, and cell multiplication in blood vessels, thickening them and promoting tumor growth.

If you can lighten the inflammation load in the intestine, you can achieve the same thing as fasting while still absorbing nutrients. You must do it in a way that doesn't produce endotoxin, lactic acid, or serotonin excess. This means using a very easily digested diet, avoiding undercooked vegetable matter that feeds bacteria, and having antimicrobial foods like raw carrots or boiled bamboo shoots.

**Caller:** It is popular to approach eating based on what we evolved to eat, like the Blood Type Diet or Paleo. What do you think about this approach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That whole approach assumes that we really know what the species ate while evolving. There are a lot of fantasy theories; whatever people enjoy eating, they tend to read into history. No one is really sure. I am inclined to think that fruit eating was a good candidate for supporting evolution to be more human than ape-like, supporting a big brain and the kind of digestive system we have.

**Caller:** I've noticed that people who are cerebral or creative seem to have a lower tolerance for stress, especially if they are exercising heavily or doing low-carb diets. Do people who place high mental demands on themselves have different nutritional needs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some have commented that the brain of the average person might weigh 2% of their body weight but uses 40% or 50% of their metabolic energy. If a person has a bigger than average brain—and human brains vary tremendously in size and metabolic requirements—and they spend a great amount of mental energy, that makes a tremendous metabolic difference.

**Caller:** It is popular to recommend high-intensity interval training or heavy weightlifting to induce a lactate threshold. Are there ways to attenuate the ill effects of that exercise?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was an experiment 30 years ago where people walked on a treadmill without letting their heart rate go over 120 beats per minute. They measured active thyroid hormone (T3) at the beginning and after 40 minutes. The average person's T3 had gone to zero in just 40 minutes of moderate exercise.

Normally, as soon as you have some sugar, your T3 would snap right back. But the longer the stress, and the more inhibitors present (like polyunsaturated fats or bad bacteria), the more delayed the recovery of the liver and T3 production will be. With some people, a little extra stress sticks them down in that low T3 condition. Studies showed that giving a low-thyroid group a tentative dose of a thyroid supplement for two or three days helped them snap back, and their own gland would take over.

**Caller:** Finally, what is your favorite joke? Or barring that, what did you eat yesterday?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What I ate yesterday would be easier than remembering a joke. I had steak—it happened to be rib steak day—eggs, lots of milk and coffee, orange juice, and Coke.

**Caller:** I want to know your thoughts on the connection between schizophrenia and hypothyroidism, as well as nutritional deficiencies like niacin and copper. Also, how much does gluten intolerance have to do with it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since the intestine is involved in everything, gluten is one of the basic things that will cause problems once you get sensitized to it. High estrogen sensitizes the intestine and system to gluten. The transglutaminase enzyme, activated by estrogen, activates immune reactions that can cause celiac disease, psoriasis, arthritis, and is now known to be involved in cancer and brain conditions, including schizophrenia.

Stopping the inflammatory process is basic. I think that was behind the orthomolecular approach to treating schizophrenia. The niacin approach was working on protecting cells energetically against inflammation. Niacin inhibits the release of free fatty acids from tissue stores, and free fatty acids poison our energy apparatus. Schizophrenics are almost always heavy smokers; nicotine has a brain-protective effect against degenerative inflammatory diseases, likely overlapping with niacin pathways.

Keeping thyroid function up supports energy, and keeping toxins down—avoiding polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) and intestinal irritants like gluten—will help.

**Caller:** Would you say hypothyroidism would be the greatest factor in schizophrenia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I would guess so. Puberty is a major time for schizophrenia onset, and that is when rising hormones often interfere with thyroid function.

**Caller:** Is coconut sugar from the coconut tree okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it is extracted from the sap, it is likely fine. If it is made from the starch chemically, I would want to know the process. Generally, if it starts with a natural sugar extract, it is fine.

**Caller:** What about parasite overgrowth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 100 years ago, it was common to use a spoonful of flowers of sulfur maybe once a year. A huge dose like that will clean out parasites. I've experimented with very small amounts of flowers of sulfur; a pinch a day for two or three days has a fungicidal effect and can discourage amoebas and worms. It is very safe for people in small amounts. Some organisms have exoenzymes that act on the sulfur, oxidizing it to sulfuric acid, and the pH change eliminates them.

**Caller:** Is it possible that parasites contribute to autoimmune functions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people think they have a beneficial effect, advocating catching worms to prevent autoimmune disease. I'm not convinced. I am on the Metchnikoff side, seeing cells as the central activity and immunity as a developmental process rather than specific chemotherapy against the environment. Every time we affect our developmental system, we take our whole self in a different direction. In Africa, for example, a lot of so-called AIDS is really just from being exposed to too many stimulants of the immune system.

**Josh Rubin:** What could it mean if someone is sweating all the time, even from an early age?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes it is a developmental overbalance of the parasympathetic or sympathetic nervous system. Sometimes hypothyroid people compensate with extremely high adrenaline production, causing sweating even when they are not hot.

**Caller:** I believe I picked up parasites in 2006 swimming in a river. I had symptoms similar to low thyroid and tested positive for Hashimoto's. Four years later, I passed a two-foot tapeworm. I'm still having digestion and energy problems. What tests should I run?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are doctors who specialize in parasites, especially in coastal tropical areas.

**Josh Rubin:** I recommend the GIFX test from Metametrix.

**Caller:** Any advice on restoring digestive function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Diet to keep your metabolic rate up, and thyroid supplement if necessary. If your metabolic rate is low, you tend to get fungal infections and parasites because the IgA antibodies on membranes are deficient in low-thyroid people.

**Josh Rubin:** There is a lot of hype about fungal infections. Doug Kaufmann promotes the fungal diet, saying mycotoxins feed on sugar, so you should cut sugar. You have a different view.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a case of a Japanese man who got drunk when he ate sugar because yeast in his stomach fermented it. However, getting drunk is the only major harm there. The real problem is poor digestion from being low thyroid. Taking thyroid would likely activate digestive enzymes and eliminate the yeast.

Rene Dubos did experiments showing that when yeast in the intestine is starved for sugar, it sends out pseudo-hyphae filaments to reach through the intestine wall to get sugar from the bloodstream. They become invasive when starved. If you feed them sugar, they don't put out those invasive filaments. A sugarless diet is dangerous if you have a yeast problem. Avoiding sugar also risks depriving the liver of sugar needed to activate thyroid hormone. Fungus loves unsaturated fat but can be killed by saturated fats.

**Caller:** What is your feeling on liver flushes and general cleansing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments on cattle showed that while 30-35% had toxins in muscle and fat, only 6-7% had toxins in the liver. The liver has the equipment for excreting toxins. If you slow down the liver's activity—which happens in a fast—your brain and organs are exposed to chemicals diffusing out of fat and muscles. The best cleansing diet is one that increases your liver's action. Tasty food, sugar, and thyroid activate the liver.

**Caller:** When you say sugar, do you mean any kind?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Manufactured sugars like high fructose corn syrup often contain other substances intermediate between sugar and starch that can be harmful. White sugar is safe regarding allergens, but nutritionally, fruit is the best way to get sugar because it comes with minerals like potassium and magnesium.

**Caller:** What about swollen feet in a relatively young person?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is likely from excess permeability of blood vessels; water leaks into tissues. Sometimes all it takes is eating enough salt to make your albumin function to bind water and keep it in the blood vessels. People on low-salt diets are susceptible to this. In pregnancy, high estrogen and low thyroid make blood vessels permeable. Studies showed that giving pregnant women with toxemia extra salt cured their symptoms.

**Josh Rubin:** There is bad hype about fructose being turned into fat. Why do you recommend tropical fruits?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ideal amount of fructose seems to be maybe a third as much as glucose. Fructose raises the metabolic rate, increases carbon dioxide production, and catalyzes the ability to burn glucose. Experiments comparing sugar/Coke to starch showed that sugar improved calcium assimilation, increased metabolic rate, and decreased obesity.

The calcium-sparing effect of sucrose or fructose comes from the metabolic stimulation imitating active thyroid hormone, which produces carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide keeps calcium out of the soft tissues and puts it in the bones. This reduces the need for Vitamin D.

**Caller:** You've written that tryptophan converts to niacin if a person is healthy. Can a healthy person tolerate more muscle meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The high phosphorus content in meat is important. The ratio of calcium to phosphorus should be high. Meat and whole grains are major sources of phosphate. Tryptophan can be handled if you have a good diet, but estrogen decreases the production of niacin from tryptophan and sends it down the serotonin pathway.

**Caller:** Is that why you recommend milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because of the high calcium-to-phosphate ratio.

**Caller:** Are there spices you don't recommend? My girlfriend craves garlic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main problem with onion and garlic is if you are allergic to them. Low thyroid people often have symptoms like gallbladder spasms when they eat them, especially if cooked. But as foods, they are fine if tolerated. Many spices are allergens.

**Caller:** Can you elaborate on the proper way to take Cytomel (T3)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you are in a temporary stress state, sometimes 10 micrograms will break the stress. If you need it longer, the body normally makes 4 or 5 micrograms of T3 per hour. If you take more than 10 micrograms at once, your liver activates enzymes to destroy it.

If you take 10 micrograms with a meal, the food delays absorption, so you get maybe 2 or 3 micrograms per hour. Taking 10mcg with each meal is a smooth way to take it.

**Caller:** Does it have to be taken with thyroxine (T4)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just occasionally. If someone wants to lower cholesterol quickly, frequent small doses of T3 work. T4 depends on the liver for activation. In women, estrogen often keeps the liver from making enough T3 from the thyroxine.

**Caller:** What is your opinion on raw vs. cooked foods?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With animal products, cooking kills parasites and microorganisms. There is no nutritional benefit to cooking them, but safety is key. With fruit, a typical apple is likely unripened and contains pectin. Pectin isn't digestible by humans but feeds bacteria. Eating raw, unripe fruit feeds bacteria.

**Caller:** Is there nutrient loss in cooking?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. An experiment in the 1940s fed rats either canned vegetables or raw vegetables. The animals eating the canned vegetables thrived; the ones eating raw did not.

**Caller:** What about enzymes in raw food like papaya?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those enzymes are biologically active, but the production of pancreatic digestive enzymes isn't a stress; it's a natural function. I don't think there is a benefit to supplementing enzymes for the pancreas's sake.

**Caller:** My four-year-old had leukemia and his CO2 levels are low (16-19). Doctors want to use bicarbonate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Bicarbonate (baking soda) is very helpful. It helps regulate minerals and can bring up systemic CO2. However, the most effective thing is to check the thyroid function, which controls CO2 production. The AACE (American Academy of Clinical Endocrinologists) has a TSH range of 0.3 to 3.0, but I think the ideal is toward the low end, 0.3 or 0.4.

**Caller:** He also has chronic diarrhea despite diet changes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Are his vegetables cooked? Salads cause diarrhea or constipation in many people.

**Caller:** I was diagnosed with MS eight years ago. I have recurrent fungal/yeast symptoms.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first five or six people I saw with an MS diagnosis recovered instantly when they took thyroid. A common symptom of low thyroid is pituitary enlargement (prolactin-secreting tumor), which presses on the optic nerve and causes vision loss, often misdiagnosed as brain disease. It is good to check prolactin and thyroid.

**Caller:** How can I check for bad bacteria holistically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Try eating a raw carrot every day—shredded with olive oil, vinegar, and salt. It has a germicidal action. In well-diagnosed MS, endotoxin is a factor causing blood vessels in the head to leak. Endotoxin can be drastically reduced by the raw carrot. Also, ensure you get enough protein (at least 80 grams) from milk, cheese, eggs, and shellfish.

**Josh Rubin:** When starting a pro-thyroid diet, does the body go through a detox? Would you see increased cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person has low cholesterol, they shouldn't start a thyroid supplement full force because thyroid converts cholesterol into hormones. Low cholesterol must be fixed first (fruit helps).

If cholesterol rises, it usually means the liver is getting enough energy to make it. Cholesterol is a protective, adaptive substance. The Framingham study found that people over 50 with cholesterol under 200 were more likely to have dementia. Longest-lived people in nursing home studies averaged around 270 or 280 cholesterol.

**Caller:** Do you have advice for learning a second language?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin B1 and coffee can make a tremendous difference. When I learned French for my graduate exam, I did it over a weekend with plenty of coffee and a few hundred milligrams of Vitamin B1. B1 makes you produce energy faster (more CO2) and increases circulation to the brain.

**Caller:** Is coffee estrogenic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hops in beer are estrogenic. Coffee is a major dietary source of niacin and magnesium. It is beneficial.

**Josh Rubin:** What is the upper limit of eating liver, and what about raw eggs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lightly cooking them reduces the risk of infection. Eating them raw doesn't protect you from the polyunsaturated fats in them. Liver should be eaten maybe once a week (six ounces).

**Josh Rubin:** Some people get bloating from gelatin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you eat it undissolved, it feeds bacteria. It must be dissolved. Regarding liver, if I eat it without enough fat and sugar, I get low blood sugar symptoms because of the high protein. I cook it in a large amount of butter or coconut oil.

**Josh Rubin:** What do you think about the therapeutic potential of tryptamine drugs like psilocybin and LSD?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In early studies, patients reported chronic migraines disappeared after LSD sessions. Migraines were identified as an excess serotonin problem, and LSD counteracted the serotonin.

The pharmaceutical industry wanted to market antidepressants, so they created the myth that serotonin is a "happy drug" and demonized anti-serotonin hallucinogens. Actually, serotonin is the misery drug—excess produces nausea, fibrosis, dementia, etc. LSD-type drugs imitate serotonin to trigger the feedback system that turns *off* the nerves that make serotonin. They are serotonin antagonists. Research is starting up again on using these for cluster headaches and organic diseases.

**Caller:** Is sunscreen necessary?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some sunblocks are carcinogenic. It is best to get sunlight but avoid sunburn. Rabbits on an unsaturated fat diet got sun-damaged skin; those on saturated fats did not. Polyunsaturated fats in the skin amplify UV damage. Coconut oil, caffeine, and aspirin applied to the skin can offer protection.

**Caller:** How do you take gelatin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I make oxtail or lamb shank soup. If using powder, I mix it with sugar, heat it until clear, and add orange juice to make gummy candies. Or I use it in mousses or marshmallows. It must be fully dissolved.

**Caller:** Is wireless internet a source of radiation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Cell phones and wireless devices emit radiation that affects nerve function and likely increases brain cancer incidence. I use wired connections.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, anything new going on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My recent newsletter talks about biological processes excluded from science. Luca Turin has lectures on the internet about how molecules and cells interact electronically rather than mechanically. Gerald Pollock also has lectures on the structure of water.

**Josh Rubin:** Great show. Thanks for tuning in. Check out our website at EastWestHealing.com. Thanks, Ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye.

title: EastWest Healing Serotonin and Endotoxin
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** What up everyone? This is Josh Rubin and Jeannie Rubin of Holistic Living. We're here today to share our radio show with Dr. Raymond Peat. Today's show is on serotonin and endotoxin distress. Ray Peat is a teacher, educator, and researcher, and today he is going to school us on these topics. How are you doing, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good.

**Josh Rubin:** How are you doing, Jeannie?

**Jeannie Rubin:** I'm doing great, Josh. Thanks.

**Josh Rubin:** Before we start, Ray, did you want to announce anything or add anything to your intro before we start talking about serotonin and endotoxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not really. I've just been finishing another newsletter that includes stuff on serotonin. This one is on osteoporosis, and serotonin turns out to be a major factor in causing that and other aging degenerative changes.

**Josh Rubin:** I've gotten a lot of requests to talk about serotonin. A lot of people don't know what endotoxin is, but you correlate it with serotonin in the gut. Most people understand serotonin as a brain chemical. Is it a hormone? Where does it come from? Why is there so much focus on serotonin in your research?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can't understand the other things that I'm working on unless you know where serotonin fits in. For example, estrogen does a lot of its work by way of serotonin. To understand unsaturated fatty acids versus saturated, you have to understand estrogen and serotonin. To understand thyroid, you have to understand all of those.

It is one of the emergency defense systems. You can't begin to understand stress or compensating for stress without seeing where serotonin fits in.
