Hans Selye was one of the early researchers on the biological effects of serotonin, and Aldous Huxley was another person that got me interested in its variety of effects.

**Josh Rubin:** Most Western research refers to serotonin as a brain chemical. Where do you find most of the serotonin in the body, where is it produced, and what are its main functions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Roughly 95% of it is produced in the intestine. The biggest concentration in the digestive system is in or around the appendix.

Part of how I got interested in the pattern of thyroid, estrogen, and serotonin was when I was about nine years old, I started becoming nearsighted and occasionally had migraine headaches. I noticed that things I ate would tend to bring on the headaches. I saw that nearsightedness was much more common among girls, especially starting around puberty, and several of the nearsighted girls I knew had migraines.

I started thinking about what I had in common with girls in puberty, and it was the thyroid question. Estrogen and serotonin happen to be anti-thyroid factors. If you are borderline for thyroid function, you are very susceptible to excesses and imbalances in estrogen and serotonin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ergot, a fungal disease of grains, was used for thousands of years to induce abortions. In the 19th century, attempts were made to use it to accelerate labor, but it was dangerous. It causes spasms not only in the uterus but in blood vessels. When people were poisoned by this ergot fungus, they would develop gangrene, insanity, nausea, and vomiting.

In the early 1900s, people started studying the chemistry of ergot. Histamine was the first thing they identified that caused muscular spasms. In the 1920s and 30s, continuing study of ergot turned up a dozen different categories of amines. Hoffman at Sandoz was working on this when he accidentally discovered the nervous properties of LSD.

In the 1930s, an Italian researcher identified an amine in the intestine that caused intestinal contractions. Later, an English group studying beef blood found an amine they thought caused blood vessel contraction. It turned out to be the same thing found much more abundantly in the intestine.

The English group gave it to someone to develop an assay. This person happened to have experienced Sandoz's LSD and knew about its mental effects. He found that serotonin would cause uterine contractions, and LSD would block that contraction. Serotonin would block kidney function; LSD would restore it. Since he saw a straight-across antagonism between LSD and serotonin, he proposed that the brain contains a small amount of serotonin and that LSD has its effects by antagonizing this serotonin.

**Josh Rubin:** So we should all take a little dose of LSD every day to be anti-inflammatory and down-regulate serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a new interest in LSD as a protective chemical. They are finding that it prevents nerve damage caused by some of the serotonergic excitotoxic chemicals.

**Josh Rubin:** Interesting.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By 1960, people were already proposing LSD to cure or prevent migraine headaches. But then the government banned research on LSD. Someone developed the idea that since LSD was an antagonist of serotonin, and the reason for banning LSD was supposedly that it made people insane, therefore serotonin must make you sane. That reasoning spread like a plague through the national culture. That seems to be the extent of the reasoning behind the idea that serotonin is the "happy drug."

**Josh Rubin:** Why is most of it found in the appendix? Isn't there a lot in the small intestine as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a gradient increasing as you go down the small intestine. Normally, the upper part starting at your stomach is sterile. As you go down, the likelihood of having bacteria increases. As a person's thyroid function decreases, their intestinal secretions and peristalsis are reduced, and bacteria tend to creep farther up.

The gradient of bacterial infection increases parallel to the gradient of serotonin. The toxins from the bacteria interacting with the physiology of the person stimulate the production of serotonin. The function of serotonin is to cause contraction of the intestinal muscles to cause diarrhea and get rid of the irritant.

**Josh Rubin:** What foods encourage that bacterial growth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The things that are slowest to be broken down by your own enzymes. Since we don't have enzymes for fibers such as pectin or lignans, the bacteria live on those. The less cooked a vegetable is, the better food it is for bacteria. Even firm fruits with fibrous material, like crisp apples or pears, are very good bacterial food and very poor human food.

**Josh Rubin:** Could something as simple as a blood sugar handling issue stimulate serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you have an acute blood sugar decrease, you put out a lot of adrenaline. That cuts the circulation for the fight-or-flight reaction. You stop digestive processes and don't deliver much blood to the intestine. The food sits there, letting the bacteria have a chance at it. Then, any kind of irritation will trigger the serotonin release.

**Josh Rubin:** What other hormones does serotonin synthesize with? What is its correlation with estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen activates the enzyme that turns tryptophan into serotonin. It is inhibited by progesterone. The route *out* of serotonin—monoamine oxidase type A—is inhibited by estrogen, so it doesn't break down serotonin. So, the "in" route is increased by estrogen and the "out" route is decreased by estrogen.

In our lab, we saw that estrogen treatment would cause animals to enlarge their adrenal cortex, activate it, and then the adrenal cortex would start bleeding and dying. The mechanism is that stress increases serotonin; serotonin increases the release factor that drives the pituitary hormone, which drives the adrenal cortex. So stress, acting through estrogen or serotonin, ends up overworking your adrenal cortex.

**Josh Rubin:** This is dangerous because a lot of women are on SSRIs and synthetic estrogens.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's where the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) come in too. They are specifically effective at releasing tryptophan to enter the brain or other cells to produce more serotonin. The serotonin activates the enzymes that convert PUFA into prostaglandins, which are executors of the inflammatory process.

**Josh Rubin:** So the unsaturated fats increase brain uptake of L-tryptophan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Josh Rubin:** Is that why Western research shows serotonin as a brain chemical?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That orientation comes exclusively from the drug industry. They don't want people noticing the diseases that would be cured or prevented if people understood what tryptophan, serotonin, estrogen, and polyunsaturated fats are doing.

**Josh Rubin:** A lot of people taking SSRIs think they are helping themselves because they have "low serotonin." You're saying there is actually an excess.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Instead of measuring the amount of serotonin in the serum, they measure the breakdown product in the urine. If your lungs are working effectively to destroy serotonin, you'll see the breakdown product. If the lungs aren't working effectively, you won't see the breakdown product. So it looks like you might not be experiencing serotonin stimulation when that's exactly why you *are* experiencing it—because you aren't forming the breakdown product.

Men with more than 100 nanograms per milliliter of serotonin in their blood serum tend to be imperfectly fertile or impotent. I would infer that everyone who has more than 25 nanograms per milliliter is experiencing some sort of inflammatory, degenerative process.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on the correlation between melatonin and serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** An Italian researcher has seen melatonin closely associated with rheumatoid arthritis. High melatonin goes with high rheumatoid symptoms. I interpret that not to mean that melatonin is causing the inflammation, but that serotonin is turned into melatonin as a detoxifying process when stressed.

**Josh Rubin:** So people supplementing with melatonin or 5-HTP might be making it worse?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you take 10 milligrams of melatonin, that's going to be a problem. But 5-HTP turns massively into serotonin. That's where people are going to get the problem. That is much more dangerous than melatonin.

**Josh Rubin:** What about people taking 5-HTP for mood who feel it helps?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it happens to drive up their cortisol, cortisol makes everyone feel good temporarily by stopping inflammation. They have treated aggressive dogs with SSRIs and found that they work to decrease aggressive viciousness. At the time the dogs become friendly, they measure the serotonin in the blood and find that it has *decreased* greatly.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about serotonin's correlation with the thyroid and CO2 levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you are low in thyroid, your serotonin goes up. The TSH is partly increased by the rising serotonin. Low thyroid people very often have increased prolactin as well.

The absence of carbon dioxide is a place where you can start. If you hyperventilate for a minute, the loss of CO2 in your blood raises the pH in the blood platelets. The loss of carbon dioxide causes the platelets to spill their serotonin, causing blood capillaries to dilate and become leaky. Within a minute, you can create a hyper-serotonemic, edematous condition.

**Josh Rubin:** So people diagnosed with asthma might actually just be hyperventilating?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Women taking estrogen will tend to hyperventilate and have a slightly alkalotic condition. That increases the release of serotonin and histamine, causing contraction of the muscles in the breathing system.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about what light or darkness has to do with serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The peak serotonin in the blood is at midnight in the winter. The enzymes that produce it and detoxify it are under the influence of light. People get sick, tend to have strokes, and depression is exacerbated under the influence of darkness and high serotonin.

**Josh Rubin:** So light is more stimulatory to progesterone, and darkness is more stimulatory towards estrogen and serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It's the increased day length in the spring that makes animals fertile from rising progesterone.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asked about serotonin and exercise. Popular articles say aerobic exercise is good because it raises serotonin. What is the best kind of exercise to make sure excess serotonin is not produced?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Resistance exercise of a very moderate sort—muscle building—is best for lowering inflammation and serotonin. You want to stay below the lactate threshold.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend anything nutritionally during a workout?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugars. Keeping your cell energy up and producing carbon dioxide is the best way to minimize the serotonin. Orange juice.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's move on to endotoxin. What is it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Its technical name is lipopolysaccharide (LPS). It is some fatty acids attached to a short starch-like molecule. It's made by a variety of bacteria, specifically the gram-negative type. Animals have evolved to recognize the presence of lipopolysaccharide as the presence of bacteria. It activates the innate immune system.

It seems to have a soaping type of action on cells that destabilizes them. That physical irritation is enough to activate the production of serotonin, release of histamine, and nitric oxide. We normally can destroy all of it that gets into the bloodstream by the time it gets to the liver. But if your liver is overworked or under-energized, the endotoxin gets through into your bloodstream.

**Josh Rubin:** So something as simple as the stress reaction could cause an increased production of endotoxin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Increased absorption of it, yes. A lot of starchy food, undercooked cereals, and poorly cooked vegetable material will feed the bacteria and increase their production of it.

**Josh Rubin:** What foods protect against it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Calcium happens to suppress the fermentation of fiber and starch in the intestine. High calcium intake will reduce the production of endotoxin. Saturated fats also help; fatty acids have a germicidal effect that helps keep the intestine sterile.

**Josh Rubin:** What are the best sources of calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Powdered eggshells are by far the next best to milk and cheese. Calcium carbonate from eggshell is very pure.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you explain why you recommend a raw carrot versus a cooked carrot?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cooking makes the carrot fiber acceptable to bacteria, and bacteria will thrive on cooked carrots. Almost no microorganism can multiply on a raw carrot. The point of the carrot isn't nutrition; it's to help cleanse your intestine.

**Josh Rubin:** What about keto proteins? You mention them in your articles.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** These are keto acids. They are the equivalent carbon framework of the essential amino acids, but they lack the ammonia needed to make the complete amino acid. Potatoes happen to be very rich in these. If you juice a potato, you get these keto acids. When you eat it, they change into essential amino acids in your bloodstream by absorbing ammonia. This allows you to recycle ammonia instead of making it into urea that needs to be excreted.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asked about a correlation between raised moles and unsaturated fat or serotonin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've had a lot of experience with the effect of thyroid on moles. Every time I have become hypothyroid, I notice I get moles growing. Adjusting the thyroid, progesterone, pregnenolone, and DHEA causes them to disappear in a matter of hours or days.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about anemia in correlation with the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Broda Barnes believed that hypothyroidism was usually the cause of anemia. It's simply a matter of temperature. If your extremities are cold, the bones are too cold to make blood cells.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asked about Candida or yeast overgrowth.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Candida normally is harmless in the intestine. Low thyroid people sometimes have Candida growing even in their stomachs. If you want to make a yeast angry, don't feed it sugar. When it is deficient in sugar, it will drill holes in your intestine to find glucose in the blood. If you keep feeding the yeast sugar, the worst you will get is a little drunk. The raw carrot is a very good antiseptic for Candida.

**Josh Rubin:** What about bamboo shoots?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I like them cooked with cheese or egg. They are also helpful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ergot derivatives and serotonin are involved in impaired fertility, birth defects, and difficult delivery. The whole preeclampsia syndrome is centered on high serotonin.

**Josh Rubin:** What about vitamin E and aspirin? You talk about aspirin increasing circulation in the uterus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Aspirin is very powerful against serotonin in many of the ways that thyroid works. Aspirin, thyroid, and fructose work in the same ways against serotonin. In an animal model of pulmonary artery hypertension, they can cure it just with aspirin.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asked about niacinamide. Have you ever seen it cause GI upset?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The nicotinic acid form—the kind that makes people turn red—increases the release of serotonin and histamine. Even the "no flush" niacin releases nicotinic acid. Niacinamide doesn't do that.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on fibrosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hans Selye demonstrated that serotonin would calcify the skin. It increases the parathyroid hormone, which takes calcium out of your bones and puts it in your blood vessels and kidneys. Eating excess calcium is helpful for regulating the parathyroid hormone.

**Josh Rubin:** What about salt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I use Morton's canning and pickling salt because it has no additives. The red color in Himalayan salt is mostly iron, and where you find iron, you are likely to find heavy metals. Gray Celtic salt is basically French mud.

**Josh Rubin:** We have a caller. Justin from Tacoma.

**Justin:** I live in the Pacific Northwest where we have stressful winters with not much light. I was looking for practical applications for the use of red light.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With mercury vapor ultraviolet lights, you have to be careful not to get sunburned. I prefer to use a vitamin D supplement rather than fiddle with UV light.

For light, you can get 130-volt reflector bulbs. They are designed to run on a higher voltage, so on standard voltage, they produce an orange-colored light that is rich in the red spectrum. They are usually about 250 watts. I have two of them aimed at the area where I work. They call them infrared, which just means they are designed for a different voltage.

**Josh Rubin:** We are running out of time. Anything else you want to add?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The current newsletter is going out in about a week on osteoporosis and how serotonin fits into that. The next one will be on sugars, especially fructose, because of the craziness telling people to fear fruit.

**Josh Rubin:** It is pretty crazy. Just a quick question on osteoporosis: is it the correlation with parathyroid hormone and prolactin that leads to it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They noticed that people on SSRIs were getting exaggerated degrees of osteoporosis. One group researching this said they "rediscovered whole animal physiology" when they realized the intestine was the source of the serotonin causing the osteoporosis.

**Josh Rubin:** One last thing regarding mood. You mentioned the dog study.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The things that lower your serotonin are likely to make you less aggressive but happier. The behavioral system for harm avoidance and inhibition is what serotonin is doing. When you reduce your overproduction of serotonin, you stop thinking about harm avoidance and have a more positive, constructive, exploratory attitude.

**Josh Rubin:** So the lower the better.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the lower the better.

**Josh Rubin:** Great show. Thanks for coming on, Ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye.

title: EastWest Healing: Cholesterol and Saturated Fats
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Today we are hosting a great show with Dr. Raymond Peat. The show is on cholesterol and saturated fats, so we will cover why cholesterol is so important, why doctors try to lower it, why our physiology needs it, and what it means if it is high or low. We will also discuss why the right types of saturated fats are so important in our diet. Dr. Peat, could you give a brief history of who you are and where you come from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Before I studied biology, I was mostly studying language, literature, and painting. I had been interested in biology for a very long time, but I had a bad impression of academic biology from my high school experience. In the 1940s, there was a very big change in the nature of American biology that was powered by industry and government promotion of the gene theory as opposed to the field theory in development and health.

I waited until 1968 to enter a graduate program in biology. I had learned enough about universities to manage to get through the program without having too many conflicts with professors. Most of the professors were committed to the genetic determinist idea of what an organism is. I was interested in the field concept and environmental influences on the organism. Nutrition is one of the most important environmental influences. I see our nature as being a matter of potential being realized according to the conditions of the environment, rather than the expression of a predetermined genetic program.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do you think America is so afraid of cholesterol and saturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is driven primarily by the food industry wanting to sell their products. The seed oils were already seen to be toxic—causing sterility, degeneration of the brain and the gonads—probably from 1925, but especially in the 1930s and 40s. The very oxidizable seed oils were known to be toxic. That was one of the factors in researching Vitamin E as something to counteract the toxicity of the seed oils, as well as the toxicity of estrogen, which happens to synergize with unsaturated fats.

The pig industry had been looking for ways to make their animals gain weight and eat less food. George Burr, who is identified as the inventor of the essential fatty acid concept, discovered that the essential fatty acids slow the metabolic rate. Deficient animals eating sugar instead of unsaturated fats had about a 50% higher metabolic rate. They found that feeding soy and corn to the pigs, because of the unsaturated fats suppressing their metabolic rate, increased the profit—less food in, more pig out. At the same time, they noticed that it was lowering cholesterol as one of its biological, toxic effects.

Around 1950, paint and plastic chemists discovered how to make their products from petroleum, which decreased the market for seed oils. They wanted to find new markets to replace the paint and plastics market, so they started promoting the health idea of their soy oil, cottonseed oil, and safflower seed oil. The only biological effect established for the seed oils, other than sterility and dementia, was that they lowered blood cholesterol.

For several decades, people had noticed that cholesterol accumulated in the walls of blood vessels—atherosclerosis. The first person who discovered that in rabbits had dissolved the cholesterol in unsaturated vegetable oil. He realized that cholesterol by itself wasn't causing the disease. However, the seed oil industry argued by association: if cholesterol is in the hardened arteries and the blood, and their oil lowers the level in the blood, then you can prevent the disease. But the very people who had made those discoveries realized that wasn't so. In the 1930s, people found that thyroid was enough to prevent atherosclerosis, and at the same time, it lowered cholesterol.

Over the last 10 or 15 years, a Swedish doctor named Uffe Ravnskov has shown that there is no causal connection between atherosclerosis, heart disease, and the triglycerides and cholesterol in the blood. The experiments done in the 30s showed that hypothyroidism and the associated metabolic changes caused the atherosclerosis. The cholesterol seems to be there as a defensive reaction to protect the injured blood vessels.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on the difference between saturated and unsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It refers to the chain of carbon atoms in the fatty acid. In one case, they have all of the hydrogen atoms attached to them that are possible; they are saturated with hydrogen. If some of the carbon atoms lack the hydrogen, they have their electron bonds more exposed to the environment. The absence of the hydrogen makes them more flexible. Instead of being like a bottle brush bristling with the hydrogen surrounding the chain of carbons, it's more like a necklace of beads—flexible.

Where the hydrogens are missing, the bonds can rotate more freely. If you get several of those double bonds, the chain is bent at each place. That flexibility is biologically important. Coconut oil is hard at room temperature because it is relatively saturated. Olive oil has to be cooler before it solidifies. Canola and corn oil have to be extremely cold before they solidify.

If an organism lives at 40 degrees Fahrenheit and contained butterfat, its fats would be solid and unmanageable. In the tropics, even fish in the Amazon river have fat as saturated as butterfat. Chocolate and coconuts grow in places where the temperature averages close to 90 degrees, so they need to have very saturated fat just for biochemical manipulation. If you had unsaturated fat in a fish in the Amazon river, the fish would oxidize its fats in just a couple of days.

Even with a medium unsaturated oil, such as soy or corn oil, if you put a rubber hose into a cork in the top of the bottle and put the other end in water, the water will rise up the tube as the oil consumes oxygen. It is a constant process. At body temperature (98 degrees), the process is much faster, and you get sticky, rancid oil very quickly.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your thoughts on atherosclerosis and heart disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) we unavoidably get in our diet are constantly breaking down, producing free radicals and tending to cause inflammation and tissue injury. If anything disturbs the metabolism of a cell, that is more likely to happen.

The normal, healthy oxidation through the mitochondrion keeps electrons tightly controlled. But if you take away some of the oxygen, the electrons will escape as free radical potentiators. Any stress on a cell puts out these electrons that can attack the exposed electron bonds in unsaturated fats. Saturated fats aren't open for stray electrons.

These reactions form lumps of material called age pigment or lipofuscin. These oxidized fat fragments attach to proteins and collect bits of iron. These lumps of age pigment, because of their iron and fat fragments, can catalyze the consumption of energy and waste oxygen. This creates a false mitochondrial effect.

Before that happens, signals go out changing the conditions of the organism—activating hormones such as cortisol, estrogen, and growth hormone. These three hormones are closely connected to rising triglycerides and damage to the blood vessel wall. Cortisol increases estrogen, estrogen increases cortisol, and they both increase growth hormone. All of these tend to break down triglycerides into free fatty acids, which are more reactive and tend to become oxidized more quickly.

**Josh Rubin:** Why does cholesterol go up when one is stressed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pituitary senses something wrong and increases ACTH, which drives the adrenal glands to take up cholesterol and synthesize it into pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, and finally cortisol. Cortisol has a short-term defensive reaction against stress; one of its main effects is to turn protein into sugar for energy.

The increased production of cholesterol itself is a primitive, defensive, anti-stress system. Starting around 1920, people tried to purify cholesterol to see its biological effects. They used about 10 different toxins—from pus to snake venom to heavy metals. They found that if they gave a lethal dose of the poison to an animal but also gave it a good dose of cholesterol, it would survive. Cholesterol has a direct activating effect on producing defensive steroids and interfering with the toxic effects of chemical and physical stresses.

**Josh Rubin:** If cholesterol goes up under stress but never comes down, is that a conversion issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40 years ago, researchers found that if thyroid hormone and Vitamin A nutrition were adequate, the amount of progesterone coming out of an ovary or adrenal gland exactly corresponded to the amount of cholesterol going in. A very big portion of cholesterol is turned into protective hormones. This depends largely on thyroid and Vitamin A.

In the 1930s, it was noticed that when the thyroid gland was removed, cholesterol immediately went up. If you gave a thyroid supplement, the cholesterol would decrease. Blood cholesterol was a mirror image of thyroid function.

If you lack something needed to turn energy into cholesterol, such as sugar, or if you are overloaded with unsaturated fats, you might not produce enough cholesterol. Sometimes a supplement of sugar is needed to bring up your production of cholesterol. You don't want your cholesterol to get below 160. A Hungarian study found that when they chemically lowered cholesterol, mortality increased from all causes—accidents, suicide, and cancer.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on pregnenolone's effects on our brain chemistry?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several signals tell your brain that you are suffering stress, such as low blood sugar. The stressed brain will activate enzymes to produce GABA, which sedates the brain. Valium acts on the GABA stabilizing system. If something prevents glutamic acid from being turned into sufficient amounts of GABA, Valium will fill in.

Progesterone and pregnenolone act on the GABA receptor system. Pregnenolone is basically a stabilizer at all levels of cells in the brain. Its effect is to imitate Valium, telling your pituitary that the stress is under control and to stop producing so much cortisol. In early experiments, animals given a huge dose of pregnenolone were more normal after the dose than they were before, even if they had been stressed.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend using a pregnenolone supplement to help balance that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on how far the system has deteriorated. Russians found that giving isolated mitochondria pregnenolone would structurally restore damaged mitochondria and allow them to begin producing more pregnenolone. There is a positive feedback: you give it some, and it makes more.

**Josh Rubin:** Why is growth hormone inflammatory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Most research is designed to praise its beneficial effects, but people who have been chronically deficient in it have a remarkable absence of atherosclerosis. Mice that are genetically deficient in pituitary hormones live two or three times as long as normal mice.

When you have hypoglycemia, you increase your growth hormone. It tends to come with other pituitary stress-responsive hormones. They are beneficial in the right amount at the right time, but harmful when they go on too long. People with acromegaly (overactivity of the pituitary) have an extremely high incidence of atherosclerosis.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you explain the differences between HDL and LDL?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Both are able to participate in detoxification. The protein that helps carry the cholesterol has specific anti-stress and antiviral activity. LDL is mostly the one that carries cholesterol into the places where it is needed—the brain, ovaries, testicles, and adrenal glands. HDL has some more specific antitoxic effects. Toxins will tend to increase HDL relative to LDL because of those antitoxic effects.

**Josh Rubin:** How does lack of light cause an increase in cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As soon as the lights go off, cortisol begins rising. The stress system recognizes immediately that darkness is stress. Intrinsic oxidation and free radical production get out of control in proportion to the exposure to darkness.

When you measure cytochrome oxidase—the enzyme that delivers food electrons to oxygen—during darkness, it degrades. After 12 to 15 hours of darkness, mitochondria swell up and some explode. Red light penetrates tissue and restores the copper in the cytochrome oxidase enzyme to its proper functional role. It recharges the enzyme.

**Josh Rubin:** So light stimulates cellular respiration and progesterone, while darkness is more stimulatory towards estrogen and stress hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Caller (JP):** I have a friend who contracted HIV. His last blood test showed CD4 and CD8 dropped. Do you have something to help him? What about niacinamide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People with HIV often have very high polyunsaturated fats circulating. Niacinamide is something that will help lower the free fatty acids. Sugar, niacinamide, and aspirin are all things that help to lower the stress and keep the immune system up.

**Josh Rubin:** You are a huge proponent of coconut oil. Can you elaborate on why?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Any of the saturated fats have an anti-inflammatory, protective effect. A group studying liver disease found that fish oils and seed oils increase liver inflammation and fibrosis. This can be blocked by saturated fats. Alcoholics in India who consumed ghee or butter didn't develop liver cirrhosis despite being alcoholic. Alcohol activates unsaturated fats to react with iron and produce liver damage.

Coconut oil is in the medium chain length. The shortness of the chain means it is very mobile. The shorter saturated fats can be handled in the mitochondria without relying on the transport systems used for longer chains. They can be oxidized as easily as glucose. They interfere with the anti-metabolic effects of unsaturated fats, allowing the mitochondria to run at full speed. This works as if you are giving a thyroid supplement.

**Josh Rubin:** Does coconut oil affect the pancreas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coconut oil and sugar work similarly to keep the system working to allow insulin both to function and to be produced.

**Josh Rubin:** Why is milk so important?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the calcium content is what makes it anti-inflammatory. Calcium increases the oxygen-using ability of the mitochondria, similar to thyroid. Systemically, it suppresses the parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH is a stress hormone that, when continued too long, contributes to degenerative diseases. Having a chronically high calcium intake gives you a chronically low parathyroid level, which protects your arteries, kidneys, and bones.

**Josh Rubin:** Why are eggs an important staple?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With the industrialization of the egg industry, the cholesterol content went down and the polyunsaturated content went up. If you can get non-industrial eggs from chickens that have pastures, they are going to be a lot better. The cholesterol in the egg seems to be one of its important nutritional values. 600 milligrams of cholesterol in your diet increases the oxidative stability of your lipid particles in your bloodstream.

**Caller (Danny Roddy):** A lot of people in the Paleo sphere are under the impression that free fatty acids in the blood are a good thing. Can you explain why that might be harmful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is my main argument against eating a high meat diet. Free fatty acids are one of the means by which stress causes its damage. Just about everything that goes wrong involves free fatty acid increase. Even if they are totally saturated, they still tend to shift the mitochondrial metabolism away from using glucose and fructose, lowering carbon dioxide production.

**Caller (Liam):** What does cholesterol have to do with mitochondrial respiration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, it stabilizes and protects the mitochondria against free fatty acids. It actually stimulates respiration and oxygen consumption. The proteins that make up the mitochondrion have a very liquid property; that protein structure is reinforced and stabilized by binding with cholesterol molecules.

**Caller (415):** A lot of coconut oil makes some people feel sick or achy. Is that because of salicylates? Is it better to get refined oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I recommend the completely deodorized coconut oil. The research was always done with the filtered kind that had no odor. Some people are allergic to the aromatic compounds in the coconut. Also, low thyroid people have very touchy gallbladders. It just takes a little grease to trigger a gallbladder reaction.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asked about butyric and propionic acid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those are produced in the intestine by fermenting bacteria. They have a protective effect against cancer, but since they are produced by bacteria, and healthy people have no bacteria in their small intestine, ideally we shouldn't be making them there. Both butyric and propionic acid have some pro-inflammatory effects as well.

**Josh Rubin:** What is the risk of taking a statin and lowering cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The tendency to become violent, suicidally depressed, or demented. Cholesterol is an intrinsic part of chromosome and DNA function. Statins interfere with the whole chain of synthesis, including Coenzyme Q10 production. This is likely a factor in why they cause muscles to break down (rhabdomyolysis).

**Josh Rubin:** To summarize, what can people do to normalize their cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A daily raw carrot will tend to lower cortisol and estrogen; stopping that stress will let your thyroid work better. Avoiding polyunsaturated fats is essential for your thyroid to recover. Everything that increases your metabolic rate, such as calcium and sodium, is essential.

**Josh Rubin:** Any final thoughts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The important thing is not to think of unsaturated fats as essential. That has never been proved. George Burr proved that unsaturated fats slow the metabolic rate. When you shift to a pro-thyroid saturated fat diet, your metabolic rate increases, which means your nutritional requirements for things like copper, selenium, and B vitamins will increase.

**Josh Rubin:** Thank you, Ray. That was an awesome show.

title: EastWest Healing: Questions and Answers II
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** All right everyone, welcome to today's show with Ray Peat, Ph.D. I want to thank everyone once again for tuning into our show every month. Last month's show with Lita Lee was great, so if you didn't have a chance to listen to that, go to our Blog Talk Radio show and check that out.

Today we're doing a question and answer show with Ray Peat. I know a lot of people have been really waiting for this show. If you want to learn more about Ray, his website is RayPeat.com. He has tons of articles on his site that will probably keep you busy for the next 50 years. He has books you can order, and a newsletter that is well worth the money.

Ray has his Ph.D. in Biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He has taught at many schools including the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, National College of Naturopathic Medicine, and Blake College. He started his work with progesterone-related hormones in 1968, did a paper on physiology, chemistry, and physics in 1971, and his dissertation at the University of Oregon in 1972, outlining his ideas regarding progesterone and the hormones closely related to it as protectors of the body structure and energy against harmful effects of estrogen, radiation, stress, and lack of oxygen.

Ray, are you on the line?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Josh Rubin:** Is there anything else you want to add before we get going?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that covered everything.

**Josh Rubin:** I have a lot of questions here. I have been getting a lot of questions from people regarding iron. A lot of people want a summary on your thoughts about iron because you believe it's a heavy metal, it's toxic, and it has all these effects on the body. Could you clarify the dangers of iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Wherever iron gets loose, it is available to react with things like polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs), but also protein and nucleic acids. The reactive form of iron is the reduced ferrous form rather than the fully oxidized ferric form. That means that if you don't get enough oxygen to your tissues, the iron tends to get reduced by glutathione. People talk about oxidative stress, but reductive stress is really what you have to worry about in relation to iron.

Alcohol, for example, interferes with the use of oxygen and causes the reduced glutathione to accumulate, shifting the ratio towards reduction. That activates iron, reduces it to the reactive ferrous form, and causes damage.

Iron accumulates faster than it should under the influence of estrogen. Inability to use oxygen properly intensifies the absorption of iron, and that seems to be what estrogen is for: to create the illusion of an oxygen deprivation so that you absorb more iron. They've tested the absorption percentage of a dose of iron in women versus men, and women absorbed nine times as much iron. That's primarily the influence of estrogen.

Unfortunately, besides making the body absorb it, estrogen also tends to create the conditions that make iron toxic and puts it into the reduced reactive form. One of the main things that activated iron attacks is the polyunsaturated fatty acid. That creates a vicious circle in which the estrogen increases the most reactive PUFA, which activate and increase the quantity of estrogen. Both of those contribute to the activation and intensification of iron toxicity. You can break the cycle in different ways: donating blood to get rid of iron or doing things to interrupt the estrogen-fatty acid cycle.

**Josh Rubin:** If you have low hemoglobin, is it still safe to donate blood, or are there alternatives?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's no blood test that I know of that will really say anything meaningful about your iron status because the iron tends to hide in your liver and bone marrow. The fact that an iron supplement increases red blood cell count or hemoglobin doesn't mean they were deficient in iron. They used to treat anemia with doses of arsenic; the arsenic creates the stress that tells your body you need more iron and more blood. Any stress that interferes with oxygen use will drive up the blood production system.

**Josh Rubin:** When you see low hemoglobin, would that be due to estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, in all animals that have estrogen, the female tends to look slightly anemic because it slows the production of red blood cells. Lowering the body temperature is one of the actions of estrogen, as is slowing down thyroid function. Probably the most common cause of apparent anemia, as Broda Barnes pointed out, is hypothyroidism.

He mentioned an experiment where they folded a rat's tail back and stitched it into the abdomen so it was kept at core body temperature. It quickly began producing red blood cells just by raising the temperature. So, the safest way to treat anemia might be to wear long wool socks to warm the extremities.

**Josh Rubin:** What is copper's role in regards to iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Its primary role is in the respiratory enzyme cytochrome oxidase. That is probably the reason that copper is essential for constructing the hemoglobin molecule.

**Josh Rubin:** So you feel that most people actually have higher amounts of iron in the liver and bone marrow, and they might be showing up low on a lab because of absorptive issues or hypothyroidism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In men, it accumulates continuously with aging. Menstruation probably helps women avoid the accumulation until they stop menstruating, and then the curve is maybe even steeper than men's. I think menstruation is one of the factors that makes women have a greater longevity.

There was a study of immigrant fruit pickers' children in California. They didn't get a good diet, but they ate lots of oranges. They had an average hemoglobin of 10, which is considered tending towards anemia, but they found that these kids didn't get infectious diseases like the well-fed city kids who had lots of hemoglobin. They've seen that same thing in Africa; when they would have campaigns to give iron supplements, lots of people would come down with malaria because iron activates the growth of germs and weakens our immune system.

One of the tests that is meaningful in the blood, but seldom done, is the iron saturation. People tend to be resistant to cancer development if the saturation is somewhat low, like 25%.

**Josh Rubin:** We have a caller. Chris Dillon, you're on the air.

**Caller (Chris):** I have two questions. Regarding ADD and ADHD, as we've been seeing a rise of these diagnoses in the last couple of decades, do you feel that sugar is the problem, or could it be more of the polyunsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's the unsaturated fats. The sugar tends to move everything in the right direction, away from brain malfunction. The polyunsaturated fats interfere with attention and increase adrenaline, the sympathetic nervous system, and the stress hormones. I think that's probably the main thing, as well as hypothyroidism, that keeps the front part of the brain from getting enough energy to focus.

**Caller (Chris):** My second question is regarding Hashimoto's disease. Can you explain the proper way for it to be diagnosed? I realize that sometimes the anti-thyroid antibodies found in blood really don't have any relation to the thyroid gland.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, those antibodies interact with cartilage of the joints just about as well. It's really a connective tissue inflammatory disease which goes with hypothyroidism. The cartilage is one of the first places that you see hypothyroidism in children. It accounts for why hypothyroid kids tend to be knock-kneed. The cartilage in the knees and the elbows is basically swollen.

**Caller (Chris):** So basically a lot of people walk around being misdiagnosed for this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Josh Rubin:** I was reading one of your old articles on Hashimoto's and thyroiditis. You talk about how estrogen affects the colloid and stimulates it, but inhibits the proteolytic enzymes to break it down. Is that why a lot of people are getting diagnosed with Hashimoto's?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The whole idea of autoimmune disease is off the mark. I think of the immune system as a clean-up system. The antibodies help the phagocytes remove debris. If the debris is caused by low thyroid causing the connective tissue to swell, the immune system has to come in and try to help clean out the junk that builds up.

**Josh Rubin:** Caller from the 678, you're on the air.

**Caller (678):** How long would you say it would take someone whose body temperature has historically been in the low to mid 97s for that to stabilize if they institute some of your recommendations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen a couple of people do it in three or four days—very skinny people who had been on a pure soy tofu diet. As soon as they started eating eggs and oranges, they just popped up out of there. A couple of people who had been diagnosed as having broken pituitary glands with no function at all saw all of their pituitary hormones pop back as soon as they started eating rationally.

**Caller (678):** My second question is regarding Hans Selye's work. It seems like he believes we have an absolute reserve of energy to deal with stress and that any stressful event can deplete this. What do you think of that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think where he left it is where the issue of cumulative buildup of iron and PUFA comes in. Both long-chain polyunsaturated fats and iron accumulate with aging, stress, and under the influence of estrogen. He wasn't looking far enough to see how those factors interacted with stress.

During prolonged adaptation, estrogen, growth hormone, and inflammatory mediators accumulate. Estrogen buildup begins to directly drive the adrenal gland. When that reaches a certain point, you can actually get bleeding in the adrenal gland and death of the cortical cells just from an excess of estrogen. The systemic effect of stress is what he neglected to think about when he talked about the reserve, innate amount of energy.

**Josh Rubin:** In one of your old newsletters regarding autoimmunity, you talked about Metchnikoff. You argued that inflammation was a pathological reaction rather than being a healthy part of a defensive immune system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's mostly me. For Metchnikoff, he saw the white blood cells going in and curing the problem. But after the medical establishment took it over, they created the idea of inflammation being the curative process. But the swelling, the redness, the pain—these are pathological.

The immune system should work like it does in the prenatal state. In the embryonic and fetal state, injury is corrected without inflammation. The cells just repair the damage in an efficient way and don't leave a scar. When you keep the carbon dioxide and sugar where they should be, you basically get fetal or embryonic healing without a scar and without inflammation. I see inflammation as an inability to deliver what's needed to repair the damage.

**Josh Rubin:** I have a lot of questions on weight loss. People begin to follow your philosophies and notice their energy goes up, but they actually gain weight. Can you elaborate on why?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gaining weight probably isn't the issue; it's gaining inches and bulging. When you're doing everything just right, very likely you will rebuild muscles that were damaged by stress and poor nutrition. As those muscles grow, the circumference of your thighs, hips, and belly should be decreasing even though your weight is increasing.

When I first experimented with DHEA, I noticed after a week or two that my waist seemed to be reappearing. My pants were getting looser, but I was exactly the same weight. I was simply growing more lean tissue and burning up some of the fat.

**Josh Rubin:** So for a lot of people, it's actually a sign that your body is moving in the right direction?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. But if someone is putting down fat rather than muscle—their pants are getting too tight—they're just eating too much, probably too much fat or total calories. I've averaged over the years probably a gallon of milk a day, but that's always been 1% milk. Even at two quarts of milk, a person doesn't want to have whole milk at 3 or 4% fat.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your feelings on aromatase inhibitors? People suggest taking calcium D-glucarate or DIM.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically, they're usually selling just powdered cabbage leaves. That has been tested and found somewhat estrogenic in itself.

The estrogen aromatase activating effect of PUFA is antagonized when you shift the balance to saturated fats. Aspirin, by blocking the formation of prostaglandins and reducing inflammation, interrupts the effect of the PUFA. Aspirin is a very effective aromatase inhibitor, but the drug companies don't want people to know that.

**Josh Rubin:** If people just eat a diet void of unsaturated fats, wouldn't that inhibit aromatase enzymes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Thyroid inhibits aromatase. Anything that lowers cortisol inhibits it, because cortisol is a major activator.

**Josh Rubin:** If people start to eat this way—increase saturated fats, take a thyroid glandular—is it dangerous because you're detoxing the liver? Is it dangerous because of stored iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The iron, if it's in the oxidized state, is just sitting there doing no harm. It forms little granules and doesn't get out to do anything.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you summarize your thoughts on coffee? Many say coffee causes adrenal fatigue, but you say it has benefits.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Do you have any idea who started the idea of adrenal fatigue? I've been trying to find out who is responsible for that word.

Coffee contains a lot of good things besides the caffeine. It's an extremely concentrated source of magnesium, niacin, and other B vitamins. The caffeine has an antioxidant effect. As long as you use it with food, it tends to stabilize your blood sugar and reduce inflammation.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding adrenal fatigue, I feel people took Hans Selye's work on the General Adaptation Syndrome and ran with it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know where "exhaustion" is, where the adrenal gland dies. You don't want to get to exhaustion, but the idea of fatigue seems to be something else.

If you have enough cholesterol, are eating a good diet with vitamin A, and your thyroid is okay, you will be able to produce pregnenolone and progesterone. Progesterone in itself has all of the functions of the adrenal hormones. Hans Selye took out animals' adrenal glands, and if they were pregnant, they didn't have any symptoms at all until they gave birth. That led him to give progesterone to animals that had their adrenal glands removed, and they lived fully normal lifespans.

With adequate vitamin A and thyroid, you will convert cholesterol into pregnenolone and progesterone. Also, the adrenals are very good at repairing themselves.

**Josh Rubin:** You talk about how using coffee is important—sipping it after a meal with cream and sweetener.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Taking it with or after the meal has basically none of the harmful effects. I've known several people who said a sip of coffee would make them feel shattered, but I told them to put some heavy cream and sugar in it and take it only with a meal. Within three or four days, these people were happy coffee drinkers.

**Josh Rubin:** There are people like Dr. Mercola promoting that fructose causes diabetes and fatty liver.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just a few days ago, I heard from someone in New Zealand who had been diagnosed with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. He started a diet that included 300 grams of fructose every day. He now has a new diagnosis: his liver has no fat problem.

**Josh Rubin:** So everyone saying fructose causes fatty liver is missing the boat because it's the unsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. My newsletter on sugar questions goes through the history of how that fructose phobia evolved. It's very closely connected to the cholesterol doctrine of heart disease and the idea of essential fatty acids being beneficial. Meanwhile, science was showing that the so-called essential fatty acids are toxic and carcinogenic.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener asks: You mentioned that pigs fed soybeans have unsaturated fat. If their fat was truly unsaturated, how come bacon is still solid at room temperature?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was a kid, I would get blocks of lard and they were definitely solid at room temperature, just like butter. But the lard I've seen in recent years, which is now slightly over 30% PUFA, is soft at room temperature. The fat droplets in bacon are enclosed in cells and connected by connective tissue, so even if it was 100% PUFA, it would still have a white, firm appearance.

**Josh Rubin:** What is your opinion on time-released T3 versus basic Cytomel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've heard from several people who were having either overdose effects or no effects from time-release. A lawyer had compounded time-release T3 analyzed by laboratories, and no T3 could be found in it. If you compound it carelessly, T3 is easily destroyed or oxidized. With the wrong time-release agent, it might permanently bind the T3 or release it as soon as it hits stomach acid. Generally, I don't think the idea of a patented brand name medicine is good, but in the case of T3, I haven't seen a good other product besides Cytomel.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend eating the carrot before, with, or after a meal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually it's just eating the carrot. If you eat it with a meal, you might slow digestion to the point that you aren't getting your food as expected, and you might feel shaky. But if a person wants to reduce their fat absorption, eating the carrot with the meal will accelerate weight loss.

**Josh Rubin:** Can adding baking soda to orange juice help increase carbon dioxide levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you put it in acid, baking soda is going to bubble off most of the carbon dioxide. Some will dissolve in the water, and it might increase your systemic CO2 a little bit. There have been experiments with bicycle racers where they took a tablespoon of baking soda before the race and performed better, either due to increased sodium or CO2.

**Josh Rubin:** If someone doesn't have a gallbladder, is coconut oil the best source of fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think just eating things in a mixed form in small amounts is important. If you don't have a gallbladder, the bile is still going to be there, but it's coming out in dribbles rather than surges.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding detoxing from PUFAs, does it take four years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments found that it depends on the size of the fat cell. It's a slow process to randomly renew the composition of the fat cells.

**Josh Rubin:** If someone feels they are getting worse—more hypoglycemic—is that because of PUFA detox?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping your blood sugar steady and adding some saturated fat helps. Saturated fats inhibit the stress hormones, which means they also tend to inhibit the release of fat from stores. Sugar, saturated fats, niacin, and aspirin inhibit the release of fat.

One of the ways the body safely eliminates stored PUFA is through the liver. The liver recognizes the PUFA as toxins and will selectively attach glucuronic acid to them, just as if it was dioxin, and send it to the kidneys for excretion. That's the safe way to get rid of it.

**Josh Rubin:** Can high blood pressure be looked at as an adaptation to stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. When your body senses it's not getting enough oxygen or glucose, it tells the heart to pump more blood. But when you're loaded with PUFA, they give chronic signals to the brain that nothing is getting the glucose and oxygen it needs.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about the benefits of salt, especially for pregnant women and eclampsia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The eclampsia problem is closely connected to high PUFA, low thyroid, low carbon dioxide, and poor ability to retain sodium. As sodium is lost, the adrenals try to correct things by increasing aldosterone. Aldosterone retains sodium but at the expense of losing magnesium faster.

If you just increase your sodium intake, you're compensating for low thyroid function, but you're turning off the aldosterone. Getting the aldosterone down directly lowers inflammation and stops some of the magnesium loss.

**Josh Rubin:** How does albumin play into that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen interferes with the liver's synthesis of albumin. If you're producing less albumin and have more unsaturated fats, the albumin becomes saturated with fats. When albumin is loaded with fats, it passes right through the kidneys into the urine.

Albumin's function is to retain water in association with sodium. If your albumin is low, you get water retention problems. The first thing that happens when you correct your fats, thyroid, and estrogen is that you let water out of the body while retaining the sodium, magnesium, and albumin.

**Josh Rubin:** Caller from the 415, you're on the air.

**Caller (415):** What do you think of heavy metal detox? If you get amalgams out, do you need IV glutathione or vitamin C drips?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hans Selye did experiments poisoning animals with mercury. He showed that a given dose would cause death, but if he gave them the same amount of mercury plus vitamin C, they had no toxic effects.

Mercury in its reduced form isn't toxic. It's like iron. Caffeine is associated with getting heavy metals out of tissues. Vitamin C from regular foods is an important defense. But if you take reducing agents like glutathione in an unphysiological way (IV), they can activate iron. Glutathione is the agent of making iron toxic. If you put glutathione into the blood, it can increase free radical damage.

**Josh Rubin:** Caller from the 386.

**Caller (Debbie):** Is there an advantage to shredding the carrot versus eating it whole?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been experiments with the length of fiber. If you put a carrot in a blender, you're destroying a lot of the water-retaining function of the fibers. Your teeth leave large sections of the fiber intact. Just chewing it is very good.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding male fertility: if someone has low sperm count, what can they do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid is probably the main cause of both male and female infertility. In the 1940s, people saw that pregnenolone alone was enough to greatly increase sperm quality. Polyunsaturated fats are a major villain in male fertility.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding sleep: people follow your principles but have trouble sleeping or wake up with a high pulse. Why?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Taking too much thyroid too soon can do that. Your liver should store enough glycogen to let you fast for eight hours. Before the liver has regenerated its ability to store glycogen, the thyroid makes your brain and muscles need more sugar. You have to eat more often until your liver adapts. Having some fat with your carbohydrate makes it absorb more slowly. Salt is also very effective at lowering adrenaline.

**Josh Rubin:** Caller from the 718.

**Caller (718):** I started taking pure fructose and felt great, but recently started having sleep problems. I switched to starch and my sleep normalized.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the starch is getting digested and assimilated more slowly. Eating fiber and fat with your carbohydrate will extend the absorption. Sugar is absorbed quickly in the upper intestine. Starch, if it's slow to break down, can feed bacteria lower in the intestine and cause inflammation. The combination of fat and fiber might be a way to make your blood sugar steadier.

**Josh Rubin:** Question about dental health. Some recommend eliminating fruit, but you talk about carbohydrates.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw a recent article on dental health in Sweden. During the time that cavities decreased radically, sugar and candy consumption had actually increased. Old studies showed that increased estrogen increased dental decay, and increased thyroid reduced it. Stress will very quickly cause an outbreak of cavities. Mainline dentistry completely neglects the chemical and immunological function of saliva. I think saliva is a mediator of stress.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your thoughts on fasting to upregulate autophagy to starve off diseases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Activating your metabolism is going to eat up proteins that shouldn't be there. One of the main things interfering with the breakdown of protein is the PUFA. Accumulating long-chain unsaturated fatty acids with aging changes the way the cell functions at the deepest levels.

**Josh Rubin:** What about carb restriction for longevity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the short range, fasting will reduce endotoxin absorption. But dropping your carbohydrate intake will raise your cortisol production. People feel better initially because cortisol produces a sort of anesthetic euphoria. But in the long run, it's stressful to turn protein into the carbohydrate your brain needs.

**Josh Rubin:** Are cell phones really unhealthy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Microwaves are a threat. There have been experiments for over 50 years showing biological effects from even moderately weak fields. The standard medical doctrine relies on the cell membrane theory—that a cell needs a barrier to seal in chemicals. They believe radiation must heat the chemicals to cause damage.

But in the cell, there is no such barrier membrane. The whole cell is highly organized and responds to very low levels of electromagnetic energy.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend thyroid glandulars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person's cholesterol is down around 100, they are very fragile. You have to get cholesterol up to at least 160 before increasing metabolic rate.

Traditional thyroid glands (like in fish head soup) consisted of about three parts T4 to one part T3. As the liver gets energy (glucose), it converts T4 to T3. If you don't have sugar and take your glandular, you only experience about 25% of the potential effect.

The glandular is safer because it lets your liver handle your physiology. If you try to take just T3, your TSH goes down. If you don't take T3 during the night, TSH revs up and turns on inflammatory processes.

The trouble is the technology of making a glandular product seems to have been lost. Armour was making their traditional product for 90 years, but then Revlon bought it and decided to extract calcitonin. So the new glandular is no longer what it used to be.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about the roles of magnesium and calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your thyroid is low and you don't produce ATP fast enough, the cell doesn't have the main thing that binds magnesium intracellularly, so it gets lost in the urine. Thyroid status is the main thing that determines how much magnesium you need.

You can't talk about the ideal ratio of minerals in the abstract. William Frederick Koch found that he could cure muscle spasms from parathyroid removal with any of the minerals—calcium, potassium, sodium, or magnesium. It's a matter of having a total of these alkaline minerals.

A lot of Americans get seven times as much phosphate as calcium. One of the functions of fructose is to make you lose phosphate faster, improving the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio. The ratio in milk (1.3 to 1) is very safe.

**Josh Rubin:** Any final thoughts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin E has undergone radical changes. When ADM bought the old distillation factory, they changed the methods. Old vitamin E research showed beneficial effects, but recent research shows ineffectiveness.

Wheat germ oil was a common starting material, rich in long-chain saturated alcohols like octacosanol. I suspect the original vitamin E research might have been effective because of these saturated fats neutralizing the PUFA, similar to how cocoa butter protects against canola oil damage.

**Josh Rubin:** Last caller from Washington.

**Caller (Justin):** I was reading about how Mexican children didn't get polio and its correlation to diet. Do you have comments on vaccinations or the infectious disease model?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect the Mexican immigrants were immune to childhood infectious diseases just because of their relative iron deficiency. Also, traditional tortillas are very high in calcium because they boil the corn in lime. That has an undoubted anti-stress effect.

**Josh Rubin:** One last question emailed in: What do you feel about research regarding cell membrane signaling?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very good business because they can sell anything if they say it's working on signals via the cell membrane. But basically, the membrane is not very relevant to actual cell physiology.

People in the 1930s showed large molecules like albumin entering cells freely. Fritiof Sjöstrand, who was a professor at UCLA and editor of the *Journal of Ultrastructure Research*, did work that is completely incompatible with the popular doctrine of plasma membranes.

**Josh Rubin:** Thank you, Ray, for this great show.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: EastWest Healing: Energy and Metabolism
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Welcome everyone to our new episode of Holistic Living. Today we are talking about energy metabolism. We have Dr. Raymond Peat back on the show. For those of you who don't know who he is, Ray got his PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He has taught in many schools, from the University of Oregon to Montana State University and the National College of Naturopathic Medicine. He also does private nutritional counseling. He started his work with progesterone and related hormones in 1968. Ray, is there anything you want to add about what you are currently working on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At the moment, I've been working on some of the similarities of the different organs. Recent newsletters were on the heart and the typical solid tumor as an organ, having some of the properties of other organs during stress. Currently, I'm working on the organization of the eye and the brain as they express some of those same properties of the failing heart and tumor physiology. You see some of the same processes showing up in such different places. I am trying to generalize things so that various treatments, diets, and programs don't seem arbitrary, but so you can see what is in common.

**Josh Rubin:** Let's move on to the show. Today we're going to be talking about energy metabolism. A lot of people talk about macronutrients; some say high protein is good, or high fat, or high carb. I think we all agree that all macronutrients are important, though we have different views on the ratios. Can you talk about the cells and metabolism and why it's so important when we talk about energy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the themes I've been interested in for a long time is the function of carbon dioxide in cells. In some observations, people have seen that the most improbable organism is unable to live without carbon dioxide, even though they can live without oxygen. Ordinarily, we think of oxygen turning into carbon dioxide as a waste product, but it really seems to be even more essential for life than oxygen.

Carbohydrates are a very good source of carbon dioxide. They oxidize and produce a lot of carbon dioxide. If carbon dioxide is that essential to life, then obviously the best food to produce it is going to be carbohydrates.

In recent newsletters, I've been pointing out some of the things that are becoming fairly common knowledge now regarding the failing heart. If you look at what happens when you exercise: when you're sitting at rest, the quiet muscle burns almost pure sugar and oxygen—pure glucose and oxygen. But as soon as it starts exercising, it shifts over to fat oxidation. At maximum exercise, it's burning mostly fat and very little oxygen. It produces quite a bit of lactic acid because it's wasting sugar. It's burning the fat pretty thoroughly, but it's wasting the sugar and turning it into lactic acid.

The failing heart does the same thing. It's exerting its maximum, and in doing that, it's burning fatty acids primarily rather than sugar. This process of substituting fat burning for sugar burning was called a cycle by P.J. Randle. It isn't really a cycle, but now it's called the Randall Cycle. This means that if you burn fatty acids, that stops you from oxidizing glucose; instead, you'll turn it into lactic acid.

Diabetes consists of living on fatty acids and not being able to oxidize glucose, but still turning glucose into lactic acid, so that lactic acidemia becomes a problem in diabetes. Obviously, to make lactic acid out of glucose, it has to get into the cells. So this whole idea that transporting glucose into the cell is the failure in heart disease or diabetes just isn't the case. If you're making lactic acid, the sugar is getting into the cell. Something goes wrong in the oxidation process and the cell begins to favor the oxidation of fat rather than glucose. That doesn't produce as much carbon dioxide, and that seems to be a basic problem for the cell that leads it down the path of reduced function and eventual non-survival.

A very similar thing happens in cancer cells. They begin turning glucose into lactic acid or fat, and then they oxidize the fat. In treating heart disease over the last five years, there's been a movement towards thinking of ways to stop the oxidation of fatty acids, allowing the heart to avoid the Randall Cycle and get back to oxidizing glucose instead of turning it into lactic acid.

**Josh Rubin:** When you say carbohydrates are the most important because they increase the production of energy (CO2), can you define what you mean by carbohydrates? Some people might hear that and think you're talking about eating a high-fat diet because our bodies are using fat for energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We can turn protein into both sugar and fat equivalents. So when you're talking about energy, you have to consider that some of it might come from protein. But oxidizing protein is very wasteful. Besides being expensive, it produces a lot of waste material—ammonia, for example—and it turns on machinery which resembles the stress reaction. When we're in stress, we break down protein and turn it into energy materials.

The mechanism of oxidizing fat also gets into the process of creating stress. Especially the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) activate the same stress-responsive enzymes that burning too much protein will activate.

By carbohydrate, people generally mean both starches and sugars. It's simply anything that's made up of that same proportion of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Starches are just long chains of sugars. In the case of most food starches, they're composed of pure glucose molecules. So when you're getting energy from starch, you're really burning pure glucose. Sucrose, the standard table sugar, is also the main sugar of sweet fruits. It consists of half glucose and half fructose. Fructose happens to be able to metabolize without relying on the use of insulin. So it has been used for feeding diabetics and for avoiding some of the stresses produced by the ups and downs of the insulin reactions.

**Josh Rubin:** So getting the right amount of carbohydrates in relation to protein and fat is one way to increase glucose oxidation. If you're relying on fat, you're inhibiting glucose oxidation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, fructose and glucose, assuming you're eating a sugar such as fruits.

**Josh Rubin:** You talk about how antioxidants allow oxygen to be used productively rather than destructively. We could say CO2 is an antioxidant. Are there more specific examples you could give regarding antioxidants to help with the production of CO2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Running the oxidative process through the mitochondria very fast happens to be an antioxidative process in terms of avoiding toxic free radicals. The faster you burn oxygen usefully oxidizing sugars, the less you have to worry about taking care of the free radical toxic products that develop when you slow down the respiratory process by burning fats, especially polyunsaturated fats.

Vitamin E, vitamin C, and uric acid (which is produced in our body) are major antioxidants. But the marketing of the idea of antioxidants has created a big confusion. The antioxidants in our body have to fit together with uric acid and the enzymes which naturally break down free radicals. If you put things in that don't fit, an apparent antioxidant in a test tube can become a pro-oxidant in the body.

Things have to fit together so that vitamin A and vitamin E lock together, vitamin E and vitamin C lock together, and uric acid and vitamin C lock together. The glucose and other sugars have to be streaming through the systems of enzymes, turning into carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide has to be flowing out of the cell properly. The whole antioxidant system is really one piece. If you try to stuff in any "super antioxidants" like they're selling as health products, you're likely to create more oxidation than you had without it. A recent publication showed that cataracts are twice as common in men over the age of 65 who took big supplements of vitamin E and vitamin C.

**Josh Rubin:** When you talk about progesterone, vitamin E, and vitamin C, are you talking more from a food sense or a supplemental sense?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin E has a peculiar history. It started out in the 1930s being called a fertility nutrient. The Shute family of doctors studied it in treating women with clotting problems and fertility problems. They saw that it prevented abnormal clotting, which is a feature of excess estrogen. Estrogen has many problem side effects when it's excessive and unopposed. The Shutes and others in the 1930s saw that vitamin E restored fertility and prevented heart disease by functioning as an anti-estrogen.

Around that same time, the polyunsaturated fats were being seen to have estrogen-like effects and to cause clotting and circulatory problems. Animals that were fed on a high polyunsaturated fat diet were sterile. Various forces, such as the estrogen industry, didn't want estrogen associated with sterility and heart disease. Various pressures turned vitamin E into an "antioxidant" rather than an anti-estrogenic material. By 1950, the whole history of vitamin E had been turned into an antioxidant.

I don't see it as primarily an antioxidant. I see it as anti-inflammatory and anti-estrogenic, with this potential side effect of protecting against free radicals if it's in the right concentration and balance with other chemicals.

**Josh Rubin:** Because estrogen creates that hypoxic environment at the cell level, and vitamin E does the opposite, you're saying it allows oxygen to be used more efficiently. In a sense, because of that, it's anti-estrogen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Both estrogen and anything that creates inflammation wastes oxygen and tends to lead to lactic acid production. Vitamin E, by stopping the inflammation and estrogen effects, is also making more oxygen available and reducing the lactic acid problem.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about free fatty acids? How they can cause a sluggish liver, inhibit T4 to T3 conversion, and lead to edema?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid is the hormone that activates our whole oxidative system and leads to the production of carbon dioxide when it's working properly. Estrogen, besides working at the cell level to waste oxygen, happens to block the enzymes that secrete thyroid hormone.

The fatty acids that are saturated happen to oxidize with fair safety. The polyunsaturated fatty acids are the ones that are more likely to break down and produce free radicals. Cells distinguish between these two types of fatty acids and prefer to oxidize the saturated fats. That means that anytime you eat a little bit of excess unsaturated fat, it primarily goes into storage because the cells prefer not to oxidize it.

However, estrogen prefers those oxygen-wasting, free-radical-producing fats. It preferentially causes them to be liberated from storage. So under the influence of estrogen, all of the free fatty acids increase. Women have, on average, a higher level of free fatty acids circulating. Estrogen preferentially brings the polyunsaturated fats out of storage, especially the very long-chain polyunsaturated ones. These are the ones that most interfere with other levels of thyroid function—not just the secretion, which estrogen directly does, but with the transport and metabolism of the thyroid hormone. So at many levels, estrogen and the polyunsaturated fats are working together to inhibit the function of the thyroid hormone and the oxidative system.

**Josh Rubin:** Does that also have to do with estrogen stimulating the adrenal cortex, putting yourself into that sympathetic state which causes the breakdown of proteins and increases free fatty acids?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen directly stimulates the secretion of insulin, and that tends to lower blood sugar and create fat storage if you've eaten more than enough. But it also directly stimulates the adrenal cortex, increasing aldosterone and cortisol, and that causes the whole system to go into the emergency reaction process. The cortisol tends to bring blood sugar up where the insulin tends to lower it. So the more estrogen is increased and unopposed by protective things such as progesterone, DHEA, pregnenolone, and thyroid, the more system stresses and tendency to failure there are.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding endometriosis and body temperature, you've talked about the work of Desjardins and how estrogen's interactions with unsaturated fats cause damage to brain cells. Is that a major factor in endometriosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Desjardins and his group were interested in many of the side effects of estrogen on the brain, pituitary, endorphins, iron accumulation, and fatty acids. Because of the estrogen-thyroid effects and the constant pushing up of growth hormone from the pituitary, the liver is feminized from an early age. This shows up in studies of liver transplants.
