They found that because of this process of stress hormones and growth hormone feminizing women's livers, they make poor candidates relative to the livers of men for transplant.

**Josh Rubin:** So you're saying endometriosis is more of the inability to detoxify this excess estrogen versus a low progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It involves the liver and the pituitary, but estrogen is very central to the actual lesion or abnormal tissue of endometriosis. Simply by reducing estrogen exposure, you can alleviate the symptoms.

The cells begin producing estrogen; they express the enzyme aromatase, which manufactures estrogen. They used to think aromatase existed only in the ovary, but it turned out to exist in fat cells, breast cells, skin cells, bone, and muscle. Everywhere that is under stress will begin to produce estrogen molecules.

In endometrial tissue, it should be exposed to estrogen for only about 12 hours each month. Then progesterone should surge up to 50 or 100 times higher concentration and cause the cells to give up their production of estrogen. But instead, the aromatase keeps churning out estrogen. The estrogen excites the tissue and turns on the cyclooxygenase enzyme, which turns polyunsaturated fatty acids into prostaglandins, creating inflammation that causes the pain and contractions. The inflammation from the prostaglandin in turn creates more aromatase. So it gets a vicious cycle going.

The simplest, most physiological way to stop it is to eat a diet with adequate protein, sugar, trace minerals, and vitamins, and to make sure your thyroid is functioning. I've seen people who had been suffering painful endometriosis for years who, in two or three days, completely stopped the symptoms permanently just with quick-acting thyroid, a good diet, and aspirin. Aspirin or other blockers of prostaglandin production all by themselves can greatly reduce the formation of estrogen and break the cycle.

**Josh Rubin:** So eliminating unsaturated fats will help reduce estrogen production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they are central to endometriosis.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on aspirin therapy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In cancers, the cells that are stressed begin to produce estrogen. As long as there is polyunsaturated fat available, the estrogen is going to activate the cyclooxygenase enzyme that makes prostaglandins, which keep the aromatase active, producing more estrogen. Even if you aren't eating it currently, the polyunsaturated fat that was incorporated into your tissues is going to break down under stress, flow into the bloodstream, and feed the production of estrogen.

Sugar is one of the things that can reduce the flow of polyunsaturated fats out of your tissues into your bloodstream. Niacinamide is another thing that limits the release of these fatty acids. So both sugar and niacinamide back up the function of aspirin.

**Josh Rubin:** So for endometriosis: get the right amount of carbs, regulate thyroid, use niacinamide, and possibly aspirin therapy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Josh Rubin:** How does estrogen relate to body temperature and pulse?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even though estrogen turns on the stress hormones, and the stress hormones tend to protect the body temperature, at a certain point of estrogen dominance, even the adrenaline and cortisol aren't enough to keep your body warm. So your temperature falls after a certain total exposure to unopposed estrogen.

Progesterone, all by itself, can drastically and quickly increase your temperature while at the same time lowering the stress hormones. Progesterone blocks the estrogen's effect, simply letting you return to a more normal set point. In doing that, it stops mechanisms that cause flushing, such as nitric oxide, which causes vasodilation and heat loss.

**Caller (David):** I remember reading about Lewis and Clark being offered salmon by Northwestern Indians and being repulsed by it because they were used to ruminants. How did these tribes survive or thrive on salmon? Have they learned to balance it? Also, animals like bears gorge on salmon and then hibernate. Is it possible animals stumble into this polyunsaturated fat thing and realize it puts them into a state where they can just sleep through the winter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Northwest Indians had a lot of varied foods. I don't know how much salmon they ate year-round, but they dried quite a bit of it. Mixtures of bear fat, berries, and fruits were able to survive storage. Those were usual staples.

**Caller (David):** Bear fat would be pretty saturated, wouldn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, because bears like to eat a lot of fruit and grass; they aren't primarily carnivores.

**Caller (David):** I know squirrels and other rodents eat nuts. Has that been studied regarding metabolism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Squirrels have been studied pretty well. They found that when they kept them from eating the acorn-type, highly unsaturated things in the fall, they didn't hibernate. The PUFA increased the serotonin and put them to sleep. It wasn't even good sleep; typically they'll wake up a few times during the winter to sleep normally. It's a type of torpor.

**Caller (David):** So it appears we try to make the best of whatever situation we are in.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is gradual adaptation to seasonal stress. People get depressed in the winter, but they aren't able to spend four or five months sleeping it off.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your thoughts on hot flashes? We know the mechanism behind them, but why do some women get estrogen therapy and it actually eliminates their hot flashes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have a little bit about that in my last newsletter. I think it just creates a stress that keeps them from experiencing the ups and downs.

**Josh Rubin:** So it's almost like taking that excess estrogen pushes them over the edge and shuts things down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think it slows the metabolism enough that they aren't going in and out of the state.

**Josh Rubin:** Regarding mothers and babies with colic or eczema, doctors often suggest food intolerances. What are your thoughts on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In animal experiments, some people saw that the mildest allergen would produce a deadly allergic reaction if they lowered the blood sugar. The mother's system can pass allergens through the milk. But with these animal studies, they found that if they increased the blood sugar artificially, the deadliest allergens that had killed normal animals would just cause a little sniffling. Lowering the blood sugar from whatever cause would cause a mild allergen to kill the animal in shock.

I've seen many times in people who used to rush to the hospital for a shot or who carried an adrenaline pen for an allergic exposure, instead, they would keep a big bottle of Coke in the fridge, drink the Coke quickly as soon as they had the exposure, and stop going to the hospital.

**Josh Rubin:** So postpartum, it's more of a hypoglycemic reaction? If someone was able to regulate their blood sugar and increase thyroid production, doing that alone would heal them and the baby?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Even when a woman has had a very happy pregnancy, because the pregnancy itself is driving her hormones, as soon as she has the baby, there's a letdown in which she discovers her own hypothyroid, progesterone-deficient state. This becomes excessively estrogen-dominated. That causes the postpartum depression syndrome along with a whole range of other possible consequences such as rheumatoid arthritis, MS, allergies, and seizures.

**Caller (Carmen):** I've been on the Ray Peat plan with orange juice and food for about 23 days. Within three days, I was able to stop taking my thyroid medicine. My temperatures went up to 98.1–99.2 and have stayed up. My pulse is about 65 in the morning and goes up to 85 during the day. Is that okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think 85 is a very good daytime pulse rate. You should stay alert to possible fluctuations in your stress hormones, but those numbers sound very good.

**Caller (Carmen):** I had my labs pulled yesterday. What can I expect with my labs, or does it matter as long as I feel good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You want to keep your eye on TSH if you have the opportunity. You don't want it to go too high because it will start creating the symptoms of hypothyroidism, inflammation, and heart rhythm issues. It's safest to keep your TSH down.

**Caller (Carmen):** How high is too high? The highest mine was was 3.0.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would say that three is always too high. Below one is where I feel more comfortable. In a big population, the freedom from thyroid cancer is best when the TSH is below 0.4.

**Caller (Carmen):** How do you actually get rid of the stored PUFA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That really is a problem. It's worse than storing DDT, I think. We do have the ability; the liver can treat them like a poison and excrete them so they pass out through the urine without having to be oxidized. But if the liver isn't very well supported, the polyunsaturated fats can block those enzymes in the liver the way estrogen does. So you have to make sure that your liver isn't under stress. Don't go too long without eating.

**Josh Rubin:** What do body temperature and pulse tell us about energy metabolism? Do you find that to be more accurate than a thyroid panel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As long as you do it in the same way, in the same place, it doesn't matter very much. The mouth is quicker than the armpit usually. I found that some people had fat armpits and it would take about two hours to get the temperature up through that thick layer of fat.

Also, in hot, humid weather, I saw hypothyroid people with normal temperatures. So I checked their pulse. These people coming in with 98.6 temperatures had 45-minute pulse rates. You have to look at more than one indicator.

The Achilles reflex relaxation test is a very quick and definite indicator of thyroid function. You want the toe to hang freely and relaxed when you kneel in a chair. If you thump it and get a twitch, the foot should relax with complete, instantaneous relaxation. It should look just like a piece of jelly flopping there after the outward twitch. If your thyroid is good, the relaxation should be utterly relaxed and floppy.

**Josh Rubin:** With temperature and pulse, we're looking at how our cells are using glucose, oxygen, and thyroid. It shows you that you're going in the right direction, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If you add a supplement of pregnenolone and thyroid to a good diet, you can get there pretty quickly. To get there just with diet depends on how much PUFA you have stored in your tissues. A big fat person has a lot of work to get rid of some of the toxic stuff. A very skinny person can sometimes pop out of a chronic state of stress in as little as a week.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, we really appreciate it. We learned a ton from your research. Thank you for your time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You're welcome. Thank you.

title: EastWest Healing Cholesterol and Saturated Fats
transcriptText:
**Guest:** Dr. Raymond Peat
**Hosts:** Josh Rubin (Jeannie Rubin is absent for this episode)

**Josh Rubin:** What up everyone? This is Josh Rubin from East West Healing and Performance. Today we are hosting a great radio show with Dr. Ray Peat. Jeannie will not be joining us today, so it's just me and Dr. Peat.

We do this show for the listeners because I know a lot of people are really into Ray’s philosophy and information. The show is on cholesterol and saturated fats, so try to revolve your questions around that.

Today’s topic is huge. We're going to get Ray Peat's philosophy on this. We'll cover why cholesterol is so important, why doctors are trying to lower it, why our physiology needs it, what it means if it's high or low, and why the right types of saturated fats are so important in our diet.

Ray, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hi.

**Josh Rubin:** I wanted to know if you wanted to take a couple of minutes just to give a brief history of who you are and where you come from.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Before I studied biology, I was mostly studying language, literature, and painting. I had been interested in biology for a very long time, but I had a bad impression of academic biology from my high school experience.

In the 1940s, there was a very big change in the nature of American biology that was powered by industry and government promotion of the gene theory as opposed to the field theory in development and health. I waited a long time, until 1968, to actually enter a graduate program in biology. I had learned enough about universities to manage to get through the program without having too many conflicts with professors. Most of the professors were very committed to the genetic determinist idea of what an organism is. I was interested in the field concept and environmental influences on the organism. Nutrition is one of the most important environmental influences. I see our nature as being a matter of potential being realized according to the conditions of the environment, rather than the expression of a predetermined genetic program.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do you think America is so afraid of cholesterol and saturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's driven primarily by the food industry wanting to sell their products: the seed oils. The seed oils were already seen to be toxic—causing sterility, degeneration of the brain and the gonads—probably from 1925, but especially in the 1930s and 40s. The very oxidizable seed oils were known to be toxic. That was one of the factors in researching Vitamin E as something to counteract the toxicity of the seed oils (unsaturated fats), as well as the toxicity of estrogen, which happens to synergize with unsaturated fats.

The pig industry had been looking for ways to make their animals gain weight and eat less food. George Burr, who is identified as the inventor of the essential fatty acid concept, himself discovered that the essential fatty acids slow the metabolic rate. Deficient animals eating sugar instead of unsaturated fats had about a 50% higher metabolic rate. They found that feeding soy and corn to the pigs, because of the unsaturated fats suppressing their metabolic rate, increased the profit—less food in, more pig out. At the same time, they noticed that it was lowering cholesterol as one of its toxic biological effects.

Around 1950, paint and oil chemists discovered how to make paints and plastics from petroleum. That decreased one of the big markets for soybeans. Henry Ford had imported soybeans to use in the car industry for plastics, but when the petroleum chemists learned how to use petroleum, that freed up the soybean market for pigs. Their production was great enough that they wanted to find new markets to replace the paint and plastics market. So, they started promoting the health idea of their soy oil, cottonseed oil, and safflower seed oil.

The only biological effect established for the seed oils, other than sterility and dementia, was that they lowered blood cholesterol. For several decades, people had noticed that cholesterol accumulated in the walls of blood vessels (atherosclerosis). Although the first person who discovered that in rabbits had dissolved the cholesterol in unsaturated vegetable oil, he realized that cholesterol by itself wasn't causing the disease. But the seed oil industry argued by association: if it's in the blood vessel and the blood, and their oil lowers the level in the blood, then you can prevent the disease.

However, in the 1930s, people had found that thyroid was enough to prevent atherosclerosis, and at the same time, it lowered cholesterol. Over the last 10 or 15 years, a Swedish doctor named Uffe Ravnskov has shown beautifully that there is no causal connection between atherosclerosis, heart disease, and the triglycerides and cholesterol in the blood. The experiments done in the 30s showed that hypothyroidism and the associated changes were what caused the atherosclerosis. The cholesterol seems to be there as a defensive reaction to protect the injured blood vessels.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on the difference between saturated and unsaturated fats for the listeners?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It refers to the chain of carbon atoms in the fatty acid. In one case, they have all of the hydrogen atoms attached to them that are possible; they are saturated with hydrogen. If some of the carbon atoms lack the hydrogen, the absence makes them more flexible. Instead of being like a bottle brush bristling with hydrogen surrounding the chain of carbons, it's more like a necklace of beads—flexible.

Where the hydrogens are missing, the bonds can rotate more freely. If you get two, three, or five of those double bonds, the chain is bent at each place. You can get very flexible shapes when you have the highly unsaturated molecules.

You can see that flexibility when you put a bottle of oil in the refrigerator. Coconut oil is hard even at room temperature. Olive oil has to be much cooler before it starts solidifying because it's relatively saturated. Canola and corn oil have to be extremely cold before they solidify.

This is biologically important. If an organism lives at 40 degrees Fahrenheit and contained butterfat, its fats would be solid and unmanageable. In the tropics, even fish in the Amazon river have fat as saturated as butterfat. Chocolate and coconuts grow in places averaging close to 90 degrees, so they need to have very saturated fat just for the biochemical manipulation of the molecules. If you had unsaturated fat in a fish in the Amazon river, the fish would oxidize its fats in just a couple of days.

Even with a medium unsaturated oil, such as soy or corn oil, if you put a rubber hose into a cork in the top of a bottle and put the other end in a cup of water, leaving the bottle at room temperature, the water will rise up the tube as the oil consumes oxygen. It's a constant process. If you raise it to body temperature (98 degrees), the process is much faster, and you have sticky, rancid oil very quickly.

**Josh Rubin:** Most Western medicine literature talks about cholesterol and heart disease. What are your thoughts on atherosclerosis and heart disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) that we unavoidably get in our diet are constantly breaking down, producing free radicals and tending to cause inflammation and tissue injury. If anything is disturbing the metabolism of a cell, that's more likely to happen.

For example, normal oxidation through the mitochondrion keeps electrons tightly controlled. But if you take away some of the oxygen, the electrons will escape as free radical potentiators. Any stress on a cell puts out these electrons that can attack the exposed electron bonds in unsaturated fats. Saturated fats aren't open for stray electrons.

Every time you are limited in your delivery of oxygen to a cell, you're putting the unsaturated fats in the way of these stray electrons. Those start chain reactions that form lumps of material called age pigment or lipofuscin. These oxidized fat fragments attach to proteins and collect bits of iron. These lumps of age pigment, because of their iron and fat fragments, are able to catalyze the consumption of energy and waste oxygen. This accelerates the process because the real mitochondrion is further deprived of oxygen.

Before that happens, signals go out changing the conditions of the organism—activating hormones such as cortisol, estrogen, and growth hormones. These three hormones are closely connected to rising triglycerides and damage to the blood vessel wall. Cortisol increases estrogen, estrogen increases cortisol, and they both increase growth hormone. All of these tend to break down triglycerides into free fatty acids, which are more reactive and tend to become oxidized more quickly.

**Josh Rubin:** Why is cholesterol so important for our physiology, and why does it go up when one is stressed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pituitary senses something wrong in the organism and increases its ACTH, which drives the adrenal glands to take up cholesterol and synthesize it from raw materials. It directs the cholesterol into the mitochondrion to turn it into pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, and finally cortisol.

Cortisol has a short-term defensive reaction against stress. One of its main effects is to turn protein into sugar for energy. But if you keep your cortisol up too long, you'll destroy too much of your protein tissues. Before the cortisol stage, the adrenal tissue will first produce pregnenolone, progesterone, and DHEA. It's only when those aren't enough that the progesterone will be converted into cortisol.

So, the increased production of cholesterol itself is a primitive defensive anti-stress system. Starting around 1920, people found that if they gave a lethal dose of poison to an animal—everything from pus to snake venom to heavy metals—if they gave it a good dose of cholesterol, it would survive. Cholesterol has a direct activating effect on producing more defensive steroids and interfering with the toxic effects of chemical and physical stresses. It is an incredibly broad-spectrum protective substance.

**Josh Rubin:** With most people, cholesterol goes up and never comes down. Is that a conversion issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40 years ago, researchers found that if thyroid hormone and Vitamin A nutrition were adequate, the amount of progesterone coming out of an ovary or adrenal gland exactly corresponded to the amount of cholesterol going in. A very big portion of the cholesterol is being turned into protective hormones. But it depends on thyroid and Vitamin A.

The higher your thyroid function, the more cholesterol you're consuming. In the 1930s, someone noticed that when the thyroid gland had been removed, cholesterol immediately went up. When they gave a thyroid supplement, the cholesterol would decrease. The blood cholesterol was a mirror image of their thyroid function.

If you have, say, a 500 mg cholesterol level, you can bring it down in a week to 200 or 180 just by giving frequent small doses of a quick-acting thyroid. That is protective because it allows them to produce progesterone and pregnenolone.

If you lack something needed to turn energy into cholesterol—for example, sugar—or if you are overloaded with unsaturated fats, you might not produce enough cholesterol. Sometimes a supplement of sugar is needed to bring up your production of cholesterol. You don't want your cholesterol to get below 160. Studies have shown that very low cholesterol levels make you susceptible to developing cancer, accidents, homicides, and suicide.

**Josh Rubin:** Some people say when they start following your philosophy, their cholesterol actually goes up. Is that because they are producing more T3 and utilizing more?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No one is really sure what the optimal level of cholesterol is. Looking at old people in rest homes, the ones that lived the longest had pretty high cholesterol—I think 270 was the number that corresponded to the longest survival. In the Framingham study, people over the age of 50 who didn't have at least a 200 cholesterol level were more likely to develop dementia. In a study of violence, violent offenders were clearly connected with cholesterol levels below 180.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you elaborate on pregnenolone's effects on our brain chemistry?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several signals can tell your brain that you're suffering stress. Low blood sugar is one. Stress acts on the stability regulators of brain cells. GABA is a sleep-inducing peptide, a fragment of the amino acid glutamic acid. Glutamic acid excites the brain. If you take off the acid, it becomes Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid (GABA), which sedates the brain.

A stressed brain will activate enzymes to produce GABA to turn off the excitation. Valium acts on the GABA stabilizing system. If something is preventing glutamic acid from being turned into sufficient GABA, Valium will fill in.

Progesterone and pregnenolone act on the GABA receptor system. Pregnenolone is basically a stabilizer at all levels of cells in the brain. Its effect is to imitate Valium, telling your pituitary that the stress is under control and to stop producing so much cortisol.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend using a supplement of pregnenolone to help balance that and lower cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on how far the system has deteriorated. Russians found that giving isolated mitochondria pregnenolone would structurally restore damaged mitochondria and allow them to begin producing more pregnenolone. This is a positive feedback loop: you give it some, and it makes more.

Ordinarily, you can make enough from converting sugar to cholesterol, and with thyroid and Vitamin A, converting cholesterol to other hormones. But when you have been poisoned with unsaturated oils or heavy metals, it helps to use all supports possible: thyroid supplements, pregnenolone, possibly DHEA and progesterone, saturated fats, sugar, and salt.

**Josh Rubin:** Why is growth hormone inflammatory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Most research is designed to praise its beneficial effects, but people who have been chronically deficient in it have a remarkable absence of atherosclerosis. Mice that are genetically deficient in pituitary hormones have no growth hormone; they aren't very big, but they live two or three times as long as normal mice.

When you have hypoglycemia, you increase your growth hormone, and it tends to come with other pituitary stress-responsive hormones. They are all harmful when they go on too long. People with gigantism or acromegaly have an extremely high incidence of atherosclerosis.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you explain the difference between HDL and LDL?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Both are able to participate in detoxification. The protein that helps to carry the cholesterol has specific anti-stress and antiviral activity.

The LDL is mostly the one that carries cholesterol into the places where it's needed: the brain, ovaries, testicles, adrenal glands, and skin. The HDL has some more specific anti-toxic effects. Toxins will tend to increase the HDL relative to the LDL. Chlorinated hydrocarbons, radiation, estrogen, and alcohol will increase HDL relative to LDL because of its anti-toxic effects.

**Josh Rubin:** How does lack of light cause an increase in cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Someone took blood samples every 15 minutes during the night. As soon as the lights went off, cortisol began rising. It shows that the stress system recognizes immediately that darkness is stress.

It seems that intrinsic oxidation and free radical production get out of control in proportion to the exposure to darkness. When you measure cytochrome oxidase—the enzyme that delivers food electrons to oxygen—during darkness, it degrades. After 12 to 15 hours of darkness, mitochondria swell up and some explode.

Cytochrome oxidase contains copper in the blue state of oxidation. Blue copper absorbs red light. Red light passes freely through tissue and is delivered to the copper in the oxidative enzyme, restoring the copper to its proper functional role. That's apparently what is lost during exposure to darkness. The enzyme wears out in the dark and needs to be recharged by light.

**Josh Rubin:** I have a listener question: "It is possible to live entirely without eating fats because your body can make all the saturated fat it needs. What's the importance of consuming saturated fats?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One thing is that it makes the food much pleasanter to eat. It makes it digest more efficiently. Experiments with a loop of intestine found that digestion was poor until you had proteins, carbohydrates, and fats present at the same time. It’s a signal of satisfaction that helps to lower stress.

In experiments with rats using a purified diet, when saturated fats were added, they had cancer-free results similar to fat-free diets. It's a very small amount of unsaturated fat that is responsible for stress and cancer production—about a teaspoonful per day is enough to show a threshold increase in cancer.

When we eat natural foods, we're always getting some unsaturated fats. It's hard to get below that threshold. That is one argument for using carbohydrates as a major part of your energy supply. If we have extra carbohydrates, they will turn into saturated fats and extend the proportion, effectively lowering the unsaturated proportion below the carcinogenic threshold.

**Caller (JP):** I have a friend who contracted HIV. I recommended saturated fat and aspirin, but his CD4 and CD8 counts dropped. Do you have something to help him? What about niacinamide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People with HIV often have very high polyunsaturated fats circulating. Niacinamide is something that will help lower the free fatty acids. Sugar, niacinamide, and aspirin are all things that help to lower the stress and keep the immune system up.

**Josh Rubin:** You are a huge proponent of coconut oil. Can you elaborate on why?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Any of the saturated fats have an anti-inflammatory, protective effect. A group studying liver disease found that fish oils and seed oils increase liver inflammation and fibrosis. This can be blocked by saturated fats.

Coconut oil is in the medium chain length. The shortness of the chain means it is very mobile. Shorter saturated fats can be handled in the mitochondria without relying on the transport systems needed for longer chains. They can be oxidized as easily as glucose. They interfere with the anti-metabolic effects of unsaturated fats.

Unsaturated fats interfere with thyroid function at all points—secretion, transport, and cellular response. Coconut oil gets in the way of these suppressive effects, especially in the mitochondrion where it is quickly burned for energy.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about coconut oil's effect on the pancreas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Bernardo Houssay saw that the pituitary would activate the adrenals to increase cortisol and raise blood sugar, while the pancreas was making insulin to lower blood sugar. Coconut oil and sugar worked very similarly to keep the system working to allow insulin both to function and to be produced.

**Josh Rubin:** Why is milk so important? Many nutritionists say it's inflammatory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the calcium content makes it anti-inflammatory. Calcium increases the oxygen-using ability of the mitochondria, similar to thyroid. Systemically, it suppresses the parathyroid hormone (PTH).

PTH is a stress hormone that, when continued too long, contributes to degenerative diseases. Having a chronically high calcium intake gives you a chronically low parathyroid level. Keeping PTH down protects your arteries, kidneys, and bones, and allows your insulin to keep free fatty acids under control.

**Josh Rubin:** Why are eggs an important staple?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With the industrialization of the egg industry, the cholesterol content went down and the polyunsaturated content went up. If you can get non-industrial eggs from chickens that have pastures, they are much better. The cholesterol in the egg seems to be one of its important nutritional values. About 600 milligrams of cholesterol in your diet increases the oxidative stability of your lipid particles in your bloodstream.

**Caller (Danny Roddy):** A lot of people in the Paleo sphere are under the impression that free fatty acids in the blood are a good thing. Can you explain why that might be harmful to the liver and thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's my main argument against eating a high meat diet. Free fatty acids are one of the means by which stress causes its damage. I've known people eating two or three pounds of meat a day who were getting sicker as their free fatty acids increased.

Just about everything that goes wrong involves free fatty acid increase. If they are totally saturated fatty acids, such as from coconut oil, those are less harmful, but they still tend to shift the mitochondrial metabolism away from using glucose and fructose, lowering carbon dioxide production.

**Caller (Liam):** What does cholesterol have to do with mitochondrial respiration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First, it stabilizes it and protects it against free fatty acids. Besides stabilizing, it actually stimulates respiration and oxygen consumption. It functions as an antioxidant.

The proteins that make up the mitochondrion have a very liquid property. If you remove all the oil-soluble materials, you still have a mitochondrion there, which shows the membrane is really a protein structure. That protein structure is reinforced and stabilized by binding with cholesterol molecules.

**Caller (415):** Coconut oil sometimes makes people feel sick or achy. Is that because of the salicylates? Is it better to get refined oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I recommend the completely deodorized coconut oil. The research was always done with the filtered kind that had no odor. Some people are allergic to the aromatic, tasty things in the coconut. Making it completely odorless is safest. It just takes a spoonful of the very odorous stuff to make me sick for about three days.

**Josh Rubin:** Could it be that people aren't used to eating saturated fat and have an overburdened liver?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid people have very touchy gallbladders. It just takes a little grease to trigger a gallbladder reaction. Getting the estrogen down is the basic thing to help the gallbladder.

**Josh Rubin:** What is the risk of taking a statin and lowering your cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The tendency to become violent or suicidally depressed, or increasing the tendency towards dementia. It makes your red blood cells less stable. Cholesterol is an intrinsic part of chromosome and DNA function and cell division regulation.

Statins interfere with the whole chain of synthesis, including Coenzyme Q10 production. That is likely a factor in why they cause bones to rot and muscles to break down catastrophically—rhabdomyolysis.

**Josh Rubin:** To summarize, what can people do to normalize their cholesterol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A daily raw carrot will tend to lower your cortisol and estrogen. Stopping that stress will let your thyroid work better and increase progesterone, accelerating the conversion of cholesterol into protective hormones. Avoiding polyunsaturated fats is essential for your thyroid to recover. Everything that increases your metabolic rate, such as calcium and sodium, is essential.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, anything else you want to add?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The important thing is not to think of unsaturated fats as anything essential. That has never been proved. George Burr himself proved that unsaturated fats slow the metabolic rate. The increased metabolic rate from a pro-thyroid diet will increase your nutrient need for copper, selenium, and B vitamins. Your activity level governs the amount of saturated fat, carbohydrate, and protein that you need.

**Josh Rubin:** Thank you so much, Ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye.

title: EastWest Healing Milk, Calcium and Hormones
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Welcome everyone. This is Josh Rubin from East West Healing and Performance. Jeannie and Ray will be joining us in a couple of minutes. It's been a little bit of trouble getting Ray back on, but I think the break was good and we have a good show ahead of us on milk, calcium, and hormones.

Ray Peat has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon. He specializes in physiology and has taught at many schools around the U.S. and Mexico. He actually started his work with progesterone-related hormones back in 1968. As you know from reading his articles and books, he is a humble genius. You can learn more about him at raypeat.com.

Today’s show is on milk, calcium, and hormones. We’re going to be talking about dairy, the degradation of it, where it comes from, and why Ray recommends so much of it. We will talk about calcium, blood labs, parathyroid hormone, and how to regulate those levels to down-regulate inflammation.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, I guess we need to rewind a little bit. There are so many people out there that say, "Stay away from milk, we're not cows." Others say, "Only drink raw milk." Why do you think there is so much degradation of milk itself, and why are we seeing so many allergies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been interested in milk for a long time, probably 55 years or so. I've been studying the cultural antagonisms. In the 1950s, the government had been collecting samples of organisms from around the world to monitor the effects of the atom bomb tests. They wanted to know how it was accumulating in young people, so they started collecting baby teeth. The isotope that concentrated most in teeth happened to be Strontium-90.

After they had been doing that for years, it came out that Strontium-90 was causing leukemia in children, among other cancers. When that got into the news, people said, "Well, baby teeth show the radioactive isotope which is similar to calcium, and milk is rich in calcium. Milk is probably the main place babies are getting their Strontium-90." A whole wave went through the culture advising people not to drink milk.

However, already in 1956 or 1957, people had analyzed the composition of diets. They found that the fallout into the soil produced a high ratio of Strontium-90 to available calcium. Plants extracted the calcium, since that was what their cells needed, but left behind a good proportion of the strontium. When cows ate the vegetation, they again extracted a high proportion of calcium and filtered out a lot of strontium.

So, when you add it up, if you get your essential nutrients from vegetable matter rather than milk, you're getting extremely high concentrations of the fallout isotopes. Milk is a good filtering process to eliminate all kinds of contaminants. Especially in a period of high radiation, it filters out the radioactive isotopes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The United States cleaned up the commercial dairy industry 40 or 50 years ago, cutting out the use of the most dangerous insecticides that were known to cause breast cancer. In the 60s, the EPA and FDA banned the use of these insecticides around cows and dairies. Israel was slower to ban one of these insecticides, but when they did, their breast cancer rate plunged. The U.S. has been leading the world in cleaning up the milk supply, far ahead of cleaning up the meat supply. Dairy is still probably the cleanest food available.

**Josh Rubin:** In your milk article, you talked about plants producing enzymes when stressed. How do you pronounce it? Chitinases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Chitinase. That's a plant enzyme that is protective against insects, but it is strongly allergenic to any animal. In small amounts, it's produced in a stressed animal under the influence of estrogen. It's possible that is a factor in meat, eggs, and milk, but probably not in a practical sense.

The main allergens that get into the milk come from cows grazing on pastures that have allergenic weeds. That will go right into the milk. You can usually taste the funny food in the milk. Some small dairies aren't very alert to what their cows are eating, and that can cause an individual dairy's milk to be more allergenic than average.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about the validity of food intolerance labs regarding dairy? I know you talk about how having a damaged metabolism or blood sugar issues can create the mechanism in the GI system to create the intolerance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The tests for allergens are really just a vague indicator that your immune system reacts to everything you are exposed to. Usually, finding antibodies to a particular substance means that you have become tolerant to that substance. I don't pay any attention to the lab tests for allergies.

The intestine adjusts its enzymes within just a few weeks. Until your intestine has adjusted its enzymes to a new kind of diet, much of that food is going to be undigested, and it will feed bacteria rather than feeding the person. The strange new growth of bacteria will produce chemicals that can be toxic and allergenic. Much of the food sensitivity issue is just failing to adapt because they change diets too suddenly.

**Jeannie Rubin:** So you're saying when somebody introduces milk back into the diet, take it very slow to allow the body to adapt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Even if a person has lactose intolerance from a lactase deficiency, tests have found that if they drink a cup per meal or less, they don't have the diarrhea produced by drinking a pint on an empty stomach. Even if biopsies show a deficiency of the lactase enzyme, that can be induced in about two weeks just by introducing an occasional small amount of milk. The cells sense the presence of a nutrient and the enzymes are gradually induced.

Bacterial infections and inflammation can cause the loss of lactase enzymes. Experiments with supplementing thyroid or progesterone have found that you can induce or restore the lactase that has been deficient just by increasing those anti-stress hormones.

**Josh Rubin:** Does that have to do with their effect on increasing metabolism, regulating blood sugar, and down-regulating estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Inflammation is probably the basic problem there. Thyroid and progesterone, by restoring energy and normal function, bypass the inflammatory processes. Inflammation shifts the cell function to an emergency state, and you tend to lose a lot of functional enzymes in an inflamed state.

**Josh Rubin:** Why do you feel dairy is so important?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The biggest part is probably the alternatives. In 1960, the focus against milk was Strontium-90, but it turned out milk was the best food for *avoiding* Strontium-90. It's the same with industrial additives and accidental pollutants. Just about every place you look in the food industry, things are far worse than milk. Some fruits, like bananas, are one of the worst products for chemical use. But if you can find unstressed fruits, those are very free of toxins relative to most other food products.

**Josh Rubin:** It would be safe to say dairy is like a complete macronutrient—carb, protein, fat—and very balanced regarding blood sugar and inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it even contains some testosterone. Thyroid, progesterone, and testosterone are important for the young animal. In human milk, they found enough thyroid hormone that babies whose thyroids were destroyed by living near Three Mile Island during the accident didn't suffer symptoms of hypothyroidism as long as they were being breastfed.

**Jeannie Rubin:** Can you elaborate on how calcium and the parathyroid work together in assisting the body with chronic stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's a subject for a week of seminars. Calcium is potentially the thing that causes all of the problems—allergies, cancer, heart attacks—but when calcium is regulated properly, it protects against all of those things.

One of the central things in regulating calcium is parathyroid hormone (PTH). When you are deficient in calcium in your foods, your PTH increases. It keeps your blood calcium up to the proper level, but it does that by taking it out of the bones. When you eat an excess of calcium, that tends to suppress the PTH.

Since they've been doing dialysis for kidney disease, they found that if they remove the parathyroid gland entirely, they can solve many of the deadly effects of chronic kidney dialysis, such as hypertension and insomnia. When you look at the effects of PTH excess in dialysis patients, you get an idea of the range of things that eating extra calcium can correct by suppressing the hormone. Insomnia is just one of them. Probably everywhere calcium is involved in an excitatory, inflammation-promoting way, you can reverse it just by increasing the calcium in your diet.

Two vitamins are important for making the tissue handle calcium properly and lowering PTH: Vitamin K and Vitamin D. Other nutrients, like Vitamin A and niacinamide, work in the same direction, helping to balance the ratio of calcium to phosphorus.

**Josh Rubin:** There are so many people listening who think because their lab results say their calcium levels are low, they need to pump calcium. But you're saying we need to down-regulate PTH first. Can you take too much calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I often see people with a blood calcium of 11, 12, or 13 (when it should be 9 or 10). By getting them to eat *more* calcium, and maybe take Vitamin D and K, they can very quickly get their calcium down to normal. The reason it is high is generally because they are eating too much phosphate and over-driving their parathyroid hormone.

**Josh Rubin:** Could eating a lot of muscle meats and tryptophan facilitate PTH?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, many things increase the parathyroid. Serotonin has a direct action. Estrogen, cortisol, and prolactin all have promoting effects on PTH. Progesterone and thyroid are the main things that help to inhibit it.

Part of that mechanism is carbon dioxide (CO2). As CO2 is produced in the cell and flows out, it forces calcium to leave the cell. That relaxes the cell, because calcium should be outside the cell. When it's inside, it tends to excite the cell and cause inflammation and lactic acid production. PTH activates glycolysis and the formation of lactic acid. That's a big part of how it dissolves the bone to provide more calcium for the bloodstream.

Everything that shifts the balance away from lactic acid production and towards carbon dioxide production helps get the calcium back into the bloodstream and back into the bones.

**Josh Rubin:** Can we use things like baking soda or carbonated water to facilitate that process?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The exchange between bicarbonate and carbon dioxide is so quick that when you give a person a dose of sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), the exchange is quick at the cell surface of a stressed cell. You can restore a stressed cell with baking soda because the sodium will quickly get lost out the urine, leaving the body acidified with the intracellular carbon dioxide, which puts the cell back into its anti-inflammatory resting state.

**Josh Rubin:** You talk about how some people can't handle raw milk, and you actually recommend pasteurized for them. Why?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Every cow has its particular balance of bacteria. A healthy cow will have a very high bacteria count in its milk, and the individual cow will change its bacterial balance according to what it's eating and the season. If a person has a bad reaction to some of the bacteria they're getting from the cow, simply trying a different dairy might work.

I know a few people who get gas or diarrhea from most supermarket milks, but if they drink only the ultra-pasteurized milk, they tolerate that nicely. Ultra-pasteurized milk has somewhat lower vitamin content and doesn't taste as good, but some people do tolerate it better.

**Josh Rubin:** What about yogurts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first concern is to make sure it doesn't contain carrageenan and gums. Those are showing up in more foods, even roast beef. Carrageenan is a sulfated polysaccharide, similar to our own connective tissue breakdown material. It can cause acute immune reactions and is used experimentally to cause inflammation in research.

If it says it's just fermented milk yogurt, that's the safest kind. Still, it's better not to eat more than a few spoonfuls per day because any lactic acid is extra work for your liver. The liver has to consume glucose to turn lactic acid back into glucose, so it is a drain on your blood sugar reserves.

**Josh Rubin:** Why are the saturated fats in dairy important?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A liver disease research group led by A.A. Nanji demonstrated a curative effect on hepatitis and cirrhosis from adding saturated fats—from coconut oil through butter fats. Similarly, they showed that fish oils and seed oils (polyunsaturated) exacerbate liver diseases. The breakdown products of unsaturated fats produce inflammatory diseases. Just by substituting saturated fats, you have an anti-inflammatory effect.

**Josh Rubin:** Dairy is also low in iron, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. During pregnancy, the mother's estrogen causes the intestine to absorb more iron. The fetus is in a situation of low oxygen tension, so it accumulates iron. The fetus is born overcharged with iron and typically doesn't need to eat any iron for about six months to a year. Milk is designed to let the baby grow into its potentially toxic overcharge of iron.

Men, by the time they're 50, are generally overloaded with iron, which contributes to free radical oxidation and heart disease. Women are protected as long as they are menstruating. Milk and cheese are foods deficient in iron, so adding them helps prevent that chronic tendency to overcharge.

**Josh Rubin:** What about cheeses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Recently, I saw an advertisement stating that over 60% of cheeses now made use commercial cultures from bacteria and fungus as cheap substitutes for traditional methods. Almost all commercial cheeses are now risky because of those microorganisms, besides any additives for texture.

**Josh Rubin:** What about whey protein powders?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 40 or 50 years ago, dairies would give fresh liquid whey to hog farmers. It produced healthy pigs. But when it is dehydrated into a powder, the process oxidizes the fragile amino acids, including tryptophan and cysteine. This increases toxicity and allergenicity.

Also, the casein in cheese is anti-inflammatory and anti-stress. You get the opposite effect from the whey fraction. Whey is easily degraded, lacks the anti-stress factors, and is deficient in calcium.

**Josh Rubin:** A lot of people say milk makes them fat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All the research on animals, and as far as it goes with humans, shows that milk is probably the best reducing food there is. The calcium inhibits the fat-forming enzyme, fatty acid synthase. At the same time, it activates the uncoupling proteins in the mitochondria, which burn calories faster. Milk is the only food I know that does both of those things simultaneously.

**Josh Rubin:** Can a high protein diet, or a diet low in carb or fat, create overstimulation of parathyroid hormone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because most protein comes with lots of phosphate. Grains, beans, and meats are high in phosphate. The ratio between phosphate and calcium is the main thing that activates the parathyroid hormone.

**Josh Rubin:** What about osteoporosis? Does estrogen play a part?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Parathyroid hormone increases with the menstrual cycle when estrogen is dominant. Estrogen, prolactin, serotonin, and cortisol all dissolve bones. It's interesting that they promote estrogen as a bone strengthener, yet in the 50 or 60 years women have been taught to use estrogen, the rate of breaking hips has increased.

**Josh Rubin:** What are some other nutritional sources of calcium besides dairy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eggshells. If you boil your eggs to get any additives off, eggshells are the purest form of calcium carbonate. It is probably the ideal form to use as a supplement.

**Josh Rubin:** How would you recommend ingesting them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pulverize them into a powder and take a fourth to a half teaspoon if a person is not getting their milk calcium.

**Caller (520):** I haven't seen anything about fluoride on your site. Where is fluoride on your radar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I avoid fluoridated water carefully. During a stay in San Francisco, I wasn't aware the water was fluoridated and I started getting extreme hypothyroid symptoms. The water had enough fluoride to totally destroy the thyroid supplement I was taking. It just takes one fluoride atom to ruin the T3 molecule. It is a thyroid toxin. Also, studies have shown that fluoridated populations have a higher cancer rate.

**Caller (360):** I've noticed an increase in acne every time I ingest dairy. What are your thoughts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Dairy increases your metabolic rate. Calcium is a powerful stimulant to metabolism. The increased metabolic rate makes you consume Vitamin A and probably several other nutrients. Vitamin A is usually the limiting nutrient. People who do anything that increases their metabolic rate often find they need more Vitamin A. If you increase Vitamin A, you can often prevent the acne.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend plant or animal sources for Vitamin A?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Plant sources (carotenes) aren't really Vitamin A. They depend on Vitamin B12 and thyroid function to be converted. If you overload on carotenes, they can have an anti-thyroid action. I recommend liver (once a week), eggs, and milk.

**Caller (617):** A lot of anti-milk articles argue that milk drains calcium from your bones because it has a higher phosphorus-to-calcium ratio than the human body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, the ratio in milk is very high towards calcium. Even if you are eating meat (high phosphate), drinking a good amount of milk will put those phosphates into proportion. Milk is, next to eggshells, our best source of calcium.

**Caller (111):** Is there a difference between natural trans fats in dairy and synthetic ones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you heard of conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)? It has therapeutic benefits—anti-inflammatory, anti-obesity. CLA is a natural component of milk fat. The trans fats in dairy are just in process on the way to forming CLA.

Bacteria in the cow's rumen detoxify the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) from the grass. In the process, they create small amounts of trans fats and CLA. I think there is good evidence showing that these natural trans fats have a protective effect and block the toxic effects of linoleic acid (PUFA).

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, do you have anything you want to elaborate on before we shut it down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, no.

**Josh Rubin:** Ray, once again we really appreciate you taking the time out. Thanks for tuning in, everyone. You can learn more about us at EastWestHealing.com. Have a great weekend.

title: EastWest Healing Questions and Answers I
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** Alrighty, welcome back to a great show with Dr. Ray Peat. Today we're going to do a question and answer session. I know a lot of you have been awaiting this type of show. Jeannie's not going to be on the call today; it's just going to be me once again.

Let's get back to Ray Peat. He has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He has taught at many schools, from the University of Oregon to Montana State University, to naturopathic schools in Mexico. You can take a look at his website at RayPeat.com to learn more about him and his background. He started his work with progesterone and related hormones in 1968.

Ray, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Josh Rubin:** I think the first question everyone keeps emailing me about is: do you have a timeline when you're going to start taking new subscribers to the newsletter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think we changed that notice and they are available now.

**Josh Rubin:** Okay, there you go. If you want to sign up, go to his website, RayPeat.com.

**Josh Rubin:** A lot of people out there are so gung-ho crazy about probiotics. That's all you hear: "People have gas? Take probiotics. Anything wrong? Take probiotics." You don't really talk too much about probiotics. Can you elaborate on your thoughts about them, specifically Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are probably okay to try. One thing that has made me skeptical about them was an article published in *Nature* probably 35 or 40 years ago. It showed that there are antigenic regions on these lactobacilli that exactly match proteins associated with female reproductive action. From puberty to menopause, roughly, there's the risk of having an autoimmune or immunological interaction between intestinal bacteria and body tissues. There hasn't been much follow-up on that, but that is the period when autoimmune-type problems show up in women. Estrogen is probably the main factor involved in that, but it just happens that there is this antigen parallel between the bacteria and the person.

The bacteria do have a direct anti-inflammatory effect on the membranes of the intestine, but one problem is that they produce lactic acid. If you provide them with enough fuel, they can produce lactic acid, which is a potential toxin. It stimulates inflammation and the formation of collagen fibrosis.

**Josh Rubin:** I think that's the biggest thing for everyone to understand—that Lactobacillus is lactate-producing. If you take it and you don't need it, you're actually causing more of a problem than helping yourself.

**Josh Rubin:** From a health perspective, is there any time you would recommend fasting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies in which rheumatoid arthritis and similar things are completely relieved during a week-long fast. But then it would come back as soon as the person eats again. That's partly because your cortisol increases tremendously when you're not eating. What the cortisol is doing is converting your muscle tissue into fuel to live on. At the same time, it's having an anti-inflammatory effect.

However, the bowel is really the basic cause of most degenerative inflammatory diseases. So there is a good reason for thinking that fasting is therapeutic. I've seen animals with huge tumors that just refuse to eat. If their owners let them sit around not eating, they would recover and live for years. The lack of appetite during sickness is a natural opportunity to fast.

Since the bowel is so connected to inflammatory diseases—producing lactic acid, endotoxin, and a tremendous amount of serotonin—if you can lighten the inflammation load in the intestine, you can achieve the same thing as fasting while still absorbing nutrients. You just have to do it in a way that doesn't produce endotoxin, lactic acid, or serotonin excess. Partly, that means using a very easily digested diet, avoiding undercooked vegetable matter that can't be digested by human enzymes, and having other easily digested or slightly antimicrobial foods. Raw carrots or boiled bamboo shoots, for example, have germicides that prevent bacterial growth.

**Caller:** It's really popular these days to approach eating based on what we evolved to eat, like the blood type diet and the paleo diet. What do you think about this approach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That whole approach assumes that we really know what the species ate while evolving. There are a lot of fantasy theories. Whatever people enjoy eating, they tend to read into the history of human evolution. No one is really sure what people were eating.

There is direct present experimental evidence that supports fruit eating better than some of the currently popular ideas, such as Cunnane's ideas about fish eating. I think fruit eating was a good candidate for supporting evolution to be more human than ape-like, supporting a big brain and the kind of digestive system we have.

**Caller:** I've noticed that people who are really cerebral or have jobs where they use their brains a lot seem to have a lower tolerance for stress, particularly if they are exercising or doing a low-carb regimen. Do people who place a lot of mental demands on themselves have different nutritional needs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some people have commented that the brain of the average person might weigh 2% of their body weight, but it uses 40% or 50% of their metabolic energy. If a person has a bigger-than-average brain—and human brains vary tremendously in size and metabolic requirements—and if they spend a great amount of mental energy compared to the average, you can see what a tremendous metabolic difference that can make.

**Caller:** Is there a way to attenuate the ill effects of high-intensity interval exercise or heavy weightlifting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was an experiment 30 years ago where they had people walk on a treadmill and didn't let their heart rate go over 120 beats per minute. They measured their active thyroid hormone, T3, at the beginning and after 40 minutes. The average person's T3 had gone to zero in just 40 minutes of moderate exercise.

Normally, as soon as you have some sugar—if your liver had a lot of glycogen—it would replenish the T3 quickly. But the longer the stress is, and the more inhibitors there are in your tissues (like polyunsaturated fats) or bad bacteria in your intestine, the more it delays the recovery of your liver and T3 production. With some people, it just takes a little extra stress to stick you down in that low T3 condition.

**Caller:** Finally, what is your favorite joke? Or barring that, what did you eat yesterday?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What I ate yesterday would be easier than remembering a joke. I had steak—it happened to be rib steak day—eggs, lots of milk, coffee, orange juice, and Coke.

**Caller (Sandy Soto):** I'm calling to know your thoughts on the connection between schizophrenia and hypothyroidism, as well as nutritional deficiencies like niacin and copper. Also, how much does gluten intolerance have to do with that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since the intestine is involved in everything, gluten is one of the basic things that will cause problems once you get sensitized to it. High estrogen is one of the things that sensitizes the intestine and system to gluten. The transglutaminase enzyme is activated by estrogen and activates the immune reactions that can cause celiac disease, psoriasis, arthritis, and is now known to be involved in causing cancer and brain conditions, including schizophrenia.

Stopping the inflammatory process is the basic thing. I think that was behind the orthomolecular approach to treating schizophrenia—the niacin approach. I think [Abram] Hoffer was opening up a whole area of science that is valid: that you can treat schizophrenia metabolically.

One of the basic effects of niacin is to inhibit the release of free fatty acids from our tissue stores. Free fatty acids poison our energy apparatus. You've probably noticed how schizophrenics almost always are heavy smokers. Nicotine happens to have a brain-protective and therapeutic effect against a lot of degenerative inflammatory diseases. I think that's because it overlaps with the niacin pathways that are natural energy producers.

I don't have any particular therapeutic ideas for schizophrenia, but keeping the thyroid function up so that energy is supported, keeping toxins down, and avoiding polyunsaturated fats and intestinal irritants like gluten and indigestible starches will help.

**Caller:** Would you say that hypothyroidism would be the greatest factor in schizophrenia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would guess that the conditions under which it comes on—puberty is a major time for schizophrenia—is when rising hormones very often interfere with thyroid function.

**Caller:** What about coconut sugar? Is that an okay sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never tried it, but if it's extracted from the sap or the core of the tree, it's likely fine. If it's made from the starch chemically, I would have to know the process. If it starts with a natural sugar extract, it's going to be fine. But if it's processed heavily with heat and chemical catalysts, it can leave irritating residues.

**Caller:** What is your approach to parasites?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on the kind. The old-timers 100 years ago commonly used a spoonful of flowers of sulfur maybe once a year. A huge dose like that will pretty much clean out any kind of parasite. I've experimented with very small amounts of flowers of sulfur; it has a fungicidal effect. If there's a mild yeast infection, a pinch a day for two or three days will clear that out. Sometimes that is enough to discourage amoebas and worms. It's very safe for people in small amounts.

**Caller:** Is it possible that parasites could contribute to autoimmune functions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people think they have a beneficial effect on the immune system, but I'm not convinced. I'm inclined toward the Metchnikov side, which sees the immune system as a developmental process rather than specific chemotherapy against organisms. In Africa, for example, a lot of the so-called AIDS is really just from being exposed to too many stimulants of the immune system.

**Josh Rubin:** What could it mean if someone is just sweating all the time, even from an early age?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes it's a developmental overbalance of the parasympathetic or sympathetic nervous system. Either way can activate your sweat glands. Sometimes hypothyroid people compensate with extremely high adrenaline production, and that can cause sweating even when they're not hot.

**Caller:** I believe I picked up parasites in 2006 while swimming. I had symptoms similar to low thyroid and tested positive for Hashimoto's. Years later, I passed a two-foot tapeworm. I'm still having digestion and energy problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you had tests specifically looking for various parasites?

**Caller:** The first tapeworm tests came back negative even though I was putting segments of worms in the stool samples.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are doctors who specialize in that, especially in coastal tropical areas.

**Josh Rubin:** I would recommend Metametrix (GI Effects profile).

**Caller:** Is there anything to look at for restoring digestive function if I get rid of the parasites?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Diet to keep your metabolic rate up, and if necessary, a thyroid supplement. If your metabolic rate is low, you'll tend to get infections. Fungal infections really tend to specialize in hypothyroid people. It's the same with intestinal parasites; the IgA antibodies on membranes in the intestine are deficient in people who are low thyroid, so all membranes are susceptible to attack.

**Josh Rubin:** There is so much in our industry about fungal infections. Doug Kaufmann promotes the fungal diet, saying mycotoxins feed on sugar, so take out sugar to starve them. I know you have a different view.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I used to read about people who got drunk when they ate sugar because yeast were growing in their stomach. Their digestive enzymes were so weak that the organisms weren't killed by stomach acid. But getting drunk is really the only major harm done by that. The real problem is that their digestion is poor from being low thyroid. Taking thyroid to activate digestive enzymes would probably spontaneously get rid of the yeast.

René Dubos did experiments showing that when yeast in the intestine is starved for sugar, it sends out pseudo-hyphae filaments long enough to reach through the intestine wall to get sugar from the bloodstream. They actually become invasive when starved. If you feed them sugar, they don't put out those adhesive, invasive filaments. So a sugarless diet is really a dangerous thing for someone with a yeast problem.

Also, when you avoid sugar, you risk not giving your liver the sugar it needs to activate the thyroid hormone, making the hypothyroid problem worse. Fungus loves unsaturated fat but can be killed by saturated fats.

**Caller:** What is your feeling on liver flushes and general cleansing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There were experiments on cattle showing that while 30-35% had toxins in muscle and fat, only 6-7% had toxins in their liver. The liver has the equipment for excreting toxins. It is the cleanest organ. If you slow down the liver's activity—which happens in a fast—your brain and other organs are exposed to chemicals diffusing out of your fat and muscles. The best cleansing diet is one that increases your liver's action. Tasty food, sugar, and thyroid are the main things that activate the liver.

**Caller:** What about swollen feet in a relatively young person?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They probably also have puffy eyelids and faces when they wake up. That's from excess permeability of their blood vessels. Water leaks out into the tissues. Sometimes all it takes is eating enough salt to make your albumin function to bind water and keep it in your blood vessels. People on a low-salt diet are very susceptible to that.

In pregnancy or premenstrually, high estrogen and low thyroid make blood vessels permeable. Albumin can't retain sodium. In one experiment with women with toxemia, they gave them over 20 grams of salt extra per day and almost immediately cured their symptoms.

**Josh Rubin:** There's a lot of bad hype about fructose being turned into fat. Why do you recommend utilizing fruits?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ideal amount of fructose seems to be maybe a third as much as glucose. What fructose does in the cell is raise the metabolic rate, increase the production of carbon dioxide, and catalyze the ability to burn glucose. It's a catalyst that increases cell activity in constructive ways.

Experiments comparing sugar or Coke to starch found that sugar improved calcium assimilation, increased metabolic rate, and decreased obesity. There was something like a 50% increase in the ability to burn calories with a sucrose-based diet. The calcium-sparing effect of sucrose or fructose comes from that metabolic stimulating effect, imitating active thyroid hormone which produces carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide keeps calcium in the bones where it should be.

**Caller:** If a person is healthy, is the majority of tryptophan converted to niacin? Can they eat muscle meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The high phosphorus content in meat is important. The ratio of calcium to phosphorus should be very high. If you're under stress, phosphate becomes more of a problem. Meat and whole grains are major sources of phosphate. You have to be concerned with your calcium intake if you have a meat or grain-based diet. Women are much more susceptible to pellagra because estrogen decreases the production of niacin from tryptophan and sends it down the serotonin pathway.

**Caller:** What about spices? My girlfriend is craving garlic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main problem with onion and garlic is if you're allergic to them. Low thyroid people often have symptoms like gallbladder spasms, especially if the garlic and onion are cooked.

**Caller:** Can you elaborate on Cytomel (T3) and thyroxine (T4) dosing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ideally, the body should make 4 or 5 micrograms of T3 per hour. If you take much more than 10 micrograms at once, your liver activates enzymes to destroy or excrete it. If you take 10 micrograms with a meal, the food delays absorption, so you get maybe 2 or 3 micrograms each hour. That is a smooth way to take it.

Just occasionally, someone might need to get their cholesterol down quickly and use frequent 5 microgram doses. But someone with a heart condition doesn't want to take more than one microgram at a time. The trouble with relying on thyroxine (T4) is that in women, estrogen often keeps the liver from making as much T3 as you need.

**Caller:** Raw vs. cooked foods?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With animal products, cooking kills parasites. There's no nutritional benefit to cooking meat, but safety is the issue. With fruit like an apple, it contains a huge amount of pectin which isn't digestible by humans but feeds bacteria. Cooking breaks this down.

There was an experiment in the 1940s where rats on a diet of canned vegetables thrived, while those on raw vegetables didn't.

**Caller:** What about enzymes in raw food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The production of pancreatic digestive enzymes isn't a stress; it's a natural function. I don't think there's any benefit to supplementing extra enzymes for the pancreas's sake.

**Caller:** My four-year-old had leukemia. His CO2 levels are low (16-19). Doctors want to use bicarbonate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Baking soda (bicarbonate) is very helpful. It helps regulate minerals and can bring up systemic CO2. But the most effective thing is to check the thyroid function, which controls CO2 production. 16 to 19 is too low.

**Caller:** He also has chronic diarrhea. We feed him squash, spinach, green leafy vegetables.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Are the vegetables well cooked? Salads are a problem for lots of people. They cause diarrhea or constipation.

**Caller:** I was diagnosed with MS eight years ago. I get fungal infections, white spots in the throat, itchy skin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Most of the first five or six people I saw with an MS diagnosis recovered instantly when they took thyroid. A common symptom of low thyroid is enlargement of the pituitary because of a prolactin-secreting tumor. That can cause pressure on the optic nerve and is often misdiagnosed as brain disease.

In well-diagnosed MS, they know that endotoxin is a very important factor in causing blood vessels in the head to be too permeable. Endotoxin can be drastically reduced just by eating a good-sized raw carrot every day. Getting enough protein (at least 80 grams) is also very important.

**Josh Rubin:** Does the body go through a detox when starting a pro-thyroid diet? Will cholesterol go up?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person has low cholesterol, they shouldn't start a thyroid supplement full force. You need cholesterol to make hormones. Fruit is the best way to raise cholesterol.

If you are just starting a diet change, improvement is gradual. The first thing is to lower toxin production in the intestine (cut out undercooked starches/salads, use carrot fiber). Avoid polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) because they block thyroid hormone production.

Rising cholesterol usually means the liver is getting enough energy to make it, and that toxins have gone down. Cholesterol is a protective, adaptive substance. A Framingham study found that people over 50 with cholesterol under 200 were more likely to have dementia.

**Caller:** Any advice for learning a second language?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin B1 and coffee can make a tremendous difference. When I learned French to pass my graduate exam, I did it over a weekend with plenty of coffee and a few hundred milligrams of Vitamin B1. I sat down and memorized 4,000 words. B1 makes you produce energy faster and increases circulation to the brain.

**Caller:** What about phytoestrogens in coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hops in beer are estrogenic. But coffee has many good things; it is a major dietary source of niacin and magnesium.

**Josh Rubin:** What is the upper limit for raw liver, and what about raw eggs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You're less likely to catch an infection if they're cooked. They should be lightly cooked. Exposure to oxygen breaks down the polyunsaturated fats. Eating them raw doesn't protect you from the PUFA.

**Josh Rubin:** How much liver do you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Six ounces once a week is enough. If I eat 6 or 8 ounces of liver with ordinary foods, I often wake up with low blood sugar. I've learned to cook it in a large amount of butter or coconut oil. It's so high in protein that it disturbs blood sugar if you don't have fat and sugar with it.

**Josh Rubin:** What do you think about the therapeutic potential of tryptamine drugs like psilocybin and LSD?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In early studies, patients reported their migraines disappeared after LSD sessions. Migraines were identified as an excess serotonin problem. LSD acted as an antagonist to serotonin.

Because the government demonized hallucinogens, the pharmaceutical industry wanted to distance their antidepressants from them. They created the myth that serotonin is a "happy drug" you want to increase. Actually, it's the misery drug. Excess serotonin produces nausea, diarrhea, high blood pressure, fibrosis, and dementia.

LSD-type drugs imitate serotonin in a way that triggers the feedback system to turn off the nerves that make serotonin. So their basic function is anti-serotonergic. Research is starting up again recognizing that these drugs work by being anti-serotonin.

**Caller:** Perspective on sunscreens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some are directly carcinogenic. There is a phobia about ultraviolet light. It's best to get sunlight but avoid sunburn. Experiments on rabbits showed that animals on a saturated fat diet weren't hurt by sunlight, while those on unsaturated fats got sun-damaged skin. The polyunsaturated fats in your skin act like an amplifier for damage. You can apply coconut oil or a solution of aspirin to the skin for protection.

**Caller:** How do you take gelatin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you eat it undissolved, it causes gas. I mix sugar with it, moisten it, heat it until clear, and add orange juice to make gummy candies. Or I use it in mousses or soups.

**Caller:** Is wireless internet a source of radiation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I don't use wireless things; I have wire connections. Cell phones and WiFi are a serious dose of radiation that affects nerve function and probably increases brain cancer incidence.

**Josh Rubin:** That does it for today. Ray, anything new going on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My recent email talks about biological processes excluded from science. There are lectures on the internet by Luca Turin on how molecules and cells interact, and Gerald Pollock on the structure of water. It's bringing back "quantum biology"—the idea that interactions of hormones and drugs can be understood on the electronic level rather than the mechanical lock-and-key conception.

**Josh Rubin:** Great show. Thanks for tuning in. Check out our website, EastWestHealing.com. Thanks, Ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye.

title: EastWest Healing Questions and Answers II
transcriptText:
**Josh Rubin:** All right everyone, welcome to today's show with Ray Peat, Ph.D. I want to thank everyone for tuning in. Check our website at eastwesthealing.com if you want to learn more about what we do. We have a lot of free information there, including our "Metabolic Blueprint" program launching soon.

Today we are doing a question and answer show with Ray Peat. If you want to learn more about Ray, his website is RayPeat.com. He has tons of articles, books you can order, and a newsletter that is well worth the money. Ray has his Ph.D. in Biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He started his work with progesterone-related hormones in 1968 and wrote his dissertation in 1972 outlining his ideas regarding progesterone as a protector of the body's structure and energy against the harmful effects of estrogen, radiation, stress, and lack of oxygen.

Ray has been incredibly generous with his time answering emails from listeners. If you feel inclined, sending a donation or a gift to his house to say thank you would be greatly appreciated. Ray, are you on the line?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Josh Rubin:** Is there anything else you want to add before we get going?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that covered everything.

**Josh Rubin:** I have a lot of questions here. I’ve been getting many questions regarding iron. Could you give a summary of your thoughts on the dangers of iron? You believe it acts like a heavy metal and is toxic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Wherever iron gets loose, it is available to react with things like polyunsaturated fats (PUFA), proteins, and nucleic acids. The reactive form of iron is the reduced *ferrous* form rather than the fully oxidized *ferric* form.
