This means that if you don't get enough oxygen to your tissues, the iron tends to get reduced by glutathione.

People talk about oxidative stress, but *reductive* stress is really what you have to worry about in relation to iron. Alcohol, for example, interferes with the use of oxygen and causes reduced glutathione to accumulate. This shifts the ratio towards reduction, activates iron by reducing it to the reactive ferrous form, and causes damage.

Iron accumulates faster than it should under the influence of estrogen. Inability to use oxygen properly intensifies the absorption of iron, and that seems to be what estrogen is for—to create the illusion of oxygen deprivation so that you absorb more iron. They’ve tested the absorption of iron in women versus men, and women absorbed nine times as much iron. That is primarily the influence of estrogen.

Unfortunately, besides making the body absorb it, estrogen also tends to create the conditions that make iron toxic. One of the main things that activated iron attacks is polyunsaturated fatty acids. This creates a vicious circle: estrogen increases the most reactive PUFAs, which activate and increase the quantity of estrogen. Both contribute to the activation and intensification of iron toxicity. You can break the cycle by donating blood or doing things to interrupt the estrogen-fatty acid cycle.

**Josh Rubin:** What would be a normal lab value for iron? If you have low hemoglobin, is it safe to donate blood?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is no blood test I know of that will really say anything meaningful about your iron status because iron tends to hide in the liver and bone marrow. The fact that an iron supplement increases red blood cell count or hemoglobin doesn't mean the person was deficient in iron. They used to treat anemia with doses of arsenic; the arsenic creates stress that tells your body you need more iron and blood. Any stress that interferes with oxygen use will drive up the blood production system.

**Josh Rubin:** When you see low hemoglobin, would that be due to estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In all animals that have estrogen, the female tends to look slightly anemic because estrogen slows the production of red blood cells, partly by lowering body temperature and slowing thyroid function. Probably the most common cause of apparent anemia, as Broda Barnes pointed out, is hypothyroidism. He mentioned an experiment where rats—whose tailbones normally don't make red blood cells—had their tails stitched into the abdomen to keep them at core body temperature. They quickly began producing red blood cells just by raising the temperature. So, the safest way to treat anemia might be to wear long wool socks to warm the extremities.

**Josh Rubin:** What is copper's role in regards to iron?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Its primary role is in the respiratory enzyme cytochrome oxidase. I think that is the reason copper is essential for constructing the hemoglobin molecule.

**Josh Rubin:** So you feel that most people actually have higher amounts of iron stored in the liver and bone marrow, which is toxic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In men, it accumulates continuously with aging. Menstruation probably helps women avoid the accumulation until they stop menstruating, and then the curve is perhaps even steeper than men's. I think menstruation is one of the factors that makes women have greater longevity.

There was a study of immigrant fruit pickers' children in California. They didn't get a "good" diet, but they ate lots of oranges. They had an average hemoglobin of 10—which is considered tending towards anemia—but they didn't get infectious diseases like the well-fed city kids who had high hemoglobin. They've seen the same thing in Africa; when they campaigned to give iron supplements, malaria rates spiked because iron activates the growth of germs and weakens the immune system.

One meaningful blood test is iron saturation. People tend to be resistant to cancer development if the saturation is somewhat low, around 25%.

**Caller (Chris):** Regarding ADD and ADHD, we've seen a rise in diagnoses. Do you feel sugar is the problem, or is it polyunsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's the unsaturated fats. Sugar tends to move everything in the right direction, away from brain malfunction. Polyunsaturated fats interfere with attention and increase adrenaline, the sympathetic nervous system, and stress hormones. That, along with hypothyroidism, keeps the front part of the brain from getting enough energy to focus.

**Caller (Chris):** Regarding Hashimoto's disease, can you explain the proper way for it to be diagnosed? I realize the anti-thyroid antibodies found in blood sometimes don't have any relation to the thyroid gland.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those antibodies interact with the cartilage of the joints just about as well as with the thyroid. It's really a connective tissue inflammatory disease which goes with hypothyroidism. The cartilage is one of the first places you see hypothyroidism in children; it accounts for why hypothyroid kids tend to be knock-kneed. The cartilage in the knees and elbows is basically swollen.

**Josh Rubin:** So people are being misdiagnosed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The whole idea of autoimmune disease is off the mark. I think of the immune system as a clean-up system. The antibodies help the phagocytes remove debris. If the debris is caused by low thyroid causing the connective tissue to swell, the immune system has to come in and try to clean out the junk.

**Caller:** How long would it take for someone with a low body temperature (mid-97s) to stabilize if they institute your recommendations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen a couple of people do it in three or four days. Very skinny people who had been on a pure soy/tofu diet—as soon as they started eating eggs and oranges, they popped right up.

**Caller:** I read Hans Selye's work. He seems to believe we have an absolute reserve of energy to deal with stress and that any stressful event depletes this. Is that correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think where he left it is where the issue of the cumulative buildup of iron and PUFA comes in. Both long-chain polyunsaturated fats and iron accumulate with aging, stress, and under the influence of estrogen. Selye wasn't looking far enough to see how those factors interacted with stress.

During prolonged adaptation, estrogen, growth hormone, and inflammatory mediators accumulate. Estrogen buildup blocks thyroid function and begins to directly drive the adrenal gland. When that reaches a certain point, you can get bleeding in the adrenal gland and death of the cortical cells just from an excess of estrogen. The systemic effect of stress is what he neglected to think about when he talked about the innate reserve of energy.

**Josh Rubin:** In a 2006 newsletter, you discussed Metchnikoff and argued that inflammation was a pathological reaction rather than a healthy part of a defensive immune system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Metchnikoff saw the white blood cells going in and curing the problem—clearing up the mess. But after the medical establishment took it over, they created the idea of inflammation—the swelling, redness, and pain—as the curative process. I think these are pathological.

The immune system should work like it does in the prenatal state. In the embryonic and fetal state, injury is corrected without inflammation. The cells just repair the damage efficiently and don't leave a scar. When you keep carbon dioxide and sugar where they should be, you basically get fetal or embryonic healing without a scar and without inflammation. I see inflammation as an inability to deliver what's needed to repair the damage.

**Josh Rubin:** I have questions about weight loss. People follow your philosophies, notice their energy goes up, but they gain weight. Can you elaborate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gaining weight probably isn't the issue; it's gaining inches and bulging. When you're doing everything right, very likely you will rebuild muscles that were damaged by stress and poor nutrition. As those muscles grow, the circumference of your thighs, hips, and belly should be decreasing even though your weight is increasing.

When I first experimented with DHEA, I noticed after a week or two that my waist seemed to be reappearing. My pants were getting looser, but I was exactly the same weight. I was simply growing more lean tissue and burning up fat. However, if someone is putting on fat—their pants are getting too tight—they are just eating too much, probably too much fat or total calories. I've mentioned averaging a gallon of milk a day at times, but that was always 1% milk.

**Josh Rubin:** What are your feelings on aromatase inhibitors like calcium D-glucarate or DIM?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically, they're usually selling powdered cabbage leaves. That has been tested and found to be somewhat estrogenic in itself.

Saturated fats antagonize the estrogen-aromatase activating effect of PUFA. Aspirin, by blocking prostaglandins and reducing inflammation, interrupts the effect of PUFA. Aspirin is a very effective aromatase inhibitor, but drug companies don't want people to know that because aspirin costs a penny. Thyroid also inhibits aromatase, as does anything that lowers cortisol.

**Josh Rubin:** Many people say coffee causes adrenal fatigue. You have the opposite view. Can you elaborate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been trying to find out who started the idea of "adrenal fatigue." Coffee contains magnesium, niacin, and B vitamins. The caffeine has an antioxidant effect. As long as you use it with food, it tends to stabilize blood sugar and reduce inflammation.

Regarding adrenal fatigue: Hans Selye took out animals' adrenal glands. If they were pregnant, they had no symptoms until they gave birth because progesterone alone covers the spectrum of adrenal hormones. With adequate Vitamin A and thyroid, you will convert cholesterol into pregnenolone and progesterone. The adrenals are also very good at repairing themselves.

**Josh Rubin:** How should people use coffee?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Taking it with or after a meal has basically none of the harmful effects. I've known people who felt shattered by a sip of coffee, but when they put heavy cream and sugar in it and took it with a meal, within three or four days they were happy coffee drinkers.

**Josh Rubin:** There is a lot of controversy claiming fructose causes diabetes and fatty liver.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just a few days ago, I heard from someone in New Zealand diagnosed with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. He started a diet that included 300 grams of fructose every day. He now has a new diagnosis: his liver has no fat problem.

The fructose phobia evolved over the last 50 or 60 years and is closely connected to the cholesterol doctrine of heart disease and the idea of essential fatty acids. The actual science showed that the so-called essential fatty acids are toxic and carcinogenic.

**Josh Rubin:** You’ve mentioned that pigs fed soy have unsaturated fat. A listener asks: if their fat is unsaturated, why is bacon solid at room temperature?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you extract the fat, it isn't solid. When I was a kid, lard was solid like butter. The lard I've seen in recent years, which is now over 30% PUFA, is soft at room temperature. The fat droplets in bacon are enclosed in cells and connected by connective tissue, so even if it was 100% PUFA, it would still have a white, firm appearance due to the structure.

**Josh Rubin:** Is time-released T3 better than basic Cytomel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've heard from people having either overdose effects or no effects from time-release. A lawyer sent me documents where they analyzed compounded time-release T3 and found *no* T3 in it. If compounded carelessly, T3 is easily destroyed. The wrong time-release agent might permanently bind the T3 or release it all at once. There hasn't been good research on how to compound time-release T3. Generally, I don't think patented brand-name medicine is a good idea, but in the case of T3, I haven't seen a good alternative to Cytomel.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend eating the carrot before, with, or after a meal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually just eating the carrot is fine. If you have low blood sugar or thyroid issues, eating it with a meal might slow digestion too much, making you feel shaky. However, if a person wants to reduce fat absorption, eating the carrot *with* the meal will accelerate weight loss.

**Josh Rubin:** Can it cause constipation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very rarely. If the intestine has been sluggish, stimulating it with the raw carrot changes the rhythm of peristalsis. It sometimes takes a week to set up a new rhythm.

**Josh Rubin:** Does adding baking soda to orange juice help increase carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you put it in acid (like juice), the baking soda will bubble off most of the carbon dioxide. Some will dissolve, and it might increase systemic CO2 a little. Experiments with bicycle racers showed that taking baking soda improved performance, either due to the sodium or the CO2.

**Josh Rubin:** If someone doesn't have a gallbladder, is coconut oil the best fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just eating things in a mixed form in small amounts is important. If you don't have a gallbladder, the bile is still there, but it comes out in dribbles rather than surges.

**Josh Rubin:** A listener feels they are having hypoglycemic reactions since starting your recommendations. Is this due to PUFA detox?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping blood sugar steady and adding saturated fat helps. Saturated fats inhibit stress hormones and the release of fat from stores. Sugar, saturated fats, niacin, and aspirin all inhibit the release of fat. You want to keep the stored fat in place while the body slowly oxidizes it.

**Josh Rubin:** What about supplements like niacinamide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Niacinamide is an anti-fat liberating substance. Usually, 100mg twice a day is all it takes.

One safe way the body eliminates stored PUFA is through the liver. The liver recognizes PUFA as toxins and will selectively attach glucuronic acid to them—just as if it were dioxin—and send them to the kidneys for excretion.

**Josh Rubin:** Can you talk about the benefits of salt, especially regarding pregnancy and eclampsia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eclampsia is closely connected to high PUFA, low thyroid, low carbon dioxide, and poor ability to retain sodium. Sodium is constantly lost, as is magnesium. As sodium is lost, the adrenals increase aldosterone to retain sodium, but at the expense of losing magnesium faster.

If you increase sodium intake, you compensate for low thyroid function and turn off the aldosterone. Lowering aldosterone reduces inflammation and stops magnesium loss. Tom Brewer showed that sodium alone would commonly cure the problem.

**Josh Rubin:** How does albumin play into this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen interferes with the liver's synthesis of albumin. Under stress, PUFAs circulate, and albumin picks them up. If albumin is loaded with fats, it passes through the kidneys into the urine. Albumin's function is to retain water in the blood. If sodium is low, albumin can't work. If albumin is low, you get water retention issues. Correcting fats, thyroid, and estrogen lets water out of the body while retaining sodium and magnesium.

**Caller:** What do you think of heavy metal detox, like IV glutathione or Vitamin C drips, after removing amalgams?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hans Selye showed that mercury plus Vitamin C prevented toxic effects in animals. Mercury in its reduced form isn't toxic; it depends on the state of reduction. Caffeine is associated with getting heavy metals out of tissues. Vitamin C from food is an important defense.

However, taking reducing agents like glutathione in an unphysiological way (IV) can activate iron and increase free radical damage. I don't think IV drips are necessary.

**Caller (Debbie):** Is there an advantage to shredding the carrot versus eating it whole?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments on milling bran showed that the length of the fiber matters. Putting a carrot in a blender destroys the water-retaining function of the fibers. Chewing it leaves large sections of fiber intact, which is very good.

**Josh Rubin:** regarding low sperm count, what can be done?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid is probably the main cause of infertility. In the 1940s, they saw that pregnenolone alone greatly increased sperm quality. Polyunsaturated fats interfere with steroid production and thyroid function. I've seen couples get pregnant in just a few weeks after the man used pregnenolone and thyroid.

**Josh Rubin:** Some people following your principles have trouble sleeping or wake up with a high pulse.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Taking too much thyroid too soon can do that. The liver needs to regenerate its ability to store glycogen to fast through the night. Before that happens, thyroid makes your body demand more sugar. You have to eat more often. Having fat with your carbohydrate at bedtime makes it absorb more slowly. Salt is also very effective at lowering adrenaline to help sleep.

**Caller:** I felt great on pure fructose but developed sleep problems. I switched to starch; my sleep normalized, but my digestion got worse.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Starch is digested and assimilated more slowly. Eating fiber and fat with your carbohydrate will extend the absorption. Pure sugar is absorbed quickly; starch, if slow to break down, can feed bacteria lower in the intestine and cause inflammation. The combination of fat and fiber might be a way to make your blood sugar steadier without the digestive issues of starch.

**Josh Rubin:** There is conflicting info on sugar and dental health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A recent article on dental health in Sweden showed that while cavities decreased, sugar and candy consumption had actually increased. Old studies showed that increased estrogen increased dental decay, while increased thyroid reduced it. Stress will quickly cause an outbreak of cavities. Mainline dentistry ignores the chemical and immunological function of saliva, which is a mediator of stress.

**Josh Rubin:** What about protein restriction and fasting to induce autophagy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Activating your metabolism will eat up proteins that shouldn't be there. Fasting drops carbohydrate intake, which raises cortisol. Cortisol breaks down proteins to turn them into sugar. You are running on stress.

**Josh Rubin:** Are cell phones really unhealthy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Microwaves are a threat. There have been experiments for over 50 years showing biological effects from weak fields. The medical doctrine relies on the "cell membrane" theory—that a cell is a bag of water needing a barrier. They assume radiation must heat the cell to damage it. But the cell is highly organized, and regions have antenna-like functions that respond to low levels of electromagnetic energy.

**Josh Rubin:** Do you recommend thyroid glandulars?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If cholesterol is low (around 100), you must be careful increasing metabolic rate. Get cholesterol up first. Then, thyroid will help. Traditional diets included the thyroid gland (fish head soup), which had a ratio of about 3:1 or 4:1 (T4 to T3).

The liver converts T4 to T3 if it has enough glucose. Glandulars are safer because they let the liver handle the conversion. However, the manufacturing of glandulars has changed. Armour was bought by Revlon, and they began extracting calcitonin, changing the product.

**Josh Rubin:** What is the optimal ratio of calcium to magnesium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can't talk about the ideal ratio in the abstract. Thyroid status determines how much magnesium you need. If thyroid is low, cells can't retain magnesium.

Calcium lowers excitatory inflammatory things. William Frederick Koch found he could cure muscle spasms with calcium, potassium, sodium, or magnesium. It's a matter of having a total of these alkaline minerals. Milk has a ratio of 1.3 to 1 (calcium to phosphorus), which is very safe. Fructose helps you lose excess phosphate, supporting the parathyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wanted to comment on Vitamin E. When ADM bought the old distillation factories, they changed the methods. The old Vitamin E (from the 1930s-50s) was rich in long-chain saturated alcohols like octacosanol and policosanol. These have endurance effects and likely contributed to the original beneficial research on Vitamin E. Modern Vitamin E lacks these.

**Caller (Justin):** I read in your book about Mexican children not getting polio.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect the Mexican immigrants were immune to many infectious diseases because of their relative iron deficiency. Also, traditional tortillas are very high in calcium because they are boiled in lime. That high calcium intake has a strong anti-stress effect.

**Josh Rubin:** What do you feel about research regarding cell membrane signaling?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's good business, but the "membrane" isn't relevant to actual cell physiology. Experiments 80 years ago showed large molecules like albumin zipping in and out of cells freely. The work of Fritjof Sjöstrand, a professor at UCLA, showed that the conventional ideas about plasma membranes are incompatible with the actual structure of the cell.

**Josh Rubin:** Thank you, Ray, for this great show. We really appreciate your work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Josh Rubin:** All right everyone, thanks for tuning in. Check out EastWestHealing.com for updates.

title: ELUV: Good Fats
transcriptText:
**ELUV:** This is the Ultrasound Show and my name is ELUV. We're going to be speaking with Dr. Raymond Peat, who has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon. He specializes in physiology and has taught at several universities, including the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, and the National College of Naturopathic Medicine. He also conducts private nutritional counseling. We're going to be speaking with him about the benefits of good oils, with a focus on coconut oil.

Greetings and welcome to the Ultrasound Show. You've done some extensive research on nutrition, how oils affect the body, and the toxic effects of polyunsaturated fats. I wanted to start by defining: what is a good oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically, saturated fats are safe and even therapeutic. A man named Nanji, who has been working with liver diseases, has demonstrated some of the toxicities of the unsaturated fats in a very comprehensive way. He showed that coconut oil and other saturated fats can be used therapeutically to treat liver disease, hepatitis, and cirrhosis.

The liver happens to be his specialty, but people have demonstrated similar effects in all systems, including brain protective effects and preventing aging of the skin. There were some very old experiments where they shaved rabbits; the rabbits given unsaturated vegetable oil in their diet got aged, wrinkled skin when exposed to sunlight. The rabbits given coconut oil tolerated the sun exposure without aging effects.

**ELUV:** This really goes against what we have been taught here in the United States about saturated fats—that they were bad.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the coconut industry doesn't have a good lobby in the United States.

**ELUV:** What is that all about? Because years ago, apparently, we used to use coconut oil for many of our food processes. What happened to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For 100 years, it was a good, cheap oil. They made crackers, tortilla chips, and potato chips with it. It was very popular because you could store it in a barrel as long as you wanted and it never got rancid.

But in the Second World War, the islands weren't accessible, so they started experimenting with using other seed oils. Animal food was one of the first places they experimented with unsaturated fats. They started seeing rats and other lab animals dying with softening of the brain and degeneration of the gonads. They found that it was one of the effects of getting too much of the polyunsaturated fats.

Mink farmers were another early experience. They were feeding the mink a lot of fish, and the mink were getting a specific disease of their fat tissues that would ultimately be fatal. It was called "yellow fat disease," and that was traced to the unsaturated fats in the fish.

Early Vitamin E studies showed that it would protect to a great extent against overexposure to unsaturated fats. That led to Vitamin E being thought of as an antioxidant. Originally, research showed Vitamin E was an anti-estrogen, but it came to be described only as an antioxidant because it protected against polyunsaturated fat excess. The reason there is a connection is that estrogen excess causes the oxidation of polyunsaturated fats. An excess of either estrogen or polyunsaturated fat amounts to the same thing as a Vitamin E deficiency, leading to sterility, brain problems, skin aging, and so on.

**ELUV:** Is Vitamin E a saturated oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin E is somewhat unsaturated, but it happens to stop the chain reaction that proceeds if you have too much of the polyunsaturated fats. If you don't have any polyunsaturated fats in your diet, you really don't need Vitamin E. The requirement for Vitamin E is directly related to how much unsaturated fat you're eating. When they feed animals coconut oil, they find that they hardly need any Vitamin E at all. Coconut oil works very much like Vitamin E in stopping the chain reactions of oxidation.

**ELUV:** Let's go back to fish oil. There is a huge industry move promoting fish oil as brain food. You're saying that's actually not true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I have several articles on my website describing the history of the concept of unsaturated fats being "essential" nutrients. That was revived around 1950, despite research that had knocked it out because they were proven *not* to be essential nutrients. You could cure the disease that had been called an "essential fatty acid deficiency" by giving Zinc and Vitamin B6. So, it wasn't a fat deficiency at all; it was a vitamin deficiency brought on by intensified metabolism.

When you don't eat the fats, you simply need better nutrition because your metabolism is running at 100% activity, the way it should. Following the discovery that polyunsaturated fats slow the metabolism—so you don't need as many vitamins and proteins—pig farmers found that very valuable. If they fed pigs a lot of polyunsaturated fat, strictly a corn and soybean diet, the pigs didn't eat as much because their metabolism was suppressed. They could fatten the pigs very cheaply. Since they sold the pigs young, it didn't matter that it also caused accelerated aging, cancer, and heart disease.

After it became an established part of the American diet, it had the same effect on people. It started making them obese, even though they weren't eating as many calories as previously, because it poisons the thyroid system. The thyroid makes you able to produce energy, use a lot of oxygen, and eat a lot of food without getting fat. Polyunsaturated fats block the function of the thyroid hormone at three or four separate points.

**ELUV:** This is interesting because people go to their doctor and are told they have a hypothyroid condition. They concentrate on that, whereas that is almost an effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Textbooks 60 years ago used to say that anyone could lose weight if they ate less than 1,700 calories a day. But women have been kept in closed wards where they could maintain their weight on 700 calories a day—less than half of what used to be maintenance. That is simply because the American metabolic rate has drastically slowed over the last 50 years.

The first time I experimented with coconut oil, I had been at about 186 pounds for 20 years. I started putting a tablespoon of coconut oil on my supper. I noticed right after eating that I felt like I had been exercising. I was pink and breathing hard for about two hours. I did that every day. Gradually, that leveled out, and I found I was losing a pound a week. By adding another 100 or 200 calories a day in the form of coconut oil, over a period of several weeks, I stabilized at a new weight of about 176 pounds.

**ELUV:** There have got to be people out there going, "He's eating oil and losing weight. Does this make sense?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Years before, I read research with rats where they did the same study methodically. They divided rats into groups consisting of pure saturated fat (coconut oil) and the other extreme, pure corn oil. At the end of their lifetime, the obesity didn't correspond to the number of calories they had eaten, but only to the ratio of saturated to unsaturated fat. The rats who had a low-calorie diet but pure corn oil were the most obese. It was strictly the ratio of fat, not the quantity.

**ELUV:** Going back to livestock fed with these unsaturated fats—how does that affect us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have analyzed lard. Scientists used to think of it as a saturated fat, and it was when pigs ate well. But for the last 50 years, pig fat has been chemically the same as corn oil or soy oil because that's what they eat, and it gets stored in their tissues. When you eat pork from industrial pigs, you're basically having a high vegetable oil intake, which is extremely fattening.

Beef and lamb evolved to eat vegetable material. They evolved a stomach which specifically destroys polyunsaturated fat. They have enzymes which use Vitamin E to destroy about 98% of the vegetable oil in their food, turning it into saturated fat.

**ELUV:** That's fantastic to know for making diet choices.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's why milk, even whole milk, is not associated with obesity. I first noticed this on a trip to Russia, where everyone was fat. When I crossed the border into Finland, everyone had milk and cheese in their stores, and everyone was slender and healthy-looking. Research shows milk drinkers have a very low incidence of obesity.

**ELUV:** What if they're drinking low-fat milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's fine, but they need to keep the fats in proportion. If you eat beef, you're getting a large proportion of saturated fat. Even if you don't eat the fat part of the meat, the muscle tissue incorporates a pretty good percentage of saturated fat.

**ELUV:** Would that be the same for duck or pheasant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, those animals reflect exactly what they eat. They don't have the detoxifying system, so they are pretty unsaturated. However, they live at a very high body temperature. Poultry is not as bad as pork or rabbits because the higher the temperature of the organism, the more saturated the fat has to be. The extremely unsaturated fats oxidize and break down so fast that in a chicken or pheasant, they don't make it into the tissue the way they do in a colder animal.

**ELUV:** What about fish? If fish oil isn't good, is the fish itself okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have ever had a piece of fatty fish laying around at room temperature, it gets rancid very quickly—even worse than leaving corn oil out. That's because the fish evolved to live in cold water. At room temperature, it starts oxidizing.

Anyone can do a simple experiment: put a cork in a bottle of unsaturated vegetable oil with a small rubber tube leading into a glass of water. At room temperature, the oil acts like it's respiring. It burns oxygen, breaks down into a varnish-like material, and sucks water up the tube. Fish oil is even worse than standard seed oils. An Amazon river fish, where the water is warm, has fat very similar to olive oil and is much safer, but we rarely get those in the United States.

**ELUV:** What about fish from Florida, since it's warmer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Undoubtedly they are safer. Any organism reflects the temperature of the tissue; warmer tissue has more saturated fat. A biochemist put sweaters on pigs and found their fat became more saturated just by keeping their skin warmer.

**ELUV:** I was speaking with someone in Israel who gets organic olive oil from the mountains. Is that a good oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's one of the best oils we can get next to coconut oil, but it still has about 10% of the toxic polyunsaturated fat. You don't want to use more than just enough for flavoring.

**ELUV:** Is there a particular quantity of coconut oil someone should consume daily?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually a tablespoon once or twice a day. That will intensify your metabolism and make you lose weight easier. I've known people who ate ounces a day to treat brain tumors or epilepsy, or to lose weight quickly, but too much can make you feel extremely hot.

**ELUV:** You mentioned it reduces estrogens. Is that through the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The thyroid activates the liver. Assuming there's enough protein and B vitamins in your diet, the liver should destroy 100% of the estrogen in the blood that passes through it. If your thyroid is low, the liver allows estrogen to pass through. This raises your systemic exposure to estrogen, which blocks the secretion of thyroid hormone. It starts a vicious cycle.

In the estrogen-stimulated state, the body selectively favors polyunsaturated fats. Women normally have a much higher concentration of polyunsaturated fats circulating because estrogen causes them to be released. Those fats then activate the estrogen receptor and intensify the effect of estrogen.

**ELUV:** Does this affect cellulite?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There's usually a lot of water in the tissue under the influence of estrogen because both estrogen and polyunsaturated fats cause cells to be more permeable. Water leaks out of capillaries easily. Even if you don't have a lot of fat, the estrogen specifically around the thighs intensifies leakiness, causing water accumulation.

**ELUV:** Why is it so difficult for women to get rid of it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mostly because they keep their thyroid suppressed by the percentage of unsaturated fats in the diet. The gland is unable to break down stored thyroid hormone, the transport protein is competed against, and the action of the hormone in the tissues is blocked by polyunsaturated fats.

**ELUV:** What is the best way to take coconut oil? Cold pressed, virgin, expeller pressed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For thousands of years in tropical climates, they filtered it to remove the debris produced when crushing the coconut. This was done because particles cause the oil to go rancid by liberating enzymes. The research on the benefits of coconut oil was done using the highly filtered, tasteless, pure product. It is the oil itself, not the nutrients in the natural product, that has the benefits.

**ELUV:** So it's not the actual pulp?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that is removed so the oil will be stable. The nutrients are there in the fresh oil—it's delicious for ice cream or cookies—but it doesn't keep well. For weight loss, anti-cancer, and liver-protecting effects, the plain, tasteless, filtered oil is fine.

**ELUV:** How long does it take to see benefits?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can feel the effect usually in about 30 minutes after eating it; your pulse rate goes up and your hands get warmer. However, a complete change of body fat takes about four years. If you've had a very unsaturated diet, your thyroid is going to be suppressed for two or three years even after changing to saturated fats.

**ELUV:** If the thyroid is fast, does it help balance it out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually, when the thyroid is overactive—pulse over 100, temperature around 99, sweaty hands—that is a self-correcting process. After about six weeks, the thyroid has unloaded the excess. In the last 50 years, people are frightened by that heat and doctors kill the thyroid gland, but it really is a self-corrective process.

**ELUV:** So given the right fats, the body has the capability to regenerate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A researcher in Israel, Gershom Zajicek, calls it "the streaming organism." He cites evidence that all tissues—brain, eye, liver, adrenal glands—are constantly regenerating. All you need is energy to keep that regeneration going, and the thyroid provides that energy.

**ELUV:** How exactly does coconut oil help the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main value is that it interrupts the anti-thyroid effects. When you eat coconut oil, it gets into your bloodstream and relieves the suppression of metabolism by getting in front of the suppressive molecules. The short-chain saturated fats (6, 8, and 10 carbon molecules) are very active metabolically. They can be taken up by the mitochondria without using the carnitine transport system. It bypasses that system and gets metabolized immediately. It's like little kids crowding in line ahead of the big fat people.

**ELUV:** It sounds like it's acting more like a carbohydrate than a fat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. It is as easily metabolized as a sugar molecule. Also, those short-chain saturated fats have a hormone-like effect. They have an antihistamine effect, quieting immune cells. When metabolized, they release ketones. These short fatty acids and ketones act like GABA transmitters in the brain to calm overexcited cells.

**ELUV:** That seems like an anti-stress effect.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The GABA system helps slow excess cell division in tumors. That's probably one of the reasons saturated fats are protective against tumors—it applies the brakes the way the GABA molecule would.

**ELUV:** I use coconut oil for skin care.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The rabbit experiment showed it protected against skin aging and sunburn. If you are sunburned, you can apply coconut oil to get a protective antihistamine effect. The sun causes excitation that spreads to the polyunsaturated fats in skin cells. Saturated fats interrupt that spreading of destructive oxidation.

**ELUV:** Weren't there studies in Asia regarding skin and sun?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was consulting with a couple in San Diego—an older man and his attractive young Filipino wife. They had been married for 40 years. She cooked her meals in coconut oil and his in standard American food. She looked 30 or 40 years younger than him.

**ELUV:** There you go—fringe benefits externally. Thank you so much for coming on the show. For people who would like to read more, where can they find you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The website is raypeat.com. There are about 50 or 60 of my articles on there.

**ELUV:** Are you available for nutritional counseling?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they can email me through the website.

**ELUV:** Excellent. Thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ray Peat. Many blessings.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: ELUV: Effects of Stress and Trauma on the Body
transcriptText:
**ELUV:** Tonight we have special guest Dr. Raymond Peat, who has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He has taught at several universities, including the University of Oregon, Montana State University, the National College of Naturopathic Medicine, and Blake College. He also conducts private nutritional counseling. Today we are speaking with him about the effects of stress and trauma on the body.

Let's dive in. Tonight's theme is really about how the body reacts to stress and trauma. Let's first talk about day-to-day stress and what happens to the body and the brain physiologically.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first thing is that if you're really healthy, you can meet challenges without experiencing something that Hans Selye would have called stress. For example, if you are not very healthy, just skipping a meal can put you in really serious stress. However, a healthy person stores something like 7 or 8 ounces of glucose in the form of glycogen in the liver, muscles, and brain. Since at rest the muscles can burn primarily fatty acids, your brain is the main thing that consumes glucose. If you are more or less inactive and relaxed, you can easily go 12 to 15 hours without eating and without having any stress at all.

But if you're not able to store that much glycogen—for example, low thyroid people or people with a history of severe stress aren't able to store very much—then when you run out of sugar, whether it's from going all day without eating or because your liver isn't very efficient, your body tries to increase the available glucose.

Normally, just being awake makes enough adrenaline to mobilize as much of the glucose from your stores as you need. But when you run out of that stored sugar, your brain still requires sugar to function properly. Instead of just increasing the adrenaline more and more, when the adrenaline reaches a certain level and can't get the blood sugar up out of your storage, then you turn on the cortisol. That's the classic stress that can be harmful because the cortisol dissolves tissues.

First, tissues like the thymus, which are very fragile, start turning to sugar immediately when you run out of stored glycogen. The thymus is gone in just two or three hours of intense stress. That happens to be one of the reasons they think adults don't have thymus glands; by the time they are dead and analyzed, the thymus has been eaten up by stress. They might have had a perfectly normal thymus until they were sick and dead.

After the thymus is consumed and turned to sugar, the cortisol starts breaking down your muscles. Then the skin, brain, lungs, and heart are spared from stress, partly because they are very saturated in a healthy person with androgens—testosterone and DHEA especially—which block the breakdown function of cortisol. If your brain, lungs, and heart are short of those protective steroids, then that's where the stress really starts causing severe, deadly damage.

Post-traumatic stress disorder is produced when someone has had such terrible stress, such as being tortured or being in terrific catastrophes. They not only deplete stored glycogen and break down the expendable tissues like thymus and liver, but then the cortisol starts damaging the brain and heart. They get very severe chronic symptoms. Once the stress is completely resolved, the brain can massively regenerate itself. For example, they've seen MRIs of girls who had been in anorexia for months; their brain shrinks from living on the cortisol breaking down their tissues, but once they start eating, the brain can rebuild itself in just a few weeks.

**ELUV:** How often does one have to eat, or is it recommended to eat, in order to not have this stress reaction happen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The famous Argentine biologist Bernardo Houssay, in the 1940s, was the first one to show that if he fed his animals only once a day, they not only tended to get fat on the same amount of calories, but they had a high incidence of diabetes. But if you fed them at least three times a day or more, then they were very resistant to diabetes and were less fattened on a given number of calories. So, more or less nibbling all the time is the safest thing. But if you have a really good diet and aren't under emotional pressure, then a person can get along on one or two meals a day.

**ELUV:** Let's talk about a really good diet. What is a really good diet for the optimal health of the body, brain, and organs? There are a lot of disputes about optimal diets. Does it differ with different people, or is there an overall optimal diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Blood type has almost no effect because you can see in even very different species of animals that have very different ways of living, the same processes occur. So there's a universal animal diet that is optimal, but the proportions vary with the type of activity, body size, metabolic rate, and personal history. Your previous stresses will affect what you need.

**ELUV:** Let's talk about someone who perhaps is not that healthy and does have stress. What would be the recommended diet for them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the reasons that the single-meal eaters tend to get fat and diabetic is that it triggers a great surge of insulin, and the insulin then triggers cortisol. If you can eat foods that don't trigger insulin, that's the ideal thing.

Fruit happens to be the best single type of food for not triggering the stress reaction because it combines very small amounts of protein with large amounts of sugar. The mineral potassium happens to handle sugar in place of insulin, and the fructose component of fruit sugar doesn't require insulin. So eating a lot of fruit, even in one meal a day, produces a much smaller amount of insulin, obesity, and cortisol than eating just one big meal of meat and potatoes. Meat powerfully stimulates insulin and cortisol, and starches are more stimulating to insulin than sugars.

**ELUV:** It's almost counterintuitive when you're talking about taking in fructose in the form of fruit with people that are insulin sensitive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, for about 100 years, fructose has been recognized as the ideal sugar for diabetics because they can metabolize it without needing insulin. It used to be sold in health food stores all across the country for diabetics.

**ELUV:** Let's talk about high fructose corn syrup and the difference between that and fructose from fruit.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The funny thing about that is that if you look at the fructose and glucose content, it seems to be not very different from any old sugar—maybe 45/55% rather than an exact 50/50 balance of fructose and glucose. But people actually thought to analyze what is in the stuff *other* than fructose and glucose. It turns out that the reason people get fat on soft drinks that contain it is that it contains a huge amount of calories that are neither glucose nor fructose. It's the syrupy component—basically a type of corn starch or corn syrup. They don't count it because it isn't fructose or glucose, but it's there as calories.

**ELUV:** Now they're using this in so many different things, from salad dressings to soft drinks.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was a trick. Because of the boycott of Cuban sugar starting in the 60s, the price of sugar went up because they wouldn't buy it from where it was cheap. So the corn starch producers learned how to produce something resembling sugar. It's really like the old Karo syrup, which was not a very appetizing way to sweeten things. During the Second World War, I think the Germans pioneered it, but in the United States sugar was scarce, and corn syrup started being used in canned things and even in homes as a substitute for sugar. But the sweeter, more palatable form that they call high fructose corn syrup was developed in the 60s in response to the increased price of sugar.

**ELUV:** It's amazing. They've done similar things with oils too, using oils that are quite toxic in our foods.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The cottonseed industry was a major power behind that. Way back in the end of the 1800s, with the gin to make cotton textiles more economical, they had machines to get the seeds out of the cotton. In proportion to the production of cotton, they were accumulating seeds that were too toxic to feed to animals. They found that they could squeeze oil out of the cottonseed, and by chemically hardening it, they could sell it as artificial butter.

For about 20 years, the butter industry required them to sell it in a colorless state, and the person had to add color so that it wouldn't ruin the butter industry. But the seed oil industry gradually got powerful enough to convince people that it's better than butter. In fact, it has many toxic effects that butter doesn't have.

**ELUV:** Is this the same as rapeseed oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first rapeseed oil happened to cause severe heart disease, and the industry wanted to sell it for margarine and cooking oil. There was a particular oil in that plant that they decided to blame the heart injury on. But Hans Selye did experiments studying the type of lesion in the heart produced by rapeseed oil. He found that it was the linoleic acid in it—which is still in it—that caused the damage. They took out the peculiar, unusual fatty acid, but the essential fatty acid, linoleic acid, is heart-toxic.

Hans Selye showed that if you added cocoa butter—highly saturated stearic acid—to the rapeseed oil, it no longer caused death of the heart cells. So it's just the excess of polyunsaturated fat that made the rapeseed, canola, or cottonseed oil toxic. All of those are actually toxic if you eat very much of them.

**ELUV:** What about soybean oil? Because they're all GMO now.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's still the polyunsaturated component. It turns into prostaglandins, which promote all kinds of inflammation and degenerative diseases. As early as 1964, a Dutch researcher named Böttcher sliced open the lesions in atherosclerotic arteries at all different stages of development and analyzed the fats in them. He called it a primitive idea that cholesterol got diffused out of the blood into the artery and damaged it. He said that the situation is very different from that. In the most advanced lesions—the farthest advanced atherosclerosis—he found that the content of linoleic acid was highest. After that, many other people demonstrated that the oxidation products of these unstable, highly unsaturated fats are found increasingly in atherosclerosis.

**ELUV:** It's very interesting that things like seed oils, canola oil, soybean oil, high fructose corn syrup, and butter substitutes are being advertised as better for your health. It's really about the consumers educating themselves.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They have to think of some excuse for claiming that people should buy them because they don't taste good. So the idea is that if they are "essential" in some sense, then the more you eat, the better they are. But in fact, it's very questionable whether they're essential as a nutrient at all. Animals can live more or less indefinitely—you can grow cells forever in a dish—without any of those, which I think proves that they're not essential nutrients. The more you increase them in the diet, there's a direct relationship with the incidence of spontaneous cancer. That was first demonstrated in 1927 and over and over since, but the industry keeps publicizing them as health foods.

**ELUV:** There's been a big resurgence of grass-fed beef, for example.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Beyond fruits, in the ideal diet, the ruminants are able to detoxify the polyunsaturated fats in grains or grasses. It happens to be vitamin E in the grass which enables them to convert polyunsaturated linoleic acid into the trans fatty acids. There is one of the components of butter or beef fat that is being sold as a drug or a health food because it counteracts the toxic effects of the polyunsaturated fats: conjugated linoleic acid (CLA). You get some of that in beef, butter, cheese, and milk.

The high ratio of calcium to phosphate in butter and cheese comes from the fact that green leaves—if the cows are allowed to eat at least some hay and grass—contain a low amount of phosphate and a high amount of magnesium, calcium, and other safe minerals. Too much phosphate, which you would get on a grain-based and meat-based diet, becomes toxic when it isn't balanced by at least as much calcium and other minerals, including magnesium. So milk, fruit, and cheese give you the main nutrients. Then there are just the regionally deficient things such as iodine and selenium; if you eat some kind of seafood, then you're getting the basic things for anti-stress foods.

**ELUV:** For vegetarians, would you say that it's a little more difficult because they're not eating these products?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you concentrate on well-cooked greens, the protein and mineral balance in cooked green leafy vegetables is essentially the same as in milk. It's just less concentrated because of the high cellulose diluting it. But you must cook away, wash away, or skim away the anti-nutrients. For example, too much spinach contains oxalic acid that tends to take the calcium out of your teeth. Some leafy vegetables have chemicals that block your stomach's digestive enzymes. But a variety of cooked greens will provide the same type of protein that milk provides, as well as the very favorable balance of magnesium, potassium, and calcium in relation to phosphate.

**ELUV:** Aside from spinach, what other vegetables would be better off cooked as opposed to raw? Do you advocate any raw foods or raw salads?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The very juicy fruits are best raw, but if they're starchy like bananas or plantains, they should be cooked by preference because the starches can enter the bloodstream and trigger allergic reactions. Too much undercooked starch causes "persorption." The particles enter the bloodstream and can block capillaries and arterioles, causing cells to die until the particle can be broken down. But it can stay in place long enough to kill cells in the heart, brain, and lungs.

Feeding mice on a very high raw starch diet, a biologist in Germany found that they were very prematurely aged because of the death of cells in all of their organs that were blocked by starch grains. So starch, like potatoes, is almost a perfect food if they're very well cooked because you want to break down the starch. The non-starch ingredients of a potato have almost a perfect balance of nutrients—B vitamins, essential amino acids, and carbohydrate in the right proportion. The only things lacking in a pure potato diet would be vitamin A and vitamin B12.

**ELUV:** Are you speaking about sweet potatoes or white potatoes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** White potatoes. Some white potatoes contain enough carotene that they could provide the requirement of vitamin A. But sweet potatoes often contain so much carotene that it interferes with digestion. Too much carotene has anti-hormonal effects that can slow down your production of thyroid hormones, progesterone, and adrenal hormones if it accumulates to the point that it's making your palms turn orange.

**ELUV:** Which it does with some people who are juicing carrots a lot.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I constantly warn people about that. There are good chemicals in the juice, but unless your thyroid is pretty active, it's going to accumulate the carotene because you convert carotene to vitamin A. If you have vitamin B12 in proportion to how active your thyroid hormone is, you are fine. But if you're getting more carotene than your vitamin B12 and thyroid can handle, then it turns off thyroid function. I experienced that myself about 40 years ago; eating so many carrots that I suppressed my thyroid.

However, if your thyroid is good, then having a whole carrot every day has some very important anti-stress functions. Yesterday I heard from a woman who said that she had started a daily carrot salad and had almost immediate relief from all of her premenstrual and digestive problems. We've measured the blood hormones in a few people after they started a daily whole carrot. It's the stimulating effect on the intestine. The fiber in the carrot isn't digestible. The excretion of bile into the liver carries all kinds of detoxified chemicals and hormones. If you have fiber in your intestine, these toxins that the liver has gotten rid of will be carried out, bound to the carrot fiber. Without enough fiber, they can be reabsorbed and recycled. So your estrogen tends to go up as the fiber in your diet goes down. That in turn turns off your thyroid and progesterone, causing all the symptoms of estrogen and cortisol excess. In just three or four days, we've seen the cortisol and estrogen level in the blood drop as the progesterone comes up just from eating a daily carrot.

**ELUV:** It's so interesting how the food that we eat influences everything about our body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of people, partly because of a bad industrialized diet, are now going around in a chronically stressed condition. It's sort of like learned helplessness or post-traumatic stress syndrome. The diet keeps people in a high cortisol, high estrogen state. Before you have to do any important work, you should make sure that your diet isn't creating the stress day by day.

You can check your thyroid function just by measuring your temperature and pulse rate when you wake up and then in the middle of the day. They should rise so that your pulse is maybe 80 per minute at rest, and your temperature should be around 98.6 at rest. In the morning, it's okay for them to be about 10% lower—pulse rate and maybe 97.8 degrees or so.

**ELUV:** This can also be influencing the fact that men are having hormone issues as well, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When a man is on a very bad diet or is under stress or has an accident, the estrogen level rises sharply. In old age, with any of the degenerative diseases, men tend to have a sharp increase in estrogen.

**ELUV:** So they can avoid this or monitor this by their diet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And your temperature is the quickest way, because estrogen lowers your temperature. Thyroid, progesterone, and DHEA help to maintain a good, steady high metabolic rate, even at rest.

**ELUV:** So when people get cold when they're sitting there in front of their desk or at home, that may indicate that the hormones have changed and the thyroid is dropping.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And one of the tricks of the body is that increasing the adrenaline can compensate for hypothyroidism. Some people are hyper-alert, anxious, and have a high heart rate, even though their thyroid is really low. Their temperature can be held up and look normal, except that it's likely to be higher when you first wake up in the morning and then decrease when you eat something.

**ELUV:** So it switches.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because the nighttime is when you aren't eating and your adrenaline and cortisol rise. Those can tear down your tissues at such a rate that they keep your temperature up. Then when you eat something and lower the stress, you see that your metabolism is really not so high. When the adrenaline is very high, even though your oral temperature might seem normal, your hands and feet will be cold—maybe even the tip of your nose—because the body is directing the energy so that your brain, lungs, and heart aren't deprived or chilled. But your body can consider your hands and feet somewhat expendable and let them get very cold.

**ELUV:** If we up the stress levels—someone has a surgery, for example—there are more severe chemical changes. Some of the symptoms in post-surgery can include low energy, weight gain, hormonal changes, depression, and sleep disorders.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And even dementia. Lately, they've been measuring mental function after major surgery. For months, even years after major surgery, people's mental function is often slowed down. That's because of the chronic effect of cortisol, which slows nerve conduction. It protects some of your tissues from inflammation, but it progressively damages your immune system and your nervous system.

**ELUV:** What would be the best way for recovery?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The thing about surgery, as opposed to a car accident, is that you can prepare for it. Even standard medical sources are now saying that you should check thyroid function before you schedule someone for surgery, because a hypothyroid person doesn't do well. Their cortisol is already high.

Before Hans Selye made stress famous, an American surgeon named George Crile in Cleveland over 100 years ago was studying shock from surgery. Shock, as he understood it, came to be part of stress as Hans Selye interpreted it. For Selye, an excess of estrogen was enough to create the whole shock syndrome.

In 1908, the mortality rate from surgeries at Crile's hospital was 4.4%. After he devised a way to reduce stress, in five years of application, it had cut the mortality to 1.8%. His basic procedure was to convince the brain that nothing had happened. He called it "anoci-association," meaning getting the brain to not notice the noxious events. He found that histamine was released by morphine when it was used to control pain, and that histamine brought on all of these other stress hormone changes. So he added an antihistamine—an herbal drug called scopolamine—to go with the anesthesia. Then he used a local anesthetic as the skin was cut, so that he was not letting the brain receive any of those harmful signals.

But careless, quick surgery nowadays often is very rough. The patient wakes up with changes in the brain from that powerful noxious stimulation. If you can get the doctor to reduce the trauma of the surgery, that's a very important part of recovery.

Since the surgery turning on the stress hormones turns off the thyroid function, temperature tends to drop drastically during and following surgery. In proportion to how the temperature falls, the person's recovery is impaired. So everything that will keep your temperature up during and after surgery helps. Preparing with at least two weeks of adjusting thyroid so that you're not hypothyroid makes the recovery a lot faster.

A study in Mississippi found that if the emergency intensive care people checked the patient's vitamin D levels as they came in, they found that out of 278 cases, only three people had normal vitamin D. Some of them had as low as 8 or 10 nanograms per milliliter, where it should be 50 or 55. When he got the dietician to supplement vitamin D, the length of stay in intensive care was cut in half, survival increased, and the expenses saved the hospital more than half.

**ELUV:** You mentioned an herbal antihistamine earlier. What was that again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was scopolamine. That is sometimes available if a person is nauseated after surgery. That's a very safe anti-nausea drug which does several things. It helps to hold up the body temperature besides stopping the nausea.

**ELUV:** And what can people do as far as specific diet for post-surgery recovery?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same foods that are generally good, but emphasizing the things that are lost specifically by high stress, which are protein, zinc, and some of the B vitamins. Foods like liver, oysters, and eggs, which are rich in the trace minerals and protein, are ideal as long as you're getting adequate carbohydrate and calcium. These happen to be high phosphate foods along with the protein, but they have the highest concentration of the healing minerals and vitamins.

**ELUV:** I wanted to ask you a question relating to pasteurization. You mentioned that there are beneficial nutrients in milk. Does this get discounted once the milks or cheeses are pasteurized?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, it's such a tiny amount. They pasteurize it now in something like three seconds at a high temperature and then drop it immediately. So there's very little oxidative damage done now by pasteurizing. It might lower the vitamin A content 3 or 4%, but since it's such a rich source of all these nutrients, no one is going to suffer deficiency if they're eating pasteurized milk and cheese.

**ELUV:** What's your feeling about exercise during that recovery time for people that have gone through surgery?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it is better just to regain flexibility and mobility in a gentle way, not to worry about muscle-building exercise. The time to think about that is before surgery. In one study of old people, they found that the fatter they were, the better their long-range survival was. In the six months following the surgery, the death rate was much higher in the lean, low body mass people.

It isn't just the fat that is a buffer against stress, but mainly the mass of the muscles. Exercises such as deep knee bends and mild weightlifting with dumbbells—just a few minutes a day of mild resistance exercise—can keep your muscles sound and relatively massive. Muscles are themselves a hormone source. They can produce testosterone instead of cortisol when you're doing these resistance exercises. So muscle building is protecting your heart and brain as well as building up the reserves of tissue that are part of your resistance against stress.

**ELUV:** You mentioned that cortisol damages the brain once the trauma has happened. Is that reversible over time if someone is following a protocol that would support their greater health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's probably just the same as following anorexia. Young women can have great and quick regrowth of the mass of the brain substance just by stopping the stress and starting to eat well. I think that would happen with old people who are partially demented by the stress of very serious surgery.

**ELUV:** Lastly, I wanted to chat a little bit about adrenals, as many people these days seem to be suffering from low adrenals or adrenal fatigue.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I mentioned that the muscles are an important source of steroid synthesis. Our biggest endocrine gland is our brain, and the brain stabilizes all of the organs. If your brain is experiencing stress, that shifts the adrenal function to cortisol rather than DHEA, progesterone, and the androgens. The adrenals shouldn't produce simply the stress-promoting hormones; they should be putting out some of the defensive, protective progesterone, DHEA, and pregnenolone as well. But when your broken brain gives them the super stress signals, then they will overact.

Hans Selye defined adrenal failure as when the adrenal gland begins bleeding and the cells die that make steroids. But the adrenal cortex is extremely able to regenerate, as fast as the thymus and thyroid gland. If you're well fed and if you stop the stress signals, it can regenerate.

What Selye was talking about was an acute stress causing immediate bleeding of your stomach and intestines. That's because of the high cortisol production. If you continue that too long without feeding some of the curative nutrients—sugars, zinc, magnesium, calcium, vitamin D—then the adrenal glands can't keep up the intense work and they start bleeding and tissue dies. Too much estrogen is one of the things that can contribute to overacting of the adrenal cortex. In animal experiments, we saw that just injecting a big dose of estrogen would cause adrenal enlargement in a moderate case, or bleeding and death in an extreme dose.

**ELUV:** Absolutely amazing how everything is so connected.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I should mention that cholesterol, thyroid, and vitamin A are the important things for keeping the adrenal cortex from getting stressed to death. Cholesterol is the raw material for making cortisol and the other stress-adaptive hormones. Without enough cholesterol, thyroid, and vitamin A, these cells are stimulated but can't work, so they just give up and atrophy.

**ELUV:** What sources of cholesterol would you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A good diet. Plenty of fruit and milk in the diet will allow your tissues, especially the liver and brain, to make as much cholesterol as they need.

**ELUV:** And speaking of liver, would you recommend for people to eat liver?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Except for the ratio of calcium to phosphate, the liver has the highest concentration of the anti-stress nutrients. So at least twice a month there should be a good meal of liver for stress resistance. Maybe once a week. Four ounces a week is a safe and effective amount.

**ELUV:** Dr. Ray Peat, thank you so much for joining us tonight on the Ultrasound Show. If people would like to get in touch with you and find out more about your services, where do they go?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My website is raypeat.com.
