transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Okay, and we're live. Hello, everybody. Welcome. We have Georgi and Mr. Raymond Peat on the line, and we are talking about Aristotle. We were talking about forms, matter, and deep politics. I'm not going to interrupt what we were talking about, but Georgi, go ahead.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Yeah, I was curious what Dr. Peat thinks made specific parts of the world amenable to such contradictory ideas. Is it something in the way people saw reality in those different parts of the world? Why would Eastern Europe or the Eastern world be so amenable to change, while the Western world would be like, "Nope, we're firmly controlled; that's the only theory that we accept is true"? Change must be happening everywhere. Why would it take root in certain parts of the world and not others?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the '50s, I was considering the Whorfian hypothesis—that the structure of language has evolved in remote history and contributes to that. But I fairly quickly realized that cultural things, such as the difference between Aristotle and Plato in the available literature when people were just starting to get literate, played a role. The church was a force for literacy, and it happened that the Eastern Christian church got the good Aristotle literature, and the West was influenced by Platonism.

So I still tend to think that there are slight differences from the structure of language. There's a linguist at Stanford who is the contemporary Whorfian apologist. I think that can be seen in the difference between English and German, for example, and between Chinese and Hindi. Chinese has, through use, reduced the superstructure of grammatical form and depends greatly on context. I think that there's a noticeable difference between English and the older European languages, with more context dependence in English grammar.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Are you familiar with the ideas of the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. The thing I liked about him was that he numbered his paragraphs instead of trying to make a grand argument that progressed logically. He simply made statements and numbered them because he believed that every statement implies a metaphysical surrounding.

I had been studying Bertrand Russell and the linguistic philosophers who followed him—like John Wisdom—who I saw as trying to sneak in the old Platonism entities, logical atomism, for example. Wittgenstein blew that up and showed somewhat a resonance with the old Leibniz: a universe being implied in every statement, or every event implying the surrounding context.

**Georgi Dinkov:** The thing that made the most impression on me is that he said there's no such thing as private language. There are no private thoughts; they can all be expressed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, but when you try to work out the implications of "there is no private language," you're always guessing statistically that you're understanding the other person. If you can't remember for sure, your own language is consistent and testable. When you look at the other person, you're just making a statistically sounder guess, but there's no essential difference between shared language and the private language once you realize that they all depend on memory and interpretation.

**Georgi Dinkov:** That leads me to the next question. You had a discussion with Danny about Lenin, memory, and matter. You said Lenin stated that knowledge is memory and it's coming from matter, but it's not matter. Matter is everything we don't know. So what is knowledge then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the physiological presence of matter, and the info is the matter itself that hasn't been incorporated into our perspective.

**Georgi Dinkov:** So would you say that knowledge is simply the structure of matter that we incorporate into ourselves?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It's living matter and it's always open to living a new phase, and that openness to new life is matter. Info is all we can say about matter. It's not denying the materiality. It's saying that this is the living matter that is our consciousness, and that's like an internal fountain. It's always going on, going ahead, becoming something else. And that's the nature of matter, that it's creating this constant flow of knowledge.

**Georgi Dinkov:** In another interview, you basically said that nothing is stored. Basically, how we feel about our memories and knowledge depends largely on thyroid function and metabolism. If knowledge isn't stored, where is it? When we access a memory, what does that process physiologically look like?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's some trace in our facial muscles, viscera, posture. We work through a series of reinventions, finding these pictures, which are arrangements of excitations. We don't go straight to a picture; we work by inference and traces to reconstruct it. And so every time we bring up the past, we're creating a new past. It's always newly experienced.

The idea that something is stored becomes part of that Platonist idea that ends up saying atoms are timeless entities and can be accurately described only by changeless units of logic. You can't let change into the system if you're in that logical atomism range. Platonism is denying that an individual atom has a history. The memory as reconstruction is that we're like a whirlwind of consciousness; the shape of our individual whirlwind is always ongoing but is moving ahead with some degree of deduction from our previous states. Looking back, it's like a reverse deduction to reconstruct that we must have experienced that being where we are.

**Danny Roddy:** In one of those same conversations, I was asking you some philosophical questions and you said something like you have to start and end with being an animal. Can you talk about that a little bit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** An animal experiencing nature or people around it is aware of its needs and hopes, and also any fears that it has. It interprets particular objects or processes as either hopeful or fearsome. Otherwise, it's in the process of going through the present situation with the intention of finding the realization of what it wants.

Culture has piled up belief and stories that complicate that so that we don't see ourselves as surrounded by future possibilities and threats. I think anytime you're going to get back on the track of realizing yourself, the larger intention—the thing that religious people feel as some kind of overarching meaning—is for the biologically amplified animal to do things that some animals can't do.

By our energy amplification, we can have the animal intentionality encompassing future possibilities on a transpersonal scale, seeing the need for the ecosystem, for the society, for other individuals, and even for different kinds of organisms. Taking responsibility in a straight line with yourself, feeling that you're responsible for all of the stuff around you, seeing it all as hopeful moving towards the future, and not having any of these cultural kinks that say, "I own this," or "I have to destroy this to do this."

**Georgi Dinkov:** Are you saying that amplified rate of metabolism coexists with a sense of solidarity with other humans, or the Kropotkin mutual aid, assuming your basic needs are met?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I see Kropotkin blending in with Vernadsky. Vernadsky said that the flow of energy from the sun into the earth is creating a living structural system that is assimilating and accumulating the interactions of the different levels of the ecosystem. This permits optimizing the metabolism of the big animal, developing a big brain, and doing the things that are appropriate. Like animals tearing through the jungle are improving the fertility of the system, not damaging it. Like Alan Savory—his rough idea is compatible with Vernadsky, that the big animals are a big part of the ecosystems that they develop in and they are helping to pull the whole ecosystem forward.

**Georgi Dinkov:** On the "being an animal" concept, are you referring to Pavlov's ideas of the first and second signal system? The first signal system being the animal raw perception of reality?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't see it as being strictly second. P.K. Anokhin, a colleague younger than Pavlov, developed the picture of consciousness in this unified sense. He called it the "acceptor of action." It's the present state of the organism in a pictorial, space-filling model of the world.

The second signal system, in Pavlov's term, gets its structure by acting as names for structures in this acceptor of action. You have a little three-dimensional holographic movie going on with your intentions cycling through this movie model of the world. The words—the second signal system—attach to each part of the model of the world. Marx or Engels referred to it as a "name of a ghost." The second signal system gets its structure exclusively from this pictorial model of the world.

**Georgi Dinkov:** To me, the way I understood your book was that intuition was part of the first signal system, and then this capacity for rigid, analytical, abstract thought felt like it didn't even need images. That was part of the second signal system. The authoritarian mind tends to really emphasize the second signal system—purely abstract thought without any connection to reality.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was studying psychology at the university, I did a survey asking people how they dreamed as well as their waking thought processes. I found that there were people who didn't know what it was to dream in pictures. They said a dream was like listening to someone tell a story. Those people were absolute zero on a scale of creativity. They followed verbal rules. Somehow they could talk to people and seem to communicate in English, but they had no ability to think with any innovation.

When your acceptor of action is de-energized, it tends to disappear, leaving just these solidified units of language. You can't learn a language without having some fluidity in this model of the world. But by the age of six or seven, people are often losing enough biological energy that they start seeing reality in terms of only the cliches that they can say.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I stumbled upon a symptom in psychiatry called Logorrhea—literally verbal diarrhea. Older studies show it's overwhelmingly connected to psychiatric conditions driven by excess estrogen and serotonin. Do you think that this excessive verbalism is partly mediated by estrogen and serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Women in general produce many more words per minute than men on average. Starting at the menstrual phase, when estrogen is highest, they can't stop talking. I think that involves a short circuit of the pictorial, space-filling thought and directing the energy through these repetitive verbal patterns.

The thing about the acceptor of action, the pictorial model of the world, is that it's always changing. There's nothing repeated. Anything you try to do twice, it's always different the second time. The word consciousness—the estrogen-driven, lubricated word machine—doesn't get any newness admitted. It's always repeating, tending to be cliched.

**Georgi Dinkov:** In one of your older interviews, you mentioned that you try to spend at least one day a week not uttering any words or reading, just painting and doing non-verbal activities. Do you think that excessive verbalization, when it's voluntary, can be detrimental?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not if you keep your energy up. When I had to teach 12 hours a week, after just two or three weeks, my verbal fluency went up tremendously just because I was exercising that. But I never repeated any idea twice through the whole series of lectures. If you keep your energy up, you can verbalize fairly fluently, but always bending the message a little so there's nothing repeated.

**Danny Roddy:** Is that a unique aspect of your personality, or do you think that's a metabolic thing of trying to always stay in a creative mindset?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I first noticed it when I was three years old and helping my father with a repetitive task. I realized that every time I repeated the task, I was a new person. And ever since then, I've never been able to have the illusion of doing something twice.

**Georgi Dinkov:** If that's the case, then don't you think that schools are really harmful because they emphasize this routine at every step of the educational process?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If a person lets themselves be tortured constantly... you just have to be quiet and let them do their thing.

**Danny Roddy:** I feel like one of the worst parts about school was sitting down. Now learning about restraint stress, that seems part of the torture.

**Georgi Dinkov:** My only concern is that you once said that "faint stupidity becomes real stupidity." So I guess a person just has to be sitting there and hoping that they're not going to be stuck in the educational system long enough to become an idiot like all the other people being turned into mental slaves.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People who did IQ tests on New York City schools found that every year the students were given more IQ tests, their IQ went down.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, do you see vaccinations, besides the food and the polyunsaturated fats, as a major problem for society?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Until fairly recently, I hadn't realized that kids are now getting 50 shots by the time they grow up. Robert Kennedy Jr. mentioned that until 1980, only 2.5% of kids had allergies. Starting in the 1980s, over half of the kids now have serious allergies.

If you want to create an allergy in an animal, you give it an injection. Intramuscular is ideal to include some little thing like an egg protein or milk protein, or any of the various proteins that are in the culture media that they make vaccines in. So they are replicating animal allergy creation every time they give a shot. There's no way to deny it sensibly.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think they take on a different meaning nowadays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think the money—billions of dollars, 50 billion a year in profits—is mostly from the sale of just vaccines.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I was shocked to see CNN last week putting a headline news that basically said, "CDC is warning: It's not a question of if, but when coronavirus will create a massive epidemic in the United States." Why would a health agency issue such a statement? It seems like scaring all of its citizens.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The CDC has been saying that the annual deaths produced by influenza range from 9 million to a high of 57 million deaths worldwide per year. Now they expect us to get excited when a dozen people die.

**Danny Roddy:** I have a Twitter application on my phone. When I turn it on, there is a new huge bar on the screen just updating me on coronavirus. I've never asked for updates on coronavirus. It just seems like the marketing campaign is palpable.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and the World Health Organization is sharing in the corruption and conflicts of interest. You can't trust any of the big organizations because they manage to profit in some way from the huge amount of wealth that's being directed through the vaccines.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I was reading some older studies showing that the more hydrophilic the cell is, the greater its susceptibility to a viral infection. Doesn't that suggest that the presence of polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) in the blood would increase susceptibility to the virus? Studies published before the 1950s made that exact claim.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That whole subject of polyunsaturated fats is worse than any organized crime campaign. Estrogen and polyunsaturated fats are gigantic criminal businesses, and the omega-3 fats are especially powerful in immune suppression, but they market that as being anti-inflammatory.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Wouldn't something as simple as taking some aspirin and niacinamide essentially greatly reduce the risk of catching any viral infection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think so. And aspirin happens to be an antiviral agent in itself, antibacterial and antiviral. There was a study around Washington, DC, that tested it on AIDS patients. Just big doses of aspirin, and it was working, but no one was interested.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, one of the papers you cited said, "It is perhaps surprising that essential lipids that are supposed to be so good for health are so potent at killing cells."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Immunodeficiency is a big thing apart from any virus. Sepsis has been growing along with other degenerative diseases. Young people never used to get sepsis practically, but now sepsis is affecting younger and younger people in bigger numbers. I think it's largely the stress cumulative effects on PUFA.

**Danny Roddy:** Something that's popular among my group of friends is the idea of herd immunity. Do you want to speak about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It sounds very much like a Nazi program. It doesn't have any convincing weight for me. It just makes me fear the people that say we're a herd that has to be treated one way or another.

**Danny Roddy:** Have you seen any of that movie *Vaxxed*? They talk about the military vaccinating people and creating Gulf War syndrome with the anthrax vaccine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I hadn't read that specifically, but Diana Dutton wrote a book called *Worse Than the Disease* where she details the swine flu. One guy was routed out of bed to go on a forced march, collapsed, and died. He was diagnosed as having swine flu—the only death acknowledged by the head of the CDC. But there were thousands of paralytic reactions and around 300 deaths from the vaccine. So hundreds of times worse than the disease.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I wanted to mention something about HIV. A study around 2014 showed that you cannot develop AIDS unless there are high levels of endotoxin in your blood. A subsequent study in 2018 showed that the single most reliable predictor of death in HIV positive people was the level of soluble CD14, which is a biomarker of endotoxin. I never see virologists talk about the role of endotoxin in viral disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm inclined to think that even cancer is largely an endotoxin problem. Chronic year after year of bad food irritating the intestine, causing increased histamine, serotonin, and estrogen, but a constant stream of endotoxin flowing through the system. This shakes up chromosomes, creates inflammation, and fatigues the repair systems. Finally, when the repair systems are down, the cancers that are constantly popping up stop being removed.

**Georgi Dinkov:** So would you say the specific organ where the cancer appears is simply because that particular organ was the most energetically compromised?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. When I've mentioned the idea of systemic disease to cancer doctors, they can't grasp it. They've been so indoctrinated with the idea that it's a clone—that one single mutant cell develops into the clone. But way back 80 or 90 years, people have been seeing precancerous gradations surrounding any tumor. The field concept of cancer goes way back almost 200 years.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Have you seen the study from 2015 regarding the Warburg effect? It basically said that metabolic disturbances and specifically lactic acid precede the genomic abnormalities and are actually the cause of them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Lactic acid creates a reduced state, shifts the balance towards increased sulfhydryl, NADH ratio to NAD. All of the electronic and energetic properties of cancer are initiated just by putting a lot of lactic acid into the system.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I saw doctors chiming in on social media saying, "Oh my God, if this is true, it means in my practice as an oncologist, I've been killing people."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Did you ever read Max Gerson's book, *59 Cases*? Coffee enemas were one of his staples. He generally gave people thyroid and tried to get their metabolism towards oxidative energy production. But cleaning the intestine was probably his single most effective thing. He actually cured numerous advanced cases of cancer. I think chronically keeping the endotoxin down gives the recuperative system a great chance.

**Georgi Dinkov:** That would explain why recent studies with tetracycline and doxycycline are reporting such remarkable effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In 1965, a doctor sent me an argument that he was curing cancer with antibiotics. I didn't at that time think of it in terms of cutting out the endotoxin, but people have been doing it repeatedly over several decades.

There have been a couple of studies in which people accidentally noticed that women given an antibiotic course recovered from their headaches, but blood tests found that before the antibiotic, they had high estrogen and cortisol and low progesterone. After the course of antibiotics, their progesterone went up and both cortisol and estrogen went down—both of which would favor recovery from cancer.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Did you know that cortisol is given to pretty much any cancer patient as a standard treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Along with morphine. And morphine increases histamine release. Histamine is a powerful tumor promoter, so they usually adjust the dose so that they're dead before they notice that the tumor has grown faster.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, would you put Paul Ehrlich in the pantheon of people that have ruined science?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He popularized the whole idea of lock-and-key receptor specificity. That whole receptor idea is perfect for selling chemicals. Every chemical can have a receptor. The holistic, ongoing whirlwind picture of the organism—where a large dose of a chemical can have an opposite effect of a small dose—is no good for the chemical industry.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I looked at all the hormones and their receptor structures. There is a significant overlap in the amino acid sequence. Is it even possible to develop a truly selective receptor compound?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I don't think so. The whole idea of receptors derives from Ehrlich and I think it's corrupt right down to its foundation. Pavlov and Szent-Györgyi were familiar with the idea that the dose determines the effect. A small amount of caffeine is sedative, a large amount is stimulating, and an even larger amount is narcotic. The typical curve has been tested on hundreds of substances and it consistently contradicts the idea of a specific receptor doing a specific thing.

You have to think of the cell as a substance which can move from one phase to another, potentially a series of phases, each having a characteristic behavior. The differentiation occurs in the cytoplasm as a whole.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Have you seen the recent news about the resurgence of hormone replacement therapy with estrogen? They're trying to put down the findings of the Women's Health Initiative (WHI).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About every five or ten years, the actual science makes a little headway. The big headway was the WHI, and within five years, the people at Stanford were explaining why estrogen didn't really cause cancer, strokes, and heart attacks. Their favorite explanation is that it's really progesterone.

Originally, estrogen was recognized as doing certain things, and they identified the estrogen receptor. Even though hypoxia in the absence of estrogen will cause the receptor to behave the same. Estrogen creates hypoxia. When they needed to explain away that estrogen does everything that it does, they discovered the estrogen receptor beta. It turns out that almost everything that estrogen *doesn't* do, the beta does—it stops growth and parallels the actions of progesterone. They're just thinking wildly of ways that they can say that progesterone is responsible for all of the bad stuff that has been blamed on estrogen.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I emailed one of the authors of a big study calling for the reintroduction of estrogen. I asked, "How can you argue that estrogen is good considering that your own organization [NIH] has a webpage which says estrogen is a carcinogen and a mutagen?" He said, "Estrogen has non-genomic effects that are actually beneficial... if we give it at lower dosages, it acts as a powerful antioxidant."

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, people say all sorts of things about why you do what you do. What is your perspective of what maintains health and what differentiates it into the state of sickness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are two simple choices. One: the genes have been laid out, creating a blueprint, and all the energy has to do is keep them running. That orientation leads to the idea that the less you live, the longer you will live—that you're going to burn up the apparatus the faster you use it. That comes from the reductionist idea of a machine laid out in genetic blueprints.

The other picture is the developmental picture: that energy flowing from the sun through the atmosphere is creating structures. The flow of energy itself generates structures. The faster the energy flows, the more complex the structure becomes, and the more energy is saved in the system in the form of complexity. It's the speed with which you can waste the energy while responding to it, building your complexity, that is holding up the whole structure. It's simply a picture of an ecosystem responding physically to energy.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, do you think there's a way forward with the system we have? Do you see glimmers of hope?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Do you know who Ann Coulter is? I think of her as the personification of goofy reactionary philosophy. But weirdly, she has made some of the most insightful comments about what's going on now. Comparing Bernie Sanders and Trump, she pointed out that the very things Trump campaigned on but didn't fulfill—keeping us out of war, taxing the untaxed corporations, and stopping immigration—Bernie has identical policies to what people were perceiving as Trump's campaign promises. She says that he is Trump's real threat.

**Danny Roddy:** I'm torn on the immigration issue. I read Bucky Fuller saying there shouldn't be borders.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Bucky Fuller would say that the corollary is that you stop creating horror experiences at home. Like imposing a fascist on Honduras. Obviously, it's an improvement for them to try to get into the United States, but simply stopping the oppression of third-world countries would stop the immigration. Hondurans would rather live in Honduras with a better standard of living.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Do you think this empire or any empire can be reformed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think theoretically a controlled collapse of the empire is possible—withdrawing the army more or less quickly. If you freed up the Pentagon budget, 90% of it, that amount of money removed from military destruction could far more than finance any kind of Bernie Sanders programs.

**Georgi Dinkov:** What would be your response to a person who understands the system is killing them but is shaking with anxiety? Where do they start?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think organizing. That's exactly where the power system exists—any impulse towards organization gets interrupted. New ways of organizing have to develop.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Do you think the cultural push towards extreme individualism is an attempt at implementing this isolation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. That's at the heart of preventing organization.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Where is the middle ground?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the first thing is to just start lots of organizations. Two or three people in a group deciding on possible courses of action. Create networks of just little personal interaction groups. If you have two million little groups developing, it will overwhelm the FBI's manpower advantage.

**Georgi Dinkov:** There have been studies suggesting that medicine has been looking at consciousness the wrong way—the "hard problem." Is consciousness a basic property of matter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. I formulated it that way in 1957. I think of consciousness as a substance in itself. I think the donor-acceptor relationship activates a constant oscillation of excited electrons through the neurons. It's a substance analogous to the conductive electron bands in metal, but the electrons are existing on the soft cytoplasmic material.

P.K. Anokhin saw his "acceptor of action" consciousness model as existing as an excited electron substance which follows the rules of Gestalt psychology. It is actually space-filling material of electron plasma.

**Georgi Dinkov:** So the frequencies of nerve firing are nothing really related to consciousness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are like the infrastructure of maintaining energy production and substance distribution, but the experience is floating over the infrastructure.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Speaking of resonance, Rupert Sheldrake writes about morphogenetic fields. If two people's consciousnesses are resonating, is there a limit to the distance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the communication can probably be carried on like a carrier wave on the Earth's resonance frequencies—the Schumann resonant frequencies.

**Georgi Dinkov:** What do you think time is in terms of a physical entity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My best guess is that Forrest Dudley was right and he described it as the neutrino sea. He proposed that neutrinos have energy and associate with matter according to its mass. Being through time, passing through time as a mass, allows these neutrinos to interact. My inference is that the brain, this structure of donor-acceptor activated gel of electrons, is able to tap into the energy of the neutrino sea. This is where the introduction of novelty as well as energy comes from.

**Georgi Dinkov:** If the stars are perhaps the most intense entities with the most intense metabolism, would you say that they possess a type of consciousness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would think a galaxy, the streaming shape-creating forces of galaxies, are probably conscious. There's no more streaming energy through matter than a galaxy in action. But I think our brains are rivaling the galaxies for the complexity of activated substance.

**Danny Roddy:** We're up to about two hours. Ray, Georgi, thank you so much for making this possible. Any parting words, Ray? Can you tell people how to obtain your newsletter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can email raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com. And see if you can have people come up with ideas and create new organizations.

**Danny Roddy:** I love it. Georgi?

**Georgi Dinkov:** I'm privileged enough to start being able to make my own studies. I was thinking of doing one on essential fatty acid depletion to prove that the symptoms seen in the 1930s were just deficiencies of specific nutrients or calories.

**Danny Roddy:** I think in our last conversation you were saying whether calcium was sedative or excitatory depended on carbon dioxide.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I was going to say, have you seen the news of the Moderna and Pfizer vaccines? How many people started suddenly dying in Norway and in Israel? **Ray Peat:** And in one county of New York, which had been free of the so-called virus for a whole month, vaccination started in one nursing home on December 22nd. They vaccinated 198 old people, and in about two weeks, 23 or 24 of those had died. That is a huge statistical indication. The nursing home people said, "Well, they had a local epidemic of the virus that happened to kill only the vaccinated people."

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think they're dying from the lipid adjuvant or from the actual mRNA operating system?

**Ray Peat:** I think it's the adjuvant, and no one is talking about that. I think they falsely labeled it as a carrier for the RNA when those same things have been sold for years as adjuvants.

**Danny Roddy:** So the RNA aspect of the vaccine is less dangerous than the polyethylene glycol lipid adjuvant?

**Ray Peat:** I would guess so. But regarding the long-range possibility of having the RNA for making the spike protein—which creates inflammation—if we become permanent factories for inflammation proteins, that isn't a good thing.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Did you see the news about the Australian vaccine? It's already been terminated, but it contains a portion of the HIV virus. As soon as they started giving it to people, people started testing HIV positive. So they freaked out and shut down the vaccine. They said, "Don't worry, it's not causing HIV infection." But you have only two choices: either the vaccine causes HIV infection, or the tests that are detecting HIV positive people are useless.

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, it's nice that there are frauds being put to the test.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Now Lin Wood, the lawyer, is saying that apparently some of his friends that got vaccinated with the Pfizer vaccine—which shouldn't contain any HIV particles—are also testing HIV positive. Do you think that maybe the mRNA is somehow activating our internal retroviruses, and that's what's causing the positive tests? Remember, Luc Montagnier, the French Nobel Prize winner, claimed that he identified some HIV in the stretch of RNA that's used.

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. I agree with Peter Duesberg, though, that there has never been any evidence that such a virus causes the AIDS condition.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Right. But in any case, it's probably not a positive sign that the retrovirus is activated by this vaccine.

**Ray Peat:** What will activate a positive test might only take a stretch of two or three nucleotides to indicate a similarity to the HIV virus.

**Georgi Dinkov:** For the PCR test, if its sensitivity is cranked up all the way to the max—I think right now they're using 40 cycles for the coronavirus—if you crank it up even more, can you come up with positive tests for pretty much any virus? Because they're so similar. There's probably an overlap of at least 10% across all viruses.

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. I think they ordered people to test all across the country using that many turns of the cycle because they knew it would create supposed evidence of a big epidemic. I'm sure that if they can get a large number of people vaccinated, then they're going to change the instruction, go back to actually measuring something rather than producing false positives, and then use that to claim that the vaccine eliminated the epidemic.

**Danny Roddy:** Probably one of the darkest things I've read is the idea that if you deny a vaccine—you don't want to be a guinea pig for an experimental new technology—you'll be labeled as a public health threat or a domestic terrorist. Do you think that will be part of this whole thing, gathering people together that refuse to get vaccinated?

**Ray Peat:** They're already doing something like that by having the communication websites censor and prevent those people from posting. The general public is being designated effectively a domestic terrorist if they want to post dissenting information. That was one of Biden's proposals, to have a new category of domestic terrorism so the government could enforce all of the internet to identify these people and keep them from posting anywhere.

**Danny Roddy:** Georgi, do you have any questions? I was going to try to go as far back as possible regarding history. My main question was, does this go back 200 years to the Battle of Waterloo and how the Rothschilds formed their fortune, and then the industrialists like the Rockefellers? Is that an effective way of understanding how we arrived here?

**Ray Peat:** I think so. One strand of culture is coming out in insane ways. In the last several years of getting emails, I've had only maybe half a dozen really insane-sounding people. Just in the last week, I've had more letters like that than in all 20 years that I've used the internet.

I've had people blaming numerology on the Jesuits, even though it originated in the Old Testament. But the Jewish Kabbalah in particular promoted and amplified this essentialist idea that God spoke Hebrew, and that every letter and word of Hebrew is a coded message from God. People like Noam Chomsky studied the Kabbalah as a kid. That philosophy says that you can assert anything that numerology confirms, and you don't need any real-world evidence because the Hebrew word defines reality.

Chomsky used it to bypass the people who wanted to explain language as a matter of the brain dealing with the world. He said, "No, you don't need any evidence at all." The way you get that scientific view of language is to treat the person and the brain as an absolute black box. Don't try to look for any information coming from the people who use language and experience it constantly.

So if you don't have words, you can't think. For example, he said that his dogs—he called them "canines"—don't understand what he is saying because they have no words. But then he explained that he used the word "canine" because if he spoke the word "dog," they would make the "wrong" conclusion that one wanted to do something with them. So he demonstrated that they *are* thinking and would draw a conclusion if he used the word dog, but then denied that thought is possible without words.

This is a deep scientific heresy cutting out empiricism. This is the greatest danger happening now. Everyone is being discouraged from looking for evidence. That forces you to rely on the experts and whoever is running the cult of the time.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Something I didn't realize is that Rothschild wealth is two centuries older than the Rockefellers. In that case, were the Rockefellers agents of the Rothschilds, or did they work together?

**Ray Peat:** I don't know how much of a mental overlap there was at the time they got in cahoots, but I think essentialism is what they all develop in context and then reinforce each other's tendency in that direction.

**Danny Roddy:** And what is essentialism?

**Ray Peat:** It's the idea that you don't need empirical evidence to develop true knowledge of the world. Exactly what Chomsky did with the brain, treating it as a black box. For example, they treat the history of an atom as not existing. This "essence" of what an atom is applies for all time, everywhere in the universe. So you don't want to look for the effect of time on individual atoms. Reductionism is generally making that claim: that we already know what chemical reactions are and what atoms are. If the organism is nothing but atoms, and atoms aren't to be investigated temporally, then we have essential knowledge. Ultimately, if we reduce the organism to atoms and reactions, we already know everything we need to know.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I have a question on economics. It's related to Marx and his theory of why the modern state seems to always lead to wars and destruction. He calls it the "tendency of the profit rate to decline." Basically, as capitalists make production more capital-intensive and shun labor, the profit rate declines because, according to Marx, value is only produced by labor. Ultimately, this leads to conflict. Are you familiar with his thought on that?

**Ray Peat:** Not in detail, but he thought that process would lead automatically to socialism. Lenin's insight was that as long as you can keep developing colonies, including the whole world in the process, every time capitalism is failing, you have to open up new populations. Lenin thought that imperialism was the result: every time capitalism would have died, they expand and organize new markets.

**Georgi Dinkov:** If there are no more colonies, because we live in a fairly developed world, then ultimately that would have to lead to a conflict. The only option is to start the destruction of the wealth that was already produced inside of that country—specifically the wealth of the middle and lower classes—so they can usurp it at pennies on the dollar.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, regarding surviving the "Great Reset," you've mentioned having a chicken or a goat or being able to produce your own food. Is there anything else you're doing to protect yourself or would recommend?

**Ray Peat:** In the short term, having storable food is logical. But because electricity is essential for ordinary living, you can't store perishable food in the freezer because they just have to turn off the electricity for a week and everything is spoiled.

**Danny Roddy:** I have a list here: UHT milk, honey, white sugar, canned oysters, canning salt, frozen meat (if you have power), Mexican Coke, coffee, powdered gelatin, powdered milk, applesauce with no additives, canned fruit without citric acid, baking soda. Is there anything else?

**Ray Peat:** Ordinary granulated white sugar, ghee, and coconut oil are intense calorie sources that are good for a medium-term shutdown.

**Danny Roddy:** And that UHT milk, does it last longer than the six months on the label?

**Ray Peat:** Oh yeah, that date is basically so they can keep selling powdered milk. The taste gradually deteriorates if it's exposed to oxygen, but if it's well sealed, I've had some five-year-old powdered milk. I've eaten ultra-pasteurized milk far beyond the expiration date and didn't notice the taste was any worse.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Did you see the recent changes by the FDA in food safety regulations? They explained they had to do it because of the pandemic, but now they're allowing vendors to replace most ingredients as they see fit without changing the label. For example, replacing coconut oil with cottonseed or canola oil in mayonnaise.

**Ray Peat:** Even five years ago, the Department of Agriculture was allowing horrible things to bypass labeling requirements as "processing agents."

**Georgi Dinkov:** I actually got some organic milk brands that were giving me digestive issues. I sent samples to a lab, and they came back saying these milks contained silica and gums, even though neither was listed on the label. I called the vendor, and they said as long as it's under a limit—I think less than one gram per serving—they aren't required to report it.

**Danny Roddy:** Let's take a listener question from Abraham regarding the aging process. He asks: "What would it take to stop aging and reverse the process? What therapies or technologies do we need?"

**Ray Peat:** I think the basic process is epigenetic, and it involves small adaptations constantly to an improper environment for our type of organism. If we can cause all of our adaptations to be directed by our central intention—what we feel ourselves to be and the need—aging could basically be stopped.

Every little adjustment to stress leaves an epigenetic residue in the tissues, slowing metabolism, lowering oxygen consumption while increasing glycolytic energy production. The consequences are a gradual increase in proteins like heat shock protein and collagen, and a progressive lowering of mitochondrial processes. The organism gets drier and drier, but the individual cells inside this dehydrating framework become more and more inflamed.

I think of running downhill as an extreme example of adjusting in the wrong direction. If you stretch a muscle under tension, that leaves damage behind and very quickly lowers the oxidative ability of the cell. Some Canadian exercise physiologists have old people do exclusively concentric exercise in which you don't have any adjustment to the forced extension of muscles. Our culture is forcing our organism to go ways that it really doesn't want to go.

**Georgi Dinkov:** If an organism is depleted of PUFA (Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids), wouldn't the maladaptive process be much slower?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, all kinds of experiments have demonstrated that PUFAs accelerate all of the bad processes.

**Georgi Dinkov:** A study just came out finding that simply blocking the prostaglandin E2 receptor basically fully reverses signs of brain aging. I thought, what a politically convenient way to not implicate PUFA. But to knowledgeable people, it means that without PUFA there can be no brain aging. Does that apply to every tissue?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. The prostaglandin system is the final amplifier of the stress-intensifying function.

**Georgi Dinkov:** In terms of controlling the stress reaction, it starts at the hypothalamus with hormones like CRH and TRH. Several studies show these peptides are highly inflammatory. Do you think there's any benefit in suppressing the reaction of the hypothalamus to stress?

**Ray Peat:** Good conditions will do it. Thyroid supplements are one of the important things for keeping down the stress produced by TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone). There's a gradually increasing awareness that TSH is what causes the circulatory damage of hypothyroidism. As TSH goes up, the deterioration—atherosclerosis, hypertension—is created by the TSH itself.

**Danny Roddy:** This question is from Oren: "Can you speak on the history of philosophy? Does the Hegelian idea of progress and post-Enlightenment rationalism lead to our current situation? How does this tie in with neo-Darwinist views, and how should we correctly conceptualize the human organism?"

**Ray Peat:** I think the idea of intentionality is what governs the organism. In philosophy, there was a jump where Edmund Husserl and Alexius Meinong proposed concentrating on intentional processes. Around the same time, early 20th-century embryology showed that if you split an early embryo, you get two complete organisms. This showed it's not just a mechanical process; there is an intention to become a certain sort of thing.

Every undesirable experience the developing organism has diverts it from its best intentions. Bertrand Russell brought back a lot of the rationalist and hidden essentialism. His idea of "logical atoms" semi-consciously incorporated ideas of strict reductionist Darwinism, racism, and imperialism.

**Danny Roddy:** When I was reading about the Rockefellers and Rothschilds, Immanuel Kant came up a few times. Is that one of the undesirable philosophies?

**Ray Peat:** Yes. It started about 1900 and was one of the most evil but widespread influences. Kantianism is sort of the ultimate denial of empiricism. In practice, we always find a way to remain essentialist and rationalist.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Would you say that the physical basis of intentionality in the human organism is a potential difference between the organism and the environment?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. I think the degree of success that the organism finds in keeping its basic purpose despite the slight deviations is what leads to delayed aging.

**Danny Roddy:** Austin asks about vellus hairs turning to terminal hairs. Babies have thin hair that turns thick; balding people have the reverse. Is it possible to turn vellus hairs back to terminal hairs?

**Ray Peat:** I've experimented several times with using DHEA in oil on the sides of my eyebrows that have gradually gone through aging and disappearance. It took about six months to create new, dark, normal hairs. Using a topical copper solution, the very next day I could see the colored hair beginning at the base. In the case of lost hairs, it was a very slow process.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I think there's a difference between the hair type a baby has and a balding person has. Babies have low androgens and high pregnenolone. Balding people tend to have high levels of estrogen and prolactin in the scalp. Both prolactin and estrogen are known to destroy the follicle.

**Ray Peat:** There have been interesting studies on dogs. Certain dogs became completely bald when their owners started supplementing estrogen on their skin.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Isn't a good indication that estrogen and prolactin are involved in hair loss the fact that most menopausal women start having serious problems with hair thinning?

**Ray Peat:** Yes. The whole "menopause is estrogen failure" idea is a total fraud created by the industry to sell a product. First, they prescribed estrogen to prevent miscarriage, even after it had been demonstrated to cause miscarriage.

In rat studies, when ovaries are removed, within a week the rats were right back to their normal estrogen level but without progesterone. My dissertation was based on the fact that sterility in the middle of the lifespan is caused by unopposed estrogen. But the drug companies have kept this misguided idea that there's a lack of estrogen at menopause. All of the symptoms of menopause can be produced by too much estrogen or too little progesterone.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Do you think there's a reason studies always focus on estradiol as if it's the only type of estrogen?

**Ray Peat:** There have been studies calling for endocrinology to evaluate its position because they only measure estradiol. If you measure estrone sulfate in menopausal women, it is very, very high. Stress and lack of progesterone shift the enzymes so every cell becomes able to convert estrone into the 10 times more active estradiol.

The most important measurement made was comparing the estrogen content in the vein coming out of the ovary to the vein coming out of an arm. They found the arm was producing just as much estrogen as the ovary. The whole body is always producing estrogen, and it's the whole body's stress-induced estrogen that has to be controlled.

**Danny Roddy:** Daniel asks about a flare-up of Crohn's disease. Any recommendations besides glycine and collagen?

**Ray Peat:** Undoubtedly estrogen is involved. I've been recommending both thyroid and progesterone for about 45 years, and everyone that has tried it has improved their symptoms.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Is the estrogen shifting the redox balance of the intestine, causing inflammation?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. Increased reduction is the same as failed oxidation.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Older studies demonstrated that you can put inflammatory bowel disease in remission by gonadectomizing animals. If they administered androgens or progesterone, they stayed in remission, which proves estrogen is the direct cause. Also, studies in the 80s treated Crohn's and ulcerative colitis with 100,000 units of Vitamin D weekly to induce remission.

**Ray Peat:** Yes, I think Vitamin D is effective taken orally. The things that reduce inflammation cure all sorts of chronic diseases. This could be a dose of 50,000 or 100,000 units of Vitamin D orally to get started. Progesterone and aspirin—everything that is a safe anti-inflammatory agent—has been used against these diseases.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, didn't you know Vitamin D was toxic?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, I've heard that a thousand times. The receptor is a good sign of deficiency of Vitamin D. As you become deficient in the storage form (25-hydroxy), you begin to produce both the receptor and the so-called "active" Vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxy). People get confused and fail to see that the "active" form and the receptor are associated with toxic effects that are reduced by adequate calcium and the storage form of Vitamin D.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Does intracellular calcium turn on aromatase?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, excitation of the cell generally turns on stress and the tendency to be on the estrogen pathway. That is part of the aging process. But a deficiency of dietary calcium also increases aromatase because it increases PTH (Parathyroid Hormone). Like a deficiency of good Vitamin D, calcium deficiency increases stress and activates the whole system: endotoxin, aldosterone, parathyroid hormone, and estrogen.

**Danny Roddy:** Will asks: "For someone who has utilized the carrot salad, mushrooms, and antibiotics yet still has chronic endotoxin symptoms and low cholesterol, what are good strategies?"

**Ray Peat:** Great care with what you eat is part of it. Anything that irritates your bowel is a risk. Sometimes you have to be fairly extreme to start improving the situation. Trying different forms of fiber can help find one that reduces inflammation.

**Danny Roddy:** What about antibiotics like penicillin or tetracycline?

**Ray Peat:** All of those sometimes help.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I know you've spoken favorably of charcoal, but cautioned against it absorbing into the bloodstream. Wouldn't combining charcoal with the carrot salad reduce those risks?

**Ray Peat:** It does seem logical, but it's something I would prefer to leave to rat experiments because any kind of unmetabolizable particle, if it gets persorbed, basically kills off part of your whole system.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you have confidence in *Biosporin* (probiotic)?

**Ray Peat:** *Biosporin* can be very powerful because the bacteria in it are producers of antibiotics. When I used it, I would let it sit in a glass of milk at room temperature until there was a delicate coagulation, then put it in the refrigerator and use only a spoonful per day. That way, the extreme dilution of the preservative wouldn't be a factor.

**Georgi Dinkov:** How long does it take for a sterilized gut to get recolonized?

**Ray Peat:** It sometimes happens in a week, but sometimes people don't manage to get it.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I've had people report that eating a few tablespoons of coconut oil daily gave them loose stools, but then they felt blissfully well for a week. Do you think that's the antibiotic effect?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, it's effective against both fungus and bacteria, but you have to make sure you aren't allergic to it.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, what are you working on right now?

**Ray Peat:** Aging of the cell. Following up on the effect of temperature. I concentrated on cold last time; this one is going to concentrate on the energy deficit effect, which can be produced by heat stress, reductive stress, or any stress that goes with energy deprivation.

**Danny Roddy:** You mentioned to Patrick Timpone that the likely cause of many deaths is just the temperature getting too low.

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. A lot of people don't bother checking the temperature of the mouth, eardrum, and extremities. Old people in particular might have a brain at a good temperature, but they're producing less energy, and that shows up as an extreme gradient from the extremities to the brain.

The indoor temperature might be 70 degrees and seem safe, but even through insulated walls, the outside temperature can profoundly drain your body's energy-producing ability. That's because a large percentage of our biological energy goes out as radiation—microwaves and infrared. If it isn't reciprocated by returning radiation from something approaching body temperature, your body is draining vastly more energy. That's why aspirin, a snack before bed, progesterone, and thyroid are so important right before sleep.

**Danny Roddy:** Brandon asks about "Kototama" or sacred sound mantra practices to tone the vagus nerve as a top-down approach to modulating stress.

**Ray Peat:** Shock is the extreme degree of most of these things we've been talking about. Hans Selye was the first to propose that estrogen imitates a shock reaction. I think that applies to many of the stimulating techniques of the vagus nerve. You have to be very watchful for estrogenic influences when you specifically stimulate the vagus.

**Danny Roddy:** Jake asks about your previous comment that a large release of carbon dioxide from the earth could lead to a planetary shift in consciousness.

**Ray Peat:** I think the earth is basically doing the best things it can. Melting tundra ice is releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide. If the earth is expanding, as some measurements suggest, that would dilute the atmosphere, resembling high altitude.

At high altitude, you see both acceleration and reduction of stress hormones. When T3 increases, cortisol doesn't increase at high altitude. Brain oxidative metabolism increases with higher CO2. That greater consumption of electrons is tending to keep the brain in a positive, productive, more conscious condition.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, we seem to have been inundated with recent UFO news. What is your take on the general UFO agenda?

**Ray Peat:** I think it's a risk in a time of crisis. A lot of us will be declared domestic terrorists for doubting Fauci. It will be a welcome distraction to get people's minds off the critics.

**Danny Roddy:** Is it purely an agenda for control?

**Ray Peat:** It functions that way. It's hard to tell whether it's just the silliness of broadcasters who know what they shouldn't write about. It's on the safe list.

**Danny Roddy:** Could any of these be extraterrestrial?

**Ray Peat:** It's a possibility, but I would give priority to all kinds of government fraud over actual evidence of aliens. The fact that it's being released specifically now makes it that much more suspect.

**Danny Roddy:** Nick asks: "If the mechanism of MDMA (Ecstasy) is a big release of serotonin, and serotonin is a stress chemical, why do people feel so happy and loving on it?"

**Ray Peat:** Obviously, it's releasing a lot of processes in the brain. The fact that it damages the brain comes from the excess serotonin. But I would guess that the good feeling comes from the general over-excitation of the brain.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Is it a cultural cliché to say "this drug makes me happy, therefore it's increasing serotonin"?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, it is strictly a cliché.

**Georgi Dinkov:** I think it's a dose-dependent effect. MDMA is in clinical trials for PTSD, and at very low doses, it has a powerful antidepressant effect tied to a large release of dopamine and a drop of cortisol. My opinion is that MDMA is serotonergic only if you abuse it in very high doses.

**Danny Roddy:** Tim asks about a comment you made previously: "If you're not in the euphoric state, then there's something wrong with you." Can you expand on that?

**Ray Peat:** Things like carbon dioxide and adequate oxidation of glucose should give you a 24-hour-a-day euphoria. Anything that interferes with this highly efficient energy production is amplifying damage.

**Danny Roddy:** How do you define euphoria?

**Ray Peat:** That life feels good. Feeling your breathing, feeling your heartbeat, and feeling the blood circulate through your tissues—all of that is background. All of it feels good. It gives a general tone to everything you're thinking and doing.

Doctors have been thinking of euphoria as something dangerous. If thyroid leads to euphoria, they'll tell you to stop taking it because they think of those good feelings as not quite compatible with life.

If you ask a person to pay attention to their heart beating, they often get nervous. But a typical response to the exactly right dose of thyroid is, "Thyroid is love." A feeling that radiates out of the chest. If you're low in thyroid, those same areas of your body report anxiety. The experience of love is probably the best description of what the euphoria of metabolism is doing.

**Danny Roddy:** That's awesome. Ray, thank you so much for joining us tonight. Georgi, thank you as always. Stay safe everyone.

transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Hey everyone, we just wrapped up live stream number 51 with Ray Peat. We had issues with bandwidth and the sound is popping, so it is imperfect, but I stitched together the silence and I thought the content was excellent.

We have Dr. Raymond Peat and Georgi Dinkov. Ray, your newest newsletter just came out: "Cumulative Damage, Degeneration and Aging: Possibilities of Reversal." It had a lot to do with heat shock proteins. Do you want to talk about your motivation for writing it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is part of the general picture of how to understand biology usefully. The reductionist approach of breaking it up into parts provides an infinite amount of knowledge that you can never do anything with. But if you understand the principle of how the organism works, you see that bacteria don't have our analytic abilities, yet they have the intelligence to redesign themselves radically to meet a challenging environment.

Barbara McClintock showed that the same sort of redesigning of the genome happens in plants. If bacteria and plants can radically change themselves to do better in the world, there is no reason people should feel weighted down by the ballast of genes inherited from reptiles.

The factors of this simplifying picture are the physics of phase change—essentially what Gilbert Ling was talking about. This was a major movement early in the 20th century for understanding the origin of life. That view sees life as a substance rather than an accumulation of 20,000 independent pieces of DNA. Life as a substance can change phase in the direction of losing energy, or, with good luck, come back to a high-energy state because all parts are subordinate to the flow of energy managed by the whole organism.

**Danny Roddy:** You talked about Le Chatelier's principle. Is this related to the cave fish example you’ve mentioned before? Where river fish diverted into a cave lost their eyes and became clear to adapt to their environment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When I was in graduate school, people were still doing experiments of that sort. One experiment fed fruit flies a very high salt diet, and they adaptively changed their cuticle so it wasn't irritated by the flow of salt. Another put them under very hot artificial light, causing the wing structure to thicken. These were first-generation adaptations to a stressful environment.

Then, they turned off the light, gave them a normal diet, and cross-bred them. From then on, they had a Mendelian-like inheritance of these traits. They sorted out generation after generation with the thickened scales and veins. When I asked my professors, the standard reaction was, "Those were hidden genes. They were there all along." That is the scientific method genetics is based on: if it happens, it must have already been there in these immortal genes because nothing new happens.

**Danny Roddy:** In your newsletter, you discuss Gilbert Ling and ATP as the "cardinal adsorbent." ATP has to be present in the cell for this phase transition to happen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I mentioned that it functions as a protein solvent. If you lower your energy and don't have the ATP binding it and keeping the cell together, some proteins come out of solution and go into a different phase. These become stress-induced organelles.

The practical use of that idea has been noticed since experiments by Albert Szent-Györgyi showed that ATP has a softening, relaxing effect on isolated protein material. It keeps everything together and in solution in the cytoplasm.

In a fatigued muscle, the muscle gets harder. When fully energized, the cytoplasm is flexible and soft but can contract to do maximum work. A fatigued heart gets harder, but on stimulation, it is already tight, so it can't do much more. ATP functionally represents the flow of energy. The energized, well-nourished cell is in a relaxed state. This relates to insomnia, muscle cramps, and even cancer.

Cancers can be diagnosed by their hardness. If a lymph node is hard to the touch, it is likely cancerous. The hardness involves the inability to relax and the stabilization of a fibrous form of actin. Depleted energy turns on collagen synthesis; the actin attaches to this growing collagen, and you get a system that is harder the more energy-depleted it is.

**Danny Roddy:** Was Szent-Györgyi the person who injected ATP into dead animals to reverse rigor mortis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, rigor mortis is the phase change. When you get smaller degrees of that phase change, you get chronic issues like intracellular bodies that produce inflammation, dementia, or prions—proteins that are no longer soluble.

**Danny Roddy:** This precedes cellular division when a cell is stressed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Promoting cell division is one alternative. You want to lose the complex, energy-consuming cell functions like thought and secretion. To escape the stress, the cell turns off differentiated functions and resorts to simple cell division. The hardening process is broken by activating the de-differentiating, cancer-producing property.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Are you familiar with studies from the 80s showing that niacinamide is a great substance for increasing solubility? I saw studies showing that mixing niacinamide with something lipophilic like progesterone increases its solubility in water by a few thousand percent. Considering the importance of niacinamide as an NAD precursor and its relationship with ATP, can niacinamide fill in for some of those roles ATP has as a solubility increaser?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it does. It is able to stop the energy loss. It turns off some of the deranged DNA repair mechanisms and can let the cell die peacefully rather than draining tremendous amounts of energy. It plugs the leak.

**Danny Roddy:** Would gelatin have some of those effects as well, increasing the solubility of intracellular proteins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It would probably depend on the starches present. Gelatin is bound to run into things like RNA and polymer carbohydrates that will affect the water-holding properties.

**Georgi Dinkov:** If I'm reading this correctly, an excess of unpaired electrons—which happens when metabolism is impaired—would greatly inhibit the solubility of proteins inside the cell. So things that accept those electrons, like quinones or other oxidizing agents, should improve solubility and retain the gelatin-like structure of the cell.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and that should involve a constant flow. When the excess electrons are being drained away quickly enough into the electron vacuum of oxygen, that is the living state.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Do the effects of estrogen on activating heat shock proteins and decreasing protein solubility relate to its activity as a reductant?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Oh, yeah. I guess that's a more physiological way. You just blow up with fat instead of calcifying and cutting off a part.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Right. So people gaining weight during middle age is a very common process. Then fibrosis, deterioration, losing muscle mass, and getting saggy tissue seems to be the process that happens later on if metabolic things are not recovered.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** It's doing on the systemic, whole-organism level what the local fibrosis does. It's preserving the organism at the expense of losing its functional tissue, such as muscle, and replacing it with fat. Exactly the same processes are involved. Intense calcification will cut off an area and turn it to stone. The process of aging is a very, very slow turning to stone. It involves calcification but in a diffuse way that increases inflammation as it lowers function.

But if the cells are de-energized, then calcium starts to accumulate too much. Then, under the influence of parathyroid hormone (PTH), it starts to become part of the fibrotic tissue. **Dr. Ray Peat:** Yeah, the parathyroid hormone is working by amplifying the de-energized situation that starts it all. **Georgi Dinkov:** What's the signal in the organism that decides between killing off and separating a particular tissue, or turning into a tumor? Is there a threshold, or is it a chance event?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Yeah, and it can do the same with invasive bacteria or parasites.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Is there a situation where this process is adaptive and should not be interfered with? If you're lowering parathyroid hormone, is there a situation where the body says, "No, I need that in order to wall that tumor off"?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Yeah, and those follow-ups to the Michelson-Morley experiment carefully controlled for temperature, because that had been brought out as a defense of the space-time thing. They absolutely showed that temperature wasn't involved.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** I think it's important to get pleasure from looking at the world. Intrinsically, the process of being involved and learning gives pleasure. **Georgi Dinkov:** If the environment is crappy and oppressing us, isn't it abnormal to try to force ourselves into positive thinking?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Not force, but to find the route to get to the different state where you aren't being oppressed by the world.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** My experience of the world right from the beginning was that it was a process I was involved in. **Danny Roddy:** A question from Phil Greaves: "What does Ray think of Marx's scientific method and social revolution?"

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Several Christians and capitalists have said Marx's science was very useful. **Danny Roddy:** People are going to say all this COVID stuff and riots are driven by Marxist ideology.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** I don't see any connection at all. You could say it's the Rockefeller world controlling class. They might understand Marx and use Marx, but Marx had the ethics that you should not kill off billions of people.

**Danny Roddy:** "How much does intuitive thinking coincide with intellectual processing, and why does intuition at times lead us to poor choices?"

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Analysis and reasoning can lead to horrible outcomes. Intuition is different from simple reasoning because instead of starting with postulates and leading to logical conclusions, you're always open. When you change your postulates, you have a flexible, open view of the world. The organism is absolutely not a bunch of algorithms. It's a process that is constantly revising itself.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Do you think one of the reasons for intuition leading to bad outcomes is because some people live in a world that's been deliberately engineered to disfavor such an approach?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** Yeah, it's trying to implant its doctrines and ways of reasoning.

**Danny Roddy:** A listener asks: "Is the desire for revenge always serotonergic, or can it have a place in a healthy person's psychology?"

**Dr. Ray Peat:** If you've been injured, you have to process the damage. Mentally, you can think of getting revenge as restoring your wholeness. It's a mental process of understanding why a person would injure you. You can have thoughts of revenge as part of the process of how to interpret that and go on without actually having to do destructive retaliatory things.

**Georgi Dinkov:** There was a study with prisoners of war in Vietnam. The ones who fantasized about getting back at their captors but without acting upon it did the best psychologically.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** That kind of mental imagery is part of a healing process, activating your creative ability in a bad situation.

**Danny Roddy:** A listener asks about how the mind affects biological processes, along the lines of your book *Mind and Tissue*.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** The way we think about the body and its organs, we've been indoctrinated to think in terms of substance and energy as different things. But the body we experience is a unitary process. The organs, tissues, cells, and conscious experience are really all one substantial phenomenon.

**Georgi Dinkov:** If you're doing something repetitive, wouldn't that give a signal to the cells that they don't need to produce as much energy?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** You can't really do anything twice. Like Heraclitus said, you're always changing. If you're trapped in that kind of repetitive behavior, you either have to escape or go to sleep. People tend to put themselves to sleep rather than escaping from pointless work.

**Danny Roddy:** Last question: "What are Ray's thoughts on planes of existence beyond our physical world, such as the etheric and astral planes?"

**Dr. Ray Peat:** I don't think there is any "elsewhere." Part of those categories derive from thinking about matter as inert substance. If you have a metaphysical idea about what matter is, then you have to have an idea of what animates matter, so you get involved in separate energy and planes. But there are all different levels of subtle interactions.

Insects and probably dogs can detect at a distance a single vibrating molecule. The environment is constantly offering us information about itself. By tuning in, you can find out that our world is full of lots of information and messages that are ignored if you believe in inert matter.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Why do you think the "second signal system" (language/abstraction) evolved? It seems to be a largely pathological development.

**Dr. Ray Peat:** I think it has practicality to make remote things something you can talk about, rather than having to stay with the surrounding immediate reality. But it is very easily pathological.

**Georgi Dinkov:** Is there a way to gauge a society by how much of each system is at play?

**Dr. Ray Peat:** I think the countries that have lost their grammar to some extent have opened up their ability to receive messages in a more realistic and biological way. If you have a language that is more fluid and flexible, that lets you have better perceptions.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, thank you so much. Stay on the line. Georgi, thank you for being my partner in crime. We'll talk to you guys soon.

**Danny Roddy:** Can you run through the calcium metabolism and how that leads to the accumulation of iron? What does parathyroid hormone (PTH) have to do with iron overload?

Some people refer to that as bloat. But when it's digestive, if you aren't digesting your carbohydrate, the bacteria can produce a large amount of gas. The test for that is just to thump your belly with your fingers. You can tap it in different places and find exactly where there's a gas deposit if there is.

**Danny Roddy:** I think that's all the questions I have for you. What are you working on right now, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cholesterol and then progesterone will be my next newsletters. Thinking about the evolutionary, in every sense, implications and meaning of cholesterol and progesterone.

**Danny Roddy:** Awesome, you have been so generous with your time. My sincere thanks. Thank you so much, Ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks.

title: Carbon Dioxide, Redox Balance, and The Ketone Body Ratio with Ray Peat  [Generative Energy #26]
transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Today I'm talking with painter, philosopher, and biologist, Raymond Peat. In this hour-long episode, we'll talk about the passing of May Wan Ho, Vladimir Vernadsky, carbon dioxide, the NAD+ to NADH ratio, new and old hormones, thyroid brands, how Ray makes his coffee, and so much more.

Ray, I thought we'd start off talking about May Wan Ho. I just ran across a review of *The Rainbow and the Worm* about 15 years ago. Did you think of her as an ally in your fight against mainstream science?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, sure. That coherence thing is where I've been going since the 60s.

**Danny Roddy:** In her photos in *The Rainbow and the Worm*, had you ever seen anything like that? I feel like talking to people about this idea of science is hard, but when you show them those photos, they almost immediately think there's more to the picture than the materialist science we've been sold.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was about 1958 or 1955 when I was in Mexico first. In the square in Pátzcuaro, people had laid out the different fish they had caught. Two different kinds of them were transparent, sort of like green jello. They called them white fish. I had some delicious fried transparent fish that were just like ordinary white fish when they were cooked—opaque, on bones, everything.

I was intrigued by how something with bones, blood, guts, heart, and all the standard organs could be perfectly transparent when it was uncooked. That made me think about the light being carried in channels to bypass the bones, effectively making bones and liver and everything disappear.

**Danny Roddy:** And that could only happen if the organism was liquid crystalline, like she talks about?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, that got me interested in how water works all by itself. Around the same time, I was interested in electrical fields in organisms and water. The idea of light conductivity in special ways in cytoplasm connected to the idea that organisms are sensitive not only to electrical currents and fields, but to magnetic fields, because we have our own electrical currents inside. A moving charge is sensitive to the magnetic environment.

The first person's research that I studied in any depth was Yuri Holodov. I went to Moscow in 1968 to talk to him about his biomagnetics or magnetobiology approach. Through him, I got interested in Madeline Barnothy and her work on magnetobiology. She and her husband applied good physics to studying the dowsing phenomenon and found that organisms could detect extremely weak magnetic fields—for example, caused just by water oozing underground. Slow movement of slightly ionized water is enough for an organism like a person to detect.

I was trying to understand how that works. Then I found Solco Tromp's book, *Psychical Physics*. It was published in 1945 or so. He reviewed the old literature on liquid crystals and argued that the cytoplasm is like liquid crystals. You know how the computer monitor screen operates on the principle that a weak electrical field will reorder the liquid crystal? The biology behind that was before the industry's technology application of it, using that as the argument to explain the extreme sensitivity to electrical and magnetic fields.

**Danny Roddy:** Was that post your discovery of Vernadsky or pre?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I found Vernadsky after that.

**Danny Roddy:** Did that tie in perfectly with what you were interested in?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure. He just gave the bigger picture of how energy guides these intricate structures in the cells of an organism. He used Le Chatelier's principle to show that when you disturb a system, it finds a new equilibrium by adjusting whatever needs adjusting. Just by thinking in that context—that the organism is responding to the available energy with the sun or volcanic energy as the source—he reasoned with that simple physical-chemical principle that the complexity and intensity of energy flow both would tend towards a maximum. He said that big trees develop under big energy flows. Big brain mammals develop when there's an opportunity for high energy flow.

**Danny Roddy:** When you were talking about magnetism, that reminded me of when you said you thought that he called himself a "geocosmic realist"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, he had various composite names for what he was doing. Solco Tromp called himself a bio-geo-meteorologist or something like that.

**Danny Roddy:** Last time we talked, we covered a lot of ground on *Nutrition for Women* (1973–1975), which you reissued in 1993, and *Generative Energy* in 1994.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, actually I was writing on generative energy through the 80s. It accumulated. *Mind and Tissue* was the first one I wrote, actually. I gave it to a flaky publisher who lost all the references. I think the chapter on Pavlov was lost too, so I had to rewrite that, but never bothered to fix the missing references because the books were all in different libraries.

**Danny Roddy:** We discussed some of the motivation behind *Nutrition for Women*. Was *Mind and Tissue* what you were truly interested in at the time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that was my intense interest. *Nutrition for Women* was just practical things that some women friends told me would make a useful compilation.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think *Generative Energy* was a marriage of those two things?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was probably Vernadsky that was the kernel for putting those together.
