**Danny Roddy:** I search your older work for carbon dioxide, and although you're constantly talking about thyroid, it seems that the emphasis on carbon dioxide might be a little less a couple of decades ago versus more now. Did things shift in the early 2000s?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was sometime in the late 90s.

**Danny Roddy:** What spurred that interest?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think people asking me about Buteyko. I had read some of Buteyko's articles in 1969 or so, but I didn't really think very much of it except it seemed valid. I was interested at that time in several gases—the way nitrogen fixation by chickens and mammals and people from the atmosphere was what got me interested in Buteyko. The Russians were using nitrogen in their space vehicles with oxygen, where the Americans were using helium. There were some publications arguing that you should always breathe some helium along with your oxygen because of the fact that it can be fixed. Hemoglobin is apparently a nitrogen-fixing molecule in birds and mammals as well as bacteria.

Thinking about how the gases are metabolized—for example, how does a fish keep its swim bladder inflated? The idea of pumping gases in or out. And the negative space between the lungs and the pleural membrane; there's in effect a vacuum there. The membranes are tightly in contact, but if you get a leak, your lungs collapse. If you punch a hole in the lung, the air goes out into that space and the lung shrivels up. So something is pumping absolutely all of the gas out of that space between your chest and the lungs.

Most of the air volume is nitrogen, so it's easy to see that you can subtract the oxygen from that space, but that would leave nitrogen bubbles around your lungs. So something apparently is pulling the nitrogen out of that space constantly, and none of my professors would even talk about that issue.

That left me thinking about the metabolism of all of the gases. I was worried about the turtles that have salt glands on their nose or eyes to excrete excess sodium. The membrane pump people were saying, "See, that proves that there are these marvelous little pumps that throw the ions out of the cells." On investigating that, I saw that there's carbonic anhydrase in there. Just by changing the association of carbon dioxide with water, you affect its solubility. If the acid moves out of the cell, to maintain electric neutrality, it takes a positively charged ion with it. So every time carbonic acid leaves the cell, so does some sodium. Then the carbonic anhydrase, if needed, can liberate the carbon dioxide as gas, leaving just the sodium.

**Danny Roddy:** You said that carbon dioxide is the context for all life processes. In *Mitochondria and Mortality*, you said carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increasing can cause the spontaneous creation of mitochondria. Do you find that is a pivotal thing for higher evolution?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At the time of the Carboniferous period, geologically, the carbon dioxide was 12% or something really intense in the atmosphere. That really stimulated a great abundance of life.

The way I see the ATP synthesis, I don't think it's anything fancier than the fact that if you write out the equation, you see H2O and phosphate becoming ATP. If you look at the equation and subtract water, it gives you ATP. Since carbonic anhydrase is in the mitochondrion closely associated with the formation of ATP, I think its purpose there is partly to turn the newly formed carbon dioxide into carbonic acid, which then leaves, taking away water and creating ATP by dehydrating the phosphates.

**Danny Roddy:** Speaking of carbon dioxide, a lot of people are talking about ketogenesis and ketosis diets. I think I read that carbon dioxide stimulated NADH oxidase. Would that be something, besides supporting mitochondrial respiration in general, that would support the NAD+ to NADH ratio?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think it's the function in Gilbert Ling's sense: an adsorbent that pulls electrons out of the system and makes a protein more actively acidic. I think it has that effect all through the cell. One of the effects of that is to let the cell release any excess water, so it has an anti-swelling effect.

The retraction of the electrons by that cardinal adsorbent action on the proteins shifts the whole electronic state of the cell, making electrons scarcer. That ends up shifting the ratio between NAD and NADH towards the oxidized NAD side.

After reading Gilbert Ling, I read Ephraim Racker and Albert Szent-Györgyi talking about electrons in cells. Szent-Györgyi's book was called *Bioelectronics*. Ephraim Racker coined the phrase "Nothing Dehydrogenases." Szent-Györgyi, working in England in the 1920s, studied related things—that there seems to be electrons or the equivalent of hydrogen from unidentified sources in living cells. Ephraim Racker removed all of the known fuel sources from cells, but his indicators of reductants kept getting reduced. He said the dehydrogenases were causing these chemicals to be reduced, but without a known source, it seemed to be an endless supply of electrons. So he called them the "nothing dehydrogenases."

Szent-Györgyi theorized that these were some of the mobile electrons in the cytoplasmic protein-lipid systems and nucleic acid systems. Some of his associates were showing semi-conductive properties for both nucleic acids and proteins based on this mobility of electrons.

**Danny Roddy:** Normally, protein, fat, and carbohydrate are the substrates for the electron flow. You're saying that because the electrons were in the cell without any substrates, that led Szent-Györgyi to think there was an electric conductivity to the cell that wasn't previously thought?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that proteins of the cell might be catching electrons from the environment. In the last 15 years, people are now talking about the trans-plasma membrane oxidases. Many people are experimenting with these indicators of dehydrogenase activity. They turn red or purple when they get reduced. Using chemicals that don't enter cells because they're strongly electrically negatively charged, they show that oxygen is removing electrons from the cell—oxidizing NADH to NAD, taking electrons out and changing color without entering the cell. So they're showing that cells don't need mitochondria for oxidative metabolism. It can happen right at the surface of the cell. Someone designed cells lacking the gene necessary to make mitochondria and still the cell respired.

**Danny Roddy:** In your *Receptors, Fields, and Therapies* 2014 newsletter, I wanted to talk about the ketone body ratio. Some people think that the NADH should be increased relative to NAD+. Is that where the confusion about the ketone body ratio is? For example, Veech says beta-hydroxybutyrate as a substrate increases NADH relative to NAD+.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that's where I absolutely disagree. It involves everything—bioelectronics and electrode physiology. I think Gilbert Ling might be the only person who would agree with me on this, and Robert Becker of *The Body Electric*.

May Wan Ho in her article "Cancer as a Redox Disease" makes the common mistake of seeing cancer as not having enough electrons. I think its essential problem is it has *too many* electrons in the form of too much NADH and all of the pairs of redox—like too much lactic acid and not enough pyruvic acid. Everything that is in balance is shifted in cancer heavily towards the lactic acid side. Beta-hydroxybutyric acid is just one of those redox couples that can, if you get too much of it, shift you in the direction of cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** May Wan Ho cited a study in which the charge on a tumor was reversed. She cited this article saying that they regressed the cancer by applying a negative field, or it was measured as having a positive charge rather than a negative charge. But Robert Becker, my own measurements, and many other people see a tumor or a cancer as an injury and inflammation. The traditional language for this kind of electric charge is called the "injury potential." If you cut your skin or any tissue is damaged, it's increasing inflammation and lactic acid, and there's a strong shift to electric negativity.

Gilbert Ling explained the so-called resting electric potential—which is highly negative in a healthy cell—as a battery effect. The way you measure it traditionally is with a concentrated solution of potassium chloride. He said that just this high concentration is enough to account for the potential. When you measure a cancer cell, you get very little charge when you poke an electrode in it. But if you measure *outside* of the cancer cell, you have this negative field. That's the injury potential.

One of my projects in graduate school was cell electrophoresis. I built my own apparatus and put cancer cells in one end of a little glass tube and applied a mild electric DC potential. With a microscope, you would look at the cancer cells as you turned on the electric field. If the cell has a high surface negative charge, it moves quickly towards the positive pole. I got very clear evidence that the cancer cells moved towards the positive pole. Other people have measured highly malignant cancer cells versus mildly malignant ones and found that the higher their surface negative charge, the more malignant the cancer is.

A healthy cell is oxidizing, subtracting electrons, creating basically a positive, slightly acidic condition. If you poke one electrode into it, you disturb that and you get a difference between the oxidizing region and the broken, not oxidizing region, which measures as a negative field.

Dan Mazia, for a long time at UC Berkeley, showed that sulfhydryl groups—which are normally oxidized to a fair degree, causing proteins to stick to each other by covalent sulfur-sulfur bonds—change during cell division. If you take away the hydrogens, they stick together. If you put the hydrogen back (reduce the proteins), they become separated and more mobile. Dan Mazia showed there is a tremendous increase in the reduced condition of sulfhydryl groups that appears at the beginning of cell division and disappears when the cell division is completed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Szent-Györgyi was working on muscles and nerves through the 40s and 50s. His theory of muscle contraction was that it was powered electronically by the conduction of electrons through these semiconducting proteins.

Just by accident, in connection with estrogen metabolism and quinone physiology, I was working along the estrogen side of the system in which estrogen shifts away from quinone oxidative physiology to a reductive physiology. In extracting stuff from liver, I was looking for ubiquinone-related things. I found that Vitamin E in a very pure form (with its neutral amber color) and ubiquinone (with its orange color), when I combined them, they turned instantly inky black.

When I put dots of this black combination on paper chromatography and passed a solvent up the paper, the Vitamin E and the quinone moved at different speeds and separated. It wasn't a covalent bond causing this color change. That's called a donor-acceptor bond, in which an electron momentarily leaves the Vitamin E and moves over to the quinone but then snaps back. You get an oscillation of the electron which acts like a system of double bonds within most pigment molecules.

Szent-Györgyi used a variety of these donors and acceptors. He wondered why the liver is dark purple/blackish colored. If you try to extract anything colored from the liver, you immediately get a white solid material. He was saying, "Here's the living liver in a very dark, intensely pigment-like condition. When you kill it, it's immediately colorless." He suggested it's a donor-acceptor relationship involving the electron moving along the protein.

He found that if he put a donor in a muscle preparation, nothing happened. If he put in the acceptor, nothing happened. But if he put in a donor and acceptor pair with just the right relationship to each other, the muscle contracted. That was his argument that the muscle contraction is essentially an electronic process.

**Danny Roddy:** You wrote somewhere that a group was using the estrogen myth to verify the nitric oxide myth, then to verify the serotonin myth. They were using a series of myths to substantiate their claims. That's what it sounds like with the NADH/NAD issue. The whole thing would go off the rails if you thought that the NADH should be higher than NAD+.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And it extends all the way to if the cancer cell and the nerve cell have this deficit or excess of electrons, then you're making a statement about how your electrometer is working, and even about how your redox and pH measuring meters are working. It involves a misinterpretation all along the line.

**Danny Roddy:** Why wasn't Szent-Györgyi taken seriously at the time? Was his work not conducive to making products?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The commercial level of science just couldn't do anything with him. Pretty much the same with Warburg. I think Szent-Györgyi was really on the right track. Everything that he proposed practically was validated 30 or 40 years later.

**Danny Roddy:** In an old interview, you said that serotonin might be a very old hormone. Yesterday I was reading that prolactin also was thought to be a pretty old hormone. Do you think of the hormones as having a layered effect in evolution?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. And that's the problem with therapies. They forget that when they fix one layer, the organism can go wrong above and below it in many other ways. If they're thinking in terms of a molecule acting locally on the receptor, they're forgetting the whole big picture of this electric state. An excess of electrons, for example, will activate hormones at all of these levels, the oldest and the newest, in a coordinated way.

The fact that the organism is coherent in May Wan Ho's sense makes the therapy basically possibly coherent and very simple—something like changing the environment in a coherent and appropriate direction rather than trying to act on parts of the organism in a reductionist way.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you look at the growth hormones and the ones that inhibit oxidative metabolism as the oldest, and then the ones that promote differentiation and oxidative metabolism as newer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I think the healthy organism in a healthy environment in the Vernadsky sense—something that's making good energy available—in that condition, you hardly need your hormones. The flow of energy is the whole thing. The movement of electrons forming water, and of oxygen and fuel forming carbon dioxide, will be having the differentiating, structuring, hormone-like action.

**Danny Roddy:** Karen asked you a while ago if there is a necessity to aging, and you replied that you hadn't seen any evidence of that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's our particular environment—more specifically, the temperature and oxygen pressure. The temperature makes many of the organisms produce unsaturated fat, but our brain development to use the energy that's available doesn't like polyunsaturated fats. They oxidize and antagonize oxygen. They're contrary to the flow of energy from sugar to carbon dioxide. So in this environment with relatively high oxygen pressure and very unstable fats, the process of living has a kind of negative hormonal influence. It's giving us signals to take emergency measures, and those emergency measures don't let us realize the proper Vernadsky organism.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think there's a time in a person's life that represents that ideal metabolic state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have observed that newborn humans and cows—the newborn calf has an essentially saturated fat brain. People have said this is dreadful, that babies are born with an essential fatty acid deficiency in their brain. But it happens that when you increase the unsaturated fats in the pregnant animal or human, the brain is smaller and less functional at birth.

In the healthy situation where you're born with a saturated tissue, as you eat these environmental fats, they are constantly slowing your metabolism, constantly having an estrogen-like effect, tending to reduce the differentiated cell and turn everything into a fibrous lump eventually. The ideal state would be something that could be foreseen from maybe an early fetus if you could keep the environment providing energy and carbon dioxide, but with fuels that weren't contaminated with unsaturated fats and heavy metals.

**Danny Roddy:** I had a couple of questions about antibiotics. A lot of people are interested in your take on antibiotics like the macrolides, tetracyclines, and penicillin VK. How do you even know that you might benefit from an antibiotic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experimenting is good. I was prejudiced against medicine and so I was reluctant to ever use such things. But once I was sick and the landlady gave me something, I had this characteristic penicillin odor in my mouth and nose, and it went with a kind of euphoria. I've always noticed that just about the time I can smell penicillin on my breath, there is this euphoric sense of well-being. I think that means that before that, I was always in a slight state of stress and emergency from whatever bacteria were producing irritants and toxins.

**Danny Roddy:** You suggested two to four days of using penicillin versus a longer dose. What was the rationale behind that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was eating a sandwich and mangoes in Mexico. I got a very bad intestinal condition and an abscess on my jaw, and I realized there was a very quick connection between intestinal inflammation and oral health.

Later, I knew a dentist, Earl Cleary, who gave presentations on various things. He said that he had stopped his very profitable practice treating periodontal disease with surgery. He said now he just gives them a laxative and he doesn't have to do periodontal surgery. So if the bowels aren't right and something's wrong with your teeth, that could be a big indicator. For something like a massive putrid material, it can take two or three days before a moderate dose of penicillin can kill that off.

**Danny Roddy:** I get this question every day. Do you have any confidence in other current thyroid brands because Cynoplus and Cynomel are not being sold anymore?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For a while in Mexico when I wasn't able to get Cynoplus or Cynomel, I found other brands that were regularly sold there. One was Proloid S. Proloid used to be the concentrated thyroglobulin, the colloid material without the rest of the gland, but it was at least as good as the old Armour product. Like Armour created their Thyrolar as a synthetic equivalent, Proloid created Proloid S, and I think that's still available at least somewhere in the world. Novothyral is another of the synthetic imitations, except it has a 5-to-1 ratio of T4 to T3 instead of the more ideal 4-to-1 or 3-to-1.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you know any replacement for Cynomel? T3 Pro is mentioned frequently.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the Saudi company, Profound Pharmaceutical, I think. I think that's the one I used for about a week and it did feel pretty normal to me, so I would guess that it's what they advertise it to be.

**Danny Roddy:** Synthetic versus desiccated—you would expect the desiccated, like a WP Thyroid, to work much slower than the synthetic version?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A little slower. It only takes two or three hours to digest.

**Danny Roddy:** Can you explain how you make your coffee? A lot of people are extremely interested.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Really, whatever is convenient. Usually filling a paper filter, sometimes a coffee sock, but currently the little paper cones. When the water is getting hot, I start and moisten the coffee without really getting it very hot. As the water gets hotter and hotter, I keep adding. So the first coffee that drips through is cool and very mild tasting, with very little caffeine in it, but it doesn't evaporate or degrade some of the delicate aldehyde-type flavor molecules. Supposedly, they're the most antioxidant part and they're destroyed if you put the boiling water directly onto the grounds.

I like to get some of the mild, low-temperature extract for flavor and then put a little of the fully boiling water at the very end to get all the caffeine.

**Danny Roddy:** So you do boil it at the end?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, just the last half cup or so of water.

**Danny Roddy:** At what point is the magnesium most readily available?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it comes out all along the way. I think it's loose so you get it even if you soak it and make cold coffee.

**Danny Roddy:** That's obviously a big thing to your approach. You often say you're drinking five cups of coffee. To me, that's always demonstrated that you were very pro-food and trying to get the most out of accessible foods versus a complicated regimen of pills.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, partly it's because the industry has gone towards profit and cheapness. Vitamin E is no longer anything like it was 70 or 80 years ago. The stuff I used in the lab that reacted with the ubiquinone to produce the black color—I tried that with various more recent types of Vitamin E and it didn't work. So we know that they're taking out different fractions from the Vitamin E. I think a big part of why the old Vitamin E in the 1930s and 40s was so much more therapeutic is that the recent Vitamin E studies show it's really nothing but an antioxidant that doesn't have any of those extremely therapeutic effects that it did 60 years ago.

**Danny Roddy:** I was just going to ask you what you were working on next and if you wanted to talk about your newsletter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The next newsletter, I think I'll write about cancer and probably some of this electronic stuff. The cancer industry, I think, is starting to realize some of the problems. Last week in JAMA, there was an article questioning whether so much emphasis on breast mammograms was really productive.

The prostate doctors in the 90s—someone did a survey and asked these specialists what they would do if they had prostate cancer themselves. A majority of them said they wouldn't do anything. Before that, in the 80s, the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) was just being researched. At that time, the mortality was 20 per 100,000 population per year. Then they discovered the PSA, told everyone to have that measured, found lots of people with very high PSA, and told them to have biopsies. So suddenly, the diagnostic rate for prostate cancer surged hugely. But by 1992, the death rate from prostate cancer increased 50% to 30 per 100,000. So the more diagnosis and treatment in that situation really very clearly showed that the more medicine you have, the more deaths you have.

John Gofman, the radiation specialist, did nationwide statistical studies and showed that breast cancer and heart disease correspond very closely to the access to medicine.

**Danny Roddy:** Was it Harding Jones that went around the world and thought that if you just did nothing, you'd live a longer and healthier life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And currently, Gershom Zajicek is saying something very similar. He has suggested that the tumor itself might be an ad hoc organ trying to defend the body against whatever is the problem. For example, he showed studies where when a mole or a melanoma was removed, suddenly they popped up all over the body.

Knowing that sort of study, a couple of times doctors told me that I definitely had to have a biopsy of a big, ugly mole. I happened to be experimenting with DHEA at one time just after a doctor had mentioned that. Just two or three days after I had been fooling around with some DHEA, the mole swelled up like a maraschino cherry and basically ate itself up.

Every time after that when I would get a diagnosable melanoma—big, ugly, huge; one thing was as big as a jumbo olive in front of my ear—I would just put a little bit of either progesterone or DHEA and Vitamin E on the skin near it, not touching it with it. Within a few days, those things would radically change. For example, a color would change from spotty blue and white to a nice tan color, or the big black thing would start shrinking. The one like a jumbo olive took almost two weeks, but the last little bit of it was like a gray-green little dry mushroom which fell off, leaving no scar.

**Danny Roddy:** That's it for me, Ray. Thank you so much. It's a total pleasure.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good. Thank you. Bye.

title: Optimizing The Environment with Ray Peat [Generative Energy #33]
transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** I loved your quote, "Without a realistic view of where you are, you can't expect to go anywhere." I thought of not only optimizing the environment, but also thinking about how you formed as an individual from your early life to now. A lot of times I'll be talking to somebody and they'll say, "My health problem started a year ago," or "It started two years ago." Then you talk to them more and realize things have been happening their whole life, unraveling this relationship with stress.

Going through your work, I highlighted *aromorphosis* from the evolution of the biosphere—the general idea of energy inducing complexity. I also highlighted Le Chatelier's principle of restoration and disturbed equilibrium. I looked into György Csaba's view of hormonal imprinting as a point of reference. From there, I looked at the precautionary principle of modifying the environment and trying to erase the imprints to maintain a good sense of euphoria. I love that quote by José Ortega y Gasset, who says, "I am myself plus my circumstances."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Pavlov, everyone seems to end up at that point, realizing that you can't separate yourself as something separate from your circumstances.

**Danny Roddy:** In your newsletter, you were just talking about progesterone being this main substance guiding the development of the individual.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the thing that holds you together while you respond in an energetically directional way. The progesterone prevents the energy from disintegrating you. It's one of the most powerful stabilizers. Carbon dioxide has a similar structurally stabilizing effect. That creates the unified system which can respond in a unified and directional way.

**Danny Roddy:** If something is interfering with the general energy production or the steroids, is that when the structure becomes imperfect? Le Chatelier's principle—that a system adjusts in ways which restore a disturbed equilibrium—is behind this idea. Every part of the flow can be seen as a disequilibrium, and the complexification of the structure tends to absorb the disturbing energy. So the more energy, the more complex.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We're always having a flow of energy. That flow itself is disturbing the equilibrium, and it's tending to absorb energy and turn it into structure. Anytime you flow energy through a system, it is creative and creates structure. Structure is always going to form, but it has the option to take on different shapes according to the shape of the stress that you're putting on the system.

There's a young physicist, Jeremy England, who has been demonstrating that the universe isn't controlled by the second law of thermodynamics. He says that if you start with a random clump of atoms and shine light on it long enough, it shouldn't be surprising that you end up with a plant. That is basically restating what Vernadsky said: that the sun generates large-brained animals.

In Jeremy England's phrase, if you create a plant by shining light on random atoms, and if you shine enough bright light, you'll eventually get large-brained mammals because the ordering principle of a directed flow of energy is going to create complexity. Whatever the surrounding conditions are where you're disturbing the equilibrium, it's going to conform to those boundary conditions. It will take a shape responding to everything in the environment, but it's the flow of energy which is responsible for the growing complexity.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, I had sent you an older quote of yours that said, "I came to see literary periods or styles—classical, realist, romantic, surrealist, et cetera—as reflections of a society's energy and structure." That got me thinking. So many people say things like, "I would like to shape the world in this point of view," or "I would like this system." Given that quote and the idea behind energy complexifying forests as a general rule of nature, I wondered how much of this is even within our control? How much should I even worry about it if the Earth's metabolism or the universe's metabolism is guiding the direction of everything?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The natural tendency of things—to have dinosaurs grow up to a huge size and then mammals come in and grow bigger brains—those are guided by the surrounding competitive innovations of matter. The sun and the internal energy of the Earth are supplying the streaming energy, and the particular shape that things take is a reflection of who else is around absorbing that energy.

So plants come up, and if the Earth is warm, the plants will make not only carbohydrates but saturated fats. The expanding brains of the contemporary animals eating those plants with saturated fats will thrive, integrating the saturated fats into their brain. But if for some reason the big brains move into a cold climate and eat plants that are defending against freezing, they'll start ingesting polyunsaturated fats into their brain. Their brains will suffer and be limited in proportion to how much of the cold climate polyunsaturated fats get into their brains. That creates accelerated aging and lots of other problems.

If everyone had stayed put, we might have just been on a straight line to a very happy, big-brained population eating nice tropical oily fruits. But besides going off into very inhospitable environments at the poles, under those tense circumstances, people started exploiting each other. Instead of having a more or less egalitarian situation in a favorable climate, they started getting competitive and creating control situations where some people would work as slaves so that a few people could have a better life.

The authoritarian, warlike, sadistic cultures reflect the distorting power of scarcity, natural scarcity, and natural competition. If those populations survive, they tend to conquer and become dominant. As they become a unified authoritarian civilization in the temperate zones, they will create ideologies that justify what they're doing—ideologies of caste systems, slavery, and competition. You'll come up with the idea of "survival of the fittest." Then, applying those ideas, various forms of education, advertising, and indoctrination will expand and complexify those authoritarian exploitative processes.

**Danny Roddy:** So it altered the course of human history by singing the praises of competition and making an institution out of it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Danny Roddy:** I reread Stephen Jay Gould's *Kropotkin Was No Crackpot*, and I've been reading more about cooperation in general. I think a lot of people have a knee-jerk reaction to it; they think it's a utopian hell when you say "cooperation." My friend Eric Lépine translated an article from Raoul Vaneigem, and a phrase that stuck out to me was the question: "How do we reconcile the greatest individual liberty possible while preserving the greatest equality within a community?" He called this a fundamental political paradox. Do you think it is a paradox, and what does cooperation look like on a grand scale?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's just a matter of being able to step back from the culture. In one of these authoritarian societies, when someone steps back and questions, they tend to get kicked out and have to go look for some other tribe to belong to because the authoritarians don't tolerate questioning and opposition. They indoctrinate everyone that competition is good, but they do everything to eliminate competition. The ideology of the United States has been "competitive free enterprise," but the basic business reality has been the elimination of competition—using government whenever possible to eliminate the competition, but also forming non-competitive, anti-competitive economic organizations.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, I know you've written favorably about Stalin, Lenin, Marx, and the general idea of communism. I was curious if you thought those terms or people's ideas were being misrepresented or perverted in some way? In the news, you hear terms like "cultural Marxism" or people talking about Stalin as being the worst person on the planet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 65 years ago, I saw a book called *Communism and Christianity*. I don't recall who wrote it, but it observed that Marx's basic ideas apparently came from Christian ethics. If you take Christian ethics seriously, then you start thinking like Marx, or at least the anarchists or communitarians of the 19th century. You think, "If those ethics are valid, what can we do to observe them?"

**Danny Roddy:** Can you get into more of the ethics? I feel like people play semantics a lot of times here.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at the "do unto others" ethic, and then you look without a Darwinian bias... Darwin believed that everything English was superior—that English plants would displace other species when transplanted, the way the "superior" Englishmen would displace other races. If you can get away from that fairly psychotic view of biology and actually look at the behavior of squirrels, mice, or birds, they are all aware of their surroundings and are inclined to be altruistic and benevolent, not destructive and aggressive. Aggression is a very peculiar and unusual part of behavior in most species. When their intelligence is allowed to act, they make it obvious that they are experiencing empathy, even with different species, but especially with their own.

**Danny Roddy:** Just to play devil's advocate, sometimes people say that when the complex apparatus of the US government tries to intervene—like using welfare to help people—it becomes a nightmare situation. Do you think that's accurate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is just a story that has been invented to put down the do-gooders. There have been people supported by big corporations and governments to write popular stories and make movies to illustrate that. Ronald Reagan got his ideology from some of these political fictions that promoted an anti-Dickens approach to society.

**Danny Roddy:** I was watching a conversation between Webster Tarpley and a libertarian, and Webster was explaining how if you cut food stamps, you basically have a genocide on your hands. It was the idea of the government being the problem, but if you get rid of the government programs, you're immediately in a worse position.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you do that, a bunch of corporations will disappear, and rich people will be desperate to find a new way to undo that, because the corporations are constantly being defended by government power. Police and armies are there to make the corporate ruling class stable and secure. They talk about welfare keeping people from starving, but it's the government keeping them poor that creates the starvation by following the rules of whatever the corporations want to write into the economic system. Every aspect of the culture has been designed to favor corporate exploitation. Poverty expands in proportion to the power of corporations over government. The story that people need welfare to prevent starvation is a very downstream part of the story. First you create the starvation, and then you decide whether to alleviate it slightly.

**Danny Roddy:** I've been reading about structural violence. James Gilligan defines structural violence as the increased rates of death and disability suffered by those who occupy the bottom rungs of society, contrasted with the relatively lower death rates experienced by those above them. He attributes these excess deaths to stress, shame, discrimination, and the denigration resulting from lower status. Do you think that's a worthwhile concept?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. Just look at the rules regarding corporations and labor unions. Unions have very restrictive things they can do collectively. Corporations now have absolutely no restrictions; they can spend whatever they want controlling political information. Just removing the organizational rules built into the system would make a tremendous difference. The whole structure is there for the purpose of exploitation, and the alleviation of suffering is just a way of preventing hysterical uprisings here and there.

**Danny Roddy:** If people were to rise up and oppose the imposed systems, is violence sometimes necessary, or is it always vile?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When Martin Luther King said that white people are being exploited and sent to kill foreigners for the good of the corporate class, that was very antagonistic to the military and corporate factions and led to his being killed. Anytime someone suggests even moderate approaches to changing the system, they suffer violence. They don't have to propose violence. He was absolutely against violence from either side, but no matter how much you advocate nonviolence, you're going to experience it if you do anything that threatens the system.

**Danny Roddy:** Stepping back a little, can we talk about hormonal imprinting? The basic idea is a cellular protein binding to certain substances while they have an effect on other cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** György Csaba, who has done so much research on hormonal imprinting, has evidence showing that the receptor is created specifically for what the cell is experiencing. That reminds me of a study from the 1930s I saw in a developmental biology seminar. Someone had presented a protein to a culture of bacteria, then removed the protein, washed the bacteria, treated them with an enzyme to break down the protein, washed them again, and cultured them. Large amounts of that same protein kept appearing in the culture, strongly showing that the bacteria had learned to copy a foreign protein. After I mentioned that and went back to make a copy for myself, the article had disappeared from the box. Someone cleansed the document box.

**Danny Roddy:** These systems are imposed on us and we're being actively harmed. Csaba mentioned serotonin frequently as being a switch back to the primitive metabolism, having a profound effect on our perception of ourselves and the world. What is your general thinking on erasing these imprints and maintaining euphoria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Euphoria consists of a balance in which structure is at least maintained by the flow of energy. It's only in that state where you can advance to increase your structure and perfection. If you are far from the euphoric condition, it means you're basically degenerating structurally—aging and deteriorating. Maintaining the euphoric state is therapeutic. That's what happens when you eat progesterone, take active thyroid (T3), pregnenolone, sugar, or breathe the right amount of carbon dioxide. Everything that doesn't cause injury and does cause energy or stability is going to lead you towards a greater stability.

**Danny Roddy:** Besides thyroid, pregnenolone, DHEA, progesterone, testosterone, cholesterol, vitamin D, and sugar, is there anything you're very concerned with? EMF, air quality, water quality?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The estrogenic toxins in the water are a major thing, but the corruption of the food supply is probably the most important for the most people. The miseducation of people to think that vegetable oil is better than butterfat, and to think that complex carbohydrates are good or sugars are bad. It's a perversion of the government intervention to help poor people survive in the Great Depression. They said, "Here are beans and grains that are very cheap," but by the 1970s, they were saying even middle-class people should eat these for their health.

**Danny Roddy:** One of my favorite quotes from you regarding trauma is: "Nothing is stored. It's like the pasts are all present in the same room and we periodically have a different perspective on them. When the present balance of stuff—toxicants, euphorians, etc.—is good, you can think and feel what you want to about things."

If somebody had a very traumatic childhood or event, is there any therapy you think is especially useful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think even the big traumas are processed in the same way. Everyone is massively traumatized by being born into Europe or America. Having a deformed body part or an intense emotional experience are fairly minor compared to the big framework that is institutionalized traumatism. Look at Gabor Maté and how well he turned out after surviving Nazism.

**Danny Roddy:** He's incredible. I don't know of anybody as articulate as him on these topics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He wasn't harmed permanently by terrible experiences. Everyone who survived had the possibility of realizing those same forces are around us all the time and we have to constantly overcome them.

**Danny Roddy:** In Ernest Schachtel's book *Metamorphosis*, he discusses how the drive to explore is strongest in childhood. As mammals mature, we see a slackening of this curiosity, and the open world turns into a variety of objects of use. I think of you as a good example of someone who has maintained that excitement. Do you see it similarly to Schachtel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. I think it's the language culture—the language bearing the story they are trying to indoctrinate us with—that turns adults away from exploration and innovation. The reason I got interested in studying linguistics was that from puberty, I started experimenting with language and the actual machine of my consciousness. For 65 years, I've been experimenting with how to separate myself from the English language, and language in general, to see the processes of consciousness.

That's what Kropotkin couldn't avoid seeing when he studied nature. If you really watch animals, you see they are behaving more intelligently than most people we read about. I've watched ants and birds; each is an individual and very communicative. People create the illusion that communication happens through words, whereas basic communication is being aware of where you are. Language is often a way of making people less conscious rather than actually communicating. It tends to reinforce indoctrinated patterns and suppress the urge to explore.

**Danny Roddy:** Is this one of the reasons you do sculpting, painting, and music? To turn off the language?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And just paying attention to sleep. That's what your consciousness machine is doing for you. For Pavlov, the cortex of the brain was an interface between everything happening in the world and everything happening inside your body. It's a constant adjustment. If you step out of the language culture, you come in contact with your cerebral cortex, which is an interaction between your kidneys, pancreas, intestine, heart, and everything around you. You select the part of your past that you think will be useful for what is to come.

**Danny Roddy:** On days you do more arts and less reading, do you notice an effect on your dreams?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. Everything affects the dreams—hormones, sugar, etc.

**Danny Roddy:** If someone wasn't dreaming at all or having nightmares, would that be a feature of hypothyroidism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Deep sleep doesn't necessarily involve dreams. If something is disturbing you, you will try to work it out in the dreams, just as you work things out in reality. When the dream catches some emotional energy, if you can remember that and become conscious with it, the dream can make the emotional energy available to you during the day to work out parts of reality.

**Danny Roddy:** Is dreaming part of the innate animal intelligence as opposed to the cultural caricature we look through during the day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the animal intelligence is always there offering itself, and our daily cultural consciousness is distracting us from watching. I see it like a set of projectors working with resources from inner body senses and stored images. The body is projecting possibilities, trying to bring them to your attention. But ordinarily, the consciousness that tries to handle those intrinsic body deliveries tends to stop the process or deform it. A passive attitude towards watching what your body is trying to do is similar to watching what ants or birds are trying to express. Treat your body as if it was a bit of nature and watch what it's trying to tell you.

**Danny Roddy:** It's funny you mention a passive approach. I always felt I had an aggressive "salt the earth" approach, treating every problem like a nail.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can have a tremendous amount of energy in the passivity, but it's passivity in relation to the fictional character—the role society tells us to play. If you detach yourself from that cultural self, then the passivity actually gains energy so that you can appreciate the full intensity of the problem you're confronting.

**Danny Roddy:** Besides the arts, is there anything else that fosters those feelings? Avoiding the news?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Being around people who are open to consideration of actual parts of reality. I think a very powerful part of our nervous system is how we feel ourselves resonate with other people. If you have a random clump of people, the natural process of resonance is going to create interesting things. There's more freedom to become yourself when you can resonate with other people. For example, brain cells isolated in a culture dish start vibrating together; they learn to act like a brain. If you put people together without pressure and demands from the outside, they will come up with solutions.

**Danny Roddy:** Tolstoy said that everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself. Do you think focusing on yourself creates a ripple effect in society?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The culture has taught people that the "self" they need to concentrate on is this fictional role, like their caste or social position. Realizing that the culture telling you who you are is also killing you is an essential starting point. You want to be able to get together with other people who are aware of the hostile nature of our bigger society.

**Danny Roddy:** So it's essential to have a group to put ideas into action?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The traditional ways of organizing are now being monitored so carefully that they can shoot them down the moment they start to take effect. The wariness of the culture is the most infectious thing that can precede organization. If the recognition that medicine is mostly harming people and that the foods are leading to an early diseased death spreads, that suspicion and rejection of the system is what can precede the actual search for what to do next. The ultimate goal should be something on the order of "gathering culture"—having such a fruitful environment that we can just pick what we need.

**Danny Roddy:** You said in an article that deleting medicine, the legal system, and education were three things that would move in a good direction.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The government and corporations are enforcing those things. Ivan Illich studied how medicine and schooling are enslaving people. One of the worst aspects of schooling he identified was the compulsory need to be taught—disengaging somebody's autonomy.

When I first went to college, I came across a professor who was teaching five different departmental subjects: comparative religion, contemporary philosophy, German literature, English literature, and others. He was an excellent teacher in everything. I saw a letter he received from a dean at Harvard inviting him to teach literature there, but he didn't want to be limited. The fact is, when you can teach a subject other than what you've been taught specifically, you're going to teach that subject probably better than someone who has been drilled in it for 10 years.

**Danny Roddy:** I would regularly encounter people in San Francisco that studied medicine, and I could never have a normal conversation with them. Wasn't it Marx who thought that there were many different aspects of a person and that you weren't just one thing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Gabor Maté was an English major. I think he's a good example. Before he studied medicine, he taught high school English. If you know one subject to a pretty saturated degree and then approach another one, you learn the essential way to get at that subject. Someone who is teaching in five departments can make each one more valuable than someone who teaches a single subject all their life.

**Danny Roddy:** Before we wrap things up, did you want to talk about "ontogeny anticipates phylogeny," pedomorphism, and juvenilization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's that same thing—Le Chatelier and Vernadsky. The energy available to flow through the system is extremely intense in the first processes away from the ovum. The oxygen, carbon dioxide, and glucose are generously available. Your demand is small because you're only a few cells big, so you can suck up the environment at a terrific rate. The environment is pretty ideal until you get up to about the size of a peanut, and then the environmental limitations start being felt.

So the aromorphosis processes, where flowing energy generates complexity, are zooming through your processing system, producing a huge head and eyes. Then you start running into what your mother didn't eat and finding the need to specialize and limit your development. You start out inventing future species, trying out what the simple flow of energy does to your cells, and it expands you as a knowing being. Then, as you run into the limits, you start adapting to those limits. The worse your mother's condition is, the more you become prematurely "adultified."

**Danny Roddy:** Can this be thought of as puberty being a major landmark in aging, and the reproductive years being a slow decline to death, while pre-puberty is a time where the organism is more evolved physiologically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think at six months of gestation is when we're at our peak. The present atmosphere limits the amount of carbon dioxide and oxygen you can use. So at six months of gestation, I think is where we're the most pedomorphic, and then that tapers off. It sets up a pattern predicting how much of a crocodile or primate you're going to be. If you were early deprived, you're going to be an eating machine more than an experiencing machine.

**Danny Roddy:** And women are more resistant to these negative effects because of the progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Progesterone keeps the oxygen and carbon dioxide towards an ideal for as long as you can supply all of those things together.

**Danny Roddy:** Because women naturally have more progesterone, and you talked about progesterone being responsible for temporal long-range thinking, do you see women as having a unique place in society?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1946, I read Ashley Montagu on the biological superiority of women. I've been conscious of that ever since and thought of myself as a feminist until the Gloria Steinem/CIA brand of feminism came on the scene.

**Danny Roddy:** I was shocked when I saw the video of her talking about her CIA operative days. Some people say feminism was used to destroy the basic nuclear family. Do you think that's right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, to expand the labor market to lower wages was a basic function. To as peacefully as possible dispose of the excess population that isn't needed to run the factories. With automation, the population excess is going to be a higher percentage. Fewer and fewer people will have authorization to live.

**Danny Roddy:** You think getting into feminism is reasonable, but the modern idea is misdirected towards the ruling class?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Women want to be as bad as men. We've had three terrible women Secretaries of State, like Condoleezza Rice.

**Danny Roddy:** It was ironic. People pointed out that women tend to gravitate to nurturing professions, and critics said, "No, they should want to be CEOs." But CEOs are some of the worst people. Why aspire to be like them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly.

**Danny Roddy:** What are you working on right now? You sent me your Sleep and Aging newsletter, which was fantastic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think I'll do something related to autism. That has been coming up in my thinking increasingly. Autism is something that everyone is periodically inclined to. The lack of that resonance among individuals—which is a natural property of life—as the death culture imposes itself, it shows up in more and more visible things that are diagnosed as autism. It is the deprivation of sugar, carbon dioxide, progesterone, thyroid, and the possibility of life opportunities.

**Danny Roddy:** I saw a reference to Dr. John Cannell's "Science is More" on medicine, invoking an old-school approach to act on the observation that vitamin D was deficient in autism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Many things are deficient. Breastfeeding is deficient. Prenatal happiness is deficient. Security of both father and mother before conception is deficient. Our culture is creating deficiencies of everything good. Autism is an increasingly epidemic expression of deprivation.

**Danny Roddy:** Interesting way of looking at it. Ray, thank you so much. I sincerely appreciate it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay. Thank you.

**Danny Roddy:** Take care, Ray. Bye.

title: Safe Supplements with Ray Peat [Generative Energy #31]
transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Hello everyone, I'm Danny Roddy, and today I'm talking with painter, philosopher, and biologist, Raymond Peat. In this episode, we'll talk about the benefits and risks of various commercial pharmaceuticals and supplements.

**Danny Roddy:** The conversation with Gavin was extremely enlightening. I'm not especially interested in politics, but I am interested in your painting of physiology. Knowing some of the things that you talk about, I was interested in anarcho-capitalism. After reading that Gavin article, it kind of shook me out of that mindset and got me thinking that capitalism wasn't the best thing for health and society. Was that similar to what you were saying in that article?

**Ray Peat:** The idea of accumulating capital so you can build machines—people wouldn't have built steam locomotives and ships if they hadn't accumulated capital. Lots of good things come from accumulating capital and putting it in one place. But the trouble is, as Marx pointed out, it tends to accumulate all in a few hands. Then the system stops running because no one can buy what is produced so efficiently in factories. So, you have business cycles.

Lenin said they discovered that you can cure the business cycle by having imperialism and invading countries to make them buy your product and keep the system running. As long as you have wars, capitalism has no problem. But that's the problem. It has its internal contradictions and tends to cycle down to a crash every few years if you don't have some way to break out of that.

**Danny Roddy:** It almost perfectly put things into perspective regarding something Bucky Fuller said. He was trying to shake the notion of everybody having to earn a living. I was confused at what he was talking about, but he was saying that technology was getting better and better, and that would free up more people from this barbaric idea of having to earn your place on the planet.

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, that was Fuller. I admired him. I listened to one of his lectures when he came to Oregon. He talked, I think, six hours steady until they closed the shop. He and Fidel Castro were experts at putting the whole world story in one lecture.

**Danny Roddy:** I was reading two other papers by a guy named Paul K. Piff. He was talking about the social and stress consequences of capitalism. He has papers called "Having Less, Giving More" and "The Influence of Social Class on Pro-Social Behavior." It seemed to tie into what you were talking about.

**Ray Peat:** The culture has functioned as a system of illusions to help keep a dysfunctional system working—to make the people think that they're better off than they are. I think working on the culture is really where political work should be done. Propaganda analysis everywhere, including science and philosophy.

**Danny Roddy:** It's almost like the food pyramid and the political system synergize to destabilize a person. Like the undigested starches and the capitalism are a perfect storm for a weird culture.

**Danny Roddy:** Let's get on to supplements. I don't remember when I first heard you say that you preferred using the oily supplements on your skin, but I initially rejected it because it didn't fit my life. Recently, I started putting them on my legs and stopped eating them, and various small things resolved themselves. You’ve mentioned before that you were known for getting people *off* of their supplements.

**Ray Peat:** In the late sixties, when I came to Eugene, I knew someone who started the local free clinic. In Eugene, the fields all around were growing grass for the seed industry. At the end of the summer, they would burn their fields, and all of the pesticides would be vaporized and blow into town. People with asthma were more likely to die during the smoky seasons.

My friend with the free clinic was constantly sending allergy people to me. I found that they were all taking ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) and Vitamin A—the usual things people take for allergies. I had just been trying out Linus Pauling's idea of big doses of Vitamin C. My first bad experience with Vitamin C was in the mid-1950s when it suddenly got very cheap. I tried a 500-milligram tablet and woke up the next morning with a sore throat and cold symptoms. Over the years, I saw that repeatedly: a big dose of Vitamin C always gave me some kind of cold symptom reaction.

Around 1968, when I started seeing these allergy people, they were all taking Vitamin C and other supplements. I suggested they try stopping them. Almost without exception, they would come back and say that their allergies were gone for the first time in years within a week of stopping.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you suspect it was due to some kind of endotoxin or irritation from the intestine?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. One of the things endotoxin does is impair oxidation of the lining of the intestine and create a reduced state—too many electrons. Sulfites and ascorbic acid are very powerful reductants. I think the combination of endotoxin and a massive chemical reductant can interact and set up a big inflammation in the intestine. Reflexes from that cause the nose to run and eyes to water.

**Danny Roddy:** Did that shift your thinking to be much more careful about supplements?

**Ray Peat:** Yes. I had previously found that after dental x-rays, I had leukoplakia on the inside of my cheek for six months. The third time it happened, it occurred to me that Vitamin A would be destroyed by x-rays just as much as it is by sunburn. I took a big dose of Vitamin A and it immediately cleared up the leukoplakia overnight.

However, as I continued taking Vitamin A as a regular supplement, I started getting headaches from it. I found that just a touch of it on my lips would give me a migraine the next morning. I tried out a series of individual supplements and found that riboflavin (Vitamin B2) was almost as powerful as ascorbic acid for giving me an immediate headache or asthma symptoms. Rutin was another intense one. Talking to people with allergies confirmed that ascorbic acid was the number one problem, but Vitamin B2, rutin, and sometimes Vitamin A also caused problems.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you suspect these substances are made in a cheap way that poses risks?

**Ray Peat:** When Vitamin C was first on the market up until 1953 or '54, it was sold in very small 50-milligram tablets. That was during the time when all of the classical amazing results were published. I think that was because it was free of contaminants. The new cheap way of making it from glucose involved sulfuric acid, which was almost always contaminated with lead.

Over the decades, there have been chemical innovations for making it even more cheaply, but each introduces some kind of chemical adulterant. In the *Journal of Free Radical Biology* in the late '90s, someone published a study of reagent-grade, high-purity ascorbic acid. They dissolved a gram in a liter of distilled water and measured it in an electron spin analyzer. The researcher said that spontaneously, upon dissolving, the content of free radicals was as high as would have been produced by a killing dose of x-rays. He said it was amazing this amount of free radicals didn't kill the intestines. It was apparently from traces of heavy metals like iron.

**Danny Roddy:** That's just one problem. I imagine the casings and fillers are added variables.

**Ray Peat:** Every additive has its own manufacturing history, and every reagent used in making that thing has its own history. When you look at every excipient in a product, each one has many components, each of which has its own history and opportunity for contamination.

**Danny Roddy:** What is your general process for evaluating if something is safe?

**Ray Peat:** My thinking got started in 1960 when they were analyzing the amount of strontium-90 from atomic bomb fallout. They were collecting baby's teeth to measure exposure. Strontium-90 concentrates in the bone, and radiation exposure to the bone marrow promotes leukemia. Because strontium-90 is similar to calcium, it associates in milk. The government was warning parents not to feed their children so much milk.

I looked at how the strontium-90 got into the milk. It falls onto the ground in the rain. The plants absorb both calcium and strontium-90. When the cow eats the grass, the cow purifies and selects for the calcium over the strontium. If you look at the ratio in grass versus cow meat and milk, the milk has the least strontium-90 in proportion to calcium.

Every organism is a purifying system, getting what's good and excluding what's bad. The safest thing is to get the purest food possible from an animal like a cow producing milk, which is multiply filtered from the environmental source. When they talk about chemical purity, that's only a reality in the mind of the chemist. In relation to biological nutrients, it's wildly out of the ballpark in terms of contamination. Any natural food is extremely purified. Any supplement made chemically is going to be dirty in principle.

**Danny Roddy:** Sometimes I get an email from someone saying, "I'm not eating liver, but I'm taking Vitamin A and the B vitamins." It seems like a non-sequitur.

**Ray Peat:** You get lots of unnamed and unidentified nutrients in any living tissue. For example, in mushrooms, the content has hardly been sketched out. There are thousands of potentially valuable nutrients that simply haven't been identified.

**Danny Roddy:** That was a motivator for me. Substances like apigenin and naringenin in foods became more interesting than supplements.

**Ray Peat:** Some fruits, like the cherimoya, have amazing still-unidentified substances. Mark Twain said it was the best-tasting substance in the universe.

**Danny Roddy:** And marmalade, too. Something you would normally throw away that is full of naringenin.

**Ray Peat:** Orange peel is usually thrown away, but if they're good oranges and well prepared, the marmalade is like a super drug. The sugar itself is part of the nutritional wonder drug.

**Danny Roddy:** When health gets in a really serious condition and drugs would be of value, are there certain ones you think of that have a proven safety record?

**Ray Peat:** A general rule is that the oldest ones are best. They've been tested for more years. Since the pharmaceutical industry took over, they have 20-year cycles where they talk about a new generation of drugs. The first generation is usually the safest and most effective. The subsequent generations are more weirdly dangerous, but the toxic side effects haven't been published yet.

**Danny Roddy:** Is there any way of understanding side effect data to understand the real risks?

**Ray Peat:** I assume most middle-term side effects would have been noticed after 50 years. If it's going to bring on cancer, you have to use it for at least 20, preferably 40 years to know.

**Danny Roddy:** Finasteride is probably a good example. It seems like it's ruining lives.

**Ray Peat:** I hear from a lot of people who have had trouble from that. Brain chemistry depends on it. The metabolism of progesterone as well as testosterone in your brain—if you block any of the enzymes used in making it, you're going to have a weird brain.

**Danny Roddy:** There's a famous quote from the FDA saying that dihydrotestosterone (DHT) apparently wasn't used in the organism or had no function.

**Ray Peat:** It works on the progesterone system too. They said progesterone is only a pregnancy-related chemical, neglecting that the brain absolutely depends on making it. It's a major brain hormone that you're messing with when you try to stop the production of DHT.

**Danny Roddy:** So restoring pregnenolone, DHEA, and thyroid function would be a good start to resolve that?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, and even better to start with increasing your cholesterol production, which means keeping your intestine and liver in good condition.

**Danny Roddy:** Can we talk about nutrient deficiencies?

**Ray Peat:** I had interesting experiences. 50 milligrams of Vitamin C cured horrible cases of poison oak for me. Around that same period, I was feeling gloomy and took a tablet of Vitamin B1; in minutes, I had a clear, happy perspective.

When I worked in the woods, I was getting acne. I realized that my retina uses a lot of Vitamin A. The eye is the main regulator of your reproductive hormones. Light activates your adrenals and gonads to produce steroids, and the production of steroids is a heavy consumer of Vitamin A. From that insight, I took a big dose of Vitamin A and immediately the pimples subsided.

Another time, a friend's niece was in the hospital with uncontrollable diarrhea. I gave him a tablet of Vitamin B6 (10 milligrams). He gave it to the little girl, and within an hour, her diarrhea stopped. Instant recovery.

A neighbor of mine had a big alcoholic nose—red, large, and shiny. He had a problem with vocabulary; he would struggle to find the right word. I described how Vitamin B2 is essential for oxidation. He finally got a shot of vitamins from the doctor. Within a day or two, he was talking fluently, and his nose was a normal pink color.

**Danny Roddy:** Basically, it's endless what could be considered a deficiency—any kind of abnormal behavior?

**Ray Peat:** A friend had a four-year-old kid who would have violent tantrums every afternoon and wake up screaming with a nosebleed at night. We made cookies with 10 milligrams of Vitamin B2. He ate them that afternoon, slept through the night without the nightmare or nosebleed, and never had those horrible tantrums again.

**Danny Roddy:** What are your thoughts on the versatility of the body? Does it need everything every day?

**Ray Peat:** Someone did experiments on rats using the cornea to test Vitamin B2 deficiency. They found that the mitochondria were essentially collapsed or structurally changed so that they no longer would take up Vitamin B2 when it was given. Your nutritional requirements depend on your parents, your grandparents, and every generation before that. Something that makes your mother low in thyroid or high in estrogen during your gestation sets a pattern that will greatly increase your requirements.

**Danny Roddy:** You've mentioned that meat eaters would normally get a fourth to a half a grain of thyroid in their food every day. Do you look at thyroid like eating oysters and liver?

**Ray Peat:** Seeing the ways country people ate in Mexico, I realized that a traditional diet was nutritionally very complex and included hormones, especially the thyroid gland. People would eat chicken necks, fish heads, and save all the glands from pigs to use in sausages. The blood, for example, carries a lot of hormones and is a frequent component of food in traditional diets.

**Danny Roddy:** I recall you used to have people read books on thyroid before they took anything. Do you think that's a good approach?

**Ray Peat:** When you don't know the client very well, it's best to give them the information to take responsibility for themselves. But if I saw someone in a suicidal condition, I would intervene by giving them quick-acting thyroid or progesterone. If you are just consulting random people, it's better if you make them get informed so they can watch themselves undergo the changes.

**Danny Roddy:** Is something like magnesium especially important for the hypothyroid person?

**Ray Peat:** Thyroid is required to retain magnesium by cells. When you're hypothyroid, the slightest stress makes magnesium fall out of your cells and get lost in the urine. A constant daily supply is essential to prevent cramps and depression. But once your thyroid is up where it should be, you can go for two weeks or more without the required amount of magnesium.

**Danny Roddy:** That Traskin study on Vitamin A—he thought healthier people needed more Vitamin A?

**Ray Peat:** Yes, because you're turning over your cholesterol to progesterone and testosterone chemistry constantly. That uses lots of Vitamin A. When your thyroid is low, you have a very low requirement for Vitamin A.

**Danny Roddy:** Is there any dead giveaway for a Vitamin A or K deficiency?

**Ray Peat:** I think experimentation is best. When a person has extremely high pulse pressure—the difference between systolic and diastolic is 70 or more—I figure they should try big doses of Vitamin K. It is needed for keeping calcium out of your arteries. As they become Vitamin K deficient and calcium overloaded, the arteries become stiff. I've seen people bring their top and bottom numbers much closer in just a week or two from a big Vitamin K supplement.

**Danny Roddy:** Can you explain the process for using Vitamins D, A, and K topically?

**Ray Peat:** You have to use about 10 times the oral dose. If you're going to bathe every day, you need more because it takes time for Vitamin D to soak in. The faster your skin is being replaced, the more Vitamin D is lost with shedding cells.

**Danny Roddy:** So if you wanted to use 5,000 IU of Vitamin D per day, you should put 50,000 IU on your skin?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, but you should still have a blood test after doing it for a while. Some people with sensitive, thin skin might absorb as much as 30 or 40% of what they put on.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you use a combination of those every day?

**Ray Peat:** In the winter, I try to do it every day. In the summer, the food supply is usually fresher, so I often don't use them every day.

**Danny Roddy:** What are your thoughts on the probiotic strains *B. licheniformis* and *B. subtilis*?

**Ray Peat:** There are safe antibiotics that can work for people with bowel dysbiosis. But the first thing is to cut out the foods supporting the bad bacteria—usually polyunsaturated fatty acids and hard-to-digest starchy fibrous foods. Disinfecting foods such as cooked mushrooms and raw carrots are natural antibiotics. But when you have a really intense bacterial problem, *B. subtilis* and *B. licheniformis* are useful.

**Danny Roddy:** Would this be useful in place of antibiotics like penicillin?

**Ray Peat:** Yes, but I've seen just carrot salad every day work just as well as penicillin for reducing the stress causing a hormone imbalance.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think aspirin should be dissolved in water? And what is the relationship between aspirin and Vitamin K?

**Ray Peat:** It's not an acute thing. The effect of aspirin knocking out clotting platelet function is trivial regarding the actual benefit. The effect that can cause uncontrolled bleeding is by interfering with proteins produced by the liver under the influence of Vitamin K. If you have taken antibiotics and have a deficiency of the bacteria that produces Vitamin K, you're susceptible to aspirin knocking out this clotting protein. Just as insurance, it's good to have a source of Vitamin K in your diet.

**Danny Roddy:** These are proteins S and C?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, those are made under the influence of Vitamin K. They are anticoagulant factors. People with excess clotting problems are sometimes told to avoid Vitamin K, but if you haven't measured proteins S and C, that might be the worst thing to do. Vitamin K is required for the normal resolution of stimulated clotting.

**Danny Roddy:** Does the inclusion of mushrooms change your diet recommendations? Can you replace the carrot if you eat mushrooms?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, I've done that. I got tired of carrots after eating one a day for 20 years. Bamboo shoots are another alternative.

**Danny Roddy:** Would it be risky to replace eggs with mushrooms?

**Ray Peat:** Mushrooms have good broad-spectrum nutritional value, but you just have to eat an awful lot of them.

**Danny Roddy:** How much have you been averaging?

**Ray Peat:** Sometimes ridiculous amounts. Once every week or two, we'll have a big bowl of mushroom soup, which is almost like porridge—probably eight ounces. Other days, much less, like liver with mushrooms, probably four ounces.

**Danny Roddy:** If you could take any substance on a desert island, what would it be?

**Ray Peat:** Probably either pregnenolone or progesterone. If you fall off a cliff, get sunburned, or get bitten by a strange animal, you want to have a lot of progesterone. It's kind of a universal antidote.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, thank you so much for talking with me. Can you let people know how they can purchase your newsletter?

**Ray Peat:** The email is raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com. No apostrophe in Ray Peat.

**Danny Roddy:** That's one issue every two months. Thank you so much, Ray.

**Ray Peat:** Okay, thank you. Bye.

title: Talking with Ray Peat [Generative Energy #19]
transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Hello everyone, I'm Danny Roddy, and today I'm talking with painter, philosopher, and biologist, Raymond Peat. In this hour-long episode, we'll talk about Ray's interest in nutrition, the lead-up to writing his 1973 book, *Nutrition for Women*, and his latest newsletter, "Mushrooms, Observations, and Interpretations."

I wanted to start with your interest in nutrition and end up at recipes. I was trying to put a timeline together of when you graduated with your degree in linguistics and then Blake College.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I got my bachelor's degree at Southern Oregon College in 1956. Then I worked in the woods for a while and got a job teaching. First, I studied at the University of Oregon in 1957 and '58, starting in the English department, then switched to philosophy and psychology. After about one or two terms in each department, I decided I couldn't stay to finish a master's in that area. I even tried art history.

During this time, I was looking around for some program that would let me integrate all of these areas. It looked like linguistics would allow me to bring together what the brain is doing when it speaks and thinks. Every time you reach a word that seems appropriate, you're putting that word into a new context that never existed before. So really, every act of communication is a creative invention. It seemed to me that the approach to how consciousness works would be possible through analyzing language.

I found that Ohio State University had a PhD program called the Interdepartmental Linguistics Committee that would grant a PhD on the basis of interdepartmental language studies. Since that seemed just what I wanted to do, I applied there and looked for a job to support myself nearby.

I found a little Swedenborgian college called Urbana University, founded in 1859. They had a really good hundred-year-old library. I enrolled in English, Russian, and philosophy department courses there, but did most of my studying and thinking at Urbana College.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What I was teaching at Urbana was introduction to biology intended for physics majors. The president of the college said he wanted a non-technical approach to the subject to let the students understand current magazine and newspaper articles in their field. At that time, 1959 and '60, the most interesting current science topics were the biological effects of radioactive fallout from atmospheric bomb testing and the development of computers.

So, I built the course largely around how to interpret the biological effects of radiation in the most general sense, and how information works in the organism analogous to how information is handled in computers.

Because of the physics part of my courses, a conservative priest who was head of the board of directors didn't like the students asking questions about how safe atmospheric bomb testing was. They went looking for a new biology teacher. They had Leo Koch come in from the University of Illinois as a prospective replacement for me. He chose to give his lecture at Urbana on the dangers of radiation and the biological effects of atmospheric bomb testing. So, he was discarded as a possible replacement. Within a week or two, he lost his job at the University of Illinois too.

I realized that even though they hadn't told me I wasn't going to have a job the next year, when he wasn't hired—and in fact got fired at Illinois—I would have to look for another job. That started me thinking about organizing a college that would be run by the students and teachers jointly without any priests or boards of directors.

**Danny Roddy:** To try to understand your orientation, had you already read Szent-Györgyi and were you familiar with Otto Warburg? What was the tip-off that radiation was something that was really harmful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yeah. I had been reading for seven or eight years. Actually, it started in 1947 or '48; people were circulating mimeographed pamphlets pointing out the age acceleration of any kind of ionizing radiation. So that had been in my mind for a good 12 years.

Linus Pauling was in the news as opposing the bomb testing. That was why they took away his passport, so he couldn't get outside the U.S. to talk to other people about it. He was strongly influenced by Szent-Györgyi. I think it was through Linus Pauling's writings that I got interested in Szent-Györgyi.

I think it was about 1950 that Szent-Györgyi was traveling around the country doing his demonstrations. He had a stroboscopic arrangement in which he could flash an ultraviolet light, cut off the flash, and reveal the fluorescent delay. He was demonstrating the effect of the living state versus the frozen state on electronic behavior.

Between 1959 and '60, Linus Pauling started explaining anesthesia on the basis of structuring water.
