Under pressure, even nitrogen causes anesthesia, but the heavy noble gases at moderate pressure will cause shutting off of nerve activity without harming the cell. There's no chemical reaction involved. Szent-Györgyi was saying that this probably explains all anesthetics. The hydrophobic molecules that aren't noble gases are likewise not chemically interacting with the cells or the water; they were simply offering a surface changing the crystalline properties of the water. He gave a clathrate analogy.

That was part of how I was interpreting the toxic effects of radiation: by affecting this interaction between the electron state of molecules and the water structure. Linus Pauling was talking about the dangers of high-energy radiation going directly into the chemical bond of DNA. I was thinking about it in terms of Szent-Györgyi's very subtle effects on the electronic state—stabilizing a higher energy state of electrons when the water is organized. I was more extreme in my concerns about radiation even than Linus Pauling was.

**Danny Roddy:** When you left Ohio with the idea of starting Blake College, you were around 25 or 26?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Since Leo Koch didn't have a job either, he was on a lecture tour about academic freedom. In his talks, he would say, "We're starting a college that won't be susceptible to censorship." He gathered up some interested students.

I found that California would let us grant degrees if we had $50,000 invested. But they wouldn't let us even acknowledge that a student had studied with us if we didn't have the money put up. I found that was the rule in all of the states I contacted. The Assistant Secretary of Public Instruction at Oregon told me, "It doesn't matter what students know."

I decided to set it up in Mexico City because of the peso difference and the political difference. They had a secular government at that time and would approve of any science-based curriculum as long as you kept the church out of it.

**Danny Roddy:** Is that when Madalyn Murray O'Hair was involved?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. My parents sent me an article about her being persecuted by the Maryland police. It said that she and her old mother had assaulted a group of cops and caused one to have a heart attack. It sounded so ridiculous that she could beat up the cops that had come to arrest her. Everyone assumed she was being persecuted. She fled to Hawaii.

My girlfriend at Blake College took pity on her. I wrote to her and asked if she wanted to be a teacher at Blake College. Madalyn said yes, but asked for help with transportation. My girlfriend Cheryl went to San Francisco, bought an old car, and Madalyn put on a nun's habit and got out of Hawaii dressed as a nun.

**Danny Roddy:** By that time were you totally into nutrition?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Reading Adelle Davis in the 50s was what really influenced me. A friend of mine in Mexico City said that his niece, 18 months old, was in the hospital with intractable diarrhea. I told him about Adelle Davis' experience with vitamin B6. I happened to have a bottle with me and gave him a 10-milligram tablet. On the third or fourth day, when the doctor said she wouldn't last more than another day, he gave her 10 milligrams of vitamin B6. Within an hour or so the dysentery stopped and she completely recovered. That was my first experience with Adelle Davis' suggestions and it impressed me.

**Danny Roddy:** I wanted to ask about the interference you faced. Was it because of Blake College, Madalyn, or both?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The U.S. was basically occupying Mexico during this period, continuing all of the intelligence agencies: Naval intelligence, military intelligence, CIA, FBI. Just a couple of weeks after opening the school in Mexico City, the cultural attaché of the embassy came to visit. He asked, "Since you're a graduate student in linguistics, why aren't you with the Summer Institute of Linguistics?" I said I wasn't interested in Bible translations. The Summer Institute for Linguistics was basically a CIA front to subdue the native populations of Central and South America.

Around the time of the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964, a man in an American uniform—which was illegal in Mexico at that time—came to our new location in Valle de Bravo. He identified himself as the military attaché of the embassy. He had private interviews with me and each of the students, asking us what our opinion was about the war in Vietnam.

**Danny Roddy:** Were you freaked out at all the attention, or did you expect it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wasn't aware of how totally covered with US intelligence agents Mexico was at that time. Madalyn Murray had a very organized thing working with the embassy to time the takeover for when I was going to be on the road driving to the US for a job in Montana. She was having a report given to the embassy, the federal police of Mexico, and the English-speaking newspapers about what was going on at Blake College.

They basically framed the college to look like some kind of drug lab. For example, the landlady had a German Shepherd with an ear infection. One of the students, who knew about injecting things, gave the dog a shot of penicillin and cured the ear. The students organized under Madalyn told her that story, and she turned it into "drug orgies," giving morphine even to the dog.

Alejandro Jodorowsky, the filmmaker, came to visit. He organized the maids' children into a "Panic Theater" thing where they played clay flutes. The police confiscated the tape recording of his flute music and claimed it was part of the drug orgies.

Just before I reached the Mexican border, an old unshaven guy with a striped shopping bag imposed himself on me for a ride. As we drove, we talked politics and were absolutely sympathetic. When we came to the border checkpoint, the soldier asked for his ID. He said, "I'm just an ignorant peasant." The soldier let us go. As we pulled away, my passenger said, "That guy ought to be fired," reached in his bag, and pulled out his ID showing he was a federal police agent. He had been there to make sure I got out of the country because the federal police had arrested all the students and teachers back at the college.

**Danny Roddy:** Why did they let you go?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the teachers was a friend of the daughter of the Mayo Clinic people. The Mayo Clinic had a team of lawyers arrive on their private jet to talk to the president. The students were immediately let out and sent to the border.

**Danny Roddy:** I read about your own health journey. A major discovery of yours was pregnenolone and vitamin E. Was that before you wrote *Nutrition for Women* in 1973?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that was after. *Nutrition for Women* started when I was talking to a girlfriend about how hormones interact with nutrients. She said this ought to be more widely available, so I started writing up little short bits.

**Danny Roddy:** The idea of oxidative metabolism reinforcing structure and vice versa—was that obvious to you early on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was nine or ten, I had been having periodic migraines. I became nearsighted and noticed that some of my classmates—girls who were nearsighted—also had migraines. I saw that it was not only myopia and migraines, but that these girls were often hypothyroid. So for many years, I considered whether I was hypothyroid.

However, when I was 16 and worked in the woods, people joked that my lunch weighed five pounds. I calculated that I was eating something like 10,000 calories a day while weighing 160 pounds. So, I was convinced I couldn't be hypothyroid.

**Danny Roddy:** Did you think the hyperthyroid state was the result of adrenaline?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think of it as metabolic inefficiency. I evaporated water many times faster than other people. When I worked on a surveying crew, I would refill two canteens every hour. I found that I couldn't urinate from breakfast until after supper, even though I had drunk typically 12 liters of water during the day. I was easily metabolizing 10,000 or 12,000 calories per day. It was inefficient, wasteful youth metabolism.

When I first tried thyroid—for some odd reasoning, despite being so hypermetabolic—suddenly my metabolism slowed down, became more efficient, and I could be comfortable on 3,000 or 4,000 calories a day. That was 1976.

**Danny Roddy:** When did the pregnenolone discovery happen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1983, I started having migraine equivalents—artery inflammation and throbbing inside my mouth, nose, or beside my eye. Thyroid wasn't enough.

I had a bottle of vitamin E that I had used to try and dissolve pregnenolone. It didn't seem to dissolve much, so the powder was sitting at the bottom. When I took that, thinking it was just vitamin E, I was in perfect health. But then I went on a trip and took a different vitamin E supply. I got sick with the migraine equivalent. When I got back, I realized the difference was the bottle. I took a dab of pregnenolone, and the pain stopped within several minutes. That was 1984. I immediately began taking pregnenolone and the symptoms never recurred.

**Danny Roddy:** Were you always thinking about unsaturated fats and their connection with pregnenolone and thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In *Nutrition Reviews*, probably in the early 70s, there was an experiment feeding rats different quantities and proportions of saturated and fatty acids. The unsaturated fatty acids produced obesity over a lifetime regardless of the quantity, and the saturated fats produced leanness regardless of the quantity. That convinced me it was acting on the oxidative system, the same thing thyroid works on.

In my estrogen research for my dissertation, I had seen studies from the 1940s showing that polyunsaturated fats were causing both testicular and brain degeneration, and that vitamin E was an anti-estrogen as well as protecting against that degeneration.

**Danny Roddy:** The foods you originally thought of as constructing a good diet—was that originally for low-income people?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was in Mexico, I saw the effects of extreme malnutrition. I found that eggs, milk, and wheat germ were a good way to get protein and vitamins. However, the wheat germ gave me a terrific calcium deficiency and extreme temperature sensitivity in my teeth, which went away when I took a huge calcium supplement.

In 1962, thinking about how to economize on food—getting a survival diet for maybe $15 a month—potatoes turned out to be one of the best answers. Potatoes and milk. Later, I saw that if you combined orange juice with eggs in sufficient quantity, you could get both your calories and all essential nutrients.

**Danny Roddy:** One of the things I love about your most recent newsletter is that you didn't usually recommend mushrooms, but then you basically changed your mind based on empiricism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the 1970s, I had been a mushroom lover. But then I saw articles by Bela Toth showing there were liver toxins in all of the mushrooms. He didn't mention that they were destroyed by heat, but I was so impressed by the ubiquity of liver toxicity and carcinogenicity that I stopped eating them.

**Danny Roddy:** What brought you back to them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The immune function. They are like an animal turned inside out as far as immunity goes. We live with rotten stuff on the inside (in our intestine), and they live embedded in rotting stuff. They have to have mechanisms that allow them not to be destroyed by toxins and pathogens in their environment.

For many years, I've been interested in endotoxin. Walter C. Alvarez, a gastroenterologist, showed that pressure in the intestine was enough to trigger a migraine in some people. But the pressure works in an environment already destabilized by endotoxin. The combination of low blood sugar and endotoxin predisposes you to any kind of other stress. Since the mushroom develops essentially in a bath of endotoxins, they are an inspiration to think about how our immune system works.

**Danny Roddy:** And they're very anti-estrogenic, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. They have anti-aromatase ingredients. One thing I didn't talk about in the newsletter was their anti-nitric oxide activity, paralleling the anti-aromatase.

The change in thinking about the immune system—from the early 20th-century idea of antibodies fighting "not self" to the ideas of Jamie Cunliffe and Polly Matzinger—focuses on protecting the self. The integrity of the self is based on keeping the cytoplasm in its well-energized state in which the water has a relatively hydrophobic quality.

There are at least three classes of things in mushrooms I think we should concentrate on:
1.  **Steroids:** Lanosterol in mushrooms (cholesterol in ourselves) and progesterone stabilize the cytoplasm so proteins stay in solution.
2.  **Anti-estrogens:** These defend against the low-level defense system. In a crisis, you turn on estrogen and nitric oxide to stimulate cell renewal. If you have mechanisms that prevent the formation of estrogen and nitric oxide, you remove forces that tend to disrupt the cytoplasm.
3.  **Trehalose:** This is a mushroom sugar that stabilizes against endotoxin.

**Danny Roddy:** Is there an amount of mushrooms you need to get those effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's probably around a cup a day. The study I saw in China showed that a very small amount, combined with green tea, lowered breast cancer rates by 87%.

**Danny Roddy:** You suggested in the newsletter to cook them for three hours. Do you have any recipes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I'm going to eat a large amount, like a cup, I like to put cheddar cheese or something meltable on it and melt it in the microwave. It makes a really scrumptious dish.

**Danny Roddy:** Could mushrooms replace meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think they would completely replace meat. The typical dietician chart shows potatoes and mushrooms as having insignificant amounts of protein because they compare the dry state of grains to the wet state of mushrooms. If you multiply the mushroom protein by five or ten to account for the water, you get something comparable to bean protein. I would compare it to milk; they are down in the range of 3% protein, like milk.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you try to get a certain amount of calcium per day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Over the years I've averaged 2,500 milligrams of calcium at least, and around 100 to 120 grams of protein. Milk, cheese, and eggs are my staples, along with all the good tropical fruits I can manage.

**Danny Roddy:** Are you working on anything else right now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** More on the nitric oxide stuff. It's a huge topic. I've been following it since the 1980s. At that time, I was interested in carbon monoxide as an endogenous toxicant. It turns out that even carbon monoxide is protective sometimes against nitric oxide. I see nitric oxide as one of the few things worse than carbon monoxide.

**Danny Roddy:** Ray, I cannot thank you enough for doing this.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay. Thank you.

title: The CIA's Mighty Wurlitzer with Ray Peat [Generative Energy #32]
transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Hello everyone, I'm Danny Roddy of DannyRoddy.com, and today I'm talking with painter, philosopher, and biologist, Raymond Peat. In this hour-long episode, we'll talk about the creation of the CIA and its primary role in shaping U.S. culture through painting, music, language, literature, economics, philosophy, religion, social activism, and politics.

I feel like I just crammed for a test. I read your newsletter, I read the article by Paul Green—I forget his name—and I read a few people distilling down that book because I couldn't get a hold of it. I read the David Talbot book and reviewed that. Then I found a list of CIA atrocities, which was mind-blowing.

When you talked about the Indonesian genocide, I had no idea that's what *The Act of Killing* and *The Look of Silence* were about. I knew the general idea, but I didn't put it together. Those movies made a huge impact on me a few years ago, so I was pretty shocked.

To start things off, it might be interesting to get your current read on the political situation. For me, that was the thing that got me interested in exploring the past—how did we end up here? In your newsletter, you said that the CIA was "treating the world like an orchard, fertilizing some trees, pruning others, and removing unwanted trees and weeds." That was really interesting to me. So, if you go back in the past, maybe you can figure out how we got here.

What are your general thoughts on free speech, this left-right thing, the media, and race tensions? It’s interesting coming from you because you've lived through Vietnam, civil rights, and so on.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the place you decided to start is sort of arbitrary. My consciousness started early during the Roosevelt time.

**Danny Roddy:** I was going to get your general thoughts on the current situation and then jump right back into Pearl Harbor. Do you want to go with Pearl Harbor first or go from the place that you wanted to go?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One perspective I have that brings things up to the present is looking at the coup against FDR in 1933 and '34, as described to Congress by Smedley Butler. The coupists—the great corporations of the country that wanted to get rid of Roosevelt because he was committing treason to their class—went quiet for several years. They focused on Harry Truman in the late 1930s as their guy, whom they put in place finally in 1944.

As I see it, they opportunely killed Roosevelt just before he found out what Allen Dulles was doing with the Nazis. So they had Truman in place when they shifted over to the Nazi-Dulles side.

During that time, Fletcher Prouty was involved in a lot of the secret plans going on in Asia during the Second World War. He tells a little about that in his book, *The Secret Team*, which refers to the privately operated CIA as related to Nixon and the Kennedy assassination. Along this stretch of time, you have people like Ted Shackley and Ronald Reagan getting put in place with the assistance of George H.W. Bush and the October Surprise.

**Danny Roddy:** The October Surprise was where he went to Paris to make deals with the Iranians not to release the hostages until they got Jimmy Carter out of office?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. On the airplane to Paris with Bush were high officials that everyone knew: Senator John Heinz and John Tower, conservative right-wing Republicans. Several years later, on successive days—April 4 and April 5 of '91—they both died in airplane crashes. People who were in a position to know what George Sr. and his associates were doing all came to bad ends.

Nixon and Schlesinger got put out through Watergate, and Carter got put out by various manipulations, such as the October Surprise. All of these things interact. Periodically, someone starts to string the pieces together, and they very thoroughly get wiped out as far as anything taken seriously goes. Do you know about Daniel Sheehan and the Christic Institute?

**Danny Roddy:** No.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He did a lot of putting together and sued the government for murder and assassination. Even though he had the evidence, his organization was destroyed because the judge said it was frivolous. He had to pay all of the legal expenses, and that bankrupted his organization.

**Danny Roddy:** Is this along the same lines as the JFK stuff? I'm skipping far ahead, but Edward J. Epstein was one of the biggest critics. The idea was that the CIA set up their critics—set up opposition to the ideas—so that it would be controlled.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was Braden who called it his "Mighty Wurlitzer" that could play any tune he wanted. Their best loudspeakers were the *Washington Post* and *New York Times*. The *Washington Post* was one of the most effective in wiping out people like the Christic Institute.

**Danny Roddy:** And that's Operation Mockingbird?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was one of its names at the time. But basically, it's just what they do.

**Danny Roddy:** When I was reading David Talbot’s book, he said Henry Luce, the Time-Life guy, was so interconnected to everybody. These major news outlets just had hardcore agendas and were all being manipulated by Dulles.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're all the same people. The CIA guys were recruited from among those. It's the scum of the ruling class.

**Danny Roddy:** Stepping back a little bit, you mentioned that you thought the culture had changed in 1947. That coincided with the creation of the CIA.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The 1944 Democrat Convention—I knew several people who were there, and they stayed furiously bitter for 50 years afterwards about what happened. Fake tickets were printed up for people who had never been in the election, and the real delegates were shut out. So it was a completely funny convention that chose Truman to be the next president.

**Danny Roddy:** Who do you think was behind that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That same group that started the coup in '33 and '34. Morgan and DuPont were the only names that I recall, but it was the top powers in the corporations. They got Truman in position.

Dulles had been a Nazi finance agent between the banks and the corporations of Germany—Rockefeller and Farben. He was a buddy with all of the top Nazis. He was in Switzerland dealing with the Nazis, arranging for them not to fight the Americans coming up the Italian peninsula so that they could go hold off the Russians to keep them from getting all the way through Germany.

Stalin, through his spies, found out what was going on in the first week or two of April 1945. Roosevelt said, "Maybe Stalin is losing it because this couldn't be happening. Stalin must be making it up that Dulles is letting the German-Italian branch of the army head to the Eastern Front." Before FDR found out that Stalin was right, he was dead.

If he had found out, that would have revealed that Dulles was leading a pro-Nazi army, dealing with the Gehlen Intelligence Organization and the top army people to unite the Americans with the Nazis against Russia to keep control of Western Europe.

So, the whole denazification thing in Germany was fraudulent. They just changed their party labels. As many of the technical people as possible were brought into the U.S., like Wernher von Braun for the rockets. Instead of denazifying Germany, the U.S. was Nazified.

**Danny Roddy:** You were actually there. Were there any people asking, "What is going on? How are these Nazis being brought over here?" Was the press just not doing its job?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Almost no one was concerned. They said they were denazified, so they're okay; they were really the "good underground Nazis." The Nazi reality never sank in.

Take Konrad Lorenz getting the Nobel Prize. He was the architect of genocide. Even in his post-Nobel book, he kept using all of the ideas that he had presented to Hitler as the reason for exterminating Black people, Gypsies, Jews, and Slavs. All of the people that got killed wholesale were justified by the specific things that Konrad Lorenz wrote, and he kept writing them. In his newer book, he used a German word slightly milder than "extirpated"—something like "weeded out."

**Danny Roddy:** It reminds me of Obama getting the Nobel Peace Prize for dropping bombs for eight years.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** [Laughter]

**Danny Roddy:** So, 1947, the creation of the CIA under Truman. President Truman signs the National Security Act of 1947, and that gives no rules to the CIA.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By that time, he knew who Allen Dulles was, if he had any brain at all. That whole thing became fairly public, except it didn't get to Roosevelt in time to save his life.

**Danny Roddy:** Why was it necessary to kill Roosevelt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Because Dulles and his people were committing horrible treason and setting up the Cold War—setting up Europe to make war against Russia.

**Danny Roddy:** If Stalin was aware of everything, was there no way for him to penetrate the propaganda?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, because the jukebox was being operated by Dulles and his people.

**Danny Roddy:** Is that the Congress for Cultural Freedom?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That, and radio stations and the great newspapers. 95% of the newspapers followed the *Washington Post* and *New York Times*. There were only three newspapers known for being independent out of thousands in the U.S.: the *St. Louis Post-Dispatch*, *Medford Mail Tribune*, and the *Valley News* in California.

**Danny Roddy:** Frances Stonor Saunders says, "Whether they liked it or not, whether they knew it or not, there were few writers, poets, artists, historians, scientists, or critics in post-war Europe whose names were not in some way linked to this covert enterprise." So even if you didn't know you were part of this cabal, you were actually part of it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If all the newspapers, radio stations, and foundations in the U.S. said it was criminal to think otherwise, you were just quiet because everyone around you seemed crazy.

**Danny Roddy:** Did you keep your thoughts to yourself at that time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. I was in the seventh grade in a social studies class. The seventh-grade boys were supposed to spend their recess time cleaning the grounds. I put up posters showing a reclining gopher and organized the "Loafer Gophers" instead of the "Eager Beavers," and got scolded for that.

Then in social studies class, a kid who was kind of a goofy, nice kid asked Mrs. White, the teacher, "Are they going to kill Raymond Peat for being a communist, if that's the policy?" She said, "I don't think so. He's a nice little boy."

**Danny Roddy:** Was Eisenhower following the same line of being put in the presidency like Truman, or was he the real deal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically, he was very stupid. But yeah, he was just following the ruling class, whatever they said.

**Danny Roddy:** And Allen Dulles was CIA director in 1953 under Eisenhower.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eisenhower came out by witness many years later that he had specifically given orders to kill Patrice Lumumba. At the time, I considered both Eisenhower and Kennedy—who had been elected by that time—as having been involved. Kennedy, as President-elect, should have been aware of what was happening.

I started out being very negative towards Kennedy. A few months later, Dag Hammarskjöld was killed in a plane crash. I figured Kennedy must have been responsible because it was right in his administration, under his direct authority, that the CIA was there in charge of things.

Hammarskjöld had been facilitating the imperialists in the Congo—the Belgian, British, and American agents. But after Patrice Lumumba was killed, Hammarskjöld suddenly started being even-handed. He was going to arrange peace discussions between the two sides. That was when he got killed. It was obviously an assassination.

**Danny Roddy:** I want to get to Dag Hammarskjöld and George de Mohrenschildt. But first, what are your thoughts on the antagonism between JFK and Dulles? I'm confused how somebody like that even got into office if they hated him so much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Kennedy's point was to go after Eisenhower and Nixon for being weak on communism. He said he would lead a great military buildup, which he did. He was the militarist's candidate. He said that Eisenhower had let him in on the fact that they were going to invade Cuba. Part of his militarism was saying, "Eisenhower has let Castro get away with everything. We'll go after Castro." So he was the right-wing extremist in that election. That really annoyed Nixon because Nixon had told him what they were going to do, and Nixon couldn't say, "Wait, we're already planning that."

**Danny Roddy:** That conflicts with the idea from David Talbot and others that JFK was anti-war or a reasonable person.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He might really have been upset over the Hammarskjöld killing because of what Hammarskjöld had in mind for Indonesia, which was to make Sukarno a puppet of the U.S. rather than leaving it with the Netherlands. Kennedy had his way of controlling Indonesia without the formality of colonialism. But despite whatever relative good he saw for Indonesia, he was still thinking imperialism. Twice he talked to his ambassador to Brazil asking if it was basically time to do a coup yet against João Goulart. The ambassador said when the time was opportune, but there was nothing urgent right then.

**Danny Roddy:** Paul Green describes some plot where they discovered some mineral that they wanted, and Dulles was friends with George de Mohrenschildt.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Neither Kennedy nor Hammarskjöld, nor just about anyone in the world, knew about the high-quality oil or the gold and copper—two huge deposits in Indonesia. The Dulles-de Mohrenschildt people had been secretive about that so none of the authorities knew. They wanted to get the Dutch out before they let it become public. The Rockefeller people bought up the properties, and I think they still own it through a Phoenix-based company.

**Danny Roddy:** So under the guise of anti-communism, the CIA overthrows the democratically elected Sukarno with a military coup. The CIA had been trying to eliminate Sukarno since 1957. According to Paul Green, Sukarno not siding with Dulles enraged him.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was all it was with João Goulart in Brazil. Kennedy said, "He's looking slightly neutral. We'll have to get rid of him right away or later."

**Danny Roddy:** When I read the list of atrocities through the CIA, it seemed bonkers. Do you see Dulles as the person driving all of these different things? It seems so complex to manage all these regime changes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You have to visualize the ruling class and how it works. It has these upper levels of academics and political lawyers for the big corporations working like secretaries of state and intelligence agency heads. There's a whole crop of these very well-informed people at the heart of both economic and political affairs. They are like a worldwide coarse mesh—only a few hundred people on that level sitting on top of thousands of corporations. Maybe 3 million or so ruling class people in America and Europe. They already have the power, so the state power is fairly trivial compared to how we think of it. They see the state officials as inconveniences, but not too hard to get rid of.

**Danny Roddy:** The creation of the CIA gave this oligarchy a tool to do whatever they wanted.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you see the Neo-Darwinian marriage with Malthusianism as a type of elite religion for them to justify their actions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The science world is very similar to the finance-politics world and has its intersections. A few of the top science people are closely connected to the political power. It's all the same recognition of power: where they're going and who they want to control for what purposes.

**Danny Roddy:** We talked about the Indonesian mass genocide in 1965-66. Do you want to talk about the connection between Obama, his mom Ann Dunham, and his stepdad Lolo Soetoro?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The reporter Wayne Madsen, I think his picture is basically right. His grandmother was probably connected with the CIA as a paymaster for people in the Pacific. A friend of mine was a tool of the Nugan Hand Bank, which was the CIA funnel for drug and weapons money in Vietnam and Iran-Contra through the '60s and '70s. That opium and weapons money was handled through Australia and Hawaii.

I assume there's been some interaction between the bank that Grandma Obama—Madelyn Dunham—worked for. She was a vice president of the bank that was handling CIA money.

His mother was in that anthropology study. Pretty much the anthropology profession was serving the CIA, mapping out people to either exterminate or control. In Mexico and Latin America, it was the Summer Institute of Linguistics, which codified native languages to give them instructions. Anthropology and religious missionaries were tied into the CIA to gather information on populations. In Indonesia, the anthropology people were helping make surveys of who was to be exterminated by the new government to make sure they didn't go neutral or favor China.

**Danny Roddy:** You mentioned opium. How much of that is involved in the power elite funding things? I perused a book on Skull and Bones saying that whole thing is tied to the sale of opium.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They use whatever has force. Religious missionaries are one way of doing it, drugs are another, and just force is another.

**Danny Roddy:** In 1966, the *Ramparts* affair happened, where the magazine began untangling the nefarious acts of the CIA.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people say the CIA was subsidizing them and promoting them to do a partial "limited hangout." The facts are so much worse that they want to make it seem that everything has come out, to make people stop looking at the connections.

When you start putting things together—like conservative senators Heinz and Tower having that connection to George Bush—it becomes inconvenient. That ties into John Kerry and his investigation, and why he didn't pursue it. It shows interconnectedness in government. On the surface, it seems crazy to connect extreme right-wing senators to extreme left-wing organizations like the Christic Institute. But when you weave the strings together, you get a thousand parts that fit snugly. The official explanation starts sounding crazy.

**Danny Roddy:** What year was it when Bush and Kerry ran against each other, and they're both Skull & Bones members? What a coincidence.

**Danny Roddy:** I was interested in Zbigniew Brzezinski, David Rockefeller, and the Trilateral Commission.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Brzezinski was controlling Carter, basically. Rockefeller was controlling Brzezinski. Brzezinski cooked up the plan to get Saudi Arabia to start sending people into Afghanistan with U.S. weapons.

The Soviets had set up a secular government in Afghanistan with education for women and basically democratic practices. Every time a secular government is created in the Muslim world, it's as bad as being neutral. Brzezinski was one example of that; the overthrow of Mossadegh was their first big anti-secular case.

The most fanatic anti-secularism came when the Soviets had set up a non-religious government in Afghanistan. The Cuban Missile Crisis had the outcome of the U.S. agreeing to take their rockets out of Turkey, and the Soviets hoped to get another buffer state without rockets in Afghanistan. To prevent that, Brzezinski got the fanatics armed with the best weapons to fight the Afghan democracy and the Soviets who supported it. That went on until Carter was out of office, and eventually, the fanatics won under extreme support from the U.S.

**Danny Roddy:** There are articles showing what Afghanistan looked like in the 1970s, and it looks like modern people walking around. Today it's just rubble.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The religious extremism was all created by Brzezinski. They brought the same sort of people into Serbia and took over Kosovo.

**Danny Roddy:** It's interesting that Brzezinski was so tied to Obama. He was in Obama's inner circle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the same sort of thing as Hillary Clinton praising Henry Kissinger. It revealed who she really is. You've heard about her newest book in which she explains the real meaning of George Orwell's *1984*? She says it means we should trust our leaders, experts, and the press more.

**Danny Roddy:** That reminds me of Mayor Giuliani saying, "Real freedom is about obeying authority."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. The meaning of *1984*.

**Danny Roddy:** Having been through so much, do you see the current situation as incomprehensible, or is it a logical continuation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The only pleasant thing about it is that so many other people are starting to see the loose ends. Before, if you had an economic theory of why wars were fought, you were ignorant, crazy, or subversive. But the atmosphere has changed; lots of people are questioning things now.

**Danny Roddy:** If you talked about the deep state before, you would be labeled crazy. Now it is being talked about openly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People always prefer surfaces, but now the surface is being slightly redefined. Before, the state said it wasn't true that the state was really rotten all the way down. Now they analyze it and say, "Here's the surface and there's a deep state." But it's always been just one rotten state. Now people are starting to break it down into its parts and seeing the illusion—how consent is manufactured.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you see the creation of the CIA as the real issue, not necessarily the government per se?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. People started separating the CIA from the government when Eisenhower had scheduled peace talks with Khrushchev. Everyone was expecting big things. Then, with Lee Harvey Oswald—a U-2 expert—in place in Russia, Dulles sent a U-2 plane over Russia. He knew they had the expert who knew exactly the recipe for shooting it down and overcoming their radar defenses.

Sending this U-2 plane over to be shot down just days before the peace talk sabotaged the talks. Eisenhower knew who Dulles was and still let it happen. Eisenhower was stupid, but he was also the one who kept Dulles in place. So you could say there were different factions working, but they weren't really separate. They were just slightly inconvenient to each other.

**Danny Roddy:** I watched a video by Lisa Pease, and she echoed what you just said—that Oswald was incredibly good at radar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was what he was trained for, as well as speaking Russian in Japan. The information that has come out provides a complete, fine-grained picture of what was going on in the assassination. All of the context fits: who was murdered, the official story, the function of the Warren Commission. There's not really any mystery anymore.

**Danny Roddy:** What is your general thought on Trump? Do you see him as part of this oligarchical cabal or a free agent?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think he's a free agent with some good instincts, but also an instinct of self-preservation. His thing about not wanting nuclear war is his basic good impulse. But what can you do with just being president?

**Danny Roddy:** Some people said when he met with Kissinger, "Oh, this guy is no good."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think he's insincere about most of what he does. But over the years, he seemed to come up with some insights. About 20 years ago, he suggested having a one-time wealth tax. He said it would cost him $200 million or something, but it would pay off the national debt, and we'd be almost tax-free from then on.

**Danny Roddy:** Truman said to his biographer Merle Miller in 1973 that the creation of the CIA was a mistake.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Recognizing any of its evil, how could he say otherwise?

**Danny Roddy:** He said the CIA makes their own wars. He also has a quote saying that they killed Dag Hammarskjöld.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A witness to the cabinet meeting where Eisenhower told them to do it didn't come out for 50 years, but everyone knew it at the time. I suppose Truman had much better information than the public.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you have any thoughts on Lyman Lemnitzer, who wrote Operation Northwoods? Reading through that is sobering on how crazy things can get.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually, the most disgusting things they do in conversation; they don't do stupid things like keeping records. Even the act of keeping records, I'm sure they don't do it with the really vile stuff. In that situation, people are free to imagine, and their imagination can seldom catch up to what's really happening right now.

**Danny Roddy:** To end on a positive note: Are things so bad that you don't see them getting better, or do you see some hope?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you get a lot of people with some very simple insights—like abuse of power is going to be the rule, so there should never be power exercised in private or in secret—people will automatically start moving in the right direction. Just insist on complete openness. With the control systems through the media, schools, and legal system, everything is going to have to happen outside of all of those channels.

**Danny Roddy:** James Angleton, CIA counterintelligence head, said in his testimony to the Church Committee, "It is inconceivable that a secret intelligence arm of the government has to comply with all the overt orders of the government."

Ray, what are you working on right now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm working on an article on milk, putting milk in a cultural context. Looking at the false assumptions and thinking about how to start rethinking things from a new point.

**Danny Roddy:** Awesome. I cannot wait to read it. Ray, you've been so generous with your time. I sincerely appreciate it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay. Fun to talk to you. Thank you.

**Danny Roddy:** Bye, Ray.

title: The Origins of Authoritarianism with Ray Peat  [Generative Energy #28]
transcriptText:
**Danny Roddy:** Hello everyone, I'm Danny Roddy of DannyRoddy.com and today I'm talking with painter, philosopher, and biologist, Raymond Peat. In this episode, we'll talk about the history and origins of authoritarianism and how the philosophy is baked into our cultural, political, and medical systems.

Ray, thank you so much for doing this. I've been interested in this topic for a while. I had a chance to read through your newsletter "Public Passivity and the Screw" from September 2003. I thought it was fantastic.

Authoritarianism seems to be an ambiguous term to a lot of people. Before we get into the weeds, could you talk about what it means to you and your general experience with it, scientifically and academically?

**Ray Peat:** Academically, there has been a study for about 50 years now. Bob Altemeier's book, *The Authoritarians*, came out on the internet maybe five or ten years ago. John Dean, the Watergate lawyer, became a fan of it and helped to publicize it because it was about the psychology of political authoritarianism primarily. His main focus is on what he calls "right-wing authoritarians."

My understanding of it started long before that. It was the intuitive thing of seeing that in the culture, there is an unreasoning submission to the ideas of anyone in power, and conformism around what is taken to be the power-enforced authoritative doctrine.

In reacting to Bob Altemeier's version of it, I have seen that in some ways, publicizing these traits of the right-wing authoritarian might be adding to the confusion somewhat. One of Altemeier's images for how this can be conceptualized comes from Theodor Adorno, a group at Berkeley who made the subject popular in the 1960s. Adorno's image was that it's the posture for riding a bicycle: bowing from the waist up and kicking from the waist down. In other words, submission to the authority of those above you, and knocking down anyone below you to keep them there.

Bob Altemeier says that isn't a very good image. He used questionnaires and got really clear results. But other people using a scale of social prestige-seeking or power-seeking identified people who, rather than conforming and fitting into wherever they find themselves on the scale, are only driven towards rising. You can think of the sociopath or the psychopath who cares about nothing but winning and isn't satisfied until they come out owning everything and controlling everyone.

**Danny Roddy:** Throughout the 20th century, there were different views on fitting into the system.

**Ray Peat:** Yes. Freud said repression is a good thing—fitting into the system. From the time I was in high school, people were saying, "You have to work within the system." My first thoughts on that were imagining that if you cooperate in the system for 10, 20, 30, or 40 years, look at the pile of criminal activities you have participated in. Then, when you finally have the power to do something, the first thing you do puts you out of the system. So you have a huge accumulated pile of bad stuff, and the first chance you have to do good stuff might result in a noticeable achievement, but it's always going to be smaller than what you did in the opposite direction getting there.

I wasn't sold on the idea that you have to work within the system because it's really just a way of buying people into it. Freud really allied with the oppressing class. He created this idea of the ego mediating between the id and the superego. It has to balance these forces, but he really came down on the side of the superego, smashing the id when necessary.

Around 1929 or 1930, Wilhelm Reich realized what Freud was doing. He believed that Freud was very conscious of the rightness of Reich's position—that you're never going to have a healthy individual as long as they're being oppressed—but believed Freud simply wanted to save his movement from Nazism and make it able to survive by giving in to the oppression.

From the 1920s, Reich was saying that there's an emotional plague all through the world. Not just fascism, but the plague of authoritarianism. At first, he said education, medicine, and psychiatry can cure people of this. But then he realized that first, you have to cure the doctors and the teachers of the emotional plague.

I think Reich was essentially right, but I think it is more than just an emotional plague. I think it's something like a historical, intellectual, epistemological plague built into the way we believe knowledge works.

**Danny Roddy:** Did it originate from Plato and Aristotle? Do you see an origin for this type of oppressive society?

**Ray Peat:** As soon as I started looking into encyclopedias trying to find explanations, I think it goes even before Plato. Parmenides and Zeno, the Greek school located in southern Italy (the Eleatics), argued that there is only one reality and it doesn't change. It doesn't do anything. There is no movement.

Someone as smart as Bertrand Russell praised the subtlety of Zeno's paradoxes, but Russell struggled for years in what seems like very stupid arguments. However, he was smart enough to work himself out of that set of paradoxical mental activities that Western philosophy had been trapped in for 2,500 years.

Plato essentially gave in to the Parmenides school of thinking that at least the knowledge part of existence—which is the "real" part of existence—is unchanging, eternal, and perfect. He was really making the crude ideas of Parmenides worse.

Aristotle acknowledged some of the reality of Heraclitus. Heraclitus said everything flows—exactly the polar opposite of Plato and Parmenides. Heraclitus said everything is moving, and reason (meaning) steers everything through everything. So it wasn't a jumbled, random movement. It was a developmental process which, as a whole, is steered by meaning.

Aristotle tried to formalize this using some of the concepts of Plato but putting it into a sensible scheme in which he had different kinds of causality, including the final cause principle: that things are moved according to meaning or intention. The universality of motion has no randomness in it. Everything is meaningful.

**Danny Roddy:** That goes back to your newsletter. You say laws were written in the past, and since the past isn't accessible, it's almost as though a foreign power ruled from a distant imperial capital. Is that the problem with not only these laws but politics in general?

**Ray Peat:** Oh yeah. The Platonic idea is creating a false reality for everything that we have in our memory. Seeing everything in terms of the past—something that we have at one time generalized—and then saying that is absolute and unchanging. What it does is say that all of these current events are random happenings. They don't contain the meaning in themselves; they only get the meaning from these generalizations, and those are all eternal, out of time.

This was taken up in physics with the assumption of randomness, which can then be treated statistically. But it's a belief about current events and the nature of substance and experience that is proclaimed to be of a lower order and essentially lacking meaning or purpose.

Plato argued for tyranny, that the people who "know" would have the power, and the power would be logic and mathematics. When this was put into action by the physicists, they proclaimed themselves as those who knew the ultimate fundamental truth. When biology wanted to gain status, they said they would model themselves on the true basic science of physics.

To find the eternal ruling class elements of the world, the physicists looked for timeless, unchanging atoms. The individual atom had no unique features, no history, and was an absolute and pure Platonic thing. The only way they can be treated is by assuming that all of their later developments and movements are meaningless and random and have to be described only statistically.

In modeling biology on physics, the equivalent of the timeless, unchanging atom was the timeless, unchanging gene. Again, the soma—the body that we experience—was said to be basically just mortal junk that would be cast aside every generation, while the immortal germline collection of genes was what was really important. This was developed very closely with people like Herbert Spencer, who identified that even Darwin was a racist that believed that English plants, animals, and people were the best in the world.

**Danny Roddy:** You mentioned psychopaths before, and in a previous interview, you mentioned the Dulles brothers. I think you were alluding to a book by David Talbot called *The Devil's Chessboard*.

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, I think that's his name.

**Danny Roddy:** You mentioned Reich before, and the connection with Dali and the persistence of memory in Dali's shift, integrating himself into the fascist culture. I was curious to unpack your thoughts on the CIA and the Dulles brothers.

**Ray Peat:** Well, 20th-century history pretty much involved the Dulles brothers. They were working with Hitler and the fascist Germans right from the beginning. One of them was declared to be an enemy agent. The German government had put their American properties in his name, so the U.S. government, to confiscate the U.S. properties, identified him as an illegal foreign agent.

But that didn't take away from their prestige or power, because Roosevelt himself was a great admirer of Mussolini. Even after he took office, he was saying what a great statesman Mussolini was. Fascism wasn't a bad word until they needed to go to war on the side of England to save the British Empire because Hitler had double-crossed the West. He wanted to knock out England and take their empire, whereas the West had figured that he would take over the Soviet Union, and then the British Empire and the American Empire could expand.

**Danny Roddy:** Going back to saying the Dulles brothers shaped the current predicament we're in, do you see authoritarianism as a pathology? Like this is basically a sickness, and people are imposing their sickness?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, in a sense. A philosopher might say it's a sickness of method or of conclusions. But if you look at it historically, Parmenides, Plato, and Hegel were all part of the ruling class. It was the purpose of their thinking that way—even though that probably seemed spontaneous and truthful to them—it happened to be a way of defining who deserves power and defining their class as an eternal, justified controller of property and power.

The idea of class was very conscious in most of history. In the 20th century, one of the tricks of the ruling class has been to teach the public that there are no classes in America. I had a professor in graduate school around 1959 or 1960 talking about the effect of class in literature. He interrupted me to say, "In America, we have no classes."

It's truly either a mental disease or defect of some sort for people to grow up, study, and be able to say something like that. It's because the ruling class learned to manipulate language and control the people that they need to be controlled. They don't want to necessarily define them as useless rubbish—which they believe they are—unless they can get away with it. But if they can make the people feel that they are equals with the royalty and keep them happy while they're living like garbage, that's the best thing for them.

So they have taught people that in America there are no classes. People who are really in the bottom 30 or 40% of income call themselves middle class, and people who are more or less in the middle income range think of themselves as being in the upper 5%. Everyone seems to have this escalated delusion of where they are in the social hierarchy.

**Danny Roddy:** It almost seems like any movement is infiltrated by authoritarianism. Is the environment essentially bracketing our current progress as a civilization right now?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, environment in every sense. There are penalties of many sorts for getting out of it, and rewards of various kinds for reinforcing it.

**Danny Roddy:** I first heard about Nicole Foss's ideas of "degrowth" through you. Do you think there will be an inevitable degrowth in our society and a move back to a simpler direction?

**Ray Peat:** No. There will be a rejection or loss of much of the trashy part of our culture, but there is no need to go as far as she suggests—going back to isolated tribalism.

What's creating the "one-worldism" at present is a really degraded concept of human interaction and the interaction between people and their environment. It's all based on this polluted kind of philosophy or religion. It's a religion of emptiness and abstraction that is telling people that this is all there is.

But leaving out all of these promotional, consumerist, economic functions, if you simply stop having wars, stop crooked advertising, and stop promoting consumerism through schools and the way university research is directed and funded—if you simply stop the craziest practices—what will be left will still be international, but without suppressing the individual flavor of ethnicities.

The natural interactions and trade, I think, will keep a unified world economy existing. Even if Foss is right about peak oil—my opinion is that the world is creating petroleum about as fast as it's being used, and it just takes a while to refill the wells after they're pumped out—but even if she was right, there are alternative sources of power that can keep a really high-level culture going more or less permanently.

At present, I think about a dozen species are being made extinct every day. That's an idea of what "progress" means in this current period. If you stop that kind of progress, it's like you stop falling into a hole. As soon as you stop falling, then you can see what kind of possibility is really there.

**Danny Roddy:** So increasing the people's knowledge, ability, and power could restrain the authority of power?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah, making people conscious of the lies that they're having imposed on them. That involves things as drastic as saying that most of the theoretical physics that we're taught to admire has been very clever technical adaptations with a gigantic, fraudulent hierarchy of mathematical theories built on that. A little bit of empirical technical stuff has been given a mythic sort of importance because it's used economically and in war. But the implications in theory, I don't think, are at all what we're being told by the theoretical physicists in Europe and America.

**Danny Roddy:** Obviously you focus a lot on food. Do you think that's a way in to shift the consciousness of the people towards lower serotonin, if that relates to somebody's authoritarianism?

**Ray Peat:** First, a person who is chronically sick and malnourished just doesn't have much energy or stamina to study and be critical. So first, you just have to stop poisoning yourself by eating what the government and dieticians are selling as a healthful diet. Once you have the strength to read and think, then you realize who is doing what to you.

You start investigating the food industry, the agricultural production industry, the science industry that supports the agricultural imposition, and the political system that justifies the medical and agricultural economic imposition. All of these are very clearly wound together in a system to maintain class dominance.

It's very healthful to eat lobster once in a while, but you don't see dieticians or the government recommending that. It started in the 1930s Depression with the government having a three-tiered diet: one to prevent starvation in the very poor, an economical diet to get along on very little, and then at the top, a healthy diet. If you look at the bare survival and economic minimal diet of the Great Depression, the dieticians in the 1960s and 70s adopted those survival diets as the "healthy" diet. Lots of beans and grains as the basic diet.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think that was on purpose, as a form of control?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. Part of it was that the government had been buying milk, dehydrating it, and making cheese and butter to keep American farmers working to support the prices. So they were warehousing huge amounts of powdered milk, cheese, and butter, and giving them away first as foreign aid. The precursor to food stamps was to have a monthly giveaway to poor people of cheese, eggs, powdered milk, and so on.

In the 70s, there was a big movement to stop helping the poor people in other countries as well as the poor at home. One of the arguments that came up in the pseudoscientific dietetic community was that people outside the United States hardly ever can tolerate lactose, so you should stop giving them powdered milk. That argument—that only certain white people can tolerate lactose—was heavily promoted as a racist change of foreign policy against foreign aid and food aid in general. Sending them beans was okay, except we didn't need to support the price of American beans that way.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you think this tendency to be authoritarian—or as Altemeier would have said, "right-wing authoritarian"—do you personally see it more in Americans versus other places? I know you've mentioned Mexico as a different type of environment and being a little more cheerful.

**Ray Peat:** A lot of it is the specific policy choices of the government and corporations indoctrinating Americans in a certain way. One of my main criticisms of Bob Altemeier is that he has focused on the right-wing authoritarianism. It would be okay to call it right-wing if you define "right" in the sense of the fascism that Winston Churchill and FDR subscribed to.

Americans generally think of FDR as an extreme leftist president, but definitely his admiration for Mussolini says there was no leftism at all. He said what he was doing was saving his class—saving the ruling class—because there was such a threat of revolution in the United States. So he was saving capitalism, and that would fit in as modified fascism. It was an inventive way of keeping the corporations lightly out of sight, letting them buy the various regulatory agencies, but keeping them out of the executive for their own good.

He was fixing the economy with Keynesian economics. The people who organized a coup in 1933 to get him out considered even the borrowing and spending to be a communist plot of government. They wanted to get Roosevelt out, but what he was doing was using finance to prevent revolution.

Immediately when it came out that Allen Dulles was working closely with the Nazis at the end of World War II, Stalin informed Roosevelt that his spies were aware that Dulles was collaborating with the Nazis. Roosevelt's comments suggested that he thought maybe Stalin had gone crazy to tell him such a thing. But within two or three days, Roosevelt surely would have found out that Stalin was right, and that would have put Dulles in line for the war crimes trials.

Luckily for Dulles, right at that moment, Roosevelt chose to die, saving Dulles from criminal treason prosecution. The powers in the Democratic Party who had connections both with Adolf Hitler and with the DuPont gang that had organized the 1933 coup attempt were in charge of the big city Democratic Party machine. They knew that Harry Truman had expressed himself many times as wanting Hitler to go fight the Soviets. Since that was the preferred American policy, they had installed him as vice president in 1944. So Roosevelt's death in '45 not only saved Dulles, but it put Truman in position to continue the pro-Nazi policy.

We have Project Paperclip, where the top Germans were not only helped to move to Argentina and adjoining countries, but a lot of them were brought to the U.S., the scientists in particular.

**Danny Roddy:** It seems like Dulles was involved in a lot of sketchy stuff like MKUltra. I know you've talked about LSD and its effects on the physiology. Do you see him as an integral part of suppressing that specific substance?

**Ray Peat:** Oh, for sure. One of the people who invented the idea of communist brainwashing said that when prisoners of war had confessed their crimes and wanted to stay with the enemy, it proved that they had amazing powers of brainwashing. I think it was two or three days after a big speech on that, he approved the MKUltra project for testing LSD and other drugs to see if they could wipe out a person's moral restrictions and give complete power over them.

**Danny Roddy:** Do you see the disestablishment of medicine as a central tower to turn over to enable the people to resist the authoritarian ideas imposed on us?

**Ray Peat:** Yeah. For example, you could still have very strong government control, but if it was rationalized so that a person had to pass a test—had to know certain empirical facts before they could get a license—they would have to know something about blood circulation and how respiration works so that they wouldn't inject things into the wrong part of the patient. With just a reasonable control, you could open up the whole field so that you would have not only more accessible medicine, but also better medicine. It would give people a choice between rational and irrational treatment.

**Danny Roddy:** If you were thinking of an optimal society, would it include medicine or government at all?

**Ray Peat:** Tolstoy and Kropotkin are my oldest political influences. One of Tolstoy's lines was that a person should be ashamed to use government power.

If you have an organization that has simply deleted the threats and the craziness that presently is saturating our culture for maybe five or ten years, I think you would very easily have a powerless society that would function without visible power.

There's a town in Andalusia, Spain, where I think in 1989 they elected an anarchist mayor. It's just an amazing town. They've reelected him ever since. They gradually, piece by piece, expropriated unused land. Within just a very few years of his first election, they had eliminated poverty, eliminated the town police, and had everything cleaned up. That's still going now, 25 or 30 years later. I think that's an example of how any place can work if you just remove the most horrible, oppressive parts of the system.

**Danny Roddy:** We'd probably end there. Ray, thank you so much. That was amazing.

This is actually the end of my stay in San Francisco. I'm going to head to San Miguel de Allende on July 1st. I think Siqueiros is the artist that you enjoy there? I think some of his big stuff is there.

**Ray Peat:** Oh, yeah. I don't think he ever finished a mural in San Miguel. I've always wanted to see that. I heard about the process of starting it and the conflicts that interrupted it.

**Danny Roddy:** Awesome. Yeah, I'll send you a picture. Thank you so much again, Ray. Total pleasure. I appreciate your time.

**Ray Peat:** Okay, great. Thank you.

**Danny Roddy:** Bye, Ray.

**Ray Peat:** Bye.
