title: It's Rainmaking Time: Life Supporting Substances
transcriptText:
**Kim Greenhouse:** Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to It's Rainmaking Time. This is Kim Greenhouse, and I have invited Raymond Peat, Ph.D., who has a background in biology from the University of Oregon and specializes in physiology. He has taught at the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, the National College of Naturopathic Medicine, and in Mexico. He has written many papers on physiological chemistry and physics. His key idea is that energy and structure are interdependent at every level.

He is known for his views on progesterone, balancing female hormones, radiation, growth, cholesterol, natural estrogens, pregnenolone, and memory. He has written hundreds of articles and has very robust views on human health, including some that will defy common beliefs about fish oils, saturated fats, and bioidentical hormones. Welcome, Raymond Peat, to It's Rainmaking Time. You have been one of the big proponents early on of natural progesterone. Could you speak about your early findings regarding it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1968, I decided to go back to graduate school in biology. I had been working in linguistics, and I decided that to understand anything, it would help to understand how the brain works. But I found that the brain researchers were just as dogmatic as the people in linguistics. I found the least dogmatic area in biology was reproductive physiology and aging research because there were so few people getting big money to do it, so they were relatively free.

My thesis advisor, Arnold Soderwall, had studied the effects of vitamin E on reproductive aging. I was going to specialize in how the oxidative process changes during aging and whether that affects reproductive efficiency. It turned out that it looked as if estrogen increased with aging, while progesterone decreased just about the time infertility sets in. That was contrary to all of the textbooks. But being an actual scientist, Soderwall said, "If it's repeatable, go ahead and do it."

In other areas of biology, if I observed something that seemed to violate the textbook description, the professor would just pretend he hadn't seen it because they were getting funding to develop a certain line of thinking. But since there was so little money put into reproduction and aging, actual science was allowed to go ahead. Other people working in the same lab eventually did the same kind of tests and found that in various situations, the tissues of other animals actually increased their estrogen content with aging.

Since progesterone is decreasing, and progesterone happens to be what inhibits the formation of estrogen inside cells all through the body, if you don't have very much progesterone, the estrogen goes on being synthesized. However, it can't escape from the cell into the bloodstream where it could be excreted. So, while the body is actually loading up inside the cells with estrogen during a progesterone deficiency, the blood shows a very low level of estrogen because it can't leave the cell. It needs things such as progesterone to loosen it from the binding proteins called receptors.

The estrogen excess causes a wasting of oxygen in the tissues that basically suffocates the embryo trying to implant and grow. This prevents pregnancy. That explains how the birth control pill works: it creates an excess of estrogen in the tissues, suffocating the fertilized egg. Stress, malnutrition, and various stressors that decrease your thyroid and progesterone production have that same effect as aging or taking an estrogen supplement. It leads to the progressive increase of estrogen inside cells, creating an oxygen deficiency which leads to a progressive loss of differentiated functions.

**Kim Greenhouse:** I imagine that during the time you were writing about this, when Dr. Lee came around, you got a lot of confirmation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I used to give talks to medical groups. There were organizations of orthomolecular doctors on the West Coast. I think it was the second time I talked to his group in the San Francisco area, I noticed one of the doctors actually seemed to wake up and pay attention, and that was John Lee. The others just couldn't hear anything that said estrogen wasn't the female hormone that decreases at menopause.

**Kim Greenhouse:** He got heavily attacked when he came out with what you were proposing. I think he front-ran it in the public domain, even though you were out there for years talking about it.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Regarding the orthomolecular and anti-aging focus—like the Life Extension Foundation—DHEA has been around forever. A lot of women are supplementing with progesterone and adding a little bit of DHEA. Even though DHEA can convert to testosterone and estrogen on low levels, women are using it. What do you think about it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In a 1971 article, I mentioned DHEA as being one of the basic protective hormones like progesterone. Progesterone happens to be the main thing that protects against the conversion of DHEA into estrogen. Testosterone is really just as much a female hormone as a male hormone. Estrogen is somewhat more a male hormone; it is responsible for differentiating the male brain. So if I had to call it a gender hormone, I would say estrogen is probably more a male hormone.

**Kim Greenhouse:** How interesting. I don't think most of us would associate it with that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Progesterone is the real feminizing hormone. It protects against an excess of anything, including excess estrogen, testosterone, cortisone, or aldosterone. Progesterone makes up for a deficiency of any of those, but it also protects against a toxic excess of any of them.

**Kim Greenhouse:** So if someone is taking a low level of DHEA and progesterone, it's a nice combination?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. As long as you're watching your general diet and thyroid function. It's possible to override the protective effect of progesterone if you eat a lot of unsaturated fat and not enough protein and calcium.

**Kim Greenhouse:** And unsaturated fat for the public would mean what? Corn oil, soy oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Corn oil, soy oil, canola, grapeseed oil—everything that is liquid has a lot of polyunsaturated fat. Olive oil, which will harden at refrigerator temperatures, still has about 10% polyunsaturated fats. I don't think a person should eat more than an average of a teaspoonful or two of olive oil per day. Butter and coconut oil are really the only very safe fats. Beef fat, lamb fat, butter, and coconut oil have only maybe 2% polyunsaturated fat. Macadamia is another one that has a moderate amount, but they still have several times as much unsaturated fat as coconut and butter.

**Kim Greenhouse:** You've been talking about the benefits of coconut oil way before Bruce Fife produced his books on the coconut oil miracle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1970s, I saw a study where groups of rats were put on lifetime diets of low fat, high fat, and medium fat. In the low-fat diet group, the fat was corn oil or some highly unsaturated oil. The high-fat animals were given either pure unsaturated fat, pure saturated fat, or blends. At the end of their life, their tissues were analyzed. The obese animals were the ones that had the high ratio of unsaturated to saturated fat. It wasn't at all the quantity of fat they ate. The low-fat eaters who got the corn oil were overweight with high body fat content. The high-fat eaters who had only the saturated fat were lean.

**Kim Greenhouse:** That is so interesting because so many people are learning about the benefit of saturated fats now, but it's taken years for this to come forward.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the early 90s, a millionaire in Nebraska started buying full-page newspaper ads saying that Oreo cookies and other traditional products were killing people because they had coconut oil in them. We had been using some very nice products, like tortilla chips fried in coconut oil. We ate huge amounts of those, and the more we ate, the leaner we got. After his national campaign against tropical saturated fats, all of these products disappeared. That really annoyed me, so I wrote an article in 1996 on coconut oil. I think that started a lot of the people selling it and talking about its benefits.

Most recently, coconut oil is being used to treat Alzheimer's patients. A woman is using MCT (medium-chain triglycerides), which are extracted from coconut oil, combined with coconut oil to make it less irritating to the intestine. A lot of people are getting good results. Previously, high saturated fat diets had been used to treat epilepsy, brain cancer, and degenerative liver diseases like hepatitis and cirrhosis.

**Kim Greenhouse:** My mom died in 2008 of Alzheimer's, and I wish I had put it together about the coconut oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My website has articles on Alzheimer's giving attention to the role of polyunsaturated fats in causing brain degeneration. There is another article that covers the role of polyunsaturated fats in scrapie or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (Mad Cow Disease). I think polyunsaturated fats have a major role in all of the degenerative brain diseases, including Huntington's and Lou Gehrig's disease.

**Kim Greenhouse:** I know you have a very different view about taking flaxseed oil and DHA. In the anti-aging industry, it is heavily touted as brain food. Please share your perspective.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The way people reason is to identify fish oils (DHA and EPA) or the Omega-3 oils as "essential fatty acids," and then say since they are essential nutrients, they can't be toxic. Some of the articles on my website deal with that issue of essentiality.

The basic studies still being cited were done in 1929 by George Burr and his wife. At the time, they neglected to mention several well-known articles published in the same journal showing that those very fats the Burrs claimed were essential were actually life-shortening—that animals lived longer on a fat-free diet. One study showed a fat-free diet eliminated almost all cancers and slowed the aging process.

The Burrs ignored the contrary evidence and pronounced that linoleic and linolenic acid were essential to prevent a certain disease in rats—scaly tail disease. About 17 years later, Roger Williams' lab recognized the Burrs' rat disease as a Vitamin B6 deficiency. Vitamin B6 wasn't known at the time the Burrs were doing their study. Williams' lab gave the rats the exact same diet the Burrs used, created the deficiency symptoms, and then cured it with Vitamin B6 without adding any fats at all.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Did you know the FDA took B6 off the market so most people can't sell it individually anymore?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I didn't know that. But no one talks about the disproof of the Burr evidence. To bring the issue up to date, they cite babies and old people on intravenous feeding. At the time those studies were done, IV nutrition didn't include zinc, which has been known for 70 years to be essential. It wasn't added until the late 1970s. So again, they are confirming that deficiencies are created when you give a limited diet.

George Burr himself demonstrated that his fatty acid-deficient rats were burning fuel and consuming oxygen at a rate 50% higher than the rats on his "adequate" diet. He didn't understand that the fats were lowering the metabolic rate, drastically suppressing thyroid function so the rats could get along on fewer calories and vitamins.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What does that mean to us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you poison your thyroid gland, you don't need very many calories. They put women in closed wards and found that many overweight women were burning only 700 calories a day—about 35% as much fuel as they should. This means if you do anything to poison your thyroid function, you won't need as many calories or vitamins.

Polyunsaturated fats happen to be very general and effective blockers of thyroid function. A series of papers in French Annals of Endocrinology showed that thyroid secretion is inhibited by polyunsaturated fats. The transport proteins in the blood are blocked by these fats, and the more unsaturated, the more perfect the blocking. If the cell manages to receive thyroid hormone, the polyunsaturated fats block the cell's ability to respond to it. This leads to increased estrogen, decreased progesterone, and fat accumulation.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Why do they call flaxseed and fish oils "brain food"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you grind up someone's brain, you find it is full of chicken fat and fish oil-like stuff; it reflects exactly what we've been eating. Animals like pigs, chickens, and fish—who don't have a rumen to detoxify fats—will have tissues that reflect the composition of the fats they eat. The brain, being composed more of fat than any other substance, will have a high concentration of these unsaturated fats.

A group in France decided to measure fetal response to sounds. They found that the brain learning response was retarded in proportion to the mother's consumption of fish fat and highly unsaturated fats. After birth, the babies were underdeveloped, including the brain. This matched animal experiments from the 1970s: babies exposed to high prenatal unsaturated fats had smaller brains and didn't learn as well as those exposed to saturated fats.

Studies in the 1960s and 70s showed that sugar and progesterone are factors that increase brain growth. Zamenhof found that a chicken embryo's brain grew rapidly as long as glucose was present in the egg. When he injected extra glucose, the brains kept growing, and the chickens were born with uniquely large brains and were smarter than ordinary chickens.

**Kim Greenhouse:** So your final take is that essential fatty acids are not necessary and not useful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been asking people for about 40 years for the evidence of the essentiality of any of these fats. The only things ever mentioned are those odd few studies. You can grow cells in a culture dish in a completely fat-free mixture, and they divide and act like normal cells. It can't be essential for making membranes.

**Kim Greenhouse:** I take it you have your coconut oil every day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not every day, but when I think of it. I try to keep my calcium intake high. Calcium and thyroid are closely connected. A hypothyroid person tends to have hyperactive parathyroid function, which dissolves the bones and puts calcium where it doesn't belong. Chronic low intake of calcium or low thyroid function will eventually make your bones weaker.

**Kim Greenhouse:** How do you get your calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Milk and cheese mostly. I average maybe a little over two quarts of milk a day with some cheese.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about gelatin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I advocate having a lot of gelatin if you are a meat eater. In the US, chickens are processed with a chlorine-based antiseptic foot bath, so chicken feet are often contaminated. If you buy tough, bony cuts—like lamb shoulder chops or oxtail—those are rich in gelatin. Gelatin only comes from animals. If you don't eat meat, milk, eggs, and cheese combined with fruits and vegetables can provide a balance of nutrients.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Let's talk about pregnenolone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I accidentally discovered its value in 1984. I had been experimenting with progesterone and DHEA in vitamin E. I got very sick on a trip where I didn't have my vitamin E mixture. I took a pinch of plain pregnenolone powder, and in 30 or 40 minutes, all my symptoms disappeared.

I bought a kilogram to experiment with. I would take 3,000 or 4,000 milligrams at a time. It didn't feel different than 30 milligrams, but the main side effects were that it tightened up loose skin, made me look younger, and prevented migraine-like symptoms.

I gave it to a friend who was 82 and suffering from emphysema and oxygen starvation. I gave him an average of 500mg a day. Two weeks later, his skin color was normal, and he was walking around the city showing me projects, whereas before he could hardly stand up.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What does it do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It seems to cause waterlogged, swollen tissues to release the water causing the malfunction. Connective tissues tend to become inert and waterlogged when deprived of energy and under the influence of estrogen. Pregnenolone helps them contract and return to normal confirmation.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Can women on progesterone also take pregnenolone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A large dose of progesterone is an anesthetic—it can sedate you. Pregnenolone doesn't have those anesthetic actions, so you can take it without that side effect.

**Kim Greenhouse:** It is also known for being good for the brain.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies during WWII showed that factory workers given pregnenolone produced more and coped better with boring work. I've seen depressed men become happy and productive within 15 minutes of taking it.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Do you want to speak about memory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Progesterone and pregnenolone improve all mental functions, including memory. Estrogen excites the brain much like cocaine; overdosing causes seizures. Progesterone produces calmness.

Thyroid and progesterone work together to stabilize body temperature. Raising body temperature and available energy improves mental functioning. I've seen demented people become normal in days with thyroid, progesterone, and pregnenolone. One woman who had been epileptic and considered demented for 18 years became completely normal in five days with progesterone. She went back to graduate school and got straight A's.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Let's talk about T3, T4, and thyroid testing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The "Free T3" test corresponds fairly well to functions, but you have to look at the function itself. To interpret Free T3, you need to know the Reverse T3. I think the TSH is useful; a population with the lowest thyroid cancer had a TSH of 0.4 and below. Health improves when you lower TSH to that range.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about thyroid medication? Armour vs. synthetics like Cytomel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw a woman in a coma who had been given increasing doses of T4 (thyroxine). She woke up when given intravenous T3. The brain keeps a 1-to-1 ratio of T4 to T3. If T4 gets too high, it can displace T3 and cause hypothyroid symptoms because T3 is the active hormone.

Cytomel (T3) is very fast-acting. If I can't remember a name, I chew a 5-microgram chip of Cytomel, and in minutes I remember. However, if you take a whole day's dose at once, it peaks and drops, potentially causing arrhythmia. Small doses throughout the day work better.

Armour Thyroid used to be the standard, but ownership changes led to processing changes, like removing calcitonin and adding binders that didn't dissolve well.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What do you suggest people take now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A mix of Cytomel and a thyroxine product works. A ratio of 4:1 or 2:1 (T4 to T3) is practical. For example, 40 micrograms of T4 and 10 micrograms of T3. Taking the T4 at bedtime helps hold down TSH.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Can we finish with a talk about coffee? We used to be told it was bad.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A monograph around 1970 defined the safety and protective qualities of caffeine, including anti-cancer effects. Coffee provides about 20% of the vitamin and mineral intake in some diets. It is a concentrated source of niacin and magnesium. Studies find that people who drink the most coffee—more than five cups a day—have the least Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and thyroid cancer.

**Kim Greenhouse:** You also spend time in Mexico for the high altitude.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** High altitude cures everything if you can get high enough. It relates to carbon dioxide (CO2). As oxygen gets thinner, CO2 is retained in your tissues. We are all being slightly oxygen-poisoned at sea level. Hospitals often harm patients by giving pure oxygen; it should have 5-7% carbon dioxide added.

Carbon dioxide therapy can cure mountain sickness. On Everest expeditions, breathing inside a bag provided CO2 therapy.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Is there anything else about the eyes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ultraviolet and blue light are damaging, especially if tissues are saturated with unsaturated fats. The blue light contributes to retinal damage.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Raymond Peat, thank you for your time. If you would like to read Dr. Peat's articles, you can go to raypeat.com. Thank you so much.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. If people want to get a perspective on what that means—a new attitude towards what life is—the works of Albert Szent-Györgyi and Gilbert Ling are the best places to start.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Let's create a context for the listeners about a new perspective on living matter. Flesh that out for us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It probably got its best start with a biochemist named Bungenberg de Jong. He demonstrated that compositions of fat, protein, and carbohydrate made things much more complex than colloids; he called them "complex coacervates." They had many of the functions of living cells.

A generation later, Sidney Fox demonstrated that he could create things like cells so simply that his students could create replicating cells that had many of the functions of bacteria in just an afternoon lab. He would throw amino acids on hot lava, imitating a prehistoric situation, and then splash a little water on them. He was creating them from a dry environment in which water was under the control of amino acids, rather than in a wet, ocean-like environment.

He showed that in this relatively dry condition, the water and the amino acids catalyzed themselves to form protein-like molecules which spontaneously formed little spheres about a micron in diameter. These were very uniform and would assimilate other proteins from the environment, grow, and bud like yeasts. They simply lacked nucleic acid to resemble living bacteria. When he added the precursors to DNA, these things would catalyze polymers of DNA-like material spontaneously. He showed that simply by not overwhelming the molecules with too much water, the water was an essential part of organizing proteins and DNA-like material.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What does that mean to us in the context of a new perspective on living matter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you look at the substance of a cell, rather than having to be assembled through a billion years of evolution, it means that the principles governing the way we function also govern the way the organism holds itself together. Rather than a cell being isolated from the environment by a lipid membrane—the famous bilayer lipid membrane—the functional principle is what Bungenberg de Jong demonstrated: these complex mixtures of protein, fats, and carbohydrates spontaneously separate things from the environment.

For example, if you take a piece of hair made up of completely dead cells, wash it free of ions, and dip it into serum, it will pull out the potassium and bind it to itself against a gradient, excluding sodium. It will bind magnesium, excluding calcium. This demonstrates that you don't need membrane pumps. It's simply an ion exchange phenomenon that dead cells can do. Gilbert Ling and Bungenberg de Jong represent the real mainline of science, while the membrane school is the peripheral, irrelevant part, except they are more numerous.

**Kim Greenhouse:** So that's the big paradigm change in the way we understand the cell? There is so much said about hydration and needing to get through the membrane of the cell. Do you agree with that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I agree that is the paradigm, but it has been disproven many times. The idea of the membrane is that the arrangement of chemistry inside is unstable relative to the outside. This view is that we are a stable form of matter as long as energy runs through us. It is a chemically favored arrangement of matter that doesn't need pumps in the membrane to maintain it; it is simply the composition which maintains itself.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Is what you're saying that the cell is a self-maintaining organism versus needing things from the outside?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The whole idea of the membrane and the pumps is based on the idea that it's an improbable, accidentally arranged thing. The fact that Sidney Fox could make cell-like things in a couple of hours shows what a different perspective it is on the nature of substance.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What is your view on cell hydration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gilbert Ling has demonstrated that the amount of energy the cell is producing regulates hydration. Energy prevents the cell from taking up too much water, but binds water and prevents its loss below a certain level. If you lose the adequate amount of energy, the cell loses control of the water. The water starts to take over and control the cell.

This explains many medical problems involving edema and swelling. The membrane theory is totally confused about this. Doctors will tell you to stop eating so much salt to reduce your edema, but in many situations, restricting sodium is exactly the wrong thing. It will make the edema worse, especially in premenstrual women and very old people. I've seen people solve their swelling problems, high blood pressure, and appetite control just by salting their food according to taste rather than what the doctor advises.

**Kim Greenhouse:** I have friends with high blood pressure, and I tell them to take real salt, but their doctors tell them not to have salt at all.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of doctors still tell people to drink two quarts of water, disregarding whether they might be drinking milk, coffee, or orange juice. Experiments show that if you put a little too much water in the intestine, it will promote inflammation. A little beyond that, and it can start causing a shock reaction.

Sodium stimulates energy production of the cell and respiration. If something interrupts that balance of salt, magnesium, and calcium, and the cell loses energy, the cell takes up too much water. The excess water stimulates cell growth, but not energy production. That tends to create an anabolic condition with possibilities including diabetes, obesity, cancer, and inflammation.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What do you think about the aquaporin channel discovery?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gilbert Ling has written quite a bit about the channel idea. Since Ling explains the balance between proteins and water adequately to take care of everything, the channel idea is unnecessary. The channel idea goes with the concept of a membrane acting as a barrier to salt and water. But Ling demonstrated that there is no such barrier. As soon as isotopes became available in the 1940s, it was discovered that sodium freely leaves and enters the cell. There is no semi-permeable membrane keeping sodium out.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about keeping water out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the same thing. One of the early critics of the lipid membrane idea commented that lecithin—which the membrane is supposedly made of—has a great affinity for water and will swell in its presence. It is a very bad choice for postulating as the limiting membrane barrier.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Would you talk a little bit about CO2? Since the EPA declared war on carbon dioxide, people are scared to death of it. However, I just realized that oxygen isn't everything. Explain what carbon dioxide is and what it has to do with aging and health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 60 years ago, researchers found that although some bacteria and protozoa can survive without oxygen, even those organisms cannot live without carbon dioxide. It really should be considered the basic material of life, not oxygen. The purpose of oxygen, from that point of view, is to make carbon dioxide.

If you consider Gilbert Ling's cell structure, the protein itself is a weak acid with a negative charge, which attracts positive ions like potassium, sodium, magnesium, and calcium. Carbon dioxide is one of the factors that cause our proteins to prefer potassium over sodium.

By having the right amount of carbon dioxide, the cell produces a steady stream of it flowing into the blood. As it leaves the mitochondrion, it reacts with water, forming carbonic acid. This carbonic acid has a negative charge, so as it flows out of the cell, it drags positive ions (calcium and sodium) with it. As we exhale, that carbonic acid in the blood changes back into carbon dioxide and leaves the lungs, leaving those calcium and sodium ions stranded in the blood. That accounts for the blood having a more alkaline pH than the inside of the cell.

One of the functions of carbon dioxide is to regulate the acidity of tissues, prevent the uptake of too much water, and keep energy intake going. Shock is a typical extreme situation in which cells become unable to make energy and take up too much water.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Can you elaborate on the relationship between CO2 and shock?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yandel Henderson, a Yale professor in the early 20th century, was one of the first to see that carbon dioxide relaxes the arterioles and allows blood to flow freely. If you turn off energy production and stop producing carbon dioxide, you have less relaxed blood vessels, and the heart has a harder job pumping. He showed that you could cause quicker recovery of oxygenation by adding 8% or 10% carbon dioxide to oxygen.

However, largely as a result of war research, the elimination of carbon dioxide metabolism became institutionalized. Hospitals simplified things by supplying pure oxygen in an emergency.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Do you agree that if we got more carbon dioxide in our systems, we would be healthier?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Up to a certain point. The insurance industry recognized more than 100 years ago that all degenerative diseases—cancer, brain diseases, heart disease—caused fewer deaths at altitudes of 8,000 to 10,000 feet.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Why do you think that is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yandel Henderson showed that oxidation of the tissues depends on carbon dioxide. If you have too much oxygen in your environment, as we do at sea level, it pushes too much carbon dioxide out of our blood. This shifts the balance so that red blood cells don't give up enough oxygen to the tissues. You will starve your peripheral tissues.

If you hyperventilate for a couple of minutes, you might notice your fingers and toes cramp. That same process happens under any circumstance that deprives you of carbon dioxide. Giving 100% oxygen will create the same situation. In the brain, too much oxygen and the deprivation of carbon dioxide shrinks the blood vessels. Imaging has shown that breathing too much oxygen lowers the availability of oxygen in the brain by constricting the blood vessels.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What would you suggest for listeners to get their carbon dioxide levels up? I noticed you mentioned the Buteyko breathing method.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Buteyko was a Russian doctor who noticed that sick and dying people tended to hyperventilate. He found that if he could calm them down and get them to breathe more slowly, they often recovered.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What else do you suggest?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Diet is very important. Some foods interfere with metabolism and cause you to produce lactic acid, which displaces carbon dioxide. Polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) block respiration and thyroid function.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about pH balance? It's very confusing for people.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The function of oxygen is to make carbonic acid (CO2), which gives the healthy cell a mild acidic condition. As the CO2 drags minerals out of the cell and drops them in the blood, the blood becomes alkaline. To maintain that alkaline bloodstream, the kidneys should ideally be producing acidic urine. People with alkaline urine tend to deposit minerals.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What do you think about hyperbaric oxygen chambers?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If circulation is destroyed, like in gangrene, high-pressure oxygen can keep tissue alive by diffusion. But in the brain, too much oxygen shuts down blood vessels. I knew someone treating cancer patients with high-pressure oxygen who tried adding carbon dioxide. One patient, who couldn't speak due to throat cancer, lost consciousness because of too much CO2. When he woke up, he was soaked in perspiration and the windows were steamed up. The carbon dioxide helped his cells excrete the water they had been holding. When he woke up, he could talk normally.

**Kim Greenhouse:** So, living at high altitude helps. What else?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anything that supports thyroid function, avoiding polyunsaturated fats, and avoiding electromagnetic fields. Estrogenic materials and estrogen pills stimulate hyperventilation.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Could you talk about the distinction between progesterone, pregnenolone, and estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen is essentially anti-thyroid. Thyroid is our basic oxygen-using hormone. Estrogen changes the way oxygen is used, diverting it from making carbon dioxide to fat metabolism, and stimulating the uptake of water. Estrogen causes the breasts and uterus to swell by taking water into the cell, which stimulates cell division.

**Kim Greenhouse:** I take it you are not into anti-aging bioidentical estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely not. The older and more stressed a tissue is, the more estrogen it tends to produce. A young, healthy person produces estrogen primarily in the ovaries. With stress and aging, every cell in the body develops the ability to make estrogen and loses the ability to excrete it. Simply by becoming deficient in progesterone, your blood test won't show that you are deficient in estrogen, because progesterone is needed to get the estrogen from the cell into the bloodstream.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What do you think of the fat cell relationship to estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** P.K. Siiteri was the first to demonstrate that fat becomes a major source of estrogen production after menopause. With stress, diabetes, and inflammation, the aromatase enzyme increases, producing more estrogen.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Doctors are giving women bioidentical estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone creams vaginally. What do you think about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Early studies showed that vaginal estrogen produces very immediate high levels all through the body because the membranes absorb it so easily. It increases the exposure of all cancer-sensitive organs. It has been known since the 1940s that all tissues will develop a risk of cancer with continuous exposure to estrogen. If you interrupt it regularly with progesterone, that reduces the carcinogenic effect.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about libido?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lowering the stress hormones, including estrogen, will very typically normalize libido.

**Kim Greenhouse:** So it's a whole system. You have to include the thyroid and nutrition.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the liver isn't supplied with adequate protein and B vitamins, your estrogen level will stay elevated. If you don't eat enough fiber, estrogen excreted into the intestine is reabsorbed. Eating a carrot every day can normalize hormones in a lot of people by preventing that reabsorption.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Let's talk about coffee. Weren't you one of the first to say coffee is good for you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1970s, a monograph showed the cancer-protective effects of caffeine. Researchers found that adding caffeine to carcinogenic smoke reduced cancer rates in mice from 95% to 5%. It protected against radiation, viruses, and chemical carcinogens.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1970s, I read an article where they fed rats different diets. The leanest rats were the ones that ate the saturated coconut oil diet, regardless of whether it was high or low fat. The fat animals were the ones that had the pure polyunsaturated fat. The "saturation index"—the proportion of saturated fats to polyunsaturated in your tissues—is important. Cancer patients are very low on the saturation index.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Do you use refined or unrefined coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I use the refined, deodorized kind because a lot of people are allergic to the extraneous material in the unrefined oil.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Do you recommend Armour thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The original Armour product was stable for 90 years, but after the company was sold multiple times, the price went up and the formulation changed. I stopped using it in the early 90s because some people found the pills were going through undigested. I started using synthetic products like Cynoplus or Cytomel (Cynomel).

**Kim Greenhouse:** Why recommend a synthetic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Armour company invested a lot in research to ensure consistency. Smaller companies don't have those resources. Synthetics like Cynomel have been very consistent.

**Kim Greenhouse:** How should we test for thyroid? Blood or urine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The blood isn't a great test because hormones travel with proteins and fats. Broda Barnes advocated morning temperature as a very important indicator. Other indicators include cholesterol (high cholesterol often means low thyroid), carotene levels, and the speed of muscle relaxation (Achilles tendon reflex). Quick relaxation corresponds to good thyroid function.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Is serotonin the "happy hormone"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The name means "serum tonic," or pressure increaser. It was identified in the 1950s as a cause of emotional disturbances and circulatory problems. 95% of the body's serotonin is made in the intestine. If the intestine is irritated, it produces excess serotonin. If the lungs and platelets don't destroy it, it gets to the brain and causes anxiety, aggression, and depression. It stimulates the adrenal stress reaction.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What is your take on mammograms and dental X-rays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** John Gofman, a former government spokesman, later showed that medical radiation was a major cause of breast cancer and heart disease. The incidence of these diseases corresponds to the availability of medical services. Radiation and estrogen synergize to increase cancer risk.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about airport scanners?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low-energy radiation is more easily absorbed by tissues and is much more carcinogenic than high-energy radiation. The industry claims flying exposes you to radiation, but cosmic rays at high altitude are high-energy and pass through the body mostly harmlessly. At sea level, those rays collide with the atmosphere and release radioactive particles, so you actually get more harmful radiation at sea level.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Tell us about pregnenolone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pregnenolone is produced from cholesterol under the influence of thyroid and Vitamin A. It is the precursor to progesterone and DHEA. If you are deficient in thyroid, Vitamin A, or cholesterol, you will be deficient in pregnenolone. Pregnenolone inhibits the stress process and blocks the production of cortisol. It stabilizes cells.

**Kim Greenhouse:** How do you get enough pregnenolone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** By eating foods that keep my cholesterol production high. Orange juice is my main one. I've seen people raise their cholesterol to healthy levels just by drinking an extra quart of orange juice a day.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Won't the sugar cause a problem with glucose metabolism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, you need sugar to make thyroid hormone and to regulate cholesterol. When sugar comes in the form of fruit like orange juice, the potassium takes on the function of insulin, so it is not fattening the way starch is. Starch is a powerful insulin stimulant, and insulin tends to turn carbohydrate to fat.

**Kim Greenhouse:** How should we prevent osteoporosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** X-rays poison bone metabolism, so bone scans can contribute to osteoporosis. Ultrasound is many times more valid for checking bone density and actually stimulates bone strengthening.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What about thyroid and bones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies show that T3 (active thyroid hormone) stimulates bone cell metabolism, causing the production of carbon dioxide, which crystallizes with calcium to form new bone. Hypothyroid women often have more osteoporosis.

**Kim Greenhouse:** What do you think of the Affordable Care Act?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'd rather pay the fine than be forced to buy insurance. I avoid doctors as much as possible.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Is there anything else you'd like to say to the audience?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Looking at the big context is the important thing. You are constantly subjected to misinformation. It is necessary to look at concrete experiments and see whether someone has done counter-experiments that would invalidate those.

**Kim Greenhouse:** Ladies and gentlemen, we have been learning from Dr. Ray Peat. You can find out more about him and his articles at RayPeat.com. Dr. Peat, thank you so much for being with us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Jodellefit: Stress and Your Health
transcriptText:
**Jodelle:** Welcome to the Get Fit with Jodelle show. I am so excited to have Dr. Raymond Peat with me today. He has a PhD in Biology from the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology. He has taught at the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, National College of Naturopathic Medicine, Universidad Veracruzana, the Universidad Autónoma del Estado de México, and Blake College.

He started his research in 1968—long before many of us so-called nutrition nerds were born—mainly regarding progesterone and the hormones closely related to it as protectors of the body's structure and energy against the harmful effects of estrogen, radiation, stress, and lack of oxygen. He is also the editor and writer of his famous newsletter, an author, and an artist. Dr. Peat, I am so excited to speak with you today. How are you doing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good, thank you.

**Jodelle:** Will you please tell my listeners briefly what got you into this passion for all things related to stress, hormones, and the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s and 60s, I was interested in psychology and language. I started a school in Mexico, Blake College. In the process, I noticed that many local people were eating a very bad diet. A couple of my friends had family members who were very sick. Having read Adelle Davis's books, I suggested some of her nutritional therapies.

For example, a friend's nephew had been in the hospital for two or three days with diarrhea that they couldn't control. They said he wouldn't live through the night. My friend decided there was no harm in trying the vitamin B6 supplement, which was one of Adelle Davis's recommendations for diarrhea. He gave the child a 10-milligram tablet of vitamin B6, and within the hour, the diarrhea stopped. He recovered in just a couple of days. A single vitamin did what the whole hospital staff couldn't manage with intravenous treatments.

I realized that a lot of information wasn't getting into the medical system. I decided to study biology instead of the humanities. In graduate school, I ran into the same dogmatism. I had planned to study brain biology, but I saw that the professors were locked into a dogmatic view of how a nerve works. I found that the reproductive physiology department at the University of Oregon was actually doing open research, trying to discover the causes of infertility in aging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I shifted from brain biology to reproductive physiology. In examining the factors that make it possible for a fertilized ovum to develop into a whole organism, I found that the brain is governed and formed by the same factors that govern fertility. The same things that cause infertility cause bad development of the brain.

I realized that the drug industry had been propagandizing the public with the idea that estrogen is the "female hormone." In our lab, we saw that estrogen was the contraceptive hormone, not the hormone of fertility. The pharmaceutical industry knew that estrogen made a good contraception pill—it was actually causing abortions—but they called it the anti-conception pill.

The real hormone of fertility and brain development turns out to be progesterone. It works by providing energy to the developing embryo in the form of oxygen and glucose. Estrogen is a factor that interrupts that process. Estrogen creates a local inflammation in the uterus—a kind of wound that allows the ovum to embed—but if the estrogen stays dominant, it kills the ovum. The function of progesterone is to knock the estrogen out of the tissue and shift that inflammatory physiology into a supportive, oxidative, sugar-rich environment.

**Jodelle:** That is not at all what we've been taught. I was always taught the importance of estrogen. A lot of your work is done around these hormones, but you also talk about stress. Would you say that stress is the driving factor behind most disease and that it contributes to the rise in estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would say stress is the factor in all disease. If you define it as a mismatch between the organism and the environment, then even so-called genetic diseases are diseases of stress. For example, sickle cell anemia is a defensive mutation against malaria in Africa. If people eat a diet that maintains an oxidative condition, there is no sickle cell disease. But when you don't have that environment, it shows up as a disease.

Inflammation is the basic factor in why stress causes disease. Heart disease and obesity, for example, are seen to originate with stress physiology. Stress leads to inflammation, and that leads to specific diseases.

**Jodelle:** When you say stress, you aren't just talking about day-to-day living. You're talking about environmental stressors like radiation, pollutants, and emotional stress, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It is when the environment puts demands on you that you don't have the internal resources to meet smoothly. An 18-year-old who is well-fed can meet changes in weather or physical exertion without stress. That same activity might kill someone who wasn't well-nourished or was elderly. It is a matter of what resources you have internally in proportion to the stress.

**Jodelle:** Can you help us understand the stressors of our modernized society?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The drug industry and other technological industries have tried to cover up the fact that they are causing disease. There has been a propaganda movement to convince the public that pollution is not harmful. Fifty years ago, the government had a campaign to tell people that radiation was good for you—the idea of "radiation hormesis," that a little poison is good for you. That is a perversion of the idea of stress.

A teenager meeting a challenge—like a tennis game or building something—builds the body and skills. That is not stress. Stress is a demand put on you that you didn't ask for and don't have the ability to do easily and with pleasure. Doing a boring, stupid job that you don't love is poisoning your tissues constantly because you aren't getting pleasure out of the activity.

**Jodelle:** I read in Hans Selye's book *Stress Without Distress* that many people live lives trying to appease others or doing jobs they don't like, and they usually die of disease because of that chronic existence.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the early 1960s, Marian Diamond found that rats in an enriched environment—with toys and things to explore—had brains that functioned better. Their enzymes changed, and their babies had bigger brains. More recently, it was found that the enriched-environment rats produced more progesterone and had lower levels of estrogen. Conversely, if you gave pregnant animals estrogen, the babies' brains were shrunken because it stopped growth by causing stress.

**Jodelle:** I found you when I went through a bad toxic mold exposure. My thyroid was hugely affected. How does the thyroid get affected by chronic stress or acute stressors like toxic mold?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The oxidative sugar metabolism controlled by estrogen and progesterone requires thyroid hormone to work. You don't have oxygen metabolism without thyroid.

Someone cultured a slice of thyroid gland and added hormones to it. If they added progesterone, the thyroid gland secreted active thyroid hormone. When they added estrogen, it blocked those enzymes and stopped secretion, but allowed the cells to synthesize thyroglobulin (colloid). This explains why women often have a swollen thyroid gland around menopause or puberty when estrogen risks becoming dominant. The pituitary drives the gland to produce hormone, but because of the estrogen, it just swells up. Many women have had their thyroid destroyed when all they needed was to lower estrogen or take a progesterone supplement.

**Jodelle:** My thyroid damage led to cellulite appearing in three months, even though I exercised and ate the same. What was the mechanism behind that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When your thyroid isn't adequate, your cells act as if they are under the influence of estrogen. Estrogen's metabolic effects can't be distinguished from the effects of radiation, suffocation, or poisoning with cyanide. They all poison your oxidative system.

Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) are the source of age pigment. Estrogen, radiation, and oxygen deprivation all accelerate the formation of age pigment, causing PUFAs to spontaneously oxidize. Poisons, such as your mold poisoning, end up acting like estrogen in that they poison your ability to use oxygen.

**Jodelle:** I didn't think about mold acting like an estrogen. Are there other things acting like estrogens in our body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s, soot was found to be highly estrogenic. That explains why smoke is a carcinogen. Any irritant that stimulates the cell so intensely that the oxidative system can't keep up acts as an estrogen.

Nanoparticles are a major issue. These occur in smoke, traffic exhaust, and tire dust, but industry also uses them as additives—titanium dioxide and silicon dioxide—to thicken shampoo, toothpaste, and food. When absorbed, these insoluble particles act as a constant irritant to the cell. That disproportion between irritation and energy supply has an estrogenic and carcinogenic action.

**Jodelle:** Would those be in supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you look at the ingredients of vitamins and drugs, you very often see titanium dioxide or silica. Even if they claim to use larger granular material, they often contain the toxic nanoparticles.

**Jodelle:** Are there diets that are estrogenic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs) are made more active by estrogen, but they also intensify estrogen activity. Both Omega-6 and Omega-3 PUFAs promote the effects of estrogen.

**Jodelle:** What are the most offending PUFAs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around 1950, the food industry had surplus cottonseed oil that was no longer needed for paint. They turned seed oils into a basic food material, calling them "heart protective." However, studies found that cancer and heart disease increased with this diet.

People then turned toward Omega-3s (fish oil). The only advantage Omega-3s have over Omega-6s is that they are extremely unstable and block the production of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins. You get an anti-inflammatory effect initially because it poisons the enzymes that make prostaglandins. However, the oxidative instability of Omega-3s leads to toxic breakdown products like acrolein. Acrolein poisons sperm cells and oocytes, increasing the risk of birth defects.

Despite evidence showing toxic effects on the developing brain, they still add fish oil to baby formula. As a person ages, PUFAs accumulate in the brain. In proportion to the amount of PUFA in the brain, the metabolic rate slows down. This corresponds to the decline of cognitive ability and oxidative metabolism.

**Jodelle:** If people realized that breast milk is 50-60% saturated fat, they would see that PUFAs don't have a place for us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And the amount of PUFA in a mother's blood corresponds to the amount of estrogen. If she has too much estrogen, she won't produce enough milk.

**Jodelle:** What about intermittent fasting? Is that a beneficial stressor?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Blood sugar normally falls during the hours of darkness. This is compensated by a rise in free fatty acids in the bloodstream. That is the same pattern that happens when you are under stress. When glycogen is depleted, you mobilize free fatty acids to oxidize for energy. This requires more oxygen and is inefficient.

When you aren't getting enough oxygen, your body starts turning protein into glucose. Lactic acid rises, which is a sign of stress. Every night, as you mobilize free fatty acids, you go into this stress state, causing damage to mitochondria. Bone loss in women happens primarily at night; the calcium shows up in the morning urine. This degeneration happens because we run out of glycogen. The longer you go without eating, the more you rely on inefficient fat oxidation.

**Jodelle:** You are not a fan of fat burning for energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at blood tests, women have about 80 times greater growth hormone than men. This is an effect of estrogen causing chronically high mobilization of free fatty acids. The high growth hormone is a compensation. To the extent you can minimize that, you reduce the chronic degenerative process.

**Jodelle:** So you advocate for consuming carbohydrates to build glycogen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. At the end of the 19th century, doctors cured patients wasting away from diabetes by feeding them as much sugar as they desired—about 12 ounces a day. Free fatty acids kill the beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin. Glucose supports the regeneration of insulin-producing cells. Those doctors found that normal sugar-regulating functions came back when they interrupted the destructive process of fat oxidation.

**Jodelle:** The mainstream is pushing Keto and low carb, but people are coming to me exhausted.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The brain and muscles must store glycogen to work. If you are forced to make glucose, you do it at the expense of your body—turning muscle tissue into glucose. This degrades your functional tissues.

**Jodelle:** When I did carnivore, I felt better initially, but then my sleep suffered. When I added carbs back, my sleep dialed in.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding meat-eating: The parathyroid gland is activated by phosphate. Meat, beans, and grains have an extremely high concentration of phosphate relative to calcium. Milk and green vegetables have a favorable high calcium-to-phosphate ratio, which suppresses the parathyroid hormone.

When parathyroid hormone is high, it mobilizes calcium out of your bones and puts it into soft tissues—arteries, brain, etc. This calcification is a sign of aging. High parathyroid hormone also activates the rancidity of PUFAs. Many fad diets emphasize meat and nuts (high phosphate) rather than green vegetables, fruits, and milk (high calcium).

**Jodelle:** What can we do to start mitigating this stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:**
1.  **Frequent snacks:** Don't let yourself go too long without eating. Have fruit, milk, or cheese at hand.
2.  **Sunlight:** The red and orange waves reduce free radicals produced by PUFA. Ultraviolet makes vitamin D, which helps handle sugar and calcium.
3.  **Diet:** Completely eliminate liquid vegetable oils (canola, soy, cottonseed) and reduce seeds, nuts, and fatty fish. Oysters and shellfish are safer.

**Jodelle:** And lifestyle strategies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The most important thing is to figure out what is important in your life and work toward that. Consider the necessities—like a horrible job—as only a stepping stone to doing something more sane and productive. If you have a long-range perspective that is meaningful, it makes the immediate stress disappear.

**Jodelle:** Dr. Peat, you've been generous with your time. How can people learn more about you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They can go to RayPeat.com. My newsletter is published every other month.

**Jodelle:** I will include that information in the show notes. May I ask your age?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 82.

**Jodelle:** I wish I had a penny-sized amount of the knowledge in your head. Thank you so much, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Jodellefit: Cortisol, Low Testosterone
transcriptText:
**Jodelle:** I am pleased to have Dr. Peat on with me again today. For those of you who have not familiarized yourself yet with Dr. Raymond Peat, you can check him out at RayPeat.com. We're going to be talking today about testosterone and high cortisol. I wanted to touch on this because I am seeing a lot of clients coming in with their blood work showing too high of cortisol and too low of testosterone—even women. I think it's a pretty important topic. Dr. Peat, how long have you been learning and teaching on this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Altogether as early as 1960, when I was doing it independently. Then I concentrated on the hormones between 1968 and 1972, when I got my PhD.

**Jodelle:** I know you've taught at numerous schools, including the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, the National College of Naturopathic Medicine, and internationally in Mexico. I consider you the leading authority based on everyone I've looked into over the years. I want to talk specifically about this tag team of symptoms: low testosterone and high cortisol. Could you talk about why cortisol is so high in so many people right now and the sex hormones are down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, it isn't the sex hormones as a group, because estrogen rises when you're under stress along with cortisol. When the androgens in general decrease, that usually goes with a decrease of progesterone, and that creates a susceptibility to stress. Practically everything harmful will increase both your estrogen and cortisol.

The first barrier to harm is the group of steroids: pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone. All of these have broadly overlapping protective effects that protect your energy apparatus and sensory apparatus, keeping things stable and working. Injury simply doesn't happen when you have a great abundance of those things. You can run a marathon or swim in ice water and do all sorts of things that could kill a more fragile person. If you're really well supplied with pregnenolone and its derivatives down to testosterone, you've got endurance, so you don't experience stress.

When something happens where you're not abundantly producing the protective steroids, then any little thing becomes stressful. Just walking can be a stress. Breathing harder, you will shift over to the lactic acid metabolism. With increasing age or malnutrition—anything that interferes with the production of these protective steroids—you shift over to the emergency production of cortisol.

All of these protective steroids block the effect of cortisol. You can take a cortisol pill or prednisone and have very little harm from it if you're fairly saturated with progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone, because they prevent the action as well as taking care of some of the things that cortisol would produce.

**Jodelle:** What does cortisol do to the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cortisol maintains your blood sugar level so that you can keep working, but it does it by converting your protein. Tissues, muscles, skin, thymus gland, lymphatic tissues in general, and finally the digestive system—liver and intestine—will be cannibalized to make sugar and energy under the influence of cortisol.

The protective effect of testosterone was demonstrated once using radioactive testosterone molecules. They injected it into athletes and thought that they would see radiation coming out of their muscles. But what they saw was most of the radiation was coming from their heart. Testosterone is most concentrated in the organs that are most vital to survival. So it concentrates in the heart, lungs, and brain at the highest ratio to protein. Even though it's responsible for making an athlete's muscles bigger, what it's doing is preventing those from being used up for energy.

With age, if you're producing less of the protective steroids, a given amount of cortisol might not look extremely high in relation to the standards. But if your pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone are lower than average, even a moderate amount of cortisol begins eating up your muscles and skin, and eventually, it can start deteriorating your heart, lungs, and brain.

**Jodelle:** Is it the chicken or the egg? Is it a high cortisol response that leads to low progesterone and testosterone, or is it something happening that causes the low hormones which leads to the stress response?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's usually a gradual deterioration from poor nutrition, eating foods that are irritating or toxic, or foods that suppress your thyroid function. Thyroid is necessary to produce these protective steroids. Cholesterol is converted pretty massively into pregnenolone and the other protective steroids if you have Vitamin A and thyroid hormone adequately. But if you're deficient in either of those, the cholesterol will rise in your blood. That generally means that you're not making enough DHEA and testosterone.

So, low thyroid, which causes high cholesterol, really means you're not making enough of the protective testosterone and related steroids. When that happens, your cortisol and other stress hormones rise. Low thyroid is the most common thing responsible for a bad ratio of cortisol to testosterone.

**Jodelle:** Could overtraining or over-exercising also lead to this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Someone did an experiment putting people on a treadmill and measuring their active thyroid hormone, T3. They had them walk very mildly, keeping their pulse rate at 120 beats per minute or less. In an hour, they had become hypothyroid in the sense of reducing their activation of thyroid into T3.

Doctors are now being taught that they should ignore T3 (the active hormone) and think about only Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) and thyroxine (T4). But when an athlete depresses their T3, their thyroxine will actually rise in a reaction. Doctors are being taught things that will make them miss the effects of stress on your thyroid.

When your thyroid goes down from stress, your estrogen normally is being excreted and kept at a low level systemically by the thyroid activating liver metabolism. The liver solubilizes estrogen, making it leave through the kidneys. If your thyroid drops from stress, very quickly your estrogen will rise. Then the estrogen acts directly on the adrenals; it increases cortisol production. It activates your pituitary to stimulate cortisol production and activates your brain to release Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH). So just dropping the active thyroid, you very quickly turn on both the estrogen and the whole cortisol stress system.

**Jodelle:** Are you familiar with CrossFit? Imagine these people doing intense overexertion.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Russians, 50 or 60 years ago, were being accused of using testosterone because they had worked out the way to under-train—avoid overexertion—and so keep their stress hormones down and their testosterone up. It takes a very moderate amount of muscle-building exercise to increase testosterone and lower cortisol.

The muscle itself becomes an endocrine organ. If you're under stress, your muscle will actually produce cortisol and not testosterone. When it's properly stimulated, the muscle becomes a testosterone-producing organ. It isn't just the gonads that produce testosterone if you're doing things right.

**Jodelle:** So this chronic output in CrossFit classes or heavy-duty weight training might be harmful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A woman doing just one or two minutes of mild dumbbell lifts and a few squats for the big leg muscles can shift her balance from cortisol to testosterone.

**Jodelle:** So it is beneficial to lift heavy things, but we don't need to do these hour-long classes that push the body to the limit.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Jodelle:** Can you talk a little bit about Sex Hormone Binding Globulin (SHBG)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that is the body's defense against estrogen. When it's high, a woman has a lower risk of breast cancer because it keeps the estrogen out of cells. But when it's high in response to defending against estrogen, it can also interfere with the testosterone effect.

**Jodelle:** How does adrenaline fit into this mix with cortisol and estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the stress hormones interfere with the conversion of T4 to T3. Instead of making the effective, respiration-promoting T3, they convert thyroxine into Reverse T3. They dispose of the precursor and turn it into an interfering, inactive suppressor of respiration.

Those same stress hormones that produce the inactive Reverse T3 also tend to suppress the pituitary TSH, making it look like you're even hyperthyroid. Doctors are taught to diagnose hyperthyroidism in terms of abnormally low TSH. But in fact, the stress which is lowering most people's TSH is caused by hypothyroidism. So a low thyroid person raises their estrogen, cortisol, and adrenaline, and these add up to lower your TSH and make it look like you have too much thyroid.

**Jodelle:** That explains why so many people go to the doctor and are told they have too much thyroid, yet they exhibit signs of low thyroid like weight gain and hair loss.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For 65 years it's been known how it works, but doctors are increasingly misinformed. Even if a person isn't hypothyroid in the sense of not having enough T3, if their TSH is increased, they will get the worst heart disease signs of hypothyroidism. TSH itself is an inflammation-promoting hormone.

**Jodelle:** I don't think people understand the importance of women having adequate testosterone. With low testosterone, I see additional weight gain.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has to be balanced in both men and women with DHEA and cortisol. Especially DHEA is an activator of fat oxidizing. Your muscle is the organ that is most equipped for oxidizing fat. Your brain and heart don't do well oxidizing fat compared to glucose, but the muscles are perfectly adapted for it. Everything you do to increase your muscle's production of testosterone and reduction of cortisol is favoring that fat burning. Just the right amount of exercise to build muscle will shift your metabolism to safely consume fat in your muscles while leaving adequate glucose for your brain and lungs.

**Jodelle:** What are other symptoms of high cortisol and low testosterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Depression. The whole stress system that ends up increasing your cortisol and decreasing DHEA, progesterone, and testosterone is related to inflammatory and degenerative processes. Depression is how we experience that process. The body senses that it's being destroyed by the stress hormones and it wants to stop everything to sort of hibernate until the stress is over. Sometimes you see anxiety and aggression. Aggression comes up when you're being overstressed. But when your body is being damaged, you get these negative emotions: aggression, anxiety, and depression.

**Jodelle:** You hear a lot about fasting and intermittent fasting as a way to improve hormones. Do you see fasting as a way to lower cortisol, or is it contributing to the stress response?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In one day of fasting, the body stores several ounces of glucose in the form of glycogen. If you're healthy, you can go up to 24 hours before you are short on glycogen. As the body senses stress, lowering the T3 slows the rate of fuel use. When your glycogen is gone, you have to start using your tissue to make glucose out of your muscles. If your thyroid didn't slow down during this prolonged stress, you would eat your whole body up in just a few days. But since the depressive process turns off metabolism, it slows the rate of degeneration.

If you give a little bit of glucose and minerals—sodium, calcium, magnesium, potassium—during the low-calorie period, you can greatly reduce your tissue loss. On a complete water fast for 10 days, they found that 80% or more of the weight loss came from the destruction of muscle and skin. But if they had a 500 or 600 calorie diet with adequate minerals, almost all of the weight loss was in the form of fat loss. So a complete fast is very destructive to the body.

**Jodelle:** Fasting in nature would mean we didn't find food, so it would be a stress response.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some professors advocated fasting for detoxification, but that got me interested in what really happens. The liver is the organ of detoxification. When you deprive the liver of sugar and expose it to cortisol, not only does estrogen rise, but the liver loses its ability to detoxify other things. Estrogen rises because the sulfation and glucuronidation detoxifying systems are shut down by fasting.

In Mexico, I was exposed to a type of insecticide used on buses. When I realized I was being poisoned, I left. Driving home, every time I got hungry, I would smell this insecticide in my exhaled breath. For about two months, every time I had low blood sugar at 3:00 AM, I would wake up smelling this Pine-Sol insecticide odor. As soon as that odor stopped leaving my body when I got hungry, I went into a hyperthyroid state. It had been suppressing my thyroid.

When you're starving, you're living on your body tissues, including fat, and that can mobilize toxins that had been stored away. A fast is a way to maybe clean up your liver eventually, but definitely, it's not good for your brain and immune system.

**Jodelle:** The liver is also important for testosterone production, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the case of progesterone, a woman produces maybe 30 milligrams a day during the premenstrual time. The liver adapts to that very large production. After two weeks, the enzymes increase and start excreting progesterone as well as estrogen and testosterone. At menstruation, the synthesis of new progesterone stops. For two weeks, the liver has very low exposure, meaning it has a chance to reset its detoxifying enzymes to zero.

If a man is supplementing testosterone every day and exceeds the liver's normal preference, the liver experiences the same thing a woman's liver experiences with high progesterone. After a week or two of high testosterone exposure, he is now excreting it very fast and probably getting about as much estrogen effect as testosterone effect. In medical use, they sometimes give 50 or 100 milligrams at once. The liver goes into a testosterone-destroying condition.

**Jodelle:** My mom died of stomach cancer at 45. She lived a very stressful existence—over-exercising, hardly sleeping, starving herself. How does chronically elevated cortisol relate to cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Behind the rise of estrogen and cortisol and the fall of thyroid is the tissue level of stress. In the alimentary canal, histamine and serotonin are massively produced. 95% of our serotonin comes from the intestine. Stomach ulcers can be produced just by an excess of serotonin.

As histamine and serotonin increase in the digestive system, that allows endotoxin and nitric oxide to rise. All of those interfere with our ability to produce respiratory energy. You shift over to lactic acid production. Lactic acid activates the stress hormones, promotes inflammation, and is carcinogenic in itself.

Serotonin is one of the most powerful activators of the cortisol stress hormone system. It acts powerfully on the hypothalamus to make CRH. Stomach cancer and intestinal cancer are very deeply involved with excess serotonin.

**Jodelle:** Are there certain habits, like being an overachiever or over-analyzer, that create this stress response?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regular sleep is a powerfully protective thing. It should be somewhere in the range of six to nine hours every night, but the *regularity* is very important. It becomes a built-in, almost machine-like regulator. Any variation of that schedule puts the whole 24-hour cycle into a stress pattern.

High progesterone, testosterone, and DHEA are promoters of restorative sleep. Cortisol interferes at all levels of sleep restoration.

Regarding habits like starvation or anorexia nervosa: they have done MRI pictures of brains during anorexia and during recovery. During anorexia, the brain—especially the frontal lobes—shrinks. When they repeat it during recovery, it rebuilds itself. So it's actually causing brain damage to fast too much. A stressful pregnancy with too much exposure to estrogen and cortisol does the same thing. Androgens protect the brain, heart, and lungs, but prolonged exposure to high estrogen will shrink the frontal lobes that handle long-range perspective.

**Jodelle:** I like that you said it can be rebuilt.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very much like exercise, but you have to stop the stress first. Taxi drivers have a bigger part of the brain that handles memory because they know every street in a big city. That kind of exercise works best if you maintain the protective hormones—even supplementing pregnenolone, progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone—combined with the kind of mental activity that you want to develop. That will, in a relatively short time, rebuild.

**Jodelle:** Can you expand on "learned helplessness"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That can be repaired with protective hormones or behavioral insight, but stopping the stress is the first thing. That requires good nutrition. Good nutrition should include plenty of carbohydrate so that you don't have to rely on cortisol to convert protein into glucose. Usually, something more than 100 grams per day of carbohydrate—preferably in the form of sucrose—is needed. If you're very active physically, 200 or 300 grams a day of carbohydrate, especially sugar, can be restorative to the brain.

**Jodelle:** I wanted to talk about the dangers of a sugarless diet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All of the things that trigger the stress hormones involve interference with glucose metabolism. Hypoglycemia itself is a powerful activator of the stress system. Excess of free fatty acids, which block the ability to use glucose, will activate the stress hormones. Lactic acid results when you're not using your glucose properly; it's a sign of a deficiency of glucose that activates cortisol production.

The obvious way to stop the stress reaction is to provide enough glucose and oxygen along with the other nutrients. If you provide only protein and fat, you're going to increase your cortisol just to convert the protein to the amount of glucose that your brain and blood cells need.

**Jodelle:** Are there specific foods that help lower cortisol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The reason I talk so much about milk and orange juice is that they are the most available foods that have the most components that tend to shut down excess cortisol production, lower adrenaline, and reduce serotonin and nitric oxide.

Everyone can usually find good milk and sweet orange juice. The calcium in milk and the minerals—potassium and others—in orange juice lower the stress factors. Most people have a borderline calcium and Vitamin D deficiency. When you are borderline, you increase your parathyroid hormone. If you're borderline in sodium, your aldosterone increases. Parathyroid hormone and aldosterone interact to turn off your energy production, shift you over to wasting sugar, increasing cortisol, and destroying your tissues. Getting your aldosterone and parathyroid hormone as low as you can will increase your metabolic efficiency.

**Jodelle:** What about fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoiding the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) is a universal benefit. Do not add fish oil, algae oil, safflower, or canola oil to your diet. Those are all anti-thyroid, anti-progesterone, and anti-DHEA. They increase your stress hormones. Just cutting out the polyunsaturated fats shifts you to increased thyroid function.

**Jodelle:** That leaves us with saturated fats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at the ratio of saturated fat to polyunsaturated in your tissues, the saturation index corresponds to lifespan. Animals with the highest saturation index have the longest life expectancy.

In the 1930s, a man did a lab experiment intended to demonstrate that taking out all of the fat would cause a deficiency of essential fatty acids. But this guy had lifelong headaches and blood pressure problems. After three or four months on this fat-free diet, he stopped having headaches and his blood pressure normalized. He never had a recurrence of his health problems. Far from producing deficiency diseases, this extreme fat-free diet cured his lifelong health problems.

**Jodelle:** What are your favorite sources of protein for lowering cortisol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gelatin happens to be fairly close to an ideal protein for an adult. Milk protein has a fair amount of tryptophan and cysteine. These are pro-inflammatory amino acids that are used in growth. Milk is ideal for growing, but for an adult, I think it should be supplemented with something like gelatin, which lacks the pro-inflammatory growth-related amino acids.

**Jodelle:** So you could blend your morning coffee with collagen/gelatin and milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I use about 8 or 9 ounces of milk with an ounce or two of extremely concentrated coffee for my breakfast meal.

**Jodelle:** Dr. Peat, I appreciate your time. Listeners can sign up for your newsletter by emailing raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com. It is $28 for the email version or $38 for the mail version for 12 issues. I also encourage everyone to check out the articles at RayPeat.com. Thank you, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: Jodellefit: How to Fix Your Digestion & Poop
transcriptText:
**Jodelle:** Welcome to the Get Fit with Jodelle podcast. I am happy to have Dr. Ray Peat with me here today. Dr. Peat is my go-to source for all things nutrition and health. He has a PhD in biology and has taught at many renowned schools regarding nutrition and women's health. You can learn more about him by visiting raypeat.com.

Dr. Peat, I am honored to have you back. I wanted to pick your brain about digestion today. From what I understand, digestion is one of the top five reasons people come to see their doctor. Why do you think there is so much digestive distress in our modern society, and was it this bad 40 or 50 years ago?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One general problem is physical inactivity. People who live in apartments have to take their dogs out for a walk every day because the digestive system tends to slow down when you aren't walking. There are reflexes between the legs and the intestine. In general, physical inactivity affects the whole process of appetite, digestion, and elimination.

The change from a crude diet to a very refined diet was also a factor.
