Around the beginning of the 20th century, health organizations emphasized using whole grains rather than refined flour because of the bulk-forming effect of the bran. Studies comparing Africans and Americans found that because there was a lot of potato and fibrous foods in the African diet, their transit time was about 12 hours. The average American at the time had a transit time of 72 hours. That is a tremendous difference. The rising incidence of bowel cancer in America has been huge, whereas there is almost no colorectal cancer in the undeveloped parts of Africa where they still eat a fibrous diet.

**Jodelle:** Do you think a lot of our digestive distress comes from a society of sitting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. Everyone who takes up the habit of walking for an hour or so a day notices improved digestion. The general sense of well-being is largely because of the improved movement of the intestinal muscles, but also improved secretions. Relaxing and moving around reduces nervous tension, which increases secretions. You can see it even in saliva. When you're very anxious, your mouth tends to go dry because the shift in the nervous system shuts off secretions starting in the mouth and affecting all the way down.

**Jodelle:** So there is a north-to-south process. Would you say saliva is just as important as stomach acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anyone who has taken a drug that shuts down saliva production has generally had an outbreak of cavities. Anticholinergic drugs and some antihistamines reduce the production of saliva so much that the chemical composition changes. Instead of washing away and inactivating bacteria, it tends to favor their growth. You see it in increased deposits on the teeth and the extremely fast development of cavities.

**Jodelle:** I didn't realize digestion translated to teeth health. I assumed you were going to say that lacking saliva leads to poor digestion because of the enzymatic breakdown in the mouth. Is that also the case?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a little digestion that begins in the mouth. 50 to 70 years ago, some people were fanatical about chewing food many times to liquefy it. However, the quantity of enzymes in saliva is not very great compared to some animals. Those same enzymes are secreted later in the stomach. If you miss getting some digestion started in your mouth, your stomach can make up for it by secreting starch breakdown enzymes.

**Jodelle:** Let's talk about that north-to-south process. I've always been an advocate for adequate stomach acid. What are your thoughts on keeping it adequate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is regulated strongly by nerves and hormones. The ultimate source of the acidity is in oxidation and the production of carbon dioxide, which is involved in the secretion of hydrochloric acid. It is essentially a respiratory process. If your thyroid is very low, your stomach acid is going to be low. The muscles become weaker at the same time the secretions are weaker.

Slowing down the transit time allows abnormal yeast to develop in the stomach. Around 1955 or 1960, there were cases of people thought to be drunkards because they reeked of alcohol. It turned out they had a little brewery in their stomach. If they ate starch, their enzymes produced enough sugar for yeast to grow, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide.

When you look at the population, only a small percentage—maybe 10%—have a completely germ-free stomach and small intestine. A large proportion, 30% or 40%, have infections in the lower half of the small intestine. Another third has detectable germs all the way up to where the pancreatic enzymes enter. Slow transit and weak secretions allow organisms to survive. A very high proportion of the population suffers from microorganism overgrowth between the stomach and the beginning of the colon. When they grow only in the colon, they are pretty harmless.

**Jodelle:** I assume the liver and gallbladder are important here. I see many people with liver stagnation or who no longer have a gallbladder. How important is it to keep the liver functioning well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver absorbs nutrients, but along with nutrients come toxins. If you have bacteria growing where they shouldn't be, they produce toxins that burden your liver. One of the first things that goes wrong when digestion slows is that high endotoxin levels start slowing down liver function.

Fiber helps because it binds and moves along some of the bacteria, reducing the absorption of endotoxin. The liver also keeps hormone levels under control. It attaches sulfuric or glucuronic acid to hormones like estrogen to make them water-soluble for excretion. If you overload the liver, these hormones are excreted into the bile, reabsorbed, and give you a chronic excess of circulating estrogen. Fiber helps bind and move along the endotoxin, bacteria, and excreted hormones.

**Jodelle:** Can you explain endotoxin in layman's terms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Its chemical name is lipopolysaccharide (LPS). It is a group of fatty acids attached to a carbohydrate that has a physical "soaping" action. The fat is absorbed in the cells and drags in this carbohydrate that acts as an irritant. Every tissue is damaged by endotoxin.

In the gallbladder, receiving chemicals like estrogen and endotoxin causes inflammation. If estrogen is high—such as in pregnancy—cholesterol tends to accumulate, forming sludge or stones. Thyroid deficiency is extremely closely associated with gallbladder problems because of the lowered detoxifying function of the liver. Estrogen can also cause spasms in the smooth muscles, starting with the gallbladder duct or the small intestine.

When you get into that over-excited, under-energized state, local irritation can send out waves of contraction that go backwards. This is reverse peristalsis. Embryologists experimented on medical students by putting microscopic particles—club moss spores—into their rectums in the afternoon. In the morning, they took swabs from their mouths. Those who regularly had morning breath found the spores in their saliva, showing it is extremely common to have reverse peristalsis all the way from the rectum to the mouth during the night.

**Jodelle:** What are some digestive symptoms someone might experience if they have high levels of endotoxins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the intestine is in bad shape, the blood vessels in the intestinal wall become over-permeable—the so-called "leaky intestine." Toxins get into the general circulation and go straight to the brain, heart, and lungs. It can contribute to obstructive pulmonary disease, emphysema, shock-like symptoms, reduced heart function, heart failure, insomnia, and sleep apnea.

**Jodelle:** What about gas and bloating? Is that a clear-cut issue of endotoxins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you tap on your belly and it sounds like a drum, that is the accumulation of gas. When you are in a spastic state, the sphincters don't let it out. That pressure itself can cause migraines.

Walter Alvarez, a professor around 1910, inserted big wads of cotton into the rectums of medical students. Those susceptible to headaches developed one just from the pressure. He used this to argue against the concept of auto-toxicity, blaming it on pressure rather than the nature of the food.

**Jodelle:** Do you think anxiety has anything to do with endotoxin or gut distress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It goes both ways. Experiments feeding soluble fiber to rats found it increased fearfulness and aggression. Conversely, emotional experiences shift blood away from the digestive system to the muscles for the fight-or-flight reaction. The intestine suffers oxygen and sugar deprivation, leading to increased permeability and toxin absorption. This can cause chronic brain syndromes, mood changes, aggression, anxiety, and even contribute to epileptic seizures.

**Jodelle:** Let's talk about the trend of prebiotics and probiotics. What do you think about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Dr. Denis Burkitt showed Africans were free of bowel cancer because of fiber, specifically potatoes. Americans wasted cereal fiber to sell bran, starting the oat bran craze. However, oat bran breaks down into bowel carcinogens and estrogenic breakdown products. Clean cellulose fiber, like wheat bran, is practically resistant to bacterial breakdown, so it functions only as fiber to stimulate peristalsis and bind estrogen and endotoxin. The current prebiotic trend focuses on short-chain fatty acids like butyric and lactic acid, but these can contribute to systemic problems.

**Jodelle:** What about probiotics? I used to advocate for Bifidus bacteria, but now I don't advocate for probiotics because I don't understand the mechanism of adding bacteria when we are already in a world of bacteria.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The small intestine shouldn't have bacteria. Even if you eat yogurt-type bacteria, the stomach and pancreas secretions usually keep them from growing. You need something that produces a competitive antibiotic to compete against irritating bacteria.

In WWII, Germans in North Africa noticed indigenous people didn't suffer from dysentery because they ate small amounts of camel dung, which contained specific bacteria. These soil-based bacteria produce strong antibiotics. Unpasteurized cow's milk also contains these, making the milk resistant to bacterial growth.

**Jodelle:** Is our poo a marker of how our digestion is doing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It should be basically the color and odor of a baby's. If it starts smelling rotten, usually you are feeling rotten. Getting that through you quickly is one of the functions of a good inert fiber.

**Jodelle:** What are some fiber foods you recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Root vegetables typically contain intrinsic antibiotics to survive underground. If you put lettuce in a warm bag, it rots quickly. A carrot will remain unchanged, showing it has a powerful antibiotic system.

This led to the carrot salad idea. Shred the carrot finely lengthwise to maximize the surface area. This acts as a physical binding agent. If you eat it with olive or coconut oil and vinegar, you have three types of antibiotic substances in a pleasant salad. Doing that every day kept my intestine healthy for 20 years. Bamboo shoots (well-boiled) and well-cooked mushrooms are also good alternatives.

**Jodelle:** What foods would someone want to eliminate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoid things that are hard to digest. All raw vegetables, except for carrots, are generally not good. Experiments showed rats thrived on canned, well-cooked vegetables but wasted away on raw ones.

**Jodelle:** Would eliminating gluten be another recommendation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Seeds contain proteins in a storage form. These storage proteins concentrate ammonia and potential irritants like arginine. When digested, arginine can feed the increase of nitric oxide associated with an irritated intestine. Legumes and cereals have low-quality protein compared to milk (70%), egg yolk (100%), or potatoes (higher than 100% because they recycle waste nitrogen).

**Jodelle:** What other advice would you give for someone looking to improve their digestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoid eating while working or anxious. Pavlov showed that the setting in which you eat is crucial; unexpected stress can delay digestion significantly. Keep nutrients in balance—milk is designed to facilitate digestion. Mood is very powerful.

**Jodelle:** Can you let listeners know how they can get your newsletter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you email raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com, you can get information on how to subscribe. It is $28 for 12 bi-monthly issues.

**Jodelle:** Thank you, Dr. Peat. I hope this gives people insight on how to improve their digestion.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: Jodellefit: Listener Q&A: Calories, Cortisol, Cellulite, Exercise, Ephedra & More
transcriptText:
**Jodelle:** Well, welcome to the Get Fit with Jodelle Show. I am super stoked because it's time for another mind-blowing episode with Dr. Raymond Peat. Dr. Peat and I decided to do listener questions today, so I can hardly wait to hear his responses to some really great questions that people put up on Facebook. Dr. Peat, I appreciate you because, once again, I'm so honored beyond words to have you with me. Thank you so much. Are you ready for this slew of questions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep, go ahead.

**Jodelle:** Great. We'll start with a person who wanted to remain anonymous. They asked: Can you give us your opinion on the current fitness trends and also what your daily exercise looks like?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, I never exercise. Well, once about every 10 years, I do some exercises just to see how things are working. But the idea of "exercise," I think, is not biologically sound. I think all of your activities should be intentional in some way—constructive, or at least pleasure-giving. The idea of exercise seems to be more fulfilling a duty or obligation rather than doing something just because it's fun or productive.

**Jodelle:** That takes me a little further down my list to a similar question. This woman likes to run. She asked: If a woman would like to run on a regular basis for enjoyment, is that beneficial, and does she need to be more vigilant regarding PUFA intake and environmental estrogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have a very pretty place to run—like the natives of northern Mexico who have canyons and interesting scenery to run through just to do their social visits and tend to their chores—running is part of their lives, but it's also meaningful in many ways. It isn't just running down the street to a certain point and coming back. The rote nature of it, the predictability and the sameness of it, I think is actually somewhat harmful to your nervous system.

**Jodelle:** So you're thinking more in terms of movement. People need to move their bodies, but not necessarily getting on a treadmill or an elliptical machine to hash out 45 minutes just because they feel like they should.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the mind has to move at least as much as the body. When you're on a treadmill or running down a certain track, your mind is not moving. Your body is moving, but your mind is in a rut. And being in a rut is biologically harmful from a stress standpoint.

**Jodelle:** Right. So if we don't enjoy the exercises we are trying to do to get in shape, they can actually be stress-inducing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And it deepens the rut. A habit of doing something that isn't pleasurable or meaningful deepens your tolerance for meaninglessness. You're at risk of sinking into routine behavior and a routine life.

**Jodelle:** I like that. We need to have meaning in everything we do.

**Jodelle:** The next question is: Could you please tell us the difference between a dairy allergy and lactose intolerance? What different symptoms would we expect, and what can we do if it is actually a dairy allergy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** An allergy can be deadly. A mild allergy is just annoying; if it's on your tongue or mouth, it makes it burn and maybe swell up a little. If it's serious, it will make your membranes swell up to a hideous extent so that you can't move your tongue or swallow. If it's a real allergy, it can stop function and make it impossible to breathe, which is fatal.

Lactose intolerance is simply the inability to absorb and digest milk sugar. If you have a sugar in your intestine that can't be absorbed, it has a laxative effect and tends to run through you. Or, if you have the wrong kind of bacteria, the bacteria can convert it to gas. Gas is the most common symptom for lactose intolerance.

**Jodelle:** I've heard you mention before that if somebody has an intolerance, different nutritional approaches can help that individual develop a tolerance.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. A deficiency of thyroid hormone creates various metabolic inefficiencies. Low production of digestive enzymes is typical, as is low stomach acid. The enzymes to digest lactose will be low when your thyroid hormone activity is low. So, low-thyroid people, as a rule, have some extent of lactose intolerance. Just fixing the thyroid function will improve their digestion of milk.

There were studies of people who were theoretically genetically unable to digest lactose because of their race. They tested these people by starting with half a glass or a quarter of a glass of milk every day. After a few weeks, they found that these genetically intolerant people were able to induce the enzyme. The enzyme is there in infancy; it's just a matter of keeping it active or re-inducing it as an adult by giving your intestine exposure to a daily amount of lactose.

**Jodelle:** So if someone had the ability to digest dairy since infancy but suddenly can't digest it in their older years, would the cause be low thyroid, low stomach acid, or a vitamin deficiency?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin deficiencies and thyroid deficiencies often go together. As your digestive system slows down from low thyroid, you will absorb poorly and be more likely to get a vitamin deficiency.

**Jodelle:** That's helpful. Hopefully, that listener can start to address their thyroid and replenish their ability to take in dairy. That actually happened to me; once I got my thyroid working after toxic mold exposure, I was able to do dairy again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known people who recovered from a variety of very different kinds of allergies or sensitivities. Aspirin sensitivity is another thing that is supposed to be genetic, but I have a friend who was thought to be aspirin intolerant for 55 years of his life, and now he takes aspirin every day.

**Jodelle:** The next question is: What is the root cause of grinding of the teeth, or bruxism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Serotonin excess is one of the things that happens during the night, usually due to an irritation in the intestine. As your blood sugar goes down, your nerves and immune system become more irritable because of the falling energy supply. That irritability during the night—even though the food wasn't causing an allergic reaction during the daytime—makes you start sensing relatively toxic or irritating things in your intestine. That causes the intestine to increase its production of serotonin. Serotonin is closely connected with bruxism.

**Jodelle:** So someone would want to get their serotonin levels down to prevent that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually just looking at your diet and finding things that are not well digested. Green salads are the worst offenders. They never can be digested by a human being, so they feed whatever bacteria or fungus happens to be in your system. Then the fungus or bacteria will make toxins that irritate the intestine so that it overproduces things such as histamine, serotonin, and nitric oxide.

**Jodelle:** I can't tell you how many women say, "I have a green salad every day," and yet have digestive issues.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We simply don't have enzymes to digest them. There were experiments with rats feeding them fresh raw vegetables versus the same vegetables that had been canned at very high temperature and pressure. Supposedly, nutrients are lost by high-temperature cooking, but because it breaks down the cellulose, it actually makes more nutrients available. The rats wasted away when fed fresh vegetables but thrived on the canned vegetables.

You can do an experiment: put a bit of green salad into a plastic bag and keep it at body temperature for two or three days—which would happen after you ate it. See what happens to the fresh green salad. It's usually a foul mess.

**Jodelle:** Rachel asks: What does Dr. Peat feel are the better exercises, foods, and supplements for middle-aged women in regards to lowering chronic stress or cortisol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you live in a woodsy, cold climate, cutting wood and stacking it in the summer months is a good, useful exercise that uses your muscles. In the winter, or if you don't have wood to cut, dumbbells are the closest thing to getting muscle use.

**Jodelle:** I love that. I went camping recently and learned how to chop wood. It was a great workout, fun, and a stress reliever.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With a good cross-cut saw, you can saw logs for the fireplace and get push-and-pull exercise on your arm muscles, like a very expensive exercise machine.

**Jodelle:** She also asked what supplements or nutrition you recommend for lowering chronic stress and cortisol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Things that are easy to digest and that don't lower your blood sugar are the most powerful anti-stressors. Keeping the ratio of calcium to phosphate very high in your diet has a relaxing, anti-stress effect.

When your muscles are active and growing, they actually produce some testosterone. When they're under stress and not being used properly, they tend to convert cholesterol into cortisol and actually create the stress syndrome. The unused muscle is slightly toxic under some conditions, whereas the used muscle adds to your steroid protective hormones.

**Jodelle:** Since you have a history in Mexico, I wanted to ask about my favorite starchy vegetable, jicama. What are your thoughts on jicama for digestion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've eaten a lot of it. I don't generally tolerate starches well—for example, cucumbers give me terrible gas and even cantaloupes are too gas-forming for me—but I never had trouble with jicama. I don't know what it is; it is starch, but it isn't famously gas-producing.

**Jodelle:** I noticed that too. I wonder if it's because it may be part of the tuber family, like a potato?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's in a very different family, but it probably has a different set of allergens and antigens.

**Jodelle:** Tina asks: Does Dr. Peat advise those coming from calorie-restricted eating and intermittent fasting protocols to slowly increase food intake and possibly count calories?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The important thing is to watch your temperature and pulse rate as indicators of how energetic your metabolism is. It's normal for your metabolic rate to go down during the night, but after breakfast, you should pop right up to a working temperature of 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) and a pulse rate of more or less 80 or 85 beats per minute.

**Jodelle:** Her second question was: Should we take T4 with T3, or do you advise just taking T3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The value of T3 in a free form is that if you're in a hurry to correct a problem, you can use a physiological replacement amount of T3, such as between 1 and 4 micrograms per hour. With a meal, where you're going to be absorbing food for two or three hours, 10 micrograms is a pretty physiological amount. You can see if that relieves your symptoms.

I've seen very serious symptoms disappear in as little as a minute after taking a 5 or 10 microgram dose of T3. Insomnia will very often disappear five minutes after chewing up a bit of T3. Pains, arthritic pains, or breast pains will disappear in 5 to 15 minutes. It is valuable for its essentially instantaneous repair functions, but it goes away almost as fast as it takes effect.

I was taking 25 micrograms in the morning all at once for a time. After doing that for a couple of weeks, at sunset, my heart would begin stopping every 10 seconds for two or three seconds at a time. Once it stopped so long that I started blacking out. I realized that taking an outsized dose all at once causes your liver to start eliminating the T3 at an exaggerated rate. After 12 hours of the liver excreting it at that high rate, if you don't replace it, you suddenly go into an extremely hypothyroid state, which leads to heart arrhythmia.

If you take T4 only, a very healthy person can handle it. They tested it in the 1940s on male medical students and said thyroxine (T4) had exactly the same effect as the full thyroid substance. But they didn't test it on women. It happens that estrogen affects the liver and the thyroid gland, blocking secretion of the hormone and slowing the metabolic process of the liver. It turns out that women have about five times the incidence of thyroid-related disease. Autoimmunity is closely connected to that feminine thyroid-estrogen interaction.

So, T4 is fine as a replacement for healthy people, but for people with a metabolic problem—mostly women—it's exactly the wrong thing to use. However, since you don't want to take 4 micrograms of T3 half a dozen times a day, taking T4 in the evening can help sustain things through the night. But it should be accompanied by, ideally, one or two doses of T3 during the daytime. The sustaining effect of T3 means that it activates your liver, keeping estrogen from accumulating. The active liver will then activate the thyroid gland, protecting it from the blocking effect of estrogen. Given the supporting effect of T3, a woman's liver can metabolize T4 just like a man's.

**Jodelle:** I have seen people take T3 and say that after a couple of weeks they no longer notice the difference. Is that because the liver is pushing it out and they need to up their dose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, if you take 5, 10, or 20 micrograms at once, your liver is going to develop super excretory enzymes to lower it faster than normal.

**Jodelle:** And taking T3 sounds like a way to remove excess estrogens from the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, and that will help you handle the T4.

**Jodelle:** Diego asks: What do you think of anti-aromatase products like Exemestane (Aromasin)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those generally have fairly serious side effects. The steroid-based one is the least toxic of the aromatase inhibitors, but there are safe aromatase inhibitors. Aspirin and progesterone, for example, do a very good job.

**Jodelle:** Christy asks: I'm losing weight, but my hands and feet are cold even with natural thyroid medication, and I'm getting colder. Why is that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's important to check temperature and pulse rate as well as how you're feeling. If you have been reducing your intake of nutrients, you might have reduced some essential nutrient so much that you're in a stress state. High cortisol can make you lose weight under stress, but it will be primarily muscle weight.

Dieters used to go on very low-calorie diets or fasts and find they could lose 10 or 12 pounds quickly. Someone did a study analyzing this and found that on an extremely low-calorie diet, the weight loss was about 80% protein and only 15% or 20% fat. But if they took a moderate amount of nutrition—enough to reduce the stress hormones—they could lose 80% fat and only 15% or 20% protein tissue. It's essential to keep adequate nutrition while lowering calories. The adrenaline will come up and bring cortisol after, and the cortisol is what makes you lose muscle.

**Jodelle:** So she might try adding some more calories. If her adrenaline is high, would it serve her to add carbohydrates?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. Carbohydrate at the right amount will spare the protein. If you are getting 80 grams of protein a day, getting carbohydrate from orange juice, for example, helps. It comes with minerals; potassium has a sparing effect on the protein besides the sugar. So fruit juice plus the adequate amount of protein will keep your metabolism up and tend to promote fat loss rather than protein loss.

**Jodelle:** That's a good tip. Anytime I drink orange juice, I feel warmer right after.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You have to allow time for the effect of the cold orange juice to wear off. If you drink warm orange juice, you'll see the warming effect immediately.

**Jodelle:** The second part of Christy's question: She had her uterus removed. Her doctor told her she doesn't need to take progesterone if she doesn't have a uterus. Is that true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many doctors thought that was true 60 years ago, but I didn't know anyone still said that. It's a horrifying thing to think that a doctor still believes progesterone has use only to the uterus.

Progesterone is one of the most basic molecules in the universe. Starting right from the ovum itself, it is involved in the structure which organizes the genes and the cell division mechanism. As the organism matures, even before puberty, progesterone is in charge of brain development. If progesterone is low during gestation, the brain fails to develop. When it's given as a supplement in animal experiments, the brain becomes super-able, bigger, and more functional.

In the mature adult brain, progesterone is a major steroid—10 times higher in the brain than circulating in the blood. You might say the uterus is a very minor field of operation for the progesterone molecule. It governs brain growth and function. If it's low, a woman will experience epileptic seizures, mood depression, etc. A deficiency of progesterone affects every aspect of life.

**Jodelle:** Christy also asks: Are sulfur supplements good or bad, such as in the form of MSM?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When people email me that question, I send them a couple of articles from about 40 years ago. A woman in a California hospital was brought in, and she exploded in the operating room. She died, and several of the staff were injured. Analyzing the chemistry, the best hypothesis seems to be that she was using MSM to treat cancer in very large amounts. Some fluke in the way it metabolized led to that toxic explosion.

That only happened once, but I think it's good for people to be aware of that chemical analysis as an indicator of how little is known about the supplements people commonly use.

**Jodelle:** She literally exploded?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, or the gases around... they had opened a big incision and a surge of emissions occurred. I think it was described as an explosion, but the fumes quickly knocked out several of the staff.

**Jodelle:** Why do people take MSM?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they're doing it as an anti-inflammatory, there are lots of other anti-inflammatory things. The safest approach is to look at causes. Low blood sugar leads to inflammation. Too much unsaturated vegetable oil amplifies inflammation. Too much phosphate in the diet relative to calcium is a very powerful promoter of inflammation. Things that over-activate the parathyroid gland will lead to inflammation, fibrosis, and calcification—things these supplements are recommended for. Supplementing calcium and avoiding things over-rich in phosphates—like too much meat, beans, or nuts—is better.

**Jodelle:** Trudy asks: What is Dr. Peat's stance on colostrum powder and powdered milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Something I just ran across a few months ago was that the dehydrating and powder-producing industry has begun using nanoparticles to prevent clumping. Colostrum is a good idea, and powdered milk is a wonder food for convenience—I've used hundreds of pounds of it myself. But recently, I found this info on the new technology. Just so the powder will flow easily, they're coating it with nanoparticles.

I haven't found any industry source which admits they're using it, but you can find articles about the technology being sold. These nanoparticles, if they're in a particular size range, are carcinogenic and pro-inflammatory. So for several months, I haven't been recommending some of my favorite recipes, like powdered milk pancakes, because of the uncertainty of how these powders are being produced.

**Jodelle:** That happened with Vitamin C too, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, in the mid-1950s. The research that made it famous was done in the 40s and early 50s. I used it myself; with two tiny tablets of 50 milligrams each, I ended a very intense poison oak allergy. But the next time I took it, the price had dropped by 90% and tablets were 500 milligrams. It caused cold symptoms and allergy symptoms when I took it. I started mentioning my experience to people with chronic sinus inflammation, runny nose, and hemorrhoids. A huge percentage of these people solved their problems when they stopped taking their synthetic Vitamin C supplements.

**Jodelle:** This is a loaded question: Can you ask Dr. Peat about pheochromocytoma, paragangliomas, and adrenal tumors? What can we do, and is there a connection to thyroid disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I suspect that there is. The people I've known with that diagnosis were actually hypothyroid. In the absence of good thyroid function, the body looks for alternative ways to keep working. One way is to over-activate that particular kind of cell. It can go in different directions—excess serotonin or excess adrenergic chemicals. I think of it as the body inventing ways to get around an energy block.

For example, years ago they found that if you removed one ovary of an animal, the other ovary was likely to develop cancer because the pituitary gland was producing enough activating gonadotropin for two ovaries. It over-stimulated the remaining one.

There is good evidence that the same thing happens with the thyroid. When you're deficient in nutrients or have something blocking hormone production, your pituitary becomes hyperactive. TSH rises and chronically over-stimulates the thyroid gland, leading to cancer. Women are more susceptible because estrogen blocks the secretion of the hormone, making the pituitary work harder.

I think if you keep the pituitary under control so it isn't over-stimulating your adrenals, you reduce the risk. Once you get a tumor, it's too late to work on the pituitary level. But low thyroid leads to increased prolactin and TSH. Serotonin happens to drive all the pituitary hormones, so a stress that leaves you with chronic serotonin excess can contribute to all the tumor developments driven by the pituitary gland.

**Jodelle:** John asks: What are your thoughts on the herbal form of ephedra, also known as Ma Huang?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've used it from the time I was four years old and first had migraine-like headaches. My grandmother made me Ma Huang tea—"Desert Tea" it was called. It's a powerful stimulant. Some people have used it in an excessive, chronic way for weight loss. In chronic excessive use, it contains things that are toxic to the liver. But if it's used just occasionally, for example, to treat nausea or a headache, it's fine.

**Jodelle:** Regarding weight loss, it stimulates the beta receptors, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, but free fatty acids are the result, and free fatty acids are what make fat toxic. So it's better to eliminate the fat slowly and carefully rather than pushing it out with a stimulant.

**Jodelle:** Ann asks: What is your remedy for cellulite?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The immediate thing is to check your temperature and metabolic rate. Look at your calorie and water consumption. You should be evaporating at least 2 liters of water every day that you can't account for. If you drink two quarts of orange juice and two quarts of milk, you should produce a moderate amount—maybe a quart—of urine per day. If most of your water intake appears as urine, you're not evaporating at a proper rate, meaning your metabolic rate is low.

Your temperature should be around 98.6°F during the day, and pulse rate preferably in the 80s. To do that might require supplementing extra calcium and making sure you're getting enough sodium. Having a Vitamin D blood test is a good idea; levels should be around 50 ng/mL. Vitamin D and thyroid work closely together.

If you still have a tendency toward cellulite, supplementing progesterone and DHEA—rubbing it into those areas and taking 5 or 10 milligrams orally—can activate the connective tissue metabolism to toughen up the tone of the tissue and help it get rid of the water.

**Jodelle:** Last question: What is your favorite pastime?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think painting is my favorite thing. Whenever I can get someone to sit for me, I like to take portraits.

**Jodelle:** That's great. We have to get "Vitamin P" (Pleasure) as well as all these other vitamins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. It's really the key to the whole thing—to make it work pleasurably.

**Jodelle:** Dr. Peat, this has been so interesting. I really appreciate your time. Make sure you check out Dr. Peat's newsletter at raypeat.com or email raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com. Thank you once again, Dr. Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you. Goodbye.
