transcriptText:
**Jodelle:** Welcome to the Get Fit with Jodelle show. I am Jodelle, and Dr. Peat has honored us with his presence on the podcast yet again. It’s a treat, Dr. Peat. Thank you. What is new in your world currently?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been writing a newsletter on vaccinations—sort of the history of vaccination and explaining some of the physiological points that are being misrepresented.

**Jodelle:** I am so excited to read that. For those of you listening who haven't signed up for his newsletter, it will blow your hair back when you read it. I highly encourage you to sign up as a way to show your support for Dr. Peat. You can send an email to raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com. If you are new to the podcast, you can read a plethora of research-based articles that Dr. Peat has written at RayPeat.com.

We had such a good podcast last time where people got to write in and ask questions, so we decided to do that again. The first question comes from Reba. She asks: How can someone get rid of endotoxins in the body since we know how detrimental they are?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A fiber diet, such as a raw carrot, is effective. If you shred a carrot fairly fine and add olive oil, vinegar, and salt, it is a pleasant enough food that you can eat every day. The carrot contains germicidal but harmless substances. Root vegetables growing underground have to resist mold and bacteria attacks, and that material has the same disinfectant effect in the intestine. Olive oil and vinegar also have a germicidal effect.

So, the salad is a good, protective, daily stimulating food. The bulk stimulates the intestine, generally reducing transit time. According to one survey, the average American had a three-day transit time, while the average person in Africa had less than a one-day transit time.

If you can get your intestinal activity increased, that has benefits far beyond reducing endotoxin. Your liver is constantly processing toxins and hormones. Estrogen, especially, is instantly inactivated when it reaches the liver. Some of it goes into the bile, and some is eliminated through the kidneys. However, if you don't have enough fiber in your intestine, the estrogen in the bile can be reabsorbed and return to the liver. When the liver is exposed to too much estrogen, it slows down and loses its ability to detoxify estrogen. Having a good flow of fiber through your intestine not only suppresses the endotoxin, but it binds the bile and the estrogen content of the bile, preventing its reabsorption.

**Jodelle:** So any kind of fiber has that anti-estrogen effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but raw carrot is a very safe one.

**Jodelle:** When you said salad, you are talking about the raw carrot salad, not necessarily a dark leafy green salad, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. I did an experiment putting lettuce in a closed plastic bag to imitate the intestine's absence of oxygen and kept it at about 90 degrees. After two or three days, the lettuce was horribly rotten, supported terrible bacterial growth, and was foul-smelling. Since we don't have enzymes to break down cellulose, that same kind of process happens when you eat raw leafy material such as lettuce.

**Jodelle:** So stick to just the raw carrot salad if you really want to remove those endotoxins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can get fairly safe fibers in other ways. For example, well-cooked oat bran is a functional alternative, although research in Australia found that chronic use of oat bran itself has some estrogenic and carcinogenic effects on the intestine.

**Jodelle:** What about coconut flour? That is high in fiber.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In studies on pigs, it didn't work so well. It supports either bacterial or fungal growth.

**Jodelle:** That's interesting since most other coconut products we can trust because they help mitigate fungus and yeast in the colon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the coconut oil, if it is well refined and clean, is a good antifungal.

**Jodelle:** Reba also asks: What do you think about bone broth, specifically chicken broth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is one of my favorites. Backs, necks, wings, and feet are all high in collagen. If you cook them thoroughly, let it stand, and skim off the fat, that is very good, high-gelatin food.

**Jodelle:** I've done the wings and the neck. I've never done the feet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You have to be careful getting them from a farmer that you know. A big processor is likely to have processed the chickens with antiseptics, and sometimes the feet soak up a lot of the antiseptic.

**Jodelle:** Ben asks: Do we need to do regular weight training for bone density, or is there something else we can do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The diet really is the main thing. Keeping your stress levels low and your activity comfortable is key; it doesn't have to be anything special. Stress involves several things that interfere with bone repair and renewal. Even a deficiency of salt can create stress that harms the bone. Old people have been told to keep their salt down for blood pressure control, but that adds to their stress, increases adrenaline, and brings up the parathyroid hormone, which tears down the bone.

Keeping a very high ratio of calcium to phosphate in your diet is helpful because that helps to suppress the parathyroid hormone. Parathyroid hormone blocks the use of oxygen in all of your tissues, leading to the production of lactic acid in the bone, which dissolves the bone and contributes to osteoporosis. That same bone-destroying effect lowers the energy production in all of our cells. Therefore, high calcium intake increases our metabolic rate and efficient oxidative metabolism all through the body, not just the bone.

**Jodelle:** Would you also say that being outside in the sun helps with bone density?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, for the Vitamin D. The older a person is, the less cholesterol the skin contains, and it is the ultraviolet light interacting with the cholesterol that makes Vitamin D. A person over the age of 50, especially a dark-skinned person, needs a lot more exposure to sunlight to get their Vitamin D level up adequately.

**Jodelle:** I like how last time you mentioned chopping wood is actually a really great form of exercise.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is something that feels productive and isn't stress-inducing just by boredom. You can see the product of your labor, and that is anti-stress.

**Jodelle:** Sergey asks: How would Dr. Peat recommend dealing with insulin resistance and early type 2 diabetes? Should one be afraid of elevated blood glucose after saying goodbye to low carb or keto?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The chronic stress that elevates the free fatty acids in the blood is the issue. Women in particular have the problem of chronically high free fatty acids because estrogen causes a great activation of the growth hormone, which is a major producer of free fatty acids. It is free fatty acids in general, and especially unsaturated free fatty acids, that interfere with the use of glucose.

Keeping your fat intake low is somewhat helpful, but anything that lowers stress and lowers estrogen is going to increase your insulin sensitivity and your ability to use glucose. Everything that lowers stress tends to lower estrogen and improve your ability to use oxygen productively, converting sugar to carbon dioxide. When you are stressed, have high estrogen, or have too much free fatty acid in the blood, any sugar that is present tends to produce lactic acid instead of carbon dioxide. Lactic acid itself has many toxic, degenerative effects.

**Jodelle:** I've heard a lot of people who went keto for a vast amount of time are now saying they have insulin resistance. It sounds like the stress of going into ketosis is part of the problem.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The ketogenic diet is always stress-promoting, and that means it is diabetogenic to some extent. It isn't strictly generating ketones; hydroxybutyrate is included as a ketone, but it is actually an alcohol, not a ketone. Studies looking at the difference between actual ketosis and the presence of a high proportion of hydroxybutyrate show that hydroxybutyrate stimulates cancer growth and other stress-related things. If you had an artificial source of real ketones, that would probably be beneficial. But when you generate them yourself, you are under stress and creating a cancer-promoting, degenerative situation.

**Jodelle:** I am picking up a trend: stress is the main cause. What is your favorite way to de-stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Playing a musical instrument, painting, or just doing anything interesting. If there is wood to chop, that's a good activity. The culture is designed pretty much to keep people under maximum stress—sort of like "idle hands are likely to get in trouble." The economy is designed to keep everyone under maximum stress so that they don't get in trouble, but naturally, it doesn't work that way.

**Jodelle:** An anonymous listener writes regarding adrenal insufficiency: "All I hear is that cortisol is evil and must be reduced. But isn't a certain amount necessary? Can you address those who have low cortisol?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Out of thousands of people whose blood tests I've seen, I have only seen one or two that were actually deficient in cortisol. Hundreds were diagnosed as having an adrenal deficiency, but their blood tests showed they were doing fine on cortisol.

The adrenals use cholesterol to turn into pregnenolone, and then into DHEA, progesterone, cortisol, and aldosterone. Cortisol and aldosterone are increased by almost any stress. Only a very small fraction of your pregnenolone, cholesterol, or progesterone makes it into cortisol. So, there has to be a great deficiency of cholesterol, pregnenolone, and progesterone before you experience an actual deficiency of cortisol. By the time you reach a real deficiency of cortisol, you are experiencing a whole range of symptoms and problems from low pregnenolone and low progesterone. You can tolerate lots of stress-induced cortisol if it is backed up with plenty of pregnenolone, progesterone, and DHEA.

**Jodelle:** Would that be something they would want to look into supplementing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In experiments on rats 60 years ago, they looked at the hormone levels of rats under stress. Some had higher than average cortisol. They gave them a gigantic dose of pregnenolone—equivalent to a cup full of powder for a person. There were no changes in their steroid hormones except for the ones who were under stress to start with; it brought their cortisol down to normal.

You can't "push upstream" in the adrenals. The more pregnenolone or progesterone you take, the more normal you become. It is the endpoint hormones—like aldosterone, estrogen, and cortisol—that are produced normally only in extreme situations to deal with specific problems. If you supplement those beyond what the body would be making, then you have potential problems.

**Jodelle:** So supplementing pregnenolone might be an easy fix rather than cortisol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There was a well-known book about 20 or 30 years ago on the natural use of hydrocortisone (cortisol). The data he based it on showed that a tiny supplement, like 5 or 10 micrograms, could improve a woman's menstrual cycle. However, I happen to know some of his patients who were given what he called a "physiological dose" of natural cortisol—about 20 milligrams per day, which is what the body normally makes. After two or three months, they all started getting puffy faces—typical Cushing's disease symptoms. Supplementing that can be risky.

**Jodelle:** Leanne asks: What is a good strategy to help with my immune system? I recently found out I have Cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus expressed.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably the majority of people have those viruses. It is a matter of keeping them from expressing themselves and keeping your ability to handle stress optimized.

When you look at studies of general infections—measles, mumps, and so on—if you supplement Vitamin A and Vitamin D alone, those two are just about as effective as a huge vaccination campaign. The viruses that are resident in the majority of people aren't doing any harm if the immune system is okay. However, if you are overweight, your blood level might show a normal amount of Vitamin A and D, but your tissues can be very deficient.

A person will benefit from bringing their Vitamin D and A levels up. With Vitamin D, a serum level of 50 or 60 nanograms per milliliter corresponds to a low rate of diabetes and various infections. Flu infections practically disappear when a person keeps their blood level at least at 50 nanograms per milliliter.

**Jodelle:** I was recently in Hawaii and noticed they don't have a cold and flu season. I wonder if that is because they get Vitamin D every day from ample sun.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known several people who used to have maybe five episodes of colds or flu every fall and winter. When they started taking Vitamin D, they didn't have another episode for several years.

**Jodelle:** What do you think about colostrum?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That probably is helpful in an emergency situation, but I don't think you need it. Magnesium is another nutrient that many people are deficient in. If your diet has too much phosphate, you can't get enough calcium and magnesium to balance it. If your thyroid is low, your cells don't retain magnesium. Magnesium deficiency opens up your immune system to flare-ups of these endangered viruses like Herpes and Epstein-Barr.

**Jodelle:** What about monolaurin, derived from lauric acid in coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The guy who was popularizing that asked me to join the campaign to promote it. I asked him if there had been any safety studies, and he got huffy and said I was anti-scientific. I've looked for safety studies, and I'm not convinced. Any of the lipid things that are germicidal can also be disturbing to our digestive system.

When we eat a fat like butter or coconut oil, it is in the triglyceride form. Our digestive system is equipped to handle that; it breaks the particles up into tiny chylomicrons which pass into the lymphatic system. Chylomicrons are formed only when you have the right amount of the right type of triglycerides. If you put other emulsifying things or very abnormal lipids in, it can disrupt our ability to make chylomicrons. Since chylomicrons are the major pathway for absorbing Vitamins A, K, D, and E, if you disturb them for too long, you can become deficient in the fatty vitamins.

**Jodelle:** An anonymous listener asks: With kidney issues such as frequent urination and dumping minerals, what do you suggest to calm down the kidneys?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The two hormones most protective for the kidneys are progesterone and thyroid. The vitamins I mentioned, especially Vitamin D, are extremely protective. Making sure you get the essential minerals—sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium—in a generous amount every day is protective.

Drinking too much water rather than milk or juices can wash the minerals out of you. It fills up your stomach and satisfies thirst, but it doesn't provide nutrients. It is better to only drink water when you are thirsty. Milk, juice, and coffee are accompanied by essential nutrients.

**Jodelle:** Are you a fan of coconut water?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you open up a fresh green coconut, it is very nice. But I don't trust any of it commercially sold because I've seen some containing preservatives.

**Jodelle:** Allison asks: Can white willow bark be taken instead of aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It works for some people, but it does have other ingredients. The tannin-type substance in any herb can be irritating to the intestine. It is a personal matter whether it works for you.

**Jodelle:** Can you tell people about the benefits of aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has many functions, but the thing that has been studied most is blocking the production of prostaglandins. Any inflammation tends to trigger the formation of these short-acting hormones. Most of them are simply amplifiers of inflammation. They are produced in the brain, heart, and other tissues in response to a minor trigger.

They are produced in proportion to the amount of polyunsaturated fat (PUFA) incorporated into these tissues. As we age, we very efficiently keep adding polyunsaturated fatty acids into our tissue structures. From age 20 to 40, we are probably doubling the amount of PUFA in our tissues. PUFA is what converts to prostaglandins in the event of inflammation.

A fetus or newborn heals an injury without scars. But as the PUFA in our tissue accumulates, wounds heal more slowly, cause more inflammation, and leave scars. Whenever you have systemic inflammation producing lactic acid and prostaglandins, both increase the deposition of collagen. With aging, the body approaches something like a big scar with very high collagen content. Aspirin, by blocking prostaglandins and several other inflammatory mechanisms, is important protection from inflammation and aging.

**Jodelle:** It also helps to lower excess cortisol, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it lowers the pituitary ACTH production. ACTH also brings up the adrenal aldosterone, which contributes to collagen production and deterioration. So, it protects against not just cortisol, but a whole range of degenerative processes.

**Jodelle:** Nick asks: I've been taking cod liver oil pills for Vitamin A and D. He says in a previous interview you said to avoid fish oils. Does that include cod liver oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cod liver oil is at least giving you A and D, which is beneficial if you don't have another source. But I think it is good to use a fish oil-derived Vitamin A and D where most of the other fish oils have been removed.

Studies on the fate of ingested fish oil are interesting. I did experiments with a bottle of unsaturated oils; I put a rubber tube in the bottle and the other end in water. Every day the water climbed up the tube because of the oxygen consumption of the unsaturated fat. Fish oils are extremely quick to react with oxygen. In studies, they found that before they reached the bloodstream, the majority of them had been oxidized.

With aging, the brain accumulates these oxidizable fatty acids, and the oxidation continues in the brain. "Neuroprostane" is what they call the breakdown product when it happens in the brain. The neuroprostanes are made from the type of fatty acid that predominates in fish oil. Before they reach storage, a large part of these fish oils are already oxidized and are immunosuppressive. That toxic effect on the immune system can temporarily reduce inflammation by damaging the cells that would react to harm. So, for about six months they are anti-inflammatory, but after that, the immune deficiencies start showing up.

**Jodelle:** I was never comfortable promoting fish oils because of the processing required.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Historically, it made very good varnish because it oxidizes so thoroughly. If you imagine that happening in your body, you don't want varnished blood vessels.

**Jodelle:** Victoria asks: Can women who are vegans or vegetarians successfully follow Dr. Peat's nutritional guidelines and maintain a healthy menstrual cycle?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It happens that the only non-animal proteins that are really adequate for human needs are potatoes and mushrooms. You can thrive as far as protein goes with either. Mushrooms generally have more trace minerals than potatoes. You can get iron from mushrooms and all other nutrients except B12 and Vitamin A from potatoes.

Adequate bacteria in the intestine will make Vitamin B12. Vitamin A is the main problem. You need carotene, good thyroid function, and Vitamin B12 to convert carotene into the actual Vitamin A needed for making progesterone. The problem becomes that so many vegetables block your thyroid function. As long as you can keep your thyroid function up and have Vitamin B12, you can convert carotene adequately to Vitamin A to make your hormones.

**Jodelle:** Are there foods that naturally promote more progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The only things that provide energy—sodium, calcium, and sugar—are necessary for making the thyroid hormone that you need to make progesterone. But there are no foods that directly go to the progesterone system.

**Jodelle:** I wasn't convinced of the yam thing being a promoter of progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People were trying to sell yams as a progesterone promoter, but the crude sterol in yams is actually estrogenic and very toxic. Russell Marker, who developed the production of progesterone from yams, decided to try the raw yam powder. The next morning he said he looked like he'd been run over by a truck; he was all black and blue. He had broken so many blood vessels that he was bleeding internally.

**Jodelle:** Elisa asks: What does Dr. Peat think of stevia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is very sweet, but I'm not sure it is safe. In a pinch, it can lower blood pressure, but I don't think there is any real problem with hypertension if you are eating well and keeping your thyroid function alright. Hypothyroidism is almost always behind hypertension.

**Jodelle:** I remember reading studies linked to infertility with stevia. Finally, do you have a favorite quick and easy recipe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I make a lot of custards. When I was confident there were safe sources of powdered milk, I had a recipe for pancakes with nothing but egg and powdered milk fried in butter. But you have to be sure your powdered milk doesn't have an anti-caking agent.

I am experimenting with recipes using Masa—nixtamalized corn. That is a very safe and digestible way to use a cereal. The processing in lime eliminates most of the toxins and breaks down the protein and starch.

**Jodelle:** How do you do your custard?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just eggs, milk, sugar, and vanilla.

**Jodelle:** That sounds easy enough. Dr. Peat, thank you once again for your time and sharing your vast knowledge. We appreciate you.

title: One Radio Network: Patrick Timpone: Dr. Peat Answers Questions Regarding Health, Diet and Nutrition Part 2
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** What does cloudy urine indicate? Is it the body wasting calcium or a yeast infection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you are drinking lots of milk or eating a high meat diet, the phosphate has to get excreted. The phosphate shows up in the urine and precipitates in the presence of either magnesium or calcium. It only precipitates if the pH is above a certain point.

If you have a very high protein diet, most of the time your urine will be acidic and it will be clear despite having a tremendous amount of phosphate in it. But when something raises the pH of your urine—which can be eating a lot of fruit or vegetables, or hyperventilating—it changes. If you blow out too much carbon dioxide, the pH of your urine goes up to keep your blood at the right pH, slightly alkaline. When your urine is neutral or higher on the alkaline side, then any phosphate and calcium is going to precipitate and make it cloudy.

**Patrick Timpone:** Here's an email from Brenda: "I recently started taking Progest-E and it's helped my cyclical mood symptoms very much. I've been taking it for days 14 through 28 in my cycle. I hate to stop taking it because I have PMS moodiness the day after I stop. Would there be any harm in just continuing to take it nonstop for a while, even if it means I miss a period or two?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known quite a few women who took some every day and kept cycling without any problem. But what they should be aware of is that if you take a little extra just before the expected time of ovulation, it will trigger early ovulation. Then, if you stop taking it or take less, it will bring on an early menstruation. So if you're going to take it every day, it has to be the same amount every day.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about someone perimenopausal where the cycle takes a long time? The period just doesn't want to come. You get the bloating, but it doesn't want to come. Are there any safe herbs or anything you can do to let it go so you can feel better?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Behind the problem with the balance of progesterone and estrogen, the basic thing is almost always low thyroid. Some women will use a quick-acting thyroid so as soon as they start getting a symptom of PMS, they take just a little extra. They can adjust the hormones on a day-to-day basis that way. Other people increase their glandular thyroid starting at ovulation just knowing that they don't want to have PMS.

The opposite happens when a person is hypothyroid. They might not have any ovulation at all, or they might have extreme and prolonged menstruation. It's a very reliable treatment for prolonged menstruation to just get the right amount of thyroid. You can usually turn off a hypothyroid excess menstruation in two days with a supplement.

**Patrick Timpone:** A quick-acting thyroid is generally a prescription?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually in the US. It's a T3, such as Cytomel.

**Patrick Timpone:** And that's just a pig or cow thyroid, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, it's purely synthetic, but it's exactly the same chemical that we make or would get from an animal.

**Patrick Timpone:** Mark wants to know: "Why is burning sugar for fuel healthier for the human body than burning ketones? Also, if a diabetic wants to use fructose medicinally, how can fructose be used by the cells if the cells need glucose? Does the body convert fructose to glucose?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The body can exchange them. The fructose enters the glycolysis process at almost the same place glucose does and then is oxidized the same way glucose is. A lot of doctors say that the brain, muscles, and heart can't use fructose. But actually, there is evidence that they do have the particular fructose transporter or glucose transporter that works for fructose. So the brain and heart can use fructose.

Ketones are good if you get them from fruit or vegetables such as potatoes. But if you have to produce the ketones yourself, they are only produced under stress in the body. They're good when you can get them from food, but it's hard to make them yourself without stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why does the Budwig diet against cancer have so much success when it uses Omega-3 flaxseed oil, given that your work has concluded that unsaturated fatty acids are not good for us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1954, a professor from the University of Guadalajara had an article in *Prevention* magazine describing his success using laxatives for his patients to get their intestine clean. It's been known for probably 3,000 years that laxatives are helpful for cancer patients because of the toxins produced in the intestine. He happened to use a cup of linseed oil, or flax oil, as the purge. It would rush right through and clean out the intestine.

Until that time, Johanna Budwig had published as a co-author a couple of articles in a soap and fat journal and wasn't doing anything unconventional. But right after that article came out in *Prevention*, she started developing her theory of the N-3 fats. My theory was that she had gone insane during that period when she stopped being a research associate for the soap professor. Shortly after that, several little booklets came out published by a Disney subsidiary in Europe describing her theory in very crazy terms. Anyone interested in doing her program should look at those books because they were radically changed when they were presented in English to make it sound much saner than they were.

Her diet consisted of mostly cottage cheese or the equivalent curds. Because of the low iron content of cottage cheese, both milk and cottage cheese are very good protective foods for people with cancer. Fruits and milk, because of the low iron content and low PUFA content, are good for cancer patients. I think as far as the flax oil can work as a laxative, it's beneficial, but when it's working as a food, then it has the risk of suppressing your metabolism.

**Patrick Timpone:** John asks for Ray's opinions on Hans Nieper's mineral transporters. Why does nobody talk about them anymore?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For one thing, we don't really need mineral transporters. People like Gilbert Ling many years ago showed that the doctrine that the cell is enclosed in an impermeable or semipermeable membrane simply isn't so. When they got isotopes where they could actually see the type of sodium atom that was being added to a system, they could demonstrate that the sodium atoms were freely moving in and out of cells. There was no barrier function at all at the surface. This applies to all of the dissolved minerals and other substances. There's just no barrier there to deal with. So that's the basic thing: we don't have any need for a mineral transporter because minerals move freely in and out.

**Patrick Timpone:** Jesse writes: "I don't know if Ray Peat knows anything about the organic sulfur you've been talking about. I've been taking the sulfur and iodine (Lugol's) together. My thyroid hormones have gone down. I need to know if the sulfur will take iodine out, too. Should they be taken at opposite ends of the day?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Too much iodine is probably the problem.

**Patrick Timpone:** Too much iodine can actually lower the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do you know what's a good amount of iodine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've got a list of about 70 articles from around the world looking at the incidence of thyroid cancer and thyroiditis. They see that above half a milligram (0.5 mg) of iodine per day chronically increases the incidence of thyroid disease.

**Patrick Timpone:** Wow, 0.5 milligrams is not a lot, is it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but that's over a period of many years where it is chronically high.

**Patrick Timpone:** I wonder how many drops of Lugol's that is. Do you have any idea how many milligrams are in one drop?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's a few milligrams.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you wouldn't want to do more than just a couple drops.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**Patrick Timpone:** "I'm a follower of Mr. Peat's. I haven't seen anything mentioned about uterine fibroids. What is his suggestion for the best way to get rid of them? Serrapeptase and other enzymes have not worked for me."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think normalizing thyroid is the best thing. I had an experience with a woman who was about 40 at the time, hadn't had any kids, and wanted to get pregnant. She had a fibroid plugging the end of her uterus by the fallopian tubes about the size of a tennis ball. I explained the physiology to her. She adjusted, taking enough thyroid that she could keep her estrogen level down while keeping the other hormones up.

It happens that her pulse averaged about 110 per minute. Her doctor told her she would die from keeping her pulse that fast. But she had an ultrasound every month, and every month that she kept her thyroid at that level, the fibroid shrank. I think she started around March or April, and by August the fibroid had disappeared and she was pregnant.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is a slower pulse necessarily better?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, generally it's not.

**Patrick Timpone:** We've been told it is. I've been exercising a lot and my resting pulse is sometimes 50 or so. That could actually be a sign of weakness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, very often it's hypothyroid. Long-distance runners, for example. If you put a person on a treadmill—in one experiment they had them walk so their pulse stayed about 120 beats per minute—in less than an hour, their blood showed almost no T3, the active hormone. If a person is healthy, as soon as they catch their breath and rest for a day, their T3 is right back where it should be. But if there's anything wrong with their diet, just that moderate amount of exercise every day can push your thyroid lower and lower.

One of the ways that you might see a bad effect of a low pulse is if the distance between the top and the bottom blood pressure is very great. It should be no more than 50 points difference. It's called pulse pressure. So the systolic minus the diastolic should be 50 or less.

**Patrick Timpone:** But isn't your heart stronger if you're beating less per minute?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not necessarily. You can give a person an anti-thyroid drug and their heart rate will just go slower and slower. I've known people who had a pulse of 40 or 50 at rest and who were really very miserable. When they got their pulse up to 70 or 80 at rest by taking thyroid, they felt much better.

**Patrick Timpone:** You can often do that just by diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, avoiding the foods that are blocking your thyroid function. In America, it's mostly the polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs). But I've known people who were eating a pure soy diet or a lot of raw cabbage and broccoli. Just stopping that diet for a week or two, they popped right back.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the PUFAs and soy are definitely anti-thyroid. What about broccoli and cauliflower? If you cook them, are they okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're still slightly anti-thyroid. If a person wants to really test what low thyroid is like, they can juice some raw cabbage or broccoli and drink a glass or two of that per day.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are some things that boost thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Milk and orange juice.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you talk a bit about Hashimoto's? Is that overactive or autoimmune?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's underactive. Most of the so-called autoimmune things—the antibodies—really are part of a recovery process. Anytime you injure a tissue, your immune system will try to eat up the junk. It treats the tissue as if it had been infected. That's why they started calling it thyroiditis.

**Patrick Timpone:** It's not the immune system attacking your thyroid; it's doing what it's supposed to do.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If you block the thyroid function for some reason, then you have to stimulate it more strongly with TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone). Just that stimulation creates a type of inflammation. If that goes on too long—for example, blocking it with too much iodine, too much PUFA, or estrogen—then your immune system will come in and clean up some of the junk.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ann says: "I'm 44 years old and the day before my period I start to get a headache. I'm assuming the headache is caused by low progesterone. I have been doing the Paleo diet for over three years now. Any suggestions?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually some good tropical fruit, orange juice, and milk or cheese will get the thyroid back to normal functioning. In the short run, a thyroid supplement can help. There have been studies where just giving even a synthetic thyroid for five or six months will correct the antibody problem in Hashimoto's.

**Patrick Timpone:** What if somebody has a hard time with casein or lactose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's no lactose in cheese, so if there's a lactose problem, cheese will take care of it. Preferably raw, grass-fed without additives.

**Patrick Timpone:** And the casein in the milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's a good protein and has many good features. But an even better protein is the juice out of a potato. In a few extreme cases where a person had no digestion for any kind of ordinary protein, if they juiced some raw potatoes and then cooked that juice, they could instantly assimilate it and got over their sensitivity to other proteins.

**Patrick Timpone:** Please ask your guest about bioidentical hormone replacement. Which testing protocol would be best?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That term can apply to testosterone, progesterone, DHEA, thyroid—any of those. But it is also applied to estrogen. It happens that the most dangerous of the estrogens, estradiol, is bioidentical. So it doesn't make it safer. Whether it's synthetic or natural estrogen, you still have to be very careful.

**Patrick Timpone:** What does Mr. Peat think about the ketogenic diet? Also, what about "Bulletproof coffee" where you whip up coconut oil or butter into your coffee? And refined vs. expeller-pressed coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Regarding the ketogenic diet, I already talked about that. It's a matter of stress. Anything that stresses you can turn on your production of ketones. It's better to have some sugar in your diet so you don't have the stress that makes the ketones. But if you can get ketones from fruit and potatoes, they're fine.

Regarding the coffee, a lot of people tell me they're doing that. But cream in the coffee is so good and it mixes nicely, whereas the coconut oil and butter just float on the surface.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about refined vs. expeller-pressed coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Refined is the only thing I've used. I used to occasionally get some homemade coconut oil that was just delicious for making coconut ice cream, but it happens to be allergenic. If you have any stress problems or digestive problems, it's better to use the refined, deodorized coconut oil.

**Patrick Timpone:** Brian asks: "I would like to know what to do to overcome radiation therapy for prostate cancer. I did not finish the total number of treatments, but following the treatments I'm still having radiation issues."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies of people 60 years after Hiroshima and 20 years after Chernobyl in which they could still see inflammatory processes in the blood traced to the radiation exposure. It's really a lingering inflammation that you have to deal with. With that kind of radiation, nothing is actually placed in the body like with fallout. The lingering effect of external radiation puts you into an inflammatory state.

All of the things we've been talking about—the good high-energy foods like milk and cheese—help to heal that. Keeping your thyroid function up activates the repair system which lowers inflammation. Anytime your energy falls, you move towards inflammation. So don't hyperventilate. Do everything to keep your blood sugar steady and the inflammation will gradually subside.

**Patrick Timpone:** William is a naturopathic doctor and wants to know what you think about Brian Peskin's claims that Omega-3s and fish oils are unnecessary.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, he's right about the fish oil. There's no evidence that it's an essential fat. But also, there's no evidence that I've seen that the "Parent Essential Oils" (PEOs) are needed either.

**Patrick Timpone:** Catherine writes: "My heart rate is about 85 sitting down, but standing up it's about 110. I was told I had POTS (Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome). What is the best way to test for food allergies?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Blood tests are often misinterpreted. You can see a reaction in the blood, but sometimes it's just showing that the person has been exposed to a food; it doesn't really correlate with symptoms. I think testing a food by leaving it out of your diet entirely for at least a week is best. If the symptoms go away, then you can guess that you're allergic to it.

Regarding the heart rate sitting down and standing up: High estrogen affects the nervous system so that your sympathetic side is weak and the parasympathetic is overactive. That's why women get varicose veins so much more often than men. High estrogen weakens the wall of the vein; progesterone tones up the veins. When the veins aren't returning the blood to the heart—when the blood falls into your legs—then your heart has to beat faster. Progesterone and thyroid are needed to tone up the veins and return the blood to the heart.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does Dr. Peat have any recommendations for rebuilding or healing the vagus nerve?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My last few newsletters have been talking about the problems of stress, for example, "learned helplessness." If an animal is restrained and doesn't have the experience of being able to escape, they might let themselves drown in a tank of water in two or three minutes, whereas a normal rat would swim for days. That's from too much parasympathetic activity.

I've been working out some of the implications of what happens after middle age that are equivalent to learned helplessness. The body has experienced so many problems it can't deal with that it starts shifting too strongly to the parasympathetic. When we go to bed at night, normally we don't need to spend a lot of energy, so the parasympathetic lowers our blood sugar. But after middle age, it can lower the blood sugar so much that the other side of the nervous system reacts with surges of adrenaline and cortisol. That's where the degenerative things come in.

In liver disease, for example, they found that they can prevent inflammation and fibrosis of the liver just by cutting the vagus nerve so it doesn't reach the liver. So you don't want to overstimulate the parasympathetic. The Gulf War syndrome had to do with exposure to organophosphate nerve gases, but people are being exposed to similar chemicals in insecticides or even in the air in airliners. All of these exposures are creating an overactive vagus syndrome.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the underlying cause of severe allergies like runny nose and sneezing that occur after a meal?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's usually something in the intestine, not necessarily what you ate in this meal, but sometimes what you ate yesterday or the day before. Eating starts the peristalsis and it moves an irritant down to a sensitive place in the intestine. Runny nose and sneezing are the most common symptoms. Animal experiments showed that just pressure in the rectum or intestine can trigger migraine headaches, runny noses, coughing, sneezing, and even epileptic seizures. Disturbed blood sugar intensifies the sensitivity of the intestine.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there such a thing as thyroid resistance or high Reverse T3 that doesn't show up on blood tests?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's important to measure Reverse T3 if you're going to measure the thyroid hormones at all. You can't interpret the T3 itself, which is the active hormone, unless you know how much Reverse T3 there is because that can interfere with the active hormone. So you have to look at the ratio of active to Reverse T3.

**Patrick Timpone:** Here's an email that says after eating peanuts, his mouth cracked and he had inflammation lesions. A lab said he had fungus/candida. Was he just allergic to peanuts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That could be. But when it lingers for a long time, there could be several things. A nutritional deficiency might have been co-acting with the allergy. A lot of B-vitamin deficiencies can make sores around the mouth. Inflammation in the intestine can activate viruses to break out inside the mouth or on the lips. Benzocaine ointment, which you can get at a drugstore, happens to be an antiseptic as well as an anesthetic and will often clear up a little skin problem, whether it's a virus, germ, or fungus.

**Patrick Timpone:** Lindsay says she has low thyroid and is on 120mg of Nature-Throid but still experiencing many symptoms.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a particular brand of thyroid doesn't work, I think it's good to change brands. Armour Thyroid is fairly reliable. There's a synthetic called Proloid S which is an old established brand available in many countries. Cynoplus is made by companies related to the ones that make Cytomel. Cynoplus is very similar to Nature-Throid and Armour, but being synthetic, it lacks some of the potential allergens that the natural thyroids might have.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the ideal diet for Type 2 diabetes? Also, I'm taking 1000mg of L-tryptophan at night for sleep. Do you recommend I discontinue this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, discontinue the tryptophan. There are articles on my website explaining how unsaturated fats are an essential problem in causing diabetes and sugar is not a problem and has been used as a cure. Getting the right diet and making sure the thyroid function is optimized are the basic things. Aspirin is well known to help regulate blood sugar and lower inflammation problems associated with diabetes.

**Patrick Timpone:** Stella says: "I keep getting acne. I sweat in saunas and take chlorella, but still have issues."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid and Vitamin A are the basic things, but the skin and the intestine are very closely connected. You want to make sure you aren't eating any foods that aren't well digested or that irritate your intestine.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about using the far infrared sauna and niacin together for rosacea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Niacin sometimes refers to nicotinic acid. Nicotinic acid happens to increase your histamine, serotonin, and prostaglandins, all of which are inflammatory. I don't think it's good for anyone to take nicotinic acid other than as occurs in food. Niacinamide is a form of that same vitamin (B3) that is active in cells and doesn't release those inflammatory materials.

**Patrick Timpone:** Brenda writes: "Could you please ask Dr. Peat about natural ways to reverse high prolactin levels? I recently started taking Progest-E."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes progesterone does help, but thyroid is the basic thing. Tryptophan and serotonin happen to turn on a trigger that increases prolactin and TSH; they tend to go together. If your thyroid doesn't respond adequately to the rising TSH, it isn't able to lower the prolactin. Without thyroid, sometimes increasing the salt in your diet and using a Vitamin B6 supplement can correct the prolactin.

**Patrick Timpone:** Carl in Urbana is in his 70s. He tried a high fat diet (70%) and stopped feeling cold, but now he seems to be in an adrenaline state early in the evening. He wakes with a higher temperature and pulse rate, then cannot get back to sleep. He asks: "Since my cortisol state is the highest in the morning, would it be best for me to avoid any foods that would stimulate insulin production in the morning?"

The ones that ate saturated fats, such as coconut oil, were lean at the end of their lives, no matter how much they ate. **Patrick Timpone:** These are the classic things Ray Peat calls PUFAs.

**Adam Bergstrom:** Polyunsaturated fatty acids, highly unsaturated fatty acids, Omega-3s mainly—DHA, EPA, ALA.

**Patrick Timpone:** We've been told that toxic substances steal electrons and cause oxidation. Is that correct?

**Patrick Timpone:** Does eating cholesterol raise your levels?

**Patrick Timpone:** We have a caller, Mike, with severe digestive inflammation. He juices beets and carrots but reacts to fibrous foods.

Recent theorists have proposed the "danger or damage" theory: the immune system recognizes damaged tissue as foreign. If you damage your thyroid by taking too much iodine or PUFA, that is structural damage the immune system tries to clean up. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Aspirin activates thyroid function and mitochondrial oxidation. 1mg of Vitamin K per day is adequate to keep the liver making clotting agents, which aspirin might affect.

title: One Radio Network: Health of the Human Body
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Raymond Peat has been kind enough to come on the show from time to time the last few months. He started his work with progesterone and related hormones in 1968. His website is RayPeat.com. Good morning, Dr. Peat.

They found that with each generation, the symptoms were worse, until the third generation was sterile. That's something biologists have been covering up for at least 50 years—probably much longer. When something mildly harmful persists beyond one generation, it is intensified every generation. Even without modifying or mutating genes, it accumulates epigenetic changes and alters the course of development. In just three generations of eating whatever had gone wrong with that grain, the animals were sterile.

**Patrick Timpone:** So they gave animals GMO grain and by the third generation, they were sterile?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, most had very small litters, and the few that survived were sterile. Similar experiments were done 50 or 60 years ago. They would make a small nick in the egg of a frog, and there would be slight changes as that animal grew up, but its offspring would be even more damaged. The third generation wouldn't be able to reproduce at all.

**Patrick Timpone:** Through what mechanism does that work epigenetically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mechanists say that if it doesn't change your genes, it doesn't hurt you, because they claim everything is permanently built into the genesis. They believe you simply print out what is inherited. But that isn't the way life works. That was a dogma starting in 1890 called Neo-Darwinism.

Until about 1975 or 1980, doctors insisted that a woman could be starved, stressed, or very sick, but as long as the baby stayed in the uterus, it wouldn't be affected. In fact, animal experiments showed that if your grandmother was stressed or poorly nourished, your health is going to be affected. The whole body changed its form—smaller brain, higher blood pressure—for generations after a serious stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** So we know that with ongoing dietary and lifestyle changes, genes express themselves differently?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Everything is constantly being checked against what's going on elsewhere in the organism and its environment. Our genes are constantly being expressed according to the present situation. The doctrine of immutable genes was a fantasy imposed for political reasons.

This has positive implications, too. A group in Berkeley in 1960 gave lab animals playgrounds instead of little boxes. The parents grew up happier and slightly more intelligent, but the offspring were even more intelligent. The third generation had bigger brains than had ever been measured before.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there anything in particular that has been top of mind for you recently?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For years I've noticed that drugs, nutritional supplements, foods, and cosmetics are being modified for the manufacturer's ease with silicon dioxide powder. I finally decided to bring together some concrete information about that.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is silicon dioxide something we definitely want to keep out of our bodies?

**Patrick Timpone:** What does silicon dioxide do in the body?

A particle of a certain size is interpreted by the cell's inflammasome the same way as an asbestos crystal. As it gets smaller towards a nanoparticle, it becomes more toxic and enters cells more easily.

These particles pass through the wall of the intestine. Cells in the intestine are designed to sample antigens in the food, so they deliberately take up particles. However, they can't digest silica, so they accumulate it. Their immune function is gradually destroyed by accumulating this indigestible fibrous material.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are other common additives in supplements we should avoid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anything other than sugar, salt, or other relatively pure edible substances shouldn't be there. For example, magnesium stearate. It sounds chemically like an edible substance, but it is manufactured and accumulates contaminants.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there anything you take regularly to hedge your bets?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have stopped using any nutritional supplement orally. I found that I could consume gallons of orange juice—huge amounts of vitamin C—without issue. But the smallest amount of a vitamin C supplement gave me a bad cough, intestinal inflammation, and headaches. When I stopped taking it, those symptoms went away. It would take only about 2 milligrams of synthetic ascorbic acid to make me sick, whereas I could consume 4,000 milligrams of ascorbic acid in natural food forms.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you don't feel it's necessary to supplement vitamin C?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. After I stopped taking it, I checked how much ascorbic acid was coming out in my urine. I was excreting between 1,000 and 2,000 milligrams daily. I was extracting vitamin C from meat and milk. Nutrition charts show meat has very little ascorbic acid, but the same molecule in the oxidized form—dehydroascorbate—is concentrated in the cells. In the cells, ascorbic acid acts as an essential oxidant. We get this form in meat, eggs, and milk.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks: How does canned milk compare to fresh milk? And are goat milk and cheese good sources of calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cheeses are great sources of most nutrients—calcium, magnesium, B vitamins—though deficient in iron. Canned milk is slightly lower in vitamin C and some B vitamins. The main concern historically was lead soldering, which was corrected 20 or 30 years ago. However, you must be alert to can liners, as estrogenic plastics are sometimes used.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do some people do better on goat or sheep cheese?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, the fat particle is more thoroughly homogenized in goat milk. Also, goats are pickier about what they eat, so it is a more certain source of nutrients like vitamin E because they don't like stale food.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about thyroid supplementation. Is it daily? For life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1940, the US Agriculture Department declared that thyroid glands must be removed at the slaughterhouse. Before that, everyone who ate animal products—fish heads, organ meats, sausages containing glands—was getting thyroid in their diet every day. Suddenly, our meat supply was deprived of it. Milk became one of the rare sources because the mother puts hormones into the milk.

For example, after the Three Mile Island incident, women breathing leaking isotopes did not have thyroid-deficient babies as long as they were breastfeeding, because the milk provided the hormone.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a concern with mercury when consuming fish?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All food is getting mercury now because smoke circulates it around the world. However, studies found that the brightest kids had the highest mercury content, showing that if they are well-nourished, the mercury can pass through them.

Hans Selye did experiments poisoning animals with mercury until their kidneys were damaged. When he gave them a good dose of vitamin C combined with the mercury, their kidneys looked normal. He showed that mercury was reduced to a non-toxic form. A good balance of oxidizing and reducing substances—like flavonoids in fruits and vegetables—helps the body eliminate it.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks if soaking grains is similar to the lye process you talk about.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not exactly, but it is another way of creating a more nutritious product. If the grain hasn't been killed by heat, wetting it activates sprouting enzymes. The seed stores starch or oil for energy and concentrated nitrogen (arginine, lysine) to grow the sprout. When you activate those enzymes, you reduce toxic proteins and starches and increase the nutritional value. The alkali (lye) process doesn't activate the proteins, but it chemically reduces toxins and increases niacin.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can we do the lye process at home?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You cook it until it swells up and the husk comes off the seed.

**Mike (Caller):** I'm taking 30 milligrams of Armour Thyroid—about 10 pills a day—and I don't feel any heating. My lab reports say I'm within range, but I feel no change.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Broda Barnes, a pioneer in thyroid therapy, found that low thyroid regions had high rates of cancer and heart disease. He put his patients on thyroid supplements and in 30 years had no patient die of heart disease. His average dose was 120 milligrams (2 grains) of Armour Thyroid.

Barnes found several things interfere with thyroid. He would increase the dose while watching the patient's temperature. If the temperature didn't rise to normal (98.6°F after breakfast), he looked for interferences. Too much protein, specifically muscle meat rich in methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan, inhibits the thyroid. Calcium in milk protects against that anti-thyroid effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** Mike, have you checked for dental issues like cavitations? Even if you don't have root canals, old extraction sites can have infections on meridians that affect the thyroid.

**Mike (Caller):** My dental is good, no root canals. My pulse stays around 58 to 60.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some people have stored enough polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) in their tissues that it can take six months or more of thyroid supplementation before their tissues respond. The fats interfere with the use of glucose to activate thyroxine. Sometimes it takes a temporary large dose to get the system going.

**Patrick Timpone:** What can we do for the heart muscle itself?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Inflammation is the worst thing for the heart and arteries. Polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) are the key to the inflammatory process. They convert to prostaglandins, which amplify any problem. This leads to the trapping of fatty acid esters of cholesterol. It isn't pure cholesterol that causes the problem; it's the accumulated fatty acid ester.

In animal experiments, a T3 (active thyroid) supplement would energize an enlarged, fibrous heart so it could clear out the excess collagen. Broda Barnes found that heart diseases were essentially prevented when patients were kept on the right amount of thyroid.

**Patrick Timpone:** Did he use T3 or a combo?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He used only Armour Thyroid. The industry convinced doctors that pure thyroxine was more scientific, but it isn't the same. Healthy young men can convert thyroxine to T3, but people under stress, aging, or with high estrogen cannot produce T3 adequately. Armour provides the T3 everyone needs during stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** How can we remove age spots?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw a woman who developed brown age spots after six months on an estrogen supplement. Within a few weeks of using progesterone, they disappeared. It was a sensitivity to estrogen excess.

In the brain, vitamin E can activate the removal of lipofuscin (age pigment). Eating vitamin E gets it into the bloodstream in the proper form to stop and reverse age pigment.

**Patrick Timpone:** How much clay or charcoal should we use for detox?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1970s, Gerhard Volkheimer showed that particles up to 10 times the size of a red blood cell can pass through the intestine into the bloodstream. This includes charcoal, clay, and minerals. Particulate matter should be taken with food containing cellulose fiber, which prevents those particles from passing into the bloodstream.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about using a teaspoon of Clorox in water to soak vegetables?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, dilute Clorox disinfects. Ideally, you use hydrogen peroxide because it leaves no chemical residue.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about navigating diet issues. Is it just trial and error?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone has a different internal ecology of bacteria. If you are low in thyroid, digestion is slow, allowing bacteria to live farther up the intestine than they should. Healthy people keep bacteria confined to the colon.

Using fibrous foods that are resistant to bacterial degradation helps control overgrowth. Raw carrots are an example; they contain antiseptics. A carrot salad—shredded carrot with olive or coconut oil, vinegar, and salt—acts as a broad-spectrum antiseptic for the intestine.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does stomach acid actually digest, or just keep bacteria down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Both. But digestion requires the exact anatomy of the intestine—the micro-projections—along with the enzymes. People deficient in hydrochloric acid are usually malnourished and low thyroid. You need carbon dioxide (from thyroid metabolism) to produce stomach acid.

**Patrick Timpone:** So reflux could be tied to thyroid?

**Patrick Timpone:** Why do doctors still prescribe fish oils?

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener is concerned about the fructose in orange juice being equivalent to soda.

Problems arise in experiments where they feed a diet high in PUFA combined with excess fructose. The PUFA blocks the proper handling of sugar. If we deprive ourselves of PUFA, our bodies handle sugars properly.

**Patrick Timpone:** Should we check fasting blood sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your thyroid is good and you didn't overeat protein at bedtime, stress hormones rise only slightly during the night. If sugar is used up, cortisol and adrenaline rise in the morning, causing high morning glucose. Eating fruit or milk helps keep morning cortisol to a minimum.

**Patrick Timpone:** How can we lower cortisol at night for better sleep?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A fibrous diet helps. Irritation in the intestine escapes control when blood sugar dips. A mild fibrous food in the afternoon—like a carrot salad or cooked mushrooms/bamboo shoots—protects against irritation. Aspirin late in the day reduces inflammation. Having carbohydrate like orange juice or milk with sugar at bedtime helps maintain sleep and reduce the cortisol rise.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about accessory thyroid glands. Are they effective if the primary gland is removed?

By the time George Crile Jr. took over, they were doing almost no thyroid surgeries. They would supplement with thyroid to suppress TSH, allowing patients to live perfectly well without surgery.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener has high barium and high blood pressure. Suggestions?

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the best way to activate our own stem cells?

In the pancreas, for example, PUFA and nitric oxide kill newly born beta cells. Sugar helps stem cells survive. It is a competition between polyunsaturated fats and glucose for whether the newly born cells will survive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A healthy liver can store glycogen, so a healthy person can go 12 to 18 hours without eating. But if you have too much PUFA in your body, as soon as blood sugar dips, you pull PUFA into circulation and start damaging tissues.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does coffee help?

**Patrick Timpone:** Does decaf coffee still have benefits?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, if it is decaffeinated with carbon dioxide rather than solvents. Coffee contains potassium, magnesium, niacin, and B vitamins. It is a significant nutritional source.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Armour used to test every batch on mice for potency. In the 1990s, the company was sold and changed. There are other products using pure beef or pork thyroid. The shortages are often powered by regulators; the FDA has been serving the pharmaceutical industry to remove traditional products.

title: One Radio Network: Natural Healing
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Ray Peat is a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon, with a specialization in physiology. He has taught at schools all over the place, including the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, and the National College of Naturopathic Medicine. He started years ago with progesterone-related hormones in 1968 and has been working on both the practical and theoretical aspects of this work for a very long time. Dr. Peat, good morning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good morning.

**Patrick Timpone:** How are you doing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are you really 85 revolutions around the sun?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, no. Yesterday I saw a thing on the internet saying I'm 83, but I'm really only 82. One place said it was 114.

**Patrick Timpone:** Who are some of your real heroes in the field of health, nutrition, and healing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I read lots of old books that the family had, early 20th century and mid-19th century. Lots of the people were not very well known, but there was a lot of good information in the medical culture that was pushed aside. Starting around the Second World War, the pharmaceutical industry really took over medicine.

One of my early interests was a doctor who wrote columns in the newspapers for many years, Walter C. Alvarez, a gastroenterologist. He was, in a way, pushing a conventional line. For example, the 19th-century doctors believed in food digestion poisoning—bacterial poisoning in the intestine. He wanted to disprove that, showing that toxins didn't cause headaches. To show that it was just a myth, he stuffed his medical students' rectums with cotton wads. All of those who were susceptible to headaches got a headache just from the cotton pressure. He said this disproves the idea that headaches are caused by toxicity in the intestine. But of course, that didn't logically prove anything, just that pressure is enough, and toxins often lead to pressure in the intestine.

A lot of Russians were showing the interaction of the nervous system with the intestine around that same time. "Nervism" was a 19th-century theory of medicine in Russia. They saw the nervous system as controlling sickness, so the interaction of the digestive system and the brain was a big topic of research. They showed that if you put a balloon in an animal's intestine and inflated it, nothing would happen if the animal's blood sugar was good. But if you lowered the blood sugar and inflated the intestine, it would cause all kinds of things: asthma, seizures, the equivalent of a headache, and vascular distortions throughout the organism.

The combination of energy in the form of blood sugar and stress in the intestine will cause that whole range of so-called psychosomatic ailments. Some French Canadians, following Hans Selye, showed that the immune system similarly interacts with the intestine and the energy supply. If you drop the blood glucose level, the intestine becomes extremely sensitive to allergens that otherwise wouldn't be noticed. The energy and the brain, which has the highest requirement for glucose as its energy source, are behind the psychosomatic and allergic ailments.

**Patrick Timpone:** So it's fair to say there are many different components in the nervous system contributing to gut issues, including blood sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. About 20 or 30 years ago, some psychologists were demonstrating learned helplessness. Training the brain to believe that escape is impossible made the whole organism shut down. The heart would stop beating in a few minutes rather than a few hours if the animal was convinced that escape was possible. The whole organism is either energized or shut down by the perspective of what is possible. Insight becomes a life-saving matter.

**Patrick Timpone:** You can extrapolate that out and think of all the physiological things going on with people who feel trapped in their life, job, or relationship.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen that happen. Just with medical diagnosis, the doctor tells a person that they have an incurable disease and they pretty soon die.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it any surprise to you that we're so inextricably connected with everything that we think, believe, and feel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. I never was committed to any particular so-called scientific view of the world. It all seemed perfectly reasonable to an ignorant kid looking at the world and hearing these different experiments. Scientific medicine always seemed like a closed, dogmatic way of seeing things. Since about the 1940s, the pharmaceutical industry has shaped medical ideas so that it's really an outlet for their products. You get a diagnosis, and then you can funnel the drugs in. Anything curative, like the old medical practice of giving people bran to cure constipation—like the Kellogg Institute—isn't profitable to the pharmaceutical industry.

**Patrick Timpone:** Isn't that how Kellogg started? His whole thing was constipation, wasn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In the mid-19th century in England and France, the autopsy cause of death was often given as inflammation of the intestine. Now, having an inflamed colon is a very common thing in a dying person, but they don't think of it as the cause of death. It was people like Walter Alvarez who said, "See, it isn't toxins causing a headache, it's just the pressure." That took attention away from the intestine as a constant source of toxins and allergens. But it's really our most susceptible interface with the outside world. We're constantly putting these risky substances into our system.

**Patrick Timpone:** That's why some folks get constipated and get a headache. Those two tend to go together.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure. And asthma attacks and seizures. When I was about 10, our dog found a coffee can full of bacon grease that had been saved to make soap. The dog liked the taste and ate the whole quart of bacon grease and had a seizure. That made Walter Alvarez's publication so interesting—to see a seizure brought on by eating fat. Lots of people had experimented showing that the intestine could trigger a seizure, headache, runny nose, or sore throat. Just about any symptom you can think of can be triggered from the intestine.

**Patrick Timpone:** We have a question from Dennis: "I've heard so much about this classic autoimmune issue. Could Dr. Peat give us his theory on this autoimmune problem?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For a long time, people noticed that women have far more autoimmune problems than men, and about five times the incidence of thyroid disease. There is a very close connection. Estrogen sensitizes your immune system. It acts on your brain and your glucose supply. For example, it activates insulin secretion, but it shifts your metabolism away from glucose towards fat oxidation. That makes you less able to oxidize glucose, turning it to carbon dioxide.

In the absence of high production of carbon dioxide, you produce lactic acid. Lactic acid promotes inflammation. Starting with the fact that estrogen slows liver function by reducing the thyroid hormone, the slowed liver production shifts you into that lactate-favoring metabolism away from carbon dioxide. Lactate causes inflammation of everything. Autoimmune thyroid disease is just the tip of the iceberg. Once the estrogen slows your thyroid down and starts inflammation there, all of your other tissues are susceptible to chronic inflammation, ultimately leading to calcification or fibrosis—excess collagen production.

**Patrick Timpone:** And all this is cascading, starting from high estrogen levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Women normally cycle. For two or three days, there's a surge of estrogen around ovulation. Then, if they're healthy and well-fed, the ovary shifts strongly to progesterone production. The diagrams in medical books often show estrogen and progesterone on the same chart using a different scale. The production of progesterone is about 1,000 times greater than the production of estrogen in a healthy person, but they show them on the same graph misleadingly.

This little moment of dominant estrogen should be suppressed by a massive pouring out of progesterone for the rest of the month. But if anything interferes—like eating too much vegetable oil or starchy vegetables that are hard to digest—their energy level decreases so that they don't produce the normal amount of progesterone. It starts with premenstrual syndrome (PMS), where they don't have the energy and sense of well-being of the progesterone-controlled condition. In the absence of progesterone, everything tends to shift in an inefficient direction towards oxidation of fat rather than glucose. That takes a lot more oxygen. Every carbon requires two oxygens if it's fat, and only one oxygen if it's carbohydrate, which already comes with one oxygen. You get a double supply of carbon dioxide, in effect, when you're using sugar as a fuel. Carbon dioxide has a stabilizing, protective effect that suppresses inflammation and turns off lactate production.

**Patrick Timpone:** So if women change their diet, they could feel better during their periods?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the short run, eating a lot of carbohydrate will make them feel better because it provides glucose. But at some point, their liver needs a good supply of protein to keep working. I've seen women eating 15 or 20 grams of protein a day, whereas an Army study found that even average or small women needed 100 grams of protein a day to work efficiently. Women are often told that 35 grams a day is fine, but competent studies show that 85 to 100 or more grams per day are needed for the liver to function well.

Just a protein deficiency makes the liver underproduce. In the 1940s, studies on prisoners who were starved noticed that when they were let out and given food, the men fairly often grew breasts in the first year. That was because their liver had been damaged from the prolonged protein and vitamin deficiency. The liver normally destroys or causes excretion of 100% of the estrogen reaching it. If you starve the liver for B vitamins or protein, the estrogen accumulates. So a man will grow breasts just from a prolonged nutrient deficiency. That happens in women, and that's a basic cause of PMS.

The estrogen industry, starting in the 1940s, convinced the government and the public that these PMS and menopausal problems were the result of a deficiency of estrogen rather than an excess. At the very same time, researchers were showing exactly how the liver keeps estrogen under control when your diet is good. The estrogen industry totally reversed that situation. They even sold estrogen to prevent miscarriage. All through the late 40s and 50s, doctors at Harvard were convincing doctors to prescribe estrogen to pregnant women. That created the DES (diethylstilbestrol) syndrome—cancer in the next generation.

**Patrick Timpone:** Was that whole syndrome blamed on the drug?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, diethylstilbestrol, a synthetic estrogen. In the 1930s, my professor, Soderwall, was a student of one of the people who showed very early that estrogen causes miscarriage. He gave animals graded doses and showed that the number of miscarriages exactly corresponded to the dose of estrogen. So estrogen as a contraceptive or abortion producer was defined before 1940. But in 1941 and 1942, the estrogen industry started promoting it to *prevent* miscarriage—exactly 180 degrees opposite of what it does. That has created more than 50 years of total confusion. For 50 years, they prescribed estrogen to men with prostate cancer. It turns out that it is a major cause of prostate cancer. High testosterone men in middle and old age are relatively free of prostate cancer; the ones who develop it are the ones with lower testosterone and more effective estrogen.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does it matter if women get animal protein or vegetable protein to balance this out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does. Gelatin is one protein that is very safe because it lacks the three amino acids which can be very toxic if you're eating more than is needed: cysteine, methionine, and tryptophan. They are used for growth until you're about 20 or 25. After that, they are just needed for replacing skin. If you eat a young person's requirement of those amino acids when you're 40 or 50, they tend to promote overgrowth, inflammation, excitotoxicity of the nerves, and tumor growth. They are associated with shortening the lifespan. Gelatin lacks those, so it's a very safe protein to add to other proteins to balance it out.

**Patrick Timpone:** Like the Great Lakes gelatin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's a good one. Gelatin is basically the stiffening glue that holds our other cells together. A lot of people are selling gelatin calling it collagen. Collagen is the raw form in your tissues; to buy actual collagen is very expensive.

**Patrick Timpone:** So if you want collagen, you should get it from pigs' feet and ham hocks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that's a natural way to get it. Chicken backs, wings, and feet are traditional ways. When a person is sick, giving them a gelatinous chicken soup is therapeutic.

**Patrick Timpone:** And the excitatory amino acids are what again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine. Glycine and proline are the protective, energy-providing, and stabilizing amino acids found in gelatin.

**Patrick Timpone:** Jeremy asks: "I just love eggs. I might eat three or four a day. Is it okay?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They used to be the perfect food. I've seen the cholesterol and polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) content analyzed in the 30s, 50s, and 70s. There has been a constant decrease in cholesterol content and a constant increase in PUFA content because of the feed. In the pork industry in the 40s, they found that highly polyunsaturated fats made the pig gain fat faster with less food. That spread to other branches of agriculture. Chicken feed has become more and more polyunsaturated.

**Patrick Timpone:** If our listeners have access to really good yard eggs, organic with no soy, is it a perfect food then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When I'm in Mexico and know where the eggs come from—chickens getting tortillas, vegetables, and bugs—I'll eat four or five eggs a day. It's okay to eat more. The cholesterol myth was created by the seed oil industry, especially cottonseed. People wanted to sell their product on the basis that it lowered cholesterol. Things that lower cholesterol generally cause cancer and degenerative disease.

In an experiment many years ago, medical students were fed eggs. It took 22 eggs a day to show an increase in serum cholesterol. At 15 eggs a day, there was no increase because their natural liver production of cholesterol was inhibited. The body recognizes it doesn't have to make cholesterol when it's getting that amount.

**Patrick Timpone:** Aajonus Vonderplanitz used to promote a raw egg diet. He claimed a dozen raw eggs a day could straighten out stomach problems.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen several people recover using that. One was a year-and-a-half-old kid, another a man about 70. Both had a diagnosis of leukemia. I suggested an eggnog or "Orange Julius" formula: egg, milk, sugar, orange juice, or vanilla. Both had a recovery. I've suggested that several times for lymphoma and leukemia.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a big difference between raw or cooking the eggs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been experiments showing that something in the raw egg yolk is germicidal and helps disinfect the intestine. That is somewhat decreased by cooking, but you still get almost all the benefit from a cooked egg. It's better to cook it as little as possible so the yolk is still runny because the polyunsaturated fat is easily oxidized by heat.

**Patrick Timpone:** Any issues with pork if it's well-tended?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For about 50 years, the Department of Agriculture called lard a saturated fat. They hadn't checked their figures since the 1930s. A more recent study showed that lard is about 32% or 33% polyunsaturated fats, so it ranks up with the worst of the liquid oils for oxidizability. When I was a kid, grocery stores had blocks of lard sitting out at room temperature like butter. Recently, I saw lard in a plastic bag looking like a liquid fat. That shows the change of diet on the fat. When the source of energy is mostly starch and protein, the animal turns it into mostly saturated fat. Solid lard stimulates your metabolism rather than poisoning it.
