If you eat a vegetable fat that grows in the tropics, it will be more saturated because the temperature of the organism governs the saturation. Cocoa butter and coconut oil are highly saturated because polyunsaturated fats are extremely unstable at 90 or 100 degrees Fahrenheit. Plants producing those fats in the tropics would die of oxygen reaction poisoning.

**Patrick Timpone:** An email asks: "Can Dr. Peat recommend foods for recovering from long-term inflammatory bowel disease causing hair loss, drop in lean body mass, and skin that doesn't heal?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Avoid things that produce inflammation. The basic things that amplify inflammation are polyunsaturated fats and the bacteria that feed on indigestible plant matter. We don't have enzymes to break down cellulose and lignin. If starches and fats are associated with those indigestible polysaccharides, they will feed bacteria in the lower intestine and cause the absorption of bacterial toxins like endotoxin.

Lettuce in a salad is an ideal bacteria food. If you are prone to inflammation, lettuce or undercooked vegetables are going to feed the bacteria that produce bowel inflammation. Overcooked vegetables are actually more nutritious than raw ones. Experiments with rats showed they couldn't live on raw vegetables but thrived on canned vegetables that were overcooked. A milk and egg diet is often therapeutic for colitis.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener's mom underwent a mastectomy and was prescribed an anti-estrogen medication which caused severe reactions. What is Dr. Peat's opinion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The anti-estrogen drugs have many effects other than suppressing estrogen. You can powerfully decrease estrogen production by inhibiting aromatase naturally. Cutting out polyunsaturated fats is key because they produce prostaglandins, which are the main force activating aromatase and estrogen production. Aspirin is a natural substance that blocks aromatase and is very safe to use in breast cancer. Progesterone is another.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener in Switzerland asks about bone necrosis in the jaw caused by X-rays. Can X-ray damage actually cause bone necrosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. About 30 or 40 years ago, I noticed a circle of white whiskers on my face where the X-ray gun had been used for dental X-rays. Right after that, I would get leukoplakia on the inside of my cheek. X-rays destroy vitamin A, E, and B2—the light-sensitive nutrients—first. These essential regulatory factors are destroyed in the bone because X-rays penetrate well.

Getting essential nutrients up would be the first defense. Vitamin D and calcium are anti-inflammatory and restorative for the bone. Keeping cortisol and prolactin down is important. Having energy come from carbohydrate rather than fats is protective. And again, aspirin keeps prostaglandin production down. An anti-inflammatory program protects against bone loss as well as cancer.

**Patrick Timpone:** Being an artist, a listener asks: "If high testosterone gives men attractive traits, and high estrogen gives women attractive broad hips and narrow waists, what does Dr. Peat think about estrogen as a factor in attractiveness?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It does increase fat on the thighs and hips when everything else is in balance. But if it comes at the wrong time, it is a masculinizing factor. It will shift a balance in an embryo towards male development. Progesterone protects the female against the masculinizing effects of estrogen. You have to have a generous supply of progesterone to keep down the cortisol, which is promoted by estrogen. If estrogen isn't blocked by progesterone, you get stress syndromes, including belly fat.

**Patrick Timpone:** A question about a 10-year-old daughter entering puberty with poor appetite, dental issues, and coldness. Should they measure thyroid or steroid hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's good to check her temperature and pulse rate. As estrogen starts rising after age 6, and especially 9, 10, and 11, the estrogen blocks the thyroid gland. In teenage girls, you often see puffiness at the bottom of the neck. The gland enlarges under the influence of estrogen because it's trying to produce hormone but isn't able to release it. Vitamin D and calcium work closely with the thyroid in sugar metabolism. Getting lots of milk, cheese, and eggs is important. Not a lot of high phosphate foods like nuts, beans, and meats.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is your opinion on using pure pine gum spirits or turpentine internally?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known lots of people who used it, and it isn't as dangerous as doctors lead you to believe, but you have to be careful because it can be irritating. I always painted with it and enjoyed the smell. The research has been biased against it by the pharmaceutical industry.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it okay to take bioidentical hormones if one has breast cancer that is ER+ (Estrogen Receptor positive)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The receptors just mean that the cell is able to respond to hormones. The presence of those receptors is almost always misinterpreted by doctors. When you have an irritation, the breast itself begins producing estrogen internally. You need to reduce that by reducing polyunsaturated fats and inhibiting it with aspirin. Progesterone inhibits cell division and knocks out the estrogen receptor. So where they tell you to avoid progesterone because you have receptors, the receptor actually means it's able to be *inhibited* by progesterone. Bioidentical estrogen is just as harmful as synthetic estrogen.

**Patrick Timpone:** What would you recommend for rheumatoid arthritis? This listener eats organic, bone broths, and cottage cheese.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With cottage cheese, make sure it doesn't have added lactic acid, as that is pro-inflammatory. Regarding bone broth, the collagen—which is the main benefit—is around the knobby end bones and joints, not the long bones. The long bone contains marrow which is rich in iron, and you don't want excess iron with arthritis.

I met a woman who was convinced her doctor was right to prescribe estrogen for her rheumatoid arthritis, yet she couldn't get off the couch. When she finally tried giving up her estrogen pills, she immediately recovered. Another woman with joint replacements used progesterone topically and her symptoms vanished. An Italian researcher named Cutolo has shown that estrogen is produced in the arthritic joint and the problem is to reduce the estrogen. Aspirin helps because it turns estrogen production down and progesterone up.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you explain the connection between volatile organic compounds and nanoparticles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nanoparticles are efficient at activating inflammation, but larger particles—up to 10 times the diameter of a red blood cell—can pass through the wall of the intestine into the blood vessels. This process is called persorption. These particles can obstruct arterioles and kill a region of cells.

Plastic particles are getting into our food supply. The larger particles can be coated with volatile organic compounds, especially polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are carcinogenic. They stick to the surface of particles and get carried into the bloodstream. This happens whenever you eat undercooked starch. Starch particles pass into the bloodstream unless they are in the presence of enough food to energize the intestine cells to keep them from being leaky. A leaky intestine isn't just holes between cells; it's that the individual cell is weak and becomes tolerant of particles passing through its substance.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the takeaway for avoiding this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Clothes are treated with silver nanoparticles that can pass through the skin. Toothpaste often contains particles. Salad dressings are thickened with fumed silica (glass particles) or titanium dioxide. Even if they aren't "nano," microparticles can still contain the pro-inflammatory nanoparticles. Processed foods are increasingly contaminated. For example, "food grade lubricants" containing Teflon microparticles are used on machinery and can contaminate food but don't show up on the label.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you recommend removing mercury amalgams for neurodegenerative issues?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they are old, they have probably released almost all of the mobile mercury. I think it's better not to mess with it. You're going to damage the tooth more by taking it out. In rat experiments, memory was impaired with each molar extraction because the nerves are closely related to brain function.

**Patrick Timpone:** We have Brenda on the line. She's been using bioidentical estrogen and testosterone pellets for four years and feels great, but is confused by your stance on estrogen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Testosterone makes everyone feel good, male or female. But women get the same effect from DHEA (the precursor of testosterone) and pregnenolone. Both will optimize your progesterone and testosterone without as much risk of excess estrogen. After age 35, fat tissues produce estrogen continuously rather than cyclically. Uninterrupted estrogen has a higher degree of cancer risk. Progesterone is normally produced cyclically, and the liver throws off the excess.

There's really no need to supplement estrogen because tissues start to produce it as they age. Testosterone has protective effects, but progesterone is more protective in aging because it can't be converted to estrogen, whereas testosterone can.

**Patrick Timpone:** How does canned milk compare to fresh milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It used to be that they soldered cans with lead, but I think they've revised that. Now, all you lose is a little vitamin quality and you have a little oxidized fatty material from the heat. It's a gradient from fresh raw milk to pasteurized, to ultra-pasteurized, to canned. Each time it loses a little value. I use pasteurized milk almost always.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are goat milk, kefir, and goat cheese good sources of calcium and protein?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener says taking iodine gives them energy, but heard you say it doesn't help the thyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Iodine can interact with polyunsaturated fats in your body producing an anti-thyroid substance. I have a file of about 70 articles showing that increased iodine in the diet from iodized salt is correlated with increased thyroid disease and cancer. In some people, iodine has an anti-inflammatory value, but taken chronically in large amounts, it tends to have an anti-thyroid effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can it cause Hashimoto's?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you explain how the male hormone system works?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's simpler than female hormones because there isn't that powerful cyclic effect. Testosterone acts as an anti-stress effect for most of the lifespan. But if the thyroid is interfered with, a slow thyroid will shift you to the conversion of testosterone to estrogen. That's where degenerative problems start.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you recommend supplemental testosterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A pellet is probably better than an oily injection. Injections usually contain testosterone esters dissolved in vegetable oil with solvents like benzyl alcohol, which are toxic. I don't often recommend it because pharmaceutical forms provide huge excesses. DHEA as a precursor is easily available. A full replacement dose is around 15 milligrams, which an 80 or 90-year-old man might need.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you recommend effective natural antibiotics?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The two I think are safest are flowers of sulfur and aspirin. Flowers of sulfur can be used on the skin or intestine. 200 milligrams orally in two or three days can kill off the most toxic intestinal bacteria and fungus. Candida, for example, converts the sulfur to sulfuric acid and poisons itself. It is very harmless to the intestine in small amounts.

Aspirin, when used with standard antibiotics, increases their effectiveness. But all by itself, it has antibiotic, antiviral, and antifungal effects.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is taking aspirin preventatively okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, anywhere from 100 to 300 milligrams. You can buy pure USP grade aspirin powder cheaply.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is Dr. Peat familiar with NR (Nicotinamide Riboside) for improving lifespan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm skeptical that those reduced substances make it into the cells without being oxidized en route. Just taking niacinamide will increase your intracellular NAD. That's very simple, economical, and harmless.

**Patrick Timpone:** How does one know when progesterone supplementation is required?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pregnancy has an anti-aging effect. Studies in rabbits and humans show that lifespan increases in proportion to the number of babies, likely due to the residual high progesterone level reversing the pro-aging effects of estrogen.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener who is post-menopausal shows no estrogen or progesterone on tests. Her doctor wants to put her on hormone replacement. Would just progesterone help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Typically it does. With aging, serum estrogen goes down, but that doesn't reflect the biological situation. Estrogen is formed in cells under stress and bound there. It can't get into the bloodstream without progesterone. Progesterone knocks out the estrogen receptor and releases the estrogen from the cells so the liver can detoxify it. So, a woman who is most under the influence of estrogen will often show almost zero estrogen in the serum because it's all trapped inside the cells.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is your take on the gluten sensitivity explosion in the last 15 years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gluten interacts with stress and estrogen. The gluten molecule has a stretch of amino acids that resembles proteins involved with stress and inflammation. If you are stressed and have high estrogen, you create a condition that responds to gluten. If you are in good condition, gluten is digested properly.

Also, it relates to bad diet and improperly leavened bread. The old-fashioned 12-hour sourdough leavening process destroys almost all the gluten and converts it to nutritious protein. Modern bread is made quickly, leaving the gluten intact. That gluten is allergenic. When I baked my own sourdough bread, I could eat a whole loaf and sleep perfectly, whereas a slice of store bread would disturb my sleep.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thanks for being with us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: One Radio Network: The Goods
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** Hello, Dr. Peat. Good morning. How are things with you, sir?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pretty good.

**Patrick Timpone:** What did you have for breakfast?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just coffee and milk.

**Patrick Timpone:** Coffee and milk. It's funny, there are so many people out there who say you shouldn't drink milk. They say we are the only mammals that drink milk after weaning and it's going to kill you. All of that hasn't killed you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nope. It's actually one of the cleanest foods available because the cow filters it through many layers. Chemically, the rumen processes the toxins out of the plant material. When you eat the same leaves that a cow eats, you absorb many allergens and toxic materials that the plant puts into its leaves defensively to kill bugs or anyone who would damage them. There are chemical pesticides naturally in plant material.

Seeds are the most precious to the plant. Their whole generation depends on seeds being viable and not being eaten by microorganisms or large organisms, so they have the most intense toxins and blockers of the digestive system. When you look at the chemicals in seeds, it turns out that they block the digestive enzymes of mammals and insects, but they don't affect that same type of enzyme in plants. It is obvious that they are directed towards defense against being eaten. Unless you have very sophisticated lab equipment, you can't separate the good stuff from the toxins. However, the cow's rumen is such that the microorganisms do the chemistry of eliminating the bad stuff and increasing the good stuff.

**Patrick Timpone:** At the local store, they have a few choices of organic milk. I just got some organic half-and-half. That's pretty fun to drink; getting a lot of good fat in there.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I use cream or half-and-half in my coffee.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the deal with A2 cows? Is a Jersey A2 cow easier to digest? And talk about the difference between goat milk and cow milk.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a big difference between the milk of different species, but they still have in common the rumen milk. Camels, goats, sheep, cows, and llamas—that type of animal produces the safest milk. The reason people don't drink pig milk or bear milk is that they don't have rumens, so all the plant toxins go into their milk.

**Patrick Timpone:** Explain what rumens are exactly.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's an extra stomach where the vegetable material goes and soaks at body temperature. This favors the growth of microorganisms which ferment and degrade the plant material, basically digesting it with protozoa, fungi, and bacteria. All of the major types of microorganisms get a chance to break down the plant material. Then, that broken-down material goes through the regular digestive system analogous to what we have. People, bears, and pigs don't have that extra stomach, so whatever they eat goes with minimal filtering into the bloodstream.

**Patrick Timpone:** You mentioned pigs, and I often think about how they do testing on animals like rats and mice. Is it viable to do something on a mouse or rat and say, "That's the way it is for humans too"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One great difference between mice and rats and humans is that they are mainly nocturnal animals. If the experimenter is working in the lab in the daytime and they keep the rat or mouse awake to do their experiments, they are creating intense stress in the animal. To do something analogous to what happens in a human, the experimenter would have to stay up all night to work with the nocturnal animals, and they don't do that. So, automatically you have to question what time of day they were doing their experiments.

Very often, if someone is selling a product, they will try out very different animals so they can get the kind of results they want. In the 1960s and early 70s, the estrogen industry was testing their products on dogs and found that estrogen would damage the dog's bones. By using a species that lives oppositely—in the nighttime rather than daytime—they found that estrogen would strengthen the bones of mice and rats. Conversely, cortisol, which weakens dog and human bones, stimulates the growth of bones in these nocturnal animals. They choose the animal that is specific to get the result they want.

**Patrick Timpone:** I've often thought that these mice and rats are probably surrounded by a huge amount of electromagnetic fields and weird lights that aren't good for them. That would put a fly in the ointment regarding the accuracy of the results.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They commonly use a very standardized controlled diet, but there are prejudices built into what they call the standard diet. Often they will put in 6% of so-called "essential fatty acids," which aren't at all essential. When someone experiments by leaving out those essential fatty acids, they get "super rats" or "super mice"—very resistant to poisons, trauma, shock, venoms, aging, diseases, and diabetes. All kinds of biological damage is less in the animals that are deficient in the so-called essential fatty acids. But since they build those fats into the standard diet, when they compare an experimental diet to the standard diet, they are already biasing the experiment. They are making sick animals their reference.

**Patrick Timpone:** I wonder who came up with the term "essential fatty acids."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was Burr. He and his wife, around the late 1920s and early 1930s, got the idea that maybe fats were like a vitamin. Even though two or three research groups at big universities had demonstrated that you could have a totally fat-free diet and the animals actually lived longer, the Burrs created a fat-free diet.

At that time, most of the B vitamins hadn't been discovered. They were feeding a diet deficient in unsaturated fats, but also deficient in several B vitamins. They said they had created a deficiency disease in which the animals got sore tails and rashy, cracked skin around their mouths. They called this the fatty acid deficiency symptom.

However, 15 years later, a Texas research institute discovered Vitamin B6. They created the Burr essential fatty acid deficient animals, gave them only Vitamin B6—with no fat—and cured the deficiency symptom. In 1945 or 1946, they proved that there was no essential fatty acid.

Meanwhile, the petroleum industry was working on how to make plastics and paint. Synthetic plastics were being engineered, and seed oils like linseed oil, which had been the bulk of plastics and paints, were replaced by petroleum chemistry. There was no longer a paint and plastics market for linseed oil and cottonseed oil. They had to figure out some way to dispose of their product, so they decided to sell it to the public as a food.

The same thing happened in the 60s and 70s with fish oil. Fish oil had been primarily used as varnish or fuel because it hardens on exposure to oxygen, like linseed oil. Fish processing factories were throwing away the skin and fatty parts when canning salmon, causing horrible pollution in bay areas. The EPA told them they had to figure out something to do with their waste material to reduce pollution. Thus, fish oil as a health food came on the market.

**Patrick Timpone:** Let's just give it to the people; they'll eat it. But wasn't fish oil used early on, like in the 1800s?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For hundreds of years it was known to make a good varnish. Whale oil was a major fuel oil for lamps.

**Patrick Timpone:** I've heard that parents gave their kids cod liver oil around 1900.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I got some when I was a kid. That was only the liver oil, and it is very different from regular fish oil. What they are selling now isn't from the liver, so it has practically no vitamin value—very small contamination with Vitamin D and A, but not enough to be therapeutic like the liver oil.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is cod liver oil healthy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you don't have other sources of Vitamin A and Vitamin D. It started in Norway where the winters are so dark. People found that they benefited from it.

**Patrick Timpone:** But we can get plenty of A in our food and D in the sun, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Eggs are a good source of Vitamin A, and getting sunlight is the best way to get your D.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is your take on water? We hear about drinking half an ounce of water for every pound of body weight. What does your research show regarding dehydration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Salt is one of the important factors in keeping us hydrated. In the 50s, drug companies came out with diuretic pills to make you lose water, and they sold them to pregnant women to prevent water retention. It turns out that is a very bad idea. During pregnancy, you have to retain water in your bloodstream and expand your blood volume tremendously to take care of the growing fetus and new systems of blood vessels.

What retains water in the bloodstream is largely the protein albumin. But albumin doesn't retain water unless there is an associated cloud of sodium atoms attached to the negative charges on the albumin protein. The combination of sodium and albumin retains water within the system. If you take a diuretic that makes you lose sodium, the water that goes with the sodium reduces the blood volume and reduces the ability of the albumin to keep water from going out into your tissues.

Without enough sodium, the albumin itself goes out of the blood vessels into your tissues, creating a kind of edema and swelling. It isn't the typical pitting edema; it is very firm, resembling the myxedema of hypothyroidism. It is caused by the lack of sodium needed to keep water in the proper compartments. You dehydrate your circulatory system but waterlog the functioning tissues.

In experiments, researchers gave women with toxemia of pregnancy—who had great water retention and high blood pressure—extra salt instead of diuretics. With this supplement (in one case six grams a day, in another 20 grams), their blood pressure quickly came down to normal and their toxemia was cured.

**Patrick Timpone:** So for the edema or puffiness around the ankles, what is the difference between the kind where you press in and it leaves an indentation, and the other kind?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have protein leaking out of your blood vessels into the tissue cells, that protein is slow to move under pressure. If it is from salt deficiency causing leakage of albumin, or from hypothyroidism causing accumulation of sugar-containing protein, either of those makes the water stick around your tissue cells. It doesn't get easily pushed back into your blood vessels. Once it gets into your feet by gravity, it doesn't all come out during the night. Simple edema will correct itself during the night, but when you stand up, if you don't have enough sodium and albumin, your blood loses water into your lower extremities.

**Patrick Timpone:** So people with puffy ankles could try taking more salt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You want to make sure your protein intake is adequate. When you increase your protein, make sure you are not overloading on phosphate. Phosphate is now being recognized as a kidney toxin. In kidney failure, too much phosphate is one of the most toxic things. Meat, fish, and seed proteins are the highest in phosphate. Leaves, milk, and cheese are the lowest.

**Patrick Timpone:** Here is an email from Eric. He wants to build more muscle. What are some foods that help muscle building?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Protein is essential, but again, you have to make sure it is not excessive in phosphate. You need B vitamins, Vitamin D, and Vitamin A to make protein. However, you don't want too much carotene. Carotene turns off your metabolism and blocks testosterone production. You want natural animal Vitamin A, such as in eggs and liver—though not too much liver either, because that can be toxic to your thyroid. But it is needed for making muscle protein and steroid hormones like progesterone and testosterone.

**Patrick Timpone:** We had a guest who said guys could safely use a little bit of progesterone from wild yam. Do you agree?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you take the amount a woman would use for menopause replacement (about 30 milligrams a day), that can antagonize a man's testosterone. But if you take 5 or 10 milligrams, that is in the range normal for a man. By reducing estrogen production in a man, it can make the testosterone effect much more potent. Both testosterone and progesterone are capable of reducing the synthesis of estrogen. However, testosterone can be converted into estrogen. If you don't have progesterone and thyroid hormone, you are liable to convert your testosterone into estrogen and lose the masculinizing effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are beans estrogenic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many years ago, they found that sheep would miscarry if they grazed on leguminous plants like clover, alfalfa, beans, and peas. They all have enough estrogens to act as a birth control pill for sensitive animals.

Beans also have other toxins designed to make them indigestible. People have developed technologies for cooking them properly. If you soak beans (or grains) for a day at room temperature, enzymes start sprouting. Those enzymes activate detoxifying processes. Soaking a bean detoxifies it quite a bit. Then, very long cooking until it softens further reduces the toxicity.

**Patrick Timpone:** So there are ways to make beans and grains digestible?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but they are still a very low-grade protein compared to leaf protein. The quality of protein in a leaf is similar to milk, or about 70% as perfect as egg yolk protein. Bean and grain proteins are way down on the scale, around 5% to 10% in quality. For muscle building, they function as nothing more than energy. You might as well eat sugar as beans.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about grass-fed whey protein?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Whey isn't quite as nutritionally balanced and safe as casein (the solid part that goes into cheese), but it is a good quality protein. Compared to beans, it is extremely good.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does Dr. Peat have insights on leg vascular insufficiency or lipedema?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Swelling of the legs and feet creates pressure from the tissue outside the blood vessels, making it hard for blood to get through. If you have extremely high fats in your blood, that increases viscosity. Interestingly, having high albumin increases the fluidity of your blood, while fibrinogen makes blood thicker. So, fat and fibrinogen increase viscosity; albumin and salt make blood more fluid.

You can correct fibrinogen and fat content by lowering stress. That includes avoiding excess phosphate and ensuring good thyroid function and Vitamin D levels. Those are the three most neglected anti-stress factors: low thyroid, low Vitamin D, and excess phosphate.

**Patrick Timpone:** Kevin emailed regarding a high PSA test. He doesn't want to take drugs. What is your opinion on PSA testing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1980s, they decided this antigen was a sign of prostate issues. Actually, this protein is a defensive reaction to irritation. Cancer does lead to an increase, but the protein itself has an anti-cancer protective effect.

When PSA testing came on the market around 1990, there was approximately a 50% increase in deaths from prostate cancer over the next few years. That is a general effect of diagnosis leading to aggressive treatment. Later, a journalist asked prostate specialists what they would do if they had prostate cancer. Almost all said they would do nothing—"watchful waiting"—because they knew treatments like estrogen and surgery weren't curing it. When this became public, the mortality rate dropped. It's okay to diagnose it if you don't treat it aggressively just because of the diagnosis.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the connection between pumpkin seeds, zinc, and the prostate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually people eat pumpkin seeds well-salted, and I think increasing salt is beneficial for many people. Generally, thyroid function decreases with aging or stress. When your thyroid is low, you lose salt in your urine. When you lose sodium, aldosterone increases. Aldosterone causes high blood pressure and fibrosis of the heart and blood vessels.

When I worked in the woods, the cook put a tablespoon of salt in our morning porridge because he knew we lost salt sweating. I would get white salt crystals on my eyebrows. The body adapts by lowering aldosterone so salt is lost easily. After I told the cook I was on a low-salt diet and stopped eating the salty porridge, I immediately stopped sweating crystalline salt. The adrenals adjust quickly. But in aging, thyroid deficiency causes sodium loss. The salt craving in most people is biological. You can correct it by correcting thyroid function, which helps you retain salt efficiently.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener in Switzerland asks what laboratory tests you advise for a health assessment.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doctors are often reluctant to do the patient's requested tests. Vitamin D should be done regularly. Free fatty acids are extremely important but rarely done; stress increases them. The common tests that are beneficial are Progesterone, DHEA, Pregnenolone, Testosterone, TSH, and thyroid hormones. Prolactin is a good indicator of stress. Lactic acid is another test that should be done more often; a rise in lactic acid indicates something is going wrong.

Also, the Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) test reflects your status of phosphate, calcium, and Vitamin D. It is rarely done but extremely relevant. PTH, like aldosterone, poisons the function of your mitochondria.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there anything to the recent talk about Vitamin A toxicity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1973, drug companies were releasing synthetic Vitamin A and found professors to tell stories about toxicity to make people fear natural Vitamin A. One popular story is about explorers eating polar bear liver and their skin falling off. Polar bear liver likely contains toxins from algae blooms concentrated through the food chain (fish/seals), which got blamed on Vitamin A.

In animal experiments, huge doses of Vitamin A caused brain deformities in chicks, but if they gave them a moderate amount of Vitamin E, the Vitamin A was no longer toxic. At very high levels, Vitamin A stimulates its own oxidation. Vitamin E prevents this breakdown.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about reducing endotoxins from gut bacteria using garlic, ginger, or cloves?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those have their own allergens. It is safest to use fibrous foods. Rinsed bran from wheat or oats, cooked mushrooms, or bamboo shoots can stimulate the intestine and chemically reduce bacterial population. Raw carrot is another; it grows in a microorganism-rich environment and powerfully reduces endotoxin production. Olive oil and vinegar are bactericidal, so a carrot salad with dressing is effective.

**Patrick Timpone:** Adam Bergstrom asks: Does oxidative stress cause lipofuscin accumulation in autism, or is it the other way around?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's both. Lipofuscin lowers oxygen tension, creating an oxygen deficiency that imitates stress. This low oxygen catalyzes the degradation of polyunsaturated fats (PUFA). Excess Vitamin A without Vitamin E interacts with unsaturated fats to lead to accelerated lipofuscin production. Vitamin E prevents lipofuscin.

**Patrick Timpone:** Would soaking wheat work for making healthier bread?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. I experimented with soaking wheat for 12 to 24 hours. Ordinary bakery bread would cause gas, but I could eat a whole loaf of my homemade soaked bread with no problem. Soaking activates enzymes that turn the storage gluten into growth proteins, doubling the protein value and making it digestible.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a fungal connection to prostate or breast cancer?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Most tumors contain fungus because the immune system is deranged. The fungus produces estrogen, stimulating growth. If you view a tumor not as a mutant cell but as a wound that is failing to heal, treatments like biopsy, chemotherapy, and radiation just add to the organism's problems.

A healing wound can look identical to cancer structurally. The cancer lacks something to get beyond that stage of healing. One thing it lacks is carbon dioxide. Simoncini's use of baking soda provides carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide stops the production of lactic acid (the Warburg effect) and allows the tissue to mature and heal. Low thyroid, low calcium, and low sodium limit the ability to make enough carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it reasonable to take a little baking soda?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Athletes find endurance is increased with baking soda. Even a quarter teaspoon in water can help. It provides carbon dioxide which re-acidifies the cell and stops it from producing lactic acid.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about A1 versus A2 casein milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is a difference in peptides, but I haven't seen convincing research that it is important for health. Our digestive systems are usually efficient enough to break them down to amino acids, which have no endocrine effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are new digital X-rays less dangerous?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They claim they are more sensitive, but in practice, they take more pictures, so the exposure is likely the same. CT scans deliver hundreds of times more radiation than a chest X-ray. Medical X-rays are a major cause of heart disease and breast cancer.

**Patrick Timpone:** Jill asks: If someone has a problem converting T4 to T3, are they better off taking Armour or Cytomel?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For most people, combination products like Armour are reliable. Women have much more thyroid disease than men because estrogen interferes with thyroid function. Estrogen increases cortisol, which blocks the conversion of T4 to T3. Therefore, most women with a thyroid problem are deficient in T3. Progesterone helps because it blocks estrogen formation and the anti-thyroid effect of cortisol.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener stopped taking Armour when starting probiotics, but their blood pressure went up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When thyroid function is low, TSH is high. TSH has a pro-inflammatory effect that creates circulatory problems. Hypertension is often caused by low thyroid (and high TSH). Correcting the low thyroid often cures the hypertension.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thanks for spending time with us today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: One Radio Network: Milk
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** We're going to have fun now. We are talking to Dr. Ray Peat, and it is great to have him on the show again. We've been inviting him about once a month, and he keeps saying yes. He is a renowned nutritional counselor. He acquired a PhD from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He started his work on hormones in 1968 and wrote his dissertation in 1972, where he outlined his ideas on progesterone and hormones. Closely related to this, his main thesis is that energy and structure are independent at every level. Dr. Ray Peat, good morning, sir. How are you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good.

**Patrick Timpone:** You always sound good, Doc. What did you have for breakfast this morning?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coffee, milk, and orange juice.

**Patrick Timpone:** I like your breakfasts. It's funny, after hanging out with you and doing these shows, I started thinking, "I'm going to try some milk too." I have access to raw goat's milk. I never did really well with it my whole life, but I'm doing great with it now after a couple of months. I'm wondering what could change in the body? If I wasn't able to do even raw goat's milk before, what would change to make it work for me now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The body is always changing to adapt to circumstances. They've done experiments with people who thought they were intolerant of lactose. By introducing an ounce or two—or three or four ounces—of milk per day, within their tolerance, they found that in a few weeks, even lactose-intolerant people were able to drink regular amounts of milk. The enzymes take a couple of weeks to adapt. That applies to any food. When you change to a different kind of major energy source, your intestine takes weeks to really adjust to it.

**Patrick Timpone:** So if you are going to change and introduce something that you haven't had for a while, it would be best to go just a little bit every day and let the body know what's going on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, you give it signals of what's happening, and it starts making new enzymes to handle the new material. That happens most easily when you have all of the essential nutrients in adequate amounts and your thyroid is working efficiently so that you have lots of energy to do the new protein synthesis.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is milk that good of a food for folks to even consider?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The only major deficiency it has is iron. During pregnancy, high estrogen causes the woman to absorb iron with extreme efficiency—I think they say nine or ten times more efficiently than a man extracting it from food. That charges up the woman's body with high amounts of iron. The baby is born overloaded with iron stores; their liver stores enough iron for almost a year of life living on milk. Milk lets them adjust to that newborn state of iron excess. It is designed to be deficient in iron, so you can't live indefinitely on just milk.

However, the estrogen also makes the woman absorb calcium very efficiently because the bones of the baby are going to require lots of calcium. So, milk has an excess of calcium for adult requirements. It turns out that even in an adult who doesn't need it for growing bones, that excess of calcium has a very powerful anti-inflammatory, anti-stress effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** I have access to raw cream, too. To take a big hit of that, like an ounce or two, sure feels good.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have good coffee with fresh heavy cream, that's delicious.

**Patrick Timpone:** If you have warm milk or cream before bed, and it soothes you, that goes a long way, doesn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. During the night, the lack of light causes a developing stress. After about the age of 30, all of the changes related to aging happen during the night because of the stress that requires sleeping to get through it. The pituitary hormones all zoom up during the night—growth hormone, the gonadotropic hormones, and cortisol.

The parathyroid hormone rises during the night, and it exacerbates things because it inhibits energy production, which makes you need the cortisol. The combination of parathyroid hormone and cortisol rising very steeply during the night takes your energy down and breaks down your bones. Morning urine is full of the calcium that you've torn out of your bones during the night. Experimenters have found that milk at bedtime greatly lowers the night stress and prevents some of the surge of those stress hormones.

**Patrick Timpone:** Maybe that's where the old idea of warm milk at night comes from.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably.

**Patrick Timpone:** Gandhi did pretty well, and I think he lived on goat's milk. Do you know any big difference between goat's milk and cow's milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has several differences. Partly it's because of the goat's favored diet; they won't eat everything. Basically, it's creamier, and the cream is emulsified in a different way, so it's slower to separate. This makes it easier to digest for a lot of people.

**Patrick Timpone:** I was on a call with a doctor regarding a blood test, and he said I could use some more fat in my brain. How can people make sure we're getting plenty of good fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The interesting thing is that if the mother keeps her blood sugar up, babies make their own fat. It is all saturated, except for the polyunsaturated omega-9 fatty acids that are synthesized in the baby's liver. Babies are born with a highly saturated brain. In that state, in their first few years—when the brain contains only our native polyunsaturated fats and lots of saturated fats—they have their highest metabolic rate and a tremendous rate of learning. By the age of five or six, they know five or six thousand words. Imagine an adult trying to learn five or six thousand words in five years.

**Patrick Timpone:** Wow. So how do we humans pony up on more of that good fat in our brain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar. Just like a baby.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Starch and sugar both turn to fat when you eat enough of them.

**Patrick Timpone:** What would be the difference between having coconut milk ice cream with sugar versus some really well-tended pork fat? Does the brain like them equally?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It actually prefers saturated fat. But since our diets have been industrialized, pigs now have highly unsaturated fat. For about 50 years, the Department of Agriculture published lists calling pork fat, or lard, a saturated fat. But it turned out to be extremely polyunsaturated because they feed them so much soy and corn to make them fat. Those polyunsaturated corn and soy oils are highly fattening. Coconut oil is more like natural human fat; it is not so fattening.

**Patrick Timpone:** There is a person at the farmers market who feeds their pigs food thrown away at Whole Foods—mostly vegetables and grass.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone used to feed their pigs that way. When I was a kid, the creameries would make cheese and give away huge amounts of whey. The farmers would mix whey with apple crops or waste vegetables and fruit. That was really an ideal diet: milk protein, fruit, and vegetables.

**Patrick Timpone:** She was saying there's a huge difference between what she's doing and standard pigs. Even if you get organic pork, you don't know what they're feeding them; it could be organic soy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I used to really like pork when I lived in Mexico because the farmers would feed them that sort of food. When I was a kid, my grandmother sent me to the store to buy lard for her cooking. At room temperature, it sat in square cubes, just like butter—nice and solid. The last time I saw lard in a meat store, it was almost liquid.

**Patrick Timpone:** Here's an email: "Is reduced-fat, ultra-filtered milk that is lactose-free good to drink?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It can be if there are no serious additives in it. They put an enzyme in that breaks lactose down into glucose and another monosaccharide. It's a perfectly good sugar and makes it taste sweeter.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there an issue with drinking organic, grass-fed milk that has been homogenized and pasteurized? Is that a negative?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not really.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you recommend folks get as high a fat content as they can in the milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, you can get fat. I used to drink a gallon a day of whole milk when I was working easily. But when I became sedentary going to school, I started getting fat on that, so I reduced it to 1%. I could drink a gallon of 1% milk without getting fat. One of the virtues of milk is that the high calcium content stimulates heat production, the same way sodium, protein, and sugar stimulate your metabolism. Calcium is a major factor in maintaining a high metabolic rate.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it the calcium that gets into the mitochondria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Both sodium and calcium stimulate the cell to counteract their stimulating effect. The rising energy production relaxes the cell, but in the process, it burns up a lot of energy.

**Patrick Timpone:** One of the biggest complaints when people go to the doctor is low energy. Talk a bit about that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mostly that turns out to be a low thyroid state. Even in the 30s and 40s, experts estimated that probably 40% of the population was practically hypothyroid. Since then, the diet has deteriorated. Using those same standards, probably 60% or 80% of people are suffering from hypothyroidism.

However, the standards for measuring it have changed since the 1940s to revise the definition of "normal." The standard they use now is TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone). What they overlook is that the stress caused by hypothyroidism and bad diet produces stress hormones that lower TSH, the same way an excessive thyroid hormone would. So, a stressed, tired, low-energy person will have very low TSH production because of the stress hormones.

**Patrick Timpone:** Wow.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Quite a few people have had a diagnosis of *hyperthyroidism* because their TSH is so low, but their symptoms—water retention, fatigue, hair loss—are typical of hypothyroidism. Several people have told me, "I'm both hyperthyroid and hypothyroid." It makes absolutely no sense, but doctors are actually saying that.

**Patrick Timpone:** Which marker should people pay attention to?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's good to look at all of them, but Free T3, Free T4, and TSH are all ambiguous under stress. I look at:
*   Is hemoglobin and hematocrit up to normal?
*   Is cholesterol above normal?
*   Are liver enzymes a little bit off-center?

Temperature and heart rate are pretty good indicators. The real indicator that was abandoned after the pharmaceutical companies took over in the 40s was measuring actual oxygen consumption and heat production. If a person was only burning two-thirds as much energy as a healthy person, they were given a thyroid supplement to bring their oxygen consumption up to normal, and their symptoms went away.

Women who diet a lot have been found to maintain their weight on 700 calories a day because of low thyroid function, instead of the textbook 1,700 calories.

**Patrick Timpone:** It's fair to say that stress and angst change a lot of things in the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid people chronically have anxiety. When energy production goes down—which happens to everyone during the night—the body compensates with increased adrenaline and cortisol. When your thyroid is chronically low, you run around in the daytime with elevated adrenaline and cortisol. I've seen people with several times the normal amount of adrenaline production. Some people can function normally with four times as much adrenaline as normal, but that's why some low thyroid people tend to get anxious or have atrial fibrillation. Especially at sunset, when stress hormones normally rise, a low thyroid person can go into a very anxious, worrying state.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why do stress hormones come out at night?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments on rabbits in Leningrad found that as soon as the lights were turned out, the mitochondria started swelling. Halfway through the long winter night, the mitochondria were extremely enlarged. About 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, they started exploding, collapsing, and stopping energy production altogether.

In humans, there was a study where they took blood samples every 15 minutes during the night. They found that when they turned the lights out, within 15 minutes there was a rise in cortisol. For those who went to sleep, the rise was much slower than if they stayed awake. So, sleep is a way of reducing our need for cortisol.

**Patrick Timpone:** We've been told it's beneficial to go to bed early, like 10:00 PM versus 1:00 or 2:00 AM. Is there something to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. People who spent the summer months in Antarctica, where daylight is constant, said they felt the best of their lives and didn't feel that nighttime stress. Getting to sleep early minimizes the stress of nighttime.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about near-infrared lights?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Infrared is basically heat. It helps keep your metabolic rate up just by staying warm. However, red light at the fairly narrow band from orange to red passes right through water without heating it. When it runs into a blue protein or blue enzyme—we have quite a few containing copper—the red light is absorbed. Under stress, free radicals reduce that blue copper. The red light re-oxidizes the copper, putting the mitochondria back to work because the copper enzymes are the final enzyme of the mitochondrial energy-producing system.

**Patrick Timpone:** So red lights can be beneficial?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, within just a minute or two, they can restore enzyme activity. They've measured rats' cognitive ability and oxygen consumption in their brains just by shining red light through their head. It restores mitochondrial oxidation very quickly.

**Patrick Timpone:** We're hearing a lot about the 600 to 800 nanometer range.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 600 to 700 is the most important band.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you shine it in your eyes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Experiments with welders who burned their eyes with ultraviolet light found almost instant pain relief when they looked at red light. Also, experimenters gave frogs a deadly dose of gamma rays. When they gave them red light immediately after the radiation, it didn't kill them. The red light restored the enzymes that would have led to fatal inflammation.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener writes: "I fall asleep well with my chicken light shining on me."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That looks like an ordinary incandescent bulb, but they are designed to run on 130 volts. On standard 120-volt lines, they are less blue-oriented and richer in red light. I have one over my head all the time.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a benefit to the more expensive 600-800nm lights versus the cheap "chicken lamp" bulbs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, the $5 ones are fine. Even with serious neurological diseases, they can help restore mitochondria.

**Patrick Timpone:** Jerome in Germany, age 65, asks about numbness in his toes and feet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With age, one of the things that becomes chronic is inflammation from slow digestion. The intestine releases inflammatory signals into the bloodstream. The nerves that pass through the pelvic area are being poisoned by the intestine emitting serotonin, histamine, nitric oxide, and endotoxin into the general pelvic area. This can affect the bladder and poison the nerves and blood vessels passing through the pelvis, slowing down circulation and energy production in the legs and feet.

**Patrick Timpone:** What can he do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The accumulation of polyunsaturated fat in the tissue means that any inflammation—for example, from a green salad, which isn't digestible by humans and feeds bacteria—will produce things that activate inflammation. The more polyunsaturated fat you have stored, the more inflammatory prostaglandins (especially PGE2) will be produced.

Cutting your polyunsaturated fats or using aspirin chronically can help. Aspirin will block the formation of prostaglandins and reduce that amplifying effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** How much aspirin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Enough to make the symptoms go away. If you are going to do it chronically, especially if you have used antibiotics and disturbed intestinal bacteria, you want to make sure your diet has some Vitamin K. Chronic aspirin use can cause excess bleeding. I noticed that if I scratched myself, I would bleed longer. So I took Vitamin K, and now I can take aspirin—1,000 milligrams a day—without bleeding abnormalities. If you eat liver two or three times a month, you get the whole range of Vitamin K.

**Patrick Timpone:** Carol asks if you prefer certain types of protein powders.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. Powdered proteins contain two or three amino acids that are very unstable. When they break down, they can produce inflammatory toxins. Cysteine and tryptophan are the worst for breaking down during processing. The only protein that doesn't have these unstable amino acids is gelatin.

**Patrick Timpone:** Just gelatin from the store?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It isn't a complete protein for a growing animal, but an adult who isn't growing has a very small requirement for tryptophan, methionine, and cysteine. If you reduce methionine alone in an adult animal's diet, experiments found a 40% extension of lifespan. Gelatin is a good source.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about taking tyrosine, cysteine, and 5-HTP for Parkinson's and sleep.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think 5-HTP is good at all; it can lead to increased inflammation. Cysteine produces inflammation and can damage mitochondria. Tyrosine is okay in moderation; it leads to adrenaline. But gelatin has a generous amount of the precursors to adrenaline and dopamine.

**Patrick Timpone:** Where do you get gelatin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Great Lakes Gelatin is an old company. 30 grams a day is fine. The soluble one (green label) is easier to dissolve.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener's fasting blood glucose came back at 127. Should he be concerned?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wouldn't be concerned, but you should pay attention to temperature, pulse rate, and cholesterol. In the long range, glucose will probably come down when thyroid function is optimal.

**Patrick Timpone:** Talk about the pulse rate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When adrenaline rises to compensate for low thyroid, it prevents the very slow pulse rate of classical hypothyroidism. Often a person waking up in the morning when cortisol is high will have a racing heart which slows to normal after breakfast.

Healthy, high-IQ kids in studies had around an 85 beats per minute pulse rate. Studies on older people found that pulse rate varied with IQ. Very low thyroid people have lower mental functioning. They tested people with heart implants: when they turned the stimulator up from 70 to 85 beats per minute, mental functions, calculation, and memory increased.

**Patrick Timpone:** So as thyroid gets more in balance, pulse rate generally increases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, in the range of 80 to 90 is good for most people. That tends to go with a stable blood sugar around 90 and stable blood pressure around 120/80.

**Patrick Timpone:** If someone starts supplementing thyroid, what happens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first week or two, if you are running on adrenaline, the thyroid feels like speed—it makes you anxious. But if you go very slow, like a fourth of the standard dose for several weeks, you'll find your pulse slowing down and temperature creeping up. When you are fully oxidizing energy, it relaxes the nerves and muscles.

However, increasing thyroid requires magnesium. Cells begin making more energy and need to retain magnesium because it binds to ATP. A low thyroid person is breaking down ATP because there isn't enough magnesium to stabilize it. If you don't have a good reserve of magnesium, increasing thyroid just increases stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is a reasonable dose of magnesium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the first few days, a gram or two of magnesium carbonate is okay. But a good diet—coffee, milk, orange juice, meat, and fish—are all good magnesium sources.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is T3 different from standard thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. T3 works within seconds if you chew it, or maximally in an hour and a half if swallowed. It fades off quickly, losing half its activity in 12 hours. You can't take it just once a day because of the ups and downs. That's why glandular powder is often better.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ellen asks about Chlorella.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wouldn't touch it. All of those organisms have irritating components, and the lakes can become contaminated with toxic versions. Same caution for Spirulina.

**Patrick Timpone:** Gio asks about bloating caused by sugar.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That indicates slow digestion. Bacteria should stay in the colon, but when digestion is slow, they move up into the small intestine (SIBO). Bacteria in the small intestine will eat sugar before you can absorb it, producing gas. The first thing is to accelerate the transit of food. Thyroid is the main thing behind the energetic quality of the intestine.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about turpentine for the stomach?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since I was a kid, people put a drop on a sugar cube. I think it's basically harmless, though you can be allergic to it. You have to ensure it is pure gum spirits of turpentine, not the stuff from the hardware store which can be gasoline.

**Patrick Timpone:** Leslie asks about iodine. Should she take it daily?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. Milk and eggs are guaranteed sources of iodine because cows and chickens stop producing if they are deficient. Seafood is also a good source.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you test digestive enzymes by putting food in a solution?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not really. Experiments showed that enzymes in a test tube were extremely slow. But when they added a piece of intestine lining, the reaction went at top rate. The enzymes need to be laid out on the fuzzy lining of the intestine to work properly.

**Patrick Timpone:** What source of progesterone do you suggest?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The kind I designed is Progest-E complex. It is progesterone in an oily solution that works well through the skin and orally.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there any reason for men to look at progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Stress hormones cause testosterone to turn into estrogen. Progesterone and pregnenolone stop the formation of estrogen from testosterone. At small doses, progesterone frees up the natural functions of testosterone by blocking the stress conversion to estrogen. However, a large dose (like 100mg) can have an anti-androgen effect. I took 100mg for a migraine once; the headache stopped, but the following day I didn't have any whisker growth.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you tell us about the protein and Vitamin C content of potatoes?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies on Pacific Islanders found they were healthy eating nothing but potatoes for 50 weeks of the year. Potatoes seem to have low protein by analysis, but in animal feeding experiments, the protein turned out to be higher quality than egg yolk.

This is because the potato juice contains keto acid versions of essential amino acids. As soon as the body absorbs them, any available ammonia attaches to the keto acid, turning it into an essential amino acid. They are also a good source of Vitamin C, B vitamins, and most minerals, though low in B12 and iron.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about eggshell calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the next best thing to milk. It is calcium carbonate. If it isn't finely ground, it can be irritating.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about regrowing hair lost due to digestive disorders.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is an association between hair loss and heart disease due to stress hormones. High parathyroid hormone (PTH) is very destructive to the hair follicle. Lowering PTH with Vitamin D and calcium is probably the most protective thing for both heart disease and hair follicles.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you elaborate on why calcium forms harmful plaque?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the same mechanism. Parathyroid hormone blocks mitochondrial metabolism and turns on lactic acid production. Lactic acid takes calcium out of the bones, and in the process, shifts the balance to deposit it in soft tissues where it shouldn't be. Increasing calcium in the diet lowers PTH and protects against calcification.

**Patrick Timpone:** We were talking about a machine that makes hydrogen gas for water.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it would be good to experiment with carbonated water combined with your hydrogen water. I would bet it would be about twice as effective.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the science behind that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Joseph Priestley, who discovered oxygen and carbonated water, found that carbonated water and CO2 gas alleviated breast cancer and healed ulcers. The Japanese are currently using it experimentally against cancer. There is a thin line of research suggesting we can assimilate gaseous hydrogen from the environment for energy.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, we burned through it. Thank you for joining us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

title: One Radio Network: Vitamin D, Thyroid, Evolving Consciously
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** We're happy to tell you that Dr. Peat says, "Yeah, I can come on once a month." We're going to do the third Tuesday, and that's today. Dr. Raymond Peat, PhD, University of Oregon. His specialization is in physiology. He started his work with hormones back in 1968 and wrote his dissertation in 1972, in which he outlined his ideas on progesterone and the hormones closely related to it. Dr. Peat, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Good morning.

**Patrick Timpone:** Have we had our coffee today?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep, had two cups already.

**Patrick Timpone:** You lived down in Mexico for a while?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah, years down there. The first time I went down was 1955 for summer school studying painting, and many times since then. I had a school down there for a few years, an experimental college from 1961 to 1965.

**Patrick Timpone:** What kind of things were you teaching down there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was intended to be a sort of open curriculum in which teachers could teach anything they wanted, and students could study anything they wanted. The student would propose an idea and try to get teachers interested, or the teacher would give a lecture and see what the students thought.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you still spend time painting now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah, almost every day. A few landscapes, lots of faces and figures—sort of integrating figures into the landscapes. It completely gets me out of the words and from reading too much.

**Patrick Timpone:** Talk a little bit about your ongoing research. How do you find research that you think is valuable?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have a general thought in mind: understanding how everything works. Things that don't fit the established theories or paradigms just stick with me. Some of them have been in the back of my mind for 50, 60, or 70 years. That was what finally shifted my main activity from painting and literature to biology—these unanswered questions that no one was working on.

Currently, the idea is around stress, energy, and structural development. There's a young professor at MIT, Jeremy England, who a few years ago proposed a new way of looking at the origin of life rather than it being governed by chance. The really kind of silly idea behind Neo-Darwinism is that everything is random and life developed by chance. Jeremy England is saying that the flow of energy very quickly creates order, and the order will begin self-organizing.

His idea is really just a new mathematical version of the Russian Vernadsky, who started that same idea at the end of the 19th century. He was integrating the development of soil with the development of organisms in the context of the continuing flow of energy from the sun. He showed very clearly why organisms develop big brains simply by responding to the flow of energy from the sun.

**Patrick Timpone:** That's how we evolved, is what he argued?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, but my interest is in how it governs development from the ovum up through the adult form. It's really the same principle: the flow of energy, ultimately derived from the sun in the form of sugar made by plants. The sugar which the mother consumes is provided to the fertilized ovum. It is that flow from glucose to oxygen that shapes the human organism. It follows that same principle that the flow of energy through the system creates order.

**Patrick Timpone:** So would that argue then that this energy has an order to it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And that's what really went wrong with Neo-Darwinism. They were horrified by the idea of spirit guiding things, so they said, "No, it's all blind and random. Matter is utterly stupid and mindless." The alternative is that matter isn't alien to spirit.

**Patrick Timpone:** I like that. It feels right.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Philosophers since before Plato's time have been onto that. It's fairly continuous through philosophy and all the cultures. It's only this fairly recent Neo-Darwinist worldview that has put things off the track. The basic horrible assumption is that the universe is random and that variation happens only by chance.

Sidney Fox, a biologist about 40 or 50 years ago, doubted that timescale had any reality. Instead of thinking of random changes in a primordial soup, he looked at volcanic energy. He took some hot lava, dropped some amino acids on it, and then splashed water on the hot rock. He looked under the microscope and had what looked like bacteria. In an afternoon, he developed a process so that high school students could create self-replicating, energy-consuming, cell-like structures in a lab class. Basically, he demonstrated that chance is not at all involved in making proteins and DNA. It's sort of a self-guiding or cosmically guided process rather than random chance over time.

**Patrick Timpone:** We've been talking a bit about parasites and bacteria. As a biologist, are we just made up of a lot of bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but they can coexist with us harmlessly. One of the people I got interested in was Frederick Koch. He developed a cancer treatment around 1920. He was a professor at the University of Michigan, and the AMA didn't like his attitude, so he was written out of science and medicine.

He showed that the treatment he used for cancer patients worked for infections. It worked simply by activating the oxidative energy system—restoring mitochondrial energy production—which activated the immune system and prevented inflammation. In the process, it made any bacteria present harmless by providing them what they needed, preventing stress to the bacteria at the same time it prevented stress to the host organism.

Some of his followers in Canada tested his materials on cows with infected udders (mastitis). When the cow was treated, their oxidative metabolism improved, and the infection disappeared. The udder became uninflamed and normal, but the number of bacteria present increased. The bacteria had become harmless and thrived without hurting the organism at all.

**Patrick Timpone:** So what does that mean for us when we think about oxidative stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's exactly the wrong idea. People in the 1960s had already demonstrated that it was a wrong approach, but for 50 years, the mainstream has gone crazy on the idea of preventing oxidative stress with antioxidants. Vitamin C was a cultural icon, the basic antioxidant, but in cells, it is present in an oxidized form.

I experienced this myself in the 1960s. I decided to stop eating all Vitamin C-rich foods or supplements and analyzed the amount of Vitamin C in my urine. It dropped slightly, but I was still putting out 2,000 milligrams a day weeks after I had stopped eating any. That got me interested in what's going on energetically. Where was it coming from?

Meat and milk turn out to have a lot of Vitamin C in them, but it isn't present in the form that ordinary tests can detect. It's almost all present in the form of dehydroascorbate, a fully oxidized form of the molecule, rather than ascorbic acid. It functions in the cell as an *oxidant*, protecting against oxidative damage by maintaining normal oxidation—which is the flow of electrons all the way down to oxygen.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the takeaway regarding Vitamin C is that our body is making all that we need?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but we're getting it from unsuspected sources like meat, milk, and eggs. The organism is making it and having it right inside their cells, but in an oxidized form, which is stabilizing their oxidative system.

**Patrick Timpone:** But scientists say you have to have so much Vitamin C from oranges and whatever.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're saying it acts as an antioxidant, but its real function is as an oxidant. One of Vitamin C's main functions is to keep the oxidized state in the endoplasmic reticulum for folding proteins properly. Without Vitamin C, the protein folding goes wrong.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you take any extra Vitamin C supplementation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I stopped in 1967 or 1968. I stopped having a habitual cough right after I stopped taking the Vitamin C. After that, when I would see someone with a habitually runny nose or cough, I would suggest they stop Vitamin C, and it generally worked.

**Patrick Timpone:** We talked to Professor Michael Holick regarding Vitamin D. He suggests 6,000 to 10,000 units. Dr. Stephanie Seneff wondered if supplemental Vitamin D does something different than the sun.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think she's very wrong and he's very right. He has pretty much turned the culture around on the issue of Vitamin D. I think its main function—not the calcium bone-building function—is that it reduces the parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH is an activator of the kidney production of what they call "activated Vitamin D" (1,25-dihydroxy).

Several years ago, a mutant mouse was found that aged very fast—osteoporosis, dementia, wrinkles, gray hair. The mutant gene was called Klotho. The Klotho gene is now recognized as a regulator of calcium metabolism, and it has an anti-parathyroid hormone effect. The Vitamin D that we take, or get from sunlight, works to reinforce Klotho, the anti-aging protein. At the same time, it lowers the parathyroid hormone.

The overriding large purpose of the organism is to be conscious. The emergency purpose is to repair tissue damage. Hormones such as parathyroid hormone work on the emergency scale and divert energy from our big biological function: consciousness.

**Patrick Timpone:** So are you on board with Holick saying 6,000 to 10,000 units is reasonable? And regarding the blood test, he prefers the upper scale.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I think the upper end of the scale is right. Maybe 50 to 80 on the 25-hydroxy test.

**Patrick Timpone:** I get out in the sun every day, but my level was 38. How can I explain that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The older you get, the less cholesterol there is in your skin. It's basically a cholesterol deficiency in the skin that makes older people need much more sunlight.

**Patrick Timpone:** So if I take supplemental D, would that be a good thing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cholesterol can be rubbed into the skin and helps restore the youthful function. Eggs are also a very good source of cholesterol.

**Patrick Timpone:** How is parathyroid hormone tied in with TSH levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** TSH is increased by stress hormones. A person with low thyroid doesn't make their oxygen turn into carbon dioxide. They don't have the carbon dioxide needed to retain sodium, so they lose sodium. That activates the adrenals to produce aldosterone. Aldosterone directly blocks your mitochondrial energy production and increases the parathyroid hormone activity.

TSH itself is a signal of stress as well as a product of stress. TSH goes around creating inflammation. For example, parathyroid hormone shifts calcium out of the bones into the blood vessels; TSH works in that same direction, calcifying the blood vessels and increasing blood pressure.

Stress creates more adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones will suppress the TSH. So, in a defensive condition, you will look like your thyroid is normal because the cortisol is holding the TSH down. This makes TSH useless as an indicator of your thyroid status because it's just as much an indicator of your stress status.

**Patrick Timpone:** So when folks take a little bit of Nature-Throid and get their TSH level to lower, they're on the right path?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I think it's good to have close to zero on TSH, as long as everything else is going smoothly—stable blood sugar, feeling good, sound sleep.

**Patrick Timpone:** You mentioned starting slow with thyroid supplementation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Traditional thyroid doctors like Broda Barnes usually started with 30 milligrams of a well-standardized product. I have seen two people who reacted surprisingly to 15 milligrams with heart pain. What's happening is that your biggest muscle cells retain magnesium and calcium in a balance. Thyroid is needed for the muscles to retain the proper amount of magnesium. If you suddenly increase thyroid when you've been deficient, your leg muscles will compete with your heart muscle for that trace of magnesium, and your heart arteries will constrict. It's very important to make sure your diet includes plenty of magnesium when you're starting to use thyroid.

**Patrick Timpone:** Just magnesium-rich foods?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, milk and meat will provide the magnesium.

**Patrick Timpone:** Masha asks: What is the purpose of the endogenous unsaturated fats, and why are they not harmful like ingested PUFAs (Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Omega-9 series that we manufacture out of saturated fat, sugar, or starch means there are nine saturated carbons lacking double bonds at the tail end of the molecule. The Omega-9 series has the unstable, water-loving unsaturated carbon bonds closer to the active end of the molecule where the acid end is. The acidic end of the fat molecule is like a carbon dioxide group, which protects against free toxic electrons.

The Omega-3 system is the least stable because it has only a short 3-carbon hydrophobic tail. It has less contribution to the film property of water. The water is less tough and protected when you have these fats. At the same time, the risky, easily oxidized double bonds are farther away from the protective acid group.

**Patrick Timpone:** So olive oil is one of the safest oils?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, because it has only 8% to 12% of the Omega-6. It provides pretty much the same fat composition that sugar would provide. Any fat we make from sugar is all Omega-9. Olive oil is something like 60% to 80% this safe monounsaturated fat.

**Patrick Timpone:** I thought HDL was good to have high?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** HDL is a protective reaction to stress. But if it's too high for too long, that is associated with some degenerative problems, like being a precursor to cancer.

**Patrick Timpone:** Linda asks about Vitamin K for babies. Is there an oral form instead of the injection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It works even transdermally. You need a bigger dose, but it is absorbed through the skin. If the mother was eating Vitamin K while pregnant, the baby wouldn't need a supplement.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about K2?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's involved in energy production, not just clotting. It's needed to make anti-clotting proteins. A Vitamin K deficiency can cause excess bleeding but also leads to abnormal clotting and strokes. It protects blood vessels against calcification.

**Patrick Timpone:** When we use the term strokes, is it usually blood clots?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Officially, clotting-type strokes are several times as frequent as bleeding-type strokes. But if you look at the data, any extremely old person is likely to be having small, microscopic bleeding strokes in their brain. I think Vitamin K, progesterone, thyroid, and Vitamin D protect against that.

The so-called "transient ischemic attack" is a constriction of small arteries caused by reduced energy production. Carbon dioxide is the normal vasodilator in the brain. If your brain isn't getting enough sugar or oxygen, it stops making enough carbon dioxide, and the arteries constrict.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do we increase this carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In an emergency, rebreathing in a paper bag. I've seen people lower crisis-level blood pressure in just a few hours by breathing for one or two minutes in a paper bag every 30 minutes. Increasing carbon dioxide relaxes blood vessels, especially in the brain.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about processed thyroid supplements. He didn't get results from desiccated thyroid and asks about a grass-fed supplement from New Zealand.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 30 years ago, the standard was Armour Thyroid. But the company sold their trade name, and the formula started changing. Before that, someone sent 10 products to an analytical lab, and they found that 8 of the 10 samples bought in a drugstore as prescription thyroid contained no thyroid tissue at all.

It's a refined technology to make a good thyroid product. You have to know you're getting the actual thyroid gland—I've seen people mistake lymph nodes for thyroid glands. You have to process it carefully, simply removing the fat with a solvent so it's stable.

**Patrick Timpone:** Where can we get the good stuff now?
