**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have told me recently they were having good results from Nature-Throid and WP Thyroid. But for about 30 years, I've been using the synthetic equivalents based on the old Armour composition. Cynoplus exactly copied the Thyrolar proportions. I've been using Cynoplus now for about 35 years. It is a mixture of a 4-to-1 ratio of T4 to T3. The same company makes a pure T3 called Cynomel.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are there any good food sources of tyrosine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Glycine and proline are the main reasons for using gelatin. Gelatin is completely free of the amino acids that are pro-inflammatory, anti-thyroid, and even carcinogenic: tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine. Gelatin is a very protective protein for a mature person who isn't growing.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you take a lot of it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. A book on the medical use of gelatin published around 1940 described treating diabetes and colitis with 30 grams a day. I've known people to use 60 grams a day with very good results.

**Patrick Timpone:** And bone broth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you cool it and it becomes solid, that's what you want.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks: If powdered eggshells are pure calcium carbonate, why not just buy calcium carbonate tablets?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the manufacturer used oyster shells or eggshells, they would get a pure, safe product. But you can't count on that. When people have analyzed various calcium carbonate products, the eggshell was always the purest.

**Patrick Timpone:** He also says his joint pain subsided by putting a quarter teaspoon of baking soda in his coffee.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's actually filling in for potential calcium deficiency. The sodium tends to lower your adrenal aldosterone production. Aldosterone is an age-promoting, inflammation-promoting hormone. The bicarbonate is turned into carbon dioxide, acidifying cells and keeping them in the protected, oxidizing state.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is sulfated castor oil (Turkey Red Oil) safe for soap? Is lanolin safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Turkey Red Oil is probably okay. Lanolin is a very stiff oil, so it helps to thin it with coconut oil. Besides being a sealing agent, it is more than 50% a precursor steroid to cholesterol. To the extent it can dissolve into the skin, it's going to have an anti-aging effect.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about high altitude living?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Studies in New Mexico and Switzerland have shown heart disease decreases in proportion to increasing altitude. Every thousand feet, there was about a 2% decrease in mortality. Your body retains more carbon dioxide when you adapt slowly.

There is a myth about high altitude causing suicide by lowering serotonin. Actually, that is totally wrong. Serotonin does go down as altitude goes up, and that's why mortality from heart disease and cancer goes down. If you look at the countries with the highest suicide rates—South Korea, Lithuania, Bangladesh—they are very low altitude. The lowest suicide rates are generally in Mexico, Colombia, and Bolivia—high altitude countries.

**Patrick Timpone:** Thoughts on a carnivore or strictly animal foods diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If that includes milk, cheese, eggs, and oysters, that's a pretty good diet. But if you eat only the muscle meats, then you have something like a 10-to-1 ratio of phosphate to calcium, which is very pro-inflammatory.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about rice or quinoa?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fats in rice are very highly unsaturated and get rancid almost immediately. The traditional Chinese way of making white rice involves removing the bran and germ. The ideal way to eat corn is the lime-processed, Mexican form called nixtamalization.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is pasteurized milk okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good tasting pasteurized milk has been held at temperature only for a few seconds and then quickly cooled. It can taste just as good as unpasteurized.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about cooking meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it's overcooked, the cholesterol is progressively oxidized. Poached salmon had many times more toxic oxidized cholesterol than quickly broiled salmon. If you can bring it up to temperature in just two or three minutes, that's best.

**Patrick Timpone:** My daughter has EPP (Erythropoietic Protoporphyria). Experts recommend a higher carb diet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, sugar is the protective thing. When your sugar is low, free fatty acids go up and poison all of your tissues. Estrogen causes a drop in blood sugar and a surge of porphyrin. Having consistent sugar intake—like frequent orange juice—is usually all it takes to prevent the attacks.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener says Omega-3 is protective to the retina.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wrote a newsletter about that. In babies, it's the Omega-3 fatty acids that are damaged by blue light or ultraviolet light. Bright light causes retinal damage specifically by the changes in these highly unsaturated fats. There is a lot of literature showing they are damaging to the retina.

**Patrick Timpone:** Have you heard of Morris Krok and the all-fruit diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of fruits stimulate the intestine and accelerate movement, keeping bacteria happy and harmless. One problem with a pure fruit diet over the long run is that most fruits are very low in iron. You can tolerate a fairly low iron intake if everything else is good. In the US, you might end up eating a lot of bananas and dates, and those happen to be high in serotonin and can create problems of inflammation.

**Patrick Timpone:** How would you get more iron on a fruit diet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In studies of Pacific Islanders who live on a potato diet, once a year they have a pork feast—one week a year—and that's enough iron apparently.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thanks for being here.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks.

**Patrick Timpone:** Well, here we go. It is the third Tuesday, and that brings us to a time when we're grateful to have the lovely and talented Dr. Ray Peat on the air. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good morning.

**Patrick Timpone:** How are you doing there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very good. It has started raining. Winter weather is setting in already.

**Patrick Timpone:** You're in Oregon, right? You get a lot of rain there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The weather has been pretty variable, but we're back to the old continuous rain. It looks like the ocean is warming up, and when that happens, we get extra rain; humid air condenses. The nighttime rain is traditional Northwest weather, but we had been changing over the last 30 or 40 years until it looked more like a Midwest climate—summer rain and drier winters. But I think we're back to the old rain in the winter night.

**Patrick Timpone:** I saw with the Farmers Almanac, they use sunspots and they're predicting a cold and woolly winter this year for a lot of the country. We'll see how accurate that is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the sun and the submarine volcanoes are really the important thing changing the weather over the long term, rather than carbon dioxide. The Pacific is really pretty full of volcanoes that actually are warming the ocean, and they have cycles like sunspot cycles.

**Patrick Timpone:** So they put out a lot of heat down there and we don't really know when they're spitting up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And they're teeming with primitive life forms that can live at extremely high temperatures.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the ocean warms and that causes all kinds of things to happen in the jet stream and weather changes more dramatically.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it changes the ocean currents.

**Patrick Timpone:** It's hard to imagine that carbon dioxide is the devil. Don't we want to keep more carbon dioxide in us by not breathing so fast?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. One of the anti-climate change people gets up on a box and lectures in London with a little sign that says, "Carbon dioxide is the gas of life."

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Ray Peat is probably one of the few well-known, well-credentialed people that "got milk." You've been drinking milk for a long time now and you do good with it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. There were times, like when I was living in Mexico City, when it was hard to get good milk. The rich people would send their maids out at dawn to buy up all of the good milk. So for three or four years, I went very light on milk. But the rest of my life, I've been a big milk drinker. Gallon a day.

**Patrick Timpone:** You're still doing a gallon a day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, about two and a half quarts average now.

**Patrick Timpone:** We had an Ayurvedic doctor on a couple of weeks ago, Dr. Marianne Teitelbaum. She says dairy is perhaps the most misunderstood of all food groups. She writes: "The ancient doctors said that every food you eat spends three to five days in each tissue before progressing to the next... The only exception to the rule is milk. It nourishes all seven tissues in one day." Do you think that's accurate, going through all the tissues like that in one day?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think some of that is historical metaphor, but there is some basis to it undoubtedly. It's now known that every tissue has its rate of protein turnover. As your nutrients change, the food you eat guides the turnover of the proteins so that you get proteins suitable for the type of food you're eating.

Every tissue has its own rate. Bone is extremely slow to turn over most of its substance. Your liver is very fast; the skin and intestine are extremely fast—just a few days and they're completely remade. The heart has a slower rate of protein turnover. But everything, including the mitochondria, is turning over constantly at its own rate.

In general, the faster a tissue turns over because it's kept warm, well-nourished, and unstressed, the better. High stress will make you turn over your thymus gland, muscles, and skin very fast, but in a destructive way. But in a good, warm, well-fed condition, you do have constant turnover and renewal of your tissues. It's like a streaming; new cells are being born as the old ones are being eaten up.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ayurveda has always been a big fan of boiling the milk. They say it helps with fat absorption and gets rid of bugs. Do you find any benefit in boiling milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, sure. Outside of Mexico City where they have cows or goats, that's the custom. Everyone puts a big pot of milk on in the morning and brings it to a boil. Usually, they skim off the fat that rises and make special dishes out of that.

**Patrick Timpone:** Would there be any benefit to our listeners who get organic grass-fed milk at Whole Foods to boil it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Surprisingly, the damage nutritionally is very small. It oxidizes some of the vitamin A and a tiny bit of the vitamin C. But milk is still basically the best source of all of the nutrients for the number of calories and protein in it. It has all of the nutrients except iron.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about A1 versus A2 milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was little we had a Holstein, and then when I was about eight or nine we got a Jersey. I don't really see any difference. I think a lot of it is just marketing to sell something for a higher price.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ayurveda says goat's milk is a little better choice than cow's milk. Do you agree?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My own preference is for cow's milk just because I'm more familiar with it. When I was young, the neighbors had goats and their milk was very strong-smelling, so I learned to prefer cow's milk. But if you handle the goats right, the goat milk will taste as good as cow's milk.

**Patrick Timpone:** You are 83. What has been your experience keeping your muscles from sarcopenia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I noticed after about 10 years of just sitting and studying, my shoulder muscles were smaller because I wasn't working regularly. However, my leg muscles have stayed huge. After not going skiing for 10 years, someone told me my leg muscles must be getting weak. I tested myself doing one-legged sit-ups. Every 10 years I would do 10 one-legged sit-ups and didn't notice a significant dropping off with time.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you do any other exercise regularly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, just every 10 years I would test myself.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you still like orange juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. When good stuff is available, it should be thoroughly ripened. The commercial stuff, they are used to selling unripe oranges. If they get unripe oranges, they add acid to it. The acid etches the enamel off your teeth. So ripe oranges are safer in every way.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you would want to rinse out your mouth with clear water after orange juice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Clear water, maybe even baking soda if it's very acidic.

**Patrick Timpone:** What do you think about taking baking soda regularly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know people who do as much as a teaspoon two or three times a day and think it improves their endurance and strength. But even a fourth of a teaspoon two or three times a day helps reduce inflammation. I know people who used to get swollen legs when taking a long airplane trip; when they took a teaspoon of baking soda in water before getting on the plane, they stopped having the swollen feet.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is happening metabolically there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The sodium lowers your aldosterone very quickly. Aldosterone is a general stress hormone that tends to go up with cortisol. Aldosterone causes a shift towards inflammation and fibrosis. Chronic elevation leads to heart and circulatory disease. So, the chronic intake of a little extra sodium has an anti-stress effect, keeping your aldosterone lower.

The bicarbonate part is quickly changed. There's an enzyme, carbonic anhydrase, that changes carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and back. At the surface of your cell, when you're losing sodium through your kidneys, your cells change bicarbonate into carbon dioxide, which is more soluble in the living cell. It goes out of your blood into your cells.

It amounts to the same as breathing a little extra carbon dioxide or failing to hyperventilate. Low thyroid people hyperventilate and blow away the carbon dioxide they should be keeping. So the supplement of baking soda is imitating, to a degree, normal thyroid function—keeping your cells more charged with carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** Fascinating. So low thyroid folks tend to breathe more?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Relative to how much oxygen they need. The oxygen requirement is very low in a low thyroid person, so they don't need to move very much air. A quart of oxygen will last a low thyroid person maybe minutes, where for a high thyroid person it would be gone in seconds.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you put much stock in taking the temperature to gauge thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you're producing energy at a high rate, you're maintaining your blood sugar level because you're using the sugar efficiently. The hypothyroid person wastes sugar at a terrible rate because they aren't using oxygen properly. If you're using sugar efficiently, you don't experience hypoglycemia, so you don't produce very much adrenaline. Your stress level is low.

**Patrick Timpone:** An email from Beth: "Do you think fluoride and chloride in tap water and bromide in breads are having a major effect on our thyroids?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I didn't know they were still putting bromide in bread, but if it's there, it should be avoided. Regarding fluoride, I was using a supplement of T3, the active thyroid hormone. When I would go to an area with fluoridated water, I would get a migraine headache. A glass of fluoridated water is enough to knock out a day's portion of the active thyroid hormone.

**Patrick Timpone:** Cynthia writes: "I take 60mg of natural thyroid every day. My TSH levels are normal. Does Dr. Peat think that if I just keep doing this, my thyroid will never be able to make what it needs on its own?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen several people who were hypothyroid who, when they took the amount that brought their oxygen consumption up to the right level, had recovery of their own thyroid function and could stop taking it. The supplement restored their anti-stress metabolism, lowered the adrenaline and cortisol, and allowed the tissue to start metabolizing by itself.

However, usually a person's body is loaded up with anti-thyroid substances—polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) built right into the structure of the cell. The average person in their 20s or 30s usually benefits from taking a supplement for at least a few years until they can change the composition of their body.

**Patrick Timpone:** If one is taking thyroid meds, what's the role of taking supplemental iodine?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Foods such as milk and eggs always contain thyroid and iodine. Animals can't produce eggs and milk if they're very hypothyroid. Since food technology has started using iodine, there hasn't been an iodine deficiency zone in the US. If you take two or three times the amount needed, you start interfering with the function of the gland. Taking half a milligram per day chronically is enough to increase the incidence of thyroiditis and eventually thyroid cancer.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you think smoked salmon is a good food?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's nutritious, but you can overload on polyunsaturated fat if you eat salmon all the time.

**Patrick Timpone:** There are PUFAs in salmon?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah, a lot of PUFA. The cold water fish eat algae, and the algae is the source of the PUFAs.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you prefer warm water fish?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As far as it's available. But there are some low-fat fish that come from cold waters. Cod and sole are the lowest fat fish that I know of, and I think they're safer than salmon if you're going to eat fish every week.

**Patrick Timpone:** Mona asks about Vasovagal Syncope. She wants to know what, besides the stressor, causes the vagus nerve to react.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Low thyroid people tend in that direction. The history of shock became a major aspect of physiology a little over a hundred years ago. One of the pioneers was George Washington Crile. He showed that stimulating the vagus nerve was the basic signal for turning on shock.

What happens in shock is that signals are sent to all of your body cells, turning off the ability to use oxygen. It imitates death. When a person in shock is cut, their blood stays bright red because they aren't using the oxygen. It's like turning off the thyroid in a nervous way.

People generally compensate for that exaggerated activity of the vagal nervous system by pumping out extra adrenaline. Their adrenal glands become overactive. Surprisingly, many people are running with both sides of their autonomic nervous system running at an extremely high rate. If something interferes with their production of adrenaline, they drop into the vagal state and move towards shock or fainting.

**Patrick Timpone:** What did Crile do to lower the surgeries at his clinic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Supplementing thyroid, basically. Things they were calling thyroid cancer were just minor conditions he could turn off by giving them a full replacement dose of thyroid. He understood that TSH was driving towards thyroiditis and cancer. He would give usually three or four grains of Armour thyroid—sufficient to lower the TSH to zero.

**Patrick Timpone:** Three or four grains seems like a high dose.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Two grains was the average dose for a middle-aged person, but sometimes to have good functioning, people took three, four, or even five grains.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do you lower the adrenaline and vagal response?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ideally, use the oxygen consumption test. But you can make a good guess by taking your temperature and pulse rate before getting out of bed, and then again an hour or two after eating.

Low thyroid people often run on high adrenaline, which rises during the night. Adrenaline speeds your pulse at dawn; cortisol raises the temperature. So you might wake up with a normal 75 pulse and 98-degree temperature. But food lowers your adrenaline and cortisol. Often, these people will drop to a 55 or 60 pulse rate and 96 or 97-degree temperature at 11:00 AM. That tells you they are super low thyroid.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the ideal would be an hour after eating, around 11 AM, to have a 98-degree temp and higher pulse?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. 80 or 85 is a good pulse rate in the middle of the day. Temperature should be 98 or 98.6.

**Patrick Timpone:** How does dopamine play into this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Dopamine is similar to the adrenaline or sympathetic nervous opposition to the shock tendency. It's the body's balancing factor for serotonin. You want to keep your serotonin down and under control, and then your dopamine will take care of keeping things in balance.

**Patrick Timpone:** What's more effective: eating a whole orange, drinking its juice, or eating marmalade?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The marmalade has the extract of the peeling, which has therapeutic things like naringin and naringenin—major protective factors. The added sugar is an anti-stress factor that supports your thyroid. Ideally, the juice is best, but marmalade acts as a kind of medical substitute.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener experiences malabsorption and can't gain weight despite eating thousands of calories.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've known people who were very skinny eating 3,000 or 4,000 calories a day. When they supplemented thyroid, their calorie requirement dropped in half, and they put on muscle. Thyroid is an anabolic hormone. If it's deficient, you're running on adrenaline. Your cells can't retain magnesium, so they waste energy making ATP that breaks down immediately. Supplementing magnesium helps, but you need thyroid to retain it.

**Patrick Timpone:** Cindy asks about Hashimoto's. She's been told not to use natural desiccated thyroid because the body will attack it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The autoimmune condition is an excited, inefficient state. If TSH keeps rising, it drives the gland harder until it causes thyroiditis. The immune system comes in to clean up the damaged cells. If you supplement enough thyroid to lower the TSH, you stop producing the antibodies. The condition corrects itself after several months.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is pearl powder a good source of calcium?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, pearls are made of calcium carbonate. That is the best supplement, along with eggshells and oyster shells.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about fish bones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is a calcium source, but it is calcium phosphate. Phosphate has an excitatory effect. Most people are overloading on phosphates from meat, grains, and legumes. Calcium carbonate is more effective.

**Patrick Timpone:** How long do you sleep?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on the weather and food, but 7.5 to 9 hours. Usually, I wake up during the night and have some milk and sugar or orange juice to lower the stress. Having milk at bedtime lowers stress hormones.

**Patrick Timpone:** What kind of sugar do you use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pure white sugar is the safest. Honey is good, but if the bees eat something you're allergic to, you can react. Maple syrup is nutritious for minerals, but the heating process creates allergenic byproducts.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about using a red light at bedside for stress.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Shining red light on your blood anywhere in your body has a de-stressing effect. It penetrates very well. Also, an air ionizer running during the night is good because negatively ionized air activates your lung's ability to destroy serotonin.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is hydrolyzed collagen powder as effective as gelatin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Gelatin lacks the toxic amino acids tryptophan, cysteine, and methionine. Hydrolyzed gelatin is just short peptides and is fine.

**Patrick Timpone:** How important is thyroid for stomach acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid makes carbon dioxide. You use carbonic acid to energize the production of hydrochloric acid. So low thyroid usually means low stomach acid and slow digestion.

**Patrick Timpone:** Many Catholic monks lived past 100 on bread and water. Do you think their lack of movement conserved their carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are records of people living to 130 or 150 in the Caucasus and the Andes. These are high-altitude areas, which helps retain carbon dioxide. They also eat simple diets with milk and cheese. Meat is a pro-aging food because of the high phosphate. I think high phosphate is one of the life-shortening things.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is your take on gluten sensitivity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Seeds have plant defense systems. The worst toxins tend to be put in the seeds to block digestion. Gluten itself can block digestive processes and cause inflammation. However, if you let the enzymes activate the seed—like in sprouting or leavening—the toxins are inactivated. Leavened bread is basically detoxified.

**Patrick Timpone:** So gluten sensitivity is real?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it's an objective thing.

**Patrick Timpone:** If someone wants to do sprouts, what is best?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are all vastly more digestible than the seeds, but they should be well-cooked. A fully sprouted bean or grain develops at least twice as much protein value as the original seed.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, are you focused on any particular research right now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm trying to put together a systematic picture of how serotonin fits into stress and aging. I think intervention to lower serotonin is going to be one of the most productive things for reducing sickness and age-related degeneration.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thanks for being here. We'll see you in about a month.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: One Radio Network: A Plethora of Wide-Randing Questions
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** It is the third Tuesday on One Radio Network, and Dr. Raymond Peat has graciously agreed to come visit, take your questions, and kick around his research. He started long ago with a PhD from the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology. He started working on hormones in 1968 and wrote his dissertation in 1972, in which he outlined his ideas on progesterone and hormones closely related to it. The main thesis is that energy and structure are interdependent at every level. Dr. Peat, good morning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good morning.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you do ongoing research all the time? Are you always looking around?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep. Always reading and trying to figure things out.

**Patrick Timpone:** Have you figured anything out recently where you had an "aha" moment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, a couple of things about how serotonin works. For example, people have known for several decades—starting in the 1930s, actually—that hospital oxygen isn't good for people. A physiologist, based on how people react to altitude, tried adding 5% to 7% carbon dioxide to the oxygen. They started using it in fire departments for resuscitating people, and it worked very well. They tried it on newborn babies and found that it was good for stimulating breathing. It was used all around the country in fire departments for maybe five or ten years, then gradually went out of use.

Hospitals almost always keep plain 100% oxygen on hand for patients. But several people in the last 20 or 30 years have started looking at the outcome when they oxygenate a person. When the blood saturation approaches 100%—when it's above 90%, actually—the mortality starts increasing rather than decreasing. About twice as many of the hyper-oxygenated patients don't come out of the hospital.

I realized that this has been known as an effect of strenuous exercising. When you breathe very intensely, your blood can become very over-oxygenated. They know that increases prolactin as a stress reaction hormone. They tried having a person breathe 60% to 100% oxygen and found that drives their prolactin very high.

I realized that what is happening is the lack of carbon dioxide in the blood when you are being treated with oxygen, or just hyperventilating, raises the pH of your blood. This causes the platelets to release their serotonin, and serotonin drives up prolactin. People have rejected that idea because they believed there was a blood-brain barrier that would keep the platelet serotonin out of the brain. But in fact, I've been going over the evidence that there is no blood-brain barrier. When you have too much estrogen, for example, the enzymes in the capillaries of the brain lose their ability to detoxify serotonin, and so it goes right from your blood into your brain.

**Patrick Timpone:** So let's unpack this. If folks over-exercise, we get too oxygenated and we lose too much carbon dioxide by breathing fast? And that could be a problem for people running 25 or 50 miles who fall over with heart attacks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. There are more than 300,000 people every year just in the United States who die with cardiac arrest. It is known that serotonin increases the delay between contraction and readiness for a new contraction. The SSRIs—serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressants—increase that delay by raising your serotonin. They are actually known to be able to increase cardiac arrest frequency.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the SSRIs are falsely helping people to "feel better" by juicing up their serotonin levels?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the theory.

**Patrick Timpone:** Let's go back to prolactin. You said it increases when we over-oxygenate or over-exercise.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Starting in about 1965, when the birth control pills came on the market, there was suddenly about a hundredfold increase in the incidence of pituitary tumors that secrete prolactin. That was an effect of the birth control pill creating prolactinoma tumors. That is because estrogen causes you to hyperventilate and interferes with your thyroid gland. The thyroid makes you produce carbon dioxide, which is an anti-serotonin agent. So if you are high in estrogen or low in thyroid function, you're going to have effectively a shortage of carbon dioxide and an excess of prolactin and serotonin.

**Patrick Timpone:** So when we exercise, we want to work towards not breathing so much and retaining the carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. That can make the exercise much more effective.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why? What is the carbon dioxide doing in the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For one thing, it delivers the right amount of oxygen to the tissue. The tissue, like your muscle, produces carbon dioxide, and the blood arriving in the capillaries releases oxygen in proportion to how much carbon dioxide you are producing. Meanwhile, the carbon dioxide is keeping the pH of the blood in the proper range where the serotonin can be stuck into the platelets. The platelets lose their affinity for serotonin if you don't have enough carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the fewer breaths we take, the more carbon dioxide we're retaining?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not really, only metaphorically. If your thyroid function is low, you just don't need much oxygen in your tissues. You can be hyperventilating even when you're only taking 10 or 15 breaths per minute because your tissue needs so little oxygen. If you breathe at a normal rate, you're hyperventilating relative to your needs. The typical diabetic or hypothyroid person is going around at rest with an excess of lactic acid in the blood because they are losing carbon dioxide and producing lactic acid, as they can't use the oxygen that is in the blood.

**Patrick Timpone:** We had a fellow on the show suggest using a laser temperature gun on the bottom of your big toe. He said it should be around 90 degrees for proper thyroid function. Is that valid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've used the little infrared things that measure oxygenation of the tissues [pulse oximeters]. Hospitals say you shouldn't get below 90% saturation. I saw that in cold weather, my fingers always showed 98% or 99% saturation. But when I was warm and my fingers were actually using oxygen, I could get my fingers down to 90% saturation. So if your tissue isn't using oxygen, you can be dead and still have saturated hemoglobin. If you quick-froze a person's hand, it would stay saturated with oxygen. So those little gadgets used in hospitals just don't say very much about your physiology.

**Patrick Timpone:** But what about the temperature of the toe being 90 degrees?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure, if it's temperature. If your feet are below roughly 80 degrees, they start producing inflammatory signals, and it can cause your whole system to become stressed. Warm feet will make you sleep better by reducing inflammation.

**Patrick Timpone:** So that's the classic "cold hands, cold feet" with low thyroid people. Can you walk us through what's happening there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oxygen makes you burn fat and sugar, turning it into energy. In the process of producing ATP and using the ATP, you are producing heat in proportion to the amount of oxygen you are using. The thyroid is what makes you use oxygen to burn preferably sugar, but also fat or protein. So in proportion to the health of your thyroid, you'll be consuming oxygen and producing heat.

However, heat production can also increase under the influence of stress and cortisol, which could be breaking down your tissue rather than using oxygen properly. So with temperature alone, you have to know the actual amount of oxygen being consumed. That's almost all under the influence of thyroid function.

In the 1930s and 40s, doctors used an apparatus where you would breathe for two minutes to measure oxygen consumption. Using that test, 30% of Americans were hypothyroid. But when the drug companies came on the market with a supposed way to measure thyroid in your blood, they convinced the whole world that only 5% of the population is hypothyroid. It was a great medical disaster.

**Patrick Timpone:** I have a tale about milk. In Ayurvedic medicine, they suggest boiling raw milk to help absorb the fat and kill bacteria. I boiled some raw milk recently, added cardamom and cinnamon, and had one of the worst cases of food poisoning I've ever had. A friend told me boiling raw milk might make it more toxic if there is bacteria.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wonder about the cardamom. Are you used to using that?

**Patrick Timpone:** No, but I've been using it for a couple of months.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think boiling would make it worse. For years in Mexico, we often used boiled milk because we didn't know the cows. But when you have your own cow or know the cow, then raw milk is fine. If you don't know the source, heating it is a reasonable practice. You can inactivate the germs satisfactorily just by holding it at 160 degrees.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a difference between 160 degrees and boiling at 212?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It inactivates more proteins when you boil it. There are theories that it improves or damages digestibility, but it probably hasn't been researched enough. I have a couple of times gotten fairly sick from using an organic raw milk, and I think it was because the cows were eating weeds that I was allergic to.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks: Do you drink milk with added vitamins, and are you concerned about the emulsifiers?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't really trust them, but I drink it because it's available. I am concerned about the possible emulsifiers used to get the vitamins in solution, but I have been using commercial vitamin-added milk for many years and apparently haven't had serious problems with it.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you drink homogenized or non-homogenized?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I like the low-temperature pasteurized, but usually I drink the homogenized just because it's convenient not to have to shake it up. I don't think homogenization makes it more difficult for humans. Our digestion effectively homogenizes it; the bile acids are an emulsifier that break up the particles very thoroughly.

**Patrick Timpone:** We were taught that white sugar and white flour are terrible. But you don't seem to be against white sugar per se?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not at all. The evidence against white flour was that they were using a bleach to make it white, and the bleach was nerve-toxic. They demonstrated dogs would have convulsions. They changed to a less toxic way of bleaching flour, so it isn't a problem now.

White sugar is very highly purified—more pure than many reagent chemicals in research labs. It is washed to a crystalline purity, so it is almost perfectly free of allergenic material. Brown sugar can cause intense inflammatory reactions for sensitive people, and molasses is even worse. White sugar is very safe. Since it has none of the problems of fats, it doesn't break down into inflammation-promoting material like all fats do under stress.

It is safe for diabetics. 150 years ago in France and England, doctors cured terminal diabetic patients—people wasting away—by giving them as much sugar as they wanted. That was about 11 or 12 ounces of white sugar added to their regular meals.

**Patrick Timpone:** They were curing diabetes like that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It works because it suppresses the breakdown of fat in your body. The free fatty acids are constantly killing the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin when you are under stress. You have a stressful event, produce free fatty acids, they kill off your insulin-producing cells, and so you're unable to oxidize the fat, which keeps you under stress.

You can break the cycle, as those doctors showed, by letting them have as much sugar as they crave. That provides energy. Their blood sugar might go up to 400mg percent, but in doing that, it provides the cells the energy they need to stop the stress reaction. That stops the breakdown of fat. Glucose happens to stimulate the creation of stem cells and beta cells in the pancreas. So sugar causes the cells to be renewed; free fatty acids kill them.

**Patrick Timpone:** That is so contrary to what is going on in the world of diabetes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40 or 50 years ago in Israel, physiologists realized that it is free fatty acids that cause diabetes. Diabetics can't get glucose into their cells, so they are having the equivalent of hypoglycemia—specifically neuroglucopenia. Their brain can't get glucose, so it sends out signals to increase the food supply, leading to the breakdown of fat and production of toxins.

**Patrick Timpone:** You mentioned organic beet sugar might be a good choice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Beet sugars are often grown in Idaho, the Dakotas, and inland mountain areas. The rainfall there is depleted in deuterium. Research in the last five years has shown that heavy water—deuterium—is age-promoting. When rain falls, the heavy water rains out first. The last rain to fall inland is lighter water. So beet sugar has less deuterium than tropical cane sugar.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do we know how to get deuterium out of the water we drink?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's been done for the nuclear industry, but it's hard to do on a practical scale. For many years, I've figured that taking as much water as possible in the form of milk and orange juice is best. The cow and the orange tree act as filters. As they age, they accumulate deuterium, and the water that passes through them is somewhat deuterium-depleted.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about desiccated liver tablets for bodybuilders. Is the heme iron a problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The heme group is how we use iron in the blood. The iron atom is isolated by the carbon framework. When you eat meat or liver, the iron is isolated until it gets into your bloodstream. But if you take an iron supplement, the free iron ions react in your stomach and can destroy nutrients like Vitamin A and B12 before they are even digested.

**Patrick Timpone:** Have you seen anything bodybuilders can take to build muscle without harm?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doing the exercise in the proper way so you don't lower your androgens. The anti-stress program—everything that keeps your cortisol low—leaves the androgens, such as testosterone and DHEA, active. Keeping cortisol low is something the Germans discovered in the 1960s. They were accused of doping because their androgen levels seemed impossibly high, but it turns out if you just don't exercise so hard, your androgens are much higher.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do we do muscle work the right way?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Concentric contraction protects the muscle. If you lift a weight and then drop it without letting it down gradually, it's the lengthening of the muscle under stress [eccentric contraction] that damages the muscle. If you walk or run uphill, the dominant action is concentric. Walking downhill injures the muscle because you're stretching the muscle under pressure.

**Patrick Timpone:** So concentric is pulling the weight up. Dropping it slowly is bad?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Letting it down slowly while resisting gravity is stretching the muscle, doing microscopic damage. That produces cortisol, which damages the mitochondria. They've shown that old people doing concentric contractions *only* can create new mitochondria and restore the energy system.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about restoring dopamine and reducing serotonin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The important thing is to limit your tryptophan intake as far as you can without becoming protein deficient. That's why I advocate gelatin, because gelatin contains no tryptophan, which is the source for serotonin. It also has the precursor for dopamine.

**Patrick Timpone:** I thought we needed tryptophan to go to sleep?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not really. Like histamine, too much serotonin keeps you awake.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is missing in people with insomnia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid is the main thing. Sleep researchers found that thyroid-deficient people went through the night without ever reaching the deep sleep stages. I found that if I took 5 or 10 micrograms of T3 thyroid, I would go to sleep perfectly in about five minutes.

**Patrick Timpone:** What effect does increasing thyroid have on testosterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Too much thyroid can create stress and waste testosterone. Not enough thyroid will cause testosterone to be converted into estrogen. Estrogen blocks the secretion of thyroid from the gland. Progesterone has a powerful releasing function on the thyroid gland, so when it has been blocked by estrogen, a dose of progesterone can reactivate the gland.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about corns and calluses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Bad shoes cause the callus to form. Put something on to soften the material, like salicylic acid and urea.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do we take the edge off learned helplessness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid hormone is one thing; progesterone is another. An improved diet that shifts you away from the serotonin side of things helps, because serotonin is at the heart of learned helplessness.

With animals, researchers would put them in a hopeless situation, such as a tank of water where they were forced to swim. If they had never had the experience of escaping, animals would sometimes let themselves drown in just a few minutes. But if they had ever been in a situation where they managed to escape, that one experience would change their perspective and physiology. They would then be able to swim for many hours. It makes a total difference in the ability to survive just by changing your mental picture of how things work.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can Dr. Peat comment on how hydrogen might work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The body has dehydrogenase enzymes that usually receive electrons from fat or sugar metabolism. Some believe they can receive electrons directly from molecular hydrogen. It seems to reduce inflammation and stress, similar to how sugar provides a generous amount of electron energy.

**Patrick Timpone:** Regarding CO2 therapy, does anyone do that anymore?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have heard of a few hospitals in the US and several in Europe, particularly Germany and Eastern Europe, still using it.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does wearing a hat to keep the head warm slow the aging process?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Also putting on a soft wool cap for sleeping. The head, kidneys, and heart have a very high metabolic rate. Your head loses a lot of energy. Big animals live longer partly because their geometry has less surface area for losing heat. A mouse loses a tremendous fraction of its biological energy through radiation. Putting a woolly hat on reduces the stress. At an average temperature of 70 degrees, a person is losing more than half of their body energy by radiation.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why is wool good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The wool fiber has a catalytic function. I think the microscopic structure has a bacteria-suppressing effect, similar to how a natural wood butcher block is self-sanitizing.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is a good way to improve libido after age 40? DHEA, progesterone, pregnenolone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they are in the right quantity. I've known aging men who took 25mg tablets of DHEA, and their estrogen became as high as a young cycling woman. You don't want to take more androgen than is optimal. A young man produces about 12mg of DHEA per day. Pregnenolone is the safest. I experimented for a year taking an average of 3,000 to 4,000 milligrams of pregnenolone per day just for fun. I had no side effects, and my skin was sort of rejuvenated.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about Centrophenoxine to remove lipofuscin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One group found that Vitamin E was removing lipofuscin from nerve cells. But they did a control test with the ethanol (alcohol) used to dissolve the Vitamin E, and the ethanol control removed the lipofuscin almost as well. A very tiny amount of alcohol seems to do the job very safely, like Vitamin E.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about black cumin seed oil for Candida?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have no experience with that. But I've had a lot of experience with flowers of sulfur [precipitated sulfur] for Candida. The fungus has exoenzymes that convert the sulfur into hydrogen sulfide, which poisons the fungus locally.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does drinking milk cause mucus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mucus is our first defense barrier against alien substances. If you get bad milk or are allergic to something in it, you will produce a copious amount. But I think a lot of people just don't like the concept of consuming an animal secretion.

**Patrick Timpone:** Doesn't sugar rip arterial walls, which cholesterol then patches up?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The "sugar disease" (diabetes) was originally defined as a wasting disease where you couldn't build tissue. The glycation of proteins is not really glycation in most cases; it is a chemical reaction produced by the small fragments of polyunsaturated fats breaking down—producing things like acrolein—which is interpreted as glycation.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about honey and maple syrup?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They contain nutrients, but they are produced by high-temperature dehydration. Heating sugar in the presence of amino acids creates brown toxic material which is allergenic. Honey is fine if it hasn't been heated above pasteurization temperature.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener gets optic migraines (wavy vision).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens when you aren't getting circulation to the optic part of your brain. Blood vessel spasms and serotonin are involved. Aspirin and sugar are first aid for that. Thyroid is long-range preventive.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about Aubrey de Grey's claim that ketosis is chemically reactive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ketones found in fruits and vegetables are very good. But if you produce "ketosis" yourself [through starvation or diet], you produce ketone bodies, one of which is a reactive alcohol. The ketones you produce yourself have side effects.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about Carbon 60 (Buckyballs)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think those are risky because tiny nanoparticles can activate the inflammatory process.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are antioxidants overhyped?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the worst damage to the body is an absence of oxidative processes—reductive stress. We have to avoid an excess of electrons and keep our oxidative system working to consume them, not try to block them with antioxidants. Cancer cells are extremely well provided with antioxidant systems.

**Patrick Timpone:** In the soot which came from the wood, I guess.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. You put a piece of cold metal or porcelain in the flame of a candle burner and carbon spontaneously condenses at high temperature. Methane is a single atom of carbon with hydrogen. When it burns—like if you have a cloud of natural gas and it explodes—it creates a cloud of soot. This results when the single atom of carbon surrounded by hydrogen condenses spontaneously into very symmetrical six-membered rings.

Some of the cyclic molecules are huge, and being very large and heavy, they stick to each other and form these gobs of black material. Each molecule has this pattern, six-membered rings, which happens to be analogous to the steroid molecule. The steroid molecule has three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. The estrogen industry realized that everyone could have a patented unique molecule and sell it as estrogen, which they called the "female hormone" because it can be found in the ovary of a pregnant animal. They advertised that they were selling the female hormone, which they said would make women more fertile.

They convinced even Harvard doctors—two of them did studies giving this, basically a soot derivative, diethylstilbestrol (DES), to pregnant women, claiming that it prevented miscarriage. But the animal studies in the 1930s and early 40s had all demonstrated that every kind of estrogen creates miscarriage or stillbirth.

**Patrick Timpone:** What's the biggest piece of misinformation regarding these two hormones that most people believe is untrue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of doctors still refer to progesterone as the "pregnancy hormone." Just a couple of weeks ago, someone said her doctor told her that since she had her uterus removed, she didn't need progesterone because progesterone is only the pregnancy hormone. That is an absolutely ridiculous idea.

Going back to the 1940s, doctors were taught to sell estrogen to get pregnant. They knew that estrogen causes cancer of the uterus. That was one of the early demonstrations of soot—that of estrogens of all sorts, the most sensitive organ is the uterus, then the breast, then the brain, then the lungs.

Then someone discovered—actually about 1945 it was already discovered—that progesterone prevented uterine cancer from estrogen. So they said, if you take estrogen and don't want uterine cancer, then you should take progesterone with it. But then the profitable thing was to do a hysterectomy. Everyone by the age of 30 or 35 was being urged to have a hysterectomy. Without the uterus, they said there's no need for progesterone.

But in the 1930s, the ovaries were found to produce hundreds of times more quantity of progesterone than estrogen. Estrogen is really a minor hormone from the ovary. In experimental surgery, people have demonstrated that when they measured the amount of estrogen coming out of the ovary as a control, they measured the blood coming out of the monkey's arm and found that the arm was producing as much estrogen as the ovary. So the idea of estrogen as an ovarian hormone is really out of context. Every tissue of the animal produces a large amount of estrogen when it's under stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** So laying it out as you have been, you can see how there's so much confusion.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doctors are still being told if you don't have a uterus, you don't need progesterone. The brain is one of the biggest sources of progesterone. The placenta in pregnancy, the corpus luteum of the ovary, and the brain. The brain contains 10 times the concentration of progesterone that the blood serum does. The skin is another major source. When you take out the ovaries, you're putting an extra load on the brain and the skin to maintain the concentration of progesterone.

**Patrick Timpone:** What's the best advice you can give to our lady listeners regarding these two hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They're very likely to be told, still 60 or 70 years after it was proven false, that estrogen is a lifelong female hormone. But old men rival women of the same age in the amount of estrogen being produced because it's a stress hormone produced by tissue of any sort under stress. Question the claim that aging is evidence of a need for more estrogen. Old tissue increasingly tends to make estrogen, but the opposite is true.

Progesterone failure is the primary thing that brings on menopause. The monthly surge of progesterone produces the monthly cycle. When that stops, what is left is a surge of estrogen which is no longer balanced by progesterone.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is that a sign of health in general, the longer a lady menstruates?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so.

**Patrick Timpone:** And the hot flashes? People have said that that's due to possible toxicity in the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is stress. Even in the 20s or younger, I've known women having hot flashes that were resolved when they took thyroid or progesterone to prevent the stress.

One of the immediate chemical changes that produces the hot flash in the skin is a surge of nitric oxide causing vasodilation. Unopposed estrogen is a powerful activator of nitric oxide. I'm convinced that unopposed estrogen is the cause of the hot flashes.

Doctors looking only at a blood test of estrogen will say no, because at menopause a woman's estrogen in the serum is very low. But this has been very competently studied. If you take a bit of tissue and compare it to the serum, the tissue has 10 or 20 times more estrogen than the serum. What makes the difference—what can raise the estrogen in the serum—is progesterone.

When you have a normal cycle with progesterone, the progesterone does eight or ten different chemical actions causing the tissue content of the estrogen to decrease. As it decreases in the cell, it enters the bloodstream on its way to the kidneys and liver to be excreted. In the absence of progesterone, those changes don't happen. So the estrogen stays inside the cell at a concentration much higher than in the blood.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why do progesterone levels go too low?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For pregnancy to be safe for both the mother and the baby, the placenta must produce a huge amount of progesterone every day. But when the woman or animal is under stress, the stress changes the pituitary and all the other glands to avoid pregnancy. A stressed animal of any sort would be less likely to survive if it got pregnant. So the trick is that pregnancy is prevented by stress for the safety of the mother.

**Patrick Timpone:** Many feel like a little bit of progesterone cream helps to keep testosterone levels better for guys. What's going on there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've heard that from several men over the years. My first experiences experimenting with progesterone was that it would stop my whiskers growing for a couple of days because a good dose of it blocks hormones that could interfere with pregnancy. Progesterone puts everything down the middle. When it's high in pregnancy, you don't want any stray hormones disturbing the pregnancy.

**Patrick Timpone:** So it's not necessarily a testosterone builder or an anabolic thing?

**Patrick Timpone:** You sound like you wouldn't recommend guys mess with it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. Most of the men that I've known who used it, it did shrink the penis and stop whisker growth. It shrinks the penis temporarily because testosterone is maintaining the circulation. The right amount of testosterone maintains a certain tone in the exit vessels, allowing a considerable amount of blood to stay there, even in the passive state.

**Patrick Timpone:** How would you know what just the right amount is?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think only by trial and error. I've known men who had anti-testosterone symptoms with 10 milligrams, and others who felt an increase of testosterone with the same small dose.

**Patrick Timpone:** After all these years, do you have a milligram standard you would start guys at if they wanted to experiment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 5 milligrams.

**Patrick Timpone:** How did all these people find you over the years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 70s when I started giving out samples of thyroid and progesterone dissolved in vitamin E, people got such tremendous results just giving it away to whoever happened by. They started talking about the amazing things that happened.

**Patrick Timpone:** What kind of experiences were they having?

I gave her a bottle of progesterone in oil and told her to go in the bathroom and spread it all over her body. She came out and within five minutes had stopped sobbing. **Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks: "You recommend 2,000mg of calcium per day. A concern expressed by other nutritionists is that calcium may not go to the bones, but into the soft tissue causing systemic damage. What are the physiological assumptions you are making?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I know lots of doctors and nutritionists still have that idea. The parathyroid gland is constantly regulating. If you eat an excess of calcium and a moderate or low amount of phosphate, the parathyroid gland becomes very passive, especially if you have adequate vitamin D.

The parathyroid gland's main function seems to be to take calcium out of the bone and bring it into the blood. A side effect of taking it out of the bone is that it activates take-up by the soft tissue. Keeping the parathyroid gland as inhibited as possible leaves your bones unaltered.

When you eat an excess of calcium and have an adequate vitamin D level, the calcium passes right through your kidneys into the urine. But if your parathyroid is active, it can form stones on the way out.

Carbon dioxide is the factor that keeps the calcium in solution in the bloodstream and stable in the bones. When the parathyroid hormone is active, it forms lactic acid in the bone, and it's lactic acid that dissolves and removes the calcium from the bone. That same process happens in the blood vessels. Carbon dioxide keeps the calcium dissolved, but lactic acid precipitates calcium and forms hardening of the arteries and kidney stones. Keeping parathyroid hormone low and your carbon dioxide production high relative to lactic acid is what's going to keep bones strong and arteries soft.

**Patrick Timpone:** Jerome asks: "I have a history of family strokes. What can I do to strengthen my arteries?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are two main kinds of stroke: one in which a clot forms and plugs up the small arteries, and the other where a blood vessel breaks and leaks. Then there is a relatively harmless thing, a transient ischemic attack (TIA), where the arteries or capillaries close down because carbon dioxide isn't being produced.

**Patrick Timpone:** Let's talk about the clotting strokes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the United States, that's by far the most common type. It relates to serotonin. Excess serotonin increases when you're under stress, especially if you're hypothyroid. Hyperventilation raises the pH of your blood by blowing out the CO2. As the pH of the blood rises, your platelets lose the ability to bind serotonin. So serotonin rises in the blood.

**Patrick Timpone:** So angst and tension could be a chief cause for these strokes?

**Patrick Timpone:** I've been putting black cumin seed oil on my thyroid with a little DMSO and using a red light, and my body temperature has gone up about half a degree.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the insulin resistance thing is not the whole story?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Stress increases the liberation of free fatty acids from your tissues. It's the liberation of free fatty acids which get into the cell and block the ability of the cell to oxidize glucose. When glucose isn't being oxidized, it's likely to be turned into lactic acid.

**Patrick Timpone:** Adrian asks: "Does Dr. Peat believe the A1C blood test is a reliable metric to see if I'm taking too much sugar?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I don't think so. It relates very closely to sugar because it will be influenced by the breakdown of free fatty acids. The polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs) break down into fragments that look like sugar fragments, but fats are much more oxidizable and toxic.

**Patrick Timpone:** James asks about the best ways to improve liver health.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A good diet is the first thing. B vitamins are extremely important. Selenium is essential for being able to use the thyroid molecules to put it into the right active T3 form. And carbohydrate is very important.

**Patrick Timpone:** Trent asks: "I donate blood several times per year. What is the optimal serum ferritin blood level for someone age 70?"

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the idea of giving blood to get rid of excess iron?

**Patrick Timpone:** Elmer asks: "If I'm trying to lose fat, should we be drinking lower fat milk?"

**Patrick Timpone:** Are birth control pills estrogen manipulators, and are they dangerous?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 30s, they already knew that estrogen prevented implantation or caused miscarriages. They didn't want to sell a miscarriage pill. In the 50s, someone thought up the idea that it isn't acting on the uterus, it's acting only on your brain and pituitary to stop ovulation. If you can stop ovulation, you won't be accused of causing abortions.

**Patrick Timpone:** But that was fake news?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The first wave of them was causing sometimes fatal hemorrhages, often disabling strokes by causing clotting in the brain. They reduced the amount of estrogen by about a factor of 10 from the first wave. But the medical literature is still out there showing that depression, mood changes, movement disorders, and restlessness are associated with them.

**Patrick Timpone:** What percent of tryptophan ingested from food is converted to serotonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That depends on your level of stress. It can be very high when you're under stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is risk-taking involved in the state of learned helplessness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Serotonin turns on the stress system, but it can also turn off the adaptive things such as production of progesterone. You can break out of learned helplessness by increasing your energy. Thyroid is a crucial thing in stopping learned helplessness.

**Patrick Timpone:** What exactly is learned helplessness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The term relates to old studies where they convinced a rat that escape was impossible. The animal in that state would allow itself to drown very easily because it saw no use in swimming. But if they showed it some exit possibility, it in effect vaccinated it against stress so that when dropped into the water, instead of drowning in a few minutes, sometimes they would resist and swim for more than a day. It was a mental change.

**Patrick Timpone:** Would you talk about free will and determinism?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think we are determined to have free will. It's part of our nature. Like the formation of soot molecules—extremely complex, organized, symmetrical molecules form spontaneously. The carbon atoms have an intrinsic ordering principle. I think that spontaneous tendency to improve things, to create order out of chaos, is where determinism affects free will. I think our inherent free will is intending to create high-level order.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ellen wants to know: As women get older, what are signs of low progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just about everything. Aging. Weakening bones, loss of elasticity in the skin, loss of moisture, stiffening of joints and arteries. Reduced curiosity and initiative. Less interest in adventure, more interest in security.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is titanium ceramic non-stick cookware safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Without seeing any tests, I would refrain from using it to cook anything acidic. Ceramics aren't necessarily acid-resistant. The more it's like a simple silicon glass surface, the safer it is.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is oral micronized progesterone equal to Progest-E in its effect?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The drug companies sell progesterone usually in an emulsion of peanut oil and micronized progesterone. As your bile emulsifies the peanut oil, very little of the progesterone goes into solution. Molecules released from the crystals will go directly from your intestine to the liver and will be attached to glucuronic acid, which quickly leaves in the urine.

When it's dissolved in vitamin E (like Progest-E), vitamin E enters in the form of chylomicrons, which enter the body through the lymphatic vessels, bypassing the liver. This lets the progesterone distribute through the whole system.

**Patrick Timpone:** James asks: "I don't have set meal times and follow my hunger signals. Is this negatively affecting my circadian rhythm?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't really think so. I think it's okay to eat whenever you feel like it. The experiments on mice claim that it's good to fast for a while, but mice are nocturnal animals. It's hard to extrapolate from rodents to people.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ian asks about the cause of vertigo.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A very common cause is toxic bacterial growth in the intestine causing a surge of serotonin, leading to a balance shift of water into your vestibular apparatus. That's probably 90% of the cases. The first thing to concentrate on is cleaning up your intestine.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thank you so much. What are you going to have for Thanksgiving?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Turkey or maybe a lamb roast. I'd like to mention a book that people can find online. It was written in 1905 called *Carbonic Acid in Medicine* by Achilles Rose. It has some very interesting stuff about the history of therapeutic use of carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** Thank you. We love your work. Take care and we'll see you next month.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you. Bye bye.
