transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** On the third Tuesday of each month, we're honored to have Dr. Ray Peat, PhD, University of Oregon, with his specialization in physiology. He started his work on hormones in 1968 and his dissertation was in 1972. He has been working in this field ever since. He has taught at the university level and writes many different articles. Dr. Ray Peat is in Oregon.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I am in Eugene, about 60 miles from the coast and 100 miles south of Portland.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are you doing any particular research right now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The last few weeks, I've been particularly interested in why life expectancy is decreasing now in the US—the government is finally admitting it. That is on top of the rapid increase in autoimmune disease, degenerative disease, and cancer rates and mortality increasing in younger people. I've been looking for explanations for that.

**Patrick Timpone:** Regarding autoimmune issues, is the basic principle correct that the body gets an infection—a virus, bacteria, or fungus—and the immune system actually attacks its own tissues while trying to get after the infection?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the classic standard story. I don't think so. For example, in studies on animals trying to duplicate that process, they give them a viral infection of the brain that increases antibodies, just like in multiple sclerosis and other human diseases. They find that if they prevent those so-called autoantibodies—if they block the cells that produce them—the animal dies. The autoantibodies are actually there repairing tissues.

I've seen this in people with very high auto-thyroid antibodies. It is a common thing now to have chronic inflammation of the thyroid gland with high antibodies. Very high Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) causes inflammation of the gland, and the immune system is attempting to clean up, similar to the way it does in a viral infection of the brain in animals. The immune system needs those antibodies as part of a tissue cleanup process.

If you go back to the Nobel prizes in immunity with Ehrlich and Metchnikoff, Ehrlich worked for the chemical drug industry and created the antibody theory of immunity. Metchnikoff was an embryologist; he saw the immune system as a process of maintaining the structure of the body and removing damaged tissues so that the body remained entire and healthy. You can see that process happening in the thyroid, or if you injure cartilage. Your body will produce autoimmune antibodies, but it's a process of removing damaged tissue so the cartilage will be restored.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the body is doing what it's supposed to do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, preservation and restoration.

**Patrick Timpone:** If you go to a doctor and they see thyroid antibodies, they treat it as an autoimmune issue. You're saying the research shows that is what the body is supposed to do?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are some terrible drugs they put people on chronically to suppress or kill the cells creating those antibodies. However, for about 50 years, it's been clear from animal research that anti-estrogen is an extremely powerful factor in disrupting the immune system and creating inflammation. Women have several times the incidence of autoimmune diseases—five or possibly ten times as much thyroid inflammatory disease as men. That's because estrogen is suppressing the restorative part of the immune system and activating the inflammatory part.

**Patrick Timpone:** If you were giving advice, would you just leave that alone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Over the last 40 years, I've seen many women with that condition. If their doctor will give them a full replacement dose of glandular thyroid hormone over a period of five or six months, those antibodies fade away.

**Patrick Timpone:** That would be desiccated thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, desiccated thyroid or Thyroid USP.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In just the last few weeks, I've run across two women who, during their pregnancy, went for a checkup and were given a vaccination against their preference. Almost immediately, their blood pressure and blood sugar went up. They were diagnosed with preeclampsia and gestational diabetes. One woman was sure the vaccination had brought it on. She developed rheumatoid arthritis symptoms and found she had lupus-typical antibodies. She was diagnosed with SLE (lupus). They wanted to put her on immune system killing drugs, but she was skeptical. She started taking thyroid and progesterone and changing her diet. The arthritis and lupus antibodies faded away. I think in probably any case of autoimmune antibodies, if you remove the sources of inflammation, the antibodies will fade away after six or eight months.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there any case in the literature showing where the immune system is actually harming the body, like we've been told with arthritis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are hundreds of papers supposedly demonstrating that, but there are also hundreds of examples of people who recovered from those so-called autoimmune diseases because the body took care of the infection that was the original cause, or the hormone deficiency leading to the inflammation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the white blood cells are slightly poisoned by a bad diet and your thyroid hormone doesn't provide the energy, then there tends to be quite a bit of lactic acid in circulation. Maybe only 50% above average, but that's enough to start the inflammation process. By increasing energy production, you lower the lactic acid and reduce the basis of the inflammation. With the lactic acid removed, oxidative metabolism can energize the cleanup process.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are the causes of high lactic acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The basic general cause is anything that shifts you over to having free fatty acids circulating in your blood. Any kind of stress that runs into a limitation of energy capacity will break down the fatty acids in your tissues and put them into your bloodstream. This can keep the organism running for weeks eating its own tissues, but when fatty acids are circulating, they block the ability to oxidize glucose.

When you aren't oxidizing glucose, you aren't producing as much carbon dioxide. That lack of carbonic acid inside the cell allows the cell to shift over to the production of lactic acid. The healthy cell oxidizes glucose, which produces a lot more carbon dioxide than oxidizing fat does. That higher carbon dioxide suppresses glycolysis and lactic acid production.

**Patrick Timpone:** In simple dietary terms, what do we do unknowingly to increase this lactic acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ideally, you would get all of your energy from carbohydrates—sugars or starches—and not have to rely on burning fat. Stress turns on fat burning, and that turns on background lactic acid formation.

**Patrick Timpone:** Isn't that the whole pitch on ketosis, that you are burning fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When you make an argument by doing a particular set of experiments, you can control the frame of reference to make your point. If you advocate ketone-based brain energy, you shift your argument to make lactic acid a virtue rather than a menace. For example, medium-chain triglycerides oxidized by the astrocytes (connective tissue of the brain) cause them to produce a lot of lactic acid. If you see lactic acid as a virtue for energy, that seems to support the fat diet.

**Patrick Timpone:** It sounds like cherry-picking information.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. There is a whole line of publication saying lactic acid feeds the brain and makes you athletic, but really, the background shift towards lactic acid metabolism is the essence of stress, inflammation, and degeneration.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are the big producers of lactic acid stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Too much fat in your diet.

**Patrick Timpone:** Even good animal fat or butter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You could eat so much butter that it can have that effect. However, when you eat butter, the highly saturated fat (stearic acid) has an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect because it is so stable. Fish oil, safflower oil, and soy oil have so much highly unsaturated fat that they are spontaneously oxidizing even before reaching your bloodstream. It's the oxidized fat molecules in fish oil that will temporarily produce an anti-inflammatory effect by poisoning your immune system.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about pig fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the pigs were eating good stuff, like apples, their fat would be just like butter.

**Patrick Timpone:** Did I hear you say that sugar energy from carbs is preferable to meat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Meat should provide the protein, which is essential, and vitamins and minerals. But meat has a very high content of phosphate and almost no calcium in proportion. Phosphate imitates the stress condition. When you are under stress and break down ATP, you liberate phosphate. If you eat too much meat without calcium, you start having an average condition of over-excitation.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you could do too much meat and not enough dark greens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cooked greens are the richest source of calcium. Cows eat greens, so milk is a very good source of magnesium and calcium.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why doesn't the calcium end up in the arteries?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the phosphate excess that pushes calcium into your arteries and out of the bones. This is closely related to inflammation and immune failure. Phosphate out of proportion triggers your parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH specializes in moving calcium out of your bones into the blood to balance the phosphate.

PTH mobilizes calcium by blocking oxidative metabolism and creating local lactic acid production, which breaks down the bone. This happens anywhere in the body exposed to PTH. If turned on chronically by high phosphate intake, it becomes a chronic block to energy production. This leads to generalized lactic acid formation. In soft tissues, the dominance of lactic acid in the presence of phosphate de-energizes the tissue and allows calcium phosphate crystals to form as the mitochondria die. The lactic acid shifts the pH of the cell so the crystal becomes insoluble.

**Patrick Timpone:** What blood test connects high parathyroid hormone to this issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** High TSH, aldosterone, and the angiotensin system all go with parathyroid hormone. But the most often identified feature is low Vitamin D. Vitamin D helps shift the ratio in your body towards calcium and away from phosphate. Vitamin D, or high calcium intake, turns off the parathyroid hormone. Eating lots of calcium will prevent calcification of the soft tissue.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is taking a Vitamin D supplement the same as being out in the sun?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is better to be in the sun. Eventually, when your tissues have assimilated the calcium and Vitamin D, you become resistant to the sun. It is the de-energized tissues liberating fatty acids that make you sunburn and age in the sun. In rabbit experiments, they fed one batch corn oil and the other saturated fat. The rabbits on the corn oil diet got prematurely aged skin when exposed to sunlight; the others did not.

**Patrick Timpone:** I have an email arguing that sugar lowers Human Growth Hormone (HGH), and since HGH is good, sugar ages the body. They also argue insulin causes aging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lowering HGH is one of the great advantages of carbohydrate, sugar, or starch. Growth hormone is a stress-related hormone. It rises when blood sugar is low and liberates free fatty acids, tending towards diabetes. If you give an excess of growth hormone, it imitates most of the degenerative features of diabetes. Animals that spontaneously lack growth hormone live about twice as long as ones with normal growth hormone.

**Patrick Timpone:** So high HGH levels are pro-aging?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pro-aging and pro-diabetes. Experimenters removed animals' pituitary glands and replaced cortisol and thyroid, but not growth hormone. The animals lived twice as long.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about metabolic syndrome, where carbs raise insulin and cause inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is basically caused by eating too much fat, not enough carbohydrate. You can create it very quickly with polyunsaturated fat (PUFA).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Butter and coconut oil have about 3% bad fats (PUFA). Chronically, you accumulate and store these PUFAs because you preferentially oxidize saturated fats—they are safer and don't destroy mitochondria. You store PUFA in your tissues.

A newborn's brain is almost free of polyunsaturated fats. By age 10 or 12, the brain shows high accumulation. After age 20, when growth stops, the concentration of PUFA increases steadily for the rest of your life. They are preferentially stored and built into the brain tissue. They tie up cholesterol, making it insoluble. It's like ashes or clinkers building up in your brain throughout the lifespan.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are the popular PUFAs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fish oil, safflower, cottonseed, corn oil, soy oil. All the things that make good paint and varnish.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener in Seattle gets constipated even from raw grass-fed milk.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What the cow eats shows up in the milk. If the cow is fed something the person is sensitive to, like weeds in the pasture, it causes inflammation. I've known people who tried five or six brands. Sometimes they settle on ultra-pasteurized milk, which is basically cooked until sterile. Lots of people find they can tolerate that without constipation or asthma symptoms.

**Patrick Timpone:** So you have to find a source that works?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I tried one famous organic milk and got sick. I looked up their farm; it was downwind from a stinky factory. The cows were breathing that air. The good taste of the milk should be the most reliable guide.

**Patrick Timpone:** How much damage can be undone if one starts living healthy late in life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Blood vessels and the brain deteriorate in proportion to the amount of polyunsaturated esters of cholesterol. Estrogen makes the balance worse; progesterone helps the balance. I think prolonged dominance of progesterone tends to reverse those brain and blood vessel changes. That is part of the function of the immune system—to break down damaged tissue and let new cells form.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is the potential human lifespan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The official view accepts 122 as the maximum. But I've seen reports of people living much longer. A man in Florida was documented at 135. A man from Peru was 184. In England, "Old Parr" lived to 152. He was autopsied by the best physician in England, who found nothing wrong with his tissues.

**Patrick Timpone:** If you were on an island and could only take three foods, what would they be?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cheese, tortillas, and oranges.

**Patrick Timpone:** Cheese, turkeys, and oranges?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cheese, tacos, and orange juice.

**Patrick Timpone:** Turkey is a fairly neutral food though, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Like chicken, they tend to feed them grains, so their fat is very unsaturated. If you eat the leanest parts, like the breast meat, that's pretty good food.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you eat bread?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why not?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 45 years ago, I liked to make bread. I would soak it for about 12 hours. The long soaking period increases the protein and practically eliminates the gluten. I found that was very digestible. A slice of regular bread would disturb my sleep, likely because of the gluten.

**Patrick Timpone:** What do you make of gluten sensitivity?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Gluten has a string of amino acids with the same pattern that estrogen activates in the intestine. Like estrogen, it can activate inflammation just by that pattern the immune system recognizes as a signal of stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** But people have eaten bread through history.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They did it in the traditional way of letting it soak for hours. Or, in Asia and the Western Hemisphere, they used ashes (alkali) in the dough. This increases niacin and decreases tryptophan, making it chemically much safer and non-inflammatory.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks about the link between hypoglycemia, lactic acid, and heart conditions like AFib.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the mitochondria are damaged, usually by fat, you tend to produce lactic acid instead of carbon dioxide. That is many times less efficient than oxidizing sugar. You are producing lactic acid and consuming sugar at a high rate but not getting the energetic benefit. To get maximum energy, you use sugar at an extremely high rate and have trouble keeping blood sugar steady.

**Patrick Timpone:** An athlete asks: I have a low pulse (60) and breathe 5-6 times per minute, but good body temp. Is this okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Endurance exercise can slow your metabolism by reducing the thyroid. The tissue itself can become more efficient. People at high altitudes adapt their tissues to resist shifting to lactic acid. Endurance athletes may have a similar adaptation. Coffee drinking does something similar—increasing efficiency without going into lactic acid production.

However, if a person starts with a thyroid problem, they produce too much lactic acid just at rest. The lower your thyroid, the lower the threshold for going into lactic acid production. High altitude and good thyroid function both help you do work without producing lactic acid.

**Patrick Timpone:** What TSH number would you like to see?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 0.01. It's okay if it's 0.1.

**Patrick Timpone:** Really? Not 1, 2, or 3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A large population survey showed that populations with 0.4 and down were essentially free of thyroid cancer. I've never seen anyone free of symptoms who had a 2.0 or higher. Very few people at 1.5 are fully functioning.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are symptoms of a TSH of 2 or 3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some kind of inflammatory problem somewhere in the system. Insomnia, for example.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener in their 80s has supraventricular tachycardia (pulse 200) and ablation is recommended. What can they do to balance things out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Checking Vitamin D would be the first thing. If Vitamin D is low, you are subject to the excitatory effects of phosphate. Check calcium and magnesium in the diet. Those are the heart-stabilizing nutrients.

Also, selenium from seafood. One good meal of seafood per week provides the required selenium, which lets your tissues form the active thyroid hormone (T3). Without selenium, tissues can't produce the T3 needed for heart metabolism.

Finally, avoid a salt-deficient diet. 40 years ago, the dogma was that high blood pressure went with high sodium. Research showed that people with hypertension were actually deficient in both calcium and sodium.

**Patrick Timpone:** A 70-year-old male has estradiol levels of 15.1 pg/mL. Is that good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That is a very fine, low estrogen level. Typically, aging men get more and more estrogen, but 15 is good.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about cooking in a microwave?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It causes the same changes that boiling meat does. It has the virtue of not scorching things on the outside like a baking oven. On average, the nutrients are safer by microwave, but it doesn't taste as good.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do microscopic parasites cause calcification?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just get your immune system revved up. Keep your body temperature around 98.6 during the daytime and your oxidative metabolism going well. The immune system can take care of those.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are there safe spices?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They all have toxic levels. Chili pepper can burn you and cause serious damage in excess. Clove is a pretty safe spice. Cinnamon and black pepper are safe.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about chlorella, spirulina, or diatomaceous earth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't like any of those. Occasionally they have been found to be contaminated with toxins. If you could have each batch tested, maybe, but otherwise no.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener says sugar and juice increased dental cavities.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is good to rinse your mouth after every intake because of the acidity. The quality of saliva varies according to hormones. Some cavities start inside the teeth when you are under stress—"stress cavities"—because the tooth removes minerals under stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is bovine desiccated thyroid okay for autoimmune thyroiditis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, both bovine and porcine are good.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is A2 milk good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I tried it for a few months. It was okay, but I prefer low-fat milk (1%).

**Patrick Timpone:** Suggestions for reversing lactic acidosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Baking soda, lower fat intake, good thyroid function, and Vitamin D.

**Patrick Timpone:** What do you think of Shilajit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know anything directly about it, just what I've read.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thanks so much for being here. Merry Christmas.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

transcriptText:
**Date:** January 20, 2020
**Host:** Patrick Timpone
**Guest:** Dr. Raymond Peat

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat is with us now. He holds a Ph.D. from the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology. He started his work on hormones in 1968 and wrote his dissertation outlining his ideas on progesterone and related hormones. His main thesis is that energy and structure are interdependent at every level. Dr. Peat, good morning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good morning.

**Patrick Timpone:** How is your life, sir?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very interesting. I had an interview yesterday about philosophy. It was an interesting change of subject, but basically, everything interrelates, so it keeps things interesting.

**Patrick Timpone:** Maybe we can talk about that a little bit. Your thesis is that energy and structure are interdependent. Is that almost a spiritual idea, that spirit or chi creates all this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is going on all through the universe. The same things that generate energy and order in planets and galaxies are exactly the same things happening in our bodies. Energy flows and creates order.

**Patrick Timpone:** So as we allow the energy to flow more, we have more order in our life, body, and health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yep. Oxygen is receiving electrons. Sunlight puts electrons into the form of sugar. That is the source of all our energy: energized electrons from the sun in sugar. When we consume it, if we are really healthy, it goes all the way down to oxygen, forming water. So the cycle is complete.

But if we aren't healthy, then the sugar electron energy stops very near where it started and comes out as lactic acid. It is only half broken down, and it becomes toxic rather than constructive. When we burn the electrons all the way down to oxygen, a byproduct of the sugar is carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide is what keeps our structure finely tuned and adjusted, favoring that complete use of energy.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the lactic acid and the incomplete use of sugar could be one of the reasons why sugar is blamed for cancer cells?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. When Warburg discovered that cancer produces a huge amount of lactic acid—even when it has oxygen and should be able to oxidize it all the way to carbon dioxide—people for 100 years have been inattentive to what that means. There are still exercise physiologists claiming that lactic acid is a wonderful source of energy.

What Warburg started discovering was that it isn't just cancer producing lactic acid, but lactic acid itself produces cancer and keeps it going. It creates the energy block in other cells. When the cancer cells turn glucose into lactic acid, the lactic acid circulating in the neighboring cells disturbs their energy, interferes, and displaces the carbon dioxide and its metabolism. So the cancer spreads just by lactic acid to a great extent. It becomes systemic. Circulating lactic acid can be a test for cancer and general health. When it is circulating, it puts all of your body under stress, shifting the electronic balance away from full oxidation and displacing carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** In the perfect model, we turn sugar into carbon dioxide. What prohibits it from doing that and turns it into lactic acid? Is that how we create disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. Just about anything that interferes. The idea of stress is extremely general. It can be too much activity or too little activity. If you are put in a cage so you can't move, the same physiology happens as if you were forced to run on a treadmill. When you are strapped down, your serotonin increases, and the serotonin turns on that cancer or stress metabolism. If you are forced to run constantly, the circulating lactic acid suppresses the active thyroid hormone and interferes with your ability to finish the oxidation to carbon dioxide. It leaves you in a stress condition.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why does the body like to have this carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People have looked at all kinds of organisms, including single-cell organisms. There are simple organisms that don't need oxygen—they just need some form of energy—but it turns out that all of the simple organisms tested still need carbon dioxide. It is really in the whole picture of life; it is even more essential than oxygen. But most organisms have the oxygen and produce their own carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** When we exercise, is there a way to retain more carbon dioxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just the right amount of exercise. You don't want to overtrain; that is where the lactic acid starts melting you down, increasing cortisol, and lowering the constructive progesterone, DHEA, and testosterone. The right amount of exercise increases those constructive steroid hormones and produces more carbon dioxide than at rest. You are raising your body temperature by the right amount of exercise, and that increases the carbon dioxide.

The carbon dioxide binds to all of the cellular proteins and changes the way the hormones interact on the cell proteins. Many years ago, in explaining respiratory physiology, they always mentioned that a major way to transport carbon dioxide on the red blood cells is in the form of carbamino compounds. The carbon dioxide sticks to an amino group on the hemoglobin molecule. The acid and the base stick together instantly. Upon reaching the lungs, where there is more oxygen, that compound decomposes.

Strangely, only two or three people I found over the last 50 or 60 years have been interested in that carbamino reaction. It happens not only in the red blood cells but everywhere there is a protein with an exposed amino group. That means the so-called hormone receptors are influenced and modified by the presence of carbon dioxide.

These groups happen to be where oxidative damage happens. You've seen the diabetic way of diagnosing red blood cells when they are getting glycated. Glycation happens in the brain in Alzheimer's disease, in the blood vessels, and in aging in general. These so-called glycation compounds are sticking to the same place the carbon dioxide should be. If you have high carbon dioxide, any glycating compounds—like breaking down sugar or unsaturated fats—just don't stick because the site is protected by carbon dioxide binding.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do you utilize this information to help you stay healthy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I make sure that I take some thyroid to keep my body temperature and heart rate up. Every couple of years, I check my oxygen saturation. If I'm at a high altitude, it's easier to get my oxygen saturation down to the level that is safest. Just waking up in the morning when I'm feeling best, my oxygen saturation will go down to 90% or 89%. If I'm under stress, my finger gadget that measures the oxygen-hemoglobin saturation might go up to 98% or 99%. It isn't good to have your tissue saturated with oxygen because that is competing against the carbon dioxide. You should keep your oxygen and carbon dioxide in a good balance.

**Patrick Timpone:** That is opposite of what we are told. We are told the higher number is better.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you put your finger in warm water, you'll tend to have a lower saturation. I've experimented putting my fingers in cold water and it goes right up to 100% saturation. If you aren't using the oxygen, it will simply show a high saturation in your extremities. You want to be using the oxygen and making carbon dioxide. I think the average person ought to be around 93% to 95% saturation.

**Patrick Timpone:** If we are at 98 or 99, what would we do to move that down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would suggest relaxing and paying attention to how your body feels. If you are having a thought of things you have to do, that can tend to make you hyperventilate. Just by being anxious and hyperventilating, you breathe so fast you are blowing out too much carbon dioxide. All by itself, that will raise your lactic acid because carbon dioxide suppresses that wasteful use of sugar and protein.

Taking thyroid makes you breathe harder, but it's doing it by producing more carbon dioxide, which stimulates breathing. So the amount of oxygen you are moving isn't the question; it's how you are using that oxygen.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is body temperature still one of your main ways to look at the thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Just getting in a warm bath can solve a lot of things. If you are sure you are keeping the energy up—having some orange juice or milk and sugar to make sure you don't get low blood sugar—warming your body will improve your metabolism and lower inflammation by getting the carbon dioxide produced.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do body temperature and TSH normally correlate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very often, if the TSH doesn't easily increase your thyroid secretion, the TSH keeps rising. When it acts on other cells, the first thing it does is excite the thyroid gland. That should produce T4 and T3, which keep the TSH down at a moderate level. But if the gland isn't responding, the TSH keeps rising. TSH has an irritating, stimulating action on other cells, such as blood vessels and bone marrow cells. It will create a generalized inflammation. A lot of circulatory problems, like hypertension, are caused directly by too much TSH rather than by too little thyroid hormone.

**Patrick Timpone:** If people are working with a doctor and using TSH numbers, are they on solid ground?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. I keep seeing people being diagnosed exclusively on the basis of their TSH. You have to look at the whole metabolism and how many calories they are eating. You can't be hyperthyroid and maintain your body weight on 1800 calories a day. I keep seeing people treated for years with a thyroid suppressive drug when their metabolic rate is already too slow. Stress hormones will lower the TSH, so it looks like you are hypothyroid, but you are really just under stress.

Looking at large populations, one study found that people with a TSH of 0.4 and below were free of thyroid cancer. As their TSH went up, so did the incidence of thyroid cancer.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you map out some bullet points for thyroid health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have seen people on a raw vegetable diet—eating lots of undercooked or raw broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, and soybeans—developing multiple endocrine problems. Just by adding eggs, milk, and orange juice, their pituitary function came back to normal.

Besides raw vegetables, the two most important things for damaging thyroid function are:
1.  **Protein deficiency:** People sometimes get along on 20 or 25 grams of protein a day, but that isn't enough to keep your energy running at the proper high rate.
2.  **Polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs):** Even on an ideal diet, they tend to accumulate. Nuts, seeds, fatty fish, poultry, and pork are generally rich in PUFAs because of what the animals are fed.

PUFAs inhibit the secretion of the thyroid hormone, interfere with transport, and block the actions of the thyroid hormone in the tissues. At the same time, PUFAs intensify the actions of estrogen. Estrogen is a major inhibitor of thyroid secretion. Ultimately, PUFAs tend to degrade the mitochondria that produce carbon dioxide.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are your favorite proteins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The National Academy of Science found that even medium-sized people at desk work needed at least 100 grams of protein a day to work efficiently. The trouble is that the highest quality proteins are rich in methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan. These happen to be potentially toxic, excitatory amino acids.

Ideally, you would get more gelatin-like amino acids. Gelatin lacks those toxic amino acids. Milk happens to have anti-stress factors and proteins that counter the stress which the excitatory amino acids would promote. The high calcium content of milk is the most important anti-stress factor.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is gelatin best for older people?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For an old person, that's the best because it doesn't support tumor growth. When you are growing up, until 25 or so, you need the full protein like milk, cheese, and eggs.

**Patrick Timpone:** Regarding animal foods, fatty fish, pork, and chicken tend to have more PUFAs because of what they are fed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Soybeans and corn have a very high proportion of unsaturated fats. During the 1940s, it was discovered that those grains produced the best weight gain per dollar in animals because they suppress the thyroid.

**Patrick Timpone:** How can you find eggs that are worth eating?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My friends in Mexico would feed their kitchen scraps to the chickens—meat scraps and leftover tortillas with the fat removed. Their eggs were super. As the polyunsaturated fat content goes down, the cholesterol tends to increase and the taste is better. Supermarket eggs labeled high in Omega-3 often have a fishy taste because flaxseed is used as a supplement.

**Patrick Timpone:** Your current newsletter is on the history and mechanism of vaccination?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. It relates to how the immune system works. Most vaccines create a local inflammation at the site of injection using aluminum or other antigens. That local inflammation leads to the delivery of these irritants to the brain and reproductive organs, causing chronic symptoms. It is generally recognized that inflammation during pregnancy changes the way the fetus's brain develops.

**Patrick Timpone:** We've been told that vaccines disrupt the innate immune system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was in graduate school, the innate immune system was considered primitive and irrelevant. They focused on antibodies. But now it is coming out that the antibody system is a desperate last measure of immunity, promoted by estrogen and stress hormones. Meanwhile, the innate immune system actually does learn and is adaptive.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the innate immune system gets stronger as it is exposed to substances?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Natural exposure is through the skin, lungs, or digestive system, definitely not through the muscle via injection. Studies in India have shown that Vitamin A can reduce infectious disease on a level comparable to vaccines. Vitamin D is the other essential immune-supporting nutrient. If you simply gave everyone good nutrition, you wouldn't have epidemics.

**Patrick Timpone:** How does the antibody theory work with vaccines?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen promotes the B cells which produce antibodies, whereas progesterone supports the thymus gland and the T cells, which have intelligent adaptability. Estrogen promotes autoimmunity. Women have five or 10 times the incidence of autoimmune diseases as men because of this influence. The fact that vaccines work exclusively on that system shouldn't be surprising that autoimmune diseases are the fastest growing in the population.

**Patrick Timpone:** How does this affect a 50-year-old versus a child?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That should have been studied in aging animals, but those studies haven't been done. In 1986, the government passed a law saying drug companies have no liability for harm done by vaccines. HHS pledged to improve safety but admitted 30 years later they had done nothing. Many safety studies used the vaccine minus one antigen as the control—meaning the control contained the toxic adjuvants. They were comparing a known toxin against the vaccine.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are thyroid nodules reversible? And do you know a good source for desiccated thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know of any well-defined, reliable glandular product now. Armour changed their recipe. I've heard the fewest bad things about WP and Nature-Throid, but I haven't used them. I use a synthetic designed to be equivalent to the old Armour called CynoPlus. It is a mixture of T4 and T3. It is available in Mexico.

Regarding nodules: Yes, they are reversible. I've known people who supplemented only T4, which suppresses the gland but doesn't give the metabolic effect. One person added T3 to their T4 supplement, and within about three weeks, the nodules had shrunk.

**Patrick Timpone:** Opinion on melatonin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The body produces a fraction of a milligram. Even a 1mg dose is unphysiological. 5 or 10mg is risky. In animals, melatonin rises in winter due to darkness and causes the gonads and thymus to regress. If one is going to supplement, use very small doses, a tenth to a fourth of a milligram.

**Patrick Timpone:** Advice on constant stomach noises?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think that's good. If you are anxious, things go quiet. As soon as you relax, your intestine gets lively.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener has sinus issues triggered by cold, wind, and ice cream. She takes progesterone, B3, thyroid, and follows your diet, but still has issues.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sometimes it is the lack of a carrot salad. Carrots are antiseptic and anti-inflammatory. They stimulate the intestine while binding toxins such as estrogen secreted in the bile, preventing reabsorption. Having a good-sized carrot salad every day can shift your hormones significantly, reducing sinus inflammation.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener has half a thyroid gland left and is on Synthroid (T4). Is the other half sufficient?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It generally regrows and is adequate, but the T4 will tend to keep it suppressed. That is okay if your liver is able to turn T4 into T3. You have to have steady blood sugar to convert T4 into the active T3. Women are more likely than men to have a problem with just T4.

**Patrick Timpone:** How long can one expect to live following these ideas?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the most important thing is the accumulation of polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs), which block your ability to respond to thyroid hormone. If you minimize intake and activate elimination, I think life should be able to go on indefinitely. That is the basic motor of aging.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are nuts a good idea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nuts are generally high in PUFAs, except Macadamia. Macadamia nuts are the lowest I know of.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do you increase starch and sugar to reduce fat intake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Orange juice, tropical fruits (the sweet ones rather than starchy), and nixtamalized grains such as tortillas and tamales. Ancient cultures discovered cooking grains in lye or lime ashes (cal). The alkali turns the fat into soap, which you wash away. It partly digests the protein, increasing nutritional quality (niacin), and makes the carbohydrates less likely to feed bacteria.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you eat bread?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not for 40 years. About 50 years ago, I made bread by soaking the flour for 12 hours until the gluten was essentially gone. I would make a batter and bake it at a high temperature. It made a delicious, non-toxic bread.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about cryotherapy or cold showers?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If your thyroid function is low, getting cold can slow things down even more and put you into an inflammatory state. When your feet are around 90 degrees Fahrenheit, they start producing inflammatory signals. A cold bath in that situation can make things worse.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a link between hypoglycemia and cardiovascular disease?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Adrenaline, histamine, and serotonin rise during hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia and oxygen deficiency are almost identical in the harm they do. They bring up inflammatory stress hormones and cause heart rhythm problems. Keeping sugar stable is important. Re-breathing in a paper bag to increase carbon dioxide can lower stress, anxiety, and arrhythmia signals by suppressing lactic acid.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about alcohol?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In some physics labs, they found that ethanol at a very small amount is a powerful antioxidant. The amount it takes is on the order of a teaspoon to a tablespoon per day.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about molecular hydrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We have enzymes called dehydrogenases which can use hydrogen. I think the hydrogen molecule can be handled by enzymes that handle NADH and transmit energy. It can be constructive by reducing inflammation.

**Patrick Timpone:** Intermittent fasting?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think it is beneficial. If you have a high metabolic rate, going 20 hours without food can bring on stress.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does boiling water damage gelatin powder?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, they are very stable.

**Patrick Timpone:** How to break out of chronic inflammatory patterns?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid (specifically T3), orange juice, and milk are the quickest ways.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about peanut butter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Years ago, they found that about 30% of peanut butter samples contained aflatoxin, a very toxic fungal metabolite. That risk is enough reason to avoid it.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thank you for being here.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye bye.
