**Patrick Timpone:** We are back with our second show this morning. It is the third Monday of the month, so Dr. Ray Peat is here. He is a PhD from the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology. He started working with hormones back in 1968, wrote his dissertation in 1972, and talks a lot about progesterone and hormones. His main thesis is that energy and structure are independent at every level. Dr. Peat, good morning to you, sir.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good morning.

**Patrick Timpone:** What is going on in your life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm working on two or three new articles right now. I learned that Gilbert Ling died last summer. He's been such a big influence on my work for 50 years that I decided to write an article introducing his ideas to people who don't get them in the usual public media.

**Patrick Timpone:** What was Gilbert Ling's specialty?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cell physiology. He came over from China on a scholarship in the 1940s and very quickly developed a new kind of cell electrode, a microscopically fine tip that goes into an individual cell to measure the voltage. It's named the Ling-Gerard Microelectrode, named after him and his thesis professor. Despite being the first person to have the technology for measuring the electronic condition of a single cell, his observations were contradictory to the dogma that had been established in the 1930s. So for 70 years, his work was simply not recognized, even though he answered all objections and showed that the picture of the cell in textbooks is a big fantasy.

**Patrick Timpone:** How did his work affect what you did or what we know about health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was taking courses to work in nerve biology or brain physiology. Within the first weeks of reading the history of cell physiology, I realized my professor was talking about fantasies. So I dropped out of the brain end of biology research and looked for people closer to the actual facts. I found the reproductive system, where you can look at one cell at a time—the fertilized ovum. It was easier to talk objectively about the physiology of a single cell rather than the complexities of the mature brain.

If I had chosen to work with the first professor, he would have said, "First we threw away the bad data." What he meant was observations that didn't fit the dogma had to be discarded. When I was working in his lab, I had a microelectrode inside a cell and showed him there were different electrical potentials within a single cell. As soon as he saw it, he jerked away like he had been electrocuted. I never talked to him again. I came to see the biological world from Ling's perspective: it's a giant business structure that doesn't care about the details of reality as long as it can be turned into profit.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do they do that on a very deep level at the medical schools?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. Medical schools are hugely directed by the pharmaceutical industry. About 50 years ago, I saw biased research coming out of Yale Medical School. I wrote to the Dean asking how much funding they were getting from the estrogen industry. He wrote back saying he was insulted I would imply money influenced their research, but he wouldn't tell me the amount. At USC, I found their funding was about 99% for estrogen and almost none for progesterone. Everyone said favorable things about estrogen and unfavorable things about progesterone because that's where the money was.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you often see people do well when they take a little extra progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Both men and women equally depend on progesterone. It's a massively important brain hormone—10 times as much in the brain as in the blood. It is basically a pharmaceutical industry fraud to call it the "pregnancy hormone."

**Patrick Timpone:** And we get too much estrogen just from modern lifestyle?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you gain too much weight, eat foods that suppress metabolism, or are stressed, any tissue can make estrogen. Even if ovaries are removed, the body makes more estrogen under stress. The dogma about menopause is really a failure of the ovaries to produce enough progesterone to support the brain. In that situation, you are deficient in progesterone, leaving the body in stress. Hans Selye was one of the first people to define this in the 1940s; he said a big dose of estrogen imitates the shock phase of the stress reaction.

**Patrick Timpone:** Ania wants to know about endometriosis. Can that be helped with thyroid medication?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid and good nutrition will activate your liver to excrete every bit of estrogen arriving in the bloodstream. Being malnourished or low in thyroid means estrogen accumulates in the body, specifically in the uterus, breast, and pituitary gland. If you can establish a proper monthly cycle, the cyst along with the rest of the endometrium should be sloughed off.

**Patrick Timpone:** Jeff asks: You recommend drinking orange juice and milk. Edgar Cayce said not to combine citrus with other foods. Is he suggesting having orange juice and milk together?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You shouldn't combine orange juice with meat or an iron-rich food because it will make you absorb too much iron, and it can react to produce free radicals. But I don't know of any harm it does with milk.

**Patrick Timpone:** Mr. Kahn asks about boiling greens and drinking the water for calcium and magnesium. How much should he have?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Milk normally provides enough magnesium in balance with calcium. But if you are getting cramps, an ounce or so of that concentrated water from boiling greens is enough to relax them. If you need that magnesium supplement, it probably means your thyroid function is low, because thyroid helps your cells retain magnesium.

**Patrick Timpone:** Lynn asks if protein and sugar are best not eaten with starch? Does this mean marmalade with tortillas or eggs with rice is best avoided?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Marmalade is good with anything. The starches that cause problems are combined starches like beans, overripe peas, and grains that haven't been sprouted or turned into sourdough. Those complex starches feed bacteria and cause gas and bowel inflammation. Pure starch, like corn starch, is less likely to cause inflammation, but it has a high glycemic index and is fattening. That's why I emphasize fruit sugar over starch.

**Patrick Timpone:** She heard you say you like cheese with tortillas. What makes cheese okay with starch?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the tortilla, which is a modified starch. The Chinese and Central Americans discovered that cooking grain in lye or lime digests the grain and destroys the things that make it indigestible. Nixtamalized corn—used in hominy, tamales, and tortillas—is very rich in calcium and niacin and is easy to digest. It is not like other grain starches.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you think this coronavirus thing is going to get bigger, or will it fade out?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the CDC, the pharmaceutical industry, and the WHO have their way, it'll be big business. So far, it looks similar to old coronaviruses, possibly twice as virulent as the average flu. The average flu kills about 1% of infected people who are already sick; this one is killing 1.5% or 2%. It is a little worse than average, but the WHO and CDC blow these up as gigantic world-ending dangers to sell more vaccines. The trouble is those vaccines won't have been tested for safety. Going back to the 1970s swine flu, the vaccines caused vastly more deaths and paralysis than the flu itself.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does Dr. Peat have ideas for narrow closed-angle glaucoma? Is making a hole in the iris safe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Your physiology is a stress physiology. Increases in eye pressure are somewhat like blood pressure. Improving the balance of thyroid and progesterone against stress hormones (estrogen, cortisol, serotonin) will improve the pressure. The surgery to punch a hole in the iris has the risk of increasing pressure with potential harm.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you think it's possible that we have infections going on with glaucoma and cataracts?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, there is always a change in bacterial load. Simple things like avoiding indigestible foods that cause inflammation can help. Bacteria in the intestine send signals to other areas. The lens depends on a constant flow of liquid for nutrition. The same factors that raise pressure can decrease the flow of nutrition into the lens, leading to swelling and opacity.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a simple test to get a good overview of hormones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Life Extension Foundation has hormone panels for a good price. A blood test is the most reliable. Saliva tests for steroid hormones like progesterone aren't reliable because saliva composition changes with emotion or appetite.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener in his mid-40s has struggled with depression for 15 years. SSRIs don't help much anymore. He understands you are no fan of serotonin. What is your view on the cause of depression?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first thing to check is temperature and heart rate. Average body temperature is now well below 98.6°F. If your adrenal and thyroid hormones are low, your energy is low, making everything stressful. Serotonin is a universal indicator of stress. It, along with estrogen, acts like beating a tired horse—they increase functions temporarily but risk harming vital functions. As energy production decreases, the brain shifts to emergency drivers like adrenaline, serotonin, and estrogen. These can create mania or depression. Keeping your thyroid up is essential. Methylene blue can repair the energy system and help depression, but it is a chemical substitute for the active thyroid hormone supported by DHEA, progesterone, and pregnenolone.

**Patrick Timpone:** Do you know how to tell if a memory is a false memory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. We put things together every time we remember. The past is always with us as a potential, and we create a picture that represents what we have experienced. If you learn a new situation you weren't aware of before, you can create memories that explain what you now know to be true.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener asks: If mitochondria have a will of their own, does being a creator mean imposing personal will upon the mitochondria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't think of mitochondria as separate at all. They reflect the happy, active, energized state of the cell. Nerves are in close communication with mitochondria electronically and oxidatively. We are an energetic, oxidizing whole with purpose and perspective. The medical-pharmaceutical myth created a machine-like picture of the body with little compartments, but really it is a continuous functioning unit.

**Patrick Timpone:** If someone just rested for a long time believing the body can heal, is there a good chance it would?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Things happening around us can help us heal or make us sick. I once watched Supreme Court judges talk on TV, and my blood pressure went up to 168 over 110. Seeing possibilities open up can help everything heal. Historically, laying down and stopping the consumption of things making you sick was the basic cure. Sophia Loren was said to have spent six months in bed to ensure she had her baby.

**Patrick Timpone:** Years ago, with natural food and no pollution, literature suggests people didn't live that long. Is that true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. The Roman Empire kept good vital statistics. Men aged 20 to 30 had a short lifespan because of war, but women and those who survived their 20s had a life expectancy almost identical to 20th-century Europe and America—into their 70s.

**Patrick Timpone:** What do you recommend to detoxify the body of a chronic infection and hormone imbalance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For an internal fungus infection, a pinch of flowers of sulfur (200 or 300 milligrams) taken orally for two or three days will suppress candida and some bacteria. The fungus secretes enzymes that convert the sulfur to hydrogen sulfide locally, which poisons the yeast. In the concentration that diffuses into the intestine, it acts as an antioxidant.

**Patrick Timpone:** Amy asks if it is important to eat only organic grass-fed beef liver, or is regular beef liver okay?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't worry about organic liver. Experiments analyzed commercial animals and found agricultural chemicals in the urine, blood, and muscles. But if the animal had 24 hours of isolation from those chemicals, the liver was able to capture and destroy them. The liver was the cleanest organ in the animal.

**Patrick Timpone:** Amy also says she urinates every couple of hours. Can this be a thyroid issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If your thyroid is active, you burn calories and breathe out or evaporate about three quarts of water a day. If your thyroid is low and you're burning only 1,000 calories, you aren't vaporizing the water, so it has to be eliminated as urine.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do you keep skin moisturized in the dry winter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Don't bathe excessively. Soap dries your skin. You want to preserve the protective oils formed in the skin.

**Patrick Timpone:** What are the safest antihistamines for someone with arrhythmia?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Benadryl is safe if not taken in excess. Ma Huang (Ephedra) doesn't have the risk of stopping the heart. I think Cyproheptadine, which reduces both histamine and serotonin effects, is safe for the heart.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you suggest ways to help pulmonary fibrosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fibrosis anywhere (heart, liver, kidneys, lungs) has a common hormonal cause. Estrogen creates a condition of effective oxygen deficiency (hypoxia), which leads to collagen formation and fibrosis. Hypoxia also leads to angiotensin, which tightens blood vessels. Drugs that interfere with angiotensin are approved for high blood pressure, but they also protect against fibrosis.

**Patrick Timpone:** Amanda has poor circulation, cold hands and feet, and veiny hands.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid and progesterone can have a big effect. Estrogen activates angiotensin and creates a shock syndrome. Bulging veins often mean they aren't getting enough energy; they are in a shock-like state. I've seen progesterone make those veins disappear in less than an hour.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it possible for stress to transform saturated fat into polyunsaturated fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** To a slight degree, but the unsaturated fats we make with our own enzymes aren't as toxic as the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) we get from the environment.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can we get rid of lipofuscin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, progesterone is a big help. By blocking the estrogen that interacts with PUFA to make that pigment, progesterone can eliminate those senile brown spots.

**Patrick Timpone:** You've recommended eating potatoes with plenty of butter or cream. How much butter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I haven't eaten potatoes for a long time, but if they are very well cooked, they are less allergenic. A pat of butter will protect against persorption.

**Patrick Timpone:** Are allergies a lifelong thing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Robert Kennedy Jr. mentioned that childhood allergies were less than 3% before the 1970s, and after 1989, about half of all kids have allergies. He was saying vaccines are a major known cause.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is there a good source of pregnenolone? Many sources seem to cause side effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think some of it has been bad manufacturing leaving impurities, specifically estrogenic materials. Women have reported swollen breasts and cramps from bad brands. Good pregnenolone shouldn't have any symptoms at all.

**Patrick Timpone:** A listener has venous insufficiency. Is this related to hormone imbalance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The wall of the vein consists partly of smooth muscle. When energy is low (hypothyroid, low progesterone), the muscle is too weak to keep its normal diameter. The vein swells, and the valves don't meet, allowing blood to flow back. Getting energy up with thyroid and progesterone allows the veins to close up enough for the valves to function.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it true that some people shed more hair while taking thyroid supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1970s, a study analyzed 10 brands of thyroid glandular supplements. Only two contained actual thyroid substance. The others contained only casein and iodine to fool the USP test. I found that cats could tell the difference. My cat loved real thyroid but tried to bury the fake brands.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can a 66-year-old woman take progesterone every day without a break?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver adapts to a constant supply, so the effect gets weaker. It is good to stop for a week every month to maintain potency.

**Patrick Timpone:** How can we help our thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keep meat intake lower and use milk, eggs, and cheese for a higher proportion of protein. Before 1940, people got thyroid in their diet because fish heads were used for soup, and thyroid glands were put into sausages. Then the USDA said it had to be sold to drug companies.

**Patrick Timpone:** What do you think about drinking food-grade hydrogen peroxide?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It can cause serious burns. Even enzymes like catalase that normally dispose of peroxide are destroyed by it if there is too much, and then it starts destroying tissue.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thank you so much for being here today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you. Bye.

title: One Radio Network: What is a virus anyway?
transcriptText:
**Patrick Timpone:** Welcome to part two of our show. Dr. Raymond Peat is on the show with us on the third Monday of each month. He has a PhD and has been at this for 40 or 45 years. Dr. Peat, good morning. I was asking you off the air, but let's dig into this. We just had a guest talking about the idea that viruses like measles and herpes are already in our bodies. The root canal people we've had on have proven through biology and peer-reviewed studies that when they open up these infected root canals, they find things ranging from herpes to syphilis—stuff that is already in the body. Does any of that balance with your perspective?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you heard of Peter Duesberg and the HIV critics?

**Patrick Timpone:** A little bit. Tell folks who he is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I started graduate school in biology in 1968. I think it was in '69 that Temin and Baltimore published an article saying they had evidence that DNA could be transcribed into RNA, and RNA could be transcribed back. According to the existence of that enzyme [reverse transcriptase], there was a possibility for a virus to insert itself from RNA to DNA; it could leave its genes in the nucleus.

At the time, all of my molecular biology professors denied that was possible because they held the dogma that genetic information goes only from DNA to RNA to protein. The idea that RNA could be integrated into the genes as a virus was not supposed to be possible. But it turns out that we are full of retroviruses. Some people say a huge proportion of all of our genes consist of retroviruses. During stress, we emit these, possibly as part of a curative system.

Around just a little while after that, an acupuncturist lent me a pamphlet written by a North Korean claiming he had evidence of particles of nucleic acid circulating in our lymph. He said it looked like our lymphatic system, but was a completely separate circulatory system carrying these virus-like particles that were actually emitted by cells to repair cells in other parts of the body. He wrote that around 1965.

Just in the last 10 years or so, it is now recognized that we are full of these tiny particles carrying RNA, DNA, and proteins emitted under stress. Aging and any sort of sickness or stress cause our cells to emit particles that circulate. They can come out of stressed tissue, be carried in the blood to the bone marrow, and change cells in the bone marrow so that they are able to repair the injured cell. It is a two-way communication of viral-like particles. Since our genome is fairly full of these viral-type particles—retroviruses—it is a very plausible idea that viruses could originate from stressed organisms.

We know that epidemics originate in famines, wars, and conditions that are stressing organisms. They don't necessarily have to travel only from the "green monkey" theory of AIDS, or snake-to-monkey-to-human.

Forty years ago, there were two botanists researching plant viruses at Oregon State University. They would use pumice powder on their fingers and rub solutions of plant viruses into the leaves of plants to create the viral disease they were studying. Within a short period, both of those researchers came down with the same kind of rare degenerative brain disease. To me, that was very suggestive that a plant virus had invaded their system. I stopped eating raw vegetables at that point.

**Patrick Timpone:** If I have a virus that manifests to help repair something in my body—like herpes manifesting on the lips—and these things are already there, can I pass those on to somebody else?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A couple of publications in the last few years have found that within the body, they not only go to the bone marrow to change our immune system cells, but they can actually go to the gonads and enter our germ cells, so they can be passed on. It is exactly what Darwin proposed with his "gemmules" coming from all of the body parts, going into the gonads, and modifying them for the inheritance of acquired characteristics. In this recent research, they demonstrated that the microvesicles do enter germ cells.

A lab in Germany, going back at least 15 years, has demonstrated that if you eat beef, for example, you can trace the genetic DNA patterns—actual long pieces of DNA from the beef—into your bloodstream and into your cells. We are incorporating not only viruses but cellular DNA from the various species that we eat. It is entirely possible that when you cough on someone, they inhale not only viral infections, but your DNA is all around you, and anyone who contacts you is assimilating that. They've demonstrated that in a good number of people; after death, they can test a woman's brain tissue and find DNA traces of each of her previous husbands.

**Patrick Timpone:** Wow. Spiritually, that makes sense if you believe in reincarnation and karma—that we share these things. So was Darwin onto something?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, he had all of the principles down. He just didn't know the details, didn't know there was such a thing as DNA. But he had the idea right.

**Patrick Timpone:** What kinds of questions have you been getting about this whole Corona thing, and what insights do you have for our audience for March 16th? Where do you think this is going?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I sort of sympathize with Trump in thinking the CDC has been helping a couple of drug companies to increase their share value. The share prices of the vaccine makers are skyrocketing. Both the World Health Organization and CDC have connections with the vaccine industry.

In a typical year, the CDC says an average of about 40,000 Americans die of the flu. Now they are getting excited when a few dozen people die; it is out of proportion to what they claim to be the usual annual mortality from flu.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is it true that when they call it the flu, it's really a pneumonia that goes into the lungs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The way the CDC has built up the market for flu vaccines is to call anyone who dies of pneumonia a "death from influenza." But a very old person, say 100 years old without any particular sickness, might just eat too much raw cabbage, get gas, and that will cause pneumonia. People dying of pneumonia shouldn't necessarily be counted as flu deaths.

However, over 10 years ago, the coronavirus was known to simply activate the well-known inflammation systems, specifically the angiotensin system. For decades we've had angiotensin receptor blockers and ACE inhibitors. The Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) produces the inflammatory protein that causes blood pressure to rise. There is a close interaction between serotonin and angiotensin, and those are both well-studied causes of aging-related inflammation.

Your angiotensin exposure and production increase in old age, which increases your likelihood of getting pneumonia from anything. It's a general inflammatory system that increases contraction of blood vessels, risk of clotting, and interferes with energy production. The people who are dying at a very high rate from the coronavirus are those who already suffer from circulatory disease, hypertension, heart disease, and stroke. They already have an active angiotensin system.

It happens that ACE2 (Angiotensin Converting Enzyme 2) is the receptor for the virus. The virus attaches to that to enter a cell. ACE2 is the enzyme that undoes the work of ACE itself. ACE produces angiotensin, and ACE2 destroys angiotensin. What the virus does in binding to ACE2 seems to be inactivating the inactivator. That leaves ACE free to make angiotensin, which then doesn't have any way out. So it accumulates, causing the dry cough, high fever, increased hypertension, stroke, and so on.

**Patrick Timpone:** Someone conjectured that Asian people tend to have more of these ACE2 receptors. Is that possible?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If it is ACE2, yes. That would make them a better target for the virus. But it would also suggest that, without the virus, they would be more resistant to age-related inflammation. Since ACE2 is the protective enzyme, if you have a lot of it, you are like a young person. Young people have more of that and are less susceptible to age-related degenerative diseases.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why was there so much going on in Wuhan?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have you heard about the military games? The American soldiers left exactly 14 days before the outbreak. South Korean and Taiwanese virologists have traced the gene pattern back to find that in the US, there are five different strains of the coronavirus. The Wuhan strain is just one of those. They say logically you can derive the Wuhan strain from one of those pre-existing five strains, but you wouldn't have five descendants at this time. The inheritance goes the other way; the Wuhan strain is like a branch on the tree, and the preceding varieties were existing in the US already.

**Patrick Timpone:** And many of us already have these in us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The CDC patented the coronavirus 17 years ago. Research was being done at Fort Detrick, supposedly creating pathogens to create vaccines. The suggestion has been made that there was an accidental release.

**Patrick Timpone:** Some of these strains were lab-created. Does that pose a more substantial problem for the human immune system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the lab, you can accelerate evolutionary changes and make very improbable things that might never statistically happen in a living organism. The pathogens they create are more imaginative than nature.

**Patrick Timpone:** It seems evident someone will come out with a vaccine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's why the stock prices have gone up. But the trouble is, as the guy who exposed the non-existence of the swine flu warned, flu viruses mutate faster than you can create a vaccine and test it for safety. By the time you show a vaccine is effective and safe, there will be no flu left of that strain.

**Patrick Timpone:** There have been people conjecturing that HIV is not really a virus you can see. A German Supreme Court upheld a claim that the measles virus does not exist.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've followed Peter Duesberg's argument closely now for 40 years, and he has never been proven wrong. He lost his research grants and is officially out of the science world because he persists with his evidence. He says the genetic DNA strip is a retrovirus, but a harmless one, and we are full of such DNA. When we are under stress, it shows up in the blood. So you can have a blood test for it, but all it is showing is that you are a stressed individual.

At the time he was presenting his argument, the information about microvesicles carrying DNA and RNA through the body during stress wasn't known except in the acupuncture world. But it is now common knowledge that stress causes retrovirus material to explode into the bloodstream.

People tested blood samples taken from army recruits in the 1960s—decades before anyone suggested AIDS or HIV existed. Giving the standard DNA analysis to those samples, 0.5% of the population tested positive for AIDS every year, steady as far back as they had samples.

**Patrick Timpone:** So the argument for the gay lifestyle connection could have been fear, angst, or guilt?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Peter Duesberg said it correlated exactly with their use of particular drugs. The drug causes stress and causes the virus to come out, as well as causing the sickness. He correlated it in the Bay Area with a fad of using a particular vasodilator drug for pleasure—poppers. That particular drug creates a very intense stress reaction that causes the release of these retroviruses.

**Patrick Timpone:** We have an email from Amy. She broke three bones in her shoulder and fractured her knee. She used Tabasco for topical pain relief. What can she do to speed up healing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Tabasco idea is a traditional medical idea to increase circulation; I think it does work. Gentle, low-energy, low-frequency ultrasound greatly accelerates bone healing. You can get a cheap apparatus for around $100. Applying that a little bit every day internally probably imitates the action of Tabasco sauce. Red light also increases open blood vessels, accelerates energy production, and speeds healing. Sunlight is best because it increases your Vitamin D, which is the other essential bone healing factor.

**Patrick Timpone:** An email asks: You said potatoes, rice, and hominy are good foods. Does that mean you don't care about the glycemic index?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I am cautious about starches. Any starch, even when well-cooked, can pass directly into your bloodstream. In mouse experiments, they showed that starch grains ranging from 5 to 100 microns could pass through the wall of the intestine into the bloodstream unless there was a lot of fat and fiber taken with it. Once in the bloodstream, the particles might be bigger than capillaries and can plug blood vessels.

I stopped eating most starches about 40 years ago when I read that research. The only starch I eat now is hominy or tortillas made with the lime process called nixtamalized corn.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you buy hominy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The lime breaks down the starch. I had students experiment with it, and it didn't have any of those harmful effects. The lime also digests the protein and makes it more nutritious. It takes out most of the polyunsaturated fat (PUFA), increases the niacin content, and pre-digests the starch.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you do this at home?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can buy powdered lime at any Latino market. For a big kettle, like a gallon of water, put in a pound or two of corn kernels and a heaping tablespoon or two of the lime. Boil it until the seeds swell up to the size of an olive and get soft. That's hominy.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can you do this with wheat, like Einkorn?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Someone emailing me from Italy tried the process on different old traditional grains and said they all work very well.

**Patrick Timpone:** What if you eat a baked potato with a lot of butter and fiber?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The potato itself, especially if you eat the peeling, has enough fiber. If you have lots of cream or butter on it, that helps it to be more digestible. I mostly pass on potatoes due to the allergenic effect of the nightshade family—tomatoes, eggplant, bell peppers. Quite a few people have an allergic sensitivity to them.

**Patrick Timpone:** Beth asks: What makes a person susceptible to shingles and how to prevent them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is a stress breakout of the chickenpox virus of the herpes family. Aspirin, by reducing stress and inflammation, helps prevent recurring episodes. Once it starts, it has to play out, but during that time, do anti-stress things: Vitamin D, lots of milk and orange juice, some aspirin. Vitamin K has some anti-inflammatory effects that protect the blood vessels.

**Patrick Timpone:** If these viruses are doing things they are supposed to do, why try to kill them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's a matter of energy. You can repair yourself if you have the energy. Stress blocks oxygen use, causing you to produce lactic acid instead. Lactic acid accelerates inflammation and further reduces the ability to use oxygen. This process is part of wound healing—a reversion to a primitive state—but for the whole organism, you want to get quickly back to oxygen use.

Carbon dioxide is what should be produced in energy production. Bathing in carbon dioxide—using baking soda and Epsom salts in a bath—helps. The body absorbs the carbon dioxide, which turns off the inflammatory process and suppresses the wasteful production of lactic acid.

**Patrick Timpone:** Chris asks about hearing loss. Can it be reversed?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid is the single most important thing. Publications show that high estrogen and prolactin damage the hair cells in the hearing apparatus. Those tend to go up with aging. Thyroid and Vitamin D are among the things that prevent that damage.

**Patrick Timpone:** Larry, 73, has a 100% occluded carotid artery. His doctor wants an angiogram. Any suggestions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The angiotensin system is at the root of atherosclerosis. Experiments show you can reverse the process using ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Losartan, for example. A recent article in *The Lancet* warned against using Losartan for the virus, but the Chinese have evidence it is protective. Separate research shows Losartan helps reverse atherosclerosis and has a general anti-inflammatory process.

**Patrick Timpone:** Is Losartan a pharmaceutical?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Progesterone is the body's natural equivalent; it lowers receptor production, but it's not as immediate and powerful as the pharmaceutical.

**Patrick Timpone:** What about high-dose Vitamin C?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A little helps, but manufactured stuff is never absolutely clean. An experimenter showed that reagent-grade ascorbic acid in distilled water was as full of free radicals as a killing dose of X-rays.

**Patrick Timpone:** How do folks figure out a Vitamin D dosage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 5,000 units a day brings most people into the healthy range (50 to 60 nanograms per milliliter).

**Patrick Timpone:** Are there downsides to having too much D?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is highly exaggerated. It takes a million units a day for many days to get real calcification. The biggest misunderstanding is thinking that dietary calcium and Vitamin D go right into soft tissues. What causes calcification of soft tissues is a failure of energy.

Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and aldosterone collaborate to knock down energy production. PTH's main function is to pull calcium out of your bones for emergency use in the blood. When aldosterone and PTH are high, you get increased blood calcium and calcification of soft tissues.

If you lower your aldosterone and PTH by having enough calcium and salt in your diet—thousands of milligrams of calcium a day—it will tend *not* to calcify your arteries. It keeps calcium in the bones. Warning people not to eat calcium and restricting Vitamin D is exactly what will increase blood vessel calcification.

**Patrick Timpone:** So dark greens are good?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because they have a high ratio of calcium and magnesium to phosphate. Nuts, seeds, meat, and fish have high phosphate, which increases parathyroid hormone. However, it is best to let the cow eat the greens and then drink the milk. The cow has the apparatus to detoxify the plant toxins in the leaves.

**Caller (Mo):** I started drinking orange juice and for the first time in 25 years, my hands and feet were warm. Now they are cold again. Also, my TSH went from 2 or 3 down to 0.1.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Healthy people have the lowest TSH, but stress hormones can also lower it. If cortisol and adrenaline go sharply up, that can lower TSH. You need to check your temperature, heart rate, and T3 levels.

**Patrick Timpone:** Why did the orange juice help initially?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It contains powerful anti-inflammatory flavonoids like naringin and nobiletin that help the thyroid work. When hands suddenly get cold, look for calcium or Vitamin D deficiency, or not getting enough salt. Salt and calcium work closely to hold down the aldosterone/parathyroid system.

**Caller (Mo):** What about the progesterone formula?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The formula I designed in the 1970s—progesterone in Vitamin E and natural coconut oil—is made by a company called Kenogen.

**Patrick Timpone:** Any fiction books or movies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** None come to the top of my head.

**Patrick Timpone:** Tell us about your newsletter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can email raypeatsnewsletter@gmail.com. The latest one is about Gilbert Ling's work. He died last fall. He was one of my early influences in biology. He gave a clear, consistent explanation of cell function, whereas the standard theories are essentially impossible fantasies.

**Patrick Timpone:** Can estriol be used topically for wrinkles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It makes the skin take up water, so it plumps up, but it alters the collagen. Estriol is the weakest estrogen, but people use 10 times more to get the effect, which ends up being the same as estradiol—pro-aging. It makes the skin swell with water, looking smooth and shiny, but it isn't good.

**Patrick Timpone:** What soap do you use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Pure coconut soap.

**Patrick Timpone:** Role of norepinephrine/adrenaline?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Adrenaline has been maligned. It activates other stress hormones like cortisol, so if it persists, it is harmful. However, things that momentarily increase adrenaline can be helpful if stopped soon enough. Thyroid has a relaxing function. When you first take thyroid, if you have been overproducing adrenaline to compensate for hypothyroidism, you might experience a stress reaction. Having sugar and salt while adjusting to thyroid helps keep adrenaline under control.

**Patrick Timpone:** Leg cramps at night?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The parasympathetic system turns on when you lie down. With age, the parasympathetic system overpowers the adrenaline system, causing blood sugar to drop. Falling blood sugar turns on other stress hormones, leading to cramps or even asthma at night.

**Patrick Timpone:** Pneumonia home treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anti-inflammatory things: chicken soup (salt and gelatin), orange juice, milk, ice cream, aspirin, and Losartan.

**Patrick Timpone:** Which potato has the most ketones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Russets have the best nutrition. Yukon Golds have yellow carotene which interferes with starch breakdown.

**Patrick Timpone:** Lutefisk (fish cooked in lye)?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was just a preservative method.

**Patrick Timpone:** Magnesium carbonate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Be cautious. Many products have impurities that cause bad headaches.

**Patrick Timpone:** Venous reflux/varicose veins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually caused by a hormone imbalance—high estrogen in relation to progesterone. High estrogen weakens the vein walls.

**Patrick Timpone:** Does Ray Peat believe in God?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I am a fan of process theology. Google Alfred North Whitehead; he was one of my philosophical influences.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dental cavitations?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If there is no pain, there is almost certainly no infection. Sometimes the bone doesn't fill in the hole, but that is no problem. I don't think surgery is needed.

**Patrick Timpone:** My husband massaged my legs and swelling reduced.

**Patrick Timpone:** Dr. Peat, thanks so much for being here.

title: Hope For Health: Hope for Health: Thyroid
transcriptText:
**Dr. Dan Royal:** Hello and welcome to Hope for Health. I'm Dr. Dan Royal. Hope for Health is brought to you by New Hope Medical Center. We invite you now to enjoy this informative program on health alternatives. Today's guest is a researcher and expert in the area of female hormones. He received his doctorate of philosophy in endocrine physiology and biochemistry from the University of Oregon in 1972. He has taught courses in endocrinology, physiology, the brain, and aging at such schools as the National College of Naturopathic Medicine and the University of Oregon. He is the author of several books, including *Progesterone in Orthomolecular Medicine* and *Nutrition for Women*. He also has a monthly newsletter which he's been writing since 1980. His name is Dr. Raymond Peat. Dr. Peat, welcome.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thank you.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** It's nice to have you with us. You're in Eugene, Oregon, correct? We're here in Las Vegas where it is sunny. You're there where it's overcast. I used to live there for 15 years, so I know exactly what it's like. It's raining or drizzling constantly. Are you familiar with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), where people become depressed because they're not getting enough sunlight?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yeah. 35 years ago, when I moved to Eugene from southern Oregon where there's a lot more sun, I wondered why I was feeling lethargic and depressed. I realized we hadn't had a day of sunlight for about two months straight. That was when I really started getting interested in the hormonal effects of sunlight. When I moved back after being in Mexico for several years, I started seeing graduate student young women who had moved to Eugene and immediately started having hormonal problems, PMS, and worse symptoms.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** What did you do for yourself to correct that problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Trying to get as much sunlight as possible. But when there's no sunlight, I keep a couple of infrared bulbs—farmers use them for brooder lamps to keep baby chicks warm. They have a clear front and a reflector built-in, but they have a lower temperature than the usual incandescent bulb. That means the light penetrates more deeply. It's rich in red and orange frequencies. I keep about 500 watts shining down on me all the time when I'm indoors.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** That sounds like a very interesting approach, similar to the infrared sauna which can penetrate deeper without having to overheat the patient. What about using ultraviolet light? Isn't that also a treatment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have an 80-year-old mercury vapor lamp that I use for getting extra vitamin D once in a while. But I also take some vitamin D. I like to take it through my skin because I never have much confidence in how pure the excipients are in supplements. Taking it through my skin works fine for keeping my vitamin D up.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** We have the same concern in our clinic about using the best quality supplements because a lot of products out there, especially the ones made by pharmaceutical companies, are very cheap but ineffective. Patients read about the great results from taking certain B vitamins or vitamin E, buy it on the cheap, and wonder why they're not getting results.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thirty years ago, I was doing a lot of counseling with allergic people in Eugene. Eugene is near a big grass-growing area, and at the end of the summer, they burn the fields and release chemicals into the air, so the asthma rate is very high. I found that giving them supplements and a good diet, especially rich in vitamin A and pantothenic acid, took care of a big part of the population with allergies. However, there were many that didn't improve. I found that if I got them to use natural foods and avoid all of their supplements, all of them improved. It turned out that many people taking a lot of vitamin and mineral supplements every day were actually allergic to the excipients in the products.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** That's a good point. Our experience is that patients have a threshold. When they are exposing themselves to allergens—whether in food, air, or supplements—they all add up. They have a cumulative effect, and then you reach that threshold where they become reactive.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the total burden and the amount of energy you have to deal with the burden that produces symptoms. If your blood sugar is low, almost anything becomes a serious allergen. With animal experiments, they found that with the weakest allergen, if they lowered the blood sugar with insulin, the animals would die in shock. But if they gave them extra sugar, even the allergic animals would get nothing but mild sniffles from a deadly, super-strong allergen.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** What about reactive hypoglycemia, where patients eat something that raises their blood sugar and then it drops over a short period? Are these patients more susceptible to allergies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It can become a vicious circle. Normally, when you are exposed to a stress or an allergen, you put out a little extra cortisol to improve your immunity and lower inflammation. But that can start suppressing your thyroid function and lowering your liver's detoxifying ability. Your intestine always has allergens in it. The chronic exposure to cortisol, suppressing your liver and thyroid function, allows those toxins and allergens from your intestine to get into the bloodstream.

Endotoxin is a basic substance produced by bacteria in the intestine, and that poisons our energy-producing systems. It almost turns off mitochondrial function, which wastes blood sugar. You can create hypoglycemia by exposing yourself to too many of these stresses. The quickest way to break out of the cycle is to eat a well-balanced natural diet, emphasizing a lot of fruits—orange juice, for example—because of the high potassium content. Potassium lets you handle and absorb blood sugar without disturbing your insulin. When your liver is receiving enough sugar from the combination of potassium and sugar in the fruit, it is able to activate the thyroid hormone, restoring the poisoned function of your mitochondria. It can bring you out of a chronic allergic hypoglycemic state and get you back to a steady blood sugar, sometimes in just a day or two.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** You mentioned a couple of things most people are not aware of. Number one, orange juice has potassium. Everybody thinks about bananas, but if you're low in potassium, you can drink orange juice. You also mentioned the liver is where the thyroid is converted from the inactive to active form.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Broda Barnes wrote a very good book years ago called *Hypoglycemia: It's Your Liver, Not Your Mind*. He was one of the first to emphasize that most of the active thyroid, about 70%, is produced in your liver rather than in the thyroid gland. The gland in your neck produces about 30% of the active hormone. Anytime your blood sugar falls—if you go without eating for eight hours, for example—your liver doesn't want to convert your tissues to food, so it stops making thyroid. Your metabolism decreases and your temperature goes down so that you don't burn up your body too fast.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Doesn't that conversion also take place at the cellular level?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several tissues produce quite a bit of it. The pituitary gland can detect T4 (the inactive form). Since it can convert it, it doesn't distinguish very strongly between whether you're taking T4 or T3; it turns off its activity whenever it sees T4 or T3. Since it produces just a tiny amount for its own detecting purposes, if you accumulate too much thyroxine (T4) in your tissues, your pituitary thinks you have enough thyroid, but your liver might not be producing any active thyroid hormone from it at all.

In early experiments, they took slices of different organs and added thyroxine. They found that the liver became fully activated with a modest amount of thyroxine added. The kidneys converted a little and were slightly activated. The muscles were not activated at all. But the brain, when thyroxine was added, was actually suppressed. The brain normally has an extremely high concentration of the active T3. Locally, too much T4 affects your brain in an anti-thyroid direction. Very few doctors are aware of the risks of prescribing plain thyroxine.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** That's a very good point. The audience may not understand that thyroxine is T4, which is the same thing as Synthroid. This means the most common thyroid medicine being prescribed has no active thyroid in it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's true. Because of pressure from the pharmaceutical industry, the FDA has begun forcing the producers of natural thyroid products, such as Armour Thyroid, to put on their label the ingredients in terms of T4 and T3. But natural thyroid contains neither of those; it's a protein. When you digest the protein, your digestive system releases those hormones. When the gland digests itself in normal functioning, that protein breakdown releases about three or four parts of thyroxine for each part of the active T3. That's why your liver has to convert the thyroxine. Similarly, when you take a supplement of Armour Thyroid, you digest it in that same ratio. This means you can't go very far wrong taking the natural substance because the ratio entering your blood is within the range produced by your normal gland.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Typically, the natural thyroids have a ratio of about 4:1, T4 to T3. In our practice, we often increase that ratio to 3:1 by adding a little Cytomel, which is pure active T3. We usually do that if the patient has developed antibodies to their thyroid, or if they are taking Synthroid and have introduced a foreign substance the body attacks. I had one patient who started gaining weight on thyroid medication; every time they upped the dose, she gained more. We checked her antibodies, and they were very high.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was teaching at the naturopathic college in Portland, someone from the University of Oregon Medical School told about a woman who had been prescribed the equivalent of one grain of thyroxine (about 100 micrograms). She got more hypothyroid, so they kept increasing the dose. When they reached 400 micrograms of thyroxine, she went into a myxedema coma. They took her to the hospital unconscious and kept her alive until someone figured out she wasn't converting T4 to T3. It had turned her brain metabolism off to the point that she was no longer conscious. When they gave her T3, she recovered immediately to full functioning.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** So it's important to have a healthy liver if that's where three-quarters of the conversion is happening. If you're taking inactive thyroid and it's suppressing the brain, can't it build up and cause other symptoms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Many people have told me that when they were given supposedly the right dose of thyroxine, they began getting symptoms like ringing in their ears and prickly sensations—common symptoms of hypothyroidism. When they added T3, the symptoms would go away.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Many patients tell me their doctor checked everything, but they only looked at T4 or TSH, never the antibodies. In your opinion, what's the best test?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The way they did it in the 1930s, before the drug companies took control of the journals and medical schools, was to look at symptoms. When they saw symptoms, they would test the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)—how much oxygen they consume at rest. That is the absolute way to determine what's happening. It doesn't matter how much is in your blood if it's being blocked. For example, if you have eaten too many polyunsaturated fats or too much cabbage, you can have an excess of thyroid hormones in your bloodstream and still not be consuming very much oxygen.

Americans, on average, are about 25% hypometabolic or hypothyroid compared to countries where they don't eat so much artificial food. The practical thing is to go by symptoms and physiological indicators. For example, reflex reaction time. If you flash a light in a person's eye, the pupil is slow to respond if they're hypothyroid. Body temperature tends to be below normal, though an excess of stress, adrenaline, and cortisol can artificially raise it.

There is also the Achilles tendon reflex. If you have a person kneel and thump their Achilles tendon, a person with almost any thyroid function will have the reflex. But you watch how quickly the foot relaxes back to its resting position. A hypothyroid person's foot looks like it has a pneumatic door closer on it; it returns slowly. A person with good thyroid function has a foot that looks like a piece of rubber; it relaxes and bounces back instantly.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** I see the high blood fat issue frequently and the cholesterol industry built around it. I would think one sign of high cholesterol would be low thyroid, because with a healthy metabolism, you should process those fats effectively.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The liver is a big source of disposal for cholesterol, but the ovaries, gonads, brain, and adrenal glands all use considerable amounts of cholesterol. In one experiment, blood containing a known amount of cholesterol was pumped into an ovary, and the amount of progesterone coming out corresponded exactly to the amount of cholesterol going in. If you lowered the cholesterol, you lowered the progesterone produced.

If you force your cholesterol down with a drug, you are likely to see problems. Many studies have shown increased rates of accidents, cancer, suicide, and death by homicide in people who were drugged to lower their cholesterol. The Framingham study found that people over the age of 50 whose cholesterol was below 200 were much more likely to become demented. Cholesterol makes those protective hormones, like progesterone in the brain, which is extremely protective against injury and toxins.

**Geraldine:** When I was 16, they thought I had a broken jaw and took many X-rays. Right after that, my thyroid went out. I have trouble sleeping, gaining weight—the whole thing. What do you suggest for medication?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The usual thing is to check the diet and make sure you are getting enough good protein. A protein deficiency makes the liver unable to activate the thyroid hormone, the same way a lack of sugar does. You need at least 80 grams of high-quality protein, like milk, cheese, or eggs.

The symptoms you mentioned are classical hypothyroid symptoms because the brain needs energy to sleep properly. EEGs show that hypothyroid people never get into deep, restful, slow-wave sleep. They stay in superficial sleep. Even worse, they often have insomnia because when your nerves or muscles are not producing enough energy, fatigue accumulates and they are unable to relax. It's the same as the Achilles reflex test—you're slow to relax. A doctor I visited had insomnia for days. I suggested Cytomel. The next day he said, "That stuff's better than opium." He was sound asleep 15 minutes after taking a little bit of the active thyroid hormone.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Patients have the misconception that thyroid is some kind of amphetamine that will keep them up. They don't understand that thyroid helps you relax.

**Geraldine:** Thank you very much.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** If the thyroid is having a problem, the adrenals tend to take over. Cortisol levels can be elevated, interrupting the sleep-wake cycle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the sun goes down, the red light or sunlight that penetrates deeply into your cells activates processes that protect you against free radicals. After about an hour of darkness, your mitochondria start losing efficiency. When darkness has lasted for several hours, your blood sugar becomes a problem. That's why your cortisol rises after you've been asleep for a couple of hours; it keeps getting higher until dawn. That allows you to stay asleep because the cortisol breaks down protein into sugar, letting the thyroid function and nerve cells repair.

However, if your liver didn't store enough glycogen, you will have an adrenaline reaction trying to get more glycogen to compensate for low thyroid function. Low thyroid people often produce 30 or 40 times more adrenaline than a healthy person. That wakes you up with a start. The adrenaline triggers increasing cortisol, which starts damaging your tissues, converting muscles to sugar to keep your brain working. These low thyroid people who compensate with high adrenaline and cortisol will sometimes wake up with a temperature of 98.6 or 99 degrees. But if you take their temperature an hour after they've had orange juice and food, you'll find it drops to the hypothyroid range (95 or 96 degrees). It's only the stress hormones before breakfast that keep them up to a normal temperature.

**Yolanda:** I have a 12-year-old diagnosed with hypothyroidism. She was gaining weight that didn't correlate with her food consumption. Her T3 came back high, but she was diagnosed based on TSH and T4. She's been on 0.88 of Synthroid for two years.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** If T3 is elevated, a hypothyroid diagnosis doesn't make sense unless they are checking T3 uptake, which is a mathematical guesstimation, not T3-RIA.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are three times when women are more likely to become hypothyroid: puberty, pregnancy, and menopause. You can see the thyroid gland enlarging. As estrogen rises, the brain senses you need more thyroid hormone and puts out more TSH, but the estrogen blocks the enzymes that digest the protein in the thyroid gland, so it stops secreting the active hormone. Progesterone activates those enzymes. You can depend on the slowing down of the thyroid whenever estrogen rises, and puberty is the most common time.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** We would typically put the patient on a grain of natural thyroid twice a day. Natural thyroid has a half-life of about 8 to 12 hours, as opposed to hanging around for 24 hours waiting for conversion.

**Stan:** Dr. Wilson has done research on subclinical thyroid where the doctor says it's normal, but people run temperatures of 97 degrees, have cold hands/feet, and are sluggish. Does Armour Thyroid fix this issue by unclogging the thyroid so you get proper T3?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The stress hormones causing a falsely elevated, normal-appearing temperature is something to watch out for. If someone has a protein-deficient diet or is in menopause, they often experience excess cortisol. Cortisol accelerates dissolving of the bones and deposition of fat around the trunk. Reverse T3 rises when you're under stress and exposed to too much cortisol. A bad diet can put you into that chronic stress state. The quickest way out is with a supplement of T3. Armour Thyroid or Thyrolar will provide enough T3 for most people, but people often prefer a little more T3 to quickly get over symptoms.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Reverse T3 is difficult to document, but there are many other factors to diagnose hypothyroidism. You need a doctor who can assess whether the patient needs thyroid even if the lab is "normal."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Traditional doctors would look at signs like oxygen consumption, cholesterol, and the palms of the hands. A low thyroid person can't convert carotene to vitamin A, so they accumulate orange in the calluses of their hands and feet. Their hands and feet are almost always cold. Cold feet can cause serious inflammatory problems elsewhere. First aid for some symptoms is just to get woolly underwear and thick stockings to keep the long bones warm. You can actually cure anemia just by keeping your long bones warmer.

**Earlene:** I had a hysterectomy at 36. I'm now 73. My arthritis seemed to get worse after the hysterectomy. Does this have anything to do with hormones?

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Absolutely. As a woman goes through menopause or surgical menopause, hypothyroidism can manifest.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had a friend in his 70s who had an accident and immediately started developing arthritis. He was crippled pretty suddenly. He had a doctor educated in the 1930s who immediately tested his thyroid because stress and injury can lower your thyroid. Within two weeks of treatment, his arthritis cleared up and he lived 15 more years with no arthritis. In the 30s, it was standard knowledge that arthritis was usually a sign of hypothyroidism.

**Bill:** I was born with Wilson's disease. I've kept it under control through diet. People say you can't live without fat, but I'm living proof that you can.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I do advocate eating saturated fats; they can have therapeutic effects. However, I am also an advocate of a fruit-centered diet. The squirrel monkey lives about three times as long as other animals of its size and has an extremely high metabolic rate; in the wild, it lives exclusively on fruit. Fruit contains the things needed to stimulate thyroid function and protect against stress. It is possible to live entirely without fat in your diet because your body can make the saturated fats it needs.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Saturated fat is what the thyroid needs, like coconut oil. On the other hand, unsaturated fatty acids actually inhibit thyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The more unsaturated the fat is, the more thoroughly it inhibits the thyroid—it inhibits secretion, transport, and reaction to the hormone. In the early part of the last century, researchers showed that animals on a fat-free diet were completely free of spontaneous cancer and lived longer than normal.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** Dr. Peat, any concluding remarks?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's a book you might be able to find in a library that is a great introduction to the amazing things thyroid can do. It is *The Thyroid* by Thomas McGavack.

**Dr. Dan Royal:** *The Thyroid* by Thomas McGavack. Dr. Peat, thank you for being with us. I'm Dr. Dan Royal. You've been listening to Hope for Health. Tune in again next week.
