title: Politics & Science: On The Origin of Life
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Hello and welcome to Politics and Science. I'm your host, John Barkhausen. Today we are dipping back into the archives to a show from the 1999–2000 time period. This is a philosophical discussion with Dr. Raymond Peat talking about the origins of life. The work of Lamarck, Darwin, and Vernadsky appear in this show.

For those who don't know, Dr. Raymond Peat has a PhD in biology and has specialized in physiology and endocrinology. He has extensive knowledge about the history of science and philosophy. You can find out more about Dr. Peat and read his articles at raypeat.com.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's necessary at some point to think about the philosophical things that have fed into controversies about the origin of life, as well as national cultural differences. I've studied the Russian tradition quite a bit, starting with Mendeleev, the man who invented the periodic table. He referred to himself as a cosmic realist.

About a generation younger than Mendeleev was V.I. Vernadsky. He called himself a biogeochemist and also thought of himself as a cosmic realist. What they meant by this was that you have to always think of the context of the problem you are dealing with and try to think of as many levels of the problem at the same time as you can.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Mendeleev completed his table around 1869. During the late 1800s, Vernadsky was traveling around Europe talking to people. He got to know all the interesting people in Europe, and every time he met someone, he would incorporate their ideas. Even literature fed into Vernadsky's way of looking at the world; he thought of Tolstoy's brain as a geochemical event.

Sechenov and Pavlov were others. They set out to try to explain human consciousness in realistic and physical terms so that they didn't have to leave anything out of the system. They didn't think of the material world without consciousness or a conscious world without material. It was a tradition of looking at the hidden assumptions behind everything.

From that perspective, there are attitudes in American and German science that I think have limited the way people think about the origin of life. Pasteur, for example, is selected by American educators as a way to obscure thinking about the origin of life. Because of his famous experiment demonstrating that life didn't arise from decaying organic matter—his principle was that life comes from life—people who didn't want to accept that life came from non-living matter seized upon this. They wanted to dispose of the idea of the origin of life and say that life came *only* from life. There is a deliberate obscuring principle going on when people try to place Pasteur's thinking at the top.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like they don't want to discuss it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The same thing happened to Pavlov. A man named Watson—who I doubt even studied with Pavlov because he totally misrepresented what he claimed to have learned—was the founder of behaviorism in America. J.B. Watson denied the existence of consciousness. Even my professors in the university psychology department were still denying consciousness, or at least denying it to children. They said that consciousness was only present in speech.

This picture of Pavlov as studying "conditioned reflexes" goes back to Watson's misrepresentation. The translation of Pavlov's phrase was deliberately misleading. If you translate it back into Russian, it says "conditional reflex," meaning that you reflect on all the conditions around you. In other words, consciousness was the meaning of Pavlov's term, yet consciousness was explicitly defined out of his system by the West.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same attempt to hide the problem has been going on in genetics. Genetics has attempted to evade the problem of where life came from in the first place simply by emphasizing that units are passed on which are identical to the units that preceded them. When they are forced to recognize change, very strange devices have developed.

The idealization of randomness—random change, random mutation—took over biological genetic thinking for about 80 years. The idea was: if we have to admit that life changes, and maybe even that life originated from non-life, we are going to say it is random because we don't really want to admit that it happens.

The big controversy between the Neo-Darwinists and the Lamarckians was this same thing. The Neo-Darwinists even rewrote Darwin. They took out the Lamarckian inclinations of Darwin—that's why they call it Neo-Darwinism, because Darwin would be too Lamarckian for their preferences.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe for our listeners, you should give a brief synopsis of Lamarckianism and Darwinism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lamarck basically said that life is purposeful, and that the intention to do something is part of the process of physiological adaptation. This attempt to adapt to an environment is part of what is passed on to the offspring.

Darwin accepted that there were many sources of variation, including the Lamarckian type. Darwin didn't say that variation was just by chance; he enumerated a whole bunch of mechanisms that could cause variation. But after Mendel's work with peas—which people have pointed out wasn't even truthful; he fudged his results to make it look mathematically perfect—people reinvented Darwin to support their position that change and evolution are random.

One of the recent manifestations of this strange religion of random changes is the craze about the idea of chaos. They use purely numerical processes to argue that you can't predict the future. Then they say particles, atoms, and things in the real world are just like numbers. That is what the genetics people did: they said the particles we are dealing with are just like numbers, and individual particles don't know where they are going, so they can only change randomly. They are reducing everything to the most meaningless unit.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Meanwhile, other people were thinking about the actual physics, chemistry, geology, and cosmology operating in everyday life. Oparin is one of the people well known in the theory of the origin of life. In the 20s, 30s, and 40s, he was talking about the types of physical processes that can create things equivalent to cells. He discussed the idea of coacervation, or clumping in complex colloid-like systems that find organization in a complex way. This allows complex structures to appear out of what seem to be simple random solutions.

Probably these people talking about coacervation were the first to introduce the idea of self-organization and self-structuring, in which entropy actually decreases according to ordinary physical processes. Once you add a few complexifying ingredients to a solution of starch, oil, or protein molecules, order starts appearing. You have to see the history of denying that entropy can decrease as part of this philosophy of idealizing randomness.

Vernadsky was working along this synthesizing route. In the 1920s, he was lecturing on the place of consciousness in the cosmos. He showed that, according to well-recognized principles, consciousness is generated by physical forces. He used the ideas of the biosphere and the *noosphere*. Teilhard de Chardin happened to be in Paris where Vernadsky was lecturing, and he popularized the idea of the noosphere. But it was this cosmic realist philosophy of the biogeochemist that really generated the central idea of what the noosphere is in relation to the biosphere.

**John Barkhausen:** So Chardin used the word noosphere, but he didn't really come up with the final meaning of it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He turned it into a fairly revolutionary religious idea, but he left out the physical principles that explain it. He left it in a very abstract form.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the outcomes of Oparin's work was the American Sidney Fox. He was the fruition of some of these experiments regarding how physical conditions affect the appearance of order out of disorder.

I should mention that one of the people Vernadsky knew in Paris was Henri Le Chatelier. Everyone hears about Le Chatelier's principle: anything you do to disturb an equilibrium causes the system to adjust in a way that restores equilibrium. Vernadsky, thinking cosmologically, realized that heat is coming out of the inside of the Earth and the sun is constantly adding energy to the system. If you are constantly pushing on the system with volcanic and solar energy, you don't have a closed system. The system is being driven and steered by this constant pressure of energy. Vernadsky said the system will adjust in ways that restore equilibrium, creating bigger, smarter, more intensely metabolizing organisms to equilibrate the energy being added.

Sidney Fox used Vernadsky's principles. About 40 years ago, everyone was talking about life originating in a "tepid pond" or a warm ocean sparked by lightning—random events. Sidney Fox intended to rethink how proteins come into existence. If you have a protein floating in water, the equilibrium is to degrade into individual amino acids. The equilibrium is not favorable for large molecules if they are floating in water.

Fox put dry amino acids—deficient in water—on hot lava in a model of volcanic energy. He showed that heat in the absence of water creates protein-like long polymerized molecules. The equilibrium is absolutely the opposite in the deficiency of water.

One of my professors, Sidney Bernhard, revolutionized cell physiology by demonstrating that glycolytic enzymes are at a higher concentration in cells than the substrate sugar they work on. Everyone had been diluting these enzymes in water, but he showed that the concentration totally changes the equilibrium.

Sidney Fox demonstrated that relatively dry heat creates order and protein-like molecules. When he added water, the proteins spontaneously formed tiny bacteria-like particles, almost all the same size—he called them proteinoid microspheres. Over 20 years, he showed that these molecules have enzyme-like properties. The amino acids polymerize in a non-random fashion. The growing molecule "selects" the next amino acid.

He added the precursors of genetic material and showed that these would be catalyzed into chains. So, you have the reverse situation where genes come *last*, after you've already created cells that can metabolize and reproduce.

**John Barkhausen:** He basically originated life.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You put the proteinoid microspheres in a solution with amino acids, and they assimilate nutrients, grow, and when they reach a size where they are no longer stable, they bud or divide. He did this in the 60s, and it was mentioned in Lehninger's Biochemistry textbook (1968 edition). Now, the new Lehninger book has deleted that material because it doesn't fit their concept.

**John Barkhausen:** I would think what Sidney Fox did would be headline news.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was for me.

**John Barkhausen:** It seems this divide between the two philosophies is like the reductionist versus the holist—someone who looks at the whole organism rather than dividing it into mechanistic parts. It also seems like science is afraid of sounding religious.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fred Hoyle said it would be hard to avoid thinking of the cosmos as essentially a biological thing, except that people can't stand the thought that the universe itself is purposeful and alive.

**John Barkhausen:** I wonder why. People are drawn to religion because it gives a purpose to life.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That was where Teilhard de Chardin made a big contribution by being both a scientist and a religious thinker. Unfortunately, some people have replaced the noosphere with the Gaia hypothesis. The Gaia hypothesis says the Earth is like a conscious being, but it's not going anywhere; it's just trying to maintain itself—homeostasis versus creation.

Vernadsky's view is that the Earth and sun are driving evolution as a system. If you delete parts of the system, the whole 4 billion years might go to waste. The Gaia/randomness people tend to say whatever happens is okay because random events have wiped out species in the past.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vernadsky's principles were extensions of Le Chatelier's principle. He showed that the migration of atoms and the intensity of metabolism were subdivisions of this principle.

An astronomer, Nikolai Kozyrev, did his doctoral dissertation around 1950 on the energy of stars. He asked: What if we assume the universe is not necessarily running down? What if we assume that time physically is a real, asymmetric factor in all systems? He reasoned that the mere passage of time distinguishes one state of a system from another in a real physical way.

Using standard Einsteinian arguments, he applied this to the energy of stars. He suggested that the passage of time adds something to the system. He concluded that time itself is the source of stellar energy. He predicted that Jupiter and Neptune would be emitting more heat than they received, and that each planet would have internal heat in proportion to its mass.

Scaling it down to the Moon, he predicted occasional volcanic eruptions. He trained his spectrometer on the dark phases of the Moon and recorded hot emissions, confirming his prediction. His physics should be taken into account in thinking about volcanic energy.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a caller on the line. Do you have a question or comment?

**Caller:** Yes. I'm curious about the idea of consciousness and its relationship to the brain. The scientific paradigm is that consciousness is an epiphenomenon of physiochemical processes and is self-referential. However, no one has been able to locate memory in the brain. Penfield operated on epileptic patients and came to espouse interactionism—that mind and brain are interactive but different, and memories might exist in some type of field.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My personal history is part of where my ideas come from. Before I discovered that thyroid was very important in my metabolism, I was a hyper-metabolic individual. I would burn perhaps 10,000 calories a day. I had an electrical field around my body that would affect physical things like millivolt meters two feet away. I couldn't operate the apparatus; my lab partner had to do it because it would go off-scale when I got near.

All of this stopped when I took the right amount of thyroid. My metabolism became regulated. But I saw that oxidative metabolism generated this potentially immense field around cells. This inclined me to see the importance of bioelectric fields in development and physiology. For example, there is a field concept of cancer—research shows it is an electromagnetic field, at least in part, that creates precancerous conditions or governs the development of an embryo.

**Caller:** That idea has been taken up by Rupert Sheldrake with his theory of formative causation—that information can be shared among members of a species.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** From Vernadsky's perspective, the supplementary context is that things are ready to be discovered. When you change components in the system, many things contribute, not just the individual's consciousness. Vernadsky would emphasize multi-causal factors.

**Caller:** You seem to be skirting around a scientific taboo: the evidence for the inheritance of acquired characteristics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely, they are a fact, and Darwin knew it. People slandered Lamarck and took him down because of the implications of his empirical, physiological approach. The same thing happened to Paul Kammerer. C.P. Lindegren wrote *Cold War in Biology*, which is the best American book on the subject.

**Caller:** The public is being led to believe in genetic determinism—the "selfish gene"—where a gene is responsible for a specific quality. As far as I know, no one has proved that genes do anything except organize the synthesis of proteins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been interested in this for more than 50 years. The motivation for a lot of these ideas around 1910 to 1920 was to stop immigration of Eastern and Southern Europeans to the United States. They created IQ tests and "showed" that 85% of Russians, Jews, and others were feeble-minded. These tests were explicitly designed for racist, exclusionary purposes.

Many of these people persisted in universities. *The Bell Curve* is a recent example. When I sent a letter to *Science* magazine criticizing a genetic determination article, the referees rejected my comments citing data from Hitler's Racial Hygiene Institute. That got me interested in studying that period. I saw that Konrad Lorenz was the architect of racial hygiene; he created the rationale for exterminating "inferior" people. Lorenz was a Nazi, and in his later books, he repeated the exact arguments of his 1942 papers on genocide.

**Caller:** The ideology has survived, but shorn of terms like "eugenics."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I went to a lecture in the 70s where Gunther Stent presented Konrad Lorenz's arguments for genocide as the ultimate in understanding the brain genetically. My professors were happily agreeing. When I pointed out the logical irrationalities, they asked if I was saying the fact that he was a Nazi had anything to do with the validity of his ideas.

**Caller:** It seems the official ideology is compounded of misinterpretations of Darwin and Adam Smith. Adam Smith believed in self-interest, but also in benevolence as a counterpoint. Yet only the self-interest part is promoted. Similarly, Alfred Russel Wallace could not accept the idea of an entirely mechanical evolutionary process driven by randomness.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It isn't just Neo-Darwinism and Smith; it is everything in our intellectual history. I've read textbooks in many fields, and 99% of them are ideological distortions, rewriting history to leave out everything interesting or threatening to the established system. Adam Smith, Darwin, Pavlov—if they were good, they have to be distorted. If they were too good, they have to be left out entirely.

**Caller:** Science developed as a reaction against religious provincialism, but it seems to have turned into an ideology itself—Scientism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They got one little success, but then decided to give in to the backward cultural forces. Most scientists have accepted the fundamental assumptions of the people who used those assumptions for religious purposes. It works by eliminating all the troubling, complexifying things and reducing everything to random variation and survival of the fittest.

**Caller:** Randomness is based on infinite time. But most mutations are regressive. It seems like a series of improbabilities linked together to explain how we get flies.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vernadsky shows that species will arise quickly to the limits of the resources available. Evolution is driven in a practically instantaneous way. The driving environmental force—energy disturbing the equilibrium—is so powerful that evolution is fast and directional.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at it in the context of energy added to the system, there are physical principles like hysteresis (system memory) and long-range order. A surface projects a field or ordering influence into the surrounding environment.

Michael Polanyi's absorption isotherm was ignored, but he showed that surfaces project their influence. One of my professors showed that you can lay a plastic membrane over a crystal and evaporate a chemical on top; the atoms appear ordered, taking on the characteristics of the crystal beneath the plastic. The crystal projects a field through space that orders the atoms.

**Caller:** So there is a consciousness inherent in matter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Alexander Rothen devised a way of measuring this ordering influence projected through membranes. The mechanism seems to be that electrons on an atom resonate, inducing a field in the next atom, which projects off into space.

**Caller:** That relates to the discovery that heart cells in close proximity influence each other without touching.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s, the Gurwitsches demonstrated that cells could communicate through a quartz window.

**Caller:** We don't have a mechanism that can explain communication between cells that aren't chemically or electrically linked.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Usually the missing piece is that the researcher is too dull-minded to measure what might be relevant, such as the phase of the moon or outside conditions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are two more aspects of the origin of life I wanted to mention. The submarine vent biologists, if you link them with Vernadsky and Sidney Fox, suggest that volcanic processes are creating organisms.

Mendeleev noticed that dissolving iron in acid produced the smell of crude petroleum. He sent samples to chemists who identified it as petroleum. The carbon atoms dissolved in hot iron were catalyzed into petroleum. Thomas Gold, an American geologist, argued that petroleum is being constantly created by this mechanism in the depths of the Earth. He pointed out you can find petroleum in granite where it shouldn't be unless it is being synthesized from below.

**Caller:** He believes it's not a fossil residue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The traditional idea is that petroleum is marine biological fossil residue. But the Gold/Mendeleev/Vernadsky interpretation is that the Earth is generating new petroleum. If you think of Sidney Fox's work where cells are generated by volcanic heat, you have organic sources of energy and organisms that can eat carbon dioxide being generated volcanically.

**Caller:** That interfaces with the bion experiments of Wilhelm Reich.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sidney Fox's organisms—any high school student can produce little cells that will eat and reproduce in a few hours.

**Caller:** So spontaneous generation is not completely bad?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not at all. I think volcanoes are churning out life all the time.

**Caller:** Amazing. I'll hang up now. Thank you.

**John Barkhausen:** Thank you for calling. Ray, did you get to say everything you needed to say?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Briefly, I think I touched on everything regarding the origin of life. I might mention the work of Lancelot Law Whyte. He wrote books on the philosophy of physics and biology, talking about the formative principle as something overlooked by conventional science.

**John Barkhausen:** Are his books available?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are in good libraries.

**John Barkhausen:** That was really fascinating. I want to thank you for coming on again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay.

**John Barkhausen:** That was Dr. Raymond Peat. You can find his work at raypeat.com. Thanks for listening to Politics and Science.

title: Politics & Science: Suppression of Cancer Tru eatments
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Hello and welcome to Politics and Science. I'm your host, John Barkhausen. Today we feature an archive of my interview with Dr. Raymond Peat, recorded circa 2001. In the show, he discusses the remarkable story of Dr. Stevan Durovic and his cancer treatment known as Krebiozen. He also covers the heroic but ultimately fruitless efforts by Dr. Andrew C. Ivy, who was at the time one of America's most prominent scientists. Dr. Ivy attempted to give this promising treatment the clinical testing that its positive findings warranted.

In case you're interested in this subject, the meticulously written book that tells the story in detail is by Herbert Smith Bailey and is called *Krebiozen: Key to Cancer*. In this show, Dr. Peat also discusses the suppressed work of an earlier brilliant cancer researcher, Dr. William F. Koch, and his successful cancer treatments. If you're interested in Dr. Raymond Peat's work, many of his writings are available at his website, raypeat.com. And now, once again, here's Dr. Raymond Peat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A.C. Ivy and these people all overlap for various reasons, partly because several of the alternative health—especially alternative cancer treatment—people were working on essentially the same ideas, and they were all attacked by the established forces that were working on different assumptions.

**John Barkhausen:** What year was this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Koch started his work around 1911 or 1914, and by the twenties, he had the clinic going in Cleveland. He was a professor of medicine and chemistry, and he was the first person to take seriously for biochemistry the work on free radicals by Moses Gomberg. Gomberg demonstrated that free radicals really exist; they aren't just a hypothesis that exists only on paper.

Moses Gomberg showed that highly colored chemicals appear when you can get free radicals to separate in solution. The color appears because the electron that is no longer paired is free enough that it absorbs light in the visible spectrum. One of the simple ways to test for an unpaired electron is that suddenly the solution goes dark. Even chemists didn't take Gomberg seriously. In Russia, he was a major influence, but in the United States, for probably 40 or 50 years, free radical chemistry just couldn't take off.

The head of one of the early chemistry plastics companies told William Koch that he had better be quiet about the idea of applying free radical chemistry in medicine because people didn't even understand it in ordinary organic chemistry. They were going to say he was talking about fantasies if he talked about the free radical basis of biology.

It was around the 1950s that the instrumentation became available to demonstrate that free radicals really did exist in living tissue. Barry Commoner was one of the first people to demonstrate free radicals existing in living tissues.

**John Barkhausen:** I didn't know that. When did the free radical theory start?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 1900 to 1905 was when Moses Gomberg was demonstrating them. But immediately, Koch was putting it into theoretical thinking about what cells are doing. He applied it to the concept of polymerization and blood clotting. He knew that in healing a wound or a cancer, blood clotting is one of the first things that happens, and clotting abnormalities are characteristic of cancer.

It turned out that for places like DuPont, polymerization was a very important practical industrial principle using the free radical. But Koch anticipated even industrial thinking. Within just a few years of starting to work on it, he was applying it theoretically and practically to devise both explanations for disease and therapies.

**John Barkhausen:** He seems like quite a brilliant man.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, he was quick to apply knowledge that was very clear and definite, but other people couldn't accept it because it didn't seem to fit the low standard that was common in chemistry and biology at that time.

**John Barkhausen:** The free radical theory must have come out of the atomic theory of electrons.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. In ordinary chemistry on paper, they would show an atom coming loose, or an atom with other atoms attached to it coming loose from another group and taking one electron away, where each atom had been contributing an electron to a pair that made a stable compound. On paper, they could take away a group with one electron and allow it to combine somewhere else, but they couldn't believe that could really exist in a watery solution.

Moses Gomberg first did it with triphenylmethyl. It had three large carbon rings attached to one tiny little molecule in the center. The tendency of the benzene rings to repel because they were placed too close together, and the fact that the whole group wasn't very soluble in water, created a reaction. If you kept adding water to a solution of this compound, as it got very highly dilute, the color would suddenly change from clear to a deep purple. As you got it diluted enough, the groups would be able to fall apart from each other and exist freely in solution.

Anyone who knew homeopathy—which a well-educated doctor did in 1900—knew that the principle of homeopathy was that some compounds become chemically more reactive when they're highly diluted. It was natural for someone with a medical education to see the importance of this chemical principle. But not many people who had studied homeopathy as well as classical medicine also studied chemistry, which Koch did.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first time I heard about Koch was around 1943 or 1944. People were circulating little mimeographed newsletters about the scandal of how he was being persecuted by the FBI. Koch himself told some of the stories, and they have never been refuted; they are pretty well documented. He said that criminals who tried to kill him were later proven to be agents of the FBI. The public didn't start hearing of mob, FBI, or CIA connections until the Church Committee in the 70s brought that stuff out, but it was something that had been going on for a long time.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that pre-Hoover?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that was Hoover. Hoover was there for about 50 years.

**John Barkhausen:** Why were they going after him at that point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** His clinic in Cleveland was so successful that it was bringing a lot of attention to him. Even though he followed the industrialist's advice and didn't explain the free radical basis—he was just having objective results—he had tried to publish all of the details between 1917 and 1921. He submitted papers all over the world, but the standard medical journals wouldn't accept a free radical chemical explanation for any biological events.

The government then claimed that he had a secret method simply because he couldn't get journals to publish it. They called it a secret quack method.

Years later, after I had studied Koch's books thoroughly, and I had also been studying Otto Warburg's work and Albert Szent-Györgyi's work on cancer, I noticed dramatic parallels. I outlined over two pages the amazing similarities between Koch's work done between 1910 and 1925, and what Szent-Györgyi started doing in about 1932. I wrote to Szent-Györgyi and asked, "Is this just coincidence or were you influenced by W.F. Koch?" In all of Szent-Györgyi's work, I couldn't find a single reference to W.F. Koch. He answered that he had the highest respect for the work of W.F. Koch. This obviously meant that since he had never referred to it in print, he knew what had happened to Koch and didn't want it to happen to him.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe we could go back a little bit and talk about Koch's cancer therapy. Who was he threatening at the time?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The FDA accused him of violating the law by selling something that they said couldn't cure cancer. They had it analyzed and claimed they couldn't detect anything in it but distilled water. He made some in court according to his procedure, took this highly colored material, and diluted it until it looked like distilled water. He gave a sample to them to analyze, and they said it was distilled water. The jury could see that their own eyes had seen stuff go into it, yet the government was telling them it wasn't there. Twice he was acquitted, but he decided it was time to get out of the country with people trying to kill him and keeping him constantly in court instead of doing science. He spent the rest of his life after 1944 in Brazil.

**John Barkhausen:** Are there any remnants of his work still operating in Brazil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 15 years ago, I talked to a very old man who had worked with him. I don't think there is anyone still living who was directly connected with him. Koch died around 1968.

**John Barkhausen:** What was the distilled water solution?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People who worked with him said it was done by judgment. He used a red-hot platinum reactor heated electrically to just the right color of red. He passed a stream of alcohol vapor over that. At that temperature, the alcohol polymerized into a water-soluble chain of molecules which were unstable enough that they would release the individual carbon-oxygen-hydrogen groups or small chains into solution. That was his primary reagent. He also used benzoquinone at high dilution.

**John Barkhausen:** How was it an anti-cancer therapy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of his early publications had to do with the muscle spasms that typically follow removal of the thyroid gland. Koch experimented with the removal of just the parathyroid glands and found that if you give any salt electrolyte—such as potassium, sodium, magnesium, or calcium—generously, you prevent the spasms. He argued that the parathyroid gland was involved in detoxifying compounds derived from ammonia, and that these chemicals are poisonous and known to cause seizures and muscle spasms. He demonstrated that he was causing those to be passed off in the urine by increasing salt intake.

However, A.J. Carlson, a powerful professor at the University of Chicago, decided that one hormone has only one action. They proclaimed that the parathyroid hormone mobilizes calcium and that in a calcium deficiency you get spasms. There are terrible problems with that theory, but it became the standard.

Koch explained the toxicity of these compounds as similar to what ammonia does. The amino or ammonia group occurs in many chemicals that produce seizures, spasms, and overstimulation—we now call it excitotoxicity. Ammonia, serotonin, and a tremendous range of amino compounds have this action. The carbonyl group was the essence of Koch's treatment. Whether the carbonyl was in his polymer or part of the benzoquinone molecule, Koch explained it as drawing electrons to itself, away from the electron donors of the ammonia compounds.

During this time, the acid theory of Gilbert Lewis came out in 1914. It was a general theory of acidity and alkalinity in terms of electron withdrawal or donation. It was exactly compatible with Koch's oxidation-reduction explanation. But again, the Lewis theory was displaced by the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acid, which is what everyone now teaches—that acid is a hydrogen ion donor. So Lewis's theory, which was true and general, was displaced by a basically erroneous theory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Albert Szent-Györgyi was essentially looking for evidence of Koch's high-energy promoter of oxidation as an electron acceptor in physiology. Koch had postulated that benzoquinone was useful because there was a quinone molecule in the cell that this was a close imitation of. It wasn't until 1950 that it was discovered that there is, in fact, an essential oxidizing quinone in the mitochondria—ubiquinone.

Szent-Györgyi appreciated the logic, and while working on respiratory chemistry, he accidentally discovered big parts of the Krebs cycle and ascorbic acid.

**John Barkhausen:** Is this what he received the Nobel Prize for?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, for his discoveries that led to the Krebs cycle, ascorbic acid, and muscle studies. Methylguanidine causes muscle contraction by donating electrons to a system that should have the electrons withdrawn by the oxidative catalyst. It became clearer in Szent-Györgyi's work why he was working on both muscle contraction and oxidative metabolism.

Another theory that becomes an obstacle to understanding is the membrane theory of cell function, which explains cell electricity in terms of ions and protons. Szent-Györgyi was working on the direct involvement of electrons in respiration. For example, consciousness disappears instantly when oxygen is no longer available to accept electrons, before there is any detectable change in cellular energy levels.

One of Szent-Györgyi's experiments involved adding electron donor chemicals and electron acceptor chemicals to a living muscle. If the donor and acceptor were related to each other in terms of their oxidation potential, the muscle would contract. If they were not tuned to each other, the muscle wouldn't react. This verified what Koch was saying: donating an electron to a muscle system causes it to go into the active state, and the high-energy oxidant causes it to stabilize and go into a resting state.

For Warburg, Koch, and Szent-Györgyi, cancer, allergy, muscle spasms, and seizures were all examples of the activated state in which there are excess electrons. Oxidation was the basic answer to restoring the cell to its stable resting state. This puts the cancer problem in a different evolutionary light. They saw cell division as the basic state of any cell. At a point in evolution, oxidative respiration came in and made it possible for cells to stop dividing long enough to form a multicellular organism. The reversion to cancer became simply interference with the ability to respire on the cellular level.

**John Barkhausen:** So the problem with cancer and spasms is that your cells are not getting the oxygen or can't use it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Warburg's definition of cancer metabolically was that it is aerobic glycolysis. Ordinarily, glycolysis is a process similar to fermentation; sugar is used very wastefully, and it happens in the absence of oxygen. Glycolysis happens normally only when there is no oxygen. When you block the oxygen apparatus, you get intense glycolysis. If it is the apparatus rather than the supply which is blocked, this is what happens in disease. Aerobic glycolysis is evidence that the respiring organ isn't working right.

**John Barkhausen:** Why do you think they were so shunned by the powers that be?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the case of Koch, he makes a case for rational behavior on the part of the government and medical associations, just in terms of them being badly educated, badly motivated, authoritarian people.

To understand it, the best way is to read Herbert Bailey's book about Krebiozen. Andrew Ivy was one of the biggest establishment doctors in the country—founder of several medical associations, Vice President of the University of Illinois, and America's representative to the Nuremberg trials to testify on universal medical ethics.

When a Yugoslav doctor, Dr. Stevan Durovic, came to the United States with a cancer treatment, he took his idea to Andrew Ivy. Ivy was intelligent and had been thinking that cancer might be the loss of a restraining process. This line of thinking has been demonstrated over and over. For example, if you cut off half an animal's liver, it will regrow to the right size. These chemicals of restraint were called "chalones."

Durovic said he had vaccinated horses with an organism that causes tumors, *Actinomyces bovis*, and produced a tumor, then extracted the blood of the horses. The technique was to use absolute ethanol to extract the material and then resuspend it in water. Ivy immediately was interested in testing it. He took patients whose doctors said they had only one or two months to live. In these people, he saw dramatic results. He wasn't looking for a cure at that point, but one injection would cause a high proportion of patients to have dramatic improvement.

Ivy said this stuff had to be studied in better ways. Herbert Bailey's book documents the horrifying way the power structure started acting. Andrew Ivy's positions were taken away from him. He was fired from his vice presidency and his professorship. He was kicked out of scientific organizations he had founded. He went from being at the very top of American medicine to being basically a community college teacher for the rest of his life.

**John Barkhausen:** It makes you wonder what the motives are.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A good place to start is to look at the Congressional Record from the 88th Congress and the material that Illinois Senator Paul Douglas introduced. It documents that two big drug companies and the treasurer of the American Medical Association offered Durovic two and a half million dollars for the rights to the chemical. They refused.

Basically, it was a conspiracy. As the Senator said in the Congressional Record, if this wasn't true, why aren't these chemical companies and the AMA suing for slander? They refused to comment even on why they wouldn't sue.

**John Barkhausen:** Are you familiar with Dr. Samuel Epstein? He feels that mammograms are not only not useful but can actually spread cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. John Gofman, whose book on the prevention of breast cancer is posted on the internet, was one of the Atomic Energy Commission's defenders of radiation in the 50s. He was a top figure in medical physics. In the 60s, he started thinking about what he was saying publicly and realized it was crazy. He says that three-quarters of breast cancers are caused by radiation, primarily medical radiation.

**John Barkhausen:** I was reading something you sent me that said bone density scans are basically X-rays.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The terrible thing is that they are going to recommend you do it anyway because you're old, and old people have thinning bones. Ultrasound technology exists that is more meaningful; it will actually tell you the strength of your bones, not just how dense they are.

In the *Journal of the American Medical Association*, someone published graphs showing the tremendous inaccuracy of the bone scan because of differences in fat and water in the tissues. Estrogen, for example, affects the distribution of fat and fluid. Estrogen causes calcium retention but no increase in bone density, yet the X-ray technique used for scanning sometimes gives an apparent increase in bone density due to the fat/water artifact.

Since ultrasound measures strength as well as density, there are overwhelming arguments why no one should ever have a bone scan. Besides being harmless and accurate, ultrasound happens to stimulate bone growth, whereas X-rays accelerate bone loss. Every time you get a bone scan, your bones are going to go away a little faster.

**John Barkhausen:** So that applies to X-rays and the teeth too?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The X-rays bounce off your teeth and jawbones and accelerate the atrophy of your jawbone. But the bouncing rays go into your brain. They know that dental X-rays cause thyroid cancer and eye cancer. If they are bouncing to that extent, obviously they are going through the brain. The brain is the most sensitive of all tissues to radiation. A great way to produce Alzheimer's disease ought to be to have lots of dental X-rays.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think they could use ultrasound on your teeth?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, there are instruments already existing that give very fine resolution. All you need is a transducer that you can put in your mouth.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe you should say where to get Herbert Bailey's book or what the name of it is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It might be hard to find. Old bookstores or libraries would be where I would look. The pressure caused the first publisher to fold up within a year, and positive reviews were cancelled. The book is called *Krebiozen: Key to Cancer*.

**John Barkhausen:** Thanks for listening to Politics and Science today. If you want to find out more about Raymond Peat, you can go to his website, raypeat.com.
