**John Barkhausen:** My guest today on Politics and Science is Raymond Peat, endocrinologist and physiologist from Eugene, Oregon. Ray, how are you today?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Good.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, maybe you should give your resume, because obviously you can do it better than I.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, well, I'm not sure I can. I was a humanities person first. While I was studying painting and literature, I was interested in science and read widely in libraries and encyclopedias. My first teaching job, while I was studying linguistics at Ohio State, was in a little college where I got assigned to teach biology. Because I had been reading in it for so long, the experience of teaching it was fun.

I taught art and English for a few years after that, but finally decided to go back to graduate school in 1968 to study biology in a university. My first courses in the sciences didn't impress me that I would be able to learn much in a university. It was the same in English, philosophy, and psychology. I basically felt that the institutions were anti-educational—that their purpose was to prepare people to conform, to get a job, and go along with the system. By the time I finally decided to be a biologist, I had learned how to be quiet enough that I could get through the degree program.

The graduate school experience—I think most people having done it recognize that it's an exercise in conformism rather than anything very special about learning.

**John Barkhausen:** You mean that they're looking for certain behavioral patterns from their students?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In the 60s, psychologists at Oregon State University did a study of academic success and how students had scored on the Miller Analogies Test. It is somewhat a test of cultural knowledge—you have to know the language—but it's partly a study of mental flexibility and ability to reason about new problems. She found that the students who scored average on the Miller Analogies Test were straight-A, very successful students in graduate school. The ones who deviated from the average, either up or down, were the less successful in graduate school. This means that having an average ability and conforming really is the way to be an outstanding graduate student.

**John Barkhausen:** And after you were a graduate student, you got your Ph.D. in 1972?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1972. I actually took more courses in biochemistry than in biology, but the degree was in biology.

**John Barkhausen:** Since then you've taught at a number of universities, I believe.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I taught some courses at the University of Oregon, but also in Mexico, at the University of Veracruz and the State University of Mexico.

**John Barkhausen:** You write extensively in a newsletter called Ray Peat's Newsletter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been doing that since 1981. Having had essentially all of my research rejected by the journals, I decided just to go ahead and publish my own things and not have to deal with editors. I had sent some very simple critical things as letters to editors of, for example, *Science* magazine, pointing out that they were drawing racist conclusions from evidence that had absolutely nothing to do with their conclusions. Even a little two-sentence criticism like that was rejected as being more extreme than the authors of the study I was commenting on. I considered science to be so political that I decided to publish my own books and newsletters.

**John Barkhausen:** I think some of your writings prompted me to name the show *Politics and Science* because the two seem very closely interwoven. In fact, they seem unable to escape from each other, to the detriment of science.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In the 50s, when I first started teaching biology, my course was officially named "Biology Introduction for Physics Majors." Since the students were planning to major in physics, I thought the biological work should relate to their interests. I thought information technology—how the organism was interpreted as information—and radiation biology were things that would be important to physics majors.

When the students got interested in reading what the government was saying about the safety of radioactive fallout, that caused great turmoil in the trustees of the university. They invited a professor from the University of Illinois to apply for my job. When he arrived, his invited speech was on radiation biology. He started his lecture looking at his wrist and saying, "Notice I'm not wearing a wristwatch." He said, "I realized how much radiation was being emitted from the dial and threw my watch away in a radioactive disposal." He not only didn't get the job he applied for, but he got fired from the University of Illinois.

**John Barkhausen:** I wonder how many they had to go through before they found a proper replacement for you. It sounds like you're not alone out there. I know at one point you recommended a book called *Cold War in Biology*, which certainly speaks to the politics that go along with the science.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's a good introduction to the politics of genetics in a broader sense—not just the racist genetics that they were teaching in American universities, but the whole history way back to the 19th century.

**John Barkhausen:** I was hoping today that we'd talk about fats, seeing that's a subject that's in the news all the time. The government always makes recommendations for what kind of fats you should be eating, and they seem to change their minds about every five years. I remember when I was growing up, they told you to avoid greasy fried foods. Wesson oil was the standard in the 50s. Then at some point, they told you that those vegetable oils were good for you and that the thing to avoid was butter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Wesson oil was cottonseed oil.

**John Barkhausen:** Oh, was it? I always thought that was corn.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, maybe it was at some time, but in the 50s when I investigated it, it was cottonseed oil. That has a long history. Mark Twain, in one of his books, told about hearing a conversation in the 1860s where people were on his boat talking about how they were going to make Americans eat cottonseed oil instead of butter.

**John Barkhausen:** That's right. Talk about a fat conspiracy. I think I read that they were taking olive oil from Italy and then cutting it ten-to-one with cottonseed oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 10 years ago, the FDA did a survey of all the imported olive oil sold in the US and reported that 70% of it was adulterated still.

**John Barkhausen:** That's not too encouraging. Maybe we could start with a bit of the history of fat consumption—what's traditionally been eaten by humans and how that's evolved.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 19th century, my relatives were still preferring fat meat to lean meat, and the taste of it seemed to be an important guide. People really didn't trim the fat from their meat because it tasted good. It was fairly isolated areas where they used exotic oils like extracted oils. Usually, they just ate oily fruits, the coconut itself, avocados, sunflower seeds, and fat poultry, beef, and pigs.

Around the 18th or 19th century was when the industrial market started promoting cod liver oil and some of the seed oils. But even fish oil was primarily used for varnish and lamps right up until the time of petroleum. When petroleum became so cheap, the plant and fish oils became too expensive, and they went looking for new markets.

Coconut oil is easy to get out with primitive technology. The oriental countries where it was grown would boil the semi-dried coconut meat and float off the oil. It was being used to feed chickens and pigs in the United States and to make Oreo cookies, for example, just because of its cheapness and the fact that it didn't get rancid.

But the agricultural industry in the 40s experimented and found that even though coconut oil was cheap, it stimulated the animals' appetites and metabolic rates, causing them to eat more food and gain less weight. One reaction was to use chemical poisons to slow their metabolic rate by poisoning the thyroid glands. Another discovery was that if they used fish oil, linseed oil, or cottonseed oil—any of the unsaturated fats—they could slow the metabolic rate and make them put on fat more cheaply. So the seed oil industry now had a fairly good market in feeding pigs.

Around 1950, the petroleum chemists found a new use for petroleum other than fuel: making paints and plastics. Where fish oil and linseed oil had been the major basis for making paints and varnishes, now those markets were lost. The linseed oil industry looked for new ways to sell their products. That was when the idea of oil as an "essential nutrient" started being promoted.

The study that has been cited for many decades was performed in connection with the lard industry, claiming that unsaturated fats were essential nutrients. The linseed oil industry, because their product is rich in unsaturated fats, picked up that isolated bit of research. They ignored the studies which previously had demonstrated that animals thrived on a diet completely lacking the unsaturated fats—or any fats, in fact. But that study was so promoted by the oil industry that it created the idea that the unsaturated fats are essential nutrients.

**John Barkhausen:** So even though they claim they're essential, you're saying there was an experiment where animals thrived without them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Starting about 1910 through the 1920s, there were several experiments in which animals were actually healthier when they didn't get any of the fats. A German study published in 1927 showed that as the animals received less fat in their diet, the incidence of cancer decreased. The cancer rate was directly proportional to the amount of fat in the diet. That study, and others that showed increased longevity, were ignored in the research that claimed the essentiality of the unsaturated fats.

**John Barkhausen:** You hear from so many people that they're essential.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The University of Texas had a famous nutrition lab under Roger Williams. In his lab in the 1940s, the researchers said the rat disease supposedly caused by a deficiency of essential fatty acids looked exactly like their vitamin B6 deficiency disease.

Only one or two of the B vitamins were known at the time the original research was done. But in the 40s, they had identified the deficiency disease specifically caused by a vitamin B6 deficiency. So they reproduced the diet fed in the 1929 research to their animals but gave them vitamin B6. It completely cured the "essential fatty acid deficiency" without any essential fatty acids.

The interpretation of why the fat-free or low-fat diet caused those symptoms was that the essential fatty acids suppress the metabolic rate, as the pig farmers demonstrated. When your metabolism is suppressed, you don't eat as much food or drink as much water, so your nutritional requirements are depressed. But if you stimulate their metabolism by *not* giving them the suppressive unsaturated fatty acids, you will reveal a vitamin deficiency. As your metabolic rate increases, you eat more protein, and to process that protein, you use up your vitamin B6 faster.

**John Barkhausen:** So do you think people are blaming symptoms caused by vitamin B6 deficiency on the lack of these EFAs?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been a few other isolated studies through the 50s and 60s. Usually, one patient would get eczema, and that would get published as proof that the essential fatty acids deficiency disease existed. But at that time, when they were giving a fat-free diet, they were often giving intravenous feeding. Their concept of complete intravenous nutrition until well into the 1970s was radically deficient in several of the essential known nutrients. Zinc, for example, wasn't included. Biotin deficiency can produce some of the related symptoms. When your metabolic rate is high and you metabolize more protein, zinc, biotin, and B6 are among the first deficiencies to show up.

**John Barkhausen:** So the control group that wasn't being given the "essential fatty acids" wasn't getting any minerals and vitamins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Even hospitals were keeping babies on this intravenous feeding. Even though the nutrition journals knew what the essential nutrients such as zinc were, hospitals refused to include them because doctors weren't doing it.

**John Barkhausen:** It's a little confusing because people have a symptom, say eczema, and a naturopath tells them to eat flax oil.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you suppress your metabolism, you can get under the metabolic rate at which you need a certain amount of nutrition. So you can "cure" a vitamin B6, biotin, or zinc deficiency sometimes just by taking a toxic thing that suppresses your metabolism.

**John Barkhausen:** So you're saying in the long run, that has other bad effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same applies to fish oil to suppress inflammation. Even people who were advocating its use published reports showing radical suppression of immunity by eating a moderate amount of fish oil. David Horrobin, for example, went on advocating polyunsaturated fats therapeutically, even though he published evidence showing decisive suppression of the immune system. You can get away with suppressing inflammation for six months or a year, maybe a couple of years, just by knocking out your immune system. But it's not good in the long run.

**John Barkhausen:** On the fish oil front, you hear that some people take fish oil to fight depression. What's your take on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've read all of the publications on it. Some of them say it makes depression worse; some say it doesn't do anything.

**John Barkhausen:** These are the studies you've seen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you select the few that say it helped a certain group, you can truthfully report that this group improved, while someone else reports that their group got worse on fish oil. If there's a bias in the journal regarding who gets published, then you don't actually see the empirical data that existed in the world.

**John Barkhausen:** I read a quote you used from a former editor of the New England Journal of Medicine, Marcia Angell. It was something to the effect that you can't really tell the truth of the studies unless you know all the studies that they rejected.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have a probability at the 5% level, but you rejected 10, 20, or 100 publications with negative results, you're biasing statistics.

**John Barkhausen:** I don't think we've covered all the different fats. People probably want to know what is bad and what is good. Is canola as bad as cottonseed oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1960s, there was a lot of concern that there was a special toxic fat in mustard oil or rapeseed oil. They bred a variety that didn't have that particular fatty acid, and that became canola. But meanwhile, researchers were experimenting. They showed that giving rapeseed oil would typically cause spots of tissue in the heart to die. Mainstream medicine said that was because of the toxic fatty acid that the breeders were eliminating.

However, Hans Selye gave purified linoleic acid—a major component of rapeseed oil—and showed that *that* was the actual toxic agent to the heart, not the so-called special toxic fatty acid. It was the "essential fatty acid" itself killing heart cells. He added chocolate fat, cocoa butter, to the diet, and that protected the heart. In spite of the same amount of linoleic acid in the diet, adding stearic acid in the cocoa butter was protective.

**John Barkhausen:** I see.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the ratio that is important. One of the early rat studies that got me interested in coconut oil involved putting 15 different groups of rats on different diets. One series was pure coconut oil (high, low, and medium fat). Another was pure unsaturated corn oil (high, medium, and low). They kept them on that diet throughout their lifespan.

At the end of the normal lifespan, the fat rats were the ones on an unsaturated fat diet. The lean rats were the ones on the coconut, saturated fat diet. The quantity of fat they ate didn't make any significant difference; it was the ratio. The degree of unsaturation corresponded to the degree of obesity.

A series of French publications in the 1980s really defined what the pig farmers had demonstrated practically. The French showed biochemically how it works. They showed that increasing the number of unsaturations—two double bonds was worse than monounsaturated, and three double bonds was worse than two. The worst was the multiply unsaturated.

Every component of the thyroid system that they examined—from the secretion of the hormone from the thyroid gland, its transport on proteins through the blood, and the cell's response to it—was selectively inhibited in proportion to the unsaturation of the oil that the animal was getting. It very neatly explained what the pig farmers found out economically: by slowing down the metabolism of the pig, it would gain weight with the unsaturated fat diet.

**John Barkhausen:** This probably deserves a whole show, but perhaps you could summarize what the thyroid does for the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The real thyroid hormone, the active part of it, wasn't discovered until the 1950s, but the function of the thyroid was studied since the mid-to-late 19th century. It was known to activate all of the organs of the body to respire, consume more oxygen, and perform more perfectly. A deficiency of thyroid was very early learned to cause mental retardation, underdevelopment of the brain, idiocy, and infertility. In some areas of the world, cretins were good employees because they were passive and stupid and didn't reproduce, so the medical establishments in those areas didn't want to cure it.

Broda Barnes in the 1930s did studies on rabbits and in Europeans and showed that the "goiter belts" were highly susceptible to heart disease at a very young age. In their 30s, they started having atherosclerosis and heart attacks. When iodine was introduced to those regions, the heart disease mortality decreased considerably. But those areas also had a very high cancer rate, especially breast cancer. As recently as the 1980s, cancer biologists in Mexico were reporting that the iodine deficiency regions in the mountains around Mexico City still had a very high rate of tuberculosis, heart disease, and breast cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** Excuse me, but iodine deficiency slows your thyroid function?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. In those regions, iodine deficiency was the thing that could be remedied. But in many areas, the diet interacts with limited iodine. It isn't just an iodine deficiency, but eating vegetables that interrupt the formation of thyroid hormone. The cabbage family and the unsaturated fats are the two most famous causes of interrupting the formation of the thyroid hormone.

**John Barkhausen:** And people with low thyroid get goiters, which are big protrusions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The pituitary gland produces Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) that compensates when your thyroid is being blocked. Naturally, estrogen inhibits the thyroid release too. The body is designed so that if estrogen is inhibiting the gland, TSH increases to overcome that block and activates the thyroid to work harder. If you keep your estrogen or goitrogen high, the TSH works harder and harder, and the gland gets bigger and bigger until sometimes it gets to be as big as a cantaloupe.

Women at puberty and during pregnancy often get a fullness in the neck. That typically causes women to have creases in the skin of their neck. Most women, but almost no men, have a defining crease right above their collarbone and just above their Adam's apple.

**John Barkhausen:** And that defined crease is from a low thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, because at puberty, the thyroid gland naturally enlarges to overcome the effect of estrogen, and that makes a fullness so that the bending of the neck causes those creases to outline the puffy area where the gland is.

**John Barkhausen:** Going back to the essential fatty acids, you've said that one of the reasons it's ridiculous to call them essential is that they're ubiquitous. They're in everything, so how could we have a deficiency?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's a question of marketing. They are in every organism, even tropical organisms. Coconuts have about 1% to 2% of those fats. Ruminants—sheep, cows, and deer—have an organ to grow bacteria which detoxify those plant fats. But still, 1% or 2% of the fats get through the detox system of the rumen. So beef fat and lamb fat still have unavoidably about 2% of those unsaturated vegetable oils. Even if you ate nothing but beef, lamb, and coconut, you'd still have more than anyone ever claimed was required. So by the most extreme ideas of essentiality, it's impossible to have a deficiency unless you eat a laboratory-prepared diet.

But the marketing departments of the linseed oil and Wesson oil companies convinced people that since it's essential in a trace amount, it must be much better in a very large amount. Several more recent research studies have demonstrated that as you increase the unsaturated fats in the diet, the cancer incidence goes up more or less in proportion to the amount. When you extrapolate it to zero, the cancer incidence approaches zero.

**John Barkhausen:** When you say extrapolate to zero, you mean no unsaturated fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**John Barkhausen:** And fish oil is also very unsaturated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A few years ago, the FDA warned that the total shouldn't exceed 3 grams of DHA and EPA. But they more recently have dropped that and have begun promoting it without the warning. But it definitely becomes toxic, as the immune suppression studies demonstrated.

The odd thing about fish oil is that it's so unstable. The reason it was a good varnish is that it oxidizes almost instantly, even at room temperature. In your body, it's mostly oxidized before it reaches your bloodstream. It has to pass through your digestive system, be heated, and circulated in tiny particles exposed to oxygen. Those so-called beneficial anti-inflammatory effects are actually produced by the oxidative breakdown products of the fats. So even in the biochemistry of it, it's a toxic effect that is being sold as a benefit.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's suppressing your immune system and that's what's getting rid of some of your symptoms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it's the free radical oxidative decomposition products that are circulating in your blood system. A very small part of it reaches your tissues as the original starting DHA and EPA.

**John Barkhausen:** How much does the marketing affect the scientific research? The media seems to still be very down on saturated fats and promoting unsaturated fats.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They apparently have taken over the government because I see the government has basically a promotion of fish oil on their website. The industry, just like the soy oil industry, has subsidized research on the health value of soy oil. The fish oil industry is now rich enough that they are sponsoring conferences, paying researchers to produce studies, and getting people on editorial boards of the journals. Just like the atomic energy industry controlling the research on the safety of radiation, the health effects of fats are being promoted by the industry, not by objective science.

**John Barkhausen:** Now you mentioned cancer in terms of unsaturated oils. Does that apply to fish oil as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Except that the shorter 18-carbon oils that you get from seeds fit into our enzyme systems more powerfully and so inhibit our own enzymes more powerfully. The fish oils are very long and don't directly attack our enzymes in the same way. They're unstable and spontaneously turn into these free radical and aldehyde toxins, but they are safer to our enzyme systems because their number of carbons is very different from the fats that we make or that we get from seeds.

**John Barkhausen:** And they also come with quite a few vitamins, too.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. When you squeeze an oily fish, you can't help getting some vitamin K, vitamin A, vitamin D, and a little E. The E is pretty much destroyed quickly by the oxidative process, but the D comes through very strongly because it's harder to oxidize. The K and A probably usually have enough activity to be of some benefit.

**John Barkhausen:** We have about five minutes left. People are probably wondering, what is good to eat? Is olive oil okay? Coconut oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Coconut oil is around 10% polyunsaturated fats. If you're only going to use half a teaspoon or so for flavoring a food, or a teaspoonful every other day, that is small enough that it isn't harmful. As a minor flavoring, olive oil is fine.

But as a major part of the diet, I think butter, beef fat, lamb fat, and coconut oil are the safe ones. And cocoa butter—chocolate. Some studies have found that the longer saturated fats are very protective. They're being investigated for curing cancer and heart disease. Some of the best studies are using the long-chain saturated fats as well as ordinary butter fats for treating liver disease. Alcoholic hepatitis, for example, is being successfully treated with saturated fat. About 20 years ago, they noticed that alcoholic liver injury requires polyunsaturated fats in the diet. Some Hindus noticed that in the areas of India where they have primarily butter, alcoholics don't get liver disease at the high rate that they do in areas that get the unsaturated fats. So the animal studies finally led to human studies in Chicago in which they are finding actual cures of alcoholic liver disease just with a good diet plus the saturated fats.

**John Barkhausen:** The unsaturated oils are in everything now. You can't buy a potato chip that isn't cooked in canola oil. If you go out to dinner, is there anything you can do to protect yourself?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 15 years ago there was this big campaign to get coconut oil off the market. In recent years it is coming back. I think if people just nag the cooks in restaurants and buyers in grocery stores, they can change things. It's changing back in the last few years to people demanding that they get real butter and other saturated fats.

**John Barkhausen:** Finally, I think most people are worried about getting fat when you say butter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The animal studies, from the industrial agriculture level all the way down to lab studies, show that the polyunsaturateds are extremely fattening in proportion to their role in the diet. The proportion to the saturated fats is more important than the actual quantity of fats. I noticed in Finland, where dairy foods are very common—probably the most common food—just going across the border from Russia to Finland, you go from a starch-eating, vegetable-based diet where everyone's fat, over to a lean, healthy population where they eat lots of butterfat. In general, Americans who eat milk and milk products are lean. It's partly the calcium and vitamin D, but also the butterfat itself is helpful.

**John Barkhausen:** I guess that's the French paradox again. Well, Ray, we're basically out of time. Is there anything else you'd like to add?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People are concerned about skin health and appearance. An experiment with rabbits is interesting. Rabbits were put on either a corn oil diet or a coconut oil diet and shaved so the sun would hit their skin. Those on the unsaturated corn oil diet got wrinkly, sun-damaged skin. For the ones on the saturated fat diet, the sun was relatively harmless to their skin.

**John Barkhausen:** That's kind of telling, isn't it? Well Ray, thanks so much for being on today. The hour blew by.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

**John Barkhausen:** Thanks, Ray. Bye.

title: Politics & Science: Empiricism vs Dogmatic Modeling
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** We are speaking with Dr. Raymond Peat out in Eugene, Oregon. He's an endocrinologist and physiologist who has written a lot of books about health, nutrition, and science, and publishes *Ray Peat's Newsletter*. You can find him on the web at raypeat.com.

Just yesterday we were doing a sound check and we picked up where we left off last week, talking about fats in our diet and the use of fats by humans over the years and as animal feed. You were talking about cholesterol and mentioned a fellow named Chris Masterjohn. One of the things you said that shocked me was that for years we've heard that cholesterol is something you get from fat—from butter, beef fat, or meats full of supposedly saturated fats—and that's why we're being poisoned by cholesterol. But it turns out that perhaps cholesterol isn't the boogeyman we always thought it was. It's actually something we need to function.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but regarding eating cholesterol: if you're healthy, you have to eat a tremendous amount to raise your levels. There was an experiment where they had healthy young men eat eggs until they could see an increase in blood cholesterol. It took 22 eggs before they saw a rise in the day's cholesterol. It does rise if you're very sick and can't compensate.

In a practical situation where a person might want to raise their cholesterol, you can usually do it just by eating lots of fruit. The minerals and sugar in the fruit give the liver the energy it needs to make adequate cholesterol. There is a U-shaped curve of mortality. You have an ideal range of cholesterol for a given age, and when you're below that range, your mortality increases.

**John Barkhausen:** What are those ranges?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The people who talk about the curve usually put the bottom of the U around 160 to 180 mg/dL. But when you look at the figures, the bottom really varies with age. One study looked at people in a nursing home situation and saw that the ones who had the highest cholesterol—I think in that group those with 270—lived the longest. So you have to think about the relation of the cholesterol to the stress you're under and consider it an anti-stress hormone.

**John Barkhausen:** My father recently was told that he has to start taking statins. A lot of people are on statins. What's your opinion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Years ago they started seeing increased mortality as they used drugs to lower cholesterol. There was a Hungarian study in the 1980s that showed a great increase in cancer mortality as they lowered cholesterol. That somewhat accorded with a Veterans Administration study in the 1960s that they stopped when they saw that people on the so-called heart-protective low-fat diet were dying at a higher rate from cancer.

There are still some lingering data showing that statins might increase total mortality, but the marketing is so intense that they manage to place articles convincing people how good it is. A recent book by Melody Peterson, titled *Our Daily Meds*, gives a lot of information about how the drug industry manipulates the culture—paying doctors well, writing articles for doctors, and getting them to sign their names to publish them in prestigious journals. It gives a little bit of the inside information about how they're actually buying the medical literature.

Marcia Angell, seeing it from an editor's viewpoint at the *New England Journal of Medicine*, emphasized that editorial decisions can completely bias the results of a topic. If people choose not to submit their data because it doesn't support the efficacy or safety of a drug, a lot of studies will simply not get submitted. If the editors introduce more bias, you might have 50 studies showing a drug is harmful and useless and one that gets published showing that it's beneficial.

Melody Peterson shows how the drug industry is not only modifying the research that gets done and how universities treat their research, but how the journals publish it and finally how the doctors use it. The system is pretty well sewed up now. Anything relating to drug therapy, you simply can't trust the Anglo-American literature. Increasingly, it has spread into Italy, Chile, France, and Japan as the industries become influential in those countries. India and Russia were relatively outside the commercial pharmaceutical influence, but now they're moving in that direction too.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's an effect of globalization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, though some of the more backward economies still manage to do some real research.

**John Barkhausen:** Getting back to cholesterol, the last time you were on the air you spoke about Chris Masterjohn.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've read several of his articles that are very good. My only disagreement with him is that he persists in believing in essential fatty acids.

**John Barkhausen:** That's something a lot of alternative health people believe in. In a nutshell, what's your view on the essential fatty acids?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first claim was that it was linoleic acid. Then maybe linolenic was added. But after the Burr studies of the late 1920s and early 30s, by the 1940s their disease was shown to be nothing but a vitamin B6 deficiency. At just about the same time, agricultural researchers were showing that linolenic and linoleic acid were the causes of brain degeneration, testicular degeneration, infertility, and muscle degeneration.

Fish oils about the same time were causing mink degenerative disease. "Yellow fat disease" was showing up in more and more animals as they were fed fish waste because of an excess of the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) in the fish fats. Finally, linoleic acid was recognized to be essential for cancer, but not at all essential for nutrition.

The publicity coming out that the original "essential" fatty acids were essential for cancer discouraged marketing in that direction. That's when it shifted to marketing fish oil as the *new* version of the essential fatty acids. That's where we are now, at the peak of the fish oil promotion. They are being recommended at higher intake levels to actually function as drugs to supposedly cure a lot of diseases. But in fact, the old research going back 40 or 50 years shows that it is simply a temporary suppression of inflammatory symptoms while, in the long run, increasing the inflammatory degenerative processes.

**John Barkhausen:** So the reason people have a subsiding of their symptoms is just that their immune system has been knocked down?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** David Horrobin, who was a big promoter of polyunsaturated fats and who died of brain cancer while trying to treat himself with his own fats, published work showing that fish oil is very immune-suppressive. Others looking at why fish oil is anti-inflammatory found that it wasn't the original long-chain polyunsaturated fats found in the fish. When they are processed and hit the hot organs of a mammal, they break down. It's the breakdown products—the aldehydes and free radicals decomposed from the fish oils—which are actually the anti-inflammatory substances. It's the deterioration of the material that produces temporary relief, but it's also those things which contribute to serious long-range problems such as brain damage and vascular damage.

**John Barkhausen:** You were saying last week that fish oil does have some good properties, like lots of vitamin A and D.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Depends on how it's made, but in its crude form, it does come with a lot of vitamin D and A. There have been products on the market extracted from fish liver oil in which they concentrate the vitamin D and A so you can get your daily dose in a couple of drops of the oil.

**John Barkhausen:** Some people are taking fish oil for antidepressants.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There have been studies in the published literature—the ones I've seen were just about an equal number saying it isn't effective as say it is effective. Same with using it as a supplement to baby food. There are studies that show that it retards brain development, even though they don't get discussed very much.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that the DHA?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**John Barkhausen:** And they've started adding that to baby food. So flaxseed oil has gone out of fashion?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think so. The literature in the 1980s became overwhelming showing that linoleic acid in particular is really the basic motor for pushing cancer excess. Linolenic isn't quite as bad, so flax is as bad as some of the others.

**John Barkhausen:** If essential oils are only essential for creating disease, how is it that they're so heavily promoted by the government?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Several years ago the FDA had a warning not to use more than, I think, three grams a day of those long-chain unsaturated fats from fish oil. I think they've dropped that warning, or at least it isn't prominent like it used to be. Right from its very beginning, the FDA was captured by the food industry and then the drug industry. Now they really are working primarily as a corporate defense system.

**John Barkhausen:** It always seems like they absorb the liability for the corporations. If they approve it, then you can't sue the corporation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, same thing as government protecting the nuclear industry by saying you can't collect more than a certain amount of damages if a reactor explodes in your neighborhood. The Public Health Service has a worse record than the FDA itself. The FDA interfaces with the consumers and tries to keep them happy, but at higher levels, the agencies have been more defensive of the power structure. In the years of the fallout from atmospheric bomb testing, the Public Health Service was destroying data and putting out false data about the safety of radiation.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe you could talk about radiation for a minute and how the government's bias has made it more widespread.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For 50 or 60 years, I've been hearing from dentists and doctors that the dose they give you in examining you is very small and harmless. Then they reduce it tenfold and say exactly the same thing. The words are the same from 1940 right down to the current day. They claim they have digitalized machines and people think it's just bits of information coming through their bodies, but it's still the same old X-rays. They're exciting their cells.

Even Linus Pauling took a less than adequate biological view. He was warning about the dangers, but he was looking only at DNA damage. The damage is much subtler than breaking strands of DNA. The excited electrons cause chemical and physiological changes that linger, completely distinct from the immediate reaction of radiation with the DNA.

For example, you can give a dose of radiation to cells in a dish and then add new cells that weren't exposed to radiation to that dish. The new cells will start mutating a day or more later from something emitted by the exposed cells. That process lingers in the tissues and the blood serum. It's called the "bystander effect." You can demonstrate in the lab that cells that weren't exposed start behaving as if they were exposed by contact with the damaged cells.

People exposed to the Hiroshima bomb have been studied 60 years later, and they still showed essentially excited electronic states in their tissues. The same with people about 20 years after the Chernobyl exposure; their serum is still toxic. It can be removed from their blood and added to healthy cells, and the healthy cells begin mutating.

The safety assumptions were based on the model of how a beam of radiation will affect a molecule. It was worked out in terms of direct interaction between a molecule and radiation, but in the organism, that simply isn't how it works. Russians way back in the 60s were showing that. The Western paradigm was that if you irradiated an animal's brain it would go into estrus, supposedly because something was altered in the pituitary causing the ovaries to produce more estrogen. The Russians did a control experiment in which they irradiated the animal's foot instead of its brain, and it still went into estrus. They called it some kind of radiation toxin that was emitted by the exposed tissue.

It's the same thing that happens in the bystander effect. It's some physiological, biochemical change that is started by the radiation but then spreads and continues. The increased estrogen happens to imitate these processes started by the radiation.

**John Barkhausen:** So you're saying a little bit of radiation causes this cascading effect throughout the body?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Two or three years ago in Seattle, they were using low-level, fancy, latest well-calibrated X-ray equipment and covering the patients with lead aprons. They found that a full set of dental X-rays, if the woman was pregnant at the time—even though her body was shielded thoroughly—resulted in her baby being underweight. It showed basically the same effects as taking a dose of estrogen while pregnant: it spreads a stress influence that malnourishes the developing fetus.

**John Barkhausen:** The method you used to describe how the government assessed the dangers of radiation—where they just had a hypothetical theory about one molecule being affected but didn't take into account the living organism—you've said before that that's common in how science is conducted in the West. They do a lot of experiments in test tubes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Worse than that. If you look through PubMed, you see lots of abstracts described as *in vitro*, but now they have the concept *in silico*.

**John Barkhausen:** What does that mean?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It means they didn't have anything living at all; it was all done in a computer. But people read the article and they're used to seeing *in vitro* and think real cells were involved. *In silico* means in the computer. It's like the medieval arguments about angels—how much floor space does an angel need to dance? It is a way of amplifying your favorite hypothesis or assumption.

**John Barkhausen:** In studying science, I think a lot of people are confused. We figure it's empirical and they're testing theories all the time, so the best theory will end up on top. How come that isn't the way it works?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of reasons, but the basic thing is that it's all filtered through the culture and the system of assumptions. If you look at different cultures, the whole background of philosophy and religion influences what you think can be taken seriously as an assumption.

Because in medieval times people believed in alchemy and astrology, ordinary chemists and physiologists think it's absurd to consider the phase of the moon when doing a chemical or biological study. But several people have looked at lab results done over a period of time and have seen that the phase of the moon *does* influence many experiments.

I worked in a hamster lab at the university where the indoor temperature was kept constant and the light was artificially controlled so a person would not have any cues indoors whether it was winter or summer. But somehow the hamsters knew what was going on outside the walls because their thymuses would atrophy in the winter season and come back in the spring, just like they do when exposed to changing day lengths.

Professor Brown in Indiana did many tests with potatoes, oysters, and flowering plants. He noticed his experiments varied with the moon. He got some oysters from the East Coast and studied their metabolism in Indiana. If it had been genetically determined—as the paradigm said it must be, because hamsters can't know when it's winter if you control their lights—it must be a genetically operated clock. Brown took his oysters to Indiana, and they were still metabolically cycling as if the tides were coming into Indiana. He did the same thing with potatoes, which aren't susceptible to tides, and saw a similar metabolic moon cycle.

He took plants into a mine shaft and they kept cycling until they got hundreds of feet below the surface. Finally, they didn't receive a cue and no longer cycled. He demonstrated that some lunar or planetary influence was able to penetrate hundreds of feet of shielding. This disproved the idea that it's all controlled by an abstract genetic clock.

**John Barkhausen:** So you're saying that genetics is a dogma that's been accepted by the culture?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It really is primarily a kind of religious belief. Remember the Lamarck-Cuvier controversy? The person who took over the museum that Lamarck had been the director of was a Christian catastrophist who basically said there was no evolution; it was accounted for by a flood destroying the ancient species. In history, genetics as an anti-environmental approach was strictly a biblical orientation against the Lamarckian environmentalist orientation.

**John Barkhausen:** I always thought the genetic orientation is very convenient for liability. If you can't directly link pollution to a problem in a simple cause-and-effect, they can always just say it's genetics.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It has been very convenient for the medical profession for the last 50 or 60 years. It's either genetic or it's a virus, and there's nothing you can do to expect a cure. Especially with cancer, the government was very influential in reinforcing that interpretation. That's closely related to military medical research. The germ warfare people were getting government subsidies and were inclined to the "it's your own fault for having bad genes" theory.

Environmentalism in cancer research simply couldn't get funding after about 1945. The idea that embryos develop according to a developmental field and gradient was the dominant theory, along with the idea that cancer is a metabolic, physiological field distortion. Embryology and cancer were related to these metabolic and pattern-based ideas. The genetics and militaristic approach simply cut those off. When the government came out of the war having funded the Manhattan Project, that sort of money was directed into germ warfare research. That gradually shifted to so-called cancer research. The Fort Detrick germ warfare lab simply changed its name while not doing very different research when it shifted over to the "War on Cancer."

**John Barkhausen:** So these cultural beliefs seem to be directing research and taking some theories for truth while rejecting others regardless of empirical evidence. They are also responsible for the misinformation we've heard about cholesterol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They talk about genetically determined tendencies towards high cholesterol that you can see in the form of cholesterol receptors. The whole idea of a "receptor" is a genetic pharmacological idea. It is very much like the ads you see on TV where a drug zooms around in your body and goes right to the place where it's needed.

One drug company was collecting genes from a village in the Mediterranean where people didn't have heart disease, trying to promote gene change as a drug product. But the environmental influences simply weren't of interest. If you can identify a problem as a permanent genetic feature and then work on that gene receptor with a drug, you've got a product.

But the cholesterol receptors are regulated by hormones such as the thyroid. If a person doesn't have enough of the receptor that takes cholesterol out of your blood, you can take thyroid and increase the amount of that receptor. But that doesn't please anyone but the thyroid industry, and they haven't really taken advantage of it.

**John Barkhausen:** I know a lot of people who take thyroid. There are several products on the market—Synthroid, Cytomel, Cynoplus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s, the main product was made by the Armour Meat Company, which became the Armour Pharmaceutical Company. They had a lot of beef and pork thyroids they didn't know what to do with, so they would dehydrate and sell them as a drug product. That was the standard treatment. When they would give patients the Armour thyroid, containing both T4 and T3, the symptoms would be alleviated.

But after the war, a company came on the market with purified Thyroxine (T4), which is only a fraction of the Armour thyroid. The thyroid contains a protein and liberates two substances, T4 and T3. T4 is released by the gland about four times as much as the active T3. When the environment is right, the liver completes the activation so that most of your thyroid function is really coming from the liver.

After the war, the drug companies had an interest in promoting a product. They said the main substance, and the easiest to make, was Thyroxine. They gave it to 25-year-old male medical students—very healthy people—and said it works just like real thyroid. But they didn't test it in sick people or in women. Women's livers are much less active than men's because of the effect of estrogen. But the drug product Thyroxine was sold across the board even though it had only been tested in young men.

It was more than 10 years later that the real active hormone, T3, came on the market. The tests that determined whether you were hypothyroid disregarded all the symptoms that had been associated with hypothyroidism up until about 1945. The tests at first measured only the iodine bound to protein, which has very little to do with your thyroid function. According to those tests, the Thyroxine product would raise your protein-bound iodine, so that was compatible with marketing the synthetic drug.

After about 20 years, they saw that the protein-bound iodine test had almost nothing to do with thyroid function. If you ate seaweed, you would get a lot of protein-bound iodine, but your thyroid function would go down. So they started looking for new ways to test. But they had established over those 20 years that instead of half the population benefiting from thyroid, the tests suggested only 5% would benefit. So any new test has been standardized to that paradigm of looking at a percentage of the population rather than whether the substance cures symptoms. Now they are treating the Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) level and disregarding the actual effect of the hormone on the person's health.

**John Barkhausen:** So they're basically treating one of the markers instead of the actual symptoms. That seems to happen a lot in medicine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and they call it "subclinical" and don't even make it explicit what they mean by clinical.

**John Barkhausen:** The AIDS test is something like that, isn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There have been several traditional drugs that alleviate symptoms, but those tend to be suppressed or forgotten. The so-called virus has attracted very little attention. What they're doing now is using a lab process to amplify a substance that relates to the virus—it isn't the actual virus—but they call it the "viral load." It's something they create in the laboratory. Meanwhile, they ignore the use of other therapies or consider them simply additional therapies to be added to the profitable drugs.

**John Barkhausen:** You were going to say something else about the AIDS drugs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are a couple of very good books. One is *Inventing the AIDS Virus* by Peter Duesberg, and the other is by Harvey Bialy about Peter Duesberg. I've been following it now for 20 years, and the establishment people just don't want to talk about it. They won't let these people publish responses to articles in the major journals. So the average doctor reading it thinks they have no answer, but it's just that the editors don't want to hear their answer. The mainline virus theory people have never answered the criticisms of Peter Duesberg, who basically says the virus is harmless.

**John Barkhausen:** That begs the question, what's causing the harm?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He thinks it's a drug. I'm inclined to the idea that it's the interaction of drugs, polyunsaturated fats, radiation exposure, and other toxins in the environment.

**John Barkhausen:** So that would be another case of an environmental problem.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you graph the incidence of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome over the last 60 years, it's a straight progressive increase since the bomb tests began after the Second World War. There was no sudden jump at the time AIDS became official as a disease. It's a steady increase going back 60 years.

**John Barkhausen:** Well, we're just about out of time. We've been talking to Dr. Raymond Peat from Eugene, Oregon. He's a physiologist and endocrinologist and puts out *Ray Peat's Newsletter*. You can find him on the web at raypeat.com where you have a lot of excellent articles.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, I have another 10 or 15 that will go up in a couple of weeks, I hope.

**John Barkhausen:** Great. Even if you don't necessarily agree with everything said there, there is plenty of food for thought and a lot of medical and scientific history that I certainly have never heard before. Thanks, Ray, for your work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay.

**John Barkhausen:** We'll talk to you soon. Bye bye.

title: Politics & Science: Thyroid and Regeneration
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Welcome again to Politics and Science. Last week we were talking about oxidative metabolism and glycolysis—creating lactic acid from glucose. We were discussing this in the context of what it is to be a healthy person: having enough energy to get your tasks done, but also enough to regenerate the damage that inevitably happens to everybody as they go through daily life. You said something last week which I thought was interesting, that we regenerate 25 to 30% of the fats in our brains every night.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It might even be more than that. If you think about taking a phospholipid apart into its components and then rebuilding more phospholipids so that a chain will exist as a unit but be rebuilt into a bigger structure, that kind of turnover probably is more than 20 or 30% during the night. You can see 25% of that kind of turnover in less than an hour in some animal studies.

But if you look at the actual oxidation and renewal of particular fats—so that a fat is broken down into carbon dioxide, for example, and then new fats come in from the bloodstream—that's more like 5% per day. If you look at just arachidonic acid, for example, which makes up a considerable amount of the fat in the brain, that changes and is renewed by the bloodstream about 5% per day.

**John Barkhausen:** Why are we regenerating fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The brain is metabolically very active. When you stress a rat, the turnover in the brain is even faster than at rest. The brain is adapting for the whole organism and thinking up new ways to handle the environment. Whether you put a rat in a tumbling drum to stress it or just have it go through the eight or ten hours of darkness during the night, they are both stressful. The brain is trying to deal with the stress and make innovations or adjustments that help the body to cope with the next day's tasks.

**John Barkhausen:** So the original fats are being burned, or are they just getting oxidized?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A small amount, like 5% or so, are actually being oxidized. A larger amount, maybe 30 or 60%, is being reshuffled from one molecule to another. There are many types of phospholipids and other fats in the brain, and the subunits can change around so that the functions of the nerve cells are adjusted as the type of phospholipid changes.

**John Barkhausen:** Obviously, you need enough energy to be doing that at night. If you don't have the energy to reproduce parts of yourself that are getting worn out or need to be adapted, what happens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The brain synthesizes and stores glycogen, similar to muscles and the liver. With aging or stress, the glycogen is depleted, and it takes deep sleep to regenerate the glycogen. The glycogen seems to be essential. Even if you have circulating glucose, the glycogen is used for those stress-adaptive processes. Having all of your biochemical machinery available—thyroid, vitamins, minerals, and so on—is necessary, but then deep sleep is needed to restore the glycogen so that you can meet the next stresses.

**John Barkhausen:** You've mentioned before that some foods are particularly unhealthy to your thyroid, which sounds like the key mechanism for keeping your metabolism up so that you have the energy available to use.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You want to avoid the specific antithyroid compounds. The goitrogens that you find in a lot of vegetables, grains, and nuts are antithyroid. The polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) are antithyroid. Tryptophan and cysteine, which you find in muscle meats at a very high concentration, are also antithyroid.

**John Barkhausen:** I didn't properly introduce you. We are talking to Dr. Raymond Peat, an endocrinologist, physiologist, and science historian. As an endocrinologist, you have extensive knowledge about hormones, and the function of the thyroid gland is a key part of that. Could you explain the function of the thyroid a little bit?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People think of the thyroid as being regulated by the pituitary hormone TSH. That is a major activator, but it's responsive to practically everything in the internal environment. If your estrogen is high, the enzymes in the gland become less responsive, and the gland accumulates rather than secreting hormone. Progesterone facilitates the enzymes that are needed to secrete the hormone. Polyunsaturated fats inhibit those same enzymes.

If your body is experiencing a deficiency, your pituitary will increase the TSH—Thyroid Stimulating Hormone—to try to get the gland to compensate. If you have a lot of estrogen and polyunsaturated fats circulating, the gland will enlarge under the stimulation of the pituitary, but without secreting very efficiently.

During puberty and pregnancy, it's very common for women to have an enlarged thyroid because of the estrogen inhibiting the release of the hormone. Then, with a change of circumstances or diet, or having the baby when the estrogen goes down, sometimes there will be an episode of hyperthyroid function as that stored hormone is released. That will often scare the patient's doctor if they see their pulse running at 120 to 125 beats per minute at rest, and their hands being pink, warm, and sweaty. That's classical hyperthyroidism.

A lot of doctors will kill your thyroid with radioactive iodine or cut it out when they see symptoms like that. But it's usually just a natural adaptive process in which the enlarged gland is returning to normal size. It takes a few weeks to safely unload that amount of stored colloid thyroglobulin. Some people have told me that they never felt better in their lives than when they were in their month or two of hyperthyroidism. Unfortunately, that's the opportunity for surgeons and radiologists to destroy the thyroid.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s, it was discovered that one molecule called T3, triiodothyronine, is the active promoter of respiration. But it took decades for that information to circulate through the American medical community. The Japanese, Israelis, and Russians were the first ones to really assimilate that information.

Since estrogen inhibits the activity of the thyroid, women are about five or ten times as likely to have thyroid problems as men. But when one form of synthetic thyroid, T4, which isn't the active respiration promoter, was created chemically and became a product, it was tested on 25-year-old male medical students in good health. It was found to act just like the desiccated thyroid glands that had been used at that time for 50 years.

The marketers began selling it to females without really testing it on females, because it worked on young men. But in fact, it very often interferes because the pituitary and brain will respond to it and shut off the thyroid stimulating hormone. It's good at turning off a woman's thyroid gland without necessarily being converted in the liver into the active form.

An experimenter in the 1960s who hadn't assimilated the knowledge of the two hormones—which normally exist in a ratio of three or four to one—sliced up pieces of muscle, kidney, liver, heart, and brain, and then added what he called the thyroid hormone thyroxine, or T4, to the solution. He found that it suppressed oxidative metabolism in the heart, muscle, and brain. The liver was the only gland that was strongly responsive to increasing its respiration rate in proportion to the amount of added thyroxine.

He said he had demonstrated that respiration isn't the important thing done by the thyroid hormone, because how could it be important if the thyroid hormone suppresses the metabolism of the brain and the heart? But in fact, the liver is the source of about 70% of the active thyroid hormone that circulates in the bloodstream. The thyroid gland secretes a little bit, 25 or 30% of the active hormone, but the liver, as it senses the need for energy in the body, converts T4 to T3. The brain doesn't have much of that capacity for activating the hormone. When the T4 increases beyond a certain small amount, it displaces the active hormone and suppresses brain metabolism.

I've seen that happen in numerous women. The first time I heard about it was at the University of Oregon Medical School Hospital in Portland. A woman who had been on one grain of thyroxine for some time was getting worse. They raised her dose to two grains, and every six months or so, she would be worse, so they would increase it. They finally reached the level of the equivalent of five grains—500 micrograms of Synthroid, I think. At that point, she went into a myxedema coma, in which the skin and other tissues puff up with a gelatinous edema material. She was deeply comatose. Luckily, some doctor knew about T3 being the active hormone and gave her intravenous T3, and immediately she came out of the coma.

I've seen that happen to lower degrees in women who would lose their memory or concentration or get strange neurological symptoms when they were taking pure T4. But if they would take a balanced product like natural desiccated thyroid, their symptoms would disappear.

**John Barkhausen:** How does estrogen become a problem in pregnancy? I thought that's when progesterone was high in the cycle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person is low in thyroid going into the pregnancy, or if they don't eat enough protein and certain vitamins so that the liver can function, problems arise. In experiments, if you put a source of estrogen where it goes directly to the liver and measure the amount coming out, in a healthy person, 100% goes in and 0% comes out, meaning the liver totally inactivated the estrogen.

But if it doesn't have enough protein or certain vitamins, the liver can't inactivate estrogen. So 100% goes in and maybe 99% still comes out. The estrogen is allowed to reach very high levels. The thyroid would activate the liver metabolism and restore its ability to destroy estrogen, but it becomes a vicious cycle. If your thyroid is a little low, the liver lets estrogen accumulate to a very high level, and that makes your thyroid go lower by blocking the gland itself. Since thyroid is needed to synthesize progesterone—converting cholesterol into progesterone—what happens in that situation is that your cholesterol rises and your progesterone becomes very low.

**John Barkhausen:** That brings us to another common issue: high cholesterol.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1936, papers were published showing that if you measure the cholesterol at the time a person's thyroid gland is removed surgically, there is a steady, sharp increase in blood cholesterol over the next few weeks. When you put them on a thyroid supplement, the cholesterol returns to normal. If you chart the metabolic rate—oxygen consumption of the whole organism—it's a mirror image of the cholesterol. The metabolic rate falls as the cholesterol rises under the hypothyroid circumstance.

I've seen a couple of people who were in a hurry to get their cholesterol down hundreds of points. One had 400 milligrams percent, the other 500 and something. They wanted to have a good physical exam. They took the active T3 hormone in physiological amounts, roughly 5 micrograms per hour, and in a week they had restored their cholesterol to the normal range of around 200 milligrams percent.

**John Barkhausen:** Is it just that with a lower metabolism, you are not converting the cholesterol into the other steroids?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some cholesterol is converted to form bile acids, steroids that help to emulsify fats in the intestine. But the formation of DHEA, pregnenolone, and progesterone uses a massive amount of the circulating cholesterol. For example, an experimenter put the bloodstream into an isolated ovary and then measured the substances in the blood coming out. The amount of progesterone coming out corresponded directly to the amount of cholesterol going in. If your cholesterol level was lowered, the progesterone produced by the ovary was lowered.

**John Barkhausen:** So when they're worried about the cholesterol, it sounds like the cholesterol is just a sign that your metabolism isn't functioning well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And if you artificially lower the cholesterol, you tend to lower the adaptive hormones, especially progesterone. The early studies, I think the first big one was done in Hungary, showed that lowering cholesterol tremendously increased cancer mortality, total mortality, and increased the death rate from accidents, homicide, and even heart disease and strokes.

**John Barkhausen:** Let me just interrupt to clarify that you're talking about lowering cholesterol artificially through statins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like the cholesterol itself is protective.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since about 1920, they showed that just injecting pure cholesterol is protective against all the types of toxins they tested: bacterial toxins, mercury, plant toxins, and so on. It protects red blood cells from being broken down by mercury and enzyma toxins, spider and snake poisons.

**John Barkhausen:** And yet there is evidence that a high cholesterol rate is associated with disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's really just because you don't get a high excess cholesterol in the blood without being hypothyroid. You can correlate high cholesterol with things such as poor learning ability, but in experiments, if you inject cholesterol right into the brain, it improves learning ability and nerve function. It's the low thyroid, which is responsible for the high cholesterol, that accounts for the disease they associate with the high cholesterol.

**John Barkhausen:** So when they say strokes are caused by high cholesterol, it's actually that you're just hypothyroid and your metabolism isn't functioning.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And when you can't make the protective adaptive steroids such as progesterone and DHEA out of the cholesterol, your body does its next best adaptive procedure, which is to increase the cortisol. The chronic elevation of cortisol, which is associated with high cholesterol and low thyroid, is one of the toxic effects you see in people with high cholesterol. The chronic exposure to excess cortisol weakens blood vessels and promotes bleeding, but it also can promote clotting, osteoporosis, and various tissue degenerative processes.

**John Barkhausen:** But cortisol also has a positive purpose, doesn't it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It protects you. If you don't have enough pregnenolone, DHEA, and progesterone, you need cortisol to handle stress. But the way it handles stress is to depress inflammation. It does it at the expense of tissues such as your thymus gland, muscle, skin, and liver, converting protein to fuel to use for energy to combat the stress. It's spending your organism rapidly to get you through a crisis situation.

**John Barkhausen:** It's an emergency adaptation. That sounds like it makes you even more hypothyroid because you've explained before that when you start digesting your own muscle, that produces more antithyroid chemicals.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably. The cortisol directly signals the liver. In vitro experiments indicate that cortisol blocks the enzymes that convert thyroxine into the active T3 hormone. So it's doing many related things: increasing the circulating cysteine and tryptophan to suppress the gland itself and changing several levels of physiology.

**John Barkhausen:** You've said before that you think they've changed the way they judge people's thyroid functions. In the 1930s, what percentage of people did they think were hypothyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 40%, I think, by the end of the 30s.

**John Barkhausen:** That's a huge number. How did they decide what was normal and what wasn't?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They were measuring the ability to extract oxygen and burn calories. They saw that the lower a person's oxidative metabolism was, the more symptoms they had. They found that giving desiccated thyroid to increase their oxygen consumption alleviated the symptoms.

They had a large list of diagnostic symptoms: having yellow palms of the hands and soles of the feet from accumulated carotene; infertility, which they found was associated with red spots in the ovaries (the corpus luteum means "yellow body," but in hypothyroid people it was found to be a red body because it contains so much carotene). The carotene was blocking the conversion of cholesterol to progesterone because vitamin A is needed. Low thyroid people accumulate the carotene because they aren't using the vitamin A fast enough, and then they can't convert cholesterol to progesterone and become infertile.

Vitamin A is needed to antagonize estrogen in probably all cells, including the skin. So you could just look at a person's palms and very often diagnose hypothyroidism. Other signs included falling hair, thinning or thickening skin, sweating excessively or not at all. If a person had been chronically hypothyroid, their growth was usually either deficient or excessive. People who hadn't reached an average height were found to grow to a normal height when they took thyroid, and people with an excess of growth hormone were found to lower their symptoms of acromegaly if they took a thyroid supplement.

**John Barkhausen:** How would they explain that we went from 40% of the population being hypothyroid to the much lower level considered now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When they did that experiment on medical students and showed that the synthetic hormone supposedly worked just like the real stuff, that went with an advertising campaign. When I was in junior high and high school, all the fat kids were reciting what they had heard from their doctor: that they were just gluttonous and lazy and didn't have a hormone problem.

A blood test was circulated at that same time that measured Protein Bound Iodine (PBI). That test showed that 95% of the population were normal; only 5% had a low protein bound iodine content. Even though at least 40% of the people would have benefited according to the pre-war diagnostic methods, if they got anything, it was likely to be the inactive thyroxine rather than the real active hormone. Since people didn't benefit, that confirmed the idea that 95% of the people were not hypothyroid.

About 20 years later, the PBI test was found to have essentially nothing to do with thyroid function. But what it had accomplished was to teach doctors that only 5% at most would need a thyroid supplement. Over the years, new blood tests came out that actually measured the various thyroid substances, but they kept the doctrine that 95% of the people were not hypothyroid. Their "normal" definition made the new tests irrelevant.

**John Barkhausen:** So they adopted that foregone conclusion that a certain percentage were normal and based everything on that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the problems with the work up to the 1940s with thyroid was that everything from cancer and heart disease to dry skin and falling hair were known to be caused by hypothyroidism. That sort of ruined the medical business if you could cure practically everything with a thyroid supplement. So they said the belief in a panacea is irrational; we have to be scientific, and each disease is a separate thing that we have to study and treat with a specific remedy.

I just happened to run across an article published by a big medical publishing company, and the subtitle was something about "Panacea for the Next Millennium: Estrogen Receptor Modifier." If the industry supports a panacea, you can talk about it. But the fact that thyroid supplements had functioned as the equivalent of a panacea was used as propaganda against "irrational quacks" who wanted to cure everything with one pill.

**John Barkhausen:** If your thyroid isn't functioning, what happens to your cells when you don't have the energy to regenerate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When a cell is injured, that accelerates renewal and healing. One of the signals for starting accelerated renewal is the fact that the damaged cell doesn't respire properly and doesn't use its thyroid environment to good effect. It shifts over to the injury metabolism of glycolysis, producing lactic acid. Lactic acid stimulates the growth and invasion of blood vessels, the acceleration of cell division, and secretion of connective tissue collagen.

If the whole body doesn't have enough thyroid and other supportive hormones, the injury can develop into a tumor. But normally, if your thyroid is functioning properly, instead of having those locally accelerated regenerative processes, the whole body is renewing itself in a process of "tissue streaming" or "organ streaming."

Think of the cells as a fountain coming out of one part of the organ, growing and functioning, and then disappearing in another part. In the cornea of the eye, they've applied a dye and found that the cells literally stream over a period of days from the edge of the cornea up onto the cornea. In the liver, adrenal glands, skin, and intestine, people have demonstrated this constant renewal—streaming or flowing of new cells into the tissue and the disappearance of old cells.

Every tissue is undergoing that kind of renewal from stem cells. But even though the research was done—Alexis Carrel at Rockefeller Institute in the early years of the century, and then Polezhaev, a Russian researcher in the 40s and 50s, demonstrated regeneration even in the brain—that violated one of the main medical biological doctrines. The establishment was creating a particular business model of medicine that took over completely in the late 1940s. The idea of organ regeneration as a normal biological process was stamped out.

People thought of aging as a simple natural process in which each cell had its finite lifespan, and when that was used up, the organism would die. It's really the Leibniz monad doctrine that nothing interacts: every individual cell has its internal model of the universe running like a clock. That was the model that took over medicine after the Second World War.

**John Barkhausen:** You mentioned Hayflick last week as the person who did the experiment that ended up convincing most of science that you can't regenerate, only to a certain limit.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The fact that he worked at a very influential laboratory that sold biological material, cell cultures, and rats to laboratories all over the country helped to give him a reputation. People just assumed that an idiot wouldn't be working for a big company like that. For 30 years I thought he was just a very remarkably stupid person, but then I saw he had financial motives that might save his mental reputation.

**John Barkhausen:** It makes me wonder where the peer review process was when he came up with those results.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's pretty much where it always has been. I've been following the estrogen receptor doctrine for many years. The promoter of that, Elwood Jensen, was working in chemical warfare. He even titled one of his articles "From Chemical Warfare to Breast Cancer Treatment." In making that transition, he created the idea of the estrogen receptor.

Biologists had been demonstrating how estrogen is metabolized and integrated in cell physiology in meaningful ways relating to oxidation and reduction. But Jensen got funding and support from the Atomic Energy Commission because of his military connection. It was extremely expensive to create a molecule with radioactive isotopes, but the AEC provided the stuff. On the basis of his experiment, he claimed that estrogen is not oxidized in the tissue and only acts through this protein called the estrogen receptor.

Because of the prestige of his funding, he shaped the whole biological culture. The enzymologists that he said were ignorant, old-fashioned fools kept on working, and now everyone knows that they were right—estrogen is reduced and oxidized. But the culture served its purpose and created the whole industry of estrogen receptor selective modifiers.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think there's such a thing as a receptor as a place where things plug in?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The whole cell is a receptor. It's like a perceptual process because the state of the cell governs what the response is going to be. The cell is in charge. The receptor idea is a perfect model of reductionist biology that really has no sound scientific basis.

**John Barkhausen:** I just got a book out of the library called *The Secret History of the War on Cancer* by Devra Davis. She talks about working at the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) and how she had a theory that a lot of cancer was caused by environmental things. Her boss, Frank Press, told her, "It had better be a really, really good book... because you won't be able to work here after you write it."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wouldn't be surprised if the NSA was involved too. Following up Elwood Jensen's Atomic Energy Commission connections and germ warfare, I found that the estrogen receptor gene people have been involved in military-financed sterilization and cancer studies continuing through the University of Chicago and currently at the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory.

**John Barkhausen:** She also mentions that some of the first modern studies on workplace causes of cancer were carried out by scientists around 1936, including many who worked in Nazi Germany. She says in 1945, an army captain traveled throughout Germany gathering information on chemical and hormonal hazards for the US Army, but sixty years later, these files remain unpublished.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of American financing has gone into how to use that information as chemical-biological warfare. I think national security is the reason it has never benefited the public. It has extended into the virus theory and works against environmental causation of cancer. It's hard to separate ignorant results from deliberate propaganda results.

**John Barkhausen:** You even said in one of your newsletters that the engineering, genetic dogma school of science thought memory was a function of brain cells dying—like holes being punched in an IBM computer card. They were postulating that that is how you remember things.
