**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you look at the history of science from the wrong perspective, it looks like a big comedy that is so farcical it's hard to believe. But these are top-notch, mainline people with these stupid theories.

**John Barkhausen:** I suppose they're coming from a certain point of view. They've all been educated in universities and done very well there, so they are trying to work within those parameters. If you look at life as a machine that doesn't have any intelligence, then I suppose an IBM punch card is a good model.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It comes down to the culture that teaches us. It has been going on for 800 years or so in philosophy, teaching us that matter is stupid, inanimate, and has nothing to do with the guiding principle of spirit and life. It is an invention that came out of a particular culture sometime after the Renaissance. It is the doctrine of matter as a special "devilish" material that has none of the life or spirit properties; it is just this mortal, essentially dead material.

The gene doctrine came in on top of things like Descartes' doctrine of the mind running an inanimate machine. The idea that matter has its own tendencies and principles was submerged under a doctrine that matter is essentially stupid and can only follow randomness.

Mathematical randomness has to be invoked when matter is treated. This applies to the idea of nuclear fission; there is a mathematical oversight that governs the half-life of each type of substance. However, people who questioned that idea of matter have done experiments showing that even nuclear decay is context-sensitive.

For example, I think it was 1971 when an experimenter used radioactive carbon in an oil form and found that the decay rate was non-random when it was made into a monolayer on a metal surface. That violated the whole doctrine of inert matter following mathematical rules of randomness, so no one paid attention to it.

Lots of physical experiments violate the rules, and people ignore them the way the genetics people ignored regeneration research or cancer cures. It was only the genetic engineers and the cloning researchers that finally opened up some space in the culture. The genetic engineers didn't want it to happen, but giving Barbara McClintock recognition and finally accepting that Dolly really had been cloned forced the issue. For 50 years, they had been denying the possibility of cloning, even when people were doing it with frogs.

The culture is being opened up by their own wrong thinking. It has led them into a corner where they are forced to recognize that something like a field is sometimes involved in biology.

title: Politics & Science: Ionizing Radiation in Context Part 1
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Good afternoon everyone, and welcome to another edition of Politics and Science. Today kicks off a new series about radiation. We'll be discussing nuclear ionizing radiation, focusing on its use in our culture and weighing its potential usefulness in relation to its costs to our health and environment. I'm very happy to have on the show again Dr. Raymond Peat, an endocrinologist, physiologist, and science historian from Eugene, Oregon. You can find more information about Ray Peat on his website, raypeat.com. Ray, welcome back.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, excellent.

**John Barkhausen:** I know you have quite a bit to say about radiation. It’s a confusing subject because often when people talk about radiation—say at the dentist or the doctor's office—they try to make you feel safe about using it. They compare it to other kinds of radiation, like sunlight. They say a bone scan is no more than two days in the sun, or they compare it to a flight from Denver to New York regarding cosmic radiation. Could you address the different kinds of radiation that exist and how they compare?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The medical profession, the government, and the nuclear industry made up a lot of stories to convince people that radiation doesn't hurt them. Sunlight is probably the basic, oldest story: if it doesn't kill you to absorb so much energy of sunlight, why should it kill you to absorb the equivalent of an hour in the form of radiation?

They have known for close to 200 years that there are very different kinds of radiation. In 1800, they knew that the invisible light beyond the blue end of the spectrum was chemically active. They called them "chemical rays" because they could produce changes in silver nitrate and photographic emulsions. They knew the warm rays and colored visible rays were harmless compared to these chemical burning rays which can sunburn you.

At the end of the 19th century, when the Curies and Becquerel were exploring radium, Becquerel carried a vial of it in his pocket and got a horrible burn on his chest. The medical profession immediately saw that as something even more fun than surgery and cautery. When they saw it caused a horrible burn, they decided it was good for medical purposes, like burning off warts.

However, by 1904, Thomas Edison’s main assistant died of X-ray poisoning after years of amputations and burns. So by 1904, Thomas Edison was already an opponent of the use of ionizing radiation in any form. But the medical profession was just starting to see that it was a profitable tool. To sell it, they had a hundred years to invent stories to convince people that they wouldn't get lethal burns. They invented the story that there was a threshold below which no damage at all was done.

**John Barkhausen:** And the government expanded on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, when they wanted to show that they could explode atomic bombs in Nevada and no one would be harmed. Forty years later, Congress investigated and concluded that about 15,000 people minimum in the United States alone were killed as a result of those atmospheric tests. But the government had its agents out convincing people that below the threshold there was no harm at all.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even Linus Pauling, who opposed exposing the population to radiation, was convinced that it was worse to live in Denver than at sea level because cosmic rays and sunlight were supposedly more intense. However, the facts showed that cancer of all kinds is less common the higher you go in altitude.

Someone as sophisticated as Linus Pauling neglected the property of radiation called **Linear Energy Transfer (LET)**. It happens that cosmic rays at high altitude don't deliver much energy or damage to your tissues. But at lower altitudes, where they are less intense, they are more able to react with your tissues and cause damage. So the cosmic rays are harmful, but when you are in a skyscraper, for example, it's even worse than being at a low altitude because the cosmic rays are slowed down and produce secondary and tertiary particles. You get much more intense radiation at low altitude, sheltered by massive structure.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe we should back up just a little bit. Why is that the case? It seems like at lower altitudes, if they are going slower, that implies less energy to me. Why does that cause more damage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Ordinary photon radiation—infrared, visible light, ultraviolet—is an electromagnetic vibration. Nuclear particles are actual protons, nuclei, or whole atoms minus the electrons. Cosmic rays are typically iron atoms without their electrons. They are very massive particles going at a very high speed. They pass through the body without doing anything except leaving a trail of ionization.

If you use a cloud chamber—humid air adjusted so it is just about to condense into rain—the particles going through it ionize the air and cause nucleation. A streamer of fog appears. Cosmic rays are constantly going through, so you can visualize them. At lower energies, they will even stop in your tissue rather than passing through.

Linear accelerators put this to use; they can adjust the voltage of protons and shoot them into your body at a given energy, designing it so they slow down and stop near a tumor. Where they slow down and stop, they cause the most damage. When they go through quickly, like a cosmic ray at high altitude, they just leave a slight trail of ionization rather than a very intense cloud of secondary reactions.

**John Barkhausen:** So the cosmic rays are worse in a skyscraper because they're being slowed down by hitting the walls?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They cause nuclei to disintegrate into secondary particles, and those particles cause other disintegrations into tertiary particles. It's like a more intense shower of lower energy, but still lethal, particles.

The Chinese did experiments with rabbits, putting them in cages with lead roofs of different thicknesses. Around half an inch to an inch of lead caused the rabbits to fairly quickly become sterile and miscarry. If they were pregnant when put under the roof, they would miscarry just like you were giving them a birth control pill. If you kept them under it, they didn't conceive at all.

**John Barkhausen:** Why was that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Radiation poisoning from tertiary or secondary cosmic rays.

**John Barkhausen:** So the cosmic rays are getting through the lead, which I assumed would block them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** At a certain thickness, you maximize the tertiary and secondary particles. There's a certain probability as the lead gets thicker that one of the rays will have a direct hit on the nucleus and cause it to split into more particles.

**John Barkhausen:** And it's making them sterile because it's adding stress?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With a shorter dose, the litter would simply be reduced in weight, some animals would be dead, and others would survive. Even though that was particles, when the lead nuclei split, you get some gamma rays and X-rays produced as well.

A study of dentistry in Seattle looked at a large population of people getting different types of dental work. They used lead shields to cover the body so only the face was getting the X-ray. But when they looked at the results, a pregnant woman who got a full set of oral X-rays could expect to have a lighter birth weight baby as a result of the systemic poisoning produced by X-raying just her head.

**John Barkhausen:** That makes cosmic rays and X-rays sound somewhat equivalent biologically.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In biological effect, yes. They are equivalent to poisoning and stress. In my dissertation work, I looked through the biological effects of different kinds of radiation and found that I couldn't distinguish the biological damage caused by overdosing estrogen from the radiation poisoning effects. It's a very general type of biological damage.

Many biologists thought radiation caused the pituitary gland to make the ovaries overproduce estrogen because the radiation was so identical to estrogen poisoning. But people did control experiments; they irradiated just the head, and the whole animal would show an estrogen effect. Others X-rayed only a foot or an arm, and still the whole body went into an estrogenic state, showing that it's a toxin produced by any tissue interacting with the radiation.

**John Barkhausen:** So you don't have to target an area; it affects the whole animal.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it spreads through the bloodstream and probably in other ways.

**John Barkhausen:** X-rays are widely used medically—dental X-rays, CAT scans, bone scans. Doctors say they're invaluable. Besides the estrogenic effect, what else do they do to your tissues?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The estrogenic effect is just part of a general type of tissue excitation that involves chronic inflammation. Depending on the dose and time, that leads to tissue atrophy and fibrosis. The atrophy and fibrosis are what predispose you eventually to cancerization.

At first, the U.S. government sponsored interpretations of the atomic bomb radiation in Japan. They drew circles around the bomb and looked at people at one mile, ten miles, and so on. But the radiation went with the wind. When they took the people who really got the radiation in one part of the radius and averaged it out with the people at the same distance but in totally different directions, they made the radiation damage disappear.

When people more honestly looked at the data, they found that 20 years later, people who had been exposed as babies or fetuses had brains much smaller than normal. This is the same effect seen in the Chinese rabbit studies.

**John Barkhausen:** And with the women in the dental study?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they actually measured their heads, and the whole head was smaller if they were exposed *in utero*. That amount of radiation was being used medically for a long time in the U.S. Alice Stewart showed that it was causing more leukemia and other childhood cancers, but no one has traced brain damage to medical X-rays yet, even though it has been established in other countries.

**John Barkhausen:** You spoke of nuclear atmospheric tests. X-rays are waves, but I imagine anything carried by the wind is a radioactive particle.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and those particles get ingested. It isn't that they radiate at you from the dust outside, but they get in your food, water, and air. They enter your body as a food atom. Then they follow the course of nuclear decay inside your tissues.

If a particle emits an alpha particle (a helium nucleus) right inside the cell, it causes total damage and is absorbed within just a few cell diameters. The nuclear industry used to say, "Why worry about alpha particles?" They would show that a sheet of paper stops the beam between an emitter and a detector. But the difference is, when you have ingested the particle, there is no paper between the particle and the cell that gets poisoned.

**John Barkhausen:** So every time a nuclear facility has a leak, particles are being emitted?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And people breathe them in. Just two or three years ago, someone compared the blood serum of Japanese atomic bomb survivors. They demonstrated lingering photochemical emission differences in their blood serum 60 years after the exposure.

**John Barkhausen:** It lingers that long? Are there still radioactive particles in them?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, it's unstable biochemical material. It spreads the influence and persists unless something intervenes to correct the process.

This is something that has come up in the last 10 years: the **bystander effect**. If you irradiate cells in a dish to produce mutations and then put those cells with unexposed cells in another dish, those unexposed cells keep mutating long after, due to something emitted by the irradiated cells. If you irradiate fish, they will emit toxic materials into the water that cause biochemical disturbances in other fish.

The genetic instability is the most horrifying part. It is transmitted as a signal from the injured cell, which then injures the receiving cells. That transmitted effect destabilizes the chromosomes generations later. In the lab, it can be passed through many generations of cells as a tendency to mutate.

**John Barkhausen:** There was a study in Germany showing a higher leukemia rate among children around nuclear power plants. Why are young living things more susceptible?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The "genetics dogma" was used by physics dogma to say that if it didn't mutate your DNA, it didn't cause damage. But the bystander effect is produced by doses in the micro-gray region—a millionth of a gray—whereas they used to call 50 gray the toxic dose.

The developing organism is never simply a genetic blueprint being read out. Doctors used to say that as long as a mother ate enough to live, the baby wouldn't be affected by her poverty. That was based on the doctrine that genes determine everything. But in fact, even the formation of the ovum is environmentally determined by the mother's physiology. Once the fertilized egg starts developing, it is modified at every stage by its environment.

If estrogen is introduced during pregnancy—even a small dose—it changes the environment. For example, the cortex of the brain is thinner in proportion to estrogen exposure. The radiation exposure caused the whole brain to be smaller, but a seemingly insignificant imbalance towards estrogen causes the cortex to be thinner than normal. Because the young organism is in a developmental state, if you introduce inflammation and stress, there will be more deviation from its ideal possibilities.

**John Barkhausen:** So it sounds like it's a good idea to avoid any kind of radiation exposure, including dental X-rays.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. But even the time of day can influence your ability to tolerate stresses. If you go for a jog before breakfast, your chromosomes are going to be more susceptible to breakage than if you had some juice first. Low blood sugar makes your chromosomes break more easily. Having your radiation injury in the late afternoon, you're going to have much less risk of damage.

**John Barkhausen:** What about the efficacy of using medical radiation for diagnosis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One article published in JAMA about 10 years ago criticized the use of bone scans. They showed they were thrown off by any consistent change in the ratio of fat and water. Fat doesn't absorb X-rays as much as water does. If you reduce the fat in your bone marrow—which is normally fat-rich—and exchange it for water (which estrogen can do), you seem to have more dense bones. So, especially for measuring the effects of estrogen, X-ray bone scans are simply not scientific.

There are ultrasound bone measuring devices that determine the strength of the bone from the elastic sound transmission. It measures bone quality, not just density. Incidentally, each ultrasound treatment is likely to make your bones stronger because it stimulates healing, whereas each X-ray exposure increases stress and makes bones weaker.

**John Barkhausen:** What about CAT scans? *Newsweek* was cautionary about people having too many.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One is too many. It's a lot of radiation—the equivalent of many, many chest X-rays.

**John Barkhausen:** Is there any time when you think an X-ray would be a useful tool?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, because the other technologies are better. Magnetic resonance (MRI) and ultrasound. The technology is there, and it would be improved if people would start using it more. But they are invested in their present machines.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you say a few words about John Gofman?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was aware of him from the 1940s on as one of the main government "devils." For 30 years, he said how wonderful X-rays were and that they weren't known to be harmful. He claimed you couldn't prove bomb tests would kill people. He called people like Linus Pauling irresponsible fear mongers.

Around 1968, in the middle of a speech where he was saying it hadn't been proved that bomb tests would result in death and disease, he suddenly realized what he was saying. He said he realized he was stupid or crazy to be saying such stuff. Once he did, he became the government's greatest enemy. His last big book demonstrated that breast cancer and heart disease in the United States are caused mainly by medical X-rays.

**John Barkhausen:** That's very similar to what Samuel Epstein says about mammography.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. There was a study in Scandinavia a few years ago that showed total mortality was higher in women who got breast scans.

**John Barkhausen:** I recently heard of a metal pellet being planted during a biopsy without the patient's knowledge to mark the spot. How does that strike you?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's not an abnormal medical technique. Did you hear the NPR program broadcasting Columbia Medical School's "blessing of the white coat" ceremony? They bless the white coats and have students put them on like they're getting a diploma. It's an attitude that physicians are sanctified by their profession, so they feel they can't do any harm if they are sincerely being physicians. What I hear are mostly horror stories—women told they are having exploratory surgery and then their ovaries are removed.

**John Barkhausen:** One thing they are using ionizing radiation for now is irradiated food. They irradiate meat and fruit. What is your opinion on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It almost instantly spoils it to some extent, but it stops other enzyme and bacterial changes. It kills enough microorganisms to stop some rotting, but it also stops the natural defense processes. Apples will instantly turn color and get soft and sour.

It activates aging processes in meat; proteins are degraded into toxic compounds, and fats are made rancid. Every component is affected in proportion to its oxidizability. When they feed these processed foods to experimental animals, the animals show effects of poisoning and malnutrition. Vitamin B2, folic acid, and Vitamin A are almost totally destroyed.

At the same time, the destruction converts them into toxic reactive compounds. You can test food to show if it has been irradiated using the same tests that show lingering radiation damage in people: photochemical luminescence. The breakdown of fats causes photoluminescence. If it was an animal—oysters, chickens, fish—the bones capture the excited electrons. If you dissolve the bone in a light-detecting device, irradiated foods will luminesce.

**John Barkhausen:** Is oxidation just a side effect, or is that what's really going on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** To the extent that there is something present to receive the excited electrons, they will react, and you will have oxidation happening. Even ultraviolet light can cause processes like that. If you get too much UV from the sun, the Vitamin B2 in your skin can get into an excited state. If you have eaten a lot of polyunsaturated fats, the excited Vitamin B2 can extract electrons from the exposed double bonds on the fats, create breakage, and spread an oxidizing process that attacks DNA.

**John Barkhausen:** So that's how you get skin cancer from ultraviolet?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The wrinkles and cancerization process from sunlight highly correspond to the amount of polyunsaturated fat in your diet.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a few minutes left. What can people do if they have to go to the dentist and get an X-ray? How can they protect themselves?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first thing is to really reconsider why you need it. Dentists often think their insurance requires the X-ray record. Endodontists say you can't do a root canal without one, but I have talked to some who were proud they didn't need X-rays. It's a matter of skill and judgment.

If you are determined to get an X-ray:
1.  **Timing:** Try to schedule it in the late afternoon in the summer.
2.  **Blood Sugar:** Have your blood sugar steady and high enough. Have some gelatinous soup, orange juice, and milk ahead of time.
3.  **Hormones:** Make sure your hormonal situation is adequate; you don't want estrogen effects interacting with radiation effects. Progesterone treatment has been found to protect against X-ray damage to some tissues. Thyroid is probably the most protective single thing.
4.  **Magnesium:** You need steady blood sugar to keep magnesium in your cells. Have magnesium-rich food before and after.
5.  **Coffee:** Coffee is protective against all kinds of radiation. The caffeine is the main factor, but coffee is also a good source of magnesium and niacin.
6.  **Supplements:** Niacinamide is a general tissue protector against stress. The antioxidants Vitamin E, Vitamin K, and ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q10) are also protective.

**John Barkhausen:** Thank you very much, Dr. Peat, for coming on again and for your work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, very good. Bye.

title: Politics & Science: Ionizing Radiation in Context Part 2
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Today is the second in a series looking at the uses and abuses of radiation in our culture, with a particular focus on ionizing radiation—that is, nuclear technology. I'm very pleased to have Dr. Raymond Peat, endocrinologist, physiologist, and science historian from Eugene, Oregon, on the show. His website is raypeat.com.

**John Barkhausen:** Last week we talked about some of the systemic and long-term cumulative effects of X-rays and other types of radiation. We also discussed radiation from power plants. Many times, our medical establishment compares it to less harmful things like sunlight. You discussed that and pointed out that it's like comparing apples and oranges.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The key idea is linear energy transfer: how much of the energy actually gets into your tissue and interacts with it.

**John Barkhausen:** I see. And the ionizing radiation has far more energy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Some of it, like the isotopes that get into the air and food, release particles that have an extremely high energy transfer. Those are the worst. Others penetrate deeply and do damage along the way. But the intensity of the radiation isn't the main thing; it's how much they interact with your tissue and in what ways.

**John Barkhausen:** Could you give us a summary of how radioactive technology crept into our culture?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Almost immediately when the Curies discovered how deadly poisonous radium and related isotopes were, the medical profession became very interested. It was a fancier way to destroy tissue instead of just poisons, surgery, cautery, and acid. They had a new technique that seemed technological and impressive. It very quickly went from treating warts and tumors to all kinds of bizarre quackery.

I knew people when I was in college whose facial bones were collapsing because they had X-ray treatment for acne, or whose hair had fallen out because they were treated for ringworm with X-rays. Total ignorance and arrogance combined to use whatever turned up.

**John Barkhausen:** And who was treating them? Just regular general practitioners?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. When I was a kid, shoe stores still had X-ray machines so anyone could look at their feet bones to see if the shoes fit. It was just a technological gadget that entertained people. Regular doctors had fluoroscopes that would let you watch a person breathe, watch their heart move, and watch their stomach and intestines. They were pumping nearly lethal doses of radiation into people, just standing there talking and watching for entertainment. Some of those things were putting out 50 to 100 rads in even a short treatment. If they had come in for a weekly exam, they would have soon been dead.

**John Barkhausen:** Just to compare that to a normal exposure from a chest X-ray, how much is that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I guess approaching a thousand times more. In the last few years, I've talked to people who had a combination of heart treatments where they put a tube or a wire up into the heart to open a clogged artery, using a fluoroscope to watch where it's going. These people get a tremendous amount of exposure. It's cumulative and can cause brain degenerative diseases. The heart surgeons who do that kind of work have a high incidence of brain cancer, so they are advised to wear a lead cap.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The various types of physicians who work with radiation—radiologists and heart surgeons especially—have a higher rate of female children. That's the same as electricians who work around high-voltage power lines and the birds that nest near the high-tension lines. It doesn't have to be ionizing to have really major biological effects.

**John Barkhausen:** Why is it that they produce female children instead of male children?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Apparently, the male fertilized ovum, embryo, and fetus are weaker at all stages; the female has better resistance in general. Partly it's because all these types of radiation imitate estrogen in their biological actions, and estrogen tends to bias the sex ratio of the offspring.

**John Barkhausen:** In the 40s, did doctors have any idea of the danger of X-rays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Doctors generally only know what they're told is good practice. The information was available—chiropractors and borderline people in the medical profession had pamphlets in their offices in the 1940s giving references to the research literature showing that radiation accelerates the aging process. Meanwhile, real doctors were exposing their patients to doses that would not only accelerate aging but tremendously increase cancer mortality. Leukemia was extremely high in that period, not only from radioactive fallout from atmospheric bomb tests but from the medical X-rays of pregnant women and fluoroscoping of general patients.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like our culture was basically in love with modern technological gadgets.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just the same as it is now. Now, 60 years later, some of the best research is showing that radiation causes the formation of amyloid, the type of substance that is incriminated in Alzheimer's disease and degenerative lung, kidney, and pancreatic diseases.

**John Barkhausen:** Amyloid is a plaque?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's a type of protein that forms plaques. Normally, the very common structure of a protein involves helix structures—a spiral piece of a chain of protein. With a certain disturbance, those spirals can break down and fold over against themselves, making a sheet arrangement called a pleated sheet. Those sheets can stick to a similar sheet structure in another protein. This array of pleated sheets forms a long fibrillation, and those fibrils condense into the visible plaques called amyloid.

**John Barkhausen:** And that's a common symptom in Alzheimer's patients.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and it turns up in practically all aged tissues. It's accelerated by radiation, toxins, estrogen, and even microwaves and ultrasound.

**John Barkhausen:** We were talking to Professor Gilbert Ling a few weeks ago, and he was discussing the electrical nature of living tissue—how all the proteins and the water within a cell are in an electrical relationship.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's exactly where the problem is with all kinds of radiation and even toxins. The romantic classical physics people, who wanted to think mathematically about radiation, assured people that there was a threshold below which radiation wasn't harmful. This kind of thinking claimed that a unit of radio energy had to be sufficient to break a chain of DNA before anything happened biologically. That takes a direct hit and high energy.

But before the ionizing radiation actually has a direct hit and breaks a DNA chain, it's doing many much more subtle things, causing fluctuations in the electronic system of proteins and causing subtle changes in the way water relates to those proteins. If the medical world and physics had been paying closer attention to Gilbert Ling's work 50 years ago, most of these questions would have been settled in a very different way, with much more concern for protection than for promotion of industry.

**John Barkhausen:** So you feel the marketing side of our culture determined its medical course.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The people with an X-ray machine to sell will tell doctors that the dose is below the threshold. But these little sub-threshold doses actually modify the water structure, which directs the way the tissue develops and affects things like the immune system and the way nerves pattern themselves. In a young individual, that deviation can produce drastic and fatal effects very quickly. In mature people, it accelerates aging and degeneration.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People were already beginning to understand it in the 1930s. Thomas Edison became a great opponent of the medical use of X-rays. But the government, the nuclear industry, and the medical instrument corporations convinced the public that those researchers were unrealistic quacks.

Albert Szent-Györgyi was one of the people working on the subtle but essential biological interactions of electrons, water, and light. For 20 or 30 years, he was totally sidelined, even though he'd won the Nobel Prize. People who criticize industry become the victims of corporate government campaigns. The big nuclear corporations used to have weekly seminars to tell their staff that radiation was actually good for them. They would smear people who presented evidence of toxic effects, like Ernest Sternglass and Alice Stewart. Stewart showed that medical X-rays were probably the main cause of childhood cancer, but she was ridiculed.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think this mindset was connected to the military use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Once they started doing atmospheric tests, the military joined up with the X-ray industry. They had massive campaigns to tell the public that fallout was good for you. Campaigns were mounted using right-wing organizations like the John Birch Society to create scandals around professors who criticized the testing, getting them fired. The U.S. Public Health Service was a major player in that campaign to incriminate critics and hide evidence.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like the Cold War is when it really got bad regarding universities and public health services.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was no line between physics and biology. People with a biological orientation like Szent-Györgyi and Gilbert Ling were called quacks. The idea of acquired damage other than a random mutation was identified as a "Lysenko Soviet doctrine," so you had to be a certain kind of genetic dogmatist to teach biology in the United States after 1950.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A good place to get insight into how the system works is to start with German romantic physics in the 19th century. They wanted to subjectify physics and make it part of a spiritual quest for unity. Facts got in the way. That's where the Heisenberg principle came in—that you can't know things on the fine level; it's all ultimately random. It's a victory of subjective idealism over empirical science.

**John Barkhausen:** In terms of selling nuclear technology, it seems like Einstein's popularity played a big role.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That only becomes dangerous when they start saying that energy and information are the same, and that knowing and matter are the same. Einstein had an interesting exchange with Max Born about whether the field of a particle is part of the substance of the particle. Einstein's position was that the field should count as matter. But when you invoke the quantum ideas, you throw out matter and substitute mind and information.

**John Barkhausen:** So when you say the field is part of matter, that means the matter is part of its environment?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The whole world, including our knowledge of the world, is part of the same substantial stuff. For example, there are people who have demonstrated luminescence in the visual center of the brain; when we see a colored light, we actually light up with that color inside. You can think of our consciousness as a physical resonance. But the people who talk about information being transmitted along nerves as a simple on/off switch reduce knowledge to something mathematical.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think that scientific attitude of quantum physics is used to say that even though radiation is there, we can't really *know* it causes harm? It seems to take away liability.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For decades, John Gofman went around working for the government saying that we can't know that this is causing damage. The idea was that you shouldn't act on anything you haven't tested empirically. Now, people are talking about a precautionary principle—that you should think about what harm might happen in the future, even if it hasn't been tested in the conventional scientific way.

**John Barkhausen:** It also sounds like quantum physics is a very good physics for an authoritarian culture.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you've ever listened to physics professors, you realize the whole culture has that authoritarian, textbook quality. They don't know anything if it isn't in the textbooks. And if you read the professional science textbooks, it's as interesting as reading novels. You can see the mind of the creator at work sorting out the things to be emphasized. They are almost always wrong in the textbooks.

**John Barkhausen:** One of the arguments for bringing back nuclear power is that we should do what the French do: recycle spent fuel rods.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There's a website called "Environmental Devastation Caused by Reprocessing Radioactive Waste." They mention that the French plant has annually discharged 100 million gallons of radioactive waste into the English Channel by way of an underwater pipeline. The industry and military also used to dump hundreds of thousands of barrels of radioactive waste into the ocean. Those barrels are leaking. The food chain from the English Channel has already drifted up to the Arctic and over to Canada.

**John Barkhausen:** The waste that's coming out of the pipes from reprocessing, is it contaminated water or particles?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Particles. Huge amounts of uranium, plutonium, and strontium-90 are getting into the water, and the fish are taking it up.

**John Barkhausen:** That's really discouraging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The United States has two very contaminated areas: the Hanford plant in Washington and the dump in South Carolina. A nearby town found their well water was contaminated with uranium. I saw a huge truck coming up behind me in Northern California going about 90 miles an hour with a giant cylindrical tub on the back labeled "Greenville, South Carolina." The people who transport these giant vats of waste aren't the safest drivers.

**John Barkhausen:** What about incineration of medical waste?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In general, they don't worry much about it. When they put radioactive iodine into a person, they don't worry about the person's urine. When bodies are incinerated, that goes into the air. If they die with radium needles in their organs, or just mercury in teeth, it gets vaporized.

**John Barkhausen:** You talked about Alzheimer's being caused by nuclear waste or ionizing radiation. Does that correspond with sites near power plants?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No one is very clear about that, but I think it will turn out that it does. Cataracts are another interesting thing. They are easy to study because the cataract is a different state of living matter, probably analogous to what happens in Alzheimer's disease.

It turns out that in a cataract, the proteins aren't even denatured. The cataract is chemically almost identical to the surrounding tissue, but it has a slightly higher water content. All that happens is a slight fluctuation in the electronic state of the protein, which lets the water get out of control.

This shows how energy—not even thermal energy in the ordinary sense, but the vibrational state of water molecules—can make the difference between a lens that works and one that's opaque. Similar changes probably happen very early in cancer or Alzheimer's, long before you get the deposition of amyloid.

**John Barkhausen:** So the radiation is changing the structure in subtle ways long before visible damage.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If microwaves and ultraviolet light can do it, then relatively weak transmissions like a dental X-ray don't even have to ionize anything. All they have to do is add enough energy to cause this semi-thermal fluctuation of electrons and water vibrations.

**John Barkhausen:** Are there things people can do to fortify themselves if they have to be exposed to X-rays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keep your energy at a peak. Getting the damage done in the late afternoon in the summer is best. Keep your carbon dioxide up with adequate thyroid function, progesterone, pregnenolone, and testosterone. Magnesium is the best-established radiation-protective nutrient. Coffee happens to protect against all kinds of radiation damage because it provides magnesium and niacinamide, as well as protective caffeine and antioxidants.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, thanks again for being here and for all your work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Goodbye.

title: [RELEASED 2019] Politics & Science: Digestion
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Welcome to Politics and Science. I'm your host, John Barkhausen. This week we continue with another archive interview recorded on April 26, 2010, with Dr. Raymond Peat. He is a physiologist living in Eugene, Oregon, who has been studying health and the history of science for his entire life. Today’s interview concerns human digestion: how it works, how it affects us, and the psychological and physical repercussions of good and healthy digestion.

Dr. Raymond Peat has a Ph.D. in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. He has taught at colleges including the University of Oregon, Urbana College, Montana State University, National College of Naturopathic Medicine, Universidad Veracruzana, the Universidad Autónoma del Estado de México, and Blake College. In addition to his science research bimonthly newsletter and other writings—some of which are available at raypeat.com—he conducts private nutritional counseling. Ray, welcome back.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, hello.

**John Barkhausen:** I'm basing our discussion today on one of your recent newsletters from January 2010 entitled "Cascara, Energy, Cancer and the FDA's Laxative Abuse." I thought I'd use it as a takeoff point to talk about digestion in general. There isn't much coverage of that in the media, yet it's something we all have to do. Perhaps you could start off by defining what you consider to be digestion in a healthy organism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everything should work smoothly. The food should be appetizing so that it stimulates the whole system. Pavlov was one of the pioneers in studying digestion scientifically. He showed that the knowledge of the food and the sensory quality of the food completely dominates the digestive process. Recent experiments show that the taste of food will even affect your blood sugar. If you eat something sweet, it will raise your blood sugar even if your throat is cut—it's a nervous connection that tells you that you are ready to start using food. Even if the food doesn't get into your blood, the taste of it will start raising your blood sugar.

Pavlov isn't widely studied anymore. There continue to be some digestive experiments, but now they are mostly done by the pharmaceutical industry. However, there is a long scientific history of digestive processes, mostly on animals and a few on people. Walter C. Alvarez was a famous gastroenterologist who had a newspaper column in the 1940s and 50s, and he helped get some scientific information into the general culture regarding digestion.

**John Barkhausen:** When was Alvarez doing his scientific work?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He did much of his scientific work in the 20s and 30s, but became a popular columnist later. After his time, most good research was done on animals related to agriculture, but some of it provided basic knowledge of how the intestine and digestive organs work. For example, they would isolate a loop of intestine to measure the blood going in and out, put certain foods in that little piece of intestine, and watch what happened.

They found that the more complex the food in the intestine, the more vigorously the digestive process worked. That one kind of experiment shoots down a whole bunch of dogma regarding food mixing or eating things in certain combinations. The most complex mixture seems to be the one that digests the most efficiently.

Pre-digestion has been advocated for foods like proteins, but in one experiment, digestive enzymes were stirred with acid and some protein. Just stirring it at body temperature didn't do much digestion. But when they added a piece of the intestine that had been washed, sterilized, and fixed—so it was basically just a structural framework—suddenly the protein digestion went full speed. It isn't just the enzymes in the liquid that digest the proteins into amino acids; the protein has to be in a certain configuration, held in place by the "surface fuzz" of the intestine, before the enzymes can efficiently work on it. Since it is digested in contact with the cells, the amino acids are absorbed immediately as they are liberated from the protein.

After the age of one, a person's digestive system doesn't do very well with free amino acids compared to the whole protein. Basically, food in the close-to-living state—complex and structurally more or less just mixed by chewing—is all it needs in preparation.

Something a lot of people don't think about is that humans don't have the enzymes for digesting a lot of plant materials, such as cellulose, lignin, and other structural materials. If we simply chew vegetables, unless we chew each bite for half an hour, a lot of the material is still going to be trapped in the indigestible framework. Bacteria in the intestine can then get at it. You are supporting bacterial growth when you eat most vegetable material, depending on how fibrous it is.

**John Barkhausen:** They are always recommending we eat fiber, so that could be a problem. Before we get into solutions, maybe you can cover the basic problems, causes, and stages of digestive dysfunction. I know a lot of people who are stressed out and have trouble digesting when stress is high.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Nervous tension will make things slow down. Adrenaline will make your intestine stop moving. It's an adaptive thing, so the fight-or-flight reaction isn't interrupted by intestinal activity. High adrenaline will not only shut down the movement of the intestine and the secretion of digestive fluids, but it even reduces the circulation to the intestine. If it is too intense or prolonged, shutting off the blood supply can actually cause some of the intestine to die. Short of that, prolonged stress makes the intestinal wall become a poor barrier, so that more toxins leak through.

**John Barkhausen:** I see.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Some types of hormonal disturbances will increase the activity of the parasympathetic nervous system—the opposite of the adrenaline side—and that often goes with high histamine release. When histamine is released, serotonin is often excessive too. For example, in low-thyroid people, there is often an excess of all the transmitter substances. Sometimes it goes in the direction of serotonin, adrenaline, and histamine all exciting the muscles of the intestine, causing it to contract and even go into spasm. Sometimes the spasms will shut off function, but more often, overactivity of that side will produce diarrhea.

**John Barkhausen:** As our digestion gets out of balance, it tends towards constipation or diarrhea. Is one worse than the other?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In constipation, if it's associated with high adrenaline, it tends to cause prolonged absorption of bacterial endotoxin. In an acute case of diarrhea, things are washed through so fast that it often reduces the absorption of toxins. As a rough generality, occasional diarrhea is probably somewhat therapeutic. However, chronic constipation has been known for thousands of years to be associated with cancer and other diseases. Just recently, I've been seeing cases of people with chronic constipation having strokes, aneurysms, and abnormal clotting. Stroke hemorrhages are now known to be promoted by endotoxin and inflammatory responses to the endotoxin.

**John Barkhausen:** I know you've written about endotoxin quite a bit, but I've talked to other medical people who have never heard of it. How does that occur?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you feed the bacteria, you can grow a culture of bacteria that are especially harmful. If you are under stress, your intestine lets too much of that into your bloodstream. If you don't feed your liver and keep it well-energized with the right amount of thyroid hormone and a good vitamin, mineral, and protein supply, your liver won't be able to detoxify the endotoxin that reaches it.

A little bit of endotoxin leaking in all the time keeps us in an immunologically toned-up state—it can be like exercise. But if your liver is letting too much through, it gets you into a chronic state of inflammation. In people injured in serious accidents, often all their major organs—kidneys, lungs, liver—will suffer and lose function. Endotoxin is the main thing involved in that multiple organ failure.

In a chronic process, these same inflammatory reactions to endotoxin produce degenerative changes in the blood vessels and brain, and promote tumor formation. In the last five or ten years, this has become one of the biggest areas of medical research. There is a tremendous new understanding of endotoxin's role in degenerative diseases. Coinciding with this, the FDA has outlawed all of the traditional laxatives.

**John Barkhausen:** Before we move on to the FDA, so endotoxin is from bacteria that is always with us, but we usually keep it under control?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. With aging or stress, our liver is less able to detoxify it. Low thyroid function is one of the things that makes the liver very weak at detoxifying. Estrogen is always there too, especially in women. After puberty, the liver tends to slow down under the influence of estrogen, which lets estrogen increasingly interact harmfully with other systems. You get very similar effects from overexposure to endotoxin or to estrogen. They both activate blood vessel leakiness and inflammation leading to degenerative diseases.

**John Barkhausen:** What is inflammation in the digestive system, and how does it affect us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first thing that happens with endotoxin or estrogen is the production of too much nitric oxide. One way that makes capillaries leak is by making them take up too much water. The nitric oxide poisons the mitochondria so they can't produce energy very fast. As energy production goes down, the cell simply swells up and gets looser in structure as it fills with water. This increases leakiness and lets more toxin get through.

As this proceeds, the wall of the intestine and the blood vessels get thicker, cutting off the delivery of oxygen. As the oxygen supply goes down, the cells produce lactic acid, which triggers more inflammatory substances. The wall of the intestine takes up more and more water through all layers—muscle, connective tissue, blood vessels—until, in an extreme state, the intestine becomes so thick there is no space left for the movement of food. Many people have seen X-rays after a barium meal where there are big wads of opaque material and other areas with none at all, or just a little thread. That is often caused by the intestine swelling up with massive amounts of water. Instead of being a membrane-like, tough, muscular organ, it becomes a big, fat, heavy, sausage-like organization.

**John Barkhausen:** You're saying that swollen, watery state is basically a state of inflammation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The simplest remedy for many people is just to take some aspirin and Benadryl to lower the inflammatory mediators. Aspirin works because people have consumed too much polyunsaturated fat (PUFA), which turns into prostaglandins—one of the endpoints causing inflammation. Waterlogging and histamine release are defended against by antihistamines. To reduce the risk in the long run, it's important to minimize your intake of those precursors of the inflammatory prostaglandins.

**John Barkhausen:** Part of the digestive process is peristalsis, where the intestine has a contraction that moves food along.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and if they are waterlogged, the muscles simply can't contract. It's like if your arm swelled up to be two feet in diameter; you wouldn't be able to bend it.

**John Barkhausen:** Are there situations where peristalsis stops and you can use something to get it contracting again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar and salt are very effective because they lower adrenaline. If stress has stopped your intestine just because of adrenaline excess, sugar, salt, and maybe a little quick thyroid supplement can get it going again.

Hypothyroidism's classical symptoms include chronic constipation. But now that so many people are being drugged, there are a lot of opiates being widely prescribed. Everyone knows morphine and opium can cause terrible constipation. The intestine is normally a very rich source of endorphins—the natural endogenous opiates. Stress increases endorphins, and they act just like exogenous opiates: they tend to stop intestinal action. Several people have proposed using anti-opiates (used for treating heroin overdoses) to cure chronic spontaneous constipation, because stress often increases endorphins to the point of causing morphine-like constipation.

**John Barkhausen:** So hypothyroidism is a cause of digestive problems. Is the medical world aware of that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They used to be. Fifty years ago, all doctors knew that constipation, dry skin, and falling hair were the most common signs of hypothyroidism. But after the Second World War, medical education changed from perception to following the instructions of drug salesmen. Nowadays, it doesn't occur to most doctors to look at the common signs and see a simple endocrine solution.

**John Barkhausen:** I know some people who have been prescribed a product called Imodin [Emodin]. I was lent some once when I had diarrhea, and I don't believe I had another movement for about three weeks. What is that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know the specific product, but it sounds like the good substance in some of the natural laxatives: Emodin.

**John Barkhausen:** We should talk about Emodin and the FDA's position on that. Can you describe the history of its use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The main traditional laxatives were herbs. Sometimes minerals like Flowers of Sulfur were used, but the most common were herbs. Tobacco was sometimes a component because it increases intestinal tone. Nux vomica is an old one that contained strychnine, but that went out of the laxative world almost 100 years ago. The component that remained was Emodin, which is in cascara, aloe, and rhubarb root. It has many protective effects other than helping cure constipation.

A medical mythology grew up in the 20th century that these natural laxatives were "stimulants." If the intestine isn't swollen, you *can* stimulate it with histamine or serotonin. But the idea that natural laxatives were stimulating the nerves and muscles to contract was a mistaken definition. Because of the fear of stimulants—and the idea that stimulation might cause addiction or euphoria—doctors began advocating drinking more water and taking bulk-forming, water-binding laxatives.

To support their recommendation, they claimed the stimulating laxatives would cause the colon to turn brown or black, which was supposed to be proof of harmfulness. It turns out that in constipation, the constant irritation causes the intestine to produce a brown or black pigment as a defensive reaction. This "melanosis" of the intestine isn't scientifically supported as being caused by the laxatives themselves.

**John Barkhausen:** So doctors were using Cascara Sagrada and Aloe?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. An old laxative called "Nature's Remedy" contained just aloe and cascara for about a hundred years. About 20 years ago, the cancer drug industry started researching chemicals in the same family as the active ingredient of aloe and cascara—anthraquinones. One of these was effective at killing cancer, but it would kill the heart. It was a synthetic derivative.

When this cancer drug was found to kill the heart, research led them to reinvestigate the natural substances. It turns out that Emodin is a good cancer drug, and it doesn't kill your heart. But it's a natural substance. They are still working on how to make a synthetic, patentable version they can sell.

Because of the cancer industry's involvement, the FDA began putting out warnings that the natural substance might cause cancer because it vaguely resembles compounds that do. There was never research to support that, but the FDA used that cancer risk to outlaw the natural substances sold as laxatives.

Coincidentally, within weeks of using that argument, they granted approval to a drug called Zelnorm. This was a synthetic that intensified the serotonin effect to simply overstimulate the intestine. The FDA approved a synthetic that was nothing but a very powerful stimulant simultaneously with taking the natural laxatives off the market. The market was wide open for Zelnorm to be sold at three or four dollars per tablet. They were making something like a billion dollars a year until too many people started having their colons or other parts of their intestine die and have to be removed.

**John Barkhausen:** I see.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The drug was authorized for a maximum of four months. After that, doctors were required not to prescribe it anymore, even though the company was making so much money. The FDA knew there was no permanent good laxative solution and that Zelnorm was outlawed in Europe because it killed intestines. But the FDA let them go for about five years, making their billions, and then outlawed it.

**John Barkhausen:** From the way you describe that, it sounds like the FDA is basically working hand in hand with the industry.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It would be interesting to see how rich the people in the FDA got after that episode. Traditionally, people involved in approving bad drugs often wind up very rich.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The FDA's involvement in these chemicals goes back much further. This family of chemicals, the quinones, was found 100 years ago to be protective. W.F. Koch was experimenting with the anti-cancer effects of these materials as early as the 1910s. The FDA was determined to shut him down by the 1940s.

There were two trials, and he won both because so many of his patients testified they had been cured of cancer. He was producing variations on the quinones. The FDA's response was that quinones are toxic. In court, he demonstrated putting a certain amount of simple quinone into water and diluting it to the strength he injected into patients. The FDA claimed there was none in there because their instruments weren't good enough to detect it, but then argued that if there *was* any, it would be toxic.

About eight years after his second trial, Ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q10) was discovered and found to work exactly as Koch had described: stimulating mitochondrial oxidative metabolism with anti-inflammatory, anti-allergic, antispasmodic, anti-cancer, and anti-infective effects.

**John Barkhausen:** So his treatment was basically helping your cells go back to a healthy state?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Albert Szent-Györgyi, who won a Nobel Prize partly for his work on cellular energy metabolism, kept following the Koch approach. He believed cell oxidative processes are the proper place to focus in treating diseases of muscle, nerve function, and cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** At this point, doctors aren't allowed to prescribe Emodin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They can prescribe it, but it can't be sold as a laxative. It can be sold as a substance or supplement.

**John Barkhausen:** Where does it come from?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Rhubarb root and aloe leaf contain variations of the molecule. Cascara bark is from a very common plant across North America. In its fresh state, the bark causes stimulation and cramping, so traditionally it was aged for at least a year until it turns black, like bitter chocolate. In that state, the soapy quality has broken down and the glucose part has been removed, making it an oil-soluble molecule. In that state, it isn't an intestinal stimulant; it is an anti-inflammatory, slightly sedative, energy-increasing substance.

Just recently, malaria [drugs/mechanisms] were found to be toxic by activating a process that's essential to cancer. It could be that Emodin will turn out to be tried as a treatment for many other diseases other than cancer and constipation.

**John Barkhausen:** How does Emodin work? Does it basically get your cells to produce energy the way they are supposed to?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The actual consumption of oxygen and production of ATP is secondary to a general "tuning up." Natural substances like progesterone, caffeine, and thyroid hormones bind to proteins and cause the protein's electronic behavior to change. The respiratory chain in the mitochondria is tuned up by small molecules associated with it. Coenzyme Q10 helps it take in energy without producing destructive oxidative reactions. Vitamin K, which is a quinone analogous to Emodin, increases the effectiveness of Coenzyme Q10.

This overlap can only be explained as a tuning up of the whole cell system. Szent-Györgyi discussed substances that act on DNA and proteins as a system, increasing the "coherence" of the cell electronically. I don't think cancer or hormone actions will be understood unless the coherence of the cell's electronic system is taken into account.

**John Barkhausen:** You said in your newsletter that the approach of Koch and Szent-Györgyi—making your body healthier and able to deactivate toxins—is in contrast to the mainstream medical approach, which is a war mentality targeting cancer cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Metchnikoff saw the immune system as a developmental process of the whole organism, not just something aimed at killing germs. But the drug industry wanted to think of their product as a germ-killing analog to the immune system. They shut down the Metchnikoff approach and went to the "kill the enemy" approach. That mentality transferred to cancer: identifying the cancer as an alien mutant rather than a dysregulation of a natural process.

**John Barkhausen:** If people are hoping to improve their digestion, what natural food substances might they use?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Raw carrots, by having a germicidal effect on the bacteria, can be very helpful until you get your hormones working. A good thyroid and steroid hormone system will make your intestine have the energy to control the flora on its own. In the meantime, a daily raw carrot helps keep down endotoxin absorption. When they are available, cooked bamboo shoots are another good intestine protector.

**John Barkhausen:** So those are the fibers you would recommend?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, because grain fibers turned out to cause bowel cancer in several research settings. Keeping your general nutrition up with adequate protein is the other main thing to make your digestion work. Eating milk, cheese, and orange juice, along with one of those protective disinfecting fibers, will take care of most bowel problems.

**John Barkhausen:** We are out of time, Ray. Thank you so much for being on today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, very good.

title: Politics & Science: A Self Ordering World
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** My guest today is Dr. Raymond Peat, and I'm happy to have him back again. We're going to talk about your recent newsletter entitled "How Do You Know? Students, Patients, and Discovery." The scope of the newsletter is enormous. It ranges from discussing a unifying, self-ordering principle concerning the nature of the universe, and talks about how the same principle is reflected in our learning processes, in our culture, and in all other functional, goal-directed systems in our world.

You used the quote "One thought fills immensity" by William Blake as the motto of the newsletter. I thought that was very apt because it's such a profound subject. To bring people into this, it would be useful if you could tell us some of your personal experience as a student and then as a teacher, and how this formed your outlook toward the world.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My parents had quite a few interesting books. They had gotten some from their parents, 19th-century books like a second or third edition of Darwin's *Descent of Man*. They also had a collection of the "Little Blue Books." They were published in Kansas and were the classics in 5 and 10-cent versions. So there was quite a variety of reading material when I was a little kid, including encyclopedias.

The older *Encyclopedia Britannica* and others were pretty objective at that time on issues like Darwin versus Lamarck. They gave the research done in the early part of the 20th century in different countries. That gave me an orientation where I began preferring the non-genetic version of the adaptation of individuals to the environment. By the late 1940s, when the genetics doctrine was being imposed politically very powerfully through the US, that made me start seeing the political significance of science in general, and especially biology.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you give us some sense of time? What year were you reading the Little Blue Books?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right after I learned to read. *Alley Oop* and such, then went right to the Little Blue Books, probably 1940.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All through the 40s, my parents knew about Peter Kropotkin's political writings as well as his "mutual aid" factor of evolution. That was my first political book, Kropotkin's biological work on evolution. From that, he drew his anarchist political ideas. That fit in with the other stuff I had been reading on the true Darwin, not the pseudo-Darwinism that was promoted after the 1940s.

Neo-Darwinism really was pretty much anti-Darwin. In Darwin's introduction to the *Descent of Man*, he pointed out that his ideas were being distorted and that he didn't say that the struggle for survival and natural selection was the basic power of evolution. He named several other, more Lamarckian factors in evolution.

**John Barkhausen:** That's more in line with what Kropotkin was saying.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Kropotkin emphasized cooperation within species and even between species in symbiosis.

Although I was interested in science before I went to college, by the time I was in college, I was convinced that there was really something wrong with American and British science in particular. So I concentrated on the humanities and did my master's thesis on William Blake. That gave me a chance to spend years reading the history of philosophy and philosophy of science. When I years later finally did go back to a degree in science, I had sort of inoculated myself against being indoctrinated and forced to believe the very dogmatic ideas that make up American science.

**John Barkhausen:** What gave you the clue that it was dogmatic and not based in actuality?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You hear the joke about Aristotle having counted the number of teeth in a donkey, and that being repeated for hundreds of years. The same thing happened in American chromosome study. Even though Germans were able to count and investigate the effect of chromosomes way back in the early 20th century, major American biologists didn't even believe that chromosomes had to do with heredity until the early 1920s.

Then, all the way up until 1956, American and English scientists were still saying that humans have 48 chromosomes. I had read enough in the 40s to know that people vary somewhat in their numbers, but by far the most common number of chromosomes was 46 in normal humans. Somehow, once fixed ideas are said with great authority, Americans and British just kept saying it over and over for decades.

**John Barkhausen:** Did you have some good teachers yourself personally going through the school system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had three good teachers in the 19 years of college and university, out of about 60, I guess.

**John Barkhausen:** You write in this newsletter about teaching literature. Could you recount your experience trying to follow the school regulations and then finally giving up on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That year I was teaching two different kinds of composition. In freshman composition, the department had a list of how we had to grade papers. For each type of grammatical, spelling, or diction mistake, you would mark off so many points. The purpose was to fail about 90% of the freshmen. That was called "keeping up standards."

I saw after doing that for a few weeks that the students were writing worse and worse because they thought they tended to make mistakes when they didn't have everything under very conscious control. So they started writing like first graders. I had to read several dozen of their papers, and to save myself the suffering of reading first-grade papers, I told them that I would from then on ignore the spelling, punctuation, and the things on that list. I would grade them entirely on their ability to communicate something of interest to me.

Within just a couple of weeks, everyone was writing much better. I had my office partner, who was teaching similar classes following the rules, read some of the before and after papers. He found that when I wasn't grading for errors, the students were writing better according to his and the department's standards. They were supposedly keeping up standards while actually degrading the work output of the students. When I asked them to put their emphasis on communicating something and not think about the mechanics of it, suddenly the mechanics improved as well as the content.

**John Barkhausen:** Did you know about Carl Rogers at that point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was majoring in psychology in the 1950s and I read his *Client-Centered Therapy* sometime in the late 50s.

**John Barkhausen:** What was his influence on education?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He went from his work showing that it's the coherent personality of the therapist that makes a difference in therapy situations, not any psychiatric technique. He established that the validity of their communication with the client was the thing that made psychological therapy work. Then he extended that and began popularizing the idea of student-centered education.

**John Barkhausen:** So it was the therapist allowing the person to self-direct their own emotional recovery that was working.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It was the process of listening deeply so that the patient, in effect, began hearing what they were saying themselves by having someone understand them.

**John Barkhausen:** How was he received?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even other psychiatrists—since he showed empirically that people recovered in proportion to the coherence of the therapist's personality and that it had nothing to do with whether they were a Freudian or a behaviorist—rejected it. The doctrinaire psychologists said that isn't possible because they really believe in their theories. The medical psychiatrists were the most rejecting; they said he isn't even a psychologist, much less a psychiatrist.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Professors in general didn't like that approach because the point of being a professor is to demonstrate that you know it all. If a person goes into a physics class, the assumption is that the professor is going to transmit, bit by bit, his textbook into the mind of the student, as an absolute filling up of an empty space.

Back when I was teaching English and literature, I talked to a variety of physics people because one of my interests was how physics underlies biology, which underlies language and consciousness. I felt I had to have satisfaction that there was some rational physics behind it. I talked to a lot of physics professionals, and invariably, when I would ask them a question, they would quote word-for-word right out of their textbook. They simply couldn't conceive what I was asking if it was an attempt to know anything other than what is in the book.

Really, the most dogmatic people in science seem to be in physics. One of my professors, who I thought was intelligent, said that the average physics graduate student has trouble knowing whether a ball will roll up or down an inclined plane because they've been trained so abstractly.

**John Barkhausen:** That's a little discouraging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The physicists who tend towards the mathematical side dislike applied mathematics. One of the local professors, who was very famous, explained some nuclear particle interactions as being explainable by a particle coming from the *future* and meeting the nucleus at the moment the nucleus emits a particle. Just a most fundamentally confused person who thought time could run both ways at the same time.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that the influence of quantum physics on the scientific culture?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the abstract way everything is taught. Even getting someone to look at the history of where the idea of quantum thinking came from is difficult. There have been books treating the German physics community at that time, showing how important idealistic philosophy was in their cultural context.

For example, take Einstein's photoelectric theory. At the time Einstein thought of the necessity to quantize light to explain why a certain frequency rather than intensity is needed to liberate electrons, he subscribed to the idea that matter is an assemblage of atomic particles, each one electrically discrete. He thought there is no electrical blurring across the substance.

When Michael Polanyi in 1915 presented a description of his work in the adsorption of gases onto solid surfaces, Einstein was one of the people at the meeting who said, "Sorry, that isn't possible. You're thinking in some kind of primitive Hungarian way. Here in Germany, we know that electrons are discreetly attached to atoms." It was that kind of thinking that was background to the quantized physics that took over the world. But Einstein was simply mistaken about how matter worked.

**John Barkhausen:** So even great minds can go astray. Did he try to call it back when he realized his error?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was about 1930 when the adsorption people started creating alternative ways to explain the experimental evidence Polanyi had demonstrated. Polanyi's evidence was vindicated, but they told a different story about how it worked. From about that time on, Einstein began saying he couldn't really accept the whole quantum approach to physical reality.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like that's an example of how dogma gets legs of its own. We're also talking about learning and how it works best if it's self-organizing. Carl Rogers was postulating that things tend to be self-organizing and live up to their fullest potential.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's in the biological idea of what a cell and an organism is where you see the clearest demonstration of that principle. In biology, there has been a huge amount of data accumulated showing that things are open, but trying to explain them in terms of these quantized, eternal parts just doesn't work.

That's where molecular biology and the dominant theory of genetics came from: a belief in an otherworldly nature of the gene. What they were doing was agreeing with the theological rejection of evolution. Mendel was a monk who gained his own professional standing by seeming to have disproved evolution. He showed that traits are eternal even though the organisms seem to change; they're only changing their appearance, but their essential nature is timeless.

The church people liked Mendel's work, but then English biologists took it up for the same reason they hated some of the things Darwin said which agreed with Lamarck—that organisms can be changed by their experience. That has racial overtones. If you say the working-class people can radically fit their nature and become philosophers, that messes with the whole authoritarian social system. The English ruling class biologists loved the Mendelian approach because it said Darwin and Lamarck were both profoundly mistaken about how evolution works.

**John Barkhausen:** So genetics just grew out of a way to appease the church and maintain the status quo?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things in the 50s that made me think American biology was ridiculous was that they believed genes would specify everything, including the way we thought. They believed every synapse of every nerve cell was supposed to be genetically determined. Someone calculated how impossible that was when they realized how many brain cells there were. People started rethinking that. As the genetics people learned more about DNA, it turned out that the great bulk of the DNA isn't there for genetic purposes. The genes that make up a person or a yeast are a very small part of the DNA present.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like there's a prejudice among educators and therapists against the self-ordering idea that goes across all professional trades.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I happened to be teaching a linguistics course in the 60s, just about the time Noam Chomsky was coming out against the Vietnam War. I had been pointing out how there was absolutely no evidence in Chomsky's type of linguistics. He totally ignored evidence. It was absolutely idealistic doctrine saying that we have genes that specify the way we talk.

There's almost no difference between Chomsky's idealistic genetic idea of language and Konrad Lorenz's genetic explanation for all behavior, which Lorenz designed specifically for Hitler to justify racial extermination. Chomsky wouldn't like that comparison, but in fact, they're both committed to ignoring the actual evidence and believing that genes explain everything. Lorenz's motive was obviously to say that society is constituted the way it should be, except for the mongrelizing with bad genetic traits—such as liking jazz music—which should be exterminated.

**John Barkhausen:** I hear the dogmatists saying that everything is determined by genes, yet they also propose things like chaos theory.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The idea of randomness goes way back into the 19th century. It was a sort of compromise. They said that if anything changes, it changes only randomly. When Muller started showing that he could mutate fruit flies with X-rays, the change was seen to deteriorate almost always. That was because change is random.

If you're going to have change, it can't be meaningful. You can't say that if you feed poor people they will have healthier babies who will be more intelligent, because that would say that you have a directional change being caused by the environment. The whole point of genetics is to say the environment can't change the reality of the organism.

**John Barkhausen:** You've said that Neo-Kantian philosophy has dominated US universities, arguing that our senses are limited so we can't really know the world. Does that tie into that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, our senses are determined by our genes. Even for the Chomsky point of view, our thoughts and behaviors are determined by our genes.

**John Barkhausen:** How do languages fit into how we learn?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Chomsky says that we really don't learn our language in the structural sense. If we're born with it, all we do is learn some of the minor details of vocabulary and pronunciation. The Neo-Kantians, at the extreme, say that our perceptions are shaped by our genes. Many of them revive the Leibnizian idea of monads—that all of our knowledge and experience is in our genes, so we aren't really experiencing anything.

George Wald, a famous professor who investigated vision, explained that color vision is based on a difference of frequencies rather than an absolute color.
