By testing people who had their lenses removed from their eyes because of cataracts, he found that they could see patterns in ultraviolet light the same way bees can. That's one of the favorite examples of the Neo-Kantians: that we are determined to see the world in a certain way. But when the thick lens is removed, the ultraviolet light gets to our retina and humans *can* see it. It's just a matter of the intensity of stimulus.

Some people say that bees and birds have a genetically programmed way of thinking, so we can never really know what a bee is thinking. But people who look at animals in their natural setting see that bees and ants are solving unique, original problems that never happened before in a manner that rivals human thinking. Given a setup of instruction and arrangements in space, ants were able to learn and transmit information as competently as trained air traffic controllers.

**John Barkhausen:** I've never understood why we separated ourselves from the animals to begin with. It just seems like another form of elitism.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just a few decades ago, some of the most famous professors in the country were saying that there are subhumans and real humans, and that working-class people are genetically inferior. They argued that with an improved society, working-class people will all go to the bottom genetically and the talented people will all rise to the top.

**John Barkhausen:** Like *The Bell Curve* by Herrnstein and Murray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Herrnstein was a famous Harvard professor who said that we needed a proper meritocracy where there wasn't the confusion of trying to educate working-class people.

**John Barkhausen:** You talked about Alfred Korzybski and Paulo Freire both pointing out the use of language and abstractions in education.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Paulo Freire had an empirical view of reality. When people realized that they could define the words of their language, it caused them to start thinking rather than simply accepting what their betters wanted to impose on them. He asked people to choose a vocabulary they wanted to investigate and to define the terms themselves.

Korzybski pretty much got stuck in the idea that there were gradients of concreteness and generality, and that truth involved getting down to the specific concrete fact. He was basically an enemy of the idea that general perceptions and concepts were just as valid as concrete naming. He wanted a scientific language with marks indicating the particular individual and time, implying that generalities were always farther from reality.

But if you realize that all facts—whether an atom, an organism, or a process—are patterns of experience, if a person doesn't look for a pattern on the scale of generality, naturally they're not going to find it. It's the same as assuming everything an ant does is stupid.

For example, when people study cancer, the genetic people don't look for field phenomena, so they can't see them. But whenever someone looks for a cancer field, they see it's there. The definitive cancer cells are surrounded by a field of precancerous cells, fading off into inflamed or stressed cells. Without seeing the future phenomenon in any process, you get stuck with a reductionist jumble of meaningless particles.

The government has giant computers stuffed with observations of enzymes and genes, thinking they'll come up with something. But they're failing to look intelligently at the field behavior—the way the thing functions as a whole through time and space. That's the difference between the way von Bertalanffy looked at systems theory and the way P.K. Anokhin derived his more cybernetic approach.

**John Barkhausen:** You said Anokhin came up with the concept of feedback.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It became popularized in English by Norbert Wiener, but all of the concepts were developed about 15 years before that by P.K. Anokhin, who was one of Pavlov's colleagues. Anokhin saw that feedback was able to explain the development of an embryo meaningfully. Instead of the embryo being guided blindly by genetic reactions, each of the cells and systems was responding to the situation it found itself in at any moment and adjusting itself.

The genetic theory has this infinitely complex idea that all of these constantly changing developmental processes have to be held in the being somehow and read at the proper time. It is impossible when you try to guide it like clockwork from the inside. But when it's a matter of responsiveness to the presently perceived situation, it explains how an embryo develops.

**John Barkhausen:** So everything is self-organized from the whole right down to the cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. One of my professors of biochemistry, Sidney Bernhard, published a series of papers showing that all of the basic assumptions of biochemistry were wrong. The idea was that if you squash up a cell and float the enzymes in a solution, the particles will meet the enzyme by diffusion.

He showed that in glycolytic metabolism, the enzymes outnumber the substrate molecules. The reaction involves one enzyme handing off the product of its reaction to the next enzyme. So it isn't a random diffusion of material through water, but a totally organized enzyme-to-enzyme handoff. He did that simply by counting molecules. But they were so committed to this idea of randomness in a watery solution, they totally missed the point of what's happening in the cell.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a number of questions. One listener asks what you would recommend to a young person who wants to study biology, and another asks what research we can trust.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Don't trust anything. Just read it carefully and think about what they're doing and who they are. For example, I recently saw a discussion of the anti-cancer drug called Ukrain. Some English researchers offered to give it an objective test, but when the producer learned what they were going to do, he wanted an independent evaluation. They wrote articles in *The Lancet* saying the producer was unwilling to submit to an objective test. But when I looked at their previous publications, they were absolutely aligned with the cell-toxic chemotherapy industry.

Reading about the history of the person making the claim is part of the process. About nine times out of ten, it will show they have some ulterior motive. As for where to start, Gilbert Ling is a good place to reorient to how the biological community works and how they have ignored Ling for almost 60 years. I've looked at literature citing Ling and seen that when someone misquoted him, that misquotation went down through about a dozen repetitions. So one error led to deliberate misrepresentations of Gilbert Ling's work. When you really pay attention to Gilbert Ling, you see a lot of corruption in the biological community.

**John Barkhausen:** Another person asked if you put a book out with all of your dietary recommendations laid out in one place.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, not really. It's coming out gradually in my newsletters.

**John Barkhausen:** Thanks so much, Ray.

title: Politics & Science: Nuclear Disaster
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** We are talking to Maggie Gunderson today. This is Politics and Science on the 16th of March, 2011. Today we're discussing the nuclear catastrophe happening in Japan. Maggie Gunderson is founder and president of Fairewinds Associates and a freelance paralegal specializing in environmental nuclear safety and energy litigation in federal and state administrative law hearings. You worked in the nuclear industry for a while, right, Maggie? As did your husband, Arnie.

**Maggie Gunderson:** Yes, we both did. That's where we met.

**John Barkhausen:** I was hoping you could bring us up to date with what exactly is happening over in Japan and what the ramifications are for that part of the world and for us.

**Maggie Gunderson:** The news that just came during the last hour is that all the fuel has boiled dry in Unit 4. That was in the spent fuel pool, not in the reactor itself. That was a full offload, so that is a tremendous amount of radioactive fuel that is getting very, very hot. There is a fear that it could catch on fire. If it catches fire, those particles become airborne. It's a worse scenario than having a melt.

**John Barkhausen:** It is?

**Maggie Gunderson:** Yes, it is, because that radiation will travel anywhere. If there's a meltdown, it does get into the water table, but you might be able to corral some of the contamination and do things to mitigate it. But this is airborne, and this will go wherever the air blows. It's like if you see someone smoking a cigarette; the plume can move in whatever direction the wind is blowing—towards Tokyo, towards the US, towards mainland China, and across the rest of Japan.

**John Barkhausen:** I know Chernobyl was terrible because it was an explosion that forced the radiation out. That was a core meltdown, wasn't it?

**Maggie Gunderson:** No, there was a graphite fire. The Chernobyl plant is a graphite plant and was not a liquid reactor like we're talking about here. There was a fire in the graphite only at Chernobyl. Only 3% of the radiation escaped; the other 97% is still inside the containment, inside the sarcophagus that they built around it.

In this accident, since the containment has failed, this radiation is getting out to the environment. The US Surgeon General was on a tour in California and spoke of the fact that anyone in the US should consider getting potassium iodide to protect their thyroid. That would be a prudent thing to do. The NRC and the State Department announced today that they told all US personnel in Japan to go at least 80 miles away from what's happening. That's more than double what the Japanese are saying.

**John Barkhausen:** The NRC is usually... I never thought of them as being actually that worried about low-level radiation.

**Maggie Gunderson:** Well, it's not low-level radiation. It's not an explosion like a bomb, but it's not low-level. There are no more personnel on site operating the plants. They've had to remove them because the radiation levels are too high.

**John Barkhausen:** So basically things are just running their course.

**Maggie Gunderson:** They're running their course. They do have people who are risking their lives to keep putting water on the plant, pumping seawater up there, but there are no operational things that they can do.

**John Barkhausen:** Is Number 4 one of the reactors that was out of commission, so all the fuel rods were waiting to be moved?

**Maggie Gunderson:** Yes, all the fuel rods had been offloaded into the fuel pool. What's really scary about that is that there are no control rods to put in to slow down the reaction. The fuel rods are in the fuel pool and as the water burns off, there's nothing to keep that fuel pool cool. If the fuel gets really hot and starts a chain reaction, it cannot be stopped because there is nothing to moderate that chain reaction.

That was the difference with Chernobyl. Chernobyl is a plant where, as the chain reaction is going on inside, the operators have to work really hard to pull it back. It's like pushing a gas pedal downwards all the time. In the Japanese plants—which are the same as the Vermont Yankee plant, boiling water reactors of the same vintage and design—you have to push the reaction to happen. Usually, you have a lot of control. But they don't have control on this because this is the spent fuel all just sitting there together. There are no control rods. As the decay heat causes chain reactions, you could have a fire or a meltdown in the fuel pool itself.

**John Barkhausen:** What's the state of the other reactors? There are six of them there at the Fukushima power station.

**Maggie Gunderson:** Two of them already are in partial meltdown. When the earthquake started, the emergency systems worked and the reaction stopped. However, 5% of the heat is decay heat, and that is what has kept burning. The diesels got swamped by the tsunami, so they didn't have any backup power and couldn't cool the reactors.

My understanding—and this has been changing hour by hour—is that two reactors have had a partial meltdown. How bad that will be will depend on how much seawater these employees, who are risking their lives, can pump in. They are pumping in tons of seawater to try and make a lake under the reactors.

In a boiling water reactor (BWR), the control rods come up from the bottom into the reactor itself. In a pressurized water reactor (PWR), which I worked on, the control rods come down from the top. In the BWR, the bottom of the reactor is not as tight. The daughter products that are generating all this excess heat are slumping into the bottom and making a molten mass. That is coming out of the bottom of the reactor. That's why they're trying to make a lake between the base of the metal reactor vessel and the concrete base of the containment.

**John Barkhausen:** Is this special nuclear-grade concrete?

**Maggie Gunderson:** It's just regular concrete, like you would find on a bridge. There's not a special nuclear grade to it.

**John Barkhausen:** How long can that hold up to temperatures that I've heard are like 2200 degrees?

**Maggie Gunderson:** No one knows. We're in uncharted territory here. The fuel pool can get up to 4,000 degrees. The Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) is saying there can't be a fire in the fuel pool, but there's already been one. They say the containment can't leak, but two of them have blown their lids off.

We need to go back and look at the general design criteria on every nuclear plant. A lot of them are just too old. Vermont Yankee, Oyster Creek, Pilgrim—these are very old plants that don't have any current safety standards around them. All of the parameters under which they were built have been grandfathered in, so they don't meet the current regulations.

**John Barkhausen:** Vermont Yankee got an upgrade 10 years ago, I think.

**Maggie Gunderson:** An uprate is really a frightening thing. If there's an accident at Vermont Yankee, there is 40% more radiation than a normal accident because of the uprate. Even though the uprate was 25%, the way the daughter products act, you get 40% more radiation. The emergency evacuation plan was designed around the way the plant was built before the uprate. It is not possible to get everyone out before there would be a lethal dose if there was a severe accident.

**John Barkhausen:** People would say Vermont Yankee is not at risk because it's not in an earthquake zone and there's no danger of tsunami. But it is next to a river. Is there a flooding danger there?

**Maggie Gunderson:** Yes, there is a flooding danger. Hurricanes could knock out power or destabilize the grid. Vermont Yankee's backup power is diesel, just like the plants in Japan. If they were involved in a flood or a hurricane and couldn't operate, there is no backup power. If a huge storm knocked out the service water that cools the plant out of the Connecticut River, or if terrorists attacked the intake structures, you couldn't cool that plant. The NRC does not consider that a realistic part of its threat matrix.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you know how the fallout from what's happening in Japan might behave?

**Maggie Gunderson:** No one knows. Will a lot of that come across the Pacific to the US? There was extensive data from bomb testing done in the Pacific originally, and a lot of that strontium and cesium were carried to the US and absorbed into kids' muscles and bones. This accident is worse than Three Mile Island, worse than Chernobyl. It is the worst industrial accident the world has ever seen. With plutonium involved, there's going to be 250,000-year waste left.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like you were once in favor of nuclear power, but you have changed your position.

**Maggie Gunderson:** That's correct. I was in favor of nuclear power. I was part of Jobs for Energy Independence. I was working in the nuclear industry, in part to make sure that when there's plenty of energy available, women and minorities have jobs. The scientists had assured me it was the safest thing. I don't believe it anymore.

**John Barkhausen:** Thank you very much, Maggie Gunderson.

**Maggie Gunderson:** You're very welcome, John. Take care.

**John Barkhausen:** I'm back live with Dr. Raymond Peat, who is a physiologist, biologist, and science historian from Eugene, Oregon. Thanks for coming on today. Considering the catastrophe in Japan, I thought we could talk about radiation's effects on the body and ways it can be mitigated.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first issue of my newsletter in 1981 was about the issue of radiation damage. I read lots of mostly Soviet research; they were the ones mostly interested in how to repair damage. The main factors are the amount of magnesium in the cells and the metabolic rate. It happens that thyroid hormone is what's needed for the cells to retain magnesium at a high level.

The central idea I reviewed 30 years ago was a high metabolic rate activating repair processes so that once the damage was done, it was almost immediately repaired. Just in the last couple of years, a group studying radio-resistant bacteria found that manganese is an essential factor for the survival of these bacteria. What the manganese is doing is catalyzing a very fast metabolism of glucose. This very fast glucose metabolism is almost all turned into carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide happens to protectively stick to amino groups of proteins.

My approach to defense against aging and stress has been to keep the carbon dioxide up high in mammals. Apparently, these bacteria carry it to an extreme so that they can survive millions of rads of ionizing radiation.

**John Barkhausen:** Does this have to do with the thyroid function as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It parallels the thyroid function. The bacteria do it just by this manganese-containing enzyme system, but in mammals, it's the thyroid hormone that's primarily responsible for turning glucose and fats into carbon dioxide.

**John Barkhausen:** One of the problems with radiation is that it damages the thyroid. The American Surgeon General just recommended that people get a supply of potassium iodide.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The CDC recommended a single dose of 160 milligrams of potassium iodide for an adult, to be repeated if the iodine cloud stays around for more than one day. Kelp, dulse, or other iodine-rich seaweed—a few grams per day—will do that if you don't have the pure potassium iodide. Even antiseptic tincture of iodine painted on the skin is an alternative way of getting your iodine up.

But I think the basic thing is to keep your thyroid hormone active, if necessary by using a supplement of thyroid hormone to keep your thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) down as close to zero as you can get it. That's good for many reasons. If your TSH is kept at zero, your thyroid won't be metabolizing and won't take up the toxic concentration of radioactive iodine. Meanwhile, high thyroid activity is going to accelerate the repair processes.

If you rely on potassium iodide, that's going to dilute the radioactive contaminant so it doesn't destroy your thyroid gland, but the potassium iodide tends to suppress your thyroid gland function, lowering the whole body's metabolic rate. That makes it increasingly susceptible to radiation damage.

If you think of the inverse relationship between thyroid and estrogen: a low thyroid person usually has very high estrogen, and a high thyroid person has low estrogen. Estrogen synergizes with radiation damage. So, a low thyroid person is doing many things to make all of their tissues more susceptible to injury by all of the radiation sources—which include carbon isotopes, cesium, and strontium. The iodide suppressing your thyroid gland isn't going to do anything to protect you against strontium, cesium, or carbon, and in fact, will tend to make you more susceptible to injury by them.

**John Barkhausen:** Because if your thyroid is functioning, you'll be able to remove those quicker?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The cells are producing carbon dioxide, which forms a defensive barrier on the proteins, keeping them from suffering destructive oxidation. And the magnesium retained by the thyroid is used in the repair enzymes for DNA repair. At the same time, you're lowering the estrogen throughout your body, which avoids that synergistic effect of radiation and estrogen.

**John Barkhausen:** In terms of raising your thyroid function, most people probably won't be able to get their hands on any thyroid supplements. How can they do that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The quickest way is to make sure that you're getting enough food and fuel. Sugar, moment by moment, is used by your liver to activate the thyroid hormone. If you go hungry for several hours, your thyroid is going to decrease its function.

On an even shorter scale, coconut oil, with its short-chain saturated fatty acids, competes with the inhibiting unsaturated fats that are always tending to circulate in the body acting as a break on the thyroid. The coconut oil short-chain fats compete against the inhibitors, momentarily liberating a higher thyroid function. That only lasts a couple of hours for a tablespoon of coconut oil. So, if you add nothing else, you could eat a tablespoon of coconut oil every couple of hours.

**John Barkhausen:** What about Vitamin E and Vitamin C?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not very. In some situations, they're protective against radiation, but when I reviewed the literature, they were somewhat ambiguous. Progesterone as an anti-estrogen is probably one of the other short-range protective things.

**John Barkhausen:** You've said before that radiation is very similar in its effects to estrogen. Could you comment on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of this research was done in the late 1930s. The estrogen functions were identified as similar to suffocation, stress, and radiation. About 15 years later, when the concept of the estrogen receptor was introduced, there was a great push to distract people from the biochemical effects of estrogen and blame all of estrogen's effects on the actions of a receptor protein.

It turned out that research was supported by the Atomic Energy Commission. It claimed that estrogen is not metabolized in cells where it's acting. 20 years later, that was proven to be absolutely false. The fact that it was supported by the Atomic Energy Commission and done by a man who had been working in chemical warfare makes the whole foundation of the receptor theory suspect.

The 1930s research was very clear that any stress activates the estrogen functions, which include inflammation, water uptake, suppression of the respiratory function, and eventually atrophy, fibrosis, calcification, and cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** And radiation has those similar effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Biochemically, they seem similar. My dissertation was trying to find anything different between radiation stress and estrogen's effect, and I couldn't find any basic physiological or biochemical difference. They both interfere with oxidative metabolism and activate the stress metabolism.

**John Barkhausen:** How does the military fit into this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are the ones that promoted the concept of the estrogen receptor. Elwood Jensen went from working on chemical warfare to working on the estrogen receptor. His group formed a tradition supported by the Pentagon. Some of them have been working more recently at Lawrence Livermore Radiation Lab on the estrogen receptor. So for 60 years now, it has been of great importance to the military, the Atomic Energy Commission, and various government agencies. At different times they have been interested in its birth control effect and population control. Estrogen is really a more controllable way to sterilize the population.

**John Barkhausen:** What is the danger we face from what's coming out of Japan now? Is this particulate radiation that we're going to be exposed to?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As long as it stays very high in the atmosphere and doesn't rain out, it isn't going to do too much harm. But if it rains out, wherever it comes down, it will do a lot of damage. A few of the bombs exploded in Nevada happened to stay in the air until one of the fallout clouds rained down in New York. Ernest Sternglass happened to be on the site and saw that his radiation measurements were showing extreme contamination while the government was saying nothing had happened. That started Sternglass on his research. He showed how the U.S. Public Health Service was collaborating with the Atomic Energy Commission to put out false information. So whatever we're going to hear from the governments of Japan and the United States, I don't think there's any precedent for thinking there will be any truth in it.

**John Barkhausen:** One of the reassurances we're always told is that nuclear power emissions don't go above the background radiation. But background radiation is always going up because of their own emissions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The type of radiation is crucial in its biological effects. The industry uses tricks, comparing living in Denver or flying in an airplane with breathing fallout. They ignore the fact that the gamma rays they're counting in Denver have a low energy transfer to the tissues; they go through so fast they don't react. At sea level, you're getting tertiary and secondary cosmic rays which have more energy delivery in a toxic way to your tissues. So actually, Denver has less biologically effective radiation than sea level.

Another trick they use is to show an alpha emitter and a detector, then put a sheet of typing paper in the path to show that it stops the alpha particles. But if you inhale an alpha emitter, when that particle goes, it's going to hit a cell, not a sheet of typing paper. The fact that it will stop in a sheet of paper means that it has 100% delivery of its energy to the tissue. It's the delivery of energy that causes the tissue damage.

**John Barkhausen:** So if you inhale a particulate that's radioactive, even though it might not be that much radiation, it's the fact that you're getting all of it in one place that makes it serious.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The beta radiation from iodine, strontium, and cesium is basically all going to be absorbed when a particle decomposes in your tissues. It's not as locally intense as alpha particles, but it's much more effective at tissue delivery than X-rays or gamma rays just passing through your body.

**John Barkhausen:** Could you summarize what alpha, beta, and gamma mean?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Alpha particles are actually an atomic nucleus, so it's a big fat particle that stops easily when it runs into cell material. A beta particle is an electron, which is much more able to pass through cells without being absorbed, but it still is a particle of matter or electricity. X-rays and gamma rays are photons, analogous to light. Certain frequencies will resonate more with the living substance, but they have a very low linear transfer of energy compared to particles.

**John Barkhausen:** How does fallout compare to going in for medical or dental X-rays?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The thyroid is damaged by all of them. But if you breathe in or eat the particles, the fallout is considerably worse than just having a dental X-ray. Dental X-rays tend to cause cancer of the eyeball, the brain, and the thyroid. But the government's tendency has been to use whatever measure sounds the least threatening, such as failing to make the distinction between the local dose and the total body dose. They did the same thing with the atomic bombs in Japan; they averaged out the people at a certain distance in any direction, making the people who were actually exposed to the fallout disappear by averaging them 360 degrees around the circle.

**John Barkhausen:** We're out of time. Could you quickly summarize the things people could do to mitigate radiation problems?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Eating seaweed, kelp. If you have a bottle of iodine, you can paint some on your fingers and toes and soak up some of it through your skin. This shouldn't be done until the cloud is actually here, because excess iodine is toxic to your thyroid in itself. But if there's an intense cloud passing over, these external sources of iodine will protect the thyroid. However, keeping your thyroid function up is the ideal way to do it. That is done with sugar, coconut oil, and when possible, a thyroid supplement.

**John Barkhausen:** Dr. Raymond Peat, thanks so much for being on tonight. You can find out more about his work at his website, raypeat.com.

title: Politics & Science: Obfuscation of Radiation Science by Industry
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** I believe I have Dr. Raymond Peat here. This is Politics and Science on the 30th of March 2011. Dr. Peat is a physiologist and an endocrinologist from Eugene, Oregon, and has a website with a lot of excellent articles, mostly about physiology, at raypeat.com. **Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I didn't know it had been that long.

**John Barkhausen:** How are listeners supposed to ascertain who has the accurate data and who doesn't?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you read the references cited by T.D. Luckey or any of these people propagandizing against Pauling and Gofman, and then read Sternglass's books, you can judge for yourself. Sternglass pried some information out of the agencies, although much of it was destroyed. But the information he got was very public, simple factual population information—mortality figures and so on. It is very sound and absolutely in a different world from the political fantasies that the Luckey people cite.

**John Barkhausen:** Talking about Ernest Sternglass brings us back to some of the history you cover in this newsletter. I guess Sternglass worked with Linus Pauling, the Nobel Prize winner, and they were both working to stop atomic testing. Can you explain why they got involved with that issue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 50s, Linus Pauling was talking about the genetic effects of even one alpha-emitting atom ingested into the body. He said that an alpha particle delivers all of its energy to a very small area. If it hits a nucleus, it will either kill the nucleus or mutate it. He said that every mutation ultimately can be considered a fatality, even if it comes 100 generations later, because it's not introducing anything of value but simply destroying information.

He emphasized the mutation damage done by any radioactive isotope, natural or artificial. The terrible thing is that the fallout from nuclear reactors and atomic bombs gets into the atmosphere as particles. When ingested, if they stay in the body, they will eventually emit a particle which will either kill a cell or probably cause a mutation.

He was making the point about the absolute difference between radiation that you get while walking past a granite bank—which passes through and delivers very little energy—and any single alpha-emitting isotope that you swallow. The isotope delivers all of its energy as that alpha particle is absorbed by the cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The RAD is the absorbed dose of radiation, and the REM (or Sievert) is the equivalent in a person. The Sievert is the new unit referring to that effective dose. Unfortunately, that effective dose is part of obscuring the actual dangers because they define "effectiveness" as a killing or a mutation.

The people defending the industry use this Sievert unit against the Pauling, Gofman, and Sternglass people. Their journals are full of studies showing how harmless particular types of radiation are. If you don't kill the cell instantly and don't mutate it so that you can find a broken chromosome right after the exposure, they claim you have done no harm. That is where the situation is totally being falsified.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sternglass was forced to recognize that there is something far beyond mutation and killing effects. He saw changes happening around Three Mile Island. He found large numbers of stillbirths, thyroid-deficient babies, and miscarriages by mothers after they had ingested the isotopes.

When he followed up all across the country, he looked at the miscarriages and thyroid deficiencies, and they followed just in the number of months that you would expect from the damage to the developing embryo. It was the same with the production of leukemia; intrauterine exposure was producing leukemia.

Then he looked at the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT) scores 18 years later. In Utah, there was a 26% decrease in scores 18 years after the heaviest exposure to bomb tests. Right across the country, the scores decreased in proportion to the radiation exposure of the mothers 18 years earlier.

The first response was that more poor kids were now taking the test. Sternglass showed that was wrong. He looked at the high range; the very highest-scoring students had decreased more. They were the most sensitive to the destructive effects of prenatal radiation exposure.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even the industry people pretty much have to accept that the women exposed to the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs while pregnant had children with smaller brains and mental retardation in proportion to the radiation they got. That was blamed on the killing of brain cells.

But just recently, a study in Seattle of women getting dental X-rays showed that if they got a whole set of dental X-rays, the pregnant women delivered underweight babies. Something happened when their head was irradiated that was transmitted to their whole body and made the pregnancy less successful. When the baby is born underweight, the brain is also underweight.

Fifty years after the bomb in Japan, and 20 years after Chernobyl, samples of workers' serum were tested. Their serum was added to healthy cells, and it was able to cause mutations or chromosome breaks even 20 to 50 years after they had been exposed.

**John Barkhausen:** I would think that if somebody had survived for 20 years with those toxic effects in their blood, then the body was coping with it. Is that not true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, the exposed people had worse health and a higher rate of death from all causes—infectious diseases, heart disease, cancer. But the healthiest of them who survived a long time still were radically injured.

Studies have been done showing that radiation to a man's head will be associated with birth defects in his offspring. Something is transmitted through his body, affects his sperm, and destabilizes them genetically. Animal studies show that sort of effect can go on generation after generation, often getting worse each generation.

**John Barkhausen:** How were Ernest Sternglass and Linus Pauling received when they campaigned to stop above-ground testing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was one of the people talking about the difference between John Gofman and Linus Pauling. John Gofman was saying Linus Pauling was a neurotic and a quack. I was saying that John Gofman is either insane or a liar. Twenty years later, Gofman suddenly had an insight and said that was the stupidest thing he could have ever done. But he was doing it regularly as his profession for the government—campaigning against Linus Pauling.

**John Barkhausen:** He was one of the main spokesmen for the Atomic Energy Agency, wasn't he?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And his old stupid arguments are still found in the professional journals of radiation protection.

**John Barkhausen:** Any insight into how he happened to change his mind?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He said he was in the middle of a talk and realized it was a crazy thing to say that until we *know* we're destroying all future generations, we should go on testing. He later said that he and hundreds of other people in similar positions could be tried for war crimes.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you explain why cosmic radiation isn't the same as ionizing radiation from fallout?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The essential thing is Linear Energy Transfer (LET). The higher the velocity of a particle, the less likely it is to stop in your tissue. If you look at a track of a particle going through tissue, when you find one that is losing enough energy that it's coming to rest, the ionization becomes extremely intense. At the very last micron of movement, it delivers all of its remaining energy right in that cell.

But if it passes through you at a high velocity, very little radiation is lost. The type of radiation we're exposed to when a primary cosmic ray goes through us is the high-velocity type. It is weakly deflected, and the energy delivered is very small.

Experiments have shown that secondary and tertiary particles—the ones slowing down—are mostly ending right near the surface of the earth. Those are the ones doing most of the biological damage. So, as far as cosmic rays are concerned, it's actually worse to live at sea level. But the industry argues the reverse—that high altitude is where you get the worst radiation. They turn the evidence upside down to support their interests.

**John Barkhausen:** You're saying the radon actually ends up in your brain if you're exposed to it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The industry says since you breathe radon, you would expect lung cancer. But since people exposed to radon in homes don't have more lung cancer, they claim radiation is good for you. But it goes through your lung in a fraction of a second. Radon dissolves in fat tissue. The brain is mostly fat, so that is where you get most of the radon exposure. Figures show that dementia corresponds very closely to radon exposure.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Carmel Mothersill and her collaborators have demonstrated the "bystander effect"—what is transmitted through body fluids. They showed you can irradiate cells in a culture dish, take the fluid from those cells, add it to fresh cells, and those fresh cells behave as if they had been irradiated.

One of the transmitters they identified is serotonin. They found that serotonin produced by the radiation-damaged cells was enough to transmit genomic instability to new cells.

**John Barkhausen:** That's without any extra radiation added?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, that's just the indirect effect transmitted through the fluids. If they irradiated fish in water and then put new fish in the water, the new fish suffered similar effects transmitted from the secretions of the injured fish.

**John Barkhausen:** The World Health Organization and the IAEA have issued studies about Chernobyl that radically differ from a Russian study that came out a year ago. The UN basically said only the immediate workers were harmed. The Russian study said over a million people have died.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Western journals reviewing about 300 Western articles concluded that 28 people died, or maybe as many as 60 or 70. The group that wrote the Russian book looked at 5,000 studies and concluded that a million people were killed.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like science is a political occupation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the idea of having a "consensus" of scientists. I see it as exactly the same as people who form their political views by taking a consensus of what the network newscasters are saying.

**John Barkhausen:** George Monbiot recently wrote that the events at Fukushima convinced him that nuclear power is the answer because hardly anyone was hurt, basing that on the UN reports. Helen Caldecott thought that was an outrageous lie. Can you give us your take?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The UN is primarily the instrument of the imperialist countries. The nuclear industry wouldn't exist without the political support of the states, which represent corporate interests. The public is taxed to finance the nuclear industry, and the corporations support the universities and the media. Helen Caldecott is threatening to hurt the interests of the nuclear industry, so the whole system has to exclude people like that.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a few minutes left. Can you outline what people can do to minimize their exposure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a very intense cloud comes by with a lot of radioactive iodine, the thyroid is the first thing that can be protected. Eating iodine-rich foods or taking enough thyroid to suppress your thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) will make the gland inactive so you don't take up the radioactive iodine. A spoonful of powdered kelp will pretty well saturate your body.

However, the iodine danger passes in about six weeks. If you take too much iodine and suppress the function of your thyroid gland, you're going to slow all of your metabolic processes, including the DNA repair enzymes. So, keeping your metabolic rate high by avoiding toxic foods is very important for long-range resistance.

For long-range things like cesium and strontium, you want to help wash those out of your body. Eating a calcium-rich and potassium-rich diet will increase the turnover of these in your tissues. A thyroid-supporting diet low in polyunsaturated fats will increase the repair processes and prevent, to some extent, those long-range bystander effects.

**John Barkhausen:** And you mentioned red light before. Is that effective?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you have a CAT scan or some kind of very intense radiation, those effects will linger as excited molecules in your tissue for hours. If in the first hour after exposure you get lots of sunlight, or bright incandescent light rich in the red spectrum, it deactivates those excited electrons.

**John Barkhausen:** I suppose it would be best to avoid milk from cows eating in the field?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, I looked at the figures 40 or 50 years ago regarding radiation in milk versus vegetables. I saw that if you ate vegetables for your nutrients, you would be getting several times more strontium than you would from the milk. The cow concentrates calcium, whereas plants tend to receive a high proportion of strontium from the fresh fallout. So the cow is actually a good filter even during the fallout storm.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, thanks so much for your knowledge and advice.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: Politics & Science: Food Quality
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** This week I'm once again very pleased to have on my show Dr. Raymond Peat, who has a PhD in biology and has studied extensively in the fields of physiology and endocrinology. In my opinion, he is a very learned science historian.

This show is inspired by two articles Ray Peat wrote: "Milk in Context: Allergies, Ecology, and Some Myths" and "Vegetables, etc.—Who Defines Food?" Both take on the issue of the quality of our food and how it has evolved—or devolved—over the years. Today I'd like to discuss how our culture, food production processes, and environment have influenced these changes. Ray, you wrote that good nutrition involves much more than essential nutrients. How do we decide what is nutritious, and how are these decisions made now compared to traditionally?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Traditionally, people would eat something that tasted good. If they survived and stayed healthy, their families and descendants would keep eating it. Each area evolved pretty safe mixtures of foods. But as soon as organization got involved—pharaohs, kings, dukes, and eventually corporations—they decided people should eat what gave them the best profit. The health of the people varied according to the convenience of who was in charge of the economy.

Since World War II—well, the Germans really started it in the First World War when they were blockaded. They had an advanced chemical industry and started learning how to make substitute materials for war and civilian survival. By the Second World War, they had developed pretty good imitation foods. For example, they fed their Russian prisoners of war on sawdust bread that resembled bread but had no nutritional value.

The FDA saw the success of that and decided to agree with the corporations. Even though in the 1940s they had said that gums weren't decent for human consumption because they produced biological damage, they finally agreed it was okay to add fillers like sawdust, cellulose, seaweed gum, and various tree gums. A baker recently said that he hadn't realized he could make a good loaf of bread with 18% sawdust.

**John Barkhausen:** That's astounding. I remember when the fiber craze hit the general culture. There were breads in our supermarket advertising extra fiber, and in the ingredients, was sawdust.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Now I think they have a more diplomatic way of saying that. They call it "nutritional fiber." Anytime there's a pleasant-sounding, unfamiliar ingredient in the food, it's probably a waste product from industry. For example, chitin and various waste products from the shrimp industry are now used in food and health foods. If you look at each industry and see what they had a problem getting rid of, you'll see the food technologists learning how to make people eat it.

**John Barkhausen:** So the food waste just gets recycled into the system again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. The EPA was receiving complaints about insect infestation and the mountains of pulp waste from the orange juice industry. They told the industry to do something with their horrendous quantities of pulp. By using microbial enzymes, they found they could make it water-soluble and create creamy, pulpy, fibrous orange juice. But it happens to be a chemical that would never occur in the natural fruit, and it has very unpredictable health results in the intestine because it's something people would never have been exposed to naturally.

The fish industry had a similar interaction with the EPA. They were either dumping their fish processing waste into the ocean or hauling it inland for landfill, but it was so stinky the EPA told them to find other ways to dispose of it. That's where they came up with fish protein powders for famine areas or food additives, and fish oil—the fat and oil and protein used in health foods.

**John Barkhausen:** The saying I've heard is, "The solution to pollution is distribution." This brings us back to convincing people to eat things as food when they otherwise might not think it is. One culture will eat something that's completely abhorrent to another. For example, they eat insects in Africa and consider them a delicacy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Once when I was visiting friends in Mexico, I ate with them and there was a nice little thing that was sort of like a salmon cake patty—a mildly fishy tasting thing. I asked what it was, and they said they would tell me after I finished. It was a mosquito cake made of mosquito larvae.

**John Barkhausen:** You're kidding. They can skim off enough larvae to make a cake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They have very fine nets especially for them. It was in the eastern side near Xalapa.

**John Barkhausen:** How did that sit in your stomach after you learned what it was?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very well. It tasted just like eating a salmon patty.

**John Barkhausen:** How do we decide what food is? It sounds like you're saying that we're told at this point what is food and what isn't, and our instincts aren't really working.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's the thought process. One of the ugliest Mexican food products is the fungus-infected corn kernel that makes a big blue swelling on the corn cob. It's a mushroom growing in the corn, but it stimulates a tumor in the corn, so it's somewhere between a tumor and a fungus. But it makes a very pleasant, semi-mushroom tasting material. It is a traditional food from a very old source that occurs spontaneously, but I guess they can infect corn to make it industrially now.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you feel like a lot of the foods that we eat now are influenced by industrial marketing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Almost entirely. About 40 or 50 years ago, I read that the food industry had been testing various things against their panel of experts. They found that the public taste preferred artificial flavors over real flavors in things like ice cream, after they had been so trained.

**John Barkhausen:** Since you mentioned ice cream, I know that at one time the ice cream lobby obtained an exemption from the law regarding declaring ingredients. They can say "artificial flavors" and it's basically a bunch of chemicals.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's still the general practice. Worse than that, they don't even have to mention on the label something which is actually present if it was mostly removed. They call it a "processing aid" or "incidental ingredient." Even though they intended to remove the bulk of it, some of it is there and can cause allergic or toxic reactions, but they don't have to list it.

Even if everyone is following those extremely useless rules of the FDA, apparently the industry doesn't take the FDA very seriously. I've bought vanilla ice cream from companies that claimed "all natural ingredients." Sometimes it would have a very intense strawberry flavor. Other times, the vanilla ice cream didn't have the black flecks but was dark brown, chocolate-colored, yet absolutely vanilla tasting. That proved they use brown coloring, pink coloring, and artificial flavoring instead of the natural ingredients they claim.

**John Barkhausen:** A lot of ice cream makers use thickeners like carrageenan, locust bean gum, and guar gum. Many people have allergic reactions to foods; could these gums be the cause rather than the milk?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The FDA recognized that problem 60 years ago, and the literature is full of published reactions to all of those gums. Carrageenan and alginate from seaweed are probably the worst. Carrageenan is recognized to be carcinogenic to the intestine and liver and to produce inflammation. It's a standard lab method for producing arthritis or inflammation of any organ they want to study.

The assumption is that if it only irritates the intestine and causes cancer in the liver, that is tolerable. But they are neglecting that these particles are passed through the intestine. When a person is under stress, bacteria and larger particles—up to the size of a red blood cell—can go right from the intestine into the bloodstream. The immune system then has direct interaction with them.

Small additives aren't going to stay entirely in the intestine. For example, particles of silicon dioxide—which people say is just harmless sand—are used to create viscous consistency in cosmetics, soaps, and foods. It's basically a very finely powdered glass. At a certain size, they very easily go from the blood into tissue cells and cause sensitization. Scleroderma is probably the most common thing caused by the silica reaction.

**John Barkhausen:** In your newsletter, you mentioned carrageenan causes a pseudo-latex allergy reaction. Can you talk about that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the arguments is that in its undegraded form, fresh out of the seaweed, carrageenan doesn't cause cancer. But when you eat it, bacteria in the intestine break it down. The broken-down form of carrageenan is recognized as carcinogenic. Regulatory agencies reveal they are serving industry convenience rather than protecting the public by ignoring this.

The reaction to latex is a general phenomenon. Plants have defense reactions. When a bug bites a plant, it expresses an enzyme called chitinase to dissolve the bug. When you stress a plant—by growing it in a monoculture or forcing it with unbalanced fertilizers—it increases these defensive toxins. A plant growing in the wild might not be allergenic, but once cultivated under extreme conditions, it will produce things such as toxic latex.

**John Barkhausen:** So people are allergic to latex because the plant is producing a toxic chemical to protect itself?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Bananas and rubber trees were the first identified with this cross-reaction. People who have a reaction to surgical gloves often have a reaction to bananas. Those people will likely react to other industrialized fruits, like kiwis. They are recognizing that a person allergic to bananas is likely to be allergic to several other similar, industrialized fruits.

**John Barkhausen:** Why are some people affected by those plant toxins and others not?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The person who is under stress is more susceptible. Estrogen induces a similar protein in humans. Things like estrogen, which intensify the stress reaction, are increasing in industrialized populations. The biological function of estrogen is to stress and activate tissues to get them growing quickly. But when we are chronically exposed to industrial estrogens, it activates our stress reactions in the intestine, making it more permeable.

It also activates enzymes in the intestine that overlap with the gluten molecule. Our immune system, reacting to an overdose of estrogen, doesn't distinguish that from gluten. So, gluten interacts with chronic estrogen exposure to produce serious chronic inflammatory symptoms.

That enzyme happens to be a cross-linker. When extracted from microorganisms, it can be used to tie any protein together. The food industry uses this enzyme to make artificial fish and meat products. If you order a fish patty at a fast-food restaurant, you're probably getting a mixture of seaweed gum and fish waste fragments glued together with this enzyme. It's known as "restructured meat."

We accidentally ate squid patties once. I cooked two of them, and they shrank from about five inches across down to the size of a silver dollar. We got really sick. I found out they use seaweed jelly (alginate or carrageenan) and grind up waste products into a mush, then add the cross-linking enzyme to coagulate it.

**John Barkhausen:** I suspect that is how they achieve the uniform look of deli hams and turkey loaves.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And in studies comparing various foods, processed meats are consistently one of the most carcinogenic categories.

**John Barkhausen:** Those meats are also full of additives and preservatives.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and the aging process itself. They add deodorants to change the smell of aged meat, but the practice of aging meat probably makes it more carcinogenic. When meat starts to rot, the odor chemicals are polyamines—specifically cadaverine and putrescine. These stimulate cell growth and are connected with cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** Around here, people raise their own cattle and hang them for about five days at 40 degrees to make the meat tender and flavorful.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It definitely gets more flavor, but that's mostly advertising. I eat more meat when I'm in Mexico because it tastes better. In small towns without refrigerators, they sell it off the carcass within the first few days. It always tastes really fresh. In US supermarkets, food technologists say it gets tender after two weeks, so they don't sell it before then. But by then, it develops putrescine, spermidine, and cadaverine, which are mildly toxic and possibly carcinogenic.

**John Barkhausen:** I thought Europe was averse to chemical treatment of animals.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They are, but recently there has been evidence that they're treating living animals with big doses of glucocorticosteroids to break down the fiber while they're alive to tenderize the meat. Even though rules are in place, you can't trust anything from a big corporation because the FDA is doing its best to look the other way.

**John Barkhausen:** You said growing crops in monoculture makes plants produce more toxic chemicals. Is there a better way?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If the plant grows more slowly, the soil will more naturally release chemicals the plant can select from. When growers add chemicals to stimulate fast maturation, it distorts the physiology of the plant.

There have been experiments where corn was fertilized heavily with potassium in one case and phosphate in another. The potassium fertilizer caused the plants to emphasize their tassels (male parts), and the phosphate fertilizer made them overproduce the cob (female parts). You can change the sex ratio of the plant just by pushing one fertilizer. Since the plant's physiology is warped, it produces toxic chemicals defensively.

Roots generally have fewer defensive toxic chemicals because they defend against fungus and bacteria in the ground. The upper parts—leaves, stems, and seeds—defend against grazing animals and insects. So, the worst toxins are in the leaves and seeds. Fruits are evolved to be delicious and non-toxic to encourage animals to spread the seeds. Therefore, fruits are almost always the safest part, roots are second safest, seeds are the worst, and leaves are intermediate.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that why so many people have an intolerance to gluten and flour products?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Storage proteins in seeds pack nitrogen into a small space. Those proteins also have the added benefit to the plant of being irritating, indigestible, or toxic to predators.

**John Barkhausen:** What is your take on the effect of genetic engineering on food quality?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The most common thing is to put an insecticide protein into the plant. People and animals are known to react allergically to a strange protein that wasn't there before. Allergy is the main thing to worry about with meddling with the genetic composition of plants.

**John Barkhausen:** Allergies seem to be on the rise. What is your take on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All major allergic symptoms are increasing. Some studies show that unsaturated omega-3 fatty acids in a woman's diet when she's pregnant seriously increase the allergies of the baby.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you explain that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Seeds have more omega-6 fats, which are a little more stable. The omega-3s are often in leaves or algae in the ocean (fish oils). These are highly unstable.

A French group decided that since the adult brain contains fish oil-like fats, babies weren't getting enough. They set up an experiment to demonstrate they could make the fetus learn faster by feeding the mother fish oil. What they found was that nervous function was impaired in the women who ate the fish oil. Other studies showed the babies would be more allergic. The babies were also smaller, implying their brains and bodies grew less, probably because of the anti-progesterone effect of the fish oil. A population with suppressed progesterone and thyroid is going to be a more allergic, stressed population.

**John Barkhausen:** You're saying fish oil is included in the same category as vegetable oils like safflower and cottonseed oil?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A big difference is that the seed oils (omega-6) have a tail of five saturated carbon atoms, making them slightly more stable. Fish oils (omega-3) have only two stable carbons at the end, so they oxidize much more easily.

**John Barkhausen:** In the few minutes we have left, what foods should people be focusing on for pleasure and health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Fruits, if you know they're grown in a safe environment. It's hard to find ripe fruit in stores, but ripe oranges or tangerines are very safe. Eggs are safe if you can find ones that weren't fed linseed or soy oil, which gives them a fishy taste. Just go by the taste. Sweet oranges, eggs that taste like eggs, and meats that taste fresh.

With milk, it's important to judge the taste because of the different feeds cows get. Even organic milk can be allergenic if the cow is eating allergenic weeds.

**John Barkhausen:** What about cheese?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You have to be cautious because they are putting seaweed and other gums in them to increase water content. They can add 30% to the weight just by putting more jelly in it. I used to eat a Wisconsin Parmesan, but suddenly it got soft and moist and caused bowel inflammation. Now I use real Parmigiano-Reggiano or strange ethnic cheeses from Greece or Italy that still use traditional methods.

**John Barkhausen:** We found a Greek strained yogurt called Fage recently that seems good.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, it seems they've got most of the lactic acid out of it. The main thing wrong with ordinary yogurt is that it has lots of lactic acid, so it's basically the same as cottage cheese regarding safety. If you can strain the lactic acid, it's a good food.

**John Barkhausen:** You don't think it's a good idea to eat extra lactic acid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It should be minimized. That's why I don't advocate aerobic exercise. I think I'm going to do a newsletter on the role of lactic acid in cancerization. It also promotes inflammation, fibrosis, and degenerative diseases.

**John Barkhausen:** Well, I look forward to that newsletter. Ray, thanks so much for coming on Politics and Science today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: Politics & Science: Progesterone Part 1
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Hi, everyone. The following show with Dr. Raymond Peat was recorded on January 22, 2012. It's about progesterone. Welcome to *Politics and Science*. I'm your host, John Barkhausen. Today, once again, I'm delighted to say that Ray Peat is here to join me. Dr. Peat has a PhD in biology and has done extensive research in the fields of physiology and endocrinology. Is that enough, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, that's enough.

**John Barkhausen:** I was just saying that we've never really touched on the subject of progesterone in a pure form. I was looking back through your newsletters on your website, raypeat.com. What percent of your letters are up there at this point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I have written 300 and some, and I think there are only about 75 on the website, so about a quarter. The search device on the website helps to find them. If you put in "progesterone," you'll find lots of newsletters that talk about it.

**John Barkhausen:** I thought maybe we could start the show just talking about how you first got interested in progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I had been writing about it somewhat in the 70s, but the Proposition 65 thing in California, calling it a carcinogen, was the occasion for me writing a new bunch of newsletters a few years ago.

Before I came to Oregon, I had been studying linguistics. Moving from Mexico to Montana and then Oregon, I noticed a great change in the way my health worked and realized that it was the absence of sunlight—dark, cloudy weather. I saw the same thing happening to all the women I knew during the winter. They would get PMS and what I called "winter sickness."

At that time, I was aware of old experiments where people noticed that sparrows in Times Square mated all year round because of the bright light. In other species, the embryo is formed but doesn't implant in the uterus until the progesterone reaches a certain level. A certain day length of light exposure raises the progesterone and allows fertility to proceed.

I noticed that during bright, sunny, long days, my vitamin A requirement increased tremendously. I came to understand that the sex hormones go up in the spring with long hours of light. Vitamin A is massively used in producing pregnenolone and progesterone. Right at the beginning of moving to Oregon, I was seeing that progesterone and daylight were very powerful on the emotions and body functions. Premenstrual mood changes were evident even in men; typically, men coming from a sunny climate would be depressed all winter living in cloudy Oregon.

**John Barkhausen:** How did you link sunlight to progesterone? Was it something that was already discovered?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One night I went to sleep reading a book with a bright light shining in my face. I woke up starting to get pimples. I realized that the light shining on my eyes, activating my brain, had done something to affect my metabolism. As I read to understand how the light affected my skin, I ran across the winter fertility of sparrows and the springtime implantation of animals. I realized that everyone from birds to men experience the driving of their hormones by day length. The first steroid made is either pregnenolone or progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think there's an adjustment made whereby even with less light you can produce progesterone, or are all of us in the north depressed for that reason?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We just get used to being depressed. If you look at Scandinavian movies, you see that depression seems to be the rule.

**John Barkhausen:** When did you become aware that progesterone was useful therapeutically for cancer and other things?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was intending to study nerve biology. The very first few weeks at the university, I realized what dogmatists the brain and nerve biology people were. So I went looking around, poking into all the labs, and saw that the reproductive physiology people were open-minded and actually studying things rather than trying to confirm their dogma. I immediately switched over from nerve biology to reproductive biology.

**John Barkhausen:** What gave it away that they were open-minded?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Talking to the nerve biology people, their personalities were absolutely militaristic, rigid, and close-minded. The money went along with that—big research grants. The reproductive physiology had grants but very low prestige in the department. People were very relaxed and had a willingness to learn.

Arnold Soderwall was the person in charge of the female reproductive end. Soderwall was the link with previous students, continuing a tradition that started in the 30s and 40s. There were three graduate students working in the lab. Bev Stockton was working on implantation, which involved an age-related delay in the production of progesterone. Terry Parkening later shifted over to see that falling progesterone and excess estrogen were essential changes of aging infertility. I was working on the oxidative changes in the aging reproductive system.

As I worked with the chemicals, I noticed that handling progesterone cured my tendency to have hangnails. Being careless in the lab and getting some of the progesterone on my hands, I noticed that my hangnails disappeared and have never come back.

**John Barkhausen:** So even though it's considered to be somewhat of a female hormone, it also has an important role in males as well?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Two different groups observed that an intrauterine device (IUD) for contraception often caused systemic health problems related to falling progesterone. Animal studies showed that if you put a slight wound into the uterus, signals travel up to the ovary and block the production of progesterone, because the system recognizes that it isn't wise to get pregnant when you have a wounded uterus.

At the same time, another group found that men who had a vasectomy often suffered very serious effects, like impotency. They found that these men had very low progesterone. Replacing their progesterone levels up to normal cured their symptoms. Very often just one dose was all that was needed to start the ovaries in women or the gonads in the man to begin producing the normal amount.

**John Barkhausen:** And of course, you've mentioned before that progesterone is the hormone of fertility that promotes life.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the basic implantation stabilizer. Estrogen creates a release of histamine throughout the body, but especially where it's concentrated in the uterus. The histamine creates a site of inflammation. That inflammation prevents survival of the implanted embryo. Progesterone turns off the histamine and estrogen and makes it possible to deliver oxygen and sugar to the implanted embryo. It's the shift towards oxygen and sugar delivery that makes progesterone the preserver of pregnancy.

Interestingly, people have removed animals' ovaries at the time of fertilization and given them different hormones. They found that testosterone worked to preserve pregnancy by delivering oxygen and sugar to the implanted embryo. So you could say that testosterone is a progestin in the sense of supporting pregnancy.

The term "progestins" or "progestogens" implies that these chemicals act to preserve pregnancy the way progesterone does. But in fact, the synthetic so-called progestins are used in birth control pills exactly because they *don't* support pregnancy. They've got the naming system very confused; testosterone functions potentially as a progestin, while the so-called progestins are really anti-progestational chemicals.

**John Barkhausen:** It does seem bizarre that estrogen is considered to be the female hormone when that's actually the hormone of infertility and abortions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The estrogen industry contributed to that. It was known from the late 1930s that estrogen is an abortifacient—it kills the embryo. The industry didn't want their product known to be killing embryos, so they claimed that it stopped ovulation. That was invented just in time for them to come on the market with birth control pills. It was a complete fabrication.

Progesterone turned out to be such a basic, simple substance—the first steroid made out of cholesterol—that only that single molecule has those functions. In the 1930s, they discovered that soot could be extracted to form almost an infinite number of estrogenic substances, allowing the industry to patent various synthetics. They wanted the idea that it was a female hormone for sales purposes. However, it was known that estrogen is actually essential for male traits to develop. Testosterone has to turn into estrogen before it androgenizes the brain. So estrogen could be called the male hormone better than the female hormone because it causes hair growth.

**John Barkhausen:** Looking back at science history, when was progesterone discovered and how has it been used?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the early 30s the molecule was identified. Armour was the company that made the corpus luteum powder from pregnant pigs. I think I was probably one of the early progesterone babies, my mother having been infertile and taking the Armour corpus luteum product.

**John Barkhausen:** What is the corpus luteum?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the follicle ovulates, that area turns into steroid-producing cells and progesterone becomes the main steroid produced. In humans, that is the basic source of progesterone for the first nine or ten weeks of pregnancy. With each pregnancy, some of those cells remain in the ovary. So a woman who has been pregnant eight times will have higher residual progesterone levels and will live much longer on average than a woman who hasn't had so many pregnancies.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that perhaps why some women who get fibroids notice that the fibroids go away if they get pregnant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Progesterone was recommended for many years for treating fibroids. Partly that involves increased thyroid function. Progesterone is needed for the thyroid to work, and the thyroid working causes the liver to lower the estrogen level systemically. Sometimes just one dose of progesterone is all it takes to free the thyroid to function, stimulate new progesterone synthesis, and lower estrogen.

**John Barkhausen:** You've talked before about estrogen and progesterone opposing each other.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen's first action is to block the use of oxygen, which causes the cell to take up water. Overloading cells with water causes them to go into a growth inflammation state where they start multiplying. If that exposure continues, you increase the risk of breast and pituitary tumors. When birth control pills were first on the market in the 1960s with big doses of estrogen, there was a terrific epidemic of pituitary tumors producing prolactin.

**John Barkhausen:** How was progesterone used therapeutically?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1940s, Russell Marker devised a way to make it from the yam steroid, making it cheap. But the drug companies created synthetic forms that could be patented. They argued that real progesterone is destroyed in the stomach, so you have to take their synthetic product. They convinced doctors that natural progesterone didn't work orally, even though companies were selling tablets that worked fine.

One of the problems was that it's extremely insoluble. The only way you can market an injectable product is to use a solvent like benzyl benzoate or benzyl alcohol. Benzyl alcohol is a nerve toxin, but progesterone's powerfully detoxifying effects overrode those poisonous effects.

Katharina Dalton's results were amazing. She treated premenstrual syndrome, which was related to the tendency to miscarry. She gave injections to cure the PMS and continued giving them during pregnancy. Her patients' babies, who usually came from working-class backgrounds with average IQs of 90, tended to average 130 IQ after progesterone treatment. The intelligence of the babies corresponded to the amount of progesterone she gave the mothers.

**John Barkhausen:** What did you do after you left the lab?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was doing nutrition consulting. I was hoping that doctors would come to understand why they shouldn't give estrogen. There's really no such thing as an estrogen deficiency. Any tissue that's injured will become a source of estrogen production. The absence of estrogen in the bloodstream often means there's an excess of estrogen inside cells. Progesterone causes the estrogen to be released from inside cells into the bloodstream where it can be eliminated.

The more a tissue is injured or aged, the more likely it is to have aromatase inside making estrogen. An injured breast, an injured uterus, or fat tissue all become sources of estrogen.

**John Barkhausen:** So as we get older, we're all producing more estrogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A person tends to lose muscle and bone and replace it with fat and connective tissue. Those tissues become sources of inflammatory materials and estrogen. Progesterone inactivates the enzymes that cause tissues to catch estrogen and activates the enzymes that send estrogen back out.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** What got me started recommending it directly to people was a 52-year-old woman who had been epileptic from the age of 35. A neurologist had given her anti-seizure drugs for migraines, which made her unable to teach school. When she stopped the drugs, she had actual seizures. By the time I saw her, she was considered hopelessly demented.

I told her about the transdermal use of progesterone. She had inflamed, arthritic fingers, so she dipped her fingers in a beaker of progesterone oil. Four or five days later, her fingers were not arthritic anymore, she felt fine, and she could find her way home. She enrolled back in the university and got her master's degree with straight A's. Her seizures stopped completely.

**John Barkhausen:** That's remarkable.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After that, I started telling people about the topical use. About 30 people had essentially immediate recovery from various types of arthritis. Another woman with multiple sclerosis and optic neuritis, who had been paralyzed and blind for weeks at a time, lectured to my endocrine class about how progesterone injections helped her.

**John Barkhausen:** Are there any cautionary tales about using progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a man takes a very big dose, it has a "cold shower effect"—it simply displaces testosterone temporarily. Also, it is an anesthetic. Once, a friend accidentally put a spoonful of it in a margarita, and I couldn't feel where my hands and feet were for about half an hour. I don't think it should be used in more than a 10% solution.

**John Barkhausen:** That reminds me of the Wall Street Journal article about brain-damaged people.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was known in the 50s as a brain-preserving hormone. It's a growth factor for nerves and an anti-inflammatory, anti-edema agent. Edema is one of the factors that kills brain cells after injury. Progesterone stops the damage and promotes remyelinization of the fibers. In the 70s, I advocated that everyone should carry a bottle with them in case they were in an accident as first aid.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, we are out of time. We've been talking to Dr. Raymond Peat, endocrinologist and physiologist. You can find out more about Ray at his website, raypeat.com. Ray, thanks so much for being on.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, very good.

**John Barkhausen:** Thanks a lot, Ray. Bye bye.

title: Politics & Science: Progesterone Part 2
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Welcome to Politics and Science. I'm your host, John Barkhausen, and I'm very happy that Dr. Raymond Peat is returning to the show. This is a follow-up show about progesterone from the one we did last week. For those who don't know, Ray Peat has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialty in physiology, and he's done extensive research in the fields of endocrinology and science history.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've been reading in both of those areas since I was about 14 or 15 years old.

**John Barkhausen:** You mentioned before that when you were a little kid you were reading the *Little Blue Books*. When did you first encounter Kropotkin? This is completely unrelated to our topic, but I was curious about that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Besides the *Little Blue Books*, he was the first really political argument I read. His book on cooperation in animals as a basis for his anarchy theory—I think I was 14 when I found that at the library. That shaped my thinking both in politics and in biology.

**John Barkhausen:** Back to the subject of progesterone. We left off last week talking about the *Wall Street Journal* article regarding a doctor who had done research on the effect of progesterone on brain damage through accidents and strokes. He found it a very effective therapy; people recovered twice as fast, and there were no negative side effects.

I asked you last week about any negative side effects you knew about progesterone, and you mentioned the danger of being over-anesthetized by it. Is that a danger of actually stopping your heart if you took too much, or is that just a risk of getting into an accident if you fell asleep?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think what it would do first is stop breathing, but up to a certain point, it stimulates breathing. It's probably somewhat of an antidote to things like morphine because progesterone, as long as it's within several hundred milligrams at a time or per day, is like an imitation of pregnancy, where it stimulates breathing.

However, up in the pharmacological range of 3,000 or 4,000 milligrams all at once, instead of being a stimulant to respiration, it just puts everything to sleep. I think that would include the respiratory system at some very high level.

In Mexico, some students were experimenting with the idea that maybe progesterone works like morphine because of those sedative effects. They combined naloxone, the anti-morphine drug, with progesterone, and their experimental rat died. It was okay on a given amount of either of them alone. That pretty much said that progesterone isn't acting like morphine, because the anti-morphine chemical seemed to exaggerate the anesthetic effect of progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Is it the equivalent of saying that maybe water supports life, but if you drink too much of it, it can potentially kill you? What's the range of the dose we're talking about for overdosing on progesterone?
