**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No one really has done that. My students' rat was the only death that I know of, even experimentally. In the 1940s, Hans Selye told his technicians to experiment with very big doses of progesterone. After doing some experiments, they said those high doses had killed the rats. He didn't believe it. He said, "What did you do with them?" They went to the garbage and fished them out. He published photographs holding them by the skin on their back; they looked sort of like a wet dish rag. Just the most relaxed rat you ever saw. But they weren't dead. They were just deeply sleepy. His technicians had thought they died. So, I'm not even sure that my students were not mistaken about the naloxone and progesterone combination, but they *thought* the rat had died.

**John Barkhausen:** I see. So it's only potentially fatal in enormous quantities.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**John Barkhausen:** You also said that vasectomies in men tended to lower progesterone. What's the mechanism behind that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It wasn't consistent. When men had very distinct symptoms following vasectomies, they studied what was going on and found that the ones who had the symptoms had very low to almost zero progesterone. They recovered when they gave them progesterone. However, most of the men having vasectomies didn't have any symptoms.

My interpretation is that it's a biological analog to what's reasonable in the female. If the female has an infection in the uterus or tubes, for example, it's biologically reasonable to turn off progesterone production so that pregnancy can't happen. Irritation in the uterus or tube in the female causes sterility by turning off progesterone and increasing estrogen. I think the event in the man who had the bad reaction to vasectomy was the biological equivalent of a signal traveling up the ducts, probably to the testicle, maybe to the pituitary, turning off steroid production.

**John Barkhausen:** It's interesting that these hormones seem very complicated. When we try to name them by one purpose, it gets confusing. We think of progesterone as the female fertility hormone, but men are actually producing it in their testicles or pituitary. And the negative effects they were experiencing from their vasectomies—wasn't impotence one of the negative effects?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I've seen several men—I don't remember whether they had vasectomies or not—who were suffering from impotency. It was immediately resolved by taking very small doses of progesterone a couple of times. It's sort of like priming the pump. Progesterone has a positive feedback loop, apparently in men as well as in women.

People have experimented with slices of either ovary tissue or adrenal tissue, which makes some progesterone. They found in both cases that if you add a little bit of progesterone, it increases the organ's production of progesterone. That is positive feedback, which is unusual in hormone regulation.

**John Barkhausen:** That indicates to me that the body doesn't see it as something you can get too much of.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** From that kind of engineering, you would think that the body believes that more is always better. In the case of progesterone, it seems to be what happens in pregnancy. If a person is having some biological problem where their progesterone drops off and they start bleeding during the pregnancy, there have been studies where they would give one shot of progesterone early in the pregnancy. These were women who habitually miscarried or had monthly bleeding throughout the pregnancy and delivered prematurely.

I think two-thirds of the women maintained full, increasing production every week, higher than the preceding week, until they had a normal nine-month delivery. Another 30% required a second injection several weeks later, and they too went back to full production. There was a small group which didn't recover so completely.

**John Barkhausen:** I know a lot of people are going in for fertility therapy in this day and age. Does progesterone still play a big role in modern fertility therapies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but very few of the clinics that specialize in that really understand. If they would read more animal research, they would understand people better. But there's really a medical bias against endocrine science based on animals.

**John Barkhausen:** Why is that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the marketing has done it through 40 or 50 years. The estrogen industry said, "Don't pay any attention to the fact that estrogen causes clotting, heart attacks, cancer, brain damage, and so on. That's just in animals. It has just the opposite effects in humans."

**John Barkhausen:** That's interesting. It does seem that they've thrown out a lot of the earlier research that you write about from the early 20th century.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When the industry wants to sell something that they can't demonstrate in humans, then they will base the whole thing on animal experiments. Like the osteoporosis issue—they found there was no evidence they could demonstrate bone improvement with estrogen in people. So they looked around at different animals. They tried it on beagle dogs and found that it caused *more* osteoporosis in dogs. So they forgot about that.

They looked around and found that in rodents, it could seem to cause increased bone strength. But it happens that in rodents, even cortisol can increase bone strength. There are some situations, like prolactin in rats, which will increase progesterone, whereas in humans it generally decreases it. If you look at the interactions, it's really all the same principles that apply in people, but rodents are generally nocturnal animals and we aren't. You have to take into account what time of day you give the injections because you're either intensifying or weakening their normal rhythms. By using animals with an upside-down rhythm compared to humans, you can sometimes get very nice upside-down results.

**John Barkhausen:** You're saying that the pharmaceutical companies paying for these studies are actually engineering them that way on purpose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They like rat experiments when they can be arranged to sell a product, but they want to forget completely about the dog experiments which caused only bad effects.

**John Barkhausen:** Going back to estrogen and progesterone, I was curious if there's any effect on estrogen or progesterone production when somebody gets a tubal ligation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right at the same time that the impotency experiment saw that in men, another group saw exactly that effect in the result of the tubal ligation within just a month or two of that publication. That really helped to explain how IUDs work. Animal experiments had been demonstrating for years that if you want to have the animal become infertile, you just put a little suture in the uterus. That's usually all it takes. The signal travels up from the slightly injured uterus to turn off the ovary's progesterone production. Injuring the tubes does the same thing—not always, but often.

**John Barkhausen:** So that could lead to a progesterone deficiency in somebody who's either had an IUD or a tubal ligation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes.

**John Barkhausen:** Let's pick up where we left off in your life's path. You were teaching at naturopathic colleges after getting your PhD, and you had decided to start recommending progesterone use to some of your nutritional patients.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was teaching endocrinology at the Naturopath School, but I was doing mostly nutritional counseling at home. I found that it involved more and more hormone interactions with the foods. When I saw two or three women with such absolute recoveries from just small amounts of progesterone, I realized that I would basically be injuring people if I didn't give them the true information that I knew about in animals and was starting to see in humans.

Over a period of two or three years in Eugene, I had spoken to enough women about the effects of thyroid and progesterone on their symptoms that the local gynecologists turned 180 degrees in their practice. There were so many dozens of their patients saying that they wouldn't take estrogen and insisted on getting a prescription for progesterone or thyroid. It took a couple of years, and doctors saw that their business was being affected, so they totally reversed their practices. That went on until those doctors retired. Then I think the pressure from the industry and profession probably reverted the situation.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like those doctors were pretty open-minded.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, very, very closed-minded. It was a terrible experience for the first dozen or so women who went to them. Just awful personal attacks. The doctors would tell the patients not to come back because they had "personality defects" if they wouldn't accept their advice.

**John Barkhausen:** Oh dear. We're talking about the late 70s and early 80s at this point?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, between '76 and '82.

**John Barkhausen:** I have a quote here from the report you referred to last time by Carla Rothenberg, which is available on the web. She wrote a report when she was at Harvard about the history of hormone replacement in this country.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Barbara Seaman was my contemporary in studying estrogen and progesterone, and she wrote a lot of good stuff. *Women and the Crisis in Sex Hormones* was one of her titles. She was very good at debating; by knowing a thousand times more, when she got the opportunity to debate someone from Yale Medical School, for example, they ended up looking like complete ignoramuses. She was very influential against estrogen and for progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Here's the ad campaign for hormone replacement therapy back in the 50s and 60s. An ad for Hoffman-La Roche's Menrium says:

> "His wife has a lot of different menopausal symptoms, but only a few really irritate him. Her hot flashes, her vertigo, her palpitations, that's her problem. What really bothers him is her nervousness, her irritability, and her excessive anxiety, often expressed by endless book shuffling, chain smoking, and reading lamp insomnia. Menrium takes care of the vasomotor symptoms as well as the emotional symptoms. This means the symptoms that bother his wife the most and the symptoms that irritate him the most."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Barbara Seaman went over advertising and public relations very thoroughly. At one point she mentioned that Hitler had tested estrogen on people in the prison camps as a way to make them meek and submissive. She thought that was probably—if you put it in context with an advertisement like the one you read—a way to make a more obedient, servile wife.

**John Barkhausen:** You were helping people find out about progesterone. At some point, you patented a progesterone formulation, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A woman who lectured in my class, who had MS and optic neuritis, was using exclusively injectable progesterone. She was getting really big amounts of benzyl alcohol, which is nerve toxic. Hans Selye called it the "catatoxic" effect of progesterone and pregnenolone—that it helps the body destroy toxins and eliminate them. Progesterone's anti-toxic effect is so great that people were benefiting from these injections despite the vegetable oil and toxic solvent.

Sometimes, if a doctor didn't like those toxins in the injectable form, there was a micronized solution in water. But if they injected that in the hip, for example, the particle would cause irritation that destroyed fat cells, leaving a dent. Those "water-wettable" solutions weren't just progesterone; there was a carbohydrate-like molecule attached to the progesterone particle, making it wettable. Those particles are toxic.

Knowing about the problems with injection and the medical indoctrination that stomach acid destroys progesterone—even though the manufacturing involves boiling the steroid in acid, so your stomach couldn't make a dent in it—I decided to try something else. Since I had noticed that I could taste progesterone just by sticking my hand in the powder, I decided that if I could get doctors to use it on the skin, that would let them see what it really does.

On the first experiments, I would heat it in olive oil to get a high concentration. The olive oil would bring their blood levels up to a perfectly normal amount in less than an hour. I was thinking about old research in Italy explaining why vitamin E would protect against the sterility-producing effects of estrogen. They explained vitamin E's action as being a "progesterone sparer."

It made me think about what vitamin E is doing in the mitochondrion where progesterone is produced. I realized that for them to both act in and be produced in the mitochondrion, they have to be compatible in solubility. So I dropped some progesterone powder in vitamin E and saw that I could get a 50/50 solution with a very pure form of vitamin E. They were absolutely inter-soluble.

That was a compact, stable way to get doctors to start using transdermal progesterone. I told them about the effect in olive oil, but no one wanted to heat the solution up every time they applied it. With vitamin E, you could get a stable 5, 10, or 20% solution convenient to rub into the skin.

**John Barkhausen:** So even when it's dissolved in vitamin E, you don't have to heat it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You don't have to get it hot, just warming it so that it's thin enough to stir. Just stirring it at room temperature will do it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** However, you only absorb maybe 10% or 20% at best when you rub it into the skin. So after doctors were willing to prescribe it for their patients using it on the skin, I pointed out to them that they could take it orally and save about 80% of the cost.

**John Barkhausen:** Why is only 20% absorbed through the skin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It binds to the skin. As cells mature and prepare to shed, they collapse. Keratin fibers—protein that makes up part of the structure of the cell—are cross-linked and become a semi-tanned, hardened barrier to water. But they bind oil, so the oils in your skin link to these cross-linked keratin proteins and make a raincoat effect, closing off the surface to water. Those also bind progesterone very strongly. The progesterone will saturate those, and some of it passes on and gets into your deeper tissues, but a good part of it sticks on these superficial barrier cells and is then shed.

**John Barkhausen:** So it might be good for your skin, but if you're trying to get it in further, it's less efficient.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's more economical just to take it orally because when it's dissolved in oil, and you eat fat in your diet, your bile emulsifies it. It breaks down into very small particles about the size of a bacterium, called chylomicrons. These pass through intestinal cells into the lymphatic ducts—called lacteals because the absorbed fat particles give it a milky look. From there, it goes right into the bloodstream as little fat globules that circulate.

If you eat powdered progesterone, the cells of your intestine have the same enzymes that the liver has for adding sugar to hormone molecules and making them water-soluble. So when the crystalline progesterone hits your intestine cells directly, a lot of it is processed just as it would be in the liver. You lose a big part of your progesterone if you take it in the crystalline form. But when it's in the fat globule form, it bypasses the liver because it's taken up as these nutritional fat particles. Basically, something like 99% of it gets into your circulation quickly when you eat it in the oil form.

**John Barkhausen:** And it would be distributed in the same proportion that your circulation works?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Everywhere red blood cells go, these chylomicrons will circulate a few times.

**John Barkhausen:** When did you decide to patent it and what was your thinking on that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was constantly submitting articles to medical and science journals, and medical journals didn't want to have anything to do with it because they were doing business with the estrogen industry. Since I couldn't get anything published, I was having to give talks up and down the West Coast. I wanted to get the information out and figured that publishing it as a patent would be the only way I could get it on the record and openly distributed.

**John Barkhausen:** Was it difficult getting the patent?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. I wrote up the whole story and sent it in. The patent examiner, talking to me through a lawyer, said, "You can't say anything about cancer if you want to get the patent to issue." He said that's a standard rule; the only thing they really are concerned about regarding accuracy is a cancer claim. So I just deleted the things I said about what I had seen it do to cancer, and it went right through.

**John Barkhausen:** What is that prejudice against cancer claims?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just that it would be used as a marketing tool by the cancer industry. You can claim perpetual motion, free energy, all kinds of things in a patent—there are thousands of those crazy patents—but they have some standards regarding cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** Once you patented it, did you figure out some way to make it available to people?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I was mixing up some myself and selling it. John Lee, for example, was one of the first people who started buying my mixture. I tried to get various people to manufacture it over the years. I talked to all the big drug companies. They said, "No thanks."

About a year or two later, those drug companies came on the market with crystalline progesterone mixed with oil as they saw there was increasing interest. But probably my having the patent on vitamin E as a solvent prevented them from messing with that, even though it was the economically effective way. They would mix it with things like peanut oil.

**John Barkhausen:** That sounds rather toxic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and it's not a very good solvent.

**John Barkhausen:** Did you manage to set up your own production?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First I tried to get someone I had worked for in nutrition counseling. He got interested and dealt with the FDA, and we got a cream form available. Then he kept making it cheaper by buying things that weren't quite progesterone or weren't quite vitamin E. I wasn't connected with it after 1979.

Then I got friends to gradually develop their own business. Seeing what this other person had done with the FDA and how it's basically a crony system, I suggested that they just sell it to the doctors who were already interested. Those doctors would tell their friends. So there was never anything said about the product by the people who took it over. It wasn't necessary to ever say anything about its medical effects.

**John Barkhausen:** So basically you didn't make any claims.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No. When I was dealing with the FDA at various times, they looked at my books and said, "Those are federal crimes because you have a patent." They didn't prosecute me for writing the books, but they said that I couldn't say anything good about progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Even in your books, you couldn't say anything about it, even though it's not attached to the actual vial of progesterone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I asked them if they would put that in writing just because it seemed so ridiculous, and they said no. That's standard policy. They can be very nice people on the telephone, and then they talk to the lawyers and act like thugs when they put anything in writing.

**John Barkhausen:** I know when I first started looking for progesterone, I was able to find it in places like Vitamin Express. They were carrying "Dr. Ray Peat's Progest-E." At what point did you start managing to get it into some stores?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They got that out of John Lee's books. That's where they attached my name to it, which they weren't supposed to do. But John Lee described it as "Ray Peat's Progesterone," and so that's what the customers wanted. These places attached my name to it even though I hadn't been involved with it for 15 years at that time.

**John Barkhausen:** How is it sold under FDA supervision?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1991, I talked to a man at FDA headquarters in Bethesda who described himself as the head of the drug division. He said he had just read an internal historical article stating that in 1941, when they were getting around to enforcing the 1937 Food and Drug Act, they had a meeting in which they decided they would not take authority over natural hormones. He said, "I have it right here on my desk. I'll send you a copy when I can find it."

Months later, I got a letter, apparently written by his lawyers, which didn't mention that article at all. Under the Freedom of Information Act, I tried to get a copy of that meeting. After a very long time, I got some edited pages that cut off right at the point where they were going to say that.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like they want to take over the authority to regulate hormones. Is that what's going on?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 2002, the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) and another study announced that estrogen causes dementia, heart attacks, strokes, deep vein clots, lung embolisms, and such. The Premarin and Prempro industry sales went from over $2 billion down to a little over $1 billion over a period of about three years. That really got their attention.

They saw that progesterone sales had gone from a few tons a year up to many tons over just a few years as estrogen sales were falling. In 2005, Wyeth petitioned the FDA to prosecute pharmacists who were preparing natural progesterone. A little later, the FDA sent out letters telling pharmacists to stop making any claim for progesterone.

Also in 2005, lawsuits against progesterone started. A women's law group had a $300,000 donation—the source of which they wouldn't reveal—to claim that progesterone was causing breast cancer. They sued something like 60 companies that were selling topical progesterone. I think most of them just stopped selling it.

**John Barkhausen:** So they're going after progesterone in response to these studies blaming estrogen for serious health problems. What's the logic there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They saw the tremendous increase in progesterone sales exactly at the same time their estrogen sales were falling. It was obvious that women were shifting their menopause treatment from estrogen to progesterone. A 2009 lawsuit revealed that tens of millions of dollars were being spent by Wyeth to basically bribe doctors, medical journals, and researchers to say that estrogen is really the thing they should be using.

Looking at the University of Southern California, one of the schools that has published most of the anti-progesterone stuff since that WHI study, I looked up "estrogen" on their website and found about 150 items indicating how good estrogen was. Looking up "progesterone," I couldn't find a single article saying anything good about it.

Really, it wasn't estrogen alone that was causing those cancers in the WHI study; it was a combination with a synthetic progestin. That links into the need to attack progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** I see. They found it's basically a scapegoat by blaming progesterone for the problems of estrogen and the synthetic progestins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And that shows up in the whole history of how progesterone is labeled by pressure on the FDA. They found that the synthetic progestins were toxic and caused heart defects in babies. So the natural progesterone has to bear the label that it might cause birth defects, even though it's a completely different substance having completely opposite effects. It carries the label of these so-called progestins.

**John Barkhausen:** Labeling is a very powerful tool. Ray, we've come to the end of the hour. We still haven't gotten to the meat of what happened with progesterone under California law. Would you be willing to do a part three show to follow up?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The article on my website really covers it, but I don't know very much about what has happened since I wrote that article about five years ago.

**John Barkhausen:** I think your case regarding progesterone and the details of what happened in California is very illustrative of how our public health policy is going. Thanks so much for being on Politics and Science today. You can find out a lot more about Dr. Raymond Peat at **raypeat.com**. Thank you very much, Ray.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks. You too. Bye.

title: Politics & Science: Progesterone Part 3
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Hello and welcome to Politics and Science. I'm your host John Barkhausen and this is part three of a discussion about progesterone and Dr. Raymond Peat's work with progesterone over the years. Dr. Peat, for those who don't know, has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialty in physiology and has done a lot of research in the fields of endocrinology and science history. So Ray, welcome once again to Politics and Science.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hi.

**John Barkhausen:** In the last two shows, Ray, we covered some of the history of your work with progesterone. This week I'm hoping we'll be able to cover some of the politics and economic pressures affecting the science of progesterone. To start this off, in spite of its proven anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory effects, progesterone is now deemed a carcinogenic substance under California's Proposition 65. How did this turn of events come to pass?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The proposition says that you can sell carcinogens in any form that you want, but you just have to quote the law that says this is "known by the state of California to cause cancer and/or birth defects." It isn't a law against selling carcinogens, just that you have to warn against them.

It was partly driven by lawyers who were given the opportunity to enforce the law instead of the state; lawyers could collect the fines themselves. They chose to interpret the law to mean that the presence of anything which *could* be carcinogenic in any other situation makes a product require the warning. It ended up that parking lots had to be warned that they were carcinogenic. The public had to see a sign if they went into the parking lot.

**John Barkhausen:** What was the rationale for the parking lots, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was either the paving material or the fact that there were cars there emitting exhaust fumes. Chocolate producers were sued, manufacturers of drinking glasses that had paint on the outside, bread manufacturers, potato vendors, vegetables—anything. There was a whole wave of these insane prosecutions and lawyers made a lot of money.

The real function of that law, besides enriching lawyers, was to put the warnings everywhere—in the produce department of grocery stores, on apartment buildings, on fishing tackle and hardware—so that it became a joke. Everything was labeled a carcinogen. So, the carcinogens became invisible. The real carcinogens were submerged in this phony warning business. It was still legal to sell carcinogens, but since everything had the warning, the public basically wasn't warned against the *real* carcinogens.

**John Barkhausen:** That's a brilliant strategy on the part of business, it sounds like.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and very bad for the public. It had been brought to the attention of the Attorney General. The lawyers basically are in control of the government, so anything that would impair their ability to shake down the public doesn't interest the law enforcement people. I gathered some evidence and asked the Attorney General if nonprofit corporations aren't supposed to take money from industries to destroy their competitors. I gathered evidence that made it look pretty clear that was what was going on. They said if I can prove that they have committed a crime, they will investigate.

**John Barkhausen:** So you have to do all the work.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Then they would just investigate it and say they would prosecute it.

**John Barkhausen:** I didn't quite follow. What does a nonprofit have to do with it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The nonprofit organizations were being formed either as friends for lawyers to extort money, or... I couldn't prove it because I couldn't subpoena the documents, but on its surface, it looks very much like the competing industries are using those organizations to get rid of progesterone, among other products.

**John Barkhausen:** Sure. That makes perfect sense. So they basically form a cartel and go after their competitors. It sounds like the Wild West where anybody can deputize themselves and go after somebody else to enforce this very open-ended law.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, and the state prescribes the type of penalty that they can get. I think it was $50 for each drinking glass that was sold without a warning. A huge amount of money. Millions of dollars that lawyers have collected.

**John Barkhausen:** That's so Kafkaesque. It sounds ridiculous, but it actually has serious repercussions for somebody who's trying to sell a product that they think is helpful. What happens to you if you don't obtain the California seal of approval of not being a carcinogen?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you don't have 10 employees or more, the law doesn't apply to you. So you legally should be able to sell anything without a warning. Except the lawyers ignore that. They go ahead and extort money from people who, on the face of the law, it can't be applied to. First they threaten you, then they pursue you, then they keep it going for years.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's basically extortion.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If you Google "shakedown lawyers California," you'll get some of the history of it. The California lawyers were getting big money from foreign corporations, even outside the US, because they do business with California. California has such a big economy that they control the world.

**John Barkhausen:** When did you become aware that progesterone was going to be coming under the sights of these guys?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** About 10 or 15 years ago, some of the manufacturers started labeling the progesterone itself "known by California to be a carcinogen."

**John Barkhausen:** So it was already a done deal when you first heard about it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was 1987 when the California review happened. The Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) is what California's board is called. They weren't willing to give me the names of the people who were their "qualified experts" who made those decisions.

The law allows them to automatically list it if the World Health Organization or National Toxicology Program lists it. But in this case, they decided to have their board of qualified experts look at the relevant evidence. Out of thousands of publications on the issue of cancer and progesterone, they picked out about a dozen articles that they said were the relevant, decisive evidence.

Of those, several of them weren't even progesterone. They were birth control pills and things that contained no progesterone at all. They listed them as the relevant evidence, but when I got them to send me copies, they weren't even about progesterone in several cases. And the ones that *did* involve progesterone in the research, every one of them was totally incompetent in terms of toxicology, science, or cancer research. They were clearly manipulated to get a case against progesterone, but they failed in every case.

They had only one outside person testify during the meeting: Richard Edgren. They asked him why he had chosen to testify, and he said, "Because progesterone isn't a carcinogen." He went over some of the studies and mentioned that one of the studies using non-progesterone chemicals had produced some tumors that *weren't* metastatic. He wasn't talking about progesterone in that moment. But the chairman of the committee heard him say "metastatic," even though he had said they *weren't*. Since the topic of the meeting was progesterone—even though Edgren wasn't talking about progesterone in that case—that was the basis for making the decision. It was like the Marx Brothers. It couldn't have been sillier.

**John Barkhausen:** Or Kafka couldn't have been more surreal. You said Richard Edgren pointed out that if you call non-carcinogens carcinogens, then what's the public going to think about real carcinogens?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. You're going to ruin the whole issue of public safety if you blur anti-carcinogens with carcinogens.

One of the studies that they listed as evidence proving that progesterone is a carcinogen introduced itself by referencing some studies by Alexander Lipschutz. Lipschutz had published many papers and a book describing the anti-tumor properties of progesterone. This article referenced that and said they were checking up on Lipschutz's work. But Lipschutz, in his paper that they were referring to, had specified that progesterone given *continuously* prevents or even sometimes reverses cancer. In this paper that California considered evidence of carcinogenicity, they gave *intermittent* progesterone treatments—exactly what Lipschutz had said wouldn't prevent cancer. They concluded it doesn't prevent cancer. That paper consisted of a bad refutation of Lipschutz's evidence that progesterone prevents cancer, yet California presented this strange non-refutation as evidence that it causes cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** It's bizarre, but very effective. It sounds like nobody's going to question it because they're the experts.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** All that was there was the title "Panel of Experts." It was probably the receptionist who looked up some titles that had cancer and progesterone in them.

**John Barkhausen:** And they just figured nobody's ever going to care or look into it because there's no money behind making progesterone, as you pointed out in an earlier show.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around the time that someone petitioned to take progesterone off the list, that petition was rejected because the person in charge of responding mentioned a study done at the World Health Organization Cancer Research Agency as having shown that progesterone was a carcinogen. I looked that up, and the people at the World Health Organization said they didn't know of any such thing. They looked carefully and finally found one with the same date that California had cited. It wasn't about progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** What was that about?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Synthetic progesterone. California had cited that one obscure article, not about progesterone, to refute the petition that had presented evidence that progesterone protects against cancer. At the point that I asked them who made the decisions that were decisive—even though the decisions violated their own regulations—the head of the agency said, "We don't have the resources to answer your questions anymore."

**John Barkhausen:** Like, "Go away."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around the same time, someone petitioned to remove saccharin from the list of carcinogens. There is a lot of evidence that saccharin is a carcinogen. California decided to remove it from their list on the basis that the reason it causes cancer of the bladder in rats is peculiar to rat bladders—sort of a crystallization and the concussion caused by falling crystals onto the wall of the bladder. They had no evidence that it was the contact of crystals with the bladder, but they found the paper that said it does cause crystallization. However, there are also articles that showed that human urine crystallizes in exactly the same way the rats' did. So there was nothing special about the rat crystals. It was just, again, reaching as far as they could not to see the evidence. So they took it off the list because it's a big industry moneymaker.

**John Barkhausen:** So it sounds like they're there to represent certain interests and basically be a filter for what becomes available to the public based on those interests.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's their public. The corporations are the only public they're concerned with.

**John Barkhausen:** I recall from your newsletters that some of the tests they cited against progesterone were actually progestins. You explained last time that progestins are synthetic and often have opposite effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, they are synthetic, but they're a different molecule. So they aren't progesterone at all. The industry got the FDA to allow them to call them progestins, even though they are good contraceptives—they prevent gestation. But because there is a change in the lining of a rabbit uterus under their influence that happens to coincide with the changes caused by progesterone in one or two features, they call a non-progestin a progestin. It's a contraceptive, but they can see one feature of overlap with progesterone, so that's the strength for calling them a progestin.

**John Barkhausen:** And for those who didn't hear the first two parts of this talk, Dr. Peat was telling us that many times progestins are prescribed and people think they're taking progesterone, but they're actually taking these different molecules.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1970, when I was working on progesterone, occasionally someone would say, "Did you see the paper in some big science magazine that progesterone causes cancer?" At that time, they were actually putting it in the title: "Progesterone Causes Cancer." But they weren't working with progesterone. Even the editors of science journals were letting them get away with calling things by false names.

By the early 70s, the science world had clarified their terminology enough so that they started consistently calling the other molecules progestins or progestogens. There has been much less scientific confusion about the terms, but medical doctors are still pretty well confused about the difference between the anti-progestational progestins and the real progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Consequently, the public is also very confused.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Natural progesterone has to carry the warning that it can cause heart defects because some of the things that are called progestins cause heart defects. Something that has one property of progesterone gets to be called a progestin, and then anything toxic that molecule does gets laid over on real progesterone. For example, women with epilepsy are told to avoid progesterone during pregnancy because it will cause heart defects. But actually, the real progesterone has been reported to prevent almost all birth defects when it's used before pregnancy.

**John Barkhausen:** As we talked about in the earlier shows, most of these rulings seem to be connected to the estrogen industry. Premarin sales dropped after the Women's Health Initiative test became public, and progesterone sales were going up, which alarmed the industry.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can see it in some of the traditional centers of estrogen-promoting research; around that time, they turned against progesterone. Instead of concentrating on how good estrogen is, they're stretching to find something bad linked to progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Who is sitting on these boards?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I looked up everyone on the board. Some of them were linked to the university that was doing the anti-progesterone research. The leading anti-progesterone guy was Malcolm Pike. He and one or two others formed a company to promote a birth control pill based on his idea of protecting against progesterone. The state of California was using federal grants and other funding to support corporations, his included. So government money was flowing into his anti-progesterone business while he was sitting influential in saying that progesterone is a carcinogen.

Everyone I looked up on the board was either directly or indirectly concerned with something competing. For example, one of the people was on the board of a company promoting transdermal medical treatments—things that will administer drugs through the skin. While most of the progesterone products were being delivered through the skin, this person was representing a company that would probably be in line to market a medical progesterone transdermal.

**John Barkhausen:** What universities were they working for?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was only one biologist on the committee and several toxicologists. The University of Southern California (USC) has, I think, the biggest concentration of anti-progesterone work. I looked at the USC website about five or six years ago and I found easily 140 references to the glorious properties of estrogen. I found numerous references to progesterone, but every one of them was about its harmful properties. If you look at them objectively, you have to look hard to find an objectively beneficial effect of estrogen, and you have to stretch very hard to find a harmful effect of progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Is the contents of this library because they've culled it, or they've just always cultivated articles with the right attitude?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The things on the website were research projects in progress. They are being funded through the university, probably from pharmaceutical companies. Berkeley has more recently moved in that direction. Michigan was a big center of estrogen research and some of those people moved to UC Berkeley. Interestingly, the Lawrence Livermore Laboratory is involved in anti-progesterone research, which seems to have grown out of the chemical warfare line of thinking.

**John Barkhausen:** One of the things you've written about Elwood Jensen, who is the supposed inventor of the concept of the hormone receptor. Is that right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The idea of receptors in general was being discussed in various fields. But for estrogen, the enzymologists were progressing very quickly in understanding the effects of estrogen through the 1940s into the 1950s. One of the lines of very productive research was showing that enzymes can change estrogen back and forth between estrone and estradiol. Estrone is relatively inactive; estradiol is very active. That was classified as enzymology.

Jensen's argument was that estrogen acts by activating a genetic program. He argued it's only a female-acting substance because females are genetically determined to be female. So what estrogen does is act on a receptor that activates the genetic program. If something is acted on by enzymes, men have enzymes that are going to do the same reactions. Enzymology tended to generalize the estrogen issue and make it a masculine problem as well as female.

Jensen got the only support from the Atomic Energy Commission, which controlled the isotopes needed to do enzyme studies. He used an isotope-labeled form of estrogen and, in his experiments with uterus tissue, claimed to show that there was no oxidation or reduction of estrogen by the uterus. He said that's the end of the enzyme tradition; it's all receptor and genes now. That spread through the research world and by the mid-1960s was the dogma.

But then the enzymologists started getting the same isotopes that he had had and showed that, in fact, the old 1940s research was exactly what's happening. Now everyone knows that estrogen, estradiol, and estrone are perfectly interchangeable. That's exactly where progesterone, thyroid, and stress hormones interact with estrogen. Progesterone turns off some of the enzymes that activate estrogen and activates enzymes that inactivate estrogen.

The enzyme approach opens up the whole issue of environmental physiology—nutritional and metabolic effects on the estrogen system. But 50 years of belief in a genetic explanation of why estrogen is so good for females and harmless to everyone else persisted.

**John Barkhausen:** The reason I brought Elwood Jensen up is because you mentioned Livermore Labs and he worked in the chemical weapons industry, isn't that right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** University of Chicago, I think, is where he was working. That was a big weapons laboratory. The government doesn't say much about their chemical-biological warfare research. But if you look at the careers of some of the famous biologists, you see that you can't explain their achievements other than that they were being pushed by the Pentagon to get the information that they needed for German chemical warfare.

**John Barkhausen:** So you're saying that the fact that he was able to shift the damage that estrogen does to the genetic causes removed the liability of government and industry pollution?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Until about 25 years ago, biologists thought about estrogen working on the estrogen receptor as simply activating femaleness in genetic females. As if a man didn't share practically all enzymes and genes with women. It was just an extreme case of genetic cleaning up of the dangerous possibilities.

Estrogen has been known for about 30 or 40 years to act on every kind of tissue. You can find the estrogen receptor everywhere. But even without the estrogen receptor, you can demonstrate that it works on any kind of tissue. Some of the estrogenic compounds attach to the so-called estrogen receptor, but some have estrogenic effects without touching the estrogen receptor. Really it should have a new name. It isn't really the crucial thing because you can get estrogenic effects from radiation, cyanide, suffocation, or various stresses and infections. They'll all bring on estrus, swelling of cells, and inflammation. The overlap of stress, radiation, and industrial smoke with estrogen—that's one of the things that has been carefully avoided, and the receptor idea is crucial in covering that up.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like what he came up with was a smoke and mirrors cartoon for selling a concept of how everything works in such a way that it fit in with the popular idea of the gene being how life is directed. People may be wondering why we're talking about estrogen when this is a show about progesterone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Estrogen in the physiological situation activates the production of progesterone, and then progesterone knocks down the production of estrogen. It's a matter of an occasional stimulus from stress or estrogen which turns on a system that then definitively gets rid of estrogen. It's only the exaggerated, prolonged effect of estrogen that becomes a danger.

Progesterone is the basic thing for getting rid of estrogen. If you look at the enzymes involved, progesterone inactivates the aromatase enzyme that produces estrogen from the androgens. It activates the two types of detoxifying enzymes: the glucuronide transferase and the sulfur transferase that attach sulfuric acid to make it water-soluble. Estrogen opposes those. Progesterone inactivates the estrogen-activated enzymes that remove the detoxified sulfate and glucuronide.

So it's just an amazingly comprehensive system. Systematically, it knocks out the production, maintenance, and activation of estrogen, and it even destroys the so-called estrogen receptor protein. Progesterone even protects against radiation as part of that same system because radiation imitates estrogen. The cancers produced by either radiation or estrogen are equally protected against by progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Elwood Jensen went on to try to discover other chemicals that oppose estrogen, and he came up with tamoxifen.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A man named Daniel Lednicer gives a more insider view of where tamoxifen came from. The people who were working on the fact that estrogen is like polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in causing not only cancer but inflammation and fibrosis were looking for anti-inflammatory things. In looking for anti-inflammatory things, they accidentally found that tamoxifen was anti-estrogen as well. Out of that line of research, according to Lednicer, even Celebrex—the COX-2 inhibiting enzymes—derived from that line of research that was thinking about a more basic view of what estrogen does. The receptor wasn't involved at all in that kind of thinking.

**John Barkhausen:** The thing I didn't understand was it's been known for a long time that progesterone does oppose estrogen. Why were they even bothering to look for something else?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think you have to imagine the mentality. The person Jensen said suggested looking for how the estrogen affects the tissues was Charles Huggins. Huggins founded the lab that Jensen was working in. Even though it was the University of Chicago, they were just totally unaware of the world of biochemistry as related to cancer.

Huggins is the guy that theorized that since testosterone makes a man develop a prostate gland and estrogen makes women develop breasts, if you want to stop the growth of cancer in the breast, you will either remove estrogen or give testosterone. And for the prostate, you would either castrate the man or give the man estrogen. His simple idea was that the female and male were opposite. Basically a completely idiotic idea at the time he proposed it. That immediately started doctors all over the country castrating men by the millions. For 45 or 50 years they were giving men estrogen, with or without castration, to treat prostate cancer. All on that very ignorant early 20th-century idea of opposition of the hormones.

**John Barkhausen:** I had no idea that the castration went on.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Huggins was the one who, besides proposing castrating men to cure prostate cancer and giving them estrogen, first proposed removing the ovaries to stop the estrogenic stimulation. Then, since some of them didn't recover from that, they took out their adrenal glands as another source of estrogen. That was practiced right through the 60s. At one point, Huggins even proposed treating breast cancer with estrogen. It just didn't make any sense. But he had sort of a Frankenstein mentality: let's tinker with things and maybe we'll come up with something.

**John Barkhausen:** We only have about 10 minutes left. It would be good for people to hear about how progesterone works in combating cancer.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Alexander Lipschutz was the person who did the most comprehensive work showing that where estrogen causes fibrosis—fibroids first and eventually cancer—it acts first on the uterus, then on the breasts, then on the lungs, kidneys, brain. It's just a matter of where estrogen concentrates that it tends to cause fibromas and cancers. In every one of those situations, progesterone was protective.

The full reason why progesterone is protective against cancer requires looking at the whole spectrum of what estrogen is doing. The first thing estrogen does is cause the cell to take up water. Taking up water stimulates cell division, fat production, and a lot of other enzyme activities. These effects happen within minutes of estrogen exposure. It takes at least several hours for genes to get activated. So obviously the receptor wasn't involved in those instantaneous effects.

Those are exactly the essence of the cancer problem. If you start an inflammation that causes cells to keep taking up water, in that stressed condition of activating cell chemistry, they're using energy faster. The stimulation of cell division tends to use up the supply of oxygen and sugar. In my thesis research, one of the things I did was show that adding estrogen to a system such as the uterus lowers the oxygen tension. It just sucks the oxygen out of the system. That stimulation creates an oxygen deficiency.

As far as sugar is available, the sugar will be glycolized to produce emergency energy. In the absence of enough oxygen to meet the stimulation, the glycolysis produces lactic acid. The production of lactic acid leaving the cell raises the pH inside the cell. That increased pH keeps the swelling going on, activates cell division, and expends energy. So it needs something from the outside to stop the production of lactic acid and deliver oxygen.

Progesterone is one of the essential things for stopping that process. But once it starts under the influence of estrogen, you get the lactic acid production, which creates the vicious cycle of cell activation. The lactic acid increases the supply of blood and spreads growth of blood vessels into the environment. It activates everything that you need to produce a tumor. All that's needed is the presence of an anti-inflammatory, energy-restoring substance such as aspirin or progesterone to stop this process.

In the simplest situation, an injury causes the lactic acid to be produced, which activates the energy changes and growth to heal the wound. But at a certain point, the system should come in with the anti-inflammatory substances to finish off the healing. In the absence of the healing, the attempt at healing simply goes on and creates this swelling and oxygen-deficient situation. If you grow cells in a culture dish and deprive them of oxygen, they will eventually mutate and form other types of cells that cause a derangement of the tissue type. So all of the steps of cancerization can be seen structurally and metabolically in terms of wound healing that can't be brought to completion.

**John Barkhausen:** I think Harry Rubin, as you've pointed out, has basically proven that cancer is not from a gene gone bad, but rather the tissue itself has developed an unhealthy state.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He has just honestly summarized the real cancer research showing that the deranged metabolism and structure is what causes the chromosomal damage. So instead of genes causing the tumor, the tumor causes the genetic defects.

**John Barkhausen:** Which is the opposite of what we hear basically every day in our popular culture.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When an oncologist or pathologist says your tissue shows abnormal cell division and the wrong number of chromosomes, they say that means we have to cut it out and irradiate you. But if you look at the fate of those deranged cells, they're going to live maybe to the next attempt to divide, then they don't have the right number of chromosomes and the halves will die. So they're very short-lived once they get to that deranged state. But the death of the cell contributes to the inflammation of the area. So stopping the inflammation and energy deficit is always the solution to the problem.

It's now recognized by some oncologists that the reason a malignant cancer reforms after they've irradiated the area or cut out the cancer is that stem cells are called into the inflamed area that has been treated. Even if you irradiate a healthy area, it will call stem cells in to try to repair the wound. Whenever you injure a tissue by removing a tumor, you're just guaranteeing that the body will try to repair the wound by sending in new cells, which then turn into cancer cells if the area is still sick.

**John Barkhausen:** So the way to actually heal or to stay healthy is to make sure that your cellular environment is a healthy one. You're saying that progesterone and aspirin are actually viable cancer treatments.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And some of the antihistamines are definitely protective. Going way back 50 years, people were seeing antihistamines would occasionally cure cancer, but that just didn't catch on in the profession.

**John Barkhausen:** Well, if people want to read more about this, they can find lots of Ray Peat's ideas at raypeat.com. We have been talking to Dr. Raymond Peat. As always, it's been a real pleasure to talk to you, Ray. Thanks so much for coming on.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay. Thank you.

title: Politics & Science: Two Hour Fundraiser I
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** I don't think they've ever used progesterone itself. In a study in humans going back to the 40s, when progesterone was just barely becoming available, people were using it to treat cancer in humans, but it was just on an individual basis. There have been quite a few publications using medroxyprogesterone, which is not progesterone, to treat kidney cancer and breast cancer. It works somewhat, but it isn't progesterone; it doesn't have all of the good properties of progesterone and has some of the bad properties. So the best information is still from animal studies. Even those pretty much faded out after Lipschütz left the field in the 50s.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I thought I remembered one with women who had cervical cancer where they were injecting progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Oh, yeah, that was.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Was that medroxyprogesterone?

**John Barkhausen:** It was just a few women that got real progesterone. They had diagnosed them as being incurable, so they were willing to see what happened. They photographed and felt the condition of the cervix at the start, and then they injected what they thought were big doses. However, they never mentioned that any of the women were anesthetized, which happens when you give a big dose. So we don't really know how much the women were getting because they were injecting it in vegetable oil, which is an unpredictable solvent. If they weren't getting anesthetized to any extent that anyone noticed, they were hardly getting anything more than a physiological dose.

But still, during the course of the study, they saw a great improvement in the appearance, feeling, and symptoms. The bleeding decreased, the lumpiness decreased, and so on. It looked less like cancer after a few weeks of treatment. But since they didn't do the experiment intending to cure cancer, they went ahead and cut out the uteruses after a certain number of weeks had elapsed and concluded that progesterone had no promise as a treatment. The article is mostly interesting for the weird conclusion.

The article published right next to that in the same book was about treating breast cancer with estrogen. As many of the patients got worse as got better with the estrogen, yet they concluded that this stuff has great promise. Those two articles, published right against each other, are most interesting for the degree of psychosis that goes unnoticed in medical science.

**John Barkhausen:** And maybe in our society in general. You were pointing out the dominance of the estrogen industry over the last couple of shows. I was thinking that's kind of analogous to the dominance of estrogen in the sick person without the progesterone to oppose it. It seems like the same thing is happening in our society, which indicates to me that there's something wrong.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. This one study, I think, is still going on. D.G. Stein was the leader of the study giving progesterone within the first 24 hours after a catastrophic head injury. He found that the people survive when they get progesterone and recover remarkably well instead of just progressing to death.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's very effective, as you said, for any kind of injury. Stopping excitation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it stops edema, excitation, and deterioration of any tissue, but it is especially noticeable in the brain because edema is deadly in the brain.

**John Barkhausen:** And as Ray pointed out in the last few shows, it's not a money maker. To put it simply, progesterone is not patentable. You said they've tried to alter the molecule so they could patent it, but those artificial progestins actually have estrogenic effects.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, either estrogenic, androgenic, or in some cases, glucocorticoid effects. Just recently I saw an article emphasizing the difference between the real progesterone and the medroxyprogesterone that was used in the Women's Health Initiative study. This person was sounding annoyed that people were making the confusion, but I don't know how influential that publication will be.

**John Barkhausen:** And the medroxyprogesterone is actually what's called a progestin. If you're taking hormone replacement therapy, you think you're getting progesterone, but you're probably just getting progestin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It's similar enough to progesterone that it turns off your own production of progesterone. The odd thing about real progesterone is that if you aren't producing enough of it and you take some, you produce more. It reinforces the system for its own production—exactly the opposite of what the synthetic progestins do.

**John Barkhausen:** On the same subject of cancer, somebody brought up the point that Craig B. Thompson, president and CEO of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, has something on YouTube where he discusses new ways to think about cancer. He concludes that if you overfeed someone with fat, you do not increase their risk of cancer at all. If you overfeed someone with carbohydrates, you dramatically increase the cancer rate, and protein is halfway in between. This person would like to hear your response to that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I haven't read it, but I've seen a couple of other things that I think are equally crazy. Gary Taubes has an article in *Science* about a year ago saying basically the same thing, which I think he got from Dr. Lustig's video.

I have read lots of studies on the subject going back almost 90 years, and I think the evidence is very clear that fat—unsaturated fat—is, if not the only, at least by far the largest promoter of cancer. Not just in humans, but everywhere they look.

The interesting thing about carbohydrate is that the fats that we make out of carbohydrate when we eat an excess of it are anti-growth for cancer. They lower the amount of unsaturated fats circulating in our blood and they have a shift effect on the metabolism of cancer cells. They tend to restore oxidative metabolism and suppress aerobic glycolysis, which is the characteristic cancer metabolism. So this guy might have some bit of evidence in mind, but if he doesn't mention the 99% of the overwhelmingly opposing evidence, there's something wrong with his presentation.

**John Barkhausen:** Yeah, he doesn't distinguish between fats, he just says fat or carbohydrate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the ways they trick the experiment so it looks like they can improve their sales of fish fat or whatever is to give the most toxic fat to the control animals and their test substance, such as beef fat, to the other animals. The fish fat happens to oxidize so quickly that it doesn't reach the cells in quantity as great as the seed oil does.

If they're feeding a comparison between fat and sugar, for example, they'll make sure to add the carcinogenic required amount of linoleic acid to the diet. So then the sugar all goes into storage, but the animal is still being exposed to the crucial carcinogenic amount of linoleic acid. I've looked at probably 150 articles that claim to have results of that sort. It's hard to imagine that they weren't designing it just to get the results they want.

**Gene:** I haven't eaten much dairy food for many years. I've been trying your diet and I started drinking whole raw milk, and my sinuses got stuffed up again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wouldn't necessarily recommend whole milk or raw milk unless you're familiar with the particular cows. If you get a bad result from one dairy or one cow, try another one that feeds the cow something different. I've felt the difference myself just between local dairies and a supermarket. There was one brand of milk that was always cheaper and tasted a little funny, and I always got sick when I drank it.

There are so many things that can go wrong. The government requires the addition of vitamin A and D to all of the commercial milk supplies. Those dairies don't like to tell how they add those vitamins, but generally, there is some diluent that the vitamins are carried in, probably an emulsifier so that they don't stick to the sides of the vessels or float to the top.

**Gene:** This milk was from a local organic raw dairy with the cream mixed in. I've had the same problem drinking or eating dairy from many different sources throughout many years. I seem to have the same response whether it's from store-bought or right from the cow.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Do you get that from cottage cheese or cheese?

**Gene:** Yes.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Or from goat milk?

**Gene:** I don't like goat milk. I don't like the taste of that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's undoubtedly some kind of digestive problem. It's a matter of experimenting with different kinds of cheese. Have you noticed an effect on your sinus symptoms?

**Gene:** Usually once in a while it doesn't bother me, but most of the time it does. I don't have any digestive problems, just sinus, and I get mucus in my lungs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** How the mucus gets there is that your intestine is being irritated. The irritation is either that you have bacteria growing on the food or the food itself contains allergens. Very often just by changing the dairy or the type of cheese, or cooking it rather than eating it raw, you can find which things cause the mucus reaction. It isn't that the milk gets into your blood and causes mucus production in your head or lungs; it's a reaction from your intestine.

**Gene:** I've been working with Lita Lee, and she suggests that I drink cream instead of milk to solve the problem.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've never heard of anyone trying that, but I would say try some homemade skimmed milk cottage cheese first.

**John Barkhausen:** Is there any use in sneaking up on the milk consumption? Just doing a little bit at a time.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If a person thinks they might have a problem digesting the lactose or any food that's chemically different, then if you drink two or three ounces at a meal, that exposes the intestine to the new chemical. In a week or two, or at most a month or two, the enzymes usually will express themselves, even though they might have been gone for years. You can usually induce them in a few weeks by these small samples, just a half a glass at a time. There's not enough to feed the bacteria significantly, but enough to sort of tickle the enzyme system into getting active.

**Gene:** My second question is, I have a relative who's been diagnosed with chronic superficial gastritis and also an inflamed duodenum. What would you suggest there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Have they been checked with an endoscopy for bacteria?

**Gene:** Yes, through a colonoscopy and also through the throat.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And did they find that they had any bacterial problem growing up in the duodenum or stomach?

**Gene:** I believe so, but I'm not positive. He's had severe stomach pain for two or three years. It's been getting worse and lots of diarrhea.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's good to check things like the thyroid, but also to consider an elimination diet. There are so many foods, even natural, fresh foods; you can rank them according to their likelihood to support bacterial growth. And then there are lots of food additives. Anything with carrageenan, for example, is causing a lot of cases of inflammation of the stomach, bowel, diarrhea, and constipation. Carrageenan is showing up in an incredible number of foods, everything from organic whipping cream to squid patties.

**Gene:** Lita Lee has recommended I take a number of enzyme supplements. Are you familiar with those?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, but I'm very cautious with any kind of a pill-shaped supplement. In the process, there are so many allergens that can enter. So anything that especially involves microorganisms, you want to be very cautious. A couple of people have told me that when they took pure free amino acids they got incredibly sick. You have to be really cautious and maybe take a half a tablet as a trial and wait three days or so just to make sure you handle it. The same with any supplement. Vitamin C supplements can cause terrible problems for people. I've seen people who had terrible sinus symptoms for years, and when I suggested they lay off their vitamin supplements for a week, they didn't ever have a runny nose again.

**John Barkhausen:** Not too much of a testimonial for vitamins.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** For a while, I was counseling at an alternative health place in Eugene where allergies were a big problem because of the grass fields. For a couple of years, I had a reputation for curing everyone's allergies by getting them to stop their vitamins.

**Gene:** Are you familiar with Lyme disease and any connection with that and thyroid?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Hypothyroidism is often misdiagnosed as Lyme disease. Candida is the other thing. If you can't find the cause, then Lyme disease and Candida are the first suspects. But usually, it's just hypothyroidism.

**Gene:** What if you test positive for Lyme?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lots of people do. We all tend to be exposed to spirochetes and there's overlap with other spirochetes. A course of antibiotics for a week or two is a way to eliminate it. The Lyme disease can be eradicated, just as syphilis would be, for example. But by avoiding looking for other causes, such as hypothyroidism, some doctors make a good business out of the Lyme treatments forever.

**Gene:** I've been working with a naturopathic doctor who recommends antibiotics for the initial onset of Lyme, but then mostly herbs. He says the antibiotics force the spirochete to create a hard shell around themselves, which is why the symptoms desist after antibiotics. But then over time, the spirochetes break out of the shell and migrate around your body, especially in joints, which is why people experience joint pain years after the initial onset.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they haven't eliminated an endocrine problem, what I see is that the hypothyroid people with low immune function also get the whole range of symptoms that are blamed on that, such as arthritis. If you can cure the disease by correcting the thyroid, it's a lot easier.

About 40 or 45 years ago, a friend of mine had an accident working on his house, and the stress of it apparently brought on severe arthritis. He went to his doctor, who examined him and didn't prescribe cortisone for his arthritis; he prescribed Armour Thyroid because he saw he was hypothyroid. My friend was really annoyed and went home grumbling that the doctor had fixed something that he thought wasn't broken. After a week or two of taking the thyroid, his arthritis disappeared and never came back. Not many doctors are aware of connections such as injury, stress, arthritis, and hypothyroidism. Most doctors would prescribe cortisone to treat the symptoms. I think a lot of the Lyme doctors are doing a similar thing—making a simple problem complex.

**John Barkhausen:** Is it possible that the bite from the tick triggers some anti-thyroid response?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Probably low thyroid people have a bigger inflammatory response and are more likely to fail to throw off the infection. So if you have the diagnosis, it's good to take a course of antibiotics. A good combination of antibiotics is well established as a cure.

**John Barkhausen:** So you really think Lyme disease is just a thyroid problem that's triggered by the immune system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not the disease, but the diagnosis. I would say 80 or 90% of the people that I've talked to have been to doctors who specialize in diagnosing and treating it chronically.

**John Barkhausen:** And have you had luck treating people for Lyme?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but they get well and forget about the Lyme diagnosis.

**John Barkhausen:** So you give them nutritional advice?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I think the power of undigested food is very underestimated. Overcooking food, like people used to do 100 years ago, is much better for the digestion because we aren't designed to eat undercooked or raw vegetable matter. Bacteria can eat it. If someone happens to have just the right mix of bacteria, their bacteria can eat their vegetables secondarily and release some of the nutrients. But if you get the wrong bacteria, then they produce toxins rather than nutrients.

**John Barkhausen:** And that's the endotoxin problem that you've referred to.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, endotoxin and many other things. Allergens released from the specific plant material, as well as bacterial toxins.

**John Barkhausen:** It's always amazed me that you talk about endotoxin all the time. If you look it up on the Internet, there's a lot of information about it. It's a real thing. It actually causes severe problems. And that seems to be well recognized. But I've talked to several doctors, internists about it. Smart people. They've never ever heard of it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I guess they forgot that section in medical school during a generation or two. In the 19th century, the intestine was a big focus of Anglo-American medicine. They were very interested in what the intestine does to the whole system—the brain-intestine symptom interactions and the other organs as they're influenced by the intestine. That was still pretty big up until 1920, and then there was a campaign against it.

Walter C. Alvarez, a newspaper gastroenterologist, helped to suppress the intestine culture. In popular medicine, for example, there was a belief that migraines or headaches in general were produced by toxins absorbed from the intestine. He was of the new school that didn't want to think about the intestine so much. So he stuffed wads of cotton into his medical students' rectums and reported that the next morning a certain proportion of them had headaches caused just by the pressure in the rectum. He said, "So you see, headaches are caused by pressure, not by toxins." But he didn't put any toxins in his students' intestines, so he didn't disprove the idea; it was just a little propaganda bit.

But other people, Russians for example, studied in more detail that toxins, nutrition, and pressure interact very meaningfully. In an experimental animal, for example, they would put a balloon in the intestine and blow it up and nothing would happen. But if they gave the animal hypoglycemia and then blew up the intestine, unpredictable things would happen all through the rabbit. It would have hormonal and neurological reactions triggered just by that pressure. Blowing up a balloon in the intestine could cause seizures or wheezing or all kinds of widespread reactions.

**John Barkhausen:** And that's when you have low blood sugar. That's when it's particularly dangerous to have blockages.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. French and Canadian researchers, instead of using pressure, combined allergens. They would feed a bit of walnut to an animal and it would maybe sneeze from the allergens in it. Then they would give it moderate hypoglycemia and feed it the same thing and it would die in shock. And then if they would give another bunch of animals slight hyperglycemia by infusing some glucose and feed them the same walnut, they wouldn't even sniffle.

**John Barkhausen:** Wow. So that goes along with what you said, that sugar or glucose is protective. It's very important to keep your blood sugar up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I think the particular researcher who did that was named Adamkiewicz and it was published in a book by Gaëtan Jasmin.

**John Barkhausen:** As long as we're on the subject of digestion, how important is it that people have regular bowel movements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The person who popularized fiber 40 or 50 years ago in the US was studying the African relative freedom from bowel problems and cancer. He saw that they typically would have three bowel movements a day and that they ate lots of potatoes. He thought it was the fiber in the potato stimulating the intestine that seemed to protect their bowel. So he published things about the benefits of fiber. The cereal industry in the US started selling oat bran as the preventive of colon cancer, which caught on in the 70s. But then in the 80s, some Australians tested oat bran diets on animals and found that it promoted and increased the incidence of bowel cancer, apparently by the nature of the breakdown product.

**John Barkhausen:** I don't think that knowledge has ever gotten around.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Not very well. But in general, fiber does clean the intestine. Keeping it moving lowers the estrogen level. The bile puts out and tries to get rid of toxic materials, including estrogen. If you don't have a regular movement through the intestine, a lot of that gets recycled, reabsorbed, and raises your general exposure to toxins, including estrogen.

**John Barkhausen:** What do you think of medicinal marijuana in its relationship to cancer and AIDS? Is it efficacious?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It helps with the nausea. If a person is having symptoms and can control the symptoms with it, it's very effective for many people. When I was 10, a doctor gave me a bag, didn't say what it was, but prescribed a cup of tea every day. Years later I recognized the taste of it as marijuana. It was supposed to prevent my headaches, but it didn't do anything noticeable for me.

It used to be prescribed a lot as a tea and I think it's a lot safer that way than smoking it because the smoke itself is carcinogenic and estrogenic. The various chemicals in the leaf are themselves slightly estrogenic or anti-androgenic. So I think that's probably the main concern for someone who's using it regularly. But I think there are other probably healthier solutions for nausea. The anti-serotonin drugs and simply increasing the blood sugar, salt, and sugar very often help with nausea.

**Roger:** My question centers around omega-3 fatty acids. A couple of years ago I came across a supplement of whole salmon fish oil that contained omega-3s and it was touted as being a great supplement to help arthritis and lower triglyceride levels. Then I read your research, which sort of contradicted all of these things. I was wondering if you could elaborate on what you think the dangers are of taking supplements of fish oil. I've been seeing that these fatty acids are showing up in all kinds of organic products like organic milk and baby formula.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Someone two or three years ago analyzed the baby formulas and found that the great bulk of the omega-3 fat that had been added to it had broken down and was probably in a toxic form. So their worst feature is that they break down and oxidize very fast. A couple of researchers have looked for them in the blood at the time that they are having their anti-inflammatory actions and found that they had already broken down. Just between the mouth and the bloodstream they broke down into completely new chemicals which were what accounted for their anti-inflammatory effect.

But those same breakdown products are what in the long run suppress the whole immune system and have a lot of other toxic effects. So the short-range anti-inflammatory effect I see as analogous to the anti-inflammatory treatments I used to give with X-ray or other radiation.

**Roger:** What would some of the other negative effects be?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The whole immune system gets turned down so that it doesn't produce the inflammation that's bothering you. But in the long run, that makes you susceptible to all kinds of infections. And I think in the long run it increases the risk of cancer and all of the age-related degenerative processes.
