**Roger:** Do you think it would be important to continue to monitor people who are using these omega supplements?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A few people are doing that and warning about their increased use. It seems like a very bad idea to put it in powdered baby food because the time and oxygen exposure before it's eaten does a terrific job of degrading those fats because they're so unstable.

**Roger:** What should we look for as a symptom that this is a problem? More infections, more colds?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, more infections would be the first thing. I've seen that in experimental animals and there have been some studies in people in which their immune systems were relatively inert against various organisms. With the anti-inflammatory X-ray treatments that they used in the 40s so enthusiastically, it took from 10 to 15 years before they saw the harmful effects of them.

**Roger:** What can we do as consumers to alert others or get doctors to conduct additional research? I have called various manufacturers and milk companies who are using the product and they assured me that everything was completely fine.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the same with the additives. They're putting in so many products like the fumed silica (silicon dioxide) that you see in vitamin pills and drugs and even foods, and titanium dioxide. These things are proven risky at best. But you talk to the companies that use them and they don't want to think about it. They won't respond to sending them an article indicating that they somehow selectively misread the research incriminating material. It's hard to counter someone's occupational commitment to something that isn't helpful.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, maybe you can explain why it's come about that most of society in scientific culture is invested in these products that actually, although they might help inflammation in the short run, cause cancer in the long run. How did we get here?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The whole idea of science has been shaped by commerce and the military. The people who have something very powerful to gain from using science in a certain way support it being used that way. The people who are trying to be objective don't have any ulterior motives and that means they don't have a source of funding.

**John Barkhausen:** Like there are minority views in science about issues like this, and my understanding is they just can't get published.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh yeah. Have you looked at some of the controversies in other fields of science, such as Halton Arp and his quasar astronomy?

**John Barkhausen:** No.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He was successful in his career as long as he published his pictures in his *Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies*. As long as he just said, "Here's odd stuff I've been finding." But when he pointed out some very orderly things that related the redshift of quasars to the redshift of galaxies that they were clearly part of, they said, "You can't use our telescopes anymore." Even though he was funded by taxpayers' money, they wouldn't let him use the public telescopes.

**John Barkhausen:** I guess what I've become aware of during the show is that there are scientific dynasties. People get to the top of their career and obviously, I think it's just human nature, they don't want to be... They feel like their own reputation and status is on the line if their theory ends up being proven not to be true.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. There's a little one or two-minute video of Halton Arp talking about his experiences and he actually quotes some of the things that happened to him on his way out of the profession. Very ridiculous things that the top people in the field said and did.

**Justin:** I was wondering if Ray could elaborate on any misconceptions he thought science might have in its view of the immune system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the best answer to that is to look at the articles by Polly Matzinger and Jamie Cunliffe. I think they are inspired by the thinking of Élie Metchnikoff who was contemporary with Ehrlich, the "magic bullet" drug person.

The German view of the immune system is the one that was profitable to the chemical drug industry—looking for a magic bullet that would kill each kind of germ, and then by extension applying it to cancer, looking for chemicals that would kill cancer cells and not human non-cancer cells.

But Metchnikoff took a totally different approach to the immune system: the developmental, nutritional, morphogenic approach. That didn't find any commercial sponsors. It was the French-Russian orientation that actually was the biological orientation rather than the industrial.

title: Politics & Science: Two Hour Fundraiser II
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** We have a caller. Justin, go ahead.

**Justin:** Fascinating stuff. I’d love to hear Ray talk about the "dead universe" theory and biological fields. I was talking about the notion that the universe was dead and inert, and that most of biology was just kind of of that nature. Do you understand what I'm saying, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The field idea in biology—embryology as a model of development according to interactions with the environment—that idea continued. Some of the people who were developing experiments to understand the rules by which an organism takes form were vitalists. They believed there was something extra besides the matter. But at least they were interested in the actual events as the organism took form.

They were knocked out of biology by the gene people, who I would say are on the side of an inert cosmos. They want to explain things in terms of essentially immaterial information. They are the ones who talk about the vitalists wanting to introduce a "vital principle" as being somehow against the materialism of science. But the genetics people really want to depreciate the material world in favor of an information world.

The idea of the Central Dogma was that the information we have in our genes is immortal, can't be added to, and can only be written out into mortal, temporary, imperfect organisms. But the genes are the timeless stuff. Calling people like Hans Driesch a vitalist and saying that they weren't really biologists is kind of self-referential, because the genetics people have thrown out most of the interesting stuff in biology until the last ten years or so.

**John Barkhausen:** When they're starting to get back to the field theory again.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**John Barkhausen:** I have a question from Brittany. She asks: "If you are trying to self-treat for hypothyroid based upon blood tests and symptoms, how much T4 would be considered too much to take? And is T4 even necessary at all?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The problem with the commercialization of synthetic T4 that started in the late 1940s was that they tested it on male medical students who were about 25 years old and selected for good health. They found that it worked in them just like the real thyroid substance that had been in use for about 50 years at that time.

The trouble is that it then became commercialized. Women have at least five times the incidence of thyroid problems because of the antagonism between estrogen and thyroid. The thyroid sluggishness that's so common in women shows up as a slow metabolism of the liver. Typically, a woman premenstrually will get drunk on a fraction of the alcohol that it takes to make a man drunk because the liver is slowed down by the antagonism between estrogen and thyroid and oxidative metabolism.

It happens that thyroxine (T4) has to be activated in the liver by taking off one of the iodines in the right position to make it the active hormone called T3. If women are having low blood sugar symptoms or high estrogen symptoms—things that are the result of hypothyroidism—then T4 can very often not help or even make the problem worse.

Some experimenters tried to argue that thyroid does something other than rev up the oxidative metabolism. They took slices of muscle, kidney, liver, brain, and heart, and added thyroxine (T4) to these cultured slices. They saw that the liver had a tremendous burst of oxidative activity, but the kidneys didn't do much, the muscles didn't do anything, and added to the brain, it actually suppressed oxidative metabolism.

They said, "You see, oxidation isn't what thyroid really does. It just happens that the liver responds that way." But they were looking at the pre-hormone. The liver has to turn it into the active hormone before it can work in the muscles, kidneys, heart, and brain.

It turns out that the brain concentrates the blood; it can have 40 times as much T4 as T3. If your liver is a little sluggish, your brain will still concentrate the T3 to the point that it has a one-to-one ratio. If you put the brain slice in the dish where it can't get a new supply of T3 constantly, the added T4 can't do anything except displace some of the active hormone that the brain had been concentrating. So adding T4 to the brain in the culture dish caused suppression of metabolic activity. In people, you very often see it causing neurological symptoms—strange electrical sensations, ringing ears, worse memory—various things that are really signs of worse thyroid function.

**John Barkhausen:** So it sounds like you shouldn't be taking very much T4, if any at all, especially if you're a woman.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, it's very good if you don't need it very much.

**John Barkhausen:** A lot of people take a mixture of T4 and T3, supposedly close to the physiological dose of 1 to 5.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you take a human gland or a cow gland, it's close to a 4 to 1 ratio.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that a good mixture to take if you were supplementing?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, even a 5 to 1 mixture is okay. But the people who were insisting on still using the Armour Thyroid with its 4 to 1 ratio in the 1960s ran into issues. As the pharmaceutical companies developed tests for diagnosing thyroid, they noticed that the people taking thyroxine (T4) had maybe a 40 to 1 ratio of T4 to T3 in the blood. The people taking Armour had maybe a 10 to 1 or a 5 to 1 ratio. They defined the people taking T4 as the "normal" and the ones taking Armour as having too much T3. But most doctors at that time weren't aware at all that T3 was the active thyroid hormone.

**John Barkhausen:** So they jumped to conclusions and we're still stuck with some of those conclusions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. One of the ideas that spread quickly in the late 1940s, when the first blood tests for thyroid came on the market around the same time as Synthroid (the T4 product), was the Protein Bound Iodine (PBI) test. People like Broda Barnes had seen close to half of the population benefiting from some thyroid—which used to be part of the meat supply until the agriculture department said the meat companies could no longer sell it. In Broda Barnes' time, he saw that somewhere between 20% and 45% of the people benefited from taking some thyroid.

But these new blood tests in the late 40s found that 95% of the people had a fairly high level of iodine-bound protein in the blood. That created the idea that only 5% need a thyroid supplement. By the 1960s, new tests came about and they realized that the PBI test had almost nothing to do with thyroid function. So the standard that still persists widely—that only 5% of the population is potentially a candidate for supplement—the basis for establishing that had nothing to do with the thyroid function.

**John Barkhausen:** Lilia asks: "If you tend to constantly have excessive air, chest pressure, or feeling the need to burp, is that a sign of low stomach acid with undigested food causing problems, or too much stomach acid? And what would you do about it?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Basically no. A lot of different things can cause that. Some people can actually have reverse peristalsis. When you analyze burps, most of the time it's air that you've swallowed coming back. But sometimes you find other gases such as methane coming out.

Walter Alvarez demonstrated that it's pretty common for people to experience very intense reverse peristalsis. He put some lycopodium powder in his medical students' rectums when they went home for the evening. He had them fill out a questionnaire saying whether they typically experienced morning breath. When they came in the morning after getting the lycopodium powder, he took a swab in their mouth and found lycopodium powder in the mouths of the ones who typically had bad breath.

**John Barkhausen:** Wow, that's a little grim. So you think most of the time the burping is just from swallowing air?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the daytime. Most of the reverse peristalsis happens in the night. If you're low thyroid, your autonomic nervous system tends to rev up, compensating for the lower oxidative metabolism. It pushes it harder to increase your adrenaline in particular. The adrenaline tends to stop the forward propulsion of the peristalsis. Then random signals—irritation from something in your intestine—can probably send waves going both directions. That is probably more common when your digestive system is slightly paralyzed by a very high adrenaline level.

**John Barkhausen:** Sheila asks: "What are your thoughts on multiple sclerosis? What causes it and how do you think it should best be treated?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 70s, I saw a series of five people over a period of maybe a year or two. As they told me their symptoms, I said that sounds like classical hypothyroidism. A couple of these people went to their old-fashioned doctors with a list of the symptoms they just told me and said, "Here are my symptoms, what do I have?" The doctor said hypothyroidism and gave them thyroid. In that series of five people in a row, every one of them discovered they didn't have multiple sclerosis, but rather just needed a thyroid supplement.

**John Barkhausen:** The same person asks: "Why do I feel bad after I accidentally took too much desiccated thyroid?" She increased it a little too fast and managed to get some raw thyroid from a butcher. She would like to know how long it usually takes for the thyroid to get back to normal when you stop eating it, and is there anything to do to feel better quicker?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People probably worry too much about it. T4 has a half-life of two weeks, and T3 in different people can have a half-life as short as one day. If you got a sudden overdose and your pulse went up to maybe 150 beats per minute at rest, in 48 hours you would probably have lost at least half of your T3, which is the active stuff. Your liver would then be putting out just a disposal amount, converting the T4 to T3. Usually, if you took so much that you had a very fast heart rate, in two days you would probably be down to a fairly safe, comfortable 120 beats per minute.

**John Barkhausen:** If you wanted to intervene and make that transition quicker?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen some people who spontaneously became hyperthyroid or who had overdosed juicing raw cabbage. It just takes a glass or two of that to very powerfully suppress your thyroid functions. Usually a glass or two a day for a couple of days and the person is back down to normal. Liver is another suppressive food. If you eat two big meals of liver, you can see a big decrease in thyroid function.

**John Barkhausen:** How long does that suppression last from liver or cabbage?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A couple of days. The fear of suppressing your thyroid gland itself by taking too much thyroid has been tested using isotopes. They would dose people until they could tell there was no thyroid being produced by their own gland, and then they stopped dosing them to see if there was any concern about prolonged suppression. Everyone's gland came right back in a couple of days.

**John Barkhausen:** That's encouraging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** People farmers used who had their own animals would often eat the thyroid gland in the chicken neck. One guy I knew said that on Friday they always had fried chicken in the field for lunch. He said Friday afternoons he was always too hot to work, but he would eat five necks and get probably 20 grains of thyroid—a very suppressive dose. He would be very hot, but by the next day it would have passed.

**John Barkhausen:** Wade asks: "I would like to ask Ray's thoughts on Reverse T3. Is it really necessary to use T3 treatment only to clear out the accumulated Reverse T3, or will a combination thyroid product and proper nutrition resolve the issue?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's mostly caused by high cortisol and stress hormones. Eating a good supportive diet—plenty of fruit, orange juice, and milk—will help keep the stress down. I think it works just as effectively as taking small amounts of T3.

**John Barkhausen:** What causes Reverse T3? It is basically where your whole thyroid system shuts down, right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If your body thinks that you're having an overexposure to thyroid, it gets rid of the excess by turning thyroxine into an inactive kind of T3. It takes off the wrong iodine. If you're fasting, for example, part of the thyroid is being excreted the way estrogen or toxins are being excreted, but part of it is being inactivated in a way that has an anti-thyroid effect. It interferes with the active T3. It's an extra fast way to turn off your thyroid function.

**John Barkhausen:** I missed part of the question regarding drugs to decrease MS symptoms. I think it's called naloxone?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, naloxone or naltrexone. When you're under stress, you produce endorphins. The endorphins compensate for injury or stress and they should go away. But prolonged stress can leave you inhibited in various ways with the wrong pattern of endorphins. If a person has been exposed to prolonged stress, sometimes you can break out of the pattern and recover functions with an anti-morphine treatment. Naloxone and naltrexone are the injected and oral forms of an anti-opiate that simply keeps the endorphin from having its effect. Sometimes that can restore functions that had been suppressed.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like you don't like opiates—you think they're actually bad for you in the long run. So that sounds like it's not a bad thing to be taking.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. I think it usually has its effect in just a few days, though. If it hasn't really made a big difference in just a few days, then it's probably some other problem.

**John Barkhausen:** If you wanted to keep the inflammation low, could you just use some other anti-inflammatory?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yeah. All kinds of stabilizing anti-inflammatory things. Thyroid, progesterone, short-chain fatty acids, and sugars are all things that help restore injured, demyelinated nerves.

**John Barkhausen:** Lilia asks: "Do you have any thoughts on the efficacy of prolotherapy, in which a solution containing sugar in the form of dextrose is injected into tendons or ligaments to strengthen weakened connective tissue?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My father had it done. I think they used vegetable oil in the 1950s—a combination of novocaine and vegetable oil. It causes an inflammatory reaction and toughening up of the ligaments. It can cure some back problems without anything very invasive. So it's proven to work, but I think there are better things. It's usually a low DHEA production from low thyroid, high estrogen, and stress hormones that cause the ligaments and tendons to get weak. Correcting the thyroid function and maybe taking a DHEA or pregnenolone supplement would be the natural way to strengthen the ligaments and tendons, and it helps the bones at the same time.

**John Barkhausen:** I've heard the complaint about your writings before that "all he ever thinks is wrong with us is our thyroid," and somehow that's a put-down. How do you respond to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It doesn't apply just to people; it applies to all complex organisms practically. The difference between us and a fungus is that we've had a lot of thyroid and oxidative metabolism that the fungus hasn't benefited from. All of our functions are characterized by high-energy oxidative metabolism—the brain more than any other part.

As you look at the animal kingdom, the outstanding thing is that their oxidative metabolism increases as they go up the so-called evolutionary scale. Oxygen is driving our existence, and our existence is culminating in a bigger, more expensive brain that other animals couldn't afford because their thyroid function wasn't adequate. It's really the essential thing. Given oxygen and sugar and a few other materials, thyroid is the catalyst for making things run right.

**John Barkhausen:** The thyroid does seem like the master system in terms of energy production for everything.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If your thyroid is working efficiently, then your pituitary doesn't have much to do and you aren't likely to get a pituitary tumor. Your adrenals don't have much to do. Your ovaries don't get overstimulated. The other glands have an easy job when your thyroid is working right. If your thyroid gets interfered with, then you've got to rev up your adrenals, and then your pituitary becomes a commander-in-chief and tells everyone what to do with the stress hormones. Then you're at risk of getting tumors of the ovaries, testicles, adrenal glands, or thyroid gland because your pituitary is working them too hard.

**John Barkhausen:** In our shows about progesterone, you were talking about instances where progesterone was very helpful to women with arthritis. Is it the right substance to use for men with arthritis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. One of the first people I gave it to was a friend over 40 years ago. Every afternoon his knee swelled up—obviously rheumatoid arthritis. It looked like a football. I got some standard injectable progesterone and he rubbed the whole vial from his side down to his calf. Two or three hours later he was walking and showed me his knee was no longer swollen. Just about three or four years ago, he was still walking without a limp. I hadn't noticed arthritis in all that time.

**John Barkhausen:** So for people developing arthritis in their hands now, is that also a thyroid problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When your thyroid is down, you compensate with all kinds of other stress hormones. Your autonomic system goes up, but so does your adrenal cortical and aldosterone hormones. Estrogen increases, even melatonin gets involved. Some of these compensatory things don't quite compensate fully, and then they get involved in increasing the inflammation. That's where DHEA and progesterone—either taken orally or applied topically—are the things that are deficient as a consequence.

The other more delicate and dangerous hormones, such as estrogen and cortisol, increase because you're low in progesterone, DHEA, and pregnenolone. Supplementing any of those three, or all three of them, will usually alleviate or cure arthritis. I've known people with dogs or horses who thought the animal was so old it would never work again. Just giving it progesterone made the horse healthy and happy for several more years.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a caller.

**Caller:** Ray, in your essay on autonomic systems, you talk about 20th-century writing and painting being considered expressive rather than communicative. I was wondering if you could give some examples of 20th-century writers or painters you consider communicative and not insane? Maybe someone following in Blake's footsteps?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** David Alfaro Siqueiros was one of my heroes.

**John Barkhausen:** Why did you say that 20th-century artists are considered to be out of their minds?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They were driven out of their minds partly by the CIA's project called the Congress for Cultural Freedom, which worked with Nelson Rockefeller to glorify what Siqueiros called the "ghost artists." They were creating a culture of anti-culture. The CIA knew exactly what they were doing, and presumably Nelson Rockefeller did too, when he and his fellow philanthropists concentrated on these people because of their antisocial consciousness. They ridiculed the idea that art should have a social consciousness. The CIA pumped Marshall Plan money into creating this alternative culture of abstract expressionism.

**John Barkhausen:** What do you think the government's motive was for doing that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** To improve the power of the Rockefeller class by keeping anyone who said art should be socially conscious shown to be some kind of degenerate or subversive. Siqueiros was working around the New York crowd and saw what was happening. It was years later, I think 1968, when this CIA financing of culture was revealed. But Siqueiros had been there seeing it going on.

**John Barkhausen:** We just got another email question: "What causes moles on the skin?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I found that they were very hormonally related. In the summer of 1981, I had been watching a mole grow on my belly. It was obviously, to me, becoming a dangerous melanoma. It had grown from a little brown spot. A couple of doctors who happened to be visiting saw it and told me they thought it was a melanoma.

Around that time I was experimenting with different steroids. I happened to be tasting some DHEA. Without thinking of any connection, one night I noticed a shiny red dome on my belly where the mole had been. Over the next three or four days, the mole disappeared. Thinking about it, I realized I had been sampling the DHEA around that time.

The next time I started getting a mole that looked like it was turning into a melanoma—turning blue and white, with the spots swimming around or changing positions rapidly—I would apply a little progesterone or DHEA to that area. Immediately the color, instead of swimming around in colored spots, would level out and become just a little tan colored thing, and then it would go away.

I had a series of experiments. One was a mole as big as a jumbo olive. When I put some progesterone near it, within two weeks it had turned to a crisp and fallen off without leaving a trace of a scar. I found that I could sort of steer them. The pigment cells are extremely mobile. A huge black thing appeared suddenly on my lower arm. I put a dot of progesterone in vitamin E oil about an inch from the spot. The following day, there was a shadow of it about an inch downstream towards my hand. I put another dot on, and each time I put a dot on, the next day there would be a shadow an inch farther down. Pretty soon all of the cells had walked away from the big black spot.

In another case, putting a dot on the front of one on my forehead, the pigment cells moved out in a circumference away from it. On the third day, it looked like a bullseye. After about a week, the original spot had shrunk up and pinched off at the base.

**John Barkhausen:** Phenomenal.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Various other people who didn't experiment in such detail would just take an overdose of thyroid for a week or two, and day by day you could see their mole shrinking until, in one case, a mole an inch long disappeared from a guy's back in two weeks.

**John Barkhausen:** So you were just toying with it with that progesterone and pregnenolone.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Very entertaining to see how fast these cells can run through your body. People have studied them on cover slips. At 90 degrees, which is the average skin temperature, a cell of that type can walk about an inch per day if it's motivated. I think the reason they collect in certain spots is that they come looking for something that's missing from where they were. Like they found some cell that was emitting DHEA, possibly, so everyone moves in to take advantage.

**John Barkhausen:** And that's maybe what caused the mole to form in the first place.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Some people in the last couple of months have been thinking about the factors that guide cell migration. It's probably going to be a very interesting field in the next few years—trying, for example, to lure cancer cells back from their metastatic positions, call them back to where they should be.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a caller.

**Caller:** I wanted to talk about type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome and how it causes low testosterone. What's the best way to attack that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Get the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) out of your body as far as possible, or keep them in storage if they're there. Definitely avoid all kinds of polyunsaturated fats because those are the things that specifically interfere with the ability to oxidize glucose. One of the reasons that aspirin has been known for 100 years to help lower blood sugar in that kind of diabetes is that aspirin does several things to interrupt the effects of the polyunsaturated fats. It keeps them from turning into the inflammation-causing prostaglandins, but it also helps to keep them in storage where they don't do so much harm.

**Caller:** Does that also correlate to the weight loss curve? I found that as soon as weight is lost, the blood sugar starts regulating itself.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The fat cells are sending out signals that create inflammation. Leptin is one of the pro-inflammatory signals. You want to signal your fat to stop sending leptin if possible.

**John Barkhausen:** Jerry asks: "I eat raw vegetables out of the garden all summer. Is that a no-no? I always thought raw veggies were more nutritious than cooked."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depends on what they are. Peppers and tomatoes are really fruits; they are good raw. Carrots and some of the radishes, if you ate a lot of them, would be anti-thyroid. But there are some things called vegetables that are really fairly rich in sugar as well as the minerals. Those sweetish root vegetables are pretty healthy.

**John Barkhausen:** You're not very big on some raw vegetables, like beans?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, the raw stuff is likely to feed bacteria and cause problems. If there is a seed developing in it, that has other specific toxins. Peas and beans are not so great.

**John Barkhausen:** I wanted to ask you about eczema. Do you have any tips for how to handle that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Keeping your intestine in good condition is one of the things. Both eczema and psoriasis tend to flare up in a lot of people when they eat bread or other grains. Beans are very hard on the intestine in general. Seeds, grains, and beans irritating the intestine tend to create sympathetic reactions. The particular enzyme that reacts to gluten is involved in the maturing of the skin cells. This particular enzyme, transglutaminase, is now being studied as a link between the intestine and the skin.

**John Barkhausen:** What can somebody do about eczema if they have it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Thyroid very often helps. Sometimes pregnenolone, by balancing all of the others. It's the precursor to all of the steroid hormones and in itself it stops the stress reaction. To the extent that your stress system—from pituitary to adrenals—associates with a flare-up of skin problems, just by turning off the stress with pregnenolone, you can see a big change.

**John Barkhausen:** We are out of time. Dr. Raymond Peat, it's been a real pleasure. Thanks for handling all those questions so well.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: Politics & Science: Autoimmune and Movement Disorders
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Hello and welcome to Politics and Science. I'm John Barkhausen, your host, and today we're going to talk about some autoimmune diseases and movement disorder dysfunctions. I'm intrigued by them not only because I have friends that are suffering from these, but also because the medical world offers so little knowledge about the diseases and so little hope or practical knowledge in terms of treatment.

I'm very happy that Dr. Raymond Peat is here to join me again today. Dr. Peat has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon and extensive knowledge of science history. There are many theories as to the causes of the diseases, and one common factor that is present in all of them—and that most people agree on—is inflammation. Ray, I just want to start off by asking you: why is so little understood about these diseases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, I think there's a lot more known than the public is aware of. The medical journals aren't a good place to look if you're just wanting to find out how much is known. If you read widely in not only medical journals but general science journals, you see that people have discovered really interesting things about all of them. There are patterns that show up across the various diseases, and I think things could be put into practice more than they are.

There are people demonstrating improvement in the degenerative diseases with very simple antioxidant supplements and creatine supplements that you just don't hear about in the *New York Times* stories about advances in health. I think part of it is that when the generic substance looks like it might prevent or cure one of these horrible conditions, the drug industry isn't interested, and so there's no advertising money to be made by running publicity about it.

**John Barkhausen:** So nobody pursues it. Ray, can you explain where you're finding out this knowledge of hopeful techniques to combat these diseases?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of it you can find right in PubMed and Google, and some of it in more obscure journals. There's enough to keep a person busy for years just putting pieces together, making a meaningful puzzle out of scraps from the various lines of thinking.

If you follow one disease over 20 or 30 years, like Alzheimer's, you'll see there are styles focusing on the cholinergic nerve death, or the accumulating fibrils, amyloid and such, and explaining that as a toxin that causes the disease. Each disease goes through its styles of what they think is interesting. But the pressure on funding research pushes generally towards a genetic explanation that makes a simple drug solution conceivable—something to stop that one genetic defect from taking its effect.

**John Barkhausen:** So when you say styles, are you talking about certain fads in research that are prevalent at certain times?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, definitely fads. But the basic big fad that has lasted for 100 years is a genetic explanation. Like in Huntington's disease, it's a certain repeat that causes a series of glutamine amino acids in the protein to increase, and that creates a protein that shows up as if it's doing damage. The framework idea is that the gene expresses itself in a protein, and the protein causes the symptoms of the disease.

But there are several ways of approaching that. One is that something is causing this repeat to be formed in the gene itself. For example, even though Huntington's is thought to set in at the age of 40 or so, they notice that the children of those people develop about eight years earlier. Each generation anticipates and starts the condition earlier. So there's something causing that repeat and the protein to increase each generation.

That is something that's slow to sink into the genetic causality—that things are happening right now, each generation creating a tendency to mutate in a certain direction. There were many genetic theories that said that mutations do have a directionality. They used to explain the growth of antlers on [certain species] as getting bigger and bigger because of some tendency in the organism to go in a certain direction. Orthogenesis, they called it. But that was sort of vaguely anti-Darwinian and inclined towards Lamarckism, so it dropped out.

The idea of a defect in the gene that causes it to get worse and worse quickly with each generation is more acceptable because, in immunology, that was a solution to how antibodies can adapt so quickly to any conceivable infection or antigen. They said they have to adapt by mutating so fast that they can evolve in just a few days to match whatever antigen they're exposed to. So this idea of almost directed mutation got put into genetics by way of immunology. John Cairns and Ted Steele are the people known to be working on the idea of directed mutations in a constructive way, not just destructive.

**John Barkhausen:** I'm awfully confused by this because I think of geneticists as saying, in the past at least, that genes were a permanent thing passed down from generation to generation and could not be changed easily.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They have been open to the idea, but they're still not seeing it as anything deliberate or constructive, just a way the defect can develop. It's a way to save the genetic causality, rather than seeing that the same thing causing the symptoms of the disease might also be causing the genes to change in the same direction. That's what they don't want to see: a link between the way the gene changes and the function of the protein in the life of the individual organism. That implies Lamarckism.

**John Barkhausen:** You mean that the organism is directing the gene mutation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Or that something is causing the organism on the cellular, not genetic, level to change, and at the same time, the gene that regulates that cellular function is changing in the same direction. They shouldn't be coordinated that way so that the function and the gene change simultaneously, or even with the information going from the function into the gene.

**John Barkhausen:** Because that would mean that the organism is a purposive being on the evolutionary level.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. That's the whole point. Ever since the anti-Darwinians in the 19th century—Weismann in particular—they hated the idea that things could be changing meaningfully or purposefully, and wanted to say that there is no real change. Genes were the way of proving that. You might get a different mixture of traits, but the traits are eternal and the gene is what causes that.

One of the people questioning this, James Shapiro, was working in ordinary bacterial genetics. He noticed that individuals exposed to an antibiotic could become resistant to it and that they could pass that information on very intentionally to their neighbors. It could even cross varieties of one bacteria to another and spread through whole systems. That got him thinking about this idea of purposive change. He proposed that the organism does genetic engineering along the lines of what Barbara McClintock was talking about. He says this is the general way genetics works in the organism—that the organism is its own genetic engineer doing changes for its own benefit.

**John Barkhausen:** I can believe it. I was looking today at a physiology book trying to understand the nervous system, and it's pretty phenomenal. If you open up an encyclopedia and look at how the nervous system is laid out, it's an awe-inspiring system. The idea that some scientists and philosophers think that happened by random evolutionary trial and error seems impossible to my mind.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The establishment genetics biology system, including most of medicine, are attacking James Shapiro with his application of the Barbara McClintock way of thinking. Randomness is such a deep part of their way of thinking that they are accusing Shapiro of being a creationist. He says, well, the creationists sometimes speak very reasonably, and sometimes the so-called neo-Darwinians don't speak so scientifically and reasonably.

**John Barkhausen:** I don't personally buy into the father figure in the sky looking down on us all.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, but he's saying the organism itself has intelligence.

**John Barkhausen:** That to me has the ring of truth to it. As you look around the world and see the world organizing itself, it's a good example of the intelligence all around us. One of the things that interested me was what Carl Lindegren said in his book *Cold War in Biology*, which was that in order to practice science back in the 40s and 50s in the United States, it was very helpful to profess some kind of belief in a God in order to keep your job. He said that professors were afraid to say they were an atheist or agnostic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, all of my professors were churchgoers. In the 19th century, biologists specifically tended to be agnostics. But it really did get a religious boost in the 1940s. They considered it anti-materialist, but what it was was a different kind of materialism: randomness-based materialism rather than the idea that material is part of the purposive, intelligent life process.

**John Barkhausen:** Bringing this back to our topic today and talking about the inflammation that appears to be present in all of these diseases—whether we're talking about Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS/Lou Gehrig's disease), Multiple Sclerosis (MS), or Rheumatoid Arthritis. All these diseases involve inflammation. Maybe you could outline for us how science has perceived inflammation over the years.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the middle of the 20th century, there was a heavy concentration on inflammation as a reaction to infection. About 35 or 40 years ago, when I mentioned to a recent graduate something about "sterile inflammation," she wouldn't let me continue and said, "There's no such thing as sterile inflammation."

But 100 years before, people were demonstrating that you could extract something from infectious organisms that would create inflammation even if it was sterile. Then with radiation experiments, they found that radiation produced inflammation, or trauma. Completely sterile burns or shutting off the blood supply creates inflammation.

I think the only way to approach inflammation is to think of it as a gap that shouldn't exist between the demands made on the cells or the tissue and the resources to meet those demands. If you traumatize or overstimulate tissue, or if you don't provide enough sugar, oxygen, and carbon dioxide to meet that stimulation, then things go wrong. The tissue becomes edematous and chain reactions happen that can kill the tissue. Or, if the organism can manage to recruit enough systems to provide sugar and stop the excitation, then it can heal. A little inflammation rouses the organism to cause regeneration. Otherwise, it can lead to fibrosis and atrophy.

**John Barkhausen:** Let's use an example of one of these diseases, like Multiple Sclerosis. The myelin sheath, for some unknown reason according to the medical authorities, becomes worn away and the nerves stop functioning. They say it's caused by inflammation. How does that relate to your idea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Something that causes a lack of energy will cause tissue to swell up and take up water. As it swells up, the tissue tries to renew itself. Cells are always renewing themselves in a tremendous churning process of taking down the old stuff and putting up new stuff. Someone said that during the night, 60% of the fat substance in our brain is totally resynthesized. Just an hour after death, a massive amount of the brain substance has decomposed because it isn't constantly being reconstituted. So you have to think of a healthy, stable organism as being in extremely intense turnover processes.

If you cut off the energy supply, the first thing that happens is the cell takes up water, and that excites the restorative process to run faster. But if it takes up more and more water, that shifts the whole direction. The cell at a certain stage of excitation will de-differentiate or try to turn into a stem cell to grow new tissue as a healing process. If there's even less energy, then that process stops.

When you have just a chronic, slight energy deprivation, you get a chronic, slight edema. One of the things that happens is that the myelin swells up, and while it's being taken down, it isn't being resynthesized efficiently. Thyroid, progesterone, pregnenolone, and saturated fatty acids are things that support the reforming of the myelin. When the energy is down—for example, thyroid is low—then you can't make the pregnenolone and progesterone, so you just can't synthesize it as fast as it's being taken down.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's really a condition where you're put under stress and you don't have the energy resources to keep rebuilding yourself under that stress.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And it's remarkably similar to the processes in the degenerative brain diseases of aging, the development of cancer, deforming arthritis, chronic inflammation like pancreatitis, hepatitis, chronic kidney disease, and so on. All the same processes are involved, just in different proportions of energy supply and irritation or stimulation.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that what Hans Selye referred to as the condition of being sick?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah.

**John Barkhausen:** And that's just a shortage of energy, basically.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the gap between stimulation and energy resources has been used to define excitotoxicity that kills brain cells. But it's really the same process in your pancreas, kidney, or skin. Exactly the same energy systems, slight differences in the particular proteins.

In Huntington's disease, there's that polyglutamine repeat that accumulates, but it's really just a symptom of an inflammatory state with a particular history that leads to that being a problem. The fact that it usually waits until you're 40 years old means that—same with rheumatoid arthritis or Crohn's disease—they almost never develop in little kids. It takes a while being exposed to certain environments for each kind of thing to develop.

But there are a few common factors in the organism involved in almost all of these: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Lou Gehrig's, Huntington's, and MS. Even diabetes involves inflammation and the failure to regenerate properly. The beta cells are being killed in the same way that brain cells are being killed. Instead of making insulin as the cells are renewed, the cells are killed as fast as they're renewed, so they stop making insulin. But if you stop killing them, then they can start making insulin again. Same with the brain.

I might have mentioned a man with ALS that I talked to about eight or ten years ago. He was 70 years old and had all the best neurologists examine him. He was absolutely convinced he had Lou Gehrig's disease and was declining the same as other people he met in the neurology offices. He decided to start doing things to stop inflammation and support repair. He did them consistently for a few months while still declining, but then he stopped declining, and within a few months was repaired. Less than a year for the whole process. The people he had met in the neurology offices with the same rate of decline were totally disabled by the time he was totally recovered.

**John Barkhausen:** That's impressive. One of the things you've talked about in terms of helping your body rebuild is a very simple thing: keeping your blood sugar up. Maybe you can describe what happens when somebody is low on blood sugar. Reading you talk about the catabolic effect that happens just from low blood sugar is pretty convincing.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When your blood sugar falls because your liver hasn't stored enough glycogen to turn into glucose, the first reaction is for adrenaline to increase to try to squeeze more glycogen into your circulation for your brain. When the glycogen is absolutely gone, the adrenaline keeps activating the breakdown of fat and provides increased amounts of circulating fat to make up for the lack of sugar.

But after the fat becomes a source of energy, your cells still need some sugar to maintain their basic processes. So they turn protein into sugar. To do that, they increase cortisol, which breaks down muscle, skin, and the thymus gland. The thymus is the first to go. The cortisol will eat up your muscle, skin, and immune system pretty quickly to feed your heart, lungs, and brain to keep them alive.

Every time your blood sugar falls, you're shifting over to fat metabolism and breaking down protein. Muscles are one of the places that store glycogen, so as your muscles get smaller, more burden is put on your liver to keep your blood sugar steady. That makes your liver progressively suffer. Eventually, it gets to the point that your brain isn't getting the right energy or the right *kind* of energy.

One of the things that happens with aging is that we progressively change our fat composition. At birth, we're very highly saturated in our fats because they've been formed from glucose in utero. We can only make saturated, monounsaturated, and omega-9 unsaturated fats when we're supplied with sugar or protein. But once we start eating in the ordinary environment, our tissues start loading up on the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) from the environment.

By the time a person is 40, the brain is pretty full of either the arachidonic acid series or, if they have eaten a lot of fish, the long, highly unsaturated fats—mostly the DHA type of fish oil-derived omega-3 fats. Even with a pretty average diet, the old person's brain is very highly biased towards the DHA type fats.

If you look at Parkinson's disease, their favorite genetic protein that some people like to say is the cause—synuclein—is the Parkinson's equivalent of the glutamine repeat of Huntington's or the amyloid of Alzheimer's. Each disease tends to have its own protein that goes haywire. In the case of Parkinson's, it's the alpha-synuclein. DHA, the fish type of unsaturated fat, causes the synuclein protein to change to its toxic form that appears in Parkinson's disease. Saturated fats tend to protect against that. So very clearly in Parkinson's, you can see the role of fat in inclining the brain towards that degenerative change.

Since pretty much everyone in the environment accumulates these highly unsaturated fats, especially in the brain, by the time you're 30 or 40, you become more and more susceptible to all of the degenerative inflammatory diseases very much in proportion to the unsaturated fats. You can find the breakdown products corresponding to the seriousness of Alzheimer's, Huntington's, or MS. The specific breakdown products, such as acrolein which comes largely from the omega-3 fats, show that these unstable fats are breaking down at an increased rate in the degenerative brain conditions.

**John Barkhausen:** You've also said that in that cascade of bad effects from low blood sugar, after the free fatty acids are released, that actually pulls down your whole thyroid system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A series of studies in France about 25 to 30 years ago showed that exactly in proportion to the number of double bonds in a fat—increasing from a purely saturated fat such as stearic or palmitic acid, through oleic acid, up increasing with linoleic, and greatly with the five and six double bonds—each increased double bond impairs the thyroid function at the level of secretion, transport, and response. They looked at four different systems, but every one of these was impaired in proportion to the degree of unsaturation of the free fatty acids in the blood.

**John Barkhausen:** When was that study done, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 80s, in *Annals of Endocrinology*, a French journal.

**John Barkhausen:** Well, they are traditionally the kings of using saturated fat in their cooking. French cuisine is known for its use of butter.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The French have fallen for the propaganda against saturated fats and cholesterol. Some of their famous fat researchers were convinced that giving a fish oil supplement to pregnant women would make their babies smarter, even though animal studies showed that in proportion to the unsaturation of the fat in the pregnant animal's diet, the babies' brains were smaller and less able to learn.

The French fed some pregnant women the unsaturated fats while measuring the fetus's ability to react to sounds applied to the abdomen. They found that, contrary to what they believed would happen, the learning was impaired by the diet with more of the highly unsaturated fats. And when the babies were born, in line with the animal experiments, their growth was retarded.

**John Barkhausen:** That seems really immoral to be testing that theory out on infants and their mothers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The publicity of the animal studies has pretty much suppressed the fact that these fats didn't have consistently good effects on brain and eye development. What got publicized were the few studies showing what were interpreted to be good results. On the basis of that, the baby food industry was allowed to add these things to their powdered milk for making baby formula. But even in the powdered milk, they're so unstable that toxic oxidation fragments are tremendously increased. Still, the publicity is such that they're promoted as protective.

**John Barkhausen:** So currently, baby formula that people are using has the DHA oils in them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of them do. I don't know if there are some without it.

**John Barkhausen:** That's a little discouraging. I can see adults going along with different fads and trying things out for themselves, but when you start experimenting with infants, it seems like not a very good idea.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the things that happens at the same time these unsaturated fats are accumulating in the body is that the ratio of estrogen to progesterone is increasing. By the time a woman is 40, her estrogen is even higher in an absolute sense than it was when she was 20. But even worse is that her progesterone has decreased. So the ratio is shifted very powerfully in the direction of estrogen.

Estrogen happens to synergize with the polyunsaturated fats. These polyunsaturateds activate the action of a given amount of estrogen and at the same time interfere with the production of progesterone and suppress thyroid. Lower thyroid increases estrogen and decreases progesterone.

But the estrogen industry has convinced most doctors that estrogen is good for the brain and for preventing heart disease and strokes. So when the Women's Health Initiative pointed out that estrogen supplements increased dementia, heart attacks, and strokes—reinforcing what animal studies had shown—the medical establishment took two or three years to respond and come back and say what must have been wrong with that study.

**John Barkhausen:** That's what they're saying now, that the study was wrong.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There is very heavy propaganda to improve the sales of estrogen, which dropped off drastically when that study came out.

**John Barkhausen:** That was a very convincing study.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Especially because it absolutely corroborated the animal research going back 50 years before then.

**John Barkhausen:** And these diseases we're talking about today affect women way more than they affect men. I think MS is 10 to 1.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even Alzheimer's. In the 90s, it was already well documented that women had two or two and a half times the incidence of Alzheimer's disease as men. In spite of that, the people who wanted to sell estrogen said, "Well, that's because women's estrogen declines with aging." But in fact, by the age of 40, it has increased tremendously. And that's when the brain damage is being done by the bad ratio of estrogen to progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** I know you've covered this before, Ray, but explain how it is that people think estrogen is declining when it actually isn't. It's increasing and the tests just don't pick it up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One thing is that the estrogen is stuck. When it's in the cells working, it's bound to the things they call estrogen receptors. Progesterone's effect, which should rise right after ovulation, destroys or decomposes the estrogen binding proteins and activates enzymes that inactivate estrogen, getting it out of the cells. So if you're deficient in progesterone, you can't get estrogen out of the cells.

It not only stays there, but it tends to activate enzymes that create more estrogen. Your aromatase in your fat tissue, fibrous tissue, and various tissues increases, making estrogen outside of the ovaries as you age. Even in a young monkey, they were studying the estrogen output in the ovary and as a control, they used the blood coming from the arm veins. They found that the monkey's arm was producing more estrogen than its ovary was. That process increases with age.

When you're deficient in progesterone, most of the estrogen stays inside cells working, rather than getting out into the blood where it could be excreted. The only way you can really tell how much estrogen influence a person has when they're 50 years old is to take a snip of tissue and analyze its estrogen content.

**John Barkhausen:** And on top of our bodies producing more estrogen as we age, we have a huge environmental load coming down on us because many of the chemicals we use in our modern lifestyle are estrogenic. Plus pollution is estrogenic.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1930s, before the estrogen industry took off, people were studying what estrogen is and does. They found that soot is estrogenic. Things that produce the estrogen effect produce inflammation and cancer. Basically, it's a process of cell excitation followed or accompanied by blocking oxidative energy production. That was pretty much covered up when the estrogen industry convinced doctors that estrogen was the female hormone that would prevent infertility and aging.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The interaction of estrogen as an excitatory thing with the polyunsaturated fats—which are also excitatory things besides producing inflammation and blocking energy production—activates other systems. For example, the glutamate/glutamic acid system. That is why monosodium glutamate (MSG) produces brain injury; it excites cells to the point that if there's not enough energy supply, the cells will die.

Estrogen and the unsaturated fats both activate this glutamate excitatory system. Those interact to increase a set of enzymes called transglutaminase. This is the enzyme involved in celiac disease, the gluten sensitivity disease. This enzyme is normally involved in maturing cells that are under the influence of stress, as in the surface of the skin when it's maturing into a hardened keratinized layer, or in the uterus as estrogen is causing the lining to mature.

But in the brain, this excitation from unsaturated fats, lipid peroxidation breakdown, estrogen, and the glutamic acid system excites the formation of transglutaminase. Transglutaminase happens to form polymers and fibrils and deposits of these various enzymes that are known to accumulate in Huntington's, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and MS.

The tau protein in Alzheimer's disease, for example: transglutaminase activates a reaction that causes these proteins to accumulate and form fibrils. This enzyme works on amino groups. When the metabolism is healthy and producing energy by the use of oxidative metabolism, it's producing a constant supply of carbon dioxide (CO2). Carbon dioxide spontaneously combines with amino groups. Every protein in the body should have its supply of carbon dioxide, preventing the action of enzymes such as transglutaminase which would bind them and cause them to condense and form fibrils.

I suspect that in places where estrogen is dominant, or in the skin where the cells are exposed to pure air, the carbon dioxide is displaced either by the effect of estrogen or just by the high saturation of oxygen. The absence of the carbon dioxide allows this transglutaminase to cross-link, inactivate, and harden the proteins. But when it happens inside your brain, you get these abnormal deposits of protein that should only happen in cells that are terminally differentiating and getting ready to slough off.

**John Barkhausen:** So CO2 is very important to the health of the body.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There was a survey in Nepal at very high altitudes. They found lots of sick people, but they didn't find the degenerative brain diseases that you would expect at lower altitude, poor populations. I suspect that it's because when you adapt to high altitude, your body retains a much higher level of carbon dioxide. Your blood is more in the carbamino state, but probably all your proteins are.

**John Barkhausen:** And you've said that reduced thyroid function—not having enough of the active thyroid hormone, T3—is when you start having trouble not only with energy levels but also the myelin sheath. Your nerves can't regenerate without the T3. Is that right?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The first five people that I met who had a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, I was starting to believe there wasn't such a thing as multiple sclerosis because all of those first five people had such classical symptoms of hypothyroidism. When they took thyroid, their symptoms totally disappeared. So it's very easy to confuse hypothyroidism with multiple sclerosis.

**John Barkhausen:** In the few minutes we have left, Raymond, maybe you could just run over what are some of the simple things people can do to alleviate their symptoms or even avoid them entirely?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Well, it's known that aspirin prevents most of these degenerative conditions. People who have chronically used some aspirin are much less likely to have Parkinson's or Alzheimer's. Caffeine is another generally protective thing against inflammation, fibrosis, and degeneration.

Avoidance of the polyunsaturated fats, I think, is the basic and most important thing. And avoiding anti-thyroid foods. The worst anti-thyroid foods are these polyunsaturated fats.

**John Barkhausen:** And keeping your protein level up.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And gelatin seems to have a therapeutic anti-inflammatory effect. Eating the cheapest cuts of meat, bones, and skin. In the US, few people eat the skin, and since the fat avoidance fad, people tend to eat skinless chicken. When the animals are fed a good diet, the skin fat is more saturated. Pork rinds are a very good source of gelatin. If you boil a chicken, the skin and bones will release a lot of gelatin, which is an anti-inflammatory, protective protein.

**John Barkhausen:** And you mentioned how important it is to keep your blood sugar up to handle stresses. How should one do that? I have a feeling that a lot of our problems today are because people are avoiding sugar because it's gotten such a bad rap.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. Every day I hear at least one or two people saying what happened when they started eating sugar. One man said his hair stopped falling out a couple of days after he started eating sugar. A kid who was having seizures and had gone down to 112 pounds in just two or three weeks is back up to his normal weight for eating something like 8 or 9 ounces of sugar added to his other foods in a crisis.

Sugar in itself—just simple honey or sugar—can be very therapeutic. But in general, you want to shift your diet towards fruit rather than grains and starchy vegetables.

**John Barkhausen:** Just to finish up, you were saying that starches are a bad way to get sugar. Like wheat is bad.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Partly because of the other things they're associated with. But one of the things they do harmfully is to support bacterial growth. The poorly cooked starches or the more undercooked vegetables and complex forms of starch support bacterial growth. The bacteria produce endotoxin, and endotoxin works with these other pro-inflammatory things.

Some of the structural changes of the degenerative proteins are very similar to the structure that is defensive against endotoxin. So some of them might be provoked by the presence of endotoxin as a defensive reaction. It's well known that the polyunsaturated fats activate prion formation and so on, but the unsaturated fats are probably biologically analogous to the endotoxin produced by the bacteria.

**John Barkhausen:** Yes. And you've written a lot about the relationship of maldigestion of food creating a lot of the problems that we've been talking about or helping to exacerbate them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. And the unsaturated fats contribute even at the digestive level because they interfere with protein digestive enzymes as well as after they get into the bloodstream.

**John Barkhausen:** Well, we've filled up the hour, Ray. It's gone very fast. I really appreciate you coming on Politics and Science again. Perhaps at some point we can follow up and get into some of the details of how digestion does relate to disease because I think that's something that the medical world doesn't cover at all.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. If you go back to the mid-19th century, you see that medicine was really making progress. Then into the 20th century, the Russians were continuing digestive physiology, but after about the 1920s in the US, it was pretty much ignored.

**John Barkhausen:** All right, well, thanks so much for sharing your knowledge with us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay.

**John Barkhausen:** Thanks a lot, Ray. Bye.

title: Politics & Science: Questions and Answers I
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Thank you very much for joining me and us this afternoon. You have a degree in biology with a specialty in physiology. Do you want to add anything to that besides being a science historian?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, except maybe that I was in the humanities for years before I went to graduate school in biology.

**John Barkhausen:** That is an interesting part of your life.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it guided the way I treated science, being more critical about the texts that you refer to.

**John Barkhausen:** And maybe giving you a more humanistic attitude toward science and life.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yeah. More philosophy. Biologists think they have a philosophy of science, but it's pretty rudimentary—mechanistic, mechanical materialism, usually.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you want to define mechanical materialism for our audience who may not be familiar with that term?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is the difference between organismic thinking—in the Whiteheadian sense—or historical materialism in the Marxist sense. Mechanistic materialism makes a clear distinction between mind and matter. For them, matter is necessarily unconscious and stupid because intelligence exists only in their realm of mind or idealist philosophy.

**John Barkhausen:** I see. So it's sort of an elitism of human thought at the expense of the rest of the world.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, a clear distinction between mind and matter. In brain biology, that is changing a lot. People are realizing that you can't solve some of the problems when you think in that dualistic way. But still, it tends to be a philosophical idealism rather than a philosophical materialism.

**John Barkhausen:** I'd like to bring the show down to earth so people can relate to it. I was thinking of talking today about how we know whether we're healthy or not. I think one of the ways we judge ourselves is how healthy we feel—if we feel energized, depressed, stimulated, or stressed out. When the medical world came into being, we used professionals to judge how healthy we are. I thought it would be interesting to talk about the history of that. Perhaps you could give us your experience from childhood on regarding the health challenges you faced and how that shaped your viewpoint.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** As a little kid, I was a migrainer, periodically having combination digestive and visually affected headaches. When I was ten, a naturopathic doctor prescribed a bag of an herb to make a tea out of that was supposed to affect the migraine syndrome. Years later, I discovered from the taste that it had been marijuana, but it didn't help at all. That was about the extent of my drug treatment.

**John Barkhausen:** What year was that? I didn't know there were naturopaths back then.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** 1945. Oh, sure. They were the original doctors. The modern type of allopathic doctor was just one strand, one ideology of medicine. There were all kinds of ideologies up until the American Medical Association defined one strand of medicine.

**John Barkhausen:** How did osteopathy relate to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It was just one of the theories that the bones were the framework of health. Many strands emphasized different things. The old humor theory of medicine pretty well died out, but those things were blended into homeopathic medicine and naturopathy. The homeopathic tradition still has some of that thinking in terms of personality types—the phlegmatic and sanguine personalities—thinking in terms of the fluid related to the various organs. When you look at standard medical traditions between France and England, you see a very heavy emphasis in the Latin cultures on the liver and the English on the intestine. In Latin America, cardiology is a much bigger thing than in Europe.

**John Barkhausen:** How do you account for the emphasis on different organs from the different cultures?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's just which school of medicine happened to be most influential or successful.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think the humors were influenced by the Indian and Far Eastern traditions like the Ayurvedic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, there was some absorption. The Arabs really were the way Greek medicine came into Europe, but some of the Indian culture got into the Greek medical tradition.

**John Barkhausen:** Before modern blood tests, how did doctors assess whether a person was healthy or not?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It depended a lot on the school of medicine. Some would make judgments about which humor was dominating them or which organ. By the 19th century, different strands of biological information were being integrated into the different theories so that people started thinking about the cells making up the organs. Late in the 19th century, they were realizing that sugar was secreted by the liver to maintain a steady internal environment.

They used feel and smell and even taste—the different secretions and warmth on the body. They would examine the person as an object to see if there was anything abnormal. For example, they used to taste the urine to see if a person was diabetic. There were many ideas about what you could diagnose by smell, including diabetes and cancer. Lately, people have been talking about the ability of dogs to diagnose by smell when a person is about to have a seizure or developing a cancer.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that their heightened smell or is it telepathic?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Possibly electrical fields. Dogs can apparently detect bioelectric fields the way fish can. But Linus Pauling was probably the first person who thought of diagnosing by analyzing a person's breath and found 250 chemicals in the breath. Only a few places are now taking advantage of that. For example, nitric oxide is increased in the breath when a person has an inflammatory disease.

**John Barkhausen:** So basically they used all their senses to diagnose people.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, as well as listening to their complaints and their history. The person often knows more about their disease than they are aware. For example, their dreams will often predict some sickness that's about to come to full awareness. If a person is a good listener, sometimes they can draw out information that the person wasn't fully aware of.

**Bill (Caller):** I was fascinated with the opening about you advocating for matter to have the same kind of intelligence as the human species. Isn't it interesting that we are willing to attribute intelligence to non-material beings like spirits, but not to matter?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the attitude towards matter that exists throughout the medical profession and biology in general is basically a religious belief. It is a religious exclusion of spirit, mind, and intelligence from whatever they consider matter. So an organ or a material object can't have in itself mentality, spirit, or intelligence, and hardly deserves to be called alive. It's not at all a scientific issue.

When I was about eight or nine years old, I read about J.C. Bose's biological experiments right around the turn of the last century. Coming from the Hindu tradition, he didn't have the Christian/Jewish/Muslim attitude towards matter, life, and human intelligence. His background gave him the perspective to ask what lifelike properties exist in the different levels of organization.

Bose asked, "What are the defining features of human life?" He listed properties of sensitivity and reactivity, then did tests on plants to see if they had any of these animal-like properties. He showed that plants showed a reactive physical response to practically any stimulation. After designing instruments that would record the reactions of plant tissue, he applied the same thing to objects such as metal and minerals and showed the same properties of sensitivity, reaction, learning, or adaptation applied to all levels of existence—mineral, plant, animal, as well as human. That didn't fit into the way Western nerve biology was developing, but scientifically it was actually more soundly based.

**John Barkhausen:** And we can thank Bose for inventing the radio? Marconi got his basic ideas from Bose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. It was exactly the same kind of physical thinking about the sensitivity of material that led to the invention of the radio as to the explanation of nerve and muscle function.

**John Barkhausen:** Was the naturopath your only experience with a doctor as a child?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh no, I had one doctor give me probably almost a lethal dose of radiation by fluoroscoping me.

**John Barkhausen:** How old were you then?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Five, I think.

**John Barkhausen:** Was there any purpose given?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Entertaining the doctor and impressing the patients. That was a very popular toy around 1940.

**John Barkhausen:** I didn't realize you'd been subjected to that. I think Thomas Edison was completely against the use of radioactive technology, wasn't he?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, he was one of the pioneers in designing the apparatus, but his main technician died horribly from exposure to it. That changed Edison's attitude.

**John Barkhausen:** When did you realize it wasn't a good idea?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In 1945 and '46, I started reading about radiation because of the atomic bomb. It was already in the underground culture that the biological effects of medical X-rays were unwise, but the medical profession was hardly getting started. They had killed many people with bad apparatus and theories in the 1930s. People I knew in college were still getting horrible X-ray treatment for acne or ringworm. About ten years after the treatment, some of their skulls had begun collapsing; their sinuses collapsed so their faces were deformed. That was still being done in the 1950s.

I remember hearing about the English woman, Alice Stewart. Her study showed that X-raying pregnant women caused leukemia in the babies. That just wasn't acceptable by the medical profession.

**John Barkhausen:** Was it unpatriotic to be against the technology of radiation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That really didn't get started as a political issue until the later 50s. It became a very dangerous thing for any academic person to criticize either X-rays or atmospheric atomic bomb tests. If you said they were killing people in Utah by the fallout, you were probably labeled a communist. John Gofman was one of the main government propagandists in favor of continuing bomb tests. I considered him a government demon all through the 50s. Later, in the late 1960s, he said he was giving a speech defending atmospheric bomb testing because there had been no evidence that it caused mutations, and while he was saying that, he realized that it was a crazy thing to be doing. He simply changed suddenly from being the government's biggest propagandist.

**George (Caller):** If you're trying to turn off stress hormones, should you err on the possibility of overeating until you're stable with temps and pulses?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sugar is the single most immediately effective food for stopping stress—sometimes salt. So a food with mixed components, including enough sodium and glucose or fructose, will stop some of the worst stress hormones.

**George (Caller):** Would losing excess weight help you gain that stability because of reduced body fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you lose too fast, that is going to cause damage by oxidative decomposition of the unsaturated fats as they're being oxidized at a higher rate. I think slow weight loss is the best thing. Having enough protein and minerals in your diet during weight loss can make a tremendous difference in the amount of stress. When a person goes on a complete fast for a week or two, they lose very little fat but a lot of protein and functioning tissue. But if they eat about a 1000 calorie diet, they can lose almost entirely fat. So the minerals as well as the protein are very important to reduce the stress hormones which will take down your good tissues when you're losing weight.

**John Barkhausen:** Priscilla asks: "Can you refer me to a source of information about the workings of hormones in the body? It seems any mention of them is laughed off as having to do with sex or anxiety."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The definition of hormone has changed a lot in the last 30 or 40 years, so the classical definitions hardly apply anymore. It's good to look at one of the classical textbooks of endocrinology. One from about 30 or 40 years ago would be Constance Martin, *Textbook of Endocrine Physiology*.

Also, Hans Selye did something called the *Encyclopedia of Endocrinology* in the 1940s. His work was very influential for my thinking. He very early showed the dangers of estrogen and the protective effects of progesterone and pregnenolone. If the medical industry had really paid attention, the country would have been much healthier.

**John Barkhausen:** What was the next doctor experience you had after the fluoroscope and the naturopath?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I stayed away from doctors after that. But because of my experience with migraine, when I was nine or ten, I started getting nearsighted. I noticed that the only other kids in my school who were nearsighted were girls, and a couple of them were also migraineurs. That got me thinking: why are more girls nearsighted and subject to migraine headaches?

I started looking at people in terms of their hormones. I was thinking along the lines of the suppressive effects of estrogen on metabolism, blood sugar regulation, and thyroid function. In my early teens, I discovered that a change in my eating rhythm would invariably trigger a migraine if I was very active physically. I would draw down my glycogen supplies, and if I hadn't replenished them fast enough, I would develop a migraine.

After thinking about that for years, I realized I could intervene. It happened that I had a couple of quarts of ice cream in the fridge. Realizing I hadn't been eating enough, I ate a quart of ice cream as fast as I could when the blind spots were already starting to flash. I found that they turned right off as I absorbed the ice cream.

**John Barkhausen:** You didn't switch to ice cream headaches instead?
