**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, those were very minor. Several other things added to that. Someone told me about eating a raw carrot being a way to interrupt a headache, and I found that worked too.

I had read some of the books of a famous gastroenterologist, Walter Alvarez. He found that the intestine was involved in a very high percentage of headaches. He wanted to disprove the idea that headaches are caused by toxins; he believed they were caused by pressure in the intestine. To demonstrate, he stuffed some of his medical students' rectums with wads of cotton, and about half of them developed headaches.

Other researchers were working on the intestine with both toxins and pressure. Russian researchers would put an inflatable balloon in the intestine of a rabbit. If the rabbit was in normal health, nothing would happen. But if the rabbit had low blood sugar, blowing up the balloon would cause all kinds of symptoms, including epileptic seizures. An allergen or chemical irritant would cause a range of symptoms from seizures to shock if blood sugar was low. But if blood sugar was high, chemical irritants had almost no effect biologically.

**John Barkhausen:** So that's how the ice cream was working—to protect you with sugar?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The carrot would apparently do multiple things: absorb toxins or speed along the elimination of toxins, and prevent pressure and chemical irritation. So you could work on either side of it: keeping the blood sugar up or reducing the irritation to the intestine.

**John Barkhausen:** At some point, blood tests began to be used extensively. When did that start?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My awareness of it started around the late 1940s. Some of my fat friends in school told me they had previously been told they had a glandular problem and were given thyroid. But with the new medical science in the late 40s, they discovered they were just gluttons. They had been given a test called Protein Bound Iodine (PBI). If your PBI was okay, you just had the psychological problem of eating too much.

About half of the people who went to doctors with overweight would get a thyroid prescription and cure their problem. After science intervened with a blood test, 95% of those people were told they were perfectly normal hormonally and taken off thyroid.

At that same time, synthetic thyroxine was introduced. It was tested on medical students—who at that time were all young men in their early 20s. When they were given a dose of synthetic thyroxine, it worked exactly the same as a dose of Armour thyroid. So the pharmaceutical industry displaced the meat industry-based Armour product because it was "more scientific."

They neglected to notice that most thyroid patients were women, and that women—especially if their thyroid is low—have much more sluggish livers than men. It's easier for a woman to get drunk on a small amount of alcohol because the liver throws it off so slowly. The same applies to aspirin and other drugs. Women are more sensitive because the liver is slowed down by estrogen.

When the liver is very sluggish, thyroxine isn't turned into the active hormone, but it does suppress the pituitary. The pituitary senses the presence of thyroid hormone and stops stimulating the gland. So the frequent event throughout the 1950s and 60s was that women would actually be made worse by turning off their remaining thyroid function by dosing them with this synthetic drug.

**John Barkhausen:** So that's a case of them doing the tests, but interpreting them in such a way that it didn't help the patient.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. During this time, the PBI test showed that only 5% of the population tested low. But as new tests became possible in the 60s using immune techniques, they found that the PBI test had nothing to do with thyroid function. However, the concept had been built into the profession that only 5% of people are really biologically lacking thyroid function. So they devised new tests and standardized them on the same population framework that the meaningless test had created. Ever since then, no matter how sensitive your measurement gets, if they're stuck on the idea that the "normal" range covers 95% of results, they stretch the test to fit a bad definition of normal.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that because of money, or did they just take a wrong turn?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The drug industry controls the world. Carla Rothenberg, a law student at Harvard, wrote a very good paper on the history of the estrogen industry during those same years. The industry didn't like the way science was going—which was showing that estrogen was able to create abortions, produce cancer, inflammation, and degeneration. But they had products that could be made cheaply. A conspiracy of 12 or 13 big corporations decided to get the FDA and the population in line with mass media and public relations to sell the idea that estrogen was a fertility-promoting medicine rather than a sterility promoter. Starting in 1942, science was turned on its head for basically 60 years.

**John Barkhausen:** Paul asks: "By reducing conflict with others and within one's own mind, can kindness, generosity, and ethical conduct promote healthy metabolism?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think so.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you ever recommend meditation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Meditation in the sense of watching your own consciousness, being mindful of your body and the world in general. I think everyone should always be doing that. By being aware of yourself and the world, you can avoid confusing the two. When I was working on linguistics, I realized that people are really participating inside each other's minds. The Russian physiologist Anokhin devised a way of explaining how reflexes work in terms of the "acceptor of action," which is essentially a model of the world built in our consciousness. We adjust that according to the results of our senses.

**John Barkhausen:** Paul also asks: "Do you consider the US government's explanation for the destruction of the World Trade Center Towers plausible?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I haven't heard anything from any government official that makes sense. I think there are quite a few possible explanations that are more plausible than the government story.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you discuss the functions of oxytocin?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's one of the adaptive hormones, but it has some stress-related responses, so I don't see it as the "happiness and euphoria" hormone. It can go up under stress too. It's sort of like the parasympathetic system—it is a good relief to the sympathetic system, but you don't want to go too far in that direction.

All of the pituitary hormones are pretty expendable as long as you keep your thyroid working. Researchers removed pituitaries from animals and gave them thyroid, and found the animals were healthier without their pituitaries.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you offer any anecdotes about slow, gradual healing for people who don't respond quickly?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When it isn't instantaneous, it tends to be gradual. When you are lucky and hit the missing thing on the first try, you can see things go from miserable to perfect in an hour. But if you don't hit the one missing factor, it can involve very slow repair. Sometimes a person will supplement progesterone and feel perfect, but then hit another point in the monthly cycle and things go out of balance. The body changes so drastically cyclically that it goes through repair phases. Bones can take quite a while to repair, but I've seen people with crippling arthritis where their joint becomes painless overnight.

**John Barkhausen:** What are your plans for the next five or ten years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I expect to keep writing newsletters. Currently, I've been thinking about the importance of carbon monoxide in our endogenous regulatory processes. For 20 years I've been talking about keeping your carbon *dioxide* up. But everything I've been talking about—bright light, thyroid, coffee, fruit—acts in the same direction to decrease carbon *monoxide*.

When we are under stress, we produce carbon monoxide. The ups and downs of pituitary hormones (ACTH, TSH, oxytocin) act partly by increasing carbon monoxide production. That seems to be one of the reasons why removing the pituitary gland in experimental animals had such beneficial effects—because of the harmful, age-advancing effects of endogenous carbon monoxide.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's dangerous from outside sources as well as inside?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah. The outside adds to what's going on inside. If someone has a tendency to liver disease or seizures, going downtown where the carbon monoxide might be 20 or 30 parts per million could be enough to trigger symptoms. When I used to drive through downtown Los Angeles, I would tend to get lost on days when the carbon monoxide was up around 50 parts per million.

**John Barkhausen:** Wade asks: "Why does someone develop Alzheimer's while another gets multiple sclerosis? What determines the disease course?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The health of your other organs influences the shape of the deterioration. In multiple sclerosis, clots tend to associate with the plaques or inflamed areas. In Alzheimer's, the clotting system is involved differently. Some people think the amyloid plaques are produced to make up for the leakiness of the capillaries.

It's basically a blood vessel leaky problem being handled from opposite sides. In MS, the clot seems to start the process. In Alzheimer's, the capillaries get leaky, produce a micro-hemorrhage, and an enzyme that clears away the heme is the enzyme that forms carbon monoxide. This enzyme is associated with amyloid plaques.

Cancer develops possibly starting with the same leakage of blood vessels, leading to increased deposition of connective tissue and atrophy. Within that area of atrophy, cells convert themselves to live without the ordinary support of the environment. All are cells trying to correct a problem but not having enough energy to do it properly.

**John Barkhausen:** We often hear that genetics determines disease.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Everyone has genes, so genetics explains everything, but they haven't made a convincing case. Usually, about half the people with a disease might have genes that contribute to it, others don't. Harry Rubin, a biology professor at UC Berkeley, pointed out that very highly mutated cells can have dozens of cancer-promoting mutations, but as long as they are in a healthy organism, they don't produce cancer. It's the failure of the organism's support system first.

**John Barkhausen:** Sandy asks: "Is it useful to compare the basal metabolic rate to the daily caloric intake to gauge one's metabolic rate?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** There are many ways you can do it. The more alive you are, the more energy is running through you. From puberty to old age, oxygen consumption decreases by about 70% unless you intervene. This corresponds to the increase in mortality.

G.W. Crile and his wife went around the world with basal metabolic apparatus. They found that people in very different cultures—from Eskimos to tropical people—had basal metabolic rates about 30% higher than the average American. He saw a correspondence of brain function to adrenal, liver, and thyroid metabolism. He showed that a crocodile at rest consumed only as much oxygen as a cat at rest, despite weighing hundreds of pounds, and showed their brains were the same size. He believed the brain represented the basal metabolic rate.

**John Barkhausen:** Justin asks about chronically low blood pressure (85/60). Is this a problem?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it reflects a low metabolic rate. You could probably be more productive if you were producing more energy. When I spent time in Florida, I was miserable because of the humidity and couldn't take my usual amount of thyroid without overheating. At night, my blood pressure would go down to something like 50 over 25.

**John Barkhausen:** Robin asks: "Why are they testing for PSAs even though he has had his prostate removed?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They believe it indicates prostate cells lodged in other parts of the body. But when you measure that antigen in women, it doesn't mean they have prostate cancer. PSA stands for Prostate Specific Antigen, but it's found in women who don't have a prostate, so it's not accurately named.

**John Barkhausen:** Stefan asks about teen acne. Causes and cures?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've seen topical progesterone work almost instantly; a pimple would regress as soon as they put progesterone on it. But it usually involves a bacterial infection and the immune system reacting badly. Vitamin A and thyroid function are essential for the differentiation of skin cells. The skin is a major source of steroid hormone synthesis. Cholesterol can be turned into steroids, but thyroid and Vitamin A are needed to maintain healthy turnover.

**John Barkhausen:** A listener asks: "I've read that people with Alzheimer's don't tend to get cancer."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't know if that happens. Alzheimer's is not consistently diagnosed. Sometimes people who get to be 95 get diagnosed with Alzheimer's just for being absent-minded, when they might not have the diagnostic features a younger person would have.

**Caller:** Eating a calorie-dense meal like a pancake seems to warm me up more than drinking orange juice. Why do you not consider starch superior to liquids for raising body heat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Starch, slightly more than sucrose, triggers insulin. Insulin tends to lead to increased cortisol production, and cortisol can raise your body temperature. But that isn't the kind of increased metabolism that is generally helpful; it warms you up by a stress reaction. Some people wake up warm (stress hormones) and then cool down after eating. Cycling heat production down during the night and up during the day leads to longer-range benefit.

**Caller:** At what age can a male expect to maintain a healthy sex life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It shouldn't have any particular age relation. Testosterone, DHEA, and thyroid are all part of good sexual energy. There's no reason why those should drop off.

**Caller:** Do you consider drugs like Viagra to be helpful or harmful?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Harmful. It acts largely by increasing nitric oxide and carbon monoxide, and those have lots of harmful effects.

**John Barkhausen:** I've been reading about the supposed problem of having too much calcium causing calcification. Is that accurate?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that's the result of medical people having a mechanical way of thinking. For at least 50 years, it's been known that parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases when you're deficient in calcium. If you aren't eating enough calcium, PTH will take calcium out of your bones and put it into your soft tissues, contributing to hardened arteries, kidneys, and brain calcification.

The prevention is to get enough Vitamin D and Vitamin K, and plenty of calcium to keep PTH, prolactin, and cortisol down. The surest way to calcify your arteries is to be a calcium avoider.

**John Barkhausen:** What about intention in testing? It seems the medical industry has gotten away from treating the patient to running a business.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, with X-rays, they have to keep their equipment busy to pay for it. A lot of testing is done to prevent lawsuits.

**John Barkhausen:** A question came in by email: "Are there dangers to antibiotics modifying gut flora? What are the best factors for cleaning the gut?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The best, safest long-range things are the indigestible but antiseptic fibers of raw carrot or bamboo shoots. The whole small intestine in a very healthy person is sterile. The more active your digestive fluids and enzymes are, the more sterile your small intestine will be. Sluggish metabolism leads to bacteria living further up in the intestine. Stimulating the intestine with raw carrot helps, but keeping your metabolic rate up is the basic thing.

title: Politics & Science: William Blake and Art's Relationship to Science
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Welcome to Politics and Science. I am your host, John Barkhausen. This is a special edition starting an hour early with Dr. Raymond Peat. Dr. Peat has a PhD in biology and has specialized in physiology. Ray, are you there?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Oh, yeah, you're there.

**John Barkhausen:** If you could fill us in, maybe a little bit about your background would be great.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 1950s, I started studying William Blake around 1955. I finished my master's degree at the University of Oregon with a thesis on Blake in 1959. By chance, I taught a combination of courses, mostly biology but a painting course or two, at a little college in Urbana, Ohio. Because of political things connected to anti-war and anti-atomic bomb testing, I left Urbana and started my own college in Mexico. I named it Blake College. The government shut that down in 1965.

I taught linguistics at Montana State for a year and tried to restart Blake College in Oregon. That went on for a couple of years with the FBI constantly watching the students. Then I went to graduate school in 1968 at the University of Oregon. I had been studying Blake's ideas and theory of knowledge in relation to language. I had been thinking about concentrating on brain physiology, but at the university, I found that was the most dogmatic area in the biology department other than genetics. Nerve theory was a caricature of primitive computer theory at the time. So, I found a really physiological area of biology: reproductive and aging physiology. That's what I did my thesis on. Since then, I've been following up similar ideas in the theory of knowledge, function of the brain, and how reproductive hormones affect brain function.

**John Barkhausen:** A lot of your work has been collating research done over the last century. Maybe you could say a little bit about that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I ran into the biological dogmatism of the nerve people, they were basing everything on an "all or nothing" function of the nerve membrane. From the reading I had been doing and some experiments, I was very skeptical about the whole membrane control of cell biology.

Starting when I was about eight years old and read about the history of inheritance in encyclopedias, I saw there was very good evidence for the Lamarckian type of inheritance all the way through the early decades of the 20th century. It was essentially stamped out by not permitting teachers to describe the Lamarckian theory starting in 1947. Seeing that modern biology people were explaining everything in terms of genes and membranes, I looked around in the literature contemporary with what we were being assigned.

I saw that Otto Warburg had solved most of the problems of how cancer develops, for example, on the basis of damage to the respiratory energy-producing system. That was very convincing to me. People were ignoring him or denying his work had any validity without even understanding it; they always misquoted and misrepresented it.

At the same time, I ran into the work of Gilbert Ling in the early 1950s. I saw that he had demonstrated the irrelevancy of the so-called nerve membrane, or cell membrane in general. His work had basically solved all of the problems that my professors were working on and mystifying—creating problems where there weren't any. I wrote to him in the fall of 1968 and said, "You seem to have solved all of these problems that are confusing my professors." He said, "You just don't understand science. Science is about prestige, money, and power." I've written to him two or three times over the decades, and he's been very helpful each time.

**John Barkhausen:** I have his book, and it's way over my head in terms of math, but he is a brilliant man. On the face of it, his theory of how cells function makes so much more sense. I think a lot of your research, Ray, has been about environmental influences on life and countering mainstream science, which says it's all genetic and the environment has very little influence on why we get sick. Would you say that's true?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, except that I see the mainstream as having been exactly where I've been, except they got shut down financially and in publication. At the same time Lamarckism was extirpated from high schools and universities, the field theory of embryology was de-financed and disappeared, even though it was the mainstream based on sound facts.

The genetic control people—if you look at summaries of the classic papers in genetics, you see how hypothetical and rationalistic it is. It's a "it could happen" approach to science. They define themselves as a mainstream simply by shutting off publication to the dissidents. But now it's coming back. People like James Shapiro, with his bacterial demonstration of environmental and trans-generational influences, and John Cairns, another bacteria person who has kept alive the influence of the environment on inheritance. There has been a continuous environmental developmental field approach in all aspects of biology, but they've been systematically quieted.

**John Barkhausen:** It seems like there are ideological reasons, but also pointed financial reasons. If the environment affects our health, it means the corporations polluting that environment are doing it at our expense.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can see that over and over; every generation has its area of concentration. The behaviorist psychologists basically defended poverty and oppression because they said what happens to the brain of the fetus in utero is purely genetically determined. So, the mother can be starved half to death, and that isn't going to hurt the offspring. The medical establishment went along with that, justifying starvation living for the poor classes.

**John Barkhausen:** Science influences public policy in an enormous way.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The only time I had an actual employment contract was from the Catholic University of Chile. Under the government in the early 70s, they were encouraged to do research on the influence of economic factors on the development of intelligence. I got a job directing a project on the influence of nutrition on brain development at the Catholic University in Valparaiso. That was part of the social change that was shut down in the coup of 1973. The whole economic intellectual environment had progressed to the point where they were interested in fetal influences and nutrition, but the American influence wiped that out with Kissinger.

**John Barkhausen:** You were there for the coup in Chile?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I didn't get there.

**John Barkhausen:** That was a terrible tragedy. Not only the loss of life and the stealing of their democracy.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens constantly in the U.S. ever since 1947. It seems to be when it started in every field of biology and psychology.

**John Barkhausen:** You've discussed the Cold War in biology before. Who wrote that book?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Carl Lindegren.

**John Barkhausen:** While we're accusing Russia of having ideology mixed with their science, we're practicing it more than anything.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Even the humanities were subjects of the same influences. When Blake College was shut down, I thought I would simply shift my activity to teaching linguistics. I saw that the influence of Chomsky, with Pentagon funding, had spread across the country. By the late 1960s, it was getting into essentially every department of the humanities. I taught a course through the Honors College at the University of Oregon on interdepartmental conceptions of human nature. We got speakers from ten different departments, and each of them said, "Our department's most important insight to human nature is Chomsky's generative language theory." Speaking of totalitarian cultures.

**John Barkhausen:** Let's get to Blake. Your thesis for your master's was called *William Blake and the Mysticisms of Sense and Nonsense*.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I concentrated on his philosophy, epistemology, ontology, and ethics. The idea that he was important in all of those areas guided my thinking in science, since it went along with what I had been learning on my own. He was putting things together, creating an image of human nature that was very different from anything that dominated our cultural institutions.

**John Barkhausen:** You were introduced to him in school?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In a world literature course when I was a sophomore. I read some of his poems and saw that his language—even though the introduction described him as a Christian mystic—had irony and complexity that was unique in my experience. One of the brightest professors of the college, Arthur Christman, let me sign up for a course just in Blake for my third year. I spent that quarter reading people who had commented on Blake, like Northrop Frye and Jacob Bronowski—who happened to be a biologist—as well as Blake's own writing.

That formed my philosophical orientation: figuring out how Blake fit in with the mainline philosophers like Kant, Hegel, Marx, Locke, and Hume. Blake had commented on several of his contemporary philosophers and pretty much ridiculed them, as he did some of the scientists. Since he worked for publishers as an engraver, he was acquainted with the authors being published. He and Henry Fuseli, the painter, illustrated Erasmus Darwin's books.

Erasmus Darwin, along with Lamarck, really was the main initiator of evolutionary thinking in biology. His grandson, Charles Darwin, sort of degraded the concept and turned it into a kind of imperialism along the lines of Malthus. Capitalism and imperialism were shaping a lot of Darwin's ideas. In a later edition, Darwin said, "Well no, I'm not exclusively saying that competition... is the only thing," and acknowledged other forms of inheritance. So, in a weak, second-handed way, he recognized that his grandfather and Lamarck did have some importance. Samuel Butler, in a couple of books, put down Charles Darwin as a phony for misrepresenting who really thought of the idea of evolution.

**John Barkhausen:** Samuel Butler said that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. Samuel Butler wrote *Unconscious Memory*, which analyzed the thinking of Erasmus Darwin and Lamarck. He showed that memory and inheritance are very similar biological processes. If you look at it in terms of present biology, it would reduce to the idea that genes are always under the influence of chemical modification other than the DNA bases—they're being methylated, for example. It's a chemical and physical process that blends between memory and inheritance.

Darwin had acknowledged the idea of gemmules—something from the whole physiology affecting the inheritance—but Samuel Butler pointed out that Erasmus Darwin and Lamarck had been much more coherent in their description. It turns out that now we talk about it as epigenetic modification of the DNA, but for 150 years, the Lamarckian view sort of disappeared from the mainstream.

**John Barkhausen:** Why did everybody come down on Lamarck so much? Was it to justify the social power structure?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The French institution denounced him and said he was an anti-Christian because his ideas contradicted the Bible. There was a lot of Christian theological attack during the 19th century. The current issue tries to put evolution on the side of progress and science, and put religion against all of that. But with Darwin, he became the imperialist's philosopher; "the strong winning" is the direction of progress.

At the time I started graduate school, Konrad Lorenz was about to get the Nobel Prize. There was a whole current in science justifying militarism. Konrad Lorenz was the ideologist of the Racial Hygiene Institute, justifying genocide in Germany. That was really mainline genetic thinking in America and Germany in the 20s, 30s, and 40s. The defeat of the Nazis made it embarrassing for Americans to use those terms, but by the 60s, Lorenz was being rehabilitated.

My professors were all basically committed to the same genetic determinism. You can see that tendency in Darwin—the way he considered that botanical species from England were going to displace native species in New Zealand, or the way white people were displacing brown people. He was a real imperialist racist.

William Jennings Bryan, against Clarence Darrow, was caricatured as the backwardness of people who opposed Darwinism. But the Scopes Monkey Trial occurred at the height of the eugenics domination of biological thinking. William Jennings Bryan represented the common person and anti-racial thinking, while Clarence Darrow sided with the imperialists and racists. Bryan didn't put it in the proper political language, so he's been ridiculed ever since as an ignorant person opposing progress. But when you look at who the geneticists really were—the people who set up Hitler's genocide—you see that Bryan and the Christians were really on the right side regarding human rights. Blake was at the center of all those movements that influenced American history and scientific thinking in that underground, unofficial atmosphere.

**John Barkhausen:** Blake is an amazingly accomplished person for somebody who never went to school from our point of view.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He went to a drawing school when he was ten, and then was apprenticed to an engraver when he was fifteen. He started associating with educated people through the engraver. As a craftsman, he wasn't at the center of their movement, but he knew these people and became friends with radicals like William Godwin, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Joseph Priestley—the oxygen guy who was also a founder of Unitarianism. These people were radicals and progressives who were in danger of being imprisoned or killed by the government for their opinions.

**John Barkhausen:** Did he read science also?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. His parents attended the Swedenborgian church for a time, and Swedenborg was a real scientist who did some nerve research a hundred years prematurely. Blake knew a lot about nervous anatomy and biology. He knew all the scientists in London, at least to the extent of reading things the publishers had.

Priestley believed that matter was made up of energy. Blake saw energy as being the essence of human life. He once referred to being so inspired that sparks were coming out of his fingers. The main scientific mood of those Deists and rationalists was that reason was where attention should be put rather than on experience, and that matter was some sort of inert something without intrinsic energy. Blake was doing better thinking about the philosophy of science than even Joseph Priestley. He not only was putting energy into matter, but he wanted to see experience as a part of the nature of matter. Whether it was a piece of sand, a bug, or a person, energy and interaction were the essential properties of matter and life.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's a building aspect of matter that it actually gains complexity.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He sometimes called the principle of life or of knowing the "poetic genius." He saw this as a universal thing; a plant or an animal expressed its poetic genius through its form. It was a lively version of Spinoza's pantheism. He didn't see any separation between matter, energy, and consciousness. He believed that experience—he even said experiment—was the true form of knowing. He said the experiencing person couldn't derive anything new from previously learned knowledge. This offended the university-educated people. Blake said if you can't doubt from what you experience, you have to doubt everything people tell you is true. But experience can't be doubted because that's what it is.

**John Barkhausen:** We have an email question from Jose Gonzalez: "In your William Blake article, you briefly talk about the difference between the craftsman and the academic. Can you go into further detail describing the difference between them and the knowledge acquired by each one?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I studied etching and drypoint printmaking for a while to experience what he was doing. I saw that working on a copper plate with a needle, making fine lines to build up shapes, created a sparkly color from the refraction lines in the copper—an iridescent quality. For hours after I had been working on a plate, I would see that quality in everything I looked at.

Blake described that sort of experience: you enliven your senses by working on something. That extends to every new experience you have; you're shaping it yourself while the new stuff is coming in. The person who works only on the level of knowledge—what the book and the professor say—builds up a similar set of reflexes. They go out seeing the world in terms of what the book and the professor have said. They see the world as talking concepts to them. The craftsman feels the world in a sensory newness corresponding to how he's been using his body and mind in working.

**John Barkhausen:** Todd Mudd asks via email: "The first biography of William Blake by Alexander Gilchrist makes frequent mention of Blake's hallucinations and visions... What do you make of Blake's visions?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's that way of thinking which kids normally have, and it gets trained out of them. You can't use metaphors and imagery too much if the world around you doesn't like novel perceptions. The body has this capacity to concretize its thoughts to different extents. Most people get stuck in concretizing thoughts as words; they think of the word as the identity of the concept, and the concept as the identity of what's in the world.

If you see that your body can bring up these concrete images as you think, that gives you a much more fluid attitude towards everything you learn. You see your thought process right in front of you. The well-trained, well-educated person sees words as their consciousness, and the words tend to carry all the intentions of the educational system. That's the cage people build in their minds.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you relate that at all to Carl Jung and his idea of the unconscious and images?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Sure. Jung was on the fringes of Freudian thinking, but I think he was closer to Blake in attitude than any of the people in that psychoanalytic culture.

**John Barkhausen:** How would you relate the psychoanalytic culture to Blake?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With Freud and his superego and id, the id had to be repressed to form a rational ego. Wilhelm Reich pointed out that the superego included the Nazis—absolutely undesirable oppressors—and that the id really had most of what was good in humanity and shouldn't be repressed. Reich had sex-political organizations and got in trouble by saying people should be sexually free, combining that with socialistic political ideas. Freud pleased the authorities by saying you must repress it and accept authority. Blake, according to some biographers, was sexually a very advanced thinker and didn't believe women should be the property of their husbands.

**John Barkhausen:** Where would you fit Jung into all that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** His emphasis on imagery is very good, but he tried to stereotype it into perpetual personality types. Blake would have said that we, and worms, and everybody, have certain properties but we're always going someplace new. You can't say a person is bound to any one of these personality types.

**John Barkhausen:** I wanted to read a quote from Blake's *There is No Natural Religion*: "Therefore God becomes as we are, that we may be as he is." That seems like a dangerous thing to say, implying God is created by us.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Spinoza said it in a much more boring way. Spinoza was trying to get away from concretizing matter in a way that justified social hierarchy. When you separate spirit from matter, you tend to metaphorically separate working people from educated and powerful people. Plato, by putting knowledge in a world of forms, relegated human life to the material world, which was only temporal and not real.

People like Blake realized that's where the important argument is. Politics, medicine, and physics all take on an ideological attitude. In medicine, it's genetics on the cell membrane. In physics, it's a tendency to mystify the whole thing into non-experiential quantum mechanical theories. That's exactly why Blake said that when your reason—which he spelled Urizen—is separated from the body, emotions, and senses, it becomes tyrannical and stupid. He was referring to the chemists and physicists of his time letting the Deist idea of God and matter get into their thinking.

**John Barkhausen:** You referred to the Deists. Were they part of the Enlightenment movement?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. They wanted to displace monarchy and social hierarchy. They kicked God out of the world and said He set it running and is no longer intervening, because the kings were claiming they were God's agents. But a lot of the Deists were rationalists who wanted to protect their property and take on the role of the monarch after they kicked out the monarch. Deism was fine for justifying a new kind of tyranny. Blake was analyzing how reason, once it throws off an old tyranny, becomes a tyrant in its place.

**John Barkhausen:** Let's switch to your role as a physiologist. One question is about the ketone diet. What's your opinion on this burning off of stored fat and how it affects overall health?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's very stressful to get in that condition. For most people, extreme hypoglycemia is needed, and that typically turns on lots of cortisol production, which has many undesirable consequences. But the worst thing is that almost everyone—the older you are, the more polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) you have built into your tissue. Those being mobilized and oxidized damage practically everything. They interfere with mitochondrial respiration but also break down and cause oxidative damage to everything outside as well as inside the mitochondria. For a 10-year-old, it's not so damaging, but for a 30 or 40-year-old, it can be really harmful.

**John Barkhausen:** Somebody used the metaphor that burning fats is like a slow-burning log and burning sugars is like burning kindling.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** With a good hot fire, you don't get any smoke. Burning unsaturated fats, you get very toxic smoke. Cigarette smoke contains acrolein, for example. Polyunsaturated fats break down into these toxins similar to what you get in smoke. So it's a good metaphor: you don't want a slow, smoky, toxic fire.

**John Barkhausen:** Heart arrhythmias, Afib, and tachycardia—what are the causes and solutions?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One recognized factor is that the blood is usually more viscous than normal, making it slower to refill after the stroke. That viscosity and discrepancy between pressure going out and coming in tends to give complex signals to the heart.

The things you eat chronically, as well as hormonal balance, affect the sensitivity of the heart. Nerve impulses are affected by the balance of sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, and opposing steroids like estrogen versus progesterone and testosterone. High estrogen increases sensitivity and the likelihood to contract. Progesterone desensitizes the heart so it can build up a bigger charge of blood and have a bigger stroke before it fires.

Too much of the adrenergic side will make it oversensitive and tend to have premature contractions. Too much of the cholinergic side can simply stop the heart. The thyroid sensitizes you to the sympathetic side. If you take thyroid suddenly when you've been hypothyroid, you can get tachycardia. A person's liver governs the way the thyroid is working, so a person with liver problems can have periodic episodes of tachycardia. Combinations of high estrogen and low thyroid are very dangerous for the heart.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds difficult to get right.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you do things gradually. Estrogen has to be kept under control because, as well as exciting nerves, it increases the tendency to clot. Getting your estrogen/progesterone balance right is probably the basic thing to work on, since progesterone has a digitalis-like effect of increasing stroke volume, making the heart work more efficiently with fewer beats.

**John Barkhausen:** A listener writes: "I am a bit confused about Ray's statements about modern quantum physics... I think it is important to distinguish between the mathematical formalism and the more or less deceptive interpretation of Heisenberg and others."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's important to look around and see the many different interpretations of the slit experiment. The prediction is there, but the interpretation is the whole thing. The problem wouldn't exist except for Einstein and people of his generation making a very mistaken basic assumption: that matter is entirely local, atomic, and has no field properties extending electrically beyond individual atomic interactions.

From that peculiar atomic granular nature of matter, to produce the photoelectric effect, light also had to be granular to act locally. It's purely derived from assumptions which just 15 years later turned out not to be true. Michael Polanyi proposed an adsorption isotherm that was very simple, empirical, and not compatible with Einstein's granular theory. Through the 20s, Polanyi's work on crystals and metals tended to indicate a non-local nature of energy.

If matter has a wave-like behavior, you can explain photoelectric processes in terms of one wave interacting with another—a sort of tuning of waves in light and matter—rather than imagining a granular nature of light. The assumptions are so important to the quantum people that they don't like critics saying the assumptions have to be re-examined.

**John Barkhausen:** Michael Polanyi was ridiculed by them, wasn't he?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. He was so affected by the reaction of established physicists that even when he became a physics professor, he wouldn't teach his students the true Polanyi isotherm; he taught the Langmuir monolayer isotherm.

Halton Arp is another example. He was making photographs showing galaxies with stringers of matter between them, showing a connectedness of substance. But the galaxies had a very great redshift difference, showing they should be moving at extremely different velocities. He was denied use of the telescopes because the pictures so strongly made fun of the belief in the expanding universe explanation for the redshift.

**John Barkhausen:** What does the redshift mean?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's interpreted like the Doppler effect of sound—pitch drops as a vehicle moves away. When you get evidence that is embarrassing to committed assumptions, you have to stop the person providing the evidence.

Once my physiology professor came up behind me to see how my nerve setup was going. I showed him that as the microelectrode entered the cell, the voltage went up properly. I said, "Now notice as it penetrates to the other side of the cell, you get a dip, a rise, a dip, and another rise." He recognized that violated his whole doctrine of cell voltage. He just turned around and never spoke to me again.

**John Barkhausen:** What is extremity numbness, like in fingers, indicative of?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's common in diabetes, but often happens years before blood sugar becomes diabetic. In the case of one hand, it can be a tunnel syndrome where the nerve gets squeezed because connective tissue swells up. If that happens during the night, that's very common in anyone who has a slight hormonal imbalance away from good oxidative metabolism, causing tissues to take up water. Many people scheduled for carpal tunnel surgery have completely relieved the problem just by taking thyroid or pregnenolone.

Standard medical opinion blames it on sugar, but research connects it to toxins, endotoxin from the intestine, prostaglandins, and nitric oxide. It was recognized about 25 years ago that the brain is a major steroid organ—producing neurosteroids like progesterone and DHEA. Just recently, people are recognizing that peripheral nerves also have their nerve steroids and are just as dependent as the brain on the right balance of estrogen and progesterone.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you explain the role of electrolytes in fluid balance and their relationship to adrenal fatigue?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The medical dogma is that cells have pumps in their membranes that regulate balance. Gilbert Ling's work shows that the pump concept is irrational. His explanation is that the cytoplasm—the whole cell substance—is like an ion exchange resin.

When the cell substance is acidified, it prefers potassium. If the cell pH rises, the electron concentration increases, and the sodium atom is preferred. The main thing determining the acidic pH in a healthy cell is the oxidation of fuel producing carbon dioxide (CO2). CO2 is an acid. As it leaves the cell, it takes ions with it.

If you slow down the production of CO2 and ATP, the pH rises. Lactic acid is formed, and in leaving the cell, it takes protons out, making the cell more alkaline. That alkaline condition prefers sodium. Any shift that increases alkalinity will make that cell take up water, hydrating the gel.

In a low thyroid state, every cell tends to take up sodium and calcium and lose potassium and magnesium. The condition of being low thyroid means you lose sodium because you can't put it back into the bloodstream from the urine. A low thyroid person will tend to put more sodium into the urine, making their blood dilute, which leads to swelling of the tissues. But the swelling really started back in the cell which became alkaline.

**John Barkhausen:** So taking thyroid or increasing salt intake would help?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, salt will help the low thyroid person. When you lose too much sodium, aldosterone increases in the adrenal. That tends to exchange magnesium loss for sodium loss. Increasing aldosterone has hormonal effects, shifting the parasympathetic balance and causing inflammation. Heart failure almost always involves too much effective aldosterone.

**John Barkhausen:** If the cell gets damaged in the mitochondria—for example, too much calcium or PUFAs—does it die? Can the body make new cells to sustain energy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The mitochondria themselves can be repaired and induced to multiply in an individual damaged cell. A dying cell can be replaced from stem cells or adjoining cells given the proper conditions.

There was a demonstration of old people whose muscle mitochondria lacked the necessary DNA for proper function. By having them do concentric weightlifting—not the kind that stretches the muscle, but only has weight when the muscle is contracting—they were able to find new mitochondria in their muscle cells with all the proper DNA within a few weeks. Something as simple as concentric exercise can restore old and damaged cells.

There were experiments taking samples from people's facial skin, finding mutated damaged cells from sun exposure. When they kept the skin completely covered for several weeks, the mutated cells disappeared. Stem cells had taken over and replaced them with good cells. Stopping the continuing damage and giving the cell the necessary stimulation will repair things. I've seen people come out of dementia and epilepsy and far-advanced cases.

**John Barkhausen:** That's really hopeful, Ray. Thank you so much for being on today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay.

**John Barkhausen:** You can find out more about Ray at raypeat.com. You've been listening to Politics and Science.

title: Politics & Science: Evolution
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** This is *Politics and Science* and I'm your host, John Barkhausen. This is a special extended interview with Ray Peat, done on the 4th of March, 2015, from the studios of WMRW. The subject was evolution and Lamarck, although that hardly gets mentioned. Ray Peat has a PhD in biology and a specialty in physiology. Ray, if you wouldn't mind, maybe you could introduce yourself a little more.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My dissertation was on reproductive physiology—specifically, the influence of female aging on the oxidative processes in the uterus. I went to graduate school in biology after having studied literature and linguistics previously. I had the intention of studying the brain and how the brain can create language, because the brain biology people were the most dogmatic, next to the genetics people. I looked around and found that the reproductive physiology professor was actually a scientist, so I did my work in that area.

**John Barkhausen:** You've been interested in science your whole life. It's fairly impressive that as a child you were reading many scientific texts. When did you first run into the subject of the origin of life and evolution?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We had a little old Funk & Wagnalls encyclopedia from my parents—they got it around 1930, I think. That was where I first ran into some of the really interesting science things when I was seven, eight, or nine years old. Then in 1950, we got the new Britannica, which had bigger articles. Both of them were very objective on the issue of Lamarckism versus Darwinism. So, I had heard about the inheritance of acquired traits when I was probably eight years old.

One of the stories that stuck in my mind was done by Michael Guyer at the University of Wisconsin. I think he ground up the eyes of rabbits and injected them to produce antibodies. By treating pregnant rabbits so that they became immune to the eyeball tissue, the babies were born with defective eyes. He then cross-mated these offspring and found that the defective eyes were inherited as if they were genetic traits in subsequent generations. No one really repeated that as far as I know, and it was pretty widely accepted. He was a very standard, mostly Darwinian biologist.

He was doing that research around the same time that Paul Kammerer in Vienna was experimenting with marine invertebrates, toads, and salamanders to show that when they acquired an adaptation, the offspring would show traits that had been acquired by the parents. Paul Kammerer was viciously attacked. He committed suicide in 1926 in the midst of a very intense attack against his midwife toad experiments. Someone had apparently injected ink into the spot that was supposed to be an inherited mating pad on the toad's feet. The person who mostly condemned him as a fraud was William Bateson, a hardline English geneticist. When Kammerer sent samples of his specimens to England, he invited biologists to examine them. Several well-known biologists did examine them and reported that they were convincing, but William Bateson refused to go to the meeting to examine the specimens. He immediately resumed his attacks. Bateson really didn't want to look at the evidence because he knew it was not there.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe you could tell us why this debate over the theories of evolution is important. Why are people getting so upset about this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is essentially a religious or political argument. The whole mystique of science wants to say that there is a simple, objective science: you follow a certain method, you get an absolute result. If you don't get what you "should" get, then it has to be pseudoscience or fraud. But the context is very closely related to your social, economic, political, and religious background.

If you look at Darwin, for example, he was a pretty progressive thinker in a lot of ways—he was against slavery—but he was essentially from the upper class and had the habits and way of life of the ruling class. Despite his progressive traits, he was really in the mainline of 19th-century British imperialist thinking. That quality stuck with the idea of Darwinian evolution. The social Darwinists really developed what was an essential part of Darwin's thinking, and that was later taken up by the fascists. Eugenics had a Darwinian genetic basis—racial improvement and so on.

People who want to claim Darwin as their intellectual ancestor don't like to recognize that he was a pretty crazy imperialist racist. He believed that even English plants were better than plants in other countries and would displace them if given the opportunity. Just like he believed the English people and Europeans would finally exterminate and eliminate by competition what he called the "intermediate races" between the higher apes and the civilized Europeans. He believed that even the higher apes, along with Australians and Africans, would go out of existence because of the superiority of Europeans.

**John Barkhausen:** So the idea of where we all came from is a powerful one in manipulating people to be on the side of your ideology.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The way science is taught, it really doesn't free itself from ideology. Whatever the ideological system existed around your physics professors and their professors gets built into a belief of how science works, how the brain works, and is a philosophy of the nature of being and the creation of the universe. My professors in all of the sciences just didn't want to think about their philosophical commitments. It was "scientific," and that was that.

**John Barkhausen:** They wouldn't look at any of their preconceptions.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The extent of philosophy might have been to have read Percy Bridgman's operationalism approach, saying that if you can't measure it, it isn't real. Some professors with philosophical minds saw that as their foundation.

**John Barkhausen:** I think you are the reason this show is called *Politics and Science*. Before I read your writings, I thought science was an objective art practiced by dedicated people with integrity. I didn't think business interests, corruption, or vanity played a role, but it turns out it's just as subject to human vices as any other field.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Early in the 20th century, you could trace the personality of the academic culture to the 19th-century conflicts regarding religion—whether the old pre-Enlightenment religion should still be in power, or whether a newer 18th/19th-century loosening of religious ideas should be the rule. But the missing thing was to see that there is a conflict between *essentialism*—which was the old absolutist religious approach, the Platonic idea that species never change because they are timeless identities—and the *empirical* or *existentialist* approach, which looks at the actual historical situation in front of you.

That is where the real difference in interpreting science comes in. You can see it in every field. The anti-essentialists tend to be on the fringe. For example, in cosmology, you have the Electric Universe people providing coherent descriptions of observed facts against the Big Bang mechanistic universe. Halton Arp, the astronomer, made pictures of galaxies that were visibly connected to each other but moving at tremendously different velocities. According to the redshift Big Bang theory, you can't have things tied together that are moving at extremely different speeds (implying different distances). The reason he was able to see and think about that was that he wasn't committed to an essentialist idea that every atom is the same at every moment of time and every place in the universe.

**John Barkhausen:** It's interesting that it all boils down to your school of thought: whether you start with the essentialist form or the empirical form. You’ve said before that Aristotle was the founder of the empirical movement.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think he was just about as fully developed as anyone as a thinker. People like Leibniz were still thinking in some of Aristotle's ideas—for example, analyzing cause into different types of causality, including *final cause*. The condemnation of teleological explanations has been a big part of essentialist, mechanistic science. But Leibniz was able to explain the physics of optics using Aristotelian final causes in his mathematical descriptions and showed that it worked just as well as the mechanical "billiard ball" kind of causality. Leibniz wanted to see causality as a global, holistic way of existence.

**John Barkhausen:** You've pointed out that the Eastern Orthodox branch of knowledge—the Russians—basically went off with the Aristotelian viewpoint, and the West somehow adopted the Platonic viewpoint. That accounts for our love of modeling instead of gathering empirical evidence.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The teleological approach is fully compatible with the evidence-based, historical, fact-centered approach. It just looks at generality and laws in a different way that doesn't insist they are outside of time. It is open to complexity in a way that the essentialist, Platonist approach is not.

**John Barkhausen:** How has evolutionary thought developed over the years?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In Darwin's time, the racist approach tried to explain everything in terms of your existing present biology, which was explained in terms of your genetic nature. It said that how you came to be was a purely random affair, and the only way to change the situation is to select out the inferior—not to improve them, because things essentially aren't open to change. So, what you measure is what was destined from the start.

This leads to either intentional or incidental genocide, in which inferior plants, people, and animals go out of existence simply because improvement isn't possible. It rejects the idea of improving the world.

**John Barkhausen:** Was that ideology expressed before Malthus came along?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it developed as they realized that the moneyed class had better health and everything else. The ideology was intended to keep down the demands of the working classes. Malthus really just codified an ideology, and Darwin, being a member of the upper class, found that compatible.

In contrast, I see Vladimir Vernadsky's use of the Le Chatelier principle. If a system is in equilibrium and you disturb the system, it adjusts itself to come to a new equilibrium. Vernadsky saw the cosmos as an energy system and life as a part of the system that is adjusting the equilibrium as the system is energized from the outside. He saw evolution as having a direction—in a way, it was teleological—because he showed that it would maximize the movement of atoms, the intensity of metabolism in organisms, and the maximization of size, especially of the nervous system and the brain. The flow of energy was giving shape to his system.

**John Barkhausen:** That's what you mean by teleological—purposefulness.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, but you think about the equilibrium and the end condition as well as the starting condition. You have to think in terms of a whole system and the interactions through time. There is no place for one of these essential Platonic forms, which Mendel, for example, wanted to identify as "trait genes" so that you could have fixed species. It’s really a very pure religious imposition on pea traits in Mendel's case.

**John Barkhausen:** It seems like the pot calling the kettle black. He insists on these ideal forms, which sounds religious, but he calls the people who believe in purposeful adaptation "vitalists" or superstitious.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The people who own the schools, universities, and publishing houses are in a better position to denounce others as frauds. But actually, there is a tremendous amount of fake science hiding among the genetics culture. Eugenics was part of the biological gene culture in the United States. The *Journal of Eugenics*, after Hitler lost the war and was discredited, changed its name to the *Journal of Human Genetics*, but the people didn't change their ideas. They still worshipped the doctrines of Konrad Lorenz, who devised Hitler's genocide rationale.

**John Barkhausen:** He was lauded in this country as a great friendly scientist.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** After he got the Nobel Prize, my professors—including the Jewish immigrants who had escaped Europe around 1939—were praising Konrad Lorenz and the very ideas that were published to justify the extermination. In his book published around 1970, he used exactly the same sentences, except he used a slight euphemism instead of "exterminated."

**John Barkhausen:** Could you walk us through your conception of the history of evolution from the origin of life?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm inclined to see Sidney Fox's approach as being at least a good image or analog of how the process works. He worked in Linus Pauling's lab and was a professor in regular biology departments. His results were very clear, but they didn't resonate with the genetics biological schools.

He did variations on the Urey-Miller experiment (bubbling primitive atmosphere). He cooked ammonia and carbon dioxide in various ways in the presence of hot rocks. He found that protein-like things spontaneously polymerized, and the arrangement was non-random. If he had 8 or 10 amino acids cooking together, the proteins that spontaneously formed on the surface of the hot rocks had a non-random arrangement, as if the amino acids were interacting in such a way that they chose their position according to stability.

With a very small amount of water letting them dry out, and then adding a small amount of water to this hot, spontaneously formed protein, they spontaneously formed little bacteria-like spheres—very uniform in size. These shapes could divide like cells or bud off parts that would then grow up to the bacteria-sized particle. They could "eat" and reproduce.

To a mixture of these amino acids, proteins, and spheres, he found that adding the bases of the nucleic acids caused them to polymerize inside the little bacteria-like particles, forming nucleic acid chain polymers. Again, these were non-randomly arranged, apparently by the nature of the bases themselves and the context of the protein structures around them.

So, the ordering process doesn't require any kind of input up to this stage—neither a divine watchmaker specifying the sequence nor the infinitely long spans of time that the crude Darwinian viewpoint suggested.

**John Barkhausen:** That's amazing. So he just did that by adding amino acids to hot volcanic rock?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He simplified the procedure so that high school students could create life in an hour lab session. It seems like a very plausible way to see the first bacteria coming into existence. If you look at the underwater vents in the ocean—volcanoes spewing material into deep ocean water full of weird organisms—as an analogy to Sidney Fox's experiments, it suggests that you might get something much closer to presently existing organisms just in a matter of minutes or hours when you have extreme pressure and high temperature.

**John Barkhausen:** Is that theory of life developing gaining more acceptance?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I mentioned it to my professors in my qualifying exam. None of them had heard about it, even though it was in Lehninger's biochemistry textbook. I looked at the edition that came out in Lehninger's name after he died, and Fox's work had been removed. So I think there was a move away from it after Fox died.

**John Barkhausen:** You wrote in *Generative Energy* that the thought that life forms might just gush up out of the earth in volcanic regions makes it all seem too easy. What do you think they are afraid of?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I'm sure it's the Malthusian and Darwinian hatred of the lower classes—the feeling that if they were given a chance, they would displace the ruling class. It really comes down to politics.

**John Barkhausen:** How do you see life developing from those molecules into actual organisms?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The Sidney Fox particles could interact with each other. If you have a whole planet full of such things, every time you get something that is a little more stable, this will spread horizontally. It isn't necessarily a matter of descendants, but it will spread its influence by contact with its contemporaries. Things can spread much faster than the idea of inheritance and selection of the fittest.

Bacteria are now known to be able to spread their resistance to antibiotics horizontally. If you have a planet full of these simple things, the tendency is for them to accumulate more and more of the stabilizing, activating structures. I see it as an example of Vernadsky's principle: apply the right pressure and temperature conditions, and the system spontaneously moves in that direction.

I think it was James Shapiro who talked about the bacterial self-engineering of their genetic material. He proposed that the movement from a protozoan-type organism to a multicellular organism could also be almost spontaneous, in which this over-endowed single cell finds a situation where colonizing with its neighbors leads to a new level of metabolism and stability.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a question from a listener named Duncan: "Is it possible to fix the class warfare problem? If so, how? Will the class warfare problem always exist considering inherent human nature?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it's essentially a metaphysical problem. Around 1870, William Morris asked, "Where will this culture end?" He answered, "With a counting house on top of a cinder pile." That was very close to the way climate change seems to be leading us—ashes and money.

If you see the mechanical commitment to the past leading its way into the future, you end up with that cinder pile. To avoid that, you have to change your metaphysics to the Leibnizian or Aristotelian view in which the *final cause* has to be taken into account. Leibniz and Teilhard de Chardin saw this endpoint as a God consciousness. Vernadsky described it as a universe of consciousness—the Noosphere—in which knowledge and awareness became the governing principle.

However you see the end condition, I think you have to start thinking in terms of final causes. Once you take into account that maybe it isn't so good to reduce the planet to ashes and money, then maybe you can work on solutions. Part of the solution is to stop thinking about class superiority and racial superiority.

**John Barkhausen:** When you say the end conditions, does that mean you have to imagine how you'd like the world to be and then intend to make it that way?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. By denouncing teleological thinking, they said that the bottom line is that you want to make your money and you don't care what it costs the other person or the environment. According to that metaphysics, the outcome is always competitive degradation.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Anthropology is an area very closely connected to evolutionary thinking. Despite the fact that academic anthropology in the US has been strongly guided by the CIA, there are evolutionary lines of thinking that are promising.

Margaret Mead's approach was that cultures don't have to be static; people make the culture, so they can change the culture. Her professor, Franz Boas at Columbia, thought of himself as a Darwinist, but when he actually studied the facts, he showed that the environment rather than the genes governed even the person's biology. He measured the heads of Europeans who had moved to New York or Puerto Rico and found that the first-generation offspring had heads shaped more like New Yorkers or Puerto Ricans than like the European parents. It showed the powerful importance of the material and social culture shaping the organism.

**John Barkhausen:** Another question from Duncan: "Is empathy evolutionarily advantageous?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I see empathy as the universal principle of substance—the absolute opposite of the essentialist view. If you break the world up into Leibnizian monads, the essentialist says that the monads are closed. The existence of empathy implies that each unit of existence is open and interacting with its environment.

I see empathy as expressible in physical terms, such as *resonance*. In the case of empathizing with a person or animal, you tune your nervous system so that it is resonating with the conditions of the other's nervous system. I see it as something that explains why the amino acids take on a non-random arrangement in Fox's molecules. Resonance is a stabilizer on the atomic level, the chemical cellular level, and the organismic level.

**John Barkhausen:** And culturally too, in the form of music and ideas.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Luca Turin is a perfume expert whose theory of psychoactive drugs, hormones, and odor molecules is based on the idea that it's an electronic resonance between the molecule and the cell that accounts for the specificity. He gives examples where molecules that resonate the same have the same smell or biological effect despite having a different shape.

**John Barkhausen:** So, are we basically just an evolution of the actual material we're made out of?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the resonant properties are the properties that matter to us. We can substitute molecules that aren't exactly the same in form but have the same electronic way of interacting with us. For example, I would say methylene blue has this remarkable range of biologically valuable functions, even though it's something that we never evolved with. It has an electronic property that fits in and stabilizes or enriches our system.

**John Barkhausen:** There was a book called *Food of the Gods* postulating that our consciousness did a radical shift when we discovered psilocybin mushrooms. What do you think about the evolution of consciousness?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think things such as the amount of carbon dioxide in the air, the amount of particular nutrients in the diet, and the balance of amino acids are the main powers of increasing consciousness. But consciousness I see as simply one side of the metabolic interactive process. Anything that increases our quality of metabolism is increasing our ability to resonate with more complex systems. Things like mushrooms act as a lubricant. The organism might have a certain amount of energy available, and with just a little lubricant, it might find that it can slide up to a new metabolic level.

**John Barkhausen:** You've written about Pavlov and Anokhin, the Russian behavioral scientists. Pavlov wrote that life has a biological urge for freedom. Do you believe that is a powerful evolutionary force?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, I think it fits into the idea of the Noosphere. Pavlov's "reflex of freedom" was also the exploratory reflex—always wanting to find out more. When the culture or planet evolves beyond the urge to accumulate power to the conscious Noosphere level, that reflex will be fully activated. Everything will become a question and an opportunity for discovery.

**John Barkhausen:** You also wrote that health can be seen as the coordination of the levels of evolution.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It is analogous to Maslow's steps of development: security, food, social interactions, and finally self-actualization. It might be analogous to the freedom reflex—the opportunity to live for creative action. Carl Rogers was a sophisticated thinker with a phenomenological approach. His understanding of therapy was that it's the interactive attempt of the therapist to listen to and understand the client—it's the resonance in itself which is therapeutic.

**John Barkhausen:** A follow-up on methylene blue from Duncan: "Have you tried methylene blue? How does it feel versus progesterone or caffeine?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've only been using it transdermally. My approach to understanding new chemicals is to find what the smallest amount does and then work up. So far, I see it as a good anti-inflammatory. Quite a few people are having very powerful antidepressant effects from it with just one milligram a day. But I think it's probably going to be effective at doses analogous to thyroid hormone—20, 30, or 40 micrograms per day might be the optimal dose. It's known that it can bypass mitochondrial defects, and I think that's a big part of why it can cure serious depression at such a small dose.

**John Barkhausen:** I wanted to talk about Russian science. You went there one summer. Did you meet any scientists?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I went to the place where Trofim Lysenko was working. One of his assistants took me around. We also dropped in on Yuri Holodov, who was studying magnetobiology—the influence of magnetic fields on the nervous system. He took the time to talk to us. His first question was, "What are you studying and where?" I said I planned to enroll at the University of Oregon in nerve biology. He immediately asked, "Oh, are you going to work with..." and named a professor who had just left the university that quarter. He was up to the present year in knowing who was doing nerve research in US universities.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe you could outline what the Lysenko controversy was about.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Lysenko never was the "Czar of Genetics." Even at the height of his power under Stalin, he was always criticizing the university genetics people. He ran the state crop improvement stations. It was Lewontin, an American Marxist biologist, who examined the grain production records under Lysenko's influence and found they were actually increasing grain production steadily. The university genetics departments weren't producing anything of value.

We've been given a false history. Lysenko emphasized the predominance of the cytoplasm. The adaptation of the organism involved changes in the organization of the cytoplasm. People in the West were working on similar things with cloning experiments. For example, with a paramecium, if you take a bit of the surface and turn it around so the cilia beat in reverse, the descendants all have the reversed cilia. This shows clear inheritance of things that happen to the cytoplasm.

Barbara McClintock was finding similar things in her work with corn—that stress increased the variability and adaptability of the organism, changing the chromosomes. She came so close to Lysenko and Lamarck in showing that stress changes heredity, and she was hostilely ignored by the profession for 40 years. Then, with genetic engineering, when people wanted to patent new genes, they realized it would be good to have scientific precedent. They resurrected Barbara McClintock's work and gave her the Nobel Prize, but 40 years later.

**John Barkhausen:** Darwin did not rule out many of the mechanisms that Lamarck talked about, correct?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Darwin proposed "gemmules" or "pangenesis"—the idea that something the organism acquired through experience was shed from the organs and reached the gonads to be taken up in the germline. That idea was too Lamarckian for anyone up until Lysenko's time.

But in the last 10 or 20 years, it has been revisited. It can be traced back to a North Korean, Bonghan Kim, who in the 60s showed there were particles carrying nucleic acids through a lymphatic-like system. Only recently have people looked at particles in the plasma called exosomes or microvesicles. These are now known to carry RNA, proteins, and even DNA, and it has been demonstrated that the DNA carried in these particles can be incorporated into the germ cells and transmitted. Basically, Darwin's gemmules are now called exosomes.

**John Barkhausen:** We have a question from Prana Rupa: "Would you be willing to speculate about future evolutionary expressions, both at the level of the biosphere and in relation to optimizing our own potentialities?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the increasing carbon dioxide is going in the right direction. I think it increases adaptability, so I don't think we have to worry about carbon dioxide contributing to the extinction of species. The tendency of this increasing carbon dioxide is to support the process of cephalization. So, I think the direction will be bigger brains and further development of the imaginative types of mental processes.

**John Barkhausen:** A question from Todd Mudd: "Are evolutionary steps really spontaneous? Do they happen in a single generation, or are the changes gradual?"

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it happens intermittently. One woman will have a remarkably advantageous pregnancy and will be the forerunner of a trend. It can happen immediately in one lucky group of organisms and become more widespread when the whole situation is more fortunate.

**John Barkhausen:** Would another evolutionary step have something to do with thinking in images rather than words?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The essentialist metaphysics is literally holding back physiological functioning and evolution. The organism is impaired when it gets stuck in verbal formulas. When the brain is properly energized—Pyotr Anokhin has terms for this—there is a conductive quality to the fluids of the brain which allows a holistic kind of functioning. Any concrete thought or image brings with it an interpretive context. You see the meaning in all of its expanded qualities rather than a symbolic formulation. It is like a simultaneous picture in three dimensions and moving.

**John Barkhausen:** That's fascinating. Is that possibly where we're evolving to—telepathy? You mentioned a talk by Michael Persinger called "No More Secrets."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes, he makes some good arguments. He experimented with stimulating the brain to get what he called the "God consciousness." I think that sense of overwhelming meaning is just a natural brain process when it's properly energized. When you think of an atom, you can't think of an abstract atom out of time; every atom has its own history.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, we are out of time. Thank you so much for offering us your time and knowledge today.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thank you.

title: Politics & Science: Biochemical Health
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Today we're going to be talking about human health and the physiological implications of some of the chemical processes that happen in the body, namely reduction and oxidation. My guest today is Dr. Raymond Peat. He has a PhD in biology and a specialty in physiology. Ray, do you want to add anything to that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was studying for my degree at the University of Oregon, I got interested in oxidative processes as they relate to aging. I've been thinking about what oxidation means and all the ramifications for 40 or 50 years, and I am still curious about how it really works.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's an ongoing scientific endeavor, understanding it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Electrons moving around in matter is one of my longest standing interests. I think it started when I was a little kid, but I'm still not satisfied that anyone knows what an electron is or how it works. Without knowing that, you really don't understand what's going on in oxidation, reduction, physical free radicals, and so on.

**John Barkhausen:** Maybe you could give us a sense of the history of people trying to understand biochemistry. How did it all start?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The famous first demonstration that life processes are material chemistry was when a guy synthesized urea. People had believed that was done by something special in the life process that couldn't be imitated in the inert world. It was demonstrated that you can make urea simply mechanically.
