People started thinking about the chemical processes that make up life and gradually got away from the idea that there is something unique about the life process that is distinct from chemistry.

**John Barkhausen:** I was reading that was a Swedish person who figured out urea around the Revolutionary War. But people must have experimented with bodily fluids before then. Was there much research done?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 18th century, people were figuring out a lot about how organisms work. But the official science that got published and approved by the government was a very slow process, usually 100 years behind the people on the ground who were really thinking about how things work.

**John Barkhausen:** Science, for a large part, was actually a private affair done by wealthy people—rich cranks.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** So they often put their particular philosophical or religious bent into the physical ideas. Because of that personal quality, science was really more literary, interesting, and artistic before the universities took it over. Gradually, in physics, the universities took control away from the cranks and rich guys in the mid-19th century. That was the physics that Einstein, for example, was dealing with in Germany. Einstein resented the authoritarian dogma of the professors, so he invented something that outwitted the authoritarian physics establishment.

**John Barkhausen:** It seems like it takes the interest out of most fields once it gets franchised like that. Religion used to be more of a personal experience before the church took over, and it sounds like it's the same with science.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think Einstein himself succumbed somewhat to authoritarian attitudes in the case of saying what an electron is. Thirty years later, I think he regretted having set things in motion in that particular direction. He never accepted the quantum mechanics view that reality is based on randomness, but he was largely responsible for setting that in motion with his theory of the photoelectric effect.

The idea of the electron as a discrete particle interacting with a photon as a discrete particle was the key idea in that photoelectric effect. A photon of a given energy would dislodge an electron from the solid state, giving it a certain voltage. So you can talk about the electronic energy or voltage of a given frequency of light, and that particularized or atomized the idea of both light and electrons. That allowed theory to take over and cover up or reject a lot of empirical, factual observation relating to light, color, electrons, molecules, and I think life.

**John Barkhausen:** Once you become an icon, you have to be very careful what you say because people might take you seriously. Can you explain further how seeing the electron as an essential part of atomic structure set us on the wrong track?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Around the time of the First World War, Michael Polanyi had demonstrated a continuous potential description of how gases are bound or adsorbed on solid surfaces. That was a smooth process—a straight relationship between the pressure on the gas and the thickness of the adsorbed layer. When he went to Berlin to present his experimental work and theory, Einstein and others said, "In the advanced science world here in Germany, we know that just isn't possible because matter is particulate."

They argued you aren't going to get forces smoothly extending away from the surface. If the surface has an electrical property and the gas has an electrical property, the first layer of gas atoms hitting that surface is going to perfectly neutralize that, so there is no potential extending through space. But Polanyi's results clearly showed that a continuously thickening layer was forming. Polanyi was defeated. People like Irving Langmuir, 15 years later, got the Nobel Prize for the idea that gases can only condense in a monolayer. Polanyi knew it was wrong, but he was a physics professor and had to teach the Langmuir isotherm.

In his own experimental work, Polanyi kept seeing continuity extending. For example, working with crystals, he found that events on the surface of a crystal affected its elasticity and resistance all the way through. Physically, the surface doesn't have the meaning that it seems to in geometry. Weakening involves energy flowing over long distances. It was analogous to the idea of conduction bands in metals where electrons are delocalized. Polanyi's work suggested that maybe particulate electrons aren't the only or necessary way to think of electrons.

**John Barkhausen:** You mentioned another experiment regarding this.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When I was in graduate school, I was reading surface physics to help understand oxidation biologically. In one of the physics journals, a man named Helmut Schwartz published a description of a funny experiment. Laser light is shined horizontally through a crystal while a beam of electrons goes through the other dimension of the crystal. The electrons passing through the crystal are deflected into a certain pattern by the electronic property of the crystal atoms.

Ordinarily, this is done by exposing a piece of photographic film to the electrons to get an image. But he found that when taking the fluorescent screen away and putting a non-reflective aluminum oxide coated layer at the bottom, the electron spots were still there, but they had the blue tint of the laser light going sideways through the crystal. The spots had to be the supposedly discrete particulate electrons to be deflected to exactly the right spots, but at that spot, there shouldn't have been any light. Yet, it was the color of the laser light modulating the beam of electrons. When I tried to talk to physics professors about it, they simply said it can't happen. You can't modulate one electron.

**John Barkhausen:** When you say modulate, you mean change color?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The color of an electron is supposed to be its relationship to the atom. What it's doing is absorbing or interacting with a particular wavelength of light. An electron flying through space having a color just wasn't acceptable. They preferred to say the person was hallucinating. But it was done at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and they had the best equipment of that sort in the world at the time. A lot of people immediately trying to replicate it didn't have the same degree of vacuum, laser power, or crystal quality. It's very easy to debunk something just by doing a slightly different setup and getting different results.

**John Barkhausen:** Today's crackpot is possibly tomorrow's genius.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Very recently, Helmut Schwartz, who became the head of Germany's research granting institution, said that outsiders are important everywhere, not just in science. You don't get advanced unless you have people somewhat on the fringe.

**John Barkhausen:** I was a little confused about the particulate electrons versus the wave theory. What is the alternative?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Since you can't explain many events in terms of particles, it becomes mathematical magic to try to make up theories to explain results like Polanyi's or Schwartz's. Albert Szent-Györgyi used conventional quantum thinking about electrons and went a long way towards explaining biological phenomena, but that doesn't necessarily validate the particulate electron.

It might be that there is an electrical ether-like material which breaks up in different ways into apparently discrete electrons. Rather than being an eternally discrete particle, the electron might be an ad hoc diffusion. The wave interpretation approaches that idea. Some subatomic thinkers are saying that the great variety of subatomic particles being seen might just be an ad hoc response of matter to a particular context or environment.

**John Barkhausen:** So it might just be an aspect you're seeing depending on the medium you're using to see it with.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. That would say that in a different solar system or galaxy, the atoms are not necessarily going to have the same functionality. That is an implication of Halton Arp's comments on his galaxy photographs. He showed what appear to be continuously connected groups of stars where one part has an extreme redshift difference from the other, meaning they should be very remote in space. But his pictures show connections, like one is being shot out of the other. He suggests the one being shot out is newly created and that new matter has a different way of vibrating which shows up as a redshift. In other words, the atoms are different when they're fresh.

**John Barkhausen:** You said that a redshift usually means something's moving away from you.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the standard mechanical physics connection, like the Doppler effect.

**John Barkhausen:** But you're saying it could have other implications.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For example, light passing close to a star has a frequency shift. An Israeli physicist named Dror Sadeh was studying the light of a star passing close to the sun and a beeping pulsar passing close to the sun. He kept seeing what seemed to be a time change or frequency change depending on how close the beam came to the sun.

He got an atomic clock at the U.S. Bureau of Standards and mounted another on a truck, connected them by radio to synchronize them, and drove up the coast towards Maine. He recorded the relationship between these two clocks and saw that every morning at sunrise, Washington, D.C. seemed to be redshifted away from his truck. His argument was that something about the field of the sun coming on the scene was shifting the radio waves connecting the two clocks. Otherwise, it would have looked like you had an expanding universe to a ridiculous extent.

**John Barkhausen:** Obviously, it makes a difference how you think about electrons if you're trying to figure out how these molecular processes are happening.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The idea of the particulate nature of matter diffused into the thinking process. Just as Einstein couldn't tolerate multilayer adsorption, biochemists can't tolerate long-range processes in biochemistry.

One of the things in chemistry that resembles what Polanyi was seeing is the inductive effect. This is the basis of fundamental biological thinking about coacervates. Bungenberg de Jong founded a line of thinking that led to Gilbert Ling's way of seeing the cell as a special state of matter. One of the basic principles is electronic induction. When you have atoms that are electron-withdrawing, the charge or intensity of the electron's effect shifts down the molecular chain towards that electron-withdrawing group.

When you take that seriously, you see this effect exists everywhere in the cell. It goes to another level: the coordinated or coherent effects of the electron-inducing groups. You have a collective reaction where you pass a threshold, sort of the way liquid water passes to solid water. You can have solid water above the melting temperature or liquid water below the freezing temperature if you don't have this cooperativity. When you combine ideas of cooperativity and induction, you get group effects where you have a change of state which passes through the bulk of the material.

**John Barkhausen:** How does this apply to proteins?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** You can look at the effects of pH on a protein. A protein with its various charged groups responds to the pH so that the internal fields are intensified or decreased. You can have a protein expanding or collapsing according to the pH. But when you add other molecules binding to that protein, and those have electron-withdrawing or donating properties, then the way that protein responds to a certain pH is different.

These electron-withdrawing molecules are, in a sense, a partial oxidation. The degree of oxidation in a molecule defines how electron-withdrawing it is. The totality of molecules with that quality in the system affects the global degree of oxidation of the system. When it reaches a certain point, instead of just one protein collapsing, you get a freeze-melt transition where one protein triggers another, and you get coherent, cooperative changes throughout the system.

**John Barkhausen:** It sounds like the pH surrounding the substance and the materials attached to the substance affect how quickly a chemical change happens.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. You have to think of it as a flow from the environment in and out. Life is always maintaining a delicate balance between oxidation and reduction. Antioxidants are a dynamic process in which they are also oxidants. If you push towards a dominance of reduction, you kill the cell in a different way.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you explain the origin of the word "oxidant"?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the 18th century, they thought of phlogiston. Then Priestley and Lavoisier saw that something was being consumed from the air during burning. They saw that it generally made an acid form. Priestley named the substance that makes burning possible "oxygen"—"oxy" being the root for acid or sour.

Thinking of oxygen in relation to its ability to form acids is important to integrate with your thinking of what a cell is doing. People tend to think of carbon dioxide as simply a waste product. But if you think of the electronic balance holding the proteins of the cell in a certain state, changing the pH is crucial. Carbon dioxide turns out to be a universal balancing factor or adjuster of the acidic properties of the protein.

Carbon dioxide is an acid as defined by Gilbert Lewis. It doesn't have protons, so you needn't talk about pH really, but the arrangement—an oxygen doubly bonded to a carbon—creates that electron-withdrawing property. When it attaches to a protein, it increases the acidity of the protein, making it partially more oxidized. This changes its affinity for other things.

This is the kind of thinking that led to Gilbert Ling's orientation, accounting for cells and their metabolism without the hypothetical membrane and its pumps. You don't need a magic pump moving things in and out that would consume more energy than the cell has. The energy of the cell is produced to form carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide prevents excess electron accumulation. Since it's a continuing streaming process, you have oxygen streaming in and carbon dioxide streaming out. The carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which ionizes. You now have a negative charge on the carbon dioxide streaming out of the cell. It takes positive charges out with it—sodium and calcium.

**John Barkhausen:** Most people have heard of the membrane theory—that cells are bags holding the cytoplasm in. This is an alternative theory that it's being regulated by the products of the mitochondria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. The mitochondria produces CO2. The CO2 starts as an electron acceptor, becomes negatively charged, and in leaving, drags out the positive metal ions like sodium.

**John Barkhausen:** Why is the CO2 leaving?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just because it's being constantly formed inside and diffuses out down the gradient. When it gets into the blood, it circulates to the lungs and changes back to carbon dioxide, which goes down its gradient into the fresh air. The carbon dioxide leaves the blood, leaving behind the molecules or ions that it took out of the cells. The absence of the acidic carbon dioxide in the blood leaves the blood with a higher pH.

The normal situation is for a healthy cell to be faintly under neutrality (pH 6.9) and for the blood to be definitely over neutrality (pH 7.4).

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A lot of people have seen disease as caused by low pH or too much acidity. In stress and cancer, a tumor will become very acidic. Inflammation produces high concentrations of lactic acid and a very low pH in that area. But when lactic acid is formed, the conversion from pyruvic acid to lactic acid draws an extra proton out of the NADH catalyst. In taking away this extra proton, it raises the pH *inside* the cell.

So even though a tumor is locally acidic, inside the cell it's the reverse process—an increase in pH. If the cell gets stuck producing lactic acid because it can't produce CO2, it gets stuck at a higher pH. That's where you tend to get a self-replicating tumor because the normal acidic conditions maintained by the CO2 are lost.

**John Barkhausen:** Could you give us a cliff notes version of cellular respiration?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** We are sandwiched between the sugar energy we get from plants and the carbon dioxide we make as the final product. Each oxidation of the sugar molecule adds chemical energy to the cell. When you are unable to oxidize the sugar all the way down to carbon dioxide and produce lactic acid instead, you lose the greatest part of the energy stored in the glucose molecule.

Without oxygen, you need some kind of oxidant to continue producing that low energy from sugar to lactic acid. To do that, cells can produce fat and get rid of their electrons by building them into fat. Building fat is a bad alternative to using up oxygen and making CO2. Cancers get stuck converting glucose to lactic acid, and they also get stuck making fat. Fat becomes their oxygen, in effect. Then, when they still have mitochondrial function, the cell burns fat as its energy source. It's a deranged metabolism to produce an irritant, lactic acid, and to do that, it has to make fat, which is then used as fuel.

**John Barkhausen:** And that's called glycolysis?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's aerobic glycolysis when you make lactic acid in the presence of oxygen. Ordinary anaerobic glycolysis happens when you exercise too hard. But when you start producing lactic acid even in the presence of oxygen, as in cancer or shock, something turns the trigger so that you waste your sugar. The nervous system is involved in making that aerobic glycolysis in shock, and many suggest the nervous system is involved in the cancer transition.

**John Barkhausen:** How does the mitochondria make do with burning fat?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It produces less carbon dioxide. If you develop fat stores, you get particles of fat accumulating in the cytoplasm that probably have a disruptive effect. When a person is very sick with cancer, they get a gaunt look as their superficial fat stores are used up. At the same time, they convert amino acids to energy.

Our stores, the older a person gets, generally have a higher amount of polyunsaturated fat (PUFA). When you are oxidizing polyunsaturated fats, that produces more oxidative damage to the mitochondria. It tends to lower the oxidative part of metabolism and slow things down.

**John Barkhausen:** Then people end up feeling less energy and get run down.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That happens in midlife to lots of people; it resembles the cancer metabolism but shows up as fatigue. Some people can maintain their weight on 700 calories a day by turning off thyroid function. You're being wasteful even though you aren't using much energy. What you are using tends to be destructive, reducing connective tissue and muscle rather than living on stored fat. Basically, you're hibernating.

**John Barkhausen:** Are fats always part of the process of respiration, or is that only when you're ill?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's generally only under stress, starvation, diabetes, or high levels of stress.

**John Barkhausen:** A lot of people are on ketosis diets where they don't eat carbohydrates. Does that cause you to burn fats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** And protein. Your brain and some other tissues have an absolute requirement for glucose. They'll get it by breaking down amino acids from your tissues if you aren't eating enough. If you are eating amino acids and fats as your energy source, you turn on the machinery for turning amino acids into glucose and fat. That involves turning on stress hormones, which I think have chronic harmful effects.

**John Barkhausen:** Most people do it in a controlled setting.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Most of the proteins being eaten under those systems are too high in phosphate and usually too high in methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan. Cysteine is an excitotoxic amino acid, and methionine is involved in stress and aging. One of the most effective life-extending diets is simply to reduce the amount of methionine. The sulfur amino acids and tryptophan are stress and aging promoters.

Also, the high phosphate in popular proteins has excitatory harmful effects. The Klotho gene, deficient in animals that age quickly, is largely a phosphate-handling protein. Meat has one of the highest ratios of phosphate to other minerals. Milk and cheese are about half and half, which is safer. Fruits and leafy green vegetables have a very safe, low phosphate content relative to calcium.

**John Barkhausen:** I have a question from a listener, Paul. He is a 34-year-old male, Type 1 diabetic for 8 months. He takes insulin and supplements but wants to prolong his "honeymoon phase" or get off insulin.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Before I was born, my father had extreme diabetes. He went down to 90 pounds, couldn't assimilate food, and had high urine glucose. Looking at old naturopathic remedies, he started eating brewer's yeast as his only food—about two cups a day. He immediately stopped producing so much glucose in his urine and in a few months was completely well.

I think part of that effect is the hormones in the yeast which stimulate regeneration, the high potassium content which has an insulin-like action, and the high B vitamins. Having enough glucose so that you don't draw polyunsaturated fats out of storage is important; those fats are very toxic to the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Normally, beta cells are being renewed constantly. In a diabetic, they die quickly. Sugar is a factor that will prolong their lifespan.

Nitric oxide is specifically what kills the beta cells. You definitely don't want to do anything that would increase nitric oxide production, like supplementing arginine. I think aspirin, B vitamins, vitamin E, pregnenolone, and DHEA help. Someone gave rabbits diabetes with a chemical toxin and then gave them a supplement of DHEA; the ones that got DHEA regenerated a healthy pancreas.

**John Barkhausen:** You're actually advocating taking sugar or glucose?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In the late 19th century, doctors described cases of advanced terminal diabetes where they added about 12 ounces per day of sugar to an otherwise good diet. In just a few weeks, people came back from near death. Their reasoning was that the patients were dying so fast they were putting out the equivalent of a pound of tissue converted to sugar every day. They figured, why not let them eat what they crave to slow down the starvation? Instead, they stopped wasting away.

**John Barkhausen:** What about multiple chemical sensitivity? A listener asked about this and mentioned Luca Turin's research on odors.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it relates to Luca Turin's work. He was talking about smell and psychoactive chemicals like antidepressants. What's in common is the resonance state, or the tuning of the molecule to the oxidation state. The whole system has to be tuned to a certain level of reduction and oxidation.

The addition of a chemical, whether it's an antidepressant or a perfume, passes along the conductive pathways of the nervous system. The autonomic nervous system regulates the state of inflammation. Cells like mast cells can regulate inflammation all through the body. A slight shift in your autonomic nervous system can globally change the degree of inflammation, increasing histamine and serotonin.

When you increase your intensity of mitochondrial respiration and your level of carbon dioxide, that stabilizes the system. But when you're right on the edge, a perfume molecule or food molecule can send impulses shifting you away from the oxidative processes towards the side of the nervous system that becomes dominant in shock. I think chronic fatigue and chemical sensitivity are, in effect, a variation on the physiology of shock.

**John Barkhausen:** What can someone do if they are suffering from this?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Supplementing thyroid is the usual thing, but sometimes they are very low in cholesterol. Since thyroid works partly through converting cholesterol to hormones like progesterone, DHEA, and pregnenolone, if your cholesterol is too low, thyroid alone doesn't necessarily do it. Supplementing one or more of those will often relieve the exaggerated sensitivity.

**John Barkhausen:** You mentioned polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) causing deterioration.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The same biochemical patterns of interference with mitochondrial respiration were produced by a great variety of stresses—radiation, estrogen, and polyunsaturated fatty acids. Vitamin E was found to stop the characteristic damage from feeding animals too much unsaturated fat.

Olive oil has only 8-10% of the unstable polyunsaturated fat. Butter and coconut oil have 2-3%. The safest of them all is hydrogenated coconut oil. It eliminates the unstable quality that makes things susceptible to oxidation.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you explain hydrogenation vs. dehydrogenation?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's the movement of electrons. When we turn saturated fat into unsaturated fat in our own bodies, we dehydrogenate it. When a cow turns unsaturated fat from their food into saturated fat for butter, bacteria in their rumen are hydrogenating it.

When you take away hydrogen atoms from adjoining carbon atoms, the electrons combine to form a double bond. The absence of the space-filling hydrogen leaves that range of electrons open and more reactive. That makes access of oxygen atoms to the fat molecule easier.

**John Barkhausen:** So that's why Crisco is a liquid oil that has had hydrogen added to make it stable.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If they would complete the process the way they do in changing coconut oil to 0% PUFA, you wouldn't get the trans fats. You would have totally saturated stearic acid, which would be safe. One group of researchers found that aged, defective mitochondria were restored when given fully saturated hydrogenated peanut oil.

**John Barkhausen:** I have questions from Martin about salt. Can salt ingestion trigger migraines? Was salt restriction useful in Gerson's tuberculosis trials?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I read Gerson's book. He was very thorough. Salts are extremely important. A contemporary researcher, William Frederick Koch, found that if he removed parathyroid glands in animals, giving them extra potassium, sodium, or magnesium had the same curative effect as calcium. One can make up for a deficiency of the other.

The Gerson diet was extremely high in potassium and magnesium. It had the amount of sodium found in juice and vegetables—a physiological amount—but a large amount of potassium. I think these were the essence of Gerson's success rather than just reducing sodium. Sodium acts as a stimulant to cell respiration and causes it to un-swell. If you lower the other minerals and give too much sodium, you can force it to swell. But when balanced, sodium increases energy production.

**John Barkhausen:** What about salt triggering migraines?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When you take a sudden dose of salt, it makes you swell up and retain water until your aldosterone has adjusted downward. Anything susceptible will swell up—fingers, toes, lips. But people who would get swollen feet on an airplane trip found that if they adjusted two or three days in advance by eating extra salt, they didn't get the swollen feet anymore.

When you cut back on sodium, aldosterone is increased. Aldosterone lets you retain sodium but at the expense of losing potassium and magnesium. Chronically, high aldosterone has a pro-inflammatory effect. Getting more alkaline minerals than you need suppresses aldosterone and protects your heart from inflammation and fibrosis.

Sodium works with albumin to hold water in the bloodstream. If you are low in albumin or sodium, the blood loses osmotic quality, and water stays in the tissues (edema). The remedy for edema is often adding sodium, but the basic reason for it is often a thyroid deficiency. The absence of high carbon dioxide production means you aren't able to retain sodium in your kidneys.

**John Barkhausen:** Any final words on staying healthy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just keeping stress down and fun up. Judging food largely by how it tastes rather than by what the experts say.

title: Politics & Science: Coronavirus, immunity, and vaccines (Part 1)
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Politics and Science is live today for a change. I'm very honored to have Dr. Raymond Peat back on the line. I'm going to use the same bio I had for you years ago, which is that you have a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialization in physiology. I also consider you a science historian and ombudsman. I've wanted to get you on again because you're interesting to hear on any subject, and we particularly have this weird emergency going on that has everybody spinning: the COVID-19 pandemic. I wanted to get your take on that, talk about the science behind pandemics and viruses, and maybe cover vaccines. What do you think is going on right now?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** First of all, I'm not sure anything special is going on in the virus and infection world. It's definitely happening in the media and politics. Mexico isn't getting excited; they've had, I think, 16 mild cases.

The CDC for years has been reporting the annual respiratory or flu-like death rate as being in the tens of thousands of deaths per year in the United States—average deaths from respiratory disease being say 30,000 or 40,000. If you look at the historic percentage of those respiratory diseases, roughly 5% to 15% are historically coronavirus infections. The others are things as simple as rhinovirus or respiratory syncytial virus—things that range from mild sniffles up to serious pneumonia.

If 30,000 or 40,000 people are expected to die from flu-like respiratory disease, we would expect to have 3,000 or 4,000 deaths per year from a coronavirus respiratory infection. I don't see any evidence at all that anything is happening on the real biological level.

**John Barkhausen:** The official line is that the crisis actually hasn't happened yet. But you're saying in a given year we should still see 3,000 to 4,000 deaths from coronavirus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In an average year that could still happen. We could get up to the average mortality associated with coronaviruses, but we're not approaching that by a long way so far. Just looking at the actual numbers, it looks like we're slightly deficient in cases and deaths of respiratory problems associated with that virus.

**John Barkhausen:** Have you checked out the Chinese or the Asian data at this point? Are the corona deaths up from their average?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** They haven't talked about the average for corona; they weren't gathering that data. But they say this is just slightly more deadly than a typical influenza virus.

The problem is Italy always has had about twice as many respiratory or flu-like deaths per year per capita as the United States, so it isn't unusual for them to be especially hard hit. What makes the number go up is that they have been primarily testing sick people in hospitals.

It's the same with cancer diagnosis. If you go all out to look for cancer in a population of middle age and old age, you'll find 100% cancers if you're really thorough. The more you diagnose, the more you can find people. People die at the same rate unless you treat them. If you increase your treatment for cancer as you increase the diagnosis, the treatment is going to kill more and more. But you can make your treatments look better by diagnosing more and more cases which are harmless.

Same with the flu or the coronavirus. If you test everyone in the population, you'll get all of these people with very mild reactions. In South Korea, for example, the mortality rate was 0.6% because they tested more people. The dying people become a smaller percentage when you test a more representative cross-section of the population.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's selection bias—because they're looking for the diseases in the most vulnerable, they test the sickest people first.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. If restricted to the people in the hospital on respirators, you'll find that most of them have serious viruses, probably multiple respiratory viruses. When you're very sick, various viruses that have been carried harmlessly will pop to the surface and get measured because your immune system is compromised.

**John Barkhausen:** Can we back up a little bit? What exactly is the difference between a virus and a bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Almost all bacteria are free-living in a sense. They can generally live outside of cells if you feed them the right stuff and give them the right temperature. They have the apparatus to reproduce their own genetic material.

The virus depends on entering a cell—either a bacterium or a higher organism's cell—and taking advantage of their machinery, like ribosomes that can produce proteins from nucleic acids. These viruses put in their nucleic acid once they get into the cell. That is processed on our ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum; proteins are added to the replicated nucleic acid, and then it's excreted as a finished particle by our ordinary cell secretory system.

**John Barkhausen:** In a healthy person, if you encounter a new virus, do you think we're able to conquer that or isolate it so it doesn't do any harm?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. For example, the air sacs in our lungs are lined with epithelial cells. There are cells around the air sac that secrete mucus to cover the epithelial cells. To reduce the surface tension so that the air sac will stay open, there is a protein called surfactant protein. It has an oily, lipophilic fraction, so it acts like a soap. The water-loving part of the protein dissolves in this mucous layer, and the oily surface reduces the surface tension so the air sac can stay open without extreme tension.

That surfactant protein contains groups that will collect the sugar-like surfaces of viral proteins. Any pathogen that hits that surfactant protein will get glued down by these binding particles. It's our first layer of defense.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** In and around the epithelial layer, we have reactive parts of the immune system. The angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is one of the early parts of our immune system. If a pathogen gets through, you activate this proteolytic protein that creates angiotensin, which is like a transmitter of a panic reaction to the organism.

It happens that this coronavirus is able to bind to one of these angiotensin-converting enzymes. There is one which is only pro-inflammatory (ACE1), and another one that backs that up and inhibits the inflammatory damage done by the first one. This is called ACE2.

ACE2 happens to be attacked by this particular virus. Binding to ACE2 means that it leaves ACE1—which produces angiotensin—free to act. ACE2 is capable of inactivating angiotensin, breaking it down to the first seven amino acids (angiotensin 1-7), which is a defensive, anti-inflammatory peptide. So if your ACE2 is knocked out, angiotensin has a free range to cause damage.

The virus increases the inflammatory reaction by sticking to this defensive enzyme. That enzyme combined with the virus then acts to enter the cell by way of the angiotensin receptor, which is called the AT1. That turns on a whole range of destructive processes—nitric oxide and serotonin, for example.

**John Barkhausen:** So nitric oxide and serotonin are inflammatory mediators?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. So anti-inflammatory things are the known treatment for this kind of virus. The Chinese for years have been using Cinanserin, which is a serotonin blocker. They find that it's helpful for people with the established respiratory corona infection. Losartan, which is a high blood pressure drug, is the most well-known blocker of the angiotensin 1 receptor.

**John Barkhausen:** How do you spell those?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Cinanserin is C-I-N-A-N-S-E-R-I-N. Losartan is L-O-S-A-R-T-A-N.

**John Barkhausen:** Basically, the virus just activates an inflammatory process that many other things activate.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. Things that primarily activate nitric oxide production, serotonin, histamine, or prostaglandin production tend to end up in the same condition. Without knowing more about the nature of the infection, I think people who are taking aspirin, for example, are protected. Aspirin has a wide range of antiviral properties. It's already known to reduce infection from the standard influenza virus, hepatitis C, and rhinovirus.

Much maligned Vitamin D happens to have effects like progesterone and aspirin: all of our known protective, pro-immune but anti-inflammatory substances lower the expression of angiotensin receptor 1 (AT1), so they predispose us to be less inflammable.

**John Barkhausen:** When it enters your lungs, your cells put out a lipid of some kind?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Once we're born and start breathing, we depend on the production of this surfactant protein. It's everywhere normally. Our intestines have similar layers of defenses. Coronaviruses don't just specialize on the lungs; they can infect the mucous membranes in the nose and the intestine.

Some people have said that runny noses aren't connected as a precursor of the lung infection, but a Russian virologist looking at tens of thousands of patients saw that a runny nose was a typical precursor to the lung infection symptoms. The intestine is just as prone to infection as the lungs.

**John Barkhausen:** So eating something could make you sick? Even though your stomach acid would take care of it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you get it in your mouth and swallow it, it could infect those tissues. The stomach acid doesn't necessarily break down the nucleic acid.

**John Barkhausen:** They're telling us to wash our hands all the time. How does soap kill a virus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It dissolves the proteins, making relatively insoluble things soluble. The soap has a hydrophobic fraction that sticks to hydrophobic insoluble parts of an organism and disassembles it from the inside out.

**John Barkhausen:** Is COVID-19 better at breaking into our system than a normal cold? I've heard a cold is also a coronavirus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A cold can be caused by any of these if your immune system is weak. One study found that for almost half of all respiratory infections, they couldn't identify a particular cause. Rhinovirus was the biggest at about 30%. The coronavirus is in the range of 5% to 15% of those respiratory infections.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think the reaction of the government at this point is over the top?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Unless it was their purpose to create international chaos—for example, to try to finish off Iran by cutting off their medical supplies while they're having a crisis. If it's not really a threat otherwise, it becomes a threat when you do all of these insane things.

The media, including big science media like *Nature* and *Science Magazine*, are getting excited in denying that it was an intentionally created virus leaked from a lab. They just published a paper explaining technically why it would be impossible, but the fact that they're rushing so fast to deny it is suspicious.

Normally they say it takes over a year to produce a vaccine to a new respiratory infection, but they're already saying they have a vaccine ready to test. The purpose of the CDC patenting the coronavirus 17 years ago was deliberately to create pathogens experimentally to enable them to anticipate pathogens so they could have a vaccine ready.

**John Barkhausen:** Why would the CDC patent that?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** So they can license a vaccine, I suppose.

**John Barkhausen:** Dr. Fauci was saying it would be at least a year and a half minimum to put out a vaccine. Do you think he's out of the loop?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, that's what virologists in general say. It takes time to develop it and do actual testing. I think that's a very optimistic idea because if they really had to test it for safety, it would take a generation.

**John Barkhausen:** Because they test on animals?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The way they have tested the safety is fraudulent. In the control group, they use the same adjuvant—aluminum adjuvant, for example—which is the most dangerous component. You can't have a test without a proper control group.

**John Barkhausen:** Explain what an adjuvant is.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It creates derangement. In this case, the muscle is where they inject it. They found that just pathogen particles weren't enough to really tear up the tissue to produce a violent immune reaction. So they found that aluminum oxide particles created a terrific immunological storm. That extreme inflammation at the point of injection activates a systemic immune reaction. It turns your whole body into an inflammatory system. That's why people often have a fever for a couple of days after getting a shot.

**John Barkhausen:** They keep harking back to the Spanish Flu of 1918. I read recently that the flu might have been caused by a vaccine the Rockefeller Center was testing on soldiers.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I haven't heard that specifically, but do you know about the movie *Vaxxed*? There's information in that about the Gulf War Syndrome and the anthrax vaccine. People were getting Gulf War Syndrome without leaving the US following their anthrax vaccination.

**John Barkhausen:** I found an article looking at research on the Spanish Flu. The scientist who looked back at the autopsies found they all tested positive for bacterial pneumonia.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Definitely. The CDC counts pretty much anything that falls into the unknown category of severe respiratory syndromes as flu to get their annual 40,000 or 50,000 deaths so they can scare people into getting flu shots. It obviously isn't the flu; it's pneumonia from partly unknown causes and partly a variety of viruses.

Also, stress itself is the cause of epidemics. Shortage of food will increase the incidence of infectious diseases. If anything unusual is happening in the disease world now, I think you can blame sanctions as one of the big causes. It's dislocating the world economy. If you cause unemployment, you're going to increase infectious diseases.

**John Barkhausen:** Some people are speculating that the hot points for this viral infection coincide with sites of 5G deployment. Do you think that could contribute to a declining immune system?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw a good lecture by Devra Davis. She did a good analysis of the electromagnetic damage. They claim it's safe on the basis of absolutely no research, but the animal research that exists shows there is a real danger. Some studies found that people who had worked on an electric sewing machine for 20 years had a very high rate of dementia. Anything that affects your nervous system is affecting your immune system.

**John Barkhausen:** Caleb from Ontario asks: How much of a role does endotoxin play in regards to a viral infection, and are the effects of endotoxin increased in the presence of a virus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Endotoxin is a fatty acid with carbohydrate attached to it—lipopolysaccharide. It's part of the coating of a bacterium. Normally our intestine filters out most of it, and the liver detoxifies it. But when you're under stress, your liver gets overwhelmed, letting it produce inflammation and interfere with mitochondrial energy production.

It activates the angiotensin system. So, a viral infection and anything stressing your intestine enough to make it permeable to bacterial materials will end up in the same place: causing inflammatory symptoms.

**John Barkhausen:** It's always amazed me how connected the intestine is to other organs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It's partly chemical leaking through and partly inflammatory substances like serotonin and histamine produced by the intestine itself. A tremendous flood of serotonin circulates in the platelets, and the nerves can transmit signals—such as secretion of mucus—right up to your nose and throat.

That's why I recommend raw carrot. Because carrot is indigestible, it helps wash out some of the bacteria producing the endotoxin. If you take anti-inflammatory things with it, such as olive oil, coconut oil, aspirin, or an antibiotic, the carrot will deliver that through your intestine.

An early 20th-century gastro doctor demonstrated that in canine distemper—thought of as a respiratory disease—there was already a well-established infection in the intestine before any virus occurred in the respiratory membranes. They would start drooling and sniffling because of a signal from an inflamed intestine.

**John Barkhausen:** Another question: What about the theory that viruses are simply phages or somatids from bacteria, and viral infections are really caused by occult intracellular bacteria?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Those things do exist, but I don't think that explains it all. We are loaded with potential viruses. Several percent of our genome is identified as potential viruses or retroviruses. This is DNA that has been built into our system by exposure to the environment.

Barbara McClintock showed that stress causes genes to come out of the chromosomes and move around. Since we have these retroviruses, it's almost certain that under stress we will express retroviruses that have been in us for generations. If you look for them, it looks like you have caught a viral infection from the outside.

**John Barkhausen:** One last question: "I heard that immunity after an infection with a coronavirus is quite short-lived."

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I don't have an opinion on acquired immunity, but one thing that is known is that after this kind of severe respiratory infection, there is a great increase in the risk of pulmonary fibrosis. Inflammation leads to fibrosis and reduced lung function. I think the real thing to worry about is stopping the progression of that angiotensin-related inflammatory production of tissue fibrosis.

**John Barkhausen:** And anti-inflammatories will do that. What's the best way of delivering an anti-inflammatory to the lung?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Through the mouth. Just eating it. Losartan, Cinanserin, or Cyproheptadine are good, safe, broad anti-inflammatories.

A lot of people are recommending the old approach to viruses: killing the virus using nucleoside analogs to mutate the DNA of the virus. But studies show these definitely injure the gonads and mutate human DNA. Widespread use of that is going to create genetic damage to the reproducing population.

**John Barkhausen:** We're running out of time. What's the best course of action for people to protect themselves?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** My first recommendation is to eat well and make sure your Vitamin D level is up to around 50-60 ng/mL on a blood test, which often takes 5,000 units a day. Use a very safe antiviral such as aspirin.

If there's a sign of an infection, then I think Losartan and the anti-serotonin things (Cinanserin or Cyproheptadine) would be appropriate to limit the degree of inflammation. Don't worry about killing the virus or becoming immune to some future variant.

**John Barkhausen:** And you can get Vitamin D from sunlight if it's sunny enough.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That's the best thing.

**John Barkhausen:** Thanks for being on the air tonight, Ray. I really appreciate it.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, anytime.

title: Politics & Science: Coronavirus, immunity, and vaccines (Part 2)
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Hey and welcome to Politics and Science. I'm your host, John Barkhausen. This week we return to part two of our conversation with Dr. Raymond Peat. This was recorded on March 24, 2020, and we are discussing the Coronavirus COVID-19, which has caused a lockdown in the United States in many areas due to its expected high contagion rate and potentially serious mortality rate.

Dr. Raymond Peat has a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon, specializing in physiology and hormones. His newsletter is available at RayPeat.com.

Ray, thanks for coming back on Politics and Science today. We're in the midst of this coronavirus pandemic declared by the World Health Organization and the CDC. Everyone is having a hard time and is very scared. I just listened to a podcast with a New York Times reporter talking to an epidemiologist saying that it's going to be very bad and we're not taking enough across-the-board measures. They argued that state responses are too piecemeal and there needs to be strong federal action to make sure everybody stays home. I wonder what your take is on that.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I am still not convinced that anything special is happening. Did we talk about the German virologist Wolfgang Wodarg?

**John Barkhausen:** No, we didn't yet.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** He is a well-known expert in pulmonology and viruses. As of the last time I checked his website, he still wasn't convinced that anything different from previous years is happening. He showed that in previous years, 5% to 15% of infectious lung disease was caused by some type of coronavirus. So far, this one hasn't really been proven to be much more virulent or infectious, though that is yet to be determined. They've jumped to the conclusion that it is both more harmful and spreads faster, but you can't find that in the evidence.

According to Wodarg and another German pulmonologist and virologist named Sucharit Bhakdi, the country is causing considerable economic damage and harming older people by the measures they're introducing without real evidence that anything special is happening. Another well-known epidemiologist, John Ioannidis at Stanford, says this might be one of history's greatest evidence fiascos because they're talking about fragments of evidence, drawing huge conclusions, and taking unprecedented political and economic actions against no clear scientific evidence.

**John Barkhausen:** Could you spell the names of the German epidemiologists so people can look up their evidence?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The first one was Wolfgang Wodarg (W-O-D-A-R-G). The second is Bhakdi (B-H-A-K-D-I).

**John Barkhausen:** And the guy at Stanford is John Ioannidis. They're saying that the Trump administration isn't doing enough.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I've always been considered crazy for pointing out that Trump, in many ways, has been less harmful than the so-called progressives like Obama. He tends to be withdrawing from wars, for example. I'm inclined to see his reluctance to go ahead with the "war on the virus" as another virtue, even though everyone considers that crazy. The Pentagon wanted to go back into Iraq heavily in retaliation against a couple of soldiers getting killed, and he used the virus as an argument against renewing the war in Iraq. So even though he's being criticized for going against the grain, so far I think he's justified by the evidence.

**John Barkhausen:** What do you make of the reports from Italy where people over 65 aren't being allowed to have a ventilator? People are doing triage and some are basically told they'll have to die.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I saw a video from a hospital in Bergamo. It looked like they were stuffing people in oxygen tents and putting oxygen masks on them. If people come in with a minor respiratory ailment and they're elderly, putting them into a pure oxygen atmosphere is exactly the wrong thing to do. However, almost all hospitals in the world do this, thinking that because they are having trouble breathing, they need pure oxygen.

Carbon dioxide is anti-inflammatory. When you give them pure oxygen—five times more than normal—you are displacing the natural balance of carbon dioxide. Several good research projects have found that if you hypoventilate people who are having problems in the hospital, letting the CO2 build up reduces inflammation and produces much better outcomes.

Inflammation is a pathogen in any kind of sickness, especially in this virus infection. The symptoms are basically inflammatory. The angiotensin system and the interferon system turn on other inflammatory agents like histamine. All of the defensive reactions triggered by these respiratory infections amplify inflammation, causing congestion, constriction, swelling, and exudation of serum into the lungs. Instead of a balanced moisture economy in the lungs, the serum and proteins in the blood ooze out into the lung space and interfere with breathing.

Anything you do to increase inflammation is going to increase that pneumonia tendency. Oxygen and many of the virucidal chemicals they are given greatly intensify inflammation. That's one of the reasons old people are so susceptible. Different studies say about 85% of proven infected people have almost no symptoms. The ones who react badly are mostly the very old who already have some kind of degenerative, circulatory, or inflammatory disease.

I see the changes of aging that cause circulatory problems as essentially overactivity of the immune system—a general tissue degenerative process that exaggerates inflammatory processes. In one study where they gave a known coronavirus intended to produce common cold symptoms, they found that people with pre-existing inflammatory problems were the ones that reacted more seriously. In mice studies, they find that the virus does very little damage to young animals. The older the animal is, with a more mature immune system, the more harmful the virus is. In this situation, the so-called immune defenses are really the instrument by which the virus is damaging the organism.

**John Barkhausen:** So it's the reaction of the organism to the virus.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. A successful virus succeeds by causing something like chronic diarrhea and a chronic cough. If the person stays well enough to go around living normally but coughing, that's good for the virus to spread. A successful virus doesn't kill many of its infected hosts.

**John Barkhausen:** If you're already inflamed and the virus attacks your cells, you're much more likely to have an over-immune reaction. That reminds me of what we're doing socially or politically right now. If what you're saying is correct, we're having an overreaction to the threat of this virus which could potentially cause a lot of damage to our society.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It already is causing unemployment. It's being taken as an opportunity. Ben Bernanke and Janet Yellen proposed that the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department join up so that the taxpayers will be made responsible for everything the Fed does, allowing them to bail out big corporations at their choice. This leads to super-corporations guaranteed by the government and taxpayers, but no guarantees for employees of middle-sized and small companies. It's pushing towards total monopoly.

**John Barkhausen:** Naomi Klein has written about this in her book *The Shock Doctrine: The Rise of Disaster Capitalism*. This seems like a combination of disaster capitalism and fascism, if the definition of fascism is the combination of corporate and federal power.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Exactly. Except as it's going, it bypasses some of the nastiness of Hitlerism and Mussolini's fascism and goes directly to giving orders around the world to stop protests and interfere with elections. For example, the Yellow Vests in France aren't able to go into the streets as they've been doing for a year. It has established total quiescence and political control.

**John Barkhausen:** I see a lot of talk on social media saying, "If only we had a vaccine that would save us." Could you speak about the efficacy of vaccines in terms of flus and this virus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** During the great swine flu pandemic that didn't exist [in 1976], the man in charge of influenza vaccines at the CDC pointed out to his superiors that the time it takes to develop a flu vaccine is usually a year to a year and a half. By that time, the flu germ has spread, reached its peak, and disappeared. People are naturally immune to that particular strain by the time the vaccine comes on the market. He lost his job for saying this on television—I think it was Phil Donahue.

Later, *60 Minutes* did a detailed analysis of the failure of the epidemic. Only one soldier was confirmed to have died of the flu virus—no one else in the world, by the admission of the head of the CDC—but hundreds died from the vaccine. Now, when someone says that vaccines are confirmed to be useless and dangerous, and can't conceivably be produced in time to prevent the disease, those people are called quacks.

**John Barkhausen:** In the history of vaccines, have there been useful ones?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** When it's an organism that doesn't change faster than the vaccine can be produced. Smallpox was probably the best example of a vaccine being able to totally abolish a disease when used intelligently. They would identify outbreaks and form a ring of vaccinated people around those outbreaks, letting the disease run its course inside that ring. By repeatedly doing that, they eradicated the virus from nature.

**John Barkhausen:** Because smallpox didn't mutate quickly, they could get a handle on it?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. I think other diseases are probably slow enough to change that they could be treated similarly if the effort were made. The cost for eliminating smallpox on a world scale was microscopic compared to the annual expense on measles and the standard array of vaccines kids get in the US. The cost alone is enough to lead to a more intelligent policy.

**John Barkhausen:** I think you said the cost now is $4.5 to $50 billion a year just for vaccines for children.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yes. And they are stupidly used, trying to vaccinate the whole world rather than closing in on the virus. If you have an outbreak at Disney World, you can track those people and vaccinate everyone around them. Vaccines have a consistent and predictable rate of damage—mortality, paralysis, brain damage. Autism is one of the outcomes. The government pays at least a proportion of the people they harm, acknowledging the damage, but they prefer to pay for a stupid use of vaccines.

**John Barkhausen:** The testing is also of questionable merit.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The safety testing is absolutely crooked. Some vaccines contain harmful adjuvants like aluminum hydroxide, added because it causes a systemic inflammatory reaction. That is often more harmful than the germ itself. When testing the safety of a vaccine, you would expect them to test the vaccine against a placebo. But in some studies, they gave the adjuvant to the control group as well. So they're creating a certain level of damage in their control group and comparing that to the damage in the complete vaccine. I can't think of any way a person could design that experiment without intending to defraud.

**John Barkhausen:** In your recent newsletter, you mentioned a fellow named John Williamson, called "Johnny Notions." How did his vaccines work if they didn't have this adjuvant?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The smallpox vaccine all by itself is irritating enough; it doesn't need an adjuvant. He reasoned that if he could weaken this nasty material, it would be safer. He would take pus or scab from a person with smallpox, smoke it, pack it under leaves and a layer of camphor, and bury it for years. This was in the 1700s, so almost nothing was known about chemistry, but he intuited that he was weakening the agent.

He would then introduce it into the skin—not into the muscle or blood. He had a very fine tool to split the skin so it went into the living material but didn't reach the blood. He vaccinated thousands, and none of them died from the vaccine, whereas many would have from a modern vaccine.

**John Barkhausen:** What's the difference between a dermal application and having something injected into your bloodstream?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Experiments in the last 10 years show that when you take a particular antigen and either inhale it, eat it, rub it into the skin, or inject it carefully intradermally, the systemic results are absolutely different from injecting it into the blood or muscle. The immune system is designed to react in a maximally appropriate way when things are encountered via natural routes. We don't have an evolved immune system for proper reactions to needle injections into the muscles.

The use of needles seems to have been a matter of professionalism in the 1800s. Doctors were the only ones with access to needles and syringes. They claimed a monopoly on the "most effective" way to give medication, rather than the "crude" way of eating or inhaling it. There never was any valid scientific basis for giving medications by injection.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The reaction from injection is largely a reaction to tissue damage, leading to autoimmune-type reactions—more reactions against your tissues than against the antigen. The antibody theory of immunity is essentially a superstructure built on ignorance of how the immune system works.

The antibody theory came about more than 100 years ago with Paul Ehrlich's "lock and key" idea, which was a way to sell chemical drugs. The antibody became the model for a specific drug cure. However, there is an alternative view gaining recognition: the Danger Theory (Polly Matzinger) or Damage Theory (Jamie Cunliffe).

In this view, the immune system isn't on the outlook for "pathogens." The organism has a picture of itself that it wants to preserve. When it experiences damage, it recognizes that part of itself is out of place. In the process of correcting the damage, the pathogenic cause tends to be eliminated. But the emphasis is on maintaining or restoring the image of the body rather than learning images of potential invaders.

**John Barkhausen:** Since flus and viruses adapt too quickly for vaccines, it sounds like we should depend on the innate immune system. How do we get that to work for us?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Making people healthy and exposing them to fewer vaccines as they grow up is important. Allergic people are known to be the ones who react the worst to coronaviruses. The degenerative or autoimmune changes that happen with aging make a person more susceptible. A person with an abundant energetic metabolism, without a lot of inflammatory experiences, can produce the most organized and almost unnoticed rejection of the infection. The 80% of people who don't know they're infected are the ones with a good immune system.

**John Barkhausen:** You mentioned that a lung infection triggers angiotensin, interferon, and histamine reactions. How do interferon and histamine react with the coronavirus?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** One of the main things the interferon system does is activate the production of nitric oxide. In vitro, nitric oxide is a very good virus killer—it's a free radical that will destroy just about anything. However, in experimental infections with nerve-targeted coronaviruses, they found that blocking interferon's production of nitric oxide prevents the death of the animal. It is specifically the interferon production of nitric oxide that kills the host.

Similarly, serotonin is produced by inflammation. The Chinese are using Cinanserin, a serotonin blocker, as one of their tools against the coronavirus.

**John Barkhausen:** Serotonin causes veins to tighten up. What is the purpose of that in a healthy creature?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Tightening the circulatory system helps raise pressure and get more blood to a problem area. It's an emergency function. It's appropriate to think of these inflammatory things as wound-healing agents. If you have a hole punched in you, these are appropriate for directing healing efforts to that spot. But when they spread from your lungs into the whole organism, the organism suffers because that repair system is damaging when generalized.

**John Barkhausen:** Can you describe the angiotensin cycle again?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Stress and estrogen make the liver produce more angiotensinogen. This is a protein cleaved by renin (an enzyme from the kidney) to produce Angiotensin I. Then, Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) produces Angiotensin II. Angiotensin II leads to all these inflammatory things.

There is another enzyme called ACE2. Its main function is to destroy Angiotensin II. The coronavirus attaches to and inactivates ACE2. This leaves the body with unchecked Angiotensin II and its inflammation.

**John Barkhausen:** You said ACE2 is a sign of a youthful person. If you have a lot of that, it means you're keeping that stress hormone down. But that begs the question: why are young people not affected by the coronavirus since they have more ACE2 for the virus to attack?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** If you have enough of it, it outweighs whatever the virus does. A healthy young person can sacrifice some of their ACE2 to the virus without succumbing to the symptoms. They still have anti-inflammatory ACE2 in reserve. Components of good health—Vitamin B1, progesterone, aspirin—help keep your ACE2 levels up.

**John Barkhausen:** A listener asks about Dr. Christian Drosten, who noted that some recovered patients did not have neutralizing antibodies. What do you think of the role of neutralizing antibodies?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think the healthy young person without too many vaccinations has an immune system that reacts correctly and doesn't bother getting to the antibody stage. As I mentioned regarding the Damage Theory, the immune system is there to repair damage. If you have autoimmunity, it's because something is prolonging the repair process. You want to give it more energy to complete the repair rather than trying to poison the system that makes the antibodies.

**John Barkhausen:** Another listener asks about a paper in *Nature* regarding T-cells. It suggests COVID-19 damages CD4 T-cells and promotes exhaustion of CD8 T-cells.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I would have to read the article, but apparently something has killed part of the T-cell repertoire.

**John Barkhausen:** Do you think the reaction to the coronavirus is a response to the anti-vax movement?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It will be a good excuse for suppressing them more actively. The internet is already being biased against them communicating.

**John Barkhausen:** A listener asks about 5G and RF radiation risks being similar to coronavirus risks.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The damage done by chronic exposure to that kind of radiation weakens the basic quiet immune system, predisposing you to the inflammatory reaction.

**John Barkhausen:** Regarding ACE2, some suggest decreasing things that increase ACE2 expression, yet research suggests things like Losartan (which increases ACE2) are helpful. Can you suggest things that increase ACE2 expression?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That argument against increasing ACE2 was published in *The Lancet*, but I think those people hadn't read the relevant literature. Increasing ACE2 goes beyond what the virus infects and has a protective effect. Progesterone, aspirin, Vitamin B1, and likely anti-serotonin agents help maintain ACE2.

**John Barkhausen:** What are your thoughts on social isolation as a remedy?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It limits the spread of viruses, which would be helpful in any flu season. But I think the harm done by the pressure to enforce isolation is greater than the benefit of keeping respiratory infections lower, especially since the contagion doesn't seem that serious so far.

**John Barkhausen:** A listener mentions a British nurse warning against NSAIDs.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I wanted to mention that the approach to killing the virus is almost always worse than the effect of the virus. Three of the most often mentioned antiviral remedies—Chloroquine, Acyclovir, and nucleoside analogs—are aimed at killing the virus by damaging its DNA or RNA replication. These also happen to damage human DNA at the expense of mutating millions of people. These protections are really very serious harms; they damage the gonads and the retina.

**John Barkhausen:** A listener asks about claims that Vitamin C can increase interferon and cause a cytokine storm.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** That has been my personal experience. In 1956, when Vitamin C became cheap, I took a 500mg tablet and immediately got cold symptoms. I found that I could consume 4,000mg a day of natural Vitamin C by eating simply and eliminating grains, with no problem at all. But 2mg of the commercial stuff produced reactions.

A chemist dissolved 500mg of reagent-grade ascorbic acid in distilled water and measured the free radicals. He said that amount contained enough heavy metal contaminants to oxidize the Vitamin C into its free radical state, equivalent to a killing dose of X-rays. Just the iron contaminant alone would replicate that reaction.

**John Barkhausen:** So you should get Vitamin C from fruit and meats?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Meats, fruit, and even milk. All animals except people, guinea pigs, and primates make their own. So all animal foods are generously supplied with Vitamin C.

**John Barkhausen:** You mentioned eliminating grains. Do grains chelate the Vitamin C?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, they are just free of Vitamin C. They are the only food that is free of it.

**John Barkhausen:** So, Aspirin, B1, vitamins, and not grains. Any other suggestions for keeping the immune system up?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Vitamin D is one of the most important. It works with thyroid, progesterone, and ACE2 to quiet reactions. Also, keeping a high ratio of calcium to phosphate in your diet works with Vitamin D to hold down inflammatory reactions. Vitamin A is also important for the membranes—eyes, nose, lungs—to keep protein turnover at an ideal level.

**John Barkhausen:** Is there anything else you'd like to add?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Looking at the videos I mentioned by Wodarg or Bhakdi will help reduce the panic. Also, do you know David Icke? There is a recent video of his on the coronavirus. I never thought of him as saying anything sensible—normally I would consider him a borderline maniac—but the only thing I disagreed with in this interview was his saying that sugar is immunosuppressive. Everything else he says seems okay.

**John Barkhausen:** I'd like to talk to you sometime about the importance of keeping blood sugar at an optimal level, because a lot of people are talking about fasting to boost their immune system.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Just 24 hours of fasting is enough to damage all of your functions, especially energy production. Energy is a basic thing for maintaining your non-inflammatory immune system.

**John Barkhausen:** Ray, thanks so much for being on Politics and Science.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Okay, thanks. Bye.

title: Politics & Science: Coronavirus, immunity, and vaccines (Part 3)
transcriptText:
**John Barkhausen:** Welcome to Politics and Science. This week we're having Ray Peat, physiologist and science historian from Eugene, Oregon, back on the show. We're going to be talking about the unfolding coronavirus crisis here in the United States and around the world. This was recorded on March 31, 2020. Ray has a PhD from the University of Oregon and specialized in physiology and hormones. Is that correct, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Right. Interrelated reproductive hormones.

**John Barkhausen:** We've been having a conversation the past few weeks about the ongoing coronavirus so-called pandemic that has swept the globe and is scaring everybody, especially in the United States where the news reporting is particularly sensational. Do you watch mainstream news, Ray? I don't usually, but I've been checking it out lately. It's just plain scary, talking about bodies piling up in the backs of trucks in New York City. But today we're going to talk about the actual data. They've been predicting huge numbers of mortalities. Do you see that yet, Ray?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** No, I haven't seen any numbers that convince me that anything unusual is happening regarding virus mortality.

**John Barkhausen:** Can I ask you, where do you go for data?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Google mostly, and somewhat on PubMed. When something on Google isn't available, I often find backup material on PubMed.

**John Barkhausen:** Give us what a normal flu year would bring and where we are now.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** A little over a year ago, the CDC announced that the 2017-18 flu year had killed at least 80,000 people. But then several months later, they revised it down to a little over 60,000. It's interesting because it shows how wildly approximate their estimates of the deaths are. They say that the average has been a little over 40,000 for the last 10 years or so.

I just saw an article on HuffPost from 2014 by Lawrence Solomon, quoting CDC people in 2004 saying that they had contact from the vaccine industry worrying about their weak sales. They decided to rouse the public by convincing them that something dangerous was happening and that they should get vaccinated. That follows long after the 1976 swine flu fiasco, where they supposedly had a pandemic but only one person died in the U.S.

In this program they started in 2004, the goal was to get media excitement going on the number of flu deaths. The verified, actual immunological evidence from people dying of respiratory diseases showed very few documented cases of flu, just because they weren't doing many tests. Despite that, the national statistics based on death certificates showed several hundred people recorded as dying of influenza. With those very small numbers, they didn't have a good case for mass vaccinations. So, they started including pneumonia deaths with influenza. They called it "influenza-like diseases." That's how they managed to get up in the tens of thousands of deaths every flu season.

**John Barkhausen:** So they started including a broader category of illnesses and put it under the heading of flu.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Yeah, that way they could get approximately 10% of everyone dying. 6% on the average year was closer to everyone dying during the four months of the flu season. The old people, that's probably just about the normal proportion of very old people dying. They'll get respiratory problems. Their breathing and circulation are failing, so the lungs fail to work and accumulate water. They can put down pneumonia as the cause of death, or respiratory problems.

When the lungs are slowing down from old age and circulatory diseases, the flow of mucus—which normally runs up the tubes to the mouth to be swallowed—slows down. The bacteria that are always falling into the bronchial tubes from the air stay in place longer just because the cilia aren't sweeping them out quickly. As you're dying from heart failure, liver failure, and lung failure, the mucus allows bacteria to accumulate. You'll very likely have a superimposed bacterial infection on top of whatever is happening. A viral infection also slows the cilia movement and lets the mucus and aerial bacteria accumulate. So a typical viral infection also ends up with a bacterial infection. The bacteria can cause all kinds of damage and are pretty sure to kill a person off if they aren't getting antibiotics. But that doesn't mean that the bacteria was the cause of the infection.

**John Barkhausen:** So basically their body was shutting down to begin with, and that's why they got infected. With the new, improved statistics, where they went from several hundred people actually dying of the flu to 40,000 to 60,000 per year, how many have actually died officially of coronavirus? Where do we stand today on the 31st of March?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** I think it was probably yesterday that I looked at it, and it was about 2,400 at that time. In just a day, it had just about doubled. So it was going up fast. But since about 10% of the people dying of flu are expected to have the coronavirus, you have to look at the samples. When they were doing samples of people with respiratory diseases, they would see about half the people had no identifiable cause. Then the rhinovirus would be maybe 30%, the flu virus maybe 15%, and the coronavirus maybe another 15%.

Just on the basis of samples from previous years, you would expect maybe 10% of the dead people to have an identifiable coronavirus in them. If 45,000 people are expected to die, then 10% of those would be 4,500 expected dead people containing the coronavirus—not that it killed them, but that it was identifiably present as they were sick with respiratory disease.

**John Barkhausen:** They actually got tested of all the people who die of the flu, and they say 50% of those are of unknown flu causes. Does that mean they haven't tested them or they just can't identify the strain?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** Couldn't identify. It could have been bacteria or just simple heart disease.

**John Barkhausen:** So what you're saying is that people are dying, they're testing them for coronavirus, which they come up positive, but it's not necessarily what killed them.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** True. If you have a limited number of tests and you use them mostly in hospitals on sick people coming in, you're going to have a very high percentage of the tests showing positive just because of that known figure from previous years that 10% of respiratory infections averaged coronavirus. Therefore, of the people who die, there is also going to be a very high percentage because you're testing primarily the sick people.

As you go out into a broader part of the population and start testing healthy people, the mortality rate per infection shrinks. That happened in China; it went from something like 3.5% or 4% down to around 1%. South Korea had a very big testing program, and they had only a 0.6% to 1% mortality. I don't know if that's the situation in New York, Spain, and Italy, where they're having a high percentage of mortality, but you can't know at all what the numbers mean unless you know who they're picking out to test.

**John Barkhausen:** It seems we're operating on the assumption that it is fatal right out of the box.

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** It looks very much as if they were inclined towards that presumption by the fact that the World Economic Forum, the Gates Foundation, and Johns Hopkins University organized this pretend pandemic in October of last year. They looked at what to do and how to prepare the government and hospitals to respond if a deadly coronavirus were imported and threatened to kill tens of millions of people. They had this in everyone's consciousness. They invited people who were in influential positions politically and economically around the world and had them run through this program in October. So everyone had this implanted fear. At the first meaningless numbers, I think people jumped to the fear that this was that imaginary virus they had proposed.

**John Barkhausen:** So basically, they had a dry run for this back in October. What is the Gates Foundation's relationship to the World Health Organization?

**Dr. Raymond Peat:** The foundation is pouring a lot of money into reorganizing the world. For example, African agricultural programs.
